0001.name: A. Caglar Tas
0001.bio: Tas is an Assistant Professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms that maintain visual stability across saccadic eye movements. Their research explores transsaccadic perception and updating, specifically examining how the brain integrates information from disparate fixations into an internal representation. Utilizing behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking technology, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), Tas studies the functional relationship between visual working memory and oculomotor control. Their recent work focuses on the temporal dynamics of attention and the interaction between peripheral and foveal vision during naturalistic viewing tasks.
0001.research_direction: Dr. Tas has recently been studying how the brain keeps the world looking stable even though the eyes jump several times a second. Their recent work explores how the visual system decides which object seen before a saccade (a rapid eye movement) is the same object seen after it, and which cues help with that match. They have examined the role of color in this correspondence, and how the object at the saccade target is given priority when people view naturalistic scenes.

papers.title: The saccade target is prioritized for visual stability in naturalistic scenes
papers.authors: Jessica L. Parker, A. C. Tas

papers.title: The role of color in transsaccadic object correspondence
papers.abstract: Tests whether color information helps the visual system establish which object before a saccade corresponds to the object after it. Full journal article (JOV 23(8):5), not a meeting abstract.
papers.authors: A. Çağlar Taş, Jessica L. Parker

0002.name: A. Mike Burton
0002.bio: A. Mike Burton is a Professor of Psychology at the University of York where they research the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of face recognition. Burton examines the familiarity effect, specifically investigating why the human visual system recognizes known individuals across variable conditions while often failing with unfamiliar faces. Their research methodologies combine experimental psychology and computational modeling to determine how stable identity representations emerge from variable visual inputs. Burton also applies this research to forensic and security contexts and co-developed the Glasgow Face Matching Test (GFMT) to assess person identification in fields such as policing and passport control.
0002.research_direction: Dr. Burton's recent work explores the cognitive, neural, and applied dimensions of face perception and recognition. They have recently been investigating how the visual system builds stable representations of familiar faces, using event-related brain potentials and computational image analysis to ask how statistical variability and idiosyncratic exposure shape identity processing over time. Beyond familiar face recognition, their recent work examines the reliability of real-world perceptual matching by assessing error rates and individual differences among human officials conducting simple photo-ID checks. Additionally, they are studying the social aspects of face perception to determine how first impressions of traits like trustworthiness are formed when faces are embedded in dynamic, naturalistic approach-avoidance contexts rather than viewed as static images.

papers.title: Representations for face recognition: The 53rd Bartlett Lecture
papers.abstract: Argues that common models treat a face representation as a fixed, essentialist set of values, which cannot explain familiar face recognition. Proposes that representations must instead capture the statistics of a person's exposure to each known face, including variability and sampling. Draws on empirical and simulation work to show that each perceiver's idiosyncratic experience yields unique representations, and calls for methodological diversity.
papers.authors: A. Mike Burton

papers.title: Polling clerks' errors in face matching
papers.abstract: Tested polling clerks who checked photo ID at the UK 2024 general election on standard face-matching tests. Clerks made many errors on simple match/mismatch decisions (about 16% on the Glasgow test and 36% on the Kent test), typical of the general population. Individual differences were large, and the results show that photo-ID checking by human officials is error-prone.
papers.authors: A. Mike Burton, Izzy Dimmock, Becca Salton

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of familiar face recognition: Event-related brain potentials reveal the efficient activation of facial identity representations
papers.abstract: ERP study tracking how quickly the brain activates identity representations for highly familiar faces. Shows rapid, efficient familiarity-related neural responses, supporting the view that stable identity representations are built from experience with variable images.
papers.authors: Holger Wiese, Tsvetomila Popova, Linda H. Lidborg, A. Mike Burton

papers.title: First impressions from faces in dynamic approach-avoidance contexts
papers.abstract: Examined how first impressions of trustworthiness and related traits form when faces are seen approaching or moving away in dynamic scenes rather than as static photos. Showed that impressions depend on the context of movement, extending the study of social face perception to more naturalistic situations.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Iliyana V. Trifonova, Cade McCall, Matthew C. Fysh, Markus Bindemann, A. Mike Burton

papers.title: A narrow band of image dimensions is critical for face recognition
papers.abstract: Used image-based analysis and behavioral experiments to ask which dimensions of face images carry identity information. Found that a narrow band of image dimensions accounts for face recognition performance, connecting image statistics to what the visual system relies on for identity.
papers.authors: Timothy J. Andrews, Daniel Rogers, Mila Mileva, David M. Watson, Ao Wang, A. Mike Burton

0004.name: Aaron Schurger
0004.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of volition and consciousness
0004.bio: Aaron Schurger is a cognitive neuroscientist at Chapman University who examines the neural mechanisms underlying voluntary action and conscious perception. Schurger’s research on the readiness potential introduced a stochastic accumulator model to demonstrate that pre-movement neural buildup can be explained by subthreshold fluctuations in brain activity rather than a pre-determined intention to act. Their work also investigates the distinction between conscious and non-conscious processing, utilizing computational modeling and neuroimaging to identify neural signatures of subjective experience, such as the stability and reproducibility of cortical activity. Schurger's methodology integrates behavioral psychophysics, machine learning, and electrophysiology to investigate the interface between neural dynamics and human agency.
0004.research_direction: Dr. Schurger has recently been investigating the neural precursors of voluntary action alongside foundational theories of consciousness. Their recent work explores the predictive value of the cortical readiness potential preceding self-initiated movements, utilizing EEG, machine-learning classifiers, and carefully matched control conditions to disentangle true neural motor commitment from physiological confounds like respiratory phase. Bridging motor control and visual perception, they are also examining whether treating a stimulus as the sensory outcome of a self-initiated action can alter visual awareness, specifically probing if voluntary movement can rescue targets from backward masking. Furthermore, they are evaluating major neurobiological theories of consciousness by mathematically testing the structural limits of feedforward networks in the presence of neural plasticity and conceptually reassessing the classical divide between sensory and cognitive models of conscious experience.

papers.title: The time course of neural activity predictive of self-initiated movement
papers.abstract: Slow ramping EEG activity has long been treated as an early predictor of self-initiated movement, but it was only ever analyzed in epochs that ended in a movement. The authors added a matched control condition with no movement and trained machine-learning classifiers to discriminate the two. Early ramping was present but not predictive; decoding accuracy jumped only about 100 ms before movement, so the neural commitment to act is a late event, and the classic approach yields a spurious impression of early predictability.
papers.authors: Lucas Jeay-Bizot, Mehmet Basbug, Uri Maoz, Robert Schapire, Aaron Schurger

papers.title: No evidence for modulation of the readiness potential by respiratory phase during natural breathing
papers.abstract: Earlier reports claimed the cortical readiness potential is coupled to the phase of breathing. Re-analyzing the original dataset, a new EEG dataset and simulated null data, the authors show the effect stems from a confound in which both RP amplitude and respiratory phase are tied to movement onset. Controlling for this by grouping trials by respiratory phase at movement removes the effect, and Bayesian tests support its absence.
papers.authors: Lucas Jeay-Bizot, Raniyah Chishti, Uri Maoz, Aaron Schurger

papers.title: On a confusion about there being two types of consciousness
papers.abstract: The authors argue that the sensory-versus-cognitive divide between theories of consciousness rests on a misreading of Block's phenomenal versus access consciousness distinction. They propose that phenomenal and access aspects are two necessary components of a single conscious state rather than two types of consciousness, and lay out how this reframing could resolve a central controversy in the field.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Nathan Faivre, Michael Pitts, Aaron Schurger

papers.title: A caveat regarding the unfolding argument: implications of plasticity
papers.abstract: The unfolding argument holds that any recurrent network can be unfolded into an input-output equivalent feedforward network, undermining causal-structure theories of consciousness. The authors give mathematical proofs that when connection weights change rapidly through plasticity, the equivalence breaks down, so a static feedforward network cannot capture such systems. This sets a boundary condition on the argument for biological neural systems.
papers.authors: Vikas N. O'Reilly-Shah, Alessandro Maria Selvitella, Aaron Schurger

papers.title: Self-initiated action rescues visual targets from backwards masking
papers.abstract: When a visual target is followed by a mask, it often goes unseen. Treating the masked stimulus as the sensory outcome of a participant's own self-initiated action, the authors show that observers are more accurate about the target when the target-mask sequence follows their voluntary action than when it is triggered externally. The result links voluntary action to visual awareness and bears on how action shapes perception.
papers.authors: Amber R. Hopkins, Tian Lan, Aaron Schurger

0005.name: Aaron Seitz
0005.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Physical Therapy, Movement and Rehabilitation Sciences; Department of Art + Design
0005.lab_name: Brain Game Center for Mental Fitness and Well-being
0005.bio: Aaron Seitz is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Brain Game Center at Northeastern University, investigating the mechanisms of brain plasticity and cognitive training. Seitz's research focuses on how the human brain solves the stability-plasticity dilemma, specifically examining the roles of reinforcement, attention, and multisensory integration in driving perceptual learning. Utilizing a methodology that combines computational neuroscience, human psychophysics, and neuroimaging, Seitz develops and validates gamified ambulatory tools designed to enhance sensory and cognitive function across populations ranging from athletes to individuals with neurodegenerative deficits.
0005.research_direction: Dr. Seitz has recently been investigating the fundamental mechanisms of perceptual learning and memory, exploring how the brain acquires information incidentally through task-irrelevant means and how prior experiences computationally bias current perception and working memory toward or away from past stimuli. Their recent work also explores the intersection of sensory function and cognitive aging, examining how declines across multiple sensory modalities might interact with dementia and age-related cognitive change. To tackle these theoretical and clinical questions, they have been developing and validating scalable, digital testing platforms designed to run on everyday devices. These methodological efforts include creating open-source applications to enable reproducible, multi-site perceptual learning research and evaluating remote, tablet-based neuropsychological batteries for at-home cognitive monitoring in older adults.

papers.title: Attraction and repulsion in perception and working memory as complementary outcomes of learning
papers.abstract: This review brings together findings that prior experience can pull current percepts and working-memory contents toward earlier stimuli (attraction) or push them away (repulsion). It argues the two effects are complementary results of learning rather than separate phenomena, and links them to computational accounts of how the brain balances stability and adaptation.
papers.authors: Nikos Gekas, Joseph M. Saito, Timothy F. Brady, Ulrik R. Beierholm, Merav Ahissar, Aviel Sulem, Aaron R. Seitz

papers.title: Neuropsychological Assessment Using Portable Automated Rapid Testing in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: Test-Retest Reliability Study
papers.abstract: Evaluates the feasibility, acceptability and short-term test-retest reliability of a remotely delivered tablet-based neuropsychological battery (PART) in cognitively healthy adults aged 50 to 85 who received mailed tablets. The study speaks to whether comprehensive at-home digital testing can support scalable monitoring of age-related cognitive change.
papers.authors: Quentin Coppola, Lakshmi Kannan, Audrey Carrillo, Susanne M. Jaeggi, Aaron R. Seitz

papers.title: Tricking our brains to learn and remember; is all learning incidental?
papers.abstract: A single-author invited review arguing that a great deal of learning happens without deliberate effort or explicit goals. It draws on perceptual-learning and memory research, including work on task-irrelevant learning and reinforcement, to argue that the brain can be led into learning and remembering through incidental means. It considers what this implies for designing training and interventions.
papers.authors: Aaron R. Seitz

papers.title: PLFest: A New Platform for Accessible, Reproducible, and Open Perceptual Learning Research
papers.abstract: Describes an open-source, cross-platform application for running standardized perceptual-learning and assessment experiments on ordinary devices. The authors present the design and validation data, and argue the tool can improve reproducibility and enable larger, multi-site studies of perceptual learning.
papers.authors: Samyukta Jayakumar, Marcello Maniglia, Zhenhong Guan, C. Shawn Green, Aaron R. Seitz

papers.title: Multidimensional relationships between sensory perception and cognitive aging
papers.abstract: A perspective piece reviewing how declines in vision, hearing, olfaction and vestibular function relate to cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. It discusses whether sensory losses are causal, contributory or merely coincident with cognitive decline, and proposes broad, portable, multi-sensory assessment to clarify how the senses interact.
papers.authors: Lakshmi Kannan, Esteban Sebastian Lelo de Larrea-Mancera, Marcello Maniglia, Mariya M. Vodyanyk, Frederick J. Gallun, Susanne M. Jaeggi, Aaron R. Seitz

0007.name: Adam Reeves
0007.bio: Adam Reeves is a Professor Emeritus of Psychology at Northeastern University whose research examines the mechanisms of human visual perception, including color constancy, iconic memory, and stereoscopic depth. Reeves utilizes psychophysical methodologies and computational modeling to study how visual attention modulates perception and how the brain processes phenomena such as synesthesia and crowding. Their recent work focuses on the short-term retention of depth and the effects of environmental lighting conditions on visual adaptation and phenomenal contrast.
0007.research_direction: Dr. Reeves has recently been investigating a broad array of psychophysical mechanisms spanning early visual processing and higher-level visual cognition. Their recent work explores the interaction between mental imagery and actual visual discrimination, specifically modeling the precise signal conditions under which visualizing an object facilitates or interferes with target detection. They are also examining the methodological foundations of color vision by evaluating the mathematical limitations and systemic weaknesses of standard metrics used to quantify color constancy. Furthermore, their research spans several other distinct visual phenomena, probing how environmental lighting adaptation shapes phenomenal contrast and depth perception, modeling numerosity judgments based on normalized contrast energy rather than absolute item counts, and measuring how peripheral crowding zones and target-flanker interactions dynamically change during shifts of visual attention.

papers.title: Imagery: Interference, facilitation, and theory
papers.abstract: Reviews the literature on how mental images near a visual target either impair or help discrimination, and proposes that matching-feature images boost sensitivity at all performance levels while all image types add noise that grows with signal strength. That noise eventually outweighs the boost, producing interference (the Perky effect) at high signal levels. A new experiment shows the switch from facilitation to interference depends on signal level, not image vividness or dynamics, and derived equations for the mean and variability of d' fit this and prior data.
papers.authors: Adam Reeves

papers.title: Five problems with color constancy metrics: discussion
papers.abstract: Argues that common summary statistics for quantifying color constancy have five weaknesses: the choice of metric, dependence on chromaticity, chance-level random matches, the bounded nature of color space, and reliance on memory. The paper is a discussion piece responding to recent colour-constancy work and calls for more careful measurement.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Adam Reeves

papers.title: Environmental Lighting Conditions, Phenomenal Contrast, and the Conscious Perception of Near and Far
papers.abstract: Examines how adaptation to darkness, daylight, and prolonged very bright light changes perceived contrast and the impression of near versus far depth in visual displays. Findings suggest that lighting history shapes brain processing from retina to higher cortex and hence conscious depth perception.
papers.authors: Birgitta Dresp-Langley, Adam J. Reeves

papers.title: Numerosity depends on normalized contrast energy: Review and square-root law model
papers.abstract: Reviews studies of perceived number and shows that judged numerosity of dot displays tracks the display's normalized contrast energy rather than count alone. Proposes a square-root law model that accounts for the pattern across experiments.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Adam Reeves

papers.title: Crowding expands and is less sensitive to target-flanker differences during a shift of visual attention
papers.abstract: Tests how peripheral crowding changes while attention is shifting. Crowding zones widen during the attention shift and become less dependent on how different target and flankers are, linking attentional dynamics to the spatial extent of crowding.
papers.authors: Jeff Nador, Adam Reeves

0008.name: Adam S Greenberg
0008.lab_name: Sensory Neuroscience, Attention, & Perception Laboratory (SNAP Lab)
0008.bio: Adam S. Greenberg is an Associate Professor in the Joint Department of Biomedical Engineering at the Medical College of Wisconsin and Marquette University and directs the Sensory Neuroscience, Attention, & Perception (SNAP) Laboratory. Greenberg’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of attentional control and object perception using a multi-modal approach that includes functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling. Their work examines how behavioral goals influence sensory processing in both visual and auditory systems, focusing on the sources and targets of attentional selection. Additionally, Greenberg explores the identification of neurological biomarkers for cognitive decline resulting from aging, hearing loss, and clinical interventions such as chemotherapy.
0008.research_direction: Dr. Greenberg has recently been investigating the spatial and temporal dynamics of attentional deployment, with a particular focus on how the visual architecture guides shifts of attention. Their recent work explores the well-documented behavioral asymmetry where object-based attention shifts faster horizontally than vertically, using psychophysics and fMRI to test how visual field meridians might partition attentional resources across retinotopic cortex. Beyond strictly visual contexts, they are examining the broader, cross-modal nature of attention, asking theoretically whether attentional mechanisms are universal across sensory and motor brain maps, while also investigating how clinical auditory changes like hearing loss alter visual attentional networks in older adults. To better capture these underlying cognitive processes, Dr. Greenberg is also developing computational neuroimaging tools, including probabilistic scaling methods for multivariate pattern analysis, designed to continuously track how perceptual and attentional states unfold over time.

papers.title: Impact of Hearing Loss and Cochlear Implantation on Attentional Selection in Older Adults
papers.abstract: The study compares visual attentional selection in older adults with normal hearing, those with hearing loss awaiting a cochlear implant, and current implant users, using the Attentional Network Test. Hearing-loss groups relied less on temporal alerting cues but made greater use of spatial orienting than controls, with no difference in executive control. The results indicate that hearing status shapes attention networks even in a non-auditory task.
papers.authors: Michael S. Harris, Gennadiy Gurariy, Shannon Walsh, Kristin Kozlowski, Samiah Ziadeh, Sarah Mleziva, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Anisotropic object-based shifts of attention arise from unequal influences of visual field meridians on neural attention gradients
papers.abstract: Attention shifts within an object are faster horizontally than vertically, an asymmetry the lab has long documented. Using fMRI in retinotopic visual cortex while people shifted attention within an L-shaped object, this study tests whether the asymmetry comes from the visual-field meridians partitioning attentional resources. The behavioral asymmetry appeared only for one object placement, and cue-related activity showed attention spreading along the vertical arm while the vertical meridian impeded spread along the horizontal arm.
papers.authors: David H. Hughes, Adam J. Barnas, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Probabilistic Scaling of Multivariate Pattern Analysis Reveals Cognitive State Dynamics
papers.abstract: This short conference paper introduces a way to convert multivariate pattern classifier outputs into probabilistic scales so that fMRI decoding can track how cognitive states unfold over time. The approach is presented as a general tool for measuring dynamics of attentional and perceptual states from neuroimaging data.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE 22nd International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (ISBI)
papers.authors: David H. Hughes, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: The object-based shift direction anisotropy is modulated by the horizontal visual field meridian
papers.abstract: Shifting object-based attention is faster along the horizontal than vertical direction. In four experiments with an L-shaped object, the authors manipulated local feature contrast at the visual field meridians. Strong enhancement of the horizontal meridian reduced the asymmetry so that horizontal and vertical shifts became equally fast, whereas weak enhancements did not, implicating the horizontal meridian in reorienting attention.
papers.authors: Adam J. Barnas, Adam S. Greenberg

papers.title: Are neuronal mechanisms of attention universal across human sensory and motor brain maps?
papers.abstract: This theoretical paper asks whether attention relies on one shared neural mechanism across vision, audition, and movement or on modality-specific ones. It outlines the conceptual and methodological hurdles of cross-modal comparison and presents an experimental approach, applicable across many brain maps, for quantitatively comparing attentional mechanisms, aiming to spur a broad empirical database.
papers.authors: Edgar A. DeYoe, Wendy Huddleston, Adam S. Greenberg

0009.name: Adam W. Kiefer
0009.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
0009.department: Department of Exercise and Sport Science
0009.lab_name: Simulation, Training, Analytics and Rehabilitation (STAR) Heel Performance Laboratory
0009.bio: Adam W. Kiefer is an Assistant Professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where Kiefer co-directs the STAR Heel Performance Laboratory and holds an appointment in the Human Movement Science Curriculum. Kiefer’s research applies a complex systems approach to sports performance and injury prevention by integrating immersive technologies like virtual reality and mobile eye-tracking with artificial intelligence to model human behavior. Kiefer focuses on the digital transformation of athletic training, utilizing nonlinear dynamics and machine learning to analyze the 'vision-in-action' loop and develop personalized interventions for elite athletes and clinical populations. This work involves the automation of perceptual-cognitive data analysis for application within the fields of digital health and behavioral dynamics.
0009.research_direction: Dr. Kiefer has recently been investigating how humans pick up and use visual information to guide complex motor actions in highly dynamic, ecologically valid environments. Using methods like mobile eye-tracking, overground virtual reality, and explainable machine learning, their recent work explores visuomotor strategies in sports, specifically examining phenomena such as spatial scanning patterns for collision avoidance and "quiet eye" fixations during targeted actions. Additionally, they are evaluating the methodological strengths and limitations of head-mounted eye trackers for real-world vision-in-action assessments. Beyond visual-motor control, their broader research applies nonlinear time-series modeling and large-scale data integration frameworks to study complex, emergent biopsychosocial phenomena, including dynamic human resilience and traumatic brain injury.

papers.title: A proposed organization of multifaceted knowledge in data repositories: structuring record collections and evidence sets for data lakehouses and moonshots
papers.abstract: The paper describes PHENOM, a cloud-based lakehouse platform that pools historical and ongoing traumatic brain injury studies spanning clinical, physiological, behavioral and environmental data. It proposes organizing such heterogeneous data into a small number of bins based on how and when data are captured, using automated ETL pipelines, metadata templates and standard biomedical terminologies for FAIR integration. The framework is mapped to TBI datasets and to exposome-moonshot efforts to support precision neurohealth research.
papers.venue: Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology
papers.authors: Adam W. Kiefer, Snigdha Sompalli, Jason P. Mihalik, Robert Hubal

papers.title: The Utility of Head-Mounted Eye Gaze Tracking for Vision-in-Action Assessments to Enhance Skill Acquisition and Sport Performance: A Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats Analysis
papers.abstract: This review weighs the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of using mobile eye trackers to assess how athletes pick up visual information to control action. Ecological validity is a key strength, while tracking fidelity problems (eye morphology, squinting, device slippage, lens fogging) are weaknesses. The authors outline opportunities such as studying performance under pressure and personalizing training, and cautions for adopting the technology.
papers.venue: Journal of Motor Learning and Development
papers.authors: Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: Visuomotor strategies for collision avoidance in athletes: Insights from virtual reality
papers.abstract: Thirty-nine athletes pursued a virtual target in an overground virtual reality environment while avoiding two to five virtual defenders, with head movements recorded throughout. A measurement model built from head-motion data captured two aspects of visual scanning, its overall amount and its temporal pattern. Athletes who avoided collisions successfully showed larger head rotations in the two-defender condition and more varied temporal scanning patterns, suggesting efficient environmental scanning underlies collision avoidance and that VR can be used to study and train it.
papers.venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
papers.authors: Adam W. Kiefer, Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Cortney N. Armitano-Lago, Ryan MacPherson, Dominic Willoughby, Paula L. Silva

papers.title: Predicting Basketball Shot Outcome From Visuomotor Control Data Using Explainable Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Twelve basketball athletes took 200 shots from six court locations while wearing mobile eye-tracking glasses. Decision-tree and random-forest models used eight predictors, including shot location, arm extension time and the onset, offset and duration of the quiet eye (the final steady fixation before the shot), to classify makes versus misses. The models predicted outcomes above chance, showing that the quiet eye carries usable information about performance and could guide training.
papers.authors: Nikki Aitcheson-Huehn, Ryan MacPherson, Derek Panchuk, Adam W. Kiefer

papers.title: Biopsychosocial Resilience through a Complex Adaptive Systems Lens: A Narrative Review of Nonlinear Modeling Approaches
papers.abstract: The review argues that human resilience is better treated as a dynamic, emergent property of self-organizing systems than as a fixed trait. It surveys four classes of nonlinear tools for studying it: univariate dynamics, bivariate coupling, topological modeling (bifurcations, attractors) and network modeling. Each is presented as a way to read system flexibility, stability and integrity from time-series data.
papers.venue: Nonlinear Dynamics, Psychology, and Life Sciences
papers.authors: Adam W. Kiefer, David Pincus

0011.name: Adrian G. Palacios
0011.department: Instituto de Neurociencia, Facultad de Ciencias
0011.bio: Adrian G. Palacios is a Full Professor at the Universidad de Valparaíso and a principal investigator at the Centro Interdisciplinario de Neurociencia de Valparaíso (CINV). Palacios utilizes multielectrode electrophysiology and patch-clamp techniques to investigate retinal physiology and the mechanisms of the neural code. Their research examines the intersection of sensory biology and neurodegeneration, specifically how aging and Alzheimer’s disease affect synaptic plasticity and visual processing in transgenic and natural models. Additionally, Palacios incorporates computational modeling and complexity science to analyze neuronal population dynamics and inform the development of gene-based therapeutic interventions for nervous system repair.
0011.research_direction: Dr. Palacios has recently been investigating the physiological and molecular intersections of aging, neurodegeneration, and retinal function, particularly in the context of Alzheimer's disease. Their recent work explores how the retina can serve as a noninvasive biomarker for central nervous system decline, using multielectrode arrays to measure the complexity of retinal responses to visual stimuli and probing the unfolded protein response as a potential therapeutic target. Beyond the visual system, they are examining the mechanisms of cognitive resilience by combining behavioral testing and hippocampal electrophysiology in natural models of aging like the Octodon degus to understand the role of inhibitory GABAergic circuits in memory preservation. To support these functional studies, Dr. Palacios is also developing scalable computational methods for detecting co-firing neuronal ensembles within large-scale spiking networks. Overall, their integrative approach combines retinal population dynamics, central circuit physiology, and molecular biomarkers to identify new early diagnostic readouts and preventative interventions for age-related neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Blood-retinal biomarker integration for precision prevention of Alzheimer's disease: Lessons from retinal aging and the unfolded protein response
papers.abstract: This perspective proposes combining blood-based markers with retinal measures to detect and prevent Alzheimer's disease earlier. It draws on what is known about retinal aging and the unfolded protein response to argue for an integrated, precision-prevention approach.
papers.authors: Monica L. Acosta, Sarah X. Zhang, Adrian G. Palacios

papers.title: XBP1s as a Therapeutic Target to Preserve Retinal Function During Aging and Neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: The authors record retinal responses with multielectrode arrays to chirp and white-noise stimuli in wild-type, XBP1s-overexpressing, 5xFAD Alzheimer model and crossed mice at about 3 and 7 months. Entropy-based complexity and wavelet coherence between stimulus and response fall with age and disease in WT and 5xFAD retinas but are preserved when XBP1s is expressed. The work positions retinal signal complexity as a scalable, noninvasive readout for testing therapies against neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Leonel E. Medina, Joel Barria, Max Chacon, Maximiliano Orellana, Daniela Ponce, David Neira, Francisco Miqueles, Claudia Duran-Aniotz, Joaquin Araya-Arriagada, Bruno Cerda, Claudio Hetz, Christian Rojas, Adrian G. Palacios

papers.title: Cognitive Resilience in Aging Degus is Linked to CA3 Hippocampal GABAergic Integrity
papers.abstract: Using Octodon degus, a long-lived rodent that ages naturally with Alzheimer-like features, the study combines behavioral testing with hippocampal electrophysiology to ask why some aged animals keep their memory. Cognitively resilient old degus retain intact inhibitory (GABAergic) function in CA3, while impaired animals lose it. The findings point to inhibitory circuit integrity as a marker of resilience to age-related cognitive decline.
papers.authors: Cristobal Ibaceta-Gonzalez, David Neira, Nicolas M. Ardiles, Nicol Baeza-Araya, Alfredo Kirkwood, Pablo Moya, Adrian G. Palacios

papers.title: Diabetic retinopathy and Alzheimer's disease: Convergence of the unfolded protein response in neurodegeneration
papers.abstract: This review argues that diabetic retinopathy and Alzheimer's disease share mechanisms of oxidative stress, inflammation and disrupted proteostasis centred on the unfolded protein response. It contrasts the IRE1-XBP1 and PERK-eIF2a arms, discusses retinal biomarkers for early Alzheimer detection, and outlines UPR-targeted therapeutic strategies.
papers.authors: Adrian G. Palacios, Sarah X. Zhang, Monica L. Acosta

papers.title: A General and Accurate Method for Neuronal Ensemble Detection in Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This methods chapter describes a scalable procedure for finding neuronal ensembles, groups of cells that fire together, in large spiking populations. It builds on the group's earlier PLoS One method and explains how to apply it to multielectrode retinal and other population recordings.
papers.venue: Neuromethods (Identification, Characterization, and Manipulation of Neuronal Ensembles)
papers.authors: Ruben Herzog-Amunategui, Soraya Mora, Garance Prada, Jean-Gabriel Minonzio, Maria Jose Escobar, Rodrigo Cofre, Adrian G. Palacios

0012.name: Adrian Nestor
0012.bio: Adrian Nestor is an Associate Professor at the University of Toronto Scarborough and the director of the Neurocomputational Vision Lab. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of face and object recognition by integrating neuroimaging techniques, such as fMRI and EEG, with computational modeling and machine learning. Nestor conducts work in neural decoding and image reconstruction, developing algorithms to visualize mental representations from brain activity. Their research program examines the relationship between physical image properties and the structural organization of neural representations within the high-level visual cortex.
0012.research_direction: Dr. Nestor’s recent work explores the behavioral and neural representations of high-level face perception, utilizing EEG decoding and GAN-based image reconstruction techniques to literally visualize subjective perceptual experiences. Specifically, they have recently been investigating how the human visual system processes dynamic facial expressions over time, asking how individual differences in memory and personality shape these affective representations. Their research also probes the visual representation of identity, examining how internal self-beliefs and subjective biases distort the mental image of one's own face. Furthermore, they are studying the well-known other-race effect, combining behavioral similarity judgments and neuroimaging to determine how viewing context—such as observing single faces versus multi-face ensembles—alters the perceptual processing and discriminability of different racial groups.

papers.title: Evidence for dimensional representations and anticipatory dynamics in facial expression perception
papers.abstract: The authors decoded EEG responses to videos of 14 emotional and 10 conversational facial expressions and showed that the representational geometry of these expressions tracks the classic dimensions of valence and arousal. EEG-based video reconstruction recovered dynamic expression content, capturing fine distinctions among related expressions. Time-resolved decoding peaked before the apex of the expression, revealing anticipatory neural dynamics.
papers.authors: Tyler Roberts, Yong Zhong Liang, Gerald C. Cupchik, Jonathan S. Cant, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: The self as an image: Appearance and belief in visual representations of one's own face
papers.abstract: Participants judged similarity among self, familiar and unfamiliar faces, and these judgments were compared with artificial neural network representations. Self-face judgments matched recognition-trained networks better than generative latent spaces. Behavior-based image reconstruction visualized self-face percepts and memories, showing they preserve identity yet are biased by self-beliefs such as perceived attractiveness and self-concept clarity.
papers.authors: Arijit De, Samuel F. Liu, Kavindu Monaragala, Moaz Shoura, William A. Cunningham, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Face ensembles reshape the neural other-race effect
papers.abstract: Twenty-two East Asian adults viewed East Asian and White faces individually and in six-face ensembles during EEG. Single same-race faces were more discriminable, more dispersed in face space and reconstructed more accurately. Ensembles kept racial-composition information but reduced the same- versus other-race decoding difference, showing that the neural other-race effect depends on viewing context.
papers.authors: Moaz Shoura, Haoyi N. Jiang, Zuhayr Azeem, Ovidiu Iancu, Marco A. Sama, Jonathan S. Cant, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Unraveling other-race face perception with GAN-based image reconstruction
papers.abstract: Using StyleGAN2 and pairwise similarity ratings from East Asian and White participants, the authors built a reconstruction method that recovers face percepts from behavior. Reconstructions were more accurate for same-race than other-race faces, mirroring the other-race effect. Other-race face reconstructions also looked younger, revealing a previously unreported age bias.
papers.authors: Moaz Shoura, Dirk B. Walther, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Perception and memory-based representations of facial emotions: Associations with personality functioning, affective states and recognition abilities
papers.abstract: In two experiments, adults rated similarity among facial expressions seen or recalled from memory, and image reconstruction produced perception- and memory-based expression representations. Individual differences in these representations were linked to self-direction impairment, positive affect and face recognition ability. A second group rated the reconstructions, tying individual variability to visual properties such as expressiveness, accuracy and valence.
papers.authors: Chi-Hsun Chang, Natalia Drobotenko, Anthony C. Ruocco, Andy C.H. Lee, Adrian Nestor

0013.name: Aihua Chen
0013.department: Institute of Brain Functional Genomics, School of Life Sciences
0013.bio: Aihua Chen is a Professor at East China Normal University and heads the Laboratory of Sensation and Action within the Institute of Brain Functional Genomics. Chen’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of multisensory integration, specifically how visual and vestibular cues combine to support self-motion perception and spatial navigation. Through single-unit electrophysiological recordings in macaque monkeys and 3D virtual reality behavioral tasks, they examine the functional properties of cortical regions including the MSTd, VPS, and STPp. Chen’s work also explores the principles of multisensory decision-making, the impact of stimulus history on perception (serial dependence), and the hierarchical control of learned saccade sequences in the prefrontal and parietal cortices.
0013.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying multisensory integration, spatial perception, and motor control using electrophysiology and targeted perturbations in macaques. Their recent work explores how the primate brain processes self-motion by probing how distinct multisensory cortical areas—such as VIP, VPS, and MSTd—combine, suppress, or dynamically recalibrate in response to conflicting visual and vestibular heading cues. In tandem with this research on self-motion, they are examining how some of these same higher-level networks extract 3D surface orientation features like slant and tilt from binocular disparity. Beyond sensory integration, Dr. Chen is also studying the hierarchical cognitive control of movement, utilizing microstimulation and cortical inactivation to determine how prefrontal and parietal regions orchestrate the initiation and transition of learned saccade sequences.

papers.title: Conflict-dependent gain control in area VIP during visual-vestibular self-motion processing
papers.abstract: Neurons in macaque VIP were recorded while the offset between visual and vestibular heading was systematically varied. Congruent cues boosted responses and larger offsets progressively suppressed gain, even in neurons classified as mostly unisensory, while heading preference changed little and population Fisher information stayed largely intact. A feedforward-gated normalization model in which conflict regulates the strength of cross-modal interaction fit the data best.
papers.authors: Huizhe Sun, Rong Wang, Fu Zeng, Aihua Chen

papers.title: Distinct role of primate DLPFC and LIP in hierarchical control of learned saccade sequences
papers.abstract: Monkeys were trained on heterogeneous saccade sequences, and neural recording, microstimulation and inactivation were used to compare dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and lateral intraparietal cortex. DLPFC neurons mainly signaled sequence initiation, and inactivating DLPFC lengthened initiation latency. LIP neurons mainly encoded transitions between subsequences, and perturbing LIP caused improper subsequence switches, indicating complementary hierarchical roles.
papers.authors: Qingjun Wang, Binchao Shi, Jing Jia, Jingyu Hu, Haoran Li, Xin Jin, Aihua Chen

papers.title: The visual representation of 3D orientation in macaque areas STPp and VPS
papers.abstract: Using random-dot stereograms defining slant and tilt, the study asked how two visual-vestibular areas, STPp and VPS, encode 3D surface orientation. Both areas carried orientation and depth information, with slant encoded independently of tilt and disparity. STPp coded plane orientation stably regardless of motion cues, while VPS responses were less stable.
papers.authors: Rong Wang, Bin Zhao, Aihua Chen

papers.title: Contrary neuronal recalibration in different multisensory cortical areas
papers.abstract: After monkeys experienced a consistent visual-vestibular heading conflict, their perceptual heading estimates for each cue shifted toward each other. The authors recorded single neurons in MSTd, PIVC and VIP during this recalibration. MSTd and PIVC tuning shifted along with the respective perceptual shifts, whereas VIP showed only a global shift in vestibular space, so its visual tuning shifted opposite to visual perception. This indicates recalibration is local in early multisensory cortex but reflects a single reference frame in higher-level VIP.
papers.authors: Fu Zeng, Adam Zaidel, Aihua Chen

papers.title: The computational rules of cross-modality suppression in the visual posterior sylvian area
papers.abstract: Neurons in macaque VPS respond to heading from both visual and vestibular cues, but vestibular signals dominate their combined responses in an approximately winner-take-all manner, unlike subadditive integration in MSTd. Population Fisher information showed VPS carries different modality information depending on cue offset. Weighted linear sums and a divisive normalization model captured the interaction in both areas.
papers.authors: Bin Zhao, Rong Wang, Zhihua Zhu, Qianli Yang, Aihua Chen

0017.name: Alan Stocker
0017.bio: Alan A. Stocker is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania who investigates the computational principles of human visual perception and decision-making. Stocker’s laboratory uses psychophysical experiments and probabilistic modeling to study how sensory information is integrated with prior beliefs and environmental statistics. Stocker focuses on the distinction between objective expectations shaped by the natural environment and subjective expectations influenced by previous perceptual choices. Their work characterizes the brain as an optimal inference engine, developing quantitative models that explain the relationships between perceptual bias and discriminability.
0017.research_direction: Dr. Stocker has recently been investigating human visual perception through the lens of Bayesian inference and efficient coding, asking how the visual system dynamically allocates limited neural resources. Their recent work explores the mechanistic origins of contextual and temporal phenomena using combined psychophysics, fMRI, and natural scene statistics, specifically examining how sensory coding precision shifts at center-surround boundaries to produce the tilt illusion and whether perceptual adaptation proactively prepares the brain for future stimuli. Additionally, they are probing the temporal dynamics of visual cognition, asking how robust ensemble coding relies on the synchronous presentation of reference stimuli and how observers balance memory maintenance and integration effort during interrupted streams of continuous evidence accumulation. Across these diverse topics, Dr. Stocker is testing computational models that reframe perception not as isolated feature estimation, but as a holistic, resource-rational inference process that operates jointly over low-level sensory inputs and higher-level categories.

papers.title: Dynamics of efficient ensemble coding
papers.abstract: Building on prior work showing that robust averaging can be explained by efficient coding whose precision adapts to the ensemble relative to a reference, this paper asks how that adaptation unfolds in time. Varying the interval between ensemble and reference, the authors find efficient ensemble coding is clearly present only when the two appear together, weaker when the ensemble comes first, and largely absent when it follows the reference. A model captures this, with reduced efficiency coinciding with lower decision accuracy in asynchronous conditions.
papers.authors: Long Ni, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: The resource-rational dynamics of evidence accumulation
papers.abstract: Human subjects estimated the angular position of a hidden source from a noisy stimulus sequence with breaks of varying length and timing inserted. They compensated for memory loss during the break by boosting integration and memory maintenance right afterward. A continuous-time Bayesian updating model constrained by performance-effort trade-offs, with two resource-efficiency parameters, predicts these schedule dependencies including individual primacy and recency tendencies, portraying accumulation as a dynamically controlled process.
papers.authors: Mengting Fang, Jiang Mao, Tobias H. Donner, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: The tilt illusion arises from an efficient reallocation of neural coding resources at the contextual boundary
papers.abstract: Using combined psychophysics and fMRI in human observers, the study measures how sensory encoding precision for orientation changes when a grating is surrounded by an oriented context. Precision rises for orientations close to the surround, and this local change in coding is enough for a Bayesian observer model to predict the behavioral tilt illusion. The effect grows along the ventral visual stream, is localized to receptive fields at the center-surround boundary, and mirrors surround-conditioned orientation statistics in natural scenes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ling-Qi Zhang, Jiang Mao, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: Adaptation optimizes sensory encoding for future stimuli
papers.abstract: The authors test whether perceptual adaptation acts proactively, tuning encoding for upcoming input rather than merely reacting to the past. Human orientation discrimination shows that adaptation reallocates coding accuracy to peak at the adaptor orientation at constant total capacity. Retinal-input statistics from freely behaving people and a next-frame-prediction network (PredNet) both show the same pattern, supporting the view that adaptation prepares the visual system for likely future stimuli.
papers.authors: Jiang Mao, Constantin A. Rothkopf, Alan A. Stocker

papers.title: Sensory perception is a holistic inference process
papers.abstract: The paper argues that perception should not be treated as a best guess of one stimulus feature but as inference carried out jointly over the whole representational hierarchy, including both a feature (such as orientation) and its higher-level category. A holistic matching model built on this idea accounts for behavior in the method-of-adjustment task across several existing datasets, beating earlier models, and it extends to categorical color perception. The authors conclude that categorical effects in perception are widespread and follow from optimal inference over holistic representations.
papers.authors: Jiang Mao, Alan A. Stocker

0018.name: Alasdair Clarke
0018.bio: Alasdair D. F. Clarke is a Senior Lecturer in the Department of Psychology at the University of Essex and is affiliated with the Centre for Brain Science. Clarke’s research integrates computational modeling, Bayesian inference, and signal detection theory to investigate how humans perceive complex visual scenes and make foraging decisions. Their work examines eye-movement biases, individual differences in visual search strategies, and the role of texture regularity and symmetry in scene analysis. Additionally, Clarke has developed standardized open-source task batteries for assessing visual performance in naturalistic environments.
0018.research_direction: Dr. Clarke has recently been developing computational and statistical models of visual search and foraging, investigating how to predict target-by-target selection and account for individual differences in spatial scanning strategies. Their recent work explores advanced analytical methods to extract more information from behavioral data, such as using Bayesian multi-level models to predict single and double feature search and applying asymptotic regression to isolate individual learning curves across repeated experimental trials. They are also examining the mechanisms behind sub-optimal decision making, specifically probing why observers continue to make variable, inefficient choices even after being exposed to simple and effective behavioral rules. Additionally, their research encompasses visual ergonomics, where they have been designing novel psychophysical methods based on signal detection theory to accurately measure subjective visual discomfort while controlling for individual response biases.

papers.title: FoMo: A unifying theory of visual foraging
papers.abstract: Presents an updated generative model of visual foraging that predicts, target by target, which item a person will select next. The new version adds spatial-structure parameters, which improve prediction for datasets in which some participants follow grid-like paths. The interpretable parameters also help explain individual differences across many descriptive foraging statistics used in earlier work.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Anna E. Hughes

papers.title: Variable and sub-optimal responses to a choice problem persist despite experience with a simple and effective decision rule
papers.abstract: Examines why people make variable, often sub-optimal choices in a decision problem even after being shown a simple and effective rule. Participants continued to respond inconsistently despite this experience, suggesting the variability is not just a lack of knowledge about the best strategy. The work links to his broader study of sub-optimal search and prioritisation behaviour.
papers.authors: Amelia Hunt, Warren R. G. James, Josephine Reuther, Melissa Spilioti, Alasdair Clarke

papers.title: Measuring visual discomfort - a novel two-step method for reducing criterion effects when measuring subjective responses
papers.abstract: Proposes a two-step procedure for measuring visual discomfort in which subjective ratings are less contaminated by individual differences in response criterion. The method draws on signal detection thinking to separate sensitivity from bias in comfort judgements. It offers a more reliable way to compare discomfort across stimuli and observers.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Louise O'Hare, Paul B. Hibbard

papers.title: Learn more from your data with asymptotic regression
papers.abstract: Argues that repeated trials in psychology experiments are not independent because participants learn, and shows how asymptotic regression can recover individual learning curves. The approach separates learning rate, starting level and asymptotic performance, so more can be learned from the same data. Demonstrated on behavioural datasets with a practical tutorial for researchers.
papers.authors: Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Amelia R. Hunt

papers.title: Bayesian multi-level modelling for predicting single and double feature visual search
papers.abstract: Applies Bayesian multi-level models to predict how people search for targets defined by one or two features. The models capture variation across individuals and conditions in search performance, giving a principled statistical account of visual search behaviour. It shows the value of hierarchical modelling for individual differences in search.
papers.authors: Anna E. Hughes, Anna Nowakowska, Alasdair D. F. Clarke

0019.name: Alejandro Lleras
0019.bio: Alejandro Lleras is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and the Beckman Institute, where they co-direct the Vision Lab. Their research investigates the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying human visual attention and awareness, focusing on the role of parallel peripheral vision in guiding goal-directed search. Utilizing a multimodal approach that integrates psychophysics, eye-tracking, and EEG, Lleras developed theoretical frameworks such as the Target Contrast Signal Theory to explain how visual features are processed and filtered during scene analysis. Their current work examines the temporal dynamics of attention and the factors that drive distractibility and attentional lapses over sustained periods.
0019.research_direction: Dr. Lleras has recently been investigating the computational and perceptual mechanisms underlying visual search efficiency. Their recent work explores how the perceptual distance between targets and distractors in color space can be modeled to predict search speed, and evaluates how multiple features—such as color-color combinations or color-shape conjunctions—are processed and integrated to guide attention. In addition to modeling these feature guidance signals, they are examining individual differences in highly difficult search tasks, such as spotting camouflaged targets. By utilizing eye tracking and decision-model analyses, Dr. Lleras investigates how an observer's raw visual search skill and their response cautiousness independently contribute to overall search performance.

papers.title: Quantifying the relationship between search efficiency and perceptual similarity in color space across different efficient search tasks
papers.abstract: The authors ask how quickly people can find a target among distractors as a function of how different the two are in color. Across several efficient-search tasks, search speed turned out to be a simple linear function of the perceptual distance between target and distractor colors in color space. This gives a quantitative, model-ready link between perceptual similarity and search efficiency, extending the group's Target Contrast Signal theory.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Alejandro Lleras, Zoe Jing Xu, Howard Jia He Tan, Yujie Shao, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Evaluating the contribution of parallel processing of color and shape in a conjunction search task
papers.abstract: Conjunction search is classically thought to be hard because features must be bound together. The authors compared parallel and serial computational accounts against data and found that color and shape are processed in parallel, with the search cost coming from how distractors are rejected rather than from binding. The results argue for a parallel account of conjunction search in which feature guidance does much of the work.
papers.authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Simona Buetti, Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras

papers.title: Color-color feature guidance in visual search
papers.abstract: The study tests how observers use two colors at once to guide search, for example targets defined by a combination of two hues. It measures how well color-color combinations guide attention compared with single-color targets and what this implies for combining features within one dimension. The findings feed models of how feature guidance signals are integrated during search.
papers.authors: Yiwen Wang, Simona Buetti, Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Alejandro Lleras

papers.title: Skills and cautiousness predict performance in difficult search
papers.abstract: Some people are consistently better than others at hard searches such as spotting camouflaged targets. Using eye tracking and decision-model analysis, the authors separate raw search skill from how cautious an observer is about responding. Both factors independently predict performance, so individual differences in difficult search are not just a speed-accuracy trade-off.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Simona Buetti, Yan Xia, Alejandro Lleras

0020.name: Alessandro Farini
0020.bio: Alessandro Farini is a senior researcher and physicist at the National Institute of Optics (CNR-INO) in Florence and directs the Visual Optics Lab (ViOLa). Farini’s research investigates the intersection of applied psychophysics, visual ergonomics, and lighting science, focusing on how ophthalmic optics and environmental illumination affect human perception. They study blue-blocking filters, colorimetry, and the visual performance of patients with macular degeneration using eye-tracking methodologies and behavioral research techniques. Farini also serves as a contract professor at the University of Florence, where they teach courses in geometrical and physical optics.
0020.research_direction: Dr. Farini has recently been working at the intersection of ophthalmic optics, visual psychophysics, and applied color vision. Their recent work explores how the human visual system processes information under altered optical conditions, combining photometric and psychophysical methods to evaluate visual performance with photochromic lenses and measuring contrast sensitivity and acuity under monochromatic yellow lighting. They are also investigating how the visual system resolves illumination ambiguity by probing the viral "Dress" illusion in observers with congenital color vision anomalies. Broadening their scope, Dr. Farini applies dichromatic vision models to simulate equine perception of show-jumping obstacles to improve animal welfare, while additionally examining the historical technological development of eyeglasses in medieval Florence.

papers.title: Perception of The Dress for different color vision anomalies
papers.abstract: The authors compare how observers with different congenital color vision deficiencies see the ambiguous colors of the viral Dress image. They relate the reported dress colors to the type of anomaly, treating the illusion as a probe of how the visual system resolves illumination ambiguity when chromatic signals are altered.
papers.authors: Daniela Ducci, Elisabetta Baldanzi, Massimo Gurioli, Paolo Antonino Grasso, Federico Tommasi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Photometric and psychophysical evaluation of photochromic lenses
papers.abstract: Combines photometric measurements of photochromic ophthalmic lenses with psychophysical testing to see how their tint transitions affect visual performance. The work links lens optical properties to what wearers actually perceive, in line with the lab's ophthalmic optics focus.
papers.authors: Aurora Piccioli, Elisabetta Baldanzi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity under monochromatic yellow light
papers.abstract: Using an art installation lit by low-pressure sodium lamps that produce near-monochromatic yellow light, the team measured visual acuity and contrast sensitivity and compared them with a normal white-lit room. Acuity was unchanged, while contrast sensitivity showed a clinically relevant but not conclusive bias, suggesting the chromatic-blur-free light merits larger follow-up studies.
papers.authors: Elisabetta Baldanzi, Paolo Antonino Grasso, Claudio Gori, Massimo Gurioli, Federico Tommasi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: Florence and the history of glasses: between fake news and technological progress
papers.abstract: Reviews the historical record on the invention and early spread of eyeglasses in medieval Florence, separating legend from documented technological development.
papers.authors: Elisabetta Baldanzi, Alessandro Farini

papers.title: A leap in the dark! How understanding horses' color perception improves their performance and welfare in show jumping
papers.abstract: Applies dichromatic vision models to simulate how horses perceive show-jumping obstacles. The authors argue that choosing obstacle and course colors matched to equine vision could improve performance and animal welfare.
papers.authors: Alessia Fava, Alessandro Farini

0021.name: Alessio Fracasso
0021.bio: Alessio Fracasso is a neuroscientist who investigates the neurophysiology of sensory-motor and visual systems, focusing on the interface between sensory stimulation, action, and perception. Fracasso utilizes ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) and psychophysical modeling to map the topographic organization of the human brain at a mesoscopic scale. Their research examines population receptive field (pRF) properties and laminar-specific BOLD responses in the visual cortex. In addition to fundamental systems neuroscience, Fracasso applies these neuroimaging and computational methods to study the neural substrates of clinical conditions, including schizophrenia, congenital chiasmal malformations, and strabismus.
0021.research_direction: Dr. Fracasso has recently been utilizing multimodal methods, including high-field fMRI, population receptive field modeling, and psychophysics, to investigate the topographic organization of the visual and oculomotor systems. Their recent work explores spatial and perceptual dynamics during active vision, mapping the tuning properties of memory-guided saccades in the parietal lobe and examining how upper-field biases in the superior colliculus shape peri-saccadic perception. They are also investigating whether map-like topographical principles extend to higher-level representations, testing how manipulable object features are organized in association cortices and probing cross-modal retinotopic plasticity in the deprived auditory cortex of congenitally deaf individuals. Additionally, their clinical research applies structural MRI to evaluate choroid plexus morphology as a potential anatomical marker for tracking the progression of schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis.

papers.title: Mapping memory-guided saccade population receptive fields reveals principles of cortical organization along the human intraparietal sulcus
papers.abstract: Using 7T fMRI and a forward-modelling (pRF-style) approach, the authors estimate not only preferred saccade direction but also tuning width for memory-guided saccade planning and execution. They report contralateral direction preference and a previously undescribed large-scale topographic organization of saccade tuning width across early visual cortex and the intraparietal sulcus. Specificity decreases along the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Alessio Fracasso, Jasper Fabius, Kristina Moravkova, Rosanne Timmerman, Rebecca Taylor, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: The Neural Organization of Visual Information in the Auditory Cortex of the Congenitally Deaf
papers.abstract: Using a retinotopy fMRI case-study design in two congenitally deaf and one hearing participant, the authors test whether deprived auditory cortex carries low-level visual spatial information. They find that visual field information is represented in the deaf auditory cortex in an organized way, extending evidence for cross-modal plasticity to spatial mapping.
papers.authors: Zohar Tal, Joana Sayal, Fang Fang, Yanchao Bi, Jorge Almeida, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Contentopic mapping in ventral and dorsal association cortex: The topographical organization of manipulable object information
papers.abstract: Using high-field fMRI and a population-receptive-field style analysis, the study tests whether mid-level properties of manipulable objects are laid out as topographic maps in ventral and dorsal visual cortex. Object-related information shows orderly, map-like organization, supporting a topographic principle for object representation beyond retinotopy.
papers.authors: Jorge Almeida, Stephanie Kristensen, Zohar Tal, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Choroid plexus morphology in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis: A cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Choroid plexus volumes were compared across participants at clinical high risk for psychosis, first-episode psychosis, established schizophrenia, and healthy controls using structural MRI. The study characterises how this ventricular structure differs across illness stages and relates it to clinical features, offering a candidate marker of psychosis progression.
papers.authors: Gina Brunner, Ruchika Gajwani, Joachim Gross, Andrew Gumley, Rosanne H. Timmerman, Rebecca Taylor, Rajeev Krishnadas, Stephen M. Lawrie, Matthias Schwannauer, Frauke Schultze-Lutter, Peter J. Uhlhaas, Alessio Fracasso

papers.title: Peri-Saccadic Orientation Identification Performance and Visual Neural Sensitivity Are Higher in the Upper Visual Field
papers.abstract: Combining human psychophysics with recordings of superior colliculus neurons in monkeys, the study asks whether perception around the time of a saccade follows the lower-field advantage typical of steady fixation or the upper-field bias of the colliculus. Orientation identification was better for upper-field targets just before and during saccades, matching stronger collicular visual sensitivity in the upper field. The result suggests that collicular representations shape perception during active vision.
papers.authors: Alessio Fracasso, Antimo Buonocore, Ziad M. Hafed

0022.name: Alex Martin
0022.institution: National Institute of Mental Health, National Institutes of Health
0022.department: Laboratory of Brain and Cognition (Section on Cognitive Neuropsychology)
0022.bio: Alex Martin is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Section on Cognitive Neuropsychology at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH). Martin’s research program investigates the neural architecture of semantic memory, specifically how conceptual knowledge about objects is grounded in the sensory and motor systems of the brain. Utilizing neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG), they explore the representation of category-specific knowledge and how these circuits are modified by learning and experience. Their work also examines the neural mechanisms underlying social interaction and communication in typically developing individuals and those with autism spectrum disorders.
0022.research_direction: Dr. Martin has recently been investigating the large-scale organization of human brain networks and cognitive representations using multimodal neuroimaging and behavioral modeling. Their recent work explores the architecture of semantic and valuation systems, employing representational similarity analysis and Bayesian embedding to map the unified conceptual space of abstract and concrete words, and to understand how the brain automatically encodes the hedonic and inhibitory properties of food images. They are also examining the neural mechanics of visual and semantic processing efficiency, utilizing simultaneous fMRI and EEG to probe how repetition suppression and oscillatory power dynamics support object naming. Additionally, Dr. Martin is charting the clinical and developmental topography of resting-state functional connectivity, investigating how whole-brain network coupling differs in high-functioning autistic adults and tracking the early maturation of hippocampal-cortical memory circuits in infants and toddlers.

papers.title: Repetition-related reductions in neural activity support improved behavior through increases in oscillatory power
papers.abstract: Simultaneous fMRI and EEG was recorded while people named objects repeatedly. With repetition, oscillatory power from theta up to gamma rose and resolved sooner in frontal and occipitotemporal regions that also showed fMRI repetition suppression. Gamma power changes correlated with behavioral priming and with left frontal suppression, supporting a blend of the Synchrony and Facilitation models of neural efficiency.
papers.authors: Adrian W. Gilmore, Leonardo Claudino, Cassandra M. Levesque, Anna M. Agron, Peter J. Molfese, Vinai Roopchansingh, Michael D. Rugg, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: A unitary representational space for abstract and concrete concepts derived from human similarity judgments
papers.abstract: The authors used a Bayesian embedding method (VICE) on more than 1.4 million human similarity judgments to embed 751 concrete and abstract nouns in a 36-dimensional space. Concrete and abstract concepts intermingle within dimensions rather than forming separate systems. The interpretable dimensions are organized along two main axes, concreteness and agency, and the model can be extended with new words.
papers.authors: Andrew Persichetti, Charles Zheng, Taylor Li, Stephen Gotts, Francisco Pereira, Alex Martin

papers.title: The Development of Hippocampal-Cortical Functional Connectivity in Infants and Toddlers
papers.abstract: Resting-state fMRI from 212 infants across the first two years of life was used to track how the hippocampus couples with cortex along its long axis. Connectivity with canonical adult memory regions increased strongly over this period, with differences between anterior and posterior hippocampus. The findings chart the early functional development of the memory system.
papers.authors: Sam Audrain, Shawn C. Milleville, Jenna M. Wilson, Jude Baffoe-Bonnie, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: A functional parcellation of the whole brain in high-functioning individuals with autism spectrum disorder reveals atypical patterns of network organization
papers.abstract: Using resting-state fMRI acquired with a sequence tuned for high temporal signal-to-noise across the brain, the authors built whole-brain functional network maps for 70 high-functioning autistic adults and 70 matched typically developing adults. Comparing the two maps showed that autistic individuals have atypical network organization, including differences in how networks are subdivided and coupled. The work supplies a comprehensive, data-driven reference map of network topography in autism.
papers.authors: Andrew S. Persichetti, Jiayu Shao, Stephen J. Gotts, Alex Martin

papers.title: Automatic engagement of limbic and prefrontal networks in response to food images reflects distinct information about food hedonics and inhibitory control
papers.abstract: Forty-three participants viewed images of 36 foods while undergoing fMRI, and representational similarity analysis was used to split food-responsive brain areas into data-driven clusters. A limbic cluster tracked how pleasant foods were rated, while a prefrontal cluster carried information about healthfulness and inhibitory control. The results show that these distinct properties of food are encoded automatically, without a task requiring judgment.
papers.authors: Jason A. Avery, Madeline Carrington, John E. Ingeholm, Valerie Darcey, W. Kyle Simmons, Kevin D. Hall, Alex Martin

0023.name: Alex S. Baldwin
0023.bio: Alex S. Baldwin is an Assistant Professor at McGill University and a Junior Scientist in the Brain Repair and Integrative Neuroscience (BRaIN) program at the RI-MUHC. Baldwin’s research investigates the mechanisms of human visual perception by combining psychophysical experiments with mathematical and computational modeling of neural processing. Their work focuses on spatial vision, specifically how the brain integrates local features into global contours and textures, as well as the dynamics of binocular vision and stereopsis in both healthy aging and clinical populations such as those with amblyopia.
0023.research_direction: Dr. Baldwin has recently been investigating the mechanisms of spatial and binocular vision in both neurotypical and amblyopic populations. Their recent work explores basic spatial processing by measuring how contrast summation scales from the fovea to the periphery using elongated gratings and personalized sensitivity maps. In the clinical domain, they are developing and applying novel dichoptic tests to quantify the depth of interocular imbalance and suppression in amblyopia. Additionally, they are probing the underlying nature of spatial and stereoscopic deficits by testing whether simulated cortical spatial scrambling accounts for amblyopic letter acuity loss, and by examining how different task demands, such as disparity detection versus depth-sign discrimination, affect the measured prevalence of stereo-anomaly.

papers.title: Summation of contrast across the visual field: a common "fourth root" rule holds from the fovea to the periphery
papers.abstract: Measures how contrast detection thresholds improve as elongated grating strips get longer, at the fovea, at 3 degrees and at 10.5 degrees eccentricity. By using each observer's own map of local sensitivity to equate local visibility across the strip, the study finds the same fourth-root summation rule at every location. A noisy-energy model is proposed to explain this common rule, tying summation to early cortical architecture.
papers.authors: Alex S. Baldwin, Tim S. Meese

papers.title: The amblyopic acuity deficit: Identification of letters distorted by spatial scrambling algorithms
papers.abstract: Amblyopic letter acuity is worse than expected from grating cut-off frequency, and cortical spatial scrambling has been proposed as a cause. The authors built stimuli that simulate subcortical or cortical scrambling, or add band-pass noise, and tested amblyopic and fellow eyes on letter identification. Efficiency did not differ overall between eyes for scrambling, but did in a subset of participants, giving partial support for a scrambling account.
papers.authors: Raffles Xingqi Zhu, Robert F. Hess, Alex S. Baldwin

papers.title: Amblyopic binocular imbalance quantified by the dichoptic contrast ordering test and dichoptic letters test
papers.abstract: Applies two dichoptic tests, DiCOT and the Dichoptic Letters Test, to people with amblyopia to quantify how strongly the two eyes are imbalanced. It examines how the measured imbalance relates to other visual function and to the depth of suppression. The work supports these rapid tablet-friendly tests as clinical measures of interocular imbalance in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Alexandre Reynaud, Marie-Céline Lorenzini, Robert K. Koenekoop, Robert F. Hess, Alex S. Baldwin

papers.title: The dichoptic contrast ordering test: A method for measuring the depth of binocular imbalance
papers.abstract: Introduces DiCOT, a tablet-based test in which observers rank the perceived contrast of stimuli shown separately to the two eyes to derive a factor that balances them. Imbalance was induced with neutral-density filters, Bangerter filters and a +3 D blur lens and compared with the Dichoptic Letter Test. Both tests were highly repeatable, but DiCOT gave smaller and partly different imbalance estimates, suggesting they capture partly distinct aspects of binocular imbalance.
papers.authors: Alex S. Baldwin, Marie-Céline Lorenzini, Annabel Wing-Yan Fan, Robert F. Hess, Alexandre Reynaud

papers.title: Stereo-anomaly is found more frequently in tasks that require discrimination between depths
papers.abstract: Reports of the prevalence of stereo-anomaly among people with normal vision range from a few percent to nearly a third.
