Using a digital stereo tool with either disparity detection or sign discrimination tasks in 228 participants, the study shows 98% could do detection but only 69% could reliably do discrimination. The task demand therefore explains much of the discrepancy in earlier prevalence estimates.
papers.authors: Alex S. Baldwin, Seung Hyun Min, Sara Alarcon Carrillo, Zili Wang, Ziyun Cheng, Jiawei Zhou, Robert F. Hess

0024.name: Alex White
0024.bio: Alex L. White is a cognitive neuroscientist and Assistant Professor whose research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual perception, selective attention, and word recognition. White’s work focuses on the limitations of processing capacity during reading, employing methodologies such as behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and functional MRI. Their research examines the functional properties of the visual word form area (VWFA), specifically how its activity is modulated by task-specific demands and top-down feedback from language regions. Currently, White explores the spatial and temporal bottlenecks that constrain the recognition of multiple words and how these constraints influence reading development.
0024.research_direction: Dr. White's recent work explores the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual word recognition, using fMRI to investigate how top-down goals, such as active reading, dynamically reshape stimulus selectivity and feedback in the visual word form area. They have recently been investigating the capacity limits of the visual system when confronted with multiple items, combining behavioral psychophysics and simultaneous-suppression fMRI paradigms to test whether multiple words are processed serially or in parallel without mutual cortical suppression. To further probe these processing bottlenecks, their research examines whether grouping separate stimuli into known compound words allows them to bypass serial constraints, while also extending computational models of redundant-target designs to predict how the presence of multiple visual targets influences response speed and accuracy.

papers.title: Serial processing of two words becomes parallel when they combine to form a known compound word
papers.abstract: Participants could judge the lexical status of only one of two unrelated words flashed briefly above and below fixation, consistent with a serial bottleneck in word recognition. When the two words together formed an existing compound word (e.g., bottle + neck), performance changed and the pair could be handled in parallel, suggesting the bottleneck is at the level of assembling separate word representations rather than at a strictly fixed capacity for two items.
papers.authors: Amritha Anupindi, Liana R. Eisler, Mariam U. Latif, Vassiki S. Chauhan, Alex L. White

papers.title: Simultaneous cortical responses to multiple written words
papers.abstract: An fMRI study that adapts the simultaneous-suppression paradigm to written words, varying how many words appear (zero, one, two sequentially, or two simultaneously) while holding visual stimulation constant. Behavioral accuracy dropped for two simultaneous words, and the cortical responses were used to test whether word-selective regions can process several words at once without mutual suppression.
papers.authors: Vassiki S. Chauhan, Krystal McCook, Mariam Latif, Alex L. White

papers.title: Negative effects of redundant targets
papers.abstract: Redundant-target designs compare responses to one versus two targets and are used to tell parallel from serial processing models. The authors extend three standard models to predict accuracy as well as speed, and show that two of them predict a reversal, with slower responses to two targets than to one. They then test this counterintuitive prediction experimentally with words and other stimuli.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Alex L. White, John Palmer, Genevieve Sanders, Jannat Hossain, Zelda B. Zabinsky

papers.title: Reading reshapes stimulus selectivity in the visual word form area
papers.abstract: Sixteen adults were scanned with fMRI while viewing words, pseudowords and unfamiliar characters under three tasks (word detection, color detection in the letters, color detection at fixation). The VWFA preferred letter strings even when ignored, engaging in reading amplified the response to words, and task demands reshaped selectivity, supporting a view of the region as flexible and shaped by reading experience and top-down demands.
papers.authors: Vassiki S. Chauhan, Krystal C. McCook, Alex L. White

papers.title: Engaging in word recognition elicits highly specific modulations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with precisely localized word-selective regions, the study shows that the visual word form area responds strongly to letter strings only when the observer is actively engaged in a word-reading task, and that this task-dependent enhancement is specific to that region and to word-like stimuli. The pattern of results indicates that language areas send targeted top-down feedback into ventral visual cortex when reading is the goal, rather than the region simply responding to text automatically.
papers.authors: Alex L. White, Kendrick Kay, Kenny A. Tang, Jason D. Yeatman

0025.name: Alexander C. Schütz
0025.bio: Alexander C. Schütz is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Philipps-Universität Marburg and investigates the bidirectional interaction between visual perception and eye movements. Their research explores how the brain maintains a stable representation of the environment despite frequent saccadic interruptions and sensory gaps like the blind spot. Schütz combines psychophysics, high-speed eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling to examine the optimization of oculomotor control for task-relevant information gathering. Their work includes studies on trans-saccadic integration, smooth pursuit eye movements, and the integration of salience and value signals in sensorimotor learning.
0025.research_direction: Dr. Schütz studies the bidirectional interaction between visual perception and eye movements, with an emphasis on how the visual system gathers and uses information to guide behavior. Earlier work showed that smooth pursuit eye movements improve visual sensitivity, that saccade choices dynamically integrate visual salience and reward value, and reviewed how eye movements and perception interact more generally. Their more recent work asks how the brain handles sensory uncertainty and missing information, focusing on metacognition and perceptual completion. Studies probe how observers assess their own perceptual inferences, using confidence judgments in tasks involving visual modal and amodal occlusion, auditory filling-in and time-constrained visual search, whether saccades preferentially target the physiological blind spot, and, with electroencephalography, how the visual system uses structural priors to estimate the number of partially occluded objects.

papers.title: Low confidence for perceptual completion of partially occluded objects
papers.abstract: Tests whether observers feel less certain about what they perceive in occluded regions than about what is directly visible. Confidence judgments in visual modal and amodal completion tasks were lower for completed than for uncovered stimuli even at matched accuracy. This suggests perceptual completion is accompanied by metacognitive awareness that the information is inferred.
papers.authors: Cemre Baykan, Pascal Mamassian, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: A review of the costs of eye movements
papers.abstract: Reviews the different costs that accompany moving the eyes, including energetic and time costs, loss of visual input around saccades, and the effort of planning and learning movements. Argues that these costs are weighed against the benefits of information gain, so that gaze behaviour can be understood as a cost-benefit optimisation. Outlines how this framework can unify findings on saccade, pursuit and search behaviour.
papers.authors: Alexander C. Schütz, Emma E. M. Stewart

papers.title: Trade-off between search costs and accuracy in oculomotor and manual search tasks
papers.abstract: Examines how people balance the effort and time of searching against the accuracy of a subsequent perceptual decision. Participants performed a combined search and discrimination task using either eye movements or manual movements. Search behaviour in both effectors adapted to costs in a way consistent with an optimal trade-off between speed and accuracy.
papers.authors: Ilja Wagner, Jan Tünnermann, Anna Schubö, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: Robust generalization of tuning to self-induced sensation
papers.abstract: Studies how the oculomotor system uses reafference signals, the expected sensory consequences of one's own movement, to tune smooth pursuit. Shows that recalibration learned for one situation generalises robustly to other conditions. This supports a flexible, prediction-based tuning mechanism for self-generated visual motion.
papers.authors: Rozana Ovsepian, David Souto, Alexander C. Schütz

papers.title: A simple optical flow model explains why certain object viewpoints are special
papers.abstract: Asks why some views of a 3D object, such as canonical or cardinal viewpoints, are perceived as special. Shows that a simple model based on 2D optical flow produced by rotating the object predicts which viewpoints people consider special. The result links viewpoint preferences to low-level motion signals rather than requiring high-level object knowledge.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Emma E. M. Stewart, Roland W. Fleming, Alexander C. Schütz

0027.name: Alfredo Spagna
0027.department: Department of Psychological and Social Sciences
0027.bio: Alfredo Spagna is a researcher at Columbia University and serves as the Director of Undergraduate Studies in Neuroscience and Behavior. Spagna’s research investigates the psychological and neural mechanisms of attention, perception, and visual mental imagery, focusing on the distinction between internally generated mental representations and sensory-driven perception. Utilizing 7-T fMRI, MEG, and EEG, they have identified a heterarchical architecture for mental imagery centered on the left fusiform imagery node. Their current work examines the interactions between crossmodal attention and consciousness, as well as the application of neuroscientific findings to interdisciplinary fields like implicit bias and theatrical performance.
0027.research_direction: Dr. Spagna has recently been investigating the neural architectures underlying visual mental imagery and conscious visual perception. Their recent work explores whether voluntary imagery relies on a traditional reverse sensory hierarchy or a heterarchical network centered on a left fusiform imagery node that integrates conceptual information from semantic regions. Using a combination of time-resolved neural recordings, high-resolution fMRI, and novel behavioral batteries, they are tracking the spatiotemporal dynamics of how the brain recruits domain-general versus content-specific imagery processes and comparing these representational spaces to actual visual perception. Alongside this focus on imagination, they are also examining the mechanisms of visual awareness, specifically investigating how pre-stimulus beta and gamma oscillatory dynamics within right-lateralized attentional networks predict whether near-threshold visual targets reach conscious report.

papers.title: Beta and Gamma Dynamics in Attentional Networks Predict Conscious Reports
papers.abstract: Using magnetoencephalography with a cued near-threshold detection task, the study looks at brain oscillations in the interval before a target appears. Whether a target is later reported depends on beta-band activity in right-hemisphere parietal and temporo-occipital regions, theta-gamma coupling and long-range gamma coherence with left temporoparietal cortex. The results link right-lateralized attentional networks to what reaches conscious report.
papers.authors: Alfredo Spagna, Jianghao Liu, Paolo Bartolomeo

papers.title: The Fusiform Imagery Node: Where vision meets concepts in the left temporal lobe
papers.abstract: A perspective integrating neuroimaging and neuropsychological findings to argue that voluntary visual imagery relies on a distributed network centred on the left fusiform gyrus. More anterior left temporal regions are proposed to supply the node with semantic and conceptual information, reconciling patient and imaging data.
papers.authors: Paolo Bartolomeo, Jianghao Liu, Alfredo Spagna

papers.title: Tracking the mind's eyes: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Domain-General and Domain-Specific Visual Mental Imagery
papers.abstract: A recent full preprint using time-resolved neural recordings to track when and where imagery recruits domain-general versus content-specific processes. It extends his lab's spatial imagery model to the temporal domain.
papers.authors: Chen He, Diane Lamarle, Jianghao Liu, Paolo Bartolomeo, Alfredo Spagna

papers.title: Probing the Imaginable: Shared and Distinct Processes Between Imagery and Perception Across Semantic Domains
papers.abstract: Introduces a computerized behavioral battery that elicits visual imagery and visual perception across five semantic domains: colors, faces, letters, maps and shapes. Tested in 75 typical imagers, it asks whether the two processes share a common semantic representational space and how imagery vividness relates to task performance.
papers.authors: Zixin Liu, Tengyu Song, Chloe Jeanne Lambert, Kassey Chang, Kezia Chuaqui, Natalie Baer, Rachel Frank, Jianghao Liu, Paolo Bartolomeo, Alfredo Spagna

papers.title: Visual mental imagery: Evidence for a heterarchical neural architecture
papers.abstract: Argues against the classic view that mental imagery is simply perception run in reverse through a top-down visual hierarchy. Drawing together 7-T fMRI, lesion, stimulation and other evidence, it proposes a heterarchical architecture in which a left fusiform imagery node interacts with semantic and frontoparietal regions, with early visual cortex playing a less central role. The paper anchors an extensive open-peer-commentary exchange in the journal.
papers.authors: Alfredo Spagna, Zoe Heidenry, Michelle Miselevich, Chloe Lambert, Benjamin E. Eisenstadt, Laura Tremblay, Zixin Liu, Jianghao Liu, Paolo Bartolomeo

0028.name: Alice J. O'Toole
0028.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
0028.department: School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences
0028.bio: Alice J. O'Toole is a Professor and holder of the Aage and Margareta Møller Endowed Chair, conducting research that integrates psychology, computer science, and neuroscience to examine human and machine perception of faces and bodies. O'Toole's work utilizes deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) and machine learning to model high-level visual representations, comparing algorithmic performance with human expertise in forensic face identification. They use methodologies such as psychophysics and functional neuroimaging to investigate how identity, gender, and viewpoint are encoded within neural populations and computational architectures. Recent investigations by O'Toole focus on the robustness of face representations in real-world viewing conditions and the potential biases inherent in automated recognition systems.
0028.research_direction: Dr. O'Toole's recent work explores the visual perception of faces and bodies across both human cognition and artificial intelligence. They have recently been investigating how to optimize human-machine partnerships in applied face recognition, testing strategies for when human reviewers—ranging from novices to forensic experts—can best improve algorithmic accuracy. In the realm of deep learning, their research dissects how neural networks represent identities, examining how foundation models can be trained to simultaneously classify faces, whole bodies, and objects, and analyzing what specific features—such as gender, viewing angle, or inadvertent facial cues—are captured within body-identification embeddings. Additionally, they are studying the social evaluation of bodies in human observers, testing how cross-cultural differences influence the personality traits and first impressions people attribute to 3D body shapes.

papers.title: Culture and conceptual influences on first impressions from body shape
papers.abstract: Tests whether body-shape-based first impressions found in Western observers generalize to an East Asian culture. American and Chinese participants rated 3D body models on Big Five-derived traits; both shared a main conscientiousness/valence dimension but differed on a secondary one, with Americans linking extraversion to thinner bodies and Chinese participants to average or sturdier bodies. A second study showed culturally embedded trait associations, rather than weight stereotypes alone, explain the differences, consistent with Dynamic Interactive Theory.
papers.authors: Ying Hu, Lan Chen, Natalie K. Bendiksen, Xiaolan Fu, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Unlocking the power of partnership: How humans and machines can work together to improve face recognition
papers.abstract: Examines when having a person review a face-recognition algorithm's decision actually improves accuracy. Testing participants from novices to professional forensic examiners, the authors show that combining human and machine judgments helps most when the two have comparable competence, and that even weaker humans can add value. A selective 'intelligent fusion' strategy that picks the reviewers most likely to help beats both machine-only and indiscriminate human-machine combination.
papers.authors: P. Jonathon Phillips, Geraldine Jeckeln, Carina A. Hahn, Amy N. Yates, P. C. Fontana, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Face, Whole-Person, and Object Classification in a Unified Space Via The Interleaved Multi-Domain Identity Curriculum
papers.abstract: Introduces a training curriculum that lets a single foundation-model backbone (DINOv3, CLIP, EVA-02) handle object recognition, face recognition at high and low quality, and whole-body person recognition at once without catastrophic forgetting. The best variants match domain-specific experts on all four tasks and outperform humans at multitasking. Analyses of the embedding space show that under 100 principal components from one task suffice for the others, implying heavy feature sharing across domains.
papers.authors: Thomas M. Metz, Matthew Q. Hill, Alice J. O'Toole

papers.title: Dissecting human body representations in deep networks trained for person identification
papers.abstract: Analyzes the embeddings of four body-identification networks trained on about 1.9 million images of roughly 5,000 identities. Facial information turns out to contribute substantially to body identification even without face training, and the embeddings also encode gender, viewing angle and even source dataset. Principal-component analysis of the embedding space can improve identification accuracy without any retraining.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG 2025); arXiv:2502.15934
papers.authors: Thomas M. Metz, Matthew Q. Hill, Blake Myers, Veda Nandan Gandi, Rahul Chilakapati, Alice J. O'Toole

0029.name: Alisa Baron
0029.lab_name: Processing and Acquisition of Language in Multilinguals (PALM) Laboratory
0029.bio: Alisa Baron is an Associate Professor at the University of Rhode Island and directs the Processing and Acquisition of Language in Multilinguals (PALM) Laboratory. Baron’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying first and second language acquisition, focusing on bilingual grammar and literacy development in neurotypical and language-disordered populations. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), Baron examines how cross-linguistic influences shape language processing and audio-visual integration. Their work aims to advance evidence-based assessment and intervention strategies for culturally and linguistically diverse children and individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders.
0029.research_direction: Dr. Baron has recently been investigating how young children learn to read and process spoken language, with a particular focus on bilingual children. Their recent work uses eye tracking, EEG, and near-infrared brain imaging to ask how early speech-sound discrimination, rapid naming ability, and gaze behavior relate to word reading in early school-age children. They also study how Spanish-English bilingual children process grammar, such as grammatical gender and sentence structure, as they hear it. In a more applied direction, they have explored an app that trains young adults with autism to look at speakers' mouths to support audiovisual speech perception.

papers.title: Rapid Automatized Naming (RAN) and Word Reading Fluency in Early School-Aged Children: A Pilot Eye-Tracking Study
papers.abstract: While rapid automatized naming (RAN) is an established clinical predictor of word reading fluency, the oculomotor mechanisms subserving this relationship in emergent readers remain poorly understood. This investigation evaluated whether behavioral alphanumeric RAN performance (rapid letter naming [RLN] and rapid digit naming [RDN]) predicted gaze metrics across discrete temporal stages of local word reading. Thirty-three English-speaking early school-aged children (ages 6–8) completed standardized RAN assessments and an eye-tracking paradigm during oral sentence reading containing embedded target words. Dependent oculomotor measures indexed early (first fixation duration), intermediate (regression path duration), and late (total word reading time) processing stages. Linear mixed-effects regression demonstrated that RLN and RDN exclusively accounted for significant variance in regression path duration, such that faster naming speed was associated with shorter regressive durations from the target words. Neither early nor late fixation durations were reliably predicted by RAN scores. These findings indicate that RAN automaticity uniquely indexes intermediate oculomotor processing during word identification, suggesting that slower naming speeds reflect bottlenecks in the real-time integration of visual-orthographic and phonological representations.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Alexia Martins, Gavino Puggioni, Vanessa Harwood

papers.title: Using the Listening2Faces App with Three Young Adults with Autism: A Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently exhibit atypical audiovisual speech integration alongside significant communication challenges. This pilot investigation assessed the feasibility, usability, and clinical implementation of Listening2Faces (L2F)—a specialized digital training application engineered to reinforce audiovisual speech perception by targeting gaze toward visible articulatory dynamics (mouth and jaw movements). Three young adults with ASD and complex communication needs completed baseline evaluations followed by multi-session computerized training using L2F within an educational setting. Individualized behavioral adaptations and behavioral supports, including cognitive picture rehearsal and token reinforcement, were implemented to maintain engagement and mitigate task-related distress. Feasibility was indexed via compliance, session completion rates, and progression through hierarchically structured perceptual difficulty tiers. All three participants successfully executed the baseline auditory noise assessment (ANA) and completed eight or more difficulty levels within the application, with one participant finishing the entire intervention protocol. Although individual trajectories and engagement profiles differed, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of application-based audiovisual speech perception training paired with tailored behavioral supports for autistic individuals with complex communication profiles.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Vanessa Harwood, Cooper Woodard, Kaitlyn Anderson, Barbara Fernandes, Jessica Sullivan, Julia Irwin

papers.title: Grammatical gender in spoken word recognition in school-age Spanish monolingual and Spanish–English bilingual children
papers.abstract: This study investigated the online processing of grammatical gender during auditory word recognition in Spanish-speaking school-aged children with varying degrees of cumulative English language exposure. Using a visual world eye-tracking paradigm with a four-alternative forced-choice visual display, children heard gender-marked definite articles followed by target nouns under conditions where distractor objects had either matching or mismatching grammatical gender, as well as grammatical versus ungrammatical article-noun pairings. Cluster-based permutation analyses were applied to fixations across the article and noun acoustic intervals. Results revealed robust lexical facilitation effects across all participants during the noun interval, alongside pronounced processing disruption and delayed target fixations during ungrammatical article-noun presentations. Furthermore, cumulative English exposure and chronological age significantly modulated gaze distributions: children with higher English exposure showed reduced overall fixations to target nouns, whereas older children demonstrated elevated target fixation rates. Additionally, lower English exposure was associated with an interaction between target noun gender (masculine vs. feminine) and competitor condition, with heightened target fixations in different-gender contexts for masculine items. These findings demonstrate that bilingual children preserve syntactic gender congruency constraints during auditory recognition, while exposure profile modulates the efficiency of lexical retrieval.
papers.authors: Alisa Baron, Katrina Connell, Daniel Kleinman, Lisa M. Bedore, Zenzi M. Griffin

papers.title: Event Related Potentials to Native Speech Contrasts Predicts Word Reading Abilities in Early School-Aged Children
papers.abstract: Fine-grained phonemic discrimination provides a neurobiological scaffolding for phoneme-grapheme correspondence and fluent word decoding; however, the precise electrophysiological dynamics linking phonological tuning to reading acquisition require clarification. This study examined auditory event-related potentials (ERPs) elicited in 33 typically developing monolingual English-speaking children aged 6 to 8 years within an auditory oddball paradigm presenting native English (/ba/ vs. /da/) and nonnative Spanish (/ba/ vs. dental /da/) consonant-vowel contrast pairs. Evoked responses were recorded over bilateral temporal and frontocentral electrode sites to determine discrimination-related components (acoustic change complex and late discriminative negativity). Standardized behavioral assessments of reading accuracy and rate were administered concurrently. Electrophysiological results indicated robust discrimination responses to native phonetic contrasts that significantly correlated with standardized single-word and pseudoword reading fluency measures. In contrast, neural sensitivity to nonnative acoustic tokens did not account for variance in English word decoding performance. These findings indicate that neuroplastic perceptual narrowing specifically optimized for native phonological categories directly supports the orthographic-phonological integration requisite for developing literacy skills.
papers.authors: Vanessa Harwood, Adrian Garcia-Sierra, Raphael Dias, Emily Jelfs, Alisa Baron

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Morphosyntactic Processing in Spanish–English Bilingual Children: A Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy Study
papers.abstract: Dual-language exposure fundamentally shapes neural specialization for morphosyntactic computation during childhood. This study employed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to delineate the cortical substrates of English grammatical processing in school-age Spanish–English bilingual children (ages 6–10), examining how age of acquisition, chronological age, and relative language usage modulate hemodynamic activity. Children listened to grammatical and ungrammatical English sentences manipulating early-acquired (present progressive -ing) and late-acquired (past tense -ed and third-person singular -s) morphosyntactic morphemes while optical absorption was recorded over bilateral inferior frontal gyri (IFG) and superior temporal gyri (STG). Bilateral frontal and temporal engagement emerged during syntactic violation detection, with greater oxy-hemoglobin (HbO) increases in left anterior cortical regions for morphosyntactic anomalies. Moreover, chronological age and greater current English exposure predicted pronounced left-lateralized IFG recruitment for later-acquired grammatical morphemes, whereas early-acquired morphemes engaged bilateral peri-sylvian networks across age cohorts. The findings demonstrate that neurodevelopmental specialization for second-language morphology is non-uniform across syntactic forms and dynamically mediated by cumulative and current environmental language input.
papers.venue: Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research
papers.authors: Baron, Wagley, Hu, Kovelman

0030.name: Allison B. Sekuler
0030.department: Rotman Research Institute; Baycrest Academy for Research and Education
0030.bio: Allison B. Sekuler holds the Sandra A. Rotman Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience, specializing in vision science and the neuroscience of aging. Their research employs psychophysical, electrophysiological (EEG), and neuroimaging (fMRI) methodologies to examine the neural mechanisms of visual perception, including face processing, motion perception, and perceptual learning. Sekuler’s work has documented functional brain plasticity, illustrating how the aging brain undergoes compensatory changes to maintain performance levels during physiological decline. Currently, Sekuler directs translational initiatives focused on developing neurotechnological interventions and biomarkers for the detection and treatment of dementia and age-related cognitive impairment.
0030.research_direction: Dr. Sekuler has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying age-related visual changes, using noise-masking psychophysics to disentangle how internal neural noise and calculation efficiency contribute to face discrimination deficits in older adults. Their recent work also explores the intersection of perception and short-term memory, examining how perceptual factors like stimulus similarity, verbal labeling, and sensory decline shape memory performance and introduce potential confounds into memory research. Additionally, they are studying visual attention in simulated three-dimensional space, testing how monocular depth cues and attended spatial distance interact to modulate peripheral target detection.

papers.title: Contribution of internal noise and calculation efficiency to face discrimination deficits in older adults
papers.abstract: The study asks why older adults are worse than younger adults at telling faces apart. Using noise-masking psychophysics, it separates the contribution of noisy internal neural processing from the efficiency with which available face information is used (calculation efficiency). The results help pin down which of these mechanisms accounts for age-related face discrimination deficits.
papers.authors: Sarah E. Creighton, Patrick J. Bennett, Allison B. Sekuler

papers.title: Perceptual Attributes in Memory Research
papers.abstract: This handbook chapter argues that perception and memory are tightly linked, especially in short-term memory, so memory researchers should design their memoranda with perceptual factors in mind. It covers stimulus similarity as a tool for framing and testing theories, perceptual confounds that can masquerade as memory differences between individuals or groups (for example due to age-related sensory decline), and the way verbal labels can support or distort remembered stimuli.
papers.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Human Memory
papers.authors: Robert Sekuler, Allison B. Sekuler

papers.title: Peripheral target detection can be modulated by target distance but not attended distance in 3D space simulated by monocular depth cues
papers.abstract: Observers detected peripheral targets in scenes where monocular depth cues created an impression of 3D space. Detection performance depended on the depicted distance of the target, but not on the distance at which attention was directed. The work informs how depth and attention interact in visual detection.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Patrick J. Bennett, Hong-jin Sun, Allison B. Sekuler

0031.name: Allison M Mckendrick
0031.department: School of Health and Clinical Sciences (Optometry and Vision Science); Lions Eye Institute
0031.bio: Allison M. McKendrick is the Lions Eye Institute UWA Chair in Optometry Research and a Professorial Fellow at the University of Melbourne, specializing in the field of visual neuroscience. McKendrick's research program investigates the mechanisms of visual processing in healthy aging and pathological conditions such as glaucoma, migraine, and visual snow syndrome. They employ a multi-disciplinary methodology that integrates clinical psychophysics, human electrophysiology, and high-resolution ocular and brain imaging to develop diagnostic tests and monitor disease progression. Their current work focuses on translating these findings into applications, particularly regarding how vision loss impacts daily activities such as night-time driving performance.
0031.research_direction: Dr. McKendrick has recently been investigating how clinical ophthalmic conditions and fundamental visual processing deficits impact both basic perception and real-world behavior. Their recent work explores Visual Snow Syndrome by developing novel psychophysical matching tasks to quantify the density and contrast of the snow-like percept, aiming to establish objective perceptual assays that could serve as clinical trial endpoints. In the domain of glaucoma, they are examining the differential vulnerability of the ON and OFF visual pathways using contrast increment and decrement visual search paradigms, alongside creating synthetic structure-function datasets of perimetry and retinal thickness to benchmark disease progression algorithms. Additionally, their research addresses applied visual processing by evaluating how basic tests of visual motion sensitivity can be utilized to assess driving safety, hazard detection, and visually guided vehicle control.

papers.title: Visual Perception in Visual Snow Syndrome
papers.abstract: Reviews the rapidly growing literature on how people with visual snow syndrome perceive the world, following the condition's recognition in ICD-11 in 2025. Because diagnosis is purely symptom-based, the authors focus on new perceptual assays that quantify individual differences in symptoms and could serve as trial endpoints. They relate these findings to candidate visual-system mechanisms and outline open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Cassandra J. Brooks, Bao N. Nguyen, Allison M. McKendrick

papers.title: Visual motion sensitivity and driving performance and safety
papers.abstract: Synthesises research linking tests of visual motion sensitivity to measures of driving performance and crash safety. The evidence indicates that motion sensitivity matters for timely hazard detection and for visually guided vehicle control such as lane keeping. The review discusses how impaired motion perception might be assessed and used to predict driving risk.
papers.authors: Joanne M. Wood, Alex A. Black, Philippe F. Lacherez, Allison M. McKendrick

papers.title: A Structure–Function Dataset With Known Rates of Glaucomatous Progression
papers.abstract: Introduces the Lions Eye Institute Structure-Function Dataset, an open synthetic collection of visual field (perimetry) and retinal nerve fibre layer thickness series built from clinical glaucoma data. Each simulated eye progresses at a known rate over ten visits across five years, giving a ground truth. It is meant for benchmarking and developing methods that detect glaucoma progression.
papers.authors: Andrew Turpin, Vasanth Muthusamy, Munis Raviselvan, Allison M McKendrick

papers.title: Contrast increment and decrement processing measured using visual search in established glaucoma
papers.abstract: Tests whether glaucoma affects the OFF (dark-detecting) pathway more than the ON (light-detecting) pathway, as suggested by animal models. In 106 people with established glaucoma, a visual search task compared performance for contrast increments versus decrements as visual field damage advanced. The study evaluates whether ON and OFF performance declines at different rates with severity.
papers.authors: Vanessa Thien Sze Tang, Andrew Turpin, William Huxley Morgan, Geoffrey Chan, Allison Maree McKendrick

papers.title: Improving Understanding of Visual Snow by Quantifying its Appearance and Effect on Vision
papers.abstract: Develops a way to measure what visual snow looks like and how much it degrades vision by having observers match and rate their percept, alongside psychophysical tests. Participants with visual snow syndrome could be characterised in terms of snow density and contrast, and these measures related to visual performance. The approach gives a quantitative handle on a poorly understood symptom.
papers.authors: Cassandra J. Brooks, Yu Man Chan, Joanne Fielding, Owen B. White, David R. Badcock, Allison M. McKendrick

0032.name: Alon Hafri
0032.department: Department of Linguistics and Cognitive Science
0032.bio: Alon Hafri is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Linguistics and Cognitive Science at the University of Delaware and the director of the Perception and Language (PAL) Lab. Hafri’s research focuses on the interface between vision and language, specifically investigating how the visual system extracts abstract relational structures—such as event roles and spatial configurations—from visual scenes. Utilizing psychophysics, functional MRI, and psycholinguistic techniques, they explore whether visual representations share a common compositional format with linguistic structures. Hafri’s work has demonstrated that relational information is processed rapidly and automatically, suggesting that perception provides structured content to higher-level cognitive systems.
0032.research_direction: Dr. Hafri has recently been investigating how the visual system extracts abstract structure from scenes, with a major focus on the compositional perception of physical relations like containment and support. Using brief psychophysical displays, their recent work explores whether the visual system constructs relational scenes in a canonical, sequential order, and whether it encodes abstract relational roles independently of the specific objects that fill them. Beyond physical relations, they are also examining how part-whole structural representations dictate what counts as a discrete unit during visual number estimation. Finally, Dr. Hafri’s research probes the interface between rapid scene perception and higher-order cognition by asking whether vision and language share abstract formats for concepts like symmetry, and how quickly observers can form complex social and moral impressions from a mere glance.

papers.title: Part-whole effects in visual number estimation
papers.abstract: The study asks what counts as a unit when observers estimate how many objects are in a display. It shows that number estimates are shaped by part-whole structure, so that items seen as parts of larger wholes are counted differently from independent objects. This indicates that numerosity perception operates over structured object representations rather than raw visual elements.
papers.authors: Chenxiao Guan, David Schwitzgebel, Chaz Firestone, Alon Hafri

papers.title: The psychophysics of compositionality: Relational scene perception occurs in a canonical order
papers.abstract: Across several experiments the authors ask whether the visual system assembles relational scenes (e.g., one object on or in another) in a systematic sequence rather than all at once. Using psychophysical measures of what observers perceive from brief displays, they show that relational elements are constructed in a reliable canonical order, such as the reference object before the relation. This supports the idea that perception builds scenes compositionally, in a way that parallels structure in language.
papers.authors: Zekun Sun, Chaz Firestone, Alon Hafri

papers.title: A phone in a basket looks like a knife in a cup: Role-filler independence in visual processing
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether the visual system represents the objects in a relation separately from the relation itself, as the roles and fillers of a symbolic structure would be. Observers viewing scenes with objects in relations like containment or support show interference patterns indicating that relation representations generalize across different objects, and that object identity and relation can be dissociated. The findings argue that perception encodes abstract relational structure independent of its particular fillers.
papers.authors: Alon Hafri, Michael F. Bonner, Barbara Landau, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Moral thin-slicing: Forming moral impressions from a brief glance
papers.abstract: The authors test how quickly people form moral impressions of others from very brief exposures to social scenes. They find that observers can judge moral character reliably from a mere glance, and that these snap impressions track the fuller judgments that emerge with more viewing time. The work extends rapid scene and event perception to social and moral evaluation.
papers.authors: Julian De Freitas, Alon Hafri

papers.title: Where word and world meet: Language and vision share an abstract representation of symmetry
papers.abstract: This work examines whether the concept of symmetry is represented in a common abstract format across vision and language. Experiments show that people map visual symmetric events and symmetric linguistic constructions onto one another, and that exposure in one modality influences processing in the other. The results support shared, abstract representations at the interface of perception and language.
papers.authors: Alon Hafri, Lila R. Gleitman, Barbara Landau, John C. Trueswell

0033.name: Alon Zivony
0033.bio: Alon Zivony is a cognitive neuroscientist and Lecturer at the University of Sheffield whose research examines the temporal dynamics of selective attention and its role in object perception. Zivony developed the "diachronic" framework of attention, which characterizes attentional selection as a process unfolding through "attentional episodes" that regulate the encoding of sensory data into working memory. Their work employs behavioral psychophysics and electrophysiological methods (EEG/ERP) to dissociate the effects of category-based expectations from attentional engagement. Prior to joining Sheffield, Zivony completed a PhD at Tel-Aviv University and conducted postdoctoral research at Birkbeck, University of London, under Newton and Marie-Curie fellowships.
0033.research_direction: Dr. Zivony has recently been investigating the temporal dynamics of selective visual attention, relying primarily on rapid serial visual presentation paradigms to track how observers process fast-paced streams of information. Their recent work explores how distractor intrusions—the phenomenon where observers mistakenly report items presented adjacent to a target—can be utilized as a robust behavioral metric to measure individual differences in the speed and timing of attentional engagement. In addition to measuring attentional speed, they are examining how selective attention shapes the temporal binding of visual features, such as color and identity, during brief perceptual episodes. Furthermore, Dr. Zivony is working to disentangle attentional allocation from other cognitive processes, probing whether factors like category-based expectations and long-term memory familiarity speed up perceptual encoding independently of attentional priority.

papers.title: Measuring individual differences in the speed of attention using the distractor intrusion task
papers.abstract: Reaction times in visual search are a common but unreliable and contaminated way to gauge how quickly people attend. The authors propose the rate at which observers wrongly report a distractor following the target in rapid serial visual presentation (distractor intrusions) as an alternative index. Across three studies this rate was highly consistent within sessions and stable across a year (above .90) even with a roughly 5-minute task, and it tracked other attention-speed measures but not attentional control, reading speed or attentional blink size.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Claudia C. von Bastian, Rachel Pye

papers.title: Long-term memory speeds encoding, independently of attention
papers.abstract: Familiar items seem to be encoded into working memory faster, which working-memory models attribute to long-term-memory template matching, but the benefit could simply reflect higher attentional priority. Using RSVP with native English and Hebrew speakers viewing letters from each alphabet, the authors found a familiarity advantage in target accuracy while familiar and unfamiliar distractors captured attention equally. The familiarity effect persisted across experiments, indicating that memory speeds encoding through a route separable from attention.
papers.authors: Abigail C. Wyllie, Claudia C. von Bastian, Alon Zivony

papers.title: A dissociation between the effects of expectations and attention in selective visual processing
papers.abstract: Expectations about what will appear and attention to what is task-relevant often go together, so their separate contributions to perception are hard to identify. The authors decouple category-based expectations from attentional engagement in fast visual streams. Their results indicate that expectations can influence perceptual processing directly, independently of how attention is allocated.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Attention and feature binding in the temporal domain
papers.abstract: The authors asked how attention shapes the binding of features such as colour and identity across time in RSVP streams. When observers mistakenly reported a distractor's identity instead of the target's, they also tended to report that distractor's colour, both within and between individuals. This suggests that attentional engagement supports binding of features that occur together, consistent with the diachronic view of attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of selective attention are reflected by distractor intrusions
papers.abstract: Observers in RSVP often report a distractor instead of the target. Manipulating whether targets appeared in one stream or unpredictably in two, the authors showed that slower engagement shifted intrusions toward items after the cue, and faster engagement toward items before it. Intrusions therefore index the timing of attentional engagement, supporting the idea that selection operates in brief attentional episodes.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

0038.name: Anastasia Kiyonaga
0038.bio: Anastasia Kiyonaga is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at the University of California, San Diego. Kiyonaga’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the interaction between working memory, attention, and action, focusing on how the brain maintains goal-directed representations amidst environmental distractions. They employ a multi-modal methodology including functional MRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and oculomotor tracking to probe the competition between internal maintenance and external processing. Their work seeks to delineate the strategic control processes that manage these representational overlaps and their consequences for human behavior.
0038.research_direction: Dr. Kiyonaga has recently been investigating the active, goal-directed nature of visual working memory, particularly how sensory representations are dynamically reformatted in the visual cortex to guide upcoming behavior. Their recent work explores how working memory content interfaces with the peripheral motor system, using eye- and hand-tracking to examine whether remembered features like orientation, brightness, and scene layout prospectively modulate pupillary responses, gaze scanpaths, and effector micro-movements based on task goals. Beyond sensory-motor integration, they are also studying the interplay between working memory and long-term storage by testing how representational competition from visual distractors during a delay period influences the durability of subsequent long-term memory encoding. By combining naturalistic stimuli with computational approaches like representational similarity analysis, Dr. Kiyonaga asks how the human brain flexibly transforms and distributes memory representations across perceptual and motor workspaces to meet shifting behavioral demands.

papers.title: Flexible working memory in the human peripheral nervous system
papers.abstract: The authors tracked eyes and stylus-holding hand while people held an orientation in working memory and reported it either by drawing a line or by adjusting a response wheel. The remembered orientation could be decoded from tiny gaze and hand-movement inflections during the delay. Which effector carried more information shifted with the response format, suggesting memory content is adaptively distributed across peripheral motor effectors according to task needs.
papers.authors: Sihan Yang, Yueying Dong, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Windows to the goal: Pupillary working memory signatures prospectively adapt to task demands
papers.abstract: The study asks whether pupil size tracks remembered brightness of real-world scenes and whether that effect depends on which features the memory test emphasizes. A feature-specific pupillary memory signal appeared only when the task encouraged visual maintenance rather than semantic categorization. The pupil response therefore looks prospective and goal-dependent rather than a passive echo of sensory features.
papers.authors: Yueying Dong, Yun-chen Hung, Connie Xie, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Competition during working memory enhances long-term memory
papers.abstract: Using a working memory task with naturalistic stimuli and a task-irrelevant distractor during the delay, the authors varied how similar the distractor was to relevant and irrelevant memory items. Moderate similarity to relevant content gave the best working memory performance, while dissimilar or near-identical distractors hurt it. Stronger interference during working memory predicted better later long-term memory, suggesting competition between internal and external representations promotes durable encoding.
papers.authors: Ian C. Ballard, Lana Gaspariani, Maytus Piriyajitakonkij, Ioannis Pappas, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Sensory reformatting for a working visual memory
papers.abstract: This review argues that visual cortex acts as an active workspace during working memory rather than passively holding a sensory copy. Early representations appear to transform from a sensory-like code into a format shaped by task context and optimized for behavior. The authors survey the kinds of transformations and their functional importance for interfacing memory with perception and action.
papers.authors: Anastasia Kiyonaga, John T. Serences

papers.title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes
papers.abstract: Participants remembered naturalistic images while their eye movements were tracked. During the delay the eyes traced item-specific scanpaths that echoed those made at encoding, resembling gaze reinstatement in long-term memory retrieval. Time-resolved representational similarity guided by a convolutional neural network showed that gaze patterns were more distinct when the task stressed visual detail and ramped up before the memory probe, showing prospective, task-flexible oculomotor memory signals.
papers.authors: Yueying Dong, Yun-chen Hung, Lana Gaspariani, Anastasia Kiyonaga

0039.name: Andrea Facoetti
0039.bio: Andrea Facoetti is an Associate Professor of Psychobiology and Physiological Psychology at the University of Padua and directs the Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience (De.Co.Ne.) Lab. Facoetti’s research investigates the psychobiological foundations of neurodevelopmental disorders, specifically the causal role of visuo-spatial and multisensory attention in reading and numerical acquisition. Their findings indicate that attentional deficits often precede and predict dyslexia, challenging strictly phonological theories. Experimental methodologies utilized by Facoetti include longitudinal behavioral studies, non-invasive brain stimulation, and the application of action video games as a remediation tool for cognitive and academic enhancement.
0039.research_direction: The Facoetti Lab investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms linking attention and perception to learning and neurodevelopment, with a major focus on developmental dyslexia and autism spectrum disorder. Current research examines how visual spatio-temporal, multisensory, phonological, and attentional mechanisms contribute to reading development and difficulties, and how they can be modulated through targeted interventions, including action video game (AVG) training. The lab also explores visual and temporal attention across neurodevelopmental traits and neurological conditions.

papers.title: The placebo effect in reading performance: A cross-over experimental study
papers.abstract: In a within-subject experiment with 102 young adults wearing sham glasses described as altering reading, the authors tested whether placebo and nocebo expectations can modulate high-level processing such as single-word reading and pseudoword decoding. It extends placebo research from perception and sensorimotor tasks to reading.
papers.authors: Sandro Franceschini, Sara Bertoni, Patrik Pluchino, Anna Panzeri, Giovanni Bruno, Martina Mancarella, Giovanna Puccio, Simona Carbone, Matteo Lulli, Cristiano Termine, Andrea Spoto, Simone Gori, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: The Benefits of Playing Action-Like Video Games on Salience Processing
papers.abstract: In a single-blind randomized crossover experiment with 60 young adults, a short session of an action-like racing game (Mario Kart) was compared with a puzzle board game. Action-like play raised positive emotion and heart rate and enhanced salience processing in typical and poor readers, with faster reading found only in poor readers.
papers.authors: Sandro Franceschini, Giovanna Puccio, Sara Bertoni, Simone Gori, Sara Mascheretti, Francesca Fusina, Alessandro Angrilli, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Action video games and posterior parietal cortex neuromodulation enhance both attention and reading in adults with developmental dyslexia
papers.abstract: Adults with developmental dyslexia received a combination of action video game training and non-invasive random-noise stimulation over the posterior parietal cortex. The combined intervention improved visual attention and reading efficiency, supporting a causal role of parietal attentional mechanisms in reading and a neuroplasticity-based route to remediation.
papers.authors: Sara Bertoni, Sandro Franceschini, Martina Mancarella, Giovanna Puccio, Luca Ronconi, Gianluca Marsicano, Simone Gori, Gianluca Campana, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia
papers.abstract: In a randomized trial with 120 pre-reading children (79 at risk for dyslexia), action video game training was compared with non-action games, speech therapy and a waiting list. Only the action game group showed a selective gain in phonemic awareness, bringing at-risk children to typical levels, suggesting that attention training can benefit language-based precursors of reading.
papers.authors: Sara Bertoni, Chiara Andreola, Sara Mascheretti, Sandro Franceschini, Milena Ruffino, Vittoria Trezzi, Massimo Molteni, Maria Enrica Sali, Antonio Salandi, Ombretta Gaggi, Claudio Palazzi, Simone Gori, Andrea Facoetti

papers.title: Action Video Games Training in Children with Developmental Dyslexia: A Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis pools studies testing action video game training in children with developmental dyslexia. It quantifies the effects on reading and related cognitive skills and evaluates how consistent and robust the benefits are, giving an evidence-based summary of this remediation approach.
papers.authors: Giovanna Puccio, Giulia Gazzi, Sara Bertoni, Sandro Franceschini, Martina Mancarella, Simone Gori, Lucia Ronconi, Andrea Facoetti

0040.name: Andreas Hierlemann
0040.department: Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering (D-BSSE)
0040.bio: Andreas Hierlemann is a Professor of Biosystems Engineering at ETH Zurich, conducting research at the interface of microelectronics and neuroscience. Hierlemann’s work focuses on the development of CMOS-based high-density microelectrode arrays (HD-MEAs) for the recording and stimulation of electrogenic cells, including neurons and retinal circuits. Their laboratory uses these platforms to examine neuronal network dynamics, subcellular signaling such as axonal action potential propagation, and the visual processing mechanisms of the human retina. This research integrates microfluidic systems and bioelectronics to investigate neurophysiology and provide tools for pharmaceutical testing and systems biology.
0040.research_direction: The group of Dr. Hierlemann has been developing advanced bioelectronic and microfluidic platforms to monitor living tissues and electrogenic cells at exceptionally high spatial and temporal resolutions. Their work is centered around engineering of high-density microelectrode arrays and integrated organ-on-a-chip devices to non-invasively track the electrophysiology and physical status of complex 3D cell culture models. Utilizing high-density microelectrode arrays and sophisticated sensors, they are investigating fundamental neural network dynamics, for example mapping how the delicate balance of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs orchestrates recurrent spiking in cortical circuits. Moreover, they recently studied how different conduction speeds in axons of the human retina ensure the coherence of nerve signals in the visual system.

papers.title: Engineering Neuronal Network Connectivity Through Precise and Scalable Electrical Modulation
papers.abstract: The paper pairs HD-MEAs with programmable stimulation to induce Hebbian-like connectivity changes in many neuron pairs in parallel, and introduces Conditional Activity Metrics to quantify stimulation-evoked shifts in spike-timing relationships. In roughly 40% of 279 tested pairs, targeted stimulation strengthened or weakened synaptic connections across in vitro and ex vivo preparations, and changes could be tracked at the axonal level. The work supports scalable, verifiable circuit shaping for neuroengineering and neurotherapeutic uses.
papers.authors: Sreedhar S. Kumar, Yannaël Bossard, Rachel Sava, Tobias Gänswein, Lorenca Sadiraj, Jean-Samuel Dupré, Manuel Schröter, J. Gray Camp, Fernando Cardes, Julian Bartram, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Functional Cell-Type Identification in Neuronal Networks Using High-Density Microelectrode Arrays
papers.abstract: The study builds ground-truth labels for excitatory versus inhibitory neurons in HD-MEA data, using chemogenetic activation of interneurons and controlled mixtures of hiPSC-derived excitatory and inhibitory neurons. A classifier using spike waveform shape and autocorrelogram dynamics separates cell types across cultures and in vivo rodent recordings. Applied to unlabeled data, it reveals cell-type-specific burst dynamics, including an inhibitory signature before burst onset.
papers.authors: Philipp Hornauer, Lorenzo Davide Dodi, Hsiu-Chuan Lin, Tobias Gänswein, Maria Pascual-Garcia, Manuel Schröter, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Advances in large-scale electrophysiology with high-density microelectrode arrays
papers.abstract: This tutorial review surveys how high-density microelectrode arrays have developed, covering chip design, readout and stimulation capabilities, and how they are used for neurons, organoids and cardiomyocytes. It discusses applications in neurodevelopment, stem cell biology, pharmacology and, increasingly, AI-driven analysis. The authors close with an outlook on remaining technical and analytical challenges.
papers.authors: Manuel Schröter, Fernando Cardes, Cat-Vu H. Bui, Lorenzo Davide Dodi, Tobias Gänswein, Julian Bartram, Lorenca Sadiraj, Philipp Hornauer, Sreedhar Kumar, Maria Pascual-Garcia, Andreas Hierlemann

papers.title: Mechanical stimulation and electrophysiological monitoring at subcellular resolution reveals differential mechanosensation of neurons within networks
papers.abstract: The authors combine atomic force microscopy, a high-density microelectrode array and fluorescence microscopy so that individual neurons in a network can be poked with piconewton force and nanometre precision while their electrical activity is recorded at subcellular resolution. Neuronal soma stiffness did not predict electrical activity, and spontaneously active cells tolerated sustained compression of the soma. Fast transient mechanical stimuli, however, evoked responses that differed between neurons, indicating differential mechanosensitivity within the network.
papers.authors: Krishna Chaitanya Kasuba, Alessio Paolo Buccino, Julian Bartram, Benjamin M. Gaub, Felix J. Fauser, Silvia Ronchi, Sreedhar Saseendran Kumar, Sydney Geissler, Michele M. Nava, Andreas Hierlemann, Daniel J. Müller

papers.title: Parallel reconstruction of the excitatory and inhibitory inputs received by single neurons reveals the synaptic basis of recurrent spiking
papers.abstract: The authors combine whole-network HD-MEA recordings with patch clamp in rat cortical cultures to estimate, for single neurons, both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs during recurrent network activity. Spiking often coincided with peaks in the fast-fluctuating input E/I ratio, driven mainly by rapid bidirectional changes in inhibition modulated by network activity. The approach also maps the circuit architecture underlying these inputs.
papers.authors: Julian Bartram, Felix Franke, Sreedhar Saseendran Kumar, Andreas Hierlemann

0041.name: Andreas Keil
0041.lab_name: Laboratory for Brain, Body, and Behavior
0041.bio: Andreas Keil is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Florida, where they direct the Laboratory for Brain, Body, and Behavior. Keil’s research examines the neurobiological mechanisms through which human sensation and perception adapt to motivational and emotional states to facilitate survival and well-being. Using dense-array electroencephalography (EEG), steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), and simultaneous EEG-fMRI, Keil investigates how aversive learning and threat expectancy modulate neural gain in the visual cortex. They also focus on developing and validating signal processing methods for characterizing oscillatory brain dynamics and establishing international guidelines for electrophysiological research.
0041.research_direction: Dr. Keil's recent work investigates how the human brain processes emotional and threatening information, with a particular focus on how sensory cortices rapidly evaluate threats and mediate fear generalization. Using electroencephalography and autonomic measures, they track the neurophysiological dynamics of aversive learning, examining how neural tuning functions adapt to threat cues and how fear responses generalize across social stimuli like faces over time. Their research also explores methodological and computational innovations to capture these sensory processes, such as introducing Ricker wavelets to summarize population-level neural tuning from non-invasive data. Additionally, Dr. Keil has recently been integrating artificial intelligence into affective science, investigating whether AI-generated pictures can substitute for naturalistic stimuli in emotion research and building deep learning models to predict synthetic electrophysiological responses to complex semantic and emotional concepts.

papers.title: Concept2Brain: an AI model for predicting neurophysiological responses to text and pictures
papers.abstract: The authors build a deep network that uses CLIP-style embeddings of a picture or a piece of text and maps them into an EEG latent space, producing synthetic electrophysiological responses to emotional and semantic content. The generated responses closely resemble empirically recorded ones. The model is released as an openly available web tool for creating reproducible EEG datasets and for testing how the brain represents concepts.
papers.authors: Alejandro Santos-Mayo, Faith Gilbert, Arash Mirifar, Anna-Lena Tebbe, Ruogu Fang, Mingzhou Ding, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Emotional responses to naturalistic and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated affective pictures
papers.abstract: The study compares how people respond to real affective photographs versus AI-generated images designed to convey the same emotional content. It asks whether generated pictures can substitute for naturalistic ones in emotion research by examining brain, bodily and self-reported responses. The work speaks to the growing use of generative models for producing experimental stimuli.
papers.authors: Faith Gilbert, Fan Yang, Ethan Smith, Sarah M. Gardy, Andrew H. Farkas, Yujun Chen, Mingzhou Ding, Ruogu Fang, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Quantifying population-level neural tuning functions using Ricker wavelets
papers.abstract: This methods paper introduces fitting Ricker (Mexican-hat) wavelets to summarize population-level tuning functions in EEG and related measures. It provides a compact, interpretable set of parameters such as width and amplitude for describing how visual cortex responds along a stimulus dimension. The approach is demonstrated on aversive generalization learning data, where tuning sharpens for threat cues.
papers.authors: Laura Ahumada, Christian Panitz, Caitlin M. Traiser, Faith E. Gilbert, Mingzhou Ding, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Neurophysiological and Autonomic Dynamics of Threat Processing during Sustained Social Fear Generalization
papers.abstract: Participants underwent social fear conditioning and generalization with faces over an extended period while cortical activity and autonomic signals were recorded. The paper tracks how visuocortical and bodily responses to threat cues and their similar faces evolve over time. It shows that generalization of fear across faces is reflected in coordinated neural and autonomic dynamics.
papers.authors: Jourdan J. Pouliot, Richard T. Ward, Caitlin M. Traiser, Payton Chiasson, Faith E. Gilbert, Andreas Keil

papers.title: Sensing fear: fast and precise threat evaluation in human sensory cortex
papers.abstract: This review argues that sensory cortices in humans do not merely relay threat information but evaluate it quickly and with fine precision. It gathers evidence from vision, olfaction and audition that aversive learning sharpens tuning and boosts gain in sensory cortex within milliseconds. The authors discuss how these findings bear on models of fear generalization and anxiety.
papers.authors: Wen Li, Andreas Keil

0042.name: Andrew B. Leber
0042.bio: Andrew B. Leber is a Professor of Psychology at The Ohio State University and serves as the Director of the Center for Cognitive & Brain Sciences. Leber’s research investigates the mechanisms of cognitive control, focusing on how the brain selects, updates, and modulates behavioral strategies in response to varying environmental demands. They utilize a multi-methodological approach, including functional MRI, electroencephalography, and eye-tracking, to examine the neural predictors of fluctuations in attentional focus and flexibility. Their recent work characterizes individual differences in attentional strategy and explores the factors that influence optimal performance in adaptive visual search tasks.
0042.research_direction: Dr. Leber's recent work explores how individuals select cognitive strategies during visual tasks, investigating why some people consistently choose optimal approaches while others do not. Using paradigms like visual search and change detection, they have recently been examining the mechanisms driving these individual differences, testing effort avoidance accounts and utilizing memory probes to separate raw ability from strategy application in both attention and visual working memory. Additionally, their research investigates experience-driven distractor suppression to understand how the visual system adapts to statistical regularities in the environment. By manipulating spatial probabilities and the temporal dynamics of visual displays, they are evaluating whether learned distractor rejection operates proactively or reactively, as well as exactly how rapidly these suppressive benefits develop during search.

papers.title: What distinguishes optimal visual searchers? Evidence from a probe procedure
papers.abstract: Some people reliably choose the more efficient of two available search strategies while others do not. Using post-trial memory probes to reveal which strategy was actually used, the authors show that optimal searchers differ from suboptimal ones in how they select and apply strategy rather than simply in raw search ability. The work sharpens the lab's account of why attentional strategy choice varies across individuals.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhang, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Learned distractor rejection: robust but surprisingly rapid
papers.abstract: Learning to suppress a salient distractor that repeatedly appears in a visual search display is often thought to build up slowly. Across experiments, the authors show that this learned rejection is robust yet emerges within very few trials, and characterize how quickly the benefit develops. The findings constrain models of statistical learning of distractor suppression.
papers.authors: Ilana Savelson, Christopher Hauck, Mei-Ching Lien, Eric Ruthruff, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Individual variation in encoding strategy optimization in visual working memory: Evidence from a change detection task
papers.abstract: Participants performing a change detection task can choose different ways of encoding items into visual working memory, and the authors test whether people adopt the encoding approach that maximizes performance. They find substantial individual differences in how well people optimize their encoding strategy. This extends the lab's strategy-choice framework from visual search to working memory.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Yin-ting Lin, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Investigating an effort avoidance account of attentional strategy choice
papers.abstract: Why do people often pick a suboptimal search strategy? The authors test whether people avoid the mental effort of the more demanding but more efficient strategy, manipulating effort-related factors during search. The results evaluate effort avoidance as an explanation of strategy selection.
papers.authors: Tianyu Zhang, Andrew B. Leber

papers.title: Learned spatial suppression is not always proactive
papers.abstract: When a salient distractor tends to appear at particular locations, people learn to suppress those locations. The authors use methods that separate proactive from reactive suppression and show that learned spatial suppression need not act in advance of the display. The result refines the prevailing view of how experience-driven distractor suppression operates.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Seah Chang, Blaire Dube, Julie D. Golomb, Andrew B. Leber

0043.name: Andrew Hollingworth
0043.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0043.bio: Andrew Hollingworth is a Professor at the University of Iowa. Hollingworth’s research investigates the cognitive architecture of scene perception, focusing on the mechanisms of visual working memory and attentional guidance. Their work explores how visual information is accumulated and integrated across saccadic eye movements to form representations of natural environments. By employing eye-tracking and behavioral paradigms, Hollingworth examines the roles of categorical learning and statistical regularities in directing visual search and the interaction between short-term and long-term memory systems in sustaining visual continuity.
0043.research_direction: Dr. Hollingworth’s recent work explores the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms underlying visual search and attentional guidance. They have recently been investigating how search templates held in visual working memory versus long-term memory interact to guide or suppress attention, including testing the sensory preactivation account of memory-based guidance. Their research also examines how goal-driven templates and stimulus-driven salience might combine within a shared spatial priority map, and how task goals and structural cues dictate exact saccade landing positions within spatially extended objects. Furthermore, they are studying visual search in naturalistic and applied contexts, utilizing dense scene inspection paradigms to understand the "satisfaction of search" phenomenon and why detecting one target often causes observers to prematurely terminate their search.

papers.title: Testing a sensory preactivation account of attention guidance from visual working memory
papers.abstract: Tests the standard view that working memory guides attention because held-in-memory features preactivate matching sensory representations. Participants briefly saw a color they either had to remember or not, followed by a search array at intervals from 0 to 500 ms, allowing the authors to assess whether purely sensory preactivation can produce a guidance benefit. The results are used to evaluate whether sensory preactivation is sufficient or necessary to explain memory-based attentional guidance.
papers.authors: Zexuan Niu, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Dissociations and interactions between attention guidance from negative templates maintained in visual working memory and long-term memory
papers.abstract: Examines how people use a template of something to avoid (a negative template) to suppress distractors during visual search, comparing templates held in visual working memory with those retrieved from long-term memory. The experiments look for dissociations between the two memory systems in how they shape guidance and for ways the two types of template interact when both are available.
papers.authors: Aditya Prakash, Andrew Hollingworth

papers.title: Satisfaction of search: evidence of premature termination in a naturalistic image inspection task
papers.abstract: Investigates why finding one target makes people miss a second one, a well-known problem in radiology. The authors built the 'Ghosts in the Forest' task, using semi-transparent faces as high- or low-salience targets in dense natural scenes, and found a robust satisfaction-of-search effect for low-salience targets in both naive observers and radiologists, supporting an account based on premature termination of search.
papers.authors: Andrew Hollingworth, Zexuan Niu, Claudia Mello-Thoms, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Saccades to spatially extended objects: The roles of observer goals and part-structure cues in determining within-object landing position
papers.abstract: Studies where the eyes land within an object that is larger than the fovea. Manipulating the observer's task goals and the availability of part-structure cues, the authors examine how each shapes within-object saccade landing position, extending object-based accounts of oculomotor control.
papers.authors: Andrew Hollingworth, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Template-Based and Saliency-Driven Attentional Control Converge to Coactivate on a Common, Spatially Organized Priority Map
papers.abstract: Asks how goal-driven (template-based) and stimulus-driven (saliency) attentional control combine. Using behavioral evidence including redundancy-gain style analyses, the authors show that the two sources of control jointly activate a shared, spatially organized priority map rather than operating as separate processes.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Zexuan Niu, J. Toby Mordkoff, Andrew Hollingworth

0044.name: Andrew Lovett
0044.department: Navy Center for Applied Research in Artificial Intelligence (NCARAI)
0044.bio: Andrew Lovett is a computer scientist at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory working at the intersection of cognitive science and artificial intelligence. Lovett's research involves developing computational models of visual perception and spatial reasoning, specifically examining how analogical mapping and qualitative spatial representations facilitate problem-solving. They model performance on visual intelligence assessments, such as Raven’s Progressive Matrices, by simulating the encoding of topological relations and abstract spatial structures. Lovett’s methodologies include the creation of software systems that integrate attention-driven processing with structure-mapping engines to generate high-level descriptions of visual scenes.
0044.research_direction: Dr. Lovett's recent work explores how the visual system detects pursuit or chasing behaviors within complex, dynamic scenes. To investigate this phenomenon, they have recently been developing novel behavioral tasks alongside computational cognitive models to measure when observers correctly or incorrectly perceive one moving object chasing another in cluttered displays. Their latest research tests whether these attention-based models can yield falsifiable theories of chase detection by generating preregistered predictions about human accuracy and response times. Specifically, Dr. Lovett is investigating the underlying decision criteria observers rely on and how distinct visual factors, such as a chaser's deviation from a direct path to its target, systematically influence perceptual errors.

papers.title: Model Predictions and Implications for Chasing Subtlety
papers.abstract: Tests whether an earlier attention-based model of chase detection generalizes by making preregistered predictions before data collection. Two experiments varied how far the chaser deviates from a direct path to its target, and the model largely predicted the response time and accuracy patterns, including which videos produced most errors. The work argues the model yields a falsifiable theory of chase detection.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Cognitive Modeling (ICCM 2025)
