papers.authors: Maria Kon, Sangeet Khemlani, Gregory Francis, Andrew Lovett

papers.title: Measuring and Modeling Pursuit Detection in Dynamic Visual Scenes
papers.abstract: The authors built a new task for measuring when people correctly or wrongly see one moving object pursuing another in busy displays, alongside a cognitive model that performs the same task. People are mostly accurate but make rare, systematic errors on particular scenes. Model strategies that match human performance reproduce those same errors, suggesting the decision criteria people rely on.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2024)
papers.authors: Maria Kon, Sangeet Khemlani, Andrew Lovett

0045.name: Andrew Mienaltowski
0045.bio: Andrew Mienaltowski is a Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Western Kentucky University and directs the Lifespan Social Cognition Lab. Mienaltowski's research investigates the intersection of cognitive aging and social cognition, specifically examining how adult development influences the visual recognition and categorization of emotional facial expressions. Utilizing a methodological framework that incorporates behavioral tasks and electrophysiological measures such as event-related potentials (ERPs), they explore the impact of emotional intensity and valence on attention and decision-making. Their work also extends to everyday problem-solving and social judgment processes across the adult lifespan.
0045.research_direction: Dr. Mienaltowski has recently been studying how people read emotion from faces and scenes, and how this differs with age and across clinical groups. Their recent work explores how younger and older adults describe the emotions they see in face-like patterns in objects, known as pareidolia, and whether the richness of their emotion vocabulary depends more on the image or on the viewer. They have also asked whether young adults with autism can identify emotions when body posture and surrounding context are available in addition to the face.

papers.title: Emotion labelling varies with lexical complexity more than age in face pareidolia images
papers.abstract: This study examines how observers verbally label the emotional expressions they perceive in face-pareidolia stimuli (objects and patterns perceived as having emotional faces), and asks whether the sophistication of the emotion vocabulary used depends more on the complexity of the eliciting image or on the age of the observer. Younger and older adults viewed pareidolia images varying in configural ambiguity and generated free-response emotion labels, which were coded for lexical/semantic complexity (e.g., basic versus more nuanced or differentiated emotion terms). Lexical complexity of emotion labels tracked stimulus-driven complexity of the pareidolia image more strongly than it tracked participant age, suggesting that image-level ambiguity constrains the granularity of emotional interpretation across the adult lifespan. Age-related differences in labelling sophistication were comparatively modest once image complexity was accounted for. The findings extend prior work from the authors' lab on age and emotion perception by showing that pareidolia stimuli can be used to dissociate stimulus-driven and observer-driven sources of variability in emotion language, and argue against a simple age-deficit account of emotion-label complexity.
papers.authors: Andrew Mienaltowski, Ellie Knapp, Brooke A. Lowe, Bailey Pruetz, J. Farley Norman

papers.title: Young Adults with Autism May Possess Typical-Level Skills in Identifying Emotions from Person-in-Context Images
papers.abstract: This quantitative investigation evaluated whether the integration of extra-facial cues, specifically bodily posture and environmental context (e.g., a person in a retail setting), facilitates emotion identification in young adults diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). While prior research suggests universal deficits in facial emotion recognition for individuals with ASD, this study utilized author-developed stimuli representing head-only, whole-body, and person-in-context conditions. Results indicated that participants with ASD (Mage = 19.47) exhibited significantly higher identification accuracy for emotions like fear, anger, disgust, and sadness when stimuli were presented as whole bodies within a relevant situational context compared to isolated head or body visuals. Furthermore, no significant performance differences were observed between the ASD group and neurotypical controls (Mage = 19.73) in the context-rich condition, suggesting that individuals with ASD may effectively leverage multi-channel visual information to compensate for facial processing difficulties in ecologically valid scenarios.
papers.authors: Nathan T. Kline, Fran C. Blumberg, Alyssa Minton, Andrew Mienaltowski

0047.name: Anna C. Nobre
0047.bio: Anna C. Nobre is the Wu Tsai Professor of Psychology at Yale University and Director of the Center for Neurocognition and Behavior, having previously led the Oxford Centre for Human Brain Activity at the University of Oxford. Their research examines the neural systems supporting human cognition, specifically investigating how the brain prioritizes and selects information from sensory streams and memory to guide perception and action. By integrating neuroimaging techniques such as MEG, EEG, and fMRI with psychophysical methods, Nobre maps the dynamic regulatory mechanisms of the human brain and their impairment in neurodegenerative diseases.
0047.research_direction: Dr. Nobre's recent work explores the interplay between external and internal attention, specifically investigating how the brain flexibly shifts its focus between incoming sensory information and representations already held in mind. Using techniques like magnetoencephalography and sequential cueing paradigms, they have recently been probing the neural dynamics that govern attentional switches within perceptual domains versus shifts across domains into working memory. Their research also expands this internal attention framework to long-term memory, developing new behavioral tasks to ask how spatial and retrospective cues can selectively prioritize specific items within consolidated contextual memories. Across these lines of research, Dr. Nobre is mapping the cognitive and neural mechanisms that allow us to allocate selective attention across perception, working memory, and long-term memory to guide future behavior.

papers.title: Orienting selective attention within long-term contextual memories
papers.abstract: Building on precue and retrocue designs from working-memory research, the study introduces a framework for probing how selective attention operates within contextual long-term memory. In three pre-registered experiments (n = 235), participants learned scenes paired with object identities and locations, then retrieved objects after spatial cues directed internal attention to the probed location. Informative cues produced retrieval benefits and costs relative to neutral cues, regardless of cue timing and even at very short durations.
papers.authors: Melinda Sabo, William Narhi-Martinez, Nahid Zokaei, Nora M. Roüast, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: How the brain shifts between external and internal attention
papers.abstract: This Perspective asks how the brain moves attention between the sensory stream and contents held in mind, a situation that everyday behavior constantly demands but that most research treats as two separate topics. It compares selective external and internal attention, sets out competing hypotheses about the principles governing shifts between the two domains, and points to candidate brain areas and mechanisms. It also reviews the few experiments that compare between-domain with within-domain shifts and closes with open questions for theory and computational models.
papers.authors: Anna C. Nobre, Daniela Gresch

papers.title: Focusing attention in working and long-term memory through dissociable mechanisms
papers.abstract: The authors developed a paradigm to compare how attentional orienting aids retrieval from spatial working memory versus long-term memory, and how focusing within each memory type affects processing of incoming sensory input. In three experiments with young adults, retrospective cues prioritized an item in WM or LTM before a retrieval or perceptual task. The pattern of cue benefits indicates that attention within the two memory systems operates through dissociable mechanisms.
papers.authors: Dongyu Gong, Dejan Draschkow, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: Neural dynamics of shifting attention between perception and working-memory contents
papers.abstract: Using magnetoencephalography, the authors compared the neural dynamics of moving attention within versus between external (perceptual) and internal (working-memory) domains. Two sequential cues directed attention to upcoming or memorized visual information, and the second cue either kept attention in the same domain or switched it across domains. Between-domain shifts showed distinct neural signatures from within-domain shifts, showing that domain switches engage dedicated dynamics.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Daniela Gresch, Sage E. P. Boettcher, Chetan Gohil, Freek van Ede, Anna C. Nobre

papers.title: Turning Attention Inside Out: How Working Memory Serves Behavior
papers.abstract: This review covers the growing literature on selective attention acting on the contents of working memory to guide behavior (inside-out), as a counterpart to attention that acts on sensory signals (outside-in). It emphasizes the functional, flexible, and future-focused nature of internal attention, and organizes the topic around its purpose, targets, timing, and neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Freek van Ede, Anna C. Nobre

0048.name: Anna Grubert
0048.bio: Anna Grubert is a Professor of Psychology at Durham University whose research examines the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual selective attention and working memory. Utilizing behavioral experiments in conjunction with electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and event-related potentials (ERPs), specifically the N2pc and CDA components, Grubert investigates how memory-based target representations, or attentional templates, guide the selection of information in complex visual environments. Their research explores the temporal dynamics and capacity limits of top-down control, including the ability of the human brain to activate multiple attentional templates and select multiple targets in parallel.
0048.research_direction: Dr. Grubert has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms that guide visual search, using ERP components like the N1pc, N2pc, and CDA to track attentional templates in real time. Their recent work explores the preparation and capacity limits of these templates, asking how individuals maintain multiple target features simultaneously and how the timing of preparatory activation shifts when rapidly switching between different search goals. They are also examining the representational format of search templates to determine whether they can operate as integrated object representations or remain strictly feature-based during complex color-shape conjunction tasks. Additionally, their research investigates how prior knowledge and statistical learning—such as spatial location probabilities or probabilistic expectations about upcoming target colors—modulate the early temporal dynamics of attentional deployment and subsequent target selection.

papers.title: Temporal acceleration drives the probability cueing effect in visual search: Evidence for early attentional deployment (N1pc) at high-probability locations
papers.abstract: Using ERPs, the study examines why targets that often appear at one location are found faster. Rather than a larger N2pc, the benefit was linked to an earlier N1pc-range negativity and earlier onset of contralateral negativity for high-probability targets. The authors conclude that location probability learning speeds up attentional deployment in time rather than increasing attentional resources.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel, Anna Grubert

papers.title: The capacity limitations of multiple-template visual search during task preparation and target selection
papers.abstract: The study asks how many attentional templates can be held ready at once before a visual search. Using N2pc responses to irrelevant colour probes flashed between search displays, the authors show that a single template is active when the target is predictable, but all three colour templates become active when the target is unpredictable. Even so, three-colour search is clearly worse than single-colour search, which the authors attribute to inhibitory interactions among simultaneously active templates.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Ella Williams, Mikel Jimenez, Roger Remington, Martin Eimer

papers.title: The Guidance of Attentional Selectivity in Visual Search Is Always Feature-Based: Behavioral and Electrophysiological Evidence From Feature and Conjunction Search Tasks
papers.abstract: This paper tests whether attentional templates can be integrated object representations when targets are defined by a colour-shape conjunction. Comparing single-target with two-target search in feature and conjunction tasks, load costs in behaviour, N2pc guidance and CDA working-memory markers were much larger in conjunction search. The authors conclude that templates remain feature-based even when object-based templates would in principle reduce memory load.
papers.authors: Ziyi Wang, Mikel Jimenez, Martin Eimer, Anna Grubert

papers.title: Target switch costs in visual search arise during the preparatory activation of target templates
papers.abstract: Borrowing the task-switching logic, the authors had people search for one of two colour targets that alternated predictably every two or four trials. Search was costlier on switch than repeat trials, and probe N2pcs showed that the relevant template was activated about 800 ms before the display on repeats but only right before target onset on switches. Switch costs therefore reflect delayed preparatory template activation, with no lingering inertia from the previous target.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Do We Prepare for What We Predict? How Target Expectations Affect Preparatory Attentional Templates and Target Selection in Visual Search
papers.abstract: The study tests whether probabilistic expectations about the upcoming target colour change how templates are prepared. Probe N2pcs showed two colour templates could be active together and were identical for expected (80%) and unexpected (20%) colours, so expectations did not alter preparation. Expectations did, however, strongly affect later target selection, revealing a dissociation between preparation and selection.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Martin Eimer

0049.name: Anna Kosovicheva
0049.bio: Anna Kosovicheva is an Assistant Professor at the University of Toronto Mississauga and co-directs the Applied Perception & Psychophysics LaboratorY (APPLY). Kosovicheva’s research uses psychophysical methodologies and eye-tracking technology to investigate mechanisms of visual localization, spatial vision, and binocular perception. They study how the visual system updates representations of object location and characterize individual differences in sensory processing. Their work also examines the application of vision science to digital readability and the clinical assessment of disorders such as amblyopia and strabismus.
0049.research_direction: Dr. Kosovicheva has recently been investigating a broad range of topics spanning applied visual search, binocular vision, and peripheral spatial coding. Their recent work explores how the low prevalence effect—the tendency to miss rare targets—manifests in naturalistic, high-stakes environments like driving, and tests whether alternative decision-making strategies can mitigate these search errors. In the domain of binocular processing, they are comparing the reliability of different psychophysical paradigms, such as Pulfrich depth tasks and flicker integration, for measuring interocular temporal delays, while also examining how these timing differences interact with contrast disparities in clinical populations like those with amblyopia. Furthermore, they are studying spatial vision in the periphery, specifically investigating how an observer's idiosyncratic biases in localizing briefly presented targets might predict their individual susceptibility to visual crowding.

papers.title: A Comparison of Methods for Measuring Interocular Delays
papers.abstract: Five psychophysical measures of temporal differences between the two eyes (two Pulfrich depth tasks, binocular flicker integration, temporal order judgements, reaction time and sensory eye dominance) were compared in normally sighted observers. Natural delays were too small to agree across tasks, but inducing a delay with a neutral density filter produced consistent correlations, with structure-from-motion Pulfrich tasks being the most sensitive and reliable. The results guide method choice for measuring interocular delays, particularly in clinical groups.
papers.authors: Brooke Lim, Anna Kosovicheva

papers.title: Reducing the low prevalence effect: Does similarity search translate to binary decisions?
papers.abstract: A recent proposal held that asking observers to pick the most target-like item eliminates the tendency to miss rare targets. This study tests whether that benefit survives when observers must also make a yes/no decision, using both T-shaped stimuli and clips of road video with hazards. Locating the target was unaffected by prevalence, but the binary decision still showed a low prevalence effect, limiting the practical usefulness of similarity search.
papers.authors: Greer Gillies, Anna Kosovicheva

papers.title: Intact Perceptual Interactions of Interocular Temporal Phase and Contrast Disparities in Amblyopia
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether timing differences and contrast differences between the two eyes, both used separately in amblyopia therapies, can be combined. Participants with amblyopia and controls judged motion direction in dichoptic flickering gratings while interocular delay and contrast imbalance were varied. Both groups showed the same pattern: a contrast imbalance reduced performance and was offset by a temporal lead for the lower-contrast eye, so the interaction is preserved in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Anna Kosovicheva, Zain Ahmed, Nikhil Chaudhry, Brooke Lim, Peter J. Bex, Emily K. Wiecek, Eric D. Gaier

papers.title: Taking prevalence effects on the road: Rare hazards are often missed
papers.abstract: Observers viewed dashcam-style driving videos in which potentially dangerous road hazards appeared either often or rarely. When hazards were rare, drivers-in-the-lab detected them much less reliably, showing that the well-known low prevalence effect from lab search tasks extends to realistic driving scenes. The work links basic visual-search theory to real-world safety concerns about missing infrequent but critical events.
papers.authors: Anna Kosovicheva, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Spatial variability in localization biases predicts crowding performance
papers.abstract: Observers systematically misjudge the location of briefly flashed peripheral targets in idiosyncratic ways. This study measured crowding strength and perceived spacing at 12 locations at 8 degrees eccentricity and found that where a person perceived items as closer together, they experienced stronger crowding. This suggests individual variability in spatial coding propagates to later stages such as peripheral object recognition.
papers.authors: Zainab Haseeb, Benjamin Wolfe, Anna Kosovicheva

0050.name: Anna Ma-Wyatt
0050.department: School of Psychology, College of Education, Behavioural and Social Sciences
0050.bio: Anna Ma-Wyatt is a Professor in the School of Psychology at the University of Adelaide and directs the Active Vision Lab. Ma-Wyatt’s research investigates the mechanisms of sensorimotor integration, specifically focusing on how visual information is utilized to plan and execute eye and hand movements. Using behavioral psychophysics and motion analysis, they explore the temporal and spatial dynamics of attentional deployment and how these processes are altered by healthy aging and clinical visual field loss. Ma-Wyatt's current work also examines human-autonomy teaming, applying principles of active vision and human performance to the design and optimization of human-AI interfaces and autonomous systems.
0050.research_direction: Dr. Ma-Wyatt has recently been studying how people coordinate vision and movement, and how that coordination copes with delays. Their experimental work looks at how delays or jitter in the feedback from a cursor affect continuous, visually guided tracking, measured with eye and hand movements. They have also been applying this human-factors perspective to space exploration, reviewing and arguing for new ways for humans and robots to work together, including the use of virtual and augmented reality interfaces for robot-assisted construction on the Moon and for living in deep space.

papers.title: The impact of varying cursor latency on visuomotor tracking
papers.abstract: The human visuomotor system typically compensates for intrinsic sensorimotor latencies to bind visual inputs with motor commands during precision tracking; however, this capacity is strained when movement feedback is subject to temporal delay or stochastic jitter. This investigation evaluated the operational thresholds where feedback latency impedes continuous manual tracking to delineate the constraints governing predictive control and error correction. Participants completed visually guided pursuit across curvilinear trajectories while ocular kinematics and cursor coordinates were simultaneously recorded under varied feedback latency parameters. Cursor position was sampled throughout each trial to compute input-to-display latency, cursor velocity dynamics, and spatial cursor–target error. In the initial experiment, cursor latency was held constant per trial across six magnitudes ranging from 0 to 300 ms. Velocity spectral power analyses showed that elevated latencies suppressed smooth pursuit submovements into lower frequency bands interspersed with sporadic, high-frequency corrective adjustments, whereas lower latencies preserved continuous tracking profiles. In the second experiment, discrete, unannounced step-changes in cursor latency were introduced mid-trial. Abrupt latency increases provoked larger instantaneous positional errors and compensatory submovement frequency, whereas sudden latency reductions prompted rapid attenuation of spatial error and swift restoration of kinematic smoothness. These adjustments demonstrate the visuomotor controller's capacity for rapid recalibration under variable feedback timing, indicating that predictive and reactive error-correction pathways adapt dynamically as a function of latency magnitude.
papers.authors: Lucy J. Turner, Steven D. Wiederman, Jessica L. O'Rielly, Anna Ma-Wyatt

papers.title: Robots Supervising Humans and Humans Supervising Robots – a Call for New Concepts in Human-Robot Teaming for Space
papers.abstract: A conceptual full conference paper arguing that human-robot teaming for space missions needs new frameworks, considering both robots supervising humans and humans supervising robots.
papers.authors: Anna Ma-Wyatt, Feras Dayoub, Melissa de Zwart

papers.title: Impact of extended reality on human-robot collaboration in lunar design & construction: A systematic review
papers.abstract: This systematic review employs PRISMA methodology to evaluate the efficacy of extended reality (XR) interfaces—including virtual, augmented, and mixed reality—in facilitating human-robot collaboration (HRC) for lunar infrastructure development. The synthesis analyzes current technological frameworks for teleoperation and supervisory control, focusing on how XR-mediated sensory feedback and spatial information visualization mitigate the challenges of extreme lunar environments, such as low gravity and latency. The study establishes performance metrics for situational awareness and mission safety, identifying critical gaps in existing HRC paradigms for off-earth construction and proposing integrated XR design principles to optimize human-robot teaming efficiency.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the International Astronautical Congress (IAC)
papers.authors: Albert Rajkumar, Amit Srivastava, Edward Palmer, Anna Ma-Wyatt

papers.title: The Challenges and Opportunities of Human-Robot Interaction for Deep Space Habitation
papers.abstract: A book chapter reviewing challenges and opportunities for human-robot interaction in deep-space habitation. It is a chapter rather than a journal or conference paper, so include it at discretion.
papers.venue: Issues in Space (Human Uses of Outer Space), Springer book chapter
papers.authors: Anna Ma-Wyatt, Justin Fidock, Jessica O'Rielly, Heidi Long, John Culton

0051.name: Anna Schubö
0051.bio: Anna Schubö is a Professor of Psychology at Philipps University Marburg and directs the Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception and Action research group. Schubö's research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual attention, focusing on how internal goals, selection history, and environmental salience guide information processing. They employ a multi-modal approach combining behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine electrophysiological markers such as the N2pc and PD components. Their recent work explores the integration of action intentions and motor planning into attentional control systems and the maintenance of task-relevant representations in visual working memory.
0051.research_direction: Dr. Schubö's recent work explores the dynamic interplay between selective visual attention, proactive cognitive control, and motor planning. They have recently been using EEG and classic visual search paradigms to examine the mechanisms of distractor suppression, specifically investigating how predictable distractor features, reward incentives, and expectations of search effort determine whether observers can strategically inhibit salient distractors. In parallel, their research investigates how attention and action influence one another in more complex environments using touch-based and real-world multi-target foraging tasks. In this applied line of work, they are asking how upcoming action intentions and motor precision demands shape which objects are prioritized during visual search and how the corresponding selection movements are physically executed.

papers.title: Picking the right piece: Action intentions shape visual search and action planning in human multi-target-foraging
papers.abstract: Participants picked up and placed LEGO bricks in a real-world foraging task while the precision demands of the placing instruction were varied. Movement analyses showed people favored nearby bricks but adjusted which bricks they chose and how they moved depending on how careful the upcoming placement had to be. The work shows that the intended action shapes both which objects get selected during search and how the selecting movements are planned.
papers.authors: Danilo A. Kuhn, Jan Tünnermann, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Neural evidence for feature-based distractor inhibition
papers.abstract: Using EEG, the study asked whether observers learn to suppress a salient distractor when its identifying feature (rather than its location) is predictable. Learning of the distractor feature reduced interference and was accompanied by lateralized ERP signatures of suppression. The results provide neural evidence that feature regularities of distractors can be exploited to inhibit them.
papers.authors: Aylin A. Hanne, Sizhu Han, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Cueing distractors is effective when the incentive to suppress is high
papers.abstract: In an additional-singleton search task, valid cues told participants the location and colour of an upcoming distractor, and correct responses were rewarded depending on distractor colour. Predictive cues sped responses, with benefits growing over the experiment, and reduced the amplitude of the distractor-related Pd component. The findings indicate that salient distractors can be suppressed proactively and voluntarily when motivation to do so is high.
papers.authors: Anna Heuer, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Attention directs actions in visual foraging
papers.abstract: The study applied a touch-based visual foraging paradigm to examine how attention and goal-directed actions interact. When one part of a two-part object was attentionally prioritized, the collecting tap was biased toward that part, and this bias combined with motor precision demands such as aiming for stable contact points. Attentional asymmetries thus feed back into motor planning.
papers.authors: Jan Tünnermann, Anna Schubö

papers.title: Effort expectation and strategic cue use in visual search
papers.abstract: Negative cues that signal distractor features are only useful if the benefit of reduced search effort outweighs the effort of using the cue. The authors manipulated whether search effort was predictable and examined how expected effort determines whether observers make strategic use of cues. Results tie cue use to effort expectation and connect it to attentional control settings.
papers.authors: Sizhu Han, Jan Tünnermann, Sara Katharina Hornung, Anna Schubö

0052.name: Anne B Sereno
0052.department: Department of Psychological Sciences and Weldon School of Biomedical Engineering
0052.bio: Anne B. Sereno is a Professor of Psychological Sciences and Biomedical Engineering at Purdue University, where Sereno investigates the physiological mechanisms of visual attention, short-term memory, and eye movements. Their research combines behavioral psychophysics, extracellular recordings, and computational modeling to examine how cortical pathways process sensorimotor and cognitive information. A portion of Sereno’s work involves translational neuroscience, specifically the development of eye-tracking and sensorimotor technologies as biomarkers for neurological disorders. These tools are designed to assist in the diagnosis and monitoring of conditions such as traumatic brain injury, Parkinson’s disease, and autism spectrum disorder.
0052.research_direction: Dr. Sereno has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying visual processing and sensorimotor function by applying artificial neural networks and machine learning to varied behavioral and neural phenomena. A central focus of their recent work explores the classical two-visual-streams hypothesis, using multi-pathway neural networks to test the computational trade-offs of segregating identity and spatial information, as well as probing how the visual system might use spatial maps to solve the feature binding problem when viewing multiple objects. Alongside these foundational architectural questions, they have been examining facial expression recognition by testing how deep convolutional networks utilize static spatial frames versus dynamic optical-flow motion cues to process naturalistic videos. Furthermore, they are extending their computational methods into translational clinical domains by applying machine learning to wearable sensor data to isolate wrist kinematics that could serve as biomarkers for age-related sensorimotor decline.

papers.title: Using neural networks to understand static and dynamic cues in facial expression recognition
papers.abstract: Trains deep convolutional networks on a large in-the-wild video database of facial expressions, using either static frames or optical-flow motion cues, in ordered or shuffled temporal form. Static cues outperformed dynamic cues, and scrambling temporal order barely hurt recognition for most expressions. Multivariate analysis of the networks' penultimate layers showed the two cue types yield different internal representations.
papers.authors: Yi-Fan Li, Elizabeth M. Edwards, Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: A spatial map: a propitious choice for constraining the binding problem
papers.abstract: Extends the authors' two-pathway network work to objects that have several attributes (identity, luminance, orientation, location). They show that a spatial map is an especially effective scaffold for keeping an object's features correctly bound together compared with maps based on other attributes. The result suggests why spatial information is retained across visual cortex and how the brain may solve feature binding.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: Understanding Cortical Streams from a Computational Perspective
papers.abstract: Reviews the history of the two-visual-streams (what/where) hypothesis and the conflicting evidence that has accumulated, such as shape selectivity in dorsal cortex and spatial tuning in ventral cortex. Using artificial neural networks with one or two pathways, the authors show how differences in encoding can reconcile these findings and why segregation is computationally advantageous. They also discuss how segregated features are rebound.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: A machine-learning method isolating changes in wrist kinematics that identify age-related changes in arm movement
papers.abstract: Uses wearable motion sensors while people perform arm movements and applies machine learning to isolate which wrist-kinematic features separate younger from older adults. The approach identifies age-related movement changes that could serve as sensorimotor biomarkers. It represents the lab's translational effort toward tools for monitoring neurological and age-related motor decline.
papers.authors: Aditya A. Shanghavi, Daniel Larranaga, Rhutuja Patil, Elizabeth M. Frazier, Satyajit Ambike, Bradley S. Duerstock, Anne B. Sereno

papers.title: Identifying and Localizing Multiple Objects Using Artificial Ventral and Dorsal Cortical Visual Pathways
papers.abstract: Tests whether networks with separate identity and space pathways still outperform single-pathway networks when images contain multiple objects. Handling the binding problem by having the identity pathway report objects in spatial order, the two-pathway networks reached higher accuracy, lower variance and faster training. Training demands grew rapidly with object count, hinting at why attention and working memory are capacity-limited.
papers.authors: Zhixian Han, Anne Sereno

0053.name: Anne Churchland
0053.department: Department of Neurobiology, David Geffen School of Medicine
0053.bio: Anne Churchland investigates the neural circuitry governing perceptual decision-making and the integration of information across multiple sensory modalities. Churchland's research utilizes large-scale neural recordings and optogenetic manipulations in rodents to examine how cortical and subcortical populations represent evidence and guide actions. A focus of their work involves characterizing the impact of spontaneous and task-related movements on neural activity, revealing that behavioral motifs often dominate signals in sensory processing areas. As a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory, they also develop standardized, collaborative frameworks to map brain-wide computations during cognitive tasks.
0053.research_direction: Dr. Churchland has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics underlying perceptual decision-making, exploring how sensory evidence is integrated with trial history, internal states, and body movements. Using cortex-wide widefield imaging and high-density recordings in mice performing visual and multisensory tasks, their recent work explores how latent engagement states and spontaneous physical movements profoundly shape cortical activity during evidence accumulation. They are also dissecting the specific circuitry of these processes, examining how distinct classes of pyramidal neurons distribute decision variables across the cortex and how the anterior cingulate cortex tracks past choices alongside ongoing motor signals. Additionally, Dr. Churchland is expanding the scope of decision-making research by investigating how autism-linked genetic mutations alter the neural use of prior expectations, while conceptually advocating for experimental paradigms that bridge highly instructed tasks with innate, ethologically relevant behaviors.

papers.title: Anterior cingulate neurons combine outcome monitoring of past decisions with ongoing movement signals
papers.abstract: Large-scale recordings in anterior cingulate cortex of freely moving mice making visual evidence-accumulation decisions reveal neurons with nonlinear mixed selectivity for the previous choice and outcome, while also being modulated by posture and movement. Trial history can be decoded from the population and occupies a component of activity separable from movement, and this code is conserved across animals and unaffected by fluctuating biases. The results show that history monitoring in ACC is a stable population code independent of environment volatility.
papers.authors: Lukas T. Oesch, Makenna C. Thomas, Davis Sandberg, João Couto, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: Spontaneous movements and their relationship to neural activity fluctuate with latent engagement states
papers.abstract: Mice performing a visual decision task drift between engaged and disengaged periods, and the study tracks how this latent state reshapes both spontaneous body movements and cortex-wide neural activity. Using widefield imaging with detailed movement tracking, it shows that movement structure and the way movements map onto cortical dynamics change with engagement, so neural signals cannot be interpreted without accounting for state. The work reframes how much of cortical activity in decision tasks reflects internal state and movement rather than the stimulus.
papers.authors: Chaoqun Yin, Maxwell D. Melin, Gabriel Rojas-Bowe, Xiaonan Richard Sun, João Couto, Steven Gluf, Alex Kostiuk, Simon Musall, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: Altered Use of Prior Expectations and Modified Neural Dynamics in a Mouse Model of Autism
papers.abstract: Mice lacking Neurexin1, a gene linked to psychiatric and autism-spectrum conditions, were tested on a visual decision task in which the stimulus side is predictable from recent trial history. Knockout animals under-used prior expectations and updated more slowly after feedback, and widefield imaging showed elevated and more correlated cortex-wide activity with a larger share of variance explained by movement. The study links a synaptic gene to how the brain combines priors with sensory evidence.
papers.authors: M. Felicia Davatolhagh, João Couto, Max Melin, Lukas T. Oesch, Charles Findling, Polo Morales, Isabelle Hong, International Brain Laboratory, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: From innate to instructed: A new look at perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: This review argues that perceptual decision-making research has leaned heavily on extensively trained, instructed behaviors, and that innate, ethologically grounded behaviors offer a complementary route. It contrasts what is learned from each approach about the neural circuits of decisions and proposes how they can be combined to reveal general principles. The piece articulates the lab's conceptual stance on task design.
papers.authors: Lukas T. Oesch, Michael B. Ryan, Anne K. Churchland

papers.title: Pyramidal cell types drive functionally distinct cortical activity patterns during decision-making
papers.abstract: Cortex-wide calcium imaging was performed in mice expressing indicators in defined classes of excitatory pyramidal neurons while they performed a multisensory decision task. Different cell types showed distinct spatial and temporal activity patterns tied to choice, sensory evidence and movement, and the cell-type-specific signals were used to model how decision-related information is distributed across cortex. The paper shows that genetically defined pyramidal populations carry different components of a decision.
papers.authors: Simon Musall, Xiaonan R. Sun, Hemanth Mohan, Xu An, Steven Gluf, Shu-Jing Li, Rhonda Drewes, Emma Cravo, Irene Lenzi, Chaoqun Yin, Björn M. Kampa, Anne K. Churchland

0054.name: Anthony Cate
0054.bio: Anthony Cate is a cognitive neuroscientist investigating the mechanisms of human visual perception and their integration with higher cognitive functions such as numeracy. Cate’s research employs functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine the neural representation of 3D shapes, focusing on how the brain differentiates between concave and convex geometry within the ventral and dorsal streams. The Cate lab explores pattern recognition in stochastic visual fields and evaluates the limitations of deep learning architectures in depicting numerical object consistency. Cate has contributed to the anatomical and functional mapping of human visual cortical fields using high-resolution neuroimaging analysis.
0054.research_direction: Dr. Cate has recently been working on how children learn algebra, in an unusual turn for a researcher with a vision and cognitive neuroscience background. Their recent work follows sixth graders through a year-long teaching experiment to ask how physical tools, such as Cuisenaire rods and linking cubes, help students move from concrete examples to general algebraic rules. A central question is how well the physical properties of each tool fit the way an individual student already thinks about multiplicative structure.

papers.title: The (activity-)effect of manipulatives on algebraic generalizations: a constructivist teaching experiment
papers.abstract: This research utilizes a year-long constructivist teaching experiment involving sixth-grade participants to investigate the cognitive mechanisms through which physical manipulatives facilitate the development of algebraic generalizations. The study specifically analyzes the interaction between students' interiorized multiplicative structures (units-coordination stages) and the physical affordances of Cuisenaire rods versus linking cubes. Results indicate that the efficacy of manipulatives is constrained by the degree of alignment between the tool's physical properties and the student's internal mental operations. Linking cubes, which enable the physical enactment of discrete units of one, supported significant transitions to generalized arithmetic, whereas Cuisenaire rods initially failed to elicit such changes until students had already mastered generalizations through discrete unit activity. These findings provide evidence for a neuro-educational model of mathematical embodiment, suggesting that the construction of algebra as generalized arithmetic is mediated by the interiorization of specific sensorimotor actions into higher-level mental operations.
papers.authors: Karen Zwanch, Brooke Mullins, Anderson Norton, Catherine Ulrich, Martha Ann Bell, Anthony Cate

0055.name: Anthony M Norcia
0055.bio: Anthony M. Norcia is a Professor (Research) of Psychology at Stanford University where they investigate the mechanisms of visual development and the neural basis of perception. Norcia utilizes high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) to measure cortical responses to spatial and temporal visual stimuli. By integrating EEG source imaging with functional MRI, Norcia maps the dynamics of visual processing in human infants and adults to understand both normal maturation and the pathophysiology of developmental disorders like strabismus, amblyopia, and glaucoma.
0055.research_direction: Dr. Norcia has recently been utilizing steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) to investigate the mechanisms and developmental trajectories of early visual processing. Their recent work explores the human binocular system, specifically probing how distinct cortical channels for absolute and relative disparity mature from infancy to adulthood and how these channels are differently modulated by contrast and blur. In a distinct line of research, they are examining spatial asymmetries in visual processing by mapping ON- and OFF-pathway responses to sawtooth luminance flicker across the upper and lower visual fields. Furthermore, they are actively working to translate these fundamental mapping techniques to clinical populations, investigating whether frequency-tagged EEG responses to ON/OFF biasing stimuli can serve as effective diagnostic biomarkers for visual system disorders such as glaucoma.

papers.title: Glaucoma Classification Through SSVEP-Derived ON- and OFF-Pathway Features
papers.abstract: The study asks whether steady-state EEG responses to luminance increments and decrements, which bias the ON and OFF visual pathways, can separate patients with glaucoma from healthy controls. Logistic-regression classifiers were trained on responses from 98 glaucoma patients and 71 controls, yielding moderate accuracy (AUC about 0.7). Response phase carried more diagnostic information than amplitude, and OFF-pathway features helped only when amplitude was used.
papers.authors: Martin T. W. Scott, Hui Xu, Alexandra Yakovleva, Robert Tibshirani, Jeffrey L. Goldberg, Anthony M. Norcia

papers.title: Late Development of Sensory Thresholds for Horizontal Relative Disparity in Human Visual Cortex in the Face of Precocial Development of Thresholds for Absolute Disparity
papers.abstract: Using steady-state visual evoked potentials in infants (about 5 months), children (about 5 years) and adults, the authors asked what limits the development of sensitivity to horizontal disparity. Thresholds for absolute disparity were nearly adult-like early on, whereas thresholds for relative disparity improved roughly tenfold over development. Equating contrast and blur visibility across ages did not equate disparity sensitivity, pointing to a protracted maturation of cortical mechanisms for relative disparity rather than limits in monocular inputs.
papers.authors: Anthony M. Norcia, Milena Kaestner, Yulan D. Chen, Caroline S. Clement

papers.title: Development of human binocular vision: An electrophysiological perspective
papers.abstract: A review of what visual evoked potentials reveal about how binocular vision develops. It covers binocular summation, dichoptic masking and intermodulation as markers of binocular interaction, the developmental motion asymmetry, and the maturation of sensitivity to horizontal disparity. The picture is one of early competence in some respects alongside quantitative and qualitative immaturities that suggest distinct mechanisms with different developmental time courses.
papers.authors: Anthony M. Norcia

papers.title: Two Disparity Channels in Human Visual Cortex With Different Contrast and Blur Sensitivity
papers.abstract: SSVEPs to dynamic random-dot stereograms alternating between zero and crossed disparity were measured across a range of contrasts and blur levels, for disparity planes and disparity gratings. The two response harmonics behaved differently: the first harmonic to gratings was more strongly affected by contrast and blur, whereas the second harmonic to planes had higher contrast sensitivity. The pattern is consistent with one channel tuned to relative disparity and higher luminance spatial frequencies and another for absolute disparity driven by lower spatial frequencies.
papers.authors: Milena Kaestner, Yulan D. Chen, Caroline Clement, Alex Hodges, Anthony M. Norcia

papers.title: Visual Field Asymmetries in Responses to ON and OFF Pathway Biasing Stimuli
papers.abstract: Using frequency-tagged steady-state EEG, the authors measured contrast response functions to sawtooth luminance flicker that biases the ON or OFF pathway, simultaneously in the upper and lower visual fields. OFF/decrement responses exceeded ON/increment responses, especially in the lower field. Lower-field ON and OFF responses followed sigmoidal nonlinearities, while the upper-field OFF function saturated less and varied more across subjects, laying groundwork for ON/OFF-based perimetry.
papers.authors: Martin Timothy Wilkinson Scott, Alexandra Yakovleva, Anthony Matthew Norcia

0056.name: Antimo Buonocore
0056.department: Department of Educational, Psychological and Communication Sciences
0056.lab_name: Experimental Psychology and Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory
0056.bio: Buonocore is an Associate Professor at Suor Orsola Benincasa University and directs the research program in Visual Cognition and Eye Movements. Their research investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms of oculomotor control, focusing on saccadic inhibition and the interference of visual transients on spatial remapping. Utilizing high-resolution eye tracking, EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Buonocore examines the role of the superior colliculus and brainstem in sensorimotor integration and target selection. Their work also encompasses the study of oculomotor dynamics in Parkinson's disease and the influence of joint attention on visual processing.
0056.research_direction: Dr. Buonocore has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual perception and motor control, with a primary focus on how the oculomotor system handles sudden sensory interruptions. Their recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms of saccadic inhibition, probing how visual transients suppress ongoing eye movement plans during both isolated sensory events and continuous, naturalistic free viewing. Beyond these oculomotor dynamics, they are using high-resolution 7-Tesla fMRI and forward modeling to map population receptive fields and characterize the topographic organization of memory-guided saccades along the human intraparietal sulcus. Additionally, their diverse research program extends into clinical neurophysiology and visual cognition, utilizing single-pulse TMS to examine pre-movement corticospinal facilitation in Parkinson's disease, and psychophysical tasks to test how spatial frequency, orientation, and familiarity influence the perceptual integration of faces.

papers.title: Sustained dynamics of saccadic inhibition and adaptive oculomotor responses during continuous exploration
papers.abstract: Uses saccadic inhibition, the reflexive suppression of eye movements after a sudden visual transient, as a probe of oculomotor dynamics during free viewing of visual arrays with gaze-contingent events. Shows that the inhibitory response persists yet adapts as stimuli repeat over space and time, indicating that the motor system balances sensitivity to novelty against predictability in naturalistic viewing.
papers.authors: Celeste Cafaro, Giovanni Cirillo, Giovanna Vermiglio, Carlo Cavaliere, Alessio Fracasso, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: Mapping memory-guided saccade population receptive fields reveals principles of cortical organization along the human intraparietal sulcus
papers.abstract: Combines 7-Tesla fMRI with forward modelling of memory-guided saccades to estimate not only preferred direction but also tuning width in human early visual cortex and intraparietal sulcus. Finds contralateral direction preference plus a new large-scale topographic organization of saccade tuning width, with specificity decreasing up the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Alessio Fracasso, Jasper Fabius, Katarina Moravkova, Rosanne Timmerman, Rebecca Taylor, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: The influence of spatial frequencies, orientation, and familiarity on face stimuli integration
papers.abstract: Tests how low and high spatial frequency content of familiar and unfamiliar faces is integrated using a face-matching task with upright and inverted faces. Finds that low-frequency content does not simply act as a fixed template for high-frequency details; integration is flexible and depends on orientation, familiarity and image contingencies.
papers.authors: Maria Cuomo, Giovanni Federico, Giovanni Mario Capolongo, Alessio Fracasso, Antimo Buonocore

papers.title: Lack of pre-movement facilitation as neurophysiological hallmark of fatigue in patients with Parkinson's disease: a single pulse TMS study
papers.abstract: Applied single-pulse TMS over motor cortex at several intervals before movement in healthy controls and Parkinson's patients with and without fatigue. Pre-movement corticospinal facilitation was intact in controls and non-fatigued patients but absent on the most affected side in fatigued patients, and its absence tracked fatigue and rigidity scores, suggesting a neurophysiological marker of PD fatigue.
papers.authors: Antimo Buonocore, Celeste Cafaro, Ciro De Luca, Giovanna Vermiglio, Giovanna Sepe, Giuseppe Rocco, Marco Aiello, Andrea Soricelli, Michele Papa, Carlo Cavaliere, Giovanni Cirillo

papers.title: The inevitability of visual interruption
papers.abstract: Argues that exogenous capture of eye movements by sudden visual events is inherently variable because such events arrive asynchronously relative to the brain's internal state. Reviews evidence from saccadic inhibition and related oculomotor phenomena, including superior colliculus involvement, to show that interruption of ongoing motor plans is a general and unavoidable feature of the system. Frames these effects as a unifying account of how sensory transients shape motor timing.
papers.authors: Antimo Buonocore, Ziad M. Hafed

0059.name: Arash Afraz
0059.department: National Institute of Mental Health, Laboratory of Neuropsychology
0059.lab_name: Unit on Neurons, Circuits and Behavior (UNCB)
0059.main_research_area: Neural mechanisms of visual object recognition
0059.bio: Arash Afraz is a Principal Investigator at the National Institute of Mental Health and leads the Unit on Neurons, Circuits and Behavior. Afraz researches the causal links between neural activity in the ventral visual stream, particularly the inferior temporal cortex, and the behavioral outcomes of object recognition. By integrating visual psychophysics with single-unit recording, optogenetics, and microstimulation in non-human primates, they aim to map how high-level cortical areas shape subjective visual perception. Recent work by Afraz on "perceptography" focuses on quantifying the hallucinatory percepts induced by neural perturbation to provide data for the development of visual prosthetics.
0059.research_direction: Dr. Afraz has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of high-level visual perception and object categorization in the macaque temporal cortex. Their recent work focuses on how neural activity in the high-level visual cortex, shapes visual perception. They are probing the causal role of the ventral stream in perception and behavior by utilizing pharmacological inactivation of face patches to study naturalistic oculomotor control, and by combining behavioral optogenetics with machine learning to reconstruct the subjective visual hallucinations induced by cortical stimulation. To facilitate these advanced neurophysiological paradigms, they are concurrently developing novel methodological tools, such as personalized, 3D-printed non-invasive head immobilization systems for awake behaving non-human primates.

papers.title: 3D-printable non-invasive head immobilization system for non-human primates
papers.abstract: Describes a personalized, 3D-printed head-immobilization system built from each animal's own anatomy, allowing stable head fixation in awake behaving macaques without surgical implants. The design is reported with fabrication steps and validation in neurophysiology-style experiments, offering a less invasive alternative to headposts.
papers.authors: Elia Shahbazi, Drew Nguyen, Tyler Swedan, Timothy Ma, Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Alvin Dinh, Reza Azadi, Amy M. Ryan, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Perceptography unveils the causal contribution of inferior temporal cortex to visual perception
papers.abstract: Monkeys were trained to report brief optogenetic pulses delivered to inferior temporal cortex through an implanted LED array. In a closed loop, a generative image algorithm searched for pictures the animal could not tell apart from the stimulation, yielding 'perceptograms' that depict the complex hallucinated percepts evoked at each cortical site. The results give the first quantitative visual readout of what artificial IT stimulation makes an animal see, and link IT activity causally to perceived object features.
papers.authors: Elia Shahbazi, Timothy Ma, Martin Pernuš, Walter Scheirer, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Inactivation of face-selective neurons alters eye movements when free viewing faces
papers.abstract: Face-patch locations in IT cortex of two macaques were identified with fMRI and then silenced by muscimol injection while the animals freely viewed face images. Inactivation changed where the monkeys fixated on faces, altering fixation patterns to specific facial features. This provides causal physiological evidence linking face-encoding IT neurons to the oculomotor system that steers gaze.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Reza Azadi, Emily Lopez, Jessica Taubert, Amanda Patterson, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Image-dependence of the detectability of optogenetic stimulation in macaque inferotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Monkeys detected optogenetic stimulation of IT cortex while viewing different background images. Detectability depended strongly on the concurrently viewed image, being higher for images containing content resembling the neurons' preferred features. This shows that the perceptual consequences of stimulating high-level visual cortex are shaped by the ongoing visual scene rather than being a fixed event.
papers.authors: Reza Azadi, Simon Bohn, Emily Lopez, Rosa Lafer-Sousa, Karen Wang, Mark A.G. Eldridge, Arash Afraz

papers.title: Behavioral optogenetics in nonhuman primates; a psychological perspective
papers.abstract: A single-author perspective on how optogenetic perturbation can be combined with behavioral measurement in primates to study cognition and perception. It argues for treating perturbation-induced experience as a psychological phenomenon to be measured with psychophysics, and reviews technical and conceptual obstacles for the field.
papers.authors: Arash Afraz

0060.name: Arathy Kartha
0060.department: Department of Biological and Vision Sciences
0060.lab_name: Multisensory Integration in Visual Impairment Lab
0060.bio: Arathy Kartha is an Assistant Professor at the SUNY College of Optometry. Kartha's research focuses on functional vision enhancement through multisensory integration and rehabilitation technologies. Their work utilizes virtual reality and real-world assessments to evaluate visual ability and develop training protocols for individuals with ultra-low vision and those using visual neuroprostheses. Kartha investigates how auditory and haptic cues supplement prosthetic vision to assist with navigation and object recognition. As a recipient of the NIH K99/R00 Pathway to Independence Award, they examine the intersection of psychophysics and clinical ophthalmology to evaluate vision restoration therapies.
0060.research_direction: Dr. Kartha has recently been investigating how to accurately assess residual visual capabilities and functional behavior in individuals with ultra-low vision. Their recent work explores the use of calibrated virtual reality platforms to safely quantify performance on complex, everyday tasks, ranging from navigating hazardous environments and gathering visual information to executing visually guided motor actions like reaching and grasping. By comparing these objective, trajectory-based performance metrics with subjective patient self-reports, they are working to establish more robust clinical endpoints for vision-restoration trials and rehabilitation programs. Additionally, their research spans into multisensory challenges, examining the unique rehabilitation needs and everyday experiences of retinal prosthesis users who concurrently navigate auditory impairments.

papers.title: Navigation behavior during visual wayfinding in people with ultra-low vision using virtual reality
papers.abstract: Using a calibrated VR platform, the study measured how people with ultra-low vision, normal vision and simulated ultra-low vision move through street-crossing, cafeteria and metro-station scenes that would be unsafe to test in the real world. Head-trajectory metrics such as onset latency, walking speed, path efficiency and turn deviation separated the groups and tracked environment difficulty, with the metro station hardest. The work argues that trajectory-based measures are more informative outcome metrics for navigation rehabilitation than conventional ones.
papers.authors: Dinesh Venugopal, Batuhan Erkat, Roksana Sadeghi, Chau Tran, Will Gee, Brittnee Livingston, Gislin Dagnelie, Arathy Kartha

papers.title: Experiences of Retinal Prosthesis Wearers with Auditory Impairment
papers.abstract: This book chapter discusses the experiences of retinal-prosthesis users who also have hearing loss (deafblindness), covering the challenges and support needs that arise when both senses are impaired. It draws on her prosthetic-vision and multisensory work to frame rehabilitation considerations.
papers.venue: Learning, Education, and Support of Deafblind Children and Adults (Oxford University Press)
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Self-Reported Visual Ability Versus Task Performance in Individuals With Ultra-Low Vision
papers.abstract: The paper compares what people with ultra-low vision say they can do on a visual-ability questionnaire with how they actually perform comparable VR and real-world tasks. Self-reports and measured performance correlated only partially, showing that questionnaires alone are insufficient outcome measures. The findings inform how clinical trials of vision-restoration therapies should pair patient-reported and performance-based endpoints.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Ravnit Kaur Singh, Chris Bradley, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Measuring visual information gathering in individuals with ultra low vision using virtual reality
papers.abstract: A set of calibrated VR tasks such as locating objects and detecting motion was used to quantify how much visual information people with ultra-low vision can gather. Performance differed clearly from normally sighted and simulated-ULV controls and scaled with task difficulty. The results show the tasks are feasible, sensitive assessments of residual vision.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Roksana Sadeghi, Chris Bradley, Chau Tran, Will Gee, Gislin Dagnelie

papers.title: Measuring visually guided motor performance in ultra low vision using virtual reality
papers.abstract: The study built VR tasks such as reaching, grasping and sorting to measure visually guided motor performance in people with ultra-low vision. Participants showed measurable but impaired performance relative to sighted controls, and the tasks discriminated between ability levels. This provides a standardized motor-function endpoint for severe vision loss.
papers.authors: Arathy Kartha, Roksana Sadeghi, Chris Bradley, Brittnee Livingston, Chau Tran, Will Gee, Gislin Dagnelie

0062.name: Arthur G Shapiro
0062.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Computer Science
0062.lab_name: Laboratory for the Study of Perception, Reality, and Illusion (SPRI)
0062.bio: Arthur G. Shapiro studies visual perception and neuroscience, focusing on the mechanisms underlying color perception, motion, and low-light vision. Shapiro uses visual illusions to investigate the computational and physiological processes that connect physical stimuli to sensory experience. Their research involves developing models of spatial and temporal contrast to explain phenomena such as lightness constancy and the peripheral-foveal processing gap. Shapiro has received multiple awards from the Best Illusion of the Year Contest and serves as the co-editor of the Oxford Compendium of Visual Illusions.
0062.research_direction: Dr. Shapiro has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying perceptual phenomena, using visual illusions as tools to probe how the visual system processes lightness, contrast, motion, and depth. Their recent work explores lightness and contrast perception, analyzing individual differences to determine whether classic lightness illusions share underlying mechanisms, and using novel chessboard demonstrations to test illumination-inference versus spatial-scale models. Additionally, they are investigating motion and shape integration by combining Kanizsa figures with edge-motion illusions to understand how local motion signals produce coherent, perpetually rotating global shapes. Expanding their methodological toolkit, Dr. Shapiro is also examining how stimulus reflectance and background brightness modulate the Pulfrich depth illusion in virtual reality, while utilizing frequency-tagged steady-state EEG to test whether the brain processes luminance and contrast modulations through distinct neural channels.

papers.title: Relationships among lightness illusions uncovered by analyses of individual differences
papers.abstract: Asks whether the many lightness illusions (simultaneous contrast, White's, Munker and others) rely on shared mechanisms by measuring how susceptible individual observers are to each one. Correlations between people's illusion magnitudes show which illusions cluster together and which are independent, constraining unified models of lightness. The pattern argues against a single common explanation for all lightness illusions.
papers.authors: Yuki Kobayashi, Arthur G. Shapiro

papers.title: Two contrast phenomena inconsistent with illumination assumptions
papers.abstract: Presents two new demonstrations to test the idea that observers infer illumination when viewing 2D images. In one, the colour of a figure changes the look of the surrounding ground; in the other, two modulating chessboards look alike although one modulates all squares and the other only half, and only the half-modulating board shifts a test patch. The results fit a network account with task-dependent spatial-scale selection better than illuminant inference.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Arthur Shapiro, Yuki Kobayashi, Joseph DeNavas

papers.title: Perpetual rotation of real and illusory shapes
papers.abstract: Combines the Kanizsa illusory square with edge-motion illusions, in which a stationary luminance-modulated edge appears to move continuously. Local edge motion signals are ambiguous, yet together they produce a coherent, perpetually rotating global shape, including for illusory-contour shapes. The work shows how global shape and motion percepts arise from local motion signals and the rigidity assumption.
papers.authors: Yuki Kobayashi, Arthur G. Shapiro

papers.title: The Pulfrich Effect in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: Examines the Pulfrich depth illusion, in which an interocular delay produces misperceived depth, in VR headsets rather than on flat panels. Across three experiments, low-reflectance stimuli produced a stronger effect than high-reflectance ones, especially against brighter backgrounds. Nulling the perceived rotation of a helix offers a sensitive way to measure the effect.
papers.authors: Anthony LoPrete, Alexander Gokan, Arthur G. Shapiro

papers.title: Separation of luminance and contrast modulation in steady-state visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: Uses steady-state EEG to test whether the brain separates responses to luminance modulation from responses to contrast modulation. Frequency-tagged signals allow the two components to be distinguished neurally, supporting separate processing channels for brightness and contrast.
papers.authors: Laysa Hedjar, Jasna Martinovic, Søren K. Andersen, Arthur G. Shapiro

0065.name: Aude Oliva
0065.department: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)
0065.bio: Aude Oliva is a Senior Research Scientist at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) and the Director of Strategic Industry Engagement at the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. Their research integrates human perception, computer vision, and cognitive neuroscience to model how the human brain encodes, processes, and remembers complex visual scenes. Oliva’s work involves research on image memorability, the development of "hybrid images," and the use of deep neural networks to map spatiotemporal brain dynamics. They also direct the MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab and lead initiatives focused on the intersection of natural and artificial intelligence.
0065.research_direction: Dr. Oliva's recent work explores the neural representations of complex visual events by leveraging massive-scale neuroimaging datasets, deep neural networks, and behavioral experiments. They have recently been building and aggregating vast fMRI datasets of naturalistic images and videos to train brain-optimized encoding models, investigating how dynamic stimuli and semantic features map onto the visual cortex and compare to artificial network hierarchies. Their research also probes the spatiotemporal dynamics of visual perception, using multimodal techniques like fMRI and MEG to track the precise temporal stages and cortical networks that underlie intrinsic image memorability. Additionally, they are investigating applied and generative aspects of human vision, ranging from training generative AI to reconstruct perceived short videos directly from whole-brain signals, to behavioral studies evaluating how real-world viewing conditions and visual UI interventions impact human susceptibility to deepfakes.

papers.title: MOSAIC: A scalable framework for fMRI dataset aggregation and modeling of human vision
papers.abstract: Pools eight large vision fMRI datasets (93 subjects, about 430,000 fMRI-stimulus pairs, about 163,000 natural and artificial stimuli) into one framework with a shared preprocessing pipeline and a train/test split filtered to avoid leakage. The authors show that more perceptually diverse stimulus sets improve decoding accuracy and stability. They also jointly train brain-optimized encoding models across subjects and datasets to predict activity across visual cortex and much of the whole brain.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Mayukh Deb, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Modeling short visual events through the BOLD Moments video fMRI dataset and metadata
papers.abstract: Introduces the BOLD Moments Dataset, whole-brain fMRI recordings from ten people watching more than 1,000 three-second naturalistic video clips, each with rich metadata. The authors show how the brain encodes word- and sentence-level descriptions of events, and find memorability-related signal reaching into parietal cortex. They also show that cortical regions line up hierarchically with video-computable deep networks and that the data capture second-scale temporal dynamics. The dataset is a resource for studying how the brain perceives dynamic events.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Kshitij Dwivedi, Polina Iamshchinina, Monika Graumann, Alex Lascelles, Gemma Roig, Alessandro Thomas Gifford, Bowen Pan, SouYoung Jin, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Kendrick Kay, Aude Oliva, Radoslaw M. Cichy

papers.title: Visual perception of highly memorable images is mediated by a distributed network of ventral visual regions that enable a late memorability response
papers.abstract: Combines fMRI with source-localized MEG through representational similarity analysis to show when and where the cortex responds to image memorability. Highly memorable images recruit a distributed set of ventral visual regions starting about 300 ms after onset, from early visual cortex to inferior temporal and fusiform areas. The effect appears after high-level feature processing and is also reflected in medial temporal memory regions. This gives the first unified space-time account of memorability in the human brain.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Yalda Mohsenzadeh, Caitlin Mullin, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Brain Netflix: Scaling Data to Reconstruct Videos from Brain Signals
papers.abstract: Presents a pipeline for reconstructing 2-3 second videos from fMRI that is designed to work across participants and across datasets. It regresses latent and conditioning vectors for pretrained text-to-video and video-to-video generative models from brain activity, and scaling the training data improves reconstruction quality. The reconstructed clips closely match the semantic content of what participants viewed.
papers.authors: Camilo Fosco, Benjamin Lahner, Bowen Pan, Alex Andonian, Emilie Josephs, Alex Lascelles, Aude Oliva

papers.title: Effects of Browsing Conditions and Visual Alert Design on Human Susceptibility to Deepfakes
papers.abstract: Online experiments show that realistic browsing conditions (low prevalence of fakes, brief exposure, poor video quality, divided attention) each reduce people's ability to spot deepfakes, so earlier lab studies likely understate the vulnerability. The authors then test AI assistance and find that a visual alert that magnifies artifacts in fake videos raises detection and confidence in the AI feedback more than text-based warnings do.
papers.venue: Journal of Online Trust and Safety
papers.authors: Emilie Josephs, Camilo Fosco, Aude Oliva

0066.name: Austin Roorda
0066.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science
0066.bio: Austin Roorda researches vision science, utilizing adaptive optics technologies to image and stimulate the human retina at a cellular scale. Roorda mapped the human trichromatic cone mosaic and developed the Adaptive Optics Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) for high-resolution retinal research. Their research combines optical engineering and neuroscience to study how the optics of the eye and the spatial arrangement of photoreceptors influence visual perception. This work also examines how these physiological factors are affected by the presence of retinal disease.
0066.research_direction: Dr. Roorda has recently been utilizing advanced adaptive optics and active retinal tracking to investigate visual perception and photoreceptor function at the scale of single cone cells. Their recent work explores a diverse array of visual phenomena, from developing optoretinography techniques that record light-evoked responses from individual cones to probing the limits of human colorspace by selectively stimulating specific cone classes. A major focus of their research also centers on fixational eye movements, specifically examining how small retinal drifts influence visual stability and the perception of relative motion. Furthermore, they are investigating how natural gaze dynamics interact with the spatial layout of the retina to optimize high-resolution vision, including how these microscopic scanning movements help preserve visual acuity under conditions of simulated photoreceptor loss.

papers.title: Revealing the benefit of eye motion for acuity under emulated cone loss
papers.abstract: To emulate retinal degeneration in healthy eyes, the authors used adaptive optics to withhold stimulation from randomly chosen cones while people read letters. Acuity fell nonlinearly with more dropout, but fixational eye motion helped substantially: at the highest dropout, moving eyes matched a static system with nearly twice as many sampling elements. Surviving cones gain information by scanning more of the letter as the eye moves.
papers.authors: Hannah K. Doyle, James Fong, Ren Ng, Austin Roorda

papers.title: How Gaze Direction and Dynamics Affect Visual Resolution
papers.abstract: Measuring where in the retina people achieve their best fine-detail vision, this study examines how gaze direction and eye movement dynamics influence resolution acuity. It characterizes an optimal retinal locus for high-resolution vision in space and time, and shows that the retinal position used for fixation is tuned to performance under natural viewing dynamics. The findings bear on why some retinal locations are favored for seeing detail.
papers.authors: Josselin Gautier, Norick R. Bowers, Martin S. Banks, Austin Roorda

papers.title: Novel color via stimulation of individual photoreceptors at population scale
papers.abstract: The authors present 'Oz', a display approach that uses adaptive optics eye tracking to deliver light to individual cone cells one at a time, so each photoreceptor's activity is controlled directly instead of through the overlapping cone spectral sensitivities. By stimulating only M cones over a wide patch of retina, they push perceived color beyond the range possible with ordinary displays. Observers described the result as a blue-green of unprecedented saturation, confirming a partial expansion of colorspace.
papers.authors: James Fong, Hannah K. Doyle, Congli Wang, Alexandra E. Boehm, Sofie R. Herbeck, Vimal Prabhu Pandiyan, Brian P. Schmidt, Pavan Tiruveedhula, John E. Vanston, William S. Tuten, Ramkumar Sabesan, Austin Roorda, Ren Ng

papers.title: Optoretinography with actively stabilized adaptive optics optical coherence tomography
papers.abstract: The paper describes an adaptive optics OCT system with real-time active retinal tracking that keeps the imaging beam locked on chosen cones despite eye motion. This stabilization makes it possible to record light-evoked optical responses (optoretinograms) from single cones efficiently and reliably. It advances functional imaging of photoreceptors toward clinical and basic-science use.
papers.authors: Jason H. Wong, Shangbang Luo, Zohreh Hosseinaee, Fabio Feroldi, Austin Roorda

papers.title: A paradoxical misperception of relative motion
papers.abstract: When the eye drifts during fixation, images slip across the retina, yet the world looks stable. Using adaptive optics stimulation with retinal image motion under experimenter control, this study finds that an object moving with the eye's drift is misperceived relative to its surroundings in a paradoxical way. The result constrains how the brain uses assumptions about self-generated motion to stabilize perception.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Josephine C. D'Angelo, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Raymond J. Weber, David W. Arathorn, Austin Roorda

0067.name: Avniel Ghuman
0067.bio: Avniel Ghuman is an Associate Professor of Neurological Surgery specializing in the neural mechanisms of high-level visual and social perception. Ghuman’s research integrates invasive intracranial EEG (iEEG) and non-invasive magnetoencephalography (MEG) with computational techniques, including machine learning and network analysis, to map the spatiotemporal dynamics of information flow in the brain. This work examines the representation of faces and objects within real-world contexts, utilizing deep learning models to reconstruct visual experiences from neural activity. Currently, their research explores real-world neurodynamics to understand how brain states and transitions support behavior during natural social interactions.
0067.research_direction: Dr. Ghuman has recently been using intracranial recordings to investigate the spatiotemporal neural dynamics of high-level vision and unconstrained natural behavior.
