Their recent work explores the visual processing of faces and words in the ventral temporal cortex, probing how domain-specific responses dynamically evolve over time and how foundational reading circuits emerge from pre-existing visual and language networks. Expanding beyond traditional controlled lab paradigms, they are also investigating real-world social vision by pairing neural recordings with wearable eye-tracking to model how the brain encodes dynamic, naturalistic facial expressions during spontaneous conversations. Additionally, Dr. Ghuman is examining broader macroscopic brain dynamics during continuous multi-day monitoring, seeking to understand how gradients of neural timescales map onto visual behavior and how the brain transitions between distinct dynamical states during everyday activities like sleeping, socializing, and consuming media.

papers.title: A week in the life of the human brain reveals stable states punctuated by chaotic-like transitions
papers.abstract: The authors recorded intracranial electrodes together with video in twenty people over a week of unconstrained hospital behavior. Deep-learning dynamical models showed brain activity tracking circadian rhythm, heart rate and behaviors like socializing, screen watching and sleep depth. Behavior changes coincided with bursts of chaotic-like neural exploration that settled into new stable states around a central attractor tied to default-mode network activity, and sleep deprivation made transitions more chaotic and weakened that stabilization.
papers.authors: Maxwell B. Wang, Max G'Sell, James F. Castellano, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel S. Ghuman

papers.title: The reading brain - Transforming vision into language
papers.abstract: This review argues that literacy emerges from specialization of pre-existing circuits rather than dedicated reading machinery. The visual word form area sits where visual input meets connections to auditory-visual speech and language networks and to visual naming circuits, which explains why it supports written word processing. The authors gather neurophysiological, anatomical and developmental evidence for this account.
papers.authors: Avniel Singh Ghuman, Julie A. Fiez, Matthew J. Boring

papers.title: Neural encoding of real world face perception
papers.abstract: Using intracranial recordings from epilepsy patients wearing eye-tracking glasses during spontaneous conversations with friends, family and others, the study models the faces people actually look at with computer vision. Brain activity alone could reconstruct viewed faces, including expression and motion, with the social vision pathway spanning parietal, temporal and occipital cortex playing a key role. Expressions appeared to be encoded as deviations from a neutral prototype, with sharper tuning for subtle than for intense expressions.
papers.authors: Arish Alreja, Michael J. Ward, Lisa S. Parker, R. Mark Richardson, Louis-Philippe Morency, Taylor J. Abel, Avniel Singh Ghuman

papers.title: Dynamic Domain Specificity in Human Ventral Temporal Cortex
papers.abstract: Intracranial recordings from 17 people across ventral temporal cortex assessed when individual words and faces can be told apart inside and outside strongly selective regions. Discrimination first appeared mainly in the strongly selective areas, then about 170 ms later also in surrounding cortex. This supports a dynamic model in which domain-specific processing is followed by distributed processing stages.
papers.authors: Brett B. Bankson, Matthew J. Boring, Arish Alreja, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel Singh Ghuman

papers.title: Interacting ventral temporal gradients of timescales and functional connectivity and their relationships to visual behavior
papers.abstract: Intracranial recordings from 4,090 contacts in 35 people were used to map gradients of neural timescales and functional connectivity across category-selective ventral temporal cortex. Spontaneous and stimulus-evoked timescales were uncorrelated, while spontaneous timescales tracked functional connectivity even after accounting for anatomical gradients. Both measures related to how strongly a population predicted behavior in a simple visual task, suggesting partly distinct mechanisms that jointly shape behavior.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Boring, R. Mark Richardson, Avniel Singh Ghuman

0070.name: Barbara Shinn-Cunningham
0070.department: Neuroscience Institute, Mellon College of Science, Psychology, Biomedical Engineering, Electrical and Computer Engineering
0070.bio: Barbara Shinn-Cunningham serves as the Glen de Vries Dean of the Mellon College of Science and was the founding director of the Neuroscience Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. Shinn-Cunningham’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying auditory scene analysis, specifically how the brain extracts meaning from complex acoustic environments like the 'cocktail party' scenario. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, neuroimaging (EEG, MEG, fMRI), and computational modeling, they investigate how top-down attention and spatial hearing facilitate the selection of specific sound objects. Their work also explores the intersection of auditory and visual attention and the impact of hidden hearing deficits on cognitive performance.
0070.research_direction: Dr. Shinn-Cunningham has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying auditory scene analysis and selective attention in complex, noisy environments. Using EEG and behavioral paradigms, their recent work explores how top-down processes like statistical learning aid in segregating competing speech streams, while also seeking to pinpoint whether the neural locus of attentional gain occurs at the cortical or early brainstem level. They are also examining the dynamics of spatial attention by testing how unexpected auditory interruptions and task-irrelevant features, such as voice continuity, impact a listener's ability to track target sounds. Broadening their scope to multisensory contexts, Dr. Shinn-Cunningham evaluates how sensory modality and spatial-temporal domains jointly drive dual-task interference between vision and hearing, and investigates the broader cognitive penetrability of perception to determine whether high-level expectations genuinely alter low-level sensory representations across different modalities.

papers.title: Attention to Pseudotone Melodies Enhances Cortical But Not Brainstem Responses in Humans
papers.abstract: Listeners followed one of two simultaneous melodies while EEG captured both cortical and brainstem-level responses. Attention clearly strengthened the cortical responses to the attended melody, but the early brainstem (frequency-following) responses showed no comparable enhancement. The result places the main locus of selective-attention gain in cortex rather than in early subcortical encoding.
papers.authors: Victoria Figarola, Yunshu Li, Adam Tierney, Fred Dick, Abigail Noyce, Ross K. Maddox, Barbara Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Effects of Task-Irrelevant Talker Identity and Continuity on Spatial Selective Attention Under Interruption
papers.abstract: Participants recalled a syllable sequence arriving from a cued direction while a competing sequence came from another direction and unexpected interrupters occasionally intruded. Giving the two streams distinct talkers improved recall and softened the damage from interruptions even though voice was irrelevant to the task. Randomly changing the talker within a stream disrupted the build-up of attention about as much as an external interrupter did.
papers.authors: Wusheng Liang, Abigail L. Noyce, Christopher A. Brown, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Prediction from Statistical Learning Aids Auditory Scene Analysis
papers.abstract: Listeners were first exposed to syllable streams with fixed transition probabilities, then detected target syllables in one of two competing streams. Targets that matched the learned statistics were detected better, especially in noise, and drove earlier neural recognition and stronger tracking of the attended stream in EEG. Predictability of the ignored stream did not help, indicating that learned schemas support scene analysis via attentional template matching.
papers.authors: Vibha Viswanathan, Srinidhi Narayanan, Ingrid S. Johnsrude, Jenny R. Saffran, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Evaluating cognitive penetrability of perception across the senses
papers.abstract: This review asks whether beliefs, expectations and other cognitive states can genuinely alter what we perceive, examining evidence from vision, audition and other modalities. The authors weigh experimental claims for top-down effects against alternative explanations such as attention, response bias and memory. They lay out criteria and cross-modal evidence for when a top-down influence counts as true perceptual change.
papers.authors: Petra Vetter, Stephanie Badde, Elisa Raffaella Ferrè, Janina Seubert, Barbara Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Sensory modality and information domain contribute jointly to dual-task interference between vision and audition
papers.abstract: Listeners performed tasks that varied in sensory modality (vision or audition) and information domain (spatial or temporal), alone and in pairs, to see what drives interference. Dual-task costs depended on both factors together rather than modality alone, with the greatest interference when tasks shared both. The findings argue that attentional resources are organized by sensory modality and information domain jointly.
papers.authors: Justin T. Fleming, J. Michelle Njoroge, Abigail L. Noyce, Tyler K. Perrachione, Barbara G. Shinn-Cunningham

0071.name: Barry Giesbrecht
0071.bio: Barry Giesbrecht is a Professor at UC Santa Barbara and the director of the UCSB Attention Lab, focusing on the neural and cognitive mechanisms of selective information processing. Their research utilizes a multimodal empirical approach, combining functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and psychophysical methods to study how attention interacts with memory and perception. Giesbrecht investigates the relationship between global physiological states, such as physical exercise, and the modulation of attentional control and sensory sensitivity. Additionally, their research explores the translational application of these findings to human performance and decision-making in complex environments.
0071.research_direction: Dr. Giesbrecht's recent work explores the dynamic nature of attentional control, investigating how cognitive performance is shaped by internal bodily states, reward history, and modern technological environments. Specifically, they have recently been examining the relationship between acute physical exertion and cognition, using both large-scale Bayesian meta-analyses and theoretical frameworks to understand how physiological arousal shifts the brain between different modes of selective attention. Their research also probes the mechanisms underlying sustained attention and task lapses, employing signal detection theory to parse the perceptual and decisional roots of the vigilance decrement and utilizing real-time, closed-loop methods to test how value-driven attentional capture influences moment-to-moment commission errors. Furthermore, they are expanding traditional cognitive methodologies into more naturalistic contexts, using electroencephalography to track how the human brain allocates attention and processes semantic meaning within augmented reality settings.

papers.title: Value-driven attentional capture prevents commission errors in real time
papers.abstract: The study tests whether reward-associated stimuli that capture attention can influence lapses during a monotonous response task. Using a real-time, closed-loop approach, it examines how value-driven capture affects the occurrence of commission errors as they unfold, linking reward history to moment-to-moment attentional control.
papers.authors: Shivang Shelat, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: Physically activated modes of attentional control
papers.abstract: This opinion piece argues that physical exertion and physiological arousal do not simply raise or lower attention but shift the brain between different modes of attentional control. It integrates human behavioral and neural findings on acute exercise, and lays out a framework and open questions for how bodily state shapes selective attention.
papers.authors: Barry Giesbrecht, Tom Bullock, Jordan Garrett

papers.title: Beyond detection rate: understanding the vigilance decrement using signal detection theory
papers.abstract: The paper reanalyzes why performance declines during long, monotonous vigilance tasks using signal detection theory rather than raw hit rate. It separates changes in perceptual sensitivity from shifts in response criterion, showing the decrement cannot be captured by detection rate alone and clarifying competing accounts such as resource depletion versus strategy change.
papers.authors: Henri Etel Skinner, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: Electrophysiological evidence for differential semantic processing of words and objects presented in augmented reality
papers.abstract: Participants viewed words and real or virtual objects through an augmented reality headset while EEG was recorded. Event-related brain responses indexing semantic processing differed between words and objects, indicating the brain links meaning to AR-presented content in distinct ways. The work brings neural measures of attention and meaning into realistic mixed-reality settings.
papers.authors: Tom Bullock, Emily Machniak, Joyce Passananti, Kangyou Yu, Radha Kumaran, You-Jin Kim, Jordan Garrett, Madhav Viswesvaran, Julia Ram, Tobias Hollerer, Barry Giesbrecht

papers.title: A systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis provide evidence for an effect of acute physical activity on cognition in young adults
papers.abstract: The authors pooled 651 effect sizes from 113 studies (about 4,400 healthy young adults) using a Bayesian hierarchical model to ask whether a single bout of exercise changes cognitive performance. They find a small but credible benefit, with faster reaction times and improvements on executive-function tasks such as working memory and inhibition. Results held across different priors and after correcting for publication bias.
papers.authors: Jordan Garrett, Carly Chak, Tom Bullock, Barry Giesbrecht

0072.name: Barry J Richmond
0072.lab_name: Section on Neural Coding and Computation
0072.bio: Barry J. Richmond is a senior researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) and serves as the Principal Investigator of the Section on Neural Coding and Computation. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual information processing, focusing on how primate brain circuits encode, categorize, and store visual stimuli. This work specifically examines the functional roles of the inferior temporal cortex subregions, TE and TEO, in visual recognition and categorization learning using rhesus monkey models. Methodologically, Richmond’s laboratory integrates multi-electrode recordings, behavioral paradigms, and computational modeling with tools such as PET imaging and chemogenetic modulations to analyze the information-carrying capacity of neural population dynamics.
0072.research_direction: Dr. Richmond has recently been investigating the neural circuits that underlie high-level visual categorization, object recognition, and associative learning in non-human primates. Their recent work explores the functional subdivisions of the late ventral stream, using targeted lesions and deep neural network models to untangle how areas like TE, TEO, and the rhinal cortex differentially support the accuracy, feature integration, and decision speed of perceptual categorization. Beyond visual recognition, they are also probing how temporal lobe structures interface with the reward system to guide behavior, specifically examining the role of rhinal-to-caudate projections in acquiring new stimulus-value associations. To enable these precise causal studies, their group is actively optimizing viral delivery protocols for chemogenetic manipulations, focusing on maximizing the reliability of DREADD receptor expression in deep primate brain structures like the amygdala.

papers.title: Chemogenetic Disruption of Monkey Perirhinal Neurons Projecting to the Rostromedial Caudate Impairs Associative Learning
papers.abstract: The authors interrupted the layer-5 projection from rhinal cortex to the rostromedial caudate in two monkeys by pairing a unilateral rhinal lesion with an inhibitory DREADD delivered by retrograde lentivirus into the contralateral caudate. Cutting this pathway barely affected performance on familiar stimulus-reward associations but strongly impaired learning of new ones. The result shows that the rhinal-to-caudate connection is causally needed for acquiring stimulus-value associations that guide reward-seeking, and it is tied to PET-verified chemogenetic receptor expression.
papers.authors: Wenliang Wang, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Tsuyoshi Setogawa, Spencer Webster-Bass, Nanami Miyazaki, Jonah E. Pearl, Jeih-San Liow, Walter Lerchner, Bing Li, Janita N. Turchi, Sanjay Telu, Sridhar Goud Nerella, Phelix Rodriguez, Robert B. Innis, Victor W. Pike, Bruno B. Averbeck, Barry J. Richmond

papers.title: Behavioral Studies Reveal Functional Differences in Image Processing by Ventral Stream Areas TEO and TE
papers.abstract: This synthesis pulls together lesion and behavioral experiments in monkeys to contrast the roles of two ventral-stream areas. Removing TEO leaves object recognition and categorization largely intact, whereas removing TE disrupts learning of categories based on perceptual similarity. The authors argue that TE, not TEO, is the region where complete images are represented and used to guide behavior.
papers.authors: Barry J. Richmond, Mark A. G. Eldridge

papers.title: Dissociation between area TE and rhinal cortex in accuracy vs. speed of visual categorization in rhesus monkeys
papers.abstract: Monkeys with bilateral TE lesions, bilateral rhinal cortex lesions, or no lesions performed a visual categorization task cued by briefly presented images. TE lesions reduced categorization accuracy but not response speed, while rhinal lesions left accuracy intact yet altered speed. The double dissociation suggests TE supports what an image is, while rhinal cortex influences how quickly decisions are made.
papers.authors: Bing Li, Kaleb Lowe, Samarth Chandra, Gang Chen, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Barry J. Richmond

papers.title: Comparing performance between a deep neural network and monkeys with bilateral removals of visual area TE in categorizing feature-ambiguous stimuli
papers.abstract: Monkeys with and without bilateral TE removal categorized feature-ambiguous images, and their performance was compared with a deep neural network trained on the same task. Intact monkeys behaved like the network, whereas TE-lesioned monkeys deviated from it, particularly for images that require integrating features. The comparison links the missing computation after TE loss to what deep networks capture, tying primate lesion data to model-based accounts of object recognition.
papers.authors: Narihisa Matsumoto, Mark A. G. Eldridge, J. Megan Fredericks, Kaleb A. Lowe, Barry J. Richmond

papers.title: Efficient viral expression of a chemogenetic receptor in the old-world monkey amygdala
papers.abstract: The paper compares lentiviral injection parameters in the rhesus monkey amygdala to get dense, well-localized expression of the hM4Di inhibitory chemogenetic receptor. A protocol of four 20 microliter injections at a slow infusion rate produced expression in roughly half to nearly all neurons within the target. It supplies a practical, validated recipe for chemogenetic circuit manipulation in primate deep structures.
papers.authors: Walter Lerchner, Kiana Dash, Deborah Rose, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Kathryn M. Rothenhoefer, Xuefeng Yan, Vincent D. Costa, Bruno Averbeck, Barry J. Richmond

0073.name: Bas Rokers
0073.department: Department of Psychology; Center for Neural Science
0073.bio: Bas Rokers is a Professor of Psychology and the Director of the Center for Brain and Health at New York University Abu Dhabi. Rokers investigates the neural mechanisms of three-dimensional visual perception, specifically focusing on how the brain integrates motion and depth cues to construct a representation of the environment. Utilizing a combination of behavioral psychophysics, neuroimaging (fMRI and tractography), and computational modeling, they explore the transformation of sensory signals into perceptual states. Their research also addresses practical applications in health and technology, including the treatment of amblyopia and the optimization of virtual reality systems to mitigate motion sickness and improve immersive experiences.
0073.research_direction: Dr. Rokers has recently been investigating the cortical representation of 3D motion, visual system plasticity, and translational neuroimaging. Using functional MRI, their recent work explores how the human visual motion complex—particularly the newly localized area FST—integrates stereoscopic and perspective cues to compute motion in depth. Beyond motion processing, they are examining late-stage structural plasticity by using diffusion MRI to track white matter changes in the visual pathways of congenitally blind patients following sight-restoring cataract surgery. Finally, their research extends into clinical and population brain health, where they are building large-scale normative multimodal MRI datasets for under-represented populations and assessing how the specific location and tissue composition of white matter lesions predict disability progression in multiple sclerosis.

papers.title: The ASPIRE Research Institute Dataset: Building a Foundation for Brain Health Research in the United Arab Emirates
papers.abstract: This data descriptor presents a large multimodal brain MRI dataset collected in the UAE, intended as a normative resource for a population under-represented in neuroimaging. It documents acquisition protocols, participants and quality checks so the data can support brain health, aging and disease research in the region. It reflects Rokers' current role building brain-health infrastructure at NYU Abu Dhabi.
papers.authors: Abdalla Z. Mohamed, Ameen Qadi, Amna Dogar, Amal Salah, Aisha Hamkari, Dana Alkalali, Gul Begum, Haidee J. Paterson, Karim Morjane, Omnia Hassanin, Puti Wen, Rawand Benour, Soumen Mohanty, Yvonne Valles, Milos Ljubisavljevic, Youssef Idaghdour, Osama Abdullah, Kartik K. Sreenivasan, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Beyond Lesion Load: Integrating Lesion Location and Composition for Explaining Disability and Predicting Progression in Multiple Sclerosis
papers.abstract: The paper argues that simple lesion volume poorly explains disability in multiple sclerosis. It combines where lesions sit along white matter tracts with their tissue composition from quantitative multimodal MRI to better account for clinical disability and to predict progression. It represents the lab's translational imaging work on brain health.
papers.authors: Osama Abdullah, Puti Wen, Abdelmalek Abdelrazeq, Mariya Matrosova, Vasiliy Bryukhov, Soumen Mohanty, Lev Brylev, David Melcher, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Single-trial fMRI decoding of 3D motion with stereoscopic and perspective cues
papers.abstract: The study asks how the human motion complex builds a representation of motion toward or away from the observer. Using fMRI decoding of single trials, it shows that 3D motion direction can be read out from V1, MT, MST and FST, but the preferred cue differs: MT favors perspective cues and FST favors stereoscopic cues. Retinotopic biases explain decoding in V1 and MST, but much less so in MT and FST, and individual skill at using stereo cues tracked decoding in FST.
papers.authors: Puti Wen, Lowell W. Thompson, Ari Rosenberg, Michael S. Landy, Bas Rokers

papers.title: Functional localization of visual motion area FST in humans
papers.abstract: Macaque area FST processes complex motion, but a clear human counterpart has been hard to pin down. The authors compared several fMRI localizers, including 2D versus 3D coherent motion, motion opponency, myelin measures and pRF mapping, in nine participants. Coherent 3D motion reliably revealed a region anterior and inferior to hMT/MST, supporting a human homolog of FST and giving a practical localization protocol.
papers.authors: Puti Wen, Rania Ezzo, Lowell W. Thompson, Ari Rosenberg, Michael S. Landy, Bas Rokers

papers.title: White matter plasticity following cataract surgery in congenitally blind patients
papers.abstract: Congenitally blind adolescents with dense cataracts were tracked with diffusion MRI before and after surgery, alongside tests of acuity and face perception. Surgery was followed by long-lasting increases in the structural integrity of late visual pathways linking occipital cortex to frontal, parietal and temporal regions. The results indicate that the visual system retains more plasticity after a critical period than traditionally assumed.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Caterina A. Pedersini, Nathaniel P. Miller, Tapan K. Gandhi, Sharon Gilad-Gutnick, Vidur Mahajan, Pawan Sinha, Bas Rokers

0074.name: Bei Xiao
0074.bio: Xiao is a Provost Associate Professor at American University and the Associate Director of the Institute for IDEAS, specializing in the intersection of neuroscience and machine learning. Xiao’s research investigates how the human visual system estimates the physical and functional properties of objects, with an emphasis on material perception and 3D shape recognition. Utilizing a methodology that combines human psychophysics, computer graphics, and deep learning, they develop computational models to simulate human-like perception and modify computer vision algorithms. Their current work focuses on bridging vision and language in material cognition, as well as employing virtual reality and EEG decoding to study multisensory and neural representations of material properties.
0074.research_direction: Dr. Xiao has recently been investigating human material perception, exploring how the visual processing of object surfaces—such as translucency and texture—connects to higher-level semantic categorization and action planning. Their recent work uses deep generative neural networks to synthesize both prototypical and ambiguous, morphed material images, pairing these stimuli with psychophysical tasks to probe how humans recognize and judge the visual similarity of complex materials. By comparing human behavioral data against unsupervised vision-only and text-guided vision-language models, they are examining the underlying mechanisms that link visual appearance to linguistic descriptions. In a distinct applied artificial intelligence strand, their lab is also utilizing large language models to predict clinical trial phase transitions directly from raw biomedical protocol texts.

papers.title: From visual appearance to material categories
papers.abstract: Investigates how people recognize materials despite huge appearance variation, using generative neural networks to synthesize both prototypical materials and ambiguous images morphing between categories. Combines behavioral tasks on these stimuli to relate visual appearance to categorical judgments. Reported as accepted at Scientific Reports in mid-2026.
papers.authors: Chenxi Liao, Filipp Schmidt, Jacob R. Cheeseman, Masataka Sawayama, Roland W. Fleming, Bei Xiao

papers.title: Material perception connects vision, cognition and action
papers.abstract: A review of how humans perceive the materials of objects and surfaces and how this ability links early visual processing to higher-level cognition and to planning of actions. It integrates work from psychophysics, computer graphics and deep learning, and argues that material perception is best modeled as a joint visual-semantic problem. It also outlines open questions for models that must capture both appearance and functional consequences.
papers.authors: Bei Xiao, Chenxi Liao

papers.title: Probing the link between vision and language in material perception using psychophysics and unsupervised learning
papers.abstract: Uses deep generative networks to build an image space of well-defined and ambiguous materials, then compares human visual similarity judgments with free-form verbal descriptions of the same images. Vision and language agree at the category level but diverge for materials morphed between categories, and visual judgments vary more across people. Human similarity structure aligns better with text-guided vision-language networks than with vision-only ones, motivating an alignment framework across modalities.
papers.authors: Chenxi Liao, Masataka Sawayama, Bei Xiao

papers.title: CTP-LLM: Clinical Trial Phase Transition Prediction Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Proposes a fine-tuned GPT-3.5-based model that predicts whether a clinical trial will progress to the next phase directly from the raw protocol text, without hand-picked features. It is presented as the first LLM-based approach to clinical trial outcome prediction and outperforms conventional baselines. The work represents the lab's NSF-funded AI-for-biomedicine strand.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
papers.authors: Michael Reinisch, Jianfeng He, Chenxi Liao, Sauleh Ahmad Siddiqui, Bei Xiao

papers.title: Unsupervised learning reveals interpretable latent representations for translucency perception
papers.abstract: Trains an unsupervised style-based generative model on photographs of translucent objects and shows that interpretable scene attributes such as shape, material and body color emerge spontaneously in different layers of its latent space. Middle layers selectively encode translucency features that correlate with human perception, suggesting that translucency is derived from mid-to-low spatial-scale image statistics. The approach is offered as a general method for finding perceptually relevant features.
papers.authors: Chenxi Liao, Masataka Sawayama, Bei Xiao

0075.name: Ben D. Sawyer
0075.department: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Systems
0075.bio: Ben D. Sawyer is an applied neuroscientist and human factors engineer focusing on the optimization of information flow within human-machine systems. Sawyer’s research integrates vision science, neurophysiology, and mathematical modeling to investigate cognitive workload, digital readability, and human performance in environments such as driving and defense. As the director of LabX and The Readability Consortium, Sawyer develops algorithms and personalized typographic systems intended to facilitate information acquisition and address distraction in digital interfaces.
0075.research_direction: Dr. Sawyer's recent work investigates the cognitive and applied aspects of readability, exploring how both typographic features and artificial intelligence influence reading behavior. Using behavioral metrics like reading speed and passage comprehension, they have recently been testing whether variations in typeface and character spacing require personalized typographic settings for children rather than a single universal format. Their research also evaluates the application of large language models in education, measuring how accurately AI can simplify texts to specific grade levels and how AI-generated passages compare to human-authored content in readability and user engagement. Additionally, their recent work explores the broader ethical and legal frontiers of generative AI, specifically examining intellectual property and creator agency frameworks surrounding human digital twins of sex workers.

papers.title: Evaluating GenAI for Simplifying Texts for Education: Improving Accuracy and Consistency for Enhanced Readability
papers.abstract: Tests how well large language models rewrite passages to a target reading grade level, examining accuracy and consistency of the simplified output. Proposes prompting and evaluation approaches to make AI text simplification more dependable for educational readability.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Jacapo Cirica, Steven R. Clapp, Veronika Penkova, Amy E. Giroux, Abbey Banta, Catherine Bordeau, Poojitha Mutteneni, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Sex worker human digital twins and intellectual property: on collaborative futures for sex thinkers, technologists, and lawyers
papers.abstract: Examines human digital twins of sex workers, AI replicas that converse in a person's likeness, and the intellectual-property questions they raise. Proposes collaborative frameworks among sex workers, technologists, and legal scholars to protect creators' rights and agency.
papers.authors: Yvette Butler, Chibundo Egwuatu, Matthew Canham, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: The Influence of Format Readability on Children's Reading Speed and Comprehension
papers.abstract: Extends adult readability research on typography to children: 51 third-to-fifth graders read narrative passages on a computer while the typeface (four serif, four sans serif) and then character spacing were varied. Reading speed and comprehension were measured for each format. The study asks whether a single best format exists for children or whether the optimal format differs by individual child, supporting personalized typography in education.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Nilsu Atilgan, Amy E. Giroux, Ben D. Sawyer

papers.title: Humanizing AI in Education: A Readability Comparison of LLM and Human-Created Educational Content
papers.abstract: Compares 300-word, 8th-grade-level reading passages written by large language models with human-written ones. Readers' speed, comprehension, and subjective ratings (familiarity, interest, perceived quality) were measured to see whether AI-generated educational text is as readable as human-authored text.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Md Mamunur Rashid, Nilsu Atilgan, Jonathan Dobres, Stephanie Day, Veronika Penkova, Mert Küçük, Steven R. Clapp, Ben D. Sawyer

0077.name: Benjamin de Haas
0077.department: Department of Psychology and Sports Science
0077.bio: Benjamin de Haas is a Research Professor of Experimental Psychology at Justus Liebig University Giessen and the head of the Indivisual Lab. De Haas investigates individual differences in human gaze behavior and the impact of visual salience on neural representations in the visual cortex. Their research utilizes eye-tracking, functional MRI, and computational modeling to examine the intersection of low-level visual features and high-level semantic dimensions such as faces and social cues. De Haas characterizes how individual viewing patterns generalize across time and stimuli, including their influence on subjective perception and social interactions.
0077.research_direction: Dr. de Haas has recently been investigating individual differences in active vision, specifically how idiosyncratic gaze behaviors during naturalistic viewing relate to neural representations and subjective perception. By combining eye tracking with fMRI, their recent work explores how a person's unique free-viewing fixation tendencies—such as a habit of looking at faces or text—shape the spatial extent and precision of category-selective responses in the ventral visual cortex. They are also examining the behavioral scope of these viewing patterns, testing whether individual gaze preferences function as stable, trait-like signatures that generalize across diverse object categories and predict the semantic content of how people later describe scenes. Furthermore, their research charts the developmental trajectory of visual exploration, using large cross-sectional datasets to investigate how these individual gaze strategies evolve and mature from childhood through older age.

papers.title: Active vision is linked to category selectivity in the individual brain
papers.abstract: Combining eye tracking during naturalistic scene viewing with fMRI in 61 adults, the study shows that people who fixate faces or text more often have more distinct and spatially larger category-selective representations for those categories in ventral visual cortex. These neural differences also predicted individual performance on face recognition and reading tasks. The work ties habitual viewing behaviour to the precision and cortical resources of category-specific coding in each person's brain.
papers.authors: Diana Kollenda, Elaheh Akbarifathkouhi, Maximilian Davide Broda, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Protracted development of gaze behaviour
papers.abstract: Using a large cross-sectional eye-tracking dataset of people from childhood to older age viewing natural scenes, the authors chart how gaze patterns change across the lifespan. Fixation tendencies keep maturing well into adolescence and beyond rather than settling early, and individual differences in viewing behaviour remain distinct at each stage. The results characterise gaze development as a long, gradual process.
papers.authors: Marcel Linka, Harun Karimpur, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Individual gaze predicts individual scene descriptions
papers.abstract: Participants viewed natural scenes and then described them, and the words they used were compared with where each person had looked. Individual fixation patterns predicted the content of individual descriptions beyond the shared image content. Gaze therefore carries information about what a person perceives and reports.
papers.authors: Diana Kollenda, Anna-Sophia Reher, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Individual differences in human gaze behavior generalize from faces to objects
papers.abstract: Participants viewed many scenes and the study tests whether a person's tendency to fixate faces carries over to other categories such as text, food and other objects. Individual gaze preferences turned out to be consistent across a range of semantic categories, indicating a broad, stable style of visual exploration rather than category-specific quirks. This supports viewing behaviour as a trait-like individual signature.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Maximilian Davide Broda, Benjamin de Haas

papers.title: Individual gaze shapes diverging neural representations
papers.abstract: Participants watched the same movie while their eye movements were tracked and their brains scanned with fMRI, and responses were aligned across people with hyperalignment. Differences in where individuals looked accounted for divergence in neural representations of the identical stimulus. The study shows that free-viewing eye movements actively shape what the brain represents.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Petra Borovska, Benjamin de Haas

0078.name: Benjamin Peters
0078.bio: Benjamin Peters is a Lecturer in Computational Cognitive Science at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Generative AI Laboratory. Their research integrates cognitive science, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence to investigate how humans and machines perceive structure and relations within complex, dynamic environments. Peters specializes in developing brain-computational neural network models that serve as mechanistic explanations for human behavior, eye movements, and neural data. Awarded a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship, Peters previously held research positions at the University of Glasgow and Columbia University focusing on the intersection of generative and discriminative computations in vision.
0078.research_direction: Dr. Peters has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying primate vision, exploring how the brain might integrate bottom-up discriminative filtering with top-down generative models to parse visual scenes. Their recent work also examines dynamic visual phenomena, such as multiple object tracking through occlusion, by combining human eye-tracking data with foveated computational models to investigate the role of selective gaze in managing limited cognitive resources. At a broader computational level, they are developing methods to identify the specific internal algorithms of both biological and artificial neural networks by using a system's transfer-learning profile as a behavioral fingerprint. Beyond empirical modeling, Dr. Peters is actively shaping the methodology of cognitive computational neuroscience by promoting generative adversarial collaborations (GACs) as a new framework for rival theorists to jointly design experiments and resolve entrenched theoretical debates.

papers.title: Using Transfer Learning to Identify a Neural System's Algorithm
papers.abstract: Many different algorithms can reproduce the same input-output behavior, so performance alone cannot tell us which one a brain or network actually uses. The paper proposes that how quickly a system learns alternative input-output mappings, its transfer-learning profile, acts as a fingerprint of its internal algorithm. Experiments with artificial neural networks across several tasks show the fingerprint can be used to recover the underlying algorithm, offering a bridge between cognitive-science algorithms, systems neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: John Morrison, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Benjamin Peters

papers.title: Generative adversarial collaborations: A new model of scientific discourse
papers.abstract: The article describes generative adversarial collaborations (GACs), in which researchers who hold competing theories jointly design and run experiments to adjudicate between them, in contrast to the usual adversarial back-and-forth of papers and rebuttals. It reviews how the format was developed and trialled in cognitive computational neuroscience, and argues it can accelerate scientific progress and reduce entrenched disagreements.
papers.authors: Benjamin Peters, Gunnar Blohm, Ralf M. Haefner, Leyla Isik, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Jennifer S. Lieberman, Carlos R. Ponce, Gemma Roig, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: How does the primate brain combine generative and discriminative computations in vision?
papers.abstract: Two long-standing views of primate vision are contrasted: a feedforward, bottom-up filtering pipeline and a Helmholtzian view in which sensory data are interpreted through a top-down generative model of causes. The authors, representing both camps, argue the brain likely runs a still-unknown hybrid algorithm that blends the strengths of both, and lay out a research program of experiments and models for pinning down that hybrid.
papers.authors: Benjamin Peters, James J. DiCarlo, Todd M. Gureckis, Ralf M. Haefner, Leyla Isik, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Talia Konkle, Thomas Naselaris, Kimberly Stachenfeld, Zenna Tavares, Doris Y. Tsao, Ilker Yildirim, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: Human-like multiple object tracking through occlusion via gaze-following
papers.abstract: Humans track several moving targets through occluders better than typical computational models. Combining human eye tracking with models that use object slots, Kalman-filter tracking and a simulated fovea, the study finds that people preferentially fixate the designated targets. Forcing the models to follow human gaze patterns yields the best match to human tracking behavior, suggesting selective gaze makes efficient use of limited visual resources.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2nd Gaze Meets ML Workshop (NeurIPS 2023), PMLR 226
papers.authors: Benjamin Peters, Eivinas Butkus, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

0079.name: Benjamin van Buren
0079.bio: Benjamin van Buren is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at The New School for Social Research and directs the NSSR Perception Lab. van Buren’s research uses psychophysical methodologies to investigate how the visual system recovers properties such as animacy, intentionality, and physical forces from dynamic environmental input. They have conducted studies on the perception of agency in simple geometric shapes and developed the "Blindfold Test" to distinguish perceptual effects from higher-level cognitive judgments. Their research program also examines the intersection of vision science with aesthetics, intuitive physics, and social cognition.
0079.research_direction: Dr. van Buren's recent work explores how high-level expectations and active selection influence visual perception, attention, and memory. They have recently been investigating whether the visual system incorporates intuitive physics—such as expected gravitational forces and surface friction—when detecting kinematic changes and allocating spatial attention. Other recent projects examine whether categorical representations distort visual working memory for facial age, and how the specific visual information selected during active scene exploration shapes a viewer's aesthetic preferences. Alongside these empirical questions, Dr. van Buren is developing conceptual heuristics, such as a thought experiment dubbed the Blindfold Test, designed to help researchers determine whether an experimental effect stems from genuine perceptual processing or post-perceptual guesswork.

papers.title: Visual information selected during active viewing is sufficient to drive aesthetic preferences for scenes (attentional transplants)
papers.abstract: Online donors explored scenes through a cursor-controlled window and rated how pleasing each was. New recipients then passively viewed the same scenes through a window replaying either the most-liking or least-liking donor's viewing pattern, and rated the scenes higher after replays from donors who liked them. Follow-up experiments showed that liked viewing patterns allow better prediction of upcoming visual content, tying aesthetic preference to attentional selection.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: The Blindfold Test: Helping to decide whether an effect reflects visual processing or higher-level judgment
papers.abstract: Many claims in vision science rest on effects that could reflect either genuine perceptual processing or post-perceptual guesswork and demand. The paper lays out a simple thought experiment, the Blindfold Test, in which one asks whether an observer who could not see the display but knew the task and stimuli would still produce the same result. It reviews how this heuristic sorts existing findings and gives guidance for designing experiments that isolate true perceptual effects.
papers.authors: Benjamin F. van Buren, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Remembering facial age: Assimilation in memory toward categories of 'Young' and 'Old'
papers.abstract: Observers briefly saw a young (30) or old (60) face and then chose between decoys 10 years younger or older. They reliably matched young faces to younger decoys and old faces to older ones, across real and artificially aged faces, observer ages, and decoy race/gender. The work indicates memory for perceived age is pulled toward visual categories.
papers.authors: Didi Dunin, Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: Rotating objects cue spatial attention via the perception of frictive surface contact
papers.abstract: Observers watched objects rotate and their attention was then probed at locations along the direction the object would travel if it were gripping a surface by friction. Attention was reflexively drawn in that direction, but only when the rotation looked like real surface contact and not when the physical cue was removed. The results suggest that the visual system incorporates intuitive physics of friction to predict where objects are headed.
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

papers.title: May the force be against you: Better visual sensitivity to speed changes opposite to gravity
papers.abstract: Observers detected changes in the speed of moving objects more accurately when the change ran against gravity's expected effect than when it agreed with it. This suggests that perception is sensitive to violations of expected physical forces, rather than simply following the raw motion signal.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Hong B. Nguyen, Benjamin van Buren

0080.name: Benjamin Wolfe
0080.department: Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences, University of Toronto Mississauga
0080.bio: Benjamin Wolfe is an Assistant Professor whose research examines the mechanisms of visual information acquisition in complex, naturalistic environments. Wolfe utilizes driving as a tool to investigate questions in vision science, specifically focusing on scene perception, peripheral vision, and the consequences of attentional failures in real-world tasks. Their methodology bridges visual psychophysics and human factors, employing eye-tracking and computational approaches to address road safety and digital readability. Currently, their work explores how the visual system integrates information across the visual field to support situational awareness and decision-making.
0080.research_direction: Dr. Wolfe has recently been investigating visual perception, attention, and prediction in dynamic, naturalistic environments, frequently using real-world driving footage as a model system. Their recent work explores how observers anticipate near-future events and localize hazards, employing methods like eye-tracking and gaze-contingent scotomas to probe the relative contributions of central and peripheral vision. Furthermore, they are examining the relationship between overt fixation and conscious awareness during dynamic scene viewing, alongside testing how specific cues like motion, scene context, and stereoscopic depth support the visual system's temporal predictions. To facilitate this research, Dr. Wolfe has also developed annotated, ground-truth video stimulus sets and is currently investigating how cross-modal information, such as imperfect auditory warnings, shapes visual hazard detection in rapidly changing scenes.

papers.title: Is the Useful Field all you need on the road? Hazard localization performance in a gaze contingent scotoma paradigm
papers.abstract: Drivers' 'useful field of view' is often assumed to be the only part of the visual field that matters for knowing what is happening on the road. Using near-collision dashcam videos and gaze-contingent scotomas that removed either central or peripheral vision, the authors test whether each region is truly necessary for localizing dangerous objects in rapidly changing scenes. The work directly tests the strong reading of the Useful Field and argues for a real contribution of peripheral vision in dynamic scenes.
papers.authors: Ido Zivli, Jiali Song, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Eye Movements Reveal That Drivers Can Predict the Location of Hazards in Dynamic Road Scenes but Gaze and Awareness Are Dissociable
papers.abstract: Recording eye movements while drivers viewed dynamic road footage, the study shows that gaze tends to go to where a hazard is about to appear, indicating drivers can anticipate hazard locations. However, where people look does not reliably match what they are aware of or report, so gaze and awareness dissociate. The finding cautions against equating fixation with perception in driver-attention research.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Ido Zivli, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: What happens next in dynamic natural scenes: Temporal discrimination is modulated by motion and scene context but not stereoscopic depth
papers.abstract: Observers judged what a road scene would look like a moment later, testing which cues support predictions of upcoming scene content. Motion and scene context shaped temporal discrimination performance, whereas adding stereoscopic depth did not help. The results speak to how the visual system anticipates the near future in natural, dynamic scenes.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Ginnie Wee, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Can unreliable auditory hazard warnings help the driver? The effect of timing errors and false alarms on road hazard detection in dynamic road scenes
papers.abstract: Licensed drivers localized hazards in real road footage while hearing non-spatial auditory warnings that were either mistimed or sometimes false alarms. Earlier cues sped responses more than later ones and any cue helped, but when hazards were rare on the road, false alarms changed how cues affected performance. The work informs how imperfect in-vehicle warning systems shape hazard detection.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Benjamin Wolfe

papers.title: Road Hazard Stimuli: Annotated naturalistic road videos for studying hazard detection and scene perception
papers.abstract: The authors present a curated set of short dashcam clips containing real road hazards, annotated with hazard locations, timing and perceived danger ratings. The stimulus set is released for vision and driving researchers who need naturalistic, dynamic scenes with ground-truth hazards. It underlies several follow-up studies from the lab.
papers.authors: Jiali Song, Anna Kosovicheva, Benjamin Wolfe

0081.name: Bevil Conway
0081.institution: National Eye Institute, National Institutes of Health
0081.department: Laboratory of Sensorimotor Research (Section on Perception, Cognition, and Action)
0081.lab_name: Section on Perception, Cognition, and Action
0081.bio: Bevil Conway is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute and leads the Section on Perception, Cognition, and Action. Conway’s research investigates how the brain transforms physical sensory signals into perceptions and cognitive categories, using color as a model system to bridge physiology and psychology. Utilizing electrophysiology, functional MRI, and psychophysics in both humans and macaques, they have characterized the parallel processing organization of the inferior temporal cortex. Conway has also established links between neural representation and the linguistic categorization of color.
0081.research_direction: Dr. Conway's recent work explores the psychological and physiological foundations of color perception, investigating how color categories emerge and whether classic models like Hering's Opponent-Colors Theory adequately explain our visual experience. They have recently been using behavioral paradigms and computational modeling in macaques to probe whether color categorization is an innate product of early visual processing or requires higher cognitive mechanisms like language. Alongside this, their functional neuroimaging research maps feature encoding across the primate brain, using macaque fMRI to identify the spatial frequency and chromatic signatures that differentiate early retinotopic areas, and to decode how distinct features like color and shape are bound into abstract object concepts in higher-order temporal and frontal cortices. Finally, Dr. Conway is also examining the perceptual statistics of art and natural scenes, comparing object colors in photographs and still-life paintings to investigate how memory and behavioral utility shape our internal visual representations.

papers.title: The origin of color categories
papers.abstract: Tests whether color categories are innate products of the visual system by measuring color categorization in macaque monkeys, who share human early color encoding but lack language. Computational modeling showed the monkeys lack consensus color categories, though one animal formed a private category. This suggests the capacity for categories is innate but consensus categories require cognitive mechanisms such as language.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Daniel J. Garside, Audrey L. Y. Chang, Hannah M. Selwyn, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: The representation of object concepts across the brain
papers.abstract: Macaques were trained for years on object-concept primitives defined by color and shape, then scanned with fMRI while holding one feature in mind cued by the other. Whole-brain searchlight decoding found cross-feature concept representations in anterior inferior temporal cortex, temporal pole and frontal cortex, with temporal pole and aIT matching color-space geometry. Extrastriate cortex distinguished color-associated shapes and congruent color-shape combinations, pointing to feedback-based binding of concepts and perception.
papers.authors: Spencer R. Loggia, Helen E. Feibes, Stuart J. Duffield, Karthik Kasi, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: Color and Spatial Frequency Provide Functional Signatures of Retinotopic Visual Areas
papers.abstract: Using macaque fMRI with gratings varying in spatial frequency, color and saturation, the study introduces a Sparse Supervised Embedding analysis to find stimulus features that best separate retinotopic parcels. Posterior (V1) and anterior (V4) parcels, and ventral versus dorsal parcels, differed in responses to chromatic and luminance contrast, with a dorsal/ventral asymmetry extending across V1 to V4. The approach is offered as a data-driven way to generate hypotheses about cortical function.
papers.authors: Spencer R. Loggia, Stuart J. Duffield, Kurt Braunlich, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: The color of fruits in photographs and still life paintings
papers.abstract: Compares color statistics of fruit in still-life paintings from a museum slide collection with color-calibrated fruit photographs. Warm object colors showed a larger chromatic-contrast advantage against backgrounds in paintings than photographs, consistent with a memory-color effect that makes familiar object colors appear more saturated.
papers.authors: Thorsten Hansen, Bevil R. Conway

papers.title: Color appearance and the end of Hering's Opponent-Colors Theory
papers.abstract: A review that argues the 150-year-old Opponent-Colors Theory is wrong on both its psychological claim (that colors are fully described by red-green, blue-yellow and black-white axes) and its physiological claim (three innate brain mechanisms encode these). It draws on evidence including cross-cultural color naming, and proposes Utility-Based Coding as an alternative, in which cone-opponent retinal signals reflect efficient spatial-information extraction and color categories are adaptive outputs shaped by behavioral demands.
papers.authors: Bevil R. Conway, Saima Malik-Moraleda, Edward Gibson

0082.name: Bianca M. van Kemenade
0082.lab_name: Systems Neuroscience of Action and Perception (SNAP) Lab
0082.main_research_area: systems neuroscience of action and perception
0082.bio: Bianca M. van Kemenade is a neuroscientist who leads the Systems Neuroscience of Action and Perception (SNAP) Lab at Justus Liebig University Giessen. Van Kemenade’s research examines how voluntary actions modulate sensory perception, specifically investigating the neural mechanisms that differentiate between self-generated and externally generated stimuli. They utilize functional MRI (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics to examine the roles of predictive coding and multisensory integration in agency and perception. Their work also addresses clinical neuroscience, investigating how disruptions in these predictive mechanisms contribute to altered perception in schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
0082.research_direction: Dr. van Kemenade studies how our own actions shape what we see and feel, and how this prediction machinery is altered in psychiatric illness. Their recent work uses high-resolution fMRI and multivariate decoding to test whether action-based predictions in early visual cortex work through sensory suppression, sharpening or pre-activation, finding pre-activation and enhanced responses to self-generated gratings. Related studies combine behavior, fMRI and pupillometry to show that action-based predictions affect visual perception and neural processing even when timing is unpredictable, and compare the timing, duration and amplitude of brain responses to self-generated versus externally generated movement feedback. They also extend this framework to clinical populations, examining predictive processing of hand and tool actions in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and the link between schizotypal traits and speech-gesture matching.

papers.title: The effects of action-based predictions in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: This neuroimaging investigation evaluates how voluntary motor activity influences neural processing and perception of contingent sensory outcomes in the primary visual cortex (V1). The study contrasts four theoretical frameworks: the classical forward model (proposing sensory suppression), pre-activation (predictive baseline shifts), sharpening (increased representational precision), and opposing processes (pre-activation followed by distinct interaction mechanisms). Using high-resolution functional MRI combined with both univariate BOLD signal analysis and multivariate pattern decoding, the researchers examined V1 activity during a preparatory window and subsequent orientation discrimination of gratings. Results revealed that the orientation of predicted stimuli could be decoded from early visual areas at levels exceeding chance before stimulus onset, supporting pre-activation across both active and passive conditions. Crucially, self-generated stimuli elicited enhanced BOLD amplitudes compared to passively presented stimuli, a finding that contradicts the neural suppression predicted by standard forward models and supports an additive or enhancement mechanism during self-initiated perception. Decoding precision did not significantly differ between active and passive conditions, providing no evidence for neural sharpening.
papers.authors: Bianca M. van Kemenade, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Predictive neural processing of self-generated hand and tool actions in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and healthy individuals
papers.abstract: An fMRI and behavioral study of people with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and healthy controls making hand movements with or without a tool and seeing delayed visual or audiovisual feedback. Both groups detected fewer delays for self-generated movements and showed reduced sensory-cortex responses, with group differences emerging in visual regions during tool use and bimodal feedback.
papers.authors: Christina V. Schmitter, Mareike Pazen, Lukas Uhlmann, Bianca M. van Kemenade, Tilo Kircher, Benjamin Straube

papers.title: Speech-Gesture Matching and Schizotypal Traits: A Network Approach
papers.abstract: In over a thousand mostly healthy adults, judgments of whether gestures matched spoken sentences were related to schizotypal traits. Poorer speech-gesture matching went with higher overall schizotypy, and a network analysis identified which trait facets link most strongly to gesture perception.
papers.authors: Bertalan Polner, Hamidreza Jamalabadi, Bianca M. van Kemenade, Jutta Billino, Tilo Kircher, Benjamin Straube

papers.title: Action-based predictions affect visual perception, neural processing, and pupil size, regardless of temporal predictability
papers.abstract: Combines behavior, neuroimaging and pupillometry to test how actions that predict a visual outcome change its perception, its neural processing and pupil size, and whether these effects depend on the outcome being temporally predictable.
papers.authors: Christina Lubinus, Wolfgang Einhäuser, Florian Schiller, Tilo Kircher, Benjamin Straube, Bianca M. van Kemenade

papers.title: The effect of self-generated versus externally generated actions on timing, duration, and amplitude of blood oxygen level dependent response for visual feedback processing
papers.abstract: Using an fMRI-compatible movement device, compares brain responses to video feedback of active versus passive movements. Self-generated movements gave smaller and earlier, shorter hemodynamic responses in supplementary motor area, cerebellum and visual cortex, supporting predictive processing of one's own actions.
papers.authors: Eleftherios Kavroulakis, Bianca M. van Kemenade, Belkis Ezgi Arikan, Tilo Kircher, Benjamin Straube

0083.name: Bilge Sayim
0083.department: Laboratoire de Sciences Cognitives et Psycholinguistique (LSCP), Département d'Études Cognitives (CNRS)
0083.bio: Bilge Sayim is a vision scientist and CNRS researcher at the University of Lille and the University of Bern who investigates mechanisms of visual information selection and compression. Sayim’s research involves the discovery and characterization of redundancy masking, a phenomenon where the visual system reduces the number of perceived items in repeating peripheral patterns. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies and appearance-based modeling, they explore how perceptual grouping, visual crowding, and prior knowledge shape conscious experience. Sayim’s current work connects neuroscience and art to develop empirical methods for studying the subjective quality of visual appearance.
0083.research_direction: Dr. Sayim has recently been investigating how the visual system processes and compresses information in the periphery, with a major focus on the phenomenon of redundancy masking, where repeated peripheral items are perceived as fewer than presented. Their recent work explores the underlying mechanisms and functional consequences of this effect using spatial cueing and foveal probe matching paradigms, questioning whether redundancy masking is driven by attentional limits, how it interacts with perceptual grouping, and whether this visual compression paradoxically improves feature discrimination. Beyond redundancy masking, they are also examining visual crowding, specifically testing whether top-down processes like targeted mental imagery can interact with degraded peripheral input to relieve crowding and improve target recognition. Finally, Dr. Sayim is extending these inquiries into clinical populations by having observers replicate the appearance of flanked letters to investigate how crowding—independent of baseline acuity—alters the structural perception of foveal targets in amblyopia.

papers.title: Compression of visual information in redundancy masking follows grouping and segmentation
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether the peripheral phenomenon in which repeated items are perceived as fewer than presented (redundancy masking) operates before or after perceptual grouping. Using arrays of 3-5 lines with different contrast-polarity patterns, they find that lines are merged mainly within segmented subgroups of identical lines. Key features such as the polarity present, the odd edge item and their relative frequency are still reported accurately. This suggests the visual system compresses redundant items after grouping and segmentation while preserving essential stimulus information.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Wolf M. Harmening, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: Compression of redundant visual information improves feature discrimination in human vision
papers.abstract: Asks whether redundancy masking, where several peripheral identical bars are perceived as fewer, is merely a loss or has a functional benefit. Observers reported how many bars they saw and matched perceived width and spacing with a foveal probe. When fewer bars were perceived, perceived width was closer to the true width, and modeling showed this could not be explained by simple feature averaging. The authors conclude that compression reduces the item count while improving feature discrimination.
papers.authors: Li L-Miao, Doğukan Nami Öztaş, Nihan Alp, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: Improvement of peripheral visual discrimination through mental imagery
papers.abstract: Crowding by neighboring elements impairs peripheral object recognition, and long-range grouping with a matching central item can relieve it. This study tests whether merely imagining an item can do the same. Discrimination of a crowded peripheral target improved when observers imagined an item matching the target, but not when they imagined a different item or one matching only in meaning. Imagery therefore appears to engage detailed visual representations that interact with degraded peripheral input, with possible applications in sports and clinical settings.
papers.authors: Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles, Rahel Aschwanden, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: Impact of crowding on visual appearance and performance in amblyopia
papers.abstract: Observers with amblyopia and controls replicated the appearance of isolated and flanked letters shown foveally, with size scaled to each eye's acuity threshold. Amblyopic observers were less accurate and less structurally similar in their reproductions, especially for small and flanked targets. A Group x Crowding interaction remained after controlling for acuity, indicating that stronger foveal crowding, not acuity alone, contributes to appearance differences in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Ângela Gomes Tomaz, Wolf Harmening, Dennis M. Levi, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: Attention in redundancy masking
papers.abstract: Tests whether redundancy masking, the underreporting of repeated peripheral items, is caused by limited attention. Participants counted lines in arrays under single-cue, double-cue and no-cue conditions. Redundancy masking occurred in all conditions, though reduced attention further impaired discrimination. Attention modulates performance but does not explain redundancy masking.
papers.authors: Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles, Daniel R. Coates, Bilge Sayim

0084.name: Billy Hammond
0084.bio: Hammond’s research examines the intersection of nutrition, vision science, and neuroscience, focusing on how dietary factors influence the central nervous system across the human lifespan. They specialize in the study of macular carotenoids, specifically lutein and zeaxanthin, and utilize psychophysical methods such as heterochromatic flicker photometry to measure macular pigment optical density and its role in neuroprotection. Hammond’s work employs behavioral and neuroimaging techniques, including critical flicker fusion, to assess visual processing speed as a biomarker for cognitive health and to investigate preventive approaches for age-related neurodegenerative diseases like dementia. Additionally, their research covers infant visual development and the optimization of visual performance in sports.
0084.research_direction: Dr. Hammond's recent work explores how optical filtering and intraocular scatter shape visual performance, particularly investigating whether dense macular pigment or high-energy-visible-filtering contact lenses can improve contrast sensitivity and extend visual range through simulated atmospheric blue haze. They have recently been examining the wavelength dependence of spatial vision, using psychophysical two-point separation tasks to map how short-wavelength light impacts fine detail resolution when controlling for factors like chromatic aberration and retinal pigment density. In addition to their core focus on visual optics and spatial acuity, their research also evaluates perceptual associations of color, such as testing the hue-heat hypothesis to determine how varying the physical intensity of saturated primary lights influences psychophysical judgments of perceived warmth.

papers.title: The relationship between the macular carotenoids and simulated visual range
papers.abstract: Tests whether people with denser macular pigment (lutein and zeaxanthin in the central retina) can see farther through simulated atmospheric blue haze. Visual range is measured with a psychophysical set-up that adds short-wavelength veiling light to a distant target. The work links an individual retinal pigment measure to real-world outdoor vision, extending the lab's glare and scatter hypothesis of macular pigment function.
papers.authors: Cameron J. Wysocky, Jacob B. Harth, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, Billy R. Hammond Jr

papers.title: Visual performance measured under simulated atmospheric blue haze conditions is improved through the addition of a HEV-filtering additive to soft contact lenses
papers.abstract: In a large double-masked crossover trial of 121 adults, peak contrast sensitivity was measured while wearing clear or high-energy-visible-filtering contact lenses, under increasing simulated blue-haze veiling light. Filtering short-wavelength light helped preserve contrast performance as haze intensity grew, across spherical, multifocal and toric lenses. It gives applied support for the idea that blocking scattered blue light extends visual range.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, John R. Buch, Patricia Martin, Wright Shamp, Jacob B. Harth, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: Wavelength dependence of fine spatial resolution in human vision
papers.abstract: Measures two-point separation thresholds in 60 young adults using narrowband lights, with luminance equated by an equal-energy approach and ocular factors such as chromatic aberration and scatter controlled, to map an action spectrum for fine spatial resolution. It clarifies how wavelength itself shapes spatial acuity once common confounds are handled.
papers.authors: Yaw Buabeng, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: The influence of macular pigment on the fine spatial resolution of light of varying wavelengths
papers.abstract: Examines how the density of a person's macular pigment relates to their ability to resolve fine spatial detail under lights of different wavelengths, particularly short wavelengths that are most affected by intraocular scatter and pigment filtering. It tests whether the pigment's optical filtering translates into sharper fine-detail vision.
papers.authors: Yaw Buabeng, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: Increasing intensity directly increases the perceived warmth of primary colors
papers.abstract: Revisits the hue-heat hypothesis (reds and yellows feel warm, blues and greens cool) by varying the intensity of highly saturated primary lights. Twenty young adults judged perceived temperature, and warmth ratings rose with intensity across colors, suggesting brightness rather than hue alone drives the association.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, Colin R. Gardner, Billy R. Wooten, Lisa Renzi-Hammond

0085.name: Blaire Dube
0085.bio: Dube is an Assistant Professor at Memorial University of Newfoundland whose research investigates the reciprocal interactions between visual attention and working memory systems. Utilizing a multi-methodological approach that includes behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, eye tracking, and functional MRI, Dube examines the cognitive filters that prioritize behaviorally relevant information while mitigating sensory competition. Their work includes the development of the Filter Disruption Theory, which characterizes how salient or unexpected environmental distractors interfere with attentional filtering and memory representations. Dube’s research aims to provide a mechanistic understanding of how humans navigate complex visual environments through flexible attentional control.
0085.research_direction: Dr. Dube has recently been investigating the mechanisms of cognitive control and attentional filtering within visual working memory. Their recent work explores how this control is compromised by everyday visual dynamics, specifically testing whether the attentional filter that blocks irrelevant information from entering memory is disrupted by external distractors or the execution of saccades. Using continuous report paradigms, they are examining the timeline of these disruptions to understand precisely when memory filtering fails and how quickly it recovers following an eye movement. Additionally, Dr. Dube is exploring how the internal state of a memory representation dictates its vulnerability, asking whether actively manipulating an item—such as mentally rotating a remembered orientation—makes it uniquely susceptible to visual interference compared to passive maintenance.

papers.title: Saccades temporarily disrupt attentional filtering for visual working memory
papers.abstract: Asks whether the attentional filter that keeps irrelevant items out of visual working memory survives an eye movement. Across three experiments using continuous color report, filtering was intact under steady fixation but failed right after a saccade (50 ms delay). It recovered when the memory display came 400 ms after the saccade. The authors conclude that saccades briefly interrupt filtering control, extending the Filter Disruption Theory from distraction to eye movements.
papers.authors: Blaire Dube, Jacqueline Bao, Julie Golomb

papers.title: Distraction disrupts control over the encoding and maintenance of information in visual working memory
papers.abstract: A JoCN Forum contribution in which Dube and a MUN student, Elissa Orbasli, discuss how distraction undermines control over what is encoded into and maintained in visual working memory. It draws on the Filter Disruption Theory and related work on attentional filtering. Only the title and authors were verified (the PubPub page returned 403), so the description is inferred from the title and her research program.
papers.authors: Blaire Dube, Elissa Orbasli

papers.title: Items in visual working memory are more susceptible to visual interference while in-use
papers.abstract: Participants held two oriented bars in memory, were cued to one, and then mentally rotated it. A colorful distractor appeared either while the item was being manipulated or after manipulation was finished. Interference with the orientation report was strong only when the distractor arrived during active use of the item. This suggests memory items are unprotected while in use but can be shielded once they are no longer in use.
papers.venue: PsyArXiv (preprint, listed by Golomb lab as under revision)
papers.authors: Eva Lout, Julie D. Golomb, Blaire Dube

0090.name: Brad Wyble
0090.bio: Brad Wyble is a Professor of Psychology at Pennsylvania State University who researches the cognitive and neural architecture of visual awareness, temporal attention, and memory consolidation. Their work integrates behavioral psychophysics and electrophysiological (EEG) recordings with neurocomputational modeling to examine how the brain constructs reportable mental representations from transient visual input. Wyble conducts research on the attentional blink and attribute amnesia and developed the 'Simultaneous Type, Serial Token' (STST) model of temporal attention. Additionally, Wyble is a co-founder of Neuromatch Academy and works on the advancement of global, open-source computational neuroscience education.
0090.research_direction: Dr. Wyble has recently been investigating the flexible architecture of visual working memory, developing hierarchical models to examine how sensory inputs are decomposed, recombined, and regenerated during cognitive tasks. Their recent empirical work explores how intrinsic stimulus properties shape short-term retention, using paradigms like attribute amnesia to test how inherent image memorability and functional links between objects influence both incidental and intentional memory performance. In addition to working memory, they are studying the temporal dynamics of visual attention, specifically testing how abrupt feature transients—such as sudden shifts in orientation versus color—dictate the boundaries of attentional episodes and define object continuity over time.
