Finally, their broader theoretical work examines the intersection of cognitive psychology and artificial intelligence, exploring how foundational neural network architectures continue to inform modern computational models of cognition and machine learning.

papers.title: Memory loves company: Related object pairs benefit working memory
papers.abstract: Participants remembered four object pairs and then identified a novel object; related (functionally linked) pairs were remembered better than unrelated ones, with high split-half reliability, and the effect held when probes were pairs. Relatedness and action-compatibility ratings correlated strongly with each other and with the benefit, though ratings did not predict variability within a condition. Stable differences in object memorability also generalized across pairing conditions.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Moussa Kousa, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Abrupt changes in orientation, but not color, define the boundaries of attentional episodes
papers.abstract: Extends attentional drag theory, in which smooth feature change prolongs attentional engagement while abrupt changes trigger disengagement. Orientation transients altered when color was sampled, even when orientation was irrelevant, but color transients did not affect orientation sampling, and only transients at the attended object or location mattered. This suggests orientation plays a special role in defining object continuity over time.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Chloe Callahan-Flintoft, Joyce Tam, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Understanding the flexibility of working memory: Compositionality, generative processing, anchors and pointers
papers.abstract: Proposes that working memory is not just a store of discrete objects but a flexible system that decomposes input into parts and recombines them, and can regenerate sensory-like representations from conceptual content. Items may act as anchors or pointers to feature clusters or to several objects bundled as one, depending on task demands. The authors sketch a hierarchical model where information moves between levels of abstraction and tie it to findings on memory and visual imagery.
papers.authors: Brad Wyble, Joyce Tam, Ian Deal, Howard Bowman

papers.title: Memorability effects emerge in incidental visual working memory
papers.abstract: Using an attribute-amnesia paradigm with faces and scenes, the study asked whether intrinsic memorability affects what people unexpectedly remember over seconds. When observers had to report a just-seen image without warning, memorable targets were reported more accurately than forgettable ones, more strongly for faces than scenes. Follow-ups ruled out attentional capture and contrast differences, indicating memorability acts without long-term memory retrieval.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Joyce Tam, Taryn Green, Ryan E. O'Donnell, Brad Wyble

papers.title: Hopfield and Hinton's neural network revolution and the future of AI
papers.abstract: An opinion piece written after the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, in which an AI researcher and a psychologist reflect on how Hopfield's and Hinton's foundational neural network ideas shaped their own work. They also discuss emerging directions in AI and the challenges ahead for neural networks and machine learning.
papers.authors: James Z. Wang, Brad Wyble

0091.name: Bradford Z. Mahon
0091.department: Department of Psychology and the Neuroscience Institute
0091.bio: Bradford Mahon is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates how the human brain organizes and represents object concepts and their associated motor and linguistic information. Utilizing functional MRI and behavioral studies, Mahon examines how visual input is transformed into conceptual knowledge to guide object-directed actions and naming. Their research involves studying patients with focal brain injuries from stroke or tumors, including translational work that utilizes awake brain mapping during neurosurgery to map language and motor functions. This approach facilitates causal tests of the neurocognitive organization of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways and has led to the development of surgical decision-support tools for preserving cognitive functions.
0091.research_direction: Dr. Mahon has recently been investigating how the human brain represents manipulable objects and coordinates object-directed actions. Their recent work explores the reciprocal interactions between the dorsal and ventral visual streams, using fMRI and lesion mapping in neurosurgical patients to examine how parietal action systems might shape ventral occipito-temporal processing based on behavioral context. They are also investigating the representational geometry of these networks during naturalistic and controlled tasks, testing whether the parietal cortex encodes complex actions through componential kinematic synergies rather than purely visual features. In a distinct but methodologically related line of clinical research, they are exploring causal brain mapping techniques, testing how graded parametric variations in direct electrical stimulation during awake neurosurgery can yield more precise, personalized maps of human language organization.

papers.title: Causal parametric language mapping with electrical stimulation during awake neurosurgery
papers.abstract: Standard awake-surgery mapping treats a stimulation site as uninvolved if it causes no errors. The authors show that both the rate and the type of errors, together with response times, vary systematically with stimulation parameters and site. These graded measures give a more precise, person-specific causal map of language organization, and they support the case for personalized surgical planning.
papers.authors: J. Raouf Belkhir, Frank E. Garcea, Eduardo Navarrete, Benjamin L. Chernoff, Max H. Sims, Sam Haber, Ajay N. Mallela, Matthew Pease, Susan O. Smith, Evan B. Hintz, Thomas Aung, Eleanor M. Reedy, Kevin Walter, Tyler Schmidt, Jorge Gonzalez-Martinez, Nduka Amankulor, Webster H. Pilcher, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Visual processing of manipulable objects in the ventral stream is modulated by parietal action systems
papers.abstract: In 109 neurosurgical patients with left-hemisphere lesions, the authors relate lesion location to fMRI responses in ventral occipitotemporal cortex during viewing of manipulable objects. Damage to the left inferior parietal lobe reduces tool-related responses in ventral cortex, indicating that dorsal action systems directly shape ventral visual processing of objects.
papers.authors: Frank E. Garcea, Emma Strawderman, William Burns, Matthew Cotroneo, Steven P. Meyers, Tyler Schmidt, Kevin A. Walter, Webster H. Pilcher, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Flexibility and Invariance of Object Representations in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI during naturalistic movie viewing, the study compares the same objects when they are passive scene elements versus targets of goal-directed actions. Action targets engage a parietal action network, while passive objects engage occipito-temporal object-recognition areas, and representational geometry shows a double dissociation between action-affordance and semantic organization.
papers.authors: Julien Dirani, Shankar Chawla, Leila Wehbe, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Object-directed action representations are componentially built in parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study shows that activity in the supramarginal gyrus for complex object-directed actions can be predicted by a linear model that builds each action from a set of kinematic synergies (combinations of finger, hand, wrist and arm postures). Image-computable models from deep networks explain visual areas but not this parietal region. The parietal region is instead tuned to kinematic rather than visual properties of actions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Leyla Roksan Caglar, Jon Walbrin, Emefa Akwayena, Jorge Almeida, Bradford Z. Mahon

papers.title: Reciprocal interactions among parietal and occipito-temporal representations support everyday object-directed actions
papers.abstract: A theoretical synthesis arguing that everyday grasping and use of objects depends on integrating conceptual, visual-form, material and visuomotor information across dorsal and ventral pathways. It uses end-state comfort in grasping as evidence for two-way communication between parietal and occipito-temporal regions and lays out a framework for how the two streams cooperate.
papers.authors: Bradford Z. Mahon, Jorge Almeida

0092.name: Bradley Duchaine
0092.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0092.bio: Duchaine is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at Dartmouth College, where they investigate the cognitive and neural foundations of social perception. Their research focuses on the functional architecture of face processing, using neuropsychology, psychophysics, and neuroimaging to study conditions such as prosopagnosia and prosopometamorphopsia. Duchaine co-developed the Cambridge Face Memory Test and characterized the heritability and developmental trajectories of face recognition abilities. Their current research aims to map the broader network of category-selective visual areas and identify specific neural deficits associated with impaired social perception.
0092.research_direction: Dr. Duchaine's laboratory explores the cognitive and neural architecture of visual recognition, primarily through the lens of face perception disorders like prosopometamorphopsia (PMO) and developmental prosopagnosia. They are investigating the severe facial distortions experienced by individuals with PMO using behavioral testing and neuroimaging to understand the organization of typical face perception. Additionally, their current work on developmental prosopagnosia examines its cognitive and neural mechanisms and whether artificial neural network models can accelerate DP research.

papers.title: The first comprehensive case study of early-emerging prosopometamorphopsia
papers.abstract: Reports the first in-depth study of a man (Zed) who has had dynamic facial distortions since early life, in which features drift, droop, vanish, swell or rotate and familiar faces are sometimes misseen as strangers. Distortions occur across viewpoints, visual field locations, orientations and sizes, and he shows face-identity deficits yet accurate age and sex judgments. Imaging showed no lesion but reduced face selectivity in two right posterior face areas and lower white matter integrity in the left inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
papers.authors: Sydney Fortner, Antônio Mello, Daniel G. Stehr, Chandana Kodiweera, Heejung Jung, Krzysztof Bujarski, Tor Wager, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Developmental prosopagnosics have normal spatial integration in posterior ventral face-selective regions
papers.abstract: Tests the influential proposal that developmental prosopagnosia stems from abnormally small population receptive fields in face-selective cortex, using pRF mapping in 20 people with DP and 20 controls. DPs showed weaker face selectivity, but pRF size, visual field coverage and pRF-center distributions were strikingly similar to controls across early, intermediate and face-selective areas. The larger sample and modern method challenge a prior small-sample result and the spatial-integration account of DP.
papers.authors: Daniel A. Stehr, Yiyuan Zhang, Anusha Patgiri, Alexis Kidder, Kendrick Kay, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Improving diagnosis of developmental prosopagnosia: The role of exclusion criteria
papers.abstract: Examines the exclusion criteria commonly applied when diagnosing developmental prosopagnosia, such as autism or other conditions, and argues that they can wrongly screen out people with genuine face recognition impairment. The authors advocate diagnostic practice that focuses on face-recognition deficits and reconsiders routine exclusions. The paper informs how DP samples are defined across the field.
papers.authors: Tirta Susilo, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: Visualising facial distortions in prosopometamorphopsia
papers.abstract: A Clinical Picture describing a man who saw everyone's faces as stretched and 'demonic' in person but not in photographs or on screens. The authors used his descriptions to build photorealistic renderings of the distortions he perceives, offering the first accurate visualization for a PMO case. The work made a rare condition tangible for clinicians and researchers.
papers.authors: Antônio Mello, Daniel Stehr, Krzysztof Bujarski, Bradley Duchaine

papers.title: The development of upright face perception depends on evolved orientation-specific mechanisms and experience
papers.abstract: Asks whether skill with upright faces reflects innate orientation-specific mechanisms, lifetime experience, or both, by testing Claudio, a man whose congenital joint disorder rotated his head so he has seen mostly inverted-relative-to-self faces. Controls showed large inversion effects, whereas Claudio showed none in face detection or identity matching, but still showed upright superiority for detecting Thatcherized faces. The pattern indicates both evolved mechanisms and experience contribute.
papers.authors: Bradley Duchaine, Constantin Rezlescu, Lúcia Garrido, Yiyuan Zhang, Maira V. Braga, Tirta Susilo

0094.name: Brett Fajen
0094.bio: Brett Fajen is a Professor of Cognitive Science and Associate Dean at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and the director of the Perception and Action Lab. Fajen's research examines the visual control of locomotion and perceptual-motor learning through immersive virtual reality and motion capture to study human navigation in complex environments. They apply ecological and dynamical systems frameworks to investigate tasks such as obstacle avoidance, target interception, and high-speed steering. This work incorporates computational modeling to explore the neural mechanisms of motion perception, specifically linking brain areas like MT and MSTd to the processing of optic flow during self-motion.
0094.research_direction: Dr. Fajen has recently been investigating the online visual control of action, specifically focusing on how humans steer and navigate through complex, cluttered environments. Using virtual reality paradigms—such as simulated driving and high-speed drone flight paired with eye-tracking—their recent work explores how humans coordinate gaze and continuous motor behavior to negotiate multiple sequential waypoints and avoid obstacles. They are currently probing how actors use prospective visual information to anticipate upcoming paths, and how this online control relies on local landmark associations when visibility is degraded by simulated fog or restricted lookahead distances. To support these detailed spatial analyses, Dr. Fajen has also been developing new methodological software tools to replay and visualize multidimensional movement and gaze data directly within 3D Unity environments.

papers.title: Learned landmark associations support online visual control under degraded visibility
papers.abstract: Two simulated driving experiments (N = 90) tested whether drivers use knowledge of road layout to steer when visibility is reduced by fog. Drivers who repeatedly drove the same road steered more stably than those on novel roads, but only in low visibility. Disrupting associations between landmarks and road segments impaired performance most, while scrambling segment order did not, suggesting that local landmark-road associations rather than a global map support moment-to-moment control.
papers.authors: Grace C. Roessling, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: The Unity Playback System: A tool for visualizing behavioral data in 3D Unity virtual environments
papers.abstract: Describes a software tool for replaying and visualizing recorded behavioral data (movement, gaze and related signals) inside 3D Unity virtual environments. It supports inspection and analysis of VR experiments like those used for the lab's steering and locomotion studies.
papers.authors: Xavier J. Marshall, Nathaniel V. Powell, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: Visual control of steering through multiple waypoints
papers.abstract: Subjects steered a simulated drone through sequences of three gates while distance, angle and orientation of the final gate were varied, and vehicle dynamics were made more or less sluggish. The data test three hypotheses about how people use information about upcoming waypoints beyond the nearest one. People adjusted their approach to the current gate in anticipation of later gates, and the results are consistent with control based on visual information rather than explicit trajectory planning.
papers.authors: A. J. Jansen, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: Coordination of gaze and action during high-speed steering and obstacle avoidance
papers.abstract: Skilled drone pilots flew a simulated quadcopter through a forest-like virtual environment while wearing a head-mounted display with eye tracking, in conditions that varied the presence of trees, hoops and a path. Pilots often looked only roughly toward where they wanted to go and fixated nearby objects and surfaces more than the path or hoops, yet they still steered fast and avoided collisions. The results indicate that steering in cluttered environments is not simply a matter of fixating the future path, and they argue for accounts of gaze that go beyond road-following.
papers.authors: Nathaniel V. Powell, Xavier Marshall, Gabriel J. Diaz, Brett R. Fajen

papers.title: Prospective control of steering through multiple waypoints
papers.abstract: Participants flew a simulated drone through a series of gates in a virtual forest while gaze was tracked, and the distance at which gates first became visible (lookahead) was manipulated. Performance and steering smoothness were good when gates were visible at least about one and a half segments ahead and degraded with shorter lookahead. Findings show that people plan steering around more than the immediate waypoint, with gaze coordinated accordingly.
papers.authors: A. J. Jansen, Brett R. Fajen

0095.name: Brian A. Anderson
0095.bio: Brian A. Anderson is a Professor at Texas A&M University and the Director of the Human Imaging Facility, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of attention. Anderson identified the phenomenon of value-driven attentional capture, in which stimuli associated with reward involuntarily attract attention even when they are task-irrelevant. His research utilizes human psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking to investigate how selection history and motivational factors influence visual processing. This work includes applications for understanding the mechanisms underlying addiction and psychopathology.
0095.research_direction: Dr. Anderson studies how selection history, such as learning that objects lead to positive or negative outcomes, changes how the brain processes those objects. Using human psychophysics (response times, accuracy and eye movements) and fMRI, the lab examines attention and perception mainly in healthy young adults, with implications for habit learning and addiction. Collaborative work extends these questions to attentional biases in substance abuse, ADHD and compulsive buying, habituation to warning signals on construction sites using virtual and augmented reality, attentional control while driving, and learning-dependent attention in non-human species.

papers.title: Statistical learning and the efficiency of visual search
papers.abstract: Examines how learned statistical regularities in the environment affect how efficiently observers find targets in search. The paper synthesizes evidence that such learning speeds search and considers how it interacts with effort and control mechanisms.
papers.authors: Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: The Attention Habit II: How selection history shapes the strategic control of attention
papers.abstract: A theoretical article proposing that learning history shapes not only involuntary attentional capture but also voluntary, goal-directed control. On this view, intentional prioritization of stimuli is itself habit-like and biased by prior experience. This blurs the boundary between goal-driven and selection-history-driven attention and raises questions about how far intentional control is shaped by learning.
papers.authors: Brian A. Anderson, David S. Lee, Niya Yan, Molly R. McKinney, Andrew Clement

papers.title: Getting a grip on visual search: Relating effort exertion to the control of attention
papers.abstract: Uses grip-force measurements during visual search to relate how much effort people exert to how attention is controlled. The experiments show that exertion tracks task demands and the use of attentional strategies, providing a physiological handle on otherwise hidden control processes. It extends the effort framework to test predictions about goal-directed and history-driven attention.
papers.authors: Brian A. Anderson, David S. Lee, Molly R. McKinney, Andrew Clement

papers.title: Trichotomy revisited: A monolithic theory of attentional control
papers.abstract: Revisits the influential division of attentional priority into goal-driven, stimulus-driven and selection-history sources. It argues instead for a single, unified priority-based mechanism in which these influences are different inputs to one control process, and it discusses how this reframing changes interpretation of distraction and capture findings.
papers.authors: Brian A. Anderson

papers.title: Visual search as effortful work
papers.abstract: Argues that searching for a target is an effortful activity and that the amount of effort exerted is itself a measurable, controllable quantity. Using a grip-force measure of exertion during search, the paper shows that effort scales with search demands and reflects strategic control over how attention is deployed. It frames search efficiency in terms of cost-benefit tradeoffs rather than fixed capacity limits.
papers.authors: Brian A. Anderson, David S. Lee

0096.name: Brian Keane
0096.bio: Brian P. Keane is an Assistant Professor at the University of Rochester whose research examines the computational and neural basis of visual perception in healthy and clinical populations. Utilizing behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking, Keane specializes in mid-level visual processes such as contour interpolation, perceptual organization, and shape completion. Their recent work focuses on identifying neural biomarkers for psychotic disorders by characterizing functional dysconnectivity within large-scale visual and somatomotor networks. These investigations aim to link specific visual processing deficits to the underlying pathophysiology and clinical progression of schizophrenia and related spectrum disorders.
0096.research_direction: Dr. Keane has recently been investigating the neural and perceptual alterations associated with severe psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and early psychosis. Their recent work explores functional brain architecture using resting-state and task-based fMRI, specifically probing how individual heterogeneity and dysconnectivity within visual, somatomotor, and dorsal attention networks relate to clinical symptoms and cognitive disorganization. At the behavioral level, they are leveraging phenomena such as illusory shape perception and depth-inversion illusions to examine how top-down predictive processing and mid-level visual integration might be altered in patients experiencing hallucinations. Additionally, their research addresses essential methodological controls in clinical vision science, investigating how subtle, often-overlooked differences in basic visual acuity can artificially mimic higher-level contour detection deficits in special populations.

papers.title: Functional dysconnectivity of visual and somatomotor networks yields a simple and robust biomarker for psychosis
papers.abstract: Using resting-state fMRI from the Human Connectome Early Psychosis Project, the study shows that psychosis patients have thalamo-cortical hyperconnectivity and cortico-cortical hypoconnectivity specifically in somatomotor and secondary visual networks, but not in auditory or primary visual networks. Combining these into a single 'somato-visual' score yields a large group difference (Hedges' g about 1.05) that is present in antipsychotic-naive patients and robust to comorbidity and demographic confounds. It generalizes across sites, works with five-minute scans, and improves classification beyond a standard neurocognitive task.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Yonatan T. Abrham, Michael W. Cole, Brent A. Johnson, Boyang Hu, Carrisa V. Cocuzza

papers.title: Increased whole-brain functional heterogeneity in psychosis during rest and task
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether brain function is more variable from person to person in psychosis. Across rest and task fMRI, patients showed greater whole-brain heterogeneity in functional connectivity and activation patterns than controls. This suggests that group averages hide substantial individual variation in psychotic illness and motivates individualized approaches.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Yonatan T. Abrham, Luke J. Hearne, Howard Bi, Boyang Hu

papers.title: Hallucinations and the depth-inversion illusion in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: The study tests whether people with schizophrenia who hallucinate differ in susceptibility to the depth-inversion (hollow-mask style) illusion. It links this perceptual measure of top-down versus bottom-up weighting to hallucination severity, offering a behavioural probe of how predictive processing may go awry in psychosis.
papers.authors: Judy L. Thompson, Steven M. Silverstein, Thomas V. Papathomas, Brian P. Keane

papers.title: Correcting visual acuity beyond 20/20 improves contour element detection and integration: A cautionary tale for studies of special populations
papers.abstract: Participants with normal vision were tested on contour detection and integration with or without refractive correction beyond the usual 20/20 criterion. Even small acuity improvements raised performance on contour tasks, so acuity differences between patient and control groups can masquerade as mid-level vision deficits. The paper argues that clinical vision studies must equate or correct acuity carefully.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Steven M. Silverstein, Thomas V. Papathomas, Bart Krekelberg

papers.title: Dorsal attention network activity during perceptual organization is distinct in schizophrenia and predictive of cognitive disorganization
papers.abstract: Participants with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or no illness were scanned while judging whether inducers formed illusory shapes or fragmented configurations. Dorsal attention network task modulations distinguished schizophrenia from the other groups and predicted cognitive disorganization across diagnoses. Activity-flow modelling suggested that attention-related feedback into secondary visual areas is disrupted in schizophrenia.
papers.authors: Brian P. Keane, Bart Krekelberg, Ravi D. Mill, Steven M. Silverstein, Judy L. Thompson, Megan R. Serody, Deanna M. Barch, Michael W. Cole

0098.name: Brian Odegaard
0098.bio: Brian Odegaard is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Florida and directs the Perception, Attention, and Consciousness (PAC) Laboratory. Odegaard’s research characterizes the behavioral, computational, and neural correlates of subjective experience, focusing on how the brain constructs awareness in the visual periphery. Through the integration of psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling, Odegaard investigates how metacognitive biases and attentional mechanisms shape perceptual decision-making. Their recent work explores reality monitoring, multisensory integration, and the development of web-based tools for reproducible vision science.
0098.research_direction: Dr. Odegaard has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architectures underlying visual metacognition, imagination, and human-AI interaction. Their recent work explores how metacognitive efficiency and decision criteria shift across the central and peripheral visual fields, as well as how an artificial system's ability to reliably signal its own uncertainty influences human trust during joint decision-making. Additionally, they are probing the neural mechanisms of visual imagery to determine whether top-down generative networks in the brain operate as strict hierarchies or flexible heterarchies. To map these internal world models, they combine fMRI, multidimensional scaling, and psychological network analysis to compare the representational geometries of human object perception and embodied imagination against the latent spaces of large language models and artificial neural networks.

papers.title: Internal World Models as Imagination Networks in Cognitive Agents
papers.abstract: Uses psychological network analysis on imagery questionnaires to compare the structure of imagination in thousands of people across three populations with that of several large language models. Human imagination networks show consistent centrality and clustering across groups, while language models show weak alignment and little clustering with humans. The authors argue that human imagery reflects memory organized through embodied experience that text training alone does not reproduce.
papers.authors: Saurabh Ranjan, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
papers.abstract: Collects large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects along eight properties, from objective features to affective judgments. Multidimensional scaling reveals three mental spaces (general object features, affective evaluation, and color), and fMRI in 80 participants links object-feature similarity to visual and prefrontal representational structure. The work then compares these human and neural geometries to artificial neural network models.
papers.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba, Megan A. K. Peters, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Metacognitive sensitivity: The key to calibrating trust and optimal decision making with AI
papers.abstract: Studies how well people rely on an AI aid when it reports its own confidence. Across human-AI joint decision experiments, the authors find that the AI's metacognitive sensitivity, meaning how well its confidence separates its correct from incorrect answers, is what best predicts whether people calibrate trust and reach good joint decisions. Raw accuracy of the AI matters less than an AI that signals its uncertainty reliably.
papers.authors: Doyeon Lee, Joseph Pruitt, Tianyu Zhou, Jing Du, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Consistent metacognitive efficiency and variable response biases in peripheral vision
papers.abstract: Tests how confidence and detection behave across the visual field. Metacognitive efficiency, how well confidence tracks accuracy, stays roughly constant from central to peripheral vision, even though observers' response biases in the periphery vary with conditions. The results separate stable metacognitive access from shifting decision criteria in peripheral perception.
papers.authors: Joseph Pruitt, J. D. Knotts, Brian Odegaard

papers.title: Heterarchy or hierarchy? Insights from a new model of visual imagination
papers.abstract: Offers a model of how visual imagery is generated in the brain and asks whether the underlying architecture is a strict hierarchy or a more flexible heterarchy. The article discusses how predictive and top-down signals, including a possible role for parietal cortex, may organize imagery and relates the model to current debates in visual cognition.
papers.authors: Saurabh Ranjan, Brian Odegaard

0099.name: Brian Scholl
0099.bio: Scholl is a Professor of Psychology at Yale University and Director of the Yale Perception & Cognition Lab, where they study the mechanisms of human vision. Scholl’s research characterizes visual awareness through phenomena such as inattentional blindness and defines how the mind represents objects and events across time and space. A focus of their work involves "visual intelligence," specifically how the visual system extracts concepts like causality, agency, and intuitive physics. Scholl employs computer-based psychophysical experiments and behavioral methods to investigate how perception provides a structure for higher-level thought. Currently, they are examining the interactions between perception and memory and how visual processing categorizes dynamic events.
0099.research_direction: Dr. Scholl has recently been investigating how the mind automatically structures and extracts rich information from dynamic sensory input. Their recent work explores basic visual processing by asking whether the visual system spontaneously categorizes events into foundational "visual verbs" (like bouncing or twisting), how observers infer material properties from non-biological point-light displays of physics-simulated cloth, and whether basic perception automatically prioritizes interrupted or "unfinished" visual events in the absence of explicit goals. Beyond basic vision, they are also examining the downstream consequences of sensory processing, testing how superficial auditory disfluency—such as poor microphone quality—might seed unintentional social biases regarding a speaker's intelligence or hireability. Additionally, Dr. Scholl has been applying concepts from sensory psychophysics to methodological questions in higher-level cognition, investigating how shifting reference sets and scale-based measurements might distort experimental research on moral judgment.

papers.title: The spontaneous prioritization of "unfinishedness" in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect
papers.abstract: The Zeigarnik effect holds that interrupted tasks are remembered better than completed ones, usually explained by goals or obligations. These experiments ask whether unfinishedness is prioritized even in basic perception, where no goals are involved, by using visual events such as paths that appear complete versus interrupted. The findings show that unfinished visual events are spontaneously privileged in perception and memory.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: How to show that a cruel prank is worse than a war crime: Shifting scales and missing benchmarks in the study of moral judgment
papers.abstract: Moral judgments are usually measured with ratings on labeled scales, but such ratings are only meaningful relative to a context, as in sensory psychophysics. The authors show how shifting the reference set can make trivial wrongs appear worse than atrocities, and argue that scale-based measurement distorts moral research. They propose psychophysics-inspired benchmarks and methods to correct this.
papers.authors: Vladimir Chituc, Molly J. Crockett, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Dynamic point-light cloths generate rich percepts beyond biology
papers.abstract: Point-light walkers are thought to reveal visual machinery specialized for perceiving other agents, but there were no non-biological displays to test that idea. The authors introduce sparse dot displays of moving cloth, simulated with physics, and show that they too give rise to rich percepts of material and event properties. A computational account suggests such percepts arise from more general inference than biology-specific processing.
papers.authors: Merve Erdogan, Wenyan Bi, Ilker Yildirim, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Superficial auditory (dis)fluency biases higher-level social judgment
papers.abstract: Videoconferencing makes some voices sound clear and others tinny, purely because of microphone quality. Across a series of experiments, listeners judged speakers with poorer audio quality as less intelligent, less hireable, less credible, and less romantically desirable, though the audio differences say nothing about the speaker. The work shows perceptual fluency can seed unintentional social bias.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Robert Walter-Terrill, Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: "Visual verbs": Dynamic event types are extracted spontaneously during visual perception
papers.abstract: Vision is usually studied in terms of objects and their categories, but this work asks whether the visual system also sorts dynamic input into a small set of primitive event types, such as twisting or bouncing. Using several paradigms that do not require participants to name or attend to the event type, the authors show that these categories are extracted spontaneously and shape downstream processing. The results support a 'language of vision' with foundational visual verbs.
papers.authors: Huichao Ji, Brian J. Scholl

0100.name: Brigitte Röder
0100.bio: Brigitte Röder is a Professor of Biological Psychology and Neuropsychology at the University of Hamburg, where they investigate the mechanisms of experience-dependent neuroplasticity and multisensory integration in the human brain. Their research explores sensitive periods of development and the extent of functional and structural brain adaptation following sensory deprivation, such as congenital blindness. Using behavioral testing, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Röder examines how early sensory experiences shape neural representations and crossmodal plasticity. Through collaboration with the LV Prasad Eye Institute in India, Röder studies cohorts of individuals who have undergone sight-restoration surgery to analyze the limitations and potential of adult brain plasticity.
0100.research_direction: Dr. Röder has recently been investigating the role of early visual experience in shaping the human visual system by studying individuals who regained sight after being born with dense congenital cataracts. Their recent work explores multiple facets of cortical plasticity and development, employing high-resolution 7T fMRI population receptive field mapping to examine how early deprivation affects the refinement of retinotopic maps and spatial scaling across early visual areas. In parallel, they are utilizing diffusion MRI to assess the limits of structural plasticity and white matter microstructural recovery in visual tracts following sight restoration. They also investigate the neurochemical consequences of transient early blindness, using magnetic resonance spectroscopy and EEG aperiodic measures to probe experience-dependent shifts in the excitation-inhibition balance of the visual cortex. Finally, their research employs multivariate decoding and occlusion paradigms to test how a lack of early visual input influences cross-modal object representations in ventral occipito-temporal cortex and feedback-driven recurrent processing in early visual regions.

papers.title: Individuals born with congenital cataracts exhibit both persisting impairment and considerable recovery of white matter microstructure after sight restoration
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI along-the-tract analysis in 20 congenital cataract-reversal individuals, plus congenitally blind, developmental-cataract and sighted control groups, shows visual-tract-specific white matter deficits. These deficits are much less widespread than in permanent congenital blindness, indicating substantial recovery after sight restoration. The pattern fits both a sensitive period for white matter development and considerable later plasticity.
papers.authors: Jordan D. Hassett, Cordula Hölig, Sunitha Lingareddy, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Early Vision Shapes Recurrent Processing in the Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Using 7T fMRI with an occlusion paradigm, the study asks whether feedback-driven scene information in early visual cortex depends on early visual experience. Individuals with reversed congenital cataracts showed poorer decoding of scene categories from stimulated cortex than sighted controls, while occluded-region decoding and connective-field analyses probe feedback flow. The work tests the idea that recurrent processing is experience-dependent.
papers.authors: Carolin Heitmann, Minye Zhan, Madita Linke, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Rick van Hoof, Rainer Goebel, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Altered visual cortex excitatory/inhibitory ratio following transient congenital visual deprivation in humans
papers.abstract: Magnetic resonance spectroscopy and EEG aperiodic measures were used to estimate the excitation/inhibition balance in visual cortex of people treated for dense congenital cataracts after years of blindness. Compared with matched sighted controls they had a lower Glx/GABA+ ratio and a steeper, higher-intercept aperiodic EEG spectrum, and lower ratios went with better acuity. This provides evidence in humans that E/I balance depends on early visual experience.
papers.authors: Rashi Pant, Kabilan Pitchaimuthu, José P. Ossandón, Idris Shareef, Sunitha Lingareddy, Jürgen Finsterbusch, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Visual and Auditory Object Representations in Ventral Visual Cortex After Restoring Sight in Humans
papers.abstract: Adults who had congenital cataracts removed were scanned while viewing and hearing movies of faces, scenes, body parts and objects. They showed reduced face selectivity in ventral occipito-temporal cortex, and a double dissociation in cross-modal decoding: auditory category patterns predicted visual categories only in the sight-recovery group. The results suggest cross-modal takeover during blindness competes with later visual specialisation.
papers.authors: Katarzyna Rączy, Madita Linke, Job van den Hurk, Carolin Heitmann, Maria J. S. Guerreiro, Minye Zhan, Ramesh Kekunnaya, Rainer Goebel, Brigitte Röder

papers.title: Early visual experience refines the retinotopic organization within and across visual cortical regions
papers.abstract: Using 7T fMRI population receptive field mapping, the study compares eight people who were born blind with dense cataracts and later regained sight against sighted controls. Sight-recovery participants show larger foveal receptive fields that fail to grow normally with eccentricity or up the V1-V2-V3 hierarchy, and reduced, flatter cortical magnification that tracks visual acuity. The authors conclude that early visual experience is needed to refine an innate, prototypical retinotopic map.
papers.authors: Heitmann C, Zhan M, Linke M, Hölig C, Kekunnaya R, van Hoof R, Goebel R, Röder B

0101.name: Bruno Olshausen
0101.department: Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute and School of Optometry
0101.bio: Bruno Olshausen is a professor at UC Berkeley and the director of the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience, where they develop mathematical models to explain the principles of biological vision. Olshausen’s work on sparse coding demonstrates how simple-cell receptive field properties in the primary visual cortex emerge from efficient coding principles applied to natural image statistics. Their research utilizes Bayesian inference and probabilistic modeling to investigate how the brain constructs stable 3D representations from high-dimensional, dynamic sensory input. Currently, their laboratory focuses on hierarchical cortical models, neural representations of 3D scenes, and the development of NeuroAI hardware that mimics the brain's analog and asynchronous computing strategies.
0101.research_direction: Dr. Olshausen has recently been investigating how the brain forms efficient, compositional representations of the world through the lenses of sparse coding and high-dimensional computing. In early vision, their recent work explores mechanistic models of perception, applying sparse coding to natural scene statistics to examine the emergence of human unique hues and linking perceptual inference in the primary visual cortex to minimal diffusion models. To understand how the visual system disentangles complex environments, they are combining convolutional sparse coding with resonator networks to dynamically factorize scenes into distinct object identities and spatial poses. Beyond the visual cortex, Dr. Olshausen is applying vector-symbolic operations and residue hyperdimensional computing to model hippocampal-entorhinal circuits, exploring how the brain binds sensory and spatial information to build flexible, compositional cognitive maps.

papers.title: Toward a mechanistic understanding of inference in visual cortex and diffusion models
papers.abstract: The authors propose a model of perceptual inference in primary visual cortex that turns out to be equivalent to a minimal diffusion model. It extends sparse coding with a non-factorial prior in the form of a pairwise interaction matrix, trained with denoising score matching. The learned interactions resemble V1 horizontal connections linking similarly tuned neurons, and the model denoises nearly as well as black-box diffusion networks, offering testable predictions for cortex and a mechanistic account of how diffusion models generalize.
papers.authors: Zeyu Yun, Alexander Belsten, Dasheng Bi, Zahra Kadkhodaie, Yubei Chen, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Emergence of unique hues from sparse coding of color in natural scenes
papers.abstract: Sparse coding is trained on chromatic natural images to see whether color-opponent representations that resemble human unique hues and color categories emerge from natural scene statistics. The learned color-tuned basis functions cluster around the unique hues and reproduce cross-cultural regularities in color naming. The paper argues that efficient coding of natural color statistics can explain why color categories are shared across people.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Alexander Belsten, E. Paxon Frady, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Binding in hippocampal-entorhinal circuits enables compositionality in cognitive maps
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a model of hippocampal-entorhinal circuitry in which grid-cell-like codes are bound to sensory or contextual information using vector-symbolic operations. This binding lets the system compose spatial and non-spatial content, so the same map can represent new environments and contexts flexibly. It gives a computational account of compositionality in cognitive maps and reproduces known cell responses.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 37)
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Sonia Mazelet, Anthony Hitchcock Thomas, Denis Kleyko, Edward Paxon Frady, Friedrich T. Sommer, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Computing with Residue Numbers in High-Dimensional Representation
papers.abstract: The authors introduce Residue Hyperdimensional Computing, which encodes integers as high-dimensional vectors built from residue numbers and does arithmetic through vector operations. The scheme supports efficient computation with superposed values, factorization with resonator networks, and works as a model of grid-cell-like spatial coding. It connects number-theoretic representations to brain-inspired computing hardware.
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Denis Kleyko, E. Paxon Frady, Connor Bybee, Pentti Kanerva, Friedrich T. Sommer, Bruno A. Olshausen

papers.title: Compositional Factorization of Visual Scenes with Convolutional Sparse Coding and Resonator Networks
papers.abstract: The paper combines convolutional sparse coding with resonator networks to break a visual scene into its constituent objects and their positions. Objects are represented compositionally in high-dimensional vectors, and the resonator dynamics search jointly over identity and pose. The approach yields interpretable, factorized scene representations and points toward efficient neuromorphic implementations.
papers.authors: Christopher J. Kymn, Sonia Mazelet, Annabel Ng, Denis Kleyko, Bruno A. Olshausen

0102.name: Bruno Rossion
0102.department: CNRS Ingénierie moléculaire, cellulaire et physiopathologie (IMoPA); Service de Neurologie; Service de Neurochirurgie
0102.bio: Bruno Rossion is a Research Director at the CNRS and Université de Lorraine specializing in the neuro-functional mechanisms of human face recognition and categorization. Rossion conducts research on the N170 electrophysiological component and case studies on acquired prosopagnosia to examine holistic face perception and the specialized nature of face processing in the human brain. Their methodology integrates multi-modal techniques including scalp EEG, functional MRI, and direct intracerebral recordings (sEEG) in patients with epilepsy. Rossion also applies fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS), or frequency-tagging, as a tool for quantifying category-selective responses across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex in neurotypical and clinical populations.
0102.research_direction: Dr. Rossion's recent work investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics and cellular mechanisms of human visual processing, focusing heavily on face recognition in the ventral occipito-temporal cortex. Using human intracerebral recordings and frequency-tagging techniques in epilepsy patients, they have recently been exploring how the spiking of individual neurons relates to broader phenomena like face familiarity and fMRI BOLD activation or deactivation. Their recent work also explores the systemic organization of this cortical network, examining whether category-selective neural activity operates hierarchically across visual areas and how the brain processes real faces compared to illusory faces in pareidolia. Additionally, they are investigating the specific roles of historically under-sampled anatomical nodes, such as the anterior fusiform gyrus, to build a more complete understanding of the architecture underlying human visual identity recognition.

papers.title: Concurrent category-selective neural activity across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex supports a non-hierarchical view of human visual recognition
papers.abstract: Intracerebral recordings from 140 epilepsy patients (over 11,000 sites) were used to measure face-selective high-frequency activity to natural images across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex. Selectivity grows along the posterior-anterior axis, but activity begins around 100 ms and ends around 450 ms at nearly the same times in all regions. This challenges the standard hierarchical model of object recognition in the human ventral stream.
papers.authors: Corentin Jacques, Jacques Jonas, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: A tight relationship between BOLD fMRI activation/deactivation and increase/decrease in single neuron responses in human association cortex
papers.abstract: Using frequency-tagging with microelectrode recordings in two adjacent fusiform gyrus sectors, the study finds that about 70% of neurons are face-selective, with neurons in the lateral fusiform increasing firing to faces while those in the medial fusiform selectively decrease it. A third of medial neurons show genuine suppression below baseline. The results link fMRI BOLD increases and decreases to the direction of underlying spiking changes.
papers.authors: Marie-Alphée Laurent, Corentin Jacques, Xiaoqian Yan, Pauline Jurczynski, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Louis Maillard, Steven Le Cam, Radu Ranta, Benoit R Cottereau, Laurent Koessler, Jacques Jonas, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: The neural basis of face pareidolia with human intracerebral recordings
papers.abstract: Frequency-tagged intracerebral recordings from 44 patients compared responses to real faces and to facelike objects across the ventral occipito-temporal cortex. Facelike objects drive selective responses in all key face-network regions, including anterior temporal lobe, but the responses are weaker and differ in space and time from those to genuine faces.
papers.authors: Begüm Cerrahoğlu, Corentin Jacques, Diane Rekow, Jacques Jonas, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Stephanie Caharel, Arnaud Leleu, Bruno Rossion

papers.title: The anterior fusiform gyrus: The ghost in the cortical face machine
papers.abstract: A review arguing that the anterior fusiform gyrus, an area strongly implicated in face identity recognition but nearly invisible in standard fMRI because of signal loss, has been systematically underrated. It draws together intracerebral, lesion and neuroimaging evidence to argue this region is a key node of the human face recognition network.
papers.authors: Bruno Rossion, Corentin Jacques, Jacques Jonas

papers.title: Single neuron responses underlying face recognition in the human midfusiform face-selective cortex
papers.abstract: Single-unit recordings from microelectrodes implanted in the face-selective midfusiform gyrus of five epilepsy patients show that face selectivity in this human region arises mainly because more neurons respond to faces than to places, rather than because individual cells are strongly tuned. Individual neurons did not prefer familiar over unfamiliar faces, but population-level decoding could tell whether a face was familiar. This offers a cellular-level account of the face-selective fMRI activations long reported in this area.
papers.authors: Rodrigo Quian Quiroga, Marta Boscaglia, Jacques Jonas, Hernan G. Rey, Xiaoqian Yan, Louis Maillard, Sophie Colnat-Coulbois, Laurent Koessler, Bruno Rossion

0104.name: Carlos Ponce
0104.department: Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School
0104.bio: Carlos Ponce is an Assistant Professor of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School whose lab studies how neurons across brain areas interact to support vision and natural behavior. Working in rhesus macaques, the lab combines large-scale neural recordings, behavioral experiments, and deep-network-guided stimulus generation to explore visual responses across a broad range of images and motion, pairing exploratory discovery with targeted experiments. Current work examines how drugs of abuse alter visual processing, how neural activity relates to spontaneous looking, and how specific cell types and pathways, including parvalbumin-expressing neurons, contribute to visual computation.
0104.research_direction: The Ponce Lab investigates how neurons across brain areas interact to support vision and natural behavior. Working in rhesus macaques, the lab combines large-scale neural recordings, behavioral experiments, and deep-network-guided stimulus generation to explore visual responses across a broad range of images and motion. Its approach connects exploratory discovery with targeted experiments that test how visual circuits work. Current projects examine how drugs of abuse alter visual processing and behavior, how neural activity relates to spontaneous looking and other natural behaviors, and how specific cell types and pathways contribute to visual computation. Current directions include investigating parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons and using intersectional AAV strategies to target defined neural projections. Computational models guide these experiments, with biological measurements and causal manipulations central to understanding the mechanisms.

papers.title: Neuronal tuning aligns dynamically with object and texture manifolds across the visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: Visual neurons respond to a vast range of images, from textures to objects, but the rules linking these responses remain unclear. Although tuning to simple features is well established in the primary visual cortex, this framework breaks down in higher areas, where neurons encode diverse and unpredictable features. To ask what features neurons prioritize, we used generative models (deep networks that synthesize new images from a learned latent space), allowing neurons in V1, V4 and the posterior inferotemporal cortex (PIT) to guide image synthesis through closed-loop optimization. We compared models that emphasize texture versus those that emphasize object structure. Although V1 and V4 aligned more strongly with texture-based spaces, many PIT neurons responded equally well to both types of optimized images, revealing a focus on shared local motifs rather than whole-object templates, and this alignment to objects emerged later in their response. These findings reveal coding principles across the ventral stream and clarify the limits of current vision models.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Brain feature maps reveal progressive animal-feature representations in the ventral stream
papers.abstract: Primate visual recognition is hypothesized to rely on object-centric representations, but cortical neurons may instead follow organizational principles based on generic features across textures and environments. This study utilized multielectrode arrays to record from V1/V2, V4, and posterior inferotemporal (PIT) cortex, employing an unsupervised heatmap approach to characterize local operations within natural scenes. We discovered that while foveal populations across the hierarchy respond to entire scenes, their activity focuses on salient subregions within object contours. Notably, there is a progressive increase in selectivity for animal-related features, such as faces and limbs, along the visual hierarchy. This trend was consistent with biological tuning but diverged from various artificial neural network architectures, suggesting that the monkey ventral stream is fundamentally organized to prioritize ethologically relevant local animal features over general object configurations.
papers.authors: Zhanqi Zhang, Till S. Hartmann, Richard T. Born, Margaret S. Livingstone, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Structure as an inductive bias for brain–model alignment
papers.abstract: The alignment between artificial neural networks (ANNs) and the biological visual system remains a central challenge in computational neuroscience. Recent evidence suggests that standard convolutional architectures exhibit inherent alignment with cortical representations even before task-specific training. This work evaluates how structural constraints in deep learning models serve as inductive biases that facilitate this alignment. We argue that the architectural regularities of ANNs, such as spatial locality and weight sharing, mirror the fundamental organizational principles of the primate ventral stream. These structural properties may be more critical for achieving brain-like representations than the specific objectives of the training tasks themselves, suggesting that future models should prioritize biological architectural constraints to improve their fidelity as digital twins of the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: A concentration of visual cortex-like neurons in prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: While visual recognition is primarily attributed to the ventral stream, recent evidence suggests that the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (vlPFC) plays a significant role in visual processing. This study investigated whether vlPFC neurons possess sensory properties comparable to the visual cortex, such as receptive fields, image selectivity, and the ability to guide the synthesis of highly activating stimuli through generative networks. By recording from vlPFC sites in monkeys, we identified a subpopulation of neurons that exhibit stable visual encoding of world statistics. These neurons appear to be anatomically clustered, consistent with functional organization identified via fMRI. The findings suggest that stable visual representations in the vlPFC may provide the necessary foundation for the integration of sensory and cognitive processes across the brain.
papers.authors: Olivia Rose, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: Macaques recognize features in synthetic images derived from ventral stream neurons
papers.abstract: Neurons in the primate ventral stream can guide generative networks to synthesize images that strongly drive them, but it was unclear whether the features in these images carry meaning for the animal. The authors trained rhesus macaques on a recognition task and then tested them with synthetic images evolved by inferotemporal neurons. Monkeys treated many of these images as containing recognizable features, such as parts of faces and bodies, linking the tuning of individual ventral stream neurons to the animal's own perception.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Katherine N. Mueller, Mary C. Carter, Jeevun A. Kansupada, Carlos R. Ponce

0105.name: Carolina Diaz-Piedra
0105.department: Department of Methodology of Behavioral Sciences
0105.bio: Carolina Diaz-Piedra is an Associate Professor at the University of Granada and co-director of the Neuroergonomics and Operator Performance Lab. Diaz-Piedra’s research examines the intersection of sleep health, cognitive load, and human performance in settings such as aviation, surgery, and military operations. They employ neurophysiological indices—including EEG power spectrum analysis, gaze entropy, and thermal imaging—to quantify mental workload and fatigue in operators. This work focuses on developing behavioral interventions and monitoring tools to address safety and efficiency in complex human-machine systems.
0105.research_direction: Dr. Diaz-Piedra has recently been working on human factors and safety in complex, high-stakes systems. Their recent work explores how safety practices from aviation can be adapted to make surgery safer within a national health system. They have also studied the ethical and legal questions raised by automated driving, asking how engineers, policymakers, and legal experts actually weigh competing values such as safety, privacy, and liability when designing and deploying these vehicles.

papers.title: Practical Tips Inspired by Aviation to Strengthen Surgical Patient Safety in the Spanish National Health System: The Use Before Surgery Initiative
papers.abstract: Describes the Use Before Surgery initiative, which adapts practical safety tips from military and civil aviation to strengthen patient safety in surgical settings within the Spanish National Health System.Book chapter, likely from conference proceedings.
papers.venue: Safer Better Healthcare, By All for All (Springer Series in Design and Innovation)
papers.authors: Carolina Diaz-Piedra, Leandro L. Di Stasi

papers.title: Ethical and legal challenges of automated driving: The prioritization of socio-political values
papers.abstract: This paper reports a qualitative, stakeholder-based investigation into how ethical and legal trade-offs in automated-vehicle design and deployment are actually prioritized by the people who must implement them, moving away from the trolley-problem framing that dominates the automated-driving ethics literature. Through workshops, semi-structured interviews, and focus groups with a diverse set of experts and stakeholders (engineers, policymakers, legal scholars), the authors elicited which socio-political values (e.g., safety, privacy, liability, equitable access, transparency) are weighted most heavily in everyday design and regulatory decisions rather than in rare extreme-harm scenarios. The results indicate that day-to-day ethical and legal concerns are dominated by mundane trade-offs—such as data governance, accountability attribution, and infrastructure equity—rather than by the moral-dilemma scenarios emphasized in prior theoretical work. The authors argue that automated-driving policy frameworks should be built around this empirically observed prioritization of socio-political values rather than around idealized dilemma cases.
papers.authors: Carolina Diaz-Piedra, Belén Liedo, Miguel Núñez de Prado-Gordillo, M. Jesús Caurcel, Leandro L. Di Stasi

0106.name: Caroline Blais
0106.department: Département de psychoéducation et de psychologie
0106.lab_name: Laboratoire de perception visuelle et sociale (LPVS)
0106.bio: Caroline Blais is a Professor at the Université du Québec en Outaouais and holds the Canada Research Chair in Cognitive and Social Vision. Blais’s research investigates how sociocultural environments modulate visual processes, focusing on face recognition and the decoding of social signals such as pain and emotion. Using psychophysical methods including the Bubbles and Reverse Correlation techniques, Blais explores cultural variability in visual strategies to identify the mechanisms underlying human social perception.
0106.research_direction: Dr. Blais has recently been investigating the visual and cognitive mechanisms underlying face perception and emotion recognition. Their recent work explores how observers form mental templates of pain expressions and use specific visual information to decode emotion intensity, frequently utilizing data-driven psychophysical methods like reverse correlation and Bubbles. They are examining the boundaries of cultural influences on vision, questioning whether known cross-cultural differences in spatial frequency tuning for faces generalize to objects and scenes, and how cultural backgrounds shape the extraction of facial signals. Broadening this focus to social and applied contexts, they are also investigating how a parent's history of childhood maltreatment affects their automatic facial mimicry of children's emotional expressions. To support these cross-cultural and individual-difference inquiries, their methodological work assesses the feasibility of migrating demanding, real-time visual psychophysics paradigms to online platforms to access larger and more diverse populations.

papers.title: Is it pain, anger, disgust, or sadness? Individual differences in expectations of pain facial expressions
papers.abstract: Pain expressions are often confused with other negative states, and earlier work suggested that people's mental templates of pain faces are imperfect. Using reverse-correlation images of what 162 White observers expect a pain face to look like, the authors had a new group rate how much each template conveyed pain, anger, disgust, sadness and fear. Expectations frequently overlapped with other negative emotions, and the degree of overlap varied across individuals.
papers.authors: Arianne Richer, Francis Gingras, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Daniel Fiset, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Cultural differences in spatial frequency tunings to faces do not generalize to visual scenes and object stimuli
papers.abstract: Earlier work found that observers from different cultures rely on different spatial frequency bands when identifying faces. This study asked whether that cultural difference is specific to faces or reflects a general visual style, by measuring spatial frequency tuning for scenes and objects in the same cultural groups. The face-related cultural differences did not carry over to these non-face stimuli, arguing for face-specific cultural tuning.
papers.authors: Francis Gingras, Daniel Fiset, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Amanda Estéphan, Michael N'Guiamba, Dan Sun, Ye Zhang, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Childhood maltreatment influences parental mimicry of children's emotional facial expressions
papers.abstract: Fifty-seven parents viewed children's emotional faces while their own facial reactions were recorded and analyzed automatically for mimicry. The study related different forms of childhood maltreatment in the parents to how much they mimicked children's expressions, a mechanism thought to support bonding. It extends the lab's line on how early adversity alters emotion processing in parenting.
papers.authors: Annie Bérubé, Rachel Pétrin, Maélie Boudreault, Gabrielle Marcotte-Beaumier, Caroline Blais

papers.title: Conducting online visual psychophysics experiments: A replication assessment of two face processing studies
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether demanding, real-time data-driven face psychophysics tasks written in MATLAB/Python can be run online using VPixx's Pack & Go platform. Two established face recognition experiments were replicated online and compared with laboratory results. The work shows the approach is workable and opens the way to larger, more culturally diverse samples.
papers.authors: Caroline Blais, Daniel Fiset, Laurianne Côté, Vicki Ledrou-Paquet, Isabelle Charbonneau

papers.title: Differences Between East Asians and Westerners in the Mental Representations and Visual Information Extraction Involved in the Decoding of Pain Facial Expression Intensity
papers.abstract: Using data-driven reverse correlation and Bubbles methods, the study compared how East Asian and Western observers imagine and decode pain expressions of varying intensity. East Asians expected more intense pain faces, needed more signal to discriminate intensities, and relied less on the same facial regions as Westerners. The results show that culture shapes both expectations and visual strategies for reading pain.
papers.authors: Camille Saumure, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Daniel Fiset, Stéphanie Cormier, Ye Zhang, Dan Sun, Manni Feng, Feifan Luo, Miriam Kunz, Caroline Blais

0107.name: Caroline E. Robertson
0107.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0107.bio: Robertson is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual perception, spatial memory, and neurodiversity. Their research identifies atypical GABAergic signaling and altered binocular rivalry dynamics as biomarkers of visual processing in autism. Robertson’s methodology integrates high-field fMRI, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), and eye-tracking with naturalistic experiments conducted in virtual reality. Their current research focuses on the interface between the visual and memory systems, exploring how the brain leverages prior knowledge and mnemonic representations to construct subjective visual experiences.
0107.research_direction: Dr. Robertson's recent work investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms bridging naturalistic scene perception and spatial memory. Using high-resolution fMRI and population receptive field modeling, they have been mapping how shared spatial reference frames, such as bivalent retinotopic codes, structure the interactions between high-level visual cortex and memory networks including the hippocampus. In parallel, their behavioral research utilizes immersive virtual reality to explore how internal scene memory generates predictions that prime perceptual judgments during active viewing behaviors like head turns. They are also investigating individual differences in visual attention by combining VR eye-tracking with deep neural networks to model how conceptual priorities shape naturalistic gaze patterns. To facilitate broader research on this perception-memory interface, they are currently developing probabilistic functional atlases that map scene and place networks across the posterior cortex.

papers.title: Conceptual priorities shape individual gaze patterns during naturalistic visual attention
papers.abstract: Sixty-one participants freely explored 100 immersive real-world scenes in a VR headset while gaze was tracked. Modeling gaze with spatial, visual and conceptual feature spaces derived from large vision and language models showed that people differ systematically in which concepts they prioritize. These stable individual differences in conceptual attention link to the lab's work on neurodiversity and naturalistic vision.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Amanda J. Haskins, Katherine O. Packard, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Positive and Negative Retinotopic Codes in the Human Hippocampus
papers.abstract: With high-resolution 7T fMRI and voxel-scale population receptive field modeling in seven densely sampled individuals, the study finds a widespread retinotopic code across hippocampal subfields and along its long axis. The code includes roughly equal proportions of positive and negative receptive fields. This extends the bivalent retinotopic framework from cortex into the hippocampus.
papers.authors: Peter A. Angeli, Adam Steel, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Memory-based predictions prime perceptual judgments across head turns in immersive, real-world scenes
papers.abstract: Using virtual reality, participants learned panoramic real-world environments and then made perceptual judgments about views that appeared after a head turn. Memory for the surrounding scene primed responses to the upcoming view, and this priming depended on the spatial layout of the learned environment. The work shows that scene memory generates predictions that shape perception during natural, active viewing.
papers.authors: Anna Mynick, Adam Steel, Adithi Jayaraman, Thomas L. Botch, Allie Burrows, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Relating Scene Memory and Perception Activity to Functional Properties, Networks, and Landmarks of Posterior Cerebral Cortex—A Probabilistic Atlas
papers.abstract: Across three fMRI datasets (44 participants), the authors map the locations of scene-perception areas and the place-memory areas anterior to them, and relate them to functional properties, large-scale networks and anatomical landmarks. The resulting probabilistic atlas gives group-level locations for these areas. It is a community resource for studying how scene perception and memory are organized across posterior cortex.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Deepasri Prasad, Brenda D. Garcia, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: A retinotopic code structures the interaction between perception and memory systems
papers.abstract: The authors show that memory-related areas at the cortical apex, which lie just anterior to scene-perception areas, carry a retinotopic (visual-field) code, but with an inverted, suppressive tuning, so that visual-field position is represented in both systems with opposite sign. This shared spatial reference frame gives a mechanism for how perception and memory areas interact and coordinate. The finding reframes the visual hierarchy as continuing into memory networks rather than ending at high-level vision.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Edward H. Silson, Brenda D. Garcia, Caroline E. Robertson

0108.name: Catherine L. Reed
0108.bio: Catherine L. Reed is a cognitive neuroscientist whose research investigates the multisensory integration of bodily, visual, and tactile information to understand how the motor system modulates perception and attention. Reed’s work focuses on the embodied attention framework, employing behavioral psychophysics and high-density electroencephalography (EEG) to examine how peripersonal space and body posture prioritize visual processing. They utilize event-related potentials (ERPs) and oscillatory analysis to characterize the neural mechanisms of action observation, social cognition, and the influence of aging on cognitive control. Current research directions for Reed involve dissociating the perceptual and motor correlates of mu-alpha and beta rhythms during emotional action simulation.
0108.research_direction: Dr. Reed’s recent work explores the intersection of social perception, cognitive aging, and executive function using both behavioral methods and electroencephalography. To understand how we perceive others, they have recently been investigating how facial expressions and body postures interact to drive social judgments of threat and emotion, as well as whether EEG mu-rhythm suppression truly reflects motor simulation during action observation once aperiodic neural activity is controlled. Additionally, their research examines cognitive-motor integration in healthy aging by testing how older and younger adults manage simultaneous parametric increases in physical difficulty and cognitive load during dual-task treadmill walking paradigms. Finally, Dr. Reed utilizes event-related potentials to probe individual differences in cognitive control, asking which specific facets of impulsivity drive error monitoring via the error-related negativity, and whether working memory capacity mediates age-related neural changes in attentional and semantic processing.

papers.title: Effects of age in a cognitive-motor dual task: parametric manipulations of cognitive load and motor difficulty
papers.abstract: Younger (n=29) and older (n=30) adults performed auditory 0-, 1- and 2-back tasks while walking on a treadmill at three inclines, so that cognitive load and motor difficulty were varied together. Higher load reduced accuracy more in older adults, though reaction-time costs were similar across ages. Age differences in gait were parameter-specific (stride length and frequency, toe clearance, double support) rather than a uniform decline, and younger adults adapted gait more fully as incline increased; RT and d-prime related to gait in different ways.
papers.authors: Chandlyr M. Denaro, Jason A. Monroy, Alan A. Hartley, Joseph Asta, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Aperiodic activity masks sensorimotor mu suppression during human action observation
papers.abstract: Using 128-channel EEG in a large sample (N=109), the study tests whether the sensorimotor mu rhythm really drops when people watch others' actions, as often claimed for a motor contribution to social perception. Mu suppression was robust during action execution, but with proper visual and attentional controls it was initially absent during observation. Once the 1/f-like aperiodic component of the spectrum was removed, a smaller but significant central mu suppression reappeared, showing that the effect is weaker than earlier reports and that aperiodic activity distorts its measurement.
papers.authors: Alison M. Harris, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: The cognitive instability aspect of impulsivity predicts the ERN: An ERP study
papers.abstract: In 261 young adults performing a flanker task, the study asked which facets of impulsivity relate to error monitoring, indexed by the error-related negativity. Total BIS-11 scores did not predict ERN amplitude, but a principal components analysis yielded planning, impetuosity and cognitive-instability factors, and only cognitive instability (racing thoughts) predicted smaller ERNs. The authors suggest this reflects individual differences in how motivationally salient errors are.
papers.authors: Folly Folivi, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Alan A. Hartley, Cindy M. Bukach, Jane W. Couperus, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Complex span measures of working memory do not mediate the effects of age on the P3 and N400 ERPs
papers.abstract: Younger (n=44) and older (n=41) adults completed three complex span working-memory tasks plus a visual oddball (P3) and a word-pair judgment (N400) ERP task. Older adults showed lower amplitudes and longer latencies, and complex span capacity did not predict P3 or N400 measures in either group, so it did not mediate the age effects. The results suggest the processes indexed by these ERPs differ from those measured by complex span, with attentional control likely more important than storage.
papers.authors: Jasmin Joshi, Chandlyr M. Denaro, Alan A. Hartley, Catherine L. Reed

papers.title: Relative contributions of the face and body to social judgements: emotion, threat and status
