papers.abstract: Two experiments had participants judge emotion, threat and status from combinations of facial expression (angry or fearful), body posture (expanded or contracted) and lean (forward or backward). Facial anger raised anger, threat and status ratings and fear lowered them, while expanded posture boosted threat and status and backward lean reduced anger and threat. When the face was hidden, posture influenced judgements more, showing that reliance on body cues depends on both the type of judgement and the availability of facial information.
papers.authors: Brittany R. Vincente, Daniel N. McIntosh, Catherine L. Reed

0109.name: Cathleen M. Moore
0109.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0109.bio: Cathleen M. Moore is a Professor and Starch Faculty Fellow at the University of Iowa and directs the Iowa Attention and Perception Lab. Moore’s research investigates mid-level visual processes, focusing on how the brain transforms retinal images into representations of objects and surfaces through mechanisms like figure-ground assignment and object correspondence. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies such as eye-tracking, virtual reality, and response-time analysis, Moore explores the interface between perception, attention, and cognitive control. Their current projects also extend to applied domains, examining attentional failures in environments such as lifeguarding and medical image interpretation.
0109.research_direction: Dr. Moore has recently been investigating how the visual system extracts mid-level object representations and utilizes them to guide attention, eye movements, and motor responses. Their recent work explores the spatial limits of perceptual organization, specifically testing whether processes like surface completion and 3D shape recovery operate in peripheral vision and whether they mediate visual crowding. In the domain of oculomotor control, they are examining how the brain programs saccades to complex visual targets, testing whether landing positions on partially occluded or spatially extended objects are determined by low-level 2D image features, part-segmentation boundaries, completed 3D object representations, or strategic observer goals. Furthermore, they are using virtual reality to investigate how spatial affordances in a 3D environment, such as the physical reachability of a stimulus, modulate stimulus-response compatibility and spatial congruence effects.

papers.title: Saccades to spatially extended objects: The roles of observer goals and part-structure cues in determining within-object landing position
papers.abstract: The study asks how a spatially extended object is converted into a single saccade vector. Landing positions in a visual search task were biased both toward task-relevant regions (a strategic bias) and toward part-segmentation boundaries (a stimulus-driven bias). A rapid orienting task showed only the segmentation bias, and the two biases combined additively when the relevant region coincided with a part.
papers.authors: Andrew Hollingworth, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Simon says "stay in touch": Reachability moderates the effect of irrelevant spatial congruence
papers.abstract: Using virtual reality, the authors compared the Simon effect for stimuli at reachable versus unreachable distances while matching image size and viewing angle across groups. The spatial congruence effect depended on whether the stimulus was within reach, suggesting that the potential to interact with an object modulates how irrelevant location information influences responses.
papers.authors: Michael L. Paavola, J. Toby Mordkoff, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Perceptual organization is limited in peripheral vision: Evidence from configural superiority
papers.abstract: Perceptual organization, the recovery of 3D surface structure from image information, is usually studied at fixation, where acuity is high. The authors measured configural superiority for four organization processes (surface completion, 3D shape, transparency/scission, and shape from closure) at central and peripheral locations. Configural superiority appeared at fixation for each process but was largely absent in the periphery, indicating that mid-level organization is limited outside central vision.
papers.authors: Cathleen M. Moore, Qingzi Zheng, Yelda Semizer

papers.title: Saccades to partially occluded objects: Perceptual completion mediates oculomotor control
papers.abstract: The paper contrasts an image-based account of saccade programming with an object-based account in which saccades are computed over 3D scene representations. Landing positions on partially occluded objects in a naturalistic search task were biased toward the center of the perceptually completed object, even when that bias was strategically disadvantageous and not explained by occluder image differences. Saccade motor programs thus draw on completed object representations.
papers.authors: Michael L. Paavola, Andrew Hollingworth, Cathleen M. Moore

papers.title: Limited midlevel mediation of visual crowding: Surface completion fails to support uncrowding
papers.abstract: The study tests whether uncrowding reflects mid-level perceptual organization by adapting displays to minimize stimulus differences across conditions while preserving the opportunity for surface completion. Surface completion did not reduce crowding, arguing against strong mid-level mediation of crowding and favoring image-level accounts.
papers.authors: Cathleen M. Moore, Qingzi Zheng

0110.name: Chai-Youn Kim
0110.bio: Chai-Youn Kim is a Professor at Korea University specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of perception, with a focus on visual awareness and binocular rivalry. Kim's research employs psychophysical methods and brain imaging to investigate how the brain resolves visual ambiguity and how multisensory inputs, such as auditory and motor information, modulate perceptual selection. Kim has published research on the mechanisms of synesthesia and neuroaesthetics, exploring how factors like familiarity and cross-modal correspondences influence aesthetic preference and conscious experience. Their recent work examines the interplay between sensory modalities in bistable perception, including the impact of musical congruence and action-based feedback on visual dominance.
0110.research_direction: Dr. Kim has recently been investigating how the brain decides what we consciously see, and how other senses influence that process. Their recent work explores whether sound can affect visual motion processing even when the visual stimulus is suppressed from awareness, and how earlier conscious experience changes this. They have also studied how touch and voluntary hand movement help resolve which image wins during binocular rivalry, when the two eyes see conflicting pictures. Beyond basic perception, they examine how expertise in art shapes preference for curved 3D shapes and how cybersickness develops during prolonged augmented reality use, measured with both self-report and physiological signals.

papers.title: Type of art expertise matters: Practical experts show a greater curvature preference for 3D shapes than theoretical experts
papers.abstract: This research investigated whether aesthetic preference for curvature in 3D shapes is modulated by different types of art expertise. The study compared three groups: practical experts (artists), theoretical experts (art historians and critics), and non-experts. Participants evaluated 3D-rendered shapes that varied parametrically in curvature. While non-experts generally preferred curved forms over angular ones, this preference was significantly more pronounced in the practical expert group than in the theoretical expert group. These findings suggest that the nature of an individual's interaction with art—whether through creative physical practice or analytic theoretical study—shapes the degree of aesthetic valuation for fundamental visual properties like curvature.
papers.venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
papers.authors: Jiwon Song, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Visuotactile object processing in binocular rivalry: The role of shape congruence, voluntary action, and spatial colocalization
papers.abstract: This study employed three-dimensional (3D) objects to investigate how visuotactile integration facilitates perceptual disambiguation during binocular rivalry. Across four experiments, the researchers manipulated shape congruence in the curvature dimension using mathematically generated 'spiky' and 'round' stimuli. The study tested the effects of voluntary action by comparing active palm exploration of 3D-printed objects with passive tactile stimulation, while spatial colocalization was manipulated through the use of video recordings as visual targets to provide bodily cues of hand-object contact. Results indicated that tactile shape congruence significantly promoted the dominance of the corresponding visual percept. This crossmodal influence was most robust when visuotactile colocalization was encouraged, suggesting that sensory integration of complex 3D features is critically modulated by spatial and motoric context during naturalistic object recognition.
papers.authors: Seyoon Song, Haeji Shin, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Cybersickness in Augmented Reality: Subjective and physiological changes with the course of prolonged exposure
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the temporal development and physiological characteristics of cybersickness induced by Augmented Reality (AR) environments. Participants were exposed to racing game videos through an AR device for 30-minute sessions across two movement speed conditions. The researchers integrated subjective data from the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), behavioral metrics of response time, and physiological signals including heart rate variability (ECG) and respiration patterns (RSP). The results demonstrated that cybersickness symptoms accumulated linearly with exposure duration, manifesting most clearly in subjective reports and significantly slowed behavioral responses. Eye-related symptoms were identified as the primary drivers of this accumulation, while movement speed had a negligible effect. Furthermore, individuals with previous AR exposure reported lower levels of discomfort, indicating that familiarity can mitigate AR-induced sickness.
papers.authors: Zion Park, Seyoon Song, Subin Jeon, Yuyeon Jung, Yeha Cha, Jiyoung Oh, Minsung Jin, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Audiovisual interactions outside of visual awareness during motion adaptation
papers.abstract: To determine whether multisensory integration can occur in the absence of conscious visual awareness, the researchers utilized a continuous flash suppression (CFS) paradigm to render translational visual motion perceptually invisible during a period of adaptation. Concurrently, participants were presented with auditory motion that was either congruent or incongruent in velocity (direction and speed) with the suppressed visual motion. The strength of the resulting visual motion aftereffect (MAE) was used as a metric for processing potency. The results showed that congruent auditory motion significantly strengthened the MAE produced by the invisible visual motion compared to incongruent or stationary auditory conditions. These findings provide evidence that auditory signals can impact visual neural processing at early, pre-conscious stages, indicating that the human brain integrates crossmodal velocity signals even when one modality is suppressed from awareness.
papers.authors: Minsun Park, Randolph Blake, Chai-Youn Kim

papers.title: Prior conscious experience modulates the impact of audiovisual temporal correspondence on unconscious visual processing
papers.abstract: The study investigated the extent to which top-down modulation from prior conscious awareness influences the integration of multisensory signals that are currently suppressed from awareness. Observers were first exposed to conscious trials where the temporal correspondence between auditory beeps and visual flashes was explicitly manipulated. Subsequently, they performed a detection task on visual stimuli suppressed by continuous flash suppression. The researchers found that the impact of auditory temporal cues on the breakthrough of visual stimuli into awareness was significantly modulated by the preceding conscious experience of audiovisual synchrony. This suggests that the mechanisms governing unconscious multisensory binding are not purely bottom-up but are instead dynamically recalibrated by recent conscious representations of crossmodal temporal structure.
papers.authors: Hyun-Woong Kim, Minsun Park, Yune Sang Lee, Chai-Youn Kim

0111.name: Chaipat Chunharas
0111.bio: Chaipat Chunharas is a clinician-scientist whose research examines the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception and working memory, focusing on how the brain maintains sensory information during distraction. Chunharas utilizes psychophysical techniques, neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), and computational modeling to investigate the representational geometry and topographic organization of the human visual cortex. Their work characterizes visual working memory distortions and the coexistence of sensory and mnemonic signals in early visual areas. Chunharas applies these cognitive and computational frameworks to clinical neurology to study the pathological mechanisms of neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions, such as mild cognitive impairment.
0111.research_direction: Dr. Chunharas has recently been bridging cognitive neuroscience and computational clinical neurology, with a dual focus on visual working memory architecture and the predictive modeling of neurological deficits. In the visual domain, their recent work explores the representational format of stored features, using fMRI to investigate how continuous versus categorical coding schemes transition along the visual hierarchy during memory maintenance, while also analyzing large behavioral datasets to model inter-item dependencies like chunking, spatial repulsion, and ensemble effects. In parallel, they are developing objective, data-driven approaches to map brain lesions and forecast clinical progression. Specifically, they use unsupervised machine learning on item-level cognitive screening scores to subtype dementia trajectories, apply automated speech recognition to structured phonetic tasks to localize corticobulbar lesions, and probe the underlying connectome principal components to determine what fundamentally drives cross-dataset replication in symptom lesion network mapping.

papers.title: Chunking, Attraction, Repulsion, and Ensemble Effects Are Ubiquitous in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: Reanalysing 11 existing datasets (about 138,000 trials), the paper shows that when many items are held in visual working memory they are not stored independently. Instead, memory reports show grouping into chunks, biases toward or away from neighbouring items, and drift toward the display average, all appearing together in the same tasks. This argues that models of memory limits should treat the display as a compressed, structured representation rather than a set of independent slots.
papers.authors: Chaipat Chunharas, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Connectome Principal Component Drives Cross-Dataset Replication and Clinical Prediction in Symptom Lesion Network Mapping
papers.abstract: Lesion network mapping projects brain lesions onto normative connectivity to find symptom-related networks, but critics argue the maps mostly reflect properties of the connectome itself. Using depression and Broca's aphasia datasets, the authors show that maps for unrelated disorders resemble each other and are dominated by a leading connectome principal component. They show this component explains cross-dataset replication and clinical prediction, and that its removal changes what the method can claim.
papers.authors: Sasin Treeratana, Arp-Arpa Kasemsantitham, Setthanan Jarukasemkit, Waragon Phusuwan, Anthipa Chokesuwattanaskul, Sira Sriswasdi, Janine Bijsterbosch, Chaipat Chunharas

papers.title: Automatic Speech Recognition and Phonetics-Informed Sentence Design for Spastic Dysarthria Detection and Corticobulbar Lesion Localization
papers.abstract: The team designed short reading sentences targeting groups of initial consonants (lip, tongue, soft-palate) based on the idea that spastic dysarthria mainly disrupts word-initial articulation. They had 37 patients with corticobulbar lesions and 37 controls read them and used automatic speech recognition errors as an objective measure. The approach detects dysarthria and helps localize the lesion, offering an alternative to subjective clinician ratings.
papers.authors: Chayoot Marukatat, Keerati Kaewrak, Sedthapong Chunamchai, Chaipat Chunharas

papers.title: A gradual transition toward categorical representations along the visual hierarchy during working memory, but not perception
papers.abstract: The authors scanned people with fMRI while they viewed or remembered oriented gratings and compared the similarity structure of activity patterns across retinotopic areas. During perception the patterns tracked the physical orientation across the hierarchy, whereas during memory they increasingly reflected categorical (cardinal vs oblique) structure moving from early to higher visual areas. This suggests working-memory contents are stored in a format that differs systematically from perceptual input, which may help the brain keep memories distinct from what is currently seen.
papers.authors: Chaipat Chunharas, Michael J Wolff, Meike D Hettwer, Rosanne L Rademaker

papers.title: Predicting mild cognitive impairment and dementia progression using MoCA score-based subtyping and cognitive decline cascade analysis with unsupervised machine learning
papers.abstract: Using item-level Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores, the authors apply unsupervised machine learning to divide patients into cognitive subtypes and to trace a typical order in which abilities decline. The subtypes differ in their likelihood of converting to dementia, showing that routine screening data can provide prognostic information beyond a single total score.
papers.authors: Dhup Bhukdee, Akarin Hiransuthikul, Sira Sriswasdi, Chaipat Chunharas

0112.name: Chaoxiong Ye
0112.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Education and Psychology
0112.bio: Chaoxiong Ye is an Academy Research Fellow and Principal Investigator at the University of Jyväskylä, where they lead research on the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual working memory (VWM). Ye's work utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potentials (ERP)—specifically the contralateral delay activity (CDA) component—alongside MEG and fMRI to investigate how attentional resources are allocated during VWM consolidation and maintenance. Ye examines how emotional valence, stimulus complexity, and individual differences in memory capacity influence the filtering of irrelevant information and the precision of stored representations. Their current research focus includes the spatio-temporal dynamics of memory processes and the interactions between long-term image memorability and short-term visual storage.
0112.research_direction: Dr. Ye's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying visual working memory, focusing particularly on how information is encoded, maintained, and protected from interference. Using behavioral change-detection tasks and EEG markers like contralateral delay activity, they have recently been investigating how intrinsic stimulus properties, such as image memorability, influence early perceptual encoding and memory formation. Their research also examines how working memory capacity is managed dynamically, probing how the perceptual grouping of identical objects alters maintenance load and how negative emotional states impact a person's ability to filter out visual distractors. Additionally, Dr. Ye explores the boundaries between memory systems, testing the conditions under which repeated visual feature bindings in short-term memory successfully transition into long-term episodic traces.

papers.title: Image memorability facilitates visual working memory formation: Evidence from contralateral delay activity
papers.abstract: Images that people reliably remember in the long run also seem to be held better in visual working memory, but a behavioral advantage could arise at encoding or merely at test comparison. Pairing a lateralized change-detection task with the contralateral delay activity, the authors show when memorability acts during working-memory formation. The results support that memorability boosts how visual information is established in working memory rather than only how it is compared later.
papers.authors: Chaoxiong Ye, Qianru Xu, Qiang Liu, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: When repeated presentation of visual feature bindings does and does not result in learning: Visual short-term and long-term memory are distinct but work in tandem
papers.abstract: Two experiments revisit why repeating the same six-item array many times in change detection yields little or no learning, unlike repetition tested by recall. The findings support a limited-capacity temporary visual cache plus a weak episodic trace that accumulates only under certain conditions. Short-term and long-term visual memory are distinct but cooperate.
papers.authors: Chaoxiong Ye, Qiang Liu, Robert H. Logie

papers.title: All identical objects reduce memory load at the late maintenance stage in working memory
papers.abstract: Grouping identical items may free up working-memory resources, but when this happens is unclear. Using the contralateral delay activity with all-same, partial-same and all-different orientation arrays, the study shows behavior improves as more items are identical. The neural load reduction emerges late during maintenance, not at encoding.
papers.authors: Lijing Guo, Hyung-Bum Park, Guofang Ren, Penglan Liu, Ruyi Liu, Dan Nie, Chaoxiong Ye

papers.title: Perceptual encoding benefit of visual memorability on visual memory formation
papers.abstract: Some images, such as certain faces, are remembered consistently across observers, but where in the memory pipeline this advantage arises is unclear. Across several experiments the authors show that memorable images are encoded more efficiently even under very brief presentation, which benefits short-term memory and carries over to later long-term retention. The work argues that memorability acts at early perceptual encoding.
papers.authors: Chaoxiong Ye, Lijing Guo, Nathan Wang, Qiang Liu, Weizhen Xie

papers.title: A negative emotional state impairs individuals' ability to filter distractors from working memory: an ERP study
papers.abstract: Working memory has limited capacity, so ignoring distractors matters. Recording EEG while participants performed a lateralized change-detection task with distractors after neutral or negative images, the authors find distractors harm accuracy in both states. ERP markers indicate that negative emotion specifically weakens the ability to filter distractors out of memory.
papers.authors: Chaoxiong Ye, Ruyi Liu, Lijing Guo, Guoying Zhao, Qiang Liu

0113.name: Charles E. Connor
0113.bio: Charles E. Connor is a Professor of Neuroscience and the Director of the Zanvyl Krieger Mind/Brain Institute at Johns Hopkins University. Connor’s research focuses on the neural algorithms that transform two-dimensional retinal images into three-dimensional representations of objects and environments. Through the study of population coding in the ventral visual pathway, specifically areas V4 and the inferotemporal cortex, their laboratory has identified how the brain encodes complex geometric configurations and structural relationships. Connor’s current work explores the integration of biological vision principles into deep neural networks and the development of neural coding strategies for visual prosthetics.
0113.research_direction: Dr. Connor has recently been working on how the primate ventral visual pathway turns retinal images into representations of object shape and structure. Their recent work reviews how 2D and 3D shape are coded across the visual hierarchy, emphasizing compression and population codes. They have also recorded from neurons in macaque inferotemporal cortex to ask how object representations remain stable when the image is partly occluded. Another thread asks how objects are represented relative to gravity, so that they look stable even when the head tilts and the retinal image rotates.

papers.title: How Shape Perception Works, in Two Dimensions and Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: A synthesis of empirical discoveries across the primate ventral visual processing hierarchy resolves how retinal afferents are transformed into rich structural representations underlying 2D planar and 3D volumetric shape perception. This review organizes ventral pathway computations around three essential computational objectives: extreme data compression to facilitate transmission through limited axonal bottlenecks and long-term consolidation in memory networks, explicit population coding to ensure high-level geometric features are linearly decodable by downstream cognitive and motor control centers, and representational invariance to preserve perceptual stability across substantial transformations in retinal perspective, illumination, and scale. We outline how the progressive cascade of receptive field properties across intermediate and late ventral cortex—spanning areas V1, V2, V4, and inferotemporal (IT) cortex—mechanistically satisfies these tripartite constraints, establishing a unified neural foundation for how primates compute continuous, high-fidelity structural shape.
papers.authors: Kristina J. Nielsen, Charles E. Connor

papers.title: An inferotemporal coding strategy robust to partial object occlusion
papers.abstract: Ventral stream visual coding is marked by hierarchical compression and increasing response sparseness, transitioning from local contour orientations in primary visual cortex (V1) to localized 2D/3D shape primitives in V4, and ultimately converging on complex multipart configurations in anterior inferotemporal cortex (AIT). Whether extensive visual familiarity drives this hierarchical trajectory to its logical extreme—yielding units dedicated exclusively to unique global objects—remains unresolved. To test this hypothesis, rhesus macaques were trained over several weeks on a delayed match-to-sample paradigm to categorize eight stylized, letter-like geometric stimuli, reaching >80% discrimination accuracy. Extracellular recordings in AIT revealed pronounced learning-induced enhancement in tuning for constituent multipart configurations characteristic of the trained symbols. Crucially, however, single units did not exhibit exclusive selectivity for intact, unique letters; instead, firing rates generalized robustly to novel, unlearned geometric constructs possessing the same sub-configurations. Although sub-maximal in terms of strict population sparseness, this multi-fragment configuration code provides an optimal trade-off for natural vision, offering intrinsic fault-tolerance against partial occlusion by allowing distinct subsets of diagnostic features to independently trigger robust whole-object classification.
papers.authors: Andrew Cheng, Sach Sokol, Charles E Connor

papers.title: Object representation in a gravitational reference frame
papers.abstract: During lateral head roll, ocular counter-rolling compensates for less than 20% of rotational displacement, exposing the retina to image rotations spanning up to 180°, despite an enduring perceptual stability of environmental objects. Investigating the neurophysiological mechanisms mediating this rotational invariance, single-unit recordings were conducted in macaque anterior inferotemporal (IT) cortex while animals performed fixation during ±25° lateral whole-body tilts, generating an approximately 40° shift in retinal orientation. Among neurons exhibiting defined 3D object orientation preferences, 63% preserved their tuning within an allocentric, gravity-referenced coordinate system rather than an egocentric retinotopic frame. Experiments modulating multisensory and contextual inputs demonstrated that this gravitational alignment relies jointly on visual scene context (such as ground-plane orientation) as well as vestibular and somatosensory signals. Constructing an internal gravitational reference frame at the terminal stage of the ventral processing stream provides not only perceptual compensation for viewer posture but also the essential mechanical coordinate space required for intuitive physical reasoning regarding equilibrium, stability, and dynamics in terrestrial environments.
papers.authors: Alexandriya M X Emonds, Ramanujan Srinath, Kristina J Nielsen, Charles E Connor

0114.name: Chaz Firestone
0114.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0114.bio: Chaz Firestone is an Associate Professor at Johns Hopkins University and directs the Perception & Mind Laboratory. Their research investigates the interface between visual perception and higher-level cognition, focusing on the functional architecture of the mind and the degree to which what is seen is influenced by what is known. Firestone’s work evaluates the evidence for top-down effects of cognition on perception and includes the study of topics such as the perception of absences, physical intuitions, and the representation of objects and events. They employ a multi-methodological approach involving psychophysics, computational modeling, and philosophical analysis to characterize the mechanisms of human vision.
0114.research_direction: Dr. Firestone's recent work explores how high-level cognitive and semantic properties intersect with basic perceptual processing. They have recently been investigating whether abstract features, such as artistic style or cross-modal information density, are extracted as fundamental perceptual quantities using classic psychophysics and reward-transfer paradigms. To determine if high-level properties like animacy directly drive perception rather than just covarying with low-level image features, their research leverages diffusion-generated visual anagrams whose semantic identities change depending on spatial orientation. Furthermore, Dr. Firestone is broadly examining the boundaries and metrics of perceptual processing, from re-evaluating historical cross-cultural data to test if the Müller-Lyer illusion is truly shaped by environmental experience, to investigating whether the physical duration of a keypress can serve as an implicit behavioral measure of subjective confidence across diverse tasks.

papers.title: Complexity is a unified cognitive kind
papers.abstract: Asks whether complexity in images, melodies, letter strings, math expressions and touch is represented by one shared cognitive quantity. Eleven experiments (N about 1500) find that reward learned for complex items transfers across very different stimulus types, intrudes automatically on unrelated judgments, and tracks individual differences in preferences across domains. This suggests a domain-general representation of information density.
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Response duration tracks confidence
papers.abstract: Beyond how quickly one responds, this work shows that how long a key is held down predicts subjective confidence, over and above initiation time. Three preregistered experiments spanning face detection, motion coherence judgments and trivia questions find longer holds for less confident responses. Response duration is proposed as a cheap implicit measure of confidence.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Hanbei Zhou, Rui Zhe Goh, Ian Phillips, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: The psychophysics of style
papers.abstract: Treats style perception, such as recognizing a Monet-like rendering of a pond, as a process that separates form from content, and applies classic psychophysical paradigms to it. Ten experiments with natural and synthetic images show perceptual tuning to stylistic information, constancy of object representations across styles, and mental rendering of novel objects in a given style. An object-recognition model also captures human similarity judgments across styles.
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Visual anagrams reveal high-level effects with 'identical' stimuli
papers.abstract: High-level properties like animacy or real-world size usually covary with low-level image features, so effects attributed to them may be confounds. The authors use diffusion-generated visual anagrams, images whose identity changes with orientation, to vary high-level content while keeping the pixels essentially identical. This offers a general method for testing whether high-level properties themselves drive perception.
papers.authors: Tal Boger, Chaz Firestone

papers.title: Is visual perception WEIRD? The Müller-Lyer illusion and the cultural byproduct hypothesis
papers.abstract: Re-examines the influential claim that susceptibility to the Müller-Lyer illusion is a product of carpentered-world experience that varies across cultures. The paper critically evaluates the century-old cross-cultural evidence and tests the cultural byproduct hypothesis. It bears on how far culture shapes basic visual processing.
papers.authors: Dorsa Amir, Chaz Firestone

0116.name: Cheryl Olman
0116.lab_name: Olman Laboratory for Imaging and Vision
0116.bio: Cheryl Olman is a researcher at the University of Minnesota specializing in high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and visual neuroscience. Olman utilizes ultra-high-field (7T) imaging and visual psychophysics to investigate how the human brain processes local image features to construct global representations of scenes and objects. Their research explores the laminar organization of the early visual cortex to differentiate between feedforward and feedback computations while examining biophysical links between BOLD signal dynamics and excitatory/inhibitory neural activity. Olman also investigates clinical applications, focusing on how visual perceptual context and neural connectivity are altered in individuals with psychotic disorders.
0116.research_direction: Dr. Olman's recent work explores how spatial context and top-down signals shape neural representations within the human visual system. Using ultra-high-resolution 7T fMRI, they have recently been investigating the depth-resolved laminar profiles of contextual modulation in primary visual cortex to disentangle the specific lateral and feedback pathways underlying surround suppression and figure-ground segregation. In parallel, their research examines the mechanistic basis of perceptual deficits in the schizophrenia spectrum, combining psychophysics and neuroimaging to test whether impaired contrast suppression arises from local gain control anomalies in early visual cortex or from disrupted priors in higher-order areas like the lateral occipital complex. Finally, their work with clinical populations extends to reading speed and visual deficits in veterans with mild traumatic brain injury, linking behavioral measures to the integrity of cerebral white matter.

papers.title: Orientation-tuned surround suppression exhibits a unique laminar signature in the human primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using 0.6 mm isotropic 7T fMRI, the authors examined how BOLD signal varies across cortical depth in V1 while people viewed grating disks embedded in surround gratings with different orientation and segmentation cues. Because feedforward, feedback and lateral pathways have distinct laminar profiles, the depth-resolved responses let them infer which pathway supports each kind of contextual modulation. Orientation-tuned suppression showed a laminar signature distinct from other forms of contextual modulation, pointing to specific intracortical circuits.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Joseph H. Emerson, Karen T. Navarro, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Reading speed, visual deficits, and cerebral white matter integrity in veterans with and without mild traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Diffusion imaging and behavioral/survey data from 63 combat veterans with and without mild TBI were analyzed for links between white matter damage and visual function. Convergence insufficiency symptom scores predicted whether a color overlay boosted reading speed in the mTBI group, and smooth-pursuit catch-up saccades related to counts of white matter potholes. The sample was too small to attribute these correlations uniquely to TBI, motivating further work.
papers.authors: Kori E. Skrypek, Philip C. Burton, Nicholas D. Davenport, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Orientation-dependent contextual modulation of contrast in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: The study used high-field fMRI and a new perceptual task to test whether weakened contextual modulation of perceived contrast in schizophrenia arises from mechanisms within V1 or from influences outside it. Participants with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, their unaffected relatives and healthy controls viewed center stimuli with near and far surrounds of matched or different orientation. BOLD responses and behavior were compared across groups to dissociate local gain-control anomalies from extrinsic input.
papers.authors: Victor J. Pokorny, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Surround Suppression of Broadband Images
papers.abstract: Most contrast surround suppression studies use narrowband sinusoidal gratings, leaving open whether the findings hold for naturalistic input. The authors built a contrast discrimination paradigm using both naturalistic broadband textures and gratings to compare suppression across stimulus types. The work tests how well grating-based accounts of contextual modulation generalize to real-world visual statistics.
papers.authors: Victor J. Pokorny, Kimberly B. Weldon, Cheryl A. Olman

papers.title: Weakened untuned gain control is associated with schizophrenia while atypical orientation-tuned suppression depends on visual acuity
papers.abstract: Weakened contrast surround suppression has been proposed as a mechanism for perceptual distortions in psychosis. By manipulating only the relative orientation of matched-contrast center and surround, the authors isolated orientation-dependent suppression from contrast-difference cues. Schizophrenia was linked to weaker untuned gain control, whereas atypical orientation-tuned suppression tracked visual acuity rather than diagnosis.
papers.authors: Victor J. Pokorny, Michael-Paul Schallmo, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman

0117.name: Chia-Huei Tseng
0117.bio: Chia-Huei Tseng is an Associate Professor who integrates psychophysics, neurophysiology, and computational modeling to investigate human cognitive functions. Tseng’s work focuses on the mechanisms of visual attention, implicit learning, and interpersonal nonverbal communication. They utilize methodologies such as steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) and EEG to map neural synchrony and "team flow" states. Research topics also include infant development, the creation of digital biomarkers for detecting cognitive decline, and the study of humanness recognition in robotic motion and human-computer interaction.
0117.research_direction: Dr. Tseng's recent work explores a diverse intersection of fundamental visual processing, multisensory development, and social cognition. They have recently been investigating the neural frameworks underlying local-to-global visual integration via "Gestalt neurons," alongside developmental studies testing how preverbal infants utilize cross-modal audiovisual congruence to learn abstract rules. In the realm of social perception, their research probes how human observers and neural networks decode embodied interpersonal intentions from whole-body kinematics, while also employing identity-shape matching paradigms to quantify implicit social bonding. Additionally, Dr. Tseng is extending these perceptual and cognitive principles into applied human-computer interaction by designing augmented reality tools to support mindfulness and cultural practices.

papers.title: Friend or Foe? Benchmarking Human Perception and ST-GCN Decoding of Embodied Social Intention
papers.abstract: Compares how people and a spatio-temporal graph convolutional network read friendly versus hostile intent from whole-body motion captured from performers. The work benchmarks human perceivers, including across cultures, against the machine decoder to see where social meaning in movement is recoverable and where the two diverge. It extends the group's motion-capture emotion database toward interpersonal, social-intent signals.
papers.venue: 2026 IEEE 20th International Conference on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG)
papers.authors: Miao Cheng, Zhan Dai, Victor Schneider, Kanta Ozawa, Yangyang Cai, Ken Fujiwara, Yoshifumi Kitamura, Chia-Huei Tseng

papers.title: HanaARrange: Designing an Augmented Reality Support System for Daily Ikebana Practice and Well-being
papers.abstract: Presents an augmented-reality tool that supports people in arranging flowers in the ikebana tradition as an everyday well-being practice. The system is designed around the experience of the practice itself, combining AR guidance with considerations of mindfulness and cultural craft. It shows the group extending its perception and social-cognition work into applied human-computer interaction.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS)
papers.authors: Xiyue Wang, Zeynep Eda Altintop, Derek Kirschbaum, Miao Cheng, Yoshifumi Kitamura, Chiahuei Tseng

papers.title: Social bonding through expressed needs: Insights from an identity-shape matching task
papers.abstract: Uses an identity-shape matching paradigm to test whether people form closer social bonds with others who express needs. The experiments probe implicit self-other association as a marker of bonding. The results link interpersonal expression of need to measurable changes in social binding.
papers.authors: Su-Ling Yeh, Ti-Fan Hung, Te-Yi Hsieh, Chia-Huei Tseng

papers.title: Social and communicative not a prerequisite: Preverbal infants learn an abstract rule only from congruent audiovisual dynamic pitch-height patterns
papers.abstract: Tests whether preverbal infants can learn an abstract rule from sequences of rising and falling pitch paired with matching visual motion. Infants learned the rule only when the sound and visual movement were congruent, and social or communicative cues were not required. This indicates that cross-modal congruence itself supports early abstract learning.
papers.authors: Hiu Mei Chow, Yuen Ki Ma, Chia-huei Tseng

papers.title: Gestalt neurons and emergent properties in visual perception: A novel concept for the transformation from local to global processing
papers.abstract: Proposes that specialized visual neurons integrate local signals into whole, emergent percepts, updating classic Gestalt principles with neurophysiological evidence. It reviews perceptual phenomena where global structure cannot be predicted from parts and links them to candidate cortical mechanisms. The paper offers a framework for the local-to-global transformation in vision.
papers.authors: Lothar Spillmann, Li-Chuan Hsu, Wei Wang, Chien-Chung Chen, Chun-I Yeh, Chia-Huei Tseng

0119.name: Chien-Chung Chen
0119.bio: Chien-Chung Chen is a Distinguished Professor at National Taiwan University and directs the Visual Neuroscience Laboratory. Their research utilizes a multidisciplinary approach combining psychophysical experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to investigate human visual processing. Chen’s work focuses on contrast discrimination, lateral inhibitory interactions in the primary visual cortex, and the neural representation of complex forms such as faces and symmetry. Currently, they examine the integration of spatial information and the role of feedback mechanisms in visual attention and object identification.
0119.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating how the visual system extracts and organizes complex spatial information, exploring higher-order pattern perception through studies on spatial pooling and symmetry. Using psychophysical masking and divisive-inhibition modeling, they are probing suprathreshold length summation for elongated features, while also examining how robust symmetry percepts can emerge from surface structure cues without strict point-to-point element matching. Their recent work also spans the dynamics and spatial constraints of form perception, measuring visual field asymmetries during the identification of complex Chinese characters and using eye-tracking to investigate how targeted fixation shifts drive perceptual reversals in bistable figures. Finally, they have been applying these core psychophysical principles to machine vision, analyzing failures of perceptual organization—such as errors in lightness anchoring and figure-ground segregation—to understand why autonomous vehicles sometimes fail to detect massive, salient obstacles.

papers.title: Varieties of higher-order symmetry
papers.abstract: The paper argues that symmetry can be perceived without any point-to-point correspondence between image elements. Symmetric modulation of random-dot carriers (via density, orientation statistics, dot-pair statistics, disparity or motion flow) yields robust symmetry percepts, which the authors call second-order symmetry. This challenges element-matching models of symmetry detection and suggests the visual system first infers surface structure before assessing symmetry.
papers.authors: Chien-Chung Chen, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Sensation without perception: The white whale effect and perceptual blindness in autonomous vehicles
papers.abstract: The authors examine why autonomous vehicles with sensors exceeding human capability still fail to detect large white obstacles such as semi-trailers against bright skies. They propose a 'white whale effect', framing these crashes as failures of perceptual organization (lightness anchoring, figure-ground segregation, global motion) rather than of sensor range. They argue safer machine vision needs architectures constrained by psychophysical principles.
papers.authors: Philip Tseng, Chien-Chung Chen

papers.title: Eye-movement patterns for perceiving bistable figures
papers.abstract: Using eye tracking during viewing of the duck/rabbit figure and the Necker cube, the study shows that fixation patterns differ between the two percepts and that fixation shifts precede perceptual reversals. Manipulating an inward bias and masking the attended region shows that changing local saliency can trigger fixation shifts and flip the percept, with inhibition of return as a candidate mechanism. The results indicate that what is perceived depends on where one looks.
papers.authors: Yi-Hsuan Hsu, Chien-Chung Chen

papers.title: Visual field asymmetries in visual word form identification
papers.abstract: Acuity thresholds for identifying traditional Chinese characters were measured along horizontal and vertical meridians from fovea to 8 degrees eccentricity at four contrast levels, monocularly and binocularly. Asymmetries were strongest along the vertical and superior visual field, and the cortical magnification factor was smaller vertically than horizontally and smaller in the upper than lower field. Low contrast and monocular viewing enlarged these meridian differences.
papers.authors: Li-Ting Tsai, Kuo-Meng Liao, Chiun-Ho Hou, Yuh Jang, Chien-Chung Chen

papers.title: Suprathreshold length summation
papers.abstract: Detection thresholds for elongated Gabor targets were measured with iso-orientation and orthogonal pattern masks. Without a strong mask thresholds showed the classic ideal-summation regime, but a high-contrast iso-orientation mask abolished it and revealed an additional very long channel. A divisive-inhibition model with second-order filters pooling local oriented channels plus a single extra-long filter (300 arcmin or more) accounts for the data.
papers.authors: Chien-Chung Chen, Chia-Hua Chien, Christopher W. Tyler

0121.name: Chris Baker
0121.institution: National Institute of Mental Health, National Institutes of Health
0121.department: Laboratory of Brain and Cognition (Section on Learning and Plasticity)
0121.bio: Chris I. Baker is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Unit on Learning and Plasticity within the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Baker’s research examines the neural mechanisms of object recognition and the ways in which experience and learning reshape cortical representations in the adult brain. Utilizing high-resolution functional MRI and behavioral psychophysics, they investigate how the human brain processes complex stimuli such as faces, scenes, and words. Baker’s work also explores the extent of cortical reorganization following sensory loss or neural damage to study the brain's adaptive capacity throughout life.
0121.research_direction: Dr. Baker's recent work investigates how the human brain represents and remembers complex visual objects and naturalistic events. To study the spatial and temporal dynamics of object recognition, they have recently been utilizing large-scale multimodal datasets—combining fMRI, MEG, and behavioral judgments—to map how multidimensional object properties are encoded over time. Their recent work also explores the theoretical foundations of the visual system, questioning whether the visual cortex is organized by strict object categories or by behaviorally relevant features. Additionally, Dr. Baker is examining the intersection of vision, action, and memory by investigating how physical interactions with real-world objects modulate subsequent neural responses to 2D images, and how eye movements and neural activity are jointly reinstated during the recall of complex narratives.

papers.title: Dynamic Representation of Multidimensional Object Properties in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: Using MEG responses from four people viewing tens of thousands of object images, the authors track how a rich set of behavior-derived object dimensions is encoded over time. Multiple dimensions become decodable within a few hundred milliseconds, with distinct timing profiles, showing that object representations are multidimensional and dynamic rather than a single category label.
papers.authors: Lina Teichmann, Martin N. Hebart, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Neural and behavioral reinstatement jointly reflect retrieval of narrative events
papers.abstract: Participants watched a narrative movie and later recalled its events while fMRI and eye movements were recorded. Gaze patterns during recall reinstated those from viewing, and this behavioral reinstatement covaried with neural reinstatement across the brain, suggesting that eye movements and neural activity reflect a common retrieval process.
papers.authors: Matthias Nau, Austin Greene, Hannah Tarder-Stoll, Juan Antonio Lossio-Ventura, Francisco Pereira, Janice Chen, Christopher Baldassano, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Rethinking category-selectivity in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: This theoretical paper questions the standard interpretation of category-selective regions (faces, scenes, bodies, tools) as being organized by object category. The authors review evidence and argue that selectivity is better understood in terms of behaviorally relevant visual features and demands, and outline how future work could test this.
papers.authors: J. Brendan Ritchie, Susan G. Wardle, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam, Dwight J. Kravitz, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Brief Encounters with Real Objects Modulate the Medial Parietal But Not Occipitotemporal Cortex
papers.abstract: Forty participants briefly handled everyday objects and then viewed photographs of those objects during fMRI. Object-selective lateral occipital and ventral temporal regions were largely unaffected, whereas medial parietal cortex showed altered responses to the previously handled items, indicating that brief real-world experience reshapes how photos are represented outside classic visual areas.
papers.authors: Susan G. Wardle, Beth Rispoli, Vinai Roopchansingh, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: THINGS-data, a multimodal collection of large-scale datasets for investigating object representations in human brain and behavior
papers.abstract: This resource paper releases a large, openly shared dataset built around the THINGS object image database. It combines densely sampled fMRI and MEG recordings with millions of behavioral similarity judgments covering up to 1,854 object concepts. The authors validate data quality and illustrate how the data can be used to study how the brain and behavior represent objects, providing a community benchmark for object-recognition research.
papers.authors: Martin N Hebart, Oliver Contier, Lina Teichmann, Adam H Rockter, Charles Y Zheng, Alexis Kidder, Anna Corriveau, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam, Chris I Baker

0122.name: Christian H. Poth
0122.department: Faculty of Health and Sport, Professorship of General Psychology
0122.bio: Christian H. Poth is a Professor of General Psychology whose research examines the functional links between visual perception, attention, and oculomotor control. Poth investigates how internal states such as urgency and phasic alertness modulate cognitive control, demonstrating that high-pressure situations can prompt stimulus-driven actions that override goal-directed behavior. Using high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and computational modeling, Poth develops experimental assessments for basic vision science and clinical neuropsychology. This research includes the application of head-mounted displays for diagnostic processing.
0122.research_direction: Dr. Poth has recently been investigating the cognitive and temporal mechanisms that govern our readiness for perception and action. Their recent work explores the nature of phasic alertness and cognitive control, using varying warning signal probabilities and conflict paradigms—such as spatial and numerical Stroop tasks—to test whether alertness relies on top-down expectations and how severe time pressure influences stimulus-driven responses. In the domain of visual processing, they are examining the temporal thresholds of conscious object recognition, utilizing masking paradigms and varying exposure durations to investigate whether the visual system extracts an object's spatial location earlier and faster than its feature identity. Additionally, their research touches on the subjective dimensions of physiological arousal, analyzing self-report data to understand how distinct low-arousal states like momentary sleepiness and relaxation relate to one another across different contexts.

papers.title: Phasic Alertness Requires Top-Down Target Expectations
papers.abstract: Tests the common assumption that phasic alertness is purely bottom-up and stimulus-driven. In two experiments with an auditory alert preceding a choice task, alerts predicted a target on 90% or 10% of trials in separate sessions. The speed-up in choice reactions from alerting appeared only when the alert predicted a target, showing that alertness benefits depend partly on top-down expectations.
papers.authors: Christian H. Poth, Nik Dietze

papers.title: Readiness for Perception and Action: Towards a More Mechanistic Understanding of Phasic Alertness
papers.abstract: Reviews how warning signals put the brain into a state of readiness for upcoming perception and action, and argues that despite abundant behavioural evidence the underlying cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. Identifies four open problems: how readiness is established as a cognitive state, whether it acts online or offline, whether it can be triggered internally without a warning, and how far it relies on bottom-up versus top-down temporal or stimulus expectations. Lays out a research program for mechanistic and computational models of phasic alertness and its neural basis.
papers.authors: Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Urgency enforces stimulus-driven action across spatial and numerical cognitive control tasks
papers.abstract: Earlier work showed that time pressure creates a window in which responses are dominated by stimulus features over task goals, but only with arrow stimuli. This study shows the same urgency effect in a spatial Stroop task with words, a numerical Stroop task, and a Simon task, where performance fell below chance on conflict trials early in the window. The results indicate that urgency compromises cognitive control in a general way rather than only for arrows.
papers.authors: Anika Krause, Christian H. Poth

papers.title: Vision of objects happens faster and earlier for location than for identity
papers.abstract: Asks whether an object's location and its identity are processed with equal efficiency for conscious report. Participants saw a target letter at one of several masked locations and reported its position and/or identity across varying exposure durations, allowing estimates of processing speed and minimum onset time. Location was processed faster and started earlier than identity, even though the two features were processed independently, pointing to an intrinsic priority of space in human vision.
papers.authors: Christian H. Poth, Werner X. Schneider

papers.title: Feeling tired versus feeling relaxed: Two faces of low physiological arousal
papers.abstract: Meta-analyses several datasets that used the Relaxation State Questionnaire to examine how momentary sleepiness and relaxation relate. Before an intervention the two states were reliably anti-correlated, dissociating them as distinct subjective states despite both reflecting low arousal. After interventions the negative relation was not consistent, suggesting that context or intervention alters their dynamics.
papers.authors: Sarah Steghaus, Christian H. Poth

0123.name: Christian Vater
0123.bio: Christian Vater is an Assistant Professor at the University of Bern and leads the Peripheral Vision Group within the Institute of Sport Science. Vater’s research characterizes the functionality of peripheral vision in high-demand, time-constrained environments such as competitive sports, driving, and aviation. They utilize experimental methodologies including eye-tracking, behavioral analysis, and virtual reality to investigate mechanisms like gaze anchoring, multiple object tracking, and the integration of foveal and peripheral information. Recent research contributions focus on the ecological validity of perceptual-cognitive training tools and the cognitive trade-offs involved in visual information pick-up during dynamic motor tasks.
0123.research_direction: Dr. Vater has recently been investigating how humans use visual information—particularly peripheral vision—to make decisions and navigate within complex, dynamic environments. Their recent work explores the perceptual and cognitive constraints of athletic performance, using immersive CAVE and virtual reality setups to test how visual eccentricity, viewing angle, crowding, and anxiety influence the real-time decision-making of basketball players and football referees. Beyond the sporting domain, they are extending their research on gaze behavior into broader spatial cognition, examining the visual strategies and navigation patterns that characterize efficient indoor wayfinding in virtual everyday spaces. Across these distinct lines of inquiry, they combine motion and eye-tracking methodologies with highly representative tasks to probe how fundamental visual processing limits interact with skill and situational context in ecologically valid settings.

papers.title: Don't get lost in the mall! Characteristics of efficient wayfinding and gaze behavior
papers.abstract: Participants navigated a large multi-level virtual shopping mall while their gaze was tracked, and efficient wayfinders were compared with inefficient ones. The work identifies gaze and navigation behaviours that distinguish successful from poor route finding in complex indoor environments. It extends the group's gaze research from sport into spatial cognition and everyday navigation.
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Panos Mavros, Jiayan Zhao, Cecile Abati, Christoph Holscher

papers.title: Peripheral Vision in Sport
papers.abstract: Book chapter reviewing what is known about how athletes use peripheral vision, including gaze anchors, visual pivots and eccentricity effects. It synthesises lab and field evidence on when peripheral information is used in sport decisions. Written for the Gaze and Visual Perception in Sport volume.
papers.venue: Gaze and Visual Perception in Sport (Routledge)
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Bozo Vukojevic, A. Mark Williams

papers.title: Viewing angle, skill level and task representativeness affect response times in basketball defence
papers.abstract: Single-author study using a CAVE with motion tracking to test how well high- and low-skilled basketball players use peripheral vision when defending. Response times were measured for stimuli up to 90 degrees to the left and right, with and without crowding, in simple reaction, choice reaction and game-simulation tasks. Responses slowed with eccentricity and differed by skill and task realism, showing that peripheral vision use depends on how representative the task is of real play.
papers.authors: Christian Vater

papers.title: That was a foul! How viewing angles, viewing distances, and visualization methods influence football referees' decision-making
papers.abstract: Football referees judged fouls in recreated real-life situations, rendered from a first-person view using markerless tracking and VR animation. Viewing distance, viewing angle and the way the scene was visualised were varied experimentally while the game context stayed fixed. The results show how referee position and presentation medium shape foul decisions.
papers.venue: German Journal of Exercise and Sport Research
papers.authors: Christian Vater, Urs Schnyder, Daniel Muller

papers.title: The role of peripheral vision during decision-making in dynamic viewing sequences
papers.abstract: Experienced basketball players viewed 4v4 defensive scenarios in a head-mounted display and stepped toward opponents threatening the basket from different eccentricities. Pressure and a working-memory load were manipulated to see how anxiety and eccentricity affect decisions and gaze. Players were slower and less accurate at larger eccentricities and under high pressure, supporting limits on peripheral processing in dynamic tasks.
papers.authors: Brady S. DeCouto, Brad Fawver, Joe L. Thomas, A. Mark Williams, Christian Vater

0124.name: Christian Wallraven
0124.bio: Christian Wallraven is a Professor at Korea University whose research synthesizes computer vision, computer graphics, and cognitive neuroscience to investigate the computational principles of human perception. Wallraven’s work utilizes immersive extended reality (XR) environments and neuroimaging modalities like fMRI and EEG to explore processes such as social face recognition, multisensory integration of vision and touch, and decision-making in high-risk scenarios. By comparing human cognitive strategies with machine learning models, Wallraven develops frameworks for human-AI alignment and creates biologically inspired artificial systems for use in robotics, computer animation, and clinical applications.
0124.research_direction: Dr. Wallraven has recently been investigating the intersection of human visual cognition, artificial intelligence, and neuroimaging. Their recent work explores human-AI attentional alignment by using eye-tracking and virtual reality to compare human gaze with the spatial attention of vision models during dynamic tasks like driving accident anticipation. In a related strand of research on explainable AI, they are examining scalable robustness metrics to evaluate the clinical relevance of model saliency maps in medical imaging without relying on costly expert annotations. Additionally, they are probing brain-computer interfaces and social decision-making, leveraging EEG recordings to decode neural markers of spontaneous deception while rigorously testing whether standard artifact removal techniques are actually necessary for the deep network decoding of neural signals.

papers.title: Mind the Gap: Quantifying and Aligning Human-AI Visual Attention for Accident Anticipation
papers.abstract: The authors build Attention-DADA, a traffic-scene dataset with human accident predictions and frame-level eye-gaze recordings. They use it to test how closely current vision-language models attend to the same scene regions as people when anticipating accidents. The work quantifies the attention gap and proposes ways to bring model attention closer to human gaze.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-26)
papers.authors: Hoe Sung Ryu, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Establishing the robustness metric as a scalable proxy for clinical relevance in medical AI explainability
papers.abstract: The study examines how to evaluate explanation (saliency) methods for medical imaging models at scale without costly expert annotation. It argues that a robustness-based metric can serve as a proxy for how clinically relevant an explanation is. This connects the lab's human-AI alignment interests to clinical AI.
papers.authors: Daehyun Cho, Sung-Hye You, Bo Kyu Kim, Arim Park, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: Seeing What Matters: Attentional (Mis-) Alignment Between Humans and AI in VR-Simulated Prediction of Driving Accidents
papers.abstract: Participants predicted accidents in virtual-reality driving simulations while their gaze was tracked, and their attention was compared with that of computer-vision models. The study reveals where human and machine attention diverge in dynamic risky scenes. It ties together the lab's VR, eye-tracking and human-AI alignment strands.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Hoe Sung Ryu, Uijong Ju, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: An EEG Dataset of Neural Signatures in a Competitive Two-Player Game Encouraging Deceptive Behavior
papers.abstract: The paper releases EEG recordings from pairs of participants playing a competitive card game designed to elicit spontaneous, genuine deception rather than instructed lying. The dataset includes role switching and behavioral labels so others can study neural markers of deceptive decisions. It is intended as a resource for decoding social decision-making.
papers.authors: Yiyu Chen, Siamac Fazli, Christian Wallraven

papers.title: I see artifacts: ICA-based EEG artifact removal does not improve deep network decoding across three BCI tasks
papers.abstract: The authors test whether removing noise components via independent component analysis helps neural-network decoding of EEG. Across three brain-computer-interface task datasets and several decomposition methods, cleaning did not improve and sometimes did not matter for classifier accuracy. The result questions a routine preprocessing step for deep decoding.
papers.authors: Taeho Kang, Yiyu Chen, Christian Wallraven

0125.name: Christian Windischberger
0125.department: Center for Medical Physics and Biomedical Engineering
0125.bio: Christian Windischberger is an Associate Professor of Medical Physics at the Medical University of Vienna and directs research on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technologies. Windischberger’s methodology involves high-resolution ultra-high-field (7T) imaging and the development of concurrent transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and fMRI systems to map and modulate human brain networks. Within vision science, Windischberger utilizes population receptive field (pRF) mapping to study the functional organization of the visual cortex and investigate retinotopic changes associated with macular and retinal diseases. Their research characterizes brain connectivity and state-dependency to develop personalized, image-guided neurostimulation protocols for clinical applications.
0125.research_direction: Dr. Windischberger has recently been developing advanced methodological tools for both visual neuroimaging and non-invasive neuromodulation. In the visual domain, their recent work explores ways to accelerate and optimize population receptive field (pRF) mapping, using novel GPU-empowered algorithms and large-scale computational simulations to study estimate variability and evaluate fMRI visual stimulation paradigms. Alongside this retinotopic mapping research, they are utilizing concurrent and interleaved TMS-fMRI to map individual neural dose-response patterns and track how acute prefrontal cortex stimulation drives brain-wide network dynamics. Furthermore, Dr. Windischberger is investigating the physical delivery of these transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) interventions by designing real-time motion compensation algorithms that dynamically adjust stimulator output to maintain stable electric fields across the cortex during prolonged treatment sessions.

papers.title: Computational simulations reproduce in vivo population receptive field mapping fMRI results
papers.abstract: Using their GEMSim-pRF framework, the authors generate millions of synthetic fMRI time courses over wide ranges of receptive-field parameters and noise levels to study why pRF estimates vary between runs and subjects. Simulated variability matches the eccentricity-dependent pattern seen in the public NYU Retinotopy Dataset. The work supports simulation as a practical way to evaluate and optimise visual stimulation paradigms before data collection.
papers.authors: Siddharth Mittal, Michael Woletz, David Linhardt, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: Reducing target E-field variability in repetitive TMS through online motion compensation
papers.abstract: Coil movement during long rTMS sessions changes the electric field reaching the cortical target. Tracking coil position continuously across 200 sessions in 20 patients with major depression, the authors show variability is driven mainly by scalp-normal displacement and rotation. They then introduce a real-time algorithm that adjusts stimulator output from precomputed E-fields, substantially reducing the variability at the target.
papers.authors: Sarah Grosshagauer, Michael Woletz, Marlen Becher, Jonas Björklund, Frank Padberg, Daniel Keeser, Lucia Bulubas, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: GEM-pRF: GPU-empowered mapping of population receptive fields for large-scale fMRI analysis
papers.abstract: Population receptive field mapping is the standard way to chart retinotopic organisation with fMRI, but its iterative parameter refinement makes it slow on large datasets. The authors reformulate the general linear model by orthogonalising the design matrix so that derivatives of the objective can be computed directly, removing the iterative step, and implement this on GPUs. Validated on empirical and simulated data, the tool matches established accuracy while cutting computation time by nearly two orders of magnitude.
papers.authors: Siddharth Mittal, Michael Woletz, David Linhardt, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: Concurrent TMS/fMRI reveals individual DLPFC dose-response pattern
papers.abstract: Fifteen participants received left DLPFC stimulation at 80, 90, 100 and 110 percent of motor threshold inside the scanner while whole-brain BOLD responses were recorded. At group level the strongest response occurred at 100 percent, yet individuals differed markedly, with some responding to subthreshold stimulation and others needing suprathreshold intensity. The results argue for individualised dosing in TMS treatments.
papers.authors: Martin Tik, Maria Vasileiadi, Michael Woletz, David Linhardt, Anna-Lisa Schuler, Nolan Williams, Christian Windischberger

papers.title: Acute TMS/fMRI response explains offline TMS network effects - An interleaved TMS-fMRI study
papers.abstract: Using interleaved TMS/fMRI with purpose-built head coils, the study maps networks activated acutely by left DLPFC stimulation. The acute BOLD activation pattern overlaps a resting-state network previously shown to change after offline TMS, including anterior cingulate regions. This suggests a causal link between DLPFC stimulation and network engagement relevant to depression treatment.
papers.authors: Martin Tik, Michael Woletz, Anna-Lisa Schuler, Maria Vasileiadi, Robin F. H. Cash, Andrew Zalesky, Claus Lamm, Christian Windischberger

0126.name: Christoph Bledowski
0126.bio: Christoph Bledowski is an apl. Professor at the Institute of Medical Psychology, Goethe University Frankfurt, where they investigate the functional and neuronal architecture of human working memory. Bledowski’s research utilizes a multimodal approach, combining behavioral psychophysics with fMRI, EEG, and MEG to delineate the neural systems responsible for mnemonic operations such as selection, updating, and feature binding. They have demonstrated the neuroanatomical dissociation between attentional focusing and mnemonic retrieval within frontoparietal and sensory networks. Bledowski’s current research programs focus on the neural representation of feature bindings in visual and auditory domains, the mechanisms of serial dependence across memory episodes, and the impact of cognitive interference on memory precision.
0126.research_direction: Dr. Bledowski has recently been studying how the brain holds information in visual and auditory working memory and what disturbs it. Their recent work explores serial dependence, the tendency for what we just saw to bias what we report next, asking whether a neural signature of that bias can be seen directly in brain activity recorded with magnetoencephalography. They have also been examining whether the memory contents stored in auditory cortex can withstand distracting sounds, and how items kept in memory for different tasks interfere with one another. Together this work probes how working memory representations are stored, updated, and disrupted.

papers.title: A direct neural signature of serial dependence in working memory
papers.abstract: While behavioral reports exhibit an attractive bias toward previous stimuli (serial dependence), identifying a direct neural correlate has proven challenging, with previous research often showing repulsive adaptation. This study utilized magnetoencephalography (MEG) and multivariate inverted encoding models to reconstruct motion-direction representations during a visual working memory task. Reconstructions of currently remembered features showed an attractive shift toward the target direction of the preceding trial, specifically during the post-encoding retro-cue delay period. This neural shift directly predicted single-trial behavioral report errors. The results provide the first evidence for a neural signature of serial dependence and suggest that attractive biases emerge at late processing stages, likely during the readout or reactivation of memory traces rather than during initial sensory encoding.
papers.authors: Cora Fischer, Jochen Kaiser, Christoph Bledowski

papers.title: Decoding of Working Memory Contents in Auditory Cortex Is Not Distractor-Resistant
papers.authors: Deutsch, Czoschke, Fischer, Kaiser, Bledowski

papers.title: Interference between items stored for distinct tasks in visual working memory
papers.authors: Czoschke, Peters, Kaiser, Bledowski

0127.name: Christopher DiMattina
0127.bio: Christopher DiMattina is a Professor of Psychology at Florida Gulf Coast University and directs the Computational Perception Laboratory. DiMattina’s research investigates the information processing mechanisms of biological sensory systems, focusing on mid-level vision, perceptual organization, and the neural basis of visual aesthetics and discomfort. They employ a methodology that integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and machine learning to analyze how the visual system classifies natural image features. This research includes distinguishing shadows from surface boundaries and segmenting complex textures.
0127.research_direction: Dr. DiMattina has recently been investigating how the visual system carves up natural images into meaningful pieces using local image cues. Their recent work explores how people tell whether an edge in an image comes from an object boundary, a shadow, or a change in surface pigment, and how texture boundaries defined by the density or the type of small pattern elements are detected. They have also been studying why some textures, such as clusters of holes, feel visually uncomfortable, testing whether that discomfort relates to resemblance to skin disease. Across these projects they combine human psychophysics with image-computable models built on natural image statistics.

papers.title: Local cues enable classification of image patches as surfaces, object boundaries, or illumination changes
papers.abstract: Parsing natural scenes into surfaces requires identifying luminance edges and inferring whether their physical origin is an object occlusion, a cast shadow, or surface material pigmentation. Although image-computable neural networks (such as filter-rectify-filter architectures) trained on natural images demonstrate that boundary sharpness and texture cues can distinguish occlusions from shadows, whether biological vision exploits these specific local achromatic cues remained unverified. Here, human classification behavior was measured using synthetic edge patches generated by quilting together natural textures, enabling independent parametric manipulation of luminance modulation, boundary sharpness (penumbral blur), and texture modulation across five stimulus sets. Observers trained with feedback on natural patches subsequently categorized synthetic patches into occlusions, shadows, or uniform textures. Psychophysical data revealed prominent nonlinear interactions among cues: for sharp step edges, increasing luminance modulation decreased texture classifications while increasing occlusion classifications, whereas for blurred edges, increased luminance modulation systematically drove shadow classifications. Boundary sharpness strongly governed edge classification under non-zero luminance modulation, suppressing shadow classifications and increasing occlusion categorizations, while texture modulation exerted negligible effects except across sharp boundaries with zero luminance modulation. Multinomial logistic regression models accurately fit and generalized across behavioral datasets, demonstrating that human visual categorization exploits the identical local achromatic cues utilized by computational vision models.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina, Eden E. Sterk, Madelyn G. Arena, Francesca E. Monteferrante

papers.title: A comparison of density-based and feature-based texture boundary segmentation
papers.abstract: The spatial density of micropattern elements constitutes a fundamental visual dimension that can support texture segmentation in the absence of luminance steps.
