Psychophysical segmentation thresholds were compared for two classes of second-order texture boundaries constructed from complementary pairs of micropatterns (such as orthogonal Gabor patches or opposite-polarity difference-of-Gaussian filters): (1) feature boundaries, which hold total micropattern count constant across opposite sides while modulating the relative proportion of each micropattern species, and (2) density boundaries, which vary the total number of micropatterns across the boundary while matching the species ratio within each side. Contrary to canonical late-pooling Filter-Rectify-Filter (FRF) architectures, which process distinct micropattern-tuned first-order channels via separate second-stage spatial filters prior to pooling and thus predict identical thresholds, human observers exhibited significantly lower segmentation thresholds for density-defined boundaries than for feature-defined boundaries. In summation experiments where two single-species density boundaries were superimposed, combining them in-phase to generate a compound density boundary produced sensitivity consistent with probability summation across channels. Conversely, superimposing them in opposite phase to form a compound feature boundary impaired performance below single-channel baselines. These findings indicate that density-based texture boundary detection operates via distinct early-pooling visual mechanisms that integrate across multiple first-order spatial filter varieties rather than relying on channel-specific second-order processing.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina

papers.title: Trypophobia, skin disease, and the visual discomfort of natural textures
papers.abstract: Trypophobia denotes the aversive emotional response and visual discomfort experienced by certain individuals when viewing clustered arrays of holes or circular geometric patterns. A prominent evolutionary account posits that this aversion constitutes an adaptation of the behavioral immune system directed toward avoiding ectoparasitic infestation and infectious dermatological pathologies. This investigation evaluated the skin-disease avoidance hypothesis by quantifying discomfort ratings across natural textures, trypophobic stimuli, and dermatological lesion imagery in participants stratified into trypophobic and non-trypophobic cohorts via the Trypophobia Questionnaire (TQ). Both cohorts exhibited congruent ordinal discomfort hierarchies across image types, with dermatological pathologies evoking maximal discomfort, followed by trypophobic patterns, and natural textures producing minimal aversion. Observers with trypophobia displayed elevated discomfort ratings across all stimulus sets, with the largest between-group divergence occurring for trypophobic and cutaneous disease stimuli. Furthermore, standard low-level image statistical metrics, including spatial frequency power spectra and deviations from 1/f spectral profiles, proved to be poor predictors of visual discomfort in natural textures and significantly under-predicted the intense aversion evoked by trypophobic and infectious imagery. These results support the skin-disease avoidance hypothesis, demonstrating that trypophobia reflects pathogen-avoidance mechanisms operating via high-level surface and material property appraisals rather than low-level early visual filter over-activation.
papers.authors: Christopher DiMattina, R. Nathan Pipitone, Martin R. Renteria, Kriston J. Ryan

0128.name: Christopher L. Striemer
0128.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of attention and visuomotor control
0128.bio: Christopher L. Striemer is a Professor at MacEwan University and an adjunct faculty member within the Neuroscience and Mental Health Institute at the University of Alberta. Striemer’s research examines the neural mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and visuomotor control in both healthy populations and neurological patients. Utilizing techniques such as kinematic analysis, eye tracking, fMRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation, they investigate how brain damage to the parietal lobe and cerebellum affects spatial awareness and motor coordination. A portion of their work evaluates the efficacy of prism adaptation as a rehabilitative tool for patients with spatial neglect.
0128.research_direction: Dr. Striemer’s recent work explores the intersection of visuomotor plasticity, spatial attention, and motor control in both healthy adults and neurological populations. They have recently been investigating the mechanisms of prism adaptation, specifically asking how the congruency between the adapting hand and the direction of visual shift influences both localized motor realignment and broader attentional biases. In the realm of visually guided action, their research examines how individual differences in executive function might influence rapid, "automatic" dorsal-stream online reach corrections during target-jump paradigms. Additionally, Dr. Striemer is investigating the cerebellum's role in these processes by studying stroke patients, using robotic exoskeletons to longitudinally track the recovery of feed-forward and feedback reaching deficits and neuropsychological screening tools to identify cerebellar contributions to spatial neglect.

papers.title: The influence of prism adaptation on spatial biases is not dependent on which hand is used to adapt
papers.abstract: Asked whether the congruency effect on prism aftereffects also produces a larger rightward attention shift after leftward prism adaptation in healthy adults (n=52). Pointing measures showed the congruency effect, but line bisection and landmark judgments did not depend on which hand was used. This suggests motor realignment and attentional biases can be dissociated, with implications for neglect rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Sophia A. Slade, Jasmine Kowalewski, Dana Cobzas, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: "Automatic" online reach corrections are associated with individual differences in executive function
papers.abstract: Eighty healthy adults did an 'automatic pilot' reaching task in which the target sometimes jumps, either correcting or ignoring the jump, plus sustained attention and executive-function questionnaires. Participants who corrected more often when told to ignore the jump differed in executive function measures, linking rapid dorsal-stream corrections to individual differences in executive control.
papers.authors: Branden T. Otte, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: Direction of visual shift and hand congruency enhance spatial realignment during visuomotor adaptation
papers.abstract: Tests whether prism adaptation works better when the hand used and the direction of the prism-induced visual shift are congruent (same side) rather than incongruent. A reanalysis of an earlier dataset and a new replication experiment both showed larger aftereffects in straight-ahead pointing in the congruent case. The authors link this to hemispheric routing of sensory input and motor output and its relevance to prism therapy for neglect.
papers.authors: Christopher L. Striemer, Adam Morrill

papers.title: Assessment and recovery of visually guided reaching deficits following cerebellar stroke
papers.abstract: Twelve patients with isolated cerebellar stroke performed a Kinarm exoskeleton reaching task from about 2 to 24 weeks after stroke. Half were impaired at baseline in feed-forward and feedback control, and impaired patients recovered substantially by 24 weeks. Lesion analyses pointed to right lobule IX and Crus II, and standard clinical scales missed much of the deficit.
papers.authors: Chella M. Robles, Britt Anderson, Sean P. Dukelow, Christopher L. Striemer

papers.title: Left Cerebellar Lesions may be Associated with an Increase in Spatial Neglect-like Symptoms
papers.abstract: Reviewed neglect screening data (line bisection, cancellation, figure copying) from 20 patients with isolated unilateral cerebellar stroke. Left cerebellar patients missed more left-sided targets than norms, while right cerebellar patients did not, with damage centered on Crus II and lobules VII and IX. The results support a left-lateralized cerebellar role in attention and visuospatial function.
papers.authors: Ryan Verbitsky, Britt Anderson, James Danckert, Sean P. Dukelow, Christopher L. Striemer

0129.name: Christopher Tyler
0129.bio: Christopher Tyler is a visual neuroscientist who invented the random-dot autostereogram and conducted research on human stereoscopic depth perception. As the Head of the Brain Imaging Center at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute, Tyler utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and electroretinography to investigate the neural processing of symmetry, motion, and 3D form. Their current research focuses on characterizing oculomotor deficits and photophobia in patients with traumatic brain injury, as well as developing computational models of the visual hierarchy. Tyler also studies the intersection of vision science and Renaissance art, exploring topics such as the perspective geometry and ocular health of historical artists.
0129.research_direction: Dr. Tyler has recently been investigating a diverse range of visual phenomena spanning higher-order form processing, motion perception, retinal physiology, and spatial motor control. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of human symmetry perception, testing whether feedforward deep neural networks trained on natural images develop selectivity for mirror symmetry and probing how observers extract symmetrical structure from second-order image statistics like disparity or motion flow rather than exact point-by-point correspondence. To understand complex motion processing, they are studying the visual perception of longitudinal traveling waves using phase-lagged oscillating dot fields to evaluate underlying motion mechanisms, velocity integration, and motion aftereffects. Clinically, they are applying a novel data-driven components analysis to full-field spectral electroretinograms in order to isolate rod- and cone-pathway contributions across mesopic intensities. Finally, Dr. Tyler is examining non-visual spatiomotor dynamics, measuring the kinematic relationship between drawing speed and trajectory curvature when blind and blindfolded individuals produce memory-guided patterns without visual feedback.

papers.title: Visual perception of longitudinal waves: theory and observations
papers.abstract: Introduces the visual study of longitudinal travelling waves, the physical basis of sound and some seismic transmission, and shows theoretically that they are strongly nonlinear. Using random-dot fields whose dots oscillate with a phase lag proportional to distance, the authors show that observers see crests moving forward and troughs moving backward rather than a single wave, and that adding a rigid velocity can cancel either percept. The work also reports the absence of a motion aftereffect unless crest contrast is reduced, revealing separate motion mechanisms.
papers.authors: Christopher W. Tyler, Joshua A. Solomon, Stuart M. Anstis

papers.title: Varieties of higher-order symmetry
papers.abstract: Challenges the assumption that symmetry perception needs point-by-point correspondence between image elements. The authors build second-order symmetric patterns in which only image statistics such as dot density, orientation, dot-pair statistics, disparity or motion flow vary symmetrically, and these still give strong symmetry percepts. They conclude that the visual system infers a surface structure before evaluating symmetry, which existing detection models do not capture.
papers.authors: Chien-Chung Chen, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: The canonical deep neural network as a model for human symmetry processing
papers.abstract: Asks whether a deep network trained only on natural images develops selectivity for mirror symmetry like the human visual system. Using object-free random-dot patterns with one, two or four symmetry axes, the authors find negligible symmetry coding in early layers and the strongest discriminability in the first fully connected layer (FC6), which they liken to human lateral occipital cortex. The results argue that a feedforward network trained on natural images mirrors the global, hierarchical processing of symmetry in the brain.
papers.authors: Yoram S. Bonneh, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Native components analysis of the spectral electroretinogram
papers.abstract: Measures full-field ERGs to seven spectral bands across mesopic intensities to test whether they can be explained as combinations of rod- and cone-pathway responses. The authors introduce Native Components Analysis, a three-stage procedure that selects representative recorded waveforms as components and fits them to the whole data set. The approach offers a way to isolate the retinal contributions to the ERG for electrodiagnosis.
papers.authors: Christopher W. Tyler, Michael Liang, Zhangziyi Zhou, Lora T. Likova

papers.title: Spatiomotor dynamics of hand movements during the drawing of memory-guided trajectories without visual feedback
papers.abstract: Examines whether the classic one-third power law relating drawing speed to curvature holds when people draw from memory without vision, using completely blind and blindfolded sighted participants from the Likova Cognitive-Kinesthetic Memory-Drawing Training. Speed and curvature follow a hyperbolic saturation relationship with an exponent near 1.0 at high curvature, well above the one-third prediction, for both groups. The authors interpret this as an adaptive approximation of minimum-jerk motor control.
papers.authors: Christopher W. Tyler, Kristyo N. Mineff, Michael Liang, Lora T. Likova

0130.name: Chuan Hou
0130.bio: Chuan Hou, MD, PhD, is an Associate Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute who researches binocular vision processing and the neural basis of amblyopia and strabismus. As a pediatric ophthalmologist, Hou utilizes VEP, fMRI-informed EEG source-imaging, and psychophysics to study interocular suppression. Their work investigates how selective visual attention influences sensory eye dominance and explores dichoptic attention-based therapies to restore visual function. Hou’s research on the role of top-down attentional influences in amblyopic suppression is supported by the National Eye Institute.
0130.research_direction: Dr. Hou has recently been investigating the mechanisms of interocular competition and sensory eye dominance, with a particular focus on how these dynamics are altered in visual disorders like amblyopia and strabismus. Their recent work explores binocular rivalry using psychophysical paradigms, testing how both low-level stimulus features—such as size and contrast—and top-down voluntary eye-based attention modulate perceptual dominance and suppression. To translate these insights into therapeutic strategies, they are also examining attention-based dichoptic perceptual learning interventions, utilizing fMRI to track functional changes in the visual cortex of adult patients. Additionally, they have been developing new methodological approaches to accurately quantify the strength of interocular suppression, providing robust tools to better characterize binocular deficits and monitor clinical treatment outcomes.

papers.title: Effects of stimulus size and contrast on binocular rivalry in adults with anisometropic amblyopia
papers.abstract: Adults with anisometropic amblyopia rarely let the amblyopic eye dominate during binocular rivalry with small equal-contrast stimuli. Making the amblyopic-eye stimulus larger or higher in contrast partly restores its dominance and reduces fellow-eye dominance, though it never reaches normal levels. Amblyopic observers also report far more mixed percepts than controls, pointing to qualitatively altered interocular interactions, and dominance bias did not track amblyopia depth, stereoacuity or suppression strength.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou, Junxian Rao

papers.title: Attentional Eye Selection Affects Perception During Binocular Rivalry
papers.abstract: Tests whether voluntarily attending to one eye biases what is perceived during binocular rivalry. Directing attention to a particular eye changed perceptual dominance and suppression dynamics, showing that top-down eye-based attention can modulate interocular competition. This supports attention-based approaches to shifting sensory eye dominance.
papers.authors: Zhangziyi Zhou, Chuan Hou

papers.title: Visual Cortical Function Changes After Perceptual Learning with Dichoptic Attention Tasks in Adults with Amblyopia: A Case Study Evaluated Using fMRI
papers.abstract: Follows an adult with amblyopia who trained on attention-demanding tasks presented separately to each eye and images visual cortex with fMRI before and after. Training was accompanied by changes in cortical responses, illustrating a neural correlate of dichoptic attention-based perceptual learning. It is a case study, so it serves as a proof of concept for this therapeutic approach.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou, Zhangziyi Zhou, Ismet Joan Uner, Spero C. Nicholas

papers.title: A new approach to measure interocular suppression in amblyopia and strabismus
papers.abstract: Describes a method for quantifying how strongly one eye suppresses the other in people with amblyopia and strabismus. The protocol is presented as a practical, reproducible measurement that can be used to characterize deficits and follow treatment effects.
papers.authors: Chuan Hou

0131.name: Chujun Lin
0131.bio: Chujun Lin examines the mechanisms, structures, and behavioral consequences of human person perception. By integrating computational tools such as deep neural networks with neuroscientific methods like single-neuron recording and fMRI, Lin investigates how individuals form social impressions from complex visual cues, including faces and naturalistic videos. Their work characterizes the high-dimensional nature of trait inferences and explores how these social judgments bias decision-making in real-world contexts such as politics and the legal system.
0131.research_direction: Dr. Lin has recently been investigating the underlying representational structure of person perception and emotion, exploring how humans extract both stable traits and transient states from faces and naturalistic stimuli. Their recent work challenges classic low-dimensional models of social cognition by testing whether high-dimensional frameworks and network models better capture the rich complexity of social inferences in real-world settings. Additionally, they are examining the intersection of person perception and mental state inference, specifically asking how our initial trait impressions of a face systematically bias our subsequent judgments of that person's transient emotions. Finally, Dr. Lin explores the methodological tools used to define the architecture of affect, evaluating how analytic techniques and deep learning can be optimized to more accurately map the structure of human emotion.

papers.title: How trait impressions of faces shape subsequent mental state inferences
papers.abstract: Across a series of experiments, the authors show that first-impression trait judgments from faces systematically bias how people then infer that person's transient mental states and emotions. The effect is explained by trait and state concepts sharing overlapping representational structure, and it persists across different stimulus sets and tasks. The work links two literatures, person perception and mental state inference, that had been studied separately.
papers.authors: Chujun Lin, Umit Keles, Mark A. Thornton, Ralph Adolphs

papers.title: A high-dimensional model of social impressions
papers.abstract: This review argues that social impressions of other people are best captured by a high-dimensional representational space rather than the few dimensions posited by classic two- or three-factor models. It synthesizes evidence from face and naturalistic-stimulus studies and proposes a framework that reconciles low-dimensional summaries with rich underlying structure. It also outlines predictions and methodological implications for future person perception research.
papers.authors: Jonathan B. Freeman, Chujun Lin

papers.title: Network models reveal high-dimensional social inferences in naturalistic settings beyond latent construct models
papers.abstract: Using naturalistic stimuli, the authors compare latent-construct (factor-analytic) accounts of social inference with network models that treat trait inferences as interconnected nodes. Network models capture high-dimensional structure that a few latent factors miss. The results argue that social cognition in real-world settings is richer than low-dimensional models imply.
papers.authors: Junsong Lu, Chujun Lin

papers.title: Investigating the Structure of Emotion: Tools, Pitfalls and Recommendations
papers.abstract: This methods-oriented paper examines how researchers infer the structure of emotion, such as dimensions or categories, and where common tools mislead. It identifies analytic and design pitfalls and offers practical recommendations. It draws on deep-learning and naturalistic approaches to make emotion research more robust.
papers.authors: Chujun Lin, Yanting Han, Umit Keles, Yue Xu, Junsong Lu, Ruoying Zheng, Ralph Adolphs

0132.name: Chunyue Teng
0132.bio: Chunyue Teng is the Dennis and Charlot Nelson Singleton Assistant Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Lawrence University and directs the Visual Memory & Cognition Lab. Teng’s research investigates the neural mechanisms governing the interaction between visual perception and working memory, focusing on how top-down cognitive control resolves representational conflicts. They utilize a multi-modal approach integrating high-resolution electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine oscillatory neural dynamics and flexible coding schemes. This work explores how the brain maintains sensory information over time and the extent to which mnemonic representations overlap with early perceptual processing.
0132.research_direction: Dr. Teng has recently been investigating how visual working memory, the brief holding of an image in mind, interacts with ongoing perception in the brain. Their recent work asks how holding an oriented pattern in memory biases what people see at the same time, and how that interference changes over the course of a memory delay. They also study the cognitive control that resolves this conflict, using EEG and computational models to test whether preparatory control settings are adjusted from one trial to the next. In addition, they examine how visual and parietal cortex separately keep track of what is being remembered versus the context in which it was encountered.

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics and Representational Consequences of the Control of Processing Conflict between Visual Working Memory and Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (WM) frequently interfaces with concurrent perceptual operations. When representational overlap induces processing conflict, cognitive control mechanisms must be deployed to attenuate bidirectional interference. In this electroencephalography (EEG) study, human observers completed a dual-task paradigm requiring perceptual orientation discrimination while concurrently retaining an oriented stimulus in WM. Employing a Bayesian feedback control model (FCM), trial-wise fluctuations were decomposed into distinct proactive (preparatory) and reactive (reflexive) control processes. Pre-stimulus preparatory control scaled with anticipated conflict and was electrophysiologically indexed by frontal midline theta-band (4–7 Hz) power. Upon presentation of the perceptual discriminandum, reflexive control was recruited proportionally to conflict prediction error. When an incongruent discriminandum appeared unexpectedly, reactive control suppressed its neural representation, as evidenced by below-baseline multivariate inverted encoding model (IEM) reconstruction fidelity; this stimulus suppression subsequently produced an inverted (repulsive) serial dependence bias in WM recall on the following trial. These findings demonstrate the dynamic coordination of proactive preparation and reactive suppression in adjudicating representational competition between visual perception and mnemonic maintenance.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Mattia Pietrelli, Jiefeng Jiang, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Proactive control CAN be updated on a trial-by-trial basis
papers.abstract: This research addresses the mechanistic distinction between proactive and reactive modes of cognitive control within the domain of visual working memory (WM) and perception interactions. Contrary to traditional accounts that characterize proactive control as a stable, list-level strategic bias adjusted over long timescales, this work provides evidence that preparatory control states are updated at a trial-by-trial resolution. Utilizing behavioral data and computational modeling, the authors demonstrate that control prediction errors (PEs)—representing the discrepancy between expected and observed conflict—dynamically reconfigure the level of preparatory control for subsequent trials. The findings suggest that the mental coordination between internal mnemonic representations and external sensory inputs is governed by a reinforcement learning-based control architecture capable of rapid, flexible updates to mitigate processing interference.
papers.authors: Brad Postle, Chunyue Teng

papers.title: Investigating the Roles of the Visual and Parietal Cortex in Representing Content versus Context in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: The binding of stimulus identity (content) to trial-specific situational variables (context) is critical for effective working memory (WM) maintenance. Prior fMRI research using dual-serial retrocueing (DSR) with oriented gratings revealed that item content was maintained in early visual cortex (EVC), whereas spatial context was tracked in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with unprioritized memory items (UMIs) undergoing priority-dependent representational transformation relative to prioritized memory items (PMIs). In this registered report, fMRI was acquired in 24 healthy participants performing a DSR task in which spatial position served as the probed content and grating orientation served as task-relevant context. We evaluated three alternative frameworks: a domain-dependent account, a functional account (content vs. context regardless of feature space), and a hybrid account wherein IPS indexes contextual variables across domains while preserving content sensitivity. Inverted encoding models (IEMs) revealed that delay-period activity in EVC supported functional predictions, demonstrating robust priority-modulated coding of spatial location (content) without decodable orientation (context) profiles. Conversely, IPS delay-period signals matched the hybrid model, actively tracking location content alongside prioritized orientation context. Exploratory analyses in IPS further demonstrated univariate BOLD sensitivity to parametric modulations in content and context load that predicted behavioral precision, underscoring the dissociable functional contributions of sensory and posterior parietal areas in structuring WM representations.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Assessing the interaction between working memory and perception through time
papers.abstract: Visual working memory (VWM) maintenance directly modulates concurrent visual discrimination, reflecting shared representational substrates in posterior perceptual cortices. However, the temporal stability of this sensory recruitment remains debated: mnemonic traces may persist continuously as sensory-like codes or be converted into abstract, categorical formats over extended delays. Here, we manipulated the inter-stimulus interval (ISI) separating memory encoding from an intermediate perceptual discrimination task to dissociate temporal decay within sensory representations from abstract recoding models. Observers encoded simple visual features (color or orientation) into VWM before performing fine-grained same/different psychophysical judgments. Task-relevant features maintained across retention intervals systematically shifted perceptual discrimination thresholds for up to 4 s, demonstrating that sensory-level tuning profiles remain functionally active across time rather than converting to non-sensory codes. In contrast, task-irrelevant dimensions of the memory item exerted only brief, rapidly decaying interference on perceptual judgments. Concurrently, perceptual comparisons introduced an attractive report bias into mnemonic representations that increased monotonically across retention intervals. These results demonstrate the persistent sensory nature of prioritized visual working memory representations throughout extended maintenance periods.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Simon M. Kaplan, Sarah Shomstein, Dwight J. Kravitz

0133.name: Cindy Xiong Bearfield
0133.bio: Cindy Xiong Bearfield is an Assistant Professor in the School of Interactive Computing at Georgia Tech, where they study the intersection of cognitive psychology, vision science, and human-computer interaction. Xiong Bearfield’s research investigates the perceptual and cognitive processes underlying data interpretation, focusing on how visual design choices influence decision-making, trust, and the mitigation of cognitive biases. They use empirical methodologies to map vision science mechanisms—such as ensemble coding, top-down salience, and visual search—to graphical perception tasks to develop visualization systems. Xiong Bearfield is a recipient of an NSF CAREER award and a founding leader of the VISxVISION initiative, which connects the visualization and vision science research communities.
0133.research_direction: Dr. Bearfield has recently been investigating the intersection of visual perception and data communication to understand how viewers extract meaning from charts and graphs. Their recent work examines the mechanistic foundations of chart reading by mapping core vision phenomena—such as ensemble coding, visual search, and top-down salience—onto complex network diagrams, while also using eye-tracking methods to link a viewer's specific gaze patterns with their overall visualization literacy. Beyond basic visual attention, they are exploring higher-level cognitive and social responses to data design, which includes developing validated psychometric tools to measure human trust in visualizations and testing how altering a chart's visual form can drive competing or polarized interpretations of identical datasets. Additionally, their research probes whether large language models are sensitive to the same structural design choices as human readers, evaluating the viability of using AI as a proxy for predicting human perceptual takeaways.

papers.title: Do You "Trust" This Visualization? An Inventory to Measure Trust in Visualizations
papers.abstract: Trust in visualizations is often measured with ad hoc single questions. This work develops and validates a multi-item inventory for measuring trust in a chart, built through a psychometric process from item generation to statistical validation. It gives researchers a reusable instrument for comparing how design choices affect credibility.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Huichen Will Wang, Kylie Lin, Andrew Cohen, Ryan Kennedy, Zachary Zwald, Carolina Nobre, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Tell Me Without Telling Me: Two-Way Prediction of Visualization Literacy and Visual Attention
papers.abstract: The paper links how well a person reads charts to where they look while doing so. Using gaze data, models predict a viewer's visualization literacy, and using literacy scores, models predict where the viewer will look. The work shows that attention patterns and skill are tightly coupled.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Minsuk Chang, Yao Wang, Huichen Will Wang, Yuanhong Zhou, Andreas Bulling, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Bridging Network Science and Vision Science: Mapping Perceptual Mechanisms to Network Visualization Tasks
papers.abstract: The authors argue that network visualization design has been guided more by intuition than by what is known about human perception. They map established vision-science mechanisms, including visual search, ensemble coding and top-down salience, onto the concrete tasks people perform with node-link diagrams. The result is a framework and set of open questions intended to let the two communities inform each other's research.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: S. Sandra Bae, Kyle Cave, Carsten Görg, Paul Rosen, Danielle Albers Szafir, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: How Aligned are Human Chart Takeaways and LLM Predictions? A Case Study on Bar Charts with Varying Layouts
papers.abstract: The study compares the conclusions people draw from bar charts with the takeaways that large language models predict for the same charts, while varying chart layout. It examines whether design choices that steer human readers have similar effects on model outputs. The findings show only partial alignment, cautioning against using LLMs as stand-ins for human chart readers.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Huichen Will Wang, Jane Hoffswell, Sao Myat Thazin Thane, Victor S. Bursztyn, Cindy Xiong Bearfield

papers.title: Same Data, Diverging Perspectives: The Power of Visualizations to Elicit Competing Interpretations
papers.abstract: When the same dataset is shown in different visual forms, people reach different, sometimes opposing, conclusions. Across experiments the authors show that visualization design can push viewers toward competing interpretations of identical data, including on contested topics. The results highlight design as a lever on persuasion and polarization.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Cindy Xiong Bearfield, Lisanne van Weelden, Adam Waytz, Steven Franconeri

0134.name: Claus-Christian Carbon
0134.department: Department of General Psychology and Methodology
0134.bio: Claus-Christian Carbon is the Chair of General Psychology and Methodology at the University of Bamberg and serves as the Dean of the Faculty of Human Sciences. Carbon’s research focuses on empirical aesthetics, the cognitive mechanisms of face processing, and the temporal dynamics of aesthetic appreciation and innovation acceptance. Carbon employs experimental psychophysics, eye-tracking, and multidimensional scaling to investigate perceptual phenomena ranging from optical illusions to haptic design. Carbon is the editor-in-chief of the journal Art & Perception and the founder of the international EPÆG research network.
0134.research_direction: Dr. Carbon has recently been exploring the intersection of high-level visual perception, empirical aesthetics, and contextual cognition. In the domain of face perception, their recent work investigates the limits of configural processing by measuring how rotation angles affect the Thatcher illusion for own- versus other-race faces. A substantial branch of their research examines the psychological experience of art, utilizing virtual reality and diverse framing paradigms to probe how physical or conceptual gallery contexts alter viewers' emotional responses, moral evaluations, and phenomenological immersion. Additionally, they are using embodied predictive-processing frameworks to model how viewers engage with and derive aesthetic pleasure from moments of unresolved semantic instability. Finally, their recent work explores applied perception in historical settings, examining how ancient militaries strategically combined camouflage and perceptual pop-out to induce psychological shock.

papers.title: Impaired configural processing for other-race faces revealed by the Thatcher illusion
papers.abstract: Participants judged how grotesque Thatcherised (eyes and mouth inverted) own-race and other-race faces looked across seven rotation angles from 0 to 180 degrees. Own-race faces showed a sharp, sigmoid-like loss of the illusion beyond roughly 120 degrees, the classic signature of configural processing. Other-race faces instead showed a gradual, near-linear change and the poorest detection of Thatcherisation, suggesting the own-race advantage rests on stronger configural face coding.
papers.authors: Sandra Utz, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Is there an Art-Specific Mode? Comparing the Experience of Art Appreciation in a Gallery and a Shop Context Using VR
papers.abstract: Thirty-two participants freely explored the same nine artworks in either a virtual art gallery or a virtual furniture shop and were interviewed right after and two weeks later. Interpretative phenomenological analysis identified five themes, with gallery visitors producing richer associations, deeper meanings, stronger emotional peaks and more personal connections. The results support the idea of a distinct art-experiencing mode triggered by the gallery context.
papers.authors: Itay Goetz, Jennifer Tesch, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Using perception as a strategy: Camouflage, surprise, and the moment of shock related to perception
papers.abstract: Using historical evidence from Roman patrol vessels on the Danube, the authors argue that camouflage was deliberately paired with a sudden reveal to produce psychological shock. Vessels painted to blend into the river became conspicuous on detection, with oversized eyes and ornamental bows amplifying a perceptual pop-out, especially in frontal attack. The paper frames concealment plus surprise as a strategic use of perception.
papers.authors: Claus-Christian Carbon, Boris Dreyer, Marcus Speck

papers.title: Art for art's sake? The influence of art framing and context on the evaluation of immoral behaviour
papers.abstract: 140 participants rated 20 depictions of immoral acts presented either in a physical gallery, online labelled as art, or online labelled as non-art. Emotional reactions stayed similarly negative across conditions, yet the pictures were rated as more beautiful, interesting and pleasing when framed as art, most of all in the gallery. Art framing also lowered perceived understanding and raised surprise, indicating that art status changes evaluation without erasing moral distress.
papers.authors: Itay Goetz, Lara Bernhardt, Friederike Margareta Karg, Alexander (Sasha) Pastukhov, Claus-Christian Carbon

papers.title: Predicting instabilities: an embodied perspective on unstable experiences with art and design
papers.abstract: The article revisits 'Semantic Instability', experiences where habitual sense-making breaks or several meanings coexist, within a predictive-processing and embodied-cognition framework. It argues that art perception differs from problem solving because viewers hold contradictory elements together dynamically without needing to resolve them. Such instability itself can produce interest and aesthetic pleasure.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Claudia Muth, Claus-Christian Carbon

0135.name: Clayton E Curtis
0135.bio: Clayton E. Curtis is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University who investigates the neural architecture of spatial working memory and cognitive control. Curtis focuses on the functional role of persistent neural activity within the frontoparietal cortex and how these signals mediate the integration of perception, attention, and motor planning. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including high-resolution fMRI, intracranial recordings (iEEG/ECoG), and computational modeling, their work characterizes the topographical organization of priority maps and the circuit-level dynamics that support goal-directed behavior. Additionally, Curtis examines how disruptions in these cognitive control mechanisms contribute to the pathophysiology of psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia.
0135.research_direction: Dr. Curtis has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and population dynamics that support visual working memory across the human cortical hierarchy. Their recent work explores how mnemonic representations are maintained and prioritized, utilizing time-resolved and high-resolution fMRI decoding to track how memory traces drift over a delay period and how frontal feedback allocates resources to high-priority items. They are also examining the spatial topography of working memory, mapping retinotopically organized mnemonic subspaces in the prefrontal cortex and tracking top-down information flow between frontal, parietal, and visual areas. Additionally, by incorporating transcranial magnetic stimulation, Dr. Curtis is testing the causal necessity of early visual cortex in preserving the precise fidelity of maintained visual memories.

papers.title: Dynamics of working memory drift and information flow across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: Using time-resolved fMRI decoding, the authors show that decoded memory content drifts over the delay toward the participant's eventual recall error in visual and parietal areas, as attractor models predict. These behaviorally predictive errors appear first in dorsal visual area V3AB and IPS0 and only later in V1. Interareal analyses indicate top-down flow of mnemonic information during maintenance, versus feedforward flow during passive viewing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of resource allocation in working memory
papers.abstract: The study develops fMRI decoding methods to separate responses to several remembered items of differing priority. In visual cortex, response gain tracks an item's priority, and higher-priority items are decoded more precisely and with less uncertainty, which predicts behavior. Frontal delay activity covaries with these priority effects, consistent with frontal feedback setting the gain of memory representations.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Thomas C. Sprague, Aspen H. Yoo, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Perturbing human V1 degrades the fidelity of visual working memory
papers.abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation was applied to early visual cortex during the delay of a visual working memory task. Stimulating V1 made memory reports less precise, giving causal evidence that early visual cortex is needed to keep memories accurate, not just correlated with them.
papers.authors: Mrugank Dake, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Mnemonic maps of visual space in human prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Scanning human prefrontal cortex with 900 micron 7T fMRI, the authors find persistent, item-specific memory activity in retinotopically organized superior precentral sulcus rather than midlateral PFC. This activity predicts memory errors and forms a stable subspace organized topographically by visual space, bearing on human-macaque homology and theories of PFC in working memory.
papers.authors: Zhengang Lu, Logan T. Dowdle, Kendrick N. Kay, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Neural population dynamics of human working memory
papers.abstract: Population-level fMRI analyses reveal how the geometry of working memory representations changes across the cortical hierarchy and over time during a delay. The work characterizes the dynamics of mnemonic codes in human visual, parietal and frontal cortex, and links them to behavior.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Clayton E. Curtis

0136.name: Clayton Hickey
0136.bio: Clayton Hickey is an Associate Professor at the University of Birmingham and directs the Motivated Cognition Lab within the Centre for Human Brain Health. Hickey's research utilizes multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, EEG, and MEG, alongside eye-tracking and pharmacological challenges to investigate how reward, reinforcement learning, and statistical regularities modulate visual attention. Their work examines incentive salience and the neural mechanisms of distractor suppression, employing electrophysiological analyses to characterize how the brain prioritizes environmental stimuli. Current research focuses on the intersection of object-based attention and reward feedback to understand the resolution of representational ambiguity in complex naturalistic scenes.
0136.research_direction: Dr. Hickey’s recent work explores the neural mechanisms of selective visual attention and its role in bridging perception, higher cognition, and action. Using human electrophysiology, concurrent fMRI, and multivariate decoding, they have recently been investigating how attention resolves representational ambiguity in cluttered scenes and how the structural properties of objects prioritize spatial attention. Beyond early visual selection, their research examines the downstream consequences of attention, specifically asking how attended percepts are translated into semantic representations across frontoparietal networks. Finally, they are also probing the temporal dynamics of cognitive and motor control, characterizing the interplay of proactive and reactive mechanisms during distractor suppression and mapping the neural feedback loops that guide continuous visuomotor error correction.

papers.title: Predictive Distractor Processing Relies on Integrated Proactive and Reactive Attentional Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Using MEG and multivariate decoding in a statistical-learning visual search task where a distractor appears more often on one side, the study shows that the likely distractor location can be decoded from temporo-occipital activity before the display appears. That pre-search pattern generalises to later post-search activity around 200 ms but not to early sensory activity around 100 ms, indicating that suppression is re-engaged at a later stage rather than simply carried over. The results argue for an integrated proactive and reactive account of distractor suppression.
papers.authors: Oscar Ferrante, Ole Jensen, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics of EEG Reflect Continuous Error Correction during Force Control
papers.abstract: Participants held a constant grip force with or without continuous visual feedback while EEG was recorded. With feedback, performance fluctuated rhythmically at about 6 Hz, consistent with ongoing correction, and these fluctuations were linked to theta, beta and alpha EEG activity. Without feedback, force decayed linearly and the neural signatures weakened, pointing to a dynamic feedback loop supporting continuous motor control.
papers.authors: Nicholas Menghi, Elio Balestrieri, Damiano Grignolio, Giorgio Coricelli, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Neural mechanisms for the attention-mediated propagation of conceptual information in the human brain
papers.abstract: Combining machine learning on EEG with concurrent EEG/fMRI, the authors trace how attended perceptual information is converted into semantic and conceptual representations. Trial-to-trial variation in the N2pc, an ERP marker of selective attention, predicts when conceptual information emerges in a network spanning prefrontal, posterior parietal and anterior insular cortex. This network appears to translate attended percepts into concepts, semantics and action plans.
papers.authors: David Acunzo, Damiano Grignolio, Clayton Hickey

papers.title: Complementary attentional mechanisms for the resolution of representational ambiguity in the human brain
papers.abstract: When several objects fall within a neuron's receptive field, the neural code for individual items becomes ambiguous, and primate work proposes that attention resolves this by biasing competition. Using a novel multivariate analysis of human EEG and concurrent EEG/fMRI, the study tests whether ambiguity recruits attention, which mechanisms act on attended versus unattended object representations, and how these unfold in time and across semantic and executive networks.
papers.authors: Clayton Hickey, David Acunzo, Damiano Grignolio

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Object Prioritization in Vision
papers.abstract: Using EEG in a spatial cueing task with task-irrelevant horizontal or vertical rectangles, the authors measure attention directly through lateralized alpha oscillations and the ADAN component. Both indices were sensitive to the rectangles' orientation, giving neural evidence that objects shape attentional deployment and countering accounts that attribute object-based effects to hemifield anisotropies or clutter.
papers.authors: Damiano Grignolio, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Joy J. Geng, George R. Mangun, Clayton Hickey

0137.name: Colin Clifford
0137.bio: Colin Clifford is a Professor at UNSW Sydney who researches the computational and neural mechanisms of human vision. Clifford examines how the visual system employs contextual information and sensory adaptation to encode features including orientation, motion, color, and social cues such as eye gaze. Using psychophysical techniques, neuroimaging, and computational modeling, they investigate the relationship between neural processing and visual awareness. Their research includes the study of gaze perception and the integration of social signals within the human brain.
0137.research_direction: Dr. Clifford has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying both high-level social vision and foundational perceptual dynamics. Their recent work explores face pareidolia and animacy by asking observers to view synthetic spatiotemporal noise, an approach used to isolate the minimal structural primitives that trigger illusory form perception and to test how observer expectations drive the attribution of social traits to unbiased stimuli. They are also studying the visual processing of human bodies and faces, using adaptation paradigms to map the population coding of walking direction in point-light figures and tracking how the integration of head and eye cues during gaze perception develops from early childhood to adulthood. Furthermore, their research examines temporal integration in low-level vision, manipulating stimulus signal-to-noise ratios and measuring observer confidence to determine how perceptual versus decisional uncertainty influences serial dependence in orientation judgments.

papers.title: Facing your expectations: perceived characteristics of illusory faces in symmetrical visual noise
papers.abstract: Using static and dynamic synthetic noise as a minimal, unbiased stimulus, the study asks what social characteristics such as gender, age and emotion people attribute to faces they see in noise. It compares these attributions across experiments to test whether previously reported face-pareidolia biases arise from image selection or from observers' own expectations. Findings show systematic social trait attributions to illusory faces even when the input contains no real facial information.
papers.authors: Lindsay M. Peterson, Kritika Sarna, Branka Spehar, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Developmental trajectories of head and eye cue integration in gaze perception
papers.abstract: Across five experiments with children aged 4-16 and adults, the authors tested how head orientation biases perceived gaze using Wollaston-illusion and natural face images. The attractive pull of head direction weakened from early childhood through adolescence, with older children not showing the classic illusion that adults do. Smaller images increased the head bias in younger children, suggesting cue weighting depends on the visibility of eye detail.
papers.authors: Yumiko Otsuka, Katsumi Watanabe, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Image primitives supporting perception of animate forms
papers.abstract: Participants viewed synthetic noise patterns that varied in spatiotemporal spectral content and symmetry and reported any shapes or structures they perceived. Patterns with natural-scene-like statistics, especially vertically symmetric ones, evoked the most animate percepts, with faces the most common but also animals and mythical creatures. The work identifies the minimal image structure sufficient for pareidolia and animacy perception.
papers.authors: Lindsay M. Peterson, Kritika Sarna, Branka Spehar, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Effects of perceptual and decisional uncertainty on serial dependence in orientation perception
papers.abstract: Serial dependence biases current orientation judgments toward recently seen stimuli and is stronger under target uncertainty. Here the authors manipulate the amount of positive evidence and signal-to-noise ratio of the preceding stimulus while measuring confidence in 33 observers. Serial dependence was greatest when the inducer had been judged with low confidence, implicating decisional uncertainty about the previous stimulus rather than its signal quality.
papers.authors: Zoë Little, Colin W. G. Clifford

papers.title: Adaptation to walking direction in biological motion
papers.abstract: The study uses adaptation of point-light walkers to probe how the brain encodes the direction another person is walking. Adapting to one walking direction produced repulsive aftereffects with tuning that depended on the adaptor-test difference, well described by a population code of channels tuned across the full 360 degrees. Further experiments showed that coding differs for figures walking toward versus away from the observer.
papers.authors: Chang Chen, W. Paul Boyce, Colin J. Palmer, Colin W. G. Clifford

0138.name: Cong Yu
0138.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0138.bio: Cong Yu is a Professor at the School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences at Peking University and a Principal Investigator at the IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research. Yu’s research utilizes psychophysical and neuroimaging techniques to investigate the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning and brain plasticity in humans and non-human primates. Yu developed the 'double training' and 'Training-Plus-Exposure' (TPE) paradigms, which challenge theories of early cortical learning specificity. Their current research involves using two-photon calcium imaging to map population-level neuronal responses in the macaque visual cortex and translating perceptual learning principles into clinical treatments for amblyopia.
0138.research_direction: Dr. Yu has recently been investigating how neural population codes in early visual processing stages support a wide array of perceptual phenomena, primarily utilizing two-photon calcium imaging in awake macaques. Their recent work explores early cortical representational geometry and decoding models to uncover the network mechanisms underlying visual uncrowding, attractive and repulsive serial dependence in orientation perception, and ocular-dominance-dependent binocular integration. They are also examining the boundaries of unconscious visual processing by probing how continuous flash suppression alters usable stimulus information within V1 populations. Additionally, their research spans human systems-level plasticity, using EEG and graph-theoretic network analyses to determine what brain network dynamics dictate whether perceptual learning remains location-specific or successfully transfers across the visual field.

papers.title: Long flankers alleviate visual crowding by enhancing population target coding in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Using two-photon calcium imaging of large neuronal populations in awake, fixating macaques, the study asks why long flanking lines produce 'uncrowding' of a target line. Long flankers reduced surround suppression and preserved orientation representational geometry and decoding accuracy in V1, whereas in V4 they produced stronger suppression and worse decoding. The results place the neural basis of uncrowding in V1 population coding rather than in higher areas.
papers.authors: Cai-Xia Chen, Dan-Qing Jiang, Xin Wang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Continuous flash suppression of neural responses and population orientation coding in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Two-photon imaging of V1 populations in awake macaques viewing gratings under continuous flash suppression showed that the masker strongly suppresses orientation responses, in a manner that depends on each neuron's eye preference. Population modeling indicated that the remaining V1 activity can support only coarse orientation classification, not accurate stimulus reconstruction. This suggests CFS largely strips V1 of usable orientation information, limiting what unconscious processing can rely on downstream.
papers.authors: Cai-Xia Chen, Xin Wang, Dan-Qing Jiang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Decoding Orientation Serial Dependence from V1/V2 Population Responses Using a Cross-Attention Transformer
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether early visual cortex carries signals for both repulsive and attractive history biases in orientation perception. Combining two-photon imaging in awake macaques with a cross-attention transformer decoder, it shows that V1/V2 population activity supports separate readouts of the two biases even though average responses show only repulsion. Attention-map analyses revealed distinct readout patterns for each bias.
papers.authors: Xin Wang, Cai-Xia Chen, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Training-induced brain network reorganization predicts location specificity and transfer in perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Reanalyzing EEG from a Vernier perceptual learning task in which some participants showed location-specific learning and others transferred across hemifields, the study finds post-training beta suppression only in specific learners. Graph-theoretic analyses tie specificity to stronger local clustering and reduced global integration, whereas transfer learners keep a stable network organization. This offers a systems-level explanation of when perceptual learning generalizes.
papers.authors: Lin Zhong, Gong-Liang Zhang, Jun-Yun Zhang, Cong Yu

papers.title: Ocular dominance-dependent binocular combination of monocular neuronal responses in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Recording thousands of superficial V1 neurons with two-photon imaging in awake macaques, the authors compared monocular and binocular responses across eye-preference classes. Binocular viewing equalized responses across neurons regardless of eye preference, keeping overall activity similar to monocular viewing. A model with ocular-dominance-dependent divisive interocular inhibition plus binocular summation accounts for the data.
papers.authors: Sheng-Hui Zhang, Xing-Nan Zhao, Dan-Qing Jiang, Shi-Ming Tang, Cong Yu

0139.name: Corey Bohil
0139.department: Department of Humanities, Social Sciences, and Communication
0139.bio: Corey Bohil is a cognitive neuroscientist and Professor of Psychology who researches the mechanisms of human categorization and decision-making. Bohil’s work utilizes computational modeling, immersive virtual and mixed-reality environments, and physiological assessments to examine how individuals classify environmental stimuli and perform in operational settings. Their research addresses the distinction between rule-based and information-integration category learning systems. Currently, Bohil employs functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to monitor cortical activity during cognitive tasks and human-technology interactions.
0139.research_direction: Dr. Bohil has recently been interested in how attention and learning shape what people see and experience. They are exploring whether a simple behavior, rhythmic finger tapping measured with sensor gloves, can track a person's sense of presence in virtual reality moment to moment, as an alternative to after-the-fact questionnaires. They also study how people learn categories, contrasting explicit rule-based learning with more implicit, intuition-like learning, and how each kind of learning guides visual search.

papers.title: Finger Tapping as a Behavioral Indicator of Presence in VR
papers.abstract: Subjective post-trial questionnaires remain the dominant methodology for evaluating spatial presence in virtual environments (VEs), whereas physiological markers often exhibit inconsistent reliability. To assess continuous behavioral tracking of presence over time, this investigation evaluated rhythmic finger tapping as an index of dynamic attentional resource allocation. Participants wearing sensor-equipped data gloves performed motor tapping at a specified pace during two distinct virtual reality experiences: a virtual plank height manipulation (elevated vs. ground-level conditions) and 360-degree vs. 90-degree immersive video displays. Positional timeseries profiles of finger kinematics—including inter-tap interval dynamics, autocorrelation, and power spectral density—were used to train a neural network classifier. The classifier achieved an 80% accuracy rate in differentiating high- from low-presence states across both task environments, establishing motor timing disruption under secondary-task constraints as an objective, continuous behavioral marker of immersion.
papers.authors: Sean Hinkle, Shayna Soares, Corey Bohil

papers.title: Explicit and implicit category learning in categorical visual search
papers.abstract: Although categorical visual search is frequently studied using naturalistic objects whose cognitive representational structures are ill-defined, category learning frameworks dissociate classification into explicit rule-based systems relying on hypothesis testing and working memory, and implicit information-integration systems mediated by procedural striatal networks. This study assessed how these dual learning systems guide and constrain visual search using parametric sinusoidal grating stimuli. Following acquisition under either rule-based or information-integration demands, participants executed categorical visual search while eye tracking was monitored. Quantitative decision-bound computational modeling verified strategy implementation across acquisition and transfer phases. Implicit category learning facilitated faster overall search responses and reduced target dwell duration relative to rule-based learning. Furthermore, participants who successfully generalized the category structure demonstrated robust search guidance, with implicit learners exhibiting a significantly greater proportion of initial saccades directly fixating the target, demonstrating distinct oculomotor and behavioral signatures between dual categorization architectures.
papers.authors: Corey J. Bohil, Ashley Phelps, Mark B. Neider, Joseph Schmidt

0140.name: Cory Miller
0140.bio: Cory T. Miller is a Professor of Psychology at the University of California, San Diego, and directs research on the neurobiology of natural primate behaviors. Miller’s work utilizes marmoset monkeys to investigate the neural mechanisms of active vision and vocal communication, employing wireless electrophysiology and head-mounted eye-tracking in freely moving animals. By moving beyond head-restrained experimental paradigms, their lab explores how cortical circuits in the visual and frontal systems integrate perceptual, motor, and social information during tasks such as prey pursuit and antiphonal calling. Miller's research aims to elucidate how the primate brain evolved to process complex, dynamic stimuli in the environments found in the natural world.
0140.research_direction: Dr. Miller has recently been investigating the neural basis of naturalistic perceptual and social behaviors in freely moving marmosets. Their recent work explores active vision outside of traditional head-fixed setups by combining wireless neural recordings with custom head-mounted eye tracking to examine how natural gaze shifts coordinate with head movements and organize activity in the primary visual cortex. In the auditory domain, they are studying the neural mechanisms of complex social communication, recording from frontal brain regions to understand how primates track turn-taking and isolate a conversational partner's vocalizations within noisy "cocktail party" environments. Additionally, their research probes the foundations of multisensory social recognition, investigating how the primate hippocampus links familiar faces and voices to build cross-modal representations of individual identity.

papers.title: Active gaze behavior organizes V1 activity in freely-moving marmosets
papers.abstract: Combining head-mounted eye tracking with neural recordings in primary visual cortex of freely moving marmosets, this preprint finds that V1 activity is strongly driven by visual input yet organized in time by natural gaze behavior. Responses are suppressed around rapid gaze shifts and enhanced during fixations, linking natural viewing behavior to cortical dynamics.
papers.authors: Jingwen Li, Vikram Pal Singh, Jude F. Mitchell, Alexander C. Huk, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Active vision in freely moving marmosets using head-mounted eye tracking
papers.abstract: The authors built a wireless, backpack-mounted eye-tracking system (CEREBRO) for small primates and used it to measure how marmosets move their eyes, head and body while freely moving. They show that gaze is organized around head movements and characterize how gaze shifts relate to behavior, establishing a method and baseline for studying active vision outside head-fixed setups.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Vikram Pal Singh, Jingwen Li, Kana Dawson, Jude F. Mitchell, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Primate ACC encodes natural vocal interactions in a 'cocktail party'
papers.abstract: In freely moving marmosets in a noisy colony-like setting, neurons in anterior cingulate cortex separate a conversational partner's calls from background vocalizations, even when sounds overlap. ACC activity also tracks turn-taking during vocal exchanges, implicating the region in managing communication in complex soundscapes.
papers.authors: Arthur Lefevre, Vikram Pal Singh, Timothy J. Tyree, Jingwen Li, Jean-Rene Duhamel, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Representing the dynamics of natural marmoset vocal behaviors in frontal cortex
papers.abstract: Wireless recordings in frontal cortex of freely moving marmosets engaged in natural vocal exchanges show that neural population activity represents ongoing vocal behavior, including hearing and producing calls and their timing. The work shows how frontal circuits encode dynamic, self-generated communication in a naturalistic setting.
papers.authors: Jingwen Li, Mikio C. Aoi, Cory T. Miller

papers.title: Cross-modal representation of identity in the primate hippocampus
papers.abstract: Recording from single neurons in the hippocampus of marmosets, the study shows that individual cells respond selectively to the face or voice of a particular familiar monkey. Beyond these single-cell responses, the population carried a shared cross-modal code that linked an individual's face and voice, indicating how the primate hippocampus supports social recognition of others.
papers.authors: Timothy J. Tyree, Michael Metke, Cory T. Miller

0142.name: Cristina de la Malla
0142.department: Department of Cognition, Development and Psychology of Education
0142.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action Group (VISCA)
0142.bio: Cristina de la Malla is an Assistant Professor at the University of Barcelona and a member of the Vision and Control of Action Group. De la Malla’s research examines the sensorimotor integration of visual and proprioceptive information, specifically how the brain processes temporal delays and predictive signals to execute interceptive actions. They use methodologies such as psychophysics, eye-tracking, and virtual reality to study the relationship between saccadic eye movements and velocity judgments. Their work further investigates the temporal dynamics of foveal and peripheral processing during ocular fixation and the role of these processes in saccade planning and change localization.
0142.research_direction: Dr. de la Malla has recently been studying how vision guides action, from catching moving targets to crossing a street. Their work asks how recent sensory history biases continuous movements, for instance how the speed of a previous target influences hand interception of the next one. They also use immersive virtual reality street-crossing scenarios to test how irrelevant variability in a scene affects decisions, confidence, and the way people sample and move. Related projects examine how the geometry of reach targets shapes learning during visuomotor adaptation, how visual sensitivity changes over time across fovea and periphery during a fixation, and, through a meta-analysis, how contrast sensitivity differs in schizophrenia.

papers.title: Serial dependence in goal-directed interceptive hand movements
papers.abstract: This study investigates how recent sensory history influences continuous sensorimotor control during manual interception. Observers executed an interception task where each trial presented sequential targets: an initial prior target moving at 5 or 15 cm/s, followed by a probe target moving at 10 cm/s in either the congruent or incongruent direction. Interception conditions manipulated motor engagement by requiring participants either to intercept both targets or to passively observe the prior before intercepting the probe. Active interception of the prior induced direction-dependent serial dependencies: probe interception errors exhibited an attractive bias for congruent movement directions and a repulsive bias for opposing directions, whereas passive observation elicited no significant modulation. Analysis of hand velocity profiles and concomitant oculomotor dynamics demonstrated an early attractive sensory bias that decayed across the movement trajectory as real-time sensory evidence was continuously acquired to guide online feedback control.
papers.authors: Cristian Muñoz-Puelman, Alexander Goettker, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Scene variability affects action decisions, confidence and behaviour dynamics
papers.abstract: This work explores how task-irrelevant environmental variability influences action decisions, subjective confidence, sensory sampling, and motor execution within an immersive virtual reality street-crossing paradigm. Observers judged their confidence in successfully crossing or decided whether to actively cross while facing six oncoming vehicles under varying levels of velocity dispersion. Elevated scene variability decreased crossing attempt frequencies and reduced confidence reports while significantly prolonging crossing initiation latencies. Participants compensated for these delayed onsets by executing crossing trajectories with increased movement velocity, preserving task performance. Furthermore, oculomotor recordings revealed that high-confidence decisions and crossing initiations were characterized by accelerated information acquisition and faster subsequent gaze disengagement, showing that environmental variability alters both metacognitive evaluations and execution dynamics.
papers.authors: David Aguilar-Lleyda, Antonio González-Del Pozo, Joan López-Moliner, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Target configuration determines how and what we learn during sensorimotor adaptation
papers.abstract: This study examines how spatial target geometry dictates learning mechanisms and coordinate frame representations during sensorimotor adaptation. Human participants completed reaching tasks under visuomotor gain perturbations (0.7× or 1.3× display scaling) across two spatial configurations: an Extent Group trained on multiple reach amplitudes along a single vector, and an Angular Group trained on fixed amplitudes across multiple angular directions. In no-feedback aftereffect assays designed to isolate implicit adaptation from cognitive strategies, the Angular Group demonstrated substantially greater implicit aftereffects, whereas the Extent Group relied predominantly on explicit re-aiming. Generalization trials to unperturbed targets revealed distinct learned models: the Angular Group acquired an extrinsic translation rule generalizing across directions but failing across amplitudes, whereas the Extent Group captured a true multiplicative gain rule that generalized to untrained amplitudes but not across spatial directions.
papers.authors: Pamela Villavicencio, Jonathan S. Tsay, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Contrast Sensitivity in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesizes visual contrast sensitivity measurements across individuals with schizophrenia relative to healthy controls. Compiling psychophysical detection thresholds across spatial and temporal frequencies from clinical studies, the meta-analysis established a pronounced deficit in contrast sensitivity among patients with schizophrenia (Hedges' g = 0.64; 95% CI: 0.40–0.88). Meta-regression indicated that stimulus duration (comparing transient ~30 ms and sustained 500 ms presentations) did not significantly moderate effect magnitudes. However, elevated antipsychotic medication dosage correlated with enhanced threshold impairment. The analysis confirms generalized degradation in early contrast encoding pathways in schizophrenia while discussing how task-unrelated attentional lapses may contribute to observed psychophysical sensitivity reductions.
papers.authors: Daniel Linares, Aster Joostens, Cristina de la Malla

papers.title: Different temporal dynamics of foveal and peripheral visual processing during fixation
papers.abstract: This study analyzes the temporal dynamics of visual sensitivity across the fovea and periphery throughout the course of ocular fixations. Utilizing dual-Purkinje-style high-precision eye tracking to ensure fixation stability, observers performed an orientation transient localization task wherein target bars flashed at varying intervals post-fixation onset within foveal, peripheral, or combined retinotopic locations. Transient localization accuracy in the visual periphery exhibited monotonic improvement as fixation elapsed over time, whereas foveal localization performance remained uniform across the entire fixation epoch. This temporal dissociation persisted when foveal and peripheral regions were simultaneously attended without dual-task interference, demonstrating that extrafoveal visual processing is selectively amplified late in fixation, likely facilitating target selection and spatial programming for subsequent saccades.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Cristina de la Malla, Martina Poletti

0143.name: Curtis L. Baker Jr.
0143.bio: Curtis L. Baker Jr. is a Professor in the Departments of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences and Biomedical Engineering at McGill University, and an Affiliate Member of the UBC Vision Cluster. Baker's lab aims to understand human visual perception, particularly the low-level neural mechanisms that perform signal processing relevant to everyday vision. Natural scenes contain objects set apart from their backgrounds not only by luminance or colour but by differences in contrast, texture and motion, and a central goal is to understand how early vision detects and uses these cues to support robust figure-ground and local depth perception. The lab combines human psychophysics with computational modeling of psychophysical and neurophysiological data.
0143.research_direction: Dr. Baker's research is now centred on human psychophysics of early visual processing: how the visual system uses contrast, texture and motion cues, not just luminance or colour, to separate objects from their backgrounds and judge local depth. Recent work uses isoluminant contrast-modulation stimuli to show that such second-order cues are hard to see when luminance information is removed, pointing to a magnocellular pathway mechanism, and looks for behavioral signatures in human vision of the nonlinear, Y-cell-like processing long studied in neurons. These experiments are paired with computational models that link perception to its neural basis. The lab's earlier neurophysiology in early visual cortex, now wrapping up, produced convolutional-network encoding models that capture simple and complex cells in one framework, showed that dark-dominance in V1 arises mainly from slower inhibition to light, and modeled how fluctuating cortical state shapes trial-to-trial response variability.

papers.title: Impaired perception of isoluminant contrast modulation stimuli: Evidence for a magnocellular pathway mechanism
papers.abstract: Nonlinear responses to contrast modulation (CM) stimuli—where a high-frequency carrier's contrast is varied by a low-frequency envelope—have been hypothesized to originate from Y-like retinal ganglion cells within the magnocellular pathway. To investigate the dependency of CM processing on this pathway, we conducted human psychophysical experiments comparing motion direction discrimination and detection for achromatic (yellow-black) and chromatic (red-green) CM stimuli. We utilized luminance masking noise to selectively interfere with luminance-driven motion mechanisms. Our findings indicate that perception of chromatic CMs is significantly more susceptible to luminance masking than achromatic CMs. While envelope motion discrimination for achromatic stimuli was robust even under high noise conditions, performance for chromatic stimuli was severely degraded. Notably, detection of the chromatic modulator remained relatively intact despite the failure of motion discrimination, suggesting that chromatic aberrations may provide spurious luminance signals that facilitate detection but not directional judging. These results support the hypothesis that second-order CM envelope motion is predominantly processed by nonlinearities within the retino-geniculate magnocellular pathway, suggesting CM stimuli as a viable tool for assessing magnocellular integrity in clinical contexts.
papers.authors: Ana L. Ramirez, Anna Shakhgildian, Ari Rosenberg, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

papers.title: Cortical state contributions to neuronal response variability in the early visual cortex: A system identification approach
papers.abstract: The responses of individual neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) to identical visual stimuli exhibit significant trial-to-trial variability, which is often dismissed as noise. This study challenges that view by demonstrating that much of this variability is driven by dynamic fluctuations in the brain's internal state. We developed a multi-pathway convolutional neural network (CNN) model that integrates a stimulus-driven pathway with a state-driven pathway. The latter utilizes indicators of cortical state fluctuations derived from simultaneously recorded local field potentials (LFPs) and multi-unit activity (MUA) in the vicinity of the target neuron. Using single-unit recordings from cat areas 17 and 18, we show that this integrated model significantly outperforms stimulus-only encoding models in predicting spiking activity. The predictive improvement was found to be heterogeneous across the population, with neurons exhibiting the highest intrinsic response variability benefiting most from the inclusion of internal state indicators.
