Furthermore, we identified neuron-specific temporal filters for LFP frequency bands, illustrating how different neurons are uniquely coupled to distinct aspects of population dynamics.
papers.authors: Jinani Sooriyaarachchi, Chang'an A. Zhan, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

papers.title: Estimating receptive fields of simple and complex cells in early visual cortex: A convolutional neural network model with parameterized rectification
papers.abstract: Characterizing the receptive fields (RFs) of early visual cortex neurons is complicated by the distinct behaviors of phase-sensitive simple cells and phase-invariant complex cells. While simple cells are well-modeled by linear-nonlinear (LN) systems, complex cells require more sophisticated hierarchical architectures to account for their nonlinear integration of subunit inputs. We present a compact CNN encoding model that employs a parameterized rectified linear unit (PReLU) to bridge the gap between simple and complex cell modeling. The architecture consists of a primary spatiotemporal filter, a PReLU nonlinearity with a single learnable gain parameter for negative inputs, and a two-dimensional Gaussian spatial map. The PReLU parameter serves as a continuous metric of phase invariance, allowing the model to smoothly transition between an LN structure for simple cells and a subunit-summation structure for complex cells. Applying this model to neurons in cat areas 17 and 18, we demonstrate high predictive performance for both natural image responses and sinewave grating tuning curves. Our results show that complex cells are intrinsically less reliable than simple cells, but noise ceiling analysis reveals that our model captures a comparable proportion of the explainable variance in both types.
papers.authors: Philippe Nguyen, Jinani Sooriyaarachchi, Qianyu Huang, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

papers.title: Model-based approach shows ON pathway afferents elicit a transient decrease of V1 responses
papers.abstract: Neurons in primary visual cortex respond more strongly to dark than to light stimuli, but it was unclear whether this dark-dominance comes from stronger excitation via the OFF pathway or from inhibition via the ON pathway. Recording simple cells in cat V1 with natural-image stimuli and fitting biologically inspired convolutional network models to their responses, the authors find that the asymmetry arises mainly from slower inhibition to light rather than stronger thalamocortical OFF excitation. Dark-dominance appeared only at early response latencies, and strongly dark-dominated neurons tended to be less orientation-selective.
papers.authors: Dominic St-Amand, Curtis L. Baker Jr.

0145.name: Daniel D. Dilks
0145.bio: Daniel D. Dilks is an Associate Professor at Emory University, where their research explores the functional organization, development, and plasticity of the human visual cortex. Dilks investigates specialized cortical regions for processing scenes, faces, and objects, as well as how these systems emerge in childhood and reorganize following brain damage or sensory loss in adulthood. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics, Dilks characterizes the neural mechanisms underlying visually guided navigation and categorization. Their recent studies examine the protracted development of scene-selective regions and the distinct cognitive systems involved in navigating environments versus recognizing places.
0145.research_direction: Dr. Dilks has recently been investigating the functional architecture and developmental trajectories of human scene recognition and navigation systems. Using pediatric fMRI, multivoxel pattern analysis, and computational modeling, their recent work explores how distinct cortical networks support different computational goals, contrasting scene categorization in the parahippocampal place area, map-based navigation in the retrosplenial complex, and visually-guided navigation in the occipital place area. Specifically, they are examining the developmental timeline of these neural representations in infants and young children to understand why scene categorization and map-based navigation emerge early, whereas visually-guided navigation—moving through the immediately visible environment—undergoes such protracted development.

papers.title: Dissociable systems for visually guided navigation versus reaching and grasping in human parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in adults, the study contrasts dynamic and static scenes with reaching-and-grasping videos to test whether parietal cortex holds separable action systems. SPL responded most to dynamic scenes, while superior parieto-occipital cortex responded most to reaching and grasping, a double dissociation echoed by resting-state connectivity with leg-motor versus arm-motor cortex. The work clarifies how parietal cortex is organized for different visually guided actions.
papers.authors: Hee Kyung Yoon, Yaelan Jung, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: A novel computational approach to isolating mechanisms of cognitive development across two systems: scene categorization and visually guided navigation
papers.abstract: Ninety-five participants aged 4 to 21 performed scene categorization and visually guided navigation tasks, and choices and reaction times were fit with a linear ballistic accumulator model to separate accumulation of correct versus incorrect evidence. For categorization only the correct-evidence rate rose with age, whereas for navigation both rates changed. This gives a formal account of why the two systems follow different developmental paths and shows the modeling approach can generalize.
papers.authors: Zvi R. Shapiro, Alexander Weigard, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: Early development of navigationally relevant location information in the retrosplenial complex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and a virtual-town paradigm in 5-year-old children, the authors ask whether the retrosplenial complex, the adult hub for map-based navigation, is already functional early in childhood. They find that RSC in 5-year-olds encodes where particular buildings are located, tracks the actual layout of the town, and predicts children's performance on a location task, whereas the parahippocampal place area instead encodes building category. The result points to an early origin of map-based navigation and a clean double dissociation between RSC and PPA.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Yaelan Jung, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: A scene-selective region in the superior parietal lobule for visually guided navigation
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that a scene-responsive region in the superior parietal lobule (SPL) joins the occipital place area in supporting visually guided navigation. In adults, SPL responds more to scenes than faces or objects, carries first-person motion and left/right sense information, and is preferentially connected to OPA at rest. Reanalysis of earlier data also shows it is engaged more by a navigation task than by scene categorization.
papers.authors: Hee Kyung Yoon, Yaelan Jung, Andrew S. Persichetti, Daniel D. Dilks

papers.title: Two cortical navigation systems and their differential development
papers.abstract: Testing the hypothesis that OPA (visually guided navigation) matures later than RSC (map-based navigation), the authors used fMRI adaptation in 5- and 8-year-old children. RSC already represented left/right information at age 5, whereas OPA did so only at age 8. Because a single system cannot have two developmental timelines, this supports OPA and RSC serving distinct navigation functions.
papers.authors: Rebecca J. Rennert, Daniel D. Dilks

0146.name: Daniel Denman
0146.institution: University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
0146.bio: Daniel Denman is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, where they investigate the neural circuit dynamics underlying visual representation and perception. Denman’s research employs high-density extracellular electrophysiology, quantitative psychophysics, and physiological circuit-tracing to study how populations of neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) interact with subcortical and cortical partners. By integrating optogenetic manipulations and computational modeling, their laboratory probes the causal relationships between large-scale neural population activity and sensory behavior across various timescales. Denman previously served as a scientist at the Allen Institute for Brain Science, where they contributed to the development and implementation of neuroengineering tools, including Neuropixels technology, for systems neuroscience research.
0146.research_direction: Dr. Denman's recent work explores neural population coding, visual system repair, and neurostimulation dynamics in the mouse cortex. Using high-density Neuropixels recordings, they have recently been investigating the relationship between single-neuron mixed selectivity and separable population-level representations of color and luminance, while also probing how trial-to-trial shared variability differs across distinct early visual areas and cell types. In the realm of neural prosthetics, their research examines the spatial and temporal population dynamics evoked by direct electrical microstimulation, a line of inquiry supported by their development of novel open-source hardware for adaptive multipolar stimulation. Furthermore, they are exploring the intersection of cortical function and pathology by evaluating how therapeutic remyelination relates to the functional recovery of in vivo visual responses in demyelination models.

papers.title: Neural population dynamics of direct electrical stimulation of neocortex
papers.abstract: Recordings across the depth of awake mouse cortex show how direct electrical microstimulation recruits neurons. The study characterizes the spatiotemporal spread and time course of evoked population activity, including the mix of direct and indirect activation and subsequent suppression, giving a mechanistic picture relevant to cortical neuroprostheses.
papers.authors: Jordan L. Hickman, Grant Hughes, Eashan Sahai, Moriah Miles, Daniel J. Denman

papers.title: Nonuniform spike count shared variability in the mouse early visual system
papers.abstract: Analyzes trial-to-trial shared variability of spike counts across neurons recorded simultaneously in mouse early visual areas. The authors find that shared variability is not uniform across the population, depending on cell type, area and stimulus, which constrains models of noise correlations and population coding.
papers.authors: Jordan L. Hickman, Juan Santiago Moreno, Grant Hughes, Eashan Sahai, Nicholas Garcia, Daniel J. Denman

papers.title: Separable neural population representations are constructed from mixed single neuron selectivity in the mouse early visual system
papers.abstract: Using high-density Neuropixels recordings in mouse thalamus and primary visual cortex with color and luminance stimuli, the authors show that single neurons have mixed selectivity while population activity can still be decomposed into separable representations of stimulus features. This links single-cell tuning to population-level coding in the early visual system.
papers.authors: Juan Santiago Moreno, Nicholas Garcia, Daniel J. Denman

papers.title: A bioelectric router for adaptive isochronous neurostimulation enables multipolar bioelectric stimulation from a single source
papers.abstract: Describes an open-source hardware device that routes the output of a single standard stimulator to multiple electrode contacts while keeping current delivery isochronous. It enables multipolar stimulation configurations at low cost and is validated in neural stimulation experiments.
papers.authors: Eashan Sahai, Jordan Hickman, Daniel J. Denman

papers.title: Incomplete remyelination via therapeutically enhanced oligodendrogenesis is sufficient to recover visual cortical function
papers.abstract: In a mouse demyelination model, drug-enhanced oligodendrogenesis leads to only partial remyelination yet is sufficient to restore visual cortical responses. In vivo recordings and imaging of visual cortex link myelin repair to recovery of neuronal function.
papers.authors: Gustavo Della-Flora Nunes, Lindsay A. Osso, Johana A. Haynes, Lauren Conant, Michael A. Thornton, Michael E. Stockton, Katherine A. Brassell, Amanda Morris, Yessenia I. Mancha Corchado, John A. Gaynes, Anthony R. Chavez, Michaelanne B. Woerner, Deidre A. MacKenna, Aryan Alavi, Anne Danks, Alon Poleg-Polsky, Rohan Gandhi, Jeffrey A. Vivian, Daniel J. Denman, Ethan G. Hughes

0147.name: Daniel Fiset
0147.department: Département de psychoéducation et de psychologie
0147.lab_name: Laboratoire de perception visuelle et sociale (LPVS)
0147.bio: Daniel Fiset is a Professor at the Université du Québec en Outaouais and co-director of the Social and Visual Perception Laboratory. Fiset’s research examines the neurocognitive mechanisms involved in recognizing faces, facial expressions, and written language through psychophysical techniques like the Bubbles method and reverse correlation. By integrating electrophysiological recordings (EEG/ERP), Fiset investigates how low-level visual properties, such as spatial frequencies and orientations, modulate the extraction of diagnostic information. Their work addresses neurotypical visual processing and clinical conditions like prosopagnosia and dyslexia, while also evaluating the impact of social factors such as the other-race effect.
0147.research_direction: Dr. Fiset has recently been studying how people recognize and interpret faces, asking which visual information the brain actually relies on. Their recent work explores whether individual differences in face recognition ability come from encoding individual facial features or from integrating the whole face, how much the eyes matter for detecting a face at all, and which spatial scales of image detail (fine versus coarse) are most useful for telling facial expressions apart. Beyond face perception, they have also examined whether verbal abuse aimed at baseball umpires biases their calls in a large real-world dataset, and developed a statistical method for drawing more accurate error bars on time-series data such as EEG and fMRI.

papers.title: The eyes are central to face detection: revisiting the foundations of face processing
papers.authors: Côté, ..., Fiset

papers.title: Part-based processing, but not holistic processing, predicts individual differences in face recognition abilities
papers.abstract: This study employs a psychophysical paradigm to evaluate the predictive validity of part-based and holistic processing for face processing ability (FPA). Defining holistic processing as the perceptual integration efficiency of multiple facial parts and part-based processing as the efficiency in identifying isolated components, the researchers used a battery of tasks (N = 64) to measure individual differences. Multiple linear regression analyses revealed that part-based efficiency was a robust predictor of FPA variance, whereas perceptual integration (holistic processing) showed no significant predictive relationship. These results suggest that feature-level encoding, rather than structural integration, is the primary driver of individual variations in face recognition.
papers.authors: Pierre-Louis Audette, Laurianne Côté, Caroline Blais, Justin Duncan, Francis Gingras, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Facial expression categorization predominantly relies on mid-spatial frequencies
papers.abstract: While previous research has debated the relative importance of low versus high spatial frequencies (SF) in emotion perception, the specific bands optimal for identifying basic facial expressions have remained unclear. This study utilizes two complementary psychophysical methods—a data-driven approach and a naturalistic distance-simulation task—to establish SF tuning profiles for basic emotions. Results demonstrate that categorization performance is highest at viewing distances corresponding to mid-range spatial frequencies (~6–13 cycles per face) and declines sharply when this information is unavailable. The findings highlight that mid-SF content is diagnostic across various expressions and suggest that its exclusion in prior studies may have led to an incomplete understanding of the visual mechanisms underlying expression recognition.
papers.authors: Isabelle Charbonneau, Justin Duncan, Caroline Blais, Joël Guérette, Marie-Pier Plouffe-Demers, Fraser Smith, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Verbal Aggressions Against Major League Baseball Umpires Affect Their Decision Making
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale ecological dataset from Major League Baseball (N = 153,255 pitches), this study assesses the impact of extreme verbal aggression—proxied by player or coach ejections—on the subsequent decision-making of home-plate umpires. The analysis reveals a significant bias following ejections: umpires were less likely to call strikes for the team that resorted to verbal abuse and more likely to call strikes for the opposing team. Statistical controls for compensation effects suggest that verbal aggression may paradoxically confer a strategic advantage by subconsciously influencing official judgments in favor of the complaining team, challenging the assumption that such behavior is purely detrimental to the aggressor's interests.
papers.authors: Joël Guérette, Caroline Blais, Daniel Fiset

papers.title: Local decorrelation for error bars in time series
papers.abstract: Confidence intervals in within-subject designs often rely on the assumption of stationary correlation across all measurement pairs. However, in time-series and electroencephalographic (EEG) data, correlations typically vanish as the temporal distance between points increases. This paper introduces a novel decorrelation technique based on local correlation assumptions. By adjusting the width of error bars using a weighted average correlation within a specific temporal radius, the method provides more precise estimates of uncertainty for contiguous data points. The authors demonstrate the utility of this local decorrelation approach using fMRI and ERP datasets, showing it effectively preserves precision in noisy temporal data without overestimating global dependencies.
papers.authors: Denis Cousineau, Anthony Proulx, Annabelle Potvin-Pilon, Daniel Fiset

0148.name: Daniel Kaiser
0148.department: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science
0148.bio: Daniel Kaiser is the Professor of Neural Computation at Justus Liebig University Giessen and directs the Neural Computation Group. Their research investigates how the human brain represents and integrates objects within structured, real-world scenes, focusing on the role of statistical regularities and top-down feedback mechanisms. Kaiser employs a multimodal approach combining functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and deep neural network modeling to explore these processes. Their work characterizes the rhythmic neural dynamics, such as alpha and beta oscillations, that support the construction of adaptive visual representations for naturalistic behavior.
0148.research_direction: Dr. Kaiser's recent work explores the neural and computational mechanisms underlying naturalistic vision, focusing on how the brain integrates complex information to form coherent percepts and evaluate visual aesthetics. Using combinations of EEG, fMRI, and deep neural network models, they have recently been investigating how distinct neural rhythms—such as alpha and gamma oscillations—route feedforward and feedback content between cortical areas during scene processing. Alongside these neural dynamics, their research probes the visual computations driving aesthetic experiences, asking how stimulus features and integrative processing stages predict the perceived beauty of both static natural images and dynamic movies. Finally, they are also examining the role of predictive processing in visual cognition by testing how person-specific internal models and learned expectations shape idiosyncratic differences in everyday scene perception.

papers.title: Visual features explain dynamic aesthetic experiences across distinct movie content
papers.abstract: Participants continuously rated their aesthetic experience while watching movie clips of different content. A combination of low- and high-level visual features, including deep network features, predicted these moment-to-moment ratings and generalized across different types of movies. The results show that dynamic aesthetic experience is partly grounded in stimulus features.
papers.authors: Mustafa Alperen Ekinci, Nina Buhlmann, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Decoding the rhythmic representation and communication of visual contents
papers.abstract: This opinion article argues that visual brain rhythms do more than modulate responses: they carry and route visual content between areas. It gathers recent decoding studies showing that alpha and beta rhythms convey feedback contents while gamma-range rhythms relate to feedforward information, and proposes a framework and open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Rico Stecher, Radoslaw Martin Cichy, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Integrative processing in artificial and biological vision predicts the perceived beauty of natural images
papers.abstract: The study asks which perceptual computations make an image look beautiful. Combining deep neural network analyses and EEG, it shows that images whose representations are more integrated across processing stages (in models and in human visual cortex) are rated as more beautiful. This links processing-fluency ideas about aesthetics to concrete visual computations.
papers.authors: Sanjeev Nara, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Individual differences in internal models explain idiosyncrasies in scene perception
papers.abstract: Predictive-processing theories hold that vision relies on internal models of what scenes should look like. The authors measured individuals' internal models (e.g. via drawings and typicality judgments) and found that these person-specific models predict idiosyncratic differences in scene perception and behavior. This ties individual variation in perception to differences in learned expectations.
papers.authors: Gongting Wang, Matthew J. Foxwell, Radoslaw M. Cichy, David Pitcher, Daniel Kaiser

papers.title: Alpha-frequency feedback to early visual cortex orchestrates coherent naturalistic vision
papers.abstract: Using combined EEG and fMRI, the authors varied how much the brain must integrate image parts scattered across the visual field, by scrambling or rearranging scene fragments. When fragments formed a coherent scene, alpha-band activity carried feedback signals into early visual cortex, and this feedback strengthened with the demand for integration. The work identifies rhythmic top-down alpha feedback as a mechanism that builds coherent percepts during natural vision.
papers.authors: Lixiang Chen, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Daniel Kaiser

0149.name: Daniel Linares
0149.department: Department of Cognition, Development and Educational Psychology
0149.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action Group (VISCA)
0149.bio: Daniel Linares is a Serra Húnter Fellow and researcher at the Universitat de Barcelona, affiliated with the Vision and Control of Action (VISCA) group and the Institute of Neurosciences. Their research utilizes visual psychophysics, computational modeling, and clinical neuroscience to examine how the brain processes sensory information and reaches decisions within the context of psychiatric disorders. Linares focuses on differentiating sensory deficits from decisional biases to identify biomarkers for glutamatergic dysfunction in conditions such as schizophrenia and anti-NMDAR encephalitis. Additionally, they developed technical tools for the field, including StimuliApp for mobile psychophysical testing and the R package 'quickpsy' for fitting and comparing psychometric functions.
0149.research_direction: Dr. Linares has recently been working on how the visual system turns physical stimulus intensity into perceptual experience, and on how that process differs in schizophrenia. In basic psychophysics, their recent work uses magnitude estimation of contrast to probe the nature of internal sensory noise, which ordinary discrimination tasks cannot fully separate from how strongly the system responds to a stimulus. They have also been pooling data across many studies to ask whether people with schizophrenia have reliably altered sensitivity to contrast and to motion.

papers.title: Magnitude estimation reveals Poisson-like noise underlying perception
papers.abstract: A foundational pursuit of sensory neuroscience is elucidating the mapping between physical stimulus intensity and internal perceptual representation. Traditional psychophysics relies heavily on discrimination sensitivity (such as two-alternative forced-choice tasks), but discrimination thresholds inherently conflate the derivative of the sensory transducer function (signal gain) with the amplitude of trial-to-trial internal noise, leaving the noise distribution underdetermined. Examining human contrast perception, this investigation establishes that the trial-by-trial response variability of numeric magnitude estimations directly exposes this internal sensory noise. Concurrently modeling empirical response means and variances revealed an internal representation governed by an asymmetric sigmoidal transducer function paired with signal-dependent, Poisson-like internal noise scaling with the square root of the internal response. Remarkably, this internal representation derived exclusively from magnitude estimations quantitatively predicted objective contrast discrimination sensitivity curves and thresholds across varying pedestal contrast levels without any free fitting parameters. This unified framework accounts for both the expansive low-contrast pedestal effect and compressive suprathreshold Weber-like behavior, demonstrating that a singular stochastic internal representation underpins both subjective appearance ratings and objective psychophysical discriminability.
papers.authors: Cristina Rodríguez-Arribas, Joan López-Moliner, Daniel Linares

papers.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis on motion sensitivity in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies measuring motion sensitivity in people with schizophrenia, following the group's earlier contrast sensitivity meta-analysis.
papers.authors: Antonio González-Del Pozo, Cristina de la Malla, Daniel Linares

papers.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Contrast Sensitivity in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Investigating low-level perceptual abnormalities in psychiatric disorders offers critical traction on disrupted neural and computational architectures. While impaired visual contrast sensitivity is widely cited as a hallmark sensory deficit in schizophrenia, existing findings across disparate spatial and temporal frequencies have not been systematically synthesized. Following PRISMA protocols, a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis was conducted across 46 studies comparing individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder to healthy control cohorts, with 43 investigations specifically evaluating chronic cohorts. Chronic schizophrenia was associated with a robust reduction in contrast sensitivity (pooled Hedges' g = 0.74, 95% CI: [0.55, 0.93], p = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁰), accompanied by marked between-study heterogeneity. Meta-regression revealed that the magnitude of contrast impairment scaled positively with antipsychotic dosage quantified via chlorpromazine equivalents, indicating medication effects may significantly mediate observed sensory decrements. Crucially, none of the synthesized studies parametrically estimated or controlled for attentional lapses during psychometric fitting, leaving unresolved the degree to which non-sensory lapse rates artifactually inflate detection thresholds. Furthermore, comprehensive visual acuity assessments were performed in only two studies, confounding inferences regarding spatial frequency dependence and the selective vulnerability of magnocellular versus parvocellular pathways.
papers.authors: Daniel Linares, Aster Joostens, Cristina de la Malla

0150.name: Daniel R Coates
0150.bio: Daniel R. Coates is an Assistant Professor at the University of Houston College of Optometry whose research examines spatial vision, letter recognition, and peripheral perception. Using psychophysical methods and computational modeling, Coates investigates visual crowding and its impact on reading and appearance. After earning a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley in 2015, Coates completed postdoctoral fellowships in Belgium and Switzerland before joining the Houston faculty in 2017. Their work focuses on stereopsis, color vision, and the development of open-source tools for psychophysical experimentation.
0150.research_direction: Dr. Coates has recently been investigating a broad array of topics spanning color vision, spatial processing, and binocular depth perception. Their recent work explores post-receptoral visual processing by using DKL color space to map spatial summation within the magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular pathways, a technique they are also adapting into a chromatic perimetry paradigm to screen for early neural changes in type 2 diabetes. In the domain of spatial vision and oculomotor control, they are examining how the preparation of voluntary microsaccades influences visual crowding at the fovea. Furthermore, their research extends into stereopsis and 3D vision, investigating how monocular and binocular optical degradations like blur and contrast loss affect the upper and lower limits of disparity processing, as well as how target and background spatial frequencies interact to shape relative depth discrimination in virtual reality environments.

papers.title: Characterizing chromatic sensitivity across the central visual field in those with and without type 2 diabetes
papers.abstract: This study asks whether early retinal neural changes in glucose dysfunction show up as local losses of colour sensitivity. Using a new chromatic perimetry paradigm that tests contrast along the DKL cardinal axes at 20 locations in the central 10 degrees, the authors compared adults with elevated HbA1c against age-matched controls. It extends the lab's colour-vision work toward a clinical screening application for early diabetic eye disease.
papers.authors: Christopher S. Wu, Bismark Owusu-Afriyie, Julia S. Benoit, Wendy W. Harrison, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Characteristics of spatial summation in the magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular pathways
papers.abstract: The authors used chromatic stimuli in DKL color space to isolate the magnocellular, parvocellular and koniocellular pathways and measured how detection improves with stimulus size across the central 20 degrees of the visual field. Complete spatial summation was found for magno- and koniocellular conditions at every eccentricity, but not within the tested size range for parvocellular conditions. A probability-summation model based on receptive-field pooling reproduced the data and suggests the critical summation area follows the dendritic field size of the underlying retinal ganglion cells.
papers.authors: Christopher S. Wu, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Alterations to foveal crowding with microsaccade preparation
papers.abstract: Perisaccadic stimuli are known to suffer less crowding, but this had only been shown for large peripheral saccades. Here observers made cued voluntary microsaccades toward a small rotated T placed 20 arcmin from fixation, with or without radial or tangential flankers. The experiments test how preparing a microsaccade changes foveal crowding and whether the effect is truly crowding-specific.
papers.authors: Krishnamachari S. Prahalad, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: The effect of target and background texture on relative depth discrimination in a virtual environment
papers.abstract: Using bandpass-filtered noise textures in a virtual environment, the authors tested how the spatial frequency of a target's texture and of the background wall combine to determine depth thresholds. Observers picked out the nearest of three squares presented at 3 m against a wall 6 m away. The results show that background texture interacts with target texture in shaping depth discrimination, which matters for designing VR scenes.
papers.authors: Wei Hau Lew, Daniel R. Coates

papers.title: Impact of monocular vs. binocular contrast and blur on the range of functional stereopsis
papers.abstract: Stereopsis is bounded by a lowest disparity threshold and an upper fusion limit; degraded contrast and blur are known to worsen the former, but the effect on the latter was unclear. Observers identified stereo letters in random-dot stereograms while contrast and blur were reduced in one or both eyes. The study compares three accounts of whether the disparity range collapses from both ends or only one.
papers.authors: Wei Hau Lew, Daniel R. Coates

0151.name: Daniel Schneider
0151.institution: Leibniz Research Centre for Working Environment and Human Factors
0151.bio: Daniel Schneider is a cognitive neuroscientist and head of the Information Processing research group at the Leibniz Research Centre for Working Environment and Human Factors (IfADo). Schneider’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of selective information processing, specifically examining how working memory acts as an interface between perception and goal-directed action. Utilizing electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and time-frequency analysis of alpha and beta oscillations, they investigate the roles of target enhancement and distractor suppression in maintaining mental representations. Additionally, Schneider’s work explores the impact of aging and environmental stressors, such as task interruptions, on cognitive resource allocation and performance.
0151.research_direction: Dr. Schneider has recently been investigating the neural dynamics of visual working memory and internal attention, primarily using EEG to track how visual representations are maintained, prioritized, and utilized. Their recent work explores how working memory interacts with other cognitive systems, asking how concurrent motor planning moderates the sensory gating of visual inputs and how attentional prioritization via retro-cues shapes subsequent long-term memory structures. In addition to traditional neural decoding, they are examining whether spontaneous eye blinks can serve as a chronometric marker to track the precise timing of internal attentional shifts toward memory items. Finally, Dr. Schneider is also investigating the cognitive control required to manage task interruptions, using electrophysiology to reveal how temporal flexibility aids both younger and older adults in successfully refocusing on memory contents after a disruption.

papers.title: Spontaneous eye blinks as temporal markers of internal attention
papers.abstract: The study asks whether the timing of spontaneous blinks reveals when attention is focused on a representation in working memory. Blink-locked EEG showed blinks aligned with neural signatures of attentional focusing, and blink-rate profiles shifted with whether the relevant item was cued early during storage or only at probe. Post-cue blinks under early selection predicted better memory, proposing blink timing as an unobtrusive chronometric readout of internal attention.
papers.authors: Daniel Schneider, Şahcan Özdemir, Edmund Wascher, Stefan Arnau

papers.title: Older adults benefit more from flexibility when dealing with task interruptions: Electrophysiological evidence from a working memory task
papers.abstract: Younger and older adults performed a working memory task with interruptions, with the option to choose when to resume the main task. EEG measures compared how age groups used this flexibility to recover and refocus. Older adults gained more from being able to control resumption timing, informing age-sensitive workplace design.
papers.authors: Stephan Getzmann, Soner Ülkü, Edmund Wascher, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: Motor control processes moderate visual working memory gating
papers.abstract: In a preregistered EEG study, participants held a colour in memory while preparing a hand-specific response and later faced an interfering task performed with the same or the other hand. Motor planning began already during encoding, seen as contralateral mu/beta suppression. The interfering task hurt memory only when it carried irrelevant colour information, and remembered colours were biased toward that irrelevant colour, showing that gating of sensory input into working memory interacts with action planning.
papers.authors: Şahcan Özdemir, Eren Günseli, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: Processing in working memory boosts long-term memory representations and their retrieval
papers.abstract: Participants learned object-location associations, then performed a working-memory retro-cue task in which some objects were attentionally prioritised and tested while others were only tested, and finally retrieved locations from long-term memory. Both prioritisation and testing in working memory improved later retrieval, with the probe role adding a further benefit visible in behaviour and EEG. Cross-phase decoding indicated a shared representational format for location across the tasks, linking working and long-term memory.
papers.authors: Melinda Sabo, Daniel Schneider

papers.title: EEG Correlates of Cognitive Dynamics in Task Resumption After Interruptions: The Impact of Available Time and Flexibility
papers.abstract: Using a retro-cue visual working memory task interrupted by an arithmetic task, the authors varied the time available before resuming: short, long, or self-determined. Interruptions impaired performance regardless of duration, but flexible resumption sped responses. EEG showed how extra or self-chosen preparation time changed the neural dynamics of refocusing on the memory content.
papers.authors: Soner Ülkü, Stephan Getzmann, Edmund Wascher, Daniel Schneider

0153.name: Daphne Bavelier
0153.department: Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
0153.bio: Daphné Bavelier is a cognitive neuroscientist and Professor at the University of Geneva, where they direct the Brain and Learning Lab at Campus Biotech. Bavelier investigates the mechanisms of human brain plasticity and learning, focusing on how the brain adapts to experiences such as deafness or training with digital media. Bavelier’s research indicates that action video games can serve as tools to enhance visual attention, perception, and spatial cognition. Utilizing fMRI, psychophysics, and eye-tracking, Bavelier currently identifies factors that promote learning and the transfer of cognitive skills across different domains.
0153.research_direction: Dr. Bavelier has recently been investigating the cognitive impacts of action video game play, specifically exploring the theoretical mechanisms through which gaming might strengthen broad attentional control and transfer to high-stakes psychomotor tasks like aviation screening. To better measure and harness these phenomena, their recent work explores methodological improvements in cognitive assessment and training, including designing multidimensional dynamic difficulty algorithms to personalize game-based interventions and evaluating how different psychometric scoring practices affect the reliability of executive function models. Additionally, they are examining the clinical aspects of heavy gaming behavior. By combining actual gameplay telemetry with psychological batteries, they are investigating whether raw gaming consumption predicts Internet Gaming Disorder, or if such symptoms are better accounted for by underlying mental health and personality traits.

papers.title: Action video game playing impacts occupational screening for high-stakes professionals
papers.abstract: Tests whether habitual action video game play relates to performance on a psychomotor battery that is part of the selection test for US Navy aviation. Among Naval Flight Students, more action-game experience predicted both better starting performance and faster learning on the psychomotor task. The link did not appear in a control group for whom the task was not occupationally relevant, suggesting that game-related skills have real-world workplace value.
papers.authors: Aaron Cochrane, Ciara Sibley, Rebecca NeSmith, C. Shawn Green, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: A novel multidimensional dynamic difficulty adjustment algorithm: Use case in a cognitive training video game
papers.abstract: Presents a modular cognitive-control training game built around an action-style hub, with an adaptive system that adjusts difficulty on several dimensions at once in real time. Data from 34 players show most reach their zone of proximal development after roughly 30-45 minutes per module, after which the algorithm keeps gameplay varied, which may aid transfer. The framework is offered as a general method for personalized game-based training.
papers.authors: Angela Pasqualotto, Marios Fanourakis, Zeno Menestrina, Friedhelm C. Hummel, Elmars Rancans, Frank Padberg, Omer Bonne, Amit Lotan, Esther Bukowski, Lena Lipskaya-Velikovsky, Mor Nahum, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: Learning and Transfer: A Perspective From Action Video Game Play
papers.abstract: Argues that action video games are unusual among cognitive training tools in producing broad benefits beyond the trained task. The authors propose that this generalization arises because play first strengthens attentional control, which lets players extract more information from new tasks and so learn them faster. They discuss theoretical and practical consequences of this learning-to-learn account.
papers.authors: Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: In search of better practice in executive functions assessment: Methodological issues and potential solutions
papers.abstract: Shows that how performance is scored in executive function tasks (single-condition scores versus difference scores, accuracy versus response time) strongly affects whether factor models of EF converge and are accepted. Using bootstrapped data from 294 children aged 8-12 across nine tasks, it finds single-task scores and accuracy measures give better-behaved models. The paper offers practical recommendations for measuring executive functions more reliably.
papers.authors: Marc Yangüez, Benoit Bediou, Julien Chanal, Daphne Bavelier

papers.title: Going beyond video game consumption when considering Internet Gaming Disorder
papers.abstract: Asks whether time spent gaming predicts Internet Gaming Disorder using two independent samples of League of Legends players, combining self-report, actual gameplay logs, mental health, personality and cognitive measures. No gaming variable showed a stable link to disorder symptoms, even around the 30 hours-per-week threshold. Anxiety, depression, ADHD and related traits were the more reliable correlates, challenging consumption-based screening.
papers.authors: Sezen Cekic, Benoît Bediou, Sophia Achab, Michael Rich, C. Shawn Green, Daphné Bavelier

0154.name: Daryl Fougnie
0154.bio: Daryl Fougnie is an Associate Professor of Psychology at New York University Abu Dhabi and the director of the Fougnie Lab. Fougnie’s research examines the structural and capacity limitations of human visual perception, attention, and working memory, focusing on how these systems interact to represent environmental information. They utilize psychophysics and computational modeling alongside neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI to characterize the precision and format of visual representations. Recent projects explore the neural mechanisms underlying internal selection from memory and external attentional selection, as well as trade-offs between the quantity and quality of stored visual information.
0154.research_direction: Dr. Fougnie has recently been investigating the architecture, control, and limitations of working memory representations across sensory modalities. Their recent work explores the probabilistic richness of these representations by developing novel behavioral paradigms, such as utilizing a spatial betting game to capture trial-by-trial uncertainty in vision, and constructing a circular Shepard-tone pitch space to translate visual continuous-report tasks into the auditory domain. In addition to measuring memory fidelity, they are examining how working memory contents are manipulated by testing whether actively dropping or deliberately forgetting specific items selectively benefits the representations that remain. Finally, they are investigating the intersection of attention and memory by probing the mechanisms of attribute amnesia, specifically testing whether the apparent immunity of meaningful objects to surprise memory failures reflects robust working memory consolidation or incidental long-term familiarity.

papers.title: Not All Forgetting Is Equal: Active forgetting has selective benefits in working memory
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether deliberately dropping an item from working memory helps the items that remain. It compares different kinds of forgetting cues and finds that the benefits of active forgetting are selective rather than uniform across conditions. The work refines theories of how working memory contents are controlled and removed.
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Introducing ART: A new method for testing auditory memory with circular reproduction tasks
papers.abstract: The authors built an auditory reproduction task using Shepard tones, which form a circular 1-360 degree pitch space, so continuous-report methods from visual working memory can be applied to hearing. They validated the perceptual circularity of the stimulus space, showed set-size effects and swap errors similar to vision, and found reproduction error correlates with other auditory and visual memory tasks.
papers.authors: Aytaç Karabay, Rob Nijenkamp, Anastasios Sarampalis, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Probabilistic and rich individual working memories revealed by a betting game
papers.abstract: Participants placed several bets on the location of a remembered color, which let the authors build a trial-by-trial uncertainty distribution rather than a single point report. Bet spread tracked accuracy, and later bets moved toward the target, so averaging across bets improved memory estimates. Even when the first response looked like a guess, later bets carried target information, arguing that memories are probabilistic and richer than a point estimate.
papers.authors: Syaheed B. Jabar, Kartik K. Sreenivasan, Stergiani Lentzou, Anish Kanabar, Timothy F. Brady, Daryl Fougnie

papers.title: Meaningful objects avoid attribute amnesia due to incidental long-term memories
papers.abstract: Attribute amnesia is the failure to report an attribute of an object one just attended to. Using a more sensitive four-alternative memory test, the authors show meaningful objects are also vulnerable, and that familiarity from earlier exposure drives choices at the surprise test. This indicates that apparent immunity for meaningful objects reflects incidental long-term memory rather than stronger working memory consolidation.
papers.authors: Edyta Sasin, Yuri Markov, Daryl Fougnie

0158.name: David Alais
0158.bio: David Alais is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at the University of Sydney, specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual and multisensory perception. Alais investigates how the brain resolves sensory ambiguity and integrates cross-modal information, focusing on the ventriloquist effect, binocular rivalry, and perceptual suppression. Recent work by Alais examines face pareidolia and serial dependence to determine how temporal context and specialized neural templates bias human awareness. Utilizing psychophysical techniques, computational modeling, and functional neuroimaging, Alais maps the spatiotemporal dynamics of consciousness and sensory integration.
0158.research_direction: Dr. Alais has recently been investigating how visual perception is dynamically modulated by bodily states, temporal context, and perceptual masking. Their recent work explores the interaction between vision and natural locomotion, utilizing wireless VR to examine how the specific phases of the walking stride cycle constrain visual detection performance across central and peripheral visual fields. In addition, they are studying temporal smoothing and contextual biases, measuring how phenomena like serial dependence and central tendency shape both basic multisensory speed perception and high-level evaluative judgments of food images. Furthermore, they investigate the mechanisms of unconscious processing by developing a novel tracking Continuous Flash Suppression (tCFS) paradigm to continuously assess breakthrough thresholds and suppression depth for visual targets of varying complexity.

papers.title: Local and global influence of contextual information: insight from auditory and visual speed perception
papers.abstract: Participants rated the speed of visual and auditory stimuli so that central tendency and serial dependence could be compared across modalities. Both biases appeared in each modality, with central tendency stronger in audition, consistent with higher sensory uncertainty, while serial dependence was an attraction to the previous trial. The two effects were uncorrelated within a modality, and only central tendency correlated across modalities, pointing to a dual-process account of contextual effects.
papers.authors: Alessia Tonelli, David C. Burr, David Alais

papers.title: Optimal phase for central and peripheral visual detection differs within the stride-cycle
papers.abstract: Extending earlier work, participants monitored parafoveal and peripheral locations for targets while walking in wireless VR. Detection performance modulated within the stride cycle at two or four cycles per stride at all eccentricities, but the optimal stride phase differed between central and peripheral targets. This suggests that walking dynamically shifts how visual field locations are prioritised over the gait cycle.
papers.authors: Cameron Kyle Phan, Matthew J Davidson, David Alais

papers.title: Positive serial dependence in ratings of food images for appeal and calories
papers.abstract: Alais and colleagues show that how appealing or calorific a food picture is rated depends on the food seen on the previous trial, with ratings pulled toward the preceding item. This attractive serial dependence appears for subjective judgements of value and for calorie estimates, not only for low-level visual features. The work argues that the perceptual system's smoothing over time extends into evaluative, high-level judgements.
papers.authors: David Alais, David Burr, Thomas A. Carlson

papers.title: Walking modulates visual detection performance according to stride cycle phase
papers.abstract: Participants detected visual targets while walking freely in wireless virtual reality, letting the authors sample performance finely across the stride cycle. Hit rate, reaction time and response likelihood oscillated at about two or four cycles per stride, with best performance aligned to the swing phase of the step. The results show that the rhythm of natural locomotion imposes phasic constraints on visual perception.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Frans A. J. Verstraten, David Alais

papers.title: A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals uniform suppression depth regardless of target complexity or salience
papers.abstract: The authors introduce tracking CFS (tCFS), in which a suppressed target's contrast ramps up until it breaks through and then down until it vanishes again, repeatedly. This yields both breakthrough and suppression thresholds, allowing suppression depth to be measured. Breakthrough thresholds differ across target types such as faces and gratings, but suppression depth does not, implying that suppression is set by the mask rather than the target and challenging claims of privileged unconscious processing.
papers.authors: David Alais, Jacob Coorey, Randolph Blake, Matthew J Davidson

0159.name: David Brainard
0159.bio: David Brainard is the RRL Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania and investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human visual perception. Their research focuses on color constancy and the process by which the visual system estimates stable object properties from light signals incident on the retina. Brainard utilizes a framework combining psychophysical experiments with image-computable modeling to study early visual encoding and the role of the retinal cone mosaic. Brainard also developed the Psychophysics Toolbox and serves as a co-editor of the Annual Review of Vision Science.
0159.research_direction: Dr. Brainard has recently been investigating the computational, neural, and behavioral foundations of visual perception, with a strong emphasis on spatial and color processing. Their recent work explores early vision by developing image-computable models of the eye's optics and retina to simulate how optical chromatic aberration and midget retinal ganglion cell mosaics affect downstream visual acuity and spatio-chromatic tuning. In parallel, they are examining the perceptual limits and temporal dynamics of human color vision, employing adaptive sampling to comprehensively map high-dimensional color discrimination ellipsoids and using continuous behavioral tracking to estimate the temporal filters of chromatic and luminance channels. Additionally, they have been combining macaque V4 recordings and human psychophysics to investigate how cortical neural populations isolate task-relevant object features from irrelevant background variation during the viewing of natural images.

papers.title: Comprehensive characterization of human color discrimination thresholds
papers.abstract: The authors measured how well people can tell apart nearby colors across a large portion of color space, using adaptive sampling together with a Wishart-process model to make this tractable in a high-dimensional stimulus space. The resulting dataset gives a far more complete picture of individual and population-level discrimination ellipsoids than earlier sparse sampling of a few color-space slices. It supplies a benchmark against which models of early color encoding and color appearance can be tested.
papers.authors: Fangfang Hong, Ruby Bouhassira, Jason Chow, Craig Sanders, Michael Shvartsman, Phillip Guan, Alex H. Williams, David H. Brainard

papers.title: An image-computable spatio-chromatic receptive field model of the midget retinal ganglion cell mosaic across the retina
papers.abstract: Using the ISETBio image-computable framework, the paper builds a model of the midget retinal ganglion cell mosaic whose receptive fields are derived from the underlying cone mosaic and anatomical constraints, varying with retinal eccentricity. The model predicts spatial and chromatic tuning of individual cells and how these change from fovea to periphery. It links retinal anatomy and physiology to downstream visual performance.
papers.authors: Nicolas P. Cottaris, Brian A. Wandell, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of human color processing measured using a continuous tracking task
papers.abstract: Observers continuously tracked a target whose color moved along different directions, allowing the dynamics of color processing to be estimated from behavior in a short session instead of many discrete trials. The analysis recovers temporal filters for different chromatic and luminance channels and compares their latencies. The approach offers an efficient way to characterize the speed of color mechanisms.
papers.authors: Michael A. Barnett, Benjamin M. Chin, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Johannes Burge, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Orthogonal neural representations support perceptual judgments of natural stimuli
papers.abstract: Recording from macaque area V4 while animals performed a task with natural image patches, the study asked how neural populations separate task-relevant object features from irrelevant background variation. Population activity encodes the two kinds of information along largely orthogonal directions, which allows a downstream readout to ignore nuisance features. Human psychophysics on the same stimuli showed behavior consistent with this organization.
papers.authors: Ramanujan Srinath, Amy M. Ni, Claire Marucci, Marlene R. Cohen, David H. Brainard

papers.title: Theoretical impact of chromatic aberration correction on visual acuity
papers.abstract: Using an image-computable model of the eye's optics and cone mosaic, the authors calculate how much visual acuity could improve if the eye's longitudinal and transverse chromatic aberration were corrected. The simulations indicate the gain is limited by the retinal sampling and other factors, giving a quantitative ceiling for optical correction strategies. The work is relevant to designing vision-correcting optics.
papers.authors: Derek Nankivil, Nicolas P. Cottaris, David H. Brainard

0160.name: David E Osher
0160.bio: Osher is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University whose research examines the intersection of brain connectivity, functional specialization, and behavior through computational modeling. Their work utilizes machine learning and multimodal neuroimaging, such as functional and diffusion MRI, to develop 'connectivity fingerprints' that predict individualized neural responses and task-evoked activation. Osher investigates how connectivity patterns constrain information processing to understand the development of specialized regions for attention and high-level visual perception. Their research also extends to predicting cognitive outcomes and identifying neural markers for developmental disorders like dyslexia.
0160.research_direction: Dr. Osher has recently been investigating how a brain region's functional specialization relates to its network wiring, using both resting-state and task-based fMRI to capture individual differences in cortical organization. Their recent work explores whether predictive modeling can accurately localize personalized functional regions—spanning high-level visual areas, language networks, and dozens of other cognitive domains—directly from connectivity data, potentially eliminating the need for traditional functional localizer scans. Alongside this macro-scale neuroimaging research, they are also exploring the cognitive mechanisms of high-level object recognition. Specifically, Dr. Osher is probing the origins of holistic processing, utilizing novel abstract stimuli to test whether classic visual phenomena like the inversion and composite effects are strictly face-specific or driven more broadly by second-order spatial configurations.

papers.title: Connectivity and function are coupled across cognitive domains throughout the brain
papers.abstract: Tests the core assumption that a brain region's specialization arises from its connections. Ridge regression models predicted activation maps for 33 cognitive domains from resting-state functional connectivity, and the coupling between connectivity and function was evaluated across the whole cortex. The results indicate the relationship holds broadly across cognitive domains rather than being confined to a few systems such as vision.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin, David E. Osher

papers.title: Task-based functional connectivity is sufficient to capture individual differences in functional selectivity across multiple cortical systems
papers.abstract: Asks whether functional connectivity computed from task-based fMRI is enough to capture how individuals differ in their functional selectivity. Across several cortical systems, connectivity-based models recovered person-specific activation patterns, extending the connectivity fingerprint approach beyond resting-state data.
papers.authors: Isaac Liao, Zeynep M. Saygin, Keara M. Ginell, Kendrick N. Kay, David E. Osher

papers.title: Face-like holistic processing in non-face stimuli
papers.abstract: Holistic processing has often been considered special to faces or acquired through expertise. Using novel abstract stimuli recognizable only through second-order spatial configuration, with matched feature-only controls, the authors found inversion, misalignment, part-whole and composite effects for configural stimuli but not featural ones. Holistic effects therefore appear when recognition depends on configuration, not on face category.
papers.authors: Yuxuan Zeng, Zitong Lu, Ren E. Hentz, David E. Osher

papers.title: Predicting high-level visual areas in the absence of task fMRI
papers.abstract: Asks how well an individual's resting-state connectivity can localize their face, body, scene and object-selective regions without any localizer scan. Connectivity-based models predicted individual functional regions with good accuracy, and the analysis probes which visual areas are most tightly constrained by their connectivity.
papers.authors: M. Fiona Molloy, Zeynep M. Saygin, David E. Osher

papers.title: A personalized cortical atlas for functional regions of interest
papers.abstract: Builds individualized resting-state parcels that identify a person's own functional regions of interest for high-level vision, language, motor control and working memory using only their functional connectome. The approach offers a fast alternative to acquiring multiple localizer fMRI tasks.
papers.authors: M. Fiona Molloy, David E. Osher

0161.name: David Fitzpatrick
0161.institution: Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience
0161.department: Functional Architecture and Development of Cerebral Cortex
0161.bio: Fitzpatrick is the Scientific Director and CEO of the Max Planck Florida Institute for Neuroscience, where their research examines the functional architecture and maturation of neural circuits in the primary visual cortex. Their work utilizes in vivo two-photon calcium imaging and anatomical tracing to identify how stimulus features such as orientation and motion are represented within the synaptic architecture of dendritic spines and population-level networks. A focus of Fitzpatrick’s research involves the 'nature-nurture' transform, specifically how early spontaneous activity establishes modular networks that are refined by visual experience to achieve binocular alignment. Previously a professor at Duke University, Fitzpatrick investigated the principles of intracortical connectivity and the role of experience-dependent plasticity in sensory processing.
0161.research_direction: Dr. Fitzpatrick has recently been studying how the visual cortex wires itself into organized, reliable circuits during early development, before and just after animals first open their eyes. Their recent work follows activity in ferret and tree shrew visual cortex over time with calcium imaging to ask how spontaneous waves of activity from the retina shape the orderly maps of preferred edge orientation that appear later. They also examine how inputs from the middle layer of cortex come to line up with recurrent circuits in the upper layers so that responses become consistent and stimuli easier to tell apart, and how the start of visual experience reshapes the excitatory synaptic inputs onto cortical neurons.

papers.title: Onset of Visual Experience Drives Rapid Expansion and Functional Re-Composition of Excitatory Synaptic Inputs in Developing Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Studies how the onset of visual experience reshapes excitatory synaptic inputs onto neurons in developing visual cortex, reporting rapid expansion and functional re-composition of these inputs.
papers.authors: Juliane Jaepel, Clara Tepohl, Rachel Satterfield, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: Development of coherent cortical responses reflects increased discriminability of feedforward inputs and their alignment with recurrent circuits
papers.abstract: The transition from immature cortical networks to reliable sensory representations requires the transformation of stimulus-driven inputs into consistent activity patterns. In the primary visual cortex (V1), layer 4 (L4) neurons provide feedforward drive to functional modules in layer 2/3 (L2/3) that are linked by strong recurrent interactions. Using longitudinal in vivo calcium imaging and electrophysiology in ferrets, this study finds that in visually naive animals, coactivity between L4 and L2/3 lacks orientation specificity, resulting in high trial-to-trial variability and poor stimulus discriminability. This state arises from low orientation selectivity in L4 and a misalignment between feedforward and recurrent circuit interactions. Following visual experience, L4 orientation discriminability increases and feedforward inputs align with L2/3 recurrent dynamics, as confirmed by whole-cell subthreshold recordings and computational modeling. This developmental alignment is essential for the emergence of reliable, modular representations characterized by interlaminar temporal coherence.
papers.authors: Augusto Abel Lempel, Sigrid Trägenap, Clara Tepohl, Matthias Kaschube, David Fitzpatrick

papers.title: Retinal waves reveal axial biases in modular patterns of cortical activity that predict future orientation preferences
papers.abstract: The formation of functional modular networks in the visual cortex is guided by spontaneous activity prior to sensory experience. This study utilizes chronic widefield and two-photon calcium imaging in neonatal tree shrews to track cortical activity before and after eye opening. The authors identified retinal-driven spontaneous waves in the immature cortex that exhibit modular structures specific to the topographic axis of the wavefront. These waves recruit neuronal populations into elongated correlated networks whose axial biases strikingly correspond to the orientation preference maps that emerge after the onset of vision. These results indicate that the structural and functional scaffold for modular orientation maps is established by retinal activity patterns well before the maturation of visually driven responses.
papers.authors: Alexandra Gribizis, David Fitzpatrick

0162.name: David Leopold
0162.institution: National Institute of Mental Health, National Institutes of Health
0162.department: Section on Cognitive Neurophysiology and Imaging; Systems Neurodevelopment Laboratory
0162.lab_name: Section on Cognitive Neurophysiology and Imaging (SCNI)
0162.bio: David Leopold investigates the large-scale neural architecture underlying visual perception, specifically how the primate brain constructs a stable interpretation of the environment. Leopold’s research integrates high-field functional MRI with laminar-specific electrophysiology and pharmacological perturbations to study thalamocortical interactions and the neural correlates of conscious visibility. Their work on bistable perception demonstrates how sensory cortical activity reflects subjective states rather than mere physical stimuli. Current research directions for Leopold include the neurodevelopment of social perception circuits and the processing of dynamic, naturalistic visual scenes.
0162.research_direction: Dr. Leopold has recently been investigating the functional and anatomical architecture of the primate visual system, examining how temporal continuity in naturalistic movies and illusory face patterns (pareidolia) drive macaque face patch neurons. Their recent work explores the underlying cellular basis of macroscopic brain networks, using simultaneous fMRI and dense single-unit recordings to test how resting-state hemodynamic connectivity relates to the spiking of specific excitatory and inhibitory interneuron classes. Beyond functional physiology, they are using multimodal neuroimaging to map cross-species evolutionary differences in vertical occipital white matter pathways linking the dorsal and ventral visual streams. To facilitate precisely targeted primate research, they are also developing novel in utero viral vector delivery methods to selectively introduce genes into developmentally defined, layer-specific neural populations without relying on transgenic animals.

papers.title: Targeted gene transfer into developmentally defined cell populations of the primate brain
papers.abstract: The authors combine in utero delivery of viral vectors with birth-dating of neuronal progenitors to introduce genes into cell populations defined by when they are generated during development. They show this works in the developing marmoset and macaque brain, giving cell-type and layer-specific expression with a single injection. The approach offers a route to genetically targeting specific primate neural populations without transgenic animals.
papers.authors: Ana Rita Ribeiro Gomes, Natalie Hamel, Surjeet Mastwal, Naim Wright, David C. Ide, Christopher T. Richie, Ted B. Usdin, Kuan Hong Wang, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Resting fMRI functional connectivity reflects fluctuations in inhibitory interneuron activity
papers.abstract: Using simultaneous fMRI and dense single-unit recordings at rest in macaques, the study sorts neurons by spike waveform and compares each class to local and brain-wide hemodynamic fluctuations. Putative excitatory cells split roughly evenly between positive and negative correlations with local fMRI, whereas all putative interneurons correlate positively, and one subclass tracks brain-wide seed-based connectivity. This suggests inhibitory activity best explains resting-state functional connectivity.
papers.authors: Daniel Zaldivar, Lea Ives, Kenji Koyano, Ryan Bhik-Ghanie, Brian Russ, Frank Ye, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Face pareidolia minimally engages macaque face selective neurons
papers.abstract: The study tested whether face-selective neurons in macaque face patches respond to illusory faces in everyday objects. Responses to pareidolia images were weak relative to real faces and often closer to those to non-face objects, even though monkeys looked at the illusory faces. The results indicate that pareidolia is not driven by the core face-selective machinery.
papers.authors: Kenji W. Koyano, Jessica Taubert, William Robison, Elena N. Waidmann, David A. Leopold

papers.title: A prominent vertical occipital white matter fasciculus unique to primate brains
papers.abstract: Combining ex vivo diffusion MRI, polarized-light imaging and tractography across species, the authors characterize a large vertical occipital white matter tract in the primate visual system. They show it is prominent in humans and macaques and absent or minimal in non-primate species. The finding highlights a primate-specific pathway linking dorsal and ventral visual streams.
papers.authors: Hiromasa Takemura, Takaaki Kaneko, Chet C. Sherwood, G. Allan Johnson, Markus Axer, Erin E. Hecht, Frank Q. Ye, David A. Leopold

papers.title: Temporal continuity shapes visual responses of macaque face patch neurons
papers.abstract: The authors recorded from macaque face patch neurons while manipulating the temporal structure of a 5-minute movie, using clips from 800 ms dynamic snippets to 100 ms static frames. Breaking temporal continuity strongly changed response profiles, especially early after stimulus onset. The results caution that models built on randomized, brief static presentations may not reflect the brain's natural mode of operation.
papers.authors: Brian E. Russ, Kenji W. Koyano, Julian Day-Cooney, Neda Perwez, David A. Leopold

0164.name: David Melcher
0164.lab_name: Perception and Active Cognition Lab (PAC Lab)
0164.bio: Melcher investigates how the human brain constructs a stable and continuous subjective experience from dynamic sensory input during active behavior. Their research characterizes trans-saccadic perception and the role of neural oscillations and temporal binding windows in organizing perception, attention, and action. Utilizing a multimodal approach including fMRI, EEG, MEG, and eye-tracking, Melcher explores the neural underpinnings of predictive remapping and how perception interacts with memory and motor control. Their work also examines individual differences in temporal and spatial processing across the lifespan and within clinical populations, such as those with autism, ADHD, and dyslexia.
0164.research_direction: Dr. Melcher has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual temporal processing and trans-saccadic perceptual stability. Their recent work explores how rhythmic alpha oscillations and aperiodic (1/f) neural noise in EEG recordings predict individual differences in visual temporal integration windows, perceptual confidence, and serial dependence. In parallel, they are examining the mechanisms of visual stability across eye movements, using gaze-contingent preview paradigms and steerable autoencoder network models to understand how the visual system predicts both the identity and timing of post-saccadic foveal inputs without relying on explicit spatiotopic maps. Furthermore, they have been studying these integration processes through the lens of neurodiversity, utilizing drift-diffusion modeling to assess how individuals along the autism-schizotypy continuum differentially weight temporal sensory evidence versus recent perceptual history during causality judgments.

papers.title: Alpha oscillations and aperiodic neural dynamics jointly predict visual temporal resolution, confidence, and dependence on prior experience
papers.abstract: With 83 participants, a sustained-integration task producing fused versus segregated percepts was combined with resting EEG. Faster individual alpha frequency went with narrower temporal integration windows, while steeper aperiodic spectra predicted more precise perception. Slower alpha and flatter spectra were associated with heavier reliance on previous judgments, tying oscillatory and aperiodic dynamics to how priors are weighted.
papers.authors: Gianluca Marsicano, Michele Deodato, David Melcher

papers.title: Steerable autoencoders underlying remapping, spatiotopy, and visual stability
papers.abstract: The article revisits how the brain keeps a stable sense of location across eye movements without building spatiotopic maps. It proposes that a small set of attended targets is tracked on retinotopic maps, and that a steerable autoencoder network shifts each target's feature activity to its new location at every saccade. This provides a unifying account of trans-saccadic integration and visual stability.
papers.authors: Patrick Cavanagh, David Melcher

papers.title: Predicting what and when across saccades: Evidence from the extrafoveal preview effect
papers.abstract: In a gaze-contingent paradigm, a face either stayed the same or changed during a saccade, and on some trials a brief blank gap was inserted at the start of the new fixation. The normal preview benefit disappeared when the blank was present. This suggests that trans-saccadic previews rely on a sensorimotor prediction of both what will appear at the fovea and when the new fixation begins.
papers.authors: David Melcher, Michele Deodato

papers.title: Atypical integration of temporal evidence and priors in causality judgment along the autism-schizotypy continuum
papers.abstract: In 150 neurotypical people spread across the autism-schizotypy spectrum, causality judgments for collision events depended on both physical timing and serial dependence on the previous decision. Schizotypy-like individuals showed the strongest reliance on prior decisions and a bias toward causal reports, whereas autism-like individuals showed the weakest history effects and a sensory-driven style. Drift-diffusion modelling supported a hierarchical account of prior use across timescales.
papers.authors: Gianluca Marsicano, Michele Deodato, David Melcher

papers.title: Aperiodic EEG Predicts Variability of Visual Temporal Processing
papers.abstract: The authors recorded resting-state and task EEG while people judged whether one or two flashes had been shown at varying intervals. Individuals with flatter aperiodic (1/f) EEG spectra, indicating greater excitation relative to inhibition, showed noisier and more variable temporal discrimination. The result links non-oscillatory neural noise, rather than rhythmic alpha activity alone, to how consistently the brain integrates or segregates events in time.
papers.authors: Michele Deodato, David Melcher

0165.name: David Soto
0165.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
0165.bio: David Soto is an Ikerbasque Research Professor who directs the Consciousness Group at the BCBL, where they investigate the neurobiological boundaries between conscious and non-conscious cognitive processes. Soto's research integrates psychophysics, functional neuroimaging, and computational modeling to examine how information influences perceptual selection, working memory, and metacognition. Their work on unconscious working memory employs functional MRI decoded neurofeedback (fMRI-DecNef) to non-invasively manipulate brain states and evaluate changes in behavior and subjective experience. Soto's laboratory extends these investigations to typical and atypical populations with the objective of translating findings into neurocognitive interventions for learning and clinical disorders.
0165.research_direction: Dr. Soto has recently been investigating the boundaries of conscious and unconscious visual processing, alongside the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying ensemble perception. Their recent work explores how the brain encodes unseen images by applying representational similarity analysis and deep neural networks to fMRI data, and tests whether non-conscious associative learning of conceptual representations can subsequently drive visual search behavior. In parallel, they are examining how the visual system extracts summary statistics like mean and variance across different visual features, combining psychophysics, drift-diffusion modeling, and multivariate fMRI to determine if these ensemble computations depend on explicit awareness of individual items. To further probe these representational spaces, Dr. Soto is also developing co-adaptive machine learning methods for fMRI decoded neurofeedback, seeking to optimize how participants are trained to induce specific neural patterns in real time.

papers.title: Neural Representations of Ensemble Mean and Variance Across Visual Features
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, this study examined how the brain represents the mean and variance of ensembles defined by orientation, shape and animacy, spanning low to high levels of the visual hierarchy. Whole-brain searchlight and ROI analyses revealed a graded division of labour between ventral and dorsal pathways, with mean and variance relying on partly dissociable mechanisms. The results speak to whether ensemble statistics rely on a common or feature-specific neural system.
papers.authors: Patxi Elosegi, Sabri Takir, Ning Mei, Yaoda Xu, David Soto

papers.title: Enhancing fMRI Decoded Neurofeedback with Co-adaptive Training: Simulation and Proof-of-principle Evidence
