papers.abstract: Decoded neurofeedback training often fails because the decoder built from localizer data does not match the data seen during training. The authors introduce a co-adaptation procedure in which the decoder is updated in real time from its own predictions across neurofeedback trials, using standard machine learning algorithms. Simulations on a previous DecNef dataset and a proof-of-principle experiment indicate that co-adaptation helps participants learn to induce the target brain patterns.
papers.authors: Najmeddine Abdennour, Pedro Margolles, David Soto

papers.title: Brain Representation in Conscious and Unconscious Vision
papers.abstract: The authors re-analysed a high-precision fMRI dataset with representational similarity analysis based on convolutional neural network features to characterise how the brain encodes seen versus unseen images. Computer vision model representations predicted responses in ventral visual cortex and fronto-parietal regions for both conscious and unconscious content, though the two conditions differed in how strongly and where these representations appeared. The work offers an information-based account beyond simple decoding of unconscious perception.
papers.authors: Ning Mei, David Soto

papers.title: Characterising the role of awareness in ensemble perception
papers.abstract: Two psychophysical experiments with a bias-free paradigm tested whether the visual system can compute ensemble statistics of a set of items without awareness of the individual features. Ensemble perception proceeded even when the relevant features were not consciously seen, and drift-diffusion modeling suggested awareness lags behind the categorization processes supporting ensemble judgments. Control analyses ruled out type-2 inefficiency as the source of the dissociation.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Patxi Elosegi, Ning Mei, David Soto

papers.title: Unconscious Manipulation of Conceptual Representations with Decoded Neurofeedback Impacts Search Behavior
papers.abstract: Using fMRI decoded neurofeedback, participants were trained to evoke brain patterns resembling a real-world category (e.g. dogs) without knowing what content those patterns represented. The procedure associated this neural pattern with initially meaningless Japanese hiragana characters, sidestepping any conscious link between the symbol and the concept. Despite participants' lack of awareness, the manipulation shifted their subsequent visual search behavior, providing evidence for non-conscious associative learning of meaning.
papers.authors: Pedro Margolles, Patxi Elosegi, Ning Mei, David Soto

0166.name: David Souto
0166.department: School of Psychology and Vision Sciences
0166.bio: David Souto is a vision scientist whose research focuses on the mechanisms of dynamic vision and the control of eye movements, specifically how humans process motion and select task-relevant information during smooth pursuit and saccades. Souto utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to investigate visuo-motor learning, adaptation, and visual stability in dynamic environments. Their work explores applied domains such as the development of gaze-controlled assistive communication technologies and the study of pedestrian visual sampling for road safety. Souto leads the VisuoMotor Lab and coordinates the Vision Science Research Group at the University of Leicester.
0166.research_direction: Dr. Souto's recent work explores the continuous interplay between oculomotor control and visual perception, with a strong focus on the sensory and motor mechanisms underlying smooth pursuit eye movements. They have recently been investigating how the visual system anticipates complex, predictable kinematics—such as biological motion in point-light walkers—and how it manages to suppress reflexive optokinetic responses to background motion during active tracking. In applied domains, their research examines the perceptual and motor constraints of using eye gaze as a direct computer input, comparing sequence planning in gaze-typing to mouse movements and evaluating how assistive technology professionals interpret feedback from commercial gaze systems. Additionally, they are studying the mechanisms behind motion-induced duration biases, using metacognitive confidence judgments to disentangle sensory and decisional contributions to how humans perceive the timing of subsecond visual events.

papers.title: Perceptual and Motor Constraints on Sequential Input in Gaze and Mouse Typing
papers.abstract: Participants learned to type on a virtual keyboard using either a mouse or eye gaze with dwell selection, providing a direct comparison of the two input modalities. Error rates and trajectories were analysed by sequence position, movement direction and eccentricity, showing largely shared error sources but systematic differences. Gaze control errors depended less on eccentricity but rose for downward selections, and mouse movements were more flexible; the authors argue gaze control imposes sequential movement planning and visual processing of targets.
papers.authors: Tom Griffiths, Simon Judge, Kevin Paterson, David Souto

papers.title: Multiple mechanisms of response suppression to self-induced sensation during pursuit eye movements
papers.abstract: When the eyes follow a moving target across a textured background, the background slides across the retina in the opposite direction, and the reflexive optokinetic response to it must be suppressed to keep tracking. By varying the contrast of a brief background motion pulse, the authors tested whether suppression reflects weakened sensory signals or a reduced visuomotor gain. Neither simple account fit; instead the data are best captured by a contrast-dependent gating combined with contrast or visuomotor gain changes, which favours stability in response to the most salient signals.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Mel Ellul Miraval, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza, David Souto

papers.title: Use of eye-gaze technology feedback by assistive technology professionals: findings from a thematic analysis
papers.abstract: Focus groups with professionals who assess and provide eye-gaze technology, and with those who work with users day to day, explored how they use the feedback tools that come with such systems. Template analysis showed existing tools are good at flagging problems but rarely suggest solutions, and that some are used to draw inferences about vision and cognition that the literature does not support. The paper calls for tiered feedback for users and professionals and for better tool design.
papers.authors: Tom Griffiths, Simon Judge, David Souto

papers.title: Tuning in to a hip-hop beat: Pursuit eye movements reveal processing of biological motion
papers.abstract: Smooth pursuit can anticipate predictable movement, but usually this is studied with a bare dot. Here participants tracked the hip of point-light walkers, and pursuit was cross-correlated with the hip's velocity oscillation across the gait cycle. Tracking was robust even horizontally, and inverting the walker or showing the hip dot alone added similar phase lag, indicating that information beyond the dot contributes to predicting hip kinematics. Pursuit thus offers an implicit readout of higher-level biological-motion processing.
papers.authors: David Souto, Jennifer Sudkamp, Kyle Nacilla, Mateusz Bocian

papers.title: A metacognitive approach to the study of motion-induced duration biases reveals inter-individual differences in forming confidence judgments
papers.abstract: Perceived duration of subsecond visual events is distorted by stimulus speed, with both sensory and decisional contributions. Participants compared interval durations containing stationary, constant-speed, accelerating or decelerating stimuli and then rated their confidence. Confidence patterns paralleled duration compression but were shifted toward longer durations, pointing to a small decisional contribution, and a simple observer model captured individual differences in confidence criteria.
papers.authors: Aurelio Bruno, Jennifer Sudkamp, David Souto

0167.name: David Watson
0167.bio: David M. Watson is a vision neuroscientist at the University of York specializing in the functional architecture of high-level visual systems. Their research integrates functional MRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and behavioral psychophysics to delineate the neural substrates of scene perception and social face processing. Watson examines how the human brain represents dynamic facial behaviors and the organizational principles of object and scene recognition. Their current work investigates the connectivity and functional specialization of the lateral and ventral visual pathways in processing complex social information.
0167.research_direction: Dr. Watson has recently been investigating the organizational principles of human visual cognition, using large-scale natural image datasets and data-driven modeling to map how the brain encodes objects. Their recent work explores how latent perceptual dimensions—such as animacy and real-world size—predict the spatial topographies and temporal dynamics of object processing across fMRI, EEG, and MEG. Beyond object representation, they have been examining the structural and functional connectivity fingerprints of face- and scene-selective cortical regions, mapping how individual nodes within these systems interact with broader brain networks during rest and natural viewing. Additionally, their methodological research scrutinizes the analytical tools used to assess these functional connectomes, specifically investigating whether cortical gradients derived from connectopic mapping reflect true neural organization or spatial autocorrelation artifacts.

papers.title: Statistically efficient neural encoding of natural object variability shapes the temporal dynamics of visual processing
papers.abstract: Applies the same PLSR framework to time-resolved EEG and MEG responses to THINGS objects, using behaviourally derived object dimensions as predictors. A small set of latent components captures the temporal dynamics and is similar across EEG, MEG and the earlier fMRI analysis. The components mix visual and semantic features and do not map onto canonical accounts of cortical organization. The result supports statistical efficiency as an organizing principle of dynamic object processing.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Richard Aveyard, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Patterns of functional connectivity differentiate individuals and individual regions in face and scene selective networks
papers.abstract: Uses fMRI from several movie-watching datasets and rest to derive whole-brain connectivity fingerprints for each core face- and scene-selective region. Fingerprints are more similar within a person than between people. They also differ across individual regions within each network. The findings show that category-selective regions have distinctive connectivity profiles and that these profiles carry individual signatures.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Kira N. Noad, Bartholomew P.A. Quinn, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Perceptual and Neural Responses to Natural Objects Reveals Organizing Principles of Human Visual Cognition
papers.abstract: Uses the THINGS image set, with perceptual similarity judgments and whole-brain fMRI responses to the same objects, and links them through partial least squares regression. A handful of components predict responses across visual cortex and form smooth, graded topographies that track animacy, real-world size and category. These components do not fit classic theories of object organization. The authors argue instead that visual cortex encodes objects in a statistically efficient way that reflects natural variability.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Mapping the functional and structural connectivity of the scene network
papers.abstract: Maps how scene-selective regions (OPA, PPA, RSC) connect to each other and to the rest of the brain, using resting-state and movie-watching fMRI plus diffusion tractography. Posterior scene regions couple with visual and dorsal attention networks, while anterior regions couple with default-mode and frontoparietal control networks and the hippocampus. Structural connectivity shows partly matching posterior-anterior and ventral-dorsal biases. The paper offers a reference map of scene-network connectivity.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Connectopic mapping techniques do not reflect functional gradients in the brain
papers.abstract: Tests whether connectopic mapping can produce illusory gradients from pure noise. Random white-noise data that were spatially smoothed or interpolated between volume and surface spaces yielded gradients that resembled those from real natural-viewing data. Global gradients were less affected but depended heavily on pipeline choices. The authors conclude that reported connectopic gradients may reflect spatial autocorrelation introduced during analysis and need cautious interpretation.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

0168.name: David Whitney
0168.lab_name: Whitney Lab for Perception and Action
0168.bio: Whitney is a Professor of Psychology and Vision Science at the University of California, Berkeley, where they direct the Whitney Lab for Perception and Action and serve as the Faculty Director of the Cognitive Science program. Whitney’s research investigates the neural and psychological mechanisms that enable stable visual perception, focusing on how the brain integrates information across space and time to overcome internal processing delays and environmental clutter. Their work involves the study of serial dependence, ensemble perception, and visual crowding, employing a multimodal approach that includes psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Whitney’s current work explores the limits of object recognition in dynamic scenes and the idiosyncratic spatial biases that influence human visuomotor control.
0168.research_direction: Dr. Whitney has recently been investigating how the brain utilizes temporal context to stabilize perception, focusing extensively on the mechanisms of "continuity fields" and positive serial dependence. Their recent work explores how observers balance incoming sensory evidence with history-driven predictive templates, testing whether this blending of past and present can explain perceptual phenomena like slow change blindness. Beyond visual perception, they are extending these questions of sequential effects into motor planning to determine whether trial-to-trial biases in reaching behaviors follow the principles of efficient coding. Additionally, their research investigates high-level social vision, testing how individuals use ambiguity-weighted Bayesian computations to integrate facial and contextual cues when inferring others' emotions in dynamic, naturalistic scenes.

papers.title: Integration of affective cues in context-rich and dynamic scenes varies across individuals
papers.abstract: Across three studies with 944 participants, the authors test whether people judge others' emotions by weighting facial and contextual cues according to how ambiguous each is, as a Bayesian observer would. Observers largely follow this ambiguity-weighted integration, but the weighting differs systematically from person to person, and the pattern generalizes to dynamic, naturalistic video. The work links individual differences in emotion inference to a common computational principle.
papers.authors: Jefferson Ortega, Yuki Murai, David Whitney

papers.title: Slow change blindness from serial dependence: slowly changing objects are perceived as biased toward the past
papers.abstract: Slow change blindness, where attentive observers miss large gradual changes, may arise because perception blends recent information into the current percept. Using a one-shot design in which each observer saw a single trial of a cartoon object gradually shifting in hue, the study shows that reports are biased toward the earlier state. This offers serial dependence as a mechanism for why gradual changes go unnoticed.
papers.authors: Haley G. Frey, David Whitney

papers.title: Sequential effects in reaching reveal efficient coding in motor planning
papers.abstract: Motor control models usually assume that prior information is integrated in a Bayesian fashion. Here reaching data show that trial-to-trial sequential biases instead follow the signature of efficient coding, where the system reallocates encoding resources according to recent statistics. The findings carry an idea that has been prominent in perception into motor planning.
papers.authors: Tianhe Wang, Yifan Fang, David Whitney

papers.title: Continuity fields enhance visual perception through positive serial dependence
papers.abstract: This review lays out the continuity field idea: perception is stabilized because current input is pulled toward the recent past over a spatiotemporal window. It integrates behavioral and neural evidence for positive serial dependence, and discusses how it improves perception in noisy, changing scenes. It also identifies open questions about mechanisms and where in the brain such effects arise.
papers.authors: Mauro Manassi, David Whitney

papers.title: Dynamic predictive templates in perception
papers.abstract: The paper argues and shows that serial dependence is not a fixed bias but alternates over time between a sensory-driven mode and a history-driven mode, in which perception is guided by a predictive template of the recent past. This dynamic account explains how observers balance expectation and incoming evidence. It refines models of how the visual system uses temporal context.
papers.authors: Veith Weilnhammer, Yuki Murai, David Whitney

0169.name: Delwin Lindsey
0169.bio: Delwin T. Lindsey is a Professor of Psychology at The Ohio State University, Mansfield, where they study the neural and cognitive underpinnings of human color vision. Lindsey integrates molecular genetics, psychophysics, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI) to examine chromatic processing and the development of color perception in infants. Their research includes computational analyses of the World Color Survey to investigate universal motifs and cross-cultural diversity in color naming systems. Lindsey also examines how linguistic categories and environmental factors affect color appearance and discrimination across global populations.
0169.research_direction: Dr. Lindsey's recent work explores the cognitive, linguistic, and biological foundations of how we categorize and communicate about color. They have recently been investigating the evolutionary and developmental origins of color naming, using comparative studies with non-human primates to parse biological from linguistic influences, and behavioral games to examine how interpersonal color communication matures across the human lifespan. Their research also tests whether behavioral color sorting mirrors proposed stages of lexical evolution and probes audiovisual crossmodal correspondences by mapping musical instrument timbre and pitch to specific color properties. Additionally, they are contributing to methodological standardization in the field by measuring and aligning physical color-sample sets with established CIE and Munsell coordinate systems to facilitate robust cross-study comparisons.

papers.title: Communication about color over the life span
papers.abstract: Children and adults aged 3 to 72 played a color communication game in which they named color samples and then picked samples matching either their own or another person's color terms. Vocabulary size and both self- and interpersonal communication accuracy matured until at least age 21, and simulations showed that producing color terms and understanding others' terms are separate abilities that develop independently.
papers.authors: Angela M. Brown, Delwin T. Lindsey

papers.title: Bridging Color Standards: Aligning the Color-Aid System with the International Commission on Illumination (CIE) and the Munsell Book of Color Coordinates
papers.abstract: Color naming studies use different physical sample sets, hindering cross-study comparison. The authors measured 65 Color-Aid Standard Set and 67 Full Set samples in two independent laboratories under D65 illumination and provide colorimetric coordinates and mappings to CIE and Munsell systems.
papers.authors: Domicele Jonauskaite, Delwin T. Lindsey

papers.title: Human and primate categorical understanding of color
papers.abstract: Asks whether the way people group colors into named categories is a product of language or of shared biology by comparing human categorization with that of non-human primates. The analysis indicates that color categories in humans and monkeys show substantial common structure, suggesting a biological basis for categorical color understanding that language then builds upon.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Delwin T. Lindsey, Angela M. Brown

papers.title: Color and tone color: audiovisual crossmodal correspondences with musical instrument timbre
papers.abstract: Participants listened to recordings of orchestral and keyboard instruments playing scales and picked colors matching each timbre, and also rated the sounds on crossmodal descriptors such as bright, dark and warm. Ratings of timbre predicted the lightness and saturation of the chosen colors, and pitch register shifted the choices in a consistent way, showing systematic color-sound mappings.
papers.authors: Lindsey Reymore, Delwin T. Lindsey

papers.title: Color sorting and color term evolution
papers.abstract: Tests whether the way people sequentially sort colors into piles mirrors the stages of color-term evolution proposed by Kay and McDaniel. Three studies with English speakers across different color palettes find that pile sorts are fairly robust to palette and reflect lexical influences more than pure perceptual similarity.
papers.authors: Delwin T. Lindsey, Angela M. Brown, Aimee N. Violette, Ryan Lange, Prutha S. Deshpande

0170.name: Denis G Pelli
0170.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0170.bio: Denis G. Pelli is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, specializing in the psychophysics of object recognition and visual perception. Pelli's research explores the phenomenon of "crowding," which they characterize as the failure of feature binding when objects are spaced too closely for individual recognition. Pelli developed the Pelli-Robson Contrast Sensitivity Chart for clinical vision testing and the Psychtoolbox software for visual stimulus presentation. Their current work employs feature-counting techniques and neuroimaging to investigate how cortical map sizes, particularly in area V4, relate to psychophysical spacing limits in humans.
0170.research_direction: Dr. Pelli has recently been investigating a diverse array of topics spanning peripheral vision, computational modeling, and empirical aesthetics. Their recent work explores the spatial constraints of visual crowding by rigorously testing the Bouma law across large observer cohorts, alongside developing novel cursor-tracking methodologies to ensure precise gaze fixation for online psychophysical testing. In the realm of high-level vision, they are examining speed-accuracy tradeoffs in object recognition by benchmarking time-pressured human categorization performance against the computational processing cycles of dynamic deep neural networks. Additionally, they are probing the psychological and emotional mechanisms underlying aesthetic experiences, investigating how well observers can predict interpersonal variance in beauty judgments and how trait empathy shapes the perceived beauty of art, nature, and music.

papers.title: Empathy strengthens beauty
papers.abstract: In an online study of 307 people rating art, nature photos and songs before and after a mood induction, the authors tested whether trait empathy shapes perceived beauty. Higher-empathy people found images and music more beautiful and more emotionally expressive, with about 45% of the effect on beauty mediated through perceived emotion, and sadness playing a special role for music. Empathy predicted beauty about as well as openness, aesthetic-reward sensitivity and art expertise.
papers.authors: Anna Bruns, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: Benchmarking the speed-accuracy tradeoff in object recognition by humans and neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors collected a new dataset from 148 people doing 16-way ImageNet categorization under enforced response times, giving human speed-accuracy tradeoff curves. They compare these with dynamic neural networks that vary the amount of computation (layers, recurrent cycles, early exits), treating repetition count as an analog of time. Cascaded dynamic networks best match human speed and accuracy, while convolutional recurrent networks, often favored as models of vision, do worst.
papers.authors: Ajay Subramanian, Sara Price, Omkar Kumbhar, Elena Sizikova, Najib J. Majaj, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: Consensus and contention in beauty judgment
papers.abstract: The universality-versus-subjectivity debate about beauty hinges on how much people differ. The authors built image quartets with matched mean beauty but high or low variance across people, and asked new participants to predict their own mean and variance. People predicted their mean beauty well but could not predict their own variability, showing that beauty variance is heterogeneous and hidden yet important for prediction.
papers.authors: Maria Pombo, Aleksandra Igdalova, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: The Bouma law accounts for crowding in 50 observers
papers.abstract: Crowding distance was measured under 13 conditions in each of 50 observers, spanning three eccentricities, four meridians, radial vs tangential flankers and two fonts. A simple two-parameter Bouma law (crowding distance grows linearly with eccentricity) explains 82% of the variance, and adding meridian, orientation, font and observer factors raises this to 94%, quantifying known asymmetries. The authors propose a standardized Bouma factor for comparing labs, show that peeking distorts estimates, and argue that crowding is a reliable individual-difference biomarker for dyslexia and visual health.
papers.authors: Jan W. Kurzawski, Augustin Burchell, Darshan Thapa, Jonathan Winawer, Najib J. Majaj, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: EasyEyes - A new method for accurate fixation in online vision testing
papers.abstract: Peripheral psychophysics such as crowding needs accurate fixation, which is hard online because webcam gaze tracking is imprecise. EasyEyes has observers track a moving crosshair with the cursor, presenting a brief peripheral target at a random moment during successful tracking, so fixation is controlled without gaze tracking. Compared against in-lab gaze-contingent testing in 12 naive observers, it gave a small fixation error (0.6 deg) and consistent crowding thresholds and individual differences at home.
papers.authors: Jan W. Kurzawski, Maria Pombo, Augustin Burchell, Nina M. Hanning, Simon Liao, Najib J. Majaj, Denis G. Pelli

0171.name: Denise Hsien Wu
0171.bio: Denise Hsien Wu is a professor and former director at the Graduate Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience at National Central University, conducting research on the neurobiological foundations of human communication and cognition. Wu’s work utilizes behavioral experiments and neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, MEG, and ERP, to investigate the mechanisms of statistical learning, bilingualism, and Chinese character recognition. Their research also includes neuroaesthetics, examining the computational principles and neural substrates involved in the perception of visual stimuli such as calligraphy and faces. Wu is a fellow of both the Psychonomic Society and the Association for Psychological Science and currently serves as the director of the Joint Research Centre for Language and Human Complexity.
0171.research_direction: Dr. Wu has recently been studying how people pick up regularities from their environment and how flexibly they update that knowledge when the rules change. Their recent work uses a sequence-learning task in which participants respond to motor patterns that later switch to new ones, measuring how sensitive each person is to emerging structure and how quickly they adapt. They also explore how this kind of statistical learning relates to reading, in particular how learners recognize Chinese characters.

papers.title: Reciprocal Relationship Between Statistical Learning and Chinese Character Recognition
papers.venue: Cognitive and Neural Foundations of Chinese Reading (Chinese Language Learning Sciences, Springer)
papers.authors: Denise Hsien Wu, Andhika Renaldi, Yi-Syuan Huang

papers.title: Rule-learning and rule-switching flexibility in motor sequence learning
papers.abstract: This study addressed the interplay between statistical rule-learning and rule-switching flexibility in dynamic environments using a modified serial reaction time (SRT) task. Participants were exposed to motor sequences where rules (Structure 1) naturally emerged and were subsequently replaced by new patterns (Structure 2). The research quantified individual differences in the sensitivity to emerging regularities and the speed of adaptation to rule changes. Quantitative analysis demonstrated that robust rule-learning does not necessarily predict high rule-switching flexibility; rather, successful learners are characterized by a specific ability to suppress previously learned dependencies when input statistics shift. These findings suggest that metacontrol over statistical learning involves dissociable mechanisms for extraction and revision of sequential expectations.
papers.authors: Yi-Syuan Huang, Ovid Jyh-Lang Tzeng, Denise Hsien Wu

0172.name: Dennis Levi
0172.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science
0172.bio: Dennis M. Levi is a vision scientist at UC Berkeley who researches the neural basis of amblyopia and the development of spatial vision. Levi’s research investigates how the adult brain retains plasticity to improve visual function through perceptual learning and video-game-based therapies. Using psychophysics, fMRI, and computational modeling, Levi’s laboratory examines the mechanisms of visual crowding and binocular depth perception to inform clinical treatments for developmental vision disorders.
0172.research_direction: Dr. Levi has recently been investigating visual plasticity and the rehabilitation of binocular vision, particularly in adults with amblyopia and strabismus. Their recent work explores whether extended reality technologies, such as virtual reality and stereoscopic video games, can be utilized to drive the recovery of depth perception and stereoacuity in both neurotypical and clinically impaired populations. Through home-based behavioral training paradigms and large-scale meta-analyses, they are assessing the therapeutic efficacy of these immersive environments in overcoming suppression and improving binocular alignment compared to traditional treatments. Additionally, Dr. Levi is examining the functional impact of oculomotor abnormalities in amblyopia, specifically questioning how deficits in fixation, saccades, and pursuit degrade visual processing and whether they might serve as diagnostic markers or novel targets for intervention.

papers.title: Recovery of depth perception in adults with abnormal binocular vision
papers.abstract: Adults with a history of strabismus, anisometropia and/or amblyopia completed 30 home-based VR game training sessions targeting stereoacuity, anti-suppression and binocular alignment, with periodic in-lab tests. Most participants improved stereoacuity substantially, while gains in binocular balance and ocular alignment were more variable, pointing to the need for personalized training.
papers.authors: Jian Ding, Michelle Y. Ma, Hilary H. Lu, Benjamin T. Backus, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Emerging therapies for improving stereoacuity in amblyopia: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Pooling 26 studies, this meta-analysis asks whether VR therapies, video games and movies improve stereoacuity in amblyopia and strabismus. The pooled gain was about 1.8-fold, comparable to occlusion, and VR did not clearly beat other binocular treatments.
papers.authors: Laura Asensio-Jurado, Marc Argilés, Lluïsa Quevedo-Junyent, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: The impact of eye movements on amblyopic vision: A mini-review
papers.abstract: Reviews the eye-movement abnormalities seen in amblyopia (fixation, saccades, pursuit), how they are measured, and how they degrade vision. It also considers whether they respond to treatment and can serve as diagnostic markers.
papers.authors: Dennis M. Levi, Susana T.L. Chung

papers.title: Playing three-dimensional video games boosts stereo vision
papers.abstract: Adults with normal vision played either stereoscopic 3D or flat 2D video games. Only the 3D gaming improved stereo vision, indicating that exposure to disparity cues in a virtual environment can drive plasticity of depth perception even after development.
papers.authors: Roger W. Li, Betty Z. Li, Sandy W. Chat, Saumil S. Patel, Susana T.L. Chung, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Applications and implications for extended reality to improve binocular vision and stereopsis
papers.abstract: Perspective on how VR/AR and other extended-reality technologies can be used to assess and treat binocular vision problems such as amblyopia. It discusses opportunities and pitfalls for depth perception and stereopsis, including cue conflicts and display limitations.
papers.authors: Dennis M. Levi

0173.name: Derek Arnold
0173.bio: Arnold is a Professor at the University of Queensland's School of Psychology, specializing in the neural and computational foundations of human perceptual experience. Their research investigates how the brain transforms sensory inputs into conscious awareness, focusing on predictive coding, temporal perception, and the mechanisms of visual imagery. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and electroencephalography (EEG), Arnold explores individual differences in visualization, such as aphantasia, and the neural correlates of confidence in sensory decisions. Their work addresses how the brain predicts environmental changes and integrates multisensory information to guide motor planning.
0173.research_direction: Dr. Arnold has recently been investigating individual differences in mental imagery, focusing particularly on the spectrum of visualization that includes aphantasia. Their recent work explores whether subjective reports of imagery vividness can be reliably captured through objective behavioral and physiological methods, testing candidates like binocular rivalry priming, EEG signatures of neural disinhibition, and pupillary responses to imagined brightness. Furthermore, they are examining the underlying neural architecture of these individual differences, questioning how top-down inhibitory feedback and sensory priors might shape both voluntary and involuntary internally generated visual experiences. Through a combination of physiological recordings, psychophysical paradigms, and survey data, they are working to redefine the boundaries of aphantasia and map the diverse ways human beings experience mental depictions.

papers.title: Vividness of mental imagery reflects a broad range of internally generated visual experiences
papers.abstract: Survey study showing that simple vividness ratings capture individual differences in imagery detail, in other internally generated visual experiences and in the vividness of dreams, and could replace longer questionnaires. Vividness is tied to whether people 'see' images or project them outward, yet many people have mental depictions without seeing them. The authors argue that aphantasia should be redefined to separate faint or unseen imagery from a complete lack of pictorial representation.
papers.authors: D. Samuel Schwarzkopf, Xinran Amelia Yu, Ecem Altan, Loren N. Bouyer, Blake W. Saurels, Elizabeth Pellicano, Derek Henry Arnold

papers.title: Imagery modulates the pupillary response, but this does not reliably index differences in imagery vividness
papers.abstract: Tests whether pupil size can serve as a physiological index of imagery vividness. Imagining dark versus bright scenes changed pupil dilation as expected, but the size of that effect was unrelated to people's vividness ratings. Pupillometry therefore shows that imagery has a physiological footprint without being a reliable measure of individual differences.
papers.authors: Daniel Gardner, Blake W. Saurels, Derek Henry Arnold

papers.title: Don't think of a pink elephant: Individual differences in visualisation predict involuntary imagery and its neural correlates
papers.abstract: Tests whether people who cannot voluntarily visualise (aphantasia) are protected from intrusive imagery. EEG was recorded while participants imagined or tried not to imagine sensory scenes; those with more vivid voluntary imagery were also more likely to report involuntary imagery. Both measures were predicted by neural signatures of disinhibition, working memory and feedback, so involuntary imagery scales with the vividness of a person's typical visualisations.
papers.authors: Derek H. Arnold, Mary Hutchinson, Loren N. Bouyer, D. Samuel Schwarzkopf, Elizabeth Pellicano, Blake W. Saurels

papers.title: Objective priming from pre-imagining inputs before binocular rivalry presentations does not predict individual differences in the subjective intensity of imagined experiences
papers.abstract: Examines whether imagery-based priming in binocular rivalry can serve as an objective measure of how vivid a person's mental imagery is. Priming of probe detection did not correlate with vividness ratings across people, although trial-by-trial priming was larger when a pre-imagined image felt more vivid. The authors conclude that the rivalry protocol is not a reliable objective index of individual differences in visualisation.
papers.authors: Loren N. Bouyer, Dietrich S. Schwarzkopf, Blake W. Saurels, Derek H. Arnold

papers.title: Deep Aphantasia: a visual brain with minimal influence from priors or inhibitory feedback?
papers.abstract: A perspective by two self-described congenital aphantasics. One author reports atypical experiences of several visual phenomena that depend on extrapolating or integrating information across space. They propose that weak inhibitory feedback and priors both prevent imagery and alter perception of real inputs, and suggest a 'deep' subtype of aphantasia.
papers.authors: Loren N. Bouyer, Derek H. Arnold

0174.name: Diane M. Beck
0174.bio: Beck is a Professor and Head of the Department of Psychology at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, where they investigate the neural and cognitive constraints of visual representation. Their research characterizes how top-down mechanisms like attention and real-world statistical regularities modulate activity in the visual cortex to facilitate scene category recognition and object awareness. Employing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Beck explores the limits of human visual processing and the role of neural oscillations in conscious perception. Recent investigations in their lab also utilize deep neural networks to model the features that define representative exemplars of scene categories.
0174.research_direction: Dr. Beck's recent work explores how the human visual system leverages the statistical regularities of natural environments to facilitate rapid and efficient perception. They have recently been investigating the perceptual advantages of highly memorable images and representative scene exemplars, questioning whether these benefits stem from early visual processing ease rather than simply memory encoding. Alongside these behavioral investigations, their lab uses deep neural networks aligned with human fMRI responses from the ventral visual stream to probe why biological vision is so robust to adversarial perturbations that typically fool artificial models. Specifically, they are using these neurally guided networks to disentangle how underlying factors, such as spatial frequency reliance and the geometry of neural category manifolds, contribute to human visual resilience.

papers.title: Dissociating spatial frequency reliance from adversarial robustness advantages in neurally guided deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Networks trained to align with human visual cortex are more robust to adversarial attacks, and one explanation is that they lean on low spatial frequencies. The authors test whether that low-frequency bias or reliance on the mid-frequency band that humans depend on for object recognition explains the robustness benefit. Their analyses separate the two accounts and clarify what neural alignment actually changes in the network.
papers.authors: Zhenan Shao, Tianyu Ren, Chengxiao Wang, Leyla Isik, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: What makes good exemplars of a scene category good? Evidence from deep neural nets
papers.abstract: Good exemplars of a scene category, the most representative examples, are recognized faster and more accurately than poor ones. The study uses deep neural networks to ask which image features make some exemplars better than others and whether network representations reproduce the human good-exemplar advantage. It ties the finding to how statistical regularities of real-world scenes are captured by visual representations.
papers.authors: Pei-Ling Yang, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: Highly memorable images are more readily perceived
papers.abstract: Across several experiments the authors show that images that people tend to remember well are also detected and categorized more easily when presented briefly or under degraded viewing. The advantage of memorable images holds up when other image properties are accounted for, suggesting memorability reflects processing ease at the perceptual stage rather than only better memory encoding. The results tie image memorability to the same mechanisms that give typical, statistically regular scenes their perceptual edge.
papers.authors: Will Deng, Kara D. Federmeier, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: Probing Human Visual Robustness with Neurally-Guided Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The paper asks why human vision tolerates small image perturbations that fool deep networks. The authors train networks to match human fMRI responses from successive stages of the ventral visual stream and find robustness improves the more the target region is higher-order. They link this to the geometry of neural category manifolds, which become smaller and more linearly separable along the stream, and show that guiding a network with manifold properties alone reproduces the robustness gains.
papers.authors: Zhenan Shao, Linjian Ma, Yiqing Zhou, Yibo Jacky Zhang, Sanmi Koyejo, Bo Li, Diane M. Beck

papers.title: The Role of Real-World Statistical Regularities in Visual Perception
papers.abstract: This review lays out how the brain exploits the statistical regularities of natural scenes to see quickly and efficiently. It covers evidence that typical, representative scenes are processed more easily, the neural signatures of this advantage, and open questions about the role of attention and deep networks. It effectively summarizes the research framework driving the lab's recent empirical work.
papers.authors: Diane M. Beck, Evan G. Center, Zhenan Shao

0175.name: Dicle Dövencioğlu
0175.bio: Nahide Dicle Dövencioğlu is an Associate Professor at Middle East Technical University and directs the Sensory Processes Lab. Dövencioğlu’s research investigates the computational and neural underpinnings of 3D vision and material perception, specifically examining how properties like softness and transparency are derived from specular motion, shading, and binocular disparity. Integrating psychophysics, fMRI, and computer graphics, they explore the interaction between active exploration and multisensory integration, including the role of linguistic sound symbolism in shaping perceptual experiences.
0175.research_direction: Dr. Dövencioğlu has recently been investigating the multidimensional perception of material properties, particularly softness, through the lens of cross-modal interactions. Their recent work explores how observing specific exploratory hand movements, such as pressing or stroking, influences an observer's visual judgments of a material's softness in the absence of direct haptic feedback. They have also been examining audio-visual-haptic links by testing how sound-symbolic onomatopoeic words alter visual material perception, probing the extent to which congruent sounds selectively shift judgments along distinct softness dimensions like deformability or viscosity. Additionally, their research integrates psycholinguistics to investigate shared cross-linguistic phonetic markers of material sounds in Turkish and Japanese, as well as how people linguistically categorize their own exploratory hand movements when touching diverse materials.

papers.title: Comparing semantic and phonetic similarities between Turkish and Japanese onomatopoeia
papers.abstract: Turkish speakers unfamiliar with Japanese rated Turkish onomatopoeia and semantically or phonetically similar Japanese ones on material-related adjective scales. Phonetic similarity predicted similar material judgments better than semantic similarity did, which was also reflected in multidimensional scaling distances. The results point to shared phonetic markers of material-related sound symbolism across languages.
papers.authors: Defne Akkuş, Fatma Nefes Tekin, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Selectively manipulating softness perception of materials through sound symbolism
papers.abstract: The authors first extracted the perceptual dimensions of softness from ratings of everyday material videos and of Turkish onomatopoeic words, finding dimensions such as deformability, viscosity, surface softness and granularity. They then paired spoken onomatopoeic words with material videos and showed that congruent words raised ratings on the matching softness dimension, while incongruent ones lowered them. Sound-symbolic words can therefore selectively shift perceived material qualities, evidence for cross-modal audio-haptic-visual interactions in softness perception.
papers.authors: Hamza Nalbantoğlu, Beyza Melis Hazır, Dicle N. Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Visual softness perception can be manipulated through exploratory procedures
papers.abstract: Observers watched videos of hands performing exploratory procedures (such as pressing or stroking) on everyday soft materials, then rated softness-related adjectives. When the observed hand action matched the softness dimension of the material, ratings on that dimension were higher than when it did not. Watching others' hand motions can thus bias visual material judgments without any haptic input.
papers.authors: Fatma Kılıç, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Dokunsal Yumuşaklık Algısına İlişkin Bir İnceleme
papers.abstract: A Turkish-language review of haptic softness perception, arguing that softness covers very different material categories such as fabric, cream, sand or fur. It surveys perceptual dimensions and the exploratory hand movements tied to them, largely from engineering and psychology literature. It serves as an entry point to the multidimensional view of touch-based softness.
papers.venue: Ankara Üniversitesi Dil ve Tarih-Coğrafya Fakültesi Dergisi
papers.authors: Müge Cavdan, Dicle Dövencioğlu

papers.title: Keşifsel El Hareketlerinin Türkçe Adlandırılmasında Dokunsal Malzeme Algısının Rolü
papers.abstract: Building on findings that softness has several perceptual dimensions each tied to a characteristic exploratory hand movement, this study asks how Turkish speakers name those movements when touching different materials. It examines how the touched material relates to the verbal labels used, extending English-language work to Turkish.
papers.venue: Ankara Üniversitesi Dil ve Tarih-Coğrafya Fakültesi Dergisi
papers.authors: Gamze Yıldız, Dicle Dövencioğlu

0176.name: Dimitris Samaras
0176.main_research_area: computer vision and computational behavioral science
0176.bio: Dimitris Samaras is the SUNY Empire Innovation Professor at Stony Brook University and the Director of the Computer Vision Lab. Their research involves developing physical and statistical models to interpret complex visual data, focusing on the interaction between 3D geometry and illumination for motion estimation and augmented reality. Samaras applies machine learning to human modeling, including the analysis of facial expressions, biometrics, and multimodal neuroimaging data such as fMRI and eye-tracking. Their work in computational pathology involves the design of foundational models for large-scale medical image analysis and diagnostic precision.
0176.research_direction: Dr. Samaras has recently been investigating the generative modeling of complex, large-scale imagery alongside the computational prediction of human eye movements. In the domain of generative AI, their recent work explores how to synthesize globally coherent, gigapixel-scale images—such as multi-magnification histopathology slides and remote sensing data—by conditioning latent diffusion models on self-supervised representations rather than costly manual labels. In parallel, they are studying human visual attention by developing transformer-based architectures that simulate foveated vision and working memory to predict where humans will look next. This line of research seeks to unify the mechanisms of top-down goal-directed visual search and bottom-up free viewing, while also exploring how to personalize scanpath predictions to specific observers using only a few examples of their unique gaze behavior.

papers.title: ZoomLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for multi-scale image generation
papers.abstract: Presents a latent diffusion model that can synthesize gigapixel-scale images such as pathology slides and satellite imagery across many magnifications. A magnification-aware conditioning scheme built on self-supervised embeddings lets one model generate both fine patches and wide fields of view, and a joint multi-scale sampling procedure keeps large images globally coherent. It sets strong results on image quality and enables tasks like super-resolution and multi-scale inverse problems.
papers.authors: Srikar Yellapragada, Alexandros Graikos, Kostas Triaridis, Prateek Prasanna, Rajarsi Gupta, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: Few-shot Personalized Scanpath Prediction
papers.abstract: Defines the task of predicting a specific individual's gaze scanpaths from only a handful of that person's examples. The proposed Subject-Embedding Network learns embeddings that separate subjects while keeping each individual's scanpaths consistent, so a model adapts to unseen viewers without heavy retraining. Experiments show it personalizes scanpath prediction effectively across tasks.
papers.authors: Ruoyu Xue, Jingyi Xu, Sounak Mondal, Hieu Le, Gregory Zelinsky, Minh Hoai, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: PixCell: A generative foundation model for digital histopathology images
papers.abstract: Presents the first diffusion-based generative foundation model for histopathology, trained on a very large corpus of H&E patches from tens of thousands of whole-slide images across cancer types. Using progressive training and self-supervised conditioning, it produces realistic images without task-specific labels and supports uses such as privacy-preserving synthetic data, virtual staining and data augmentation for downstream classifiers.
papers.authors: Srikar Yellapragada, Alexandros Graikos, Zilinghan Li, Kostas Triaridis, Varun Belagali, Tarak Nath Nandi, Karen Bai, Beatrice S. Knudsen, Tahsin Kurc, Rajarsi R. Gupta, Prateek Prasanna, Ravi K Madduri, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: Unifying Top-down and Bottom-up Scanpath Prediction Using Transformers
papers.abstract: Introduces the Human Attention Transformer (HAT), a single model that predicts human fixation sequences for both goal-directed visual search and free viewing. It combines a transformer architecture with a simplified foveated retina that gives the model a working-memory-like sense of what has been seen, and predicts dense fixation maps instead of coarse grids. HAT sets new state of the art on scanpath prediction and yields interpretable gaze behavior.
papers.authors: Zhibo Yang, Sounak Mondal, Seoyoung Ahn, Ruoyu Xue, Gregory Zelinsky, Minh Hoai, Dimitris Samaras

papers.title: Learned representation-guided diffusion models for large-image generation
papers.abstract: Shows that self-supervised representations can stand in for costly patch-level human labels when conditioning diffusion models in specialized domains like histopathology and remote sensing. The models generate high-quality patches from SSL embeddings, and a spatially consistent patch-assembly procedure extends this to large images. Synthetic data from the approach also improves downstream classifiers.
papers.authors: Alexandros Graikos, Srikar Yellapragada, Minh-Quan Le, Saarthak Kapse, Prateek Prasanna, Joel Saltz, Dimitris Samaras

0178.name: Dirk Bernhardt-Walther
0178.bio: Dirk Bernhardt-Walther is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto and a Senior Member of the IEEE. Bernhardt-Walther’s research investigates the neural and computational foundations of high-level sensory perception, specifically how humans represent and categorize complex real-world scenes. By combining functional neuroimaging, psychophysics, and eye tracking with computer vision and machine learning, Bernhardt-Walther identifies mid-level visual features—such as contours and symmetry—that facilitate scene recognition and aesthetic preferences. Their work also includes the development of computational tools like the Mid-level Vision Toolbox to model how structural image properties influence human cognition and neural representations.
0178.research_direction: Dr. Bernhardt-Walther has recently been investigating the intersection of mid-level visual processing and aesthetic perception, focusing on how structural image properties drive both neural activity and human liking. Their recent work explores how the visual system extracts mid-level structure from natural scenes, using isolated contour and texture stimuli in fMRI and behavioral adaptation paradigms to understand the drivers of early orientation tuning and phenomena like the tilt aftereffect. Concurrently, they are studying the cognitive and neural foundations of visual aesthetic pleasure, testing theoretical frameworks that propose a link between beauty, successful image categorization, and processing efficiency. By combining human neuroimaging, deep neural network modeling, and causal image manipulations that alter scene contours, Dr. Bernhardt-Walther is mapping how the brain's metabolic processing costs and mid-level feature extraction give rise to our aesthetic valuations.

papers.title: Contours drive the tilt aftereffect in naturalistic images
papers.abstract: Extends the contour account from neural selectivity to behavior. Adaptation to naturalistic images produces tilt aftereffects that are driven by their contour structure rather than by texture, linking mid-level contour properties to perceptual adaptation.
papers.authors: Seohee Han, James T. Lochbichler, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: The sweet spot of seeing: A categorization-based account of visual aesthetic pleasure
papers.abstract: A theoretical synthesis proposing that visual aesthetic pleasure arises from successful, efficient categorization of what we see. It integrates evidence on contours, processing efficiency and the neural basis of liking into one framework and lays out predictions for future work.
papers.authors: Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Less is more: Aesthetic liking is inversely related to metabolic expense by the visual system
papers.abstract: Tests whether aesthetic pleasure follows an energy-saving principle. Both a deep network (VGG19) and human fMRI responses show that images people like more incur lower metabolic cost, in early visual and scene/face-selective regions alike. The inverse relation appears only in the network trained on object and scene categorization, not a randomly initialized one, tying beauty to efficient processing.
papers.authors: Yikai Tang, William A. Cunningham, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Contours drive distinct orientation selectivity in the human visual system
papers.abstract: Uses natural images decomposed into contour and texture components to ask what drives orientation tuning in human visual cortex. Contours produce orientation-selective responses that differ from those driven by textures, showing that mid-level structure, not just local energy, shapes early orientation coding.
papers.authors: Seohee Han, Dirk B. Walther

papers.title: Changing What You Like: Modifying Contour Properties Shifts Aesthetic Valuations of Scenes
papers.abstract: Builds a contour-based model of scene aesthetics that predicts ratings from observers worldwide. By editing contour properties while keeping scene identity fixed, the authors push aesthetic judgments up or down, giving the first causal evidence that contour properties drive aesthetic value.
papers.authors: Delaram Farzanfar, Dirk B. Walther

0179.name: Dirk Kerzel
0179.department: Psychology Department, Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
0179.bio: Dirk Kerzel is a Full Professor of Cognitive Psychology who researches the mechanisms of attentional selectivity and their integration with visual working memory and oculomotor control. Kerzel’s work utilizes psychophysical paradigms and electrophysiological markers, such as the N2pc and Pd components, to investigate how stimulus saliency and top-down goals influence the selection or suppression of visual information. They study the capacity limits of the cognitive system and how distractors interfere with the execution of hand and eye movements. Currently, their research focuses on the precision of representations in visual working memory and the spatial anisotropies that affect distractor interference in complex visual search tasks.
0179.research_direction: Dr. Kerzel has recently been investigating the mechanisms of attentional control and visual working memory, focusing on how top-down templates and bottom-up salience interact during visual selection. Their recent work explores the phenomenon of optimal tuning in visual search, using eye tracking, manual responses, and ERP components like the N2pc to examine how attentional templates might shift away from nontarget features to maximize target contrast. In the realm of visual working memory, they are testing how probabilistic retro-cues and spatial pre-cues influence the flexible prioritization of stored items and whether this top-down guidance can ever fully override initial stimulus salience. Finally, their research interrogates the neural markers of distractor processing by designing context-dependent search tasks to determine whether the Pd event-related potential truly reflects active suppression or merely the selection of nontarget locations.

papers.title: Attentional tuning to color in efficient visual search: Evidence for optimal peak shifts and relational asymmetries
papers.abstract: Participants searched for a color singleton while ignoring a shape distractor whose color was varied systematically toward or away from the background color. Interference from the distractor peaked at colors shifted away from the nontarget color, as predicted by optimal tuning, and this shift was stronger for early eye-movement capture than for manual responses. Response curves were also asymmetric, and a feature-dissimilar distractor caused almost no capture, indicating that selection was governed by a feature-based template. The work suggests optimal tuning mainly shapes the guiding template rather than the template used for target verification.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel, Martin Constant

papers.title: Probabilistic tuning of attentional templates: Evidence for flexible prioritization in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Three experiments combined memory recall with visual search while manipulating how reliable retro-cues were. Higher cue validity increased both search efficiency and memory performance, and the pattern held at higher memory loads and when item shape signaled functional role. This points to flexible, reliability-sensitive prioritization of templates, without distinguishing continuous strength adjustment from probabilistic switching between discrete states.
papers.authors: Alexandre Fortuna, Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Electrophysiological evidence for the optimal tuning of attention
papers.abstract: Optimal tuning proposes that attention is shifted away from nontarget features to increase target-nontarget contrast. Using ERPs, the study found that the N1pc and N2pc were larger for cue colors deviating away from the nontarget color, as optimal tuning predicts, and less consistent with rapid disengagement or object-updating accounts. Control conditions further indicated that the early Ppc component reflects imbalanced saliency rather than sensory adaptation.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: Persistent effects of salience in visual working memory: Limits of cue-driven guidance
papers.abstract: Across four experiments, the authors asked whether pre-cues and retro-cues can offset the recall advantage that more salient items enjoy in visual working memory. Valid spatial and feature cues improved accuracy, but never removed the salience effect. The results indicate salience acts strongly during initial encoding and that later top-down prioritization cannot fully override it.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Martin Constant, Dirk Kerzel

papers.title: The PD Reflects Selection of Nontarget Locations, Not Distractor Suppression
papers.abstract: Participants were told the distractor color in advance and searched for the other-colored item. A PD appeared to a lateral distractor paired with a vertical target, consistent with suppression, but only when target and distractor could also fall on opposite sides of fixation. This context dependence suggests the PD reflects selection of nontarget locations rather than active suppression of the distractor, challenging a common interpretation of the component.
papers.authors: Dirk Kerzel, Stanislas Huynh Cong

0180.name: Dirk van Moorselaar
0180.department: Experimental Psychology, Helmholtz Institute (Faculty of Social and Behavioral Sciences)
0180.lab_name: Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (IBBA)
0180.bio: Dirk van Moorselaar is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual attention, working memory, and distractor suppression. Van Moorselaar’s research utilizes time-resolved EEG decoding, alpha-band oscillation analysis, and psychophysics to investigate how the brain uses prior expectations and statistical learning to manage sensory selection. Their work provides evidence for the existence of proactive distractor templates and characterizes the dynamic trade-offs between storage and selection within the visual working memory system. Van Moorselaar also explores the reflexive shifts of the attentional 'zoom lens' and the role of retinotopic coordinates in suppressing interference from the environment.
0180.research_direction: Dr. van Moorselaar's recent work explores how the brain proactively allocates spatial attention and prepares for upcoming visual events based on cues and statistical learning. Using EEG and inverted encoding models, they have recently been investigating the neural dynamics of spatial priority maps, asking whether the visual system adjusts the breadth and gain of its attentional "zoom lens" in response to exogenous cues or expected search difficulty, and whether phenomena like inhibition of return reflect sustained preparatory suppression. Beyond explicit spatial cueing, their research asks how statistical learning shapes visual anticipation, utilizing time-resolved decoding to track how the brain builds preparatory neural representations of predictable sequence events before they appear. Finally, Dr. van Moorselaar brings this predictive framework to affective vision by examining whether learned spatial probabilities can help individuals suppress automatic attentional capture by highly threatening fearful distractors.

papers.title: Inhibition of Return without Preparatory Suppression in Spatial Priority Maps
papers.abstract: Asks whether inhibition of return reflects sustained suppression in the brain's spatial priority map or instead arises at the motor/response level. EEG inverted encoding models reconstruct spatial tuning during the anticipatory interval, finding clear enhancement at predictively cued locations but no evidence of preparatory suppression at previously cued locations despite robust behavioral IOR. The result argues that IOR is not sustained priority-map suppression.
papers.authors: Dirk van Moorselaar, Vicky Voet, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Boosting the signal: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
papers.abstract: Examines whether observers proactively change the spatial scope of attention when they expect sparse versus dense search displays. Spatial cueing combined with EEG inverted encoding models reconstructs both the locus and the breadth of attention before search onset. Expecting difficult, crowded searches boosted the gain of the preparatory attentional signal rather than narrowing its width.
papers.authors: Dirk van Moorselaar, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Alpha-Band Activity Tracks Reflexive Changes in the Breadth of the Zoom Lens of Attention
papers.abstract: Tests whether involuntary (exogenous) attention can adjust its spatial scope like voluntary attention does. Using cues of different sizes together with inverted encoding models applied to alpha-band EEG, the authors show that the breadth of attentional tuning follows the cue extent and sharpens over time after narrow cues. Alpha activity therefore tracks dynamic changes in the zoom lens of reflexive attention.
papers.authors: Dirk van Moorselaar, Jan Theeuwes, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Learning to suppress what I fear
papers.abstract: Fearful stimuli such as spiders normally capture attention automatically, especially in fearful individuals. Here participants first learned to suppress a distractor at a high-probability location, then faced spider and butterfly distractors. Highly spider-fearful people showed more capture by spiders overall, yet could suppress them at the learned high-probability location, suggesting statistical learning can attenuate attentional bias to threat.
papers.authors: Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar

papers.title: Neural representations of predicted events: Evidence from time-resolved EEG decoding
papers.abstract: Investigates how the brain represents events it can predict from learned sequences before they occur. Time-resolved EEG decoding shows that predicted upcoming stimuli, such as the next position in a learned sequence, are represented in neural activity ahead of time. The work links statistical learning to preparatory sensory representations.
papers.authors: Ai-Su Li, Jan Theeuwes, Dirk van Moorselaar

0181.name: Dobromir Rahnev
0181.bio: Dobromir Rahnev is an Associate Professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology whose research investigates the computational and neural foundations of perceptual decision-making and metacognition. They utilize a methodology combining psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), including simultaneous TMS-fMRI protocols to establish causal brain-behavior relationships. Rahnev's work focuses on why human perception is often suboptimal, developing mathematical models based on signal detection theory and Bayesian inference to explain the divergence between objective performance and subjective confidence. Additionally, Rahnev coordinated the creation of the Confidence Database to facilitate large-scale collaborative research and open science in the field.
0181.research_direction: Dr. Rahnev has recently been investigating the computational, neural, and theoretical foundations of human perceptual decision-making and metacognition. Their recent work explores the validity of Bayesian frameworks in vision and cognition, using psychophysical experiments to test whether human confidence truly reflects optimal probabilistic computations or instead relies on simpler heuristics. To model these processes, they are developing image-computable neural networks that accumulate noisy evidence over time to simulate classic behavioral signatures, such as response times and the speed-accuracy tradeoff. Furthermore, Dr. Rahnev is examining the methodological tools and neural implementations underlying these phenomena, evaluating the reliability of widely used metacognitive metrics like meta-d' and using fMRI clustering to investigate how multiple, distinct brain-wide activation patterns can support the exact same perceptual task.

papers.title: The explicit-Bayes hypothesis for cognition
papers.abstract: This perspective questions the common assumption that the brain represents and computes with probability distributions in a Bayes-optimal manner. It proposes that Bayesian-like behavior arises only when people explicitly reason about probabilities, and reviews evidence from perception, confidence and higher cognition to argue that implicit Bayesian computation is less supported than often thought.
papers.authors: Kai Xue, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: A comprehensive assessment of current methods for measuring metacognition
papers.abstract: This sole-author paper evaluates the most widely used measures of metacognitive ability, such as meta-d', M-ratio and related indices, on a large collection of real datasets. It examines how reliable each measure is and how strongly it depends on task performance and response bias. The analysis reveals that most current measures have important limitations and gives practical guidance on which to choose.
papers.authors: Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: Multiple brain activation patterns for the same perceptual decision-making task
papers.abstract: Using fMRI data from a perceptual decision task, the authors show that group-average activation hides distinct subgroups of trials and people. Clustering reveals several reliable activation patterns that each support the same behavior, and these patterns differ in how they engage regions such as the default mode and frontoparietal networks. The results argue that one task can be implemented through multiple brain-wide solutions.
papers.authors: Johan Nakuci, Jiwon Yeon, Nadia Haddara, Ji-Hyun Kim, Sung-Phil Kim, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: The neural network RTNet exhibits the signatures of human perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: The authors build a neural network that accumulates noisy evidence over time and makes stochastic decisions with response times, unlike standard feedforward image classifiers. Tested against human behavior on a digit-discrimination task, this network reproduces the main hallmarks of human perceptual decisions, including the speed-accuracy tradeoff, effects of difficulty and of prior evidence, and confidence patterns. This shows that a fairly simple sampling-based architecture can serve as an image-computable model of human decision-making.
papers.authors: Farshad Rafiei, Medha Shekhar, Dobromir Rahnev

papers.title: Challenging the Bayesian confidence hypothesis in perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: The study tests the idea that confidence reflects the Bayesian posterior probability of being correct. Using a set of psychophysical experiments that manipulate stimulus reliability and decision boundaries, the authors find human confidence patterns that this hypothesis fails to predict. They instead favor heuristic accounts, undermining a popular normative view of confidence.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Kai Xue, Medha Shekhar, Dobromir Rahnev

0182.name: Domenica Bueti
0182.bio: Domenica Bueti is a Full Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the International School for Advanced Studies (SISSA) and directs the Time Perception Lab. Bueti’s research examines the neural mechanisms of temporal cognition and magnitude processing, focusing on how the brain encodes and integrates dimensions such as time, space, and numerosity. This work includes the identification of chronotopic maps—topographic representations of time in the supplementary motor area and parietal cortex—using ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI). Bueti integrates psychophysics, neuroimaging, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to characterize the functional architecture of the human timing system.
0182.research_direction: Dr. Bueti has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying visual time perception and the ways in which perceptual history biases current sensory experience. Using ultra-high-field 7T fMRI, their recent work explores how duration-tuned neuronal populations are organized across the cortical hierarchy and asks how the neural coding of time interacts with spatial retinotopy. They are also using EEG and computational modeling to examine the dynamic interplay between sensory timing and motor systems, specifically probing how visual time perception is warped by the learning and preparation of goal-directed actions. Additionally, Dr. Bueti investigates the phenomenon of serial dependence across multiple sensory dimensions, including numerosity, duration, and size. By tracking early visual-evoked activity and comparing visual and auditory judgments, their research seeks to uncover whether the pull of recent past stimuli on present perception relies on centralized domain-general processes or modality-specific sensory pathways.

papers.title: Neuronal populations across the cortex underlie discrete, categorical, and subjective representations of visual durations
papers.abstract: With 7T fMRI during a visual duration categorisation task, the study maps how duration-tuned neuronal populations are organised across cortex. Parietal, premotor and caudal SMA contain topographic populations tuned to every tested duration, whereas rostral SMA, inferior frontal cortex and anterior insula prefer durations near the mean and track each participant's categorical boundary. This suggests a hierarchy from discrete to categorical to subjective duration representations.
papers.authors: Valeria Centanino, Gianfranco Fortunato, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: Evolution of visual time throughout goal driven action learning
papers.abstract: Participants judged brief visual durations while preparing goal-directed reaches, and perceived time expanded in the moments before movement onset, an effect that grew as motor plans became faster and more efficient with practice. EEG representational similarity analysis and modelling link this dynamic to the interplay between timing and action systems. The paper argues that time perception is shaped by the learning of motor control.
papers.authors: Nicola Binetti, Federico Mancinelli, Marco Zanon, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: Different modality-specific mechanisms mediate serial dependence effects in visual and auditory perception
papers.abstract: Asking whether the pull of the recent past on current percepts arises from a single central mechanism or from separate ones in each sensory pathway, the authors compare serial dependence in vision and audition. Their results support modality-specific mechanisms rather than one shared process. The paper speaks to how perceptual history is implemented in the brain.
papers.authors: Irene Togoli, Michele Fornaciai, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: The neural link between stimulus duration and spatial location in the human visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high-field 7T fMRI, the authors show that neuronal populations tuned to particular stimulus durations along the human visual hierarchy are not independent of where the stimulus appears in the visual field. Duration preferences and spatial position are coupled across visual areas, providing a neural basis for why perceived time interacts with spatial location. The work ties the coding of time to the retinotopic organisation of visual cortex.
papers.authors: Valeria Centanino, Gianfranco Fortunato, Domenica Bueti

papers.title: Perceptual History Biases Are Predicted by Early Visual-Evoked Activity
papers.abstract: Combining EEG and behaviour across numerosity, duration and size judgments, the study asks whether an early neural signature of past-stimulus information really accounts for serial dependence. The behavioural bias depends on the task, yet the neural signature also reflects task-irrelevant dimensions of the previous stimulus, indicating a partial dissociation. The early visual-evoked signal predicts the size of the bias across participants.
papers.authors: Michele Fornaciai, Irene Togoli, Domenica Bueti

0183.name: Dominique Lamy
0183.bio: Dominique Lamy is a Professor of Psychology at Tel Aviv University and directs the Visual Cognition Lab. Lamy’s research examines the determinants of attentional priority, exploring how stimulus-driven salience, goal-directed targets, and implicit memory factors like priming of pop-out interact to guide selection. Lamy developed the Priority Accumulation Framework (PAF) to characterize the temporal dynamics and evidence accumulation involved in attentional deployment. Using behavioral psychophysics and event-related potentials (ERPs), they investigate the functional boundaries between conscious and unconscious vision, as well as the role of spatial and object-based mechanisms in perception.
0183.research_direction: Dr. Lamy has recently been investigating the mechanisms that guide visual attention, focusing heavily on how selection history, task switching, and priority accumulation shape ongoing visual search. Their recent work explores the timing and flexibility of these processes using behavioral and eye-tracking paradigms to measure spatial cueing, trial-to-trial repetition effects, and target-location probability cueing. Additionally, they are examining how attentional guidance driven by salience, goals, and past experience changes across the adult lifespan. Beyond attentional control, their research also probes the boundary between conscious and unconscious visual processing by using masked response priming to test the validity of subjective ratings versus objective forced-choice measures of awareness.

papers.title: Sequential effects in visual search, action control, and task switching: Evidence for distinct episodic-retrieval and priority-based mechanisms
