papers.abstract: Visual search, action control and task switching literatures each report strong trial-to-trial repetition effects, but they have rarely been studied together. In four experiments participants searched for a cued target while the task, target location and response repeated or changed at random. When people were strongly motivated to prepare for the upcoming task, the previous target location influenced performance only if the task had also repeated, while location-response binding effects were more general. The results point to separable episodic-retrieval and priority-based mechanisms that jointly shape behavior on complex tasks.
papers.authors: Daniel Toledano, Tamar Alkalai, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: Searching beyond decrements: Attentional guidance across the adult lifespan
papers.abstract: This review asks whether age-related declines in visual search reflect impaired attentional guidance or other changes such as general slowing. It examines guidance from salience, goals and past experience across adulthood. Once perceptual factors and slowing are accounted for, experience-based guidance is largely preserved and guidance by stable goals and salience is broadly intact. The main age effects are a greater reliance on past experience under demanding conditions and less efficient goal reconfiguration when past and current priorities conflict.
papers.authors: Nir Shalev, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: On the timing of overt attention deployment: Eye-movement evidence for the priority accumulation framework
papers.abstract: Most search theories hold that attention goes automatically to the location of highest priority. The Priority Accumulation Framework instead proposes that priority accumulates over successive events and that evidence about action-relevant information helps decide when attention is deployed. Using first saccades in a free-viewing spatial-cueing task with varied search difficulty and cue salience, the authors showed that the cue can bias competition late, after processing of the search display has begun, in line with the framework and contrary to standard capture accounts.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Daniel Toledano, Mor Sasi, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: Attentional guidance by target-location probability cueing is largely inflexible, long-lasting, and distinct from intertrial priming
papers.abstract: The paper examines target-location probability cueing, where search improves for targets in a region where they appear more often. Across four experiments with a learning phase followed by an equiprobable extinction phase, the bias reduced search slopes and persisted, indicating an attentional effect. Telling participants that the imbalance would end did not remove the bias, and intertrial priming did not account for all of it. The bias thus behaves as a long-lasting, largely inflexible form of selection history distinct from goals and salience.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Aidai Golan, Dominique Lamy

papers.title: Unconscious Processing Contaminates Objective Measures of Conscious Perception: Evidence From the Liminal Prime Paradigm
papers.abstract: Assessing unconscious processing requires valid measures of awareness, but subjective reports and forced-choice discrimination often disagree. Using masked response priming, the authors replicated a dissociation showing that invisibility ratings were not contaminated by conscious perception. Within the same experiment, prime discrimination was above chance for primes rated unseen. This supports the view that objective forced-choice discrimination is contaminated by unconscious processing, not that subjective reports are contaminated by conscious perception.
papers.authors: Nitzan Micher, Diana Mazenko, Dominique Lamy

0184.name: Dora Hermes
0184.department: Department of Physiology and Biomedical Engineering
0184.bio: Hermes is an Associate Professor at the Mayo Clinic who investigates neurophysiological signals to identify biomarkers for neurological diseases and develop neuroprosthetics. Their research integrates multimodal imaging techniques, such as fMRI and intracranial EEG, with computational modeling to characterize brain network dynamics. Hermes examines how human visual and motor systems respond to sensory inputs and electrical stimulation to inform the development of therapeutic devices. This work connects fundamental neuroscience with clinical application through collaborations with neurosurgeons and neurologists to treat conditions like epilepsy.
0184.research_direction: Dr. Hermes's recent work explores the causal dynamics and architecture of human brain networks by combining single-pulse electrical stimulation with intracranial EEG recordings. A major focus of their research is the visual system, where they are investigating the directional flow of information across visual streams, probing how specific subregions of the pulvinar influence distinct cortical pathways, and examining how white matter stimulation modulates visually evoked responses. Beyond visual processing, Dr. Hermes has recently been investigating fundamental properties of neural communication by measuring the developmental trajectory of cortico-cortical transmission speeds across the human lifespan. Furthermore, their recent work explores clinical applications for drug-resistant epilepsy by assessing how targeted thalamic stimulation can be used to map and alter network excitability.

papers.title: Pulvinar Subregions Influence Select Cortical Pathways in Humans
papers.abstract: Single-pulse electrical stimulation of the pulvinar in 30 epilepsy patients with stereo-EEG was used to causally map the thalamic nucleus's influence on cortex. Lateral pulvinar drove striate and extrastriate visual areas, ventral-medial pulvinar drove lateral temporal cortex, and dorsomedial pulvinar drove parietal cortex, with the effects captured by a few large-scale gradients. The maps may guide targeting of pulvinar subregions for neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Jordan A. Bilderbeek, Nicholas M. Gregg, Maria Guadalupe Yanez-Ramos, Harvey Huang, Morgan Montoya, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, Jamie J. Van Gompel, Gregory A. Worrell, Kai J. Miller, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Single pulse electrical stimulation in white matter modulates iEEG visual responses in human early visual cortex
papers.abstract: In two patients with intracranial electrodes, single electrical pulses were delivered in white matter tracts connected to visual cortex while images appeared at varied delays after each pulse. Stimulation added a transient broadband response that did not alter visual broadband responses, but it enlarged visual evoked potentials when the pulse came closer to image onset. This suggests a single pulse can boost the strength or synchrony of connected visual populations without changing their overall firing.
papers.authors: Harvey Huang, Kendrick N. Kay, Nicholas M. Gregg, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Myung-Ho In, Christoph Kapeller, Yunhong Shu, Gregory A. Worrell, Kai J. Miller, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Electrical perturbation reveals a directional architecture for communication across human visual streams
papers.abstract: Single-pulse electrical stimulation during intracranial EEG in 23 patients was used to map directed effective connectivity among 22 visual cortical areas. Feedforward influence from early visual areas to dorsal and lateral streams was more reliable than feedback, ventral-temporal interactions were balanced, and temporal-to-parietal influence exceeded the reverse. Early and ventral areas behaved like sources and dorsal and lateral areas like integrators, providing constraints for models of visual processing.
papers.authors: Maria Guadalupe Yanez-Ramos, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Harvey Huang, Nicholas M. Gregg, Jordan Bilderbeek, Morgan Montoya, Kendrick Kay, Gregory A. Worrell, Kai J. Miller, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Thalamic Stimulation Induced Changes in Network Connectivity and Excitability in Epilepsy
papers.abstract: In ten patients with drug-resistant epilepsy undergoing stereo-EEG, the authors delivered single pulses and short trials of high-frequency thalamic stimulation and tracked the evoked potentials before and after. Baseline responses showed which thalamic subfields engage seizure networks most strongly, and stimulation lasting over 90 minutes reduced response amplitude in proportion to baseline connectivity. This supports using evoked potentials as biomarkers to guide thalamic neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Nicholas M. Gregg, Gabriela Ojeda Valencia, Tereza Pridalova, Harvey Huang, Vaclav Kremen, Brian N. Lundstrom, Jamie J. Van Gompel, Kai J. Miller, Gregory A. Worrell, Dora Hermes

papers.title: Developmental trajectory of transmission speed in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using single-pulse electrical stimulation and intracranial recordings in 74 patients, the authors measured how long cortico-cortical evoked responses take to travel along association and U-fibre pathways and converted these latencies into conduction speeds. Delays shrink with age until at least the third decade of life, showing that neural signalling speed keeps maturing well into adulthood, alongside the structural development of the connectome.
papers.authors: Dorien van Blooijs, Max A. van den Boom, Jaap F. van der Aar, Geertjan M. Huiskamp, Giulio Castegnaro, Matteo Demuru, Willemiek J. E. M. Zweiphenning, Pieter van Eijsden, Kai J. Miller, Frans S. S. Leijten, Dora Hermes

0186.name: Dwight J. Kravitz
0186.bio: Dwight J. Kravitz is an Associate Professor at George Washington University and a Program Director at the National Science Foundation. Kravitz researches the relationship between neuroanatomy, experience, and neural representations, specifically focusing on the functional organization of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways. Using multivariate fMRI analysis, behavioral psychophysics, and data-driven computational modeling, they explore how the brain represents visual objects, scenes, and social concepts. Kravitz’s work addresses the intersection of perceptual processing and working memory to develop a convergent understanding of vision across humans, animal models, and patient populations.
0186.research_direction: Dr. Kravitz's recent work broadly explores how cognitive neuroscience might better organize its theories around specific task demands and generalization, which includes evaluating how these shifting demands influence processing across the classic dorsal and ventral cortical visual pathways. Empirically, they have recently been investigating spatial representations of scene layout, using behavioral experiments to test how distance perception in natural photographs varies across different observers, response parameters, and viewing durations. Additionally, their recent experimental work examines the bidirectional interference between visual working memory and perception for stimuli like faces and motion to understand representation-specific recruitment in the brain. They are also studying visual attention and learning using large-scale behavioral data, explicitly testing how repeated exposure to both target-relevant and task-irrelevant contextual information drives changes in visual search performance over time.

papers.title: Representation-specific recruitment: Bidirectional interactions between working memory and perception for motion direction and face identity
papers.abstract: Studies of how holding an item in visual working memory and perceiving new stimuli interfere with each other, tested for both motion direction and face identity. The pattern of interference in both directions indicates that memory and perception recruit shared, feature-specific representations.
papers.authors: Sanika Paranjape, Simon Kaplan, Sarah Shomstein, Dwight J. Kravitz

papers.title: Repeated exposure to task-relevant and task-irrelevant information - and their interaction - affect visual search performance
papers.abstract: Visual search experiments examining how repeated exposure to target-relevant and irrelevant context information changes performance over time. The results show that both kinds of repetition improve search and that they interact, informing how learning shapes attention in large-scale, crowdsourced-style data.
papers.authors: Chloe Callahan-Flintoft, Patrick H. Cox, Emma M. Siritzky, Stephen R. Mitroff, Kelvin S. Oie, Dwight J. Kravitz

papers.title: Distance perception in natural scene images generalize across individuals, tasks, and viewing time
papers.abstract: Behavioral experiments in which people judged distances in photographs of natural scenes. Judgments proved highly consistent across observers, across different response tasks, and across brief versus extended viewing, supporting a stable, shared spatial representation of scene layout.
papers.authors: Prachi Mahableshwarkar, Lindsay Houck, John Philbeck, Dwight Kravitz

papers.title: Centering cognitive neuroscience on task demands and generalization
papers.abstract: A perspective arguing that cognitive neuroscience should organize its questions around the demands of the tasks participants actually perform, and around whether findings carry over to other tasks and settings, instead of relying on predefined psychological categories. The authors show how task-centric framing and explicit tests of generalization can reconcile discrepant results across studies and guide more robust theories of brain function.
papers.authors: Matthias Nau, Alexandra C. Schmid, Simon M. Kaplan, Chris I. Baker, Dwight J. Kravitz

papers.title: Insights from the Evolving Model of Two Cortical Visual Pathways
papers.abstract: A commentary revisiting the classic dorsal/ventral (where/what, action/perception) account of visual cortex in light of accumulating evidence. It argues for a picture of richly interconnected, recurrent processing streams whose roles depend on task demands rather than strictly separate pathways.
papers.authors: Chris Baker, Dwight Kravitz

0188.name: E. J. Green
0188.department: Department of Philosophy; Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0188.main_research_area: philosophy of perception and cognitive science
0188.bio: Green is the Miller Associate Professor at Johns Hopkins University, where they hold a primary appointment in the Department of Philosophy and a secondary appointment in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences. Green’s research examines the intersection of philosophy of mind and vision science, specifically investigating the nature of perceptual representation and the architectural boundary between perception and higher-level cognition. Their work addresses topics including shape constancy, multisensory object perception, and the compositionality of visual formats. Green integrates empirical findings from psychophysics and perceptual psychology with philosophical analysis to model how the mind segments and interprets sensory input.
0188.research_direction: Dr. Green has recently been investigating the fundamental nature and format of perceptual representation by bridging conceptual analysis with empirical findings from psychophysics and neuroscience. Their recent work explores how the visual system achieves perceptual constancy for properties like shape, size, and color across changing viewpoints, questioning whether the brain relies on a pluralistic set of representations to balance stable object properties with perspectival appearance. Additionally, they are examining the boundary between vision and cognition by asking how fine-grained sensory inputs are transformed into abstract categories, and whether processes like perceptual categorization require the observer to possess higher-level conceptual thought. Finally, their research probes the mechanisms of constructive perception, interrogating the extent to which mental imagery acts as a working ingredient when the visual system represents hidden or occluded object parts.

papers.title: Reconsidering the Role of Imagery in Perception
papers.abstract: The paper re-examines the popular idea that mental imagery is a working ingredient of ordinary perception, for example in how we represent the hidden parts of partly occluded objects. It weighs the empirical and conceptual case for this claim against alternative accounts of perceptual completion and constructive perception. The authors argue that the role of imagery has been overstated and clarify what a defensible imagery-in-perception thesis would need to show.
papers.authors: Kevin J. Lande, E. J. Green

papers.title: A Pluralist Perspective on Shape Constancy
papers.abstract: Shape constancy, seeing an object as keeping the same shape despite changing viewpoint, is often explained by a single kind of perceptual representation. The paper argues instead for a pluralist picture in which perception represents shape in more than one way, with different representations serving constancy and perspectival appearance. It draws on psychophysical findings about shape perception to motivate this view.
papers.venue: The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science
papers.authors: E. J. Green

papers.title: Perceptual Abstraction
papers.abstract: The paper asks how the fine-grained information delivered by the senses is turned into the simpler, more abstract categories that we perceive and judge, such as a color category like red. It analyzes what perceptual abstraction consists in and how it differs from conceptual thought. The account is developed with reference to research in perceptual psychology and neuroscience.
papers.authors: Mason Westfall, E. J. Green

papers.title: Perceptual Categorization and Perceptual Concepts
papers.abstract: The paper examines whether categorization within perception requires the perceiver to possess concepts. It distinguishes perceptual categorization from conceptual classification and argues about what, if anything, the notion of a perceptual concept adds. The discussion bears on how far perception is structured like thought.
papers.authors: E. J. Green

papers.title: Perceptual Constancy and Perceptual Representation
papers.abstract: The paper considers how the phenomenon of perceptual constancy, stable perception of properties like size, shape and color under varying viewing conditions, bears on theories of what perception represents. It argues that constancy has implications for the format and content of perceptual states. It engages with both philosophical positions and psychological findings.
papers.authors: E. J. Green

0190.name: Edward Awh
0190.bio: Awh is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and co-directs the Awh/Vogel Lab, which focuses on the cognitive neuroscience of attention and memory. Their research characterizes the architectural and neural constraints of visual working memory, specifically investigating why storage is limited to a small number of individuated items. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) to track alpha-band oscillations and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), Awh explores the functional overlap between spatial selective attention and online memory maintenance. Their work employs multivariate decoding and computational modeling to differentiate between spatial orienting and object-based storage while examining content-independent pointer systems in the human cortex.
0190.research_direction: Dr. Awh has recently been investigating the fundamental architecture and capacity limits of working memory, specifically exploring the theoretical framework that storage relies on a small set of content-independent "pointers" to index individuated items. Using EEG decoding and behavioral paradigms, their recent work examines whether neural load signals track the number of items held in memory regardless of sensory modality or the specific cortical regions processing disparate visual features like color and orientation. Furthermore, they are probing how this storage system interfaces with broader cognition by investigating the temporal dissociation between directing spatial attention and memory encoding, as well as testing whether the apparent working memory advantage for meaningful objects is actually driven by contributions from long-term memory.

papers.title: Contributions from Long-Term Memory Explain Superior Visual Working Memory Performance with Meaningful Objects
papers.abstract: Working memory tends to look better for meaningful objects than for simple stimuli. These experiments indicate this advantage arises mainly from help provided by long-term memory rather than from a larger working memory capacity. Neural and behavioral measures point to a boost that operates separately from storage limits.
papers.authors: Hyung-Bum Park, Edward Awh

papers.title: Working memory needs pointers
papers.abstract: This opinion piece argues that working memory storage depends on a small set of content-independent pointers that index individuated items, rather than on the representation of each item's features. It reviews behavioral and neural evidence, including load-dependent EEG and fMRI signals that are shared across different stimulus types, and shows how a pointer framework explains capacity limits and the interplay between memory and attention.
papers.authors: Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Neural evidence for modality-independent storage in working memory
papers.abstract: Using EEG decoding, the authors show that neural load signals track how many items are held in working memory regardless of whether the items are visual or auditory. Load signals from one modality generalized to the other, and were observed while people held mixed sets of items. The results support a pointer system that is independent of the sensory format of stored content.
papers.authors: Darius Suplica, Henry M. Jones, Gisella K. Diaz, John P. Veillette, Howard C. Nusbaum, Edward Awh

papers.title: Cortically Disparate Visual Features Evoke Content-Independent Load Signals during Storage in Working Memory
papers.abstract: The study asked whether load-related neural signals in working memory depend on the type of visual feature being stored. EEG decoding of load generalized across features processed in different cortical regions, such as color and orientation. This indicates a common load signal that is independent of memory content.
papers.authors: Henry M. Jones, William S. Thyer, Darius Suplica, Edward Awh

papers.title: Electroencephalogram Decoding Reveals Distinct Processes for Directing Spatial Attention and Encoding Into Working Memory
papers.abstract: The authors used EEG decoding to compare directing spatial attention with encoding an item into working memory. Attention-related spatial signals appeared before and independently of memory-load signals, and the two could be dissociated in time and across task conditions. The findings challenge accounts that treat attentional selection and memory storage as a single process.
papers.authors: Henry M. Jones, Gisella K. Diaz, William X. Q. Ngiam, Edward Awh

0191.name: Edward F Ester
0191.department: Department of Psychology and Institute for Neuroscience
0191.bio: Edward F. Ester investigates the neural architectures and computational principles that support visual working memory and selective attention. Their research integrates behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging methods, including fMRI and EEG, to reconstruct and track mnemonic representations across the human cortex. Ester examines how the brain maintains information in the absence of sensory input and how these representations are transformed into motor plans to guide goal-directed behavior. Their current projects explore the factors determining individual differences in cognitive efficiency and the impact of neural competition on memory integrity.
0191.research_direction: Dr. Ester's recent work explores the neural and oculomotor mechanisms underlying visual working memory, internal attention, and category learning. Using a combination of scalp EEG decoding and eye-tracking, they are investigating how behavioral priority and attentional competition influence the accessibility and selection timing of internally stored visual representations. Additionally, they have recently been examining how humans learn and make decisions about abstract visual categories, tracing these cognitive processes through neural evidence-accumulation signals and uninstructed gaze behaviors. Finally, their research probes how large-scale brain networks support cognition, specifically testing how cortical traveling waves coordinate the flow of information between visual and frontal regions during memory-guided actions.

papers.title: Human Gaze Behaviors Track Abstract Stimulus Categories
papers.abstract: Monkey studies show oculomotor structures encode learned categories and produce tiny uninstructed eye movements reflecting them. Across three experiments, this work shows that human gaze behavior likewise carries abstract category information independent of the stimulus's physical features. This links eye movements to abstract cognition and suggests gaze as a readout of category learning.
papers.authors: Ali Caron, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Neural Measures of Human Decision-Making Track Evidence Accumulation in Learned Space
papers.abstract: Participants classified oriented stimuli into discrete categories defined by an experimenter-set boundary while scalp EEG was recorded. Category-level evidence computed from learned representational transformations was tracked by neural signals that behaved like an evidence-accumulation process. This extends neural accumulation-to-bound decision mechanisms to decisions based on newly learned category rules.
papers.authors: Arianna Thoksakis, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Traveling waves link human visual and frontal cortex during working memory–guided behavior
papers.abstract: Using EEG recorded during a memory-guided action task, the study finds forward- and backward-propagating traveling waves that link visual and motor/frontal regions around the time a remembered item is used to guide behavior. The strength of these waves predicts differences in performance both between and within individuals. The authors argue that traveling waves may flexibly coordinate the timing and direction of communication between memory storage and behavior-producing areas.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Canhuang Luo, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Endogenous–Exogenous Competition Delays Internal Selection Across Cortical and Oculomotor Systems
papers.abstract: Combining EEG and eye tracking, the study asks whether involuntary capture of internal attention by cue-matching memory content occurs when cue and probe are simultaneous. Across behavior, lateralized alpha activity, and gaze biases it finds no retro-capture; instead competition between goal-driven and stimulus-driven selection uniformly delays selection of the relevant memory. The results suggest retro-capture depends on the timing between cue and action.
papers.authors: Dayana Valdez, Edward F. Ester

papers.title: Changes in behavioral priority influence the accessibility of working memory content
papers.abstract: Using EEG decoding in a retro-cue working memory task, the study tests whether unequal behavioral priority of remembered items alters the strength of their neural representations or how fast they can be selected. Probabilistic changes in relevance did not change decodability but changed the latency at which above-chance decoding emerged. Priority therefore affects how easily memories are selected rather than how strong they are.
papers.authors: Edward F. Ester, Paige Pytel

0192.name: Edward K. Vogel
0192.bio: Edward K. Vogel is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and a member of the Grossman Institute for Neuroscience. Vogel’s research focuses on the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying visual attention and working memory, specifically identifying the biological and cognitive factors that limit the capacity to maintain information in an active state. Using electrophysiological techniques such as EEG and event-related potentials, Vogel utilized the contralateral delay activity (CDA) as a neural index of memory load. Their work explores how individual differences in these neural signatures predict cognitive performance and how these mechanisms are affected by various neurological and psychiatric conditions.
0192.research_direction: Dr. Vogel has recently been investigating the structural limits and dynamic updating mechanisms of visual working memory and attentional control. Their recent work explores whether memory storage relies on content-free pointers that index items in the environment, using neural load signals like the contralateral delay activity to measure how the visual system parses both static and moving objects. In addition to storage mechanisms, they are examining the active management of these representations, probing how and under what conditions irrelevant visual information is selectively dropped during testing or spontaneously cleared when a task ends. Finally, their research asks how individual differences in these core working memory and attentional capacities continue to constrain downstream long-term memory performance even after extensive practice.

papers.title: Item-based Parsing of Dynamic Scenes in a Combined Attentional Tracking and Working Memory Task
papers.abstract: Both multiple-object tracking and visual working memory are limited to a few items, which may reflect a shared way the visual system parses scenes into discrete units. The authors recorded the contralateral delay activity while people tracked moving objects and simultaneously remembered static ones. Load signals from the two tasks combined in an item-based fashion, supporting a common indexing mechanism.
papers.authors: Piotr P. Styrkowiec, William X. Q. Ngiam, Will Epstein, Ron Gneezy, Henry M. Jones, Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Selective removal of visual working memory items at test
papers.abstract: Working memory tasks usually require comparing remembered items to a test display, yet how people drop irrelevant items at that point is poorly understood. In three experiments the authors used the contralateral delay activity to track memory load during testing. They found that participants can selectively remove items, but only under certain conditions, and not simply on the basis of spatial location or grouping.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Temilade Adekoya, Sintra Horwitz, Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Working memory needs pointers
papers.abstract: The authors argue that working memory storage depends on content-free pointers that bind stored information to locations or objects in the environment, rather than on the stored features themselves. This idea accounts for why neural load signals such as the contralateral delay activity track the number of items held regardless of their content. They review behavioural and neural evidence for pointer-based storage and lay out predictions for how this framework explains capacity limits.
papers.authors: Edward Awh, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Individual Differences in Working Memory and Attentional Control Continue to Predict Memory Performance Despite Extensive Learning
papers.abstract: The study asks whether working memory and attentional control abilities still predict memory performance once people have had extensive practice learning the material. Across repeated learning of the same items, these abilities continued to explain differences in long-term memory performance. The results suggest that individual differences in core cognitive capacities keep constraining memory even when learning is heavily repeated.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Task Termination Triggers Spontaneous Removal of Information From Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: Working memory should release information once a goal has been completed, but earlier work could not show this directly. Using neural and behavioural measures, the authors show that content is spontaneously cleared from visual working memory when the task ends. This provides direct evidence that maintenance is goal-dependent.
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Tsubomi, Keisuke Fukuda, Atsushi Kikumoto, Ulrich Mayr, Edward K. Vogel

0193.name: Eero P. Simoncelli
0193.bio: Eero P. Simoncelli is a Silver Professor at New York University and the director of the Center for Computational Neuroscience at the Flatiron Institute. Simoncelli develops computational models at the intersection of mathematics, engineering, and neuroscience to characterize the representation of visual information in biological and artificial systems. Their work includes research on natural image statistics, multiscale image transforms such as the steerable pyramid, and the SSIM index for image quality assessment. Currently, Simoncelli investigates the geometric structure of neural representations and population coding principles to analyze how the brain processes complex visual scenes.
0193.research_direction: Dr. Simoncelli has recently been investigating the mathematical structures that bridge statistical models of natural images with human sensory perception. Their recent work explores how generative frameworks, such as denoising diffusion and neural energy models, can be leveraged to estimate complex image probability densities and exploit the low intrinsic dimensionality of visual data. To better understand visual representations, they are also developing rigorous geometric methods—often utilizing Fisher information and denoising errors across noise scales—to define novel perceptual distance metrics and generate local image distortions that computationally differentiate deep neural networks from models of the early visual system. Furthermore, they are probing the foundational laws of psychophysics by building unified theoretical frameworks that link how humans judge the perceived magnitude of a sensory stimulus with their fundamental ability to discriminate between distinct stimuli.

papers.title: Learning a distance measure from the information-estimation geometry of data
papers.abstract: The paper defines the Information-Estimation Metric, a distance between signals derived from how a denoiser's error vectors change across noise levels, which ties signal log-probability to optimal denoising error. It reduces to Mahalanobis distance for Gaussian data, is proven to be a valid global metric, and has a local Riemannian approximation. Using learned denoisers on ImageNet, it predicts human perceptual judgments of image similarity competitively with supervised quality metrics.
papers.authors: Guy Ohayon, Pierre-Etienne H. Fiquet, Florentin Guth, Jona Ballé, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Blind denoising diffusion models and the blessings of dimensionality
papers.abstract: The authors show that diffusion models need not be told the noise level: the level can be inferred from a single noisy sample as a Bayesian estimation problem, exploiting low intrinsic dimensionality of image data. They prove that such blind denoising diffusion models work as sampling algorithms under this assumption, and use the analysis to justify an adaptive sampler. Experiments compare them with standard noise-conditioned diffusion models.
papers.authors: Zahra Kadkhodaie, Aram-Alexandre Pooladian, Sinho Chewi, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Learning normalized image densities via dual score matching
papers.abstract: The authors build a neural energy model whose input gradient gives the usual denoising score, and add a second objective on its derivative with respect to noise level so that the energies are properly normalized across noise scales. Trained on ImageNet64, it reaches cross-entropy competitive with state-of-the-art density models, and estimates from networks trained on disjoint data subsets agree closely. The learned probabilities show that image likelihood and local dimensionality vary substantially with image content.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Florentin Guth, Zahra Kadkhodaie, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: Discriminating image representations with principal distortions
papers.abstract: This work compares image representations, whether deep networks or models of the early visual system, by their sensitivity to small local distortions, summarized with Fisher information. It finds 'principal distortions' that most separate two models' responses, which can be rendered as images and tested against human perception. Applying it to vision models reveals differences in local geometry linked to architecture and training that global similarity measures miss.
papers.authors: Jenelle Feather, David Lipshutz, Sarah E. Harvey, Alex H. Williams, Eero P. Simoncelli

papers.title: A unified framework for perceived magnitude and discriminability of sensory stimuli
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that a single internal-representation model with noise can explain both how strong a stimulus feels (magnitude ratings) and how well two stimuli can be told apart (discrimination). It links the two through the Fisher information of the representation, letting one fit predict the other. The framework is tested on existing perceptual datasets across several sensory attributes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Jingyang Y. Zhou, Lyndon R. Duong, Eero P. Simoncelli

0196.name: Elisha Merriam
0196.bio: Elisha P. Merriam heads the Computational Neuroimaging and Perception Team within the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Their research uses fMRI and image-computable encoding models to study how the human visual system represents visual information, with a focus on primary visual cortex, motion perception, and how these representations change over time.
0196.research_direction: Dr. Merriam has recently been investigating how visual information is represented in the brain using fMRI and image-computable models. Their recent work has shown that representations in human primary visual cortex drift over months, driven by changes in neural responsivity while the population-level structure of responses stays stable. They have also used fMRI decoding to study the double-drift illusion, finding that area hMT+ carries the illusory motion trajectory. In collaboration with the Gardner lab, they have used population modeling to show that orientation maps reported in mouse superior colliculus can be explained by units with non-orientation-selective, center-surround receptive fields.

papers.title: Orientation Maps in Mouse Superior Colliculus Explained by Population Model of Non-Orientation Selective Neurons
papers.abstract: In this study, the authors employ image-computable population modeling to address recent empirical findings of radial orientation preference maps in the mouse superficial superior colliculus (sSC), which appear to contradict the computational invariance observed in primates. By constructing a model based on circular-symmetric, center-surround receptive fields (RFs) typical of lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons, they demonstrate that measured orientation selectivity is an emergent population property. The results show that these maps are critically dependent on the interaction between neural spatial frequency tuning and the vignetting effects introduced by stimulus apertures. This computational framework suggests that the apparent orientation tuning in mouse SC does not necessitate de novo orientation-selective circuitry but is consistent with stimulus-invariant RF mechanisms previously established in primate research.
papers.authors: Austin Kuo, Justin L. Gardner, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Brain representations of motion and position in the double-drift illusion
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and decoding analyses, the authors studied the double-drift illusion, in which internal motion within a moving window shifts its perceived path even when the eyes track the window. Area hMT+ was the only area where the illusory trajectory could be decoded, pointing to a role in combining retinal and eye-movement signals.
papers.authors: Noah J. Steinberg, Zvi N. Roth, J. Anthony Movshon, Elisha P. Merriam

papers.title: Representations in human primary visual cortex drift over time
papers.abstract: Analyzing a large longitudinal fMRI dataset of responses to natural scene images, the authors fit an image-computable encoding model and found that its fit degraded cumulatively across sessions over many months, attributable to changes in neural responsivity, while population-level representational dissimilarities stayed stable.
papers.authors: Zvi N. Roth, Elisha P. Merriam

0197.name: Elissa L. Newport
0197.bio: Elissa L. Newport is the Director of the Center for Brain Plasticity and Recovery and a Professor of Neurology at Georgetown University. Newport’s research involves the 'less is more' hypothesis, which posits that children's cognitive limitations facilitate the acquisition of complex linguistic structures. They conduct research on statistical learning in language and visual domains to examine how infants and adults extract patterns from environmental input. Newport’s current work focuses on the Pediatric Stroke Research Project, using neuroimaging to investigate how the developing brain reorganizes language functions following early-life neurological injury.
0197.research_direction: Dr. Newport has recently been investigating the neural plasticity and cognitive mechanisms underlying early language development. Using fMRI and diffusion imaging, their recent work explores the early anatomical lateralization of typical infant language networks and tests whether functions like auditory sentence comprehension and visual word-form processing systematically reorganize to homotopic right-hemisphere regions following perinatal left-hemisphere strokes. In a complementary line of research, they have also been examining how young children learn syntax through behavioral artificial-language paradigms. These studies ask how young learners leverage statistical and distributional cues in their auditory input to group words into phrase structures and decide whether to generalize linguistic patterns as broad rules or restricted exceptions.

papers.title: Children's acquisition of syntax from distributional cues to phrase structure
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether children can learn the phrase structure of a new language from the statistical distribution of words in the input. Building on Newport's statistical-learning tradition, it examines which distributional cues let children group words into phrases and acquire syntactic structure. The findings bear on how much syntax can be learned from input statistics alone.
papers.authors: Alix B. Fetch, Heidi R. Getz, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: 6-To-8 Year-Old Children Adjust Their Linguistic Generalizations Based on Distributional Cues
papers.abstract: Children heard artificial-language input that varied in how frequently and evenly words followed a pattern. The study shows that 6-to-8-year-olds use these distributional cues to decide whether a pattern is a productive rule or a lexically restricted exception. It supports the view that learners rationally calibrate generalization to the statistics of their input.
papers.authors: Kathryn D. Schuler, Patricia A. Reeder, Heidi Getz, Kathryn Kissinger, Richard N. Aslin, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: Right-Lateralization of the Visual Word Form Area after Left-Hemisphere Perinatal Stroke
papers.abstract: Reading normally depends on a left ventral occipitotemporal region, the visual word form area. The authors scanned people with early left-hemisphere stroke and found that word-form processing shifts to the mirror-image right-hemisphere region. This indicates that even a culturally acquired skill like reading is relocated to homotopic cortex when the usual left-hemisphere site is lost early in life.
papers.authors: Anna Seydell-Greenwald, Natalya Vladyko, Catherine E. Chambers, William D. Gaillard, Barbara Landau, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: Assessing the Early Lateralization of White Matter in the Infant Language Network
papers.abstract: Using diffusion imaging in infants, the study tracks the frontal-temporal white-matter pathways that support language and asks whether they are already lateralized early in life. The results characterize how lateralization of these tracts emerges in the first months, giving a developmental baseline for the language network. The work complements the group's stroke studies by defining what typical early organization looks like.
papers.authors: Madeline Marcelle, Venkata Sita Priyanka Illapani, William D. Gaillard, Elissa L. Newport

papers.title: One right can make a left: sentence processing in the right hemisphere after perinatal stroke
papers.abstract: The study asks whether people who suffered a large left-hemisphere stroke around birth reorganize sentence comprehension in a consistent way in the right hemisphere. Using fMRI during auditory sentence comprehension in 14 stroke participants, the authors find that language activation is reliably re-expressed in the right hemisphere in a pattern that mirrors the typical left-hemisphere language network. This shows that early plasticity follows a predictable, homotopic blueprint rather than an idiosyncratic one.
papers.authors: Kelly C. Martin, Anna Seydell-Greenwald, Peter E. Turkeltaub, Catherine E. Chambers, Margot Giannetti, Alexander W. Dromerick, Jessica L. Carpenter, Madison M. Berl, William D. Gaillard, Elissa L. Newport

0198.name: Elkan G. Akyürek
0198.bio: Elkan G. Akyürek is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience and Chair of the Department of Experimental Psychology at the University of Groningen. Akyürek's research focuses on the mechanisms of temporal integration, visual attention, and human working memory, specifically exploring how the brain parses and integrates rapid sensory input into coherent perceptual events. Utilizing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and neurocomputational modeling, they investigate the neural dynamics of memory maintenance, including the characterization of activity-silent states. Their recent work examines the adaptive nature of temporal processing and the role of oscillatory activity in attentional prioritization.
0198.research_direction: Dr. Akyürek has recently been investigating the flexible dynamics of visual processing, focusing on how temporal integration and working memory adapt to environmental demands. Their recent work explores how the brain binds successive visual inputs into a single percept, using EEG and multivariate pattern analysis to track the shifting speed and timing of these integrative stages. Beyond early perception, they are also probing the neural mechanisms of visual working memory to understand how different items are retained over delays. Specifically, they use techniques like visual impulse perturbation and neural decoding to disentangle whether memorized features are actively prioritized via alpha-band oscillations or maintained in activity-quiescent, latent synaptic states. By bridging perception and memory, their research examines how the visual system leverages statistical regularities to dynamically adjust the speed, timing, and storage format of incoming information.

papers.title: Variable Processing Shifts during Perceptual Acceleration: Evidence from Temporal Integration
papers.abstract: Using multivariate pattern analysis of EEG in a missing-element task, the study tracks when the representation of an integrated percept emerges as two successive displays are combined. Delaying the second display shifted the integrated representation correspondingly earlier, showing that the first display predictively speeds perception. The speed-up was nonlinear across processing stages, rising from early to intermediate latencies and shrinking again later, so time gained at one moment can be lost at another.
papers.authors: Michael J. Wolff, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Sustained alpha oscillations serve attentional prioritization in working memory, not maintenance
papers.abstract: Asks whether sustained alpha-band activity during a working memory delay reflects generic maintenance or attentional prioritization. With two memory items, one tested first, and short versus long delays, decoding showed only the prioritized item stayed decodable across the delay and shifted into a stable code. This persistence was tied to induced alpha power, supporting a prioritization role and leaving activity-silent maintenance for the other item.
papers.authors: Yuanyuan Weng, Jelmer P. Borst, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Temporal integration as an adaptive process in visual perception, attention, and working memory
papers.abstract: A sole-authored synthesis of the author's program on how the brain binds successive visual inputs into one percept. It argues that temporal integration is not a fixed-window mechanism but adapts flexibly to the statistics and demands of the task. The review connects evidence across perception, attention and working memory and proposes a unifying adaptive account.
papers.authors: Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Maintenance of color memoranda in activity-quiescent working memory states: Evidence from impulse perturbation
papers.abstract: Tests whether colour information held in working memory persists in a neurally quiet, activity-silent state. Brief impulse stimuli were used to probe the hidden memory traces with EEG, revealing decodable memory content even when no ongoing activity carried it. The results support synaptic or latent storage accounts of maintenance for colour features.
papers.authors: Güven Kandemir, Sophia A. Wilhelm, Nikolai Axmacher, Elkan G. Akyürek

papers.title: Adaptive Encoding Speed in Working Memory
papers.abstract: Shows that people encode information into working memory faster when they have adapted to fast recent or overall stimulus durations. Across several experiments, encoding speed tracked statistical regularities in the environment. Explicit cues, even when more informative, failed to speed encoding, suggesting adaptation is largely implicit.
papers.authors: Joost de Jong, Hedderik van Rijn, Elkan G. Akyürek

0199.name: Ella Striem-Amit
0199.bio: Ella Striem-Amit is an Assistant Professor of Neuroscience at Georgetown University Medical Center and directs the Sensory and Motor Plasticity (SAMP) Lab. Striem-Amit’s research investigates the relationship between innate brain organization and experience-dependent plasticity in individuals with early-onset sensory or motor deprivation, such as those born blind, deaf, or without hands. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics, they study how the brain maintains task-specific and topographical organization without typical sensory input or motor effectors. Their research characterizes compensatory cross-modal plasticity to inform the development of sensory aids and motor prostheses through the study of neural adaptability.
0199.research_direction: Dr. Striem-Amit has recently been studying how much the human brain can reorganize when the input it normally receives is missing from birth. Their recent work examines people born blind, asking whether the early visual cortex takes on different roles in different individuals and how stable those individual patterns are over time. They also study congenitally deaf people, asking how brain networks organize around the deprived auditory cortex depending on when language was acquired. In people born without hands, they ask how the sensory and motor cortex handles the feet used in place of hands, and whether brain areas that represent kinds of actions, including recent ones like tool use, work independently of the body part used.

papers.title: Experience-driven plasticity in the secondary somatosensory cortex in people born without hands
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the neuroplastic reorganization of the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) in individuals with congenital upper-limb dysplasia (IDs) who utilize their feet for manual-compensatory tasks. Using task-based fMRI and resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) analyses, the researchers demonstrate that foot-related motor execution and sensory stimulation drive selective activation within the former hand-selective territory of the left SII in IDs, significantly exceeding the activations observed in typically developed (TD) controls. This foot selectivity in SII cannot be attributed to intrinsic organizational biases (e.g., latent somatotopy), as the hand-selective area in TD controls shows a secondary preference for the shoulder rather than the foot. Furthermore, RSFC data reveals altered coupling between SII and primary sensorimotor regions specifically in IDs. These findings suggest a hierarchical organization of cortical plasticity where reorganization in the primary somatosensory cortex (SI) remains constrained by somatotopic principles, while SII reflects functionally dependent, experience-driven adaptation to lifelong motor demands.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Zhiqing Deng, Florencia Martinez-Addiego, Yuqi Liu, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Action-type mapping principles extend beyond evolutionarily conserved actions, even in people born without hands
papers.abstract: The research investigates whether motor association areas generalize action representations across different effectors for evolutionarily recent tool-use actions, contrasting with evolutionarily conserved actions like reaching and grasping. Using fMRI in typically developed (TD) individuals and those born without hands (IDs), the study employed univariate analyses, multivariate decoding (MVPA), and temporal signal dynamics to identify effector-independent neural architectures. While primary sensorimotor regions (M1/S1) exhibited high fidelity for concrete, body-part-specific encoding (e.g., hand vs. foot), higher-level regions in the dorsal tool-use network—specifically the left dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) and superior parietal lobule (SPL)—encoded abstract action goals regardless of whether the action was performed with the hand or the foot. Crucially, this action-type organization emerged in IDs despite the total absence of manual experience, suggesting that the hierarchical division between body-centric and action-centric representation is a fundamental organizational principle not dictated by evolutionary recency or typical sensorimotor input.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Florencia Martinez-Addiego, Yuqi Liu, Kyungji Moon, Elizabeth Shytle, Lénia Amaral, Caroline O’Brien, Sriparna Sen, Maximilian Riesenhuber, Jody C. Culham, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Unraveling the impact of congenital deafness on individual brain organization
papers.abstract: This study examines how congenital auditory deprivation and the timing of language acquisition influence inter-individual variability in brain network organization. Analyzing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from congenitally deaf individuals (including native signers and delayed signers) and hearing controls, the authors quantified inter-subject variability in functional connectivity (FC) originating from the deprived auditory cortex (AC). The findings reveal a significant increase in FC variability among deaf individuals, particularly within regions that undergo cross-modal reorganization and language-processing networks. This heightened variability was not significantly attenuated by early language exposure, as it persisted in native signers. The results demonstrate that sensory experience exerts a critical stabilizing influence on typical brain development, and its absence triggers a diversification of neural connectivity patterns, suggesting that cortical plasticity manifests through highly idiosyncratic, rather than uniform, organizational outcomes across individuals.
papers.authors: Lénia Amaral, Xiaosha Wang, Yanchao Bi, Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Can individual differences explain brain plasticity in blindness?
papers.abstract: In this theoretical review, the author addresses the long-standing debate regarding the functional role of the early visual cortex (EVC) in individuals with congenital blindness, which has been shown to participate in an heterogeneous array of tasks including language, memory, and executive control. Striem-Amit proposes that the apparent lack of a singular, group-level explanation for EVC recruitment can be resolved by considering substantial inter-individual variability in neural plasticity. The article argues that individual developmental trajectories and environmental experiences drive the formation of stable, idiosyncratic connectivity 'fingerprints.' By adopting a precision-neuroscience framework that shifts focus from group-averaged patterns to individual-specific functional architectures, the field may reconcile disparate findings and improve the efficacy of personalized rehabilitative and sensory restoration technologies.
papers.authors: Ella Striem-Amit

papers.title: Longitudinal stability of individual brain plasticity patterns in blindness
papers.abstract: This longitudinal fMRI study assesses the temporal stability of reorganized functional connectivity (FC) patterns in the primary visual cortex (V1) of congenitally blind individuals over a two-year period. By comparing repeatedly sampled FC profiles across various cognitive states (resting-state vs. task-driven), the researchers tested whether the role of blind V1 is transiently task-flexible or longitudinally consistent. Results show that V1-FC patterns are highly unique to each individual and remain remarkably stable over time, irrespective of the specific task being performed. Multivariate pattern analysis successfully decoded individual identity from these connectivity profiles with high accuracy. These findings indicate that while visual deprivation leads to diverse plasticity outcomes across the blind population, the resulting functional connectivity of V1 forms a stable individual fingerprint, challenging the hypothesis that blind V1 operates as a highly flexible, task-dependent station within the multiple-demand system.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Lénia Amaral, Peyton Thomas, Amir Amedi, Ella Striem-Amit

0200.name: Emanuela Bricolo
0200.bio: Emanuela Bricolo is a Full Professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca who researches the cognitive mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and oculomotor control. Bricolo utilizes psychophysical techniques and eye-tracking to investigate phenomena such as visual crowding, reading patterns, and the spatial representation of numbers along a mental number line. Their work has explored the neurological basis of spatial neglect and the efficacy of neuromodulation techniques, including TMS and tRNS, in cognitive performance. Additionally, Bricolo examines the psychology of virtual environments, focusing on user learning in the metaverse and the realism of computer-generated faces.
0200.research_direction: Dr. Bricolo has recently been investigating visual attention and perception across both fundamental and applied contexts. Their recent work explores how statistical learning and spatial expectations regarding targets and distractors dynamically shape the center-surround inhibition of the attentional focus. They have also extended these questions into realistic environments, developing virtual reality driving simulator protocols to examine how proactive distractor suppression impacts complex behaviors like braking responsiveness and lane-keeping precision. Additionally, their research assesses the methodological validity of using computer-generated faces in experimental psychology, investigating how factors like realism and prior exposure drive the uncanny valley effect.

papers.title: Statistical learning re-shapes the center-surround inhibition of the visuo-spatial attentional focus
papers.abstract: The study tests how learning the statistical regularities of where targets and distractors tend to appear changes the shape of the attentional focus. Learned expectations reorganised the suppressed surround that normally rings the attended location, showing that center-surround inhibition is flexibly tuned by experience rather than fixed.
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Carlotta Lega, Luca Ronconi, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Prepared for the expected but unready for the unexpected: Unmet distractor expectations slow braking responsiveness but improve lane-keeping precision in a virtual driving simulation
papers.abstract: Twenty-four participants drove a virtual circuit and braked to road-sign-like targets while distractors appeared often or not at all across blocks. Expecting frequent distractors slowed braking even when none appeared, more so when distractors resembled the target, yet it also tightened lane keeping, revealing a cost-benefit trade-off of proactive suppression in a realistic task.
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Marco A. Petilli, Carlotta Lega, Simone Fontana, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Using computer-generated faces in experimental psychology: The role of realism and exposure
papers.abstract: An empirical follow-up examining how the realism of computer-generated faces and viewers' prior exposure to them shape perception and judgments. The results inform when synthetic faces are an adequate substitute for real photographs in experiments.
papers.authors: Anna Flavia Di Natale, Stefania La Rocca, Matilde Ellen Simonetti, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: A protocol to evaluate the impact of visual distractors on driving attention using a virtual reality simulator
papers.abstract: Proposes a standardized VR driving-simulator protocol in which drivers respond to stop-sign-like targets amid distractors of varying similarity. Reaction times and lane keeping index how distractors erode driving attention, offering a safe, reproducible alternative to on-road studies.
papers.authors: Simone Fontana, Andrea Massironi, Marco Petilli, Carlotta Lega, Emanuela Bricolo

papers.title: Uncanny valley effect: A qualitative synthesis of empirical research to assess the suitability of using virtual faces in psychological research
papers.abstract: A systematic qualitative synthesis of empirical studies on the uncanny valley, evaluating whether computer-generated faces can serve as valid stimuli in psychology experiments. It identifies which realism and design factors drive uncanny reactions and offers guidance for researchers choosing virtual faces.
papers.authors: Anna Flavia Di Natale, Matilde Ellen Simonetti, Stefania La Rocca, Emanuela Bricolo

0201.name: Emily A Cooper
0201.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science (also Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute)
0201.bio: Emily A. Cooper is an Associate Professor of Cognitive Science and Computer Science at Dartmouth College, where they direct the Perceptual Reality Lab. Cooper’s research investigates the computational mechanisms of human visual perception, with an emphasis on how the brain processes three-dimensional information and depth cues in natural environments. By combining psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and natural scene statistics, Cooper examines the principles of visual encoding to inform the design of augmented reality, virtual reality, and assistive vision technologies. Their work focuses on the intersection of biological vision and digital display engineering for applications in clinical vision care and immersive graphics.
0201.research_direction: Dr. Cooper's recent research investigates the computational and physiological mechanisms underlying visual perception, bridging low-level optics, natural scene statistics, and high-level perceptual judgments. They have recently been exploring how the eye’s accommodation system integrates competing wavelength signals to focus in polychromatic environments, and how introducing monocular distortions to binocular disparities alters the perceived 3D shape of highly familiar objects. At the neural level, their recent work uses natural environment recordings and population models of area MT to probe how the visual system segregates figures from backgrounds, while also examining how the criteria for optimal neural coding transform across the processing hierarchy. Furthermore, they are studying applied perception in the era of generative AI, using signal-detection analysis to evaluate how temporal evidence and viewing duration influence human accuracy when judging the authenticity of synthetic video.

papers.title: Focusing on color: How the eye chooses which wavelength to see best
papers.abstract: Because the eye's optics cannot bring all wavelengths into focus at once, the visual system must choose which color to sharpen. Using polychromatic stimuli and measurements of accommodation, the authors show that the eye does not simply maximize overall image sharpness; the balance among different color signals also guides its focusing. The results clarify how accommodation is controlled in colorful natural scenes and have implications for lens and display design.
papers.authors: Benjamin M. Chin, Martin S. Banks, Derek Nankivil, Austin Roorda, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: Perceptual Judgments of Video Authenticity: An Examination of Viewing Duration, Confidence, Content, and Strategies
papers.abstract: Participants judged whether short videos were real or generated by current text-to-video models, with clips lasting from a single frame to eight seconds. Longer viewing raised detection of AI videos from about 58 to 75 percent, but accuracy on real videos stayed near 60 percent. Signal-detection analysis shows extra evidence leads people to reject fakes without trusting real videos more, hinting that realistic synthetic video may erode trust in all video.
papers.venue: CVPR Workshop on Authenticity & Provenance in the Age of Generative AI (APAI)
papers.authors: Catherine E. Davodi, Sarah Barrington, Hany Farid, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: Statistical regularities in natural scenes that support figure-ground segregation by neural populations
papers.abstract: The authors measured motion and distance in natural scene recordings and found that objects tend to move faster and sit closer than their surroundings. Combining this with models of receptive fields in area MT, they show that neural populations can exploit these regularities to separate figures from backgrounds. The work ties the tuning of visual neurons to the statistics of the natural environment.
papers.authors: Clara T. Friedman, Minqi Wang, Thomas Yerxa, Bryce A. Arseneau, Xin Huang, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: How small changes to one eye's retinal image can transform the perceived shape of a very familiar object
papers.abstract: A slight distortion applied to the image in only one eye can make a familiar rectangular object, such as one's own phone, look visibly warped. The experiments show how the brain combines binocular disparity with other shape cues and where that inference breaks down. This has direct relevance to optics and augmented-reality devices that alter the two eyes' images differently.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Iona R. McLean, Ian M. Erkelens, Emily A. Cooper

papers.title: Transformations of sensory information in the brain suggest changing criteria for optimality
papers.abstract: The paper compares how sensory information is represented at successive stages of the visual pathway, including binocular disparity coding. Early areas appear tuned to preserve faithful information about the world, whereas later areas reshape it to better serve perception and action. This suggests that the criterion for an optimal neural code changes across the processing hierarchy.
papers.authors: Tyler S. Manning, Emma Alexander, Bruce G. Cumming, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Xin Huang, Emily A. Cooper

0202.name: Emily D Grossman
0202.bio: Emily D. Grossman is a visual neuroscientist at the University of California, Irvine, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of biological motion perception. Grossman utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and electroencephalography (EEG) to map the cortical networks involved in integrating form and motion signals. Their research characterizes regions within the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and ventral temporal cortex that process animate movement and social cues. The Grossman laboratory currently explores how feature-based attention and perceptual learning modulate the sensitivity and invariant coding of these visual brain areas.
0202.research_direction: Dr. Grossman’s recent work explores the neural and perceptual mechanisms underlying social vision, particularly how the brain extracts cues of animacy, interactivity, and mental states from simple moving shapes. They have recently been investigating how the functional configuration of the action observation network dynamically shifts depending on the viewer's explicit task goals. To probe these phenomena, their research combines fMRI with perceptual ratings and language models to map social representations in key brain regions like the superior temporal sulcus (STS). Alongside these core cognitive questions, Dr. Grossman is also advancing neuroimaging methodology by optimizing multivariate pattern classification pipelines for rapid event-related designs and quantitatively evaluating how well standard atlas parcellations capture the highly heterogeneous functional organization of the human STS.

papers.title: Neural Representations of Social Interactivity: A Perceptual and Language Model Analysis
papers.abstract: Uses simple moving-shape animations to ask how the brain represents whether two agents appear to interact. The study compares fMRI response patterns in social-perception regions such as the superior temporal sulcus with perceptual ratings and with descriptions generated by a language model. The aim is to show which cues of interactivity are carried in neural representations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Sajjad Torabian, John A. Pyles, Hongjing Lu, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: A quantitative comparison of atlas parcellations on the human superior temporal sulcus
papers.abstract: The superior temporal sulcus is a functionally heterogeneous region, and researchers often rely on standard atlases in place of individually defined functional localizers. This paper quantitatively compares several published atlas parcellations of the STS against each other and against functional localizer data, to see how well atlases capture the underlying functional organization.
papers.authors: Brandon C. Hackney, John A. Pyles, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: Configuration of the action observation network depends on the goals of the observer
papers.abstract: Examines the network of brain regions engaged when people watch other people act, and tests whether its configuration shifts with the observer's task goals. fMRI data are analysed to show that network organization is not fixed but changes with what the viewer is trying to do.
papers.authors: Xiaojue Zhou, Daniel A. Stehr, John Pyles, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: When shapes are more than shapes: perceptual, developmental, and neurophysiological basis for attributions of animacy and theory of mind
papers.abstract: A review of how Heider-Simmel style animations of simple shapes elicit impressions of animacy and mental states. It covers the developmental shift from goal-directed to mentalistic interpretation of actions and the neural systems that support these attributions.
papers.authors: Sajjad Torabian, Emily D. Grossman

papers.title: Optimizing multivariate pattern classification in rapid event-related designs
papers.abstract: Multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI offers many analytic choices with little guidance from controlled datasets. This methods paper evaluates how those choices affect decoding performance in rapid event-related designs and gives practical recommendations.
papers.authors: Daniel A. Stehr, Javier O. Garcia, John A. Pyles, Emily D. Grossman

0206.name: Eren Günseli
0206.bio: Eren Günseli is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Sabancı University and the director of the Memory, Attention, & Cognitive Control (MACC) Lab. Their research investigates the bidirectional relationship between attention and memory, specifically examining how attentional templates are maintained in working memory and the processes driving the reactivation of long-term memory. Günseli utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) to track contralateral delay activity and alpha oscillations, alongside fMRI and eye-tracking. Their recent work focuses on the neural dissociation between selective attention and storage, as well as the cognitive mechanisms underlying event segmentation in episodic memory.
0206.research_direction: Dr. Günseli has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between working memory, long-term memory, and the structuring of continuous experience into discrete episodes. Using behavioral tasks and EEG markers like contralateral delay activity and alpha suppression, their recent work explores the cognitive mechanisms driving event segmentation, specifically testing whether memory boundaries are formed by prediction errors or by shifts in contextual stability. Additionally, they are examining how cognitive load is shared across memory systems, tracking how familiar or previously studied information is handed off to long-term memory while remaining accessible to attention. Furthermore, their research probes how environmental context binds to memory content, asking whether event transitions or simple task-irrelevant context changes can trigger the reactivation of stored representations back into active working memory.

papers.title: Working Memory Facilitates Event Segmentation Via Boundary-triggered Reactivation and Partial Accumulation during Events
papers.abstract: Using EEG markers of working-memory load (alpha suppression and contralateral delay activity), the study asks whether working memory contents build up gradually during an unfolding event or are reactivated when an event boundary occurs. Alpha suppression increased right after event transitions, supporting a boundary-triggered reactivation account, while evidence for gradual accumulation was mixed. The work links working memory directly to how continuous experience is split into memory episodes.
papers.authors: Berna Güler, Sümeyye Karahamza, Yağmur D. Şentürk, Oded Bein, David Clewett, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Passive but Accessible: Studied Information Is Not Actively Stored in Working Memory, Yet Attended Regardless of Anticipated Load
papers.abstract: Participants held novel or previously studied object-colour associations while EEG tracked contralateral delay activity, with load expectation manipulated across blocks. Studied items evoked a smaller working-memory signal than novel ones regardless of expected load, and were recalled more accurately, indicating they are handed off to long-term memory yet remain accessible to attention. The findings refine how working memory and long-term memory share the load.
papers.authors: Yakup Yılmaz, Nursena Ataseven, Wouter Kruijne, Elkan Akyürek, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Prediction error is out of context: The dominance of contextual stability in structuring episodic memories
papers.abstract: Across four experiments the authors pit prediction-error accounts of event segmentation against a contextual-stability account, measuring temporal order and distance memory. Contextual stability produced stronger segmentation than prediction errors did, and predicted and unpredicted transitions segmented equally well within stable contexts. The results argue that context, not surprise, primarily structures episodic memory.
papers.authors: Berna Güler, Fatih Serin, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Prediction error and event segmentation in episodic memory
papers.abstract: A review of the evidence on whether prediction errors drive the splitting of experience into discrete episodes and shape later memory. It weighs supporting and conflicting findings, considers alternative factors such as context change, and outlines open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Sophie Nolden, Gözem Turan, Berna Güler, Eren Günseli

papers.title: Effects of Context Changes on Memory Reactivation
papers.abstract: Participants saw the same target object across repeated trials, moving it from working memory toward long-term memory, while the background colour changed on half of the repetitions. EEG contralateral delay activity showed that task-irrelevant context changes reactivate the long-term memory in working memory. The authors link this to content-context binding and hippocampal pattern separation.
papers.authors: Şahcan Özdemir, Yağmur Damla Şentürk, Nursima Ünver, Can Demircan, Christian N. L. Olivers, Tobias Egner, Eren Günseli

0207.name: Erez Freud
0207.bio: Erez Freud is an Associate Professor at York University who researches the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying object recognition and the visuomotor control of actions. Utilizing functional MRI, psychophysics, and hand-movement tracking, Freud’s work investigates the functional organization and development of the ventral and dorsal visual pathways. This research program examines how visual representations emerge in childhood, evolve throughout the lifespan, and are affected by brain damage or aging. Freud’s research focuses on the interface between perception and action, specifically regarding how the brain processes three-dimensional structural information.
0207.research_direction: Dr. Freud has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architectures underlying high-level vision and visuomotor control, particularly how vision-for-perception and vision-for-action interact in neurodivergent and aging populations. Using behavioral psychophysics, 3D motion tracking, and classic visual illusions, their recent work explores whether the fundamental dissociation between perceptual size estimation and targeted motor grasping is altered in autistic adults or during healthy aging. They are also testing the clinical utility of these motor behaviors, specifically evaluating whether machine learning classifiers trained on precise grasping kinematics can serve as an accessible diagnostic biomarker for autism. Additionally, Dr. Freud is examining the broader interplay between visual processing and spatial attention, using fMRI to ask how attentional state modulates large-scale shape representations across the dorsal and ventral streams, and utilizing behavioral cueing paradigms to investigate how perceived 3D depth influences attentional allocation in near versus far space.

papers.title: Reduced Dissociation Between Perception and Action in Autistic Individuals
papers.abstract: This work tests whether perceptual differences in autism reflect weaker specialization between vision-for-perception and vision-for-action.
