Using a Ponzo illusion and a stimulus-history manipulation, non-autistic adults showed contextual effects only when estimating size, whereas autistic adults were also affected when grasping. The findings point to a reduced perception-action dissociation in autism.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Zoha Ahmad, Bat-Sheva Hadad, Yarden Mazuz, Tzvi Ganel, Erez Freud

papers.title: Preserved perception-action dissociation but altered visuomotor behaviours in healthy aging
papers.abstract: Younger and older adults completed size estimation and grasping tasks with objects on a Ponzo illusion background or on surfaces of different sizes. The illusion affected perceptual estimates but not grasping in both age groups, so the perception-action dissociation persisted in older age. Grasping kinematics and timing did differ with age, and surface size modulated grasping more strongly in older adults.
papers.authors: Felicia Tassone, Zoha Ahmad, Tzvi Ganel, Erez Freud

papers.title: Effective Autism Classification Through Grasping Kinematics
papers.abstract: The authors asked whether the way autistic adults reach out and grasp an object carries enough information to identify autism. Tracking just two markers on the thumb and index finger, they trained subject-wise cross-validated classifiers that separated autistic from non-autistic young adults with over 84% accuracy and AUCs above 0.95 at the participant level. The results suggest that simple, low-cost motion tracking of grasping could support accessible diagnostic tools.
papers.authors: Erez Freud, Zoha Ahmad, Eyal Shelef, Bat-Sheva Hadad

papers.title: Perceived depth modulates allocation of attention
papers.abstract: Across four Posner-cueing and Egly-Driver experiments, targets appearing on a surface that looks closer were processed more accurately, and cueing effects were smaller there. Attention also shifted more efficiently toward and within the near surface, even after controlling for background and target size. The authors argue that perceived proximity gives near space preferential attentional processing because of its relevance for interaction.
papers.authors: Tasfia Ahsan, Laurie M. Wilcox, Erez Freud

papers.title: The large-scale organization of shape processing in the ventral and dorsal pathways is dissociable from attention
papers.abstract: Two fMRI experiments presented parametrically scrambled novel objects while participants attended either to the object or to another image feature. Univariate and multivariate analyses showed that shape selectivity is organized along both ventral and dorsal pathways regardless of attentional focus. Attention changed shape sensitivity, but similarly in both pathways, indicating shape processing is partly independent of attention.
papers.authors: Yael Goldstein-Marcusohn, Rahaf Asaad, Leen Asaad, Erez Freud

0208.name: Erich Graf
0208.bio: Erich Graf is an Associate Professor in Experimental Psychology at the University of Southampton, where they have been a faculty member since 2004. Graf earned a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley, focusing on how humans integrate sensory inputs with learned priors to construct internal 3D models of the world. Their research utilizes psychophysics, computational modeling, and virtual reality to investigate scene perception, multisensory integration, and the statistical regularities of natural environments. Currently, Graf studies the dynamics of spatial and semantic processing in real-world scenes and the mechanisms of decision-making in complex visual environments.
0208.research_direction: Dr. Graf has recently been working on applied questions at the intersection of psychology and technology. Their recent work explores whether immersive virtual reality can evoke nostalgia more effectively than traditional recall tasks, and what psychological benefits such experiences bring. They have also been examining how large language models, ontologies, and knowledge graphs can be combined in robotic systems to support human-robot collaboration in industry, including guidance for choosing among language-processing and knowledge-representation approaches.

papers.title: Virtual-reality induced nostalgia: duration and psychological benefits
papers.abstract: This study investigated the efficacy of a novel nostalgia induction paradigm utilizing immersive virtual reality (VR). In a series of experiments, the authors compared a newly developed Virtual Reality Task (VRT) against the conventional Event Reflection Task (ERT). Initial validation through psychometric assessments demonstrated that the VR-based environment successfully elicited heightened levels of state nostalgia and associated psychological benefits—such as increased social connectedness and self-esteem—relative to control conditions. Subsequent longitudinal analysis using five repeated measurements at 5-minute intervals revealed that while the ERT-induced effects decayed rapidly, the augmented VRT maintained significantly higher levels of felt nostalgia over time. Although the VRT did not statistically outperform the ERT in the magnitude of immediate psychological benefit, the findings establish VR as a robust and durable medium for inducing complex emotional states in experimental settings.
papers.authors: İrem Yılmaz-Özdemir, Constantine Sedikides, Tim Wildschut, Erich Graf

papers.title: From ontologies to knowledge augmented large language models for automation: a decision-making guidance for achieving human–robot collaboration in Industry 5.0
papers.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 necessitates advanced human-centric cognitive frameworks for industrial automation. This research evaluates the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs), ontologies, and knowledge graphs within robotic systems to facilitate seamless human-robot collaboration (HRC). The authors propose a structured decision-making taxonomy to guide the selection of appropriate Natural Language Processing (NLP) and knowledge representation techniques based on task dependency and environmental complexity. Through a comparative analysis across various industrial use cases, the study demonstrates how LLMs can enhance robotic adaptability and reasoning in dynamic manufacturing environments, while emphasizing the continuing utility of traditional ontologies in resource-constrained or low-dependency sectors. The framework serves as a roadmap for developing resilient, flexible robotic architectures that prioritize human-centric interaction and task generalizability.
papers.authors: John Oyekan, Christopher Turner, Michael Bax, Erich Graf

0209.name: Erik Blaser
0209.bio: Erik Blaser is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston, where they lead the Human Vision Lab and direct the Developmental and Brain Sciences program. Blaser's research utilizes psychophysical and pupillometric methodologies to investigate the mechanisms of visual attention, object tracking in feature-space, and perceptual learning. Their work examines the developmental trajectory of visual cognition, including the study of iconic memory in infants and the underlying mechanisms of enhanced visual search in individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder. This research aims to characterize how the human visual system prioritizes and integrates sensory information to guide behavior and task performance.
0209.research_direction: Dr. Blaser has recently been studying how attention and memory work together to serve everyday goals, in both adults and children. Their recent work explores the trade-off between sampling information from the world and remembering it, and how young children adjust their strategies depending on whether an external aid, such as a device, is reliably available. They have also been investigating how accurately and precisely people remember natural scenes, using continuous walking videos as a measurable stimulus space. Another strand revisits whether mixing up examples of different categories during study really improves learning, using tests designed to remove response bias.

papers.title: Testing the interleaving effect without response bias: A forced-choice reevaluation of Kornell and Bjork (2008)
papers.abstract: In category induction, the canonical interleaving effect demonstrated by Kornell and Bjork (2008) showed that alternating exemplars of target categories during study facilitates superior inductive generalization compared to blocked schedules. However, standard identification protocols that present single test probes inherently confound mnemonic discriminability with criterion shifts and response biases, meaning that observed effect sizes could represent artifacts of decision strategies. To resolve this interpretive challenge, an online direct replication of Kornell and Bjork's Experiment 1A was conducted (N = 288), alongside a critical conceptual replication replacing the identification format with an n-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) design (N = 276) to isolate memory strength free of criterion bias. The 2AFC procedure revealed a robust interleaving benefit (t(275) = 7.19, p < .001, dz = 0.43, 95% CI [0.32, 0.55]) comparable in magnitude to that obtained in the standard identification task. These findings demonstrate that category interleaving advantages reflect genuine mnemonic differences in perceptual classification rather than response bias confounds.
papers.authors: Jamie Donenfeld, Zsuzsa Kaldy, Erik Blaser

papers.title: How attention and working memory work together in the pursuit of goals: The development of the sampling-remembering trade-off
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical investigations into visual working memory and attention have typically constrained participants to maximum-effort paradigms with static, isolated stimuli, leaving unaddressed how cognitive control dynamically manages resources to serve real-world behavioral goals. This theoretical framework advances an ecological, resource-rational approach focused on the sampling-remembering trade-off: the adaptive equilibrium struck between harvesting information from the external visual environment through active sampling (e.g., saccades, head movements) and maintaining representations within internal working memory buffers. Grounded in economic principles of cognitive effort, a dynamic feedback model is proposed in which an individual balances the subjective cost of querying external sources against the metabolic and cognitive load of internal mnemonic storage. The model generates three developmental predictions: (1) individual children seek an equilibrium between perceptual sampling and internal maintenance effort; (2) age-dependent increases in working memory capacity and executive control drive a strategic shift favoring greater internal storage; and (3) older children exhibit enhanced flexibility to re-calibrate trade-offs across shifting task structures.
papers.authors: Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: My Tablet's About to Go Dead! 5- to 6-year-old Children Adjust Their Cognitive Strategies Depending on Whether An External Resource is Reliably Available
papers.abstract: While extensive research highlights adults' propensity to offload cognitive burden onto external artifacts, the impact of external store reliability on young children's strategic trade-offs remains poorly understood. In a preregistered experiment employing a touchscreen 'Shopping Game', 5- to 6-year-old children (N = 37) retrieved target items from a virtual grocery store using a shopping list, where storefront and list could only be inspected alternately via active toggling. The reliability of the external aid was manipulated across conditions: the list remained predictably accessible in the reliable condition, whereas participants were led to believe the list might disappear in the unreliable condition. When the external store was reliable, children exhibited greater offloading, characterized by more frequent visits of shorter dwell time and fewer items retrieved per excursion. When list access was made uncertain, children adapted by expanding study duration and maintaining more items in working memory per visit. Children also identified the reliable condition as easier and reported greater subjective preference for it, demonstrating that preschool-aged children strategically calibrate internal cognitive investment according to external resource reliability.
papers.authors: Yibiao Liang, Zsuzsa Kaldy, Erik Blaser

papers.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Memory for Natural Scenes: A Walk in the Park
papers.abstract: Quantifying the accuracy and precision of natural scene memory has been hampered by the absence of metric stimulus spaces that capture naturalistic image topologies. This study exploited the continuous, metric topology of natural navigation by generating continuous video loops of outdoor 90-meter walking circuits recorded at 6 frames per second, yielding 360 ordered scenes separated by approximately 0.25 meters. In a delayed estimation, continuous report paradigm, participants viewed a target scene extracted from a circuit and localized its position using a 360-frame continuous response wheel. Memory performance was highly accurate and exhibited no systematic directional bias, indicating an absence of net boundary extension or contraction along the route trajectory. Mnemonic precision was systematically structured by environmental similarity: circuits with higher self-similarity—indexed by the spatial half-life of the Multiscale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM) metric—yielded significantly higher recall precision, demonstrating a demand-dependent similarity advantage in visual long-term memory for complex naturalistic spaces.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Leo Westebbe, Yibiao Liang, Erik Blaser

0210.name: Erik Chihhung Chang
0210.bio: Erik Chihhung Chang is an Associate Professor who integrates behavioral experimentation with neuroimaging techniques, such as functional MRI and electroencephalography (EEG), to investigate the relationship between human motor control and higher-order cognition. Chang’s research examines cognitive aging, focusing on how motor skill learning and inhibitory functions change across the lifespan and under the influence of physical exercise. They utilize information theory and machine learning to develop predictive databases for monitoring cognitive decline. Chang also employs task scenarios, such as simulated battlefield environments, to study brain responses in ecologically valid settings.
0210.research_direction: Dr. Chang has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural foundations of action representation, with a major focus on testing the functional equivalence between motor imagery and actual physical execution. To do this without relying on subjective self-reports, their recent work explores stimulus-response binding through objective behavioral assays, such as EMG-monitored repetition-priming paradigms paired with visuospatial working memory manipulations. Beyond motor imagery, they are examining broader mechanisms of motor learning, probing how the brain balances stable statistical learning with adaptive flexibility, and applying information-theoretic metrics like entropy to quantify motor control across different age groups. In a distinct line of behavioral research, their work also delves into spatial cognition, using virtual environments to measure how the availability of large-scale global versus small-scale local object landmarks supports wayfinding and the construction of spatial knowledge.

papers.title: Shared Action Binding and Differential Working Memory Demands Between Motor Imagery and Execution Under Objective Behavioral Verification
papers.abstract: Using a repetition-priming assay with EMG screening to exclude trials with muscle activity, the authors compared how imagined and executed actions bind stimulus and response. Across two experiments, imagery and execution priming were correlated across people and equivalent in size at baseline. Concurrent visuospatial working-memory load hurt imagery-based binding more than execution-based binding, suggesting complementary rather than competing functional-equivalence accounts.
papers.authors: Hsin-Ping Tien, Erik Chihhung Chang

papers.title: When Stability Meets Change: Neural Dissociation of Statistical Learning and Adaptive Flexibility in the Motor Domain
papers.abstract: This 2026 piece addresses how the brain supports both stable statistical learning and flexible adaptation to change in motor tasks, and reports a neural dissociation between the two. Details were not retrievable from the publisher page, so this summary is based on the title and venue only.
papers.authors: Erik Chihhung Chang, Chiao-En Chan, Denise Hsien Wu

papers.title: Differential contributions of global and local object landmarks in human wayfinding behavior
papers.abstract: Participants navigated virtual environments in which either large-scale (global) or small-scale (local) object landmarks were available, and the study measured how each type of landmark supports route finding and the building of spatial knowledge. The results show that global and local landmarks contribute in different ways to wayfinding performance, extending Chang's earlier work on landmark use and sex differences in virtual navigation.
papers.authors: Wen-Jing Lin, Erik Chihhung Chang

papers.title: The Application of Information Theory in Studying Motor Control
papers.abstract: A book chapter that reviews how information-theoretic measures such as entropy and information transfer can quantify motor control and learning across task difficulty and age. It connects to his earlier information-theoretic account of dedifferentiation in aging motor and executive functions.
papers.venue: Cognitive and Neural Foundations of Chinese Reading (Springer)
papers.authors: Hsin-Ping Tien, Erik C. Chang

papers.title: Inequivalent and uncorrelated response priming in motor imagery and execution
papers.abstract: The study tests the functional-equivalence view of motor imagery without relying on self-report, using a response-repetition priming paradigm in which the prime is merely observed, imagined or executed. Imagery and execution both produced repetition benefits, but they were not equivalent in magnitude and were uncorrelated across individuals, an EMG-monitored second experiment confirming this. The work challenges strong equivalence accounts of imagined and executed action.
papers.authors: Hsin-Ping Tien, Erik C. Chang

0213.name: Eva Wiese
0213.department: Institut für Psychologie und Arbeitswissenschaft, Fachgebiet Kognitionspsychologie und kognitive Ergonomie
0213.bio: Wiese is a social neuroscientist and cognitive psychologist whose research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying mind perception and social interaction with artificial agents. Their work employs EEG/ERP, eye-tracking, and computational modeling to study how ascribing intentionality to robots modulates visual attention, working memory, and trust. Wiese currently directs projects exploring the neural correlates of trust in human-AI teaming and the design of robots that trigger human social-cognitive processing.
0213.research_direction: Dr. Wiese has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying social vision in human-robot interactions. Their recent work explores whether artificial faces trigger holistic face-processing machinery—such as the face inversion effect—and tests how this is modulated both by physical facial configurations and top-down beliefs about whether a face belongs to a human or an android. They are also examining how the physical appearance of artificial agents shapes human attributions of mind, such as agency and experience, and whether non-human entities that merely imply a social presence can prompt visuospatial perspective-taking. Furthermore, Dr. Wiese is utilizing EEG methods to quantify implicit trust during human-AI teaming, tracking the N2pc component in shared visual search tasks to measure how individuals divide visuospatial attention and offload cognitive effort onto artificial partners.

papers.title: Measuring trust in artificial intelligence with the N2pc component
papers.abstract: The authors introduce an EEG-based way to directly observe how attention is divided between a person and an AI partner working on the same visual search task. The N2pc component indexes how much attentional effort the human devotes to their own share of the display versus monitoring the AI, giving an implicit readout of how much the person trusts and offloads to the AI. This offers an alternative to self-report trust scales in human-AI teaming.
papers.authors: Eva Wiese, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld

papers.title: Wall-E vs. Terminator: The relationship between physical appearance and dimensions of mind perception
papers.abstract: The study examines how a robot's physical appearance relates to the dimensions of mind that people ascribe to it, such as agency (capacity to act and plan) versus experience (capacity to feel). It compares robots ranging from cute and harmless to menacing and machine-like to see which visual features shift mind attributions. This connects robot design choices to perceived mind and thus to social engagement.
papers.venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans
papers.authors: Yasmina Giebeler, Basil Wahn, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Taken at Face Value: Do Robots Trigger Face-Typical Processing?
papers.abstract: This work asks whether robot faces engage the holistic, specialised face-processing machinery that human faces do, and how this depends on how human-like the face configuration is (number and arrangement of features). Combining behavioural and neural measures, it links robot face design to whether viewers treat robots as social partners. The findings inform the design of robots whose faces trigger social cognition.
papers.authors: Ali Momen, Tobias Feldmann-Wüstefeld, Kurt Hugenberg, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Humans take the visuospatial perspective of robots and objects that imply social presence
papers.abstract: Visual perspective-taking has mainly been studied with human-like agents. Here the authors isolate social presence from human-like appearance and test whether robots or objects that merely imply a social presence lead people to adopt their visuospatial viewpoint. Participants did take these entities' perspectives, suggesting social presence alone can be sufficient to trigger perspective-taking.
papers.authors: Basil Wahn, Eva Wiese

papers.title: Social perception of robots is shaped by beliefs about their minds
papers.abstract: Across experiments, the authors test whether believing a face belongs to an android robot rather than a real person changes how it is processed. Face-typical processing, such as the disadvantage for inverted faces in recognition, was reduced when perceivers believed the faces were robots, even though the images were identical. The results show that higher-order beliefs about mind, not just physical appearance, determine whether social-cognitive face mechanisms are engaged, with implications for robot and deepfake design.
papers.authors: Ali Momen, Kurt Hugenberg, Eva Wiese

0215.name: Fabian Soto
0215.bio: Fabian A. Soto is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Florida International University and director of the Computational Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Soto’s research examines the neural and computational mechanisms of learning and generalization, specifically focusing on how categorization training and visual representations influence one another. Through the integration of behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and EEG, Soto tests theories concerning object and face perception. Their work employs multidimensional signal detection theory and General Recognition Theory to investigate the independence of stimulus dimensions and the origins of perception biases.
0215.research_direction: Dr. Soto has recently been investigating the perceptual and neural mechanisms of face recognition, specifically exploring how facial shape and motion interact during the processing of identity and expression. Their recent work uses fMRI cross-decoding and reverse correlation with 3D synthetic dynamic faces to map how expectations of facial motion are derived from structural features, and to test whether face-selective brain networks utilize invariant or context-specific representations. Beyond high-level vision, they are also exploring metacognition in semantic memory by applying multidimensional signal detection models, such as general recognition theory, to measure how tip-of-the-tongue and feeling-of-knowing states influence metacognitive sensitivity. Additionally, their broad scholarship in cognitive modeling includes evaluating the historical impact and computational legacy of general-process associative learning frameworks like the Rescorla-Wagner model.

papers.title: Motion-from-structure in face perception: expectations of natural face motion depend on face shape
papers.abstract: Because the anatomy that makes a face unique also shapes how it moves during expression, the visual system could plausibly predict facial motion from facial shape. Using reverse correlation with synthetic dynamic faces whose shape or motion varied randomly, the authors estimated what expression speeds people expect and how that depends on identity. Expectations of natural motion were modulated by face shape, while the shape features used to recognize identity stayed stable across motion contexts, which the authors interpret as a form of motion-from-structure within an independent-pathways framework.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Raphael Tordjman, Emily Renae Martin, Fabian Aurelio Soto

papers.title: Invariant versus context-specific representation of face shape and motion in the face network
papers.abstract: Face-selective brain regions may prefer one kind of information (shape) yet still be modulated by another (motion). Using fMRI with videos of 3D synthetic faces in which shape and motion were manipulated independently, the study combined cross-decoding with context-sensitivity tests. Shape and motion were both decodable across face-selective areas, with distinct invariance patterns in OFA, FFA and IFG that challenge strict separate-pathway models and show that confounded motion types can inflate invariance estimates.
papers.authors: S. Sanaz Hosseini, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Shape information used for face identity and expression recognition is highly versatile and context specific
papers.abstract: Using reverse correlation in an anatomically interpretable 3D face shape space, participants chose the face closest to a target identity or expression, letting the authors recover templates of the features used for recognition. Recognition depended on subtle shape changes distributed across the face, and the templates shifted with context: expression changed the representation of identity, and identity changed the representation of expression.
papers.authors: Emily Renae Martin, Jason S. Hays, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Tip-of-the-Tongue and Feeling-of-Knowing Experiences Enhance Metacognitive Sensitivity of Confidence Evaluation of Semantic Memory
papers.abstract: Applying general recognition theory, a multidimensional extension of signal detection theory, the authors asked whether tip-of-the-tongue states and feeling-of-knowing judgments change how well confidence tracks memory accuracy. In two recall-then-recognition experiments (famous names and general knowledge), stronger TOT or FOK experiences were associated with higher metacognitive sensitivity of confidence. This is presented as the first evidence linking these states to metacognitive sensitivity.
papers.authors: Ali Pournaghdali, Bennett L. Schwartz, Fabian A. Soto

papers.title: Why is the Rescorla-Wagner model so influential?
papers.abstract: The Rescorla-Wagner model has shaped cognitive and neural science even though it is computationally close to earlier models and its shortcomings are well known. The authors argue that its reach comes from the learning field's sustained search for general-process theories, and review its theoretical and empirical background, its links to later developments across Marr's levels of analysis, and the breadth of research it has guided.
papers.authors: Fabian A. Soto, Edgar H. Vogel, Yerco E. Uribe-Bahamonde, Omar D. Perez

0216.name: Fang Fang
0216.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0216.lab_name: Lab of Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience
0216.bio: Fang is a Professor of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and Vice President at Peking University, where they also serve as a Principal Investigator at the IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and consciousness by integrating high-resolution fMRI, psychophysics, and transcranial electrical stimulation. Fang’s work includes the study of visual perceptual learning, cortical plasticity, and the representation of objects and faces in the human visual cortex. Their current research directions involve investigating neural prediction errors in visual reasoning and the role of subcortical nuclei in feature-based attentional control.
0216.research_direction: Dr. Fang’s recent work explores the neural dynamics of perception, memory, and language using a diverse toolkit that includes EEG, intracranial recordings, neuromodulation, and computational modeling. In the visual domain, they have recently been investigating how targeted rhythmic light stimulation modulates wakeful consolidation and plasticity in early visual cortex, and how the visual system stores and replays temporal motion sequences following passive exposure. Their research also examines rapid affective processing, utilizing intracranial recordings to probe the subcortical mechanisms by which the human amygdala detects invisible, backward-masked fearful faces. Furthermore, they are investigating the temporal and structural architecture of language, testing how auditory cortical alpha rhythms dictate speed limits for speech comprehension and using novel frequency-tagging paradigms to compare syntactic representations between the human brain and large language models.

papers.title: Alpha rhythms in the left auditory cortex set the speed limit for speech comprehension
papers.abstract: The study asks why speech comprehension breaks down once speech exceeds roughly ten syllables per second. Combining psychophysics, EEG, tACS, repetitive sensory stimulation and intracranial sEEG, it shows that each listener's individual alpha frequency predicts their maximum comprehensible speech rate, and that shifting alpha activity in left auditory cortex shifts that limit. Alpha rhythms are thus identified as a causal neural bottleneck on temporal processing in speech.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Yayue Gao, Jianing Fan, Na Xu, Libo Zhao, Lifang Deng, Ruolin Yang, Luyao Chen, Zhiwei Jing, Tingting Huang, Xiongfei Wang, Jing Wang, Pengfei Teng, Peng Cai, Guoming Luan, Yi Du, Qian Wang, Fang Fang

papers.title: Frequency-dependent photic modulation of wakeful consolidation in visual learning
papers.abstract: After training on orientation discrimination, participants viewed flickering gratings at different temporal frequencies during a wakeful rest period. 10-Hz stimulation improved later performance while 1-Hz stimulation impaired it, and the effects required patterned gratings and prior training. EEG and MR spectroscopy linked the benefit to a larger N1 and a higher glutamate/GABA ratio in early visual cortex, pointing to LTP-like plasticity and offering a non-invasive light-based way to modulate consolidation.
papers.authors: Xin-Yue Yang, Chuyue Zhao, Zhentao Zuo, Aming Li, Huan Luo, Qing He, Fang Fang

papers.title: Non-feature-specific elevated responses and feature-specific backward replay in human brain induced by visual sequence exposure
papers.abstract: Participants were briefly exposed to a fixed sequence of four motion directions and then shown the first or last direction as a cue. Cue-evoked brain activity showed a non-feature-specific elevated response together with feature-specific replay of the sequence in backward order. The results describe how the human visual system stores and reactivates temporal sequence information after passive experience.
papers.authors: Tao He, Xizi Gong, Qian Wang, Xinyi Zhu, Yunzhe Liu, Fang Fang

papers.title: Hierarchical Frequency Tagging Probe (HFTP): A Unified Approach to Investigate Syntactic Structure Representations in Large Language Models and the Human Brain
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a frequency-tagging method that probes syntactic structure at several hierarchical levels, applied both to single units of large language models (GPT-2, Llama, Gemma) and to human brain recordings. Different LLMs process syntax in similar layers, while the human brain uses distinct regions for different syntactic levels, with stronger alignment to left-hemisphere language areas. Newer model versions do not consistently align better with the brain.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Jingmin An, Yilong Song, Ruolin Yang, Nai Ding, Lingxi Lu, Yuxuan Wang, Wei Wang, Chu Zhuang, Qian Wang, Fang Fang

papers.title: Rapid Processing of Invisible Fearful Faces in the Human Amygdala
papers.abstract: Using intracranial EEG recorded in human amygdala, the authors presented fearful, happy and neutral faces rendered invisible by backward masking. Fearful faces preferentially evoked a very short-latency response beginning about 88 ms after onset, selective for low spatial frequencies. The findings offer direct human electrophysiological evidence for a fast subcortical route that processes threat without awareness.
papers.authors: Yingying Wang, Lu Luo, Guanpeng Chen, Guoming Luan, Xiongfei Wang, Qian Wang, Fang Fang

0217.name: Faran Sabeti
0217.department: Discipline of Optometry, Faculty of Health
0217.bio: Faran Sabeti is an Associate Professor of Optometry and Vision Science at the University of Canberra. Sabeti’s research focuses on developing objective functional tests for the early detection of retinal and neurological diseases. They specialize in multifocal pupillographic objective perimetry (mfPOP), employing this technology to identify physiological biomarkers in conditions such as diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration, and multiple sclerosis. Sabeti’s work explores the integration of subjective and objective perimetric measures to characterize neural damage and investigates interventions, including stochastic resonance and ocular therapeutics, to alter visual function.
0217.research_direction: Dr. Sabeti has recently been working on measuring how well the retina and visual pathway function in people with eye disease, especially diabetes. Their recent work compares objective tests that use pupil responses to light with standard visual field tests for spotting early or progressing damage from diabetic retinopathy and macular oedema. They have also run a clinical trial of how eye drops containing levodopa, a dopamine precursor, affect retinal function in healthy young adults, motivated by links between retinal dopamine and myopia. A separate strand examines how understandable and actionable online patient education about diabetic retinopathy is for Indigenous and general audiences.

papers.title: Understandability and actionability of patient education materials for diabetic retinopathy among indigenous and general populations
papers.abstract: This study evaluated the quality, readability, understandability, and actionability of online patient education materials (PEMs) addressing diabetic retinopathy (DR), contrasting resources tailored for Indigenous Australian populations against those designed for the broader community. A systematic search identified 540 educational resources, of which 54 met the predetermined inclusion criteria across printable and audiovisual modalities. Evaluated via the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT), Indigenous-targeted PEMs attained superior mean understandability scores (80%) compared to general population materials (75%). However, actionability scores were uniformly compromised across all formats: printable resources achieved mean actionability scores of 42% for the general cohort and 53% for Indigenous resources, whereas audiovisual formats demonstrated marked deficits at 29%. These data indicate that while current DR patient education resources generally communicate disease concepts comprehensibly, they substantially lack structured, stepwise instructions necessary to guide self-management and adherence to sight-preserving interventions.
papers.authors: Kam Chun Ho, Falicia Tay, Caitlin Quan, Faran Sabeti

papers.title: Retinal Function in Young Adults Following Topical Application of Levodopa to the Eye
papers.abstract: Dysregulation of the retinal dopaminergic system has been implicated in ocular pathologies including myopia. This randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled phase I clinical trial assessed whether localized topical administration of levodopa/carbidopa drops alters human retinal structure or functional topography. Twenty-nine healthy male volunteers aged 18 to 30 years received daily unilateral administration of either a low dose (1.4 μmol levodopa / 0.34 μmol carbidopa per day, n = 14) or high dose (2.7 μmol levodopa / 0.68 μmol carbidopa per day, n = 15) for 28 days, while the contralateral eye received vehicle placebo. Testing at baseline, cessation of treatment (4 weeks), and 4 months post-treatment included high- and low-contrast visual acuity, 44-zone Matrix frequency-doubling perimetry, regional multifocal electroretinography (mfERG), and optical coherence tomography (OCT) macular thickness maps, complemented by rabbit pharmacokinetic analysis. A minor, statistically significant increase in mfERG ring 5 response amplitude and localized macular thinning appeared in low-dose eyes (p < 0.05), but these remained within physiologic limits and lacked clinical relevance; no significant perturbations occurred in high-dose eyes. Pharmacokinetics demonstrated rapid clearance within 4 hours without systemic blood accumulation, verifying the safety and retinal tolerability of topical levodopa/carbidopa formulations.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Kate Thomson, Ted Maddess, Cindy Karouta, Myra Leung, Nicola Anstice, Tina Jong, Regan Ashby

papers.title: Discriminating early-stage diabetic retinopathy with subjective and objective perimetry
papers.abstract: To establish sensitive functional biomarkers capable of resolving subclinical neuroretinal impairment prior to manifest microvascular pathology, this cross-sectional study compared multifocal pupillographic objective perimetry (mfPOP) with conventional subjective automated perimetry (SAP) in type 2 diabetes mellitus (PwT2D). Subjects classified with either no diabetic retinopathy (noDR) or mild-to-moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (mmDR) underwent bilateral testing using two mfPOP configurations—the macular OFA15 (±15°) and wide-field OFA30 (±30°) variants—alongside 24-2 Matrix frequency-doubling technology and 24-2 Short-Wavelength Automated Perimetry (SWAP). Five out of eight mfPOP global indices (mean defects and pattern standard deviations) successfully discriminated noDR from mmDR eyes (p ≤ 0.02), whereas none of the corresponding SAP metrics revealed statistically significant separation. Region-specific mfPOP mapping highlighted significant peripheral hypersensitivity and response delays in mmDR, with localized distribution excluding generalized autonomic pupillary neuropathy. Discriminative power reached high diagnostic utility (AUROCs up to 0.86), confirming that mfPOP-derived response latencies and amplitude deviations serve as robust surrogate endpoints for identifying early diabetic retinal neurodegeneration.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Joshua P. van Kleef, Rakesh M. Iyer, Corinne F. Carle, Christopher J. Nolan, Rong Hui Chia, Ted Maddess

papers.title: Objective perimetry identifies regional functional progression and recovery in mild Diabetic Macular Oedema
papers.abstract: This prospective longitudinal investigation monitored neuroretinal structural and functional dynamics over a 27-month period in type 2 diabetic patients presenting with mild, non-central-involving diabetic macular oedema (DMO) versus non-DMO diabetic controls. Sixteen participants (32 eyes; 10 presenting with baseline DMO) underwent longitudinal evaluation producing 94 visits, which included Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) grading, posterior-pole optical coherence tomography (OCT; 64-region grid), 10–2 Matrix subjective perimetry, and objectiveFIELD Analyser (OFA) mfPOP 30° and 60° paradigms assessing per-region sensitivity and response latency. Structural and functional metrics were mapped to an identical 44-region topographic layout. Eyes with baseline DMO showed significant mean central thickness reduction from 237 ± 25 μm to 234.2 ± 26.7 μm (p < 0.05), which correlated with localized functional recovery toward normative OFA sensitivities and latency profiles (all p < 0.021), whereas non-DMO eyes demonstrated progressive structural thickening from 250.7 ± 24.4 μm to 255.7 ± 20.6 μm (p < 0.05). Matrix perimetry detected significant longitudinal changes in only sparse regions restricted to the central 8°, whereas mfPOP revealed comprehensive regional progression and recovery across wide visual fields, underscoring its utility as an objective functional monitor of DMO progression.
papers.authors: Faran Sabeti, Bhim B. Rai, Josh P. van Kleef, Emilie M. F. Rohan, Corinne F. Carle, Richard C. Barry, Rohan W. Essex, Christopher J. Nolan, Ted Maddess

0218.name: Felix Franke
0218.institution: Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel
0218.department: Faculty of Science, University of Basel; Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering, ETH Zurich
0218.bio: Franke is an Assistant Professor at the University of Basel and leads the Quantitative Visual Physiology Group at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel, with a continuing affiliation at ETH Zurich. Franke's research focuses on the computational principles of retinal processing, specifically investigating how distinct retinal ganglion cell types encode visual information to support oculomotor feedback loops and the optokinetic reflex. Utilizing high-density microelectrode arrays and signal processing, they develop phenomenological and digital twin models of retinal circuitry to explain how the visual system stabilizes images and synchronizes signal arrival times across varying axonal lengths. This work combines computational neuroscience and experimental physiology to study the position-dependent nature of retinal computation and the functional properties of the human fovea.
0218.research_direction: Dr. Franke's recent work explores how the early visual system processes spatial and temporal information to guide perception and behavior in mice and humans. They have recently been using a combination of high-density microelectrode arrays, eye tracking, and computational modeling to investigate phenomena such as the temporal synchronization of foveal cone signals across varying retinal axon lengths and the role of ambiguous local edge motion in reflexive gaze stabilization. To accelerate these physiological studies, their team is developing novel dynamic stimuli and reverse correlation techniques for the rapid mapping of receptive fields across large neural populations. Beyond fundamental visual neuroscience, they are also advancing recording hardware by designing CMOS microelectrode-array chips that embed cryptographic signatures directly into the sensing pipeline to guarantee the origin and integrity of electrophysiological data.

papers.title: In-sensor cryptographic signature generation to link a physical process and an immutable digital entity
papers.abstract: The paper describes a CMOS microelectrode-array sensor chip that embeds a cryptographic signature step directly into the measurement pipeline. Data leaving the chip are therefore cryptographically bound to the physical recording that produced them, allowing later verification of origin and integrity. The approach is demonstrated on electrophysiological recordings and aimed at trustworthy, tamper-evident scientific and biomedical data.
papers.authors: Fernando Cardes, Sebastian Bürgel, Xinyue Yuan, Qianchen Yu, Arianna Rubino, Jihyun Lee, Raziyeh Bounik, Vijay Viswam, Andreas Hierlemann, Felix Franke

papers.title: Mice and humans use ambiguous local motion to stabilize gaze
papers.abstract: Local edge motion seen through small receptive fields is ambiguous about global object motion. The study traces motion signals from the retina through the nucleus of the optic tract to eye movements, using retinal and in vivo electrophysiology, modelling and eye tracking in mice and humans. Stimuli that dissociate local from global motion show that reflexive gaze stabilization is driven directly by ambiguous local motion signals rather than a resolved global estimate.
papers.authors: Federica B. Rosselli, Marc Büttner, Annalisa Bucci, Felix Franke

papers.title: Rapid estimation of receptive fields across stages of the early visual system
papers.abstract: Mapping receptive fields in large populations is slow when informative stimuli evoke few spikes in feature-selective neurons. The authors introduce reverse correlation against stimulus elements (RCASE) together with a random-moving-objects stimulus that engages neurons broadly across the early visual pathway. Compared with conventional spike-triggered methods, it yields interpretable receptive-field estimates in far shorter recording times.
papers.authors: Marc Büttner, Matej Znidaric, Roland Diggelmann, Federica B. Rosselli, Annalisa Bucci, Andreas Hierlemann, Felix Franke

papers.title: Synchronization of visual perception within the human fovea
papers.abstract: Foveal cones sit at very different distances from the optic disc, so their signals travel along retinal ganglion cell axons of very different lengths. The authors combined single-cone stimulation with behavioural reaction-time measurements, high-density microelectrode recordings from human retina and modelling. They show that axonal conduction speeds scale with axon length so that foveal signals arrive at the optic nerve head at about the same time, meaning temporal synchronization of visual perception is already set up in the retina.
papers.authors: Annalisa Bucci, Marc Büttner, Niklas Domdei, Federica B. Rosselli, Matej Znidaric, Julian Bartram, Tobias Gänswein, Roland Diggelmann, Martina De Gennaro, Cameron S. Cowan, Wolf Harmening, Andreas Hierlemann, Botond Roska, Felix Franke

0219.name: Filip Děchtěrenko
0219.institution: Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences
0219.bio: Filip Děchtěrenko is the head of the Department of Cognitive Psychology at the Institute of Psychology of the Czech Academy of Sciences. Their research investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying visual memory, attention, and perception, focusing on how humans process and retain information from complex natural scenes. Děchtěrenko utilizes a methodology combining behavioral experiments and eye-tracking with computational techniques, such as convolutional neural networks, to model image similarity and predict recognition performance. Their recent work explores the role of typicality in visual recognition and the limits of detail retention in visual long-term memory.
0219.research_direction: Dr. Děchtěrenko has recently been studying how much visual detail people can actually remember, and who remembers it best. Their recent work asks whether intensive study of a small set of complex scenes leads to accurate memory for fine details, and compares art students with laypeople on recognition and on drawing images from memory. They also examine whether a fast visual matching card game can serve as a measure of cognitive or perceptual ability, and have collaborated on work relating ADHD symptoms to planning, coping, and time perspective in daily life.

papers.title: The card game Dobble as a diagnostic tool
papers.abstract: Examines whether performance on the Dobble card game, a fast visual matching task, can serve as a diagnostic measure of cognitive or perceptual abilities.
papers.authors: Anežka Šolcová, Filip Děchtěrenko

papers.title: Low detail retention in visual memory despite focused effort
papers.abstract: The research investigated whether intensive encoding of a restricted number of complex scenes could mitigate the limitations typically observed in high-fidelity recognition for visual details. The authors implemented a novel experimental design incorporating repeated memory probes for specific image segments to track mnemonic decay and long-term retention. Results indicated that despite high intentional focus and extended study time, participants failed to achieve high-accuracy detail-oriented memory. While observers reliably identified presented content and novel foils, they exhibited a pronounced failure to reject distractors sampled from unseen parts of previously studied photographs, suggesting that visual long-term memory representations for scenes lack sufficient granularity to exclude semantically and perceptually similar distractors.
papers.authors: Filip Děchtěrenko, Jiří Lukavský, Petr Adámek

papers.title: Visual free recall and recognition in art students and laypeople
papers.abstract: This study compared the visual memory capacities of art students and laypeople through a combination of surprise drawing tasks and recognition tests. While recognition memory performance was comparable across both groups, art students demonstrated significantly superior visual free recall. Analysis of memory-based drawings revealed that artists produced higher-quality representations with greater fidelity to the original spatial and object information. At the individual level, the quality of a participant's drawing was a significant predictor of their recognition accuracy, indicating that artistic expertise facilitates the encoding and subsequent retrieval of detailed visual representations from long-term memory.
papers.authors: Filip Děchtěrenko, Wilma A. Bainbridge, Jiří Lukavský

papers.title: Dopad ADHD na plánování, coping a časovou perspektivu v každodenním životě jedince
papers.abstract: Czech-language study of how ADHD symptoms relate to planning, coping and time perspective in everyday life. Off-topic for vision science, and the Crossref record lists a blank first author plus four named authors, with Děchtěrenko last.
papers.authors: Irena Smetáčková, Radek Ptáček, Martina Vňuková, Filip Děchtěrenko

0220.name: Frank Bremmer
0220.bio: Bremmer investigates the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory spatial and motion perception, focusing on how visual processing is modulated by eye movements such as saccades. Their work integrates single-cell recordings and EEG in animal models with fMRI, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling in humans to decode the integration of visual, tactile, and vestibular signals. A focus of this research involves characterizing the neural dynamics of perisaccadic perception and self-motion (heading) encoding in the primate brain. Bremmer also collaborates on clinical studies to investigate disturbances in motion processing and balance control in patients with neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease.
0220.research_direction: Dr. Bremmer has recently been investigating how the primate brain integrates visual and motor signals to represent space and guide behavior, particularly using electrophysiological recordings in macaque parietal areas to probe how neurons encode egocentric 3D distance and differentiate between voluntary saccades and reflexive eye movements. Their recent work also explores human self-motion perception, testing how active oculomotor signals shape path integration and distance estimation from optic flow. Additionally, they are investigating the network dynamics underlying early visual processing by combining marmoset primary visual cortex recordings with thalamocortical computational models to uncover the cellular basis of alpha-band perceptual echoes. Broadening their methodological scope, their research extends into clinical neuroengineering, where they apply convolutional neural networks to posturography data to identify time-frequency signatures of postural instability in Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Path integration from optic flow and the role of eye movements
papers.abstract: Optic flow supports perception of heading, speed and travelled distance, but most human path-integration experiments enforce central fixation. This study compared distance discrimination from optic flow under fixation versus free eye movements to test whether oculomotor signals help estimate distance travelled. It examines how eye movements shape self-motion-based distance perception.
papers.authors: Renate Reisenegger, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: The representation of voluntary and reflexive fast eye movements in the macaque lateral intraparietal area
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether area LIP acts as a general oculomotor controller by comparing neuronal activity around voluntary saccades and reflexive fast phases of optokinetic nystagmus. Neurons with strong peri-saccadic responses were not modulated around OKN fast phases, and local field potentials pointed to distinct network processing. The same neurons still encoded gaze position and motion direction, suggesting higher-level integration for goal-directed actions.
papers.authors: Sadra Fathkhani, Bahareh Taghizadeh-Sarshouri, Andre Kaminiarz, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Thalamocortical network dynamics can explain visual impulse responses and perceptual echoes
papers.abstract: Human EEG shows an alpha-band component in the visual impulse response (the perceptual echo), but its cellular basis was unknown. Recording marmoset V1 during broadband flicker, the authors found a non-oscillatory, low-frequency-dominated impulse response with sparse stimulus-locked spiking. An established thalamocortical network model explained this, and reducing damping reproduced the oscillatory human response, implicating thalamocortical alpha resonance in perceptual echoes.
papers.authors: Jakob C.B. Schwenk, Maureen A. Hagan, Shaun L. Cloherty, Elizabeth Zavitz, Adam P. Morris, Nicholas S.C. Price, Marcello G.P. Rosa, Andrea Alamia, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Coding of egocentric distance in the macaque ventral intraparietal area
papers.abstract: Eye movements shift the retinal image, which complicates the brain's representation of 3D space. The authors recorded from macaque area VIP while animals fixated at three vergence distances and viewed stimuli at seven disparities, asking whether neurons encode distance in an eye-position-invariant (egocentric) way. Single neurons were modulated by both disparity and vergence without the expected shift of tuning curves, yet population activity allowed egocentric distance to be decoded, supporting a role for VIP in 3D space coding.
papers.authors: Baptiste Caziot, Sadra Fathkhani, Frank Bremmer

papers.title: Sway frequencies may predict postural instability in Parkinson's disease: a novel convolutional neural network approach
papers.abstract: The authors trained a convolutional neural network on spectrogram images of body sway to separate people with early to mid-stage Parkinson's disease from age-matched healthy controls. The hypothesis was that time-frequency content of sway carries diagnostic information about postural instability. The work shows deep learning on posturography can objectively flag balance impairment.
papers.authors: David Engel, R. Stefan Greulich, Alberto Parola, Kaleb Vinehout, Justus Student, Josefine Waldthaler, Lars Timmermann, Frank Bremmer

0221.name: Frank H. Durgin
0221.bio: Frank H. Durgin is the Elizabeth and Sumner Hayward Professor of Psychology and social sciences at Swarthmore College, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying human spatial representation and figurative language. Durgin's research focuses on systematic distortions in the perception of locomotor space and slant, employing high-fidelity virtual reality and perceptuo-motor calibration tasks to study how the visual system optimizes information for action. Additionally, Durgin utilizes psycholinguistic methods, including eye-tracking and event-related potentials (ERPs), to explore the cognitive processing of metaphors and their role in implicit bias. Their work provides evidence for coding strategies that prioritize functional efficiency over geometric accuracy, which challenges theories of embodied perception.
0221.research_direction: Dr. Durgin’s recent work explores a diverse range of topics spanning visual psychophysics, spatial perception, and cognitive linguistics. In the visual domain, they have recently been investigating the perceptual primitives underlying visual numerosity, using adaptation paradigms and novel stimulus-generation methods to test whether number perception is fundamentally derived from texture density. Their recent vision research also examines how figure-ground segmentation drives subset numerosity illusions, and utilizes postural manipulations in stereoscopic virtual reality to probe the default reference frames governing angular expansion in 3D visual direction. Finally, in a distinct line of cognitive research, they are investigating the affective dimensions of language by using semantic-differential ratings to assess the emotional and dynamic profiles of figurative versus literal text.

papers.title: Density is a precursor in the perception of visual numerosity: Evidence from adaptation
papers.abstract: A preregistered study of 60 observers adapted people to dense or sparse patches of different sizes, then measured perceived density, number and size of a test patch with comparison stimuli that varied on all three dimensions. Aftereffects on perceived numerosity were tracked by density changes and not by an independent number signal. The results answer a recent claim that numerosity adaptation cannot be explained by density and support density as the primitive underlying number perception.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Frank H. Durgin, Abigail M. A. Love, G. Taylor, Alexander C. Huk

papers.title: Texture density discrimination is more precise than numerosity discrimination
papers.abstract: The authors argue earlier comparisons of density and number precision were confounded because true stimulus density was mis-specified when patch area was idealized. Using a new stimulus-generation method that fixes density independently of patch size and number, they find density judgments are more precise than number judgments, including at low numerosities. This supports density as a basic visual feature from which number is derived.
papers.authors: Frank H. Durgin, Nichole Suero Gonzalez, Ping Wen, Alexander C. Huk

papers.title: Change blindness, subset segmentation, and the perceptual underestimation of subset numerosity
papers.abstract: Six experiments test whether the impression that white dots are fewer than gray ones, when both are intermixed on a medium-gray background, arises from figure-ground segmentation by color similarity. Incomplete segmentation leads to underestimation of the foregrounded subset, and subset matching turns out to be most accurate for sets that are hard to segment. The work links a numerosity illusion to general principles of perceptual organization.
papers.authors: Katelyn Becker, Eliana Dellinger, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: Figurative language is (implicitly) more dynamic and emotionally deeper than literal language
papers.abstract: Two experiments used semantic-differential ratings analyzed with principal component analysis to compare the emotional profile of metaphoric stories and figuratively used words with literal counterparts. Figurative wording differed reliably from literal wording along three data-defined dimensions, including greater dynamism and emotional depth. The finding suggests metaphor carries distinctive affective content beyond its literal meaning.
papers.authors: Tshering Yanzom Dorji, Frank H. Durgin

papers.title: Default reference frames for angular expansion in the perception of visual direction
papers.abstract: Perceived elevation relative to a visible horizon is normally exaggerated by about 1.5. Five experiments, most with observers lying supine in a wide-field stereoscopic virtual environment so no gravitational reference was available, asked whether the exaggeration persists. It did, suggesting exaggerated angular scaling is a default property of 3D visual direction perception.
papers.authors: Prince U. D. Tardeh, Crystal Xu, Frank H. Durgin

0222.name: Frank Tong
0222.bio: Frank Tong investigates the neural foundations of visual perception, attentional selection, and object recognition using high-resolution 7-Tesla fMRI, visual psychophysics, and computational modeling. Tong applied multivariate pattern classification to decode subjective mental states and the contents of visual working memory from early cortical activity. Their research examines how early visual areas contribute to conscious awareness and the maintenance of information in the absence of physical stimuli. Currently, Tong compares biological perception with convolutional neural networks to model visual processing and robustness.
0222.research_direction: Dr. Tong has recently been investigating how realistic, ecological viewing conditions shape human visual processing and object recognition. Much of their recent work explores whether training deep neural networks under naturalistic constraints—such as exposure to progressive blur, visual noise, and occlusion—can yield computational models that are more robust and better aligned with human visual cortex and behavior. In tandem with these modeling efforts, they are examining the mechanisms of category-specific perceptual learning to understand how humans and artificial networks improve at recognizing degraded visual inputs. Furthermore, Dr. Tong uses fMRI to probe the underlying functional organization of the human ventral visual cortex, specifically testing whether high-level categorical divisions like animacy might be driven by mid-level shape properties such as spikiness.

papers.title: Ecological Vision Hypothesis: Training Deep Neural Networks for Robustness and Human Alignment
papers.abstract: A review that argues human vision is shaped by the ecological conditions of development and everyday viewing, such as blur, noise, and occlusion. It surveys work showing that deep networks trained under these more realistic conditions become more robust and more human-aligned, and lays out the hypothesis and open questions for using such training to build better models of biological vision.
papers.authors: Frank Tong, Hojin Jang

papers.title: Exposure to naturalistic occlusion promotes generalized, human-like robustness in deep neural networks
papers.abstract: The preprint examines whether training deep networks on images with naturalistic occluders helps them recognize partially hidden objects in a human-like way. Networks exposed to realistic occlusion generalize better to novel occlusion types and behave more like human observers than networks trained conventionally.
papers.authors: David D Coggan, Frank Tong

papers.title: Category-specific perceptual learning of robust object recognition modelled using deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Humans improve at recognizing degraded objects with training, and this study asks how that learning is specific to object categories. Deep network models trained on noisy images from particular categories are compared with human learners, revealing patterns of within-category learning and limited transfer that the models capture. The work links perceptual learning to the robustness of object recognition in networks.
papers.authors: Hojin Jang, Frank Tong

papers.title: Improved modeling of human vision by incorporating robustness to blur in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors train convolutional networks on images that progress from blurry to sharp, loosely mimicking early visual development. The resulting models become much more robust to noise and blur and show a stronger bias toward shape over texture. Their internal representations also align better with human behavior and with human visual cortex than standard networks do.
papers.authors: Hojin Jang, Frank Tong

papers.title: Spikiness and animacy as potential organizing principles of human ventral visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study tests whether the animate-inanimate organization of ventral temporal cortex can be explained by a simpler visual property, how spiky versus stubby an object's shape is. It compares the contributions of spikiness and animacy to cortical responses and network-model features, and argues that both are candidate organizing dimensions of category selectivity.
papers.authors: David D Coggan, Frank Tong

0224.name: Freek van Ede
0224.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
0224.bio: Freek van Ede is an Associate Professor at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and the Principal Investigator of the Proactive Brain Lab. Van Ede's research investigates how the human brain selectively prioritizes and retains sensory information in working memory to guide prospective goal-directed behavior. Utilizing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), high-resolution eye-tracking—specifically microsaccadic analysis—and virtual reality, they explore the neural dynamics of internal attention and anticipation. Their work focuses on the functional links between mnemonic representations, motor planning, and temporal expectations within a proactive perspective of cognition.
0224.research_direction: Dr. van Ede's recent work explores the continuous interplay between visual working memory, spatial attention, and oculomotor behavior. They have recently been investigating how selective attention operates on internal memory representations to guide future behavior, and whether the human brain can concurrently prioritize these internal cognitive goals while searching for external sensory targets. Using gaze biases as an implicit readout of cognition, their research examines how working memory utilizes spatial scaffolding, probing whether stored representations are anchored to their past encoding locations, their future test locations, or a flexible combination of spatial features like distance and direction. Additionally, Dr. van Ede interrogates the mechanistic link between covert attention and miniature eye movements, using EEG and eye-tracking to ask whether fixational microsaccades directly drive well-known neural markers of spatial attention like the N2pc component.

papers.title: Sparse spatial scaffolding for visual working memory
papers.abstract: Space helps keep separate memories individuated, but its format is unclear. Participants remembered items at varying directions and distances, and gaze biases during memory selection served as an implicit read-out. The results show a flexible, minimal spatial scaffold: distance is dropped when direction alone separates the items and used only when it helps distinguish them.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Zampeta-Sofia Alexopoulou, Shuai Kong, Anouk Zonneveld, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Concurrent selection of internal goals and external sensations during visual search
papers.abstract: The authors built a visual search task that simultaneously tracks which item is being selected among search goals held in working memory and which target is being selected in the visual scene, using gaze and EEG markers. Internal and external selection did not have to alternate serially; they unfolded at the same time, supported by largely distinct neural activity patterns, even when the memory item and the scene target sat at opposite locations. This challenges the idea that the brain is either in an internally or externally focused state.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Microsaccades strongly modulate but do not directly cause the EEG N2pc marker of spatial attention
papers.abstract: The study asks whether the N2pc, a widely used EEG index of spatial attention, is driven by the tiny fixational eye movements that occur in the same time window. Trials with microsaccades showed a much larger N2pc in both perception and working memory tasks, yet a smaller but reliable N2pc remained without them, and the N2pc did not time-lock to the microsaccades themselves. Microsaccades therefore shape the N2pc strongly without being its direct cause or a prerequisite.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Shuai Kong, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Jointly looking to the past and the future in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Standard working-memory tasks confound where an item was encoded with where it will be tested. The authors separated these past and future locations and tracked both through gaze biases during mnemonic selection. Gaze reflected both locations jointly, even within single saccades, showing that working-memory representations retain and give access to both past and future attributes.
papers.authors: Baiwei Liu, Zampeta-Sofia Alexopoulou, Freek van Ede

papers.title: Turning attention inside out: how working memory serves behavior
papers.abstract: This review argues that attention directed at the contents of working memory (inside-out) is as important for behavior as attention acting on sensory input (outside-in). It covers why, on what, from where and how internal selective attention operates, using visual working memory as the model system. It presents a future-oriented, flexible view of working memory in which selective attention and memory are considered together.
papers.authors: Freek van Ede, Anna C. Nobre

0225.name: Frédéric Gosselin
0225.bio: Frédéric Gosselin is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the Université de Montréal and the Co-director of CerebrUM. Gosselin developed the 'Bubbles' method, a psychophysical technique used to isolate and identify the specific visual information humans utilize during recognition and categorization tasks. Their research integrates psychophysics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational modeling—including EEG, fMRI, and machine learning—to decode mental representations. This work investigates the neural correlates of individual differences in face and object perception.
0225.research_direction: Dr. Gosselin has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of visual perception, using MEG and novel reverse-correlation frameworks to disentangle how the visual system rhythmically samples stimulus information over time from how it subsequently processes that information. Their recent work also explores the representational overlap between visual mental imagery and perception by probing whether adapting to mentally imagined faces produces measurable visual aftereffects. Additionally, they are studying basic visual development by mapping the maturation trajectories of the contrast sensitivity function across distinct spatial frequencies from childhood to early adulthood. To support the broader experimental community, Dr. Gosselin has also been developing statistical procedures that improve signal-to-noise ratios in behavioral and electrophysiological datasets by using trial-level evidence like response times to reclassify lucky guesses.

papers.title: Time^2: A framework for the neural dynamics of visual perception
papers.abstract: Argues that visual perception unfolds along two entangled time axes, the time the brain takes to process information (processing time) and the time over which the stimulus is sampled while it is viewed (stimulus time), which are usually conflated. Introduces a reverse-correlation method, Time^2, that measures both at once. Shows that it can characterize rhythmic sampling, predictive processing and coarse-to-fine sampling within one framework.
papers.authors: Laurent Caplette, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: The Development of the Contrast Sensitivity Function From Childhood to Early Adulthood
papers.abstract: Measured contrast thresholds for discriminating vertical from horizontal gratings with an adaptive QUEST procedure at seven spatial frequencies (0.5 to 30 cycles/degree) in 103 participants aged 4 to 27. Fitted developmental trajectories to determine when and how the contrast sensitivity function becomes adult-like across spatial frequencies, addressing inconsistent earlier findings.
papers.authors: Frédéric Gosselin, Jessica Tardif, Laveniya Kugathasan, Deborah Eileen Giaschi

papers.title: Aftereffects following adaptation to face mental images
papers.abstract: Tests whether adapting to a mentally imagined face produces aftereffects on subsequent face perception, comparable to those following adaptation to a physically seen face. The work probes how much visual mental imagery and perception share representational mechanisms.
papers.authors: Mathias Salvas-Hébert, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel, Ian Charest, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Rhythmic Information Sampling in the Brain during Visual Recognition
papers.abstract: Participants performed face recognition tasks while random parts of the face were revealed at random moments, and brain activity was recorded with MEG. This let the authors measure how each snapshot of stimulus information is processed across time and cortex. They found rhythmic sampling (theta, alpha, low beta) in early visual areas that contributed more to brain activity than earlier-studied rhythmic processing, alongside non-rhythmic sampling in later visual cortex.
papers.authors: Laurent Caplette, Karim Jerbi, Frédéric Gosselin

papers.title: Reclassifying guesses to increase signal-to-noise ratio in psychological experiments
papers.abstract: Introduces a procedure that raises signal-to-noise ratio in experiments using accuracy to select trials for another measure, by reclassifying some correct responses as guesses using trial-level evidence such as response time. Shows the gain is largest for hard tasks with few response alternatives, and demonstrates over 13% SNR improvement on two behavioral and ERP datasets; code is released in Matlab and Python.
papers.authors: Frédéric Gosselin, Jean-Maxime Larouche, Valérie Daigneault, Laurent Caplette

0226.name: Fuat Balci
0226.bio: Fuat Balci is a Professor of Biological Sciences at the University of Manitoba who studies the computational and neural mechanisms of interval timing and decision-making. Balci's research integrates empirical psychophysics with theoretical modeling to analyze how humans and animals perform temporal risk assessments and maximize reward rates. Through methodologies such as optogenetics, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), and drift-diffusion modeling, Balci investigates the role of the nigrostriatal dopamine system in temporal control. They also examine how these cognitive functions are affected by aging and neuropsychiatric disorders.
0226.research_direction: Dr. Balci has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying interval timing and temporal metacognition across species. Their recent work explores how midbrain dopamine circuits regulate subjective time, using optogenetics and drift-diffusion modeling in mice to determine whether dopamine alters the internal clock's speed or shifts decision thresholds. They are also studying real-time error monitoring, developing computational models of how timing errors might be prospectively anticipated within a trial, and deploying novel behavioral tasks to test whether rodents can track the magnitude and direction of their own temporal inaccuracies. Additionally, Dr. Balci is expanding the methodological toolkit for timing research by analyzing the continuous spatial trajectories of rats to map moment-to-moment temporal expectations, while simultaneously leveraging massive human datasets to investigate the psychophysics of retrospective duration judgments.

papers.title: Midbrain Dopamine Warps Subjective Time via Threshold Setting But Not Clock Speed
papers.abstract: Mice were trained to hold a lever for at least 3 s while substantia nigra pars compacta dopamine (TH+) neurons were optogenetically excited or inhibited. Excitation shifted timed responses later and inhibition shifted them earlier. Drift-diffusion modelling showed these shifts arise from raising or lowering the decision threshold rather than changing the rate of temporal integration, assigning nigrostriatal dopamine a threshold-setting role in the internal clock.
papers.authors: Alihan Erdağı, Ezgi Gür, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: Temporal foreknowledge: Anticipation and prospective correction of timing errors by diffusion
papers.abstract: Building on evidence that timing errors are read out from neural signals before the timed behavior occurs, this paper proposes a drift-diffusion model of real-time temporal error monitoring. The model lets emerging error signals adjust the timing threshold within a trial, improving precision while preserving the standard psychophysical properties of timing. Its task-representation-dependent decision element also accounts for reward-rate-maximizing timing, and it yields testable behavioral and electrophysiological predictions.
papers.authors: Fuat Balcı, Tutku Öztel

papers.title: Movement path as an ethological lens into interval timing
papers.abstract: Rather than relying on focal operant responses, this study tracked the movement trajectories of rats in a modified open field under fixed-time versus variable-time 30 s water schedules. Movement was temporally patterned under fixed-time schedules, with animals farthest from the reward grid around 15 s before returning, but not under variable-time schedules. Temporal control was stronger when water was delivered near the wall, suggesting that movement trajectory reveals moment-to-moment temporal expectancy.
papers.authors: Fuat Balcı, Varsovia Hernandez, Ahmet Hoşer, Alejandro León

papers.title: Mice monitor their timing errors
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether non-human animals can track the direction and size of their own timing errors. Mice performed a novel temporal-production task that strongly rewarded accuracy while limiting sensorimotor noise, with post-production reward-seeking as a proxy for confidence. Expected reward fell with deviation from the target for both short and long productions, indicating symmetric, human-like metric metacognition about timing in mice.
papers.authors: Tutku Öztel, Fuat Balcı

papers.title: Dynamics of retrospective timing: A big data approach
papers.abstract: Most timing research uses prospective tasks, but real-life duration judgments are usually retrospective. Using roughly 24,500 participants who estimated how long a questionnaire session took (5-90 min), the study found overestimation below about 15 min and underestimation above it, with best accuracy near 15 min.
