Variability fell with duration and many people rounded to multiples of 5 min; results replicated in a second large dataset.
papers.authors: Fuat Balcı, Hüseyin Ünübol, Simon Grondin, Gökben Hızlı Sayar, Virginie van Wassenhove, Marc Wittmann

0227.name: Fulvio Domini
0227.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic and Psychological Sciences
0227.bio: Fulvio Domini is a vision scientist who investigates how the human visual system extracts 3D information from retinal images to facilitate motor interactions with the environment. Their research addresses probabilistic inference models of depth-cue integration, proposing deterministic frameworks such as the Intrinsic Constraint (IC) and Vector Sum models to explain systematic perceptual biases. By combining computational modeling with psychophysical experiments and virtual reality, Domini examines the adaptive mapping between visual perception and motor actions like reaching and grasping.
0227.research_direction: Dr. Domini's recent work explores the mechanisms underlying 3D depth perception, sensory cue integration, and intuitive physics across both visual judgments and motor planning. They have recently been investigating how the visual system combines depth cues like disparity, texture, and shading, testing non-probabilistic models of sensory integration against standard reliability-weighted Bayesian accounts. Using virtual reality and haptic feedback paradigms, their research also probes how systematic biases in 3D spatial estimates directly influence sensorimotor actions such as planned grip size during grasping. Furthermore, they are examining how the human sensorimotor system processes dynamic physical events in real time, utilizing collision paradigms to uncover how relational kinematics, mass, and velocity jointly constrain both explicit perceptual judgments and predictive motor control.

papers.title: The online processing of dynamics
papers.abstract: Proposes the Online Processing of Dynamics model, in which mass and velocity are jointly constrained and encoded in a momentum-like representation. Three experiments confirm that initial mass impressions bias perceived post-collision velocity and that those velocity biases in turn bias mass judgments. The model fits the data better than an adapted noisy Newton model.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Alexander Fengler, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Sensorimotor adaptation reveals systematic biases in 3D perception
papers.abstract: The authors use visuomotor adaptation as a probe for whether perceptual and motor spatial judgments carry systematic errors. In a VR grasping study with haptic feedback, adaptation aftereffects showed that planned grip size overestimated object depth, and more so when multiple depth cues were present. This is taken as direct evidence for inherent biases in visual depth estimates that affect both perception and action.
papers.authors: Chaeeun Lim, Dhanraj Vishwanath, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Relational dynamics inform predictive motor planning and perception
papers.abstract: Introduces a dynamic weight illusion in which the sensorimotor system builds conservation of momentum into both motor planning and weight judgments. Using a hybrid VR and real-object paradigm with precise motion tracking, relational cues between colliding objects, and not only static object features, biased anticipatory grip force and explicit perception. The work argues that intuitive physics is directly encoded in sensorimotor processing.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Weak overcomes strong in sensory integration: shading warps the disparity field
papers.abstract: Three within-subject experiments had observers judge the shape of disparity-defined surfaces combined with different shading patterns. Shading altered perceived shape even though disparity is the stronger cue, which cannot be explained by measured reliability, cue vetoing or cue promotion. The result is presented as an instance of cue cooperation that current accounts of 3D perception do not predict.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Celine Aubuchon, Jovan Kemp, Dhanraj Vishwanath, Fulvio Domini

papers.title: Perceiving depth from texture and disparity cues: Evidence for a non-probabilistic account of cue integration
papers.abstract: The paper tests the Intrinsic Constraint theory against standard maximum-likelihood (Bayesian) cue integration. Under the IC theory, cue estimates form a vector whose norm gives the combined depth, so combining texture and disparity increases perceived depth, and just-noticeable differences do not reflect cue uncertainty. Three experiments on depth perception support the vector-sum model over reliability-weighted averaging.
papers.authors: Jovan T. Kemp, Evan Cesanek, Fulvio Domini

0228.name: Fumiko Hoeft
0228.lab_name: Laboratory for Learning Engineering and Neural Systems (brainLENS)
0228.bio: Hoeft is a developmental cognitive neuroscientist and psychiatrist who investigates the neurobiological mechanisms underlying learning disabilities, specifically dyslexia and literacy acquisition. Their methodology integrates multimodal neuroimaging—including functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging—with machine learning and genetic analysis to map brain maturation and predict individual learning outcomes. Hoeft conducts research on the 'Neural Noise Hypothesis' and investigates the intergenerational transmission of brain networks as well as the role of socio-emotional resilience in academic success. Currently, Hoeft serves as the Director of the UConn Brain Imaging Research Center and leads the brainLENS laboratory, focusing on translating neuroscientific findings into early identification tools and personalized educational interventions.
0228.research_direction: Dr. Hoeft has recently been investigating the neurodevelopmental trajectories of language and reading acquisition, focusing on how neural networks adapt as children learn to process written words. Their recent work explores the functional connectivity fingerprints of emerging reading skills, using machine learning on fMRI data to model brain age and track structural shifts toward left-hemisphere lateralization in young learners. Additionally, they are studying multisensory pathways by using simultaneous fMRI and EEG to capture how children integrate audiovisual print and speech signals in real time. To capture the broader landscape of language development and its disorders, Dr. Hoeft is also examining how exposure to typologically diverse languages shapes a multilingual child's neural processing, while modeling how neural noise and excitation-inhibition imbalances might interact to form an etiological pathway for dyslexia.

papers.title: Modeling differences in neurodevelopmental maturity of the reading network using support vector regression on functional connectivity data
papers.abstract: The authors train support vector regression models to predict age from functional connectivity in 742 participants aged 6-21, using both whole-brain and progressively reduced reading-network models. Highly weighted connections came mainly from default mode and frontoparietal control networks. Children with reading disorder showed a larger brain-age gap than typical readers in the whole-brain model, though follow-up tests mainly supported overestimated maturity in advanced older readers, suggesting reading skill relates to broader network maturation.
papers.authors: Oliver H. M. Lasnick, Jie Luo, Brianna Kinnie, Shaan Kamal, Spencer Low, Natasza Marrouch, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Functional Connectivity Fingerprints of Emerging Reading Skill in the First Months of Schooling
papers.abstract: Sixty-six kindergarteners performed a visual word task during fMRI, and individualized functional connectivity networks were estimated with a data-driven method (cs-GIMME). Pre-readers and beginning readers had similar overall network complexity but differed in centrality and hemispheric balance: pre-readers had more distributed and right-hemisphere-heavy connections, while beginning readers showed more symmetric, left-centered organization. The work characterizes the brain network shift at the start of reading acquisition.
papers.authors: Rebecca A. Marks, Florence Bouhali, Xin Sun, Jocelyn F. Caballero, Olga Kepinska, Yuuko Uchikoshi, Adriene Beltz, Ioulia Kovelman, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Audiovisual integration in reading among school-aged children: Evidence from combined fMRI and EEG
papers.abstract: Fifty-six children aged 7-10 completed letter-detection tasks with combined fMRI and EEG to study how print and speech are integrated. Additive enhancement appeared in bilateral superior temporal cortex and Heschl's gyrus, congruency effects in left IFG and STG, and EEG showed P200 and theta-power effects over left frontotemporal sites. Individual differences in these signals, and IFG-STG connectivity, related to spelling and reading fluency, pointing to complementary sensory-convergence and conflict-monitoring pathways.
papers.authors: Jin Ren, Haiwa Wang, Nicole Landi, Marc F. Joanisse, Vincent Gracco, Daniel Kleinman, Kelly Mahaffy, Aahana Bajracharya, Roeland Hancock, Kenneth Pugh, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Sensory temporal sampling in time: an integrated model of the TSF and neural noise hypothesis as an etiological pathway for dyslexia
papers.abstract: This theoretical review reconciles the temporal sampling framework, which attributes dyslexia to poor neural entrainment to speech rhythms, with the neural noise hypothesis, which links dyslexia to excitation-inhibition imbalance from genes to behavior. The authors argue the two are complementary and propose an integrated model of sensory temporal sampling as an etiological pathway, and outline open questions for testing it.
papers.authors: Oliver H. M. Lasnick, Fumiko Hoeft

papers.title: Language combinations of multilinguals are reflected in their first-language knowledge and processing
papers.abstract: In 162 kindergartners with backgrounds from monolingual to quintilingual, the authors relate the typological diversity of the languages a child is exposed to with cognition and brain function. Greater typological diversity was linked to expressive vocabulary in the dominant language and to activation in bilateral inferior parietal regions including area PGa. The study offers an ecologically valid way to describe multilingual experience.
papers.authors: Olga Kepinska, Jocelyn Caballero, Myriam Oliver, Rebecca A. Marks, Stephanie L. Haft, Leo Zekelman, Ioulia Kovelman, Yuuko Uchikoshi, Fumiko Hoeft

0229.name: Gabriel J. Diaz
0229.department: Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science
0229.bio: Gabriel J. Diaz is an Associate Professor in the Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science at the Rochester Institute of Technology and directs the Perception for Movement (PerForM) Lab. Diaz's research focuses on the intersection of vision and motor control, specifically investigating how visual information guides complex actions like navigation and object interception using immersive virtual reality and motion capture. Their current projects include developing neuro-rehabilitation methods for stroke-induced cortical blindness and using deep learning to improve eye-tracking systems through synthetic data generation. Diaz maintains research collaborations with the University of Rochester's Center for Visual Science to study the behavioral impacts of vision loss.
0229.research_direction: Dr. Diaz has recently been studying how people use vision to guide movement, especially steering through the world, using virtual reality and eye tracking. Their recent work asks how the quality of optic flow, the pattern of motion across the visual field, shapes steering in younger and older adults, and how losing part of the visual field, whether from cortical blindness or from a simulated gaze-contingent mask, changes lane position and gaze behavior. They have also examined whether combining sound with vision can speed perceptual learning of difficult motion judgments in the periphery. On the engineering side, they have been benchmarking deep learning methods that make eye tracking in head-mounted displays more accurate and robust.

papers.title: Multisensory stimuli facilitate low-level perceptual learning on a difficult global motion task in virtual reality
papers.abstract: The study investigates the efficacy of inducing visual perceptual learning (VPL) within a peripheral, 4-alternative forced-choice (4AFC) global direction discrimination task utilizing head-mounted virtual reality. Participants were trained over a 10-day period on a high-difficulty motion integration stimulus located at 10° eccentricity. The experimental design compared a unimodal visual training group with an audio-visual (AV) group provided with a pulsed white-noise auditory cue that spatially simulated motion directions congruent with the horizontal visual component. Results demonstrated significant learning and spatial transfer to untrained retinotopic locations in both cohorts. Crucially, the AV group exhibited a superior performance benefit and accelerated learning rates, an advantage that persisted into unisensory post-tests where auditory cues were omitted, suggesting that multisensory integration enhances the robustness of low-level visual plasticity.
papers.authors: Catherine A. Fromm, Ross K. Maddox, Melissa J. Polonenko, Krystel R. Huxlin, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Steering in the presence of a gaze-contingent occlusion over a quarter of the visual field
papers.abstract: This research examines the hypothesis that steering biases observed in patients with cortical blindness (CB) result directly from the loss of visual information within the blind hemifield. Using a gaze-contingent display in a virtual reality steering environment, visually-healthy participants were subjected to quadrant-based occluding masks that spared foveal vision. The study sought to determine whether healthy drivers would replicate the asymmetric lane-positioning biases characteristic of left-sided CB patients (who typically bias away from their blind field). Findings indicate that healthy participants with simulated visual field deficits did not exhibit the steering biases seen in clinical CB populations. These results suggest that CB-related steering behavior is not a mere consequence of instantaneous information omission but likely arises from complex, long-term neuroplastic adaptations or compensatory motor strategies.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Matthew Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: The effect of unilateral cortical blindness on lane position and gaze behavior in a virtual reality steering task
papers.abstract: This longitudinal assessment investigated how cortically-induced blindness (CB) affects the processing and integration of optic flow for navigation control. Steering behavior and gaze dynamics were analyzed in 21 CB drivers (11 left-sided, 10 right-sided deficits) and age-matched controls navigating a virtual winding road. Optic flow quality was manipulated by varying environmental texture density across low, medium, and high levels. While right-sided CB patients maintained steering profiles comparable to controls, left-sided CB patients exhibited significant lane position biases and were markedly less sensitive to variations in optic flow density and turn direction. This asymmetry suggests a lateralized disruption in the motion processing networks essential for steering control, indicating that left-hemifield CB leads to a systematic under-weighting of optic flow in the motor control loop.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Matthew Cavanaugh, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Optic flow density modulates corner-cutting in a virtual steering task for younger and older adults
papers.abstract: The researchers investigated the potential contribution of age-related detriments in optic flow processing to steering performance using a virtual reality winding-road paradigm. Seventeen younger (mean age 21.1) and thirteen older adults (mean age 57.3) were tasked with maintaining a central lane position while environmental texture density was systematically manipulated to vary the quality of optic flow information. Quantitative analysis revealed that both age groups exhibited 'corner-cutting' behavior, which was significantly modulated by the density of proximal motion cues (rotational flow). However, no significant interaction was found between age and optic flow density, and exploratory gaze analysis showed no age-related differences in visual sampling strategies. The findings imply that the visuomotor mechanisms for steering based on naturalistic optic flow remain functionally preserved across the healthy aging lifespan.
papers.authors: Arianna Giguere, Krystel R. Huxlin, Duje Tadin, Brett R. Fajen, Gabriel J. Diaz

papers.title: Using Deep Learning to Increase Eye-Tracking Robustness, Accuracy, and Precision in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: This study provides a technical evaluation of deep learning-based semantic segmentation for eye-feature tracking in head-mounted virtual reality systems. Recognizing the limitations of traditional computer vision in handling environmental reflections and occlusions, the authors benchmark several contemporary machine learning (ML) architectures against conventional feature-based and 3D model-based gaze estimation algorithms. Rather than relying solely on pixel-level segmentation metrics like mIoU, the paper assesses performance via downstream gaze metrics, including angular accuracy, precision, and data drop-out rates. The results demonstrate that while ML models significantly improve feature tracking robustness in diverse environments, their impact on the final gaze coordinate estimate varies depending on the underlying geometric model used for gaze calculation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques
papers.authors: Kevin Barkevich, Reynold Bailey, Gabriel J. Diaz

0230.name: Galit Yovel
0230.bio: Professor Galit Yovel researches the cognitive and neural architecture of high-level vision, specifically the mechanisms underlying face and person recognition. Yovel’s laboratory employs a multidisciplinary approach combining behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and eye-tracking to investigate how perceptual, cognitive, and social systems integrate. A portion of their current work utilizes deep neural networks (DNNs) as computational models to contrast human visual processing with machine learning algorithms, aiming to characterize the representations of facial features and body identity. Through these methodologies, Yovel explores the functional organization of the face-selective cortex and the factors that enable recognition of familiar individuals.
0230.research_direction: Dr. Yovel’s recent work investigates the neural representations of high-level visual and social information by combining functional neuroimaging with deep neural networks and large language models. Specifically, they have recently been using mechanistically interpretable voxel-wise encoding models to probe fine-grained functional selectivity in the visual cortex, capture multimodal social processing in the superior temporal sulcus during naturalistic viewing, and disentangle how representations shift between purely visual and semantic formats across perception and memory. Additionally, their research explores the developmental origins of human face specialization by building computationally plausible models of infant learning. By manipulating artificial network training regimes and employing continuous learning strategies like generative memory replay, they are testing how visual experience alone shapes hallmark perceptual phenomena such as the face inversion and other-race effects.

papers.title: Mechanistically Interpretable Neural Encoding Reveals Fine-Grained Functional Selectivity in Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: The paper introduces MINE, a framework that applies mechanistic-interpretability methods to voxel-wise fMRI encoding models built on language-aligned image representations. It identifies which image features drive each voxel's response and describes them in words. Generating and counterfactually editing images according to these descriptions shifts voxel activation as predicted, giving causal support and revealing fine-grained structure within category-selective regions.
papers.authors: Idan Daniel Grosbard, Mor Geva, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Visual and auditory deep learning models capture neural representations of naturalistic social interaction in the superior temporal sulcus
papers.abstract: Participants watched a TV series during fMRI while self-supervised visual and auditory networks provided features for movie frames and audio. Voxel-wise encoding models using the joint audio-visual representation predicted superior temporal sulcus responses better than hand-crafted social feature models. The work shows that high-dimensional deep network features can capture the multimodal social information that drives the STS.
papers.authors: Itai Peleg, Shiri Almog, Maya Kadushin, Idan Daniel Grosbard, Nitzan Guy, Ido Tavor, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Experience Alone Can Generate Human Face Specialization: Evidence From Deep Learning Models
papers.abstract: Human face recognition is specialized for upright, own-race faces, but the causal role of experience is hard to test in people. The authors manipulate training experience in deep networks and show that experience alone is sufficient to produce human-like face specialization effects such as the inversion and other-race effects.
papers.authors: Nitzan Guy, Mandy Rosemblaum, Galit Yovel

papers.title: A developmentally inspired computational model of face recognition that learns continuously through generative memory replay
papers.abstract: The authors build a face-recognition network that learns like an infant: gradually and continuously rather than in one batch, starting from few identities and limited views, and consolidating knowledge by replaying faces generated from memory. The model reproduces hallmark human effects such as inversion and other-race effects. It offers a more developmentally plausible account of how face expertise is acquired.
papers.authors: Naphtali Abudarham, Galit Yovel

papers.title: Using deep neural networks to disentangle visual and semantic information in human perception and memory
papers.abstract: The authors use visual deep networks and language models to isolate purely visual versus purely semantic information in stimuli, then use representational similarity analysis on behavioral and neural data. They find that visual information dominates representations of faces and scenes during perception, whereas semantic information gains dominance when the stimuli are recalled from memory. This shows a shift in the content of representations between perception and memory.
papers.authors: Adva Shoham, Idan Daniel Grosbard, Or Patashnik, Daniel Cohen-Or, Galit Yovel

0231.name: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga
0231.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
0231.bio: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga is an Ikerbasque Research Fellow and Associate Group Leader at the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL). Lerma-Usabiaga’s research examines the neurobiological foundations of vision and literacy, focusing on the functional and structural architecture of the ventral occipitotemporal cortex. They utilize multimodal neuroimaging methodologies, including functional, quantitative, and diffusion MRI, alongside computational modeling techniques such as population receptive field (pRF) mapping. Their work also involves the development of reproducible software tools for automated tractography and the characterization of spatiotemporal dynamics within the human visual system across the lifespan.
0231.research_direction: Dr. Lerma-Usabiaga has recently been working on how the visual system is organized for reading, and on the neuroimaging tools needed to measure it well. Their recent work uses densely sampled fMRI to map the visual-field layout of reading-selective cortex, including the visual word form area, with a stimulus designed to capture retinotopy and reading selectivity at once. They have also examined how the choice of analysis space, volume versus cortical surface, can bias estimates of population receptive fields, particularly near the fovea. Alongside this, they have contributed reproducible, containerized software for diffusion MRI that produces standardized profiles of white matter tracts.

papers.title: Design and Validation of a Hybrid Stimulus fMRI Paradigm for Simultaneous Retinotopy and Mapping of Reading-Selective Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Reading selectively recruits specialized cortical subregions within the ventral occipitotemporal cortex (vOTC), notably the visual word form area (VWFA). Interactive models of reading postulate that these functional responses arise from bidirectional exchanges between bottom-up sensory visual inputs and top-down linguistic feedback. However, resolving the visual field organization of these regions remains challenging because high-level category selectivity confounds purely retinotopic spatial signals. In this dense-sampling functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study (n = 11, ten sessions per participant), the authors investigated the visual field architecture of the cortical reading network using population receptive field (pRF) modeling and functional localizers. First, they systematically evaluated the influence of stimulus frequency, bar width, and element size (FWS) across multiple sessions to identify configurations that optimize the test-retest reliability of pRF eccentricity shifts observed for word and false-font stimuli relative to standard checkerboard carriers. Second, they developed and validated an innovative Word-Center (WC) hybrid paradigm designed to decouple sweeping spatial mapping carriers (moving checkerboard bars) from central lexical processing (continuous streams of words or false fonts at fixation). Results demonstrated that the hybrid WC design preserved stimulus equivalence, successfully isolating bottom-up retinotopic sweeps from top-down lexical influences and delivering simultaneous, highly reproducible characterizations of reading-selective functional clusters and retinotopic field maps within individual brains.
papers.authors: Miguel Martinez-Zaldivar, Yongning Lei, Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga

papers.title: Biases in Volumetric Versus Surface Analyses in Population Receptive Field Mapping
papers.abstract: Population receptive field (pRF) mapping with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) provides quantitative models that link visual field coordinates to discrete anatomical loci across visual cortex. A standard preprocessing step involves projecting 3D volumetric functional data onto reconstructed 2D cortical surfaces, an operation that typically causes spatial upsampling. Using containerized analysis pipelines, this investigation assessed systematic biases in pRF parameter estimation introduced by surface versus volumetric computational spaces. The authors identified a marked and consistent overestimation of pRF coverage in the central foveal visual field when functional data underwent upsampling onto the cortical surface relative to native volumetric processing, an artifact conserved across early visual areas V1, V2, and V3. Systematic empirical and synthetic simulations revealed that this foveal coverage bias is primarily driven by cortical magnification—the pronounced nonlinear decrease in cortical representation per degree of visual angle as eccentricity increases—alongside secondary contributions from increased contrast-to-noise ratio due to surface averaging. These findings emphasize the necessity of accounting for space-representation artifacts when evaluating visual field coverage and when interpreting cross-study comparisons across divergent preprocessing pipelines.
papers.authors: David Linhardt, Michael Woletz, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Christian Windischberger, Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga

papers.title: Reproducible Tract Profiles 2 (RTP2) suite, from diffusion MRI acquisition to clinical practice and research
papers.abstract: Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) tractography provides a critical, noninvasive window into white matter bundle architecture and microstructural tissue properties in vivo; however, the extreme sensitivity of dMRI pipelines to parameter configurations and execution environments severely compromises scientific reproducibility and clinical utility. To resolve this challenge, the authors introduce Reproducible Tract Profiles 2 (RTP2), an end-to-end, containerized neuroinformatics software suite engineered to transform raw diffusion datasets into standardized, highly reproducible along-tract microstructural profiles. RTP2 encapsulates automated preprocessing, anatomical parcellation, region-of-interest (ROI) definition, tractography fiber tracking, and along-tract tractometry into self-contained Docker and Singularity modules structured around Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specifications. The pipeline supports versatile anatomically curated ROI delineations, handles multiple diffusion modeling frameworks (from basic diffusion tensor metrics to advanced multi-shell reconstructions), and quantifies tissue indices such as fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity along tract nodes. Comprehensive validation across test-retest acquisitions and multisite cohorts demonstrated high repeatability, robust parameter management, and sensitive tracking of white matter pathways, establishing an open-source tool bridging reproducible computational neuroanatomy and clinical investigations.
papers.authors: Garikoitz Lerma-Usabiaga, Mengxing Liu, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Brian A. Wandell

0232.name: Gene Brewer
0232.bio: Gene Brewer is a Professor of Psychology and a faculty member of the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of California, Riverside, where they direct the Memory and Attention Control Laboratory. Their research focuses on the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in working memory, sustained attention, and episodic memory retrieval. Utilizing a multi-methodological approach that includes behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and neurostimulation, Brewer investigates how attention control influences performance in both theoretical and high-stakes applied contexts. Brewer’s work receives support from federal agencies including DARPA and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and includes collaborations with the Department of Defense on personnel assessment and cognitive enhancement.
0232.research_direction: Dr. Brewer's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms governing working memory, attention control, and episodic memory. They have recently been investigating how the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system regulates arousal and sustained attention, employing comprehensive theoretical modeling alongside physiological methods like pupillometry and trigeminal nerve stimulation. In parallel, their research examines how momentary attention lapses, such as state and trait mind-wandering, impact the temporal dynamics of memory encoding and free recall. Finally, Dr. Brewer is studying large-scale individual differences in working memory capacity to uncover both the underlying mediators that link it to fluid intelligence and how these capacity constraints influence strategic behaviors like cognitive offloading to external memory stores.

papers.title: Individuals with higher working memory are more strategic offloaders but also greater forgetters
papers.abstract: After a battery of working memory tasks, participants did a value-directed remembering task in which they could offload words to an external store. High working memory individuals offloaded the highest-value items more selectively. When the store unexpectedly became unavailable, they recalled those offloaded high-value words worse than low-capacity peers, revealing a paradoxical cost of strategic offloading.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Dillon H. Murphy, Myles Alucard, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: The role of the LC-NE system in attention: From cells, to systems, to sensory-motor control
papers.abstract: This review pulls together molecular, systems, human neuroimaging, electrophysiology and modeling evidence on how the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system supports attention control. It covers tonic and phasic LC firing and interprets the findings through adaptive gain theory, the network reset hypothesis and the GANE model. The central conclusion is that LC-NE activity tunes signal-to-noise in cortical and subcortical circuits to shape attention and behavior.
papers.authors: Alexis S. Torres, Matthew K. Robison, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: Individual differences in state and trait mind-wandering influence episodic memory encoding and retrieval dynamics
papers.abstract: Participants studied word lists while reporting task-unrelated thoughts, and the analyses examined how both momentary and dispositional mind-wandering relate to free recall. Mind-wandering during encoding and trait tendencies shaped what was remembered and how retrieval unfolded over time. The paper links attention lapses to the temporal dynamics of episodic memory.
papers.authors: Dillon H. Murphy, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: What makes working memory work? A multifaceted account of the predictive power of working memory capacity
papers.abstract: A large individual-differences study (N = 974) asks why working memory capacity predicts reading comprehension and fluid intelligence. Attention control, primary memory and secondary memory were tested as candidate mediators, and no single one fully accounted for the link. The pattern held whether capacity was measured with complex span or n-back, supporting a multifaceted account of what working memory measures.
papers.authors: Matthew K. Robison, Ashley L. Miller, Elizabeth A. Wiemers, Derek M. Ellis, Nash Unsworth, Thomas S. Redick, Gene A. Brewer

papers.title: The influence of transcranial direct current stimulation to the trigeminal nerve on attention and arousal
papers.abstract: The study tested whether tDCS applied over the face, which stimulates the trigeminal nerve linked to the locus coeruleus, changes attention. Using pupillometry, thought probes and a sustained attention task with sham, anodal and cathodal stimulation, it found the usual time-on-task decline but no stimulation effect on pupil dynamics, self-reported attention or performance. The null result challenges the claim that trigeminal tDCS acts through LC arousal.
papers.authors: Alexis S. Torres, Matthew K. Robison, Samuel M. McClure, Gene A. Brewer

0233.name: Geoffrey K Aguirre
0233.bio: Geoffrey Karl Aguirre is a neurologist and cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Pennsylvania whose research focuses on the functional organization of the human visual cortex. Utilizing BOLD fMRI and non-invasive neuroimaging, Aguirre investigates how the brain represents visual information and how these processes are disrupted by neurologic and ophthalmologic diseases. Their work encompasses the methodological refinement of imaging techniques, the study of melanopsin-mediated visual pathways, and the characterization of neural population coding for object and facial recognition. Aguirre also examines the plasticity of the visual system in response to blindness and conditions such as migraine, bridging basic vision science with clinical behavioral neurology.
0233.research_direction: Dr. Aguirre has recently been investigating a diverse range of topics spanning fundamental visual neurophysiology and clinical translational research. Their recent work explores the temporal limits of human color and luminance vision by using 7T fMRI and cone-isolating stimuli to map flicker sensitivity across eccentricity and the cortical hierarchy. In the clinical realm, they are examining the relationship between sensory sensitivity, daily melanopic light exposure, and circadian rhythms in migraine populations using wearable loggers and lifespan symptom analyses. Additionally, they are leveraging advanced neuroimaging for broader biomedical applications, investigating postretinal fMRI and pupillometry responses in canine models of retinal disease to assess potential gene therapies, and proposing semantic neural decoding paradigms to evaluate covert consciousness in unresponsive brain-injured patients.

papers.title: Cluster Analysis of Migraine-Associated Symptoms (CAMS) across the lifespan: a cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether a symptom-cluster measure previously developed in children and adolescents (CAMS), which aggregates twelve headache-associated symptoms such as sensory sensitivity, nausea, and autonomic and vestibular signs, generalizes to adults. Using survey data from the Penn Online Evaluation of Migraine, it examines how symptom clustering relates to age and headache burden across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Eric Kaiser, Christina L. Szperka, Andrew D. Hershey, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: Reconstructing Covert Consciousness: Neural Decoding as a Novel Consciousness Assessment
papers.abstract: This review argues that current fMRI and EEG tests for covert consciousness in unresponsive brain-injured patients are insensitive and rest on shaky assumptions about functional anatomy. It proposes that neural decoding, the reconstruction of stimuli and concepts from brain activity, could reveal what patients can actually experience, and lays out how semantic decoding might be adapted to disorders of consciousness.
papers.authors: David Fischer, Brian L. Edlow, Holly J. Freeman, Daniel Alaiev, Qichao Wu, Jeffrey B. Ware, John A. Detre, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: Daily light exposure habits of youth with migraine: a prospective exploratory study
papers.abstract: Twenty adolescents with migraine wore chest pendant light loggers for a week. They received recommended daytime melanopic light only a small fraction of the day, with distinct weekday/weekend patterns, and a delay in the timing of light exposure correlated strongly with monthly headache days. The work shows that wearable light measurement is feasible in this population and hints at a circadian link to migraine burden.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Ryan Shah, Blanca Marquez De Prado, Nichelle Raj, Christina L. Szperka, Andrew D. Hershey, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: Temporal Sensitivity for Achromatic and Chromatic Flicker across the Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Using 7T fMRI and stimuli that isolate the luminance and the two cone-opponent postreceptoral channels, the study maps how sensitivity to flicker frequency varies from LGN through V1 (across eccentricity) to higher visual areas in three participants. It shows channel-specific temporal tuning that changes with eccentricity and along the cortical hierarchy, providing a quantitative picture of the temporal limits of human color and luminance vision.
papers.authors: Carlyn Patterson Gentile, Manuel Spitschan, Huseyin O. Taskin, Andrew S. Bock, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

papers.title: Cone-Driven, Geniculocortical Responses in Canine Models of Outer Retinal Disease
papers.abstract: The authors used pupillometry and fMRI with stimuli directed at L/M cones, S cones and rods to measure postretinal responses in normal dogs and three canine models of inherited retinal degeneration. Cone-driven geniculocortical responses could be measured and distinguished across disease models, supporting fMRI as an objective readout of restored vision in gene-therapy trials.
papers.authors: Huseyin O. Taskin, Jacqueline Wivel, Gustavo D. Aguirre, William A. Beltran, Geoffrey K. Aguirre

0234.name: Geoffrey Woodman
0234.bio: Geoffrey Woodman is a Professor of Psychology and the E. Bronson Ingram Chair of Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University, where they direct research on the neural basis of visual attention and memory. Woodman's laboratory employs a comparative approach, utilizing electrophysiology and behavioral measures in both humans and nonhuman primates to investigate how the brain selects and maintains information during complex tasks. They identify neural signatures of attentional selection and study the cognitive architecture of working memory through computational modeling and brain stimulation techniques. Their current work examines the interaction between sensory noise and cognitive deficits in neurotypical and clinical populations.
0234.research_direction: Dr. Woodman has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms linking learning, memory, and visual attention using behavioral paradigms, event-related potentials, and computational modeling. Their recent work explores how both intentional and statistical learning shape visual search, specifically probing how rapidly new attentional sets can be acquired, whether observers can simultaneously deploy multiple search templates, and if learned display regularities optimize early attentional selection rather than late response stages. In the domain of memory, they are testing whether executive control mechanisms can query visual long-term memory traces that remain inaccessible to explicit conscious report. Additionally, they are developing computational models to determine if hallmark working memory phenomena, such as set-size and recency effects, can emerge purely from context-guided long-term memory retrieval without the need for a separate, capacity-limited storage buffer.

papers.title: Capacity not required: A long-term memory model that exhibits key signatures of working memory
papers.abstract: The authors build a computational model in which retrieval from long-term memory, guided by a shifting temporal context, is enough to reproduce hallmark working-memory findings such as set-size effects and recency, without positing a separate capacity-limited buffer. This challenges the standard view that working memory needs its own storage system and argues that its limits can emerge from retrieval dynamics.
papers.authors: Sean M. Polyn, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Executive control can query hidden human memories
papers.abstract: Using behavior and EEG, the study shows that memory traces which participants cannot consciously recognize can still be accessed by executive control processes when the task demands it. The results indicate that control mechanisms can probe visual long-term memory content that is invisible to explicit report.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Keisuke Fukuda, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Super rapid learning of new attentional sets
papers.abstract: The study asks how quickly people can learn what to look for in visual search when the relevant target features change. It finds that new attentional sets are acquired within very few trials, far faster than typically assumed for attentional learning.
papers.authors: Seth A. Marx, Sisi Wang, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Intentional learning establishes multiple attentional sets that simultaneously guide attention
papers.abstract: Across behavioral experiments, observers who intentionally learned multiple search targets kept several attentional sets active at once, and each set guided attention concurrently. This argues against a single-template limit on attentional guidance and shows that learning can install multiple control settings.
papers.authors: Sisi Wang, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Statistical learning speeds visual search: More efficient selection, or faster response?
papers.abstract: Combining behavior and event-related potentials, the paper asks whether learned regularities in a search display speed performance by making attentional selection more efficient or by speeding later response stages. The evidence favors changes in attentional selection, with learning shifting when target selection occurs.
papers.authors: Sisi Wang, Stanislas Huynh Cong, Geoffrey F. Woodman

0235.name: George A. Alvarez
0235.bio: George A. Alvarez is the Fred Kavli Professor of Neuroscience in the Department of Psychology at Harvard University and a visiting scholar at the Kempner Institute. Alvarez’s research investigates the computational constraints of the human visual system, with a focus on the mechanisms of attentional selection, visual working memory, and resource allocation. They employ a methodology that combines human psychophysics and neuroimaging with deep neural network (DNN) modeling to study how the brain processes visual information. Recent work by Alvarez focuses on the alignment between biological and artificial intelligence, using deep learning frameworks to model perceptual phenomena such as lightness illusions and contour integration.
0235.research_direction: Dr. Alvarez has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying classic human visual phenomena, employing deep neural networks to model processes like perceptual grouping and brightness perception. Their recent work explores whether plain feedforward architectures with large receptive fields can account for contour integration, while also examining edge-based image reconstruction as a potential computational origin for lightness illusions. They are additionally probing the representational strategies of state-of-the-art vision transformers, utilizing tools like visual anagrams to test whether these models rely on holistic shape configurations rather than local textures. To better understand how these artificial networks internally route and suppress visual information, Dr. Alvarez is developing novel mechanistic interpretability techniques—such as maximally tense images and factor decompositions of self-attention—to visualize inhibitory feature interactions and disentangle position-based from content-based communication.

papers.title: A Unified Account of Lightness Illusions via Edge-Based Reconstruction of Natural Images
papers.abstract: Proposes edge-based image reconstruction as the computational goal that gives rise to lightness illusions. Using a deep learning framework trained to reconstruct natural images from edge information, the authors show the model reproduces a wide range of classic illusions with a single mechanism. The work frames these illusions as byproducts of constructive perception.
papers.authors: Srijani Saha, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: Bi-Orthogonal Factor Decomposition for Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Presents a decomposition of self-attention in Vision Transformers that separates position-based from content-based token communication using statistical analysis and singular value decomposition. Attention is dominated by content, heads specialize in content-content, content-position or position-position interactions, and DINOv2's strong shape processing arises from intermediate layers that keep positional structure while enriching semantic content.
papers.authors: Fenil R. Doshi, Thomas Fel, Talia Konkle, George Alvarez

papers.title: A feedforward mechanism for human-like contour integration
papers.abstract: Shows that plain feedforward convolutional networks fine-tuned on contour detection reproduce human-like contour integration, without lateral connections, recurrence or top-down feedback. Two ingredients turn out to be key: large receptive fields that integrate over space and a training objective that demands the task. The resulting models match human behavioral signatures, challenging the view that perceptual grouping requires recurrent processing.
papers.authors: Fenil R. Doshi, Talia Konkle, George A. Alvarez

papers.title: Visual Anagrams Reveal Hidden Differences in Holistic Shape Processing Across Vision Models
papers.abstract: Introduces the Configural Shape Score, a benchmark using visual anagrams to test whether models recognize objects from the arrangement of parts rather than local texture. Evaluating 86 models, self-supervised and language-aligned transformers such as DINOv2 and SigLIP2 score highest. Restricting attention to local windows hurts them sharply, and the networks shift from local to global processing at mid depth.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Fenil Doshi, Thomas Fel, Talia Konkle, George Alvarez

papers.title: Understanding Inhibition Through Maximally Tense Images
papers.abstract: Examines how networks suppress features, which standard interpretability tools handle poorly because of ReLU asymmetries. Introduces maximally tense images that simultaneously excite and inhibit a feature, plus attribution inversions and an attribution atlas to visualize excitatory and inhibitory contributions. Also discusses how superposition complicates interpretation.
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (ICML 2024 workshop; DB lists AAAI-25, unverified)
papers.authors: Chris Hamblin, Srijani Saha, Talia Konkle, George Alvarez

0236.name: George R. Mangun
0236.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Neurology
0236.lab_name: Laboratory for the Neural Mechanisms of Attention
0236.bio: George R. Mangun is a Professor of Psychology and Neurology and the founding Director of the Center for Mind and Brain at the University of California, Davis. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms of selective attention, specifically investigating how top-down signals from the frontal and parietal cortex modulate sensory processing in the visual system. Utilizing a multimodal approach that integrates high-density EEG/ERP with functional MRI, Mangun maps the spatial and temporal dynamics of attentional control and selection. Mangun is also a co-author of the textbook, 'Cognitive Neuroscience: The Biology of the Mind.'
0236.research_direction: Dr. Mangun has recently been investigating the neural networks and temporal dynamics underlying various forms of attentional control. Using simultaneous EEG and fMRI, their recent work explores how the brain organizes hierarchical control networks for non-spatial feature attention and how the ventral attention network mediates cross-modal reorienting to sensory expectancy violations. Additionally, they are probing the mechanisms of internally driven, willed attention by using EEG to examine whether pre-conscious neural patterns predict overt gaze targets during visual search, and to test whether freely chosen spatial shifts still engage standard alpha-band lateralization. Finally, their research utilizes neural decoding to investigate how attention operates on internal representations, specifically tracking whether competing targets and distractors in visual sensory memory are alternately sampled at low theta-band rhythms.

papers.title: The Ventral Attention Network Mediates Attentional Reorienting to Cross-Modal Expectancy Violations: Evidence from EEG and fMRI
papers.abstract: Participants were cued to expect a visual or auditory target, and trials in which the expectation was violated required reorienting across modalities while EEG and fMRI were recorded. Reorienting engaged the ventral attention network, and the pattern of activity linked this network to the shift of processing toward the unexpected sensory channel. The findings show the ventral network acts in cross-modal, not only within-vision, reorienting.
papers.authors: Soukhin Das, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Evelijne M. Bekker, Sharon Corina, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Rhythmic sampling and competition of target and distractor representations in visual sensory memory
papers.abstract: EEG decoding was used to track how representations of a target and a competing distractor evolve in visual sensory memory right after the stimuli disappear. The two object representations fluctuate out of phase with one another at a low theta-band rhythm, consistent with attention alternately sampling the competing items. The results support a rhythmic, competitive sampling account of attention applied to internal representations.
papers.authors: Sean Noah, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Hierarchical Organization of Human Visual Feature Attention Control
papers.abstract: Using simultaneous EEG and fMRI-informed analyses during a cued feature-attention task (color versus motion), the study asks how the brain organizes control over attending to non-spatial features. Results point to a hierarchy in which frontoparietal regions carry general control signals and feature-specific information is encoded in more specialized control and visual areas. The work extends the well-studied spatial attention control framework to feature-based attention.
papers.authors: Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Mingzhou Ding, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Unconscious Neural Activity Predicts Overt Attention in Visual Search
papers.abstract: Before a voluntary eye movement in a cluttered search display, brain activity recorded with EEG was analyzed to see whether it forecasts where the person will look. Pre-search neural patterns predicted the subsequent gaze target, even though observers were not aware of having settled on it. This links willed attention to overt orienting and suggests decisions about where to look are made before conscious awareness.
papers.authors: John G. Nadra, Jesse J. Bengson, George R. Mangun

papers.title: Attention without Constraint: Alpha Lateralization in Uncued Willed Attention
papers.abstract: Participants freely chose which side to attend without any external cue while EEG was recorded, allowing a test of whether alpha-band lateralization, a marker of spatial attention, arises without instructions. Alpha lateralization emerged for self-chosen attention shifts, resembling that seen with cued attention. It shows willed attention engages the same oscillatory mechanisms as instructed attention, even in an unconstrained paradigm.
papers.authors: John G. Nadra, Jesse J. Bengson, Alexander B. Morales, George R. Mangun

0237.name: George Sperling
0237.bio: George Sperling is a Distinguished Professor at the University of California, Irvine, known for identifying iconic memory and developing the partial report paradigm to measure visual sensory storage. His research integrates mathematical and computational modeling to investigate visual processes, including the three-systems theory of motion perception and the dynamics of spatial and feature-based attention. Recently, Sperling's work has expanded into measuring perceptual attention filters and exploring substance-invariant salience processing to explain how the brain extracts information from various visual stimuli.
0237.research_direction: Dr. Sperling studies how the human visual system takes in, briefly stores and selects information, combining psychophysics with mathematical and computational models. Most recently his lab has developed psychophysical methods to independently measure the properties of the parvocellular and magnocellular pathways from the retina to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus. Related work uses rapidly masked, multi-feature displays and ideal-detector analysis to study salience maps, showing that judgments of distance, centroids and numerosity rely on substance-invariant processing that extracts spatial position regardless of luminance, color or texture, and estimating how many salience maps an observer can use at once. This builds on his discovery of iconic memory with the partial-report method and on the three-systems theory of motion perception.

papers.title: Salience maps for judgments of frontal plane distance, centroids, numerosity, and letter identity inferred from substance-invariant processing
papers.abstract: Topographic salience maps integrate multi-feature sensory inputs into continuous scalar salience values indexed by spatial coordinates (x, y). Beyond the conventional view that salience maps serve primarily to dictate action priority and attentional deployment, this study shows that they execute substance-invariant perceptual measurements analogous to physical calibration tools. Across a suite of psychophysical paradigms, observers performed four visual tasks: estimating frontal-plane spatial distance between two target tokens, computing the center of mass (centroid) of target arrays, estimating target numerosity, and identifying large alphabetic letters. The targets and distractors were systematically defined by luminance contrast, chromaticity, or grating texture orientation, including rigorous isoluminant configurations in the fovea and periphery to rule out luminance-channel contributions. Distance, centroid, and numerosity judgments exhibited strict substance invariance—performance was equivalent across homogeneous and heterogeneous feature compositions and remained intact under isoluminance, demonstrating that these metric evaluations operate solely over featureless spatial location coordinates represented within salience maps. In contrast, letter recognition was the sole task showing moderate performance facilitation with luminance information. These results establish that the primate visual system uses shared salience maps as low-dimensional coordinate representations for diverse spatial and ensemble computations independently of luminance pathways.
papers.authors: Lingyu Gan, George Sperling

papers.title: Deriving the number of salience maps an observer has from the number and quality of concurrent centroid judgments
papers.abstract: Topographic salience maps translate multi-channel visual feature inputs into scalar priority landscapes across the visual field. While observers can concurrently judge centroids of three intermixed dot colors, the upper capacity limit for parallel salience representations in the human brain has remained unresolved. Using an eleven-experiment partial-report paradigm, observers viewed tachistoscopic 300 ms presentations of 28 to 32 item arrays composed of M intermixed feature classes (with M spanning from 3 to 8), followed by a post-stimulus mask and a feature cue instructing the observer to localize the spatial centroid of only the cued feature set. Ideal detector analyses revealed that observers simultaneously sampled and pooled spatial coordinates from 12 to 17 individual items. Quantitative modeling of whether performance in an M-feature experiment could be predicted from performance in the corresponding (M-1)-feature baseline demonstrated that one observer maintained at least 7 concurrent salience maps, while two observers maintained at least 5. Computational decomposition of six potential error sources established that performance ceilings were not constrained by feature-based attentional filtering or motor execution noise, but primarily by channel capacity during multiplexed item-location encoding and working memory constraints during retention of calculated centroid coordinates.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Lingyu Gan, Peng Sun, George Sperling

0238.name: Gerrit Maus
0238.bio: Maus is a vision scientist at Magic Leap, Inc., where they apply principles of human perception to the development of augmented reality technologies. Previously, Maus served as an Assistant Professor at Nanyang Technological University and a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley, focusing on how the brain compensates for sensory delays and discontinuities. Their research includes studies on motion extrapolation, the flash-lag effect, and the automatic recalibration of gaze direction following eye blinks. Maus utilizes an approach that combines psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI (fMRI) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to investigate the neural mechanisms of spatial and temporal vision.
0238.research_direction: Dr. Maus has recently been applying vision science to the practical problem of making augmented reality displays comfortable and convincing. Their recent work explores how much misalignment between the two eyes' images people can tolerate in see-through headsets, measuring both visual search performance and discomfort, along with the resulting eye posture. They also continue to study basic perceptual illusions, such as how blue and yellow color combinations strengthen the illusory motion seen in static patterns like the Rotating Snakes.

papers.title: Eye posture and screen alignment with simulated see-through head-mounted displays
papers.abstract: Rendering virtual environments on near-eye head-mounted displays demands precise knowledge of display calibration, scene geometry, and ocular anatomy to prevent binocular disparity artifacts. In optical see-through augmented reality (OST-AR), binocular vertical misalignment (BVM) creates an incongruence between the unmediated, geometrically aligned real background and the misaligned virtual overlay. This study evaluated human tolerance to BVM during an active visual search task over random-dot stereograms while concurrently assessing subjective discomfort (via a visual discomfort questionnaire) and objective binocular posture (using Nonius alignment). Across varying degrees of vertical disparity and stimulus angular subtense, empirical results demonstrate that physiological compensation for vertical disparity is partitioned approximately evenly between sensory fusion and motor vertical vergence. Significant inter-individual differences in misalignment thresholds and symptom severity were observed, indicating that individualized calibration parameters are critical to mitigate asthenopia and maximize visual performance in see-through wearable systems.
papers.authors: Agostino Gibaldi, Yinghua Liu, Christos Kaspiris-Rousellis, Madhumitha S. Mahadevan, Jenny C. A. Read, Björn N. S. Vlaskamp, Gerrit W. Maus

papers.title: Blue-yellow combination enhances perceived motion in Rotating Snakes illusion
papers.abstract: The Rotating Snakes illusion evokes anomalous visual motion from static repeated asymmetric luminance profiles. Although chromatic variations—specifically combinations of blue and yellow—have been qualitatively reported to exacerbate this illusion, rigorous empirical verification under controlled luminance remained unestablished. Here, psychophysical nulling via a motion cancellation paradigm was employed to determine the point of subjective stationarity across blue-yellow (BY), red-green (RG), and achromatic greyscale configurations, with corresponding micropattern segments precisely luminance-matched across conditions. Results revealed a statistically significant main effect of color profile: the physical angular velocity needed to achieve perceptual stationarity was significantly higher for the blue-yellow stimulus relative to both the red-green and achromatic baselines, while the latter two exhibited comparable effect magnitudes. These quantitative findings provide direct empirical evidence that S-cone-opponent chromatic signals modulate the spatiotemporal contrast mechanisms that generate anomalous motion percepts.
papers.authors: Maiko Uesaki, Arnab Biswas, Hiroshi Ashida, Gerrit Maus

0239.name: Gi-Yeul Bae
0239.bio: Gi-Yeul Bae is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at Arizona State University and the principal investigator of the Visual Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory. Bae’s research investigates the neural architectures of visual perception and memory, employing EEG decoding and psychophysics to track stimulus-specific information in the human brain. Bae develops computational models that examine how prior trial history and categorical frameworks introduce systematic biases into visual working memory. Their work aims to describe how the brain maintains a stable and coherent visual experience by integrating sensory inputs with internal goals and past experiences.
0239.research_direction: Dr. Bae has recently been investigating how our perceptual history shapes ongoing visual processing, focusing heavily on the mechanisms underlying serial dependence and adaptation. Their recent work explores whether the attractive and repulsive biases observed across sequential trials arise from early, low-level sensory adaptation or from later, post-perceptual decisional stages, using behavioral techniques like continuous mouse-tracking and interpersonal estimation tasks to parse these temporal dynamics. In parallel, they are examining the intersection of perceptual history and visual working memory, testing how the active maintenance or disruption of memory representations influences the direction of serial biases. Additionally, Dr. Bae uses EEG decoding during delayed-estimation paradigms to understand how working memory flexibly recodes raw sensory input into action-oriented formats depending on the specific behavioral goals of the observer.

papers.title: Decisional processes balance sensitivity and stability in visual perception
papers.abstract: Adaptation makes vision more sensitive over time but pushes reports away from recent stimuli, while serial dependence pulls them toward the past. The authors test whether early adaptation produces a repulsive bias that later post-perceptual decisional processing counteracts. In two orientation tasks using continuous mouse-tracking, the bias changed direction as the decision unfolded, supporting a two-stage account of how sensitivity and perceptual stability are balanced.
papers.authors: Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Is repulsive serial bias in visual perception driven by adaptation mechanisms?
papers.abstract: The repulsive serial bias has been attributed to low-level adaptation during encoding of the new stimulus. This study compared that bias with a bias known to come from adaptation, the tilt aftereffect, using matched location-estimation tasks. The two biases behaved differently, arguing against a purely low-level adaptation account of repulsive serial bias.
papers.authors: Scott Janetsky, Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

papers.title: Beyond self-generated perceptual history: Other's prior perceptual decisions bias one's own perceptual decision
papers.abstract: Serial bias research has looked only at one's own perceptual history, but people also observe others' decisions. In pairs of students alternating trials of an orientation-estimation task, reports were biased away from the partner's previous report even when it was task-irrelevant. Follow-up experiments indicated that this between-individual bias arises from post-perceptual decision mechanisms rather than low-level sensory processing alone.
papers.authors: Gi-Yeul Bae, Kuo-Wei Chen

papers.title: EEG decoding reveals task-dependent recoding of sensory information in working memory
papers.abstract: Participants did color delayed estimation while EEG was recorded, with the response colorwheel either randomly rotated or fixed across trials. When the mapping was fixed, participants could prepare a response from the mapping instead of holding the exact color. EEG decoding tracked how the memory content changed format under these task demands, showing that working memory recodes sensory input into a format suited to the behavioral goal.
papers.authors: Gi-Yeul Bae, Kuo-Wei Chen

papers.title: Working memory flips the direction of serial bias through memory-based decision
papers.abstract: Serial biases can attract or repel a new percept toward prior stimuli, and working memory is involved in almost all such studies. This orientation delayed-estimation study used an attention-demanding intervening task to disrupt memory maintenance. It found that the state of working memory, through the decision made for the new stimulus rather than the stored representation itself, reverses the direction of the bias.
papers.authors: Kuo-Wei Chen, Gi-Yeul Bae

0240.name: Gideon Caplovitz
0240.bio: Gideon Caplovitz is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms and principles underlying human visual experience, specifically how the brain integrates features such as form and motion into coherent percepts. Utilizing psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and high-density electroencephalography (EEG), Caplovitz explores the spatiotemporal integrative processes of the visual system and the neural correlates of object-based attention. Their research employs visual illusions to isolate specific sensory mechanisms and includes the investigation of octopus cognitive processes to relate biological vision to the development of artificial intelligence.
0240.research_direction: Dr. Caplovitz has recently been studying how the visual system decides what to attend to and how it builds a stable picture of moving and partly hidden objects. Their recent work uses fMRI to ask whether attention automatically spreads across an entire object in early visual cortex, even when the task gives no reason to monitor the uncued parts. They also study illusions of induced motion, in which surrounding movement pulls the perceived path of a target, and have developed a simple computational model to capture that effect. A further line of work examines how completing the contours of partly occluded shapes biases their perceived size and location.

papers.title: Seeing smaller: Occlusion, contour completion, and biases in spatial localization
papers.abstract: Studies how partially occluded shapes, such as a triangle whose vertex is hidden, are perceived as smaller or mislocalized due to contour completion. Reports systematic biases in the perceived spatial location of occluded vertices.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Tess White, Chidera J. Abiakam, Drew G. Asborno, Jacob Crull, Chloe Leroy, Andrew Piotrowski, Elka Piotter, Madalyn C. Sawatzky, Lars Strother, Gideon Paul Caplovitz

papers.title: Invalid Trials Are Not Required to Observe Neural Correlates of Object-based Attention in Retinotopic Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the object-mediated allocation of attention is an obligatory, automatic process or a strategic behavior contingent on spatial uncertainty or the presence of invalidly cued targets. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and the known retinotopic organization of the human early visual cortex, the study measured blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal modulation at task-irrelevant, uncued locations within a cued object. Critically, the experiments employed a 100% valid cueing paradigm to eliminate strategic monitoring of non-cued locations. Statistically significant object-based attention (OBA) effects were observed in cortical areas V1, V2, and V3 during both 100% valid runs and runs containing invalid trials. The magnitude of these neural correlates was found to be comparable across conditions, providing strong evidence that object-based attentional spreading occurs automatically within the visual hierarchy and is not reliant on the inclusion of invalid trials in the experimental design.
papers.authors: Taissa K. Lytchenko, Marvin R. Maechler, Nathan H. Heller, Sharif Saleki, Peter U. Tse, Gideon P. Caplovitz

papers.title: New insights and a computational model for understanding induced motion revealed through novel variants of the Flying Bluebottle Illusion
papers.abstract: This paper explores the mechanisms of induced motion using the Flying Bluebottle Illusion, where a target's perceived trajectory is significantly distorted by the motion of surrounding context. The authors introduce the Dueling Orbit Illusion, a series of variants where a target moves in a circular orbit while surrounding inducers follow an offset orbital path. These stimuli reveal that the perceived orbiting motion of the target is 'pulled' and distorted in both direction and extent by the background motion. A straightforward computational model is proposed to quantify the magnitude of this contextual influence based on stimulus parameters. The findings suggest that induced motion reflects high-level integrative processes in the visual system and provide a predictive framework for understanding motion contrast and relative motion perception across diverse observer domains.
papers.authors: Ryan E. B. Mruczek, Gideon P. Caplovitz

0241.name: Giovanni Federico
0241.department: Department of Education, Psychology and Communication
0241.bio: Dr. Federico investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms that enable humans to understand, use, learn, share, delegate to, and be shaped by technologies, ranging from physical artefacts to digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and immersive sociotechnical systems. He combines experimental psychology, eye-tracking, structural and functional MRI, high-density EEG, and clinically oriented neuropsychological methods to develop a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology (Federico et al., 2026, Cognitive Neuroscience). This research programme links basic mechanisms to applied questions in education, ageing, digital inclusion, human-AI interaction, clinical neuropsychology, rehabilitation, and technology-informed assessment, with the broader aim of understanding how technological environments reshape human cognition.
0241.research_direction: Dr. Federico studies the neurocognitive mechanisms that enable humans to understand, use, learn, share, delegate to, and be shaped by technologies, from physical artefacts to digital platforms, artificial intelligence, and immersive sociotechnical systems. Combining experimental psychology, eye-tracking, structural and functional MRI, high-density EEG, and clinically oriented neuropsychological methods, he is developing a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology. His research programme links basic mechanisms to applied questions in education, ageing, digital inclusion, human-AI interaction, clinical neuropsychology, rehabilitation, and technology-informed assessment, with the broader aim of understanding how technological environments reshape human cognition.

papers.title: An integrated account for technological cognition
papers.abstract: Proposes a hub-and-processors framework for how the human brain creates, uses and adapts to technology, combining causal reasoning, semantic cognition, visuospatial skill, sensorimotor knowledge and social learning. Argues that mechanical and digital technologies recruit separable neural subsystems, and links technological cognition to embodied-cognition and extended-mind theories. Serves as the target article for a set of twelve commentaries.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, François Osiurak, Maria A. Brandimonte, Paola Marangolo, Ciro Rosario Ilardi

papers.title: Growing Technological Opacity and the Social Brain
papers.abstract: Develops a neurocognitive framework in which increasingly opaque technologies recruit the social brain, not only the technical brain, to support transmission of making processes, reliance on human experts, and interaction with machines as if they were intentional agents. Describes what drives switching between technical and social networks, such as perceptual cues, causal uncertainty and expertise.
papers.authors: François Osiurak, Giovanni Federico

papers.title: Two distinct neural pathways for mechanical versus digital technology
papers.abstract: In an fMRI experiment, watching mechanical tool use engaged dorsal and ventro-dorsal visual streams, whereas digital tools such as smartphones mainly engaged the ventral stream linked to conceptual and social cognition. Follow-up behavioural and priming experiments showed people readily anthropomorphize digital tools and that they activate the social brain. The results point to distinct neurocognitive systems for mechanical and digital technology.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, Mathieu Lesourd, Arnaud Fournel, Alexandre Bluet, Chloé Bryche, Maximilien Metaireau, Dario Baldi, Maria Antonella Brandimonte, Andrea Soricelli, Yves Rossetti, François Osiurak

papers.title: Left area PF as a neural marker of technical reasoning
papers.abstract: In 75 healthy adults, grey matter volume in left area PF of the supramarginal gyrus predicted individual differences in technical reasoning, independent of demographics, personality and total brain volume. Right prefrontal control regions tracked fluid intelligence and abstract reasoning but not technical reasoning. The authors suggest left PF acts as a technical hub within a fronto-temporo-parietal network.
papers.authors: Giovanni Federico, Ciro Rosario Ilardi, Paola Marangolo, Chloé Bryche, Maximilien Metaireau, Alexandre Bluet, Mathieu Lesourd, Yves Rossetti, François Osiurak

papers.title: Bringing cumulative technological culture beyond copying versus reasoning
papers.abstract: Challenges the dominant view that cumulative technological culture depends on high-fidelity copying without causal understanding. Reviewing tool-use literature, the authors show that reproducing others' tool actions requires causal understanding, and propose causal understanding as a key driver of cumulative culture.
papers.authors: François Osiurak, Nicolas Claidière, Giovanni Federico

0242.name: Gabriel Kreiman
0242.bio: Gabriel Kreiman is a Professor of Ophthalmology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at the F.M. Kirby Neurobiology Center at Boston Children's Hospital. Kreiman’s research integrates high-resolution intracranial neurophysiology in the human brain with computational modeling and psychophysics to study how neural circuits encode, process, and transmit information. This work addresses the neuronal correlates of visual object recognition, memory formation, and the development of biologically-inspired artificial intelligence models. Their current projects focus on elucidating the mechanisms of visual cognition—such as pattern completion and context-dependent recognition—while building AI architectures that mimic human-like visual perception and learning.
0242.research_direction: Dr. Kreiman has recently been investigating the neural underpinnings of high-level visual and linguistic processing alongside the closing gap between biological and artificial intelligence. Using invasive intracranial and single-neuron recordings in human patients, their recent work explores the timing and recurrent processing involved in the rapid learning of degraded images, the recognition of minimal visual configurations, and the modality-invariant representation of parts of speech. Concurrently, they are probing the limits of modern AI systems by benchmarking them against human behavior across diverse vision and language tasks. To test these computational models' capacity for high-level abstract scene understanding, they employ large-scale Turing-like tests and novel visual datasets featuring minimal counterfactual pairs to determine whether AI can truly comprehend graphical humor.

papers.title: Single-neuron encoding of rapidly learned visual information reshapes human perception
papers.abstract: Single neurons were recorded in human occipital cortex and medial temporal lobe while patients quickly learned to recognize degraded images. Neurons in both regions changed their responses to carry the newly learned image identity, and this tracked changes in what participants perceived. Population decoding suggested that occipital neurons needed extra processing time to resolve learned images, which delayed their responses. The work links fast learning to enduring changes in single-neuron codes in the human brain.
