papers.authors: Marcelo Armendariz, Julie Blumberg, Jed Singer, Franz Aiple, Jiye Kim, Nuria Dominguez-Iturza, Armin Brandt, Peter Reinacher, Andreas Schulze-Bonhage, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
papers.abstract: The study benchmarks how well 37 AI agents imitate humans on three language tasks (captioning, word association, conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection, attention prediction). It compares them with responses from 636 people and runs more than 72,000 Turing-like tests with human and AI judges. Current models can often pass as human, and simple AI judges detect AI output better than people do. Imitation ability correlates only weakly with standard performance metrics, so passing as human is a separate evaluation axis.
papers.authors: Mengmi Zhang, Elisa Pavarino, Xiao Liu, Giorgia Dellaferrera, Ankur Sikarwar, Caishun Chen, Marcelo Armendariz, Noga Mudrik, Prachi Agrawal, Spandan Madan, Mranmay Shetty, Andrei Barbu, Haochen Yang, Tanishq Kumar, Shui'Er Han, Aman Raj Singh, Meghna Sadwani, Stella Dellaferrera, Michele Pizzochero, Brandon Tang, Yew-Soon Ong, Hanspeter Pfister, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Invariant neural representation of parts of speech in the human brain
papers.abstract: Invasive recordings from 1,801 electrodes in 20 epilepsy patients were made while they read or heard two-word adjective-noun phrases. A small region of left lateral orbitofrontal cortex carried signals that separated adjectives from nouns. The signal held across visual and auditory presentation, across word length, order, frequency and meaning, and even across languages. This extends classic fronto-temporal models of language.
papers.authors: Pranav Misra, Yen-Cheng Shih, Hsiang-Yu Yu, Daniel Weisholtz, Joseph R. Madsen, Scellig Stone, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Neural correlates of minimal recognizable configurations in the human brain
papers.abstract: Intracranial recordings from epilepsy patients were used while they viewed minimal recognizable images, which are tiny image patches that can be recognized, and slightly reduced versions that cannot. Neural responses tracked the recognizable versus unrecognizable distinction, and the timing pointed to recurrent, top-down processing rather than a pure feedforward sweep. The results relate a classic psychophysical phenomenon to specific brain signals and to models of object recognition.
papers.authors: Antonino Casile, Aurelie Cordier, Jiye G. Kim, Andrea Cometa, Joseph R. Madsen, Scellig Stone, Guy Ben-Yosef, Shimon Ullman, William Anderson, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: HumorDB: Can AI understand graphical humor?
papers.abstract: The authors build a dataset of images, cartoons and sketches with minimal counterfactual pairs. In each pair, a small edit removes the humor, so models must grasp the visual joke rather than rely on surface cues. Human raters, vision-language models and vision-only networks are all tested. The models remain well below human performance, which shows a gap in abstract, high-level scene understanding.
papers.authors: Vedaant Jain, Felipe dos Santos Alves Feitosa, Gabriel Kreiman

0244.name: Gregory J. Zelinsky
0244.department: Department of Psychology, Department of Computer Science
0244.bio: Gregory J. Zelinsky is a Professor at Stony Brook University with appointments in the Departments of Psychology and Computer Science, specializing in the intersection of human vision and artificial intelligence. Zelinsky’s research focuses on the mechanisms of visual search, scene perception, and working memory, utilizing eye-tracking technology to record human oculomotor behavior. They integrate these behavioral data with image-based neurocomputational models to simulate and predict the spatiotemporal dynamics of attention and information selection. Their work aims to clarify how the brain represents object categories and manages visual guidance through the development of computational frameworks that mimic human visual processing.
0244.research_direction: Dr. Zelinsky has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying visual search, object recognition, and scene understanding. Their recent work explores how the visual system utilizes top-down, generative templates rather than fixed prototypes to guide attention, leveraging deep image synthesis and autoencoder networks to model robust target localization and recognition under occlusion. To further probe how humans process complex environments, they are using latent diffusion models to synthesize visual metamers of foveated scene representations and testing how well self-supervised Vision Transformers predict human object grouping and segmentation behaviors. Alongside these computational approaches, Dr. Zelinsky is also investigating the neurophysiology of active vision, recording from the primate superior colliculus to uncover how neural populations integrate target guidance with spatial fixation history during multi-target search tasks.

papers.title: Generating metamers of human scene understanding
papers.abstract: Introduces MetamerGen, a latent diffusion model that fuses low-resolution peripheral scene gist with high-resolution information from a viewer's fixations to synthesize images that stand in for what a person has understood about a scene. A dual-stream DINOv2-token representation handles the foveated inputs. Same-different behavioral experiments show the generated images are perceptually aligned with viewers' latent scene representations, especially when fixated regions are included.
papers.authors: Ritik Raina, Abe Leite, Alexandros Graikos, Seoyoung Ahn, Dimitris Samaras, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: Human-like Object Grouping in Self-supervised Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Builds a behavioral benchmark of over 1000 same/different object-judgment trials on natural scenes and tests many vision models on how well they predict human reaction times. DINO-trained transformers align best, and a new metric of object-centric structure in patch similarity predicts human segmentation behavior. Matching Gram matrices of supervised transformers further improves alignment.
papers.authors: Hossein Adeli, Seoyoung Ahn, Andrew Luo, Mengmi Zhang, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Gregory Zelinsky

papers.title: Guiding attention during search using generative target template matching
papers.abstract: Argues that attention in visual search is guided by generative templates that are shaped by the current visual input rather than fixed prototypes. Using deep image synthesis to build input-specific templates, the authors show they localize targets better in naturalistic arrays and capture human search efficiency, fixation probability and guidance toward similar non-targets.
papers.authors: Seoyoung Ahn, Hossein Adeli, Gregory Zelinsky

papers.title: Multiple patterns of selectivity in superior colliculus control visual search
papers.abstract: Recordings from monkey superior colliculus during a multi-target grid search show that neurons carry mixed signals combining target guidance with a history of previously fixated locations. The results indicate that SC integrates these control signals to direct efficient search, informing competing theories of neural information integration.
papers.authors: Abe Leite, Hossein Adeli, Robert M. McPeek, Gregory J. Zelinsky

papers.title: The attentive reconstruction of objects facilitates robust object recognition
papers.abstract: Proposes that the visual system aids recognition by reconstructing the object it hypothesizes to be present and using that reconstruction as a top-down attentional template. Built on autoencoder networks, the model recovers objects under noise and occlusion and improves robustness of recognition beyond feedforward networks, with behavioral and neural parallels.
papers.authors: Seoyoung Ahn, Hossein Adeli, Gregory J. Zelinsky

0246.name: Guido Maiello
0246.bio: Guido Maiello is a Lecturer at the University of Southampton specializing in the neural and computational mechanisms of visual-motor integration. They utilize psychophysics, eye-tracking, functional MRI, and virtual reality to investigate how the human visual system facilitates actions like grasping and object manipulation in 3D space. Maiello's research examines how observers judge grasp quality and integrate multi-sensory cues—including shape, material, and depth—to plan and execute motor tasks. Their work also explores the impact of visual impairments on hand-eye coordination and the development of image-computable models for visual shape similarity.
0246.research_direction: Dr. Maiello has recently been investigating the neural, behavioral, and computational mechanisms underlying visual perception and visuomotor control. Their recent work explores the sensorimotor transformations of visually guided grasping, using fMRI and representational similarity analysis to map how cortical networks represent grasp axis, object size, and mass during action planning versus execution. Alongside these neural studies, they are examining the behavioral kinematics of natural object manipulation to determine whether classic two-digit precision-grip findings generalize to unconstrained, multidigit grasping. Beyond motor control, they use psychophysics to assess how normal aging and glaucoma impact binocular disparity sensitivity and depth integration across the visual field. Furthermore, their theoretical research examines how biological brains might leverage unsupervised and self-supervised learning principles to build useful sensory representations from unstructured input.

papers.title: Does precision grip research extend to unconstrained, multidigit grasping?
papers.abstract: Most grasping studies use a two-digit precision grip, so the authors asked whether their findings hold when people may use any fingers. Participants grasped brass and wood objects either with a precision grip or freely. When free, they mostly chose multidigit grasps, yet in both conditions grasps shifted toward the center of mass and became more variable when grasp factors conflicted. The thumb and index finger landed in the same places regardless of extra fingers, implying that precision-grip results generalize to natural grasping.
papers.authors: Fabrizio Lepori, Frieder T. Hartmann, Kira I. Dehn, Manuela Chessa, Roland W. Fleming, Guido Maiello

papers.title: Distinct Neural Components of Visually Guided Grasping during Planning and Execution
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and representational similarity analysis, the study separates the brain signals for grasp axis, grasp size, and object mass while people plan and then execute grasps on L-shaped wood and brass objects. Grasp axis was represented in dorsal-stream regions during planning, grasp size moved from ventral areas to premotor cortex, and mass appeared mainly during execution. Premotor cortex also carried predictions of grasp comfort, with ventral cortex carrying comfort during execution, tracing the sensorimotor transformations behind grasping.
papers.authors: Lina K. Klein, Guido Maiello, Kevin Stubbs, Daria Proklova, Juan Chen, Vivian C. Paulun, Jody C. Culham, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Unsupervised learning in biological brains
papers.abstract: A single-author perspective on how brains can learn useful representations from sensory input without explicit labels or rewards. It reviews the computational principles and neural evidence for unsupervised learning and connects them to modern machine-learning ideas about self-supervised objectives.
papers.authors: Guido Maiello

papers.title: Despite Impaired Binocular Function, Binocular Disparity Integration Across the Visual Field Is Spared in Normal Aging and Glaucoma
papers.abstract: Psychophysics in glaucoma patients, age-matched and young controls measured disparity sensitivity across spatial frequencies and visual-field sectors, including full-field versus annular stimuli, and compared results with models of disparity integration. Glaucoma reduced disparity sensitivity in both central and peripheral vision, contrary to the view that central vision is spared. Nevertheless, integration across the field stayed near-optimal at low spatial frequencies, so patients make good use of their remaining binocular signals.
papers.authors: Guido Maiello, MiYoung Kwon

0247.name: Guillaume S Masson
0247.department: Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT)
0247.main_research_area: Visual motion processing and oculomotor control
0247.bio: Guillaume S. Masson is a neuroscientist and former director of the Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT) who researches the neural mechanisms of visual motion perception and eye movement control. Masson’s work focuses on how the brain integrates and segments local motion signals to generate reflexive and pursuit oculomotor responses, often employing short-latency ocular following as a model system. Using a multi-scale approach that combines human psychophysics, non-human primate electrophysiology, and Bayesian computational modeling, Masson investigates how nonlinear interactions within cortical areas V1 and MT facilitate visual inference under uncertainty. Their current research explores the role of predictive signals and environmental statistics in shaping the spatiotemporal dynamics of sensory integration for active vision.
0247.research_direction: Dr. Masson has recently been studying how the visual system builds perceptual and eye-movement responses to moving, naturalistic input. Their work includes developing a real-time generative toolbox for synthesizing dynamic textures whose orientation, spatial-frequency, and speed statistics can be controlled precisely, which lets them probe motion processing with well-defined stimuli. They have also been exploring whether visual search decisions can be explained by an information-theoretic strategy of prioritizing compression of sensory input. In addition, their recent work asks whether repeated smooth-pursuit tracking can correct the bias the aperture problem introduces into initial eye movements, linking perceptual error to sensorimotor learning.

papers.title: Sensorimotor learning compensates for irreducible perceptual bias
papers.abstract: Tests whether repeated smooth-pursuit tracking of tilted Gabor patches can correct the initial pursuit bias caused by the aperture problem. Initial error stays unchanged after multi-day training, but later error correction becomes faster for the trained orientation only.
papers.authors: Cléo Schoeffel, Guilhem Ibos, Anna Montagnini, Guillaume S. Masson

papers.title: DynTex: A real-time generative model of dynamic naturalistic luminance textures
papers.abstract: The study introduces DynTex, an open-source toolbox designed for the real-time synthesis of Motion Clouds (MCs), which are stochastic dynamic textures with parametrically controlled spatiotemporal statistics. MCs are characterized by their energy distribution in Fourier space, particularly across orientation, spatial frequency, and speed. The generative model employs a frame-by-frame autoregressive (AR) process to ensure temporal continuity and allows for precise manipulation of bandwidth parameters. By implementing the synthesis on GPU architectures, the authors achieve high-frame-rate rendering suitable for psychophysical and neurophysiological experiments. The paper demonstrates the toolbox's utility in bridging the gap between simple synthetic stimuli (e.g., gratings, dots) and complex natural videos, providing a calibrated method for probing hierarchical visual motion processing.
papers.authors: Andrew Isaac Meso, Jonathan Vacher, Nikos Gekas, Pascal Mamassian, Laurent U Perrinet, Guillaume S Masson

papers.title: Prioritizing Compression Explains Human Perceptual Decisions in Visual Search
papers.abstract: This study proposes an information-theoretic account of human decision-making in visual search tasks. The authors hypothesize that the visual system employs a strategy aimed at prioritizing data compression to handle the high dimensionality of sensory input. By analyzing behavioral data from search experiments where target-distractor similarity and set size were systematically manipulated, the researchers show that accuracy and reaction time distributions are well-modeled by a framework that minimizes informational redundancy. The results suggest that perceptual bottlenecks in visual search are not solely due to limited neural capacity but represent an adaptive optimization for processing efficiency. This compression-based approach provides a unified explanation for set-size effects and search asymmetries in complex visual scenes.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP)
papers.authors: Andrew Isaac Meso, Anna Montagnini, Jason Bell, Guillaume S Masson

0248.name: Halely Balaban
0248.lab_name: Cognitive Dynamics and Adaptability Lab (CDA Lab)
0248.main_research_area: visual working memory and intuitive physics
0248.bio: Halely Balaban is an Assistant Professor of Cognitive Psychology and director of the Cognitive Dynamics and Adaptability Lab at The Open University of Israel. Balaban’s research examines the relationship between visual working memory and commonsense physical reasoning, focusing on how the mind maintains and updates representations of dynamic objects in visual scenes. Using a multi-method approach that integrates EEG, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling, Balaban has analyzed how intuitive physics guides tracking mechanisms and how mental simulation is constrained by serial capacity limits. Their work identifies bidirectional links between representational content and the pointer systems underlying human visual cognition.
0248.research_direction: Dr. Balaban's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying visual working memory, intuitive physics, and mental simulation. They have recently been investigating the working memory pointer system that maps internal representations to external objects, using behavioral reset costs to determine whether these pointers are governed by physical objecthood or spatiotemporal continuity. Alongside this, their research examines how intuitive physical expectations guide online visual processing, utilizing EEG to capture moment-by-moment neural responses to physically impossible scene dynamics and theorizing a division between cognitive physics and graphics engines. Finally, Dr. Balaban has been testing the capacity limits of dynamic mental imagery, employing novel behavioral tracking paradigms to ask how many moving objects people can simultaneously simulate in the mind's eye.

papers.title: Working memory's pointer system is governed by physical objecthood, not spatiotemporal information
papers.abstract: Visual working memory relies on pointers that map each stored representation to an object in the world so that it can be updated when the object changes; when the mapping breaks, representations are reset and changes become hard to detect. This single-author study tests whether pointers are assigned by physical objecthood or by spatiotemporal continuity. The results indicate that objecthood, rather than spatiotemporal information alone, governs pointer assignment.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban

papers.title: The capacity limits of moving objects in the imagination
papers.abstract: Across nine pre-registered experiments (N=313) using a new Imagined Objects Tracking task, the authors ask how many moving objects people can simulate in the mind's eye. With one object, estimates track ground truth, but with two or more, behavior is best explained by a serial model that simulates only one object at a time while others are frozen or guessed. The work shows a severe, serial capacity limit on mental simulation that is much tighter than the limit for tracking objects in direct perception.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Tomer D. Ullman

papers.title: Physics versus graphics as an organizing dichotomy in cognition
papers.abstract: The paper argues that intuitive mental simulation splits into two components borrowed from engineered simulation systems: a physics engine that predicts dynamics and a graphics engine that renders appearance. The authors show why this division of labor arises naturally in any cognitive system and use it to organize a range of findings across perception, memory, imagery and reasoning. They also outline predictions and open questions for the framework.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Tomer D. Ullman

papers.title: Visual working memory's pointer system: Past, present, and future
papers.abstract: A review of the notion that visual working memory representations are accessed via one-to-one indexes to objects in the environment. It traces classic findings, stresses the distinction between pointers and representational content, and describes a recent approach that uses the cost of resetting to probe pointer operation, ending with open questions for future work.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Roy Luria

papers.title: Electrophysiology reveals that intuitive physics guides visual tracking and working memory
papers.abstract: Two EEG experiments used short videos similar to those in infant and AI intuitive-physics studies to ask whether physical expectations shape moment-by-moment visual processing. Neural signatures of tracking and working memory differed when objects behaved in physically impossible ways, showing that intuitive physics guides online scene processing even when no explicit physical judgment is required.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Kevin A. Smith, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Tomer D. Ullman

0249.name: Haluk Öǧmen
0249.bio: Haluk Öğmen is a Professor and Senior Associate Dean at the University of Denver’s Ritchie School of Engineering and Computer Science, where they direct the Perceptual and Cognitive Dynamics Laboratory. Öğmen’s research focuses on reverse-engineering the human visual system to analyze how the brain processes information across space and time, specifically through the study of visual masking and motion perception. By employing computational neuroscience and psychophysical methodologies, they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying non-retinotopic representations and the interaction between attention and sensory memory. Their technical work includes theoretical research on the microgenesis of conscious vision and the development of neural models that account for the temporal dynamics of human perception.
0249.research_direction: Dr. Öǧmen has recently been investigating how the visual system establishes spatial and temporal reference frames to process both static objects and dynamic scenes. Their recent work explores how structural cues, such as symmetry and elongation, guide the formation of internal reference axes for unfamiliar shapes during mental rotation tasks in virtual reality. In the motion domain, they are developing neural network models and conducting psychophysical experiments to study how the brain performs motion vector decomposition, specifically examining how Gestalt principles are used to extract relative-motion percepts from retinotopic signals in classic paradigms like the point-walker display. Broadening their methodological focus to applied clinical tools, Dr. Öǧmen is also exploring how topological data analysis—specifically persistent homology—can be leveraged to extract spatio-temporal features from raw eye-tracking recordings to screen for neural disorders like dyslexia and ADHD.

papers.title: The roles of symmetry and elongation in developing reference frames
papers.abstract: The study asks whether object symmetry and elongation determine which internal reference axis the brain adopts when viewing unfamiliar shapes. Observers learned novel textured shapes in virtual reality, removing screen-edge and familiar-object cues, and judged whether each was original or mirror-flipped. Reaction times followed mental-rotation-like linear functions of angular deviation from the axis defined by symmetry and/or elongation, revealing how reference frames are formed for new objects and how the two cues combine.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Haluk Öğmen

papers.title: Leveraging Persistent Homology of Eye Movements for Neural Disorder Screening
papers.abstract: This preprint proposes extracting topological features from raw eye-tracking recordings using persistent homology, a topological data analysis tool, instead of hand-crafted eye-movement metrics. Using only these spatio-temporal topological features and a very small perceptron classifier, the approach shows promising discrimination of dyslexia and ADHD from controls, and is designed to generalize across different eye-tracking tasks.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Shaoying Wang, Haluk Öğmen

papers.title: A neural model for vector decomposition and relative-motion perception
papers.abstract: The authors present a neural network in which the Gestalt common-fate principle is used to pick the direction and speed of a reference frame from retinotopic motion detectors. Motion vectors are then decomposed relative to that frame, giving relative-motion percepts. The model reproduces classic three-dot, rotating-wheel and point-walker displays and predicts curved target trajectories in the three-dot paradigm, which two psychophysical experiments confirmed.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Haluk Öğmen

0252.name: Hans Op de Beeck
0252.bio: Op de Beeck is a Professor in the Department of Brain & Cognition and Dean of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at KU Leuven. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object recognition and the representational plasticity associated with learning and expertise. Methodologically, the lab integrates human functional neuroimaging (fMRI) and psychophysics with rodent electrophysiology and computational modeling using deep artificial neural networks. Op de Beeck examines the topographic organization of the ventral visual stream and how neural representations are altered in neurodevelopmental disorders and following brain damage.
0252.research_direction: Dr. Op de Beeck's recent work explores the multidimensional nature of high-level object representations in the human brain. Using a combination of fMRI, behavioral tasks, and deep neural networks, they have recently been investigating how the occipitotemporal cortex organizes visual object space, testing whether this architecture is driven by shape-based features or higher-level categorical distinctions. Beyond basic object recognition, their research examines how neural representational geometry is altered by domain-specific expertise and probes how well multivariate cortical activity can predict distinct categorization behaviors. Furthermore, they are currently expanding these neural and computational frameworks to investigate the diverse perceptual, cognitive, and appraisal dimensions that underlie human aesthetic experiences.

papers.title: Rethinking neuroaesthetics: Toward a multidimensional and integrative science of aesthetic experience
papers.abstract: A Neuron perspective arguing that aesthetic experience should not be reduced to a single dimension such as beauty or reward. The authors propose a multidimensional framework spanning perception, conception and appraisal, integrating behavioral, neural and computational (deep network) approaches, and outline directions for a more integrative neuroaesthetics.
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Johan Wagemans, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: Low-dimensional and optimised representations of high-level information in the expert brain
papers.abstract: Compares how expert chess players and novices represent complex domain-specific stimuli in the brain and in models. The work shows that expertise compresses high-level information into low-dimensional, optimised neural codes, linking learning and expertise to representational geometry.
papers.authors: Andrea I. Costantino, Artem Platonov, Felipe Fontana Vieira, Emily Van Hove, Merim Bilalic, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: Can Category-selective Cortex Predict Categorization Behavior?
papers.abstract: Tests whether the multivariate activity in category-selective regions of occipito-temporal cortex can predict categorization behavior using a distance-to-bound approach. The study relates region-specific fMRI activity to performance across categorization tasks to clarify where and for which tasks such brain-behavior links appear.
papers.authors: Timothee Maniquet, Huangxu Fang, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Hans Op de Beeck

papers.title: Understanding Human Object Vision: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Representations
papers.abstract: An Annual Review that synthesizes recent behavioral, neuroscientific and computational work showing object vision is a multidimensional representational space. It argues that this complexity should be understood in relation to the wide range of behavioral goals humans pursue, and that core object recognition may be less central than assumed.
papers.authors: Stefania Bracci, Hans P. Op de Beeck

papers.title: Category Trumps Shape as an Organizational Principle of Object Space in Human Occipitotemporal Cortex
papers.abstract: Pits two proposals for object space organization in ventral visual cortex, one based on aspect ratio (stubby versus spiky) and one on face/body categories, using fMRI and a deep generative network. Both brain and network representations reflected animacy and category clusters but not aspect ratio, favoring category over shape.
papers.authors: Elahe' Yargholi, Hans Op de Beeck

0253.name: Heather Lucas
0253.bio: Heather D. Lucas is an Assistant Professor at Louisiana State University whose research focuses on the neurocognitive mechanisms of episodic and relational memory. Lucas's work utilizes event-related potentials (ERPs) and eye-tracking to investigate how individuals navigate memory constraints and employ strategic behaviors during information gathering and encoding. Lucas examines these processes across the lifespan and in clinical populations, including individuals with traumatic brain injury and neurodivergent adults, to understand how neural and cognitive factors influence learning outcomes.
0253.research_direction: Dr. Lucas has recently been studying how people encode and retrieve memories, and how attention and eye movements shape what gets remembered. Their recent work asks how anxiety, induced by threat of shock, disrupts memory by reducing how people organize information by meaning. They have also examined how gaze patterns during viewing support memory for spatial layouts, and whether visual working memory compares items as whole objects or as separate features, using EEG. A further line of their work looks at learning and communication in autistic adults, including whether retrieval practice with feedback helps them learn and how they interpret hand gestures.

papers.title: Examining the Roles of Retrieval Practice and Post-Retrieval Feedback in Learning Among Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Retrieval practice robustly enhances declarative memory retention, with performance further optimized when followed by informative feedback; however, empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of retrieval-based learning and corrective feedback in autistic individuals has been lacking. In two experiments, the authors examined retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback on associative memory in autistic and neurotypical adult cohorts. Participants encoded pairs of semantically unrelated words and subsequently reviewed them across practice conditions comprising retrieval practice with feedback, retrieval practice without feedback, or restudy. Learning modalities (auditory in Experiment 1; visual in Experiment 2) and practice formats (cued recall vs. four-alternative forced choice) were varied across experiments, with final retention assessed via cued recall. In both experiments, post-retrieval feedback yielded robust mnemonic benefits across both diagnostic groups, disproportionately benefiting items recalled incorrectly on initial practice. Additionally, Experiment 2 confirmed a significant testing effect—retrieval practice outperformed passive restudy even in the absence of feedback across autistic and non-autistic cohorts alike. These findings confirm that retrieval practice coupled with corrective feedback represents a highly viable and generalizable instructional strategy for autistic adult learners.
papers.authors: Brianna E. Cairney, Eileen Haebig, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: The impact of threat of shock on memory for threat-irrelevant information: Evidence for a role of reduced semantic organization
papers.abstract: The mechanisms through which acute state anxiety modulates episodic memory encoding remain controversial, particularly with respect to threat-irrelevant, neutral stimuli. Across two experiments utilizing a threat-of-shock paradigm, this study investigated whether anticipatory anxiety degrades episodic retention by disrupting semantic-organizational encoding strategies. In Experiment 1, participants encoded and freely recalled lists of semantically unrelated neutral words under alternating conditions of shock threat versus safety. Threat blocks resulted in significantly diminished recall accuracy alongside reduced semantic clustering, quantified via a semantic path length metric that assesses vector distance across consecutively recalled words. In Experiment 2, semantically related word lists were used to control for block-order dynamics. Threat of shock again induced significant decrements in recall volume and elicited longer, less organized semantic path lengths. Crucially, mediation analyses confirmed that anxiety-induced shifts toward longer semantic path lengths mediated the negative relationship between autonomic physiological arousal (indexed via skin conductance responses) and downstream free recall performance. These findings indicate that attenuated semantic executive control serves as a key neurocognitive mechanism underlying the adverse effects of acute anxiety on declarative memory formation.
papers.authors: Felicia M. Chaisson, Christopher R. Cox, Amber M. Alford, Lauryn M. Burleigh, Steven G. Greening, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: Interpretations of meaningful and ambiguous hand gestures in autistic and non-autistic adults: A norming study
papers.abstract: Co-speech and silent manual gestures are integral to human communication, yet existing findings on how individuals on the autism spectrum process and assign semantic meaning to gestures remain equivocal. To provide a standardized, cross-population stimulus set, this study created and normed an open database of 162 silent gesture video clips comprising iconic, emblem, and ambiguous manual gestures. Equal cohorts of autistic (N = 40) and non-autistic (N = 40) adult raters evaluated each clip for semantic meaningfulness on continuous rating scales and provided open-ended, single-word descriptors. Ratings of meaningfulness exhibited exceptional concordance across diagnostic groups (r > 0.90 across all stimuli). Analysis of naming data, however, demonstrated greater naming variability and lexical dispersion among autistic participants compared to neurotypical peers. This indicates that perceived meaningfulness remains intact in autistic adults, and that group discrepancies in gesture tasks are more likely driven by lexical access or semantic selection processes rather than atypical core semantic gesture processing. The normed database and accompanying kinematic profiles provide an open-science resource for multimodal communication research.
papers.authors: Brianna E. Cairney, Stanley H. West, Eileen Haebig, Christopher R. Cox, Heather D. Lucas

papers.title: Dynamic interactions between memory and viewing behaviors: Insights from dyadic modeling of eye movements
papers.abstract: Visual memory representations are constructed through active oculomotor exploration, but the temporal trajectory over which specific gaze metrics support encoding within individual study epochs remains unclear. The authors applied structural equation modeling via dyadic path models to evaluate spatial reconstruction accuracy based on the temporal dynamics between scanpath entropy (spatial dispersion of gaze) and item-to-item saccadic transition frequency. Trials were partitioned into early and late temporal windows to model direct contributions to memory as well as indirect pathways where early-trial viewing cascaded into alterations of late-trial viewing. Across analyses, sustained low scanpath entropy throughout the entire trial predicted superior spatial memory precision. In contrast, the functional contribution of item-to-item transitions shifted across time: higher transition rates during early-trial viewing negatively predicted memory performance, whereas late-trial transition frequency positively predicted memory accuracy. Early oculomotor sampling patterns also indirectly mediated subsequent recall accuracy via downstream effects on late-trial exploration. Furthermore, individual differences in standardized memory ability predicted gaze effectiveness, with oculomotor dynamics partially mediating this relationship. The model demonstrated strong goodness-of-fit upon validation in an independent replication dataset, emphasizing that the chronological order and dynamic coordination of eye movements critically govern encoding success.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Heather D. Lucas, Ana M. Daugherty, Edward McAuley, Arthur F. Kramer, Neal J. Cohen

papers.title: Behavioral and electrophysiological evidence for the flexible recruitment of feature- and object-based processing in visual working memory comparison
papers.abstract: The architectural debate regarding whether visual working memory (VWM) comparisons operate over integrated object tokens or isolated feature dimensions remains unresolved. Prior event-related potential (ERP) studies examining change detection have documented that the N200—an electrophysiological marker of VWM comparison—is modulated by both task-relevant and task-irrelevant attribute changes, suggesting an obligatory object-based processing bias. To determine whether VWM comparison can operate in a strictly feature-based mode, the authors introduced task constraints designed to isolate relevant features: an initial block containing purely task-relevant alterations followed by a second block featuring both relevant and irrelevant changes, alongside arrays manipulating within-display feature repetition. In Block 2, N200 amplitudes were selectively sensitive to task-relevant feature changes and remained unaffected by task-irrelevant alterations, regardless of intra-display repetition status, demonstrating isolated feature-based comparison processing. However, downstream behavioral performance and N200 latency metrics revealed that task-irrelevant variations were nevertheless processed when no relevant change was detected. These findings demonstrate that VWM comparison is computationally flexible and dynamically shifts between feature-based and object-based processing architectures depending on task goals and prior context.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Saltzmann, Katherine C. Moen, Brandon Eich, Felicia M. Chaisson, Gaojie Fan, Rebecca R. Goldstein, Melissa R. Beck, Heather D. Lucas

0254.name: Heiko H. Schütt
0254.department: Department of Behavioural and Cognitive Sciences
0254.bio: Heiko H. Schütt is an Associate Professor at the University of Luxembourg specializing in the development of mechanistic models for visual perception and cognitive behavior. Their research integrates deep neural networks, Bayesian inference, and efficient coding to explain human visual processing, particularly regarding eye movements and object recognition in natural scenes. Schütt developed open-source computational toolboxes, including Psignifit 4 for psychometric function fitting and the rsatoolbox for representational similarity analysis. Their work focuses on creating models that bridge behavioral and neurophysiological data while advancing statistical methods for evaluating representational geometries.
0254.research_direction: Dr. Schütt has recently been developing advanced statistical methods and theoretical models to better understand and decode neural population responses. Their recent work explores how to rigorously compare computational models against brain data, designing generative modeling techniques to disentangle multivariate signal from noise in large-scale neural recordings. To support these efforts, they are building open-source software and improving statistical inference for representational similarity analysis (RSA) to ensure that model evaluations generalize reliably across both novel subjects and novel stimulus conditions. Beyond methodological development, they are also investigating normative theories of dopamine physiology, testing whether efficient coding principles can explain the heterogeneous tuning properties of reward prediction error neurons.

papers.title: A Python Toolbox for Representational Similarity Analysis
papers.abstract: Presents rsatoolbox, an open-source Python package that brings together recent advances in representational similarity analysis, including improved distance measures, model evaluators, and statistical inference methods. It lets researchers characterize neural representational geometries and test neural network models against brain data. Schütt is the senior author and maintainer of the toolbox.
papers.authors: Jasper J. F. van den Bosch, Tal Golan, Benjamin Peters, JohnMark Taylor, Mahdiyar Shahbazi, Baihan Lin, Ian Charest, Jörn Diedrichsen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Marieke Mur, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Disentangling signal and noise in neural responses through generative modeling
papers.abstract: Proposes Generative Modeling of Signal and Noise (GSN), which models neural responses to repeated events as the sum of a multivariate signal distribution and a noise distribution. The signal covariance is estimated by removing the estimated noise covariance from the trial-averaged response covariance, allowing signal and noise to be studied separately. Demonstrated on simulated data and large fMRI datasets, where it improves estimates of signal structure and enables denoising.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Jacob S. Prince, Thomas Gebhart, Greta Tuckute, Jingyang Zhou, Thomas Naselaris, Heiko H. Schütt

papers.title: Reward prediction error neurons implement an efficient code for reward
papers.abstract: Asks whether the response properties of dopaminergic reward prediction error neurons can be explained by efficient coding. The model shows that a population code optimized to transmit information about the reward distribution reproduces the observed heterogeneity of tuning across neurons and the shape of their reward responses. The work links normative coding theory to dopamine physiology.
papers.authors: Heiko H. Schütt, Dongjae Kim, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Statistical inference on representational geometries
papers.abstract: Introduces inference methods for testing and comparing models that predict the representational geometry (distances among stimulus representations) of a neural population. The approach extends cross-validation and bootstrapping to two factors, so that model accuracy estimates are not inflated by overfitting to either subjects or stimulus conditions, and comparisons generalize to both new subjects and new conditions. The methods are validated in simulations and applied to fMRI and electrophysiology data.
papers.authors: Heiko H Schütt, Alexander D Kipnis, Jörn Diedrichsen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

0255.name: Heleen A. Slagter
0255.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology
0255.bio: Heleen A. Slagter is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and the Director of the Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (iBBA). Slagter's research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive functions such as selective attention and conscious perception, focusing on how these processes are modulated by mental training and prior experience. Utilizing EEG, fMRI, and computational modeling, they examine the plasticity of the predictive brain and how practices like meditation can alter information processing and self-awareness. Slagter has received VIDI and ERC Starting and Consolidator grants for this work.
0255.research_direction: Dr. Slagter has recently been investigating the tight bidirectional coupling between motor action and visual cognition, alongside foundational questions about conscious perception and sensory sensitivity. Their recent work explores whether intended manual action plans dynamically reshape visual feature representations within working memory, and if implicit spatial distractor suppression is grounded in viewer-centric coordinates. Using EEG with time-resolved decoding and representational similarity analysis, they are also examining whether predicted sensory outcomes are inherently bound into the neural computations used to select goal-directed actions. Finally, their meta-analytical and theoretical research probes the validity of classical EEG markers for visual awareness, such as the visual awareness negativity, and frames trait-level sensory processing sensitivity through a predictive coding lens.

papers.title: The neural correlates of consciousness: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the visual awareness negativity and P3b
papers.abstract: This registered-report meta-analysis pooled EEG studies of visual awareness to test whether two candidate markers of conscious perception, the visual awareness negativity and the P3b, are necessary and sufficient for awareness. Across 117 studies, both signals were reliably larger for seen stimuli, but the P3b vanished under task-irrelevant conditions and the VAN persisted even when stimuli went unseen. The authors conclude that neither component is a clean marker of consciousness and discuss how study quality and theory-driven design choices shape the evidence.
papers.authors: Brendan T. Hutchinson, James E. Pustejovsky, Kavindu Bandara, Hugh McGovern, Jolene Cox, Alexandra Voce, Michael Pitts, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Sensory processing sensitivity: theory, evidence, and directions
papers.abstract: This review synthesises the fast-growing literature on sensory processing sensitivity, a trait marked by heightened reactivity to and deeper processing of stimuli, covering how it is measured, how it relates to other personality traits, and its positive and negative outcomes. It proposes a predictive-processing account in which high-sensitivity brains consistently assign high precision to incoming sensory signals. The account links cognitive, neural and computational levels and points to future tests.
papers.authors: Corina U. Greven, MacKenzie D. Trupp, Judith R. Homberg, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Goal-directed action selection relies on conjunctive representations that bind goals, actions and expected sensory outcomes
papers.abstract: Using EEG with time-resolved decoding and representational similarity analysis, this study asked whether predicted sensory outcomes are part of the neural computation that selects goal-directed actions. Participants learned new action-outcome contingencies and chose actions to produce specific outcomes. The strength of high-dimensional conjunctive codes that included the anticipated outcome predicted trial-by-trial reaction times, supporting the idea that actions are selected to control expected sensory input.
papers.authors: Jet Lageman, Atsushi Kikumoto, David Badre, Johannes Jacobus Fahrenfort, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Grounding distractor inhibition in action control: Implicit distractor-location learning is viewer dependent
papers.abstract: Spatial attention is known to include an action component; this work asks whether learned suppression of distractors is likewise tied to the viewer. In three experiments (one preregistered) with a visual search task on a tabletop monitor, participants changed standing position while a salient distractor appeared more often at one location. The results indicate that implicit distractor-location learning is viewer dependent, so suppression is grounded in action-relevant coordinates.
papers.authors: Litian Chen, Freek van Ede, Chris Jungerius, Heleen A. Slagter

papers.title: Action similarity warps visual feature space in working memory
papers.abstract: In two experiments (one preregistered) using an interactive working-memory task, participants memorised two bar orientations and were then told which manual action they would use to report each. Orientations that looked alike were remembered as more different when tied to different action plans than to the same plan. A control experiment showed this is a true change in the visual representation rather than motor bias, so intended actions reshape what is held in visual working memory.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Caterina Trentin, Luigi Falanga, Jannik Jeske, Christian N. L. Olivers, Heleen A. Slagter

0256.name: Hendrikje Nienborg
0256.bio: Nienborg is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute and the head of the Visual Decision Making Section. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms that integrate sensory signals with cognitive factors such as attention, motivation, and prior knowledge to guide behavior. Using large-scale electrophysiological recordings, optogenetics, and computational modeling, their lab explores how cortical circuits process information from central and peripheral visual fields. Nienborg’s work examines how decision-related feedback is broadcast across the visual cortex and the influence of spontaneous movements on sensory encoding in primates.
0256.research_direction: Dr. Nienborg has recently been investigating how behavior, physiological states, and motor actions influence visual processing and decision-making across multiple mammalian species. Their recent work explores the sources of movement-related signals in early visual cortex, recording from macaques to determine whether spontaneous behaviors drive cortical activity via internal state signals—as often observed in rodents—or primarily through movement-induced retinal image shifts. In the context of 3D orienting, they are also examining binocular depth processing in the primate superior colliculus by mapping how these neurons selectively respond to natural versus unnatural disparities. Beyond sensory encoding, Dr. Nienborg is studying perceptual decision-making to understand how decoupling a sensory choice from a fixed motor action alters choice-history biases and sequence learning in non-human primates. Finally, their research investigates extreme forms of structural neuroplasticity by using Golgi staining to track how the dendritic morphology of V1 pyramidal neurons changes as ground squirrels cycle between the torpor and arousal phases of hibernation.

papers.title: Short-Latency Signals in the Primate Superior Colliculus Specialized for Real-World Disparities
papers.abstract: The study asks whether the primate superior colliculus carries binocular depth signals suited to guiding 3D orienting. Disparity-selective neurons were common, appeared at short latency and needed no task training. Responses were selective for naturally occurring (correlated) disparities and much less so for unnatural anti-correlated ones, unlike early visual cortex, in both superficial and deeper saccade-related layers.
papers.authors: Incheol Kang, Gongchen Yu, Leor N. Katz, Richard J. Krauzlis, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Decoupling Choice from Motor Response Reduces Choice-History Effects
papers.abstract: Macaques performed two perceptual decision tasks, each with a coupled version (fixed choice-to-action mapping) and an uncoupled version (mapping varied across trials). Choice-history biases were larger when choice and motor response were coupled, and uncoupling impaired learning of induced stimulus-sequence regularities. The work shows that choice-response coupling shapes how recent history guides behavior.
papers.authors: Sriram Thothathri, Bharath Chandra Talluri, S. Shushruth, Michael N. Shadlen, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Pronounced Neuroplasticity in the Primary Visual Cortex of the 13-Lined Ground Squirrel during Hibernation
papers.abstract: Using Golgi staining in hibernating and non-hibernating ground squirrels, the authors show that V1 layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons lose dendritic length and complexity during torpor. These changes fully reverse within about 1.5 hours of intertorpor arousal, implying rapid dendritic regrowth. No differences remained six months after the hibernation season.
papers.authors: Allison Fultz, Carlos A. Mejias-Aponte, Christina Jacob, Laura Castillo, Francisco M. Nadal-Nicolas, Yue Gao, Wei Li, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Is the impact of spontaneous movements on early visual cortex species specific?
papers.abstract: This review contrasts the strong movement-related signals seen in mouse visual cortex with the weak ones found in primates. It weighs candidate explanations such as behavioral state, slow neural drift, eccentricity and changes in retinal input. It also proposes a functional classification of the possible sources of movement-related signals to support cross-species comparisons during natural behavior.
papers.authors: Incheol Kang, Bharath Chandra Talluri, Jacob L. Yates, Cristopher M. Niell, Hendrikje Nienborg

papers.title: Activity in primate visual cortex is minimally driven by spontaneous movements
papers.abstract: The authors recorded from macaque visual areas V1, V2 and V3/V3A while tracking the animals' face and body movements, mirroring analyses used in mouse studies where spontaneous movements strongly drive visual cortex. In monkeys, movement-related modulation existed but was largely explained by movement-induced changes in the retinal image rather than by an internal movement signal. This suggests that primate early visual cortex is far less driven by spontaneous behavior than rodent cortex, pointing to species-specific sensorimotor strategies.
papers.authors: Bharath Chandra Talluri, Incheol Kang, Adam Lazere, Katrina R. Quinn, Nicholas Kaliss, Jacob L. Yates, Daniel A. Butts, Hendrikje Nienborg

0258.name: Herwig Baier
0258.institution: Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence
0258.bio: Herwig Baier is a Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence, where they investigate the functional architecture of neural circuits governing animal behavior. Baier's research employs larval zebrafish as a transparent vertebrate model, integrating genetic engineering, calcium imaging, and optogenetics to map sensory-to-motor transformations. The laboratory established large-scale behavioral screens and developed the Zebrafish Brain Atlas to classify neuronal cell types and their synaptic connectivity. Their current work explores the circuit-level logic of spatial attention, social interactions, and the influence of evolutionary processes on behavioral programs.
0258.research_direction: Dr. Baier has recently been investigating the neural and molecular architectures that drive visually guided behaviors across teleost fishes. Their recent work explores the functional organization of the zebrafish visual system by combining brain-wide transcriptomic atlases, two-photon imaging, and multiplexed gene expression mapping to understand how molecular cell types in regions like the optic tectum relate to specific visual tuning and morphological features. Expanding beyond established laboratory models, they are also studying comparative neuroethology, utilizing high-speed video and automated kinematic tracking to parse the diverse visual algorithms and motor syntax used during prey capture by cichlids and medaka. Furthermore, they are examining the cognitive foundations of complex spatial behaviors, investigating the neural circuitry and geometric templates that guide innate nest-building routines in shell-dwelling cichlids.

papers.title: Cognitive ethology of nest building in a shell-dwelling cichlid
papers.abstract: The study dissects nest building in the cichlid Lamprologus ocellatus, which modifies empty snail shells into shelters. Building unfolds as a chain of stimulus-response loops allowing restarts and shortcuts, shell attraction and final nest form are innate, and performance improves with experience. Shells must meet strict geometric criteria, and building engages brain regions homologous to mammalian hippocampus and neocortex, suggesting cognitive template matching.
papers.authors: Swantje Grätsch, Alessandro Dorigo, Vartika Agarwal, Ash V. Parker, Ivan Hernández Murcia, Manuel Stemmer, Abdelrahman Adel, Alex Jordan, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Transcriptomic neuron types vary topographically in function and morphology
papers.abstract: The authors built a transcriptional atlas of the larval zebrafish optic tectum, identifying more than 60 neuron types arranged in anatomical layers, and matched these to two-photon visual response measurements and single-neuron morphologies. Neurons within a single transcriptomic type turned out to differ in shape, connectivity and tuning depending on their position in the tectal volume. The work shows that position-dependent extrinsic factors subdivide molecularly defined cell types into functionally distinct subclusters.
papers.authors: Inbal Shainer, Johannes M. Kappel, Eva Laurell, Joseph C. Donovan, Martin W. Schneider, Enrico Kuehn, Irene Arnold-Ammer, Manuel Stemmer, Johannes Larsch, Herwig Baier

papers.title: Diverse prey capture strategies in teleost larvae
papers.abstract: The authors compared hunting behavior of larvae from four Lake Tanganyika and river cichlid species and medaka against zebrafish, using high-speed video and neural-network tracking of eyes and tail. Cichlids share basic features with zebrafish such as eye convergence and discrete capture bouts but have a broader movement repertoire, whereas medaka swim continuously while tracking prey. The results show how visually guided hunting syntax diverges across teleost lineages.
papers.authors: Duncan S. Mearns, Sydney A. Hunt, Martin W. Schneider, Ash V. Parker, Manuel Stemmer, Herwig Baier

papers.title: The Visual Systems of Zebrafish
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes the organization of the zebrafish visual system, from roughly 40 retinal ganglion cell types acting as matched feature filters, to the 12 retinorecipient areas and the nine-layered optic tectum. It describes topographic adaptation of the tectal map to visual scene statistics and dedicated multistation pathways for behaviors such as prey capture and loom avoidance. The authors argue that this labeled-line-like architecture serves adaptive behavior.
papers.authors: Herwig Baier, Ethan K. Scott

papers.title: A single-cell resolution gene expression atlas of the larval zebrafish brain
papers.abstract: Using multiplexed HCR in situ hybridization, the team mapped expression of a growing panel of marker genes across the larval zebrafish brain and registered the data to the Max Planck Zebrafish Brain atlas, allowing joint viewing of gene expression, single-neuron tracings and anatomical segmentations. Post hoc cfos labeling in freely swimming larvae mapped responses to prey and feeding. This revealed a previously unrecognized calb2a-expressing cluster in the secondary gustatory nucleus projecting to the hypothalamus.
papers.authors: Inbal Shainer, Enrico Kuehn, Eva Laurell, Mariam Al Kassar, Nouwar Mokayes, Shachar Sherman, Johannes Larsch, Martin Kunst, Herwig Baier

0260.name: Holger Wiese
0260.bio: Holger Wiese is an Associate Professor at Durham University whose research examines the cognitive and neural architecture of face perception and person recognition. Utilizing high-temporal resolution electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related brain potentials (ERPs) such as the N250 and N250r, Wiese investigates how the human brain transitions from image-dependent unfamiliar face processing to image-invariant familiar face representations. Their work explores social biases in face memory, including the own-race and own-age effects, as well as neuro-cognitive changes in face recognition across the adult lifespan. Wiese’s recent investigations focus on the consolidation of newly learned identities and the specific visual information, such as color and contrast, encoded within long-term facial representations.
0260.research_direction: Dr. Wiese has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying human face recognition, utilizing the high temporal resolution of EEG and event-related potentials to map out the serial stages of identity processing. Their recent work explores how distinct perceptual operations—ranging from early structural encoding to long-term memory access and domain-general person knowledge—can be isolated using experimental manipulations alongside key neural markers such as the N170, N250r and ERP familiarity effects. They are particularly interested in the structure of facial memory representations, in how we learn new faces, and in individual differences in face perception and memory.

papers.title: Neural correlates of temporal interference between faces
papers.abstract: Uses ERP repetition priming with two successive familiar-face primes to look for within-pool inhibition between face representations. A second prime wiped out effects of the first at short intervals, this did not depend on the second prime's familiarity, and longer intervals restored the first prime's effect, suggesting limited interference.
papers.authors: Linda H. Lidborg, Defne Kohen Tuncer, A. Mike Burton, Holger Wiese

papers.title: Neural correlates of familiar face recognition: Evidence in support of a serial model
papers.abstract: Two ERP experiments test whether face recognition unfolds in separable stages. Contrast-negation affected the N170, familiarity effects emerged from about 200 ms, and name primes added an identity-congruence effect at 300-400 ms, supporting distinct perceptual, facial long-term-memory and domain-general person stages.
papers.authors: Milena M. Bojdo, Deni Zakriev, Maya Schipper, Maria Ciocan, Linda H. Lidborg, Holger Wiese

papers.title: The neural dynamics of familiar face recognition
papers.abstract: Reviews EEG/ERP work on how the brain recognises familiar faces and argues earlier research was fragmented because it ignored image-independence, levels of familiarity, automaticity and domain-selectivity. Proposes a three-phase account (early visual, domain-sensitive, domain-general) that integrates multi-dimensional face representations and coarse-to-fine processing.
papers.authors: Holger Wiese, Stefan R. Schweinberger, Gyula Kovács

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of familiar face recognition: Event-related brain potentials reveal the efficient activation of facial identity representations
papers.abstract: Three ERP repetition-priming experiments varied prime duration from 500 ms down to 33 ms, including backward masking, and used different images of the same identity. Priming effects at 300-500 ms persisted even for very brief masked primes, showing that familiar face recognition is both effective and efficient.
papers.authors: Holger Wiese, Tsvetomila Popova, Linda H. Lidborg, A. Mike Burton

papers.title: Developing familiarity during the first eight months of knowing a person: A longitudinal EEG study on face and identity learning
papers.abstract: A pre-registered longitudinal ERP study followed students' neural responses to a new friend's faces across about eight months. The N250 familiarity effect grew over time while the sustained familiarity effect for identity knowledge did not change, suggesting visual face representations develop faster than person knowledge.
papers.authors: Tsvetomila Popova, Holger Wiese

0261.name: Hong XU
0261.department: School of Social Sciences, Division of Psychology
0261.bio: Hong Xu is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Nanyang Technological University. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, with a focus on face processing and self-motion (heading) perception. Xu utilizes a methodology incorporating human psychophysics, eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling to examine how sensory information is integrated and adapted across the cortical hierarchy. Their laboratory also conducts translational research applying vision science principles to virtual reality simulations and investigating the role of social cues in digital trust and fake news detection.
0261.research_direction: Dr. Xu has recently been investigating how humans perceive, trust, and interact with modern automated technologies across multiple levels of cognitive processing. In the visual domain, they explore the temporal dynamics of the uncanny valley effect, using extremely brief stimulus exposures to determine how rapidly the perceptual system evaluates and responds to artificial human-like faces. Broadening their focus to applied behavioral ethics, Dr. Xu uses driving experiments and surveys to probe whether people's stated moral preferences for autonomous vehicle algorithms actually align with their enacted choices during dynamic driving dilemmas. Additionally, their recent work examines the broader psychological mechanisms of technology adoption, utilizing structural equation modeling to identify the key factors that govern and sustain continuous user trust in digital platforms like mobile banking applications.

papers.title: Dissociating ethical dilemma preferences and actions in autonomous driving by survey and driving experiment
papers.abstract: The study compares what people say they prefer in ethical dilemmas involving autonomous vehicles (via survey) with what they actually do in a driving experiment. It reports a dissociation between stated preferences and enacted choices, cautioning against basing autonomous-vehicle ethics policy on survey responses alone.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice
papers.authors: Yuanyuan Wu, Han Yu, Zhang Yan, Hong Xu

papers.title: A stimulus exposure of 50 ms elicits the uncanny valley effect
papers.abstract: The paper asks how quickly the uncanny valley, the unease produced by almost-human faces, emerges. Participants viewed human-like faces for very brief durations, and the results indicate that an exposure of only about 50 ms is enough to produce the effect, suggesting it arises from rapid, largely automatic perceptual processing.
papers.authors: Jodie Yam, Tingchen Gong, Hong Xu

papers.title: Investigating customers' continuous trust towards mobile banking apps
papers.abstract: Using an online survey of 450 frequent mobile banking users and structural equation modelling, the study tests a model of how trust in a banking app is formed and maintained at the continuous-use stage. The model, and a reduced form of it, was supported by the data, identifying the factors that sustain customers' ongoing trust and hence retention.
papers.authors: Maohao Che, Sze Yee Ashley Say, Han Yu, Qingji Zhou, Jared Shu, Wen Sun, Xi Luo, Hong Xu

0262.name: Hong-jin Sun
0262.bio: Sun is an Associate Professor at McMaster University whose research explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human spatial perception and navigation. Utilizing immersive virtual reality technologies—including simulations of driving, biking, and walking—Sun investigates how visual spatial attention and visuospatial asymmetries are modulated by depth and distance in three-dimensional environments. Their work focuses on how behavioral relevance, semantic environmental information, and multisensory integration guide attentional prioritization in complex scenarios. Current research directions include examining the influences of depth on inhibition of return (IOR) and the interaction between top-down preparation and visual search in 3D space.
0262.research_direction: Dr. Sun has recently been investigating how visual spatial attention operates in three-dimensional environments, moving beyond traditional flat displays to understand how depth, motor constraints, and behavioral relevance shape attentional priorities. Their recent work explores the "near advantage" in visual processing, utilizing meta-analyses and behavioral experiments to ask how task demands—such as target localization versus discrimination—and 3D object structure influence spatial biases and inhibition of return across different depth planes. They are also examining the link between attention and action by manipulating peri-hand space during spatial cueing tasks to probe the mechanisms underlying the lower-visual-field advantage. Furthermore, Dr. Sun is extending this research to dynamic, ecologically valid contexts, using driving simulators to investigate how scene context, object animacy, and top-down experience guide attention toward critical real-world stimuli like roadside pedestrians.

papers.title: Inhibition of Return in Three-Dimensional Space is Modulated by Depth and Object Membership
papers.abstract: In a simulated 3D scene, inhibition of return was reduced when a cue appeared farther than the following target, but only when cue and target belonged to different objects rather than a single object spanning depth. The work shows that depth-specific IOR effects depend on object-based structure of the scene.
papers.authors: Hanna Haponenko, Noah Britt, Brett Cochrane, Hong-Jin Sun

papers.title: Distribution of attention in three-dimensional space
papers.abstract: Three experiments test whether the well-known bias toward near space is universal or depends on task goals, comparing target localization with target discrimination across near and far depth. The results indicate that the depth bias of attention shifts with the attentional priorities of the task rather than always favouring near stimuli.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hanna Haponenko, Brett A. Cochrane, Bruce Milliken, Hong-Jin Sun

papers.title: Context-dependent modulation of spatial attention: prioritizing behaviourally relevant stimuli
papers.abstract: Using a driving simulator with a peripheral cue-target task, the study shows that licensed drivers attend more to a roadside pedestrian facing the road than one facing away. This orientation-specific prioritization vanishes when the 3D context is removed, the viewpoint is static, or the target is an inanimate object, pointing to context-dependent, experience-driven attentional guidance.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Jackie Chau, Hong-jin Sun

papers.title: Lateral peri-hand bias affects the horizontal but not the vertical distribution of attention
papers.abstract: Asks whether the lower-visual-field attention advantage reflects motor demands in near space by manipulating where the hand rests during a spatial cueing task. Hand position near the display altered horizontal attention distribution, but the downward bias persisted regardless, so peri-hand manipulation cannot override the lower-field advantage.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hong-Jin Sun

papers.title: Spatial attention in three-dimensional space: A meta-analysis for the near advantage in target detection and localization
papers.abstract: A quantitative synthesis of 29 studies (about 1,260 participants) asking whether people respond faster to targets that appear near rather than far in depth. The pooled analysis confirms a near advantage for attention, and shows it depends on moderators such as task type (detection versus localization), whether retinal size is controlled, the depth environment (real, stereoscopic, monocular) and target eccentricity.
papers.authors: Noah Britt, Hong-jin Sun

0263.name: Hongjing Lu
0263.bio: Lu investigates the mechanisms of human learning and reasoning by developing computational models that emulate human-level intelligence. Their methodology integrates theories from psychology and statistics with tools from computer vision, machine learning, and computational neuroscience to perform behavioral and fMRI-based investigations. Lu’s research identifies two principles of human inference: the application of generic priors to guide learning from sparse data and the manipulation of structured representations for complex tasks. Current projects in their lab focus on biological motion perception, action recognition, and the computational underpinnings of causal and analogical reasoning in both biological and artificial systems.
0263.research_direction: Dr. Lu has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying complex cognition across artificial intelligence, visual perception, and collective social dynamics. Their recent work explores whether large language models possess emergent, generalized analogical reasoning capabilities by testing them against human performance on classic cognitive tasks and novel counterfactual variants. In the visual domain, they are using psychophysics, fMRI, and deep learning architectures to examine how hierarchical abstraction supports human-like 3D shape processing of point-cloud objects, and how motor networks enable observers to recognize their own whole-body movements from sparse point-light displays. Additionally, Dr. Lu has been employing natural language processing and agent-based modeling to understand how the topological structure of interacting groups influences the emergence of shared narrative beliefs about events.

papers.title: Hierarchical abstraction drives human-like 3-D shape processing in deep learning models
papers.abstract: Three human experiments manipulated point density, orientation, local geometry and part structure in point-cloud objects, and the results were compared with deep learning models for 3D shape recognition. Models trained on large object sets capture local geometry but fall short on global shape. Models with hierarchical abstraction over parts show the most human-like behavior and robustness.
papers.authors: Shuhao Fu, Philip J. Kellman, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Network structure shapes consensus dynamics through individual decisions
papers.abstract: Experimental online social networks show how network structure affects the emergence of shared narrative beliefs about an event. Using NLP embeddings and agent-based modeling, the study finds that fully connected groups emphasize the causes of an event, while locally connected networks emphasize its effects. Complex causal content weakens the influence of network structure by prompting longer exploration of background knowledge.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: J. Hunter Priniski, Bryce Linford, Anna Hirschmann, Sai Krishna Venumuddala, Fred Morstatter, Nancy Rodriguez, P. Jeffrey Brantingham, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
papers.abstract: Responds to critics who found that language models fail on counterfactual analogy variants designed to differ from training data. When the models can write and run code, they generalize to these altered tasks. This supports the claim that LLMs have acquired a real capacity for analogical reasoning rather than memorized patterns.
papers.authors: Taylor W. Webb, Keith J. Holyoak, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Self-Awareness from Whole-Body Movements
papers.abstract: Uses fMRI to ask how people recognize their own whole-body movements in sparse point-light displays. Frontoparietal and somatomotor regions respond more strongly and are more connected during self-generated actions, and they encode self-identity through motor familiarity even after visual cues are regressed out. Self-recognition therefore relies on motor systems rather than visual experience alone.
papers.authors: Akila Kadambi, Gennady Erlikhman, Micah Johnson, Martin M. Monti, Marco Iacoboni, Hongjing Lu

papers.title: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
papers.abstract: Tests GPT-3 on text-based matrix reasoning, letter-string analogies, verbal analogies and story analogies, comparing it with college students. The model matches or exceeds human performance on many of these problems, including ones unlikely to appear in training data. The authors argue that analogical reasoning can emerge in sufficiently large language models without explicit training, and discuss the limits of this claim.
papers.authors: Taylor Webb, Keith J. Holyoak, Hongjing Lu

0264.name: Hsin-Hung Li
0264.bio: Li is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University and leads a research program focused on the neural and computational foundations of decision-making, attention, and working memory. Li's work utilizes a multi-methodological approach—combining psychophysics, eye-tracking, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI/EEG) with formal computational modeling—to understand how the brain represents information and handles uncertainty. Previously, they conducted doctoral and postdoctoral research at New York University, investigating the dynamics of neural population codes and the intersection of visual perception and metacognition. Their current research seeks to identify the mechanisms through which top-down cognitive processes modulate sensory inputs to guide adaptive human behavior.
0264.research_direction: Dr. Li has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms, temporal dynamics, and resource limitations underlying human visual working memory. Their recent work explores how the brain allocates limited memory resources based on item priority and expected utility, utilizing a combination of fMRI decoding, computational modeling, and comparisons between human behavior and recurrent neural networks. To understand how memories are actively maintained, they track the population-level dynamics of memory representations during delay periods, specifically examining how remembered visual information drifts and flows across the cortical hierarchy from early visual cortex to frontoparietal areas. Additionally, they are probing the metacognitive aspects of working memory by using EEG to disentangle the distinct neural oscillatory rhythms that support the objective precision of a memory trace versus a person's subjective confidence in it.

papers.title: Dynamics of working memory drift and information flow across the cortical hierarchy
papers.abstract: The paper tracks how remembered visual information drifts over a delay and how it moves between cortical stages from early visual to parietal and frontal areas. Combining fMRI decoding with modeling, it links drift-like dynamics to directional information flow. This ties memory errors to the wider cortical hierarchy.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Distinct oscillatory neural rhythms support representational precision and confidence in working memory
papers.abstract: EEG-based analyses dissociate oscillatory rhythms tied to how precisely a memory is represented from those tied to how confident people are in it. The results indicate separable neural signatures for memory content quality and metacognitive access. This opens up the mechanisms of memory confidence.
papers.authors: Yang Di, Xingwei An, Hsin-Hung Li

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of resource allocation in working memory
