papers.abstract: Human fMRI combined with computational modeling tests how a limited working memory resource is divided across items of different priority. Decoded representations in visual and parietal cortex change in strength and precision with priority, and the resulting neural changes account for behavioral precision differences. The work links resource-allocation models of memory to concrete cortical mechanisms.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Thomas C. Sprague, Aspen H. Yoo, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Efficient Allocation of Working Memory Resource for Utility Maximization in Humans and Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The study asks whether working memory resources are allocated to maximize expected reward. Human behavior under different reward structures is compared with recurrent neural networks trained to maximize utility, and both show comparable resource-allocation strategies. It bridges cognitive resource models and neural network training.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
papers.authors: Qingqing Yang, Hsin-Hung Li

papers.title: Neural population dynamics of human working memory
papers.abstract: Using fMRI decoding across the delay period, this study characterizes how population-level representations in human cortex evolve during working memory. It shows that memory representations are not static, with systematic dynamics that change how information is coded over time. The findings challenge purely stable-code views of memory maintenance.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Clayton E. Curtis

0265.name: Hsin-I Liao
0265.bio: Hsin-I Liao is a Senior Research Scientist at NTT Communication Science Laboratories within the Human Information Science Laboratory. Their research focuses on decoding internal cognitive states, including preference formation, visual attention, and auditory salience, by analyzing implicit ocular behaviors such as pupillary dilation responses and microsaccades. Liao employs psychophysical methodologies to explore how these physiological markers reflect and participate in multisensory integration and attractiveness judgments. Liao earned their Ph.D. in Psychology from National Taiwan University and has collaborated with the Division of Biology at the California Institute of Technology.
0265.research_direction: Dr. Liao has recently been investigating how pupillary dynamics and non-image-forming visual pathways interact with higher-level cognitive states. A major focus of their recent work explores the pupillary light response and spontaneous pupil-phase fluctuations as real-time indices of spatial, temporal, and cross-modal attention. Specifically, they are using techniques like interocular suppression and closed-loop triggering to study whether pupillary reflexes track invisible brightness, how slow arousal cycles modulate the auditory attentional blink, and whether covert attention to auditory objects can drive visually mapped pupil changes. Additionally, Dr. Liao is examining the distinct time courses of pupil reactivity to affective versus highly salient images, alongside research using silent substitution to isolate how selectively driving intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells impacts working memory.

papers.title: Pupillary responses to invisible brightness escape from attentional modulation
papers.abstract: The pupillary light response is usually treated as a reflex, but it also tracks perceived and attended brightness. Using interocular suppression to render Gabor patterns invisible, the study finds that unseen bright or dark stimuli still drive weaker but reliable pupil responses that feature-based attention does not alter. Spatial attention modulates the response only when stimuli are visible, pointing to a cortical-subcortical gating of pupil control that depends on awareness.
papers.authors: Yung-Hao Yang, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Eye Pupil is Constricted to Attractive Images and Dilated to Salient Ones at Different Time Windows
papers.abstract: Pupils are thought to dilate to attractive, arousing pictures, but rarity or novelty may confound this. The authors selected IAPS images with matched salience or attractiveness through a large online rating study (166 raters, 942 images), then measured pupil responses in 30 participants. Attractive images produced an early constriction, while late dilation grew for both salient and attractive images, suggesting distinct mechanisms across the response time course.
papers.authors: Hsin-I Liao, Yuta Suzuki, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Real-time tracking of pupil-phase fluctuations reveals state-dependent modulation of temporal attentional capacity
papers.abstract: Using an auditory attentional blink task, the study asks whether slow pupil-linked state fluctuations shape temporal attention. Successful second-target detection was linked to smaller baseline pupil size and to the dilation phase of slow (<0.2 Hz) pupil cycles. A closed-loop experiment triggering stimuli at set pupil phases confirmed phase-dependent detection beyond baseline size, implying the attentional blink is a state-dependent limit.
papers.authors: Yuta Suzuki, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Selective activation of ipRGC modulates working memory performance
papers.abstract: Blue light can improve working memory, but it is unclear whether ipRGCs alone or combined rod/cone signals are responsible. Using silent substitution to isolate ipRGC activation while holding cone responses constant, participants did 1- and 2-back tasks under low or high ipRGC stimulation. 2-back hit rate was higher under high ipRGC activation, showing direct ipRGC influence on cognition.
papers.authors: Yuta Suzuki, Shigeki Nakauchi, Hsin-I Liao

papers.title: Seeing an Auditory Object: Pupillary Light Response Reflects Covert Attention to Auditory Space and Object
papers.abstract: The study shows that pupil light responses can index shifts of auditory attention. Pupils followed the luminance at the location of the attended talker whether attention was cued by space or by a nonspatial feature such as talker gender, and with headphones or loudspeakers. Gaze drift did not explain this, implying a unified audiovisual spatial representation in auditory object-based attention.
papers.authors: Hsin-I Liao, Haruna Fujihira, Shimpei Yamagishi, Yung-Hao Yang, Shigeto Furukawa

0266.name: Hui Chen
0266.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0266.bio: Chen is a Professor at Zhejiang University specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual processing. Their research examines the relationships between visual attention, working memory, and conscious awareness, specifically investigating how internal representations guide external selection. Chen identified the 'attribute amnesia' phenomenon and utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to map these mental processes. Their work applies these findings to examine cognitive deficits in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia.
0266.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the complex, dissociable relationship between visual attention and working memory, specifically challenging the traditional view that attending to a stimulus automatically guarantees its memory encoding. Their recent work explores phenomena like "attribute amnesia"—where individuals cannot recall a feature they just actively used in a task—to determine how expected future relevance and secondary "memory reselection" processes dictate what information is actually stored. In a reciprocal direction, they are also examining how working memory content subsequently guides visual attention, using multi-item arrays to test whether bound objects or isolated features serve as the functional units for memory-guided capture. Finally, Dr. Chen is extending these fundamental cognitive paradigms into developmental and clinical domains, probing how the capacity to filter out outdated information evolves between childhood and adulthood, and characterizing the dynamic trajectories of attentional hyperfocusing and hyperfiltering in patients with schizophrenia.

papers.title: Working memory encoding of attended information is adaptive to future relevance
papers.abstract: Attribute amnesia shows people often fail to report a feature they just attended and used, raising the question of whether it was ever encoded into working memory. The authors show that a feature which becomes irrelevant after use is not automatically encoded, but one that may be needed for later tasks is intentionally encoded. Attended information therefore does not enter working memory automatically but is encoded actively according to expected future relevance.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Ping Zhu, Chenxiao Guan, Yingtao Fu, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: The objecthood of visual working memory representations influences their interaction with attention
papers.abstract: Visual working memory content can guide attention to matching stimuli, but this capture largely disappears when several items are held at once. Across five experiments the authors show that features bound into one object jointly guide attention, whereas the same features on separate objects do not. The object effect held for more colors, across feature dimensions and across modalities, identifying objects as the functional unit of memory-guided attention.
papers.authors: Litian Chen, Jiewei Zheng, Mengjiao Xu, Ping Zhu, Yingtao Fu, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: Children exhibit superior memory for attended but outdated information compared to adults
papers.abstract: Across five experiments with 130 children and 130 adults, participants used a specific feature for a task and were then given a surprise test about it. Children reported this attended-but-outdated information better than adults, a developmental reversal, and the effect could not be explained by different strategies or attention allocation. The authors conclude that memory selection, the ability to filter out no-longer-needed information, is still immature in young children.
papers.authors: Yingtao Fu, Tingyu Guo, Jiewei Zheng, Jie He, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: The dynamic process of hyperfocusing and hyperfiltering in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Uses a task tracing how people focus on relevant features, filter out irrelevant ones, and update expectations over time to compare patients with schizophrenia and healthy controls. Patients showed excessive focusing on relevant information together with excessive filtering of irrelevant information, characterizing attentional selection abnormalities in the disorder as a dynamic process.
papers.authors: Jian Li, Bao-liang Zhong, Dongsheng Zhou, Yingtao Fu, Xiaoqi Huang, Luo Chen, Huiying Liu, Jiewei Zheng, Enze Tang, Yongqi Li, Chenxiao Guan, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen

papers.title: Attention with or without working memory: mnemonic reselection of attended information
papers.abstract: Reviews the long-held idea that attention acts as gatekeeper for working memory, and how the attribute amnesia effect (failure to report a feature one has just attended and used) challenges it. Introduces the concept of memory reselection, a second selection stage that operates on already-attended information, and argues that attention and working memory should be modeled as dissociable processes.
papers.authors: Yingtao Fu, Chenxiao Guan, Joyce Tam, Ryan E. O'Donnell, Mowei Shen, Brad Wyble, Hui Chen

0269.name: Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza
0269.department: Department of Experimental Psychology, Cognitive Processes and Speech Therapy
0269.bio: Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza is a Professor of Vision Science at the Complutense University of Madrid, where they direct the Laboratory of Visual Psychophysics. Their research utilizes human psychophysics and computational modeling to analyze the functional mechanisms of the human visual system, with specific focus on motion perception, spatial vision, and stereopsis. Serrano-Pedraza has investigated neuronal inhibitory mechanisms, such as center-surround antagonism, and their influence on motion discrimination and stereoscopic anisotropy. Their current work involves applying psychophysical findings to clinical research to identify biomarkers for sensory alterations in populations with schizophrenia, epilepsy, and depression.
0269.research_direction: Dr. Serrano-Pedraza's recent work explores the spatial and temporal mechanisms underlying stereoscopic depth and visual motion perception. In the stereo domain, they have recently been investigating stereoscopic anisotropies by measuring disparity thresholds for static and drifting depth corrugations to model V1 disparity energy and isolate orientation-selective and temporal channels using individual differences analyses. Their research also probes basic motion processing mechanisms, specifically testing how fine and coarse spatial frequencies interact in center-surround paradigms under both binocular and dichoptic viewing conditions. Furthermore, they utilize large behavioral datasets to evaluate individual and demographic variations in visual performance, such as assessing potential sex differences in duration thresholds during contrast-detection and motion-discrimination tasks.

papers.title: Orientation mechanisms in stereoscopic vision: an individual differences approach
papers.abstract: The authors measured disparity thresholds in 37 observers for depth corrugations at three spatial frequencies and seven orientations. Thresholds at low spatial frequency rose strongly from horizontal to vertical, and this anisotropy shrank at higher frequencies. Component and factor analyses of the individual differences showed that neighbouring orientations covary, which supports orientation-selective mechanisms in stereovision and extends earlier evidence limited to spatial-frequency tuning.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, David H. Peterzell, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Characteristics of the Stereoscopic Anisotropy
papers.abstract: Disparity thresholds for vertical and horizontal depth corrugations were measured across a wide range of spatial and temporal frequencies. Thresholds were always higher for vertical corrugations and low-pass in temporal frequency. A spatiotemporal cross-correlation model approximating V1 disparity energy, with a shift parameter, captured how the orientation difference depends on spatial and temporal frequency.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Center-surround motion interaction between low and high spatial frequencies under binocular and dichoptic viewing
papers.abstract: Impaired direction discrimination of fine-scale motion when a coarse static pattern is added was tested with the coarse component placed in the surround rather than overlapping the center. The strength of the interaction (cancellation speed) was bandpass in spatial frequency, grew with temporal frequency up to about 12 Hz and with contrast, and was present, though weaker, when the components were shown to different eyes. This indicates a mechanism that integrates fine and coarse scales even without spatial overlap or common monocular input.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Temporal mechanisms in frontoparallel stereomotion revealed by individual differences analysis
papers.abstract: Disparity thresholds for drifting vertical and horizontal depth corrugations were measured at temporal frequencies from 0.25 to 8 Hz in 34 observers, using stimuli with no monocular luminance motion. Factor analysis of the individual differences pointed to multiple independent temporal mechanisms in cyclopean stereomotion. A small advantage for horizontal corrugations was also found.
papers.authors: Ichasus Llamas-Cornejo, David H. Peterzell, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

papers.title: Visual motion discrimination experiments reveal small differences between males and females
papers.abstract: A new contrast-detection motion experiment and a reanalysis of four earlier motion-discrimination datasets compared duration thresholds of males and females across spatial frequency, size, contrast and temporal frequency. Overall the link between sex and thresholds was not significant and both sexes showed similar patterns. Only one reanalysed study showed a sex difference with a large effect size, so previously reported differences appear small and condition-specific.
papers.authors: Omar Bachtoula, Sandra Arranz-Paraiso, Raul Luna, Ignacio Serrano-Pedraza

0270.name: Ikuya Murakami
0270.bio: Ikuya Murakami is a Professor at the University of Tokyo specializing in the psychophysics of human vision and the neural mechanisms of perception. Murakami’s research utilizes experimental psychophysics, eye-movement tracking, and functional neuroimaging to investigate how the brain processes visual motion, achieves perceptual completion, and integrates signals across sensory modalities. Their work includes studies on the temporal dynamics of the flash-lag effect and the role of physiological factors, such as microsaccades and melanopsin activation, in modulating visual sensitivity and the subjective experience of duration.
0270.research_direction: Dr. Murakami has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying spatial vision, motion perception, and contextual modulation. Their recent work explores various motion-induced position shifts—such as the twinkle-goes and flash-grab illusions—to probe how perceived object location interacts with rhythmic neural theta oscillations and perceptual filling-in at the blind spot or behind occluders. Additionally, they are examining the visual system's processing of motion trajectories by testing adaptation to both physical and illusory motion paths. Beyond spatial positioning, Dr. Murakami's research also investigates how temporal expectation alters contextual orientation illusions, and probes non-classical photoreception by measuring how short-wavelength light stimulation inside the optic disc influences general light detectability across the visual field.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of the twinkle-goes illusion and its relationship to neural theta oscillations
papers.abstract: The twinkle-goes illusion makes the vanishing point of a moving object look displaced along its motion direction when the background is dynamic noise. The authors mapped how this position shift unfolds over time using probes along the trajectory, and related it to the phase of ongoing neural theta oscillations measured with EEG. The results tie the timing of the illusion to rhythmic sampling in the brain and support an account based on delayed accumulation of sensory evidence.
papers.authors: Ryosuke Nakayama, Kaoru Amano, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Flash grab effect within the regions of modal and amodal completions
papers.abstract: In the flash-grab effect, a briefly flashed item appears displaced after a rotating grating reverses direction. The study places the expected shifted position inside a region of perceptual filling-in at the blind spot or behind an occluder, and measures where observers perceive the flash. It probes how position shifts interact with completed, unseen parts of a scene.
papers.authors: Hoko Nakada, Yuya Seshita, Haruka Shimazaki, Sohei Kito, Tomoya Nakamura, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: The illusion of orientation repulsion is weakened in a temporally more predictable visual target
papers.abstract: Orientation repulsion makes a vertical target look tilted away from the orientation of its surround. The authors show that when the target's onset is made predictable in time, by a valid or rhythmic cue, the illusion shrinks. This reveals a phenomenological effect of temporal expectation on how contextual modulation shapes what we see.
papers.authors: Tomoya Nakamura, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Illumination by short-wavelength light inside the blind spot decreases light detectability
papers.abstract: The optic disc holds no classical photoreceptors but does contain melanopsin. Participants detected light stimuli in the normal visual field with or without extra illumination inside the blind spot. Blue illumination inside the blind spot lowered detectability, suggesting a slow melanopsin-related pathway rather than scattered light.
papers.authors: Marina Saito, Kentaro Miyamoto, Ikuya Murakami

papers.title: Aftereffect of perceived motion trajectories
papers.abstract: After adapting to several objects moving along trajectories with a shared tilt, a test trajectory looks tilted in the repulsive direction. The aftereffect arises equally whether the adapting tilt is physical or is an illusion produced by motion-induced position shifts. This suggests a dedicated adaptive process for perceived trajectories operating at the level of the perceived path.
papers.authors: Ryohei Nakayama, Mai Tanaka, Yukino Kishi, Ikuya Murakami

0272.name: Ilker Yildirim
0272.lab_name: The Cognitive and Neural Computation Lab (CNCL)
0272.bio: Ilker Yildirim is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Yale University and directs the Cognitive and Neural Computation Lab. Yildirim's research utilizes a reverse-engineering approach to study how the human brain converts sensory signals into mental representations of objects, physical dynamics, and social agents. By integrating generative models, probabilistic programming, and deep learning, Yildirim develops computational theories that are evaluated using human psychophysical behavior and multi-area neural data. This work focuses on establishing an engineering-level account of visual cognition and its function in supporting reasoning and decision-making processes.
0272.research_direction: Dr. Yildirim has recently been investigating how biological vision systems construct rich, three-dimensional physical understandings of the world from 2D images. Their recent work explores whether visual processing relies on "inverse graphics" and physics-based simulation, using neural recordings from macaque inferotemporal cortex to study 3D object inference and employing computational models to probe how humans visually process the intuitive physics of soft, deformable materials like cloth. Additionally, they are investigating dynamic visual attention during tasks like multiple object tracking, framing visual selection as an adaptive, resource-rational algorithm that allocates perceptual computation on the fly rather than a fixed capacity limit. Beyond traditional vision and psychophysics, Dr. Yildirim is also examining the cognitive capacities of artificial intelligence, questioning whether large language models develop structured, human-like world models or merely acquire task-driven instrumental knowledge.

papers.title: Adaptive computation as a new mechanism of dynamic human attention
papers.abstract: The paper proposes adaptive computation, an algorithm in which attention rations perceptual computation across objects on the fly according to a general notion of how relevant each object is to the current task. It is tested in multiple object tracking, a classic case of dynamic selection, where the model reproduces how human observers' performance and effort vary across objects and time. The work casts attention as resource-rational allocation of computation rather than a fixed capacity limit.
papers.authors: Mario Belledonne, Eivinas Butkus, Brian J. Scholl, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Visual Perception of Intuitive Physics and Its Computational Foundations
papers.abstract: This review surveys evidence that vision is tuned not only to statistical regularities of images but also to the laws of physics governing objects and materials. It covers psychophysical work showing that physical inferences are rapid, spontaneous and stimulus driven, and lays out physics-based analysis by synthesis as a computational framework. It also discusses neuroscience findings and open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Wenyan Bi, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Computational models reveal that intuitive physics underlies visual processing of soft objects
papers.abstract: Most computational models of vision focus on rigid objects, but everyday scenes are full of soft things like cloth whose folds and wrinkles constantly change. The authors build a model that perceives soft objects by inverting a physics-based simulation of how cloth moves and deforms, and compare it against standard deep networks and other alternatives. The physics-based model accounts for human stiffness judgments and for spontaneous, automatic responses to cloth dynamics better than the alternatives, indicating that intuitive physics is built into visual processing.
papers.authors: Wenyan Bi, Aalap D. Shah, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: Multiarea processing in body patches of the primate inferotemporal cortex implements inverse graphics
papers.abstract: The study asks whether higher visual cortex in macaques carries out something like the reverse of computer graphics, mapping images back to the 3D structure that generated them. Using neural recordings from multiple areas of the body-selective network in inferotemporal cortex, the authors compare an inverse-graphics model with standard deep networks trained for recognition. Neural responses across areas were better explained by the inverse-graphics account, supporting inferring 3D objects as a computational objective of biological vision.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Hakan Yilmaz, Aalap D. Shah, Ariadne Letrou, Satwant Kumar, Rufin Vogels, Ilker Yildirim

papers.title: From task structures to world models: What do LLMs know?
papers.abstract: The article asks in what sense large language models can be said to know things. The authors propose that LLMs hold instrumental knowledge, gained by using next-word prediction as a tool, and contrast it with the worldly knowledge people have through structured world models. They argue that LLMs might recover more worldly knowledge through an implicit resource-rational tradeoff between tasks and world models.
papers.authors: Ilker Yildirim, L. A. Paul

0274.name: Ione Fine
0274.bio: Ione Fine is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Washington who researches the adaptation of the human brain to long-term sensory deprivation, such as blindness and deafness. Fine uses functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling to investigate the relationship between neural function and neuroanatomical structure. Their work includes the development of "virtual patients" to model and predict perceptual experiences produced by sight restoration technologies like retinal and cortical prostheses. Fine also characterizes the mechanisms of cross-modal plasticity and the limitations of experience-dependent recovery in high-level visual processing.
0274.research_direction: Dr. Fine has recently been exploring both the computational modeling of vision restoration and the mechanisms of cross-modal plasticity following early blindness. To advance sight recovery technologies, their recent work uses "virtual patient" simulations to link physiological interventions—such as electrical cortical stimulation and optogenetic retinal therapies—to predicted perceptual outcomes like phosphene appearance and temporal contrast sensitivity. In parallel, they are investigating how early visual loss reorganizes auditory processing, testing pitch and auditory motion perception in blind individuals to determine whether compensatory sensory enhancements stem from altered cue weighting or reduced internal neural noise. Furthermore, they are developing theoretical frameworks to assess whether the recruitment of the deprived visual cortex for non-visual tasks is fundamentally governed by domain-general principles of skill acquisition.

papers.title: Using Virtual Patients to Predict Perceptual Outcomes for Optogenetic Sight Recovery Technologies
papers.abstract: Extends the virtual patient approach to optogenetic vision restoration, linking the sensitivity and kinetics of opsin-mediated retinal responses to predicted temporal contrast sensitivity. Simulations show that opsin sensitivity and speed jointly determine perceptual outcomes, and that boosting sensitivity at the cost of temporal resolution can impair perception of fast motion. The platform is meant to help choose opsins for clinical translation.
papers.authors: Vaishnavi B. Mohan, Ezgi I. Yucel, Ione Fine, Geoffrey M. Boynton

papers.title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise
papers.abstract: Tests pitch perception in early blind and sighted listeners matched for musical training, finding equal peripheral frequency selectivity but better cortical-level pitch discrimination in blind listeners. Modeling attributes the gain to lower internal noise rather than sharper tuning, and both blindness and musical training predict less noise. Internal noise is thus a key factor in experience-driven auditory plasticity.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Jasmine Awad, Ione Fine

papers.title: A virtual patient simulation modeling the neural and perceptual effects of human visual cortical stimulation, from pulse trains to percepts
papers.abstract: Presents a computational 'virtual patient' that links electrical stimulation parameters of visual cortex (pulse trains) to the phosphenes people report, combining a model of neural activation with a perceptual model. It reproduces published human data on how brightness, size and shape of phosphenes depend on stimulation amplitude, frequency and duration. The framework offers a tool for predicting and designing perceptual outcomes of cortical visual prostheses.
papers.authors: Ione Fine, Geoffrey M. Boynton

papers.title: A unified model for cross-modal plasticity and skill acquisition
papers.abstract: Proposes that cross-modal plasticity in blind individuals can be explained by the same principles that govern ordinary skill learning. It reviews evidence and shows how a skill-acquisition framework accounts for both the strengths and limits of visual cortex recruitment for non-visual tasks.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

papers.title: The perception of auditory motion in sighted and early blind individuals
papers.abstract: Compares how sighted and early blind people perceive moving sounds, testing whether blindness changes auditory motion processing. Behavioral results and modeling indicate that early blind individuals rely on different cues than sighted people when judging motion. The study speaks to how the brain reorganizes perception after early visual loss.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

0275.name: Ipek Oruc
0275.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
0275.bio: Ipek Oruc is an Associate Professor at the University of British Columbia and director of the NOVA Lab, where she investigates the neural mechanisms of higher-level vision and object recognition. Oruc’s research integrates computer science, visual psychophysics, and neuroimaging to examine how the brain develops perceptual expertise for complex stimuli such as faces. She also studies visual dysfunction in neurodevelopmental disorders like autism and conditions such as prosopagnosia to inform the development of rehabilitation paradigms. Additionally, Oruc applies deep learning and data science to create automated diagnostic tools and predictive models using retinal imaging.
0275.research_direction: Dr. Oruc’s research examines human visual perception and its intersection with computational modeling and artificial intelligence, spanning both basic vision science and clinical applications. Her work investigates how visual information is represented and used by the human visual system, including face and object perception and naturalistic visual experience. A major focus of her lab is also the development and evaluation of AI methods for ophthalmic imaging, including retinal and optic nerve biomarkers, glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, and questions of model generalization, interpretability, and demographic variation. Across these areas, the lab combines behavioral experiments, eye tracking, neuroimaging, medical imaging, and machine learning to understand visual processing and to develop computational tools that are both scientifically informative and clinically useful.

papers.title: AI-Assisted identification of sex-specific patterns in diabetic retinopathy using retinal fundus images
papers.abstract: Asks whether diabetic retinopathy looks different in male and female patients, using 2,967 fundus images matched for age, ethnicity, severity and HbA1c. Fine-tuned VGG16 models classified sex above chance, and saliency maps showed the networks relied on different retinal regions by sex, suggesting sex-specific disease patterns.
papers.authors: Parsa Delavari, Gulcenur Ozturan, Eduardo V. Navajas, Ozgur Yilmaz, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: The blur paradox: Better recognition at a distance
papers.abstract: Shows that blurred faces are recognized better when viewed from farther away, and that this holds with physical blur filters and real viewing distances rather than only digital manipulations. Accuracy improved gradually but nonlinearly with distance, with a stronger effect in older participants.
papers.authors: Caitlin Long, Lei Yuan, Claudia Wu, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: CNN-extracted features generate synthetic fMRI responses to unseen images
papers.abstract: Using BOLD5000 and a pretrained AlexNet, shows that CNN features can generate synthetic fMRI responses that correlate better with repeated real responses than the real responses do with each other under noise. A decoder trained on this synthetic data can classify real fMRI responses to unseen images and even unseen object categories.
papers.authors: Parsa Delavari, Leonid Sigal, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: Atypical daily visual exposure to faces in adults with autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: Using more than 360 hours of first-person camera footage, this study provides the first direct record of the daily face exposure of autistic adults. Compared with neurotypical adults, they saw familiar faces for less time, viewed faces from farther away, and saw them from viewpoints skewed toward profile. The authors argue this impoverished face diet may help explain reduced face expertise in autism.
papers.authors: Todd Kamensek, Grace Iarocci, Ipek Oruc

papers.title: Artificial intelligence, explainability, and the scientific method: A proof-of-concept study on novel retinal biomarker discovery
papers.abstract: Proposes a four-phase framework that combines explainable AI with hypothesis-driven science. As a proof of concept, a CNN trained to classify patient sex from retinal fundus images is interrogated with saliency tools to generate 14 hypotheses about retinal sex differences, which are then tested to yield candidate biomarkers.
papers.authors: Parsa Delavari, Gulcenur Ozturan, Lei Yuan, Özgür Yilmaz, Ipek Oruc

0276.name: Irene Sperandio
0276.department: Department of Psychology and Cognitive Science
0276.bio: Irene Sperandio is an Associate Professor who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying size constancy and the integration of retinal and extra-retinal signals for perception and action. Utilizing a multimodal approach including functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and kinematics, Sperandio explores how the primary visual cortex (V1) and higher-order cortical areas process object size relative to viewing distance. Their work employs visual illusions, such as the Ebbinghaus illusion, to examine the computational and neuroanatomical dissociations between the ventral and dorsal visual streams. Sperandio's research also addresses the developmental trajectories of visual perception and the characterization of anomalous perceptual experiences in clinical conditions such as psychosis.
0276.research_direction: Dr. Sperandio has recently been investigating the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying visual awareness, size perception, and susceptibility to visual illusions. Their recent work explores the network computations and temporal dynamics driving size constancy and apparent size, employing combined EEG-kinematics with real-world 3D objects alongside fMRI dynamic causal modeling. Additionally, they are probing the boundaries of pre-conscious visual processing by using continuous flash suppression to track how unseen stimuli, ranging from 3D targets to emotional faces, break into awareness while simultaneously monitoring physiological markers like pupillometry, skin conductance, and facial EMG. Finally, Dr. Sperandio is examining how high-level individual differences, such as psychotic-like traits and emotional distress, influence perceptual alterations during classical visual illusion tasks.

papers.title: Temporal tuning of continuous flash suppression for 3D objects reflects intrinsic dynamics of visual awareness
papers.abstract: Using a real three-dimensional disc shown to one eye against a flickering colourful mask in the other, the authors measured how long the disc took to break into awareness across ten mask frequencies. Suppression was strongest near 6 Hz, as with 2D stimuli, and did not depend on which eye saw the target. Response times were unexpectedly bimodal, hinting at distinct processing of real 3D objects.
papers.authors: Simona Noviello, Alessio Toraldo, Mirko Tommasini, Samantha Sartin, David Melcher, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Pre-conscious reactions to faces as the biological roots of emotion perception
papers.abstract: Fearful, happy and neutral faces (and scrambled controls) were hidden from awareness by interocular suppression while facial EMG, skin conductance and pupil size were recorded. Even without conscious perception, pupils and facial muscles reacted more to fearful faces, and happy faces broke into awareness fastest. Once seen, expressions evoked responses matching the perceived emotion, and pupil responses related to autistic, alexithymic and schizotypal traits.
papers.authors: Cecilia Dapor, Ronen Hershman, Daniela Ruzzante, Federica Meconi, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Temporal features of size constancy for perception and action in a real-world setting: A combined EEG-kinematics study
papers.abstract: Participants judged or grasped real disks placed at different distances whose physical size was scaled to keep the retinal image constant, while EEG and hand motion were recorded. The earliest visual evoked response (about 90 ms) came sooner and was larger for bigger disks of identical retinal size, in both tasks, and behaviour showed matching size and grip constancy. The study offers the first timing evidence that size-distance scaling arises very early, plausibly in primary visual cortex.
papers.authors: Simona Noviello, Saman Kamari Songhorabadi, Zhiqing Deng, Chao Zheng, Juan Chen, Angelo Pisani, Elena Franchin, Enrica Pierotti, Elena Tonolli, Simona Monaco, Louis Renoult, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Network dynamics underlying alterations in apparent object size
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and dynamic causal modelling during an Ebbinghaus illusion task with attention directed to one configuration, the study asked how early and higher visual areas interact to produce the illusion. Extrastriate activity tracked the illusory size, accompanied by reduced self-inhibition in extrastriate cortex and stronger feedback from the precuneus. The authors conclude that apparent size depends on top-down feedback to lower visual areas.
papers.authors: Lihong Chen, Baoyu Wu, Haoyang Yu, Irene Sperandio

papers.title: Visual illusions in young people reporting psychotic-like experiences
papers.abstract: Twenty-five young people with psychotic-like experiences and 53 controls adjusted a battery of 13 visual illusions. The clinical group showed generally stronger illusion susceptibility, but this vanished once depression, anxiety and stress were controlled, with stress the best predictor. The results suggest that altered illusion perception in this group reflects emotional distress rather than psychotic-like experiences per se.
papers.venue: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
papers.authors: Irene Sperandio, Philippe A. Chouinard, Emily Paice, Daniel J. Griffiths-King, Joanne Hodgekins

0277.name: Isabel Gauthier
0277.main_research_area: Visual object recognition and perceptual expertise
0277.bio: Isabel Gauthier is a cognitive neuroscientist who researches the neural and behavioral mechanisms of visual object recognition and perceptual expertise. Gauthier uses novel objects, such as "Greebles," to demonstrate that category-specific neural responses in the fusiform face area can be recruited through experience rather than being strictly innate. Their methodology integrates high-resolution fMRI, event-related potentials (ERP), and psychophysics to investigate the plasticity of the human visual system. Gauthier’s current research focuses on quantifying individual differences in high-level visual abilities and exploring the relationships between domain-general recognition and ensemble perception.
0277.research_direction: Dr. Gauthier has recently been investigating individual differences in a domain-general ability for subordinate-level object recognition, a construct often referred to as o. Their recent work explores how to reliably measure this generalized visual ability using aggregated cross-category scores and asks whether it represents a distinct cognitive trait compared to established constructs like general intelligence and spatial ability. Using latent-variable modeling and behavioral testing, they are examining the breadth of this general mechanism to see if it extends to auditory object recognition and the ensemble perception of visual summary statistics. Furthermore, their research tests the applied boundaries of this framework, asking whether an individual's generalized object recognition skills can predict their performance in novel perceptual challenges, such as distinguishing real human faces from AI-generated images.

papers.title: Is Domain-General Object Recognition Ability a Novel Construct?
papers.abstract: A review of the case that people vary in a general ability to tell apart objects at the subordinate level, regardless of category (called o). The authors connect vision and cognitive neuroscience work on this ability to the broader literature on individual differences in cognitive abilities and ask whether o is distinct from established constructs such as general intelligence.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Domain-general object recognition predicts human ability to tell real from AI-generated faces
papers.abstract: Tests whether people who are good at recognizing objects in general are also better at judging whether a face is real or generated by AI. Object recognition ability predicted detection performance beyond face-specific and other measures, suggesting that a general visual ability supports this new real-world task.
papers.authors: Jason K. Chow, Rankin W. McGugin, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Visual and auditory object recognition in relation to spatial ability
papers.abstract: Examines how object recognition ability in vision and audition relates to spatial ability, using latent-variable modeling. The results place domain-general recognition among established cognitive ability factors and probe how far it extends across sensory modalities.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Jason K. Chow, Andrew J. Tomarken, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: Measuring object recognition ability: Reliability, validity, and the aggregate z-score approach
papers.abstract: Presents a methodology for measuring domain-general object recognition ability by aggregating performance across several object categories into a single z-score. The authors show that the composite is reliable and valid, and that it outperforms single-category tests as a measure of general ability.
papers.authors: Conor J. R. Smithson, Jason K. Chow, Ting-Yun Chang, Isabel Gauthier

papers.title: A general ability for judging simple and complex ensembles
papers.abstract: Asks whether a shared ability underlies judging summary statistics of groups of items, from simple features to complex objects. Individual differences in ensemble judgments were related across stimulus types and to object recognition ability, indicating a domain-general contribution to ensemble perception.
papers.authors: Ting-Yun Chang, Oakyoon Cha, Isabel Gauthier

0279.name: Isabelle Boutet
0279.bio: Isabelle Boutet is an Associate Professor at the University of Ottawa and the Principal Investigator of the SCOPE Lab, where they investigate the cognitive and neural mechanisms of face perception across the human lifespan. Boutet’s research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine how individuals process socially relevant cues such as identity and emotional expression. A portion of their work focuses on cognitive aging, specifically how age-related sensory declines influence facial recognition and how familiarity affects visual scanning patterns. Additionally, Boutet analyzes the interpretation of emojis and non-verbal cues in digital contexts in the absence of face-to-face interaction.
0279.research_direction: Dr. Boutet has recently been investigating how people process visual social and emotional cues across both human faces and digital communication. In their face perception research, they utilize eye-tracking to examine how gaze behaviors, such as specific fixation patterns on the eyes versus the mouth, relate to memory consolidation during face-name learning and how emotion recognition differs across the adult lifespan. In tandem, their recent work explores how these visual processing mechanisms apply to digital environments, testing whether designing emojis with diagnostic facial-expression cues can reduce interpretative ambiguity. Furthermore, they are investigating the broader social and demographic dynamics of these artificial visual signals by measuring how emoji valence shapes professional judgments of competence and how emoji comprehension and adoption vary between younger and older adults.

papers.title: Emojis at Work: The Effects of Emoji Use on Perceptions of Competence and Appropriateness
papers.abstract: Simulated workplace instant messages were varied in sentence valence, emoji valence and sender gender, and 243 participants rated how competent and appropriate the sender seemed. Both the wording and the emoji shaped impressions, so emojis are not neutral decoration in professional messaging. The work extends the lab's program on how visual emotional cues shape social judgments in text-based communication.
papers.authors: Erin L. Courtice, Megan Lawrence, Charles A. Collin, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Getting to know you: Gaze behaviours and biographical information in face-name associations
papers.abstract: Undergraduates learned new face-name pairs, half with a biographical fact, and were tested immediately and after one and two weeks while their eye movements were tracked. Biographical information improved both face and name recognition and the benefit persisted at two weeks. It was accompanied by more fixations on the eyes and fewer on the mouth, and by fewer fixations and region transitions as pairs were consolidated.
papers.authors: Isabelle Boutet, Arda Erbayav, Bozana Meinhart-Injac, Charles A. Collin

papers.title: Emotion Processing in Late Adulthood: The Effect of Emotional Valence and Face Age on Behavior and Scanning Patterns
papers.abstract: Three experiments used a new image set of younger and older faces showing positive and negative emotions to test how older adults read emotion. Older adults differed from younger adults in emotion recognition accuracy, while gaze patterns did not differ significantly between groups. Stimulus valence and the age of the face model both modulated performance.
papers.authors: Bozana Meinhardt-Injac, Nicole Altvater-Mackensen, Alexandra Mohs, Jean-Christophe Goulet-Pelletier, Isabelle Boutet

papers.title: Are older adults adapting to new forms of communication? A study on emoji adoption across the adult lifespan
papers.abstract: Emoji use and interpretation were compared across adult age groups to see whether older adults are keeping pace with this newer communication format. The study documents how emoji adoption and understanding vary with age, linking the PI's cognitive-aging interests to digital communication.
papers.authors: Isabelle Boutet, Jean-Christophe Goulet-Pelletier, Eva Sutera, Bozana Meinhardt-Injac

papers.title: Emojis that work! Incorporating visual cues from facial expressions in emojis can reduce ambiguous interpretations
papers.abstract: Building emojis from facial-expression cues that are diagnostic of emotion was tested as a way to reduce ambiguous readings of emojis. Emojis redesigned this way were interpreted more consistently than standard ones. The paper ties face-perception findings to the design of digital emotional signals.
papers.authors: Isabelle Boutet, Joëlle Guay, Justin Chamberland, Denis Cousineau, Charles Collin

0280.name: J. Anthony Movshon
0280.bio: J. Anthony Movshon is a visual neuroscientist and the founding Director of the Center for Neural Science at New York University. Movshon’s research investigates how neural circuits in the primate cerebral cortex encode and represent visual information, focusing on the mechanisms of motion and form perception. Using an approach that integrates single-unit electrophysiology, computational modeling, and psychophysics, Movshon applied neurometric functions to link neuronal firing rates to behavioral performance. Their current work explores the hierarchical processing of naturalistic textures and the developmental impact of abnormal early visual experience on cortical function.
0280.research_direction: Dr. Movshon has recently been investigating how mid-level visual features are computed and represented across the macaque ventral stream, specifically focusing on the hierarchical processing between areas V1, V2, and V4. Much of their recent work explores the neural basis of texture and object perception, using electrophysiological recordings in awake macaques to ask how contrast-invariant representations of naturalistic textures emerge and how populations of V4 neurons transition from processing unstructured "stuff" to intact "things." To probe the computational foundations of early form selectivity, they are also fitting two-stage feedforward models to V1 and V2 responses to test the limits of these mechanistic accounts. Additionally, Dr. Movshon is studying the developmental trajectory of this visual hierarchy by examining how and when position-invariant shape and curvature tuning mature in the cortices of young macaques.

papers.title: Curvature tuning in areas V2 and V4 of the developing macaque
papers.abstract: Multiunit activity in V2 and V4 was recorded from two macaques at 30 and 58 weeks of age while they viewed shapes that varied mainly in curvature along one boundary segment. Curvature tuning already looked adult-like at 30 weeks in both areas, and position-invariant tuning appeared in V4 but not V2. Neither a boundary-curvature model nor a linear spike-triggered model showed age-related change, indicating object-centered curvature codes first arise in V4 and mature early.
papers.authors: A. Ezra Sutter, Gerick M. Lee, Timothy D. Oleskiw, Najib J. Majaj, Lynne Kiorpes, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Emergence of a contrast-invariant representation of naturalistic texture in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Multiunit recordings in V1, V2 and V4 were made while monkeys viewed textures that varied in contrast and in naturalistic statistical structure. Contrast changed responses in every area, whereas naturalistic structure boosted responses and contrast sensitivity in V2 and V4, with the most dispersed tuning in V4. Linear readout of naturalistic structure was possible in V2 and V4 and was most robust to contrast changes in V4, suggesting invariance emerges along the ventral stream.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Gerick M. Lee, Najib J. Majaj, Charlie L. Rodriguez-Deliz, Lynne Kiorpes, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Neuronal and Behavioral Responses to Naturalistic Texture Images in Macaque Monkeys
papers.abstract: Monkeys were trained to judge whether a stimulus looked more like naturalistic texture or like phase-scrambled noise while V1 and V2 neurons were recorded simultaneously. Single neurons carried far less information than the animals' behavior, but V2 cells, particularly those that prefer naturalistic textures, came significantly closer to behavioral sensitivity than V1 cells. Choice-related firing was seen in one monkey only, so the authors conclude that the neural code for texture perception keeps developing downstream of V2.
papers.authors: Corey M. Ziemba, Robbe L. T. Goris, Gabriel M. Stine, Richard K. Perez, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: From stuff to things: Responses of neurons in macaque V4 to textures and objects
papers.abstract: Images were built along a continuum from scrambled textures to intact photographs by varying the size of the region over which local statistics are preserved. V4 neurons responded equally on average to photographs and their scrambled versions, yet had a larger dynamic range for photographs, letting populations discriminate photographs better. Responses to partially scrambled images stayed texture-like until the pooling regions shrank to about half a typical receptive field, and object selectivity built up slowly, hinting at recurrent mechanisms.
papers.authors: Justin D. Lieber, Timothy D. Oleskiw, Laura Palmieri, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

papers.title: Foundations of visual form selectivity for neurons in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: A two-stage model combines the outputs of a fixed bank of V1-like oriented filters with sparse, local weights, and was fit to V1 and V2 responses recorded in awake fixating macaques to sparse 'droplet' stimuli. It explains roughly 43% of explainable variance in V1 and 38% in V2 and generalizes to gratings and spectrally varied textures. It fares worse for some form-selective responses, marking limits of the feedforward account.
papers.authors: Timothy D. Oleskiw, Justin D. Lieber, Eero P. Simoncelli, J. Anthony Movshon

0281.name: Jack Gallant
0281.department: Department of Psychology and Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute
0281.bio: Jack Gallant is a cognitive neuroscientist who develops voxel-wise encoding models to characterize how the human brain processes naturalistic sensory and cognitive information. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and machine learning techniques, Gallant’s research maps the functional organization of the cerebral cortex during tasks such as movie watching and language comprehension. This work includes the creation of semantic atlases and the reconstruction of visual experiences from brain activity. Their current research focus involves refining these computational models to decode complex mental states and individual differences in brain representation.
0281.research_direction: Dr. Gallant has recently been using high-dimensional voxelwise encoding models to map how the human brain processes complex, naturalistic stimuli during both vision and language tasks. Their recent work explores the distributed cortical networks that mediate real-world spatial navigation and investigates how visual-semantic tuning dynamically shifts when subjects switch from passive movie watching to active goal-directed behavior. In the linguistic domain, they are examining how varying degrees of narrative context influence semantic representations across the cortex. To support these naturalistic approaches, Dr. Gallant is also developing new computational methodologies, ranging from foundational tutorials on encoding models to advanced machine learning techniques that use sparse concept atoms to make dense neural embeddings more interpretable.

papers.title: Visual-Semantic Tuning across the Cortex Shifts between Tasks
papers.abstract: Voxelwise encoding models were used to compare how visual-semantic tuning differs across two naturalistic fMRI experiments, movie watching and active navigation. Tuning changed substantially between tasks: during navigation, representations of vehicles and traffic signs increased and the shifts were confined to particular functional networks. The results indicate that cortical object representations are reconfigured according to behavioral relevance.
papers.authors: Tianjiao Zhang, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: A map of the cortical functional network mediating naturalistic navigation
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while participants navigated a virtual city, the authors fit very high-dimensional encoding models (over 28,000 features) with banded ridge regression. They find that real-world navigation recruits a network of 11 functionally distinct cortical regions, spanning prefrontal, parietal and visual cortex, that transform perceptual input through decision-making into action. The regions are arranged along distributed functional gradients, giving a unified map of the navigation network. The lab reports the work as accepted at Nature Neuroscience (Sept 2026).
papers.authors: Tianjiao Zhang, Emily X. Meschke, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: The Voxelwise Encoding Model framework: A tutorial introduction to fitting encoding models to fMRI data
papers.abstract: This tutorial explains the voxelwise encoding model approach, in which stimulus or task features are used to predict activity in each voxel and performance is judged on held-out data. It argues that the framework handles complex naturalistic stimuli, produces high-dimensional functional maps, limits overfitting, and generalizes across subjects and stimuli. Hands-on tutorials built on open-source tools such as Himalaya and Pycortex are provided for newcomers.
papers.authors: Tom Dupre la Tour, Matteo Visconti di Oleggio Castello, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: Disentangling Superpositions: Interpretable Brain Encoding Model with Sparse Concept Atoms
papers.abstract: Dense word or network embeddings are hard to interpret in encoding models because distinct semantic features overlap along correlated directions, making regression weights non-identifiable. The authors map embeddings into a higher-dimensional sparse, non-negative space of learned concept atoms, so each axis corresponds to an interpretable concept. On story-listening fMRI the model predicts as well as dense models while allowing clean readout of voxel selectivity, for example separating cortical representations of time, space and number.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 38
papers.authors: Alicia Zeng, Jack L. Gallant

papers.title: Semantic Representations during Language Comprehension Are Affected by Context
papers.abstract: Four subjects read text in four context conditions (narratives, isolated sentences, blocks of related words, isolated words) during fMRI. More context raised response signal-to-noise and increased semantic representation across temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortex, and altered voxel semantic tuning. Models fit on low-context stimuli generalized poorly to natural language, questioning conclusions based on simplified stimuli.
papers.authors: Fatma Deniz, Christine Tseng, Leila Wehbe, Tom Dupre la Tour, Jack L. Gallant

0282.name: Jacob Feldman
0282.department: Department of Psychology, Rutgers Center for Cognitive Science
0282.bio: Jacob Feldman is a Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Science at Rutgers University who specializes in the mathematical and computational modeling of human visual perception and concept learning. Feldman’s research investigates how the visual system utilizes principles of simplicity and Bayesian inference to organize image data and estimate the structure of the world. Their work addresses shape representation, perceptual grouping, and the Boolean complexity of human categorization. Currently, Feldman explores the probabilistic origins of compositional mental representations and information-theoretic frameworks for signal detection.
0282.research_direction: Dr. Feldman has recently been investigating how the mind extracts structured representations from complex, noisy environments. Their recent work explores the theoretical foundations of concept learning, using information-theoretic and Bayesian frameworks to model how humans form discrete compositional features and learn probabilistically defined concepts based on their complexity. Within visual perception, they are examining how the brain uses internal skeletal models to judge shape similarity across novel objects, and how structural shape interacts with kinematic cues to support emotion recognition from naturalistic biological motion. Additionally, their research extends into applied social perception, using virtual reality to test how the trajectory curvature of passing mobile robots influences human affective responses like arousal and pleasantness.

papers.title: Simplicity and complexity of probabilistically defined concepts
papers.abstract: Extends Feldman's classic work on Boolean concept complexity from deterministic to probabilistic concepts defined by distributions over features. It develops a measure of the complexity of such concepts and links it to how easy they are for people to learn, tying concept learning to simplicity and efficient probabilistic inference.
papers.authors: Jacob Feldman

papers.title: The role of dynamic shape cues in the recognition of emotion from naturalistic body motion
papers.abstract: Examines how observers infer emotions from body motion using naturalistic clips (films, security footage) rather than staged displays. Joint positions extracted algorithmically were rendered as point-light displays, stick figures, or anatomically scrambled figures, revealing how much skeletal shape information beyond point-light motion contributes to emotion recognition across fear, joy, anger, sadness and other states.
papers.authors: Erika Ikeda, Nathan Destler, Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Effects of Mobile Robot Passing-Motion Path Curvature on Human Affective States in a Hallway Environment
papers.abstract: In a virtual-reality hallway, participants were passed by a mobile robot following Bezier-curve trajectories that varied in sharpness of curvature and starting distance, and rated how arousing and pleasant each pass felt. Moderate curvature produced the most positive affect, while very sharp or very straight passes were rated more negatively, yielding an empirical constraint for socially acceptable robot path planning.
papers.authors: Benjamin Greenberg, Uriel González-Bravo, Jingang Yi, Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Probabilistic origins of compositional mental representations
papers.abstract: Asks how discrete, combinable features can adequately capture the continuous, noisy probabilistic structure of the world. Introduces information-theoretic measures of the fidelity and efficiency of a featural representation relative to a probability model, and shows that combinations of projected features (compositionality) can represent a distribution far better than single features. The framework explains when and why the mind should carve the world into compositional discrete parts.
papers.authors: Jacob Feldman

papers.title: Skeleton-based shape similarity
papers.abstract: Proposes a principled measure of shape similarity, 'generative similarity', built on the Bayesian skeleton estimation framework: two shapes are similar in proportion to the posterior probability that they arose from a common skeletal model rather than separate ones. In experiments where subjects picked members of a shape class from 1-3 example nonsense shapes (2D and 3D), the measure predicted choices better than competing similarity measures from the literature.
papers.authors: Nathan Destler, Manish Singh, Jacob Feldman

0283.name: James Bisley
0283.bio: James W. Bisley is a Professor in the Department of Neurobiology at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. His research investigates the neural basis of visual attention and spatial processing, focusing on the lateral intraparietal area (LIP), visual working memory and saccadic eye movements in the primate brain. He studies how the brain prioritizes information during visual search and decision-making. He earned his PhD at the University of Melbourne, did postdoctoral work at the University of Rochester and Georgetown University/National Eye Institute, and joined UCLA in 2006.
0283.research_direction: Dr. Bisley has recently been investigating how the primate brain prioritizes visual information and plans eye movements. His recent work explores how neurons in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) remap their responses around saccades, showing that the timing of remapping is consistent with a wave of activity that takes longer for longer saccades. He and his collaborators also study how saccadic decisions are corrected during active visual search, where monkeys often make very short-latency second saccades to the search target, and how the priority-map concept from visual neuroscience relates to attention mechanisms in transformer-based language models.

papers.title: The timing of LIP remapping is consistent with a wave of activity and brings into question the relevance of the pre-saccadic remapped response
papers.abstract: Recording from LIP neurons while animals made saccades of different lengths, the authors found that predictive remapping takes longer for longer saccades, which points to a wave of activity as the underlying mechanism and questions whether pre-saccadic remapped responses are a fundamental feature of remapping.
papers.authors: Yelda Alkan, Alanna Morris, James W. Bisley

papers.title: A priority map is all you need: Exploring the roots of neural mechanisms underlying transformer-based large language models
papers.abstract: Draws an analogy between priority maps in visual neuroscience, which combine bottom-up salience with top-down goals to direct attention, and the attention mechanisms of transformer language models, noting shared features such as parallel processing, layered refinement and inhibition.
papers.authors: Koorosh Mirpour, James W. Bisley, Nader Pouratian

papers.title: Correction of saccadic decisions during active visual search in the monkey
papers.abstract: Monkeys performing active visual search without a pop-out target often make an ultra-short-latency second saccade that corrects an erroneous first saccade, preferentially landing on the search target; the results suggest concurrent processing of saccade goals in visual and oculomotor priority maps.
papers.authors: Anna E. Ipata, James W. Bisley, B. Suresh Krishna

0284.name: James Gordon
0284.main_research_area: Visual neuroscience of color and form
0284.bio: James Gordon is a Professor Emeritus in the Department of Psychology at Hunter College, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the processing of color and form. Gordon’s research utilizes a combination of psychophysical techniques, such as hue scaling and chromatic adaptation, alongside physiological measures including visual evoked potentials (VEP) to map the development of parallel visual pathways from infancy to adulthood. Gordon has contributed to the creation of nonlinear models for human luminance contrast and the study of color-brightness interactions in the primary visual cortex. Their current work focuses on identifying specific visual processing deficits in pathologies such as schizophrenia, glaucoma, and autism to facilitate clinical diagnosis and potential intervention strategies.
0284.research_direction: Dr. Gordon has recently been investigating the neurophysiological and psychophysical mechanisms underlying human color appearance and spatial vision. Their recent work explores how the visual cortex integrates chromatic and luminance signals arriving from the retina, utilizing scalp-recorded visual evoked potentials and psychophysical hue and saturation scaling to probe phenomena like the perceptual effects of weak luminance contrast on S-cone isolating stimuli. In a distinct line of research, they have also been examining the spatial contrast sensitivity function through the development of accessible, tablet-deliverable visual assessments. By modeling these spatial frequency measurements with receptive-field-based mechanisms, they aim to bridge the gap between behavioral psychophysics, underlying retinal and cortical processing, and clinical visual deficits.

papers.title: Cortical processing of color: Chromatic visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: Reviews and interprets scalp-recorded visual evoked potentials elicited by chromatic stimuli to understand how human visual cortex combines the separate color and luminance signals arriving from the retina. The paper relates the timing and form of these responses to cortical color mechanisms and to perceptual color appearance.
papers.authors: Robert Shapley, Valerie Nunez, James Gordon

papers.title: Low luminance contrast's effect on the color appearance of S-cone patterns
papers.abstract: Uses psychophysical hue and saturation scaling to show that weak luminance contrast in the surround or pattern shifts the perceived color of stimuli that isolate the short-wavelength cones. This reveals an interaction between luminance and S-cone chromatic signals at early cortical stages.
papers.authors: Robert Shapley, Valerie Nunez, James Gordon

papers.title: The spatial contrast sensitivity function and its neurophysiological bases
papers.abstract: Presents a tablet-deliverable test of contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies and models the resulting function with receptive-field-based mechanisms, tying the measurements to underlying retinal and cortical processing. It also discusses relevance for clinical populations with visual deficits.
papers.authors: Vance Zemon, Pamela D. Butler, Michael E. Legatt, James Gordon

0285.name: James Herman
0285.bio: Herman investigates how primate visual perception and cognitive functions such as attention and decision-making emerge from coordinated activity between the cerebral cortex and subcortical regions including the superior colliculus and basal ganglia. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms of learning-driven behavioral changes using a combination of high-density extracellular electrophysiology, psychophysics, and targeted neuronal perturbations. Recently, Herman’s work has integrated computational modeling, including recurrent vision transformers, to analyze the relationship between biological and artificial intelligence in how populations of neurons govern specific cognitive tasks.
0285.research_direction: Dr. Herman has recently been working on how the brain decides what to attend to, and how that selection is implemented in cortical and subcortical circuits. Their recent work explores a neural network model that combines the self-attention mechanism of vision transformers with working memory and reinforcement learning, asking whether reward feedback alone is enough to produce primate-like attention behavior in a cued change-detection task. They have also been examining priority maps, meaning the brain's running estimate of which locations and features matter most, and the role of the superior colliculus in shaping them.

papers.title: Priority Maps, Featureful Processing, and the Superior Colliculus
papers.authors: Wu, Gandhi, Herman

papers.title: A recurrent vision transformer shows signatures of primate visual attention
papers.abstract: The authors present a neural network model of visual attention (NNMVA) that bridges the gap between AI self-attention and biological mechanisms of biased competition. The model utilizes self-attention from Vision Transformers (ViTs) to simulate competition between representations, coupled with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for working memory and an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework. By training the system solely on reward feedback during a cued orientation-change detection task, the model develops behavioral patterns typical of non-human primates, such as reaction time benefits and accuracy improvements for attended locations. The study demonstrates that reward-driven learning signals can sufficiently organize top-down feedback to guide attentional prioritization in a manner consistent with subcortical and cortical circuits.
papers.authors: Jonathan Mark Morgan, Badr Albanna, James P Herman

0286.name: James Hillis
0286.bio: James Hillis is a research scientist at Meta’s Reality Labs, where they apply vision science to the design of augmented and virtual reality systems. Hillis’s research includes multisensory integration, 3D shape perception via disparity and texture cues, and the development of computational models for perceptual quality metrics. Previously, Hillis served as an assistant professor at the University of Glasgow and conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Pennsylvania. They use psychophysical methods and computational modeling of human perception to study display performance and human-computer interaction in immersive environments.
0286.research_direction: Dr. Hillis has recently been working on how human visual behavior and the statistics of natural scenes should inform the design of augmented reality displays. Their recent work explores what an AR system needs to sense about the surrounding environment, such as background brightness, clutter, depth, and motion, so that virtual content stays visible and legible when overlaid on the real world. They have also been building a resource-rational account of eye movements during visual search in immersive 3D scenes, treating gaze as an efficient strategy for gathering information under limited cognitive and biological resources, and testing it against human gaze.

papers.title: Environment to Bits: What do AR Systems Need to Know About the Environment to Ensure High Quality Display Experience?
papers.abstract: Unlike conventional emissive displays on mobile devices that adjust brightness based strictly on ambient illuminance, optical see-through augmented reality displays superimpose virtual imagery directly onto physical environments, making visual target detection and legibility highly dependent on local background luminance, spatial clutter, depth structure, and relative motion. Using egocentric video captured during everyday activities, this work quantifies natural environment image statistics to evaluate background variability and determine the minimal environmental sensing required for perceptual optimization. The findings outline architectural considerations for sensor integration and display pipelines, emphasizing the need for synchronized environmental capture, real-time rendering adjustment, and psychophysical evaluation to ensure robust display visibility.
papers.venue: SID Symposium Digest of Technical Papers
papers.authors: James Hillis, Lili Zhang, Takahiro Doi, Xueyan Niu, Charlie S. Burlingham, Thomas E. Yerxa, Jasmine Jan, Romain Bachy, Kavitha Ratnam

papers.title: A Resource-Rational Account of Human Eye Movements During Immersive Visual Search
papers.abstract: Naturalistic visual search requires observers to sample visual information under stringent cognitive and biological constraints. This study formalizes visual search in complex 3D environments as a problem of bounded optimal information gathering, cast as a meta-level Markov decision process (meta-MDP) defined over latent visual representations extracted by a deep convolutional neural network. Reinforcement learning agents optimized to solve this meta-MDP converge toward an ideal observer policy previously formalized only for highly simplified visual arrays. When evaluated against human gaze and fixation sequences collected during immersive visual search tasks in virtual reality (VR), the resource-rational model exhibits close qualitative and quantitative alignment with human fixation behavior, demonstrating that naturalistic scanpaths reflect the rational allocation of limited internal computational resources.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Angela Radulescu, Bas van Opheusden, Frederick Callaway, Thomas L. Griffiths, James M. Hillis

0287.name: James J. DiCarlo
0287.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0287.main_research_area: visual object recognition and computational neuroscience
0287.bio: James J. DiCarlo is the Peter de Florez Professor of Neuroscience at MIT and an Investigator at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research. DiCarlo’s research focuses on reverse-engineering the neural mechanisms of human visual intelligence, specifically how the primate ventral visual stream enables object recognition. Through the integration of large-scale neurophysiology, machine learning, and neural perturbation, their lab develops neurally mechanistic computational models to explain how the brain transforms retinal images into invariant representations. DiCarlo also serves as the Director of the MIT Quest for Intelligence, coordinating interdisciplinary work at the intersection of natural and artificial intelligence.
0287.research_direction: Dr. DiCarlo has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of primate visual processing by leveraging image-computable deep learning models to probe and manipulate brain activity. Their recent work explores how computational models of the ventral visual stream can be used to non-invasively steer targeted neural population dynamics simply by subtly perturbing the natural images an animal views. Beyond core object recognition, they are examining alternative network training objectives—such as estimating spatial features or utilizing predictive coding on natural videos—to determine which learning rules best capture cortical representations of objects and 3D shape-from-motion. Additionally, their research extends these computational frameworks to downstream regions, investigating how unconditioned visual inputs drive natural valence selectivity in the primate amygdala.

papers.title: Predictive coding yields a brain-like code for shape from motion
papers.abstract: The paper examines how the brain recovers 3D surface structure from motion using camouflaged, motion-defined stimuli. Both dorsal and ventral pathways carried information about the surfaces, but parietal neurons tracked human perception most closely. Among the models tested, only video models trained by predictive coding, i.e. filling in missing content in natural videos, reproduced both the neuronal responses and human judgments.
papers.authors: Yoon H. Bai, Thomas P. O'Connell, Yoni Friedman, Ani Ayvazian-Hancock, Hannah Maver, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: An image-computable characterization of the non-conditioned linkage of visual drive and valence in the primate amygdala
papers.abstract: Amygdala neurons are usually studied through learned stimulus-value associations, but responses to natural, unconditioned images are less understood.
