Recordings showed that many amygdala sites are selective across arbitrary natural images, and that this selectivity is well predicted by image-computable models of high-level ventral stream neurons that feed the amygdala. A subpopulation of visually selective sites also had systematically linked valence tuning, without any laboratory conditioning.
papers.authors: Alina S. Peter, Gwangsu Kim, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: Noninvasive precision modulation of high-level neural population activity via natural vision perturbations
papers.abstract: The study asks whether activity of targeted neurons deep in the primate ventral visual stream can be steered without any invasive hardware, simply by subtly perturbing the images an animal views. Using ventral-stream models to design the perturbations, the authors found that the effects recorded in macaque inferior temporal cortex matched model predictions, with strong modulation focused on the targeted sites. They further showed that experimenter-chosen population activity patterns could be injected on top of ordinary natural visual input.
papers.authors: Guy Gaziv, Sarah Goulding, Ani Ayvazian-Hancock, Yoon Bai, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: Vision CNNs trained to estimate spatial latents learned similar ventral-stream-aligned representations
papers.abstract: Rather than training on object categories, the authors trained CNNs to estimate spatial latent variables of objects such as pose and position. The resulting networks developed representations that align with ventral stream neural data about as well as category-trained models. This suggests that the ventral stream's objective may be broader than categorization alone.
papers.authors: Yudi Xie, Weichen Huang, Esther Alter, Jeremy Schwartz, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, James J. DiCarlo

papers.title: The Quest for an Integrated Set of Neural Mechanisms Underlying Object Recognition in Primates
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes what is known about how the primate ventral visual stream supports core object recognition, from single-neuron tuning to population codes and behavior. It argues that image-computable, neurally mechanistic models now provide a common framework for integrating these findings and generating testable predictions. It also outlines remaining gaps in mapping models to circuits and to causal manipulations.
papers.authors: Kohitij Kar, James J. DiCarlo

0288.name: James W. Tanaka
0288.bio: James W. Tanaka is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Victoria and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada who investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying face and object recognition. Tanaka’s research examines the 'expertise hypothesis,' which posits that face-like holistic processing is a byproduct of perceptual experience, a concept demonstrated through the part-whole effect paradigm. This work extends to clinical and applied domains, including the development of digital interventions for children with autism and studies on the 'other-race' effect in social perception. Currently, their lab utilizes EEG, eye-tracking, and psychological embedding software like PsiZ to model how individuals represent complex visual categories and to track the temporal dynamics of face familiarity.
0288.research_direction: Dr. Tanaka has recently been investigating the cognitive and behavioral mechanisms underlying high-level visual perception, with a distinct focus on face processing and visual expertise. Their recent work explores the multifaceted nature of face perception, pairing recognition memory with similarity ratings to test whether the cross-race effect is driven by representational density within a psychological face space, and utilizing composite paradigms to examine how facial and bodily cues are integrated during whole-person identity judgments. They have also been probing the temporal and applied boundaries of face processing, employing backward-masked saccadic choice tasks to isolate feedforward visual sweeps during ultra-rapid face detection, while concurrently developing behavioral training protocols to improve human detection of AI-generated faces based on global perceptual impressions. Beyond face perception, Dr. Tanaka is studying the broader nature of perceptual expertise, using gaze-contingent eye tracking to investigate whether subordinate-level object experts, such as birders, extract information from an expanded peripheral perceptual field.

papers.title: Training humans to detect AI-generated faces
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a new way to help people spot AI-generated faces: rather than teaching them specific visual artifacts, participants are trained to use their global impressions of faces, since AI and real faces evoke systematically different perceptual impressions. In a pre-post design with untrained test faces, all 45 participants improved and mean accuracy nearly doubled, with some reaching near-perfect detection and better confidence calibration after training. A test-retest control ruled out practice effects and an online replication showed the approach scales.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Amy Dawel, Tanya George, Eric Y. Mah, James D. Dunn, Clare A. M. Sutherland, Nicholas J. Argument, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Differences between the perception and the recognition of cross-race faces
papers.abstract: Tests the Face Space account of the cross-race effect by pairing recognition memory tasks with similarity-rating tasks on the same faces in Asian, Black and White participants. Similarity judgments were used to build psychological face spaces so that recognition accuracy could be linked to how densely same- versus cross-race faces are represented. The results only partly supported the density prediction, suggesting that perception and recognition of cross-race faces dissociate.
papers.authors: Deniz Töredi, Eric Y. Mah, Megan K. Lall, Hongjing Jin, Brett D. Roads, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Attending to faces and bodies in person perception
papers.abstract: Uses face-body composite pairs in a sequential matching task to ask how the face and body of a person are combined in identity judgements. When observers attended to the face, an unattended body interfered with same/different judgments, and vice versa, with congruent trials better than incongruent ones. Misaligning face and body had no effect on this congruency, suggesting whole-person perception is not a face-like holistic process.
papers.authors: Anna K. Lawrance, Nicholas J. Argument, Katelyn Forner, Eric Y. Mah, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: Fast saccades to faces during the feedforward sweep
papers.abstract: Uses a saccadic choice task with backward masking, which mainly disrupts feedback processing, to test whether ultra-fast face-selective eye movements can arise from a single feedforward pass. Accurate face saccades occurred within roughly 110-160 ms even under strong masking and even when observers reported no visual experience, though masking slowed median latencies. The findings support a feedforward account of rapid face detection.
papers.authors: Alison Campbell, James W. Tanaka

papers.title: A perceptual field test in object experts using gaze-contingent eye tracking
papers.abstract: Bird experts and novices judged whether two sequentially shown bird images were the same species while the second image was shown fully, only near gaze, or only in the periphery using gaze-contingent eye tracking. Eye-movement behavior did not differ between groups, but experts' fastest responses were less harmed when only peripheral information was available. This suggests expertise expands the perceptual field used for subordinate-level recognition.
papers.authors: Simen Hagen, Quoc C. Vuong, Liandra Jung, Michael D. Chin, Lisa S. Scott, James W. Tanaka

0289.name: Jan R. Wiersema
0289.bio: Jan R. Wiersema is a professor at Ghent University whose research focuses on the neurocognitive underpinnings of developmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD. Wiersema utilizes neurophysiological methodologies, including high-density EEG, frequency tagging, and fMRI, to investigate social perception, self-referential processing, and the mechanisms of self-other distinction. Their work explores how the visual and motor cortices represent complex social interactions and observed actions within visual scenes. Through leadership of the EXPLORA research group, Wiersema aims to identify neural biomarkers of social-cognitive challenges and characterize the dimensions of cognitive effort and uncertainty in clinical populations.
0289.research_direction: Dr. Wiersema's recent work explores the neural mechanisms of social cognition and biological motion perception, with a strong focus on how these processes operate across the autism spectrum. Using EEG frequency tagging, they have recently been investigating how dynamic visual cues, such as synchrony, group individual point-light walkers into a social whole, and how individuals process complex, third-party social interactions within naturalistic scenes. They are also examining whether specific non-social autism traits alter the spatial and temporal integration required to bind local motion signals into a global visual percept. Methodologically, Dr. Wiersema is actively refining frequency-tagging paradigms by evaluating their utility and pitfalls for clinical research and by developing novel time-resolved approaches to capture more complex, self-referential cognitive phenomena like auditory own-name recognition.

papers.title: EEG frequency tagging for studying social cognition in autism: usefulness and pitfalls
papers.abstract: A single-author article in the International Journal of Psychophysiology that reflects on the use of EEG frequency tagging to study social cognition in autism. It discusses what the method offers for measuring neural responses to social stimuli and where its limitations and pitfalls lie. Summary based on title and venue only; the abstract was not retrievable.
papers.authors: Roeljan Wiersema

papers.title: Evidence that non-social autism traits in the general population are correlated with spatial processing of biological motion
papers.abstract: In 193 general-population participants, the authors tested whether autism traits relate to biological-motion perception while manipulating spatial and temporal scrambling. Contrary to the hypothesis, temporal scrambling effects did not correlate with autism traits, but the attention-to-detail subscale correlated with the effect of spatial scrambling. This links autism-related local-global processing to how spatial information binds local motion signals into a global percept, although effect sizes were small.
papers.authors: Emiel Cracco, Danna Oomen, Jan R. Wiersema

papers.title: Using time-resolved auditory frequency tagging to capture self-preferential processing of the own (vs other) name
papers.abstract: The authors sought an EEG auditory frequency-tagging measure of the self-preferential response to one's own name, which is useful for infant and clinical work. In two studies (n=31 and n=32) conventional frequency-tagging analysis showed no self-preferential effect, but a new time-resolved frequency-tagging approach that exploits the late timing of the effect revealed a clear own-name advantage. The approach is proposed as a template for tagging other complex cognitive processes.
papers.authors: Danna Oomen, Emiel Cracco, Annabel D. Nijhof, Jan R. Wiersema

papers.title: Evidence for a role of synchrony but not common fate in the perception of biological group movements
papers.abstract: Two EEG frequency-tagging experiments tested which dynamic cues make several people appear as a social group. Neural responses to four point-light walkers were stronger when they moved in sync than out of sync, but only when presented upright, whereas shared movement direction (common fate) had no effect. The findings point to synchrony as a key driver of social grouping of biological motion.
papers.authors: Emiel Cracco, Liuba Papeo, Jan R. Wiersema

papers.title: EEG frequency tagging evidence of intact social interaction recognition in adults with autism
papers.abstract: The study asks whether autistic adults process third-party social interactions differently from non-autistic adults, using complex scenes rather than isolated faces or hands. With EEG frequency tagging in 61 adults, scenes showing two people interacting drove stronger neural responses than scenes of non-interacting people. This enhancement, previously seen in neurotypical samples, was equally strong in both groups, suggesting that basic social interaction recognition is not what underlies social difficulties in autism.
papers.authors: Danna Oomen, Emiel Cracco, Marcel Brass, Jan R. Wiersema

0290.name: Jan Theeuwes
0290.bio: Jan Theeuwes conducts research in cognitive neuroscience regarding stimulus-driven attentional capture and the interplay between top-down and bottom-up visual selection. Their work utilizes psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI to investigate how environmental statistical regularities and reward history automatically bias attention, challenging traditional dichotomies of attentional control. Theeuwes founded the Institute for Brain and Behavior Amsterdam (iBBA) and developed the 'Self-Explaining Roads' design principle for applied human factors. Additionally, they contributed to the development of the OpenSesame experiment software.
0290.research_direction: Dr. Theeuwes has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual attentional control, focusing on how implicit statistical learning and selection history compete with top-down goals and bottom-up salience to dictate what captures attention. Using a combination of behavioral search paradigms and neuroimaging methods like fMRI and EEG, their recent work explores the spatial and temporal dynamics of proactive distractor suppression to determine whether it operates at the earliest stages of visual cortex processing. They are also developing novel EEG "pinging" techniques coupled with multivariate pattern analysis to read out otherwise latent, history-driven attentional priority maps in the brain when no stimuli are on screen. Furthermore, their behavioral research re-examines classic phenomena like feature-search mode to test whether the prevention of attentional capture relies on distinct top-down control settings or arises mechanically from display-constrained serial scanning.

papers.title: Beyond top-down: Feature search as a serial clump-wise process
papers.abstract: Tests whether the absence of attentional capture in feature-search mode reflects real top-down suppression or simply serial, clump-wise scanning imposed by the display. Using a two-target compatibility manipulation, feature search showed almost no compatibility effects and no capture, whereas singleton-detection mode showed both large compatibility effects and strong capture. The authors conclude that search modes reflect display-constrained serial search rather than distinct control settings, challenging the top-down suppression account.
papers.authors: Jasper de Waard, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Attentional Capture and Control
papers.abstract: A review that lays out a three-part framework for attentional control in which top-down goals, bottom-up salience and selection history compete to set attentional priority. It asks when salient distractors capture attention and when capture is prevented, and concludes that capture can be controlled proactively, mainly through implicit statistical learning rather than volitional top-down suppression. It also surveys the remaining controversies in the field.
papers.authors: Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Proactive distractor suppression in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: An fMRI study in which one location in an additional-singleton search task frequently held a salient distractor, without participants being told. Early visual cortex showed reduced responses at that location, in a receptive-field-specific way, regardless of what item appeared there, and the suppression was also present when search was only anticipated. This indicates that learned distractor suppression is proactive and acts before stimulus identification.
papers.authors: David Richter, Dirk van Moorselaar, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Learning Modulates Early Encephalographic Responses to Distracting Stimuli: A Combined SSVEP and ERP Study
papers.abstract: Combines steady-state visual evoked potentials with event-related potentials while participants learn that a salient distractor frequently appears at one location. Evoked responses at the suppressed location differed from other locations very early after search onset, while pre-search differences were minimal apart from post hoc alpha lateralization. The findings place learned spatial suppression at the initial stages of visual processing.
papers.authors: Dock H. Duncan, Norman Forschack, Dirk van Moorselaar, Matthias M. Müller, Jan Theeuwes

papers.title: Pinging the brain to reveal the hidden attentional priority map using encephalography
papers.abstract: Uses a brief, task-irrelevant visual 'ping' during the intertrial period of an EEG experiment to read out the otherwise silent attentional priority map shaped by statistical learning of target locations. Multivariate pattern analysis of the evoked response reveals the history-driven priority landscape without any stimulus on screen. The work provides both a method for visualizing latent priority and evidence for how past experience biases future selection.
papers.authors: Dock H. Duncan, Dirk van Moorselaar, Jan Theeuwes

0291.name: Jared Medina
0291.bio: Jared Medina is an Associate Professor at Emory University whose research characterizes how the human brain constructs and maintains representations of the body and surrounding space. Their methodology integrates single-case cognitive neuropsychology in brain-damaged populations with functional neuroimaging, non-invasive brain stimulation, and the development of multisensory illusions. Medina investigates the mechanisms of somatosensory plasticity, tactile spatial remapping, and the constraints governing embodiment and the sense of self.
0291.research_direction: Dr. Medina has recently been investigating how the brain integrates visual, tactile, and proprioceptive information to construct body representation and spatial awareness. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of multisensory conflict and embodiment using mirror box illusions, probing phenomena like the visual capture of tactile motion across distinct spatial reference frames and the perceptual requirements for embodying supernumerary digits. They are also utilizing signal detection theory to examine vicarious touch, testing whether viewing tactile stimulation on a hand genuinely alters sensory sensitivity or merely shifts perceptual decision criteria. Additionally, Dr. Medina's clinical research employs fMRI in stroke survivors to understand neural plasticity, specifically asking how cortical motor networks compensate and reorganize around intact visuomotor areas following the loss of primary somatosensory input.

papers.title: Multiple trajectories of proprioceptive drift in the mirror box illusion
papers.abstract: Across four experiments with 181 neurotypical participants, perceived hand position was tracked repeatedly during the mirror box illusion while visual-proprioceptive congruence was varied. Congruence strengthened the illusion, but individuals followed distinct time courses: abrupt shifts, gradual drift, immediate onset, or none. The authors propose these reflect different causal-inference algorithms for resolving multisensory conflict.
papers.authors: Grant T. Fairchild, Yuqi Liu, Jared Medina

papers.title: Visual Capture of Tactile Motion: Evidence from a novel mirror box illusion
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a visuotactile illusion in which viewing a moving stroke across one hand alters the perceived trajectory of a simultaneous touch on the hidden hand. Across four experiments, the capture occurred independently of body ownership. Posture manipulations showed that tactile motion is computed in both skin-based and external reference frames at once.
papers.authors: Anupama Nair, Stephanie Dietz, Jared Medina

papers.title: Reweighting of visuomotor areas during motor processing subsequent to somatosensory cortical damage
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in two stroke survivors with extensive left somatosensory cortex damage but largely intact motor cortex and movement, the study asks how motor networks cope without S1 input. Both patients had impaired touch detection and localization on the contralesional hand, yet differed in how movement recruited motor and visuomotor regions. The results indicate that motor processing reorganizes, shifting weight toward visuomotor areas, when somatosensory cortex is damaged.
papers.authors: Yuqi Liu, Elizabeth J. Halfen, Jeffrey M. Yau, Simon Fischer-Baum, Peter J. Kohler, Olufunsho Faseyitan, H. Branch Coslett, Jared Medina

papers.title: Anchoring to the hand, but not spatially distinct mappings, facilitates illusory supernumerary finger embodiment
papers.abstract: Using the Anne Boleyn mirror illusion, in which a sixth finger is felt, the study tested what is needed for embodying an extra digit. Stroking only one location on the hidden finger did not weaken the illusion, whereas the starting location of the stroke mattered. Embodiment appears to depend on anchoring the extra finger to the hand rather than on distinct spatial mappings.
papers.authors: Isabel T. Folger, Jared Medina

papers.title: Viewed touch influences tactile detection by altering decision criterion
papers.abstract: Seeing a hand being touched raises tactile detection rates, which has been read as evidence for a vicarious tactile system. Applying signal detection theory in three experiments, this study shows that viewed touch instead makes observers more liberal in their reporting criterion, with little change in sensitivity. This offers a decision-level alternative to the sensory-enhancement account.
papers.authors: Anupama Nair, Jared Medina

0292.name: Jarrod Lewis-Peacock
0292.bio: Lewis-Peacock investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control and the management of information within working memory. Their research utilizes neuroimaging techniques, such as multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and real-time fMRI neurofeedback, to decode and manipulate mental representations in the human brain. Lewis-Peacock examines how the brain prioritizes, updates, and removes information from the focus of attention to support goal-directed behavior. Their work explores the intersection of memory and control, specifically how strategic shifts in attention and cognitive interventions influence long-term memory outcomes and the intentional forgetting of information.
0292.research_direction: Dr. Lewis-Peacock has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between working memory, visual attention, and cognitive control, particularly focusing on how the human brain manages distraction and interference. Using computational modeling and neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG multivariate decoding, their recent work explores how visual distractors and prior trial histories intrude upon or merge with active target representations in visual working memory. They are also examining the mechanisms of active suppression, testing how deliberately forgetting maintained items impacts subsequent hippocampal associative learning and tracking the temporal dynamics of how salient singleton distractors are converted into suppressive codes during visual search. Broadening these themes to continuous behavior, they are assessing how working memory capacity constrains individuals' ability to flexibly reprioritize spatial targets and replan navigational routes following sudden environmental perturbations.

papers.title: Rapid Inversion of Singleton Distractor Representations Underlies Learned Attentional Suppression
papers.abstract: Using multivariate decoding of EEG during visual search (N = 40), the study shows that singleton-distractor information appears in an early phase and is then transformed into an inverted code in a later phase. Stronger late representations predicted faster search, and distractor locations were suppressed relative to other locations in the spatial priority map. The results point to top-down control converting bottom-up saliency into suppression.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Working memory constraints on replanning following distraction
papers.abstract: A Snake-inspired navigation paradigm (N = 50) tested how people reallocate working memory when a sudden distraction moves them away from their plan. Without distraction, people prioritized nearby remembered targets; after a perturbation they re-prioritized targets near their new position. This flexibility shrank with memory load, and after distraction people could rely on only about one item regardless of load.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Maintenance suppression enhances subsequent associative learning
papers.abstract: Across behavioral and fMRI experiments, deliberately suppressing just-learned associations in working memory made it easier to encode new associations afterward. The benefit was tied to stronger neural pattern fidelity in hippocampal subfield CA1, and later retrieval was helped by a neural bias away from the previously suppressed content. The work frames active forgetting as an adaptive process that clears the way for new learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Signal Intrusion Explains Divergent Effects of Visual Distraction on Working Memory
papers.abstract: The authors propose a single signal-intrusion model, built on the target-confusability-competition framework, in which a distractor's sensory signal blends with the target's during memory. Fit to three delayed-estimation experiments (N = 220), it outperformed alternative models and reproduced the seemingly conflicting distraction effects on bias, precision and guess rate. Intrusion weakened as distractors became less similar to the target, consistent with sensory recruitment.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

papers.title: Integration of history information Drives Serial Dependence and Stabilizes Working Memory Representations
papers.abstract: The paper tests a reactivation-and-integration account of serial dependence in visual working memory using EEG pattern analysis (26 participants). Prior reports, rather than prior sensory inputs, are reactivated on the next trial, and the strength of that reactivation predicts the size of the behavioral bias. The reactivated content merges with the current memory representation and improves its decodability, explaining both biasing and stabilizing effects.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock

0293.name: Jason B. Mattingley
0293.department: Queensland Brain Institute and School of Psychology
0293.bio: Jason B. Mattingley is the Foundation Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Queensland, holding a joint appointment between the Queensland Brain Institute and the School of Psychology. Mattingley's research investigates the neural architecture of selective attention, multisensory processing, and executive control to understand how the brain prioritizes sensory input and coordinates motor behavior. They employ a multimodal approach combining psychophysics, functional MRI, electroencephalography, and transcranial brain stimulation to probe cognitive functions in healthy adults and patients with neurological conditions. Mattingley's recent work focuses on the influence of neural oscillations on perception and the mechanisms of brain plasticity during learning and decision-making tasks.
0293.research_direction: Dr. Mattingley has recently been investigating how the human visual system dynamically processes and stabilizes information in continuously changing environments. Their recent work explores predictive coding, using behavioral, pupillometry, and EEG techniques to test how expectation violations—both within a visual sequence and across auditory-visual modalities—alter the neural representation and perceptual fidelity of sensory features. They are also examining the neural mechanics of perceptual decision-making by tracking how sensory uncertainty is continuously resolved in the brain as evidence accumulates over time. Broadening this focus on dynamic vision, Dr. Mattingley is probing the computational mechanisms that maintain spatially stable attention across saccadic eye movements and disentangling the early and late neural processes that drive sensory adaptation.

papers.title: Dynamic reduction of neural uncertainty shapes perceptual decisions in a Bayes-optimal manner
papers.abstract: The authors ask what actually gets refined as evidence accumulates during a decision. Recording EEG while 32 people judged the direction of global dot motion, they decoded time-resolved uncertainty in the brain's motion representation. Uncertainty shrank steadily over the course of a trial, and this shrinkage tracked the timing and accuracy of decisions in a way that matches a Bayes-optimal observer. The results tie sequential-sampling models of decisions to a concrete change in the precision of sensory neural codes.
papers.authors: Dragan Rangelov, Sebastian Bitzer, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Neural effects of expectation violation generalise across sensory modalities
papers.abstract: Prediction is thought to cut sensory overload, but most work looks within a single modality. Here observers watched rapid streams of oriented gratings while ignoring an alternating high/low tone sequence, and EEG was used to read out how visual orientation was represented. Violations of the auditory pattern altered the neural representation of the visual stimuli, showing that expectation violations propagate across senses rather than staying modality-specific.
papers.authors: Dragan Rangelov, Edwina Shi, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Violated predictions enhance the representational fidelity of visual features in perception
papers.abstract: Predictive coding says that violated expectations produce prediction errors, but what this does to perception has been unclear. Observers reported the orientation of a briefly shown grating embedded in predictable or random sequences, first with a speeded categorisation and then with an untimed reproduction, while pupil size indexed surprise. When the sequence prediction was violated, orientation representations were reproduced more accurately, indicating that surprise sharpens rather than degrades perceptual fidelity.
papers.authors: Reuben Rideaux, Phuong Dang, Luke Jackel-David, Zak Buhmann, Dragan Rangelov, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: A computational account of transsaccadic attentional allocation based on visual gain fields
papers.abstract: Eye movements give only brief, fovea-limited snapshots of the world, yet perception stays stable across them. Using a psychophysical protocol with fine spatial and temporal resolution and custom analysis, the authors show that the visual system computes an object's real-world position very early, and that attention is allocated in world-centred coordinates across saccades. They propose a model based on gain-field remapping that accounts for the pattern of attentional benefits before and after eye movements.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: William J. Harrison, Imogen Stead, Thomas S. A. Wallis, Peter J. Bex, Jason B. Mattingley

papers.title: Distinct early and late neural mechanisms regulate feature-specific sensory adaptation in the human visual system
papers.abstract: Sensory adaptation may reflect neuronal fatigue or a sharpening of selectivity, and the two accounts have been hard to separate. Recording whole-brain activity before and after adaptation to gratings and applying inverted encoding, the authors found signatures of both. Fatigue-like changes arose early and sharpening-like changes arose later, indicating that adaptation is implemented by separable mechanisms on different timescales.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Reuben Rideaux, Rebecca K. West, Dragan Rangelov, Jason B. Mattingley

0294.name: Jay Pratt
0294.bio: Jay Pratt is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto who investigates the mechanisms of visual cognition and their role in guiding human action. Pratt's research focuses on how the brain selectively acquires information from the visual field and how this selection influences motor outputs, such as eye movements and limb reach. Methodologically, Pratt utilizes psychophysical testing, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological measures (EEG/ERP) to explore phenomena including attentional prioritization and inhibitory processes like inhibition of return. They also study the modulation of visual pathways by hand proximity.
0294.research_direction: Dr. Pratt's recent work investigates the diverse mechanisms that guide and shape visual attention, spanning basic feature selection, higher-order perceptual representations, and social influences. Utilizing behavioral methods like temporal order judgments and eye tracking, they have recently been exploring whether target selection during visual search obligatorily encodes information into visual working memory, and how rapidly the oculomotor system adapts to novel search features via target enhancement versus distractor suppression. Their research also examines attentional prioritization by complex stimuli, asking whether internally generated, unseen ensemble statistics or intuitive physical properties—such as object stability and orientation—can direct visual attention. Furthermore, Dr. Pratt is probing the intersection of social constructs and basic spatial orienting by testing whether internalized gendered socialization can explain established demographic differences in gaze-cueing effects.

papers.title: The mind’s average: Unseen, internally generated ensemble representations can guide visual attention
papers.abstract: The paper examines ensemble (average) representations of a set of items and shows that such summaries can guide visual attention even when the average was never shown and is only internally generated. It extends the group's ensemble-and-attention line of work to the case of unseen summary statistics.
papers.authors: Kristina Knox, Jonathan S. Cant, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Beyond the Gender Differences: Gendered Socialization Impact on Gaze-Cueing Effects
papers.abstract: Women show stronger gaze-cueing effects than men, and this study asks whether gendered socialization explains that difference. In two experiments participants completed a gaze-cueing task (Experiment 1) or a non-social peripheral cueing task (Experiment 2), plus questionnaires analysed with mixed-effects models. Internalized gendered attitudes modulated orienting to gaze cues but not to non-social cues, linking social factors to basic attentional orienting.
papers.authors: Ece Yucer, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Selectively attended information is obligatorily encoded into visual working memory
papers.abstract: The authors test whether picking out a target during visual search automatically writes that item into visual working memory. On a first search trial the target was either selected from among nontargets or shown alone, and on the next trial a distractor matching the earlier target colour captured attention and eye movements more strongly, but only after selection. Filling working memory to capacity removed this carry-over, which supports a causal link between attentional selection and obligatory VWM encoding.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Zachary Hamblin-Frohman, Jay Pratt

papers.title: ‘Not so intuitive’ physics: Orientation supersedes stability in prioritizing attention
papers.abstract: Using cueless temporal order judgments, the study asks whether an object's physical stability gives it a head start in perception. It compares stability with object orientation as cues for attentional prioritization, and finds that upright orientation outweighs stability. The work casts doubt on a special role for intuitive physics in attentional priority.
papers.authors: Ece Yucer, Andrew Clement, Jay Pratt

papers.title: Rapid development of inhibitory effects in response to novel features: It's mostly target-feature enhancement
papers.abstract: The study asks how quickly visual search adapts to a new target or distractor colour and whether the adaptation comes from boosting the target feature or suppressing the distractor feature. Using eye tracking, the authors find that within a few trials the effect is driven mostly by target-feature enhancement rather than distractor suppression.
papers.authors: Zachary Hamblin-Frohman, Jay Pratt

0295.name: Jeffrey Allen Saunders
0295.bio: Jeffrey Allen Saunders is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Hong Kong and directs the 3D Vision and Action Lab. Saunders' research investigates the computational processes and psychophysical principles governing human 3D perception and visuomotor coordination. This work includes studies on the integration of depth cues, such as texture and stereopsis, and how these factors inform the control of reaching and grasping movements. Additionally, Saunders examines the reliability of visual and nonvisual information in perceiving self-motion and heading, utilizing mathematical models to describe human behavioral performance.
0295.research_direction: Dr. Saunders has recently been investigating human perception and visual cognition, with a primary focus on spatial learning and usability in virtual reality. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of cybersickness, testing whether interventions like rendering a stationary virtual nose or restricting a user's visual attention to the central visual field can mitigate discomfort during simulated movement. In addition to VR usability, they are researching spatial navigation, specifically examining whether providing top-down maps or unobstructed environmental overviews helps individuals translate first-person egocentric experiences into accurate allocentric spatial representations. In a distinct line of visual attention research, Dr. Saunders is also investigating temporal processing limits, measuring how foreknowledge of arousing distractor images or categories modulates target suppression in emotion-induced blindness paradigms.

papers.title: Does viewing a top-down map facilitate spatial learning from navigation in a virtual environment?
papers.abstract: Across three experiments, participants explored virtual cities and villages with or without first viewing a top-down map, then were tested with pointing, judgments of relative direction and map reconstruction. Map previews, whether structural or detailed and whether or not targets were labeled, did not improve the spatial knowledge acquired through first-person navigation. The authors speculate that translating between egocentric experience and allocentric map information is hard, which limits the benefit of maps.
papers.authors: Jie Ding, Ho Ming Chan, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Knowing the upcoming distractor image or category can reduce the emotion-induced blindness effect from erotic images
papers.abstract: Emotion-induced blindness is the brief failure to see a target that follows an emotionally arousing distractor in a rapid picture stream. In three preregistered experiments (N = 48 each), warning participants about the distractor reduced this blindness. Previewing the exact distractor image cut the effect by about 78 percent, versus roughly a third for a same-category image or a text warning. This suggests specific previews prime or suppress the distractor, while category knowledge alone still offers partial protection.
papers.authors: Ho Ming Chan, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Preregistered test of whether a virtual nose reduces cybersickness
papers.abstract: Earlier work suggested that rendering a nose in a VR headset could reduce motion sickness, but the evidence came from one low-powered study. Here participants (n = 32) experienced simulated movement with and without a virtual nose in separate sessions, in a preregistered, better controlled design using standard sickness scales and Bayesian analysis. The effect was essentially zero (dz about -0.02), and any true benefit was bounded to be small. The paper is a rigorous failure to confirm a popular, simple VR intervention.
papers.authors: Sai Ho Yip, Adrian K. T. Ng, Henry Y. K. Lau, Jeffrey A. Saunders

papers.title: Restricting the distribution of visual attention reduces cybersickness
papers.abstract: The authors asked whether directing attention to the central rather than peripheral visual field can lessen motion sickness in virtual reality. In one experiment, cueing targets centrally or peripherally during VR navigation made no difference, but a second experiment using a dot-probe task found more sickness when attention had to be spread to the periphery. Baseline attentional allocation did not predict individual susceptibility, so the earlier correlational finding was not replicated. The results suggest that keeping attention central reduces cybersickness, in line with the known link between wide field of view and sickness.
papers.authors: Sai Ho Yip, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

papers.title: Does viewing an environment without occluders improve spatial learning of a large-scale virtual environment?
papers.abstract: The study tested whether seeing a virtual environment from a vantage with no occluding structures before or during exploration helps people build a better spatial representation. Participants learned large virtual spaces by navigation and were then tested on their spatial knowledge. The work examines how an unobstructed overview interacts with first-person learning of layout.
papers.authors: Ho Ming Chan, Jie Ding, Jeffrey Allen Saunders

0296.name: Jeffrey D. Wammes
0296.bio: Jeffrey D. Wammes is an Assistant Professor at Queen's University who researches how learning and experience reorganize representational spaces in the brain to facilitate memory retrieval. Wammes utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), computational tools, and behavioral experiments to investigate the mnemonic benefits of active learning tasks, particularly the 'drawing effect,' and how these activities drive representational change in the hippocampus. Their research also examines the dynamics of attention, specifically analyzing how intentional and unintentional mind-wandering impact performance in laboratory settings and educational environments.
0296.research_direction: Dr. Wammes has recently been investigating the interplay between active visual behaviors, memory, and large-scale cortical organization, with a major focus on how the physical act of drawing serves as a versatile cognitive tool that shapes ongoing thought patterns and memory encoding. Their recent neuroimaging work explores the functional architecture of visual processing, using fMRI and generative image synthesis to map convolutional neural network layers onto distinct cortical regions, while also tracking how visual statistical learning shifts whole-brain connectivity along low-dimensional network gradients. Additionally, they have been examining applied cognitive phenomena, specifically investigating how behavioral interventions like concurrent testing can mitigate mind-wandering and sustain attention during continuous educational tasks.

papers.title: Concurrent testing improves attention generally and selectively during video lectures
papers.abstract: Students watched video lectures with test questions embedded during viewing, and attention was measured through mind-wandering reports and content-specific tests. Concurrent questions reduced lapses of attention overall and boosted attention to the tested material specifically. The findings suggest a simple way to keep learners engaged with online lectures.
papers.authors: Silvia Shiwei Zhou, Aidan G. Taylor, Amy Tuer, Selena Breithaupt, Si Pan, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Synthesizing images to map neural networks to the human brain
papers.abstract: The authors build a generative image-synthesis method that decorrelates the representational geometry across layers of a convolutional network, so each layer yields a distinct similarity fingerprint. They scan people with fMRI while viewing 16 synthesized images and show that individual network layers map onto more circumscribed cortical regions than with natural images. A complementary residual method extends the approach to existing natural-image datasets.
papers.authors: Kailong Peng, Kenneth A. Norman, Nicholas B. Turk-Browne, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Visual Statistical Learning Alters Low-Dimensional Cortical Architecture
papers.abstract: Using fMRI during an implicit visual statistical learning task, the study tracks how whole-brain connectivity reorganizes along a low-dimensional manifold as people learn image pairs. Visual regions decouple from other networks while dorsal attention regions become more integrated, and violations of learned regularities shift perirhinal and entorhinal cortex toward default-mode and attention networks. The results frame statistical learning as a distributed, network-level change rather than a single-region effect.
papers.authors: Keanna Rowchan, Daniel J. Gale, Qasem Nick, Jason P. Gallivan, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Drawing behaviour influences ongoing thought patterns and subsequent memory
papers.abstract: Participants drew, wrote or did control tasks while reporting their ongoing thoughts, and memory was tested afterward. Drawing changed what people thought about during encoding, shifting the content of thought in ways that tracked later memory. The work links the drawing effect to changes in ongoing cognition rather than only to sensory or motor factors.
papers.authors: Silvia Shiwei Zhou, Keanna Rowchan, Brontë Mckeown, Jonathan Smallwood, Jeffrey D. Wammes

papers.title: Drawing as a versatile cognitive tool
papers.abstract: A review arguing that drawing is more than an artistic skill: it is a flexible tool for thinking, learning and communicating. The authors synthesize work on how making visual marks supports memory, problem solving and the externalization of ideas, and describe the perceptual, motor and conceptual processes involved. They also outline how drawing can serve as a window onto cognition and lay out open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Judith E. Fan, Wilma A. Bainbridge, Rebecca Chamberlain, Jeffrey D. Wammes

0297.name: Jelena Ristic
0297.bio: Jelena Ristic is a Professor of Psychology at McGill University and directs the Laboratory for Attention & Social Cognition. Their research investigates the mechanisms of human attention and its intersection with social cognition, specifically examining how signals like eye gaze and facial expressions facilitate interpersonal communication. Employing a combination of electroencephalography (EEG), laboratory eye-tracking, and naturalistic mobile gaze monitoring, the lab studies the divergence between controlled and real-world social interactions. Their findings contribute to the understanding of the evolutionary development of social orienting and the role of attention in mediating group dynamics.
0297.research_direction: Dr. Ristic's recent work explores how the visual system processes complex social information, investigating whether observers perceive face-to-face, interacting groups as unified perceptual wholes during visual search. They have also been examining the underlying drivers of social attention, specifically testing how classic gaze-cueing effects are modulated by higher-order inferences about another agent's intentionality. Furthermore, their research probes how emotional expressions influence attentional orienting even when the cueing faces are partially occluded. To push this subfield beyond static, screen-based paradigms, they are utilizing dual mobile eye-tracking methods to measure how mutual eye contact and natural gaze exchange actually unfold during live face-to-face conversations.

papers.title: Social attention is enhanced by facial emotions even for occluded faces
papers.abstract: Gaze-cuing effects were larger when the cueing face showed an emotional expression, and this boost persisted when the lower part of the face was covered by a mask. Emotion information carried by the eye region alone was enough to enhance orienting of attention. The findings tie together the lab's work on emotion, masks and social attention.
papers.authors: Sarah McCrackin, Florence Mayrand, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: A perceptual advantage for social groups in interactive configurations
papers.abstract: Groups of people arranged in interactive, face-to-face configurations were detected and processed more efficiently than non-interactive arrangements. The advantage depended on the configuration of the individuals rather than on low-level features. The paper supports the view that interacting groups are represented as perceptual wholes.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Francesca Capozzi, Victoria Fratino, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: Search advantages for facing social groups reflect optimal interactive group sizes
papers.abstract: Observers find groups of people who face each other faster in visual search than groups facing away, indicating that interacting groups are perceived as a unit. This advantage was strongest for small groups of roughly three to four individuals, matching the sizes at which real conversational groups tend to form. The results suggest the visual system is tuned to the typical scale of human social interaction.
papers.authors: Luowei Yan, Clara Colombatto, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: Intentional looks facilitate faster responding in observers
papers.abstract: Observers responded faster to targets when the preceding gaze shift was perceived as intentional, showing that attributed intent, not just gaze direction, shapes attentional orienting. The experiments link gaze following to inference about another agent's mental state. This connects classic gaze-cuing research to social cognition.
papers.authors: Florence Mayrand, Sarah D. McCrackin, Jelena Ristic

papers.title: A dual mobile eye tracking study on natural eye contact during live interactions
papers.abstract: Two people wearing mobile eye trackers conversed face to face while both gaze streams were recorded, allowing mutual eye contact to be measured in natural interaction. Actual eye contact was rare and brief compared with what lab studies with static faces suggest. The work provides a template for studying gaze exchange outside screen-based paradigms.
papers.authors: Florence Mayrand, Francesca Capozzi, Jelena Ristic

0298.name: Jennifer K. E. Steeves
0298.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Health
0298.bio: Jennifer K. E. Steeves is a Professor and the Associate Vice President Research at York University and holds a York Research Chair in Non-Invasive Visual Brain Stimulation. Steeves examines how the human brain reorganizes in response to altered sensory input, such as early monocular enucleation, or to specific cortical lesions like those causing prosopagnosia. By integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and MR spectroscopy, they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying object, face, and scene perception. Their current work focuses on identifying biomarkers for brain plasticity and developing neuromodulation protocols to treat clinical conditions like visual hallucinations and visual snow syndrome.
0298.research_direction: Dr. Steeves has investigated how the visual brain reorganizes and how its cortical areas interact, combining brain stimulation, neuroimaging and behavior. Using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), often combined with fMRI, their work has shown how disrupting object-, scene- and face-selective visual cortex changes processing locally and in remote networks, and how theta burst stimulation affects neurochemistry measured by MR spectroscopy. Recent TMS work uses MRI-guided neuronavigation to quantify phosphene size, phosphene thresholds and modeled electric field strengths, to map individual differences in visual cortex excitability. A second major focus is sensory neuroplasticity following early monocular enucleation, using fMRI population receptive field (pRF) mapping to examine topographic reorganization in early visual cortex, alongside survey-based methods to assess how the timing of eye loss affects vision-related quality of life. Additionally, they study crossmodal plasticity through behavioral testing of how long-term musical training influences voice recognition.

papers.title: Pulvinar and total thalamus volumes are preserved following early monocular enucleation
papers.abstract: Using structural MRI, the authors measured the volume of the pulvinar, its subnuclei and the whole thalamus in adults who lost one eye early in life versus binocular controls. Volumes were preserved in the one-eyed group, unlike the reduced LGN reported previously. The result suggests spared pulvinar and thalamic structure may help support the intact lower-level and enhanced audiovisual processing seen after early eye loss.
papers.authors: Stefania S. Moro, Remy Cohan, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Enhanced voice recognition in musicians
papers.abstract: Musicians and non-musicians learned face-voice and car-horn identity pairs and were tested on old/new recognition in auditory, visual and audiovisual conditions. Musicians were more sensitive to voices but not to object sounds, and voice sensitivity tracked years of training and weekly practice. The dissociation implies experience-driven plasticity in person-specific rather than object-specific pathways.
papers.authors: Allison J. Sletcher, Stefania S. Moro, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Timing of eye removal influences low-vision quality of life and self-perception of facial appearance in people with one eye
papers.abstract: Twenty-two people with early or late eye removal and 27 binocular controls completed questionnaires on low-vision quality of life, facial-appearance self-perception, anxiety and depression. Late enucleation was associated with lower quality of life, tied to poorer self-perceived facial appearance, while time since surgery and binocular experience were not. The authors conclude that developmental timing relative to critical periods, rather than experience, shapes psychosocial outcomes.
papers.authors: Aysha N. Kinakool, Stefania S. Moro, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Continuous and intermittent theta burst stimulation of primary visual cortex do not modulate resting state functional connectivity: A sham-controlled multi-echo fMRI study
papers.abstract: In a sham-controlled design, continuous and intermittent theta burst TMS was applied to V1 while multi-echo resting-state fMRI and phosphene thresholds were measured before and after. Neither protocol changed functional connectivity or visual cortical excitability, in contrast to the group's earlier low-frequency rTMS results. The null finding challenges assumptions that motor-cortex TBS effects generalize to visual cortex.
papers.authors: Remy Cohan, Sara A. Rafique, Karlene S. Stoby, Diana J. Gorbet, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

papers.title: Perception of the McGurk effect in people with one eye depends on whether the eye is removed during infancy or adulthood
papers.abstract: The study compared McGurk-effect perception in people who lost an eye late in life, those who lost one early, and binocular controls. Late-enucleated participants perceived the illusion like controls, whereas the early-enucleated group perceived it much less. This indicates that cross-modal compensation after eye loss depends on age at surgery relative to visual system maturation.
papers.authors: Stefania S. Moro, Faizaan A. Qureshi, Jennifer K. E. Steeves

0299.name: Jenny Bosten
0299.bio: Jenny Bosten is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Sussex and Director of the Sussex Vision Lab, where they study the biological and environmental determinants of human color vision. Bosten’s research uses psychophysics, neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), and genetic analysis to examine how phenotypic variations, such as anomalous trichromacy and putative tetrachromacy, influence individual perceptual experience. They investigate the ecological calibration of the visual system by analyzing natural scene statistics and characterize cortical representations of color through projects such as COLOURCODE and COLOURMIND. Bosten also applies vision science to clinical contexts, developing diagnostic tools for pediatric color vision deficiency and virtual reality-based assessments for patients with low vision.
0299.research_direction: Dr. Bosten's recent work explores how color is processed across multiple levels of the human visual system, from fundamental cortical tuning to subjective perceptual experience. Using high-resolution fMRI data, they have recently been investigating the organization of the ventral visual pathway, probing whether color-biased patches are fundamentally driven by behaviorally relevant objects like food and testing whether voxel-level color preferences can map distinct functional cortical boundaries. To characterize these systems at a more mechanistic level, they also use EEG steady-state visually evoked potentials to measure how hue dissimilarity shapes the tuning functions of cortical color mechanisms. Furthermore, their behavioral research examines plasticity and individual differences in color perception, testing how the visual system adapts to altered environmental color statistics and whether age-related variations in color similarity judgments can illuminate the inter-subjective nature of human color qualia.

papers.title: The colors of images preferred by individual voxels can be used to delineate functionally distinct visual regions
papers.abstract: The authors compute, for each voxel in the Natural Scenes Dataset, a response-weighted average of the images it responds to and use the colors of these voxel-preferred images as a tag for functional properties that co-vary with color in natural scenes. Mapping these onto cortex reveals structured patterns whose boundaries match those from other methods and hint at subdivisions within regions. This offers a simple data-driven way to visualize cortical organization.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ian M. L. Pennock, Chris Racey, Kendrick Kay, Anna Franklin, Jenny M. Bosten

papers.title: Effects of adaptation to altered color statistics provide evidence for calibration of color perception to the environment
papers.abstract: Observers were exposed to environments with experimentally altered color statistics, and their color perception was measured afterwards. Perception shifted in ways consistent with the visual system recalibrating to the prevailing color distribution. The results support the idea that color vision is continually tuned to the statistics of the visual diet.
papers.authors: Beata E. Wozniak, John Maule, Taysa-Ja Newman, Yasmin Richter, Anna Franklin, Jenny M. Bosten

papers.title: Do color similarity judgments vary with age, and do they reveal anything about qualia?
papers.abstract: The paper examines whether people's judgments of how similar colors look change across age and what such similarity structure can say about whether color experience (qualia) is shared. It links the developmental and individual-difference data to the philosophical question of inter-subjective color experience.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Jenny M. Bosten, Anna Franklin

papers.title: Tuning of cortical color mechanisms revealed using steady-state visually evoked potentials
papers.abstract: Four EEG experiments used intermodulation of steady-state evoked potentials to measure how hue dissimilarity affects shared neural processing of flickering checkerboards. Tuning functions were broad and similar for cardinal and intermediate color axes, implying intermediately tuned cortical color mechanisms that do not depend on spatial chromatic edges. Full 360-degree tuning functions were consistent with multiple broadly tuned mechanisms.
papers.authors: Ana Rozman, Dylan J. Watts, Lucy P. Somers, Bora Gunel, Chris Racey, Katie Barnes, Jenny M. Bosten

papers.title: Color-biased regions in the ventral visual pathway are food selective
papers.abstract: Using the large Natural Scenes Dataset of 7T fMRI responses, the authors show that the color-biased patches in ventral visual cortex, which sit between face, place and body areas, respond preferentially to images of food. Color preference in these regions is tied to the colors that characterize foods, suggesting the regions are organized around behaviorally relevant color-diagnostic objects rather than color per se. The work reframes the function of human color-biased cortex.
papers.authors: Ian M.L. Pennock, Chris Racey, Emily J. Allen, Yihan Wu, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick N. Kay, Anna Franklin, Jenny M. Bosten

0301.name: Jeremy B Wilmer
0301.main_research_area: graph interpretation, data visualization, perceptual organization, decision making, attention, spatial thinking, ensemble processing
0301.bio: Jeremy B. Wilmer is a Professor of Psychology whose research investigates the nature and origins of individual variation in human cognition, focusing on face recognition and visual perception. Wilmer utilizes large-scale, internet-based citizen science through platforms like TestMyBrain.org to examine the heritability and cognitive specificity of social-perceptual abilities. Their work extends into statistical cognition and data visualization, where they develop tools and practices, such as ShowMyData.org, to communicate individual-level data in scientific research. By using massive sample sizes and psychometric methodologies, Wilmer aims to map the architecture of the human mind through its variations.
0301.research_direction:
Jeremy Wilmer directs the I See What You Mean (ISWYM) Lab at Wellesley College, where his research examines how people see, understand, and reason from statistical graphics. His lab studies the perceptual and cognitive processes that shape graph interpretation, including systematic misunderstandings of familiar visualizations such as bar and line graphs of averages, individual differences in graph comprehension, and the ways that showing underlying data can improve the accuracy and consistency of people’s interpretations. A central goal of this work is to develop data visualizations that take advantage of the strengths of human visual perception rather than working against them.

Wilmer is also the principal creator of ShowMyData.org, a free, open-access suite of tools for creating and exploring data visualizations that emphasize individual observations and the distributions underlying summary statistics. His work on graph interpretation and data literacy has been featured on Science Friday, including an interview with Ira Flatow on why seemingly simple bar graphs can lead people to misunderstand the data they represent.

papers.title: Graphs of averages exaggerate and sow disagreement
papers.abstract: Across 40 replications, participants drew the individual data points they imagined lay behind plotted averages. Their drawings were strongly exaggerated relative to the real data and highly inconsistent from person to person, in many cases less accurate than blind guesses. The effects held across plot types, data content and education levels, and a simple remedy, showing the underlying raw data, greatly reduced both problems.
papers.authors: Jeremy Bennet Wilmer, Sarah Horan Kerns, Lily Widdup, Ken Nakayama

papers.title: Multiple object tracking is selectively linked to STEM achievement
papers.abstract: In a sample of over 25,000 people, performance on a brief web-based multiple-object-tracking task was more strongly tied to math and science outcomes than to verbal or writing outcomes. This pattern held for school performance, SAT scores, STEM majors and STEM occupations. The results suggest attention-based tracking taps a core capacity underlying STEM success.
papers.authors: Roger W. Strong, Laura Germine, Ken Nakayama, Paolo Martini, Jeremy Bennet Wilmer

papers.title: The Uniformity Fallacy: A Second Common, Severe Misinterpretation of Bar Graphs of Averages
papers.abstract: Using a drawing-based measure of viewers' mental picture of data, the paper identifies a second widespread error with bar graphs of averages: roughly one in three viewers assume data are spread about evenly across the whole range. They thus omit the rarity of extreme values that is typical of real distributions. The authors name this the uniformity fallacy and discuss its implications for graph design.
papers.authors: Jeremy Bennet Wilmer, Sarah Horan Kerns

papers.title: Multiracial Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test (MRMET): An inclusive version of an influential measure
papers.abstract: The authors built and validated a version of the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test that uses faces of diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds. The new test shows good psychometric properties in a large, diverse online sample. It offers a fairer measure of social-perceptual ability than the original, predominantly White stimulus set.
papers.authors: Heesu Ally Kim, Jasmine Kaduthodil, Roger W. Strong, Laura T. Germine, Sarah Cohan, Jeremy B. Wilmer

0302.name: Jeremy M. Wolfe
0302.bio: Jeremy M. Wolfe is a cognitive scientist who developed the Guided Search model, which explains how preattentive feature information directs focal attention during visual search. Wolfe’s research examines the interplay between bottom-up stimulus-driven guidance and top-down observer-driven goals, recently resulting in the Guided Search 6.0 framework. Wolfe applies psychophysical methodologies to real-world scenarios such as cancer screening in radiology and threat detection in airport security. Their current research investigates the mechanisms behind the 'low prevalence effect' and 'inattentional blindness' in expert observers.
0302.research_direction: Dr. Wolfe has recently been investigating the intersecting mechanisms of visual search, long-term memory, and medical image perception. Their recent work explores fundamental visual behaviors, including mapping idiosyncratic biases in covert attention around fixation and testing whether patch-leaving decisions in complex hybrid foraging tasks align with optimal foraging models. They are also examining the limits of massive visual long-term memory, specifically testing how well observers can encode the precise spatial and temporal contexts of thousands of images. In applied clinical domains, Dr. Wolfe investigates how rare target prevalence and feedback shape decision criteria in expert versus novice diagnostic search, while also exploring how human behavioral perception determines the ways radiologists integrate artificial intelligence into their visual workflows.

papers.title: Biasmapping: Idiosyncratic covert search in the vicinity of fixation
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to map where an observer tends to look covertly around the point of fixation during search, revealing a personal bias pattern in how attention is spread near fixation. These maps differ reliably between individuals. The work bears on how the functional visual field should be understood in search.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe, Injae Hong

papers.title: Mixed hybrid visual foraging is near optimal
papers.abstract: Observers collected many targets from displays containing several target types while holding a memory set in mind, a hybrid foraging task. Their decisions about when to leave one patch of items for another were compared with the optimal policy of marginal value theorem. Behavior came close to optimal even when target types were mixed, extending the foraging framing of search.
papers.authors: Injae Hong, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Effects of prevalence and feedback in the identification of blast cells in peripheral blood: expert and novice observers
papers.abstract: Rare targets are missed more often, and feedback changes how observers set their decision criterion. This study tested those effects with abnormal blast cells in blood smears, comparing expert laboratory staff and novices. It shows how target prevalence and feedback shape identification in a real diagnostic task.
papers.authors: Wanyi Lyu, Jennifer S. Trueblood, Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Behavioral Research Will Help Us Understand When AI Will Help Radiologists
papers.abstract: This invited commentary in Radiology argues that whether AI helps radiologists depends on human perception and decision behavior, not only algorithm accuracy. It calls for behavioral experiments on how readers combine AI output with their own search and judgment. It draws on the author's work on errors in visual search.
papers.authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe

papers.title: Spatial and temporal massive memory in humans
papers.abstract: Observers viewed thousands of images and were later tested on both where and when each item had appeared, testing whether the famous capacity of visual long-term memory extends to spatial and temporal context. Memory for location and for time of occurrence was well above chance across a very large stimulus set. The results show that humans store large amounts of contextual information about scenes and objects, not just what was seen.
papers.authors: Jeremy M. Wolfe, Farahnaz A. Wick, Maruti Mishra, Joseph DeGutis, Wanyi Lyu

0303.name: Jessica Cantlon
0303.bio: Jessica Cantlon is the Ronald J. and Mary Ann Zdrojkowski Professor of Developmental Neuroscience at Carnegie Mellon University, where they investigate the evolutionary and developmental foundations of quantitative reasoning. Cantlon’s research employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral paradigms to compare numerical cognition across human infants, children, adults, and non-human primates. Cantlon identified conserved neural mechanisms in the intraparietal sulcus that support approximate magnitude estimation, indicating a biological continuity in mathematical intuition that predates symbolic language. Their recent work examines the neural overlap between visuospatial processing and early mathematical learning, addressing assumptions about gender differences in cognitive development.
0303.research_direction: Dr. Cantlon has recently been investigating the evolutionary and developmental foundations of spatial and numerical cognition. Their recent work explores how non-human primates and young children represent abstract concepts, using behavioral tasks in monkeys to test whether geometric intuition and numerical learning share an ancient, continuous cognitive architecture across species. Alongside this comparative research, they are utilizing fMRI in children and adults to map how spatial and mathematical abilities intersect in the developing brain. Specifically, Dr. Cantlon is examining how early neural representations of visual numerosity, geometric shapes, and spoken number words overlap within parietal networks to support the transition from non-symbolic to symbolic thought.

papers.title: Continuity in geometric intuition between humans and monkeys
papers.abstract: Geometric intuition is often held up as a uniquely human trait, explained by humans encoding shapes with discrete symbolic features while other primates rely on continuous perceptual ones. Using match-to-sample tasks, the authors show monkeys combine high-level perceptual codes with abstract symbolic codes much as humans do, implying a graded rather than categorical divide across species. Monkeys leaned more on symbolic features for rotated shapes than preschoolers did for unrotated ones, suggesting apparent symbolic coding may largely reflect rotation-invariant encoding.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Jialin Li, Isabelle Boni, Logan R. Sandwick, Emily M. Sanford, Caroline M. DeLong, Wenjie Li, Margaret M. Henderson, Steven T. Piantadosi, Jessica F. Cantlon

papers.title: Number words recruit numerosity-related cortex in 3- to 5-year-old children
papers.abstract: The study asks when neural representations of spoken number words come to overlap with those for non-symbolic numerosity. fMRI in 3- to 5-year-olds showed that bilateral intraparietal sulcus responds to number word sequences, and that child-to-adult neural synchrony during listening tracked formal math ability. Auditory number-word responses also overlapped with visual numerosity responses, so symbolic and non-symbolic number share neural substrates very early.
papers.authors: Alyssa J. Kersey, Lauren S. Aulet, Jessica F. Cantlon

papers.title: Cognitive bridge between geometric and numerical learning in monkeys
papers.abstract: Human development links numerical and spatial cognition, usually attributed to cultural tools such as the number line. The authors trained task-naive monkeys on numerosity and geometry tasks and found that abstract quantitative features, not low-level visual similarity, predicted accuracy in both. Cross-lagged analyses showed that gains in geometry learning predicted later improvement in numerosity, implying a shared, evolutionarily older number-space mechanism.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Jessica F. Cantlon, Logan R. Brownell, Jialin Li, Caroline M. DeLong

papers.title: Intersection of spatial and numerical cognition in the developing brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in 4- to 8-year-olds and adults, the study compared numerical matching, geometric shape matching and number line estimation. Parietal specialization for number and geometry was already present in young children, who showed more overlapping activation across the two domains than adults. Number line estimation drew on both number and geometry circuits in children but mostly number-specific circuits in adults.
papers.authors: Lauren S Aulet, Caroline M Kaicher, Jessica F Cantlon

papers.title: Uniquely human intelligence arose from expanded information capacity
papers.abstract: This review argues that what sets human intelligence apart is not a set of qualitatively novel cognitive algorithms but a large expansion in the amount of information that can be represented, stored and processed. It surveys comparative evidence on number, sequence, recursion and abstraction across species, and frames human cognition as a quantitative scaling of capacities shared with other animals.
papers.authors: Jessica F. Cantlon, Steven T. Piantadosi

0304.name: Jessica K. Witt
0304.bio: Jessica K. Witt is a Professor of Psychology at Colorado State University whose research investigates the relationship between visual perception and motor capabilities. Witt examines the action-specific account of perception, utilizing empirical methodologies to demonstrate how factors such as physiological state, reachability, and performance success scale the perceived geometry of the environment. Their current research extends these principles to information visualization, applying psychophysical methods to the communication of uncertainty in datasets such as hurricane forecasts and medical risks. Witt’s work applies vision science to cognitive engineering, aiming to support decision-making through perceptually-aligned graphical representations.
0304.research_direction: Dr. Witt has recently been investigating the intersection of basic visual perception and data visualization, exploring how low-level perceptual processes influence high-level statistical reasoning and risk assessment. Their recent work explores fundamental perceptual phenomena, such as how observers estimate the spatial variability of visual dot ensembles, and tests how the perceptual grouping of icon arrays alters human performance in Bayesian reasoning tasks. Additionally, they have been examining how dynamic and narrative visualization formats—including animated storm trajectories compared to standard static uncertainty cones, or graphics depicting accumulating hazards over time—affect a viewer's ability to grasp cumulative risk and forecast uncertainty. Ultimately, Dr. Witt is studying how specific perceptual design choices in displaying probability and variance can shape human decision-making, threat interpretation, and public trust in scientific data.

papers.title: Narrative visualizations: Depicting accumulating risks and increasing trust in data
papers.abstract: The authors test graphics that show how a risk builds up over time, rather than a single static number, and ask whether these narrative-style displays help non-experts grasp cumulative risk. The displays changed how people understood the risk and increased their reported trust in the underlying data. The work links perceptual design choices to trust and decision making in risk communication.
papers.authors: Madison Fansher, Logan A. Walls, Chenxu Hao, Hariharan Subramonyam, Aysecan Boduroglu, Priti Shah, Jessica K. Witt

papers.title: Visualizing Uncertainty in Hurricane Forecasts with Animated Risk Trajectories
papers.abstract: Instead of the standard cone of uncertainty, the study shows hurricane forecasts as animated individual possible storm paths. Experiments compare how viewers interpret the threat, including where the storm might go and how likely it is to reach them, across the two formats. The results argue that animating trajectories can convey forecast uncertainty more accurately than the conventional static cone.
papers.authors: Jessica K. Witt, Zachary M. Labe, Amelia C. Warden, Benjamin A. Clegg

papers.title: Visual organization of icon arrays affects Bayesian reasoning and risk judgments
papers.abstract: Icon arrays are grids of symbols used to show how many people in a group have some outcome. This paper manipulates how the icons are laid out and finds that the visual organization changes how well people reason about conditional probabilities and how risky they judge outcomes to be. It shows that low-level perceptual grouping of a graphic can shift statistical reasoning.
papers.venue: Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition
papers.authors: Jessica K. Witt, Mandeep K. Dhami

papers.title: Variability of dot spread is overestimated
papers.abstract: Observers judge how spread out a cloud of dots is and consistently report more spread than actually exists. The experiments characterize this bias in perceived variability of visual ensembles. It provides the basic-perception foundation for later work on how people read variability in data graphics.
papers.authors: Jessica K. Witt, Mengzhu Fu, Michael D. Dodd

0305.name: Jessica Montag
