0305.bio: Jessica Montag is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and a faculty member at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology. Montag’s research examines how linguistic and cognitive abilities emerge from experience, focusing on the relationship between environmental statistics, visual salience, and language processing. They utilize eye-tracking to investigate oculomotor behavior during reading and sentence production, alongside corpus analyses and naturalistic audio recordings to quantify language input. Montag’s work demonstrates how structural complexities in picture books and individual differences in text exposure shape syntactic development and vocabulary acquisition across the lifespan.
0305.research_direction: Dr. Montag has recently been investigating the naturalistic language environments of infants and young children, focusing on the quantity, quality, and temporal distribution of the speech that early learners encounter daily. Their recent work explores how early language input is shaped by varied everyday contexts, utilizing transcribed daylong audio recordings to examine the influence of older siblings and the temporal burstiness of how words cluster over time, alongside caregiver surveys evaluating picture book reading practices. In addition to characterizing naturalistic language exposure, they also study the cognitive mechanisms underlying real-time language production. Specifically, their experimental work investigates whether the use of optional adjectives is driven by a speaker's own internal processing demands rather than a communicative need to assist the listener.

papers.title: Theoretical and Methodological Insights From Five Transcribed and Annotated Daylong Audio Recordings of Young Children's Language Environments
papers.abstract: The authors fully transcribe and annotate five day-long home audio recordings of young children and use them to examine what the language environment actually looks like across a whole day. They draw out lessons about how much and what kinds of speech children hear, and about the choices researchers face when sampling and analyzing such recordings. The paper is a methods and theory contribution for the study of naturalistic language input.
papers.authors: Jessica L. Montag, Zeynep B. Marasli, Katherine M. Koch

papers.title: The Role of Siblings on Infant Language Exposure in Daylong Audio Recordings
papers.abstract: Using day-long audio recordings from infants' homes, the study asks how having older siblings changes the language an infant hears. It compares the amount and type of speech directed to and around infants with and without siblings. The results show that family structure meaningfully shapes early language input.
papers.authors: Maily Galindo, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: Investigating the temporal distribution of words in child-centered audio using the burstiness metric
papers.abstract: The paper applies a burstiness measure to child-centered audio to quantify how words are clustered or spread over time in the speech children hear. It examines what the metric can and cannot reveal about how input is distributed across a day. The work links temporal patterns of word use to how children may learn words.
papers.authors: Zeynep B. Marasli, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: A speaker-centric motivation for the use of optional adjectives during language production
papers.abstract: The study tests why speakers add optional adjectives when describing things, and argues that the reasons come from the speaker's own production processes rather than from a purely listener-directed account. It uses language production experiments to compare the two explanations. The results bear on theories of how speakers decide how much to say.
papers.authors: Ella R. Bohlman, Jessica L. Montag

papers.title: An Online Survey of Picture Book Reading Practices with Children Between the Ages of 0 and 30 Months
papers.abstract: The authors survey caregivers about how they read picture books with infants and toddlers, including how often they read and how they talk about the books. The responses describe the range of reading practices during the first two and a half years. The findings give a baseline for how book reading contributes to children's language input.
papers.authors: Trisha N. Patel, Zeynep B. Marasli, Alyssa Choi, Jessica L. Montag

0307.name: Jiahui Guo
0307.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
0307.department: Department of Psychology, School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences
0307.bio: Jiahui Guo is an Assistant Professor at The University of Texas at Dallas whose research explores the neural mechanisms of high-level perception, with an emphasis on face recognition and social cognition. Guo’s work utilizes naturalistic stimuli and functional neuroimaging to map individualized brain topographies and investigate how specialized cortical regions support visual tasks. By integrating computational modeling, deep neural networks, and neuropsychological assessments of populations such as those with prosopagnosia, Guo aims to develop models of human functional brain organization and its behavioral outcomes.
0307.research_direction: Dr. Guo has recently been investigating how the human brain represents faces and other visual categories under naturalistic conditions, using movies rather than static images. Their recent work tests whether deep convolutional neural networks can serve as models of how people and face-selective brain regions represent dynamic faces, comparing network layers with behavior and fMRI responses. They have also been developing hyperalignment-based methods that predict an individual's own face-, place-, and body-selective brain regions from movie-watching or resting data. More recently, they have been asking whether these individualized predictions still work in people with developmental prosopagnosia, who have lifelong difficulty recognizing faces.

papers.title: Predicting Individualized Functional Topography in Developmental Prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: Tests whether hyperalignment-based estimation of individualized functional topographies, which works well in typical participants, generalizes to people with developmental prosopagnosia. Uses two independent datasets of DP and control participants. Affiliation on Crossref is UT Dallas Psychology, matching the scholar.
papers.authors: Ian Abenes, Jiahui Guo

papers.title: Modeling naturalistic face processing in humans with deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) as computational models for the neural and cognitive processing of dynamic, naturalistic faces. Using a large-scale dataset of 707 naturalistic face video clips, we conducted representational similarity analysis (RSA) across DCNN layers, human behavioral arrangements, and fMRI-measured neural responses in face-selective regions. Results indicate that late-intermediate DCNN layers effectively capture categorical face attributes (e.g., age, gender, expression) that align with human behavioral and neural geometries. Conversely, the final fully connected layers, optimized for identity discrimination, show significantly weaker correlations with human brain and behavioral data, suggesting that current DCNN architectures do not fully replicate the mechanisms underlying human face individuation and dynamic feature processing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Jiahui Guo, Ma Feilong, Matteo Visconti di Oleggio Castello, Samuel A. Nastase, James V. Haxby, M. Ida Gobbini

papers.title: Cross-movie prediction of individualized functional topography
papers.abstract: We present a novel computational framework and a normative database designed to estimate individualized functional brain topographies using naturalistic movie stimuli. By utilizing connectivity hyperalignment (CHA) to map idiosyncratic functional architectures into a shared high-dimensional model, we can predict participant-specific, category-selective regions (e.g., face, place, and body-selective areas) from resting-state or naturalistic viewing data. Our methodology demonstrates that movie-based predictions achieve high fidelity, frequently exceeding the reliability of traditional functional localizer scans. This database serves as a resource for precisely localizing specialized cortical regions in individual brains across diverse datasets, facilitating the study of fine-grained functional organization and individual differences.
papers.authors: Jiahui Guo, Ma Feilong, Samuel A. Nastase, James V. Haxby, M. Ida Gobbini

0309.name: Jian Chen
0309.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0309.bio: Jian Chen is an Associate Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at The Ohio State University and directs the Interactive Visual Computing Lab. Chen’s research integrates vision science and human-centered computing to design immersive 3D visualizations and interactive metaphors for data exploration. They utilize cognitive and perceptual experiments alongside mathematical modeling to quantify how humans process global configurations, such as ensembles and gist, within large-scale datasets. This work is applied to neuroscience and brain imaging, focusing on the representation of spatially complex biological information.
0309.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating how both humans and artificial neural networks perceive and process complex graphical information, particularly in the context of data visualization and scientific imagery. Their recent work explores the fundamental drivers of perceived visual complexity in charts and develops comprehensive, image-based typologies to categorize the visual stimuli used in data communication. To better understand the perceptual mechanics of graphical interpretation, they are employing large-scale behavioral testing frameworks to compare how convolutional networks and human observers extract quantitative information like ratios, while also evaluating how distinct glyph designs influence human perception of scientific data spanning massive magnitude ranges. Furthermore, Dr. Chen’s research extends into expert visually guided decision-making, utilizing extensive eye- and mouse-tracking to study how medical professionals navigate and extract diagnostic information from giga-pixel pathology images.

papers.title: A Rigorous Behavior Assessment of CNNs Using a Data-Domain Sampling Regime
papers.abstract: The authors build a sampling framework over the data domain to measure how convolutional networks perceive bar charts and estimate ratios. Using 16 million trials from 800 CNN models and about 6,800 trials from 113 people, they show that CNNs can beat humans on this graphical perception task and that their errors are mostly governed by how far test charts lie from the training distribution. The work gives a principled, preregistered way to compare machine and human graphical perception.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (IEEE VIS 2025)
papers.authors: Shuning Jiang, Wei-Lun Chao, Daniel Haehn, Hanspeter Pfister, Jian Chen

papers.title: What Makes a Visualization Image Complex?
papers.abstract: This study asks what drives perceived visual complexity in data visualizations. About 350 crowdsourced participants rated 1,800 visualization images, and the ratings were compared with twelve image-based metrics including two new object-level ones (meaningful color count and text-to-ink ratio). Edge and corner counts and the number of distinct colors turned out to be robust predictors, and the effects differ across visualization types.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (IEEE VIS 2025)
papers.authors: Mengdi Chu, Zefeng Qiu, Meng Ling, Shuning Jiang, Robert S. Laramee, Michael Sedlmair, Jian Chen

papers.title: Eye-Tracking, Mouse Tracking, Stimulus Tracking, and Decision-Making Datasets in Digital Pathology
papers.abstract: The paper presents PathoGaze1.0, a behavioral dataset covering the full diagnostic workflow on giga-pixel whole-slide images: 19 pathologists reading 397 slides, with about 18.7 hours of eye tracking, mouse interaction, viewport navigation and diagnostic decisions. The data were collected in an ecologically valid testbed and preregistered. The authors argue it can explain diagnostic inconsistency and help train both pathologists and AI systems.
papers.venue: arXiv (under review at Nature Scientific Data)
papers.authors: Veronica Thai, Rui Li, Meng Ling, Shuning Jiang, Jeremy Wolfe, Raghu Machiraju, Yan Hu, Zaibo Li, Anil Parwani, Jian Chen

papers.title: An Image-based Typology for Visualization
papers.abstract: The paper derives a bottom-up typology of visualization from qualitative analysis of published visualization images, identifying the main visual stimulus in each and arriving at ten image-based types. It documents the coding decisions and releases a dataset and browsing tool. The typology is meant to support research, teaching, tracking the evolution of the field, and discussion of standardization, analogous to an ImageNet-style index for visualization.
papers.authors: Jian Chen, Petra Isenberg, Robert S. Laramee, Tobias Isenberg, Michael Sedlmair, Torsten Moeller, Rui Li

papers.title: Evaluating Glyph Design for Showing Large-Magnitude-Range Quantum Spins
papers.abstract: The study tests bivariate glyphs for encoding vectors that span a very wide range of magnitudes, as in quantum spin simulations. Local tasks needing only a couple of glyphs and global tasks over hundreds of glyphs were run with participants, and the results show that separable visual dimensions with a categorical component drive effectiveness. The findings give design guidance for visualizing large-magnitude-range scientific data.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Henan Zhao, Garnett W. Bryant, Wesley Griffin, Judith E. Terrill, Jian Chen

0310.name: Jiawei Zhou
0310.department: School of Ophthalmology and Optometry, Eye Hospital
0310.lab_name: Lab of Visual Deficits and Visual Rehabilitation
0310.bio: Jiawei Zhou is a Professor and Principal Investigator at Wenzhou Medical University, where they direct the Lab of Visual Deficits and Visual Rehabilitation and the Zhejiang-Canada Joint Translational Visual Cognition Laboratory. Zhou’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual information processing and ocular dominance plasticity, specifically regarding amblyopia, strabismus, and myopia. Utilizing high-resolution 7T fMRI and psychophysical paradigms, Zhou investigates the dynamics of interocular suppression and sensory eye dominance to develop binocular treatments and perceptual learning protocols. Previously a postdoctoral researcher at McGill University, Zhou works in the fields of amblyopia treatment and visual rehabilitation.
0310.research_direction: Dr. Zhou has recently been investigating the mechanisms of adult visual plasticity and binocular dynamics, focusing particularly on sensory eye dominance in normal and amblyopic vision. Their recent work explores how interventions like short-term monocular deprivation, dark exposure, and contrast-based perceptual learning might alter cortical states to successfully rebalance ocular dominance. To uncover the underlying neural basis of these shifts, they use magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track fluctuations in excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the primary visual cortex, examining how these neurochemical dynamics predict phenomena like binocular rivalry and metaplasticity. Furthermore, Dr. Zhou is psychophysically mapping how sensory eye dominance behaves across the continuum from binocular combination to rivalry, seeking to understand how intrinsic neural oscillations and states—rather than just changes in visual input—govern plasticity in the adult brain.

papers.title: GABAergic fluctuations predict mixed perception during binocular rivalry
papers.abstract: Using magnetic resonance spectroscopy in 14 normally sighted adults, the study tests whether 60 minutes of dark exposure changes visual-cortex Glx and GABA+ and how binocular rivalry behaves afterwards. Dark exposure raised mixed perception and Glx but left group-average GABA+ and the Glx/GABA ratio unchanged. Individual differences in the change in mixed perception tracked the size of each person's GABA+ fluctuation, suggesting rivalry depends on specific neurochemical responses rather than net excitation/inhibition balance.
papers.authors: Seung Hyun Min, Rongjie Hu, Nan Jiang, Liying Zou, Xiaoxiao Wang, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Sensory Eye Dominance Remains Stable Across Binocular Combination and Rivalry in Normal and Anisometropic Amblyopic Vision
papers.abstract: Adults with amblyopia and with normal vision viewed dichoptic gratings whose interocular orientation difference varied from 9 to 90 degrees, moving perception from fusion to rivalry, at three spatial frequencies. The balance point measuring eye dominance did not change with orientation difference in either group, but amblyopes showed a consistently larger imbalance that varied with spatial frequency. Sensory eye dominance therefore appears stable across the combination-to-rivalry continuum.
papers.authors: Wenjing Wang, Yiya Chen, Yiqiu Lu, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Monocular Contrast Sensitivity Visual Perceptual Learning Rebalances Adult Amblyopes' Two Eyes
papers.abstract: Adults with anisometropic amblyopia, myopic anisometropia and normal vision underwent 10 days of monocular contrast-detection perceptual learning with the weaker or non-dominant eye, alongside untrained controls. Training improved contrast sensitivity and the interocular balance point at the trained spatial frequency, with transfer to nearby untrained frequencies, though binocular summation did not improve. The results support monocular perceptual learning as a practical way to reduce binocular imbalance in adults.
papers.authors: Wenman Lin, Zhifen He, Shiqi Zhou, Liuqing Weng, Liying Zou, Renhao Ye, Jinli Zhu, Fan Lu, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Internal neural states influence the short-term effect of monocular deprivation in human adults
papers.abstract: The authors manipulated whether the patched eye was open or closed during short-term monocular deprivation and tracked intrinsic neural oscillations. Eye-open versus eye-closed states changed baseline contrast sensitivity and the size of the ocular dominance shift in the unpatched eye. The work shows that adult visual plasticity depends on the internal neural state during deprivation, not just on the visual input change.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Yige Gao, Zhifen He, Zhouyuan Sun, Yu Mao, Robert F Hess, Peng Zhang, Jiawei Zhou

papers.title: Metaplasticity: Dark exposure boosts local excitability and visual plasticity in adult human cortex
papers.abstract: Using magnetic resonance spectroscopy in V1 and a binocular combination assay, the study shows that 60 minutes of dark exposure raises local glutamate/glutamine concentration and enlarges the ocular dominance shift produced by subsequent monocular deprivation in normal adults. No such boost occurred in amblyopic adults. The magnitude of neurochemical change, rather than its absolute level, related to the plasticity gain, questioning a simple excitation/inhibition account.
papers.authors: Seung Hyun Min, Zili Wang, Meng Ting Chen, Rongjie Hu, Ling Gong, Zhifen He, Xiaoxiao Wang, Robert F Hess, Jiawei Zhou

0311.name: jiayu Zhan
0311.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0311.bio: Jiayu Zhan is an Assistant Professor at Peking University's School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences and the Institute for Artificial Intelligence. Their research examines the computational and neural mechanisms of visual cognition, specifically the representation and categorization of complex social stimuli such as faces and dynamic expressions. Zhan has developed frameworks to quantify task-relevant information within brain activity and contributed to the identification of a specialized third visual pathway for dynamic social perception. Their work also bridges cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence by investigating the grounding of abstract concepts and human values within large language models.
0311.research_direction: Dr. Zhan has recently been studying how people recognize emotions from faces, and how that process is organized in the mind. Their recent work asks whether the individual facial muscle movements (action units) and the emotion categories they signal are processed in parallel or in sequence, and whether this differs by the observer's or the face's gender. To probe this, they combine cognitive-psychology experiments with computational modeling and a purpose-built, richly annotated 3D face dataset.

papers.title: CoEmo: Modeling Cognitive Processes in Facial Expression Recognition through Action Units and Gender Perspectives
papers.abstract: This research examines the underlying cognitive architecture of facial expression recognition at the interface of computational modeling and cognitive psychology. Specifically, the study investigates whether facial action units (AUs) and discrete emotion categories are processed through parallel or sequential neural frameworks and evaluates potential gender-based modulations of these processes. By developing a high-fidelity 3D facial dataset with comprehensive AU amplitude and emotion annotations, the authors contrast parallel and sequential architectures implemented via multi-task learning and pipelined convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Performance metrics indicate that the parallel processing model (F1 = 42.9%) significantly surpasses the sequential model (F1 = 17.1%), corroborating the parallel processing hypothesis. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) further characterizes sex-specific representational structures: female emotion recognition demonstrates alignment with social-distance metrics between emotions, whereas male performance is uniquely driven by representations of anger. These results provide evidence for parallelism as a primary cognitive mechanism and reveal distinct gender-related differences in the neural representation of facial affect.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2025)
papers.authors: Shangjing Huang, Xiaoxue Gao, Jing Wang, Yuankun Fang, Jiani Zhang, Shiwei Qiu, Jialu Ouyang, Xiaolin Zhou, Fujia Wang, Jiayu Zhan

0312.name: Jifan Zhou
0312.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0312.bio: Zhou is a Professor and doctoral supervisor at Zhejiang University, where their research focuses on the cognitive architecture of visual working memory (VWM) and its interaction with attentional mechanisms. Their work explores how mental representations in VWM guide visual search behaviors and the storage of dynamic relations between functional objects. Zhou also investigates phenomena such as attribute amnesia and the postdictive effects of choice on attention, applying interdisciplinary approaches that link cognitive psychology with artificial intelligence to model human information processing.
0312.research_direction: Dr. Zhou’s recent work explores the cognitive mechanisms of social and visual perception, particularly focusing on how we spontaneously adopt the visual perspectives of others. They have recently been investigating whether this perspective-taking relies on perceptual simulation or heuristic inference, and whether behavioral cues like gaze and reaching can induce these social responses toward non-human agents to make robot behavior more intelligible. Beyond social vision, their research examines the strategic allocation of visual working memory during active tasks, asking how individuals weigh varying sampling costs and time pressures to choose between internal memory storage and external visual re-sampling. Additionally, Dr. Zhou investigates visual ensemble perception, exploring how observers leverage underlying regularities to infer missing elements and extract complete summary representations from incomplete visual information.

papers.title: I'll believe it unless it's too absurd: Spontaneous visual perspective-taking as prior-based heuristic inference
papers.abstract: Theories disagree on whether visual perspective-taking reconstructs another's visual experience (perceptual simulation) or relies on symbolic inference from naive optics (heuristics). Because prior evidence for heuristics came mostly from explicit reports, the authors test the implicit, spontaneous form of perspective-taking. Results support a prior-based heuristic inference account, in which people accept another's line of sight unless it is implausible or absurd.
papers.authors: Xucong Hu, Yitong Zheng, Qinyi Hu, Hui Chen, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: Regulating Memory Use: Individual Differences in Working Memory Capacity in Natural Tasks
papers.abstract: Working memory capacity predicts many cognitive abilities, but little is known about how people with different capacities choose between remembering and re-sampling the display when memory use is voluntary. In two experiments (N = 120) using copying and change-detection tasks, the authors manipulated sampling cost and time pressure. Higher sampling cost increased memory use, and the work examines how capacity relates to consistent regulation of memory use.
papers.authors: Xutao Zheng, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: How Can We Make Robots Intelligible? Building Perception-Behavior Causal Links for User-Centered Explainability
papers.abstract: This paper addresses how users come to understand what a robot is doing and why. It develops the idea that robots become intelligible when their perceivable features are causally linked to their behavior in ways users can grasp, framing a user-centered approach to robot explainability. Summary based on title and metadata; abstract not retrieved.
papers.authors: Xucong Hu, Enjie Xu, Haokui Xu, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: Good to see you R2-D2: Inducing spontaneous perspective-taking towards non-human agents through human-like gaze and reach
papers.abstract: Spontaneous visual perspective-taking, the automatic tendency to represent what another agent sees, was long assumed to depend on the agent looking human. This study asks whether a clearly non-human robot can trigger it. The authors show that giving a robot human-like gaze and reaching behavior is enough to induce spontaneous perspective-taking, indicating that behavioral cues rather than a human-like body drive the effect, with implications for social robot design.
papers.authors: Xucong Hu, Haokui Xu, Hui Chen, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

papers.title: Completeness out of incompleteness: Inferences from regularities in imperfect information ensembles
papers.abstract: Perception often must cope with imperfect information, where not all elements of a set can be observed. The authors examine whether internal regularities among the elements of an ensemble can serve as clues to infer the missing items and yield a complete summary. Findings show that observers exploit such regularities to compensate for incomplete ensembles.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Jingyin Zhu, Haokui Xu, Bohao Shi, Yilong Lu, Hui Chen, Mowei Shen, Jifan Zhou

0313.name: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco
0313.bio: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco is an Assistant Professor at the University of British Columbia and the Director of the UBC Perception & Cognition Lab. Ongchoco's research focuses on the interface between perception and higher-level cognition, specifically investigating how the mind constructs discrete objects and events from continuous sensory input. They study the phenomenon of 'scaffolded attention' and how event segmentation influences various mental processes, including memory, decision-making, and the subjective experience of time. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods and computational modeling to explore how perceptual structures shape human thought and imagination.
0313.research_direction: Dr. Ongchoco has recently been investigating how early perceptual organization shapes fundamental sensory experience and higher-level cognition. A major focus of their recent work explores how the mind parses continuous information into discrete structures, examining how perceptual event boundaries alter the subjective reproduction of time, restrict cognitive anchoring biases during decision-making, and prompt the spontaneous visual prioritization of "unfinished" dynamic sequences. Beyond event segmentation, they have been studying individual differences in "scaffolded attention," using interactive matching tasks to investigate how distinct visual routines cause observers to perceive illusory geometric patterns on otherwise uniform grids. Additionally, their research spans into the aesthetics of motion perception, utilizing playback adjustment tasks to probe whether human aesthetic speed preferences for viewing dance are inherently grounded in the natural kinematic pace of everyday movement.

papers.title: The spontaneous prioritization of "unfinishedness" in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect
papers.abstract: Unfinished tasks are known to linger in memory (the Zeigarnik effect), usually explained by goals and obligations. These experiments ask whether unfinishedness is instead extracted spontaneously by visual processing itself. Across studies with dynamic events and incomplete paths, unfinished structures were automatically prioritized in perception even when irrelevant to the task, suggesting a perceptual version of the Zeigarnik effect.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Are you a visual "shader" or a "bolder"? Different visual routines create everyday hallucinations in "scaffolded attention"
papers.abstract: Looking at a uniform grid of squares, many people see patterns in which squares appear brighter or colored (shaders) or outlined and bolded (bolders). With about 100 observers and an interactive matching method, the study characterizes these individual differences and links them to distinct visual routines, extending her scaffolded-attention work on everyday illusions.
papers.authors: Andrea S. Ying, Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco

papers.title: Aesthetic speed preferences when viewing dance synchronize to a 'natural' pace of human motion
papers.abstract: In a set-the-pace task, people adjusted playback speed of many videos to what they found maximally pleasing. Across multiple experiments and replications, preferred speeds for dance tracked the natural pace of everyday human movement, suggesting a shared basis for perceiving and appreciating motion in functional and aesthetic contexts.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, David Melcher

papers.title: Visual event boundaries restrict anchoring effects in decision-making
papers.abstract: Anchoring, where irrelevant numbers bias later estimates, is among the most robust effects in judgment and decision-making. The authors show that a low-level visual feature, spontaneous segmentation of experience into events, limits it: when a visual event boundary separates the anchor from the judgment, the anchoring bias shrinks or disappears. This links early perceptual event segmentation directly to higher-level decisions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Robert Walter-Terrill, Brian J. Scholl

papers.title: Event segmentation structures temporal experience: Simultaneous dilation and contraction in rhythmic reproductions
papers.abstract: Using a rhythmic reproduction task, participants listened to irregular tone sequences containing one salient, task-irrelevant perceptual boundary and then reproduced the rhythm. Time was simultaneously dilated and contracted depending on where intervals sat relative to the boundary, showing that event segmentation shapes how time itself is experienced.
papers.authors: Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Tristan S. Yates, Brian J. Scholl

0314.name: Joan López-Moliner
0314.department: Department of Cognition, Development, and Psychology of Education
0314.lab_name: Vision and Control of Action (VISCA) Group
0314.bio: Joan López-Moliner is a Full Professor at the Universitat de Barcelona and a researcher at the Institute of Neurosciences (ubNeuro). Their research examines how the human visual system processes information for motor tasks, such as object interception or navigation, through computational modeling and optimal decision-making frameworks. Using psychophysics, 3D virtual reality, and eye tracking, López-Moliner investigates the integration of sensory feedback with internal priors—such as gravity—to explain the precision of human interceptive actions. Their current work focuses on motion-in-depth perception, optic flow, and the adaptation of perceptual systems to augmented and virtual realities.
0314.research_direction: Dr. López-Moliner has recently been investigating how the human visual system processes dynamic information to guide self-motion and interceptive actions. Their recent work explores how complex retinal flow patterns, such as the mean curl of the flow field, might serve as a direct heading signal, while also using mobile eye-tracking to quantify how 3D eye rotations—including natural ocular torsion—jointly shape these flow fields during real-world locomotion. Additionally, they have been examining the mechanisms underlying time-to-contact estimation and interceptive behavior, testing whether the brain relies on predictive internal models of gravity and integrates contextual priors when target trajectories are uncertain. Finally, their research probes the fundamental limits of spatial motion processing by comparing the precision of continuous visual tracking to evaluate the relative perceptual noise in lateral motion versus motion in depth.

papers.title: Retinal curl as a functional signal for heading estimation beyond the focus of expansion
papers.abstract: Standard accounts of heading perception assume the visual system must locate the focus of expansion while compensating for the rotation added by eye movements. This work proposes instead that the mean curl of retinal flow produced during fixation acts as a surrogate heading signal, so the focus of expansion never needs to be recovered. In a large-screen simulated-walking task with real-time manipulation of foveal curl (left intact, cancelled or over-cancelled), continuous heading reports shifted as predicted by the curl signal.
papers.authors: Kontessa I. Zorpala, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: Torsion in motion: the visual system as a three-axis gimbal
papers.abstract: Using head-mounted eye tracking, the study estimates ocular torsion (rotation about the line of sight) alongside horizontal and vertical eye rotations while ten people walk toward a distant target. It examines how all three eye rotations, together with head movement, jointly shape the retinal flow that underlies self-motion processing, a component previously hard to quantify in natural locomotion.
papers.authors: Andres H. Mendez, Jorge Otero-Millan, Cristina de la Malla, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: The predictive outfielder: a critical test across gravities
papers.abstract: The paper presents a model based on optic variables that continuously updates predictions of a ball's landing position and remaining flight time as the fielder moves, and that adapts to different gravitational accelerations by building gravity into its predictions. It pits this predictive account against closed-loop heuristics in interception across gravity conditions, testing whether the brain uses an internal model of gravity.
papers.authors: Borja Aguado, Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: A comparative analysis of perceptual noise in lateral and depth motion: Evidence from eye tracking
papers.abstract: Using eye tracking during continuous tracking, this single-author study compares how precisely observers perceive motion across the frontal plane versus in depth. It quantifies the perceptual noise in each and asks whether motion-in-depth uncertainty is substantially worse than lateral uncertainty.
papers.authors: Joan López-Moliner

papers.title: Prediction of time to contact under perceptual and contextual uncertainties
papers.abstract: The study examines how people predict when a moving object will arrive when its motion is partly hidden or uncertain, and how they combine sensory uncertainty with contextual information such as prior expectations. It probes the strategies used for time-to-contact estimation under different uncertainty conditions.
papers.authors: Pamela Villavicencio, Cristina de la Malla, Joan López-Moliner

0316.name: Jocelyn Faubert
0316.bio: Jocelyn Faubert is a professor of visual perception and cognitive neuroscience at the Université de Montréal, where they direct a multidisciplinary research laboratory focused on human performance. Faubert’s work investigates the neural mechanisms of sensory-cognitive integration, specifically how aging, neurodevelopmental conditions, and traumatic brain injuries affect the processing of complex dynamic scenes. They developed the NeuroTracker system, a 3D multiple-object tracking technology used to assess cognitive load in clinical settings and modify mental performance in athletes. Their research methodology integrates psychophysical testing with immersive virtual reality environments, such as CAVE systems and EON Icube technology, to connect fundamental vision science with real-world applications.
0316.research_direction: Dr. Faubert's recent work explores a diverse array of basic and applied questions in visual perception, human performance, and neurotechnology. They have recently been investigating how individuals manage cognitive load and perceptual-cognitive learning in demanding environments, utilizing paradigms like 3D multiple object tracking in young athletes and multimodal physiological monitoring—including EEG and pupillometry—in novice pilots. Their research also examines the role of sex and individual differences in the acquisition of trainable perceptual skills and the optimization of EEG-based machine learning models for neurological diagnostics. On a fundamental sensory level, Dr. Faubert is modeling how retinal pathways might de-multiplex signals from broad, overlapping cone sensitivities to isolate distinct color channels. Additionally, their applied clinical work extends into aging populations, focusing on the conceptual development and technological requirements of real-time systems capable of anticipating and preventing imminent falls.

papers.title: Critical role of EEG signals in assessment of sex-specific insights in neurological diagnostics via machine learning approach
papers.abstract: The study uses machine learning on EEG recordings to test whether sex-related differences in brain signals affect diagnostic performance for neurological conditions. It examines how models behave when sex is or is not accounted for, arguing that sex-specific signal patterns matter for building reliable EEG-based diagnostic tools.
papers.authors: Mohammad-Javad Darvishi-Bayazi, Mohammad Sajjad Ghaemi, Irina Rish, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: The nature of multi-channel color perception from three photodetector types with wide overlapping spectral sensitivity bands
papers.abstract: Proposes a physical signal de-multiplexing scheme in which outputs of photodetectors with broad, overlapping spectral sensitivities are combined to isolate narrower spectral zones. The authors present this as a candidate mechanism for how retinal chromatic pathways derive colour signals from the three cone types, and one that can be built into an instrument.
papers.authors: Vasile Diaconu, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: Gender comparison of perceptual-cognitive learning in young athletes
papers.abstract: Seventy-two athletes and non-athletes aged 16-22 trained on a 3D multiple object tracking task (NeuroTracker) across five sessions. All groups improved speed thresholds, and the study compares learning and baseline performance between males and females, informing sex differences in trainable perceptual-cognitive skill.
papers.authors: Isabelle Legault, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: Immediate fall prevention: the missing key to a comprehensive solution for falling hazard in older adults
papers.abstract: A perspective arguing that ageing-technology solutions underemphasize real-time prevention of traumatic falls, the leading cause of injury in older adults. It advocates systems that anticipate an imminent fall and intervene in time, and outlines what such a technology needs.
papers.authors: Khashayar Misaghian, Jesus Eduardo Lugo, Jocelyn Faubert

papers.title: Beyond performance: the role of task demand, effort, and individual differences in ab initio pilots
papers.abstract: Twenty-four novice pilots flew a simulator at three difficulty levels while heart rate, EEG and pupil size were recorded alongside NASA-TLX ratings. The work relates performance to physiological markers of effort and shows individual differences in how trainees respond to task demand, relevant for tailoring flight training.
papers.authors: Mohammad-Javad Darvishi-Bayazi, Andrew Law, Sergio Mejia Romero, Sion Jennings, Irina Rish, Jocelyn Faubert

0317.name: Jochen Triesch
0317.department: Department of Physics and Department of Computer Science and Mathematics, Goethe University Frankfurt
0317.bio: Jochen Triesch holds positions as a Senior Fellow at the Frankfurt Institute for Advanced Studies and a Professor at Goethe University Frankfurt, specializing in the self-organization of intelligent behavior. Triesch developed the 'Active Efficient Coding' framework, which provides a theory for the joint development of sensory coding and motor control in biological systems such as binocular vision. Their research integrates computational modeling, machine learning, and developmental robotics to study how neural circuits adapt through synaptic plasticity and how artificial systems can emulate human-like cognitive development. Triesch currently focuses on developmental artificial intelligence, spiking neural networks, and the mathematical principles governing neural competition for synaptic resources.
0317.research_direction: Dr. Triesch has recently been investigating the computational and developmental mechanisms that enable visual systems to learn robust representations from natural, embodied experience. A major focus of their recent work explores how human visual constraints—specifically temporal slowness, central visual acuity, and active toddler gaze behavior—guide self-supervised object learning from egocentric input. To study how multimodal sensorimotor interactions shape this cognitive development, they are also building open-source, simulated infant models equipped with vision, touch, and proprioception. At the algorithmic level, Dr. Triesch investigates biologically plausible mechanisms for early vision, such as how spiking neural networks might implement predictive coding via local spike-timing-dependent plasticity, as well as broader machine learning principles like using local-global feature alignment to improve unsupervised category learning.

papers.title: Toddlers' Active Gaze Behavior Supports Self-Supervised Object Learning
papers.abstract: Combines head-mounted eye tracking from toddlers during dyadic play with an unsupervised, slowness-based learning model. Feeding the model image crops centered on the toddler's gaze yields more invariant object representations than other views, and the small high-acuity central field turns out to be critical. The work argues that toddlers' own gaze behavior actively shapes how they learn to recognize objects.
papers.authors: Zhengyang Yu, Arthur Aubret, Marcel C. Raabe, Jane Yang, Chen Yu, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Temporal Slowness in Central Vision Drives Semantic Object Learning
papers.abstract: Simulates about five months of human-like visual experience from the Ego4D dataset, cropping frames around predicted gaze locations to mimic central vision, and trains a time-contrastive self-supervised model on them. Both restricting input to the central visual field and exploiting temporal slowness improve how well the learned representations encode object semantics. The results suggest these two properties of human vision jointly support semantic object learning from egocentric experience.
papers.authors: Timothy Schaumlöffel, Arthur Aubret, Gemma Roig, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Seeing the Whole in the Parts with Self-Supervised Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Presents CO-SSL, an instance-discrimination self-supervised method that aligns local (pre-pooling) feature representations with a global image representation to capture spatial co-occurrence of features. It outperforms earlier methods on several datasets, including ImageNet-1K, and is more robust to noise, corruption and adversarial attacks. Analysis suggests it learns highly redundant local representations, supporting local-global alignment as a principle for unsupervised category learning.
papers.authors: Arthur Aubret, Céline Teulière, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: Predictive Coding Light
papers.abstract: Proposes a hierarchical, recurrent spiking network in which higher layers learn to predict and suppress the spikes of lower layers, so that only unpredicted information is passed on rather than explicit prediction errors. Learning uses excitatory and inhibitory spike-timing-dependent plasticity in an unsupervised fashion. The network develops V1-like receptive fields and sparse, compact codes on natural and event-based visual input, and performs competitively on recognition benchmarks with low energy use, offering a biologically plausible, neuromorphic-friendly alternative to classical predictive coding.
papers.authors: Antony W. N'dri, Thomas Barbier, Céline Teulière, Jochen Triesch

papers.title: MIMo: A Multimodal Infant Model for Studying Cognitive Development
papers.abstract: Introduces MIMo, an open-source simulated infant with a child-like body and touch, vision, proprioception and vestibular senses, built for studying how cognition develops through embodied interaction. The platform is compatible with standard reinforcement-learning tooling and is presented with benchmark tasks and demonstrations. It is intended to let researchers ask how sensorimotor experience shapes learning in both humans and artificial agents.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Cognitive and Developmental Systems
papers.authors: Dominik Mattern, Pierre Schumacher, Francisco M. López, Marcel C. Raabe, Markus R. Ernst, Arthur Aubret, Jochen Triesch

0318.name: Jody C. Culham
0318.bio: Jody C. Culham is a Professor of Psychology and the Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Immersive Neuroscience at Western University. Culham’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visually guided actions, such as reaching, grasping, and tool use, using neuroimaging techniques including functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). They utilize an immersive neuroscience framework to study brain function through 3D stimuli and naturalistic behaviors in virtual or augmented reality environments. This work focuses on the human parietal cortex and the specialized roles of the dorsal and ventral visual streams in real-world contexts.
0318.research_direction: Dr. Culham has recently been exploring how high-level vision and visually guided action operate in ecologically valid, real-world contexts rather than traditional, reductionist laboratory setups. Using functional neuroimaging and virtual reality, their recent work investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying authentic, closed-loop motor behaviors, such as intercepting moving targets in 3D space or manipulating physical tools, to contrast them with the symbolic pantomimes typically used in experimental research. They are also examining how naturalistic realism shapes face and social processing by employing fMRI to test how binocular depth cues alter neural responses in face- and depth-selective cortices. Furthermore, Dr. Culham is using fNIRS to track the cognitive demands and neural dynamics of live social interactions compared to pre-recorded or animated avatar encounters, ultimately asking how real-world complexity fundamentally shifts our understanding of the visual brain.

papers.title: Bringing Vision Science Closer to the Real World
papers.abstract: The authors argue that decades of tightly controlled, reductionist experiments have served early and mid-level vision well, but understanding high-level vision requires embracing real-world complexity. They lay out strategies including richer natural stimuli and tasks, virtual reality that represents space veridically, treating participants as active agents, considering ecological and developmental goals (including for neural network models), and analytic approaches that treat natural complexity as data. Examples show how such approaches have advanced understanding of everyday visual processing.
papers.authors: Jody C. Culham, Eva Deligiannis

papers.title: fNIRS reveals that live social interactions and visual realism influence neural responses
papers.abstract: Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy, the study compared brain responses during live conversation with those during pre-recorded conversation, and with a human versus an animated avatar partner. Pre-recorded interactions produced more prolonged activation, consistent with greater cognitive effort, and right temporoparietal junction patterns differed between human and avatar partners, alongside more eye-directed looking at humans. The findings show that both liveness and facial realism shape social-cognitive processing.
papers.authors: Michaela Kent, Eva Deligiannis, Kevin M. Stubbs, Karsten Babin, Emma G. Duerden, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Binocular cues to 3D face structure increase activation in depth-selective visual cortex with negligible effects in face-selective areas
papers.abstract: Participants viewed stereo photographs of real faces under accurate, zero, reversed, or absent binocular disparity in fMRI. Faces with 3D disparity drove stronger and distinct activation in depth-selective occipitoparietal regions (V3A, V3B, IPS0/1, hMT+), while face-selective regions (OFA, FFA, pSTS) were largely insensitive to internal facial disparities. This suggests 2D images are a reasonable proxy for face-selective cortex, though dorsal-stream 3D processing deserves further attention.
papers.authors: Eva Deligiannis, Marisa Donnelly, Carol Coricelli, Karsten Babin, Kevin M. Stubbs, Chelsea Ekstrand, Laurie M. Wilcox, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Target interception in virtual reality is better for natural versus unnatural trajectory shapes and orientations
papers.abstract: In a virtual reality task, participants punched to intercept a ball moving on parabolic or tent-shaped paths, upright or inverted, in the upper or lower visual field. Reaction times were faster for more natural shapes and orientations regardless of visual field, while inverted tent paths produced worse accuracy and longer movement times. Endpoint error analyses suggest stronger expectations about final trajectory direction for natural conditions.
papers.authors: Sofia Varon, Karsten Babin, Miriam Spering, Jody C. Culham

papers.title: Human Neuroimaging Reveals Differences in Activation and Connectivity between Real and Pantomimed Tool Use
papers.abstract: Because fMRI constraints usually force researchers to use pantomime as a stand-in for tool use, the authors had participants use real plastic tools on a putty target or pantomime the same movements. Real use yielded higher execute-phase activation in sensorimotor regions and anterior supramarginal gyrus, whereas pantomime elicited more activation in classic tool-selective areas; planning-phase patterns and motor cortex connectivity also differed. Real tool use is a closed-loop process with real consequences, unlike symbolic pantomime.
papers.authors: Juan Chen, Joseph U. Paciocco, Zhiqing Deng, Jody C. Culham

0319.name: Johan Wagemans
0319.bio: Johan Wagemans is a Full Professor at KU Leuven, where they lead the Laboratory of Experimental Psychology and direct long-term Methusalem projects focused on the psychology and neuroscience of visual perception. Wagemans’ research integrates principles of perceptual organization—including symmetry, grouping, and figure-ground segregation—with psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging. Their work investigates mid-level vision and how the brain constructs representations from complex stimuli. Wagemans applies these findings to the study of atypical perception in autism and the cognitive foundations of visual arts and aesthetics.
0319.research_direction: Dr. Wagemans has recently been exploring the intersection of classic perceptual organization and modern computational modeling, investigating how principles like Gestalt Prägnanz and symmetry detection can be formalized to benchmark human-like computer vision. Their recent work also extends perception-inspired ideas into deep learning, such as developing novel tokenization approaches for Vision Transformers to preserve image composition during computational aesthetic assessment. Additionally, they have been investigating the neural mechanisms of predictive processing, utilizing fMRI and perceptual-inference models to understand how autistic and neurotypical adults encode hierarchical predictions in volatile environments. Finally, their research probes the boundaries of visual experience, employing immersive ganzfeld setups and mixed-methods approaches to characterize the phenomena of visual fading and homogeneously induced hallucinations.

papers.title: From pixels to perception: A benchmark for human-like symmetry detection
papers.abstract: Introduces a benchmark for testing whether computational models detect symmetry in images the way human observers do. It links classic perceptual-organization work on symmetry to modern computer vision, allowing systematic comparison of models with human performance.
papers.authors: Gonzalo Muradás Odriozola, Lisa Koßmann, Tinne Tuytelaars, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: And then there was light in the ganzfeld: clarifying the methods, experiences, and modulating factors of hallucinations and decays
papers.abstract: Reviews the literature on the ganzfeld, a homogeneous visual field that induces hallucinations and fading of colour and brightness, and clears up inconsistent terminology in older studies. The authors built a walk-in ganzfeld space and combined quantitative and qualitative measures to characterise the number, kinds and time course of experienced phenomena. They identify distinct types of decay and describe the factors that modulate them.
papers.authors: Eleftheria Pistolas, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Charm: The Missing Piece in ViT fine-tuning for Image Aesthetic Assessment
papers.abstract: Proposes Charm, a tokenization approach for fine-tuning vision transformers on image aesthetic assessment that better preserves image composition and native resolution or aspect ratio when forming patches. This addresses the tendency of standard resizing and cropping to distort aesthetic cues. It improves aesthetic prediction across benchmarks, tying perception-inspired ideas to computer vision.
papers.venue: CVPR 2025 (IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition)
papers.authors: Fatemeh Behrad, Tinne Tuytelaars, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Neural correlates of hierarchical predictive processes in autistic adults
papers.abstract: An fMRI study in which 26 autistic and 26 neurotypical adults learned associations in a volatile environment, with a perceptual-inference model used to extract trial-wise hierarchical predictions and prediction errors. Behavioural learning was intact in the autistic group, and predictions at multiple levels were encoded in both groups and biased perception. High-level predictions tracked activity more closely in autistic adults, and prediction-error responses differed in anterior cingulate cortex and putamen, giving neural evidence relevant to Bayesian accounts of autism.
papers.authors: Laurie-Anne Sapey-Triomphe, Lauren Pattyn, Veith Weilnhammer, Philipp Sterzer, Johan Wagemans

papers.title: Prägnanz in visual perception
papers.abstract: A theoretical review revisiting the Gestalt law of Prägnanz, the idea that perceptual organization tends toward the 'best' possible form given the conditions. It traces how the concept has been defined and often misused, and lays out its main uses: a tendency in each organizational process, a property of a good Gestalt, internal reference points, and related notions. The authors argue for a more precise, renewed role of Prägnanz in perception and beyond.
papers.authors: Eline Van Geert, Johan Wagemans

0320.name: Johannes Burge
0320.bio: Johannes Burge is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania who researches how the visual system performs tasks in natural environments. Burge utilizes psychophysics, natural scene statistics, and computational modeling to identify rules for transforming sensory signals into behavioral representations. Their work includes the development of Accuracy Maximization Analysis (AMA) for learning task-optimal filters and the investigation of depth perception cues such as defocus, disparity, and motion. By comparing human performance to ideal observer models, Burge examines how biological systems adapt to the statistical regularities of the natural world.
0320.research_direction: Dr. Burge's recent work explores the computational limits and temporal dynamics of binocular vision, depth perception, and motion processing across naturalistic, clinical, and experimental contexts. They have recently been investigating how natural scene statistics, such as variations in luminance and contrast, act as nuisance variability to constrain human stereopsis and local motion-in-depth estimation using image-computable ideal observers. In parallel, their recent research examines how these principles of binocular timing apply to clinical interventions, specifically testing how interocular blur differences from monovision prescriptions induce processing delays and real-world 3D motion illusions like the Pulfrich effect. To more efficiently measure these fine-grained perceptual dynamics, Dr. Burge is also advancing the methodology of continuous target-tracking psychophysics, evaluating whether millisecond-scale visual delays can be precisely extracted from ongoing sensorimotor behavior.

papers.title: A Common Prescription Lens Correction Causes Motion Illusions in the Presbyopic and General Populations
papers.abstract: Monovision lens corrections, in which one eye is focused near and the other far, are widely prescribed for presbyopia. The blur difference between the eyes changes signal timing, which can cause the moving-object misperception known as the Pulfrich effect. Psychophysical measurements in presbyopic and non-presbyopic adults show that this correction produces sizeable motion-in-depth illusions, with consequences for everyday tasks such as driving and sport.
papers.authors: Victor Rodriguez-Lopez, Callista M. Dyer, Johannes Burge

papers.title: Continuous psychophysics: past, present, future
papers.abstract: This review traces how continuous tracking tasks have evolved from early control-theory work into a rapid, data-rich approach for measuring perception and action. It explains the modeling frameworks used to interpret tracking data and compares the method's strengths and pitfalls with those of traditional trial-based psychophysics. It closes with open problems and directions for applying the approach to more complex perceptual questions and to clinical populations.
papers.authors: Johannes Burge, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: Optimal Estimation of Local Motion-in-Depth with Naturalistic Stimuli
papers.abstract: The authors derive an image-computable ideal observer for estimating motion toward or away from the viewer from binocular natural-image sequences. The model uses the motion signals in the two eyes and shows how natural-scene statistics and neural noise limit estimation accuracy. Model predictions are compared to human behavior, providing a normative account of biases in 3D motion perception.
papers.authors: Daniel Herrera-Esposito, Johannes Burge

papers.title: How distinct sources of nuisance variability in natural images and scenes limit human stereopsis
papers.abstract: Stereo depth judgments are limited by more than sensor noise, because natural scenes vary in luminance, contrast, and depth structure in ways that perturb the disparity signal. This study uses carefully sampled natural stereo images to separate the contributions of these distinct nuisance sources to human performance. It shows that natural-scene variability accounts for a substantial share of human stereo limits, and that its effects can be partitioned and predicted.
papers.authors: David N. White, Johannes Burge

papers.title: Continuous psychophysics shows millisecond-scale visual processing delays are faithfully preserved in movement dynamics
papers.abstract: Continuous target-tracking psychophysics, where observers follow a moving target with a pointer, is a fast alternative to conventional trial-based methods. The authors ask whether the tiny visual processing delays known from classic tasks, such as those caused by dim light or interocular differences, survive the motor system and show up in tracking responses. Across manipulations, tracking lags mirrored the delays measured with standard psychophysics to within milliseconds, supporting continuous tracking as a precise way to measure temporal processing.
papers.authors: Johannes Burge, Lawrence K. Cormack

0321.name: John A. Greenwood
0321.bio: John A. Greenwood is a Professor of Visual Perception at University College London whose research focuses on the mechanisms of spatial vision and object recognition. Greenwood examines 'visual crowding,' the disruptive effect of clutter on recognition, in both typical peripheral vision and clinical conditions such as amblyopia and nystagmus. Their methodology integrates behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to model how the brain encodes visual dimensions like motion, depth, and face identity. Currently, the lab investigates the computational topology of the visual field and the processes underlying visual imagery and hallucinations.
0321.research_direction: Dr. Greenwood's recent work explores the spatial and cortical mechanisms underlying both healthy and impaired visual processing. They have recently been investigating the phenomenon of visual crowding, using psychophysical methods to map its developmental trajectory in children and to disentangle sensory from oculomotor deficits in clinical populations with albinism and nystagmus. Their recent work also examines the fundamental architecture of the visual system by using wide-field retinotopic mapping to measure how population receptive fields in face-selective regions relate to early visual cortex. Furthermore, they are translating these psychophysical approaches into applied clinical tools, developing rapid behavioral tests to detect higher-level visual loss in neurodegenerative conditions such as posterior cortical atrophy.

papers.title: The development of visual acuity and crowding reveals the slow fine-tuning of foveal vision
papers.abstract: Tests 119 children aged 3 to 13 and adults on foveal acuity and crowding using child-friendly methods. Acuity for isolated targets reaches adult levels by about 5-6 years, whereas crowding by neighbouring elements stays elevated until roughly 7-8 years. A meta-analysis with 13 earlier studies confirms this trajectory, and developmental crowding shows the same target-flanker similarity selectivity as peripheral crowding, suggesting shared mechanisms and a slow shift from fine detail toward scene gist.
papers.authors: John A. Greenwood, Marilia Kyprianou, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Visual crowding in albinism: Evidence for a cortical sensory deficit with oculomotor influences
papers.abstract: Compares foveal crowding in adults with albinism, matched controls and prior data from infantile nystagmus. Crowding is far higher in albinism than in nystagmus alone, is stronger for flankers along the nystagmus direction, and is not relieved by opposite-contrast flankers. The authors conclude a cortical sensory deficit contributes beyond eye-movement effects.
papers.authors: Vijay K. Tailor-Hamblin, Maria Theodorou, Annegret Dahlmann-Noor, Tessa M. Dekker, John A. Greenwood

papers.title: Face-selective cortical regions inherit the visuospatial organisation of early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using wide-field retinotopic mapping with upright and inverted faces, the study estimates population receptive fields in V1-V3 and face-selective OFA, pFus and mFus. Face areas have larger pRFs, but like early cortex they sample the horizontal meridian and lower field more densely. This matches known behavioural anisotropies in face recognition and supports a hierarchical account in which category-selective areas inherit early visuospatial properties.
papers.authors: Anisa Y. Morsi, Hugo T. Chow-Wing-Bom, D. Samuel Schwarzkopf, Valerie Goffaux, Tessa M. Dekker, John A. Greenwood

papers.title: The Graded Incomplete Letters Test (GILT): a rapid test to detect cortical visual loss, with UK Biobank implementation
papers.abstract: Introduces a fast psychophysical test in which letters are shown at decreasing completeness to detect cortical visual impairment as in posterior cortical atrophy. Given to over 2,300 UK Biobank participants and to patients with PCA or typical Alzheimer's disease, it had about 83-89% sensitivity for PCA and above 94% specificity, including against people with eye conditions.
papers.authors: Keir X. X. Yong, Axel Petzold, Paul J. Foster, Andrew Young, Stephen Bell, Yuhan Bai, Alexander P. Leff, Sebastian J. Crutch, John A. Greenwood

0323.name: John Jonides
0323.bio: Jonides is the Edward E. Smith Distinguished University Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Michigan and co-directs the Functional MRI Laboratory. Their research examines the behavioral and neural architectures of working memory and executive control using methodologies such as functional MRI, PET, and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). Jonides has investigated the mechanisms of attentional capture, the dissociation between verbal and spatial working memory, and the relationship between cognitive control and fluid intelligence. Their current work focuses on the dysfunction of these mechanisms in clinical populations, including those with major depressive disorder and ADHD, and explores how environmental interventions like nature exposure may restore attentional resources.
0323.research_direction: Dr. Jonides has recently been investigating the precise temporal dynamics of visual attention and cognitive control, alongside a re-evaluation of foundational mechanisms of attentional capture. Their recent work explores whether abrupt onsets capture attention primarily due to high physical salience compared to other distractors like color singletons, utilizing explicit psychophysical techniques to probe these longstanding assumptions. To understand how visual processing and conflict resolution unfold over milliseconds, they are employing forced-response paradigms combined with computational modeling and physiological measures to trace the exact timecourse of distractor suppression. Furthermore, they are applying these temporal modeling approaches to clinical populations, investigating how delays in goal-directed processing might underlie the inhibitory control challenges observed in adults with ADHD.

papers.title: Delayed goal-directed processing underlies inhibitory control challenges in adult ADHD
papers.abstract: Using a forced-response method with computational modeling, the study separates habitual from goal-directed processing over time in response-conflict tasks (Simon and Flanker). It compares adults with ADHD to neurotypical adults, and ADHD participants on versus off medication. The findings indicate that inhibitory control difficulties in ADHD arise from delayed goal-directed processing.
papers.authors: Jahla Osborne, Jacob Sellers, Han Zhang, Wang Su, Sarah Liberatore, Chandra Sripada, Priti Shah, John Jonides

papers.title: Physiological evidence for the time-dependent resolution of response conflicts
papers.abstract: The response preparation model, applied to forced-response data, describes how goal-directed and automatic responses unfold over time during conflict resolution, but it relies on overt behavior. This study seeks physiological evidence for the same time-dependent processes, validating the model's account of conflict resolution beyond behavioral data.
papers.authors: A. Kane York, Jacob Sellers, Han Zhang, Michael Vesia, Taraz G. Lee, John Jonides

papers.title: The temporal dynamics of visual attention
papers.abstract: Across four experiments, the authors use a forced-response method, which forces participants to respond at controlled moments, to trace how attentional priority for targets and salient distractors evolves over milliseconds. Combined with a computational model, the results show when distractor suppression takes hold and how it unfolds over time. The work reframes the debate on distractor suppression as one about temporal dynamics.
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Jacob Sellers, Taraz G. Lee, John Jonides

papers.title: Attentional capture by abrupt onsets: Foundations and emerging issues
papers.abstract: This article revisits the classic finding by Yantis and Jonides that abrupt onsets capture attention in a stimulus-driven way unless attention is proactively directed elsewhere. It evaluates that conclusion against three decades of later work and identifies concepts, measurement practices, and open questions that should guide future research on attentional capture.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Han Zhang, A. Kane York, John Jonides

papers.title: Are abrupt onsets highly salient?
papers.abstract: Abrupt onsets are often assumed to be highly physically salient, which is used to explain why they capture attention more than other distractors such as color singletons. Using a recently developed psychophysical technique to measure salience explicitly, the study tests whether onsets are in fact more salient, questioning that assumption.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Han Zhang, Esha Brar, A. Kane York, John Jonides

0324.name: John K. Tsotsos
0324.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Lassonde School of Engineering
0324.lab_name: Laboratory for Active and Attentive Vision (LAAV)
0324.bio: Tsotsos is a Distinguished Research Professor of Vision Science at York University and holds the NSERC Tier I Canada Research Chair in Computational Vision. They developed the Selective Tuning (ST) theory, a computational framework for visual attention that addresses the complexity of visual information processing through a hierarchy of winner-take-all mechanisms. Their research connects computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence, focusing on the integration of top-down attentional control with bottom-up sensory processing. Tsotsos also develops active vision systems for robotic navigation and object search.
0324.research_direction: Dr. Tsotsos has recently been investigating active vision and attentional mechanisms across both biological and artificial systems. Their recent work explores how observers actively sample 3D environments, employing full-body motion tracking to study viewpoint selection during real-world visual search and translating human-like vergence eye movements into binocular stereo models for humanoid robots. They are also examining the nature of selective attention by investigating whether self-attention mechanisms in Vision Transformers truly capture biological top-down feedback, and by incorporating task and behavioral context into predictive models of human gaze during driving. Additionally, they are developing mechanistic neural models of the ventral stream to explore how hypothesized border-ownership cells might utilize equiluminant color contrast to parse figure from ground.

papers.title: Convergent binocular stereo: Depth perception for humanoid robot vision
papers.abstract: Robot stereo systems usually use fixed, parallel cameras, whereas human depth perception relies on both eyes converging on the same point. The authors present a stereo algorithm, convergent binocular stereo, that computes depth under the humanoid constraint of vergence and version eye movements. It gives robot heads a way to use active, human-like binocular geometry for purposeful depth computation.
papers.authors: Mingshi Chi, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Real-world visual search goes beyond eye movements: Active searchers select 3D scene viewpoints too
papers.abstract: Subjects moved freely in a controlled 3D room while eye and head movements were tracked as they looked for toy objects. This gave the first record of viewpoint selection during search. Searchers used their full range of body and head motion to choose viewpoints, showing that real-world search involves much more than eye movements and that passive 2D screen tasks miss this.
papers.authors: Tiffany C. Wu, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Equiluminant Border Ownership Cells as a Missing Link in Color Form Perception
papers.abstract: The authors hypothesize a subpopulation of border ownership neurons that signal which side is the figure along borders defined only by color contrast. They build a hierarchical mechanistic ventral-stream model of these cells. Simulated units show strong color selectivity along with orientation and border ownership tuning like their luminance counterparts, giving testable predictions.
papers.authors: Paria Mehrani, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Understanding and Modeling the Effects of Task and Context on Drivers' Gaze Allocation
papers.abstract: Most driver gaze models use bottom-up saliency and ignore the driver's actions and context. The authors add action and context annotations to existing driving datasets, analyze how task and context shape where drivers look, and propose a model that integrates them to predict gaze better.
papers.authors: Iuliia Kotseruba, John K. Tsotsos

papers.title: Self-attention in vision transformers performs perceptual grouping, not attention
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether the attention mechanism in vision transformers behaves like human visual attention. Analyzing the formulation, the authors show it acts as a relaxation-labeling process with similarity-grouping effects rather than attention. Unlike biological attention, it lacks feedback and top-down selective mechanisms. Experiments support this interpretation.
papers.authors: Paria Mehrani, John K. Tsotsos

0325.name: John Maule
0325.bio: John Maule is an Assistant Professor at the University of Sussex and the lead of the Statistical Perception Lab. Their research explores the intersection of vision science and cognitive psychology, focusing on the ensemble perception of color and how individuals extract summary statistics from complex visual scenes. Maule investigates the 'visual diet' through hyperspectral imaging and image analysis to quantify how chromatic statistics influence perception, adaptation, and aesthetic preference. Additionally, their work examines neurodiversity in vision, specifically studying atypical color perception and adaptation in autistic populations using psychophysical and behavioral methodologies.
0325.research_direction: Dr. Maule has recently been investigating both the developmental trajectory of human color perception and its real-world applications under complex lighting conditions. Their recent work explores how color vision, color constancy, and color categorization emerge from infancy through childhood, examining the interplay between low-level sensory development and higher-level cognitive and cultural influences. In a highly applied track, they are using spectral data and computational models of human vision to quantify the luminance and chromatic contrast of moving targets—specifically cricket balls—against various backgrounds across daylight, twilight, and floodlit environments. Furthermore, Dr. Maule is extending these models to evaluate how red-green color vision deficiencies impact object visibility during these dynamic tasks, investigating how equipment choices and ambient lighting interact to affect visual performance and inclusivity in sports.

papers.title: Not So Pretty in Pink: Computational Modelling of Cricket Ball Visibility with Colour Vision Deficiency
papers.abstract: Models how cricketers with red-green colour vision deficiency see red versus pink balls under varying match lighting, since roughly 9% of male players are affected. The simulation shows how ball colour interacts with dusk conditions and background to change visibility for these players. The results inform equipment and inclusion decisions in day-night cricket.
papers.authors: Peter M. Allen, Oliver R. Runswick, Luke Wilkins, David L. Mann, Matthew A. Timmis, J. Maule

papers.title: Difficult at dusk? Illuminating the debate on cricket ball visibility
papers.abstract: Uses measured spectral data and models of human vision to compare how visible red, white and pink cricket balls are under daylight, twilight and floodlit conditions. The analysis tests player claims that the pink ball is hard to see at dusk. It reframes the debate in terms of the ball's chromatic and luminance contrast against the background.
papers.venue: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
papers.authors: John J. Maule, Robert Maguire, Matthew A. Timmis, Oliver R. Runswick, Luke Wilkins, David L. Mann, Stephen J. Dain, Jenny M. Bosten, Peter M. Allen

papers.title: The Development of Color Perception and Cognition
papers.abstract: A comprehensive review of how color vision, color constancy, color categories and color language emerge from infancy through childhood. It integrates evidence on low-level sensory development with higher-level perception and cognition, and highlights how the visual environment and culture shape color. It also identifies open questions for future developmental work.
papers.authors: John Maule, Alice E. Skelton, Anna Franklin

0326.name: John Serences
0326.bio: John Serences is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at UC San Diego, investigating how top-down behavioral goals and attentional factors modulate visual perception, memory, and decision-making. Their research utilizes functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine population-level representations in the human brain.
