Serences employs quantitative neuroimaging techniques, including multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and forward encoding models, to reconstruct feature-selective responses within the visual cortex. Their work provides evidence for the 'sensory recruitment' theory of working memory and characterizes how spatial priority maps in the parietal and frontal cortices coordinate the selection of relevant environmental stimuli.
0326.research_direction: Dr. Serences has recently been investigating the dynamic interplay between visual working memory, feature-based attention, and immediate sensory perception. Using fMRI decoding and psychophysical recall tasks, their recent work explores how the early visual cortex multiplexes these demands, specifically testing how active memory representations are reformatted by task context and how they compete for shared neural resources with incoming sensory distractors. They are also examining the distributed nature of working memory capacity, mapping how load-related signals are represented across the cortical hierarchy and how they drift over time. Additionally, Dr. Serences uses spiking neural network models to ask how near-random, top-down prefrontal feedback can successfully drive precise feature-based attentional modulation in early sensory regions.

papers.title: Memory recall errors reflect interacting sensory and mnemonic representations
papers.abstract: The study tests whether working-memory errors reflect interaction between sensory and mnemonic representations, using an orientation recall task. Adding noise to the memorandum and presenting distractors each raised recall error independently. Distractors that shared a feature with the remembered item pulled recall toward the distractor's orientation. The size of that bias depended on stimulus noise and on whether the distractor was task-relevant. This supports partial overlap between the representations used for perception and for memory.
papers.authors: Holly Kular, John T. Serences

papers.title: Sensory reformatting for a working visual memory
papers.abstract: This review looks at how the visual cortex holds information in working memory. It argues that early visual activity does not stay a faithful sensory copy during maintenance. It can be transformed into a format shaped by task context and tuned to behavior. The authors survey evidence for these transformations, the forms they take, and why they matter, and propose that visual cortex acts as an active workspace where 'good enough' memory codes interface with perception and action.
papers.authors: Anastasia Kiyonaga, John T. Serences

papers.title: Distributed and drifting signals for working memory load in human cortex
papers.abstract: In a pre-registered, high-powered fMRI study, 12 people each completed 12 scanner-hours of a visual working memory task with 0 to 4 items. Univariate activity in parietal cortex rose with load, replicating earlier work. Activity across the visual hierarchy also changed with load, in both directions. Multivariate patterns encoded load everywhere regardless of the direction of the univariate effect, which argues against a single parietal locus. The load code also drifted across sessions, suggesting it is continually refined over time.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Edward Awh, John T. Serences

papers.title: Near-random connections support top-down feature-based attentional modulations in early sensory cortex
papers.abstract: The paper asks how prefrontal feedback can boost neurons tuned to a relevant feature in sensory cortex without also boosting neurons tuned to irrelevant features. The authors built a two-layer spiking network in which a control layer with high-dimensional tuning connects to feature-selective sensory neurons at random. Stimulating control neurons that respond to a relevant stimulus produced gain changes in the matching sensory neurons, including at locations without direct input. The results suggest that unstructured feedback wiring is enough to support feature-based attention.
papers.authors: Sunyoung Park, John T. Serences

papers.title: Manipulating attentional priority creates a trade-off between memory and sensory representations in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Participants held an orientation in memory while a distractor grating stayed on screen. They were cued to ignore it, attend its contrast, or attend its orientation, and fMRI decoding tracked the effect in early visual cortex. Memory fidelity was best when the distractor was ignored and worst when its orientation was attended. Distractor fidelity showed the opposite pattern. The results indicate a trade-off in shared early sensory representations when top-down feedback serves both remembered and currently seen features.
papers.authors: Rosanne L. Rademaker, John T. Serences

0327.name: Jonathan Cant
0327.department: Department of Psychology, University of Toronto Scarborough
0327.bio: Jonathan Cant is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto Scarborough and directs the Cant Lab. Their research integrates functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and psychophysical behavioral methods to map the neural substrates of human visual perception and cognition. Cant investigates the functional organization of the ventral stream, focusing on how the brain distinguishes between object shape, surface-based cues such as texture and color, and complex scene ensembles. Their work also examines the interactions between these perceptual pathways and their role in producing adaptive behaviors within natural environments.
0327.research_direction: Dr. Cant's recent work investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying ensemble perception across a variety of visual domains. Using multivariate EEG decoding, they have recently been exploring the temporal dynamics of face processing, specifically tracking how the brain represents individual faces versus crowd averages and testing whether facial expressions are coded along continuous, anticipatory dimensions. In tandem with this neural focus, their recent behavioral research examines how attention and spatial layout interact to shape the extraction of summary statistics from face crowds. Furthermore, Dr. Cant is investigating the broader computational principles of ensemble coding, probing how rapidly observers can extract average features from complex real-world scenes and testing whether the mechanisms for averaging low-level features like orientation are shared across distinct stimulus categories.

papers.title: Evidence for dimensional representations and anticipatory dynamics in facial expression perception
papers.abstract: This EEG decoding study asks how the brain represents facial expressions over time, testing whether they are coded along continuous dimensions rather than as discrete categories. The authors find dimensional structure in the neural signals and evidence that expression information is anticipated before it fully unfolds. The work extends the lab's face-perception and EEG-decoding line to emotional expression.
papers.authors: Tyler Roberts, Yong Zhong Liang, Gerald C. Cupchik, Jonathan S. Cant, Adrian Nestor

papers.title: Internal domain generality for ensemble perception of average orientation: Comparing and integrating information from multiple stimulus categories
papers.abstract: This paper tests whether the mechanism that averages a set of items is shared across stimulus categories or separate for each. Observers compared and combined average orientation information drawn from different categories, and performance points to a largely domain-general averaging mechanism. The work bears on a central question of whether ensemble perception is a general-purpose computation.
papers.authors: Greer Gillies, Keisuke Fukuda, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: Rapid ensemble encoding of average scene features
papers.abstract: The authors show that observers can extract the average of features such as those defining natural scenes after very brief exposures. Several experiments establish how quickly scene-level summary information becomes available. This extends ensemble perception from simple items and faces to complex real-world scenes.
papers.authors: Vignash Tharmaratnam, Jason Haberman, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: Attention and stimulus structure interact during ensemble encoding of facial expression
papers.abstract: The study asks how attention and the arrangement of a face crowd jointly shape the extraction of its average expression. Attention and stimulus structure interact rather than acting independently, so summary judgments depend on both where observers attend and how the faces are organized. The findings refine accounts of when ensemble coding is automatic and when it is modulated by attention.
papers.authors: Marco A. Sama, Moaz Shoura, Adrian Nestor, Jonathan S. Cant

papers.title: The neural dynamics of face ensemble and central face processing
papers.abstract: Using EEG with multivariate decoding, the authors track when the brain represents a single central face versus the average of a surrounding crowd of faces. The results show that ensemble (summary) information is available in neural signals on a distinct timescale from individual-face processing, and that the two kinds of information can be dissociated. This supports the idea that face crowds are summarized by dedicated processes rather than being built up from individual faces.
papers.authors: Marco Agazio Sama, Adrian Nestor, Jonathan Samuel Cant

0328.name: Jonathan Flombaum
0328.bio: Jonathan Flombaum is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences at Johns Hopkins University and the director of the Visual Thinking Lab. Flombaum’s research focuses on the computational and representational constraints of human cognition, specifically the intersection of visual perception, attention, and memory. They investigate object persistence, multiple object tracking, and the role of categorical biases in visual working memory. By combining behavioral psychophysics with mathematical modeling, their work identifies how the mind utilizes core knowledge of physics and categorization to navigate the limitations of mental computation.
0328.research_direction: Dr. Flombaum's recent work explores how the human visual system structures the representation of moving objects and processes temporal information across the visual field. They have recently been investigating the spatial reference frames used during visual tracking, specifically asking whether objects in rotational or orbiting motion are represented independently or bound together within composite, object-centered representations. To probe these representational formats and how they might conflict with task demands, their lab leverages psychophysical paradigms involving multiple object tracking, the freezing illusion, and the motion-silencing illusion. In a distinct line of research, their recent work explores how retinal eccentricity influences temporal perception, using rapid stimulus streams to investigate how processing speed differences between the fovea and periphery affect perceptual judgments of simultaneity and duration.

papers.title: The format of representation for objects in orbit: Composite and internally referenced.
papers.abstract: Asks whether objects moving on circular (orbiting) paths are represented independently, as when translating, or as parts of one composite system with an internal reference frame. Across six experiments, tracking targets was harder for rotation than for matched translation, and visible connecting lines made translational tracking worse in the same way, consistent with composite representations. The freezing illusion was also stronger for rotation, extending object-centered representation to axes and relations not physically present in the stimulus.
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: Conflict Between Representational Format and Procedure Constrains Cognitive Performance in a Simple Visual Tracking Task
papers.abstract: Preprint extending the lab's orbit-tracking work, arguing that performance in a simple visual tracking task is limited when the format in which moving objects are represented conflicts with the procedure the task demands. Summary based on the title and related conference work on tracking a single predictable, slow orbiting object; abstract not directly retrieved.
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: The Motion-Silencing Illusion Depends on Object-Centered Representation
papers.abstract: Motion silencing makes salient changes hard to notice when the changing items are also moving. The authors introduce a way to quantify illusion strength and show that rotational motion produces a stronger illusion than well-controlled non-rotating motion, which argues against a simple low-level detection-limit account. They propose that the illusion reflects a failure to attribute changes to locations under a structured object representation, and support this with a rotating external frame that weakens the illusion.
papers.authors: Qihan Wu, Jonathan I. Flombaum

papers.title: Eccentricity advances arrival to visual perception.
papers.abstract: Examines how the uneven processing speed across the visual field affects perceived timing. Participants reporting which letter in a rapid stream coincided with a cue chose earlier letters for more peripheral cues, so never-simultaneous stimuli were perceived as simultaneous. Control experiments tied this to eccentricity rather than inter-stimulus distance and showed that peripheral stimuli also appear longer, suggesting transient peripheral signals reach perception faster than foveal ones.
papers.authors: Aditya Upadhyayula, Ian Phillips, Jonathan I. Flombaum

0329.name: Jonathan Touryan
0329.institution: U.S. Army DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory
0329.lab_name: Cognition and Neuroergonomics (CaN) Collaborative Technology Alliance
0329.bio: Jonathan Touryan is a senior research scientist within the Human Research and Engineering Directorate at the U.S. Army DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory. Touryan’s research focuses on the intersection of visual neuroscience and neuroergonomics, utilizing high-density electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and virtual reality to decode neural signatures of situational awareness and target detection in complex environments. Touryan contributed to the development of the Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) and large-scale data analysis frameworks to enhance human-autonomy teaming and brain-computer interface technologies. Touryan earned a PhD in the neurophysiology of vision from the University of California, Berkeley, and completed postdoctoral training at the Yale University School of Medicine.
0329.research_direction: Dr. Touryan has recently been investigating the neural and oculomotor dynamics of unconstrained visual search in ecologically valid virtual reality environments. Their recent work explores how to continuously track latent cognitive states, such as task engagement and the processing cost of sensory interruptions, by applying machine learning to paired EEG and head-eye tracking data. At a mechanistic level, they are studying how the onset latency of fixation-locked object processing relates to the amplitude of preceding saccades, and whether multimodal gaze features can reliably decode environmental difficulty and time pressure during active foraging. Furthermore, they are examining how specialized training impacts applied visual behavior by comparing the saccade kinematics and neural attentional allocation of active-duty military personnel against civilian populations.

papers.title: The Cost of Disruption: Analyzing the Impact of New Tasks on Time-Evolving Cognitive Activity
papers.abstract: Attention and related cognitive states oscillate over time, so interrupting an ongoing process may carry a hidden cost. The authors build a predictive model that forecasts future cognitive state from a finite history of prior state, then use it to see what happens when an auditory side task interrupts an unrestricted visual search. The work is aimed at human-system integration where interruptions must be timed sensibly.
papers.authors: S. M. Gordon, J. Touryan

papers.title: Decoding target discriminability and time pressure using eye and head movement features in a foraging search task
papers.abstract: Thirty-one participants searched for targets among distractors in a virtual reality shooting scenario while difficulty and time pressure were manipulated. Support vector classifiers using eye and head movement features could tell which condition each trial came from, with the combined eye-plus-head model beating either alone. Fixation-related features were most useful for discriminability, and the results support behavior-based monitoring of operator state in high-pressure visual tasks.
papers.authors: Anthony J. Ries, Chloe Callahan-Flintoft, Anna Madison, Louis Dankovich, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Saccade size predicts onset time of object processing during visual search of an open world virtual environment
papers.abstract: The authors decode fixation-locked P300-like brain responses with convolutional networks while people search freely in an open-world virtual environment. Estimating when this response occurs after each fixation shows that its latency varies from one fixation to the next. That variability is predicted by the size of the preceding saccade, giving a behavioral handle on when object processing begins during natural free viewing.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Gordon, Bianca Dalangin, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Evidence of elevated situational awareness for active duty soldiers during navigation of a virtual environment
papers.abstract: Active-duty service members and civilians navigated an open-world virtual environment, searching and counting targets under varying cognitive load, while eye movements and EEG were recorded. Soldiers counted targets more accurately, scanned with faster and larger saccades, and showed a neural (CNN-decoded P300) response weighted more toward first fixations than refixations, suggesting more efficient allocation of attention. The study links military experience to measurable differences in visual search physiology.
papers.authors: Leah R. Enders, Stephen M. Gordon, Heather Roy, Thomas Rohaly, Bianca Dalangin, Angela Jeter, Jessica Villarreal, Gary L. Boykin, Jonathan Touryan

papers.title: Decoding neural activity to assess individual latent state in ecologically valid contexts
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether neural patterns learned in tightly controlled lab tasks can reveal internal cognitive states in complex, naturalistic settings. Domain-generalization methods from the brain-computer-interface field were used to train models on two lab paradigms and apply them to unconstrained tasks. The decoded signals tracked latent states such as engagement across contexts, supporting lab-derived neural markers as tools for real-world state inference.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Gordon, Jonathan R. McDaniel, Kevin W. King, Vernon J. Lawhern, Jonathan Touryan

0330.name: Jonathan Victor
0330.bio: Jonathan Victor is the Fred Plum Professor of Neurology and Neuroscience at Weill Cornell Medicine and directs the Division of Systems Neurology and Neuroscience. Victor’s research integrates mathematical modeling and information theory with neurophysiology to investigate sensory processing within the visual and olfactory systems. They developed metric-space analyses for neural spike trains and conduct studies on how cortical networks represent visual textures and natural scene statistics. Additionally, Victor applies computational frameworks to examine large-scale brain dynamics and cognitive motor dissociation in patients with disorders of consciousness.
0330.research_direction: Dr. Victor's recent work explores the active, dynamic nature of visual processing and the mathematical structures underlying perception. They have recently been investigating how self-generated eye movements—such as saccades, blinks, and fixational drift—fundamentally shape retinal input, including how top-down cognitive expectations can modulate ocular drift even in the absence of structured sensory information. In parallel, their research examines the geometry of neural and cognitive representations, using similarity ranking paradigms to map the dimensionality of perceptual spaces across both low-level visual textures and high-level semantic domains, while also employing hyperbolic geometry to model the temporal dynamics of neural spike trains. Furthermore, they are actively studying methodological approaches to vision science, investigating how computationally generated images can be leveraged to bridge the gap between mathematically tractable artificial stimuli and natural scene statistics.

papers.title: Narrowing the gap between analytically convenient and naturalistic stimuli
papers.abstract: An invited perspective arguing that mathematically tractable stimuli like sinusoids and noise, and natural scene images, are less far apart than usually assumed. Computer-generated images sit in between, and better understanding of natural image statistics could make them more useful experimental probes for uncovering design principles of sensory systems.
papers.authors: Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: Walks with jumps: a neurobiologically motivated class of paths in the hyperbolic plane
papers.abstract: Introduces a mathematical construct in which a point moves through the hyperbolic plane at constant velocity but is displaced by discrete jumps, as a representation of a neuron's spike train. Because hyperbolic transformations do not commute, the endpoint carries information about the timing of jumps and has a built-in point-of-no-return suited to progressive decision making, though the encoding is incomplete; the paper proves these properties with hyperbolic geometry.
papers.authors: Jordan DeBlois, Eli Einstein, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: The visual system does not operate like a camera
papers.abstract: A perspective piece arguing that vision is not a sequence of static snapshots but a fundamentally dynamic process built from the temporal signals that saccades, fixational drift and blinks generate. The authors review evidence that these self-generated motions shape retinal input and neural coding, and propose that models of vision should treat time-varying input as the norm rather than an afterthought.
papers.authors: Michele Rucci, Ehud Ahissar, David C. Burr, Igor Kagan, Martina Poletti, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: The Geometry of Low- and High-Level Perceptual Spaces
papers.abstract: Using an efficient ranking paradigm, the study collected similarity judgments across five stimulus domains ranging from colored textures to animal names and fit geometric embeddings to each participant. All domains needed roughly 5-7 dimensions with modest spherical curvature, yet the organization of stimuli within the space, such as hierarchical clustering, depended on how much semantic content the domain carried.
papers.authors: Suniyya Amna Waraich, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: Cognitive influences on fixational eye movements
papers.abstract: Subjects discriminated letter pairs while unknowingly viewing pure noise fields, allowing task knowledge to be separated from incoming sensory input. Ocular drift was systematically shaped by the expected task, showing that fixational drift is under open-loop cognitive control and is tuned to enhance the spatial information needed for the discrimination.
papers.authors: Yen-Chu Lin, Janis Intoy, Ashley M. Clark, Michele Rucci, Jonathan D. Victor

0331.name: Jonathan Winawer
0331.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0331.lab_name: Winawer Laboratory for Visual Perception and Neuroscience
0331.bio: Jonathan Winawer is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University and directs the Winawer Laboratory for Visual Perception and Neuroscience. Winawer’s research characterizes the computational principles and biological constraints of the human visual system, examining how sensory pathways encode and transform information to support perception. They employ a multi-modal approach integrating psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques, including functional MRI (fMRI), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG). Winawer’s work involves developing predictive models of cortical responses, mapping visual field organization, and investigating the neural mechanisms underlying temporal summation and perceptual adaptation.
0331.research_direction: Dr. Winawer has recently been using fMRI, retinotopic mapping, and psychophysics to investigate the functional organization of the human visual cortex and its relationship to spatial vision. Their recent work explores how fine-grained variations in cortical magnification and map surface area—such as individual differences in V4 size or the developmental emergence of visual field asymmetries in V1—relate to fundamental perceptual limits like crowding distance and spatial frequency tuning. Additionally, they are investigating how top-down cognitive processes dynamically modulate these early sensory representations. Specifically, they are examining how covert spatial attention shifts population receptive fields during target anticipation, and how feedback during visual working and long-term memory alters spatial tuning across the visual hierarchy compared to feedforward perception.

papers.title: Spatial attention selectively alters visual cortical representation during target anticipation
papers.abstract: Using concurrent psychophysics and fMRI, the study asks what covert spatial attention does to visual cortex before a target appears. Behavior improved at the cued location and worsened at uncued ones. Pre-target BOLD showed a stimulus-independent baseline increase near the cue and a decrease elsewhere, along with population receptive fields shifting toward the attended location, with both effects growing up the visual hierarchy.
papers.authors: Ekin Tünçok, Marisa Carrasco, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Human V4 size predicts crowding distance
papers.abstract: Crowding limits recognition when objects are closely spaced, and it varies about two-fold between healthy adults. Pairing psychophysical measurements with fMRI retinotopic mapping in 49 observers, the authors show that the number of letters that fit in the visual field without crowding scales with V4 surface area but not with V1-V3. This implies a roughly constant cortical crowding distance of about 1.4 mm on the V4 map across individuals.
papers.authors: Jan W. Kurzawski, Brenda S. Qiu, Najib J. Majaj, Noah C. Benson, Denis G. Pelli, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Unpacking the V1 map: Differential covariation of preferred spatial frequency and cortical magnification across spatial dimensions
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in 40 observers, the paper examines how V1 cortical magnification and preferred spatial frequency covary with eccentricity and polar angle. The two are proportional across eccentricity, consistent with a common cause such as retinal ganglion cell density, but not around polar angle. The authors conclude that V1 is not simply a tiling of identical units and that cortical variation around the visual field differs from that across eccentricity.
papers.authors: Marc M. Himmelberg, Yuna Kwak, Marisa Carrasco, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Feedback scales the spatial tuning of cortical responses during both visual working memory and long-term memory
papers.abstract: Participants viewed, held in working memory, or recalled from long-term memory a peripheral target while fMRI measured polar-angle tuning across visual field maps. Perceptual responses became broader up the hierarchy, while both memory conditions produced uniformly broad tuning, even in V1. This supports the view that mnemonic activity in early visual cortex comes from top-down feedback that scales tuning relative to perception.
papers.authors: Robert Woodry, Clayton E. Curtis, Jonathan Winawer

papers.title: Comparing retinotopic maps of children and adults reveals a late-stage change in how V1 samples the visual field
papers.abstract: Adults perceive better along the horizontal than vertical meridian and along the lower than upper vertical meridian, mirroring V1 surface area. Measuring retinotopic map area with MRI in children and adults, the authors find most map features are adult-like, but children devote similar V1 area to the upper and lower vertical meridians. This points to a late developmental change in V1 organization tied to the emergence of the vertical-meridian asymmetry.
papers.authors: Marc M. Himmelberg, Ekin Tünçok, Jesse Gomez, Kalanit Grill-Spector, Marisa Carrasco, Jonathan Winawer

0332.name: Joo-Hyun Song
0332.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0332.bio: Song investigates the behavioral and neural mechanisms that integrate cognitive processes, such as attention and decision-making, with motor control. Their research employs a multi-methodological approach—including continuous action tracking, fMRI, and EEG—to examine how humans coordinate eye and hand movements within complex, dynamic environments. Song utilizes the reach-tracking paradigm to demonstrate how real-time motor trajectories reveal internal cognitive states and the continuous interplay between perception and action.
0332.research_direction: Dr. Song's recent work explores the continuous, bi-directional integration of visual perception, cognition, and motor action, challenging the traditional view of these systems as strictly sequential processing stages. They have recently been investigating how action mechanisms interact with diverse cognitive functions, such as testing whether goal-directed attentional demands modulate seemingly automatic implicit motor adaptation and asking if practicing timed motor tasks like throwing influences baseline time perception. Additionally, their research leverages continuous reach-tracking methods to uncover the real-time inhibitory-control dynamics underlying high-level social-cognitive processes, such as how children resolve conflict during judgments of fairness. Across these varied domains, Dr. Song is ultimately probing how reconceptualizing visual attention and decision-making as integrated sensorimotor processes can reshape our fundamental theories of behavior.

papers.title: Automatic, but not autonomous: Implicit adaptation is modulated by goal-directed attentional demands
papers.abstract: Implicit motor adaptation, the error-driven recalibration of a reach to a perturbed display, is often described as an automatic process. This study shows that it is nevertheless sensitive to how much attention is consumed by a concurrent goal-directed task, so adaptation is automatic but not independent of attentional resources. The results tie implicit sensorimotor learning to general attentional control.
papers.authors: Joshua J. Liddy, Sean R. O'Bryan, Alexander Daskalopoulos, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Visual attention as an integrated sensorimotor process
papers.abstract: A target-article style commentary-invited paper arguing that visual attention should not be treated as a purely perceptual filter separate from action. It draws on behavioral and neural evidence that selection and movement planning share mechanisms, and proposes attention as an integrated sensorimotor process.
papers.authors: Sean O'Bryan, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Emergent motor timing enhances time perception
papers.abstract: Using a throwing task, this work asks whether practising a timed action sharpens the perception of time. Participants who improved their motor timing through practice also showed more precise time perception, indicating that timing skill developed through action feeds back onto perceptual judgments.
papers.authors: Jianfei Guo, Zhaoran Zhang, Mukesh Makwana, Dagmar Sternad, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Distinct Inhibitory-Control Processes Underlie Children's Judgments of Fairness
papers.abstract: Continuous reach tracking was used to follow how children and adults resolve conflict when judging what is fair. The movement trajectories reveal that different inhibitory-control processes are engaged for fairness judgments, connecting real-time motor dynamics to social-cognitive development.
papers.authors: David M. Sobel, David G. Kamper, Joo-Hyun Song

papers.title: Rethinking Vision and Action
papers.abstract: This review argues against a strict pipeline in which vision feeds a separate motor stage. It surveys evidence that perception and action are tightly and continuously intertwined, and outlines how studying behavior in action reshapes theories of attention, decision-making and visual processing.
papers.authors: Ken Nakayama, Jeff Moher, Joo-Hyun Song

0334.name: Jorge Morales
0334.department: Department of Philosophy; Department of Psychology and Neuroscience (lab housed in the Duke Institute for Brain Sciences)
0334.bio: Jorge Morales is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Philosophy at Northeastern University and directs the Subjectivity Lab. Their research combines psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and philosophy to investigate conscious experience and visual perception. Morales examines how the mind constructs visual reality, focusing on the perception of absences, the representation of perspectival shape, and the mechanisms underlying metacognitive introspection. This work addresses the relationship between subjective mental states and their neural and computational foundations.
0334.research_direction: Dr. Morales has recently been investigating fundamental phenomena in visual perception and memory, exploring whether predictive memory distortions like representational momentum apply to non-motion features such as color and brightness, and experimentally testing long-standing philosophical claims about how we perceive perspectival shape. Their recent work also explores the emergent cognitive capacities of large language models, probing whether purely text-based systems can execute visual mental imagery tasks involving shape transformations and whether they can introspectively self-report the complex internal variables driving their choices. Additionally, they are examining the methodological foundations of consciousness science by evaluating how metacognitive confidence ratings might serve as a better operational bridge between subjective experience and objective measurement than traditional introspection.

papers.title: Artificial Phantasia: Emergent Mental Imagery in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Tests whether purely language-based systems can carry out tasks thought to require pictorial mental imagery, by having people and LLMs mentally compose letter and shape transformations and name the resulting image. The best LLMs outperformed 100 human participants, and models did better with longer reasoning chains, suggesting language-like propositional representations can suffice for what looks like visual imagery. The paper weighs several hypotheses about how such emergent imagery arises.
papers.authors: Morgan McCarty, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Self-Interpretability: LLMs Can Describe Complex Internal Processes that Drive Their Decisions, and Improve with Training
papers.abstract: The authors fine-tune GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini to make choices (condos, loans, vacations) according to randomly generated attribute weightings, then ask the models to report those weightings. The models can accurately describe the quantitative preferences that drive their own decisions, even though they were never shown them explicitly, and this self-report ability improves with further training and generalizes to other tasks. The work presents introspective self-report as a route to understanding LLM internals alongside mechanistic interpretability.
papers.authors: Dillon Plunkett, Adam Morris, Keerthi Reddy, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Representational Momentum Transcends Motion
papers.abstract: Across seven experiments with US adults, the authors show that the memory distortions once seen only for moving objects, where remembered positions drift toward where things are heading, also occur for changes with no motion, such as brightness, color saturation and proportion. Minds appear to make predictions that bias what we remember about a wide range of changing properties. This reframes representational momentum as a general feature of predictive perception.
papers.authors: Dillon Plunkett, Jorge Morales

papers.title: Confidence in Consciousness Science
papers.abstract: Engages with Maja Spener's book on introspection, arguing that confidence ratings, and metacognition more generally, are a better methodological bridge between subjective experience and objective measurement than introspection as a method. Confidence has objective anchors, is easy to operationalize, and tracks both visibility judgments and neural markers of awareness. The author concludes that confidence ratings are a tractable, mechanistically informed tool for consciousness research.
papers.authors: Jorge Morales

papers.title: Empirical evidence for perspectival similarity
papers.abstract: Responds to a philosophical critique of earlier experiments showing that a tilted circle is perceived as resembling an ellipse (perspectival similarity). The authors defend both the philosophical framing and the empirical methods, and present new analyses arguing that the perspectival-shape effect stands. The paper is part of a broader effort to test long-standing philosophical claims about perception experimentally.
papers.authors: Jorge Morales, Chaz Firestone

0335.name: Jorge Otero-Millan
0335.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry & Vision Science
0335.bio: Jorge Otero-Millan’s research focuses on the mechanisms of ocular motor control and their intersection with visual perception and vestibular integration. Otero-Millan investigates fixational eye movements, specifically microsaccades, and their role in maintaining visual stability during head and eye rotations across all three axes. Utilizing computational modeling, virtual reality, and eye-tracking, Otero-Millan develops methodologies to characterize nystagmus and other oculomotor abnormalities. Their research explores the application of these metrics as non-invasive diagnostic biomarkers for neurological and vestibular disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, vertigo, and concussions.
0335.research_direction: Dr. Otero-Millan has recently been investigating the intricate relationships between oculomotor control, spatial perception, and natural scene statistics. Their recent work explores the mechanistic drivers of eye movements, using behavioral experiments and computational modeling to determine what causes horizontal saccade biases during free-viewing and whether illusory visual tilt is sufficient to trigger optostatic ocular torsion. They are also examining how the oculomotor system actively shapes visual experience, testing how eccentric gaze-holding distorts perceived spatial layouts and how eye position and velocity influence heading judgments drawn from optic flow. To support this broad methodological approach, Dr. Otero-Millan has been developing Open Iris, a modular, open-source video-based eye-tracking framework designed to make highly customizable gaze and pupil measurements more accessible to the research community.

papers.title: Horizontal saccade bias results from combination of saliency anisotropies and egocentric biases
papers.abstract: Humans make most of their saccades along horizontal and vertical directions, and the source of this bias has been unclear. Using two public free-viewing datasets, the authors show that orientation anisotropies in image saliency best predict the horizontal bias. They then build a target-selection model that mixes image-aligned (allocentric) and eye/head-aligned (egocentric) biases, which reproduces gaze distributions for upright and tilted scenes.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Reeves, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Distortion of perceived visual space after prolonged horizontal eccentric gaze holding
papers.abstract: Holding the eyes at extreme horizontal angles produces rebound nystagmus, an index of oculomotor adaptation. Using a landmark (line-bisection) task, the authors show that perceived spatial bias afterwards differs between far-left and far-right gaze holding, with a marginal change in relative-distance sensitivity. The work links oculomotor adaptation to visual space perception.
papers.authors: Terence L. Tyson, Dennis F. Perez, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Behavioral and Modeling Evidence that Eye Movements Bias Self-motion Perception
papers.abstract: The authors test how gaze position and velocity affect judgments of heading from optic flow. Heading estimates shift toward the direction of eye motion and grow with horizontal eccentricity and speed. A Bayesian ideal observer with eccentricity-dependent motion noise, underestimated eye-rotation speed and a prior toward straight ahead accounts for these errors.
papers.authors: Matt D. Anderson, Emily A. Cooper, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Illusory tilt does not induce optostatic torsion
papers.abstract: Viewing tilted images produces a small ocular torsion (optostatic torsion) in the direction of the tilt. The authors asked whether an illusory tilt (a Cafe Wall-based room) is enough to trigger it. Although observers perceived roughly 3.7 degrees of illusory tilt, three-dimensional eye recordings showed no torsion, suggesting the response follows physical image content rather than perceived tilt.
papers.authors: Mihret Girum, Ariel Winnick, Jorge Otero-Millan

papers.title: Open Iris - An Open Source Framework for Video-Based Eye-Tracking Research and Development
papers.abstract: Open Iris is an open-source software framework for video-based eye tracking with a modular design for research and development. It supports pupil and gaze tracking, integrates with common cameras, and allows customization of algorithms and hardware. The goal is an accessible, extensible alternative to costly closed commercial trackers.
papers.venue: ACM Symposium on Eye Tracking Research and Applications (ETRA)
papers.authors: Roksana Sadeghi, Ryan Ressmeyer, Jacob Yates, Jorge Otero-Millan

0336.name: Joseph DeGutis
0336.department: Department of Psychiatry, Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine (also VA Boston Healthcare System)
0336.lab_name: Boston Attention and Learning Laboratory (BAL Lab)
0336.bio: Joseph DeGutis is a cognitive neuroscientist whose research focuses on the mechanisms and rehabilitation of attention and face perception. As the co-director of the Boston Attention and Learning Laboratory, DeGutis utilizes behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation to characterize cognitive deficits and develop targeted interventions. Their work includes developing computer-based training paradigms for sustained attention and exploring the neural basis of developmental prosopagnosia. DeGutis’s current research aims to improve cognitive outcomes for individuals with traumatic brain injury, PTSD, and age-related neurodegeneration.
0336.research_direction: Dr. DeGutis has recently been investigating the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying developmental prosopagnosia, alongside broader topics in sustained attention and clinical neuropsychology. Their recent work explores the prevalence and diagnostic standards of face-recognition impairments using large-scale behavioral testing, as well as employing fMRI to probe how functional connectivity and region-specific activation in the cortical face network map onto heterogeneous perceptual deficits. Beyond high-level vision, they are developing novel continuous performance tasks to study how emotional distractors disrupt sustained attention and impact subsequent memory encoding. Additionally, their recent clinical research examines how specific psychiatric symptoms, such as anxiety and PTSD, influence negative metacognitive biases regarding cognitive performance in veteran populations.

papers.title: Perceptual heterogeneity in developmental prosopagnosia: The role of the right OFA
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in 34 individuals with developmental prosopagnosia, the study asks why perceptual deficits differ so much across people. Face selectivity in the right occipital face area and fusiform face area tracked face-matching performance, and the right OFA effect was specific to perceiving the eye region rather than the mouth. This ties a specific cortical node to a behavioral subtype of face-recognition impairment and supports the OFA's role in extracting eye information.
papers.authors: Alison Campbell, Michael Esterman, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Anxiety/stress symptoms uniquely predict greater negative global metacognitive bias in post-9/11 veterans
papers.abstract: In 601 post-9/11 veterans, the study separates the contributions of depression, anxiety/stress and PTSD symptoms to metacognitive bias, meaning the tendency to underestimate one's own cognitive abilities relative to objective testing. Anxiety/stress explained the most unique variance, depression a little, and PTSD none, and in a subsample retested two years later, changes in anxiety/stress and PTSD predicted changes in bias. The results suggest that anxiety/stress is a key driver of negative self-appraisal of cognition.
papers.venue: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society
papers.authors: Joseph DeGutis, Ethan Ng, Osaruese Megwa, Sam Agnoli, Catherine B. Fortier, William Milberg, Michael Esterman

papers.title: Left hemisphere abnormalities in face-selective activation and functional connectivity in developmental prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: An extensive fMRI comparison of 34 developmental prosopagnosics and 23 controls examined activation and connectivity in ventral and lateral face-selective regions and their links to the rest of cortex. Prosopagnosics showed reduced left FFA and left OFA activation to faces and weaker connectivity within the face network, especially between the right anterior STS and left FFA, with no broader connectivity deficits beyond the face network. The findings point to the left FFA as a key locus of face-recognition deficits.
papers.authors: Alison Campbell, Xian Li, David Rothlein, Michael Esterman, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: Characterizing the effects of emotional distraction on sustained attention and subsequent memory: A novel emotional gradual onset continuous performance task
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the emogradCPT, a sustained-attention task in which emotional background images serve as distractors while participants judge digits. Across two experiments, negative distractors reliably reduced accuracy and slowed responses relative to neutral, positive or no distractors, and the effects related to subjective distraction ratings and to later memory encoding and affect. The task offers a validated tool for studying external emotional disruption of attention.
papers.authors: Michael Esterman, Sam Agnoli, Travis C. Evans, Audreyana Jagger-Rickels, David Rothlein, Courtney Guida, Carrie Hughes, Joseph DeGutis

papers.title: What is the prevalence of developmental prosopagnosia? An empirical assessment of different diagnostic cutoffs
papers.abstract: Developmental prosopagnosia is usually said to affect 2-2.5% of people, but studies have used very different diagnostic cutoffs. Testing over 3,000 web-recruited adults on objective and subjective face-recognition measures, the authors show that applying cutoffs from 14 years of published studies yields prevalence estimates spanning roughly 0.1% to 5%, with the most common criteria implying under 1%. Cluster analyses found no natural grouping of poor face recognizers, and stricter criteria in 43 prior studies only weakly tracked better face-perception scores, arguing for more principled diagnostic standards.
papers.authors: Joseph DeGutis, Kajal Bahierathan, Kimberly Barahona, Eric Lee, Travis C. Evans, Hyun M. Shin, Maruti Mishra, Jirapat Likitlersuang, Jeremy B. Wilmer

0338.name: Joy Geng
0338.bio: Geng investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms that govern how humans prioritize visual information based on behavioral goals and prior experiences. Their work characterizes the balance between the selection of task-relevant targets and the suppression of irrelevant distractors, proposing models such as "good-enough" attentional guidance to explain search efficiency. Methodologically, Geng integrates functional MRI, electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and psychophysics to map the dynamics of attentional templates and their impact on perception. Their lab currently explores how these processes operate in complex environments, including 3D contexts and virtual reality.
0338.research_direction: Dr. Geng has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual search, focusing on how the visual system integrates diverse sources of information to minimize attentional uncertainty. Their recent work explores a "good-enough" framework of attentional guidance, examining how spatial attention is driven not only by strict target features, but by seemingly task-irrelevant cues like learned associations and layout-defining "anchor" objects within complex scenes. Using fMRI and multivariate decoding, they are also probing how preparatory attentional templates are instantiated in the prefrontal and sensory cortices before a search even begins. Specifically, they are studying how these brain regions encode the expected target identity alongside probabilistic feature uncertainty and context-associated objects to govern efficient goal-directed selection.

papers.title: Task-Irrelevant Information Reduces Attentional Uncertainty
papers.abstract: The review contends that information usually labeled task irrelevant, such as scene context, learned associations and co-occurring cues, actually carries signals that lower uncertainty about where or what the target is. It systematically catalogs these sources and the evidence that they shape goal-directed selection. The authors conclude that such information is necessary for efficient processing of complex environments.
papers.authors: Joy J. Geng, Sarah Shomstein, Qianqian Wan, Kelly E. McEvoy

papers.title: Anchor objects guide spatial attention during visual search
papers.abstract: The paper examines whether large, layout-defining anchor objects in a scene help observers find smaller objects. Search was faster and more direct when the target lay near its typical anchor, suggesting attention uses scene structure to narrow the search region. The work extends the lab's view that contextual information reduces search uncertainty.
papers.authors: Makayla Souza-Wiggins, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Preparatory attentional templates in prefrontal and sensory cortex encode target-associated information
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and multivariate decoding, the study asks what the brain holds in mind before a search begins. Prefrontal and sensory cortex were found to represent not only the target but also objects and context associated with it. This indicates that preparatory templates are broader than the target's own visual features.
papers.authors: Zhiheng Zhou, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Good-enough attentional guidance
papers.abstract: This review argues that attention during visual search does not aim for perfectly optimal target guidance but for guidance that is good enough given the task. It shows that the target template is flexibly adjusted, for example shifted away from similar distractors, and that search rests on multiple sources of information beyond the target's own features. The authors lay out a framework that explains why guidance is efficient yet often imperfect.
papers.authors: Xinger Yu, Zhiheng Zhou, Stefanie I. Becker, Sage E. P. Boettcher, Joy J. Geng

papers.title: Prefrontal Cortex Codes Representations of Target Identity and Feature Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Human participants performed visual search while fMRI recorded activity, and the work tested how learned uncertainty about the target's features is represented. Prefrontal cortex encoded both the identity of the expected target and the amount of feature uncertainty. The results tie attentional priority to probabilistic predictions held in frontal control regions.
papers.authors: Phillip P. Witkowski, Joy J. Geng

0340.name: Rhea T. Eskew Jr.
0340.bio: Rhea T. Eskew, Jr. is a Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University. Eskew's research focuses on characterizing color detection and discrimination through quantitative models and psychophysical testing, with an emphasis on S-cone pathways and higher-order chromatic mechanisms. Their work includes investigating asymmetries in ON and OFF pathways, the role of cones in border distinctness, and the effects of light adaptation on response dynamics. Eskew is a Fellow of the Optical Society of America and served as the inaugural Robert M. Boynton Lecturer.
0340.research_direction: Dr. Eskew has recently been studying how the human visual system represents color and brightness at the earliest stages of perception. Their recent work measures how strongly people perceive increases and decreases in light and in short-wavelength (blue-yellow) cone signals, asking whether the pathways that respond to increments and decrements behave symmetrically or differently. They also examine color illusions in which color appears to leak or spread beyond its true boundaries, such as neon color spreading and the Boynton illusion, where a bright contour pulls the perceived position of a nearby colored edge. Across these projects, they use careful psychophysical measurements to ask what limits how color is filled in and how contrast is scaled by the visual system.

papers.title: The Boynton Illusion: Chromatic edge attraction to a luminance contour
papers.abstract: The Boynton Illusion describes a phenomenon where the perceived location of a low-contrast chromatic edge is significantly biased by the presence of a nearby high-contrast luminance contour. This study employed a position judgment task to parametrically investigate this color spreading effect across S-cone, equiluminant red-green, and achromatic directions. Using a gap effect stimulus consisting of a bipartite box divided by a central contour, the researchers demonstrated a robust attraction effect of high-contrast boundaries on chromatic edges. When the chromatic test region was physically smaller than the demarcated area, the edge was perceived as being closer to the contour (filling-in); when it extended beyond the contour, the edge was similarly attracted (filling-out). Results showed that while S-cone and equiluminant red-green stimuli exhibited similar magnitudes of positional displacement, achromatic stimuli showed relatively smaller effects. These findings suggest that the visual system prioritizes suprathreshold achromatic contours to assign uniform surface attributes within demarcated regions, effectively using luminance boundaries to constrain chromatic integration.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Yesenia Taveras-Cruz, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: S cone increments and decrements: Nearly-linear perceptual scales and variable noise
papers.abstract: This research investigated the suprathreshold perceptual representation of S-cone incremental (S+) and decremental (S−) visual signals using maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS) and pedestal discrimination tasks. Contrary to previous findings in the achromatic domain which show strong asymmetries, the estimated perceptual scales for both S-cone polarities were found to be approximately linear and symmetric up to high contrast levels. However, a significant asymmetry was observed in the pedestal discrimination thresholds, which rose more steeply for S+ pedestals compared to S− pedestals, indicating stronger high-contrast masking in the S-ON pathway. To reconcile the linear perceptual scales with the non-linear discrimination thresholds, the authors proposed and validated a variable-noise MLDS model. In this model, internal noise in the S-cone pathways grows proportionally with the square root of the stimulus contrast, allowing for accurate prediction of forced-choice discrimination performance from scaling data and suggesting fundamental physiological differences in noise characteristics between S-ON and S-OFF pathways.
papers.authors: Yangyi Shi, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: Psychophysics of neon color spreading: Chromatic and temporal factors are not limiting
papers.abstract: Neon color spreading (NCS) is an illusory phenomenon used to study surface completion and color filling-in. This study utilized a parametric psychophysical approach to evaluate the efficacy of cone-isolating and equiluminant stimuli in generating NCS for both incremental and decremental polarities. Experiment 1 demonstrated that once differences in base detection thresholds are controlled, all cone types and polarities generate NCS at approximately twice the detection threshold level, indicating that chromatic resolution rather than specific cone-opponent circuitry limits the effect. Experiment 2 measured the temporal contrast sensitivity functions for NCS using L-cone flicker modulations from 0.5 to 8 Hz. The results showed that NCS sensitivity remains constant or increases with higher temporal frequencies, providing strong evidence against models of NCS based on slow, diffusive filling-in processes. Instead, the data support the existence of relatively fast, parallel mechanisms underlying illusory surface completion that operate on similar timescales to low-level flicker detection.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Ennio Mingolla, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

papers.title: Asymmetries between achromatic increments and decrements: Perceptual scales and discrimination thresholds
papers.abstract: Human perception of achromatic increments (A+) and decrements (A−) exhibits qualitative asymmetries, likely reflecting divergent processing in ON and OFF retinal channels. This study quantified these differences using maximum likelihood difference scaling (MLDS) and a fourfold 2-alternative spatial forced-choice (2SAFC) pedestal discrimination paradigm. The experiments revealed that A+ perceptual scales follow a modified Naka-Rushton transducer function, whereas A− scales are best described by a cubic function. Correspondingly, discrimination thresholds for A+ pedestals increased monotonically with contrast, while A− thresholds exhibited a non-monotonic 'dipper' function, initially increasing and then decreasing at high contrasts. The authors developed a unifying model where the pedestal discrimination threshold is inversely proportional to the derivative of the perceptual scale. This model accurately predicts the threshold-vs-contrast (TvC) functions from the scaling data, suggesting that the well-known asymmetries in brightness perception and contrast masking are manifestations of a shared underlying transduction mechanism constrained by the distinct statistics of ON and OFF visual pathways.
papers.authors: Yangyi Shi, Rhea T. Eskew, Jr.

0341.name: Juan Chen
0341.lab_name: Action Perception and Learning Lab (APL Lab)
0341.bio: Juan Chen is a Professor at the School of Psychology at South China Normal University and serves as the director of the Action Perception and Learning Lab. Chen's research investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms of human perception and hand actions, focusing on the functional differences between the processing of 3D real-world objects and 2D images. Using a multimodal approach that includes fMRI, EEG, psychophysics, and kinematics, Chen examines size constancy in the visual cortex and the implicit plasticity of the dorsal visual stream. Their current work explores how visually guided motor training affects sensory encoding in the absence of conscious perceptual awareness.
0341.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the bidirectional links between motor action and visual perception, exploring how goal-directed movements actively shape sensory processing. Their recent work uses EEG and fMRI to examine how the intent to grasp an object dynamically modulates early visual mechanisms like surround suppression, and how neural activation and motor-cortex connectivity fundamentally differ during real versus pantomimed tool use. Additionally, they are studying how visual and motor systems distinctively process degraded signals and multisensory inputs, testing if visually-guided action training under continuous flash suppression can drive implicit dorsal-stream plasticity, and whether auditory distance cues can support size constancy in reaching behaviors compared to perceptual judgments. Finally, their research emphasizes ecological validity in vision science, using psychophysics and computational modeling to uncover how viewpoint adaptation in the ventral stream differs when observers process real 3D objects rather than standard 2D images.

papers.title: Goal-Directed Action Planning Modulates Surround Suppression in the Visual System
papers.abstract: Using EEG frequency tagging, the study asks whether preparing to grasp a target amid flanking objects strengthens surround suppression, a mechanism for segregating an object from clutter. Planning a grasp amplified suppression relative to planning a simple key release, and the boost was greatest for the dominant hand and for relevant targets. A perceptual-judgment control task produced no such effect, indicating the modulation is specific to action planning rather than attention to the target in general.
papers.authors: Yichong Zhang, Jie Gao, Zhiqing Deng, Tianyu Wang, Wenxuan Wang, Yijin Wang, Chenxi Wang, Xiaoli Liu, Yuqing Wang, Jiaxin Long, J. Randall Flanagan, Jason P. Gallivan, Biao Han, Juan Chen

papers.title: Learning by doing: Effects of visually-guided action learning on highly degraded visual stimuli
papers.abstract: Adults trained to grasp low-contrast bars made nearly invisible by continuous flash suppression. Training improved contrast sensitivity and grasping even though perceived visibility did not improve, and individual gains tracked sensitivity changes rather than initial visibility. The results point to implicit, action-driven plasticity in the dorsal stream that requires sufficient sensory input but not conscious perception.
papers.authors: Jie Gao, Yijin Wang, Zhiqing Deng, Huiting Li, Ruoyu Zhang, Yichong Zhang, Xilin Zhang, Guofu Zhou, Juan Chen

papers.title: Contribution of auditory distance cues to size constancy in perception and grasping in restricted viewing
papers.abstract: Building on earlier work showing that proprioceptive distance cues restore size constancy in grip scaling under restricted vision, this study tests whether sound can do the same. Auditory distance information improved perceptual size judgments but did not affect grip scaling, unlike proprioception. Only after extensive auditory distance training did grasping improve modestly, suggesting the grasping system integrates cues differently from the perceptual system.
papers.authors: Chao Zheng, Gexiu Wang, Xiaoming Zhou, Jie Gao, Irene Sperandio, Melvyn A. Goodale, Juan Chen

papers.title: Viewpoint adaptation revealed potential representational differences between 2D images and 3D objects
papers.abstract: Vision research relies heavily on flat images, so this work checks whether image and real-object perception differ in ventral-stream processing. Viewpoint adaptation with faces and kettles produced stronger aftereffects for 3D stimuli (real objects or stereoscopic images) than for 2D images when adapting to rightward views. A computational model attributed the difference to broader viewpoint tuning for 3D stimuli.
papers.authors: Zhiqing Deng, Jie Gao, Toni Li, Yan Chen, BoYu Gao, Fang Fang, Jody C. Culham, Juan Chen

papers.title: Human Neuroimaging Reveals Differences in Activation and Connectivity between Real and Pantomimed Tool Use
papers.abstract: Participants in an fMRI scanner either used real plastic utensils to act on putty or pantomimed the same movements. Real tool use gave stronger activation in sensorimotor cortex and anterior supramarginal gyrus during execution, while pantomime engaged classic tool-selective areas more. Even in the planning phase, activation patterns and motor-cortex connectivity differed, showing that pantomime is not a valid stand-in for real tool use.
papers.authors: Juan Chen, Jamie U. Paciocco, Zhiqing Deng, Jody C. Culham

0342.name: Jude Mitchell
0342.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0342.bio: Jude F. Mitchell is an Associate Professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of selective attention and sensory processing, focusing on how internal brain states influence visual perception and oculomotor control. Mitchell utilizes the common marmoset as a model for visual neuroscience, leveraging its smooth cortical surface to employ techniques such as laminar electrophysiology and optogenetic circuit mapping. Their current work explores the physiological basis of foveal vision, trans-saccadic integration, and the roles of distinct neuronal classes in active visual behavior.
0342.research_direction: Dr. Mitchell’s recent work investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms of active vision and naturalistic visuomotor control in the common marmoset. They have recently been exploring how the visual system maintains perceptual stability across eye movements, using electrophysiology in extrastriate areas MT and MTC to ask how neural subpopulations utilize corollary discharge to discount saccade-generated retinal motion and enhance pre-saccadic target processing. To support these questions, their lab develops innovative paradigms for studying unconstrained vision, including mapping receptive fields in freely viewing animals without traditional fixation training and comprehensively characterizing eye-head coordination during natural gaze shifts. Furthermore, their recent work extends beyond the oculomotor system to visually guided reaching, utilizing high-speed tracking of live prey capture to study the neural basis of fast predictive motor planning in primates.

papers.title: Marmoset area MTC shows larger pre-saccadic neural enhancements than MT
papers.abstract: Compares how neurons in marmoset motion area MT and its neighbor MTC change their responses just before a saccade, when attention shifts to the upcoming target. The paper reports that MTC shows larger pre-saccadic enhancements than MT, giving a laminar and area-level account of how attention-linked signals build up ahead of eye movements. It extends the lab's earlier work on pre-saccadic feature enhancement in marmoset MT.
papers.authors: Amy Bucklaew, Shanna H. Coop, Jude F. Mitchell

papers.title: Neural subpopulations in marmoset area MT/MTC detect and discount saccade-related retinal motion
papers.abstract: Records from MT and MTC in freely viewing marmosets to ask how the brain suppresses the retinal motion produced by its own saccades. Using natural images, blank screens, darkness and simulated saccades, the authors find a mix of excitatory, suppressed and biphasic responses. Some narrow-spiking (putative inhibitory) cells combine visual and corollary-discharge signals to drive suppression, while broader-spiking (putative excitatory) cells respond to simulated but not real saccadic motion, and could therefore support perceptual stability across eye movements.
papers.authors: Amy Bucklaew, Shanna H. Coop, Jude F. Mitchell

papers.title: Probing the limited oculomotor range of common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus)
papers.abstract: Marmosets orient mostly with rapid head movements and have a restricted eye-movement range of roughly 10 degrees around the resting position. This study probes that limit across viewing contexts beyond empty arenas, testing how far the eyes will travel and how gaze is split between eye and head. It informs how marmoset active vision should be modeled and compared with humans and macaques.
papers.authors: Oviya Mohan, Alexia Nelms, Amy Bucklaew, Dora Biro, Jude F. Mitchell

papers.title: Detailed characterization of neural selectivity in free viewing primates
papers.abstract: Presents hardware and software tools for measuring receptive fields and tuning in untrained, freely viewing marmosets, avoiding the need for fixation training. Using full-field noise stimuli and precise eye tracking, the authors recover receptive fields and tuning curves from V1 and extrastriate area MT/MTC, and show that free viewing reveals how eye movements shape visual input. The approach provides a general route to studying natural-behavior vision with detailed neural characterization.
papers.authors: Jacob L. Yates, Shanna H. Coop, Gabriel H. Sarch, Ruei-Jr Wu, Daniel A. Butts, Michele Rucci, Jude F. Mitchell

papers.title: Fast prediction in marmoset reach-to-grasp movements for dynamic prey
papers.abstract: Uses multi-camera high-speed tracking of marmosets catching live crickets in the lab to study visually guided reaching toward moving targets. The results show that marmosets predict prey motion and adjust their reach online, revealing fast predictive control that compensates for visuomotor delays. It establishes a naturalistic reach-to-grasp paradigm for studying the neural basis of prediction in primates.
papers.authors: Luke H. Shaw, Kuan Hong Wang, Jude F. Mitchell

0344.name: Julie D. Golomb
0344.bio: Julie D. Golomb is a Professor at The Ohio State University and director of the Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab, where they investigate how the brain constructs a stable perceptual representation from dynamic visual input. Golomb’s research employs behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, EEG, and eye-tracking to explore interactions between attention, memory, and perception. Their work indicates that the visual system primarily encodes spatial location in retinotopic coordinates during high-level processing and examines how attention is remapped across eye movements. Current research focuses on the neural mechanisms of feature binding and the spatiotemporal representations of three-dimensional visual space.
0344.research_direction: Dr. Golomb's recent work explores how the human visual system maintains a stable perception of the world across eye movements and how it constructs high-level object representations. Using behavioral paradigms and naturalistic scenes, they are investigating the mechanisms of trans-saccadic perception, specifically asking how saccade target status influences the spatial reference frames of object-location binding, how memory interacts with stability priors, and whether eye movements transiently disrupt semantic scene categorization. Additionally, Dr. Golomb has recently been combining time-resolved EEG with deep artificial neural networks to disentangle the processing timelines of complex visual features, such as an object's real-world size versus its perceived depth. Their research also leverages these human neuroimaging signals as training constraints for machine-vision models, testing whether aligning artificial network representations with the human brain can improve downstream computer vision performance.

papers.title: Achieving more human brain-like vision via human EEG representational alignment
papers.abstract: The authors use human EEG recordings to fine-tune artificial vision networks so that their internal representations resemble those of the human brain. They present an alignment framework that uses neural signals as a training constraint and show that the aligned models are more brain-like and also perform better on several downstream vision tests. It links human neuroimaging with machine-vision engineering.
papers.authors: Zitong Lu, Yile Wang, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Post-saccadic disruption of semantic category information in naturalistic scenes
papers.abstract: Behavioral and neural measurements show that scene category information is briefly degraded immediately after the eyes land on a new fixation. The paper characterizes this window of post-saccadic vulnerability for scene perception, suggesting that each eye movement transiently disrupts high-level scene representations even as perception feels continuous.
papers.authors: Yong Min Choi, Tzu-Yao Chiu, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Human EEG and artificial neural networks reveal disentangled representations and processing timelines of object real-world size and depth in natural images
papers.abstract: Using time-resolved EEG responses to natural images and comparing them with deep neural network and language-model representations, the study separates the brain's coding of an object's real-world size from its retinal size and perceived depth. Real-world size information emerges after retinal size but is dissociable from depth, and the two follow different processing timelines. The work shows how ANN-brain comparisons can be used to isolate high-level object properties in the human visual system.
papers.authors: Zitong Lu, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: The influence of saccade target status on the reference frame of object-location binding
papers.abstract: Across several experiments, the paper asks whether the visual system binds an object's identity to its location in eye-centered or world-centered coordinates after a saccade. Whether the object is the saccade target changes which reference frame dominates binding, with target status favoring stable world-centered binding. The results refine accounts of how the brain keeps a stable perceptual world across eye movements.
papers.authors: Tzu-Yao Chiu, Julie D. Golomb

papers.title: Maintaining visual stability in naturalistic scenes: The roles of trans-saccadic memory and default assumptions
papers.abstract: Participants viewed naturalistic scenes and had to detect changes across saccades, testing how trans-saccadic memory and a default assumption of stability support perceptual continuity. The findings show that observers rely on both stored information and a prior that the scene has not changed, extending visual stability research from simple displays to real-world images.
papers.authors: Yong Min Choi, Tzu-Yao Chiu, Jake Ferreira, Julie D. Golomb

0345.name: Julie M. Harris
0345.bio: Julie M. Harris is a Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of St Andrews whose research investigates how the brain processes complex visual information to guide motor action. Their work utilizes psychophysical, behavioural, and computational techniques to explore binocular stereopsis, motion-in-depth, and the ecological principles of animal camouflage. Harris studies how the human visual system decodes three-dimensional signals and the application of these processes to tasks such as hazard perception in driving and visual communication in virtual environments. Previously, they held research positions at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute and the Universities of Edinburgh and Newcastle.
0345.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been exploring the intersection of visual ecology and early spatial vision, investigating how animal coloration and low-level image statistics influence both perception and memory. Their recent work employs biologically inspired computational models of early visual processing—incorporating features like scale-tuned receptive fields and color opponency—to objectively quantify the conspicuity of natural warning signals and camouflage from the perspective of specific predators. Alongside testing visual ecology hypotheses in animals, such as whether ultraviolet vision aids reindeer in spotting lichens against snow, they are also examining human memory and metacognition. Specifically, their research uses artificial textures and natural aposematic patterns to investigate whether early visual stimulation and low-level spatial structure can predict human metamemory ratings and actual image recognition.

papers.title: Natural warning signals unexpectedly shape human metamemory ratings but not image recognition success
papers.abstract: Observers viewed images of aposematic (warning-patterned) and non-aposematic butterflies and moths, rated how memorable each looked, and later did a recognition test. Warning patterns looked more memorable at first sight, yet were no better recognised on a second encounter, a metacognitive mismatch. Even so, observers agreed on which aposematic images they remembered, suggesting an intrinsic memorability. The work implies warning signals may work mainly through perception at first encounter rather than through memory.
papers.authors: Federico De Filippi, Olivier Penacchio, Akira R. O'Connor, Julie M. Harris

papers.title: Using biologically inspired visual statistics to predict texture memorability
papers.abstract: Uses a model of early vision (orientation- and scale-tuned receptive fields plus colour opponency) to pick textures that give either high or low visual stimulation. One hundred observers rated how memorable each looked and then took a recognition test. The paper tests whether low-level spatial structure alone predicts what people remember, independent of meaning.
papers.authors: Federico De Filippi, Olivier Penacchio, Akira O'Connor, Julie M Harris

papers.title: The Role of Vision Science in Understanding Animal Camouflage
papers.abstract: A review of how vision-science findings have sharpened the study of camouflage, which was long based on descriptions from the human viewpoint. It covers three areas: colour and texture, motion processing, and the perception of shape and depth. It argues that knowing how predators actually see is needed to understand how camouflage works.
papers.authors: Julie M. Harris, Olivier Penacchio, Daniel C. Osorio

papers.title: A computational neuroscience framework for quantifying warning signals
papers.abstract: Introduces a model of early visual processing, built from artificial neurons with realistic receptive fields and tailorable to a species, to estimate how strongly a pattern drives a predator's visual system. Applied to a bird viewing hyperspectral images of butterflies and moths, warning-signal species produced stronger activity than undefended species and than natural backgrounds. This gives an objective, neural-based definition of what makes a warning signal conspicuous.
papers.authors: Olivier Penacchio, Christina G. Halpin, Innes C. Cuthill, Paul George Lovell, M. Wheelwright, J. Skelhorn, C. Rowe, Julie M. Harris

papers.title: Reindeer and the quest for Scottish enlichenment
papers.abstract: Reindeer are unusual in transmitting a lot of ultraviolet light to the retina despite living in the day-active Arctic. The authors measured reflectance spectra of lichens eaten by reindeer in the Cairngorms. They test whether UV vision could help spot UV-absorbing lichens against UV-reflecting snow in winter twilight.
papers.authors: Nathaniel J. Dominy, Catherine Hobaiter, Julie M. Harris

0346.name: Jun-Yun Zhang
0346.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0346.bio: Jun-Yun Zhang is an Associate Professor at Peking University specializing in visual perception and cortical plasticity.
