Zhang developed the "double training" and "Training-Plus-Exposure" (TPE) paradigms, which demonstrate that perceptual learning can generalize across retinal locations and orientations. Using psychophysical methodologies, they investigate the mechanisms underlying visual crowding, rule-based learning, and top-down influences on sensory processing. This research also extends to clinical applications, focusing on the diagnosis and treatment of visual deficits in individuals with amblyopia.
0346.research_direction: Dr. Zhang's recent work explores the mechanisms of visual plasticity, spanning fundamental perceptual learning and clinical interventions for amblyopia. To understand how learning generalizes across the visual field and stimulus features, they have recently been using double-training paradigms and feature-roving visual search tasks to test the boundaries of specificity and transfer in both perceptual and category learning. They are also investigating the methodological limits of perceptual plasticity, such as testing whether brief memory reactivation can effectively substitute for full practice in texture discrimination tasks. In the clinical domain, their research assesses temporal visual deficits in amblyopic children using moving-slit contour integration tasks, while also comparing the therapeutic effects of monocular versus dichoptic stereopsis training on visual acuity and binocular function.

papers.title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is usually tied to the retinal location where it was trained, whereas category learning is assumed to generalize across the visual field, but recent work suggests information-integration category learning is also location-specific. Using a double-training design, the authors show that transfer of grating category learning to the opposite hemifield depends on the temporal order of training: passive exposure to an irrelevant task at the new location, simultaneous with or after category training, yields strong transfer, whereas doing the irrelevant task first abolishes it. The order-dependent pattern mirrors double-training effects in perceptual learning, pointing to shared principles of location-specific plasticity.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Xin-Yu Xie, Cong Yu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Comparative Effects of Monocular and Stereopsis Training on Visual Acuity and Stereoacuity in Children With Amblyopia
papers.abstract: Forty-three amblyopic children (about 7 to 15 years old) received roughly 29 sessions of either monocular training (grating acuity or motion discrimination in the amblyopic eye) or dichoptic stereopsis training, on top of standard optical correction and patching. Both regimens improved amblyopic-eye acuity to a similar degree, but stereopsis training produced larger stereoacuity gains. The results support adding binocular disparity training to conventional treatment to address residual binocular deficits.
papers.authors: Yanru Chen, Pin-Xian Li, Hui-Fang Zhang, Xiang-Yun Liu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Temporal Contour Integration Deficits in Children With Amblyopia
papers.abstract: Compared 19 amblyopic and 26 typically developing children on detecting contour paths made of collinear Gabor elements seen through a moving slit, varying slit width, orientation jitter and speed. Amblyopic eyes needed wider slits than fellow eyes, with deficits growing as acuity worsened and peaking for fully collinear contours and moderate speeds. The temporal deficit did not correlate with stereoacuity or with spatial contour-integration deficits, suggesting a separate temporal integration problem in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Yanru Chen, Shu-Qi Jiang, Xiang-Yun Liu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Brief memory reactivation may not improve visual perception
papers.abstract: A large-sample, better-controlled replication of a claim that five trials a day of texture-discrimination reactivation matches the benefit of full practice. The reactivation group did improve, but no more than a no-reactivation control that had no task exposure, and all groups still gained further with true full practice. Brief reactivation therefore seems not to contribute meaningfully to perceptual learning, and traditional training remains necessary.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Jun-Yun Zhang

papers.title: Feature variability determines specificity and transfer in multiorientation feature detection learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is often specific to the trained stimulus. Training observers on four roving orientation search stimuli, the authors find that a 5-degree spread yields learning without transfer to swapped target and background orientations, while a 45-degree spread learns more slowly but generalizes. A modified training-plus-exposure design, pairing narrow-range training with passive exposure to widely varying orientations, also produced generalization, specifying when multi-stimulus training generalizes.
papers.authors: Jun-Ping Zhu, Jun-Yun Zhang

0348.name: Justin Halberda
0348.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0348.bio: Justin Halberda’s research investigates the architectural links between visual perception, numerical cognition, and the development of language. Halberda characterizes the human 'approximate number system' (ANS), using psychophysical modeling to demonstrate how non-verbal magnitude estimation precision predicts symbolic mathematical performance across the lifespan. Their work employs methodologies such as change detection paradigms, multiple object tracking, and large-scale internet-based testing to probe the constraints of visual working memory and attentional selection. Additionally, Halberda explores the interface of vision and semantics by analyzing how the meanings of logical quantifiers are grounded in non-linguistic perceptual systems.
0348.research_direction: Dr. Halberda's recent work explores how the visual system and developing mind represent quantitative and logical information. They have recently been investigating the extraction of perceptual magnitudes and numerosity, testing whether number adaptation tracks objects across spatial displacements, whether continuous visual features like area or density drive numerical judgments in real-world scenes, and how observers efficiently isolate the minimum and maximum elements within visual sets. Beyond magnitude processing, their research probes decision-making under extreme visual uncertainty, using novel zero-signal paradigms to test if guessing behaviors reflect an observer's internal model of their own perceptual precision. Additionally, their recent work extends into cognitive development, investigating whether toddlers and preschoolers utilize abstract modal concepts of possibility and impossibility to guide their decisions under uncertainty.

papers.title: Guessing reveals internal models of perceptual precision
papers.abstract: When observers have too little information to respond confidently, they guess, and standard models treat guesses as uniform or shaped by environmental statistics. The authors propose instead that guesses reflect observers' knowledge of their own perceptual precision. They elicited guesses under extreme target uncertainty and with a novel zero-millisecond presentation in which no stimulus appeared, and compared competing accounts of the resulting response distributions.
papers.authors: Caroline Myers, Chaz Firestone, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Number adaptation survives spatial displacement
papers.abstract: Perceived numerosity shifts after prolonged exposure to a large or small set of items, and this adaptation has been taken as evidence that number is a primary visual feature. The authors ask whether the adapted signal is bound to a fixed retinal location or follows the objects when they move. Adaptation persisted when the adapting items were displaced in space, indicating that number adaptation is not purely retinotopic and operates on representations that track objects across displacement.
papers.authors: Caroline Myers, Chaz Firestone, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Logical Concepts of (Im)possibility Guide Young Children's Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Reasoning about what is possible or impossible is a core logical ability, but when it emerges in development is debated. The paper tests whether young children use modal concepts of possibility and impossibility to choose between options under uncertainty. Results show that toddlers and preschoolers' decisions are guided by these logical concepts.
papers.authors: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti, Sofia Jáuregui, Peter Mazalik, Shaun Nichols, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Observers Efficiently Extract the Minimal and Maximal Element in Perceptual Magnitude Sets: Evidence for a Bipartite Format
papers.abstract: The study asks how perceptual magnitudes such as length, size and number are represented. Across six experiments, observers found the smallest and largest items in a set faster and more accurately than inner values, even beyond visual short-term memory limits. This supports a bipartite format in which magnitudes are scaled to the dynamic range of the input, giving endpoints privileged access.
papers.authors: Darko Odic, Tyler Knowlton, Alexis Wellwood, Paul Pietroski, Jeffrey Lidz, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Non-numerical features fail to predict numerical performance in real-world stimuli
papers.abstract: Accounts of the approximate number system often argue that non-numerical cues such as area or density, rather than number, drive numerosity judgments. The authors test this with real-world stimuli and find that non-numerical features fail to predict performance, whereas number does. This supports number as a genuinely represented feature.
papers.authors: Emily M. Sanford, Justin Halberda

0349.name: Jutta Billino
0349.bio: Billino is an Associate Professor at Justus Liebig University Giessen investigating visual perception and sensorimotor control across the adult lifespan. They employ psychophysical methods, eye-tracking, and motion capture to examine the interaction and individual variation of sensory, motor, cognitive, and motivational mechanisms. Billino's research covers motion processing pathways, saccadic eye movement plasticity, and visuomotor adaptation in both healthy populations and clinical patients with cerebral lesions. They aim to identify mechanisms of functional aging and the factors involved in perceptual and motor preservation.
0349.research_direction: Dr. Billino has recently been investigating how perceptual and cognitive processes change across the adult lifespan, with a specific focus on how we process expectation violations. Their recent work explores how unexpected objects and events in both static real-world scenes and dynamic virtual environments influence object memory and drive gaze allocation during active locomotion. Beyond visual attention and memory, they are also studying cross-modal metacognition to determine whether confidence judgments across visual and tactile discrimination tasks rely on a shared, modality-general scale. Additionally, their recent scholarship extends into clinical education, examining the structural challenges and opportunities of integrating neuropsychological psychotherapy into doctoral and licensure-track training programs.

papers.title: In Theorie und Praxis: Wie Promotion und Gebietsweiterbildung in Neuropsychologischer Psychotherapie verbinden? – Spezifische Herausforderungen und Chancen für Promotionsvorhaben
papers.abstract: A German-language article on how doctoral research can be combined with postgraduate clinical specialization in neuropsychological psychotherapy. It lays out the specific challenges and opportunities for doctoral projects in this dual-track setting.
papers.authors: Patrizia Thoma, Mathias Klinghammer, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Violated expectations during locomotion through virtual environments: Age effects on gaze guidance
papers.abstract: Younger and older adults walked through virtual environments in which unexpected objects or events appeared, while their gaze was recorded. The study asks whether violations of scene expectations capture gaze differently across the adult lifespan during natural, active movement. It links age differences in gaze allocation to expectation-driven attentional guidance and locomotor demands.
papers.authors: Sophie Meissner, Jochen Miksch, Lena Würbach, Sascha Feder, Sabine Grimm, Wolfgang Einhäuser, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Neuropsychologische Psychotherapie im Approbationsstudium – Quo vadis?
papers.abstract: A German-language discussion of how neuropsychological psychotherapy is, and should be, embedded in the licensure-track psychotherapy degree programs. It considers the outlook for training in the field.
papers.authors: Mathias Klinghammer, Patrizia Thoma, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Cross-modal metacognition: Visual and tactile confidence share a common scale
papers.abstract: Participants performed comparable visual and tactile discrimination tasks and rated their confidence in each. The results show that confidence judgments are calibrated on a common scale across the two senses, which points to a modality-general metacognitive readout. The work extends her interest in individual differences and aging in perceptual confidence.
papers.authors: Lena Klever, Marie Christin Beyvers, Katja Fiehler, Pascal Mamassian, Jutta Billino

papers.title: Aging attenuates the memory advantage for unexpected objects in real-world scenes
papers.abstract: Younger and older adults viewed real-world scenes containing objects that were either consistent or inconsistent with the scene, then were tested on memory for those objects. Younger adults remembered the unexpected objects better, and this benefit was reduced in older adults. The result shows that aging weakens the way expectation violations enhance memory.
papers.authors: Lena Klever, Jasmin Islam, Melissa Le-Hoa Võ, Jutta Billino

0350.name: K. Suzanne Scherf
0350.bio: Scherf investigates the developmental trajectories of visual and social-cognitive processes, focusing on how the brain’s functional specificity for face processing emerges from childhood through adulthood. Their research utilizes multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including functional and structural MRI and diffusion tensor imaging, alongside eye-tracking and behavioral paradigms to study typical development and neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism. Scherf examines the impact of pubertal maturation on the reorganization of neural circuits involved in social information processing during adolescence. Additionally, they oversee the design and evaluation of digital serious games intended to serve as social interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder.
0350.research_direction: Dr. Scherf has recently been studying how people perceive faces and social signals, and how this differs across development and in autism. Their recent work explores how stable individual differences in face recognition are, how strongly adolescents show the own-race bias in recognizing faces, and how sensitive people are to subtle facial emotion expressions in relation to anxiety and depression symptoms. They have also been evaluating a game-based intervention for autistic adolescents, using eye tracking to see whether it changes how they attend to social cues such as gaze, and examining how well self-reports and parent reports of social behavior agree.

papers.title: Ask autistic adolescents too: informant discrepancies and test-retest reliability in social behavior
papers.abstract: This study evaluated informant discrepancies and the temporal stability of self-reported social functioning in autistic youth compared to parent reports. Across two randomized controlled trials comprising 81 parent-adolescent dyads (ages 10–18), participants completed the Social Skills Improvement System (SSIS) rating scales across a 2- to 3-month interval. Test-retest reliability was established within the control cohorts (N = 40) using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) based on two-way mixed-effects models and Pearson correlations. Autistic adolescents demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability for both social competence and problem behaviors without systematic reporting bias for social skills, whereas problem behaviors exhibited regression-to-the-mean patterns. Baseline analyses across all dyads demonstrated weak inter-rater concordance and significant systematic divergence: autistic youth reported significantly higher social competence and fewer problem behaviors relative to parent evaluations, with the magnitude of disagreement increasing as adolescent-reported social competence scores rose. These results challenge assumptions regarding the unreliability of autistic self-report and support incorporating youth perspectives into multidimensional clinical assessments.
papers.authors: Hunter Mattern, Glenn I. Roisman, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Perceiving motivational signaling and complexity in facial emotion expressions: the role of internalizing symptoms
papers.abstract: This investigation tested whether internalizing symptoms modulate early, non-linguistic perceptual sensitivity to facial expressions varying along distinct signaling dimensions. Emerging adults (N = 123) performed an online psychophysical just-noticeable-difference (JND) staircase paradigm using stimuli from the Complex Emotion Expression Database, measuring discrimination thresholds required to distinguish expressive faces from neutral counterparts. Stimuli systematically crossed motivational direction (approach vs. avoid), structural complexity (basic vs. complex), and affective valence (positive vs. negative), with concurrent assessment of depression and anxiety symptomatology. Observers exhibited lower perceptual thresholds (greater sensitivity) for approach-oriented relative to avoidance-oriented expressions, but sensitivity was not systematically structured by complexity or valence. Elevated depressive symptoms did not predict perceptual discrimination thresholds across any expression subcategory, reflecting intact early sensory encoding of affect. Conversely, heightened anxiety symptoms specifically predicted decreased sensitivity (elevated thresholds) to anger and fear displays, implicating targeted disruption of early visual processing for threat-related expressions.
papers.authors: Myles N. Arrington, Lark Caboy, Jordan Sigler, Sara Silber, Lorah D. Dorn, Glenn I. Roisman, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Investigating the stability of individual differences in face recognition behavior
papers.abstract: While individual variability in unfamiliar face recognition is widely characterized as a stable, highly heritable cognitive trait, prevailing frameworks rely predominantly on between-subject variance across extreme performers rather than evaluating intra-individual stability across task contexts. To examine intra-individual reliability and consistency, emerging adults were assessed on two structurally matched paradigms of unfamiliar face memory differing primarily in stimulus target gender (the male CFMT+ and the female F-CFMT+). Although aggregate sample-level performance demonstrated strong rank-order stability (r = 0.71), significant intra-individual discrepancies emerged: 16.7% of participants exhibited divergent recognition accuracy between male and female tests exceeding 1 standard deviation. Moreover, high behavioral stability was disproportionately confined to individuals at the upper and lower performance margins. Participant demographic and psychometric covariates—including observer sex, age, and self-reported social skills—failed to account for this task-dependent variance, challenging unidimensional models of face recognition competence.
papers.authors: Myles N Arrington, K Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: How is race perceived during adolescence? A meta-analysis of the own-race bias
papers.abstract: Adolescence involves major neurodevelopmental reorganizations in social perceptual circuitry, often indexed by emerging behavioral biases in facial processing. This study examined the developmental trajectory and magnitude of the own-race bias (ORB) in identity recognition across adolescence (~10 to 22 years of age) through a Bayesian random-effects meta-analytic framework. Synthesizing 38 effect sizes across 16 empirical studies comprising 1,321 adolescent participants, the analysis tested hypotheses derived from perceptual expertise and social-cognitive models, which predict an age-dependent expansion of the ORB driven by cumulative disproportionate contact with own-race exemplars. The meta-analytic summary effect revealed a small, positive ORB (Hedges' g = 0.24) that remained stable across varying prior distributions and levels of analytical uncertainty. However, effect magnitude was not reliably moderated by chronological age or participant racial categorization, demonstrating that adolescent ORB expression does not follow simple linear accretion models of perceptual exposure.
papers.authors: Junqiang Dai, Jason W. Griffin, K. Suzanne Scherf

papers.title: Social visual attention as a treatment outcome: evaluating the social games for autistic adolescents (SAGA) intervention
papers.abstract: Difficulty decoding dynamic eye-gaze shifts is a hallmark feature of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) hypothesized to stem from atypical social visual attention (SVA). In this randomized controlled trial evaluating the serious game intervention Social Games for Autistic Adolescents (SAGA) versus standard-of-care controls, high-resolution eye tracking was acquired during an ecologically naturalistic Gaze Perception task to establish whether intervention-driven improvements in gaze decoding were mediated by increases in foveation toward faces and target referents. Contrary to mechanistic predictions, autistic participants in the serious game condition did not show preferential increases in proportional dwell time or fixation counts to faces relative to control participants; both arms exhibited modest gains in face-directed looking across test intervals. Furthermore, baseline SVA metrics failed to predict behavioral gaze-decoding accuracy at pre- or post-test. These findings demonstrate that therapeutic enhancements in social gaze interpretation occur independently of quantitative shifts in macro-level ocular engagement with facial features.
papers.authors: K. Suzanne Scherf, Jason W. Griffin, Charles F. Geier, Joshua M. Smyth

0352.name: Karen B. Schloss
0352.bio: Karen B. Schloss is an Associate Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where they direct the Visual Reasoning Lab and hold affiliations with the Wisconsin Institute for Discovery. Schloss’s research investigates the cognitive and perceptual processes that enable humans to derive meaning from visual features, particularly color semantics and aesthetics. They developed the Ecological Valence Theory, which explains human color preferences as a product of affective associations with objects and environments. Currently, Schloss employs psychophysical methods and virtual reality to study information visualization design and methods for making scientific communication more accessible.
0352.research_direction: Dr. Schloss has recently been investigating the perceptual and cognitive mechanisms underlying how humans associate colors with meaning and interpret data visualizations. Their recent work explores the structure of "color semantic space," using behavioral ratings, color-space regression, and large language models to examine how people flexibly map colors to both concrete and abstract concepts. Beyond basic color semantics, they are studying the broader cognitive foundations of information visualization by investigating how observers translate visual features and spatial structures in charts or maps into conceptual understanding. Additionally, they have been developing affective colormaps, investigating how to balance the emotional connotations of a color sequence with the perceptual discriminability required for viewers to accurately extract spatial data.

papers.title: Color-concept associations reveal a new conceptual space
papers.abstract: Shows that people's judgments of how strongly colors go with concepts are not just noise on top of perception or affect, but reflect a compact, low-dimensional conceptual space of their own, which the authors call color semantic space. Across four experiments, this space can be captured by regression on color-space coordinates and is distinct from both affective and denotative semantic spaces as well as from perceptual color space. Color-semantic relations also predict judgments of word similarity even when those judgments have nothing to do with color, suggesting a previously unrecognized kind of conceptual representation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Kushin Mukherjee, Laurent Lessard, Michael Gleicher, Timothy T. Rogers, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Affective Color Scales for Colormap Data Visualizations
papers.abstract: Develops colormaps whose color sequences convey specific emotional connotations (for example happy versus sad) while still letting viewers read fine spatial detail in the data. Using behavioral ratings to characterize affective color scales, the authors show how to construct and evaluate scales that trade off affective expressiveness against perceptual discriminability. The work bridges basic color-emotion research and practical visualization design.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Halle C. Braun, Kushin Mukherjee, Seth R. Gorelik, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Large Language Models Estimate Fine-Grained Human Color-Concept Associations
papers.abstract: Tests whether a multimodal large language model (GPT-4) can reproduce human ratings of how strongly 71 colors spanning color space associate with concepts ranging from concrete to abstract. Model ratings correlated strongly with human ratings, including for abstract concepts, indicating that color-concept structure is learnable from cross-modal statistics without strong built-in priors. The paper also evaluates how well such estimates could scale up color-semantics data collection for visualization design.
papers.authors: Kushin Mukherjee, Ankit Mohapatra, Timothy T. Rogers, Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Perceptual and Cognitive Foundations of Information Visualization
papers.abstract: Reviews how observers interpret charts, maps and diagrams, organized around three stages: perceiving visual features and their relations, mapping those features to the concepts they represent, and comprehending information about the world. Argues that visualizations work best when their design aligns with the natural workings of perception and cognition. Synthesizes findings on color, spatial structure and biases in visualization interpretation.
papers.authors: Karen B. Schloss

papers.title: Color Semantics in Human Cognition
papers.abstract: Introduces the color inference framework, which explains how people link colors to concepts, including abstract ones like sleeping or driving, and how those associations are distinct from the meaning a color takes on in context. Shows that color semantics is flexible and context dependent, which is what makes color a useful channel for communication in charts, maps and diagrams.
papers.authors: Karen B. Schloss

0353.name: Karin James
0353.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0353.bio: Karin Harman James is a Professor at Indiana University Bloomington where their research examines the intersection of sensori-motor experience and cognitive development. James utilizes functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to study how self-generated motor actions, such as handwriting and object manipulation, facilitate the functional specialization of the brain's visual systems. By studying both children and adults, James investigates the neural correlates of learning in domains like literacy and object recognition. Their research focuses on how bodily interaction with the environment shapes neural representation and perception.
0353.research_direction: Dr. James has recently been investigating how active sensorimotor experiences shape cognition, learning, and visual perception across development. Their recent work explores multisensory-motor learning in object recognition, using real 3D objects to ask how active manual exploration and combined visuo-haptic cues influence subsequent visual and touch-based recognition. Additionally, they are examining the educational and neurological impacts of motor production tasks, specifically assessing how handwriting versus typing builds the visual-motor brain circuitry required for early literacy and mediates notetaking efficacy in students. Broadening this embodied approach to atypical development, Dr. James is also evaluating how underlying motor system difficulties interact with cognitive impairments and learning outcomes in individuals with ADHD.

papers.title: Enhancing haptic object recognition ability through a real multisensory learning environment
papers.abstract: Adults studied real 3D objects with different combinations of vision and touch and were later tested on recognizing them by touch alone. Having direct multisensory access to the object's shape, rather than only haptic information, improved haptic recognition accuracy, indicating vision contributes to touch-based recognition. Whether the visual structure came from watching one's own actions in the real environment or from a computer screen did not matter.
papers.authors: Hellen Kyler, Karin James

papers.title: Brain correlates of early writing development: The foundational role of production tasks in early childhood
papers.abstract: This chapter reviews neuroimaging and behavioral evidence on how young children's early writing skills develop and which brain networks support them. It argues that actually producing letters and symbols by hand, as opposed to only viewing or typing them, plays a foundational role in building the visual-motor and reading-related circuitry that supports early literacy.
papers.venue: Advances in Child Development and Behavior (Foundations of Literacy)
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Gabrielle Shimko, Harper Marshall, Karin H. James

papers.title: The Relationship Between Motor Development and ADHD: A Critical Review and Future Directions
papers.abstract: The review examines behavioral and neurological evidence that motor difficulties are common in ADHD across development yet are usually overlooked as a possible cause of its functional impairments. It argues that existing explanations are too simple and proposes that embodied theories of development better account for how the motor system, cognition and later impairment interact. The authors suggest this view could sharpen how ADHD is identified and treated.
papers.authors: Gabrielle A. Shimko, Karin H. James

papers.title: The effects of notetaking modality and symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) on learning
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether the best way to take notes depends on a student's level of ADHD symptoms. It compares handwritten, tablet and typed notetaking and relates each to later learning, with a focus on inattentive symptoms and the sensorimotor demands of writing by hand.
papers.authors: Gabrielle A. Shimko, Karin H. James

papers.title: The importance of multisensory-motor learning on subsequent visual recognition
papers.abstract: The study tests whether the known advantage of actively exploring objects for later visual recognition holds when people handle real objects that provide both visual and haptic information. Participants either manually explored novel 3D objects or watched another person interact with them, then were tested on rendered views. Actively explored objects were recognized more accurately, and which viewpoints were recognized best differed from earlier work with virtual objects.
papers.authors: Hellen Kyler, Karin James

0354.name: Karl R. Gegenfurtner
0354.bio: Karl R. Gegenfurtner is a professor of psychology whose research examines the interactions between low-level sensory processing, higher-level visual cognition, and sensorimotor control. Gegenfurtner investigates color vision and eye movements, specifically how color contributes to object recognition and how visual information is used to guide motor behavior. Their methodological approach combines psychophysics and eye tracking with computational modeling and virtual reality to study perception in naturalistic environments. Currently, their work focuses on the neural representation of complex scenes and the mechanisms of color constancy through an object-oriented lens.
0354.research_direction: Dr. Gegenfurtner has recently been investigating color vision with a strong emphasis on ecological validity, shifting the analytical focus from pixel-level cone excitations to how color facilitates object detection in natural environments. Their recent work explores the metric structure of color space and the mechanisms of color constancy by measuring hue and chroma discrimination thresholds for three-dimensional objects and testing perception in real-world illuminated scenes. To advance these behavioral measurements, they are developing high-throughput psychophysical methods, such as utilizing immersive VR rhythm games to assess color discrimination during continuous, engaging physical action. Alongside their color perception research, they are also examining sensorimotor integration, leveraging individual differences in saccade and smooth pursuit tasks to understand how specific visual sensory inputs drive and coordinate oculomotor control.

papers.title: Color discrimination in action: High-throughput measurement in immersive VR
papers.abstract: Embeds a four-alternative odd-one-out color discrimination task in a rhythm-game-style VR environment on a calibrated headset, where participants slice approaching cubes. Participants sustained about one trial per second, thresholds reproduced known hue versus chroma asymmetries, and motor engagement did not degrade precision while raising enjoyment and motivation. The approach offers a scalable way to map the metric structure of color space.
papers.authors: Giulia Agosti, Jacob Hadnett-Hunter, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: The Verriest Lecture: Color vision from pixels to objects
papers.abstract: Argues that color research has been too focused on pixel-wise cone excitations and that the main function of color is to help detect and recognize objects. Proposes that an object's color appearance is defined by the whole distribution of color coordinates across it, and reviews behavioral, neural and computational evidence for object-based color processing in natural scenes.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Importance of hue: color discrimination of three-dimensional objects and two-dimensional discs
papers.abstract: Compares color discrimination thresholds for rendered matte 3D objects with those for flat uniform discs using an odd-one-out task in four quadrants of DKL space. Hue thresholds were the same for both, while chroma thresholds were higher for objects, and chroma-to-hue ratios exceeded one everywhere, especially in bluish and orangish regions where natural object colors cluster. The result implies hue carries special weight for recognizing objects.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Laysa Hedjar, Matteo Toscani, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Individual differences link sensory processing and motor control
papers.abstract: Uses inter-individual differences across a balanced set of saccade and smooth pursuit tasks to show that oculomotor behavior correlates across tasks only when the same sensory information (e.g. moving targets) drives them. Within a task, saccade and pursuit coordination was tailored to each person's strengths, linking sensory processing tightly to motor control.
papers.authors: Alexander Goettker, Karl R. Gegenfurtner

papers.title: Color constancy in real-world settings
papers.abstract: Measures color constancy with real objects in real illuminated scenes and finds close-to-perfect constancy, far above the 15-80% typically reported in laboratory tasks with impoverished cues. The result reconciles the long debate over how good constancy is with the stable color appearance and consistent color naming of everyday life.
papers.authors: Karl R. Gegenfurtner, David Weiss, Marina Bloj

0355.name: Kartik K Sreenivasan
0355.bio: Kartik K. Sreenivasan is an Associate Professor of Psychology at NYU Abu Dhabi who researches the neurobiological mechanisms supporting working memory and goal-directed behavior. Using a multimodal approach integrating fMRI, MEG/EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation, Sreenivasan examines the distributed and dynamic nature of mnemonic representations across the prefrontal and visual cortices. Their work investigates how the brain maintains information in the presence of interference and how parallel memory systems contribute to behavioral responses. Additionally, Sreenivasan explores the intersection of working memory with perception and cognitive control to understand the constraints and flexibility of human mental representation.
0355.research_direction: Dr. Sreenivasan has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms and representational formats underlying visual working memory. Their recent work explores how the brain maintains multiple features and sequential items, using MEG and fMRI to test whether these complex memories are supported by alpha-band phase synchrony or organized into distinct low-dimensional neural subspaces. They are also examining the informational architecture of these memories, asking whether cortical regions encode remembered stimuli as rich probabilistic distributions that capture uncertainty rather than as single point estimates. Furthermore, Dr. Sreenivasan’s research probes the broader distributed networks that support these mnemonic processes, utilizing dynamic causal modeling to map feedback and feedforward interactions across frontoparietal and visual cortices while also investigating subcortical contributions to working memory storage in the lateral geniculate nucleus.

papers.title: Alpha phase coding supports feature binding during working memory maintenance
papers.abstract: Using MEG while people held multiple features in memory, the authors tested whether binding of features to the right object relies on phase synchrony. Trials with swap (binding) errors showed weaker phase-locked oscillatory activity during the delay, as an attractor network model predicts. The weakening came from greater variability in alpha-band phase coding across a distributed sensorimotor network, implying binding emerges from competition between memories.
papers.authors: Mattia F. Pagnotta, Aniol Santo-Angles, Ainsley Temudo, Joao Barbosa, Albert Compte, Mark D'Esposito, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Probabilistic working memory representations in human cortex guide behavior
papers.abstract: Working memory models disagree on whether a memory is a single point estimate or a full probability distribution carrying uncertainty. The authors built per-trial memory distributions from participants' iterative motion-direction reports and found their idiosyncratic shape, such as asymmetry, matched distributions decoded from fMRI in occipital and parietal cortex. The neural distribution's width and asymmetry predicted behavior, supporting information-rich memory representations.
papers.authors: Ying Zhou, Clayton E. Curtis, Daryl Fougnie, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Neural Subspaces Encode Sequential Working Memory, but Neural Sequences Do Not
papers.abstract: The study compares two accounts of how multiple sequential items are held in working memory: reactivation of neural sequences versus organization into distinct low-dimensional subspaces. Using broadband MEG with dimensionality reduction and decoding, the authors found behaviorally relevant subspaces during retention but no evidence of sequential replay in the delay. Sequential memory thus appears to rely on geometric organization of representational space.
papers.authors: Aniol Santo-Angles, Jiarui Yang, Ying Zhou, Wing Kwan Hannah Chu, Grace W. Lindsay, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Effective connectivity of working memory performance: a DCM study of MEG data
papers.abstract: MEG recorded during a multi-item delayed-estimation task was analyzed with dynamic causal modeling to ask whether WM maintenance relies on feedforward or feedback interactions. Behavioral modeling separated high-accuracy, low-accuracy and swap trials, and each showed different disruptions in frontoparietal and frontooccipital connectivity. Results support a distributed model in which visual regions store memory content.
papers.authors: Aniol Santo-Angles, Ainsley Temudo, Vahan Babushkin, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

papers.title: Mnemonic representations in human lateral geniculate nucleus
papers.abstract: Using model-based fMRI, the authors mapped the topography of human LGN and used those maps to reconstruct spatial locations held in working memory during memory-guided saccade tasks. LGN activity encoded the remembered locations, dissociated from retinal stimulation and saccade metrics. This adds the thalamic visual relay to the regions carrying WM content.
papers.authors: Masih Rahmati, Clayton E. Curtis, Kartik K. Sreenivasan

0356.name: Katharina Dobs
0356.bio: Dobs is a Professor of Applied Computer Science at Justus Liebig University Giessen and directs the Visual Cognitive Computational Neuroscience (VCCN) Lab. Their research integrates deep learning architectures with human behavioral and neuroimaging data to investigate the computational principles underlying visual recognition and the functional organization of the cortex. Dobs has conducted studies demonstrating that brain-like functional specialization, such as face-selective regions, emerges in artificial neural networks optimized for specific visual tasks. Their current research, supported by an ERC Starting Grant and a LOEWE Start Professorship, focuses on developing models to explain the organization of the human visual system into specialized domains.
0356.research_direction: Dr. Dobs studies functional specialization in the brain and in deep neural networks (DNNs), asking why the human visual system is organized into specialized domains such as faces and bodies and how face-specific phenomena arise, by combining task-optimized DNNs with fMRI, EEG, and MEG. Recent work shows that networks optimized for visual recognition develop face- and body-selective units alongside mixed-selective units that best explain activity across cortex, suggesting that face and body processing is increasingly integrated along the visual hierarchy, and that category-selective areas such as FFA, EBA, and PPA are tuned to multiple interpretable feature dimensions that link categorical and dimensional accounts of high-level visual cortex. The lab also uses DNNs to explain face-specific phenomena, showing that face pareidolia emerges in networks optimized for both face and object recognition and that the Other-Race Effect arises from homogeneous visual experience and is mitigated by diverse training. Complementing this modeling, EEG work maps how prior scene context speeds the neural dynamics of face detection.

papers.title: Multidimensional feature tuning in category-selective areas of human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Asks whether the categorical view of high-level visual cortex (face, body and scene areas) and the dimensional view (continuous feature maps) describe the same organization. A data-driven decomposition of fMRI responses finds shared, spatially overlapping activity patterns in which each category-selective area encodes several interpretable dimensions, even in its most selective voxels. These dimensions cluster within the areas yet extend as distributed maps across cortex, reconciling the two accounts.
papers.authors: Leonard E. van Dyck, Martin N. Hebart, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Faces and bodies are increasingly integrated along the visual hierarchy in humans and deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Tests whether deep networks trained for visual recognition segregate or integrate face and body processing, and compares them with fMRI during natural image viewing. Models contain face-selective, body-selective and mixed-selective units; the mixed units best explain activity across cortical regions, and the variance shared between face and body signals grows from posterior to anterior cortex. This suggests specialized yet integrated person perception in both brains and models.
papers.authors: Leonard E. van Dyck, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Human-like face pareidolia emerges in deep neural networks optimized for face and object recognition
papers.abstract: Investigates why people see faces in inanimate objects (pareidolia). CNNs trained on combinations of face and object tasks were compared with human behavior and MEG responses. Networks whose training included object categorization matched neural responses to pareidolia faces best, and only networks trained on both face and object recognition produced human-like pareidolia effects.
papers.authors: Pranjul Gupta, Katharina Dobs

papers.title: Behavioral signatures of face perception emerge in deep neural networks optimized for face recognition
papers.abstract: Human face recognition shows characteristic signatures such as a particular representational space, a large inversion cost and an other-race effect, often taken as evidence that faces are special. The authors show that CNNs trained on face identification, but not object-trained networks, reproduce these behavioral signatures. This supports the view that the signatures arise from optimization for face recognition and from the visual experience the system receives.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Katharina Dobs, Joanne Yuan, Julio Martinez, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Using artificial neural networks to ask 'why' questions of minds and brains
papers.abstract: A perspective arguing that task-optimized neural networks let researchers test why the mind and brain have the properties they do, by asking which tasks and experiences produce a given representation or specialization. It reviews cases in vision, audition and language and outlines how such why-question modeling can complement conventional how-and-what neuroscience.
papers.authors: Nancy Kanwisher, Meenakshi Khosla, Katharina Dobs

0357.name: Kathryn Bonnen
0357.bio: Assistant Professor Kathryn Bonnen investigates the neural computations and sensorimotor mechanisms supporting vision-guided behavior in naturalistic environments. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, wearable eye tracking, and body motion capture, Bonnen characterizes how the brain integrates binocular and monocular cues for tasks such as 3D motion tracking and complex locomotion. Their work examines the relationship between natural scene statistics and the development of visual processing, employing computational models to link environmental properties with neural representations and behavioral outcomes.
0357.research_direction: Dr. Bonnen has recently been studying how the visual system develops and operates in natural, everyday conditions. Their recent work uses head-mounted cameras worn by infants to see what babies actually look at and how they move their heads, including whether the horizontal and vertical bias of real-world scenes is already present in early visual input. They also work on continuous psychophysics, a method in which people track a moving target over time instead of giving many separate button-press answers. In addition, they have written about how animals such as zebrafish sample motion cues across the visual field during self-motion.

papers.title: Moving through everyday life: distinct developmental timescales for head-rotation magnitude and rotation efficiency in infancy
papers.abstract: While laboratory paradigms have documented the role of head kinematics in visual orienting and gaze stabilization during infant development, little is known about how head motor control evolves within unconstrained domestic settings. This study evaluated 383 hours of egocentric video recordings captured via head-mounted cameras from 88 infants ranging from 3 weeks to 29 months of age. Using a visual-odometry algorithm, the authors quantified rotational magnitude (comprising net and total head rotation across short temporal windows) and rotational efficiency (the directional coherence of head movement). Head-rotation magnitude exhibited substantial increases across the first year of life, reflecting expanding muscular strength and postural maturation. In contrast, rotational efficiency showed prolonged developmental gains persisting through 29 months. These divergent timescales indicate that the development of infant head control involves a progressive kinematic reorganization toward directional directness rather than a simple scaling of head movement amplitude.
papers.authors: Zachary J. Petroff, Rajat Kapgate, T. Rowan Candy, Linda B. Smith, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: The world through infant eyes: Evidence for the early emergence of the cardinal orientation bias
papers.abstract: Natural and built environments contain a pronounced anisotropic distribution of orientation energy, characterized by an overrepresentation of cardinal (horizontal and vertical) contours relative to oblique orientations aligned with the direction of gravity. In adults, this environmental structure is associated with enhanced perceptual sensitivity for cardinal orientations (the oblique effect). To test whether cardinal dominance characterizes human visual input prior to the establishment of mature postural control and gravitational alignment, the authors analyzed head-camera video recordings from 75 infants aged 1 to 12 months across two distinct environments (Indiana, USA and Tamil Nadu, India). Orientation energy was computed across multiple spatial frequency bands, including 0.5 cycles per degree. Even at 3 weeks of age, infants experienced a marked prevalence of cardinal contours, yielding an overall median cardinal-to-oblique ratio of 1.90 (bootstrapped 95% CI: 1.81 to 2.03) that remained stable across development and geographical setting. These results confirm that an anisotropic visual diet is present well before infants can reliably align their bodies with gravity, providing the sensory substrate necessary for experience-dependent tuning of visual cortical pathways.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Zachary J. Petroff, Swapnaa Jayaraman, Linda B. Smith, T. Rowan Candy, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: Continuous psychophysics: past, present, future
papers.abstract: Continuous target-tracking psychophysics has emerged as an innovative experimental paradigm that complements classical forced-choice psychophysical methodologies. Rather than gathering isolated, discrete responses over numerous repeated trials, continuous psychophysics requires participants to continually track dynamically changing stimulus properties (such as position in 2D or 3D space) using manual effectors or eye movements. Analyzing response trajectories with cross-correlation functions and Bayesian observer frameworks (e.g., Kalman filter modeling and optimal feedback control) permits simultaneous estimation of sensory noise, processing latency, and motor execution dynamics in a fraction of the testing time required by standard forced-choice protocols. The review synthesizes theoretical principles and practical applications of continuous psychophysics across spatial contrast sensitivity, motion-in-depth perception, and multisensory integration, while discussing its utility for non-traditional subject cohorts such as infants, pediatric patients, and individuals with visual impairments.
papers.authors: Johannes Burge, Kathryn Bonnen

papers.title: Motion vision: Fish swimming to see
papers.abstract: Self-motion generates dynamic optic flow fields across the visual epithelium, providing sensory information critical for navigation, speed regulation, and postural equilibrium across species. However, neural systems frequently sample optic flow with substantial spatial non-uniformities; for example, the optomotor response of larval zebrafish (Danio rerio) demonstrates prominent visual field anisotropies, preferentially relying on downward and lateral motion vectors. This commentary reviews computational modeling and behavioral experiments showing how spatial biases in optic flow sampling reflect an optimal adaptation to the physical geometry of natural habitats and the animal's locomotor state. By prioritizing visual field regions situated closest to stable environmental structures (such as riverbeds), animals maximize the signal-to-noise ratio of self-motion estimates while minimizing velocity ambiguities arising from compound translational and rotational movements.
papers.authors: Kathryn Bonnen

0358.name: Katja Fiehler
0358.bio: Katja Fiehler’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying the integration of perception and action, focusing on how sensory information facilitates goal-directed eye and hand movements. Their work explores the reference frames used for spatial coding, the role of predictive mechanisms such as efference copies in shaping sensory perception, and the interaction between sensorimotor processes, attention, and working memory. Utilizing a multimodal approach, Fiehler combines psychophysical experiments in virtual and real-world environments with kinematic motion tracking, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG). Current research directions include examining the adaptive nature of the human brain in complex environments and the mechanisms of tactile suppression during movement execution.
0358.research_direction: Dr. Fiehler has recently been investigating the sensory and cognitive mechanisms underlying action control, spanning from tactile perception to spatial memory. One major strand of their recent work explores tactile suppression during goal-directed limb movements, using EEG and behavioral paradigms to disentangle central predictive signals from peripheral sensory gating. In a distinct line of research, they are investigating memory-guided actions in naturalistic virtual reality environments to understand how scene semantics, structural grammar, and spatial proximity jointly shape allocentric spatial representations. Furthermore, their work examines visually guided locomotion in these virtual spaces, asking under what conditions humans predictively exploit probabilistic environmental regularities to navigate paths and avoid obstacles.

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of early somatosensory processing in goal-directed actions
papers.abstract: Using EEG during reaching movements with brief vibrations applied to the moving finger, the study tracks how tactile sensitivity changes across movement phases. Touch is suppressed during reaching but recovers near peak speed, and the early P45 somatosensory potential from primary somatosensory cortex follows the same pattern. Smaller P45 amplitudes went with stronger behavioural suppression, linking early cortical activity to perceptual change.
papers.authors: Elena Fuehrer, Dimitris Voudouris, Lisa K. Maurer, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Spatial proximity and scene grammar: Shaping spatial representations for memory-guided actions in naturalistic environments
papers.abstract: In a memory-guided VR task, participants placed remembered objects after landmark objects were imperceptibly shifted. The study crosses landmark proximity with semantic congruence between local objects and large anchor objects, testing how spatial and cognitive factors combine in allocentric coding. It shows that scene structure and object semantics jointly shape how spatial memory is anchored during actions in realistic scenes.
papers.authors: Bianca R. Baltaretu, Melissa L.-H. Võ, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Predictive use of environmental regularities requires action relevance
papers.abstract: Participants walked through a virtual museum corridor toward one of two exits while an obstacle appeared on a probabilistically predictable side. Many delayed their path choice until the obstacle was visible, but when a larger static obstacle made late correction costly, nearly everyone anticipated the correct route. The results suggest that learned regularities are exploited predictively only when the action makes them relevant.
papers.authors: Benedikt Kretzmeyer, Constantin A. Rothkopf, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Distinct role of central predictive mechanisms in tactile suppression
papers.abstract: Touch feels weaker on a moving limb, and the paper asks whether this suppression comes from central predictions about the movement's sensory consequences or from peripheral factors. Comparing self-generated and externally generated movements and touches, the authors show that predictive signals contribute a distinct component of suppression that cannot be reduced to movement-related sensory gating. The work helps separate prediction-based and generic mechanisms of sensory attenuation.
papers.authors: Belkis Ezgi Arikan, Dimitris Voudouris, Benjamin Straube, Katja Fiehler

papers.title: Scene semantics affects allocentric spatial coding for action in naturalistic (virtual) environments
papers.abstract: In a VR study participants viewed kitchen or bathroom scenes with large anchors and small local objects, then placed a remembered object after one anchor was shifted. Placement errors and eye-tracking showed that semantically related anchors influenced where objects were remembered, beyond simple proximity. This extends allocentric coding accounts to hierarchical scene structure.
papers.authors: Bianca R. Baltaretu, Immo Schuetz, Melissa L.-H. Võ, Katja Fiehler

0359.name: Katsumi Watanabe
0359.department: School of Fundamental Science and Engineering
0359.bio: Katsumi Watanabe is a Professor at Waseda University who investigates the mechanisms of human perception, cognition, and action. Their research utilizes psychophysics, functional brain imaging, and eye-tracking to examine interactions between explicit and implicit mental processes. Watanabe conducts research in crossmodal perception, social cognition, and the neural basis of decision-making. Their current work focuses on applying cognitive science principles to human-robot interaction and analyzing the psychological and behavioral effects of artificial intelligence and digital media.
0359.research_direction: Dr. Watanabe's recent work explores a broad spectrum of mechanisms spanning visual perception, sensorimotor decision-making, and multisensory cognition. In the visual domain, they have recently been investigating how observers process biological motion by detecting kinematic mismatches in speed-altered point-light walkers, alongside examining how numerosity and spatial perception interact within Ebbinghaus size illusions. Their research also probes motor control and social behavior, testing the subjective and objective sources of risk-seeking biases during sensorimotor tasks and mapping the developmental trajectory of automatic movement imitation across childhood. Additionally, they are examining higher-level cognitive learning, employing cross-cultural paradigms to determine how sound-shape iconicity and autistic traits influence the acquisition of novel words.

papers.title: Dissociation of the sources of the risk-seeking bias in sensorimotor decision-making based on the subjective-objective relationship in risk attitudes.
papers.abstract: Motor 'chicken game' tasks reliably produce risk-seeking relative to the Bayesian optimal aim point. Participants performed the task under instructions to be risk-seeking, neutral or averse, or freely, and their subjective risk reports were compared with model-derived objective risk attitudes. Free-choice bias reflected an explicit preference for risk, while individual differences were tied to subjective reports and deviation from optimality under risk-neutral instruction.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Ryoji Onagawa, Kazutoshi Kudo, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Detecting unnaturalness in biological motion with altered playback speeds
papers.abstract: Observers are known to tolerate large speed changes in natural videos, so the authors asked how sensitive vision is to kinematic mismatches in human action. Point-light walkers were recorded at several speeds and then replayed faster or slower so that translation speed stayed matched while gait kinematics did not. Observers could detect the unnatural motion above chance, but reliably only when the display was upright and spatially intact, pointing to configural biological-motion processing.
papers.authors: Kan Misumi, Hiroshi Ueda, Yuichiro Nishiura, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Ebbinghaus illusion changes numerosity perception independent of density perception
papers.abstract: The study tests whether number and space share visual mechanisms by using the Ebbinghaus size-illusion configuration. After equating perceived density across dot arrays, dots surrounded by small inducers looked more numerous and more spatially extended than those surrounded by large inducers. This suggests numerosity processing interacts with size perception separately from density processing.
papers.authors: Saki Takao, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: The influence of iconicity and autistic traits on novel word learning: a cross-cultural investigation
papers.abstract: An online experiment with about 1,500 adults from Brazil, India, Japan and the USA tested whether sound-shape iconic (bouba-kiki style) names help people learn novel word-image pairings. Participants learned either iconic or arbitrary names and were then tested on recognition. The work relates the iconicity benefit to autistic traits and compares it across cultures.
papers.authors: Vijayachandra Ramachandra, Kairi Sugimoto, Kelly Ziskind, Ark Verma, Irfan Ahmad, Mahayana Godoy, Katsumi Watanabe

papers.title: Automatic imitation in children: Age-related change and comparison to adults.
papers.abstract: Automatic imitation, where observing another person's movement biases one's own, was measured in children aged 5 to 12 and in adults using a stimulus-response conflict task. Reaction time, accuracy and inverse efficiency scores showed that imitation tendency was weak up to about age 7. Across childhood the tendency changed nonlinearly, following an inverted U-shape.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Kae Mukai, Ryoji Onagawa, Katsumi Watanabe

0361.name: Keisuke Fukuda
0361.department: Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences, University of Toronto Mississauga
0361.bio: Keisuke Fukuda investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human information processing, focusing on the interplay between selective attention, visual working memory, and long-term memory. Fukuda integrates electrophysiological recordings, such as EEG and ERP, with behavioral experiments and computational modeling to analyze the temporal dynamics of neural networks. Their research examines the basis of individual differences in memory capacity and explores how metacognitive accuracy and memory distortions affect information retention and retrieval. By combining an individual-differences approach with neuroscientific techniques, Fukuda studies the biological constraints of the mind and investigates methods to optimize cognitive performance.
0361.research_direction: Dr. Fukuda has recently been investigating the dynamic nature of visual memory, exploring how our mental representations are shaped by both top-down goals and bottom-up perceptual inputs. Their recent work uses behavioral paradigms and EEG decoding to examine how items in visual working memory are dynamically reconfigured by task demands, how internal prioritization alters an item's vulnerability to perceptual interference, and whether individuals can accurately monitor moment-to-moment fluctuations in their own memory performance. Additionally, they are exploring the mechanisms of memory distortion, testing whether the mere act of predicting an upcoming visual stimulus is sufficient to generate robust false memories. Finally, their research employs deep neural networks to probe the computational basis of stimulus-intrinsic image memorability, seeking to isolate the underlying visual features that make an image memorable beyond what human observers can explicitly report.

papers.title: Task goals dynamically reconfigure neural working memory representations
papers.abstract: Using EEG while participants held shapes in memory under two different task rules (exact match versus category match), the authors decode the remembered shape across the delay. Neural patterns first generalize across tasks and later reconfigure to reflect task-specific and category information. The results show that working memory representations are dynamically shaped by current goals.
papers.authors: Frida A.B. Printzlau, Olya Bulatova, Michael L Mack, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Working memory prioritization changes bidirectional interactions with visual inputs
papers.abstract: The authors ask how prioritizing one item in working memory alters the way that item and incoming visual input affect each other. They show that a prioritized memory item is pulled toward and pushes on similar perceptual stimuli differently than an unprioritized one, so influence runs in both directions between memory and perception. The results argue that attention within working memory changes how vulnerable a stored item is to interference from new input.
papers.authors: Joseph M. Saito, Frida A. B. Printzlau, Yvanna Yeo, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Prediction-based false memory: Unconfirmed prediction can result in robust false memories
papers.abstract: This work tests whether merely predicting what will appear can leave a false memory even when the prediction is never confirmed. Participants who made predictions about upcoming items later misremembered the predicted item as having been seen, and this persisted across conditions where the prediction was not confirmed. The findings indicate that prediction itself, not just exposure, can generate robust false memories.
papers.authors: Olya Bulatova, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Prospective and retrospective awareness of moment-to-moment fluctuations in visual working memory performance
papers.abstract: The paper examines whether people notice, in real time and afterward, when their visual working memory performance dips. Participants show both forward-looking and backward-looking awareness of these lapses. The work speaks to metacognition of working memory, an area central to the lab's individual-differences program.
papers.authors: Olga Kozlova, Kirsten C. S. Adam, Keisuke Fukuda

papers.title: Deep neural network decodes aspects of stimulus-intrinsic memorability inaccessible to humans
papers.abstract: The study compares human behavior with a deep neural network trained to predict image memorability. The network captures aspects of intrinsic memorability that human observers cannot access, meaning that some of what makes images memorable is not reflected in what people themselves can report or predict. This links memorability research to modern computational models.
papers.authors: Chong Zhao, Joie Kim, Tzu Hsuan Tang, Joseph M. Saito, Keisuke Fukuda

0362.name: Keith A. Schneider
0362.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0362.bio: Keith A. Schneider is a Professor and the Director of the Center for Biomedical and Brain Imaging at the University of Delaware. Schneider investigates the functional architecture of the human visual system, with a technical focus on subcortical structures such as the lateral geniculate nucleus, pulvinar, and superior colliculus. Utilizing high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and visual psychophysics, they examine how neural mechanisms of attention, perception, and awareness are implemented. Their current work explores temporal processing dynamics and the magnocellular hypothesis in clinical populations, investigating how subcortical abnormalities contribute to disorders like dyslexia.
0362.research_direction: Dr. Schneider has recently been working on how the visual system and the observer's own confidence support perceptual decisions. Their recent work develops a mathematical model that treats an observer's uncertainty about a decision using information theory, in the way signal detection theory describes accuracy. They have also been studying how the early visual pathway in the thalamus responds during binocular rivalry, when the two eyes see conflicting images and perception flips back and forth. This work uses high-resolution fMRI to ask how the fast and slow visual channels contribute to that competition.

papers.title: An entropy model of decision uncertainty
papers.abstract: Characterizing metacognitive uncertainty provides critical insights into the computational architecture governing perceptual decisions, yet decision uncertainty has lacked an analytical functional parameterization comparable to signal detection theory models of choice accuracy. In this work, an information-theoretic framework is formulated wherein an observer's subjective uncertainty is modeled as the joint entropy incorporating both the entropy of the external sensory stimuli and the entropy of categorical response probabilities across the psychometric function. Establishing this functional form permits the recovery of latent internal decision parameters that cannot be deduced from choice distributions alone. Applying the model to visual psychophysical tasks demonstrates that spatial attentional cues alter decision uncertainty profiles distinctively compared to explicit instructional response biases, despite producing identical shifts in the point of subjective equality. These findings reveal that while different decisional mechanisms can yield divergent uncertainty distributions across perceptual tasks, they can nonetheless operate over shared underlying representational parameters.
papers.authors: Keith A. Schneider

papers.title: Neural Dynamics during Binocular Rivalry: Indications from Human Lateral Geniculate Nucleus
papers.abstract: During binocular rivalry, perception alternates between incompatible monocular inputs presented dichoptically, providing a model for visual awareness; however, the relative functional contributions of the magnocellular (M) and parvocellular (P) pathways in early subcortical visual structures remain unresolved. High-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3T was employed to record blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses within the laminar subdivisions of the human lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) during spontaneous rivalry and a physically alternated replay control condition using achromatic stimuli to prevent chromatic opponent confounds. Although standard general linear model (GLM) parameter estimation showed elevated eye-specific modulation in M compared to P subdivisions during rivalry, an equivalent modulation occurred during the replay condition. Contrasting rivalry against replay by subtracting replay beta weights isolated rivalry-specific dynamics predominantly within the P subdivisions, whereas M subdivision modulation did not significantly exceed physical alternation. These results indicate that perceptual alternations during binocular rivalry are primarily governed by interocular competition localized within the parvocellular pathway of the human LGN.
papers.authors: Irem Yildirim, Keith A. Schneider

0363.name: Kelly Bijanki
0363.bio: Kelly Bijanki is an Associate Professor at Baylor College of Medicine and director of the Translational Neuromodulation Lab. Bijanki’s research utilizes invasive intracranial electrophysiology, including stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) and direct brain stimulation, to investigate the neural mechanisms of human affect and social cognition. They study the clinical application of deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant psychiatric disorders by characterizing the causal roles of the cingulum bundle and amygdala in mood regulation and anxiolysis. Their program in affective neuroscience also includes work on facial emotion perception, such as its developmental trajectory and the neurophysiological signatures of emotion processing biases within fronto-temporal networks.
0363.research_direction: Dr. Bijanki’s lab studies the neural basis of human emotion and its disorders, combining affective neuroscience, intracranial electrophysiology and neuromodulation. Using direct intracranial recordings (iEEG) and stimulation in patients, their recent work examines the spatiotemporal dynamics of emotion processing and the mechanisms of deep brain stimulation (DBS) for treatment-resistant depression. They are examining both behavioral and electrophysiological markers of depression, probing whether negative emotion processing biases and aperiodic (1/f) background neural activity can track longitudinal symptom severity and predict DBS efficacy. They are also investigating how individual macroanatomical variations, such as cortical folding in the cingulate region, influence white matter connectivity, to better understand how distinct neural networks are engaged during therapeutic neuromodulation. Facial emotion processing is one part of this program: recordings across temporal and prefrontal networks show how the brain’s encoding of naturalistic facial affect develops from childhood to adulthood.

papers.title: The representation of facial emotion expands from sensory to prefrontal cortex with development
papers.abstract: This developmental study utilizes intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) to characterize the ontogenetic trajectory of neural encodings for facial affect from childhood (ages 5–10) to adulthood (ages 13–55). Utilizing multivariate pattern analysis on neural responses to naturalistic emotional stimuli in a short film, the researchers identified that while the posterior superior temporal cortex (pSTC) reliably encodes facial emotion throughout development, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) only begins to significantly represent affective information post-childhood. This spatial expansion of emotion representation into higher-order social-cognitive prefrontal areas suggests a maturation of top-down emotional processing circuits that is absent in early childhood.
papers.authors: Xiaoxu Fan, Abhishek Tripathi, Kelly Bijanki

papers.title: Asymmetric cingulum bundle connectivity is modulated by paracingulate sulcus morphology
papers.abstract: This investigation defines the electrographic connectivity profile of the human cingulum bundle (CB) and evaluates the impact of macroanatomical variability in the paracingulate sulcus (PCS). Using intracranial single-pulse electrical stimulation (SPES) and stereotactic EEG (sEEG) to measure effective connectivity in patients undergoing epilepsy surgery evaluation, analysis of pulse-evoked potentials (PEPs) revealed significant hemispheric asymmetry characterized by leftward dominance. Critically, this asymmetry was modulated by PCS morphology: left CB connectivity was maximized in the presence of a left PCS, whereas right CB connectivity was prioritized in its absence. These results indicate that individual anatomical variations in the cingulate region fundamentally dictate the extent of white matter network engagement during therapeutic neuromodulation.
papers.authors: Isabel A. Danstrom, Joshua A. Adkinson, Meghan E. Robinson, Lu Lin, Atul Maheshwari, Ben Shofty, Garrett Banks, Mohammed Hasen, Sameer A. Sheth, Alica M. Goldman, Eleonora Bartoli, Sarah R. Heilbronner, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Affective bias predicts changes in depression during deep brain stimulation therapy
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study examines whether neurocognitive measures of affective bias can predict clinical outcomes in treatment-resistant depression (TRD) patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS). By assessing emotion recognition and affective processing alongside clinical monitoring via the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), the researchers found that baseline negative affective bias—the tendency to prioritize negative over positive valence—significantly predicted long-term symptomatic improvement following chronic subcallosal cingulate DBS. Furthermore, shifts in these behavioral biases during therapy were correlated with changes in clinical severity, suggesting that biomarkers of affective processing function can serve as objective proxies for titrating stimulation efficacy.
papers.authors: B. Cui, M. M. Mocchi, B. A. Metzger, P. Kalva, J. F. Magnotti, J. G. Fiedorowicz, A. Waters, C. K. Kovach, Y. Y. Reed, R. K. Mathura, C. Steger, B. Pascuzzi, K. Kanja, A. Veerakumar, V. Tiruvadi, A. Crowell, L. Denison, C. J. Rozell, N. Pouratian, W. Goodman, P. Riva Posse, H. S. Mayberg, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Aperiodic (1/f) Neural Activity Robustly Tracks Symptom Severity Changes in Treatment-Resistant Depression
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the utility of aperiodic (1/f) neural activity as a longitudinal biomarker for symptom fluctuations in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). Utilizing multi-month intracranial recordings from patients with deep brain stimulation (DBS) systems, the researchers analyzed the spectral properties of local field potentials (LFPs). Findings indicated that aperiodic features, specifically the spectral slope and offset, significantly correlated with depressive symptom severity across time, outperforming traditional periodic (oscillatory) band-power metrics. These correlations were most pronounced in prefrontal and amygdala-centered networks, providing evidence that aperiodic activity captures state-dependent changes in the excitation/inhibition balance associated with the pathophysiology of TRD.
papers.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Carl Hacker, Madaline M. Mocchi, Jiayang Xiao, Brian Metzger, Joshua Adkinson, Bailey Pascuzzi, Raissa Mathura, Denise Oswalt, Andrew Watrous, Eleonora Bartoli, Anusha Allawala, Victoria Pirtle, Xiaoxu Fan, Isabel Danstrom, Ben Shofty, Garrett Banks, Yue Zhang, Maria Armenta-Salas, Kourosh Mirpour, Sanjay Mathew, Jeffrey Cohn, David Borton, Wayne Goodman, Nader Pouratian, Sameer Sheth, Kelly R. Bijanki

papers.title: Brain mechanisms underlying the emotion processing bias in treatment-resistant depression
papers.abstract: This research utilizes stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) to investigate the spatiotemporal dynamics of the emotion processing bias in treatment-resistant depression (TRD). By comparing high-temporal resolution recordings from the amygdala and prefrontal cortex (PFC), the study identified a significant imbalance in bottom-up and top-down processing.
