TRD patients exhibited heightened amygdala activation to negative stimuli (bottom-up) and delayed, attenuated amygdala responses to positive stimuli associated with aberrant inhibitory signaling from the orbitofrontal cortex (top-down). Chronic deep brain stimulation was found to selectively modulate these dynamics by relieving abnormal top-down inhibition of positive information, thereby shifting the affective processing balance toward a more normative state.
papers.authors: Xiaoxu Fan, Madaline Mocchi, Bailey Pascuzzi, Jiayang Xiao, Brian A. Metzger, Raissa K. Mathura, Carl Hacker, Joshua A. Adkinson, Eleonora Bartoli, Salma Elhassa, Andrew J. Watrous, Yue Zhang, Wayne Goodman, Nader Pouratian, Kelly Bijanki

0364.name: Ken Nakayama
0364.lab_name: Whitney Laboratory for Perception and Action
0364.bio: Nakayama is an Adjunct Professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and previously served as the Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at Harvard University. Nakayama's research utilizes human psychophysics to investigate the mechanisms of mid-level vision, focusing on how the visual system constructs surface representations to bridge low-level features and high-level object perception. Their work on face recognition includes the identification of developmental prosopagnosia and the characterization of "super-recognizers" to explore the cognitive and genetic substrates of recognition. Additionally, Nakayama examines the integration of visual attention, motion processing, and visuo-motor coordination to understand the functional architecture of the human visual system.
0364.research_direction: Dr. Nakayama's recent work explores the tight theoretical coupling between visual perception and motor action, challenging the traditional "see-decide-act" pipeline often assumed in psychology. To investigate how these systems interact in practice, they have recently been leveraging large-scale, web-based citizen science platforms to gather massive datasets on sensorimotor adaptation, examining demographic predictors of the implicit and explicit components of learning during visuomotor rotation tasks. Beyond sensorimotor neuroscience, their research also investigates the cognitive psychology of data visualization, using behavioral sketching tasks to assess how viewers infer underlying data distributions from plotted averages and testing simple design remedies to improve statistical transparency.

papers.title: Graphs of averages exaggerate and sow disagreement
papers.abstract: Across 40 replications, participants sketched the data points they believed underlay plotted averages, and their drawings showed severely exaggerated and highly inconsistent interpretations of the underlying data. Accuracy was worse than blind guessing in three of four tested cases. The authors also present a simple remedy that improves how viewers read visualized averages.
papers.authors: Jeremy Bennet Wilmer, Sarah Horan Kerns, Lily Widdup, Ken Nakayama

papers.title: Large-scale citizen science reveals predictors of sensorimotor adaptation
papers.abstract: The authors used a citizen-science website to gather more than 2,000 online sessions of a visuomotor rotation task, far larger than typical lab samples. The dataset let them replicate and reconcile classic findings on adaptation and uncover demographic constraints on the implicit and explicit components of learning. It argues that large exploratory web-based datasets can complement hypothesis-driven lab studies in sensorimotor neuroscience.
papers.authors: Jonathan S. Tsay, Hrach Asmerian, Laura T. Germine, Jeremy Wilmer, Richard B. Ivry, Ken Nakayama

papers.title: Rethinking Vision and Action
papers.abstract: This review argues that psychology has treated action as a separate specialty, resting on a simple see-decide-act sequence. It surveys recent anomalous findings showing a much tighter coupling between vision and action than that caricature allows. It then highlights three theories that deserve more attention in explaining this coupling.
papers.authors: Ken Nakayama, Jeff Moher, Joo-Hyun Song

0365.name: Kenneth D. Miller
0365.bio: Kenneth D. Miller is the Peter Taylor Professor of Neuroscience and a principal investigator at the Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute at Columbia University, where they co-direct the Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. Miller's research utilizes mathematical and computational methods to investigate the circuitry and development of the cerebral cortex, with a specific focus on the primary visual cortex (V1). Miller developed the Stabilized Supralinear Network (SSN) model, which provides a framework for understanding nonlinear cortical integration and context-dependent modulation of neural responses. Their current work uses data-driven modeling to investigate principles of neural computation and the self-organization of cortical circuits.
0365.research_direction: Dr. Miller has recently been building mathematical models of how circuits in the visual cortex produce context-dependent responses, such as how a neuron's response changes when a stimulus extends into its surround. Their recent work explores how excitatory and different inhibitory cell types (PV, SST, VIP) stabilize cortical activity, and how feedforward and feedback signals combine to generate surround suppression in mouse and other visual cortex. They have also been developing methods and analyses for large neural recordings, including a transformer model that infers activity in brain areas that were not recorded, and a geometric analysis of how population activity in macaque parietal cortex represents evidence during decisions.

papers.title: Characteristics and dynamical signatures of recurrent cortical circuits during context-dependent processing
papers.abstract: This study employs data-driven computational modeling to infer the circuit architecture of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) during context-dependent sensory processing. By fitting spatially extended stabilized supralinear networks (SSNs) to the observed responses of excitatory (E), parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) neurons, the researchers find that inhibitory stabilization is a dynamic process where the dominant inhibitory cell type affecting E-cells varies with stimulus parameters and spatial location. While PV-mediated stabilization is consistently required, the necessity for SST-mediated stabilization is stimulus-dependent. The analysis reveals that traditional uniform perturbations may fail to reveal paradoxical effects in certain inhibitory subtypes; instead, patterned perturbations are required to uncover the paradoxical response modes characteristic of inhibition-stabilized networks. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that recurrent excitatory connections and nonlinear input-output transformations are indispensable for reproducing cortical spatial response profiles, especially under conditions where feedforward thalamic inputs are weak.
papers.authors: Yue Kris Wu, Ho Yin Chau, Serena Di Santo, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Inpainting the Neural Picture: Inferring Unrecorded Brain Area Dynamics from Multi-Animal Datasets
papers.abstract: The authors propose NeuroPaint, a transformer-based masked autoencoding architecture designed to reconstruct latent neural dynamics in unrecorded brain regions by exploiting the shared structure across large-scale multi-animal datasets. In typical high-density extracellular recordings (e.g., Neuropixels), only a subset of brain areas is sampled simultaneously. NeuroPaint leverages overlapping recorded regions across different sessions and animals to 'in-paint' missing activity through a cross-attention stitcher and temporal tokenization framework. Tested on both synthetic and large-scale empirical mouse datasets (e.g., the IBL brain-wide map), the model successfully infers single-neuron firing rates and inter-area interactions in unobserved regions. The results show that this approach significantly outperforms standard baselines like LFADS and enables population-level systems neuroscience analyses that transcend the physical limitations of single-subject recording sessions.
papers.authors: Ji Xia, Yizi Zhang, Shuqi Wang, Genevera I. Allen, Liam Paninski, Cole Lincoln Hurwitz, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Stabilized Supralinear Network Model of Responses to Surround Stimuli in Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research investigates the circuit mechanisms underlying visual center-surround interactions in primary visual cortex (V1) using the stabilized supralinear network (SSN) framework. The model accounts for three critical features of surround suppression: the suppression of both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents, the dominance of orientation-matched suppression (where surround suppression is strongest when the surround orientation matches the center orientation regardless of the cell’s preferred tuning), and feature-specific suppression observed in plaid stimuli. The authors demonstrate that a spatially two-dimensional SSN with strong local recurrent connectivity operates in an inhibition-stabilized regime that naturally reproduces these phenomena. The findings are further validated in a biologically realistic conductance-based spiking network, which also replicates the rapid decay kinetics of V1 activity following the silencing of thalamic inputs.
papers.authors: Dina Obeid, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: The geometry of the neural state space of decisions
papers.abstract: Through the analysis of large-scale population recordings from macaque area LIP during a motion-direction discrimination task, this study characterizes the geometric structure of decision-making in neural state space. Contrary to the standard drift-diffusion model (DDM) where evidence integration is viewed as a one-dimensional scaling of activity at choice targets, the data reveal that evidence accumulation occurs along adaptive, context-dependent directions on a curved decision manifold. The population activity undergoes a dynamical transition from sensory-driven deliberation to commitment, characterized by adaptive retinotopic shifts. The authors propose a mechanistic circuit model in which competitive interactions and self-excitation drive the 'winning' activity bump, transitioning the system from external-input-dominated to intrinsic-circuit-driven dynamics. The model’s predictions for how choice selectivity varies with trial speed are confirmed by single-trial and trial-averaged population analyses.
papers.authors: Mauro M. Monsalve-Mercado, Gabriel M. Stine, Michael N. Shadlen, Kenneth D. Miller

papers.title: Contextual modulation emerges by integrating feedforward and feedback processing in mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: This study develops a unified circuit model of the mouse primary visual cortex (V1) to explain how feedforward and feedback signals are integrated to generate complex contextual modulations. Reanalysis of V1 data reveals that increasing the spatial extent of a visual stimulus leads to only a minimal increase in the total area of the responsive neural population, a finding that challenges existing feedforward models of surround suppression (SS). The proposed model suggests that SS in Layer 2/3 is inherited from Layer 4, while 'inverse responses' (size-tuned responses to luminance-matched 'holes' in full-field gratings) are driven by wide feedback connections from higher cortical areas. Cross-orientation surround facilitation is explained by the integration of these feedback-driven inverse responses with feedforward-driven classical receptive field activity, illustrating a multi-stage mechanism for contextual processing across the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Serena Di Santo, Mario Dipoppa, Andreas J. Keller, Morgane M. Roth, Massimo Scanziani, Kenneth D. Miller

0366.name: Kevin Willeford
0366.institution: NOVA Southeastern University College of Optometry
0366.department: College of Optometry, Department of Optometric Sciences
0366.bio: Kevin Willeford is an Assistant Professor at Nova Southeastern University’s College of Optometry, where their research focuses on the neural mechanisms governing sensorimotor fusion and binocular vision. Willeford developed Limbus Segment Tracking (LST), a non-invasive image-processing method designed to quantify large-scale ocular rotations that traditional video-based eye trackers do not capture. Their work utilizes eye-movement analysis and visual evoked potentials (VEP) to investigate attentional processes, the quantification of aniseikonia, and the clinical evolution of ocular motility disorders. Willeford’s research also involves optimizing eye-tracking reliability by mitigating pupil-induced fixational drift and characterizing ocular duction patterns in both normal and strabismic populations.
0366.research_direction: Dr. Willeford has recently been investigating how eye movements and attention relate, especially in people whose eye muscles are impaired. Their recent work explores whether attention can still shift toward a cue in patients with paralytic strabismus, testing the idea that attention is tied to preparing an eye movement. They have also been developing an image-processing protocol to objectively measure how far and how symmetrically the eyes rotate in different directions, and have studied how optometry students calibrate their confidence in their own answers when given feedback.

papers.title: Exogenous spatial attention is functional in paralytic strabismics
papers.abstract: This study challenges the strict interpretation of the premotor theory of attention, which suggests an obligate link between ocular motor execution and the allocation of spatial attention. The researchers employed two experiments to measure the effects of exogenous visual cues—designed to facilitate or inhibit attentional shifts—on the response latencies of both saccadic and manual (keypress) targets in patients with paralytic strabismus. By incorporating a no-cue control condition, the study quantified the presence and direction of cue-induced attentional modulation. Results indicated that all patients exhibited classic signatures of cue-target interactions, with faster responses to proximate targets and slower responses to distal targets across both eye and hand effectors. These findings support the hypothesis that premotor structures program attentional shifts in an effector-independent manner, maintaining functional exogenous orienting even when peripheral ocular motility is severely restricted.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: A protocol to quantify cross-sectional and longitudinal differences in duction patterns
papers.abstract: The authors propose a novel clinical protocol to address the lack of established systems for objectively quantifying ocular duction patterns. The methodology integrates digital image processing with a statistical framework consisting of summary indices—specifically focusing on movement area and symmetry—to evaluate ocular motility. The protocol provides a global characterization of the motor field, allowing for the detection of monocular and binocular imbalances in synergistic muscle pairs. By establishing criteria for minimal detectable change (MDC), the researchers demonstrate the protocol's utility in evaluating both cross-sectional deviations from normative populations and longitudinal shifts indicative of pathological progression or therapeutic resolution. This systematic approach transforms subjective clinical observations into reliable, continuous biometric data suitable for tracking ocular motility disorders over time.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Victoria Copel, Hua Rong

papers.title: Feedback Changes Metacognitive Accuracy Over Different Time Scales
papers.abstract: This study investigates how optometry students utilize metacognitive feedback to improve their self-assessment accuracy during a national board examination preparation course. Third-year students were required to make sequential retrospective confidence judgments regarding the probability that their answers to board-style questions were correct. Metacognitive accuracy was quantified using indices such as error (mismatch between average confidence and correctness), calibration, and resolution. These metrics were analyzed across item-by-item, single session, and course-wide time scales to determine if providing performance feedback could dynamically alter metacognitive accuracy. The results demonstrated that while feedback delivery over varied durations provided the potential for students to refine their calibration and resolution, the degree of improvement was highly variable, suggesting that individuals utilize metacognitive feedback in distinct ways during their clinical education.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Nicole Patterson, Jamie Althoff

0369.name: Kirsten Adam
0369.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Mind and Brain
0369.bio: Kirsten Adam is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology and the Center for Mind and Brain at UC Davis who investigates the cognitive and neural constraints that limit human attention and memory. Adam's research utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine how the brain manages visual distractions and why individuals experience moment-to-moment fluctuations in performance. Their work focuses on visual working memory capacity, demonstrating how attentional lapses and stimulus history influence the representation of information in the early visual cortex.
0369.research_direction: Dr. Adam has recently been investigating the dynamic mechanisms and capacity limits of visual working memory, exploring how observers manage these strict cognitive bottlenecks. Their recent behavioral work explores whether memory retention can be optimized by aligning performance feedback with an individual's intrinsic capacity, and how observers might rapidly recruit visual long-term memory to bypass capacity limits during explicit stimulus repetitions. On a neural level, they are using fMRI and multivariate decoding to test whether memory load constraints stem from a localized parietal bottleneck or instead rely on distributed, drifting representational codes across the broader cortex. Additionally, they are investigating the true magnitude of attentional capture, utilizing single-trial surprise paradigms to measure how salient distractors disrupt visual search before observers have the opportunity to develop learned suppression strategies.

papers.title: Distributed and drifting signals for working memory load in human cortex
papers.abstract: While increases in working memory (WM) load reliably yield behavioral costs, whether the underlying neural constraints stem from a localized hub in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) or are distributed throughout the cortex remains contentious. In a high-powered, pre-registered fMRI study (N = 12 observers; 12 scanner-hours each), participants completed a visual WM delayed-estimation task under variable load (0 to 4 items). Analyses replicated classical load-dependent monotonic increases in univariate BOLD activity within parietal cortex; however, systematic bidirectional univariate modulations—both signal increases and decreases indicative of population receptive field surround suppression—were also evident across early and high-level visual areas. Crucially, multivariate pattern analyses accurately decoded WM load across visual, parietal, and frontal cortices regardless of the sign of univariate changes, challenging models of an exclusive parietal bottleneck. Furthermore, significant representational drift in multivariate load-encoding patterns was detected across sessions, suggesting that cortical load codes undergo continual experience-dependent reorganization to support efficient storage.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Edward Awh, John T. Serences

papers.title: Beyond routine maintenance: Current trends in working memory research
papers.abstract: Theoretical perspectives on working memory (WM) are evolving away from classical frameworks of static, persistent maintenance toward dynamic, flexible mechanisms of active cognition. Synthesized by the organizers of the 2024 Working Memory Symposium, this review evaluates emerging trends across four foundational themes: (1) expanding empirical investigations beyond conventional visual and verbal domains into cross-modal sensory systems to evaluate the generality of WM principles; (2) establishing the malleable and context-sensitive format of WM representations, which actively reformat to facilitate prospective motor planning and behavioral goals; (3) resolving how complex feature bindings, structural hierarchies, and modality-independent pointers (or object files) coordinate multi-item storage within capacity limits; and (4) illuminating shared computational and functional architecture between WM and related faculties, including selective attention, episodic retrieval, and executive control. The authors integrate current evidence regarding distributed sensory recruitment and dynamic population codes, outlining crucial benchmarks for developing unified models of active cognitive processing.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Laura-Isabelle Klatt, Jacob A. Miller, Marlene Rösner, Keisuke Fukuda, Anastasia Kiyonaga

papers.title: Capacity-aligned feedback enhances visual working memory performance
papers.abstract: Because visual working memory (VWM) is sharply capacity-limited, previous research has evaluated performance feedback and reward incentives to improve retention, yet findings have been equivocal. This paper proposes an optimal strategy framework postulating that feedback is maximally beneficial when incentivized goals align with an individual's intrinsic capacity limits rather than encouraging unconstrained performance maximization. Across three whole-report behavioral experiments manipulating goal difficulty (1–5 items) under blocked and intermixed conditions, optimal group-level performance occurred when goals matched average human capacity (~3 items). In contrast, supra-capacity goals (e.g., remembering 5 items) triggered an overload effect that systematically increased attentional lapse rates (chance-level recall). Pre-registered individual-differences analyses in Experiment 2 confirmed that individual performance peaked when incentive targets matched each participant's measured capacity limit, accompanied by a quantifiable trade-off between metacognitive calibration and maximal memory retrieval.
papers.authors: Olga Kozlova, Kirsten C. S. Adam

papers.title: First encounters: Estimating the initial magnitude of attentional capture
papers.abstract: Attentional capture is routinely evaluated using repetitive paradigms where participants complete hundreds of visual search trials containing salient distractors, a design that can inadvertently establish secondary task-sets for proactive distractor suppression. To estimate capture magnitude in the absence of distractor experience, large web-based cohorts performed a shape search task containing a single surprise distractor-present trial (Exp. 1: N = 970; Exp. 2: N = 1,025 across four sparse blocks). Initial capture costs were 9- to 15-fold larger (~370–580 ms) than canonical multi-trial estimates (~30 ms). Furthermore, capture was strongly modulated by stimulus history: singleton distractors rendered in a previously unseen color produced substantially greater slowdown (~585 ms) than distractors rendered in colors previously encountered during distractor-absent search (~375 ms). Reaction time mixture modeling demonstrated that capture manifests as large delays on a subset of trials rather than a small, uniform shift across the full distribution, indicating that typical laboratory estimates severely underestimate initial distraction costs.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Zi Yang, John T. Serences

papers.title: Behavioral signatures of the rapid recruitment of long-term memory to overcome working memory capacity limits
papers.abstract: Working memory and long-term memory are conventionally investigated in isolation using unrepeated abstract arrays to avoid long-term memory contributions. In contrast to incidental array repetitions, which typically fail to enhance visual working memory performance, this study evaluated whether explicit repetitions enable the rapid deployment of visual long-term memory (VLTM) to overcome working memory capacity limits. In two behavioral experiments using continuous whole-report color recall of 6- or 8-item displays, explicit array repetitions approximately doubled recall performance from baseline (~2.8 items) to over 5–6 items across eight repetitions, with substantial improvements emerging after a single repetition. Subsequent surprise recognition tests verified above-chance recognition of repeated arrays. Crucially, fine-grained inter-response time (IRT) analyses identified a distinctive temporal slowing after reporting 2–3 items that emerged exclusively for repeated arrays, providing a behavioral metric of chunk retrieval and demonstrating rapid synthesis between active working memory and episodic long-term traces.
papers.authors: Kirsten C. S. Adam, Chong Zhao, Edward K. Vogel

0370.name: Kohitij Kar
0370.lab_name: Visual Intelligence and Technological Advances (VITAL) Lab
0370.bio: Kohitij Kar is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biology and a Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience at York University. Kar’s research functions at the intersection of primate neurophysiology and artificial intelligence, focusing on the recurrent neural mechanisms underlying core object recognition in the ventral stream. Utilizing large-scale electrophysiology, behavioral assays, and deep learning, they develop computational models to analyze the relationship between biological and artificial vision. Their work investigates how these neural frameworks can be used to understand visual cognition and to model neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism.
0370.research_direction: Dr. Kar builds and tests brain-like neural network models of how the primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex supports visual recognition. Combining macaque electrophysiology, large-scale behavior and deep networks, the lab asks not only how well models predict IT responses but also how well IT predicts the models, revealing network units with no counterpart in the brain. Recent work shows that learning new objects reshapes IT in ways well captured by gradient-based optimization, that facial expression and identity are coded along partially overlapping IT dimensions, and that masked-image tests can reveal which model explanations match human and monkey recognition strategies. Low-cost home-cage kiosks make this high-throughput primate behavior practical.

papers.title: Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains
papers.abstract: Standard model-brain comparisons ask only how well a network predicts neural responses. This paper adds the reverse direction, asking how well macaque inferior temporal responses predict the network's units. Many units in high-performing networks turn out to have no brain counterpart, and this asymmetry relates to how well models track behavior and robustness, offering a stricter benchmark for brain-like AI.
papers.authors: Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Hierarchical optimization predicts plasticity in the macaque inferior temporal cortex following object training
papers.abstract: Macaques were trained on new object categories while IT cortex activity was recorded. The resulting changes in IT representations are well captured by gradient-based optimization of a hierarchical network, indicating that learning-induced plasticity follows principles similar to those used to train deep networks.
papers.authors: Lynn K. A. Sörensen, James J. DiCarlo, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Facial expression discrimination emerges from partially overlapping neural subspaces of detection and identity
papers.abstract: Recording from macaque IT cortex during facial expression discrimination, the study finds that expression information is read out from neural dimensions that partly overlap with those supporting face detection and identity. Model comparisons show that networks trained for detection and identity best predict these responses, providing a primate model for emotion perception relevant to autism research.
papers.authors: Maren Wehrheim, Shirin Taghian Alamooti, Hamidreza Ramezanpour, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: Masked attribution-based probing of strategies as a computational framework to align human, non-human primate, and model explanations
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a masked-image probing method that reveals which image regions drive recognition decisions in humans, macaques and deep networks. Comparing these explanation maps shows which models rely on strategies similar to primates, going beyond accuracy-based alignment.
papers.authors: Sabine Muzellec, Yousif Kashef Alghetaa, Simon Kornblith, Kohitij Kar

papers.title: The Quest for an Integrated Set of Neural Mechanisms Underlying Object Recognition in Primates
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes evidence on how feedforward, recurrent and feedback circuits in the primate ventral stream jointly support core object recognition. It evaluates how well deep-network models account for the data and lays out the open problems for building mechanistic, integrated models.
papers.authors: Kohitij Kar, James J. DiCarlo

0371.name: Konstantinos Derpanis
0371.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
0371.bio: Konstantinos G. Derpanis is an Associate Professor at York University and a Faculty Affiliate at the Vector Institute, focusing on computer vision, human motion understanding, and temporal sequence analysis. Their research applies deep learning and probabilistic modeling to 3D human pose estimation, motion segmentation, and point tracking through occlusions. This work connects computational vision and vision science by using neural network architectures to model human lightness and illusion perception. Derpanis also conducts research on spatio-temporal representations and weakly supervised learning for sequence alignment in video datasets.
0371.research_direction: Dr. Derpanis has recently been exploring the internal representations and interpretability of deep vision networks, developing methods to discover how models build high-level visual concepts across layers and how these semantic vocabularies can be aligned across different architectures using shared sparse autoencoders. Their recent work also investigates spatiotemporal representations in video foundation models, probing networks layer-by-layer to quantify their reliance on static appearance versus dynamic motion cues and to determine where physical properties like camera motion or intuitive physics are encoded. Additionally, they are designing geometry-aware diffusion models for 3D computer vision, specifically focusing on multi-view scene inpainting methods that maintain geometric consistency across different viewpoints without relying on explicit radiance fields.

papers.title: What, Where, and How: Probing Spatiotemporal Representations in Video Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Performs a layer-by-layer probing study of self-supervised video models (V-JEPA 2 and VideoMAE-v2) to see what temporal properties they encode and where. Camera motion is decodable with high accuracy at mid-to-late depth, anomaly detection is moderate, and intuitive-physics tasks stay near chance. Camera-motion features also lie along smooth low-dimensional trajectories, which the authors exploit for spline-based steering of video latents.
papers.authors: Sharon S. Musa, Fereshteh Forghani, Harrish Thasarathan, Sonia Joseph, Matthew Kowal, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment
papers.abstract: Trains a single sparse autoencoder whose shared dictionary can reconstruct and be decoded from the activations of several different vision models at once. This gives a common vocabulary of concepts that can be matched across architectures, letting the authors compare what different networks represent and see which concepts are universal versus model-specific. The learned concepts support coordinated activation maximization and cross-model comparison of features.
papers.authors: Harrish Thasarathan, Julian Forsyth, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Quantifying and Learning Static vs. Dynamic Information in Deep Spatiotemporal Networks
papers.abstract: Introduces a way to measure how much a video network relies on static appearance versus dynamic motion information, applying it across action recognition, video object segmentation and other tasks with many architectures. The analysis shows that many models are biased toward static cues and that the balance depends on task and architecture. The authors also show how this bias can be shifted by design and training choices.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI)
papers.authors: Matthew Kowal, Mennatullah Siam, Md. Amirul Islam, Neil D. B. Bruce, Richard P. Wildes, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Diffusion Models for Multiview Scene Inpainting
papers.abstract: Tackles filling in masked regions of a scene captured from several viewpoints so that the completions agree geometrically across views. Instead of fitting an explicit radiance field, which tends to blur inconsistent inpaintings, the method fuses cross-view information in a learned space using a geometry-aware conditional diffusion model with reference-based cues. It reaches state-of-the-art results on SPIn-NeRF and NeRFiller and works with only a few views.
papers.authors: Ahmad Salimi, Tristan Aumentado-Armstrong, Marcus A. Brubaker, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

papers.title: Visual Concept Connectome (VCC): Open World Concept Discovery and their Interlayer Connections in Deep Models
papers.abstract: Presents an unsupervised method that discovers human-interpretable concepts in a vision network's layers and then measures how concepts in one layer feed into concepts in later layers. The result is a graph-like map (a connectome) of how a model builds up high-level concepts from simpler ones, applied to several classifiers. Quantitative tests and case studies illustrate how the map exposes model behaviour.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Matthew Kowal, Richard P. Wildes, Konstantinos G. Derpanis

0373.name: Kowa Koida
0373.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0373.bio: Kowa Koida is an Associate Professor at Toyohashi University of Technology and directs the Visual Neuroscience Lab, focusing on the neural substrates of color perception and object recognition. Their research integrates primate electrophysiology, human psychophysics, and neurotechnology to examine how the cerebral cortex transforms visual stimuli into subjective experiences. Koida contributed to the development of high-precision tungsten microelectrodes and investigated how cortical microstimulation influences behavioral color judgment. Current research directions include mapping the functional structure of the lateral geniculate nucleus and examining how material properties like gloss and transparency affect three-dimensional shape perception.
0373.research_direction: Dr. Koida has recently been investigating the mechanisms of color vision across the primate visual hierarchy, alongside developing advanced methodological tools for in vivo neurophysiology. Their recent work explores how color signals are processed in the macaque brain, using electrical microstimulation to test the causal role of the anterior inferior temporal cortex in color judgment, and employing cone-isolating stimuli to map the precise anatomical distribution of blue-ON cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus. Beyond neural mechanisms, they are also investigating optical contributions to visual phenomena, specifically examining how chromatic aberration and blur might drive hue and luminance dependencies in color assimilation illusions. To support this diverse research program, Dr. Koida has been developing novel experimental techniques, including a minimally invasive tungsten marking method to rigorously link single-unit recording sites to fine-scale anatomy and integrated hardware systems to synchronize stimulus presentation with precise data acquisition.

papers.title: Localization of blue-on cells in the lateral geniculate nucleus of the macaque monkey using a tungsten marking technique
papers.abstract: The authors recorded single units in macaque LGN, classified them with cone-isolating stimuli, and marked the recording sites with a high-resolution, minimally invasive tungsten deposition method to verify locations histologically. Cells receiving S-cone ON input were found mostly in the koniocellular layers or at the koniocellular/parvocellular border, with one case in the pregeniculate nucleus. This gives direct anatomical-physiological evidence for where blue-ON signals live in the primate LGN.
papers.authors: Tatsuya Oikawa, Kowa Koida

papers.title: Digital Signal Processor Integrated Recording System for Visual Neurophysiology using a Single Personal Computer
papers.abstract: The authors describe a recording setup that combines a digital signal processor with a single PC to handle both visual stimulus presentation and neural signal acquisition. This replaces multi-computer rigs and keeps stimulus and recording timing synchronized for visual neurophysiology experiments. It is an enabling tool for his lab's macaque recordings.
papers.authors: Tatsuya Oikawa, Kowa Koida

papers.title: 色同化の色相依存性と輝度依存性をもたらす眼光学的要因 (Optical factors contributing to the hue and luminance dependency of color assimilation)
papers.abstract: This study asks how the eye's optics contribute to color assimilation, the shift of a target's apparent color toward its surround. Simulating optical aberration, the authors show that blur and chromatic aberration can account for part of the dependence of assimilation on hue and luminance. It points to optical rather than purely neural origins for some assimilation effects.
papers.venue: VISION (Journal of the Vision Society of Japan)
papers.authors: Natsumi Tsuji, Tama Kanematsu, Kowa Koida

papers.title: Effect of microstimulation of the inferior temporal cortex on color judgment behavior
papers.abstract: Monkeys performed a color judgment task while electrical microstimulation was delivered to anterior inferior temporal cortex. Stimulation shifted the psychometric function strongly in a restricted sub-region whose extent matched where color-selective neurons are found. Surprisingly, the direction of the behavioral shift was negatively related to the color preference of nearby neurons, supporting a causal role for an anterior IT color-selective area in color perception.
papers.authors: Kowa Koida, Hidehiko Komatsu

papers.title: A Fine-Scale and Minimally Invasive Marking Method for Use with Conventional Tungsten Microelectrodes
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to mark recording sites by passing biphasic current pulses through ordinary tungsten electrodes, depositing tungsten oxide spots of 10-100 micrometers that show up bright red under dark-field imaging after Nissl staining. The marks cause little tissue damage, persist in vivo for at least two years, and work in both mouse and macaque brains. It lets physiological recordings be tied precisely to anatomy.
papers.authors: Tatsuya Oikawa, Kento Nomura, Toshimitsu Hara, Kowa Koida

0374.name: Krista A. Ehinger
0374.department: School of Computing and Information Systems
0374.bio: Krista A. Ehinger is an Associate Professor at the University of Melbourne whose research explores the interface between biological and artificial vision, focusing on scene recognition, visual search, and depth perception in naturalistic environments. Ehinger utilizes a methodology that integrates psychophysical experiments and eye-tracking with computational modeling techniques such as Bayesian inference and deep neural networks. Their work investigates how scene context and peripheral encoding facilitate navigation and object detection in both humans and machines. Ehinger has developed large-scale scene understanding databases and models for predicting human attentional allocation.
0374.research_direction: Dr. Ehinger has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying both visual and abstract reasoning across a variety of artificial intelligence systems. Their recent work explores amodal perception, employing diffusion and generative vision-language models to segment hidden object regions, infer occlusion orders, and visually reconstruct occluded parts based on open-ended text queries. Additionally, they are developing multi-stage benchmarks to evaluate abstract visual reasoning in multimodal large language models, seeking to isolate basic perceptual processing from higher-order rule inference. Finally, their research extends into structured automated planning, investigating step-by-step verification workflows to improve LLM code generation and physics-simulated spatial search algorithms for complex 3D object disassembly.

papers.title: Open-World Amodal Appearance Completion
papers.abstract: Presents a training-free framework that reconstructs the hidden parts of partially occluded objects in a scene from open-ended text queries, rather than being limited to a fixed set of object categories. The system handles both direct object names and abstract descriptions, which the authors call reasoning amodal completion. It combines large vision-language and generative models and is evaluated on open-world benchmarks.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Jiayang Ao, Yanbei Jiang, Qiuhong Ke, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Planning-Driven Programming: A Large Language Model Programming Workflow
papers.abstract: Proposes LPW, a two-phase workflow for LLM code generation. The model first drafts a solution plan and checks it against visible tests, then writes code from the verified plan and, if tests fail, refines it using the plan's verification as guidance. This improves both first-attempt and refined code accuracy over prior refinement methods on standard code-generation benchmarks.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
papers.authors: Chao Lei, Yanchuan Chang, Nir Lipovetzky, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Beyond Perception: Evaluating Abstract Visual Reasoning through Multi-Stage Task
papers.abstract: Introduces MultiStAR, a RAVEN-based benchmark that decomposes abstract visual reasoning into several stages, and a metric that credits correct intermediate steps rather than only final accuracy. Testing multimodal LLMs shows they cope with basic perception stages but fail at the higher-order rule inference that the task needs.
papers.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025
papers.authors: Yanbei Jiang, Yihao Ding, Chao Lei, Jiayang Ao, Jey Han Lau, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: State-Based Disassembly Planning
papers.abstract: Presents a planning approach to taking apart complex 3D assemblies that prioritizes physics-simulated translational motion and stores intermediate motion states to make the search scale. Two new evaluation functions built on state-enriched Directional Blocking Graphs guide the search, and experiments show it solves harder disassembly tasks more efficiently than earlier simulation-based methods.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI)
papers.authors: Chao Lei, Nir Lipovetzky, Krista A. Ehinger

papers.title: Sequential Amodal Segmentation via Cumulative Occlusion Learning
papers.abstract: Develops a diffusion model that segments both visible and hidden regions of objects of unknown category and recovers their occlusion order. A cumulative-mask strategy during diffusion captures uncertainty about occluded regions. The approach is motivated by how humans infer complete objects and outperforms prior methods on standard amodal segmentation benchmarks.
papers.authors: Jiayang Ao, Qiuhong Ke, Krista A. Ehinger

0375.name: Krista Kelly
0375.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science
0375.bio: Krista Kelly is an Assistant Professor at the University of Waterloo and directs the Vision and Neurodevelopment Lab. Kelly's research examines the impact of atypical early-life visual experiences, such as amblyopia, strabismus, and pediatric cataracts, on brain development and functional skills. Utilizing psychophysics, binocular eye tracking, and motion capture for gait analysis, they investigate the mechanisms behind reading delays and motor coordination deficits in children. Their work focuses on identifying biomarkers for vision-related impairments and developing interventions to address functional outcomes for pediatric patients.
0375.research_direction: Dr. Kelly has recently been investigating the broader functional and real-world consequences of amblyopia and strabismus, framing them as systemic neurodevelopmental disorders that affect the whole child. Their recent work explores how early unbalanced visual input impacts complex everyday behaviors beyond simple visual acuity deficits. To capture these effects, they employ diverse behavioral and kinematic methods, such as using rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) to isolate the role of fixation instability in reading, tracking eye and limb kinematics during targeted reaching, and utilizing pressure-sensitive walkways to evaluate visually guided gait. Ultimately, Dr. Kelly's research seeks to deeply phenotype the cascading impacts of childhood visual impairment on motor control, skill execution, and overall health-related quality of life.

papers.title: Gait kinematics during walking in children with impaired binocular vision due to amblyopia or strabismus
papers.abstract: Children aged 7-13 with amblyopia or strabismus and normal-vision controls walked on a pressure-sensitive walkway, either straight or stepping on targets while avoiding distractors. Average gait measures were similar between groups, but affected children missed more targets, were more variable step to step, and showed no learning across trials. The authors interpret this as immature gait development after unbalanced early visual input.
papers.authors: Lauren E. Hoare, Krista R. Kelly

papers.title: Slow binocular reading during rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) in children with amblyopia and the role of fixation instability
papers.abstract: Tests whether children with amblyopia read slowly because of the need for saccades between words, by using single-word-at-a-time RSVP reading. Even without inter-word saccades, amblyopic children read slower than controls, and both eyes showed unstable fixation. Only children with stable fellow-eye fixation read at control speed, implicating fellow-eye fixation instability as a source of slow reading.
papers.authors: Dorsa Mir Norouzi, Norah M. Nyangau, Yi-Zhong Wang, Lori M. Dao, Cynthia L. Beauchamp, David R. Stager Jr., Jeffrey S. Hunter, Krista R. Kelly

papers.title: Eye-hand coordination during visually-guided reaching in children with monocular deprivation amblyopia
papers.abstract: Children aged 7-15 with amblyopia after a unilateral congenital or infantile cataract were compared with controls while eye and reaching movements were recorded during reach-to-touch of targets. The cataract group showed poorer saccade and reach kinematics, including slower and less accurate reaches, with the worst performance in those with poorer visual acuity outcomes. Extra reach-related saccades and prolonged final approach suggest impaired online control and no efficient compensatory strategy.
papers.authors: Krista R. Kelly, Mina Nouradanesh, Reed M. Jost, Christina S. Cheng-Patel, Eileen E. Birch, Serena X. Wang, James Y. Tung, Ewa Niechwiej-Szwedo

papers.title: Functional consequences of amblyopia and its impact on health-related quality of life
papers.abstract: A review of recent evidence that amblyopia affects everyday functioning beyond acuity, spanning contrast sensitivity, attention, reading, eye-hand coordination, body composition, physical activity and health-related quality of life. It argues that clinicians, educators and researchers should account for these broader effects when managing patients and designing treatments and interventions.
papers.authors: Krista R. Kelly, Yi Pang, Benjamin Thompson, Ewa Niechwiej-Szwedo, Carolyn D. Drews-Botsch, Ann L. Webber

papers.title: Amblyopia and the whole child
papers.abstract: A high-profile review arguing that amblyopia is a neurodevelopmental disorder whose consequences reach well beyond visual acuity. The authors note large, unexplained individual differences in treatment response and propose deep phenotyping of each child's deficits to select treatments. They also synthesize evidence on knock-on effects on visually guided skills, self-perception and quality of life, advocating a whole-person approach to care.
papers.venue: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research
papers.authors: Eileen E. Birch, Krista R. Kelly

0377.name: Kristina J. Nielsen
0377.department: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience
0377.bio: Kristina J. Nielsen is an Associate Professor of Neuroscience at Johns Hopkins University who researches the neural circuits responsible for object recognition and motion perception. Nielsen's laboratory uses two-photon calcium imaging and high-density electrophysiology to map the functional transformations occurring between primary and higher-level visual cortical areas. By studying non-human primates and ferret models, Nielsen investigates how these representations emerge during development and the extent of adult plasticity. Their work aims to bridge the gap between pixel-level visual inputs and the invariant object representations formed in the brain.
0377.research_direction: Dr. Nielsen has recently been investigating how the higher levels of the visual system develop, and whether they simply mature after early areas or follow their own timeline. Their work in young ferrets tracks when neurons in a motion-processing area become selective for the direction an object moves, and compares this with primary visual cortex. They have also been developing a network-level view in which the visual hierarchy emerges from changing patterns of connectivity rather than a strict step-by-step build-up. In parallel, they explore how the primate visual system represents shape in two and three dimensions, framed as a set of computational goals for the ventral visual stream.

papers.title: Early development of direction selectivity in higher visual cortex
papers.abstract: The computation of motion direction is an essential element of visual processing represented in both early cortical stages, such as primary visual cortex (V1), and higher-tier motion areas, such as middle temporal area (MT) in primates and posteromedial lateral suprasylvian (PMLS) cortex in ferrets. Tracking the developmental time course of directional tuning in the ferret visual pathway revealed that direction selectivity emerges earlier in PMLS than in V1, contradicting standard bottom-up hierarchical maturation models. While sensory experience influences direction selectivity across both cortical areas, the sensory requirements differ fundamentally: drifting gratings that provide coordinated spatiotemporal cues are necessary for the development of direction selectivity in V1, whereas spatially stationary flickering stimuli containing only temporal modulation are sufficient to induce direction selectivity in PMLS. These findings indicate that motion pathway maturation is governed by complex network-level interactions that do not depend strictly on feedforward drives from V1.
papers.authors: Dallas C. Khamiss, Augusto A. Lempel, Brandon R. Nanfito, Kristina J. Nielsen

papers.title: Development of Higher-Level Vision: A Network Perspective
papers.abstract: Whereas extensive neurodevelopmental research has mapped the mechanisms governing early visual processing through primary visual cortex (V1), the developmental principles shaping downstream extrastriate and higher-order visual cortex remain poorly understood. The conventional model presumes a sequential, feedforward maturation process that mirrors the hierarchical ordering observed in adult cortex. However, an evaluation of structural, physiological, and behavioral evidence across species indicates that the mature hierarchy arises from an evolving series of distinct, transient network configurations rather than simple incomplete variants of adult connectivity. Adopting an interactive, network-level perspective across multiple cortical stages will be necessary to resolve the biological rules governing higher visual development, uncover specific temporal windows of susceptibility to neurodevelopmental disorders, and design effective clinical interventions.
papers.authors: James A. Bourne, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Lynne Kiorpes, Maria Concetta Morrone, Michael J. Arcaro, Kristina J. Nielsen

papers.title: How Shape Perception Works, in Two Dimensions and Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: The primate ventral visual stream executes a succession of nonlinear transformations that convert retinal light patterns into high-level structural representations supporting 2D pattern recognition and 3D volumetric shape comprehension. This review outlines an integrative computational framework defining three primary objectives governing ventral stream coding: radical dimensional compression to facilitate transmission across white-matter tracts and enable compact mnemonic storage; explicit linear readouts allowing downstream circuits to directly access shape features for executive control; and representational invariance to preserve perceptual constancy across changes in size, orientation, illumination, and retinal position. Analyzing neural encoding across early visual cortex, intermediate area V4, and inferotemporal cortex (IT) demonstrates how successive receptive field transformations fulfill these computational objectives to yield detailed, stable object perception.
papers.authors: Kristina J. Nielsen, Charles E. Connor

0378.name: Kristina Visscher
0378.bio: Kristina Visscher is an Associate Professor in the Department of Neurobiology and Associate Director of the McKnight Brain Institute at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. Visscher's research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and psychophysics to investigate how cognitive control mechanisms modulate sensory processing and adapt to environmental changes. A focus of their work is cortical plasticity following central vision loss, specifically exploring how the brain reorganizes to utilize peripheral vision in patients with macular degeneration. Visscher also leads efforts within the McKnight Brain Aging Registry to characterize neural network dynamics and cognitive health in the oldest-old population.
0378.research_direction: Dr. Visscher's recent work explores experience-dependent plasticity in the adult brain, with a major focus on how central vision loss drives structural and functional reorganization in the visual cortex. Using neuroimaging methods like resting-state fMRI and microstructural mapping, they have recently been investigating how foveal deprivation and the compensatory, attention-demanding use of a peripheral preferred retinal locus alter cortical thickness, reshape functional routing to category-selective visual areas, and drive idiosyncratic whole-brain connectivity patterns. To pinpoint the behavioral drivers of this adaptation, they are also using gaze-contingent simulated scotomas to test which specific attentional mechanisms—such as habitual versus dynamic attention—underlie performance improvements following peripheral vision training. Broadening their focus on large-scale brain organization, their recent research additionally examines healthy cognitive aging by investigating how the functional segregation of cortical networks relates to preserved processing speed in the oldest-old.

papers.title: Increased Attentive Use Is Linked to More Idiosyncratic Functional Connections
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether parts of cortex that are used more often for attention-demanding tasks develop whole-brain connection patterns that are more individual-specific. In healthy adults, connectivity of central-vision cortex is idiosyncratic while peripheral-vision cortex connectivity is similar across people. In patients with central vision loss, the cortex representing the preferred retinal locus, which is used heavily, also shows more idiosyncratic connectivity than a control region or matched controls.
papers.authors: Pinar Demirayak, Leland L. Fleming, Pauline Stewart, Rachel Chua, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Network segregation is associated with processing speed in the cognitively healthy oldest-old
papers.abstract: Using resting-state fMRI from 146 cognitively healthy adults aged 85 and older in the McKnight Brain Aging Registry, this study examines how cleanly the brain's large-scale functional networks are separated. Greater network segregation, particularly in association systems, tracks with faster processing speed. The work links brain network organization to preserved cognition in the oldest-old.
papers.authors: Sara A. Nolin, Mary E. Faulkner, Paul Stewart, Leland L. Fleming, Stacy Merritt, Roxanne F. Rezaei, Pradyumna K. Bharadwaj, Mary Kate Franchetti, David A. Raichlen, Cortney J. Jessup, Lloyd Edwards, G. Alex Hishaw, Emily J. Van Etten, Theodore P. Trouard, David Geldmacher, Virginia G. Wadley, Noam Alperin, Eric S. Porges, Adam J. Woods, Ron A. Cohen, Bonnie E. Levin, Tatjana Rundek, Gene E. Alexander, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Impact of Deprivation and Preferential Usage on Functional Connectivity Between Early Visual Cortex and Category-Selective Visual Regions
papers.abstract: The study tests whether, after central vision loss, the brain preferentially routes information from the retinal region patients use instead of the lost fovea. Connectivity between early visual cortex and face-, place- and other category-selective regions differs depending on whether the retinotopic sector is deprived or preferentially used. It shows that both loss and compensatory use shape large-scale visual networks.
papers.authors: Leland L. Fleming, Matthew K. Defenderfer, Pinar Demirayak, Paul Stewart, Dawn K. DeCarlo, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Constraining the Possible Mechanisms Underlying Performance Improvements Following Peripheral Vision Training
papers.abstract: Using a gaze-contingent simulated scotoma, the study tests whether training peripheral vision improves performance by changing habitual, exogenous or endogenous attention. Gains were consistent with increased habitual attention to the trained location, while dynamic attention improvements transferred to untrained locations. This narrows the possible mechanisms behind retinotopically specific learning after central vision loss.
papers.authors: Mandy K. Biles, Marcello Maniglia, Ishant S. Yadav, Paul D. Stewart, Brody C. DeSilva, Kristina M. Visscher

papers.title: Cortical plasticity in central vision loss: Cortical thickness and neurite structure
papers.abstract: In late-stage macular degeneration, cortex tied to the lesion is deprived while cortex tied to the preferred retinal locus is used more. The paper measures cortical thickness and neurite-related microstructure in these regions to see how structure changes with deprivation and increased use. It provides structural evidence for use- and deprivation-dependent plasticity in adult visual cortex.
papers.authors: Matthew K. Defenderfer, Pinar Demirayak, Leland L. Fleming, Dawn K. DeCarlo, Paul Stewart, Kristina M. Visscher

0380.name: Krystel Huxlin
0380.bio: Krystel Huxlin is the James V. Aquavella Professor of Ophthalmology at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the capacity for repair and neuroplasticity in the damaged adult visual system. Huxlin’s research utilizes psychophysical training paradigms, non-invasive brain stimulation, and advanced perimetry to develop rehabilitation strategies for patients with cortical blindness resulting from stroke. In the field of physiological optics, they work on the development of non-surgical laser refractive index change (LIRIC). Huxlin also studies the molecular mechanisms underlying corneal wound healing and nerve regeneration.
0380.research_direction: Dr. Huxlin has recently been investigating visual plasticity and rehabilitation following primary visual cortex (V1) damage, alongside distinct research into the cellular mechanisms of corneal fibrosis. Their recent work explores how perceptual retraining can recover visual processing in the cortically blind field of occipital stroke patients, focusing on functional limitations like contrast sensitivity and the spatial specificity of perceptual learning. To optimize clinical interventions, they are testing whether exogenous spatial attention cues can accelerate rehabilitation by promoting learning transfer to deeper, untrained blind-field locations, while also using longitudinal perimetry to track the natural baseline evolution of these visual field defects over time. Furthermore, their research extends to the anterior eye, where they have been exploring how manipulating mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic states in corneal myofibroblasts might provide new therapeutic targets for treating fibrosis and scarring.

papers.title: What V1 Damage Can Teach Us About Visual Perception and Learning
papers.abstract: Reviews what is known about adults who lose conscious vision after occipital stroke damages primary visual cortex, and how perceptual retraining in the blind field can bring back lost abilities despite the long-held view that such damage is irreversible. Summarizes the main training approaches, the mechanistic insights they have provided about residual visual processing and plasticity, and the current limitations and opportunities for clinical translation.
papers.authors: Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Exogenous Spatial Attention Helps Overcome Spatial Specificity of Visual Learning in the Blind Field After V1 Damage
papers.abstract: Training in cortically blind fields usually improves performance only near the trained location, so recovering vision deeper in the field takes months. Here, twenty patients trained on global motion discrimination with or without exogenous spatial-attention pre-cues placed deep in the blind field. Cues induced transfer of learning to deeper locations in over half of participants, at the cost of somewhat smaller gains at the primary location, suggesting attention can be used to accelerate rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Marisa Carrasco, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Evolution of Visual Field Defects After Occipital Stroke: A Quantitative Analysis
papers.abstract: Retrospective chart review of 73 hemianopia patients with repeated, reliable Humphrey perimetry quantifying how visual field defects change over time after occipital stroke. More than three quarters improved spontaneously in the first six months, especially those with partial defects, while chronic-phase measurements were mostly stable although about half still shifted by more than 1 dB. The work provides an empirical baseline against which rehabilitation effects can be judged.
papers.authors: Elizabeth L. Saionz, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Brent A. Johnson, Donald Harrington, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Limited Restoration of Contrast Sensitivity with Training after V1 Damage in Humans
papers.abstract: Tests whether luminance contrast sensitivity for orientation and motion direction discrimination is preserved in the blind field of subacute and chronic V1-stroke patients, and whether training can improve it. Training raised contrast sensitivity more often in subacute than chronic patients, but nobody reached normal sensitivity even with flicker or motion added. This indicates contrast sensitivity is a fundamental limit on restoration, unlike the near-complete recovery of high-contrast discrimination.
papers.authors: Jingyi Yang, Elizabeth L. Saionz, Matthew R. Cavanaugh, Berkeley K. Fahrenthold, Michael D. Melnick, Duje Tadin, Farran Briggs, Marisa Carrasco, Krystel R. Huxlin

papers.title: Manipulating mitochondrial pyruvate carrier function causes metabolic remodeling in corneal myofibroblasts that ameliorates fibrosis
papers.abstract: Examines how blocking the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, with troglitazone or UK5099, changes metabolism and epigenetic state in TGF-beta-treated corneal fibroblasts turning into myofibroblasts. A metabolic shift alone did not drive loss of the myofibroblast phenotype; instead sustained carbon flux into the Krebs cycle appeared prioritized over proline synthesis for collagen, and higher acetyl-CoA and histone acetylation pointed to downstream epigenetic remodeling. The findings identify metabolic targets for treating corneal fibrosis.
papers.authors: Kye-Im Jeon, Ankita Kumar, Paul S. Brookes, Keith Nehrke, Krystel R. Huxlin

0381.name: Lana M. Trick
0381.lab_name: DRiVE Lab (Driving Research in Virtual Environments)
0381.bio: Lana M. Trick is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Guelph and the director of the Driving Research in Virtual Environments (DRiVE) Lab. Trick’s research examines the mechanisms of visual attention and memory, focusing on how these operations change across the lifespan and in neurodivergent populations such as those with ADHD or autism. Using driving simulators, Trick investigates the impact of cognitive load, distraction, and vehicle technologies on collision risk and driver performance. Their work also provides data on spatial enumeration processes, including subitizing and multiple-object tracking, to identify the capacities and limitations of human visual processing.
0381.research_direction: Dr. Trick has recently been investigating the allocation of visual attention and cognitive resources across both applied transportation contexts and basic visual cognition paradigms. Their applied work uses high-fidelity driving simulators, eye-tracking, and physiological measures to explore how hazard perception and vehicle control are affected by internal states like unintentional mind-wandering, external cognitive loads such as complex audiobooks, and neurodivergent sensory processing in autistic drivers. Their recent basic research utilizes dual-task paradigms to examine the cognitive architecture shared between multiple-object tracking (MOT) and visually guided touch. Specifically, they are testing whether spatial indexing mechanisms—such as those proposed by the FINST framework—compete for the same representational resources as the preparation and execution of reaching movements.

papers.title: Multiple-Object Tracking and Visually Guided Touch: Dual-Task Interference Reveals Distinct Effects of Target Indexing and Target Report Method
papers.abstract: Building on Pylyshyn's proposal that the same indexing mechanism supports both tracking moving targets and directing actions to them, this study asks why tracking and touching interfere. Participants touched items that changed colour during tracking while the way they reported the tracked targets afterward (touching versus a different response) was manipulated, separating competition for a shared item-individuation resource from mere similarity between motor responses. The results show that indexing and response-method effects are distinct contributions to dual-task interference.
papers.authors: Mallory E. Terry, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Multiple-object tracking in displays where each item is unique: Do competing organizations impair the ability to track targets that share a common colour or shape?
papers.abstract: Featural grouping has been proposed to automatically help or hinder multiple-object tracking depending on whether targets share features with distractors. Here participants tracked four targets among sixteen items, comparing identical items with displays where every item was a unique colour-shape combination that created competing colour and shape groupings. The work tests whether grouping benefits survive when groupings conflict, bearing on how automatic featural grouping really is.
papers.authors: Rachel A. Eng, Jessica Swayze, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Does a “wait-and-search” strategy account for the item heterogeneity benefit in multiple object tracking?
papers.abstract: Tracking is often easier when items are visually distinct than when identical. This paper evaluates whether that benefit arises from a strategy of waiting and then searching for targets rather than continuous tracking, using behavioral manipulations to test the account against alternatives.
papers.authors: Rachel A. Eng, Naseem Al-Aidroos, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Driving performance is better predicted by unintentional rather than intentional mind-wandering in high density traffic
papers.abstract: Using a driving simulator, this study compares intentional and unintentional mind-wandering and how each relates to driving performance across traffic densities. Unintentional mind-wandering emerges as the better predictor of poorer driving in dense traffic, suggesting that not all lapses of attention carry equal risk.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Heather E. K. Walker, Lana M. Trick

papers.title: Easy listening or driving distraction? The relationship between audiobook complexity level and driving performance on simple routes
papers.abstract: Drivers in a simulator listened to audiobooks of differing complexity while driving simple routes, testing whether cognitive load from listening degrades vehicle control and hazard response. It addresses the common assumption that passive audio is harmless distraction-wise.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: Jessica M. Kespe, Lana M. Trick

0382.name: Lars F Muckli
0382.bio: Lars F Muckli is a Professor of Visual and Cognitive Neurosciences and Director of fMRI at the University of Glasgow's Centre for Cognitive Neuroimaging. Muckli’s research examines the predictive processing framework, investigating how internal models and cortical feedback modulate sensory perception in the early visual cortex. They use high-resolution, layer-specific fMRI techniques at ultra-high fields (7T) to isolate top-down signals in the superficial layers of the primary visual cortex. Their work combines neuroimaging with computational modeling to identify the mechanisms by which the brain anticipates visual input and processes contextual information.
0382.research_direction: Dr. Muckli has recently been investigating the dynamics of predictive processing and top-down feedback in the early visual cortex. Using techniques like multivariate decoding and high-resolution laminar 7T fMRI, their recent work explores how V1 integrates incoming sensory evidence with various internal priors, such as surrounding scene context and self-generated actions. They are also examining the cortical architecture of internally generated experiences to determine whether mental imagery and visual illusions rely on distinct layer-specific feedback pathways. Additionally, their research probes the limits of cross-modal processing, specifically testing whether auditory inputs still evoke decodable activity patterns in the primary visual cortex of aphantasic individuals who lack voluntary visual imagery.

papers.title: The effects of action-based predictions in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: An fMRI study that pits four theories of how self-generated actions change visual processing against each other: forward model, pre-activation, sharpening and opposing processes. Predicted grating orientation was decodable from early visual cortex before stimulus onset in both active and passive conditions, and self-triggered stimuli evoked larger rather than smaller BOLD responses. The pattern best fits the opposing-processes account and argues against simple suppression.
papers.authors: Bianca M. van Kemenade, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Context-sensitive V1 activity that depends on both coherence and surprise
papers.abstract: This 2026 study examines how activity in primary visual cortex reflects the surrounding context of a scene or stimulus. It reports that context-sensitive V1 responses depend jointly on how coherent the context is and on how surprising the input is, rather than on either factor alone. The work fits with the lab's account of cortical feedback and predictive processing, and is co-authored with W. A. Phillips on context-sensitive pyramidal cell theory.
papers.authors: Zirui Zhang, Clement Abbatecola, Angus T. Paton, Christiaan N. Levelt, William A. Phillips, Lucy S. Petro, Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Priors, evidence, and memory: Dynamics of predictive processing in a hierarchical visual system
papers.abstract: A single-author synthesis of the lab's work on how the visual hierarchy combines memory-based priors with incoming sensory evidence. It integrates findings on cortical feedback to V1, layer-specific signals and time-distant mnemonic information into a dynamic predictive processing account, and outlines open questions for the framework.
papers.authors: Lars F. Muckli

papers.title: Cortical depth profiles in primary visual cortex for illusory and imaginary experiences
papers.abstract: Using laminar 7T fMRI in two studies, the authors asked whether illusory percepts and mental imagery leave distinct signatures across cortical depth in V1. Imagery content could be decoded mainly from deep layers, whereas illusory content was decodable mainly from superficial layers. Illusory content also shared information with veridical perception, while imagery content did not generalise to either, indicating partly separate feedback pathways for 'real-seeming' versus internally generated experiences.
papers.authors: Johanna Bergmann, Lucy S. Petro, Clement Abbatecola, Min S. Li, A. Tyler Morgan, Lars Muckli

papers.title: Decoding sound content in the early visual cortex of aphantasic participants
papers.abstract: The study asks whether people without voluntary visual imagery still show cross-modal feedback into early visual cortex. Listening to natural sounds produced decodable activity patterns in early visual cortex of aphantasic participants, at levels comparable to controls. This suggests that auditory-driven feedback to V1 does not depend on the ability to consciously visualise.
papers.authors: Belén M. Montabes de la Cruz, Clement Abbatecola, Roberto S. Luciani, Angus T. Paton, Johanna Bergmann, Petra Vetter, Lucy S. Petro, Lars F. Muckli

0383.name: Laura Dugué
0383.bio: Laura Dugué is a Professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience whose research examines the periodic nature of human perception and attention. Utilizing a multimodal framework that integrates EEG, MEG, fMRI, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Dugué investigates how brain oscillations and traveling waves organize information sampling across the visual field. Their work provides causal evidence for the role of alpha and theta rhythms in attentional selection. This research is supported by the ERC-funded SAMPLING project and an appointment to the Institut Universitaire de France.
0383.research_direction: Dr. Dugué has recently been investigating the large-scale spatial dynamics of cortical oscillations, with a particular focus on how macroscopic traveling waves and neural rhythms support visual cognition. Their recent work explores how to reliably detect and characterize these propagating waves across different spatial scales using diverse human recording methods, including intracranial stereotactic EEG and model-based MEG-EEG approaches informed by fMRI retinotopy. To understand the functional role of these dynamics, they are testing the causal links between anterior-to-posterior traveling waves and inter-areal communication during visual search using combinations of double-pulse TMS and EEG. Additionally, Dr. Dugué is examining how specific oscillatory signatures relate to attentional processes, parsing whether theta rhythms uniquely index the active exploration of visual space while alpha rhythms reflect sustained attention.

papers.title: Traveling waves support rhythmic attentional search
papers.abstract: Whether large-scale cortical traveling waves play a causal role in cognition has been largely untested. The authors used double-pulse TMS over right frontal eye field to induce anterior-to-posterior theta traveling waves detectable with EEG during a visual search task. The strength of induced waves varied rhythmically with stimulation latency, and behavioral search performance followed the same rhythm, giving causal evidence that global waves support inter-areal communication in attention.
papers.authors: Yue Kong, Kirsten Petras, Philippe Marque, Rufin VanRullen, David M. Alexander, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Theta Oscillations Selectively Support Attentional Exploration of Space
papers.abstract: Using EEG and a cueing paradigm, the study tested whether theta oscillations index attentional exploration across both spatial and feature dimensions. Decoding of the cued dimension showed alpha rhythms for sustained attention regardless of dimension, but theta only when locations were being explored. Post-stimulus theta power also rose when attention had to reorient and predicted performance, indicating theta is specific to spatial exploration.
papers.authors: Mehdi Senoussi, Laurie Galas, Niko A. Busch, Laura Dugué

papers.title: The dominance of large-scale phase dynamics in human cortex, from delta to gamma
papers.abstract: The authors estimate the spatial frequency spectrum of cortical phase dynamics using stereotactic EEG to quantify the poorly known large-scale range. They find that phase organization is dominated by large spatial scales across frequency bands from delta to gamma, and assess how much scalp recordings can resolve of it. This supports the relevance of global traveling waves for inter-areal communication.
papers.authors: David M. Alexander, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Traveling Waves in the Human Visual Cortex: An MEG-EEG Model-Based Approach
papers.abstract: Detecting cortical traveling waves with MEG or EEG is hard because sensor signals mix many sources and no ground truth exists. The authors built a model-based approach in which propagating oscillations are simulated in V1 using fMRI retinotopic maps, projected to sensors, and compared with measured MEG-EEG responses to a rotating stimulus. The results indicate that traveling waves in visual cortex can be reliably identified non-invasively and their propagation characterized.
papers.authors: Laetitia Grabot, Garance Merholz, Jonathan Winawer, David J. Heeger, Laura Dugué

papers.title: Traveling waves across scales: Different mechanisms but same canonical computation?
