papers.abstract: This review-style theoretical article proposes that traveling wave patterns seen at different cortical scales arise from distinct generative mechanisms, which it categorizes as first- and second-order waves. It argues that despite differing origins, waves at all scales serve a canonical computation, ordering neuronal processing to impose a computational syntax. The framework yields testable predictions at mechanistic and functional levels.
papers.authors: Laura Dugué, Frédéric Chavane

0384.name: Laura Lewis
0384.department: Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES); Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
0384.bio: Lewis develops multimodal neuroimaging technologies to investigate the neural and physiological mechanisms governing sleep and arousal states. Their research integrates fast fMRI, electroencephalography, and computational signal processing to characterize subsecond brain dynamics and the activity of deep subcortical circuits. Lewis identified synchronized cerebrospinal fluid flow during sleep, a process that facilitates metabolic waste clearance and brain maintenance. Their current work examines how these neural and fluid dynamics are modulated by sensory inputs and how they are altered in neurological and psychiatric disorders.
0384.research_direction: Dr. Lewis has recently been investigating the deeply interconnected dynamics of neural activity, vascular hemodynamics, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow across different states of arousal. Their recent work explores how neural rhythms, such as sleep slow waves, drive macroscopic fluid movement in the human brain, examining both how these mechanisms degrade with aging and how they can be causally manipulated using closed-loop auditory stimulation. Beyond sleep, they are utilizing simultaneous fast fMRI and EEG to map these neurovascular and fluid interactions during wakefulness, testing whether targeted visual stimulation can directly drive large-scale CSF flow. Additionally, they are applying machine learning to predict electrophysiological rhythms from brainwide hemodynamics and probing how coordinated, system-wide shifts in neural and fluid physiology give rise to attentional lapses following sleep deprivation.

papers.title: Closed-loop auditory stimulation in phase with slow waves during sleep enhances cerebrospinal fluid flow in humans
papers.abstract: The team built a system that delivers sounds locked to EEG slow waves during sleep while the person lies inside an MRI scanner, using real-time denoising and a neural-network targeting strategy. Stimulation increased slow waves and evoked larger waves of CSF flow, but only when sounds were aligned to slow-wave peaks, and it also produced widespread hemodynamic waves. This provides causal evidence that neural slow waves drive CSF flow and a tool for modulating it.
papers.authors: Joshua Levitt, Xiangjian Zeng, Zinong Yang, Leandro P. L. Jacob, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: Attentional failures after sleep deprivation are locked to joint neurovascular, pupil and cerebrospinal fluid flow dynamics
papers.abstract: Using simultaneous fast fMRI and EEG in sleep-deprived people, the study shows that lapses of attention during wakefulness coincide with a coordinated brain-and-body event: neural activity shifts, pupil constriction, and pulses of cerebrospinal fluid flow. The CSF pulsations follow the attentional impairment, consistent with a vascular mechanism governed by neuromodulatory state. The authors propose that sleep-deprivation lapses reflect an irrepressible need for a rest-like state driven by a system that regulates both neuronal and fluid physiology.
papers.authors: Zinong Yang, Stephanie D. Williams, Ewa Beldzik, Stephanie Anakwe, Emilia Schimmelpfennig, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: The aging human brain exhibits reduced cerebrospinal fluid flow during sleep due to both neural and vascular factors
papers.abstract: Combining fast fMRI and EEG during overnight sleep in young and older adults, the study finds that sleep-related CSF flow is smaller in older adults, tied to weaker frontal delta power and global hemodynamic oscillations. Daytime sensory and vasoactive experiments show both neural and cerebrovascular changes contribute, and lower CSF flow is associated with gray matter atrophy.
papers.authors: Sydney M. Bailes, Stephanie D. Williams, Baarbod Ashenagar, Joseph Licata, Massinissa Y. Bosli, Brandon J. Dormes, Hannah J. Yun, Dabriel Zimmerman, Alejandra Hernandez Moyers, David H. Salat, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: Brainwide hemodynamics predict EEG neural rhythms across sleep and wakefulness in humans
papers.abstract: Using simultaneous EEG and fast fMRI in people who fell asleep in the scanner, the authors trained a machine-learning model that predicts fluctuations in alpha and delta EEG power from fMRI in held-out subjects. The approach maps which regions and networks carry the information, with alpha tied to arousal- and visual-related networks and delta spread broadly across cortex.
papers.authors: Leandro P. L. Jacob, Sydney M. Bailes, Stephanie D. Williams, Carsen Stringer, Laura D. Lewis

papers.title: Neural activity induced by sensory stimulation can drive large-scale cerebrospinal fluid flow during wakefulness in humans
papers.abstract: The authors drove neural activity with a flickering visual checkerboard and observed macroscopic CSF flow in the human brain, with timing and amplitude matched to the evoked hemodynamic response. This indicates neural activity can modulate CSF flow through neurovascular coupling, extending earlier sleep observations to a causal test during wakefulness.
papers.authors: Stephanie D. Williams, Beverly Setzer, Nina E. Fultz, Zenia Valdiviezo, Nicole Tacugue, Zachary Diamandis, Laura D. Lewis

0386.name: Laure Pisella
0386.bio: Laure Pisella is a CNRS researcher at the Lyon Neuroscience Research Center (CRNL) who studies the neural substrates of human action and perception. Pisella’s work focuses on the role of the posterior parietal cortex in visuomotor integration and the mechanisms of optic ataxia, hemispatial neglect, and Bálint syndrome. Using clinical neuropsychology, eye-tracking, and prism adaptation, they investigate how the brain processes spatial information for motor control and maintains visual stability during trans-saccadic remapping. Their current research explores the influence of aging on the distribution of spatial attention and the competitive mechanisms underlying target selection in the visual periphery.
0386.research_direction: Dr. Pisella has recently been investigating how the dorsal visual stream integrates spatial, attentional, and peripheral inputs to guide motor action, spatial cognition, and reading. Their recent work explores visuomotor transformations in peripheral vision, utilizing spatial cueing paradigms to examine how pointing hypometria is modulated by covert attention. It also explores visual field loss and attentional field utilizing gaze-contingent masking, and specialized sensorimotor expertise like juggling. In clinical contexts, they are studying the real-world impact of visual crowding and stimulus eccentricity on functional visual acuity in patients with Posterior Cortical Atrophy.

papers.title: Attentional modulation of size perception in peripheral vision
papers.abstract: Objects look smaller the further into the periphery they are, a bias tied to cortical magnification. Using a size-comparison task with predictive arrow cues at three eccentricities, the study shows that valid endogenous attention substantially reduces this underestimation, especially far out, and sharpens discrimination. Misplaced attention worsens the bias in a way that resembles optic ataxia, leading the authors to propose that dorsal parietal regions rescale peripheral representations.
papers.authors: Tristan Jurkiewicz, Alexandre Foncelle, Yaffa Yeshurun, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Dorsal Posterior Parietal Cortex Lesions Disrupt Spatial- but Not Motor-Based Inhibition
papers.abstract: Two stroke patients with unilateral or bilateral dorsal posterior parietal damage and 21 matched controls performed saccade tasks separating spatial inhibition (inhibition of return) from motor response inhibition (stop-signal). Patients lost inhibition of return in their ataxic hemifields yet stopped movements normally. This is a clean dissociation implicating dorsal parietal cortex in spatial attention-based inhibition rather than motor inhibition.
papers.authors: Julie Ouerfelli-Ethier, Tristan Jurkiewicz, Isabella Comtois-Bona, Thomas Carrier, Aarlenne Z. Khan, Laure Pisella

papers.title: From Visual Attention to Literacy: Symbol Search Deficit Predicts Future Reading Difficulties From Age 3
papers.abstract: A visual search screening test contrasting symbol search with colour search yields a 'Temporal Gap' index of visuo-attentional fragility. In a longitudinal cohort screened in kindergarten and reassessed in third grade, the index predicted later reading performance from as early as age 3. Children with a pathological score at age 3 were about 5.7 times more likely to have later reading difficulty, offering lead time for early intervention.
papers.authors: Audrey Vialatte, Eric Chabanat, Pierre-Emmanuel Aguera, Agnes Witko, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Attentional modulation of peripheral pointing hypometria in healthy participants: An insight into optic ataxia?
papers.abstract: Optic ataxia after superior parietal/intraparietal damage produces pointing that undershoots targets in the affected peripheral field. This study asks whether that bias reflects impaired attention by manipulating cue validity while healthy participants and two patients pointed to peripheral targets. Without endogenous attention, healthy participants showed an eccentricity-underestimation bias reminiscent of optic ataxia, suggesting the deficit partly stems from impaired attentional orienting.
papers.authors: Tristan Jurkiewicz, Audrey Vialatte, Yaffa Yeshurun, Laure Pisella

papers.title: Validation of a screening test based on symbols visual search to detect visuo-attentionnal reading difficulties
papers.abstract: A quick visual search test compares finding a target among symbols versus among colours, giving an age-standardised 'Temporal Gap' index. Tested on 2015 children aged 3 to 11, it was feasible from kindergarten and reliable on retest. In 769 fourth and fifth graders the index correlated with reading speed and errors, flagging severe reading-efficiency deficits with moderate sensitivity and good specificity.
papers.authors: Audrey Vialatte, Eric Chabanat, Agnes Witko, Laure Pisella

0387.name: Laurence Harris
0387.bio: Laurence R. Harris is Professor Emeritus of Psychology at York University, associated with the Multisensory Integration Laboratory and the Centre for Vision Research. Harris is not taking on any students or postdocs. Their research investigates how the brain synthesizes visual, vestibular, and somatosensory information to maintain a sense of self-motion, body orientation, and the "perceptual upright." Employing methodologies such as virtual reality, parabolic flights for microgravity simulation, and specialized apparatuses like the "Tumbling Room," Harris explores human adaptation to unusual gravitational and sensory environments. Their work extends to the temporal aspects of perception, examining how the brain synchronizes disparate sensory signals to create a unified experience of the world.
0387.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been investigating how gravity, vestibular signals, and visual motion shape human spatial and temporal perception. Their recent work explores how altered gravitational states—studied using microgravity exposure in astronauts, supine terrestrial postures, and galvanic vestibular stimulation—affect a variety of perceptual phenomena, including multisensory duration perception, estimates of object height, and the prediction of parabolic object motion. Additionally, they are utilizing novel continuous psychophysics paradigms in virtual reality to examine the temporal dynamics and precision of heading perception through optic flow. By manipulating environmental and physiological cues to self-motion and gravity, Dr. Harris seeks to disentangle how the brain relies on online vestibular feedback versus learned terrestrial priors to interpret the physical world.

papers.title: No Evidence for a Vestibular Contribution to Object Motion Prediction
papers.abstract: Observers predict the motion of objects better when it is consistent with gravity, and this study asks whether that reflects a learned Earth-gravity prior or on-line vestibular gravity signals. In virtual reality, participants judged when a ball on a normal (1g) or inverted (-1g) parabola would return to launch height while standing or supine, and with disruptive galvanic vestibular stimulation or sham. Surprisingly, performance was no better for 1g than -1g and vestibular manipulations had no significant effect.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: The Vestibular System Influences the Perceived Duration of Lights But Not of Sounds or Touches
papers.abstract: Using a new psychometric procedure with adaptive staircases, the study measured how long a 'one second' visual, auditory or tactile event is judged to be while changing the reliability of gravity cues via posture or galvanic vestibular stimulation. Auditory and tactile durations were unaffected, but a visual second was perceived about 45 ms longer when supine or under disruptive vestibular stimulation than when upright or sham. The result links vestibular/gravity signals to time perception in vision specifically.
papers.authors: Fatemeh Ghasemi, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: Can visual acceleration evoke a sensation of tilt?
papers.abstract: Twelve astronauts on long-duration missions on the International Space Station, plus Earth controls in upright and supine postures, viewed visually simulated linear acceleration in a virtual corridor and then adjusted a virtual ground plane to report any change in perceived orientation. The hypothesis that visual acceleration could act as an artificial gravity cue was not supported: no systematic tilt was induced in microgravity or on Earth. The study did replicate that microgravity and supine posture both make judgements of upright more variable.
papers.authors: Laurence R. Harris, Björn Jörges, Nils-Alexander Bury, Meaghan McManus, Ambika Bansal, Robert S. Allison, Michael Jenkin

papers.title: Precision and temporal dynamics in heading perception assessed by continuous psychophysics
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a continuous-psychophysics approach in virtual reality in which observers use a joystick to track a randomly walking heading direction through optic flow for 90 seconds at a time. Faster and denser optic flow reduced variability, as expected, and, using cross-correlogram and Kalman-filter analyses, also made observers respond faster. This provides the first empirical support for model predictions that richer optic flow speeds up processing, and validates the method for studying the time course of self-motion perception.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Ambika Bansal, Laurence R. Harris

papers.title: The impact of gravity on perceived object height
papers.abstract: Twelve astronauts judged the height of a virtual square against a hand-held reference before, during and after a stay on the ISS, alongside supine and seated tests on Earth and Earth-bound controls. Microgravity exposure had no immediate effect, but astronauts systematically underestimated height, more so 60+ days after returning to Earth, and supine posture also reduced perceived height in controls. Precision was unchanged, and the authors explored sex/gender differences.
papers.authors: Björn Jörges, Nils-Alexander Bury, Meaghan McManus, Ambika Bansal, Robert S. Allison, Michael Jenkin, Laurence R. Harris

0388.name: Laurent Madelain
0388.department: SCALab (UMR 9193 CNRS-Université de Lille), Faculty of Psychology; team AVA (Action, Vision et Apprentissage)
0388.bio: Laurent Madelain is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Lille and serves as the Deputy Director of the SCALab research unit. Madelain’s research focuses on the operant control of human eye movements, specifically investigating how saccades and smooth pursuit are modulated by their consequences rather than acting solely as reflexive responses. Utilizing psychophysical methodologies and reinforcement paradigms, they explore the mechanisms through which motor patterns emerge from environmental contingencies and biological constraints. Madelain's current work examines the role of motor planning in contextual adaptation and the influence of reinforcement on sensorimotor variability and active vision.
0388.research_direction: Dr. Madelain has recently been investigating the mechanisms of oculomotor learning, specifically exploring the boundary conditions of contextual saccade adaptation. Using a double-step paradigm, their recent work examines which types of cues—ranging from motor and spatial signals to visual, auditory, and statistical features—can successfully guide simultaneous adaptations to different intrasaccadic target shifts, probing the dissociation between conscious perceptual awareness and automatic motor updating. Alongside these fundamental studies of sensorimotor control, they have also been developing open-source methodological tools to advance web-based vision science. To this end, Dr. Madelain recently introduced a Python-based framework designed to facilitate complex online behavioral experiments utilizing Bayesian adaptive psychophysical measurement procedures like QUEST+.

papers.title: PyBOLE – A General Python Based Framework for Behavioral Online Experiments: A Case Study Using the QUEST+ Adaptive Method
papers.abstract: PyBOLE is an open-source, Django-based Python framework for building and deploying fully programmable online behavioral experiments with controlled stimulus presentation and response collection. It integrates Bayesian adaptive psychophysics through the QUEST+ procedure and reduces the JavaScript development normally needed for web experiments. A case study demonstrates its use for adaptive psychophysical measurement online.
papers.authors: Vasiliki Myrodia, Jérôme Buisine, Samuel Delepoulle, Laurent Madelain

papers.title: Ineffective cues for contextual saccade adaptation
papers.abstract: Using a contextual double-step paradigm in which two directions of intrasaccadic target steps are signalled by different cues, the study tests nine kinds of contextual cue for driving two simultaneous saccadic adaptations. Only motor-related cues (first-step amplitude, target starting location) produced robust contextual learning, whereas color, shape, symbolic, auditory, timing and statistical cues did not. Participants could accurately report the nonmotor cues yet still failed to adapt, showing a dissociation between perceptual report and oculomotor learning and implying that the saccadic system selectively learns from spatially relevant cues.
papers.authors: Maxime Martel, Laurent Madelain

0389.name: Laurie M. Wilcox
0389.department: Department of Psychology, Faculty of Health
0389.bio: Laurie M. Wilcox is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at York University and a core member of the Centre for Vision Research. As the York Research Chair in 3D Vision, Wilcox investigates the neural mechanisms underlying stereoscopic depth perception and surface interpolation using psychophysical methodologies. Their research addresses the role of disparity in 3D shape perception, the integration of depth cues in complex environments, and the evaluation of image quality in stereoscopic displays. Wilcox also serves as the Scientific Director of the Vision: Science to Applications (VISTA) program.
0389.research_direction: Dr. Wilcox has recently been investigating human depth perception and spatial vision, with a primary focus on how sensory cues interact in both natural and mixed-reality environments. Their recent work explores depth cue conflicts in augmented reality, specifically examining how mismatches between metric cues like binocular disparity or motion parallax and ordinal cues like occlusion influence distance perception and visually-guided motor action. To model these phenomena, they utilize behavioral distance-matching paradigms, active reaching tasks, and Bayesian cue-combination frameworks. Broadening the scope of their applied spatial vision research, they are also investigating aviation-related visual illusions, utilizing flight simulators to assess how factors like mental rotation ability and sex influence pilot susceptibility to the "black hole" spatial disorientation phenomenon during night approaches.

papers.title: Reexamining the Relationship Between Stereopsis and Motion Parallax
papers.abstract: A review of how binocular disparity and motion parallax, which share geometric foundations, differ in practice. Disparity generally gives finer discrimination and more accurate depth magnitudes, while parallax is hampered by head movement and scene motion. Cue-combination studies show nonlinear interactions with stereopsis often dominant, and the authors relate this to immersive displays where head tracking and optical mismatches distort perceived depth.
papers.authors: Laurie M. Wilcox, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Depth Cue Conflicts Between Real and Virtual Objects Disrupt Visually-Guided Reaching in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: Participants placed a virtual ring around real or virtual posts at varying distances in an AR headset. Placements on real posts were less accurate because virtual object distances were systematically underestimated relative to real ones. The distortion persisted during active reaching despite disparity, proprioception, occlusion and motion parallax being available, which matters for AR design.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Conflicting ordinal and metric depth information interferes with depth matching
papers.abstract: A HoloLens 2 virtual letter was superimposed on a physical occluder of variable transparency while observers matched its depth. Placing the letter beyond the surface caused progressive distance underestimation, scaled by occluder opacity and surviving added retinal size cues. A Bayesian cue-combination model with a non-uniform prior for positions beyond the surface accounted for the data.
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Jonathan Tong, Robert S. Allison, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Visual Illusions in Aviation: Simulating the Black Hole Phenomenon
papers.abstract: Trainee pilots flew approach-and-land scenarios in a Transport Canada Level 2 flight training device by day and night. Most flew shallow night approaches consistent with the black hole illusion, especially pilots with lower mental-rotation scores, and men showed smaller errors than women, regardless of flight experience. The results show the illusion can be reproduced in a relatively low-cost simulator for training.
papers.authors: Arleen Aksay, Brittney Hartle, Robert S. Allison, E. L. Irving, S. Jennings, Laurie M. Wilcox

papers.title: Misperception of the distance of virtual augmentations
papers.abstract: Using distance-matching and reaching tasks in AR both within and beyond arm's reach, the study tested how occlusion and binocular disparity combine when they conflict. Observers consistently underestimated the distance of a virtual letter rendered beyond a real surface, with errors growing with distance, even with proprioceptive feedback. The authors conclude designers must position virtual content carefully to avoid such errors.
papers.venue: IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces (VR)
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Robert S. Allison, Iroshini Gunasekera, Laurie M. Wilcox

0390.name: Leslie Carver
0390.bio: Leslie J. Carver is a Professor at UC San Diego who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying social cognition, memory, and reward processing during early development. Carver’s research utilizes event-related potentials (ERP) and longitudinal behavioral paradigms to study typically developing infants as well as those with or at risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). They focus on identifying neurophysiological markers of joint attention and predictive coding to evaluate the social motivation hypothesis and understand how early brain function shapes social trajectories.
0390.research_direction: Dr. Carver has recently been studying how infants make sense of the physical and social world during the first year of life. Their recent work explores whether babies as young as four to five months can use the motion of a colliding object to predict when the matching sound should occur, which probes their early intuitions about physical events. They also examine joint attention, the ability to share focus on an object with a caregiver, in infants with a family history of autism, asking how gaze-following and hand-following routes to shared attention develop across the first year.

papers.title: Infants Anticipate the Timing of Sounds From Dynamic Collision Events
papers.abstract: Dynamic visual motion regularly provides predictive sensory evidence that allows observers to forecast ensuing auditory consequences. This study examined whether infants between 4 and 5 months of age possess intuitive physical event representations enabling them to utilize dynamic visual trajectories to predict the precise temporal onset of collision sounds. In a moderated remote testing paradigm, looking times were assessed across two infant groups presented with an animated two-dimensional disk colliding with a barrier. One cohort observed alternating multimodal conditions manipulating audiovisual (AV) temporal congruence: an AV-synchronous condition where the auditory transient coincided with physical contact, and an AV-asynchronous condition where the auditory transient preceded collision. A second cohort viewed amodal visual control conditions in which the disk altered color either synchronously at barrier contact (visual color change; VCC synchronous) or asynchronously prior to contact (VCC asynchronous). Offline behavioral coding of looking times demonstrated that infants exhibited significantly increased fixation duration toward AV-asynchronous relative to AV-synchronous trials. This looking-time divergence was absent in the visual-only color-change control conditions. Additionally, infants displayed significantly longer looking times during AV-asynchronous events than during VCC-asynchronous events. These findings reveal that 4- to 5-month-old infants formulate precise temporal expectations regarding the alignment of kinematic collisions and resulting sounds, indicating that early crossmodal predictive frameworks operate to scaffold physical reasoning within multisensory environments.
papers.authors: Andrew Marin, Zara Fearns, Melanie Dratva, Lindsey J. Powell, Viola S. Störmer, Leslie J. Carver

papers.title: Multimodal pathways to joint attention in infants with a familial history of autism
papers.abstract: Joint attention (JA) is a foundational socio-communicative behavior emerging early in ontogeny that allows infants and adult caregivers to coordinate shared focus on an external referent. While disruptions in JA mediated by face-following pathways represent an early behavioral marker of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) detectable by 12 months, emerging evidence demonstrates that JA can also be successfully established via manual and hand-following pathways. This study examined the developmental dynamics of multimodal JA pathways in 6-, 9-, and 12-month-old infants with (FH+) and without (FH-) an elevated familial likelihood of ASD. Naturalistic caregiver-infant play interactions were recorded remotely in domestic settings and subjected to fine-grained offline behavioral coding of gaze directions and manual actions. The total cumulative duration of time spent in coordinated JA did not significantly differ between FH+ and FH- dyads. However, significant group differences emerged in the preparatory cues preceding JA episodes: caregivers of FH+ infants engaged in greater scaffolding behavior to establish triadic attention and relied more heavily on face-following than hand-following pathways relative to caregivers of FH- infants. These findings indicate that underlying infant motoric and sensorimotor variations alter the structure of multimodal interactive cues, suggesting that early motor differences can cascade into altered parent-infant social coordination.
papers.authors: Lauren M. Smith, Julia Yurkovic-Harding, Leslie J. Carver

0391.name: Leyla Isik
0391.lab_name: Isik JHU Computational Cognitive Neuroscience Lab
0391.bio: Leyla Isik is the Clare Boothe Luce Assistant Professor of Cognitive Science at Johns Hopkins University and directs a research program on the neural and computational basis of social vision. Isik's work examines how the human brain converts visual input into social representations, including the recognition of actions and complex social interactions. They employ a multi-disciplinary approach involving human neuroimaging with fMRI and MEG, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling such as deep neural networks and graph-based AI. Current research directions include studying the development of social perception in neurotypical and autistic populations and creating artificial intelligence systems designed to emulate human social intelligence.
0391.research_direction: Dr. Isik's recent work explores the computational and neural mechanisms underlying dynamic social vision, specifically investigating how humans so rapidly perceive and understand everyday social interactions. Using fMRI and naturalistic viewing paradigms in both children and adults, they have recently been mapping how relational and social action features are hierarchically organized along the lateral visual pathway toward the superior temporal sulcus. To formalize how the brain extracts this information, their research tests whether neural responses in core social and mentalizing regions are best modeled by fast, bottom-up computations—such as those captured by graph neural networks—or by generative inverse-planning models. Furthermore, they are investigating the current computational gaps between human behavior and artificial intelligence by evaluating whether modern deep learning models can successfully capture the explicit relational features, such as gaze and physical contact, that drive human social scene understanding.

papers.title: Bottom-up and generative computations uniquely explain neural responses across the social brain
papers.abstract: This preregistered fMRI study tests whether social perception regions (pSTS) run fast bottom-up computations while mentalizing regions (TPJ) run inverse-planning. Participants watched animated-shape social interactions, and responses were compared with a graph neural network and a generative inverse-planning model. Both models explained activity in both regions even after controlling for each other, with a later shift toward higher-order reasoning suggesting a temporal rather than spatial hierarchy.
papers.authors: Manasi Malik, Minjae Kim, Tianmin Shu, Shari Liu, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Modeling dynamic social vision highlights gaps between deep learning and humans
papers.abstract: The authors collected human similarity judgments on short videos of everyday social interactions and compared them with the outputs of hundreds of image, video, and language models. Human judgments were best predicted by a small set of social features, while most deep networks captured them poorly, with video models doing somewhat better than image models. Models that explicitly encode relational information such as gaze and contact did better, pointing to what current AI lacks in social scene understanding.
papers.authors: Kathy Garcia, Emalie McMahon, Colin Conwell, Michael F. Bonner, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Hierarchical organization of social action features along the lateral visual pathway
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while people watched naturalistic videos, the study mapped how features of social actions are represented across the brain. Low-level visual features were strongest in early visual cortex, while social and action features increasingly dominated along the lateral visual stream toward the STS. This supports a hierarchy in which social information is extracted within a dedicated visual pathway.
papers.authors: Emalie McMahon, Michael F. Bonner, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Early Neural Development of Social Interaction Perception: Evidence from Voxel-Wise Encoding in Young Children and Adults
papers.abstract: The study asks how the brain's social interaction representations develop by scanning young children and adults during naturalistic movie viewing. Voxel-wise encoding models show that social interaction features are already represented in the lateral visual/STS regions in young children, with development refining rather than creating these responses. This gives an early developmental picture of social perception in the human brain.
papers.authors: Elizabeth Jiwon Im, Angira Shirahatti, Leyla Isik

papers.title: Relational visual representations underlie human social interaction recognition
papers.abstract: Humans quickly recognize social interactions in simple animated scenes, and the authors ask what representations support this. They show that a graph neural network using relational information between agents predicts human behavior better than standard feedforward visual models. The results argue that relational, graph-like visual representations are key to social interaction recognition.
papers.authors: Manasi Malik, Leyla Isik

0392.name: Li Zhaoping
0392.department: Werner Reichardt Centre for Integrative Neuroscience (CIN)
0392.bio: Li is a professor at the University of Tübingen and a department head at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics. Li developed the V1 Saliency Hypothesis (V1SH), which posits that the primary visual cortex creates a bottom-up saliency map to guide exogenous visual attention. Their current research focuses on the Central-peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory, exploring how the brain manages an information bottleneck by specializing peripheral vision for gaze selection and central vision for object recognition. Li’s methodology integrates theoretical modeling with experimental techniques, including human psychophysics, fMRI, and electrophysiology in multiple species.
0392.research_direction: Dr. Li's recent work explores visual perception through the framework of an information bottleneck, investigating how the brain divides labor between peripheral "looking" and central "seeing." They have recently been examining how the primary visual cortex acts as more than a simple feature filter, questioning how V1 generates bottom-up saliency maps to guide peripheral gaze shifts while leaving detailed recognition to central vision. To probe the neural mechanisms underlying this dichotomy, their behavioral experiments employ psychophysical techniques like backward masking and random-dot stereograms to investigate top-down feedback and phenomena like the reversed depth illusion in the central visual field. Additionally, their recent theoretical research investigates whether this fundamental functional division between peripheral orienting and central recognition extends to multisensory processing across different species.

papers.title: Vision as looking and seeing through a bottleneck
papers.abstract: A short synthesis arguing that vision is best framed as looking and seeing through an information bottleneck: only a small fraction of retinal input gets recognized. Looking, done mostly by peripheral vision and gaze shifts driven by a V1 bottom-up saliency map, selects what enters the bottleneck, while seeing, mostly central vision aided by top-down feedback, recognizes it. The author calls for falsifiable theories linking behavior to neural substrates and for experiments that avoid forced fixation.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: What are the functions of primary visual cortex (V1)?
papers.abstract: Argues that V1 does more than Hubel-and-Wiesel feature filtering: it acts as a motor-like area that builds a bottom-up saliency map guiding saccades, it starts the visual information bottleneck, and it supplies extra information requested by top-down feedback that targets central-field representations. These roles are tied into the looking-and-seeing framework with peripheral versus central vision.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Testing the top-down feedback in the central visual field using the reversed depth illusion
papers.abstract: Tests a prediction of the central-peripheral dichotomy theory: the reversed depth illusion in random-dot stereograms is normally visible only in the periphery because central vision has feedback that vetoes it. Using backward masking to disrupt this feedback, the illusion becomes visible in central vision, supporting the feedback privilege of the central field and analysis-by-synthesis.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Peripheral vision is mainly for looking rather than seeing
papers.abstract: Reviews evidence that peripheral vision mainly serves looking (deciding where to shift gaze, often via a V1 saliency map and with limited awareness) rather than seeing. Peripheral vision is poor in resolution, prone to crowding and illusions, and lacks the top-down feedback that central vision enjoys, so saccades hand selected content over to central vision for recognition.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

papers.title: Peripheral and central sensation: multisensory orienting and recognition across species
papers.abstract: Extends the peripheral-versus-central dichotomy beyond vision, proposing that across senses and species, peripheral sensation orients the animal toward relevant stimuli while central sensation supports detailed recognition. It links this division to the information bottleneck and to differences in neural processing and feedback.
papers.authors: Li Zhaoping

0393.name: Liad Mudrik
0393.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0393.bio: Liad Mudrik is a researcher at Tel Aviv University who investigates the neural substrates and functional roles of conscious experience. Mudrik utilizes adversarial collaborations to compare theories of consciousness, such as Global Neuronal Workspace and Integrated Information Theory. Using psychophysics, EEG, and augmented reality, they explore how semantic knowledge shapes perception and whether consciousness is required for complex information integration and volition. Mudrik’s background in neuroscience and philosophy informs their work on the mind-body problem and the limits of unconscious processing.
0393.research_direction: Dr. Mudrik's recent work explores the boundaries of conscious awareness, with a strong focus on refining the methodological rigor of unconscious processing research and testing theories of consciousness. They have recently been developing novel psychophysical calibration methods to accurately estimate participant-specific subliminal thresholds, evaluating how trial-by-trial awareness reporting impacts unconscious response priming, and building large-scale meta-scientific databases to track how different visual suppression paradigms influence empirical outcomes and how theories of consciousness have been tested. Their research further investigates the neural correlates of consciousness. They also studied the cognitive penetrability of vision by probing whether high-level semantic priming can bi-directionally modulate low-level perceptual integration, such as the formation of illusory contours in the Kanizsa illusion. Additionally, they are examining the broader epistemological challenges of consciousness science, evaluating philosophical frameworks for attributing subjective experience to non-standard entities like artificial intelligence, animals, and neural organoids.

papers.title: On a confusion about there being two types of consciousness
papers.abstract: The paper takes on a proposal that there are two distinct types of consciousness and argues that it rests on a conceptual confusion between conditions for consciousness. The authors clarify how the conditions relate to one another and what empirical evidence would be needed to support any such distinction.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Nathan Faivre, Michael Pitts, Aaron Schurger

papers.title: Unpacking the complexities of consciousness: Theories and reflections
papers.abstract: Seven leading consciousness researchers, spanning the major theoretical camps, each lay out their theory and then respond to shared questions on what each theory explains and how it could be tested. The exchange highlights where the theories converge, where they truly conflict, and which empirical results might arbitrate between them. It serves as a snapshot of the state of the field and a guide for designing future adversarial tests.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Melanie Boly, Stanislas Dehaene, Stephen M. Fleming, Victor Lamme, Anil Seth, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: Studying unconscious processing: Contention and consensus
papers.abstract: A large group of researchers who disagree about unconscious processing worked together to find where they agree. They cover how to define and measure unawareness, which effects are robust, and which methodological pitfalls, such as regression to the mean and unreliable awareness measures, most often cause disputes. The paper offers shared recommendations for future studies.
papers.authors: François Stockart, Maor Schreiber, Pietro Amerio, David Carmel, Axel Cleeremans, Leon Y. Deouell, Zoltan Dienes, Patxi Elosegi, Surya Gayet, Alon Goldstein, Adelina-Mihaela Halchin, Guido Hesselmann, Ruth Kimchi, Dominique Lamy, Leyla Loued-Khenissi, Sascha Meyen, Nitzan Micher, Michael Pitts, Roy Salomon, Kristian Sandberg, Iris A. Schnepf, Aaron Schurger, David R. Shanks, David Soto, Amir Tal, Darinka Trübutschek, Miguel A. Vadillo, Simon van Gaal, Itay Yaron, Zefan Zheng, Nathan Faivre, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: Tests for consciousness in humans and beyond
papers.abstract: The authors ask how one can tell whether a system is conscious when it cannot report, as in infants, patients, animals or AI. They review candidate tests and argue for an iterative natural-kind strategy, in which tests are validated in humans and then cautiously extended to progressively different systems. The paper lays out a practical framework for building and refining such tests.
papers.authors: Tim Bayne, Anil K. Seth, Marcello Massimini, Joshua Shepherd, Axel Cleeremans, Stephen M. Fleming, Rafael Malach, Jason B. Mattingley, David K. Menon, Adrian M. Owen, Megan A.K. Peters, Adeel Razi, Liad Mudrik

papers.title: Taking consciousness for real: Increasing the ecological validity of the study of conscious vs. unconscious processes
papers.abstract: Most consciousness research uses simple, artificial stimuli and tasks, which may not generalize to real life. The authors argue for more ecologically valid paradigms, using richer and more naturalistic stimuli, tasks and settings such as virtual reality, and discuss how this would sharpen both theories and empirical findings on conscious versus unconscious processing.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Rony Hirschhorn, Uri Korisky

0394.name: Lihui Wang
0394.bio: Lihui Wang is an Associate Professor and Principal Investigator at Shanghai Jiao Tong University who researches the neural substrates of visual perception through the framework of enactive cognition. Wang’s work investigates how the interaction between the body and the environment shapes cognitive processes, focusing on the functional roles of eye-movement patterns in face recognition and emotional processing. By integrating multi-modal neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI, EEG, and MEG with machine learning, they develop diagnostic algorithms for psychiatric disorders and compare human embodied intelligence with artificial systems. Their recent research identifies dynamic representations of facial information in the human ventral pathway to characterize oculomotor-perceptual coupling.
0394.research_direction: Dr. Wang's recent work explores the active nature of visual perception, focusing on how sequential eye movements structurally guide information sampling during face processing. Using eye-tracking and MEG, they have recently been investigating the specific functional roles of early fixations and how top-down gaze representations are dynamically encoded along the ventral visual pathway. Their research probes oculomotor behavior across spatial scales, examining whether large-scale saccades and tiny microsaccades rely on shared sampling mechanisms when humans distinguish between visual categories. Beyond human neuroimaging, Dr. Wang is evaluating whether artificial neural networks, such as CNNs and Vision Transformers, align with these sequential human fixation strategies during facial expression recognition. Additionally, they are investigating how active action selection and reward interact to dynamically modulate perceptual performance and motor preparation.

papers.title: Dynamic face-related eye movement representations in the human ventral pathway
papers.abstract: Using MEG, participants followed a dot that replayed gaze tracks recorded earlier while they freely viewed faces and houses, so no face image was ever shown. Face-related gaze tracks were represented mainly in the ventral stream, beginning in orbitofrontal cortex and anterior temporal lobe and extending to medial temporal and ventral occipitotemporal cortex. The authors read this as top-down face-category prediction that guides face perception through the ventral pathway.
papers.authors: Zhongbin Su, Xiaolin Zhou, Stefan Pollmann, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Alignment of Artificial Neural Networks with Human Eye Movement Patterns in Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: The study tests whether CNN and Vision Transformer models trained for facial expression recognition reproduce the roles of humans' first two fixations. Both VGG16 and ViT matched the separate functions of the two fixations, but only the ViT showed a synergistic benefit when both were combined. Layer-wise analysis suggests the CNN relies on feedforward detail processing while the ViT integrates across fixations in a feedback-like way.
papers.authors: Meng Liu, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Active action selection in reward-modulated visual perception
papers.abstract: The paper continues the lab's line on how reward and action choice shape visual perception and motor preparation. It examines how actively selecting an action interacts with reward to modulate perceptual performance. Abstract not retrievable in this session; the summary is based on the title and the lab's stated research direction.
papers.authors: Tingjuntao Ni, Li Zhang, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Specified functions of the first two fixations in face recognition: Sampling the general-to-specific facial information
papers.abstract: Eye-tracking showed the first fixation on a face lands near the nose bridge and takes in broad facial information. The second diverges to the eyes, nostrils and lips to collect local detail. The second fixation tracked face-distinguishing information and recognition responses better than the first, and the two together discriminated face categories best. Perception is framed as an active process driven by structured motor programs.
papers.authors: Meng Liu, Jiayu Zhan, Lihui Wang

papers.title: Common structure of saccades and microsaccades in visual perception
papers.abstract: Twenty-seven adults viewed faces and houses in free-viewing and fixation-controlled conditions. Saccade patterns and microsaccade patterns each distinguished faces from houses, and classifiers trained on one generalised to the other. People with more distinctive saccadic patterns also had more distinctive microsaccadic ones. Both showed a shared preference for the eye region, suggesting a common sampling mechanism.
papers.authors: Zhenni Wang, Radha Nila Meghanathan, Stefan Pollmann, Lihui Wang

0395.name: Lili Sahakyan
0395.bio: Lili Sahakyan is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, where they direct the Control of Memory & Forgetting Lab and maintain affiliations with the Beckman Institute and the Neuroscience Program. Their research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human long-term memory, focusing on the strategic control of memory and the processes underlying intentional forgetting. Sahakyan utilizes functional MRI, EEG, and eye-tracking to examine how internal mental context and executive functions modulate memory retention and suppression. Their work also explores these memory control mechanisms in populations at risk for psychopathology, specifically investigating how schizotypy relates to episodic memory deficits.
0395.research_direction: The Control of Memory & Forgetting Lab studies how the mind decides what to hold on to and what to let go, treating forgetting not as a failure of memory but as an adaptive tool of cognitive control. A central question is why intentional forgetting differs from everyday forgetting: the lab first showed that shifts in mental context, such as mentally travelling to another time or place, can themselves cause forgetting, and uses directed-forgetting paradigms to separate active from passive forms of it. Eye tracking and pupillometry reveal memory traces that behavior misses and distinguish incidental from intentional forgetting, while EEG (including frequency tagging) and fMRI with multivariate pattern and representational similarity analyses track how context is reactivated or flushed over time. Newer work uses music as a dynamic, cross-modal retrieval cue, applies computational models of memory competition, and examines individual differences in memory control in young adults at risk for psychopathology.

papers.title: Pupil Old-New Effects Reflect an Early Match Between Perceptual Input and Memory Representations
papers.abstract: Pupil diameter grows more for correctly recognized old items than for new ones, yet grows more for falsely recognized new items than for missed old ones. Two experiments dissociated these objective and subjective pupil old-new effects. The findings support an early, rapid match between incoming perceptual input and stored memory representations as the source of the pupil signal.
papers.authors: Johnathon Whitlock, Ryan Hubbard, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Delayed testing in directed forgetting dissociates active and passive forms of forgetting
papers.abstract: Two experiments used item-method directed forgetting with Remember, Forget, and Thought Substitution cues and tested memory after several retention intervals. Forgetting produced by the different cues changed at different rates over time, separating an active form of forgetting from a passive, time-dependent one. The work sharpens the lab's central claim that intentional forgetting is not a single mechanism.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Jonathon Whitlock, Huiyu Ding, Ryan Hubbard, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Pupil Fluctuations Signal Intentional Forgetting of Natural Scenes
papers.abstract: Using an item-method directed forgetting task with natural scenes, the authors tracked pupil size, a proxy for locus coeruleus-norepinephrine activity, while participants were cued to remember or forget each scene. Pupil responses differed as a function of the memory cue and predicted later recognition, indicating that pupillometry provides a physiological signature of intentional forgetting. Findings extend the approach from words to complex visual images.
papers.authors: Huiyu Ding, Jonathon Whitlock, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: The role of prior familiarisation and meaningfulness of verbal and visual stimuli on directed forgetting
papers.abstract: Stimuli were pre-exposed zero, two, or six times before a directed forgetting task, using verbal or pictorial and meaningful or meaningless materials. The study tested how the nature of the material and its prior familiarity shape the size of the directed forgetting effect. Results clarify the boundary conditions under which intentional forgetting operates.
papers.authors: Yi-Pei Lo, Huiyu Ding, Jonathon Whitlock, Lili Sahakyan

papers.title: Differential Recruitment of Inhibitory Control Processes by Directed Forgetting and Thought Substitution
papers.abstract: People can intentionally forget either by suppressing encoding of an item (directed forgetting) or by mentally substituting another thought or context (thought substitution). The study asks whether encoding suppression genuinely draws on prefrontally mediated inhibitory control while thought substitution works through changing contextual representations instead. The results indicate that the two forgetting strategies recruit inhibitory control processes differently, supporting distinct mechanisms for intentional forgetting.
papers.authors: Ryan J. Hubbard, Lili Sahakyan

0396.name: Linda B. Smith
0396.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0396.bio: Linda B. Smith is a Distinguished Professor at Indiana University who researches developmental cognitive science and vision. Smith's work utilizes a complex systems approach to examine the interdependencies between perceptual, motor, and cognitive development, focusing on how infants' active exploration structures their visual input. Through high-resolution egocentric data from head-mounted eye-trackers, they investigate the statistical regularities in the developmental environment that support visual object recognition and word learning. Their current research links human development with machine learning by modeling how sensory-motor experiences create pathways for cognitive acquisition.
0396.research_direction: Dr. Smith’s recent work explores the naturalistic statistics of early developmental environments and how these specific inputs scaffold human learning. Using head-mounted cameras to capture egocentric infant vision, they have recently been investigating the visual properties of everyday experience, asking how phenomena like early edge-simplicity biases and repeated views of a few individual objects might enable data-efficient generalization in both the developing brain and artificial machine learning models. Beyond vision, their research examines the multimodal and environmental foundations of language by tracking the temporal coupling between infant vocalizations and body movements, as well as investigating how the specific verbs children naturally hear shape cross-linguistic differences in early word acquisition. Additionally, they are studying early mathematical cognition, specifically exploring how kindergartners gradually acquire multidigit place-value concepts to support later arithmetic.

papers.title: A solution to generalized learning from small training sets found in infants' repeated visual experiences of individual objects
papers.abstract: Infants see far fewer distinct objects than machine-learning datasets contain, yet they generalize well. The authors analyze head-camera video of infants' natural experience and show it consists of many repeated, varied views of a small number of individual objects. Training vision models on this kind of input yields strong generalization from very small training sets, suggesting that the structure of infant experience is itself a solution to data-efficient learning.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Frangil M. Ramirez, Elizabeth M. Clerkin, David J. Crandall, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Rethinking the Origins of Cross-Language Effects: How Heard Verbs Influence Japanese- and English-Speaking Children's Learning
papers.abstract: The paper asks why children's early word learning differs across languages such as Japanese and English. It examines how the verbs children actually hear in their language environment shape what they learn, offering an experience-based alternative to accounts that attribute the differences to language-specific biases.
papers.authors: Hiromichi Hagihara, Monica Barbir, Hanako Yoshida, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: An edge-simplicity bias in the visual input to young infants
papers.abstract: Using head-mounted cameras and image analysis, the study measures the visual statistics of what infants see across the first months of life. Infants' input is dominated by simple, low-complexity edge structure, and the simplicity is strongest in the youngest infants and declines with age. This developmentally ordered input may scaffold early visual cortex tuning and object learning.
papers.authors: Erin M. Anderson, T. Rowan Candy, Jason M. Gold, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Infant vocal productions coincide with body movements
papers.abstract: Analyzing naturalistic recordings, the authors show that infants' vocalizations are tightly coupled in time with their body movements. Vocal production is thus embedded in a multimodal, sensorimotor system rather than isolated speech development, which bears on how early language is scaffolded.
papers.authors: Jeremy I. Borjon, Drew H. Abney, Chen Yu, Linda B. Smith

papers.title: Place value learning in kindergarten
papers.abstract: A study of how kindergartners come to understand multidigit numbers, tracking the development of place value knowledge and its role in later arithmetic. It shows that understanding grows gradually and that structured instruction can build on partial knowledge.
papers.authors: Kelly S. Mix, Corinne A. Bower, Gregory R. Hancock, Sandra Crespo, Linda B. Smith

0400.name: Lisa M. Oakes
0400.bio: Lisa M. Oakes is a professor in the Department of Psychology and the Center for Mind and Brain at the University of California, Davis. Oakes’s research investigates developmental cascades in infant mental abilities, specifically the integration of visual attention, memory, and categorization during the first years of life. Utilizing eye tracking, representational similarity analysis, and looking-time paradigms, Oakes examines how infants scan naturalistic scenes and whether their gaze is directed by physical salience or semantic meaning. Their work focuses on how early attentional mechanisms interact with environmental experience to influence long-term cognitive and perceptual development.
0400.research_direction: Dr. Oakes has recently been investigating the development of infant visual attention, framing it as a cascade of interacting systems where infants learn how to look in order to learn about the world. Their recent work explores how gaze allocation during natural scene viewing matures over the first year of life, specifically questioning how and when fixations transition from being guided by low-level visual features to higher-level semantic meaning. To map this trajectory, they employ infant eye-tracking in conjunction with adult-derived meaning maps and representational similarity analysis linking infant looking behavior to adult fMRI cortical activation patterns. Additionally, they are examining the embodied nature of visual development by studying how emerging motor milestones, such as crawling, and varying physical vantage points influence how infants prioritize visual information in their everyday environments.

papers.title: The role of motor development and point-of-view on infant attention to naturalistic scenes
papers.abstract: Fifty-two infants around 6 months old viewed photographs of household scenes from different vantage points, and gaze was analyzed against adult-rated local meaning. Crawling and non-crawling infants prioritized meaningful regions under different viewpoints, with crawlers favoring meaning from higher vantage points. The findings suggest that self-locomotion tunes how infants allocate visual attention.
papers.authors: Christian M. Nelson, Brianna K. Hunter, Taylor R. Hayes, John M. Henderson, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: Relating infant fixations to adult cortical activation patterns using the Natural Scenes Dataset
papers.abstract: Gaze patterns of 5-7 and 10-12 month-old infants and adults viewing Natural Scenes Dataset images were compared with adult fMRI responses to the same scenes using representational similarity analysis. Younger infants' fixation similarity matched only low-level visual cortex, whereas older infants and adults matched mid-level regions. The result supports a shift in attention guidance from simple to more abstract features over development.
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, John E. Kiat, Steven J. Luck, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: What have we learned about infant visual attention in the first 25 years of the 21st century?
papers.abstract: This review contrasts the early-2000s view of infant attention as a shift from stimulus-driven to goal-driven control with current understanding of multiple interacting systems with cascading effects. It highlights how infant eye tracking, saliency models, computational vision models and head-mounted egocentric views have changed the field, and sets out directions for the next 25 years.
papers.authors: Brianna K. Hunter, Erim Kızıldere, Shannon M. Klotz, Christian M. Nelson, Julie Markant, Lisa M. Oakes

papers.title: The role of local meaning in infants' fixations of natural scenes
papers.abstract: Infants aged 4 to 12 months viewed photographs of everyday scenes while their gaze was tracked, and fixations were related to adult ratings of how much meaning each scene region carried, with physical salience and center bias held constant. Infants looked more at higher-meaning regions, like adults, and this effect grew with age. This is the first evidence that semantic content increasingly shapes infants' scene viewing over the first year.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Oakes, Taylor R. Hayes, Shannon M. Klotz, Kelsey I. Pomaranski, John M. Henderson

papers.title: The cascading development of visual attention in infancy: Learning to look and looking to learn
papers.abstract: This theoretical article argues that infant visual attention is a set of interacting systems rather than a single ability. Changes in attention, the visual system, motor control and learned knowledge cascade over time, so infants learn how to look, and their looking in turn supplies the input from which they learn about the world.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Oakes

0401.name: Lisa Renzi-Hammond
0401.department: Department of Health Promotion and Behavior, College of Public Health
0401.bio: Lisa Renzi-Hammond studies the functional relationships between sensory integrity, neurological health, and cognitive vitality across the human lifespan. Their research utilizes psychophysical, electrophysiological, and neuroimaging methodologies to investigate how visual function serves as a non-invasive biomarker for central nervous system health. Renzi-Hammond examines how dietary carotenoids, such as lutein and zeaxanthin, influence neural processing speed and protect against neurodegenerative diseases. They serve as the Director of the Institute of Gerontology and co-director of the Cognitive Aging Research and Education (CARE) Center, translating vision science into public health initiatives for dementia prevention and education.
0401.research_direction: Dr. Renzi-Hammond's recent work explores how specific light spectra and optical filters influence visual performance, while also maintaining a distinct line of research on cognitive interventions for aging. They have recently been investigating the functional and perceptual effects of high-energy visible (HEV) and blue-light-filtering lenses under ecologically realistic conditions, utilizing brightness-matching tasks with natural images, simulated atmospheric blue haze, and masked assessments of glare and dysphotopsias in pseudophakic patients. In the realm of multisensory color perception, their recent work examines the hue-heat hypothesis by measuring how varying the physical intensity of primary colors alters psychophysical ratings of perceived warmth. Broadening their focus to cognitive health, they are also using EEG and neuropsychological testing to evaluate whether active musical training impacts memory, reasoning, and brain activation in older adults differently than passive music listening.

papers.title: Visual performance measured under simulated atmospheric blue haze conditions is improved through the addition of a HEV-filtering additive to soft contact lenses
papers.abstract: Atmospheric blue haze veils distant objects and cuts outdoor visual range. In 121 adults tested under simulated veiling light shaped like the blue-haze spectrum, wearing a contact lens with a high-energy-visible (HEV) filtering additive improved visual performance compared with a clear lens. The gain scaled with the optical density of the HEV filter, suggesting that HEV-filtering contact lenses can help vision in hazy outdoor conditions.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, John R. Buch, Patricia Martin, Wright Shamp, Jacob B. Harth, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: The effects of a HEV-filtering contact lens on the brightness of natural images
papers.abstract: Yellow and HEV-filtering lenses are often said to make real-world scenes look brighter, but lab results have been mixed. Using a brightness-matching task adapted to present natural images with broad-spectrum light, the authors compared a clear contact lens with one containing an HEV-filtering additive. The work tests the brightness-enhancement claim under ecologically realistic viewing.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, John R. Buch, Patricia Martin, Wright Shamp, Jacob B. Harth, Cameron Wysocky, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: The Effects of Piano Training on Cognitive Function and Brain Activation in Older Adults
papers.abstract: Twenty older adults were randomized to weekly piano lessons with daily practice or to a music-listening control condition. After training, the piano group outperformed controls on reasoning and composite memory tests and showed differences in EEG-measured brain activation. The results suggest that learning to play an instrument may boost cognition in later life.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond, Jade Dandurand, Kassidy Hogan, Peter Jutras, Jenay M. Beer, Billy R. Hammond

papers.title: Visual Function Under Bright Light Conditions Tested Using a Blue-Light Absorbing or Clear Lens in Pseudophakic Patients
papers.abstract: Twenty-five pseudophakic patients with UV-only intraocular lenses were tested in a masked crossover design with a control filter or a blue-light-absorbing filter matched to common BLF IOLs. The blue-light filter improved glare disability, chromatic contrast and light-threshold measures, and shrank perceived dysphotopsias (snowballs and spokes) by roughly a fifth. This supports blue-light filtering as a way to ease bright-light problems after cataract surgery.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, Jacob B. Harth, Lisa M. Renzi-Hammond

papers.title: Increasing intensity directly increases the perceived warmth of primary colors
papers.abstract: The hue-heat hypothesis says reds and yellows feel warm while blues and greens feel cool, but past work used fixed-intensity light. With saturated primary colors at five intensity levels, 20 observers rated perceived temperature. Red and yellow were warmest and blue coolest, yet every color grew warmer as intensity rose.
papers.authors: Billy R. Hammond, Colin R. Gardner, Billy R. Wooten, Lisa Renzi-Hammond

0402.name: Lisa S. Scott
0402.bio: Lisa S. Scott is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Florida and the director of the Brain Cognition & Development Lab. Scott’s research examines the neurobiological and behavioral mechanisms of visual attention, perception, and learning, with a focus on how early experience influences face and object recognition across the lifespan. Utilizing a multimodal approach including electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials (ERPs), and eye-tracking, Scott tracks the specialization of neural circuits and the acquisition of perceptual expertise. Their recent investigations include longitudinal studies of brain development and the visuocortical foundations of learning from infancy into childhood.
0402.research_direction: Dr. Scott has recently been investigating how early visual experience shapes the developing brain's organization for category-specific processing from infancy through early childhood. Using EEG and behavioral paradigms, their recent work explores how exposure to specific stimuli—ranging from newly trained objects to naturally encountered face groups—modulates visuocortical responses and influences competitive cortical prioritization for limited processing capacity. They are particularly focused on the development of face expertise, advancing a domain-relevant framework to test how everyday visual experience, rather than an innate module, specializes face perception and differentiation over time. Additionally, their research tracks the emergence of oscillatory neural signatures, such as alpha-rhythm desynchronization, to understand the developmental timeline of how the infant visual system categorizes faces versus objects.

papers.title: Experience Modulates Visuocortical Responses to Faces in 3- to 6-Year-Old Children
papers.abstract: This study extends the lab's work on face experience from infancy to early childhood, measuring visuocortical responses to faces in 3- to 6-year-olds with EEG. It tests how familiarity with different face groups modulates those responses.
papers.authors: Grace Wallsinger, Maeve R. Boylan, Ryan Barry-Anwar, Gabriella Silva, Stefania Conte, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Competitive Cortical Prioritization Emerges for Trained Objects across the First Year of Life
papers.abstract: Infants were given experience with a set of objects and their visual cortical responses to trained versus untrained items were tracked with EEG at several ages across the first year. The study shows that cortical prioritization of trained objects appears as a competitive process in which learned objects come to win out over other stimuli for limited processing capacity. It gives a developmental account of how early experience tunes the visual system.
papers.authors: Maeve R. Boylan, Anna-Lena Tebbe, Jamie Newland, Jessica Sanches Braga Figueira, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Infant dominant rhythm desynchronization to faces and objects
papers.abstract: Using EEG in infants across the first year, the authors examined desynchronization of the dominant (alpha-like) rhythm when infants viewed faces versus objects. The work links a developing oscillatory signature to category-specific visual processing. It builds on their earlier characterisation of how this rhythm emerges with age.
papers.authors: Mina Elhamiasl, Maeve R. Boylan, Ryan Barry-Anwar, Zoe Pestana, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: Experience With Face Groups Impacts Face Processing, but Not Face Differentiation in 6- and 9-Month-Old Infants
papers.abstract: Six- and nine-month-old infants with differing amounts of everyday exposure to face groups were tested on face processing and on differentiating individual faces. Familiarity with a face group shaped how faces were processed but did not change the ability to tell individual faces apart. The results clarify which aspects of face perception are experience-dependent in early infancy.
papers.authors: Grace Wallsinger, Maeve R. Boylan, Jessica Sanches Braga Figueira, Ryan Barry-Anwar, Gabriella Silva, Andreas Keil, Lisa S. Scott

papers.title: A domain-relevant framework for the development of face processing
papers.abstract: This review lays out a framework in which face processing develops through experience with domain-relevant input across infancy and childhood, rather than from a fixed face-specific module. It integrates behavioural, neural and comparative evidence on how early face exposure narrows and specialises perception and cortical organisation. It also sets out predictions for how experience shapes face expertise.
papers.authors: Lisa S. Scott, Michael J. Arcaro

0403.name: Lotfi B. Merabet
0403.institution: Harvard Medical School (Massachusetts Eye and Ear)
0403.department: Department of Ophthalmology; Laboratory for Visual Neuroplasticity
0403.bio: Lotfi B. Merabet is a clinician-scientist and Professor of Ophthalmology at Harvard Medical School who investigates the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in response to vision loss. Merabet’s research characterizes how the brain's structural and functional architecture reorganizes following both ocular blindness and brain-based visual impairment. By employing neuroimaging techniques such as functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging alongside behavioral tasks, Merabet explores how the visual cortex is recruited for non-visual processing and identifies the neural correlates of visual search deficits. Their current work focuses on translating these findings into rehabilitative strategies and assistive technologies designed to improve functional outcomes for individuals with visual disabilities.
0403.research_direction: Dr. Merabet has recently been investigating the behavioral and neurophysiological mechanisms underlying higher-order visuospatial processing deficits in cerebral visual impairment (CVI). Their recent work explores how early brain damage alters the recruitment of the dorsal and ventral visual streams by combining functional neuroimaging with psychophysical measures of global motion and form coherence. Additionally, they are examining the functional consequences of these neural changes on real-world visual behavior and clinical assessments. Using both stationary and wearable eye-tracking during naturalistic scene exploration, Dr. Merabet studies how individuals with CVI allocate their gaze, specifically questioning how a disrupted interplay between bottom-up image salience and top-down semantic cues impacts visual search efficiency and scanning strategies.

papers.title: Assessing visuospatial abilities related to visual scanning in cerebral visual impairment using the star cancellation test combined with wearable eye tracking
papers.abstract: Sixteen individuals with CVI and 19 controls completed the Star Cancellation Test while wearing a mobile eye tracker. Accuracy was not clearly lower in CVI, but they took longer, verified their work more, and had lower cancellation efficiency, with more fixations and longer scan paths, though normalized gaze metrics did not differ. The work shows how wearable eye tracking can quantify functional visual scanning in a clinical test.
papers.authors: Madeleine Heynen, Alyssa W. Sullivan, Claire E. Manley, Serena Micheletti, Elisa M. Fazzi, Lotfi B. Merabet

papers.title: Higher-Order Visuospatial Processing Abilities in Cerebral Visual Impairment: Behavioral Assessment and Neurophysiological Mechanisms
papers.abstract: A review arguing that visuospatial processing deficits are a core feature of cerebral visual impairment (CVI), drawing on behavioral work on complex motion perception and visual search plus structural and functional neuroimaging. The authors propose that higher-order visual dysfunction in CVI arises from a disrupted interplay between bottom-up stimulus-driven and top-down goal-driven processing.
papers.authors: Lotfi B. Merabet, Claire E. Manley, Zahide Pamir

papers.title: Visuospatial processing in early brain-based visual impairment is associated with differential recruitment of dorsal and ventral visual streams
papers.abstract: Individuals with CVI and neurotypical controls performed a naturalistic visual search task (following a walking person) with eye tracking and in the fMRI scanner. CVI participants were slower and less accurate, showed reduced dorsal-stream activation consistent with dorsal stream dysfunction, but unexpectedly stronger ventral-stream activation, with no differences in early visual or frontal cortex. This points to impaired selective attention and altered stream recruitment.
papers.authors: Zahide Pamir, Claire E Manley, Corinna M Bauer, Peter J Bex, Daniel D Dilks, Lotfi B Merabet

papers.title: Visual search patterns during exploration of naturalistic scenes are driven by saliency cues in individuals with cerebral visual impairment
papers.abstract: Compared gaze behavior of people with CVI and controls while searching naturalistic scenes for a cued target, testing how well image-salience and semantic models predict where people look. CVI participants were slower, less successful, and searched wider areas with more fixations, and their search was driven mainly by image salience rather than meaning, with performance related to verbal IQ for text cues.
papers.authors: Kerri Walter, Claire E. Manley, Peter J. Bex, Lotfi B. Merabet

papers.title: Motion and form coherence processing in individuals with cerebral visual impairment
papers.abstract: Used a response-adaptive psychophysics paradigm (FInD) to measure global motion and form coherence thresholds as indices of dorsal and ventral stream function in 20 people with CVI and 30 controls. Motion, but not form, thresholds were elevated in CVI, consistent with dorsal stream dysfunction, and thresholds did not track lesion severity. The paradigm may help characterize perceptual deficits in CVI.
papers.authors: Lotfi B. Merabet, Claire E. Manley, Zahide Pamir, Corinna M. Bauer, Jan Skerswetat, Peter J. Bex

0406.name: Lucia Melloni
0406.department: Predictive Brain Department, Faculty of Psychology (University Alliance Ruhr / Research Center One Health Ruhr)
0406.lab_name: Neural Circuits, Consciousness, and Cognition Research Group
0406.bio: Lucia Melloni is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural and computational foundations of consciousness, perception, and memory. Melloni’s research examines how the brain utilizes predictive mechanisms to interpret sensory input and shape subjective experience through a multimodal approach that integrates invasive electrocorticography (ECoG), non-invasive MEG/EEG, and computational modeling. They coordinate large-scale adversarial collaborations designed to empirically arbitrate between competing theories of consciousness as part of an open science framework. Their work also explores the neuroethological aspects of experience, examining how memory and prediction contribute to the continuity of conscious life in real-world contexts.
0406.research_direction: Dr. Melloni has recently been leading large-scale adversarial collaborations to empirically test competing theories of consciousness, pitting models like Integrated Information Theory against Global Neuronal Workspace Theory. Using multimodal neuroimaging techniques including fMRI, MEG, and intracranial EEG, their recent work explores the neural correlates of visual awareness and investigates how the probability of conscious access fluctuates over long timescales. Alongside this focus on visual consciousness, they are also studying predictive processing in audition, using MEG to examine how frontoparietal networks integrate hierarchical predictions about the content and timing of speech sequences.
