Broadly, their research advocates for resolving profound questions about conscious experience through rigorous, collaborative empirical testing rather than a priori philosophical assumptions.

papers.title: What consciousness is should be determined empirically, not a priori
papers.abstract: An opinion piece arguing that the nature of consciousness, and which systems have it, should be settled by empirical investigation and theory testing rather than by a priori definitions or philosophical stipulation. It connects to her broader push for theory-neutral, adversarial and evidence-driven consciousness science.
papers.authors: Lucia Melloni, Jaan Aru, Tobias Schlicht

papers.title: Long-timescale dynamics shape visual conscious awareness
papers.abstract: Analyzing 20 datasets (N=335), the study shows that subjective visibility and confidence reports carry long temporal autocorrelation (over 5 s, exponential decay), whereas objective accuracy decays slowly and linearly, yet both share common underlying fluctuation dynamics. Causal TMS indicates the temporal dependency is read out in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which has similarly long neural timescales. The authors argue models of conscious access must explain how access probability evolves over time.
papers.authors: Zefan Zheng, Darinka Trubutschek, Yongchun Cai, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
papers.abstract: A large preregistered adversarial collaboration pitted two leading theories of consciousness, integrated information theory and global neuronal workspace theory, against each other using fMRI, MEG and intracranial EEG in 256 participants viewing visual stimuli of varying duration. Conscious content was decodable in visual, ventrotemporal and inferior frontal cortex, and the data supported some predictions of each theory while substantially challenging core tenets of both, such as the lack of sustained posterior synchronization for IIT and of ignition at stimulus offset for GNWT. The paper also argues for principled, collaborative, theory-driven testing as a model for cognitive neuroscience.
papers.authors: Cogitate Consortium, Oscar Ferrante, Urszula Gorska-Klimowska, Simon Henin, Rony Hirschhorn, Aya Khalaf, Alex Lepauvre, Ling Liu, David Richter, Yamil Vidal, Niccolo Bonacchi, Tanya Brown, Praveen Sripad, Marcelo Armendariz, Katarina Bendtz, Tara Ghafari, Dorottya Hetenyi, Jay Jeschke, Csaba Kozma, David R. Mazumder, Stephanie Montenegro, Alia Seedat, Abdelrahman Sharafeldin, Shujun Yang, Sylvain Baillet, David J. Chalmers, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Francis Fallon, Theofanis I. Panagiotaropoulos, Hal Blumenfeld, Floris P. de Lange, Sasha Devore, Ole Jensen, Gabriel Kreiman, Huan Luo, Melanie Boly, Stanislas Dehaene, Christof Koch, Giulio Tononi, Michael Pitts, Liad Mudrik, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: Unpacking the complexities of consciousness: Theories and reflections
papers.abstract: Following the adversarial-collaboration results, leading theorists in the field reflect on the state of consciousness science, comparing where major theories converge and diverge and discussing how the community should evaluate and refine theories going forward. It serves as a field-level perspective on methodology and open questions.
papers.authors: Liad Mudrik, Melanie Boly, Stanislas Dehaene, Stephen M. Fleming, Victor Lamme, Anil Seth, Lucia Melloni

papers.title: "What" and "When" Predictions Jointly Modulate Speech Processing
papers.abstract: Using MEG with syllable and pseudoword sequences, the study manipulated content (what) and timing (when) regularities at two hierarchical levels. Temporal regularity amplified mismatch responses for content deviants with hierarchical specificity, yet the effects localized to the same frontal and parietal regions, with connectivity changes consistent with gain modulation. This suggests the brain integrates level-matched what and when predictions through a shared distributed network.
papers.authors: Ryszard Auksztulewicz, Ozan Bahattin Odul, Saskia Helbling, Ana Boke, Drew Cappotto, Dan Luo, Jan Schnupp, Lucia Melloni

0408.name: M.D. Rutherford
0408.bio: M.D. Rutherford is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology, Neuroscience & Behaviour at McMaster University, where he holds a Canada Research Chair in Social Perception. Rutherford’s research investigates the developmental and evolutionary foundations of social cognition, focusing on how humans process visual social cues such as eye gaze, facial expressions, and biological motion. Using eye-tracking and psychophysical methodologies, Rutherford studies social perception in typically developing infants and the early identification of autism spectrum disorders. His work examines the mechanisms of visual adaptation, animacy detection, and the ontogeny of specialized cognitive systems for social navigation.
0408.research_direction: Dr. Rutherford’s research focuses on the development of social perception and social cognition across infancy, childhood, and neurodiverse populations, with a particular emphasis on autism spectrum disorder. His work examines how humans perceive and interpret socially relevant information, including faces, facial expressions, biological motion, and social group cues, and how these processes emerge and change over development. Using a combination of longitudinal studies, meta-analyses, neurocognitive approaches, and experimental investigations, he seeks to identify early markers of autism risk, understand the perceptual mechanisms that support social understanding, and characterize typical and atypical developmental trajectories in social information processing. Rutherford’s research also explores the broader cognitive processes through which people form representations of social categories and identities, illuminating how perceptual and developmental mechanisms shape social understanding from infancy through adulthood.

papers.title: Different event-related potential responses during face processing between siblings of autistic individuals and neurotypical infants: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled infant ERP studies of face processing in younger siblings of autistic children, up to 12 months of age. Siblings showed slower N290 responses, a reduced P400 and hints of altered N290 amplitude and left-hemisphere dominance compared with neurotypical infants. Responses to the mother's face also looked different. The results point to early neural markers of face-processing differences in infants at elevated likelihood for autism.
papers.authors: Esin Gürcan, Sarah Watson, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Face perception and social cognitive development in early autism: A prospective longitudinal study from 3 months to 7 years of age
papers.abstract: The authors followed infants from 3 months onward, comparing 22 who later developed autism with 131 typically developing infants, and tracked their social-cognitive outcomes to age seven. Less interest in direct gaze and the eyes in infancy was linked to weaker adaptive behavior at age four and weaker theory of mind at age seven. Infants who developed autism also integrated facial features and gaze information less holistically. The work ties early face perception differences to later social-cognitive development in autism.
papers.authors: Xiaomei Zhou, Hasan Siddiqui, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Preference for Eyes Predicts Later Autism-Related Characteristics in Children with a Family History of Autism
papers.abstract: Nine-month-old infants with and without a family history of autism viewed side-by-side faces with open versus closed eyes, and were later assessed for autism-related characteristics. In infants with a first-degree relative with autism, a stronger preference for open eyes predicted lower autism-related scores later on. The finding suggests early eye preference could serve as a marker of later outcomes in infants at elevated likelihood for autism.
papers.authors: Esin Gurcan, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Picture a scientist: classification images of scientists are perceived as White, male, and socially inept
papers.abstract: Using a two-phase reverse-correlation method, participants chose faces that best matched 'scientist', 'hero', 'genius' and 'person', and the averages became classification images. In a second phase, 251 naive raters scored these images. The scientist image was seen as predominantly White and male, and was also rated more negatively and as less sociable than the other categories. The study shows how the method can expose stereotypes in mental face representations.
papers.authors: Maheen Shakil, Hasan Siddiqui, M.D. Rutherford

papers.title: Religious labels and food preferences, but not country of origin, support opposing face aftereffects
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether explicit religious labels, food preferences or country of origin could make face aftereffects specific to Christian versus Muslim face sets. Contingent aftereffects appeared with religious labels and food preferences but not with country of origin. The results suggest that some social categories create perceptually meaningful groups whose face templates adapt separately, so social categorization shapes visual processing.
papers.authors: Maheen Shakil, M.D. Rutherford

0410.name: Manish Singh
0410.department: Department of Psychology; Rutgers Center for Cognitive Science (RuCCS)
0410.bio: Manish Singh is a Professor of Psychology and Cognitive Science at Rutgers University who investigates the computational and psychological foundations of human vision. Singh’s research focuses on how the brain constructs three-dimensional representations of objects and surfaces from two-dimensional retinal images, specifically examining part-based shape representations, skeletal models, and object completion. By integrating psychophysical experiments with probabilistic Bayesian modeling, Singh examines phenomena such as transparency, illusory contours, and the visual prediction of physical object behavior. Their work also addresses theories of perception, including the interface theory of perception and the evolutionary logic of perceptual systems.
0410.research_direction: Dr. Singh has recently been studying how the visual system recovers the shape and depth of objects from motion and contours. Their recent work explores how people interpret objects that change shape while moving, and why the visual system tends to favor certain interpretations over others. They also examine how the shape of an object's outline and the motion of surface texture combine to decide which surface appears in front of another. On a more conceptual level, they have been considering what evolution implies about whether perception tracks reality and how that limits scientific theorizing.

papers.title: Perception, Evolution, and the Explanatory Scope of Scientific Theories
papers.abstract: This work evaluates the Interface Theory of Perception (ITP) and its implications for the foundational constraints of scientific theorizing. ITP suggests that natural selection has not tuned perceptual systems for veridicality but has instead shaped them into species-specific 'interfaces' designed to optimize fitness-payoffs. The authors argue that this evolutionary trajectory imposes a conceptual and structural bottleneck on scientific understanding, as theories are inherently formulated within the data formats provided by these interfaces (such as spacetime and discrete objects). Consequently, the explanatory reach of any scientific theory is fundamentally delimited by the non-veridical nature of human perception, suggesting that objective reality remains largely outside the representational scope of our current theoretical frameworks.
papers.authors: Donald D. Hoffman, Manish Singh

papers.title: Perceptual Biases in the Interpretation of Non-Rigid Shape Transformations from Motion
papers.abstract: This study investigates the computational constraints and perceptual biases that govern the recovery of 3D shape from non-rigid motion. While structure-from-motion (SFM) research typically focuses on rigid objects, many ecological entities, such as biological organisms, undergo non-rigid transformations. Through psychophysical experiments using stimuli with dynamic length changes during rotation, the authors demonstrate a systematic bias in the human visual system toward interpreting non-rigid motion as part-wise rigid. Specifically, observers reinterpreted image-plane length changes as variations in the angular orientation of a rigidly attached part relative to a main body. The findings are modeled using a geometric framework that suggests the visual system prioritizes interpretations consistent with the biological constraints of articulated motion over mathematically possible but ecologically rare non-rigid deformations.
papers.authors: Ryne Choi, Jacob Feldman, Manish Singh

papers.title: Interaction of contour geometry and optic flow in determining relative depth of surfaces
papers.abstract: This research examines the integration of boundary geometry and texture motion in the perception of dynamic occlusion and figure-ground assignment. Utilizing random-dot kinematograms, the authors manipulated the speed profile of texture near a boundary (accretion/deletion) and the geometry of the occluding contour (convexity vs. concavity). The experiments reveal that contour geometry (specifically convexity) acts as a dominant cue that can override traditional depth-from-motion indicators, such as the speed-gradient and accretion/deletion of texture. The results indicate that the visual system employs a complex interaction between local optic flow signals and global contour shape to resolve depth ordering, suggesting a Bayesian-like integration where shape-priors (convexity) exert significant influence on the interpretation of ambiguous motion signals.
papers.authors: Ömer Dağlar Tanrıkulu, Vicky Froyen, Jacob Feldman, Manish Singh

0412.name: Margaret Livingstone
0412.bio: Margaret Livingstone is the Takeda Professor of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School and studies the functional organization and development of the primate visual system. Livingstone’s research, conducted in collaboration with David Hubel, identified parallel processing pathways for color, form, and motion within the visual cortex. Their current work investigates the plasticity of the inferotemporal cortex, examining how early visual experience and learning influence the formation of specialized domains such as face-selective patches. Using functional MRI, single-unit electrophysiology, and behavioral modeling, Livingstone explores the biological basis of object recognition and visual perception, including the neurobiology of artistic illusions and developmental dyslexia.
0412.research_direction: Dr. Livingstone has recently been investigating the computational principles, spatial organization, and development of high-level visual representations in the macaque inferotemporal cortex. Their recent work explores the fundamental nature of feature selectivity, using deep-network models to ask whether classic face cells encode strict semantic categories or general visual features, while also probing the specific spatial topography of object features within individual receptive fields. Additionally, they are studying how this neural tuning operates dynamically during natural, active vision as subjects freely saccade across complex scenes. Finally, their research broadens to developmental and cross-species questions by examining how early visual deprivation impacts the long-term formation of face-processing circuits, and by using natural image responses to create functional, non-anatomical mappings between the macaque and human visual systems.

papers.title: Early face deprivation leads to long-lasting deficits in cortical face processing
papers.abstract: Macaques raised without visual experience of faces were examined for face processing in inferotemporal cortex. The paper reports that the lack of early face exposure leaves lasting deficits in face-selective cortical responses, supporting the view that experience during development is needed to build normal face-processing circuits.
papers.authors: Saloni Sharma, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Spatial organization of faces and bodies in single neurons
papers.abstract: IT neuron receptive fields mapped with upright versus inverted faces shift vertically depending on where the eyes fall within the field, rather than through remapping. Responses to isolated eyes, mouths, hands, bodies and faces reveal a systematic feature topography inside receptive fields, and an encoding network recovers factors tuned to feature-location combinations. IT face cells thus act as spatially structured subunits and not translation-invariant templates.
papers.authors: Margaret Livingstone, Akshay Jagadeesh, Sohrab Najafian, Binxu Wang, Michael Arcaro

papers.title: Mapping macaque to human cortex with natural scene responses
papers.abstract: The work aligns macaque and human visual cortex by comparing neural responses to a shared set of natural scenes rather than relying on anatomy alone. This yields a functional cross-species map showing which macaque regions correspond to which human areas, and provides a basis for translating macaque electrophysiology to human fMRI.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Kasper Vinken, Saloni Sharma, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: Feature-selective responses in macaque visual cortex follow eye movements during natural vision
papers.abstract: The authors recorded from inferotemporal and related visual cortex of macaques freely viewing natural images and found that neurons keep their feature preferences across saccades, with responses following the features that land on the fovea at each fixation. Selectivity measured during free viewing agreed with that from conventional fixation tasks, and neural responses could be predicted from fixated image content. This links classic tuning results to natural active vision.
papers.authors: Will Xiao, Saloni Sharma, Gabriel Kreiman, Margaret S. Livingstone

papers.title: The neural code for "face cells" is not face-specific
papers.abstract: Face-selective neurons in macaque inferotemporal cortex are usually described as coding for faces as a category. Using large sets of natural images and deep-network feature models, the study shows that face-cell responses are well explained by general visual features and are driven by many non-face images, so their code is not specific to faces. This challenges category-specific accounts of face processing.
papers.authors: Kasper Vinken, Jacob S. Prince, Talia Konkle, Margaret S. Livingstone

0414.name: Maria Robinson
0414.bio: Robinson investigates the mechanisms of visual cognition and memory using computational modeling and mathematical psychology. Their research focuses on the architecture of visual working memory, employing signal detection theory to evaluate discrete-slot capacity models and analyze how memory fidelity evolves across timescales. Robinson also examines ensemble perception and the integration of sensory evidence into cognitive representations through quantitative frameworks. In the field of metascience, they contribute to the development of measurement practices and the evaluation of auxiliary assumptions in psychological theory assessment.
0414.research_direction: Dr. Robinson has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying visual working memory and ensemble perception. Their recent work explores how the full distribution of memory errors and gist-driven biases can be predicted using a priori measures of representational geometry derived from human similarity judgments, deep neural networks, and generative AI. They are examining these predictive models across diverse visual inputs, from simple features and faces to systematically structured spaces of real-world objects. In addition to building new representational frameworks, they are critically evaluating the foundational methods of the field by probing the hidden auxiliary assumptions used to test continuous-resource against all-or-none memory models. Ultimately, they are working to formally link individual item representations to higher-level phenomena like statistical summaries and categorical memory biases.

papers.title: Predicting visual working memory errors with a priori measures of representational geometry from human and artificial systems
papers.abstract: Measures the representational geometry of faces and simple features from human similarity judgments and pretrained deep networks, independent of any memory experiment. With a single-parameter decision rule, these geometries predict the full distribution of working memory errors, including which items get confused, without fitting to the memory data. The pipeline transfers to thirty new face sets and other feature types, and beats standard mixture and tuning-function models with fewer parameters.
papers.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: Bridging Bayesian and representational theories of memory to predict memory bias
papers.abstract: Integrates a Bayesian account of how gist and item-specific information combine with representational models of item and category memory. Fidelity parameters measured from separate gist and item tasks, together with independent stimulus-representation measures, are used to predict the full distribution of gist-driven memory errors in a third task, including bias magnitude, direction, skew and individual differences.
papers.authors: Anxin Miao, Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: Controlled real-world object generation for visual memory experimentation and theory-building
papers.abstract: Uses a generative AI model grounded in human similarity judgments (CoCoG) to build systematically structured spaces of real-world objects, and combines its embeddings with a computational memory model to predict error distributions. Across seven online experiments (N = 1,019) it reproduces known phenomena such as object-state versus exemplar memory and reveals new effects for novel object morphs.
papers.authors: Jiachen Zou, Chi Zhang, Deng Haotian, Quanying Liu, Chen Wei, Maria Martinovna Robinson

papers.title: Zooming in on what counts as core and auxiliary: A case study on recognition models of visual working memory
papers.abstract: Argues that theory tests always carry hidden auxiliary assumptions and shows this by reanalysing a seminal study and its replications that supported all-or-none recognition models of working memory. Many practical and theory-general assumptions were unchecked or violated and the original comparisons were often non-diagnostic. Once these are addressed and diagnostic conditions identified, continuous-resource models outperform all-or-none models.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Jamal R. Williams, John T. Wixted, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: A quantitative model of ensemble perception as summed activation in feature space
papers.abstract: Proposes that an ensemble summary of a set of items arises from simply summing the activation signals of all the individual items in feature space. Using memory performance for single items to generate zero-free-parameter predictions, the model accounts for both between-person and within-person differences in ensemble judgments across five experiments and outperforms alternative accounts. It thereby formally links memory for individual items to ensemble perception.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Timothy F. Brady

0415.name: Marianne Maertens
0415.department: Institute of Computer Engineering and Microelectronics, Department of Computational Psychology
0415.bio: Maertens is a Professor of Computational Psychology at Technische Universität Berlin, where they investigate how the human visual system transforms retinal stimulation into perceptual categories. Their research examines the mechanisms of lightness, transparency, and edge perception to analyze the relationship between objective visual performance and subjective experience. By combining experimental psychophysics with computational modeling, Maertens develops image-computable theories regarding how the brain interprets complex visual scenes. Maertens previously held research positions at New York University and the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences and received the Emmy Noether and Heisenberg fellowships.
0415.research_direction: Dr. Maertens has recently been studying how humans detect and localize edges, a basic step in seeing the shapes of objects. Their recent work tests whether the standard model of early spatial vision, built from channels tuned to orientation and spatial frequency, can explain how sensitive people are to edges under visual noise. They also examine how tiny involuntary eye movements during fixation reshape the input to the visual system and whether accounting for them improves models. In addition, they use line drawings that people trace on natural images as a way to measure edge sensitivity beyond simple lab stimuli.

papers.title: Line drawings as a tool to probe edge sensitivity in natural scenes
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the utility of human-generated line drawings as a metric for assessing edge sensitivity within naturalistic visual environments, moving beyond the traditional reliance on simplified, parametric stimuli. Observers performed a contour-tracing task on natural images subjected to various types of two-dimensional visual noise. Using a signal detection theory framework, individual edge traces from noise-free conditions established a ground-truth signal to quantify performance in noisy conditions through metrics such as d-prime and response bias. Findings indicate that noise interference patterns in natural scenes mirror those observed in traditional psychophysical studies using Cornsweet edges, particularly for edges whose spectral profiles align with natural image statistics. This consistency suggests that mechanisms identified in controlled paradigms generalize to complex scenes, positioning line drawings as a high-fidelity tool for characterizing real-world visual behavior and individual variability in edge perception.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Anna L. Haverkamp, Marianne Maertens

papers.title: Ocular drift shakes the stationary view on pattern vision
papers.abstract: The role of involuntary fixational eye movements, specifically ocular drift, is investigated in the context of human edge sensitivity. While traditional spatial vision models assume stationary retinal input during fixation, ocular drift dynamically redistributes stimulus power, emphasizing high spatial frequency content. The authors combined empirical edge sensitivity data obtained under visual noise with neural modeling to test if incorporating drift improved model predictions. Analysis revealed that drift-induced spectral shifts align with the human contrast sensitivity function (CSF), leading to superior data fitting compared to stationary assumptions. Mechanistic modeling further demonstrated that standard multi-scale architectures may artificially compensate for the absence of drift by redistributing activity across spatial frequency channels. These results argue for a transition from purely spatial models to spatiotemporal frameworks that recognize the active nature of visual sampling during fixation.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Marianne Maertens

papers.title: Standard models of spatial vision mispredict edge sensitivity at low spatial frequencies
papers.abstract: The standard model of early spatial vision, which employs orientation- and spatial frequency (SF)-selective channels followed by nonlinear recombination, is tested for its ability to account for psychophysical sensitivity to high-contrast edges. Using a 2-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) localization task, the authors measured sensitivity to Cornsweet edges (peak SFs: 0.5, 3, and 9 cpd) in the presence of broadband and narrowband noise. Although single- and multi-scale versions of the standard model successfully predicted performance in many conditions, significant and systematic deviations were observed for the lowest SF edges and in the presence of pink noise. These failures suggest that the standard linear-nonlinear filter bank architecture may lack necessary components for processing broadband, behaviorally relevant stimuli, potentially indicating a shift from contrast-based to luminance-based detection mechanisms at low spatial frequencies.
papers.authors: Lynn Schmittwilken, Felix A. Wichmann, Marianne Maertens

0416.name: Marieke Mur
0416.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Computer Science; Brain and Mind Institute
0416.bio: Mur is an Assistant Professor at Western University with joint appointments in the Department of Psychology and the Department of Computer Science. Their research integrates psychology, neuroscience, and artificial intelligence to study how the human brain transforms visual input into representations. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and deep neural networks, Mur investigates the neural population codes and representational geometries that support object recognition. Mur contributed to the development of representational similarity analysis (RSA), a framework used to connect brain-activity patterns, computational models, and behavioral measures.
0416.research_direction: Dr. Mur has recently been investigating the functional organization and representational dynamics of both the visual and prefrontal cortices using a multimodal approach that spans fMRI, MEG, and primate electrophysiology. In the visual system, their recent work explores how the ventral stream processes visual features and semantic information over time by comparing brain activity to deep neural networks, and asks how the cortex balances stimulus-driven representational stability against task-driven flexibility during object categorization. Parallel lines of research examine the functional architecture of the prefrontal cortex, investigating whether it is organized by smooth gradients or discrete functional boundaries using individualized human neuroimaging, as well as probing the task-specific spatial topography of macaque prefrontal population activity. To better capture these complex spatial and temporal patterns, they have also been developing novel methodological tools, such as dual-frequency-tagged fMRI protocols, to map fine-grained computations across the cortical hierarchy.

papers.title: Individualized parcellation reveals functional boundaries in human prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Task-evoked organization of human prefrontal cortex varies considerably between people, which limits what group atlases can reveal about whether PFC is organized by smooth gradients or discrete subdivisions. The authors build individualized functional parcellations by combining a group atlas with subject-specific task data, and use them to test for sharp functional boundaries. The results bear on the long-standing gradient-versus-modularity debate in prefrontal organization.
papers.authors: Jinkang Derrick Xiang, Da Zhi, Bassel Arafat, Caroline Nettekoven, Joern Diedrichsen, Marieke Mur

papers.title: Stimulus effects dwarf task effects in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Human participants categorized object images and written words under different task rules while fMRI was recorded, to ask how the visual system balances a stable representation of the world against task-driven flexibility. An ANOVA-style decomposition of representational variance across the cortical hierarchy shows that stimulus identity explains the overwhelming majority (over 95 percent) of explainable variance in ventral visual cortex, with task and stimulus-by-task interaction contributing very little. The work argues visual representations are far more stable than the task-modulation literature suggests.
papers.authors: Marieke Mur, Daniel J. Mitchell, Stephan Brueggemann, John Duncan

papers.title: Task-specific topographic maps of neural activity in the primate lateral prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Multi-electrode array recordings were made from macaque lateral prefrontal cortex during three different cognitive tasks. The spatial topography of population activity was stable within a task but changed across tasks, at a spatial scale consistent with anatomical afferent input patterns. The authors conclude that prefrontal maps are stable, task-specific codes that support task specialization, and that variability in map layout tracks task demands.
papers.authors: Jinkang Derrick Xiang, Megan Roussy, Benjamin Corrigan, Roberto A. Gulli, Rogelio Luna, Maryam Hasanzadeh Mofrad, Lyle Muller, Joern Diedrichsen, Taylor W. Schmitz, Julio Martinez-Trujillo, Marieke Mur

papers.title: Frequency-tagged fMRI: A platform for fine-grained spatiotemporal analysis of cortical function
papers.abstract: The paper introduces and validates a dual-frequency tagging protocol in which oscillating stimuli drive BOLD responses at known frequencies, at 3T and 7T. It reliably recovers fundamental, multiplexed and nonlinear intermodulation responses at single-vertex resolution across human visual cortex, with spatially distinct topographies and reproducible dynamics across sessions. This establishes frequency-tagged fMRI as a tool for fine-grained study of cortical computation.
papers.authors: Geoffrey N. Ngo, Reebal W. Rafeh, Lyle E. Muller, Ali R. Khan, Ravi S. Menon, Taylor W. Schmitz, Marieke Mur

papers.title: Deep neural networks and visuo-semantic models explain complementary components of human ventral-stream representational dynamics
papers.abstract: Time-resolved MEG representations of the human ventral stream were compared with deep neural networks and with visuo-semantic models built from human-labelled object properties. Each model class accounts for a different portion of the representational dynamics, with the two together explaining more than either alone. The findings suggest the ventral stream carries both visual-feature and semantic information that current DNNs only partly capture.
papers.authors: Kamila M. Jozwik, Tim C. Kietzmann, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Marieke Mur

0417.name: Marion Rouault
0417.institution: Paris Brain Institute (Institut du Cerveau, ICM)
0417.department: Motivation, Brain and Behavior (MBB) Team (CNRS / Sorbonne Universite / Inserm)
0417.bio: Marion Rouault is a Chargée de Recherche at the CNRS, based at the Paris Brain Institute (ICM), where they investigate the neurocognitive architecture of human metacognition. Rouault's research explores how individuals monitor their own cognitive processes, specifically focusing on the computational mechanisms that transform local confidence signals into global self-beliefs and self-esteem. Using behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and MEG, Rouault examines the functional roles of these signals in learning and decision-making. Their work also addresses the clinical implications of metacognitive efficiency in psychiatric disorders, aiming to characterize how self-evaluation impairments relate to mental health symptoms.
0417.research_direction: Dr. Rouault has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architectures underlying metacognition and subjective confidence judgments. Their recent work explores how our overall sense of confidence is constructed, using behavioral experiments, fMRI, and computational modeling to isolate the domain-specific versus domain-general brain signals that track self-assessment across diverse tasks like perception and memory. Beyond basic cognitive mechanisms, they are also examining how metacognition operates in high-stakes applied contexts, specifically testing how accurately practicing physicians monitor their own diagnostic decisions to identify potential sources of clinical error. Furthermore, their research extends these computational measures of self-monitoring to clinical populations, investigating how altered metacognitive and interoceptive bodily awareness might drive the subjective experience of fatigue in conditions like multiple sclerosis.

papers.title: Decision-making for clinicians
papers.abstract: A review-style article summarizing what cognitive science says about how decisions are made and where they go wrong, aimed at practicing physicians. Covers biases, confidence and metacognition in clinical reasoning. Intended to translate laboratory findings into practical awareness for clinical practice.
papers.authors: Benjamin Rohaut, Marion Rouault

papers.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
papers.abstract: Asks how the overall sense of how well one is doing (global confidence) is built from confidence in single decisions, and how much of it depends on the task domain versus a general self-assessment signal. Uses behavioral experiments across cognitive domains combined with computational modeling to separate the domain-specific and domain-general components. The work bears on how self-beliefs and metacognitive ability generalize across tasks.
papers.authors: Sophie Bavard, Andrew McWilliams, Flora Chartier, Karim N'Diaye, Stephen M. Fleming, Marion Rouault

papers.title: Physicians' metacognition in medical decision-making
papers.abstract: Examines whether physicians accurately monitor their own diagnostic decisions, testing for overconfidence and how well confidence tracks correctness in clinical scenarios. Compares confidence and accuracy across clinicians and links the findings to models of metacognition. Highlights implications for reducing diagnostic error in high-stakes medical settings.
papers.venue: PsyArXiv (Preprint; listed as Neuroscience of Consciousness, in press 2026)
papers.authors: Camille Lakhlifi, Rayan Kouzy, Francois-Xavier Lejeune, Nicolas Beuzon, Jerome Mawet, Caroline Roos, Mehdi Khamassi, Benjamin Rohaut, Marion Rouault

papers.title: Interoceptive and metacognitive facets of fatigue in multiple sclerosis
papers.abstract: Investigates how fatigue in multiple sclerosis relates to bodily (interoceptive) awareness and to metacognitive self-monitoring. Combines heartbeat-based and perceptual tasks with computational measures of metacognition in patients and controls. Suggests that fatigue is associated with altered self-monitoring rather than only with basic sensory sensitivity.
papers.authors: Marion Rouault, Ines Pereira, Herman Galioulline, Stephen M. Fleming, Klaas Enno Stephan, Zina-Mary Manjaly

papers.title: A shared brain system forming confidence judgment across cognitive domains
papers.abstract: Uses fMRI to ask whether confidence judgments in different cognitive tasks rely on common brain regions. Finds that a shared set of regions, including prefrontal and value-related areas, tracks confidence across domains such as perception and memory. Supports a domain-general system for forming metacognitive judgments.
papers.authors: Marion Rouault, Mael Lebreton, Mathias Pessiglione

0418.name: Marisa Carrasco
0418.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0418.bio: Marisa Carrasco is the Julius Silver Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, where they investigate the relationship between the psychological and neural mechanisms of vision. Carrasco’s research utilizes human psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), neurostimulation (TMS), and computational modeling to characterize how attention modulates early visual processing and alters the subjective appearance of stimuli. Their work distinguishes between endogenous and exogenous attention and documents how attentional mechanisms interact with sensory factors like spatial resolution and contrast sensitivity to shape perceptual performance.
0418.research_direction: Dr. Carrasco has recently been investigating the structural, computational, and neural mechanisms that shape how visual perception and attention operate across space and time. A major focus of their recent work explores performance asymmetries across the visual field—specifically variations across eccentricity and polar angle—by utilizing equivalent-noise modeling, contrast adaptation paradigms linked to individual V1 surface area, and cross-species behavioral comparisons between humans and macaques. In parallel, they are investigating the cortical dynamics and causal neural networks underlying voluntary attention. To examine these top-down processes, their lab uses MEG with steady-state visual probes to track how temporal expectation modulates anticipatory neural activity, and employs TMS to map the respective causal roles of frontal and occipital cortices in deploying endogenous spatial attention.

papers.title: Distinct system-level computations underlie perceptual variation across the visual field
papers.abstract: Using the equivalent-noise method and a perceptual template model, the authors decomposed orientation discrimination into gain, internal noise and nonlinearity across eccentricity and around polar angle. Worse performance in the periphery came from reduced gain and nonlinearity plus increased internal noise, whereas polar-angle asymmetries (horizontal over vertical, lower over upper meridian) were explained by gain alone. This separates the computational bases of the eccentricity effect and polar-angle asymmetries and ties them to known neural architecture.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Shutian Xue, Antoine Barbot, Jared Abrams, Qingyuan Chen, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Visual adaptation stronger at the horizontal than the vertical meridian: Linking performance with V1 cortical surface area
papers.abstract: Adaptation to repeated stimuli was measured for contrast sensitivity at the fovea and perifovea across the four cardinal meridians. Adaptation was stronger along the horizontal than the vertical meridian, which reduces the usual horizontal-vertical performance anisotropy and promotes perceptual uniformity around the visual field. Perifoveal adaptation strength correlated with each observer's V1 surface area, linking behavior to cortical structure.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Hsing-Hao Lee, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Opposite asymmetry in visual perception of humans and macaques
papers.abstract: Human adults and macaque monkeys performed the same motion-direction discrimination task at isoeccentric locations. Humans showed the familiar advantage of the horizontal over the vertical meridian, while macaques showed the opposite pattern. This challenges the assumption that macaques are a straightforward model of human perception across the visual field.
papers.authors: Ekin Tunçok, Lynne Kiorpes, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Anticipatory and evoked visual cortical dynamics of voluntary temporal attention
papers.abstract: The authors recorded MEG while observers directed temporal attention to one of two predictably timed targets, with a steady-state visual probe tracking cortical activity throughout. Before the target, the probe ramped up with expectation and showed a low-frequency modulation whose phase shifted depending on which time point was attended. After target onset, attention transiently modulated the response, revealing both periodic anticipatory and transient evoked mechanisms.
papers.authors: Rachel N. Denison, Karen J. Tian, David J. Heeger, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Transcranial magnetic stimulation to frontal but not occipital cortex disrupts endogenous attention
papers.abstract: TMS was applied over right frontal eye fields (rFEF+) or V1/V2 while observers did an orientation task under manipulated endogenous attention. Occipital stimulation left attentional effects intact, whereas rFEF+ stimulation reduced the overall attention effect, removing both benefits and costs. This gives causal evidence that frontal rather than early visual cortex is critical for voluntary attention, in contrast to exogenous attention.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Antonio Fernandez, Nina M. Hanning, Marisa Carrasco

0419.name: Mark B. Neider
0419.bio: Mark B. Neider is a Professor and the Interim Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Central Florida and directs the Applied Cognition and Aging Laboratory. Neider’s research examines the mechanisms of human perception and cognition in complex contexts, focusing on the interaction between attentional and memory systems. Neider utilizes methodologies such as high-fidelity driving simulation, virtual reality, eye tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to study behavior throughout the lifespan. Their work focuses on developing evidence-based training interventions and technological solutions intended to improve performance and safety in high-stakes environments.
0419.research_direction: Dr. Neider has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual search and attentional guidance, exploring how top-down categorical templates are used for distractor suppression and how the proportional surface area of a target color influences search efficiency in both simple and naturalistic stimuli. To support these inquiries into ecologically valid vision, their recent work includes developing open-source computational tools to quantify and control the dominant colors of complex, real-world objects. Beyond foundational vision science, they are also examining how fundamental attentional limits operate in applied human-computer interaction contexts. Specifically, their applied research investigates how workplace task interruptions impact a user's ability to identify phishing emails, as well as how icon realism and visual complexity affect search performance within digital interfaces.

papers.title: MATCH: A toolbox to assess the primary color of real-world objects and generate color-matching stimuli
papers.abstract: The paper presents an open toolbox for determining the dominant color of photographs of real-world objects and for building stimulus sets whose colors are matched across objects. It is aimed at visual search and attention researchers who need to control or manipulate object color, which is otherwise hard to specify for natural items. The authors describe the method and validate it against human judgments of object color.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Top-down categorical information can be utilized in distractor suppression
papers.abstract: Using visual search experiments, the study asks whether observers can use advance knowledge of a distractor category (rather than a specific distractor image) to suppress those items and speed up finding a target. Results indicate that categorical templates for rejection can be used to reduce distraction, extending suppression beyond specific features. This bears on theories of how top-down knowledge shapes attentional selection.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Proportion of colour proportionally affects guidance in search for conjunction and real-world objects
papers.abstract: The experiments manipulate how much of an object's surface is the target color and measure how strongly that color guides search, both for simple conjunction stimuli and for real-world objects. Guidance from color scaled with the proportion of the object that carried that color, giving a graded rather than all-or-none picture of feature guidance. The work links laboratory feature-search findings to natural objects.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Phishing interrupted: The impact of task interruptions on phishing email classification
papers.abstract: The study tests whether being interrupted while sorting emails changes people's ability to tell phishing messages from legitimate ones. It links attention and memory limits under interruption to cybersecurity behavior. The findings inform how workplace interruptions may raise vulnerability to phishing.
papers.authors: Elisabeth J.D. Slifkin, Mark B. Neider

papers.title: Keep it real, keep it simple: the effects of icon characteristics on visual search
papers.abstract: Experiments examined how icon realism and visual complexity change how quickly people find a target icon on an interface. The results show that realistic, simpler icons are found more efficiently than abstract or complex ones. The paper offers design guidance grounded in visual search theory.
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider

0421.name: Mark D. Lescroart
0421.bio: Mark D. Lescroart is a neuroscientist and associate professor at the University of Nevada, Reno, specializing in the computational modeling of human visual perception. Lescroart’s research employs voxel-wise encoding models, fMRI, and deep neural networks to investigate how the brain transforms retinal input into representations of 3D scene structure, object geometry, and human actions. They have conducted studies on the neural encoding of medial axis structures and the identification of body-selective regions in the visual periphery. Their current research, supported by an NSF CAREER award, explores how task-related attentional states modulate visual representations and involves the development of the Visual Experience Database (VEDB).
0421.research_direction: Dr. Lescroart has recently been working on how the human visual cortex represents complex natural scenes, particularly bodies. Their recent work uses large fMRI datasets and voxelwise encoding models, which predict brain responses from image features, to map how body parts and their locations are represented, including newly identified regions that respond to bodies in the periphery. They have also been developing methods that use deep neural network models of the brain to generate images that drive specific brain regions, making these models easier to interpret. In addition, they have built a deep learning tool for tracking eyelids and pupils in video under difficult imaging conditions.

papers.title: Novel Body-Selective Regions Responsive to Bodies Away from the Center of Gaze
papers.abstract: This study identifies two previously unidentified cortical regions in the human visual system that exhibit specialized selectivity for images of human bodies located in the visual periphery. Utilizing high-resolution 7T fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and voxel-wise encoding models, the researchers localized the Ventromedial Body Area (VMBA) and the Medial Body Area (MBA). Unlike the well-known Extrastriate Body Area (EBA) and Fusiform Body Area (FBA), these regions—situated posterior to the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and superior to the retrosplenial complex (RSC) near the parieto-occipital sulcus—respond optimally to bodies viewed away from the center of gaze, suggesting a neural substrate for processing social and action-related information in the peripheral field.
papers.authors: Yu Zhao, Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: Visualizing and Controlling Cortical Responses Using Voxel-Weighted Activation Maximization
papers.abstract: The authors introduce Voxel-Weighted Activation Maximization (VWAM), a technique for interpreting deep neural network (DNN)-based encoding models of the human brain. By mapping activations from multiple layers of a pretrained Inception V3 network to fMRI BOLD responses using linear regression, the method creates an image-computable model of the visual cortex. VWAM utilizes gradient-based optimization to synthesize stimuli that maximize predicted responses in individual voxels and entire regions of interest (ROIs). Validation in an fMRI study demonstrated that these generated 'superstimuli' reliably and selectively drive activity in both early and higher-level visual areas, providing a flexible framework for characterizing and modulating human cortical representations without the need for natively generative models.
papers.venue: 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW)
papers.authors: Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: Voxelwise Modeling Reveals Selectivity for Body Part Identity and Location in BOLD fMRI Responses to Complex Naturalistic Stimuli
papers.abstract: This research investigates the representation of human body parts and their spatial locations in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC) using a large-scale encoding model approach. The researchers employed a deep neural network (OpenPose) to parameterize the identities and positions of body parts across diverse stimulus sets, including natural movie clips and computer-rendered scenes. Regularized linear regression was used to fit these quantified features to BOLD fMRI signals. The findings reveal a complex, distributed pattern of tuning within LOTC that encompasses both the identity of body components and their retinotopic or relative coordinates, challenging simple modular accounts of body representation and providing evidence for a more integrated topography of body-related features in the human brain.
papers.authors: Matthew W. Shinkle, Mark D. Lescroart

papers.title: A framework for generalizable neural networks for robust estimation of eyelids and pupils
papers.abstract: This paper presents pylids, a deep learning framework designed to improve the accuracy and robustness of video-oculography under challenging imaging conditions. Built upon the DeepLabCut architecture, the model addresses the scarcity of labeled training data by leveraging algorithmic annotations from high-quality eye videos and employing domain-specific data augmentation, such as simulated reflections and occlusions. The authors demonstrate that the performance of the DNN can be predicted based on the distributional distance between training and test data. By implementing guided sampling strategies and data pruning, the framework achieves state-of-the-art results in pupil and eyelid localization while requiring significantly fewer training samples and enhancing generalization to real-world, noisy datasets.
papers.authors: Arnab Biswas, Mark D. Lescroart

0422.name: Mark Greenlee
0422.department: Department of Experimental Psychology and Methodology
0422.bio: Mark Greenlee is the Chair of Experimental Psychology and Methodology at the University of Regensburg and co-director of the institution's Magnetic Resonance Imaging Center. Greenlee’s research examines the neural mechanisms underlying human visual and vestibular processing, focusing on self-motion perception and visual-vestibular integration. Using high-field fMRI, EEG, and psychophysical techniques, Greenlee investigates cortical plasticity, population receptive field mapping, and the effects of training on visual crowding. Their work also includes the study of cognitive functions such as visual short-term memory, attention, and the neural correlates of perceptual filling-in.
0422.research_direction: Dr. Greenlee has recently been exploring the foundational mechanisms of visual perception and memory, ranging from the spatiotemporal properties of contour erasure and perceptual filling-in to how visual short-term memory for motion is encoded by action video game players. Their recent work also extensively investigates multisensory integration and the cortical representation of self-motion. By combining fMRI with caloric and visual-motion stimulation, they are mapping distinct vestibular and visual regions within the medial cortex, while parallel behavioral studies test how congruent olfactory sensations influence visual search accuracy and speed. Furthermore, they are investigating the neuromodulatory drivers of visual perceptual learning, specifically asking how the structural integrity of the locus coeruleus governs the spatial transfer of reward-paired feature discrimination.

papers.title: The integrity of locus coeruleus modulates reward-induced visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Participants trained on a contrast categorization task in one visual quadrant while one task-irrelevant orientation was secretly paired with a probabilistic monetary reward. Only the reward group improved orientation discrimination for the reward-paired feature, and this learning transferred to untrained quadrants. Structural integrity of the locus coeruleus predicted how much learning transferred, pointing to neuromodulatory control of reward-driven perceptual learning.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Sinah Wiborg, Lea Hemesath, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: Visual search performance depends on the congruency of olfactory sensations
papers.abstract: Participants searched for a cued fruit among fruit distractors while being exposed via an olfactometer to a matching, non-matching or no odor. Matching smells improved accuracy and speed, most strongly in people with poor baseline search, while mismatching smells hurt good searchers. The size of the effect tracked individual olfactory discrimination ability.
papers.authors: Serena Castellotti, Marija Soldo, Tina Plank, Maria Michela Del Viva, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: The spatial and temporal properties of the contour erasure effect and perceptual filling-in
papers.abstract: Brief flicker adaptation at a disk's outline can make the disk vanish into the background. The authors systematically varied eccentricity, adapter size, flicker rate, adaptation duration and interstimulus interval and measured detection-threshold elevation. The results link contour erasure to filling-in, forward masking and contrast adaptation, emphasizing the role of edges in surface perception.
papers.authors: Yih-Shiuan Lin, Chien-Chung Chen, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: Visual short-term memory in action and non-action video game players: A focus on short and long delay intervals
papers.abstract: Action and non-action video game players memorized the directions of one to four random-dot motion stimuli and reproduced a probed one after a short or long delay. Action players showed higher precision at long delays for a single item and needed less initial training, while resource-rational modelling suggested different encoding strategies between the groups.
papers.authors: Andrea Pavan, Seyma Koc Yilmaz, Hulusi Kafaligonul, Julia Föcker, Mark W. Greenlee

papers.title: Vestibular and visual brain areas in the medial cortex of the human brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with caloric vestibular, thermal and visual-motion stimulation in 36 participants, the study maps the medial-cortex network for self-motion. Beyond the known visual-vestibular area CSv, it identifies a vestibular-only region in the pericallosal sulcus (vPCS) distinct from retrosplenial motion regions, and characterizes V6 and precuneus motion areas as visual-motion driven.
papers.authors: Anton L. Beer, Markus Becker, Sebastian M. Frank, Mark W. Greenlee

0423.name: Mark J. Fenske
0423.bio: Mark J. Fenske is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Guelph and directs the Cognitive-Affective Neuroscience Lab. Fenske’s research investigates the neurocognitive interface of attention, emotion, and motivation, specifically how cognitive control mechanisms like inhibition influence the emotional evaluation of stimuli. Using functional MRI and psychophysiological measures, Fenske has found that the act of ignoring distractions can result in their subsequent affective devaluation. Their broader research program also addresses the cognitive and perceptual impacts of states such as boredom and the neural foundations of performance.
0423.research_direction: Dr. Fenske has recently been studying boredom and how it relates to attention, emotion regulation, and everyday behavior. Their recent work explores why some people are more prone to boredom, examining links to difficulties regulating emotions, attention lapses, and cognitive flexibility. They have also tested whether doodling during a lecture helps people stay engaged and remember material. A related thread looks at older adults with hearing loss, asking how boredom proneness and attention difficulties shape how much hearing problems bother them and whether they adopt hearing aids.

papers.title: The Cognitive-Affective Hearing Aid Paradox: Boredom Proneness and Attentional Difficulties Predict Worse Age-Related Subjective Hearing but Lower Rates of Hearing Aid Adoption
papers.abstract: Untreated age-related hearing impairment significantly elevates risks for depressive symptoms, social isolation, and accelerated cognitive decline, yet adherence to rehabilitative intervention remains notably low. Although audiometric thresholds inform clinical severity, self-reported subjective hearing handicap is historically a stronger determinant of hearing aid acquisition. Building upon evidence that individuals high in trait boredom proneness and attentional lapses perceive hearing loss more negatively, this longitudinal investigation examined whether these cognitive-affective individual differences mediate the pathway between subjective auditory impairment and actual hearing aid adoption. Older adults (aged 50+) recruited from hearing-health clinics completed pure-tone audiometry alongside standardized self-report measures of hearing handicap, effortful exertion while listening, boredom proneness, and spontaneous mind-wandering, with device adoption tracked across a 5-year follow-up period. While boredom proneness and spontaneous mind-wandering did not independently predict device acquisition in direct univariate models, parallel mediation models demonstrated that both traits significantly mediated the relationship between subjective hearing handicap (as well as listening effort) and hearing aid purchase. Crucially, whereas heightened hearing handicap and listening strain increased the probability of device purchase, elevated boredom proneness and spontaneous mind-wandering functioned as suppression variables that predicted reduced rates of adoption, demonstrating a paradoxical barrier in hearing healthcare decision-making.
papers.authors: Alyssa C. Smith, Carolyn M. L. Crawford, Gurjit Singh, Mark J. Fenske

papers.title: Boredom Proneness Is Predicted by Difficulties in Emotion Regulation that Are Mediated by Corresponding Problems with Attention and Cognitive Flexibility
papers.abstract: The well-established links between boredom proneness and dysfunctional behaviors—including substance misuse, pathological gambling, and problematic smartphone engagement—have been hypothesized to reflect emotion-dysregulation mechanisms driving maladaptive coping with negative affect. However, empirical investigations clarifying how specific facets of emotion regulation relate to boredom proneness remain sparse. This investigation examined whether trait boredom proneness is predicted by maladaptive emotion-regulation strategies (specifically expressive suppression and rumination) and whether such relationships are underpinned by executive function impairments (attentional control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility). Undergraduate participants (N = 219) completed a comprehensive psychometric battery evaluating trait boredom proneness, emotion-regulation profiles, and perceived cognitive failures across attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility domains. Structural and mediation analyses revealed that generalized difficulties in emotion regulation significantly predicted boredom proneness, an effect that was partially mediated by self-reported attentional difficulties and diminished cognitive flexibility, but not by memory failures. Furthermore, individual propensities for expressive suppression and rumination positively predicted boredom proneness, whereas cognitive distraction showed no significant association. These findings highlight distinct cognitive-affective pathways through which executive dysfunction and maladaptive emotion regulation interact to heighten vulnerability to chronic boredom.
papers.authors: Natasha Vogel, Mark Fenske

papers.title: Note-taking for the win: Doodling does not reduce boredom or mind-wandering, nor enhance attention or retention of lecture material
papers.abstract: Although doodling and incidental motor fidgeting are traditionally categorized in educational settings as behavioral indices of inattention, recent proposals have framed them as functional coping mechanisms that may preserve performance by mitigating boredom and attenuating mnemonic deficits. To rigorously evaluate these competing hypotheses, two experiments (combined N = 222) assessed the influence of concurrent doodling on state boredom, attentional allocation, spontaneous mind-wandering, and episodic retention of lecture content. In Experiment 1, participants engaged in a repetitive auditory monitoring task while either performing structured doodling (shading geometric templates) or listening passively. In Experiment 2, participants listened to a 45-minute academic lecture assigned across four distinct conditions: structured doodling, unstructured (free-form) doodling, intentional note-taking, or a listen-only control. Throughout the lecture, intermittent thought probes measured real-time fluctuations in state boredom, mind-wandering, and focused attention, followed by an objective post-lecture comprehension test. Across both paradigms, doodling failed to alleviate state boredom or mind-wandering and conferred no benefits to sustained attention or information retention relative to control listening. In contrast, focused note-taking optimized cognitive engagement, generating significantly higher attentional focus and superior test scores alongside the lowest observed levels of state boredom and mind-wandering.
papers.authors: Emily Krysten Spencer-Mueller, Mark J. Fenske

papers.title: Subjective Impact of Age-Related Hearing Loss Is Worse for Those Who Routinely Experience Boredom and Failures of Attention
papers.abstract: Despite demonstrable psychosocial and cognitive benefits associated with audiological interventions, many older adults experiencing presbycusis fail to pursue auditory rehabilitation. A critical contributor to low treatment uptake is the persistent discordance observed between objective pure-tone audiometric thresholds and subjective evaluations of auditory disability. This investigation tested whether individual differences in cognitive-affective vulnerability—namely trait boredom proneness and everyday attention failures—account for variance in the subjective burden of age-related hearing impairment. A clinical sample of older adults completed diagnostic pure-tone audiometry and self-report instruments quantifying hearing handicap (Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly), subjective listening effort, boredom proneness, and spontaneous attentional lapses. Regression and mediation analyses revealed that individuals with greater susceptibility to boredom reported significantly more severe perceived hearing handicap and heightened listening strain. Crucially, parallel mediation demonstrated that this relationship between boredom proneness and subjective hearing handicap was mediated by individual differences in sustained task-focused attentional control, an effect that remained consistent regardless of the severity of objective audiometric hearing thresholds. These findings identify distinct neurocognitive-affective traits underlying subjective hearing distress that may inform clinical counseling and improve rehabilitation uptake.
papers.authors: Carolyn M. L. Crawford, Kalisha Ramlackhan, Gurjit Singh, Mark J. Fenske

0424.name: Mark W. Becker
0424.bio: Mark W. Becker is a Professor in the Cognition and Cognitive Neuroscience program at Michigan State University who investigates the mechanisms governing visual attention and its application to real-world tasks. Their research utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysical methodologies to explore how visual search is influenced by target prevalence, emotional stimuli, and individual differences in working memory. Becker has examined 'panic search'—where threat-related stimuli improve search efficiency for non-threatening items—and has conducted interdisciplinary studies on the efficacy of medical and nutritional labeling. Becker’s current work focuses on the processes guiding the allocation of attention and the cognitive factors that lead to errors in critical visual search environments.
0424.research_direction: Dr. Becker has recently been studying how people search visual scenes and why they sometimes miss what they are looking for. Their recent work explores how the visual system implicitly learns regularities, such as where or in what color targets tend to appear, and how several of these learned biases combine to steer attention. They have also been investigating why rare targets get missed so often, testing whether the cause is quitting the search early or a higher bar for deciding an item is a target, and whether occasional practice trials with feedback can reduce the problem. Related work examines how bright, irrelevant distractors change the way evidence accumulates during search, and how a mental template of the target's color and shape guides eye movements.

papers.title: Guidance of attention by statistical learning when multiple guidance mechanisms compete
papers.abstract: Observers implicitly extract environmental statistical regularities to bias visual attention toward spatial coordinates and surface features correlated with target occurrence; however, empirical investigations have typically evaluated these statistical biases in isolation. In Experiment 1, a visual search paradigm tested whether human observers simultaneously acquire and implement dual independent regularities—one mapping target probability to a spatial quadrant and another to a surface color. The behavioral results demonstrated that both statistical regularities were acquired implicitly, exerting independent, additive influences on attentional guidance. Experiments 2 and 3 investigated how volitional goal-directed control interacts with implicit statistical learning by presenting endogenous feature cues while maintaining implicit spatial contingencies. Endogenous cuing along one feature dimension did not attenuate the implicit learning of contingencies in the other. Crucially, the deployment of statistical regularities was contingent upon the validity of volitional cues: statistical biases facilitated performance during neutral or valid cuing but were eliminated under invalid cues. These findings demonstrate that volitional control and statistical learning operate within an integrated hierarchical framework where volitional guidance takes precedence over implicit statistical biases during selection conflicts.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Morgan Dodd, Tristan Janisse

papers.title: Reducing the low-prevalence effect with probe trials
papers.abstract: Target scarcity during visual search triggers an elevated miss rate termed the low-prevalence effect (LPE), presenting a persistent operational hazard in visual screening. Across four experiments, this study examined whether distributing artificial 'probe' trials—target-present trials paired with post-response feedback—effectively mitigates the LPE. Experiment 1 used a low-prevalence T-among-Ls search task and demonstrated that interleaved probe trials substantially attenuated target miss rates. Experiment 2 evaluated dual-target search (T and O targets among L and Q distractors) while manipulating the proportion of probe trials dedicated to each target; the observed probe benefit scaled strictly with the frequency of the probed target exemplar, showing minimal generalization to unprobed targets. Experiment 3 used eye tracking to dissociate whether probe trials shift trial-level quitting thresholds, alter item-evaluation decision criteria, or enhance attentional guidance. Gaze metrics demonstrated that probe trials selectively improved top-down attentional guidance toward features matching frequently probed targets, without altering quitting thresholds (number of inspected items) or conservative shifts in decision criteria. Finally, Experiment 4 showed that performance improvements persisted without explicit trial feedback, confirming that probe trials alleviate the LPE by shifting perceived target prevalence rather than reinforcing accuracy through feedback alone.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Andrew Rodriguez, Derrek T. Montalvo, Chad Peltier

papers.title: Salient distractors influence information accrual rather than quitting threshold in visual search
papers.abstract: The addition of an irrelevant salient singleton to visual search arrays has previously been observed to increase target misses while accelerating target-absent reaction times, an effect typically interpreted as a reduction in the global quitting threshold. Across two experiments, this investigation demonstrates that this behavioral profile persists when the salient singleton shares no critical dimensions with background distractors, but reverses when the salient singleton shares orientation features with the search target, producing prolonged target-absent response times and reduced miss rates. This crossover effect contradicts a unitary quitting threshold explanation. Instead, the empirical patterns align with a drift-diffusion framework wherein a salient stimulus provides a rapid burst of evidence accumulation toward its associated decision boundary: when sharing target features, evidence accrues rapidly toward the 'target-present' boundary, whereas non-target salient features drive evidence toward the 'target-absent' boundary. This evidence-accrual account offers a parsimonious alternative to global threshold shifts and specifies the conditions under which salient singletons enhance or disrupt target detection.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Jeff Moher, Derrek T. Montalvo, Andrew Rodriguez

papers.title: Activation thresholds, not quitting thresholds, account for the low prevalence effect in dynamic search
papers.abstract: The low-prevalence effect (LPE) describes the marked reduction in detection accuracy that occurs when search targets are rare. Standard visual search models attribute this deficit to lowered quitting thresholds, where observers abort search after inspecting fewer items on discrete trials. However, this quitting threshold account cannot directly explain performance in continuous monitoring tasks involving dynamic displays that lack discrete trial terminations. In Experiment 1, a 2 (display dynamic: continuous moving vs static) × 2 (target prevalence: 10% vs 40%) design demonstrated that while baseline detection was lower in dynamic displays, an LPE of equivalent magnitude occurred in both display types. In Experiment 2, participants searched for either of two targets (Ts and Ls) where prevalence was varied within-display (10% vs 40%), an arrangement eliminating trial-level quitting threshold adjustments even in static searches. Replicating Experiment 1, a pronounced LPE persisted across both static and dynamic modalities. These results demonstrate that the LPE in continuous and multi-target search is not governed by quitting thresholds, supporting instead an activation-threshold model wherein target infrequency raises the internal evidentiary threshold required for an attended item to trigger conscious detection.
papers.authors: Mark W. Becker, Andrew Rodriguez, Jeffrey Bolkhovsky, Chad Peltier, Sylvia B. Guillory

papers.title: Isolating the impact of a visual search template's color and form information on search guidance and verification times
papers.abstract: Visual search guidance relies on preparatory attentional templates, with pictorial cues consistently providing greater search benefits than linguistic text cues. However, pictorial cues provide both detailed structural form and chromaticity, leaving it ambiguous whether picture benefits arise from peripheral guidance via chromatic signals or spatial form resolution. Given that spatial visual acuity drops precipitously with retinal eccentricity while color discrimination remains relatively robust, high-fidelity form information may contribute minimally to peripheral oculomotor guidance. Using eye tracking across a 2 (cue modality: pictorial vs text) × 2 (color information: chromatic vs achromatic) factorial design, this study separated search guidance (latency and saccadic steps before target fixations) from target verification (post-fixation dwell time). Experiment 1 cued search targets using full-color images, grayscale images, color-descriptive text, or neutral text. Experiment 2 matched text cue font colors to the target's dominant hue. Oculomotor metrics demonstrated that high-fidelity form information predominantly improved target verification dwell times, whereas chromatic information drove efficient attentional guidance across the visual periphery, indicating distinct functional dissociations between form and color components within the search template.
papers.authors: Derrek T. Montalvo, Andrew Rodriguez, Mark W. Becker

0425.name: Markus Lappe
0425.bio: Markus Lappe is a Professor of General Psychology at the University of Münster who researches the computational and biological mechanisms of visual perception in relation to motor activity. Lappe’s work examines how the visual system integrates retinal information with eye movement signals for spatial stability and how humans utilize optic flow and biological motion for navigation and action recognition. By combining psychophysical experiments with quantitative computational modeling and neurophysiological data, Lappe explores the plasticity of perceptual space and the neural processes involved in perceiving the environment during active movement.
0425.research_direction: Dr. Lappe has recently been investigating how the visual and motor systems interact to maintain perceptual stability and adapt to spatial errors. A major focus of their recent work explores oculomotor learning, using computational population-based models and intra-saccadic target displacements to probe how global spatial errors versus local feature errors drive saccade adaptation. They are also examining complex motion processing, analyzing how the visual system parses optic flow to simultaneously estimate self-motion and object trajectories, and how dissociations between smooth pursuit and saccadic control during nonrigid motion affect spatial perception. Additionally, their research extends these principles of sensorimotor plasticity to whole-body locomotion, testing how individuals acquire and retain long-term motor adaptations to altered spatial contingencies during redirected walking in virtual reality.

papers.title: Global spatial errors and local feature errors drive oculomotor learning
papers.abstract: Comparing subtle and obvious intra-saccadic target displacements, the study shows two distinct sensory errors can drive oculomotor learning: a global spatial error that shifts perceived object location and a local feature error that does not. Adaptive saccade changes do not strictly depend on these sensory errors and instead appear to minimize an overall task error.
papers.authors: Frauke Heins, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Long-term Adaptation in VR: Retention of Altered Sensorimotor Contingencies through Redirected Walking
papers.abstract: Ten participants walked with a fixed curvature gain across nine sessions over two weeks.
