Adaptation of locomotion was retained across days, with curved paths when told to walk straight, while pointing stayed stable and detection thresholds for curvature gains were tracked. The results show newly acquired sensorimotor settings persist and are available on re-entering VR.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Niklas Hypki, Taravat Anvari, Frank Steinicke, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Flow parsing as causal source separation allows fast and parallel object and self-motion estimation
papers.abstract: A computational model of flow parsing uses heading likelihood maps to separate the causes of retinal motion into self-motion and independently moving objects. It estimates heading, detects and localizes a moving object, and recovers its scene-relative motion at the same time. Simulations reproduce human perceptual biases and show that the separation can be done quickly and in parallel.
papers.authors: Malte Scherff, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Adaptation across the 2D population code explains the spatially distributive nature of motor learning
papers.abstract: A population-based gain-field model is proposed in which saccade adaptation acts on maps of visual, motor and corollary-discharge signals rather than on a single movement vector. Fitted to saccades and target localization data, it explains the spatial spread and radial shape of adaptation fields and their asymmetries through population coding and polar-angle error encoding.
papers.authors: Jana Masselink, Markus Lappe

papers.title: Inability to pursue nonrigid motion produces instability of spatial perception
papers.abstract: The authors describe a class of nonrigid motion that is perceived accurately during fixation but cannot be smoothly pursued. Catch-up saccades still land on the moving target, yet the stimulus seems to jump with each saccade. This dissociates pursuit from saccade control and shows that perceptual stability of moving objects depends on motion mechanisms shared with pursuit.
papers.authors: Krischan Koerfer, Tamara Watson, Markus Lappe

0426.name: Markus Meister
0426.bio: Markus Meister examines the principles of information processing within large-scale neural circuits, focusing on the mammalian retina and the superior colliculus. Their research utilizes high-density multielectrode arrays and optogenetic techniques to investigate how sensory inputs are transformed into behaviorally relevant neural representations. By integrating experimental findings with mathematical modeling, Meister aims to define a standard model for retinal computation and identify the circuit mechanisms behind rapid learning and task coordination.
0426.research_direction: Dr. Meister has recently been investigating the computational principles of early and midbrain visual processing, seeking to establish a unifying circuit model for the vertebrate retina while also using high-density recordings to systematically catalog functional cell types in the awake mouse superior colliculus. Their recent work also explores the neural mechanisms of rapid spatial cognition, observing how mice navigate complex 3D labyrinths to test whether structures like the neocortex and hippocampus are strictly necessary for these behaviors. To further probe how animals map environments and learn goals, they are developing neuromorphic algorithms that rely on simple neuron-like units and local plasticity rules to simulate natural navigation and patrolling. Finally, they are examining the profound informational bottlenecks of the central nervous system, asking what architectural constraints limit human behavior and thought to a mere ten bits per second despite the brain receiving billions of bits of sensory input.

papers.title: A standard model for the vertebrate retina
papers.abstract: Argues that early visual processing in the vertebrate retina is now understood well enough that one comparatively simple circuit model, run with different parameter settings, accounts for a wide range of retinal computations. The paper lays out the model, shows how it explains diverse phenomena across cell types, and notes how unusual such a consensus framework is in systems neuroscience. It also sets out the baseline assumptions and the remaining open puzzles to guide future retinal research.
papers.authors: Markus Meister

papers.title: Rapid spatial cognition in mice, with and without neocortex and hippocampus
papers.abstract: Mice navigating a reconfigurable 3D labyrinth solved a complex route within a few rewards, generalized to similar mazes, and learned to prefer a decision made far from the reward, all within hours. Modeling suggests much of the learning happens before the first reward as the animal builds a model of the environment. Mutants lacking neocortex and hippocampus retained these abilities and remembered the task for weeks, with only slower learning from inefficient exploration, indicating rapid spatial learning does not strictly require those structures.
papers.authors: Jieyu Zheng, Rafael Guimaraes, Zeynep Turan, Anup Das, Jimmy Y. Hu, Kelly Sadorf, Pietro Perona, Markus Meister

papers.title: The unbearable slowness of being: Why do we live at 10 bits/s?
papers.abstract: Points out that human behavior and thought proceed at roughly 10 bits per second even though the senses collect information at around a billion bits per second, and asks what limits this throughput. Proposes that the brain has an 'outer' fast high-dimensional sensorimotor mode and an 'inner' slow mode handling the few bits needed for behavior. The authors argue the large neuron count of the inner brain is unexplained and suggest new research directions.
papers.authors: Jieyu Zheng, Markus Meister

papers.title: Endotaxis: A neuromorphic algorithm for mapping, goal-learning, navigation, and patrolling
papers.abstract: Presents a brain-inspired circuit that lets an animal or robot learn a map of its environment, learn goals, and navigate to them. The algorithm uses simple neuron-like units and local plasticity rules to build the map while exploring and to compute routes toward targets, and can also support patrolling. It provides a neural-circuit hypothesis for rapid learning and navigation.
papers.authors: Tony Zhang, Matthew Rosenberg, Zeyu Jing, Pietro Perona, Markus Meister

papers.title: Functional cell types in the mouse superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Uses high-density electrode recordings in awake mice to survey visual responses of neurons across the superior colliculus and clusters them into functional cell types. The study characterizes how these types differ in their receptive-field properties and how they are distributed across collicular layers. It offers a systematic catalog of visual computation in this midbrain structure.
papers.authors: Ya-tang Li, Markus Meister

0427.name: Marlene Behrmann
0427.bio: Marlene Behrmann is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the psychological and neural mechanisms of visual processing, including object, face, and word recognition. Behrmann’s research investigates how the brain transforms retinal signals into coherent percepts by integrating functional neuroimaging, psychophysics, and computational modeling. They study neurotypical populations and individuals with brain damage or neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism and prosopagnosia, to examine cortical organization and plasticity. Recently, Behrmann’s work has focused on the developmental trajectory of hemispheric specialization and the structural connectivity of neural circuits underlying high-level vision.
0427.research_direction: Dr. Behrmann has recently been investigating the functional organization, plasticity, and lateralization of high-level visual cortex. Their recent work explores how the visual system adapts following severe early brain injury, using longitudinal fMRI and naturalistic viewing paradigms to track category-selective regions in children who have undergone extensive cortical resections. In parallel, they are examining the computational and developmental mechanisms that drive the topographic layout and hemispheric asymmetry of ventral temporal cortex in typical populations, with a particular focus on face and visual word processing. By combining neuroimaging with computational modeling, their research probes how factors like local neural competition, long-range interhemispheric coupling, and wiring constraints collectively shape the distributed, bilateral networks underlying visual recognition.

papers.title: Individual variation in the functional lateralization of human ventral temporal cortex: Local competition and long-range coupling
papers.abstract: The paper examines why face and word selectivity are lateralized differently across individuals. Combining individual-level fMRI analyses with computational modeling, it shows that local competition and long-range interhemispheric coupling jointly explain variability in lateralization patterns.
papers.authors: Nicholas M. Blauch, David C. Plaut, Raina Vin, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Cross-sectional and longitudinal category-selectivity in visual cortex following pediatric cortical resection
papers.abstract: Category-selective regions for faces, places, objects and words were tracked in children after cortical resection, both across groups and within individuals over time. The regions were largely preserved and stable in the remaining hemisphere. The work shows how robust visual specialization is after early brain injury.
papers.authors: Tina T. Liu, Michael C. Granovetter, Anne Margarette S. Maallo, Sophia Robert, Jason Z. Fu, Christina Patterson, David C. Plaut, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: The Emergence of Topography and Hemispheric Lateralization in High-Level Vision
papers.abstract: This theoretical and empirical synthesis asks how the topographic layout and hemispheric asymmetry of high-level visual cortex emerge. It integrates neuroimaging findings and computational modeling to argue that shared learning pressures and wiring constraints give rise to these organizational features.
papers.authors: Marlene Behrmann, Nicholas M. Blauch, David C. Plaut

papers.title: Investigation of hemispheric functional organization after pediatric epilepsy surgery with naturalistic neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Children who have had one hemisphere's occipitotemporal cortex removed for epilepsy were scanned while watching naturalistic movies. Functional organization and connectivity in the remaining hemisphere were compared with typically developing controls. The results show that the surviving hemisphere retains largely typical functional organization, indicating substantial resilience of the visual system after early surgery.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Sophia Robert, Michael C. Granovetter, Christina Patterson, Marlene Behrmann

papers.title: Visual word processing engages a hierarchical, distributed, and bilateral cortical network
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in adults, the study maps how reading-related word processing unfolds across ventral cortex. Word responses are found to be hierarchically organized and to recruit regions bilaterally rather than only in the left hemisphere. This challenges strictly left-lateralized accounts of visual word recognition.
papers.authors: Raina Vin, Nicholas M. Blauch, David C. Plaut, Marlene Behrmann

0428.name: Martin A. Giese
0428.department: Section Computational Sensomotorics, Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research
0428.bio: Martin A. Giese is a Professor of Computational Sensomotorics at the University of Tübingen and leads a research section at the Hertie Institute for Clinical Brain Research and the Centre for Integrative Neuroscience. Giese’s research combines computational neuroscience and psychophysics to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying biological motion recognition and social perception. Their work involves the development of physiologically-inspired neural models and the use of computer animation to study how the brain represents body movements and facial expressions. This research applies these frameworks to clinical studies of movement disorders and social cognition deficits in psychiatric conditions.
0428.research_direction: Dr. Giese has recently been investigating the perceptual mechanisms of social vision and action recognition in both biological systems and artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores how primates process bodily and emotional cues, using parametrically controlled 3D avatars to test for uncanny-valley effects in macaques, and utilizing motion-capture stimuli to examine how emotions are jointly perceived across interacting individuals rather than isolated actors. They are also translating biological principles into computer vision, testing human zero-shot generalization to appearance-free motion to inform two-pathway video classifiers, and implementing brain-inspired norm-referenced encoding to help models transfer facial expression recognition to unnatural domains like cartoons. Additionally, Dr. Giese is probing the interpretability of large Vision Transformers by analyzing how specific architectural tokens influence the integration and separation of local and global image features.

papers.title: Realistic monkey body animation reveals an uncanny valley in macaque body perception
papers.abstract: The authors build a pipeline that tracks macaque body motion from synchronized multi-camera video using data-driven pose estimation and a small set of hand-labelled keyframes, and use it to drive a realistic 3D monkey avatar with life-like movement. Because the avatar's realism can be parametrically degraded, they can test how monkeys respond to bodies of varying naturalness. Macaques show an uncanny-valley effect in body perception, giving a controllable tool for studying primate social vision.
papers.authors: Lucas M. Martini, Anna Bognár, Rufin Vogels, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Facial expression recognition based on multi-domain norm-referenced encoding
papers.abstract: People easily read expressions on unnatural head shapes such as cartoon characters, but machine learning models transfer poorly across such domains without large training sets. The authors add a brain-inspired norm-referenced encoding, which represents inputs as deviations from a domain-specific reference face, to a vision model. This enables data-efficient transfer of learned expressions to new head shapes.
papers.authors: Michael Stettler, Alexander Lappe, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Appearance-free Action Recognition: Zero-shot Generalization in Humans and a Two-Pathway Model
papers.abstract: Human participants trained on ordinary action videos were tested on videos stripped of appearance and containing only motion, and still performed well above chance. The authors then built a two-pathway 3D CNN that combines RGB and optical-flow streams with a coherence-gating mechanism. It beats existing video classifiers on this test and narrows the gap to human performance, supporting multi-stream architectures.
papers.authors: Prerana Kumar, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Register and [CLS] tokens induce a decoupling of local and global features in large ViTs
papers.abstract: The paper examines attention artifacts in DINOv2-style Vision Transformers. It shows that register tokens give cleaner-looking attention maps, but those maps do not faithfully reflect how local image information is integrated. Both register and [CLS] tokens cause local and global feature processing to separate, which matters for interpreting large vision models.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)
papers.authors: Alexander Lappe, Martin A. Giese

papers.title: Perceptual encoding of emotions in interactive bodily expressions
papers.abstract: Most work on emotional body perception uses single actors, although real emotional behaviour involves interactions. Using motion-capture-based stimuli of interacting people, the study shows that the emotion perceived in one agent depends on the emotional style of its interaction partner. The results indicate that emotion perception is jointly encoded across both agents.
papers.authors: Andrea Christensen, Nick Taubert, Elisabeth M. J. Huis in 't Veld, Beatrice de Gelder, Martin A. Giese

0429.name: Martin Arguin
0429.lab_name: NeuroCVL - Laboratoire de neurocognition de la vision
0429.bio: Martin Arguin is a Professor at the Université de Montréal and a researcher at the Centre de recherche de l’Institut Universitaire de Gériatrie de Montréal (CRIUGM). Arguin investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual processing, focusing on shape perception, object recognition, and the spatiotemporal dynamics of attention during reading. They utilize psychophysics, EEG/ERP electrophysiology, and computational modeling to study visual function in healthy populations and individuals with neurological impairments. Their research examines the impact of aging on visual encoding and the development of optimized typography intended to improve reading performance in developmental dyslexia.
0429.research_direction: Dr. Arguin has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of visual word and object recognition, frequently utilizing random signal-to-noise modulation and classification images to track how perceptual processing unfolds over time. Their recent work explores fundamental mechanisms of human vision, such as whether letters are processed serially or in parallel, how spatial frequency utilization shifts during a brief word exposure, and which specific sparse image features observers extract to recognize objects across varying 3D viewpoints. Additionally, they are applying these psychophysical methods to study individual differences and neurodiversity by mapping the time-frequency profiles of visual efficiency. Specifically, Dr. Arguin is examining how perceptual oscillations and the rapid timing of visual processing for non-social stimuli are altered in both healthy aging and autistic adults.

papers.title: The features subtending visual object recognition
papers.abstract: Five experiments use classification images from a coarse spatial-sampling technique to reveal directly which image features human observers rely on to recognize objects, across object classes differing in familiarity, form, and viewpoint demands. Human diagnostic features turned out to be very sparse, concentrated on edges, vertices and occasionally shading, and they differed consistently from those of ideal observers. The same features were reused across 3D viewpoints, and humans showed amodal completion that let them beat an ideal observer lacking capacity limits.
papers.authors: Martin Arguin, Marie-Audrey Lavoie, Youri Tasse, Melanie Levesque, Marc-Antoine Akzam-Ouellette, Penelope Pelland-Goulet

papers.title: Temporal features of visual processing efficiency in autistic adults
papers.abstract: Using random temporal sampling of noisy targets shown for 200 ms, the study compares time-frequency profiles of visual processing efficiency between autistic and typically developing adults in object and word recognition. Accuracy did not differ between groups, but strong group differences appeared in the temporal patterns of efficiency in both tasks. A subset of temporal features reliably discriminated the groups regardless of task, suggesting altered timing of visual processing for non-social information in autism.
papers.authors: Martin Arguin, Jade Desrosiers, Lili El Khalil, Laurent Mottron

papers.title: Spatiotemporal letter processing in visual word recognition uncovered by perceptual oscillations
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether letters in a word are processed serially or in parallel by randomly modulating the signal-to-noise ratio over the 200 ms exposure, either uniformly across letters or independently per letter position. Accuracy was clearly higher when the SNR varied together across all letters, and classification images computed per letter position and for letter conjunctions, analyzed in both time and Fourier domains, revealed distinct temporal signatures. The results point to substantial parallel letter-processing capacity across the word along with position-specific temporal dynamics.
papers.authors: Martin Arguin, Simon Fortier-St-Pierre

papers.title: The processing of spatial frequencies through time in visual word recognition
papers.abstract: Sixteen adult readers identified briefly presented words whose signal-to-noise ratio fluctuated randomly over 200 ms, with the word filtered into four spatial-frequency bands. Contrary to coarse-to-fine accounts, the highest spatial-frequency band dominated early processing and processing shifted toward lower frequencies later in exposure. A machine-learning classifier separating data patterns by frequency band worked best when the time dimension was recoded into its Fourier transform.
papers.authors: Clemence Bertrand Pilon, Martin Arguin

papers.title: The oscillatory features of visual processing are altered in healthy aging
papers.abstract: Young and elderly adults performed object and word recognition while the signal-to-noise ratio of the target oscillated randomly during a 200 ms exposure, yielding classification images of efficiency over time and SNR-oscillation frequency (5-55 Hz). The two age groups differed substantially, yet individuals within a group shared key features, letting a classifier assign participants to their age group with 100% accuracy. The work shows that perceptual oscillations change with normal aging.
papers.authors: Melanie Levesque, Martin Arguin

0430.name: Martin Eimer
0430.bio: Martin Eimer is a Professor of Psychology at Birkbeck, University of London, and serves as the director of the Brain and Behaviour Lab. Their research program utilizes event-related brain potentials (ERPs) and behavioral paradigms to study the cognitive and neural architecture of visual attention, visual search, and face perception. Eimer has characterized electrophysiological signatures of attentional selection, including the N2pc component, and investigated structural encoding processes associated with the N170 face-sensitive component. Their work focuses on the temporal dynamics of attentional control, the integration of multisensory information, and the neurocognitive basis of face recognition deficits such as developmental prosopagnosia.
0430.research_direction: Dr. Eimer has recently been investigating the real-time dynamics of preparatory attentional templates during visual search, utilizing the N2pc event-related potential to track how observers maintain and switch target features before a search array even appears. Their recent work explores the capacity limitations of holding multiple templates simultaneously, as well as whether these feature-based expectations operate globally across the visual field or can be restricted to specific spatial locations. Beyond preparatory templates, they are examining the relationship between perceptual expectations and selective attention, using rapid serial visual presentation tasks to determine if anticipating a high-level target category alters perception directly without engaging attentional guidance. Finally, Dr. Eimer's research probes the mechanisms of proactive suppression, utilizing the distractor positivity (Pd) electrophysiological component to test whether the visual system can concurrently inhibit multiple salient distractors to optimize search performance.

papers.title: Rapid Changes of Attentional Priorities in Visual Search: Tracking Covert Switches of Preparatory Attentional Templates in Real Time
papers.abstract: Using N2pc responses to rapid streams of irrelevant probe colours, the study tracks in real time which target template is active while people wait for a search display whose timing is unpredictable. A template for the early target colour is activated shortly before the earliest possible display and is then covertly swapped for the late target colour when no display arrives. Switches driven by internal time expectations unfold more slowly than cue-driven ones, and cues even trigger a brief template shutdown when the target colour stays the same.
papers.authors: Gordon Dodwell, Rebecca Nako, Martin Eimer

papers.title: EEG evidence for spatial selectivity in feature-based preparation for visual search
papers.abstract: Asks whether the feature-based attentional templates that observers activate before a search begins are spatially global or restricted to relevant locations. Colour probes presented during preparation produced later and weaker N2pc components when they fell at task-irrelevant locations, showing that spatial expectations can shape preparatory feature-based attention. The spatial filtering was only partial, so preparatory templates are not fully location-specific.
papers.authors: Gordon Dodwell, Rebecca Nako, Martin Eimer

papers.title: The capacity limitations of multiple-template visual search during task preparation and target selection
papers.abstract: Tests how many colour templates can be held ready at once by tracking N2pc responses to probe colours during the preparation interval. When the upcoming target colour was predictable only a single template was active, but when three colours were equally likely all three were activated together. Multi-template search nonetheless carried clear costs for guidance and performance, apparently from inhibitory competition between active templates.
papers.authors: Anna Grubert, Ziyi Wang, Ella Williams, Mikel Jimenez, Roger Remington, Martin Eimer

papers.title: A dissociation between the effects of expectations and attention in selective visual processing
papers.abstract: Whether expectations alter perception directly or only by capturing attention is hard to settle because the two are usually confounded. Using RSVP streams with expectations about the target's alphanumeric category (a high-level feature that should not attract attention) and behavioural plus EEG indices of attention, four experiments show expected targets are reported more accurately without any change in attentional guidance or engagement. Expectation effects thus arise at later encoding stages, not through attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Martin Eimer

papers.title: Proactive suppression can be applied to multiple salient distractors in visual search
papers.abstract: Extends the signal-suppression account by asking whether several salient distractors can be inhibited at once. Search performance improved as the number of salient distractors grew, and the distractor-related PD component appeared for a weaker distractor even alongside a stronger one when displays were intermixed. Multiple concurrent salient signals can therefore be proactively suppressed.
papers.authors: Brandi Lee Drisdelle, Martin Eimer

0431.name: Martin N. Hebart
0431.department: Department of Medicine and Independent Research Group Vision and Computational Cognition
0431.bio: Martin N. Hebart is a computational neuroscientist who researches the latent representational dimensions underlying human object recognition and semantic knowledge. Hebart directs the Vision and Computational Cognition group and participates in the THINGS initiative, utilizing large-scale behavioral and neuroimaging datasets to map multidimensional spaces of visual perception. Their methodology integrates multivariate pattern analysis and representational alignment techniques to compare human neural representations with deep neural networks and artificial intelligence. Hebart’s current research investigates the transformational cascade from low-level visual input to high-level semantic reasoning and how these processes are altered in psychiatric conditions involving visual phenomena.
0431.research_direction: Dr. Hebart studies how the human brain and artificial neural networks represent the visual world of objects. Their most influential work built the THINGS initiative, including the THINGS image database and THINGS-data, a multimodal collection of fMRI, MEG and 4.7 million behavioral similarity judgments, and used those judgments to identify the interpretable dimensions underlying human object similarity. Follow-up work maps these behavior-derived dimensions across visual cortex, showing that they explain brain responses better than categories and that category selectivity emerges as a special case of sparse tuning. More recent studies compare human and deep-network representations, showing that humans weight semantic dimensions while networks lean on low-level visual ones, develop high-throughput methods for predicting perceived similarity, and examine the fine-grained image and category information in visual cortex, foveal V1 encoding of saccade targets and individual functional topography predicted from structural MRI.

papers.title: Feedback of peripheral saccade targets to early foveal cortex
papers.abstract: Combining fMRI decoding with saccade paradigms, the work tests whether information about a peripheral saccade target is fed back to foveal early visual cortex. It shows that foveal V1 carries content-specific information about the upcoming target, extending the idea of foveal feedback to active vision. The results link eye-movement planning with predictive processing in early visual areas.
papers.authors: Luca Kämmer, Lisa M Kroell, Tomas Knapen, Martin Rolfs, Martin N Hebart

papers.title: Dimensions underlying the representational alignment of deep neural networks with humans
papers.abstract: The authors ask which underlying dimensions drive the agreement between deep network representations and human judgments. They extract interpretable dimensions from both systems and compare them, finding that humans rely mostly on semantic dimensions while networks lean more on visual and low-level ones, even when overall alignment scores look similar. The framework gives a more granular way to diagnose and improve human-AI representational alignment.
papers.authors: Florian P. Mahner, Lukas Muttenthaler, Umut Güçlü, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: A high-throughput approach for the efficient prediction of perceived similarity of natural objects
papers.abstract: Collecting human similarity judgments at scale is costly, so the authors build a method that predicts perceived similarity of natural objects from a small amount of behavioral data combined with model features. It reaches high accuracy with far fewer trials and is validated against the large THINGS similarity dataset. This makes similarity measurements feasible for many more stimuli and populations.
papers.authors: Philipp Kaniuth, Florian P. Mahner, Jonas Perkuhn, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: Distributed representations of behaviour-derived object dimensions in the human visual system
papers.abstract: Using the THINGS fMRI data, the study maps the behaviorally derived object dimensions onto cortex. Dimensions are found to be encoded across widespread, overlapping regions rather than in isolated modules, and they explain brain responses better than category labels. Category selectivity emerges as a special case of sparse tuning within this distributed multidimensional code.
papers.authors: Oliver Contier, Chris I. Baker, Martin N. Hebart

papers.title: THINGS-data, a multimodal collection of large-scale datasets for investigating object representations in human brain and behavior
papers.abstract: This resource paper releases a large multimodal dataset built around 1,854 object concepts: fMRI and MEG responses to thousands of natural images plus millions of human similarity judgments. It documents data quality and shows example analyses linking behavior and neural responses. The datasets serve as a common community benchmark for studying object representations.
papers.authors: Martin N. Hebart, Oliver Contier, Lina Teichmann, Adam H. Rockter, Charles Y. Zheng, Alexis Kidder, Anna Corriveau, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam, Chris I. Baker

0432.name: Martin Rolfs
0432.bio: Martin Rolfs is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, where they lead the Active Perception and Cognition Lab and serve as a principal investigator in the Science of Intelligence (SCIoI) Cluster of Excellence. Rolfs's research examines mechanisms linking sensory processing to motor control, focusing on how eye movements, such as saccades and microsaccades, shape visual experience and attentional allocation. Their work addresses the predictive remapping of attention and the functional role of corollary discharge signals in maintaining visual stability. Using a combination of psychophysics, eye tracking, EEG, and computational modeling, Rolfs investigates how motor kinematics and the incidental sensory consequences of movement contribute to perception in active observers.
0432.research_direction: Dr. Rolfs has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying trans-saccadic perception and visual stability, focusing on how the brain handles the extreme sensory disruptions caused by rapid eye movements. Using a combination of psychophysics and image-based modeling, their research examines the processing of visual information during the saccade itself, characterizing the spatial and temporal properties of saccade-induced retinal smear and asking how invisible, high-speed motion signals might actually help support object continuity. They are also exploring how pre- and post-saccadic visual representations are linked, investigating the dynamics of pre-saccadic foveal prediction and using retinal afterimages to measure the precision of spatial updating across eye movements. Ultimately, their recent work seeks to reveal how the stereotyped kinematics of oculomotor behavior are fundamentally tied to the limits of high-speed motion perception.

papers.title: High-fidelity but hypometric spatial localization of afterimages across saccades
papers.abstract: Afterimages are fixed on the retina, so they offer a way to measure how the brain tracks visual locations across eye movements without any external stimulus change. The study finds that observers localise afterimages across saccades with high precision but systematically undershoot their true displacement. This points to an accurate yet incomplete compensation for eye movements in visual stability.
papers.authors: Richard Schweitzer, Thomas Seel, Jörg Raisch, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: Lawful kinematics link eye movements to the limits of high-speed perception
papers.abstract: The paper asks why fast eye movements do not impair vision even though they sweep the image across the retina at extreme speeds. Combining psychophysics and modelling, it shows that the regular relation between saccade amplitude, duration and peak speed places retinal image motion in a range the visual system can handle. The stereotyped kinematics of saccades thus tie oculomotor behaviour directly to the limits of high-speed motion perception.
papers.authors: Martin Rolfs, Richard Schweitzer, Eric Castet, Tamara L. Watson, Sven Ohl

papers.title: Saccadic omission revisited: What saccade-induced smear looks like
papers.abstract: Using a combination of psychophysics and image-based modelling, the authors characterise the retinal smear that a saccade produces and how it appears to observers. They show that the visual system's failure to notice the blur during saccades cannot be explained by simple masking alone, and they describe the spatiotemporal properties of the perceived smear. The work revisits a classic question about saccadic omission with a new quantitative account.
papers.authors: Richard Schweitzer, Mara Doering, Thomas Seel, Jörg Raisch, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: Object continuity through invisible retinal motion at saccadic speed
papers.abstract: During a saccade, objects move across the retina too fast to be seen, yet the world appears stable and objects keep their identity. The authors show that this invisible high-speed retinal motion can still support object continuity, letting the visual system link the object seen before and after the movement. It reveals a functional role for motion signals that never reach awareness.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Melis Ince, Carolin Hübner, Martin Rolfs

papers.title: The magnitude and time course of pre-saccadic foveal prediction depend on the conspicuity of the saccade target
papers.abstract: Just before a saccade, the visual system appears to predict what will land at the fovea. This study tracks how strong and how early that foveal prediction is, and finds that both depend on how conspicuous the saccade target is. The results refine the account of predictive processing that underlies stable perception across saccades.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Kroell, Martin Rolfs

0433.name: Martin Szinte
0433.department: Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT)
0433.lab_name: inVibe (Integration of Visual and Behavioral Diversity)
0433.bio: Martin Szinte is a CNRS researcher at the Institut de Neurosciences de la Timone (INT) who examines the links between visual perception and oculomotor behavior. Their research focuses on the mechanisms of visual stability and retinotopic remapping, investigating how the brain maintains a constant representation of the environment during eye movements. Szinte utilizes a multi-modal approach combining behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and high-field (3T/7T) fMRI mapping. Szinte also contributed to the development of the Eye-Tracking-BIDS standard, an international initiative dedicated to standardizing eye-tracking data within neuroimaging frameworks to enhance scientific transparency and reproducibility.
0433.research_direction: Dr. Szinte has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of visual-spatial processing while simultaneously advancing the methodological and open-science frameworks used for eye-tracking in neuroimaging. Their recent work explores how the human visual cortex updates spatial reference frames across eye movements, using 7T fMRI and population receptive field modeling to test whether the brain constructs a world-centered map or relies strictly on eye-centered coordinates. Alongside this fundamental research, they are developing robust computational tools for experimental designs, such as optimizing deep-learning models to decode gaze position and eyelid state directly from the magnetic resonance signal when traditional camera-based tracking is impossible. Furthermore, Dr. Szinte is actively shaping community data standards by leading the extension of the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) to formalize how raw gaze and pupillometry recordings are organized and shared alongside neuroimaging datasets.

papers.title: A retinotopic reference frame for space throughout human visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study asks whether the brain builds a stable, world-centred (spatiotopic) map of space across eye movements or keeps everything in eye-centred coordinates. Using 7T fMRI with voxel-wise population receptive field modelling while varying gaze position and where attention was directed, the authors found that receptive fields across all visual field maps stay locked to the retina regardless of attention. Bayesian decoding of stimulus location from whole-area response patterns also failed to reveal a spatiotopic code, supporting a fully retinotopic account of visual-spatial processing.
papers.authors: Martin Szinte, Gilles de Hollander, Marco Aqil, Ines Verissimo, Serge Dumoulin, Tomas Knapen

papers.title: Eye-Tracking-BIDS: the Brain Imaging Data Structure extended to gaze position and pupil data
papers.abstract: This paper presents the community specification (BEP20) that extends the Brain Imaging Data Structure to eye-tracking recordings. It defines how raw gaze position and pupil data and their metadata should be organised, and adds a mechanism for asynchronous model parameters, messages and trigger events emitted by the device. Worked examples show it in use across different experimental setups, aiming to make eye-tracking data open, standardised and reproducible alongside neuroimaging data.
papers.authors: Martin Szinte, Dominik R. Bach, Dejan Draschkow, Oscar Esteban, Benjamin Gagl, Remi Gau, Klara Gregorova, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, Scott Huberty, Sina M. Kling, Sourav Kulkarni, Christopher J. Markiewicz, Mark Mikkelsen, Robert Oostenveld, Julia-Katharina Pfarr

papers.title: Optimizing MR-based gaze-decoding for eyes-closed eye-tracking in fMRI
papers.abstract: Camera-based eye tracking is impossible when the eyes are shut, so the authors use DeepMReye, a deep-learning tool that reconstructs gaze from the MR signal of the eyes. Fine-tuning the network on eyes-open visuomotor calibration data, without needing concurrent camera recordings, improved decoding, and the model generalised to eyes-closed periods in a new auditory-guided gaze task. Fine-tuning also allowed eyelid state (open versus closed) to be decoded directly from the MR signal, making gaze monitoring in eyes-closed fMRI studies feasible.
papers.authors: Sina M. Kling, Uriel Lascombes, Matthias Nau, Guillaume S. Masson, Martin Szinte

0434.name: Martin Wiener
0434.bio: Martin Wiener is an Associate Professor at George Mason University and directs the STAR Lab, focusing on the neural foundations of time and space perception. Wiener’s research integrates functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), Electroencephalography (EEG), and Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) to investigate how the brain constructs temporal and spatial dimensions. Their work explores the intersection of vision and timing, specifically how image features like memorability and visual hierarchy clutter modulate perceived duration and memory encoding. By combining these neuroimaging techniques with computational modeling and psychophysics, Wiener aims to map the sensory and motor circuits that enable rhythmic processing, navigation, and decision-making.
0434.research_direction: Dr. Wiener has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms of human time perception, focusing on how visual features, rhythmic entrainment, and metacognition shape our sense of duration. Their recent work explores the visual determinants of time, using psychophysics and recurrent neural networks to ask how stimulus properties like image memorability, spatial clutter, and shape geometry systematically distort how long an image appears to last. In parallel, they are examining rhythmic timing, employing EEG, neuromodulation, and coupled-oscillator models to investigate how neural systems synchronize to competing tempos. Additionally, Dr. Wiener is probing the metacognitive dimensions of temporal processing, utilizing fMRI and EEG to determine how the brain monitors its own sensorimotor timing errors and whether subjective confidence actually tracks temporal illusions induced by visual motion.

papers.title: The symbol of time: Efficiency and meaning of shape stimuli drives time estimates
papers.abstract: Four experiments test how the geometry of shapes and symbols alters time perception. Angular, Kiki-like shapes were timed more precisely and quickly, and symbols that are edgier, vertically asymmetric or thicker were judged as lasting longer. The work extends the lab's stimulus-feature program to shape as a basic determinant of perceived duration.
papers.authors: Giuliana Macedo, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Blinded by motion: Electrophysiological decoupling of time dilation and confidence
papers.abstract: Using EEG during a temporal bisection task with a walking figure, the study replicates that faster motion dilates perceived duration and shows that confidence does not track the illusion. Occipital onset responses tracked the dilation, while frontocentral responses tracked confidence. The authors conclude that the illusion arises in sensory processes that never reach metacognition.
papers.authors: Tutku Öztel, Martin Wiener

papers.title: A coupled oscillator model predicts the effect of neuromodulation and a novel human tempo-matching bias
papers.abstract: Participants judged and matched two simultaneously presented tempos. EEG showed neural entrainment to both rhythms drifting into alignment, and tACS that strengthened one tempo causally improved matching. A coupled-oscillator model explained the entrainment and a new tempo-matching bias.
papers.authors: Chloe Mondok, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Memorability shapes perceived time (and vice versa)
papers.abstract: Across a series of experiments, the authors show that the perceived duration of a scene image depends on its properties: larger scenes and more memorable images seem to last longer, while cluttered images seem shorter. More memorable images are also timed more precisely, and conversely images judged as longer are remembered better. A recurrent convolutional network trained on the images reproduced these effects, suggesting time perception can emerge from visual processing itself.
papers.authors: Alex C. Ma, Ayana D. Cameron, Martin Wiener

papers.title: Neuroimaging Signatures of Metacognitive Improvement in Sensorimotor Timing
papers.abstract: Participants underwent fMRI while reproducing suprasecond intervals, with each trial repeated after feedback so they could redo it. Behavior replicated that people improve on redo trials, indicating awareness of their own timing errors. The neuroimaging identified networks supporting this error monitoring and improvement.
papers.authors: Farah Bader, Martin Wiener

0435.name: Martina Poletti
0435.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0435.bio: Martina Poletti is an Associate Professor at the University of Rochester who investigates the mechanisms of active vision and fine-scale oculomotor control. Poletti’s research demonstrates that visual perception and selective attention are non-uniform and modulated within the 1-degree foveola. Utilizing high-precision eye tracking and adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy, they examine how microscopic eye movements, such as microsaccades, are controlled to facilitate high-acuity tasks. Their research focuses on the interplay between sensory processing, motor behavior, and attentional allocation at the arcminute scale to study the perception of fine spatial details during active exploration.
0435.research_direction: Dr. Poletti has recently been exploring the ultra-fine sensory and motor dynamics of the central one-degree foveola by combining adaptive optics retinal imaging with arcminute-precision, gaze-contingent displays. Their research investigates the spatial limits of this microscopic region, probing whether established peripheral phenomena like visual field asymmetries and spatial crowding operate differently at the scale of individual cones. Additionally, they are examining the active oculomotor components of foveal processing, asking how continuous ocular drift contributes to foveal crowding and how pre-saccadic attention shifts at ultra-fine resolutions prior to microsaccades. Furthermore, their recent work investigates fine-scale sensorimotor plasticity by introducing tiny artificial foveal scotomas to observe how the visual system balances sensory and motor factors to rapidly adjust the preferred retinal locus.

papers.title: Rapid fine-scale sensorimotor plasticity in human foveal vision
papers.abstract: The authors use an adaptive optics scanning light ophthalmoscope to create a tiny artificial scotoma (about 0.03 deg squared) in the foveola. Observers show perceptual deficits and, without reporting awareness of the loss, quickly shift their preferred retinal locus by roughly 5 arcmin toward visible retina, even into regions of lower cone density. This indicates that fixation control balances sensory and motor factors, and suggests oculomotor markers for detecting early retinal disease.
papers.authors: Benjamin Moon, Krishnamachari S. Prahalad, Ashley M. Clark, Austin Roorda, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Wolf Harmening, Aleksandr Gutnikov, Samantha K. Jenks, Sanjana Kapisthalam, Michele Rucci, Jannick P. Rolland, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Non-Uniform Signal Pooling Across the Foveola
papers.abstract: Crowding is usually studied in the periphery and blamed on cortical pooling; its mechanism in the one-degree foveola was unclear because of optical blur and constant fixational eye motion. Combining adaptive-optics retinal imaging with retinal-contingent stimulus rendering, the authors show that at the preferred retinal locus the critical spacing is about one cone diameter. Only 0.25 deg away, mislocalization errors appear and crowding extends beyond cone spacing, pointing to a cortical-magnification-like gradient inside the fovea.
papers.authors: Krishnamachari S. Prahalad, Ashley M. Clark, Benjamin Moon, Austin Roorda, Pavan Tiruveedhula, Wolf Harmening, Aleksandr Gutnikov, Samantha K. Jenks, Sanjana Kapisthalam, Michele Rucci, Jannick P. Rolland, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Asymmetries in Foveal Vision
papers.abstract: Peripheral vision is better along the horizontal than vertical meridian and along the lower than upper vertical meridian, and these asymmetries shrink toward the center of gaze. Using gaze-contingent presentation with arcminute control, the authors tested fine discrimination at isoeccentric locations across the foveola and parafovea in 12 observers. They probe whether such perceptual asymmetries persist inside the foveola.
papers.authors: Samantha K. Jenks, Marisa Carrasco, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Ultra-fine resolution of pre-saccadic attention in the fovea
papers.abstract: Microsaccade-linked attention was measured across the one-degree foveola using arcminute-precision eye tracking and gaze-contingent display. The attentional spotlight at this scale can be as fine as about 0.17 deg. When a microsaccade is prepared, fine vision is enhanced at the target location but drops at the very center of gaze where acuity is normally highest.
papers.authors: Yue Guzhang, Natalya Shelchkova, Ashley M. Clark, Martina Poletti

papers.title: Oculomotor Contributions to Foveal Crowding
papers.abstract: Foveal crowding was thought to be purely cortical, but this study shows fixational eye movements matter. Retinal stabilization, which removes the image motion caused by ocular drift, reduces the harm of crowding in 13 observers. Drift therefore lets target and flankers stimulate the same pooling region over time, adding a temporal component to crowding at this scale.
papers.authors: Ashley M. Clark, Aaron Huynh, Martina Poletti

0436.name: Marvin Chun
0436.bio: Chun is the Richard M. Colgate Professor of Psychology at Yale University, where they investigate the neural substrates of visual attention, memory, and perception. Their research utilizes functional MRI and machine learning to decode brain activity, enabling the prediction of individual differences in cognitive performance through connectome-based predictive modeling. Chun’s work on contextual cueing demonstrates how implicit memory for environmental regularities guides spatial attention. They also conduct research on the functional architecture of the human visual system.
0436.research_direction: Dr. Chun has recently been studying how the human brain represents and holds visual information using fMRI. Their recent work explores how object identity, attention, and memory load are coded differently in visual cortex, which is stable, and parietal cortex, which is adaptive. They also ask how features like shape and color are combined in working memory, and how the pattern for several remembered objects relates to the patterns for each object alone. A separate line uses whole-brain functional connectivity to predict individual differences in executive functions such as inhibition, shifting, and updating.

papers.title: Connectome-Based Predictive Models of General and Specific Executive Functions
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the unity and diversity of executive functions (EF) by applying Connectome-based Predictive Modeling (CPM) to whole-brain functional connectivity data. Utilizing fMRI datasets from the Human Connectome Project, the researchers developed neuromarkers to predict individual differences in task performance across the Flanker (Inhibition), Dimensional Change Card Sort (Shifting), and 2-back (Updating) paradigms. Results identified a common executive function factor represented by a dense functional connectome spanning the frontoparietal, default-mode, and dorsal attention networks. While the Updating-specific component demonstrated high cross-prediction with the general EF factor, specific models for Inhibition and Shifting exhibited more specialized connectivity profiles, supporting a hierarchical architecture of cognitive control in the human connectome.
papers.authors: Shijie Qu, Yueyue Lydia Qu, Kwangsun Yoo, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Interactive shape and color representation in visual working memory for colored objects in the human occipitotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI pattern decoding and cross-decoding techniques, this research investigated whether visual features such as shape and color are maintained independently or integrated within the human occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) during visual working memory (VWM). While these features are represented in a largely orthogonal and independent manner during initial perceptual encoding, the study found a significant drop in cross-decoding performance during the VWM delay period within shape-selective and ventral color areas. This finding provides the first evidence for interactive coding of shape and color in VWM, suggesting that sensory representations are actively transformed into a more integrated format to support efficient information storage and retrieval.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Benjamin Swinchoski, JohnMark Taylor, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Representing Visual Objects, Attention, and Load in Human Occipito-temporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: This study explores the neural mechanisms by which the brain manages stability and adaptability in visual processing across varying task demands. Using fMRI pattern decoding, the authors examined the representational overlap of object identity, attentional priority, and cognitive load in the human occipito-temporal cortex (OTC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC). Findings reveal that OTC maintains relatively invariant object representations despite fluctuations in attention and load, providing stability in identification. In contrast, PPC representations are highly adaptive and modulated by task context. The interaction between these regions facilitates a balance between maintaining object identity and flexibly responding to changing goal-directed demands.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin M. Chun

papers.title: Using fMRI representations of single objects to predict multiple objects in working memory in human occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortices
papers.abstract: This research quantifies the relationship between neural representations of individual items and multi-object arrays within visual working memory (VWM). By analyzing fMRI response patterns in the occipitotemporal and posterior parietal cortices, the study demonstrates that the VWM representation for a pair of objects can be accurately modeled as the linear average of the representations for each item presented alone. This averaging relationship held even after accounting for the modulatory effects of task load. These results suggest that VWM capacity and representational space are governed by competitive interactions and a normalization mechanism that approximates the mean of individual component representations in high-level visual and parietal areas.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin M. Chun

0438.name: Mary Hayhoe
0438.lab_name: Vision, Cognition, and Action Virtual Reality Lab
0438.bio: Mary Hayhoe is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and works in the field of active vision. Hayhoe utilizes virtual reality and motion-tracking technologies to study eye movements and visual perception during natural, goal-directed activities. Their research investigates the interplay between gaze control, working memory, and sensory-motor decision-making. This work demonstrates how task-specific demands and internal rewards dictate the allocation of visual attention in dynamic environments.
0438.research_direction: Dr. Hayhoe's recent work explores visually guided behavior in its natural ecological context, specifically investigating how dynamic visual information is actively sampled and utilized during real-world locomotion. To understand the sensory input walkers actually receive, they have recently been recording eye, body, and 3D scene data during free movement to examine how gaze and gait actively shape natural retinal motion statistics. Their research also investigates the visual control of foot placement and steering, utilizing virtual reality manipulations to isolate the role of ground-plane optic flow, and employing head-mounted cameras with photogrammetric 3D terrain reconstructions to measure precisely where gaze falls relative to chosen footholds. Broadly, Dr. Hayhoe is working to reframe the study of natural vision by modeling these dynamic behaviors as sequences of decisions made under uncertainty, advocating for experimental approaches that integrate active planning, changing goals, and noisy motor actions.

papers.title: Visual control of walking using terrain reconstructions
papers.abstract: Using photogrammetric 3D models of terrain built from a head-mounted scene camera, the study measures how closely gaze falls relative to actual footholds during walking. On medium and rough terrain gaze clustered around individual steps within a few tens of centimetres, indicating that vision is used to select specific footholds in the time allowed by the gait cycle.
papers.authors: Daniel P. Panfili, Karl Muller, Kathryn Bonnen, Mary M. Hayhoe

papers.title: The Role of Retinal Flow in Walking
papers.abstract: Goal-directed walking was tested in virtual reality with a prism manipulation that separated visual direction from ground-plane and wall texture flow. Adding ground texture straightened paths about as much as full-scene texture, while wall texture did little, suggesting that flow on the ground plane, through its effect on balance and foot placement, influences steering rather than visual direction alone.
papers.authors: Nathaniel V. Powell, Daniel Panfili, Youjin Oh, Jonathan S. Matthis, Mary Hayhoe

papers.title: Approaches to understanding natural behavior
papers.abstract: This perspective argues that vision must be studied in its natural context and that this needs better measurement of natural visually guided behavior. It proposes treating diverse behaviors as sequences of decisions made under uncertain world states, changing goals and noisy actions, involving memory and planning, which provides a way to design controlled yet ecologically valid experiments.
papers.authors: Alexander Goettker, Nathaniel Powell, Mary Hayhoe

papers.title: Retinal motion statistics during natural locomotion
papers.abstract: The authors recorded eye, body and 3D scene during real-world walking to measure what retinal motion signals a walker actually receives. They show that gaze behaviour and gait shape the flow field in structured ways, producing statistics that differ markedly from the classic textbook optic-flow patterns. These in situ measurements provide constraints for models of motion processing and neural organization.
papers.authors: Karl S Muller, Jonathan Matthis, Kathryn Bonnen, Lawrence K Cormack, Alex C Huk, Mary Hayhoe

0439.name: Mary Peterson
0439.bio: Mary A. Peterson is a Professor Emerita at the University of Arizona whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and the organization of visual input into objects and backgrounds. Peterson’s findings show that high-level semantic knowledge and object memories influence early figure-ground assignment through reentrant processing, which contrasts with traditional hierarchical models. Utilizing psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI, Peterson investigates competitive inhibitory processes during object detection and the role of the perirhinal cortex in perceptual organization. Their current research examines how past experience, context, and unconscious knowledge shape conscious visual experience and attentional allocation.
0439.research_direction: Dr. Peterson has recently been investigating the dynamic, interactive mechanisms underlying figure-ground organization and object detection, challenging the traditional view of a strict feedforward visual hierarchy. Their recent empirical work explores how high-level priors—such as semantic labels and familiar object configurations—shape early perceptual assignment, using behavioral paradigms and drift diffusion modeling to isolate whether meaning alters sensory evidence accumulation or decision thresholds. To probe the neural architecture of these effects, they have also been utilizing backward and dichoptic masking to decouple how cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamic recurrent processes help resolve local and global visual ambiguity. Broadly, Dr. Peterson's theoretical work seeks to reframe Gestalt perceptual organization as a highly interactive Bayesian process where multiple semantic interpretations implicitly compete via inhibitory feedback loops well before yielding a conscious percept.

papers.title: Does exposure within an experiment affect the influence of familiar parts versus wholes on figure assignment?
papers.abstract: Observers reported which side of a border appeared as figure when one region showed a familiar object as an upright whole, inverted, or with rearranged parts. Upright familiar configurations were the strongest figural priors, inverted ones were weaker but still stronger than part-rearranged ones, implying inter-part connectivity matters. Performance also improved across blocks, pointing to a role for familiar parts, while exposure to one configuration type did not carry over to another.
papers.authors: Colin S. Flowers, Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Gestalt Perception
papers.abstract: An invited entry in the Open Encyclopedia of Cognitive Science, written as a sole author, surveying Gestalt perception and perceptual organization. It reflects her view of how grouping and figure-ground organization are shaped by dynamic, interactive processing.
papers.authors: Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Ambiguity and Reentrant Processing in Object Detection
papers.abstract: A single-author review arguing that object detection is not a strict feedforward sequence of stages. Evidence from her lab suggests several interpretations of an image, along with their semantics, are activated at high levels before conscious detection, so ambiguity exists even for displays that later look clear. Inhibitory competition resolves this via cortico-cortical and cortico-subcortical reentrant loops, which she frames as global dynamic Bayesian interaction.
papers.authors: Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Semantic influences on object detection: Drift diffusion modeling provides insights regarding mechanism
papers.abstract: Reanalyzes earlier figure-ground experiments in which a word label preceded bipartite displays, using drift diffusion modeling to ask how meaning acts. Labels matching the display raised the drift rate (stronger effective signal), whereas mismatching labels mainly raised the evidence threshold, especially for within-category conflicts. The results support semantic networks being engaged during familiar-object detection.
papers.authors: Jingming Xue, Robert C. Wilson, Mary A. Peterson

papers.title: Backward masking implicates cortico-cortical recurrent processes in convex figure context effects and cortico-thalamic recurrent processes in resolving figure-ground ambiguity
papers.abstract: Three backward-masking experiments tested whether convex-figure context effects and the resolution of figure-ground ambiguity depend on recurrent processing. Delaying recurrent activity with masks at different intervals, including dichoptic masking that delays interference in the thalamus, indicated that cortico-cortical recurrence generates the convex context effects while cortico-thalamic recurrence helps resolve ambiguity in homogeneous convex displays, with the two operating in parallel. The work shows that displays that look unambiguous can still be ambiguous during perceptual organization.
papers.authors: Mary A. Peterson, Elizabeth Salvagio Campbell

0440.name: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam
0440.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0440.lab_name: Movement and Visual Perception Lab (MVP Lab)
0440.bio: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural and computational architectures supporting real-time interactions with objects and social agents. Using methodologies such as fMRI, body movement tracking, and machine learning, Vaziri-Pashkam examines how the human brain integrates visual information with motor control across the dorsal and ventral processing streams. Their research has identified object and action representations within the parietal cortex and compared these biological representations to artificial convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to evaluate models of the visual system. Currently, their work focuses on the neural mechanisms involved in action prediction, object affordances, and the extraction of shape features for grasping.
0440.research_direction: Dr. Vaziri-Pashkam studies how the human brain represents objects and actions, how these representations support interactions with the natural environment, and how they are shaped by attention. A central theme of this work is that object processing is not confined to the ventral “what” pathway. Instead, the research supports the existence of two parallel “what” networks, with dorsal parietal regions carrying object shape and category information that is more task-dependent than that represented in the ventral pathway. Using “object kinematograms,” which isolate motion information by transferring the movements of real objects to random-dot displays, the lab has shown that motion alone evokes robust category representations across occipitotemporal and parietal cortex. These representations generalize to static images, and object recognition from motion also exhibits inversion effects. Related fMRI work has identified position-tolerant representations of observed actions in distinct occipitotemporal and parietal networks that differ in their representational content. In work on attention, the lab has shown that object-based attention sharpens neural tuning rather than producing a simple multiplicative gain, with attentional effects becoming smaller as targets and distractors become more similar.

papers.title: Object Recognition from Dynamic Cues: Examining the Inversion Effect
papers.abstract: Object kinematograms, random-dot displays carrying only the motion of real videos of four animate and four inanimate categories, were shown upright or inverted in an online experiment. Participants categorized the animacy and identity of the items, and inversion impaired recognition from motion alone. This extends the inversion effect beyond faces and bodies to a broad range of object categories defined by dynamic cues.
papers.venue: PsyArXiv preprint (Journal of Vision, in press)
papers.authors: Niloufar Faridani, Shifa Maqsood, Sophia Robert, Amirali Soltani Tehrani, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Altered causality perception in Parkinson’s disease
papers.abstract: Using a Michotte launching-effect psychophysics task, the study compared causality judgments in Parkinson's patients and age-matched controls while varying spatial overlap between two moving objects. Patients showed a shifted point of subjective equality and shallower psychometric slopes, biasing them away from causal interpretations. Control experiments ruled out low-level deficits in overlap or speed perception.
papers.authors: Hadi Choubdar Parvin, Zahra Rostami, Mehri Salari, Arash Soltani, Maryam Vaziri Pashkam

papers.title: Attention Modulates Human Visual Responses to Objects by Tuning Sharpening
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with four object categories (bodies, cats, cars, houses), the study asks how similarity between an attended target and a distractor changes attentional modulation across visual cortex. Attentional effects were smaller when target and distractor were more similar in neural representation, and the pattern was better explained by sharpening of neural tuning than by a simple multiplicative gain. This offers a mechanistic account of object-based attention in human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Narges Doostani, Gholam-Ali Hossein-Zadeh, Radoslaw M Cichy, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Two “What” Networks in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: A sole-author review revisiting the classic ventral 'what' versus dorsal 'where' division of visual processing. It gathers evidence that parietal (dorsal) cortex carries robust object shape and category information that is more task-dependent than that in ventral cortex, and argues for two parallel 'what' networks with distinct roles.
papers.authors: Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

papers.title: Disentangling Object Category Representations Driven by Dynamic and Static Visual Input
papers.abstract: The authors built 'object kinematograms' that transfer the motion of real objects onto random dots, isolating motion from luminance-defined form. fMRI showed that motion alone evokes robust category representations across occipitotemporal and parietal cortex, and these representations generalize to those evoked by static images.
papers.authors: Sophia Robert, Leslie G. Ungerleider, Maryam Vaziri-Pashkam

0441.name: Masataka Sawayama
0441.department: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology (Information Media Environment Laboratory / IME lab)
0441.bio: Masataka Sawayama is an Associate Professor specializing in visual 'Shitsukan' (material perception), investigating how humans recognize complex surface qualities such as gloss, wetness, and translucency. Sawayama’s work integrates human psychophysics with computational modeling and deep neural networks to identify the image cues and neural mechanisms involved in material recognition. Their research also explores the intersection of computer vision and cognitive neuroscience, including the development of brain-decoding models and the analysis of semantic representations in the visual cortex.
0441.research_direction: Dr. Sawayama's recent work explores the computational and image-based mechanisms underlying visual representation and material appearance, commonly referred to as Shitsukan. They have recently been investigating how early visual efficient coding of color and luminance supports the perception of complex material optics, using image quantization algorithms and behavioral tasks to isolate the visual statistics required for material classification versus shape-based object recognition. In parallel, their recent work explores human-model alignment in visual processing by developing novel adaptive image-generation frameworks that use human perceptual feedback to map multidimensional metameric spaces across different hierarchical levels of convolutional neural networks. Broadening their methodological scope, they are also investigating applied cognition, having systematically reviewed the efficacy and transfer effects of using artificial intelligence to individualize computerized cognitive training programs.

papers.title: MAME: Multidimensional adaptive metamer exploration with human perceptual feedback
papers.abstract: Metamers are physically different stimuli that look identical, and they are used to compare brains with artificial models, but researchers have lacked a direct way to search human metameric spaces. The authors introduce MAME, an online image-generation framework that adaptively modulates images along several dimensions of hierarchical CNN responses using participants' discrimination feedback. In a single experiment it maps human metameric spaces and finds that humans are less sensitive to Gram-matrix metamers built from low-level CNN features than from high-level ones, indicating weaker human-model alignment in early visual computation.
papers.authors: Mina Kamao, Hayato Ono, Ayumu Yamashita, Kaoru Amano, Masataka Sawayama

papers.title: Human Visual Perception of Shitsukan
papers.abstract: This book chapter gives an overview of how humans perceive Shitsukan, the perceived quality and material appearance of objects, including properties such as gloss, translucency and wetness. It reviews the image cues and computational accounts proposed to explain material perception and frames the topic for the volume on understanding and manipulating material and quality perception.
papers.venue: Shitsukan: Understanding and Manipulating Material and Quality Perception (Springer Nature)
papers.authors: Shin'ya Nishida, Masataka Sawayama

papers.title: Revisiting Color Efficient Coding through Material Perception
papers.abstract: Early vision is usually thought to split cone signals into luminance and color to remove redundancy in natural scenes, but for materials with complex optics the two channels stay highly redundant. The author shows that median cut, a classic computer graphics quantization algorithm, yields a more efficient decomposition that keeps information diagnostic of material while discarding fine geometry. Behavioral experiments show that this color reduction disrupts material classification yet leaves object recognition intact, suggesting shape is available from low-bit information while material relies on image sub-space summary statistics.
papers.authors: Masataka Sawayama

papers.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence in individualized cognitive training: A systematic review
papers.abstract: This systematic review examines computerized cognitive training that uses AI to individualize the curriculum for each learner, addressing heterogeneity in how people respond. Nineteen studies were analysed for training setup, adaptive approach (macro versus micro adaptive), intra-training performance and near, far and everyday transfer effects. Evidence for benefits was promising but limited by small samples and lack of controls.
papers.authors: Maxime Adolphe, Marion Pech, Masataka Sawayama, Denis Maurel, Alexandra Delmas, Pierre-Yves Oudeyer, Helene Sauzeon

0442.name: Mathew Diamond
0442.lab_name: SENSEx Lab (SISSA Explorations into the Neuronal foundations of Sensory Experience Lab)
0442.bio: Mathew Diamond is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at SISSA, where they direct the SENSEx Lab and coordinate the PhD program in Cognitive Neuroscience. Diamond’s research investigates the neuronal algorithms underlying tactile perception, specifically examining how the rodent whisker system and human sensory pathways encode stimulus features such as texture, intensity, and duration. By integrating multi-channel electrophysiology, optogenetics, and psychophysics, their work characterizes the transformation of sensory signals into subjective percepts and explores the role of working memory and sensory history in decision-making. Diamond is a co-author of the textbook From Neuron to Brain.
0442.research_direction: Dr. Diamond has recently been investigating how the mammalian brain processes tactile information and time, utilizing both rat whisker neurophysiology and human vibrotactile psychophysics. Their recent work explores the neural mechanisms of time perception, testing whether regions like the dorsolateral striatum encode elapsed time and how the primary somatosensory cortex serves as a shared gateway for judging both stimulus duration and intensity. Additionally, they are examining how perceptual decisions are shaped by prior context, asking how current sensory inputs are integrated with feature-specific history traces via population coding across sensory and frontal cortices. Finally, Dr. Diamond is studying temporal attention by tracking how sensory-motor networks support the distinct behavioral strategies animals use to filter out irrelevant, out-of-sequence distracting stimuli.

papers.title: Cortical population codes for embedding sensory inputs into the prior context
papers.abstract: Rats categorizing vibrissal stimuli were recorded simultaneously in primary sensory cortex and a frontal target region to ask how current input is combined with prior experience. Behavior was history-dependent, but sensory cortex encoded the present stimulus largely independently of past stimuli and could not account for that dependence. Frontal cortex instead embedded the current input within a representation of previous sensory information, via collinear coding dimensions largely carried by fast-spiking neurons, which explained trial-to-trial variability in choices.
papers.authors: Iacopo Hachen, Sebastian Reinartz, Alisea Stroligo, Alejandro Pequeño-Zurro, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Independent history traces for distinct percepts derived from a single stimulus
papers.abstract: Human participants judged either the intensity or the duration of vibrotactile stimuli, with the relevant feature cued at random on each trial. Within a trial the two features influenced each other, implying a shared sensory representation, but across trials serial dependence was feature-specific and drew on several past trials in which the same feature was relevant. A model with parallel, task-gated memory traces captured the behavior, placing history effects downstream of a common sensory encoding stage.
papers.authors: Alessandro Toso, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Individual strategies for ignoring irrelevant information are reflected in distinct neural signatures during temporal attention
papers.abstract: Rats were trained to categorize a relevant vibration while ignoring an irrelevant one delivered to the same whiskers at a different time, a temporal-attention task. Animals split into a small number of reproducible strategy classes rather than one common solution, with some learning to suppress the distractor almost completely. Recordings in a few animals showed motor cortex separating relevant from irrelevant input and stronger high-gamma coupling between sensory and motor cortex in effective performers.
papers.authors: M. Gironimi, K. I. Ryom, T. Potracov, A. Orsini, F. Pulecchi, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Direct contribution of the sensory cortex to the judgment of stimulus duration
papers.abstract: Whisker somatosensory cortex was recorded and optogenetically driven while rats judged how long a vibration lasted. Exciting the cortex made stimuli feel longer, and in a second group of rats it also made vibrations feel stronger, showing that sensory cortex is a shared gateway for both time and stimulus-feature processing. A biophysical model starting from membrane currents reproduced the animals' choices, arguing that time perception is intertwined with sensory coding.
papers.authors: Sebastian Reinartz, Arash Fassihi, Maria Ravera, Luciano Paz, Francesca Pulecchi, Marco Gigante, Mathew E. Diamond

papers.title: Time coding in rat dorsolateral striatum
papers.abstract: Neuronal recordings from the dorsolateral striatum in rats performing a timing task were used to ask how the region represents elapsed time and whether such activity provides a temporal basis for organizing behavior.
