The paper is part of an ongoing debate over striatal time representations, which the lab followed with a reply letter in Neuron in 2024.
papers.authors: Alessandro Toso, Sebastian Reinartz, Francesca Pulecchi, Mathew E. Diamond

0443.name: Matteo Valsecchi
0443.bio: Valsecchi is an Associate Professor at the University of Bologna whose research examines the mechanisms of human visual perception and oculomotor control. Their work focuses on how the brain maintains a stable and continuous perceptual experience despite the resolution differences between foveal and peripheral vision and the interruptions caused by saccadic eye movements. Using psychophysics, eye tracking, and electrophysiological techniques such as SSVEPs, Valsecchi has investigated phenomena including saccadic suppression, transsaccadic integration, and the influence of prediction on peripheral appearance. Recent studies by Valsecchi explore the metacognitive aspects of vision, specifically analyzing confidence biases and the perceived uniformity of the visual field across eccentricities.
0443.research_direction: Dr. Valsecchi has recently been investigating a diverse range of mechanisms underlying visual attention, oculomotor behavior, and spatial metaperception. Their recent work explores how the visual system habituates to irrelevant luminance transients and onset distractors during visual search, specifically probing whether this suppression relies on spatially selective expectation or operates via independent temporal mechanisms within and across trials. They are also examining the allocation of spatial attention across the visual field, utilizing EEG alpha oscillations to measure the covert tracking of moving targets and testing how perceptual confidence compares between central and peripheral vision during rapid scene categorization. Furthermore, Dr. Valsecchi investigates the relationship between involuntary eye movements and internal cognitive states, testing whether spontaneous microsaccade dynamics can serve as an implicit behavioral marker for mind wandering during sustained attention tasks.

papers.title: Peripheral overconfidence in a scene categorization task
papers.abstract: Observers judged which of two intervals they were more confident about, one showing a scene only in the periphery (central scotoma) and one only in the center (window), while the difficulty was varied by size. Confidence did not track performance equally: matched confidence needed noticeably higher central performance, i.e. people are overconfident about peripheral vision even for a task suited to it (rapid scene categorization). This extends earlier mixed findings on metaperception across the visual field.
papers.authors: Nino Sharvashidze, Matteo Toscani, Matteo Valsecchi

papers.title: Within-Trial and Across-Trials Habituation Mechanisms to Irrelevant Visual Transients
papers.abstract: Repeating an irrelevant luminance transient at the same location several times within a trial reduced its interference with visual search, just as repeated feature singletons do. This within-trial benefit was independent of how often such repeats occurred across trials, indicating two relatively independent habituation mechanisms for attentional capture. A control showed the effect is not just a warning or spatial-predictability cue.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Matteo Valsecchi, Massimo Turatto

papers.title: Attentional tracking reduces cortical alpha oscillations
papers.abstract: Sixteen observers kept fixation while covertly tracking a target moving at different speeds in the left or right periphery, with EEG and eye movements recorded. Alpha power fell more when the target moved farther into the periphery, regardless of speed, showing alpha tracks the allocation of covert attention during tracking. The result links covert tracking to the mechanisms of overt smooth pursuit, in line with the premotor theory of attention.
papers.authors: Songlin Qiao, Xuemei Xia, Jing Chen, Matteo Valsecchi

papers.title: Is mind wandering reflected in microsaccade dynamics?
papers.abstract: Participants did a sustained attention go/no-go task prone to mind wandering, and microsaccade rates were compared in windows before commission errors versus correct withholds. Microsaccade rate was consistently lower before errors, a pattern robust in cluster-based analyses. Because microsaccades are involuntary, this suggests they may offer an implicit marker of mind-wandering episodes.
papers.authors: Matteo Valsecchi, Mario Dalmaso, Luigi Castelli, Eleonora Baldini, Giovanni Galfano

papers.title: Habituation to onsets is controlled by spatially selective distractor expectation
papers.abstract: By varying how probable an onset distractor was at a fixed location without changing how many distractors were shown, the study tested two accounts of habituation. Results favored an expectation-based (Sokolov-type) mechanism over simple stimulation count, and showed habituation is governed by local rather than global distractor rate and is spatially specific.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Massimo Turatto, Matteo Valsecchi

0444.name: Matthew Davidson
0444.department: School of Psychology, Graduate School of Health
0444.main_research_area: Neuroscience of consciousness and active perception
0444.bio: Matthew Davidson is a cognitive neuroscientist and Lecturer at the University of Technology Sydney, where they are a member of the Behavioural Sciences and Technology research group. Davidson’s research examines the neuroscience of consciousness and active perception, specifically investigating how neural activity and subjective experience are influenced by natural movement. Using a combination of mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and virtual reality (VR), they study how perceptual sampling and multisensory integration are phase-locked to the human gait cycle. This research, supported by an ARC Discovery Early Career Researcher Award (DECRA), has been published in journals including Nature Communications, eLife, and PLOS Biology.
0444.research_direction: Dr. Davidson’s recent work explores how natural body movements and automatic neural mechanisms shape visual perception, awareness, and metacognition. Using wireless virtual reality, they have recently been investigating how visual target detection and continuous sensorimotor tracking rhythmically fluctuate according to the phase and speed of the human stride cycle during free walking. In a distinct line of research on visual awareness, their work introduces a novel continuous flash suppression (CFS) tracking paradigm to continuously measure suppression depth, testing whether complex, upright, or emotionally salient faces genuinely receive privileged access to consciousness. Additionally, they use multivariate EEG decoding to examine metacognitive monitoring, investigating whether automatic, post-decision error signals generalize across visual and auditory domains to inform perceptual confidence.

papers.title: An Automatic Domain-General Error Signal Is Shared across Tasks and Predicts Confidence in Different Sensory Modalities
papers.abstract: Using multivariate decoding of EEG, the study tests whether a post-decision error signal generated without explicit confidence reports generalizes between visual and auditory tasks. A classifier trained to detect errors in one task and modality transferred to others, and its output tracked later self-reported confidence. This supports an automatic, domain-general metacognitive monitoring mechanism.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Sriraj Aiyer, Nick Yeung

papers.title: Priority access to awareness? A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals no priority for fearful faces or a face inversion effect
papers.abstract: Applying the tracking CFS method to faces, the authors tested whether upright or fearful faces gain privileged access to awareness compared with inverted or neutral faces. Suppression depth did not differ between these conditions, and the classic breakthrough advantages were not replicated in the tracking measure. The findings argue against special priority for emotional or upright faces under interocular suppression.
papers.authors: David Alais, Lina Ye, Jacob Coorey, Matthew J. Davidson

papers.title: Walking modulates visual detection performance according to stride cycle phase
papers.abstract: Participants walked freely along a linear path in a wireless virtual reality setup while detecting brief visual targets. Accuracy, reaction time and response likelihood all oscillated across the stride cycle at about twice the step rate (~2 Hz), with a phase preference consistent within individuals and matched to step timing. The results show that visual perception during natural locomotion is rhythmically gated by the phase of the gait cycle.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Frans A. J. Verstraten, David Alais

papers.title: A new 'CFS tracking' paradigm reveals uniform suppression depth regardless of target complexity or salience
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a tracking version of continuous flash suppression in which a hidden target ramps up in contrast until it breaks through and then ramps down until it vanishes again, repeating over many reversals. This yields a measure of suppression depth rather than only breakthrough time. Across a range of target types, depth of suppression was essentially the same, challenging claims that complex or salient stimuli get privileged access to awareness.
papers.authors: David Alais, Jacob Coorey, Randolph Blake, Matthew J. Davidson

papers.title: Continuous peripersonal tracking accuracy is limited by the speed and phase of locomotion
papers.abstract: In a body-tracked wireless virtual environment, participants performed continuous reaching to track a moving target while walking at different speeds. Tracking accuracy and reaction time worsened at slower walking speeds and varied rhythmically with the phase of the step cycle. This shows that sensorimotor performance, not only perception, is coupled to the rhythms of locomotion.
papers.authors: Matthew J. Davidson, Robert Tobin Keys, Brian Szekely, Paul MacNeilage, Frans Verstraten, David Alais

0445.name: Maurice Ptito
0445.department: School of Optometry; Department of Applied Mathematics and Computer Science
0445.bio: Maurice Ptito researches the development and functional plasticity of the visual system in humans and animal models. Their work addresses sensory substitution, specifically the use of the Tongue Display Unit to enable blind individuals to process spatial information through tactile pathways. Ptito employs neuroimaging and electrophysiological techniques, including diffusion MRI tractography, fMRI, and PET, to investigate how the brain reorganizes in response to congenital or acquired blindness. They currently hold the Harland Sanders Research Chair in Vision Science and investigate the neural mechanisms of cross-modal reorganization and spatial navigation.
0445.research_direction: Dr. Ptito’s recent work explores how the human brain adapts to early and late-onset blindness, focusing on cross-modal plasticity and the neurocognitive mechanisms of spatial navigation. Using magnetoencephalography, they have recently been investigating the specific neural pathways by which auditory and tactile signals reroute to the primary visual cortex after visual loss. A major branch of their research also examines how blind individuals acquire spatial knowledge and construct cognitive maps over time, utilizing virtual navigation paradigms, real-world sensory substitution devices, and diverse two- and three-dimensional tactile displays. To ground these behavioral phenomena in neuroanatomy, Dr. Ptito utilizes structural MRI volumetry to probe how the sizes of distinct hippocampal subfields contribute to spatial learning, pattern separation, and route inference in the absence of sight.

papers.title: Pathways of Cross-Modal Access to the Visual Cortex in Late Blindness
papers.abstract: Using magnetoencephalography, the authors traced how touch and sound signals reach primary visual cortex in adults who lost sight later in life versus sighted controls. Tactile input evoked earlier and stronger V1 responses in late-blind people (about 35 vs 59 ms), pointing to a fast thalamo-cortical route, while auditory cues followed a shared thalamus to A1 to V1 sequence in both groups. Thalamus-to-V1 connectivity was enhanced in the late blind, showing cross-modal reorganization in adulthood independent of blindness duration or onset age.
papers.authors: Samuel Paré, James Isaac Lubell, Sylvain Baillet, Ron Kupers, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Hippocampal Subfield Volumetry and Navigation in Congenital Blindness
papers.abstract: The study compared volumes of hippocampal subfields (CA, dentate fascia, subiculum, HATA) in congenitally blind and sighted adults and related them to learning of obstacle detection and avoidance with a tactile sensory substitution device in a real-world course. Congenitally blind participants had smaller left CA and dentate volumes, and the subfields linked to learning differed between groups. Hippocampal-navigation links are therefore selective and task-component dependent rather than uniform without vision.
papers.authors: Daniel-Robert Chebat, Fabien C. Schneider, Ron Kupers, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Tracking acquisition of cognitive maps in early- and late-onset blindness
papers.abstract: The authors built a multisensory virtual navigation paradigm to follow how cognitive maps form over repeated learning of a tactile maze, using pointing and navigation tasks in early blind, late blind and sighted participants. Early blind people accumulated spatial knowledge more slowly and both blind groups struggled when viewpoints changed, yet everyone improved and some blind participants reached expert level. Cognitive map formation in blindness appears experience-dependent and variable across individuals.
papers.authors: Maxime Bleau, Quentin Dessain, Laurence Dricot, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Ron Kupers, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Subfield-specific hippocampal contributions to cognitive map-based navigation in early- and late-onset blindness
papers.abstract: Hippocampal T1 MRI was segmented into CA1, DG/CA3 and subiculum in early blind, late blind and sighted adults and correlated with performance on a non-visual cognitive-map navigation task. Volumes did not differ by group, but DG/CA3 size tracked navigation in early blind and (pre)subicular volume tracked performance and learning rate in both blind groups, with no relation in sighted controls. The results suggest hippocampal output, head-direction and pattern-separation circuitry support cognitive mapping in blindness.
papers.authors: Maxime Bleau, Mats Donbrowe, Ron Kupers, Laurence Dricot, Nikolai Axmacher, Daniel Robert Chebat, Maurice Ptito

papers.title: Cognitive map formation in the blind is enhanced by three-dimensional tactile information
papers.abstract: Early blind, late blind and sighted participants learned maze layouts presented as 2D tactile, 3D tactile or visual displays and then inferred routes from memory. Early blind people formed stronger cognitive maps with 3D tactile mazes, late blind people did equally well with 2D and 3D, and sighted people did as well with 3D tactile as with visual mazes but worse with 2D tactile. 3D tactile maps may therefore reduce cognitive load and aid spatial learning in blind and newly blind people.
papers.authors: Maxime Bleau, Camille van Acker, Natalina Martiniello, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Maurice Ptito

0446.name: Maximilian Riesenhuber
0446.bio: Maximilian Riesenhuber is a Professor of Neuroscience at Georgetown University and Co-Director of the Center for Neuroengineering. Their research integrates computational modeling with human behavioral data, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG) to examine the neurocomputational mechanisms of object recognition and learning. Riesenhuber developed hierarchical, biologically plausible models of the visual cortex to show how neural populations extract invariant features from complex stimuli. Their current research investigates cross-modal sensory processing in vision, audition, and touch to translate biological insights into neuromorphic artificial intelligence and augmented cognition technologies.
0446.research_direction: Dr. Riesenhuber has recently been studying how the brain turns letters and sounds into whole-word representations, and whether the visual (reading) and auditory (speech) pathways are organized in parallel. Their recent work examines the visual word form area and a proposed auditory counterpart in the anterior temporal lobe, and how the two language systems interact during reading and listening. They also explore how the brain can take on speech information delivered through touch, by matching vibrotactile signals to the acoustic structure of natural speech. In a separate line of work, they ask how extensive practice on visual categorization changes brain circuitry, shifting the task away from a slow frontal-cortex bottleneck toward more automatic processing.

papers.title: Evidence for hierarchical representations of written and spoken words from an open-science human neuroimaging dataset
papers.abstract: Reading and speech recognition both require multi-tier hierarchical cortical processing that transforms sensory features into whole-word representations; however, the degree of organizational homology between the visual and auditory pathways remains incompletely characterized. To resolve lexical and sublexical representations across modalities, the authors performed parametric regression analyses on the Mother Of all Unification Studies (MOUS) open-science fMRI dataset (n = 204), assessing cortical responses to variations in whole-word frequency alongside sublexical unit frequency (bigrams and syllables) during reading and listening tasks. Analysis of the reading data demonstrated significant inverse correlations with lexical frequency in the visual word form area (VWFA) of the left mid-fusiform gyrus and with bigram frequency in posterior occipital cortex, confirming hierarchical orthographic encoding. In the auditory modality, spoken word frequency parametrically modulated BOLD responses in the left mid-superior temporal gyrus within the auditory word form area (AWFA), whereas syllable frequency selectively modulated activity in posterior superior temporal gyrus. Furthermore, cross-modal convergence was identified in the left inferior frontal gyrus, which correlated with both visual and auditory word frequencies. These findings indicate parallel posterior-to-anterior processing hierarchies within the anteroventral visual and auditory processing streams, progressing from sublexical structures to lexical hubs that connect to frontal language regions.
papers.authors: Suneel Banerjee, Kimberly Jin, Plamen Nikolov, Philip Cho, Vishnu R. Pendri, Lillian Chang, Srikanth R. Damera, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Distinct cross-modal coupling between the written and auditory language networks during reading and spoken word processing
papers.abstract: The development of lexical representations in the visual word form area (VWFA) is hypothesized to be driven by top-down scaffolding from the auditory language system, particularly via putative lexical representations in the anterior superior temporal gyrus (the auditory word form area, AWFA). The authors examined functional responses and functional connectivity (FC) between individually localized VWFA and AWFA regions of interest (n = 18) during visual reading and spoken word perception, alongside MEG sensor-level and beamforming coherence analyses from the MOUS dataset. The fMRI results revealed marked cross-modal asymmetry: the VWFA responded selectively to spoken words and exhibited heightened functional coupling with the AWFA during auditory processing, whereas the AWFA showed no comparable recruitment or cross-modal connectivity during reading. MEG source analyses demonstrated significant signal coherence between the AWFA and VWFA emerging approximately 300 ms post-stimulus onset during spoken word comprehension. These findings elucidate an asymmetric cross-modal architecture wherein spoken language representations in the anterior temporal lobe provide direct scaffolding to ventral occipito-temporal reading circuits without reciprocal engagement during standard visual orthographic processing.
papers.authors: Lillian Chang, Philip Cho, Suneel Banerjee, Srikanth R. Damera, Laurie S. Glezer, Benson Stevens, Kimberly Jin, Plamen Nikolov, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Extensive Experience Remodels Neural Task Circuitry to Escape the Frontal Bottleneck and Increase Automaticity of Categorization
papers.abstract: Standard models of perceptual categorization propose a two-stage hierarchy in which early sensory cortices represent physical shape features while prefrontal cortex (PFC) units encode task-dependent category boundaries. However, executive processing in the PFC creates a processing bottleneck that limits concurrent task execution. To examine how extended training alters this circuitry, human subjects completed over 30,000 categorization trials with parameterized morphed car stimuli across 5 to 10 weeks. Using longitudinal fMRI and EEG rapid adaptation paradigms, neural tuning and connectivity were tracked following initial acquisition (~4 hours) and extensive practice (~16 additional hours). Although category selectivity was initially confined to the PFC with shape tuning in the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOTC), extensive training induced an emergence of discrete category selectivity directly within the vOTC. Concurrently, vOTC showed marked reductions in functional connectivity with the PFC and enhanced coupling with motor output cortices. This functional disconnection from the prefrontal bottleneck directly predicted preserved categorization performance under dual-task interference, demonstrating that prolonged sensorimotor experience can physically bypass executive prefrontal circuits to achieve automated processing.
papers.authors: Patrick H. Cox, Clara A. Scholl, Marissa L. Laws, Nelson E. Jaimes, Xiong Jiang, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Evidence for a Spoken Word Lexicon in the Auditory Ventral Stream
papers.abstract: A core premise of spoken language comprehension models is the existence of an auditory lexicon housing neural representations of complete spoken words, yet its anatomical locus has remained controversial. Drawing an architectural parallel to the visual word form area (VWFA) in reading, the authors used fMRI rapid adaptation (fMRI-RA) to probe whether the anterior superior temporal gyrus harbors an auditory word form area (AWFA) selective for individual spoken words. In 26 participants, adaptation profiles in response to pairs of real words, unfamiliar pseudowords, and experimentally trained novel words were evaluated. The putative AWFA demonstrated robust release from adaptation for single-phoneme substitutions that was indistinguishable from the release evoked by completely different words, confirming fine-grained neural tuning for specific real words rather than sublexical acoustic overlap. Furthermore, targeted phonological training with novel spoken words selectively sharpened neuronal tuning within this region. These findings locate the auditory word-form lexicon within the anterior superior temporal gyrus, illustrating that the auditory and visual ventral processing hierarchies employ convergent mechanisms for whole-word representation.
papers.authors: Srikanth R. Damera, Lillian Chang, Plamen P. Nikolov, James A. Mattei, Suneel Banerjee, Laurie S. Glezer, Patrick H. Cox, Xiong Jiang, Josef P. Rauschecker, Maximilian Riesenhuber

papers.title: Metamodal Coupling of Vibrotactile and Auditory Speech Processing Systems through Matched Stimulus Representations
papers.abstract: Sensory substitution technologies seek to compensate for sensory loss by translating information across modalities, but the neurocomputational principles governing whether non-native sensory inputs can access established cortex remain unclear. This study investigated whether matching the representational format of vibrotactile speech to the acoustic feature hierarchy of natural speech promotes the metamodal recruitment of auditory speech networks. Sighted, normal-hearing human participants were trained to identify words delivered through vibrotactile stimulation using either a vocoder-based algorithm (designed to match the spectrotemporal modulation patterns of acoustic speech) or an unaligned token-based mapping scheme. Pre- and post-training fMRI experiments revealed that only subjects trained on the vocoded algorithm exhibited recruitment of speech-selective regions in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) by vibrotactile input. Moreover, this condition was uniquely accompanied by strengthened functional coupling between primary somatosensory cortex and auditory speech areas. These findings demonstrate that representational alignment is critical for facilitating cross-modal functional reorganization, offering computational constraints for the design of neurobiologically grounded tactile speech sensory substitution systems.
papers.authors: Srikanth R. Damera, Patrick S. Malone, Benson W. Stevens, Richard Klein, Silvio P. Eberhardt, Edward T. Auer, Lynne E. Bernstein, Maximilian Riesenhuber

0447.name: Meenakshi Khosla
0447.bio: Meenakshi Khosla is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at the University of California, San Diego. Khosla’s research operates at the intersection of artificial intelligence and computational neuroscience, focusing on the development of data-driven models to analyze information processing in the human brain. They use deep neural networks and functional neuroimaging (fMRI) to characterize structured neural representations in the visual cortex, including the identification of food-selective neural populations. Their work also involves building interpretable machine learning tools for large-scale brain mapping across sensory and cognitive domains.
0447.research_direction: Dr. Khosla has recently been investigating the representational geometry of the human visual system and its alignment with artificial neural networks. Their recent work explores the functional organization of higher visual cortex, using data-driven, sparse decompositions of fMRI responses to natural images to test whether category-selective pathways operate as isolated modules or broadly applicable filters. Alongside this neuroimaging research, they are critically examining the theoretical and methodological foundations of neuro-AI comparisons, specifically questioning whether brains and artificial models share privileged representational axes and auditing how the choice of similarity metric shapes our understanding of brain-network alignment. Furthermore, they are probing the dynamics of convergent learning within deep vision models themselves, tracking how internal representations evolve across network depth, training time, and distribution shifts.

papers.title: Higher visual areas act like domain-general filters with strong selectivity and functional specialization
papers.abstract: The paper decomposes fMRI responses across human higher visual cortex in a data-driven way and asks whether regions such as face, body, and scene areas are best seen as category-specific modules. It finds that these areas behave like broadly applicable filters that nonetheless show sharp selectivity, and that their functional profiles are specialized rather than interchangeable. Encoding models built from these findings connect the observed organization to how visual information is transformed along the cortical hierarchy.
papers.authors: Meenakshi Khosla, Leila Wehbe

papers.title: Conclusions Drawn From Neural Network to Brain Alignment Depend Strongly on the Chosen Similarity Measure
papers.abstract: This study shows that conclusions about which neural networks resemble the brain depend heavily on which similarity metric is used, with different metrics ranking the same models very differently. The authors compare popular measures across many models and brain datasets and reveal where they agree and disagree. The results argue for careful, multi-metric evaluation in brain-model alignment work.
papers.authors: Ansh K. Soni, Sudhanshu Srivastava, M. Maechler, Konrad P. Kording, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Sparse components distinguish visual pathways and their alignment to neural networks
papers.abstract: The work applies a sparse component decomposition to fMRI responses to natural images to separate distinct visual pathways in human cortex, including ventral, dorsal, and lateral streams. The recovered components are more interpretable than those from standard methods, and the authors then examine how well they align with the units and layers of deep neural networks. The result gives a cleaner picture of cortical organization and of how models map onto it.
papers.authors: Ammar I. Marvi, Nancy Kanwisher, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Bridging Critical Gaps in Convergent Learning: How Representational Alignment Evolves Across Layers, Training, and Distribution Shifts
papers.abstract: The paper audits dozens of vision models to see when and why different networks converge on similar internal representations. It tracks alignment across depth, over the course of training, and under distribution shifts, identifying where convergence emerges and where it breaks down. The results clarify the limits of the idea that networks learn universal representations.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Chaitanya Kapoor, Sudhanshu Srivastava, Meenakshi Khosla

papers.title: Privileged representational axes in biological and artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors test whether individual neural axes carry special meaning in brains and deep networks, or whether representations are freely rotatable. Using fMRI and vision models, they show that some axes are consistently privileged and shared across systems, and that this structure supports meaningful comparison between cortex and networks. The work argues that rotation-invariant similarity measures can hide a real aspect of representational organization.
papers.authors: Meenakshi Khosla, Alex H. Williams, Josh H. McDermott, Nancy Kanwisher

0448.name: Megan A. K. Peters
0448.bio: Megan A. K. Peters is an Associate Professor of Cognitive Sciences at the University of California, Irvine, and a Fellow in the CIFAR Brain, Mind & Consciousness program. Peters' research investigates how the brain represents and utilizes uncertainty to support adaptive behavior and metacognitive evaluations, focusing on the computational mechanisms of conscious awareness. They employ a methodology combining psychophysics, functional neuroimaging, and computational modeling to characterize how biological and artificial systems monitor internal noise and model their environments. Additionally, Peters is a co-founder and board chair of Neuromatch, a nonprofit organization focused on education in computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence.
0448.research_direction: Dr. Peters' recent work explores the computational and neural mechanisms underlying metacognition, uncertainty representation, and conscious subjective experience. They have recently been developing formal methodological frameworks to rigorously study these phenomena, such as extending signal detection theory to model optimal strategies for confidence judgments and proposing an introspective psychophysics to empirically quantify subjective reports. Additionally, their theoretical research investigates how the brain might build metacognitive estimates computationally, focusing on how higher-order Bayesian representations of first-order sensory reliability could be implemented neutrally. Finally, they are applying these computational and behavioral insights to novel domains, both by comparing uncertainty monitoring in large language models against human metacognition and by developing domain-adaptation machine learning techniques to improve predictive modeling on small, heterogeneous neuroimaging datasets.

papers.title: How brains build higher order representations of uncertainty
papers.abstract: Proposes that metacognitive estimates of uncertainty reflect a read-out of higher-order Bayesian posteriors about the reliability of first-order representations. The authors discuss what such higher-order representations might look like computationally and how they could be built and identified in the brain. The account is tied to metacognition, learning and theories of consciousness.
papers.authors: Megan A. K. Peters, Hojjat Azimi Asrari

papers.title: Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Humans and Large Language Models
papers.abstract: A review of what is currently known about whether large language models can monitor and report the reliability of their own outputs, and how that compares with human metacognition. The authors outline methods for testing LLM metacognition and show that while humans and LLMs sometimes look similarly calibrated, the underlying mechanisms and failure modes differ in important ways. They discuss implications for how uncertainty should be communicated to users in high-stakes settings.
papers.authors: Mark Steyvers, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Introspective psychophysics for the study of subjective experience
papers.abstract: Argues that introspective reports can be treated as measurable quantities in the tradition of classical psychophysics rather than dismissed as unreliable. The paper lays out which limitations of introspection are truly damaging and proposes a framework for making subjective experience an empirical target. It is a methodological manifesto for consciousness and perception research.
papers.authors: Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Domain adaptation in small-scale and heterogeneous biological datasets
papers.abstract: Machine-learning models tend to overfit when biological datasets are small and come from heterogeneous sources. The authors present a domain-adaptation approach that transfers structure learned across datasets to improve prediction on small target cohorts. They demonstrate gains on human neuroimaging and other biological data where sample sizes are limited.
papers.authors: Seyedmehdi Orouji, Martin C. Liu, Tal Korem, Megan A. K. Peters

papers.title: Optimal metacognitive decision strategies in signal detection theory
papers.abstract: Extends signal detection theory to metacognitive (type 2) judgments by deriving what normative strategies for confidence ratings look like. The paper gives a formal account of how an ideal observer should set metacognitive decision criteria and shows how observed behavior can deviate from that optimum. It provides a theoretical foundation for interpreting confidence data.
papers.authors: Brian Maniscalco, Lucie Charles, Megan A. K. Peters

0450.name: Megumi Kobayashi
0450.department: Department of Psychology and Human Studies
0450.bio: Megumi Kobayashi is an Associate Professor at Niigata University who researches the developmental trajectory of person recognition and face processing during infancy. Kobayashi utilizes behavioral preferential-looking methods and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to investigate how infants integrate facial and body cues to identify individuals. Their recent work examines the influence of environmental factors on visual development, including the impact of mask-wearing during the COVID-19 pandemic and the role of scenic context in shaping facial preferences.
0450.research_direction: Dr. Kobayashi has recently been investigating the development of face perception in infancy, focusing on how environmental exposure and visual contexts shape early visual processing. Their recent work explores the impact of real-world visual diets on face recognition, specifically using preferential-looking paradigms to examine how restricted exposure to unmasked faces during the COVID-19 pandemic influenced infants' preference for their own mother's face. Additionally, they are studying the integration of faces within broader visual environments to determine at what developmental stage infants begin relying on surrounding scenic context to support upright face processing. By manipulating variables like facial masking and scene intactness, Dr. Kobayashi aims to uncover the external visual conditions that guide the typical maturation of the human face processing system.

papers.title: Variations in face experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic affect infants' preference for their mother's face
papers.abstract: Because masks were worn outdoors in Japan for about three years, infants born during the pandemic saw few unmasked faces. The authors tested 5-8-month-olds in Tokyo and in provincial cities on their looking preference for the mother's face versus an unfamiliar woman, with faces unmasked or masked. Provincial infants preferred their mothers in both conditions, whereas Tokyo infants did so only when faces were masked, and parent-reported exposure to unmasked faces predicted preference at the individual level. The results indicate that everyday face experience shapes the development of face preferences.
papers.authors: Megumi Kobayashi, Machi Sugai, So Kanazawa, Masami K. Yamaguchi

papers.title: The role of scenic context on upright face preference in infancy
papers.abstract: Using a preferential-looking task, the study asked whether infants use surrounding scene information when processing faces. Infants aged 6-7 months preferred upright over inverted faces only when the face appeared in an intact scene, not a scrambled one, while 4-5-month-olds preferred upright faces in both. A control experiment showed the difference was not due to distraction by the scrambled images. Scene context therefore begins to support face processing around six months of age.
papers.authors: Megumi Kobayashi, So Kanazawa, Masami K. Yamaguchi

0451.name: Melchi M. Michel
0451.bio: Michel is an Associate Professor at Rutgers University who investigates the human visual system through the lens of probabilistic inference and ideal observer modeling. Their research examines how the brain integrates sensory data to form perceptual judgments, focusing on mechanisms of visual search, saccadic eye movements, and transsaccadic integration. By comparing human performance against mathematically optimal standards, Michel explores how observers exploit statistical regularities in both natural and artificial environments. Their work also extends to clinical domains, including the evaluation of visual performance in medical imaging and the development of training interventions for retinopathic patients.
0451.research_direction: Dr. Michel has recently been studying how people identify a visual target when its appearance is unpredictable, for example when its contrast, size, and position all vary from one presentation to the next. Their recent work compares human observers with a mathematically optimal Bayesian observer for this kind of categorical identification problem. The aim is to understand how the visual system copes with uncertainty about what a target will look like and where it will appear.

papers.title: Target identification under high levels of amplitude, size, and position uncertainty
papers.abstract: This research investigates how human observers classify image patches into categorical targets under significant within-category variability across multiple dimensions, including amplitude (contrast), size, and spatial position. The authors treat the problem as categorical identification from a set of mutually exclusive categories, which are further partitioned into subcategories representing specific target configurations. By deriving a mathematically optimal Bayesian observer for this identification task, the study provides a baseline to evaluate human performance and information integration strategies. The findings reveal the computational mechanisms humans use to resolve high-dimensional uncertainty during target identification in complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Yelda Semizer, Melchi M. Michel

0452.name: Melissa Beck
0452.bio: Melissa R. Beck is a Professor of Psychology at Louisiana State University and a member of the Multidisciplinary Institute for Neuroscience Discovery (MIND). Beck utilizes eye-tracking, behavioral psychophysics, and cognitive modeling to investigate how the human brain maintains stable visual representations across eye movements and shifts of attention. Their research examines change blindness, visual search efficiency, and the role of metacognition in perception. Beck applies cognitive science to applied domains, including the optimization of human-computer interfaces for aviation and the development of spatial reasoning training protocols for STEM education.
0452.research_direction: Dr. Beck has recently been studying how memory shapes what people look for and find in visual scenes. Their work asks how the priority of a search target held in working memory changes the stages of searching real objects, using eye movements to separate starting a search from scanning and verifying a target. They also explore hybrid search, where people look for any of many remembered targets, and whether holding those targets in long-term memory interferes with remembering distractors. Related projects examine how the meaning of a scene affects global versus local processing and whether the attentional blink differs for nature and urban scenes.

papers.title: Effects of template priority on working memory-guided search for real objects: evidence from eye-movements
papers.abstract: This research investigates how the prioritization of attentional templates in working memory (WM) influences different stages of visual search in realistic scenes. Utilizing eye-tracking to segment reaction times into initiation, scanning, and verification phases, the study compared performance for current versus prospective templates. The results demonstrated that template priority specifically facilitates the scanning and verification epochs—evidenced by fewer object fixations and reduced gaze duration on targets—but does not affect the latency of search initiation. These findings suggest that higher-priority templates are characterized by increased representational precision, which optimizes the matching process between external stimuli and internal memory representations during complex search tasks.
papers.authors: Hanane Ramzaoui, Melissa R. Beck

papers.title: Activated long-term memory and visual working memory during hybrid visual search: Effects on target memory search and distractor memory
papers.abstract: Hybrid visual search involves the simultaneous search of the environment and a memory set maintained in activated long-term memory (aLTM). This study explored the extent to which loading aLTM with target templates interferes with visual working memory (VWM) maintenance of distracting information. Across seven experiments, the authors measured distractor memory (via revisits and recognition) and target memory search (via dwell times and error rates). The data revealed that increasing the memory set size in aLTM does not directly impede VWM for distractors; however, the presence of a hybrid search task itself reduces VWM capacity by a fixed amount. These results support a model where VWM acts as a bottleneck for passing visual representations to aLTM for comparison rather than serving as the primary storage for search templates.
papers.authors: Stephanie M. Saltzmann, Brandon Eich, Katherine C. Moen, Melissa R. Beck

papers.title: Semantic Meaning Impacts the Relationship between Global and Local Visual Processing
papers.abstract: Investigates how the semantic meaning of stimuli changes the relationship between global and local visual processing.
papers.authors: Gaojie Fan, Brandon Eich, Stephanie Saltzmann, Melissa R. Beck

papers.title: Differences in the duration of the attentional blink when viewing nature vs. urban scenes
papers.abstract: Tests whether the attentional blink lasts a different time when the stimuli are nature scenes rather than urban scenes.
papers.authors: Brandon Eich, Melissa R. Beck

0454.name: Micaela Mitolo
0454.bio: Micaela Mitolo is a researcher at the University of Parma specializing in the neuroimaging and neuropsychology of aging and neurodegenerative disorders. Mitolo utilizes multimodal imaging techniques, including structural and functional MRI, proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and quantitative susceptibility mapping, to identify biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies. They investigate the neural correlates of visuospatial processing and the melanopsin retinal ganglion cell system, alongside the predictive value of sulcal morphometry in cognitive decline. This research also explores the relationship between sleep quality, gray matter atrophy, and functional connectivity in patients with mild cognitive impairment.
0454.research_direction: Dr. Mitolo has recently been focusing on characterizing visuospatial and visuomotor dysfunction in neurodegenerative conditions, particularly Lewy body disease. To investigate the posterior-cortical networks underlying these cognitive and motor deficits, they are combining task-based fMRI, structural volumetry, and kinematic tracking of reaching movements and saccades. Their recent work also explores the clinical relevance of specific perceptual anomalies by examining "minor visual phenomena"—such as pareidolias and passage hallucinations—to understand how these symptoms relate to broader visuospatial decline and major visual hallucinations. Broadening their focus on clinical neurodegeneration, they are investigating multi-modal diagnostic and therapeutic frameworks, including mapping blood-based protein biomarkers to structural MRI changes in Alzheimer’s disease and evaluating non-pharmacological interventions like neurostimulation and cognitive rehabilitation.

papers.title: Sustained attention in dementia with Lewy bodies: a task-based fMRI study
papers.abstract: Thirty DLB patients and 25 controls completed neuropsychological testing and an auditory psychomotor vigilance task during 3T fMRI. Patients had more lapses and slower responses, with worst performance in visuospatial tests. They showed reduced activation in precuneus, intracalcarine cortex, angular gyrus and cuneus, pointing to posterior-cortical attention network dysfunction.
papers.authors: Davide Braghittoni, Greta Venturi, Lucia Guidi, Elettra Capogna, Giovanni Sighinolfi, Luca Baldelli, Giulia Amore, Chiara La Morgia, Luisa Sambati, Annalena Venneri, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Visuospatial performance and its neural substrates in Dementia with Lewy Bodies during a pointing task
papers.abstract: Combines mixed-effects modelling and machine learning on reaching/pointing kinematics, saccades and superior parietal lobule volumetry to tell dementia with Lewy bodies patients apart from healthy controls. Patients showed slower and less accurate pointing, delayed and hypermetric saccades with direction-specific asymmetries, and left-lateralised parietal volume loss. The multimodal visuomotor signature is proposed as a biomarker framework beyond standard visuospatial tests.
papers.authors: Annalisa Bosco, Caterina Foglino, Lucia Guidi, Davide Braghittoni, Greta Venturi, Luisa Sambati, Luca Baldelli, Giovanna Calandra-Buonaura, Patrizia Fattori, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Minor Visual Phenomena in Lewy Body Disease: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Reviews 44 studies on minor visual phenomena in Lewy body disease, such as illusions, pareidolias, sense of presence and passage hallucinations. These phenomena are highly specific to LBD versus Alzheimer's disease and seem to relate to visual hallucinations, but whether they are precursors is unclear. Pareidolia tends to associate negatively with visuoperceptual and visuospatial ability, though causality remains open.
papers.authors: Elettra Capogna, Virginia Pollarini, Alessia Quinzi, Lucia Guidi, Luisa Sambati, Maria Sasca Criante, Elena Mengoli, Annalena Venneri, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

papers.title: Association between blood-based protein biomarkers and brain MRI in the Alzheimer's disease continuum: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Systematic review of 33 studies linking plasma biomarkers (Abeta, p-tau, NfL, GFAP) to MRI measures across the Alzheimer's continuum. Amyloid ratios track hippocampal volume, p-tau181/217 track temporal grey matter and cortical thickness, NfL tracks white-matter integrity, and GFAP tracks posterior cingulate myo-inositol. Suggests combining biomarkers improves early diagnosis and monitoring.
papers.authors: Micaela Mitolo, Gemma Lombardi, Riccardo Manca, Benedetta Nacmias, Annalena Venneri

papers.title: Non-Pharmacological Treatments in Lewy Body Disease: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: PRISMA-based review of 23 studies (231 patients) on physical therapy, cognitive rehabilitation, light therapy, tDCS, TMS, ECT and DBS in Lewy body disease. Physical therapy helped motor symptoms and cognitive rehabilitation improved mood, cognition and quality of life. Light therapy showed partial benefits for mood and sleep, and tDCS for attention.
papers.authors: Lucia Guidi, Stefano Evangelisti, Alessandra Siniscalco, Raffaele Lodi, Caterina Tonon, Micaela Mitolo

0455.name: Michael A. Crognale
0455.bio: Michael A. Crognale is a retired Professor of Visual Neuroscience (retired July 1, 2026) and former Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Nevada, Reno, and continues to do consulting. Crognale’s research investigates the physiological mechanisms of sensory processing, focusing on color vision, comparative visual capacities, and neural development across the lifespan. They utilize methodologies such as high-density electroencephalography (EEG), electroretinography (ERG), and adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to examine visual function ranging from photoreceptor genetics to cortical attention. Their work is applied to the clinical diagnosis of color vision deficiencies and human factors in aviation visibility.
0455.research_direction: Dr. Crognale has recently been investigating how the human visual system responds to color and brightness, using both brain recordings and perceptual experiments. Their recent work explores how to get stronger and cleaner visual evoked potentials, including stimulus designs that limit neural adaptation and tripolar electrodes that reduce electrical noise, and whether attention changes early responses to chromatic versus achromatic patterns. They have also been developing tablet-based tests of color vision that can identify color deficiencies more efficiently than traditional clinical tests. In addition, they have been asking how the visual system computes the apparent brightness of a patch from its surroundings, and how this depends on whether the patch is lighter or darker than its background.

papers.title: Alternating pattern orientation or phase can increase the amplitude of the visual evoked potential
papers.abstract: The research evaluates the cortical response characteristics to pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs), which typically yield robust signals for achromatic stimuli but attenuated responses for isoluminant chromatic stimuli. This attenuation is hypothesized to result from contrast adaptation within the sustained parvocellular and koniocellular visual pathways, which exhibit higher time-averaged contrast under reversal paradigms compared to pattern-onset paradigms. To address this, the authors implemented a novel stimulus protocol that modulates pattern orientation or phase in addition to luminance reversal to minimize steady-state adaptation. Findings demonstrate that these spatio-temporal modifications significantly increase the amplitude of the chromatic VEP, providing a methodological enhancement for electrophysiological studies of the sustained chromatic pathways in the human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Jawshan Ara, Alireza Tavakkoli, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Comparison of tripolar and traditional EEG recording of the visual evoked potential
papers.abstract: This study conducts a comparative performance analysis between traditional disc electroencephalography (EEG) and tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCRE/tEEG) in the recording of pattern-reversal visual evoked potentials (VEPs). The authors characterized the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and noise profiles, finding that tEEG exhibits significantly enhanced robustness against non-physiological interference, particularly 60 Hz line noise and its harmonics, due to its inherent Laplacian spatial filtering properties. While the qualitative morphology of the VEP waveforms was preserved across both electrode types, systematic shifts in the latencies of primary peaks (N75, P100, N135) were observed, suggesting that the TCRE configuration isolates a more localized subset of the spatiotemporal neural generators involved in early visual processing.
papers.authors: Mackenzie V. Wise, Gideon P. Caplovitz, Gabriel Foster, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Application of the angular indication measurement and foraging interactive D-prime paradigms to tablet-based color vision testing
papers.abstract: The authors developed and validated a tablet-based platform for screening color vision deficiencies (CVD) using two advanced psychophysical paradigms: the Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) and the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD). The study benchmarked these automated paradigms against traditional clinical assessments, including the Farnsworth-Munsell 100-hue (FM-100) test and the Hardy-Rand-Rittler (HRR) plates. Using Spearman’s rho and linear mixed models to analyze total error scores (TES) and discrimination thresholds, the researchers demonstrated that these computer-based paradigms accurately categorize observers into superior, average, and deficient color discrimination groups. The findings support the use of mobile tablet technology as a reliable and high-throughput alternative to legacy clinical color vision testing methods.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Christabel Arthur, Jingyi He, Peter J. Bex, Jan Skerswetat, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Dependence of brightness induction on the contrast polarity of a disk–annulus stimulus
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural computations underlying brightness induction by testing a model based on edge integration theory coupled with contrast gain control. Using a disk-annulus paradigm, observers performed brightness matches across varying annulus luminance levels. The data was used to construct achromatic color appearance matching functions (ACAMFs), which were found to be non-linear and well-modeled by second-order polynomial functions. The analysis revealed that brightness induction is highly dependent on the contrast polarity (increment vs. decrement) of the target disk relative to its annulus. These results support the existence of distinct gain control mechanisms for the ON and OFF pathways in the human visual system that regulate the strength of induction from luminance edges.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Osman Kavcar, Michael E. Rudd, Michael A. Crognale

papers.title: Pattern reversal chromatic VEPs like onsets, are unaffected by attentional demand
papers.abstract: The study examined the susceptibility of early chromatic and achromatic cortical processing to attentional modulation using visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and a multiple object tracking (MOT) distractor task. Participants were presented with pattern-reversal stimuli in CIE color space along isoluminant (L−M and S−(L+M)) and achromatic axes while performing varying levels of the MOT task. Frequency tagging and FFT analysis showed that while achromatic VEP amplitudes were significantly modulated by attentional demand—exhibiting a decrease in response during the distractor task—the chromatic VEP responses remained robust and invariant. These findings indicate that while top-down attention influences luminance-based spatial pathways in the primary visual cortex, the chromatic pathways are largely resistant to such attentional filtering.
papers.authors: Christabel Arthur, Osman B. Kavcar, Mackenzie V. Wise, Michael A. Crognale

0456.name: Michael A. Webster
0456.bio: Michael A. Webster is a Foundation Professor in the Department of Psychology and Director of the Center for Integrative Neuroscience at the University of Nevada, Reno. Webster’s research examines visual adaptation and how the human visual system recalibrates its sensitivity in response to changes in the stimulus environment and observer physiology, such as aging or ocular disease. They utilize a methodological approach integrating psychophysical experiments, computational modeling, and natural image statistics to study color constancy, image focus, and high-level perception, including facial recognition. Their work characterizes forms of adaptation across various visual domains and investigates how these processes function to optimize vision for specific ecological contexts.
0456.research_direction: Dr. Webster's recent work explores the perceptual and neural mechanisms underlying human color vision, ranging from early cortical coding to applied visual ecology. They have recently been investigating how fundamental color spaces are structured, using behavioral scaling and visual evoked potentials to probe the origins of hue asymmetries, the perceptual reality of the warm-cool color axis, and how the representational coordinates of color fundamentally differ from those of motion. Additionally, their research examines how the visual system adapts to impoverished or altered chromatic signals, particularly in the context of color vision deficiencies. By measuring chromatic contrast adaptation aftereffects and visual search performance, they are testing whether sensory-level gain compensation explains near-normal color experiences in anomalous trichromats and evaluating how color-enhancing notch filters alter target salience in naturalistic foraging environments.

papers.title: Asymmetries in hue percepts and early cortical color coding: Evidence from chromatic visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: Hue appearance changes faster in some directions of color space (near yellow) than others (near green), but the reason is unknown. The authors recorded occipital visual evoked potentials to gratings varying in hue at fixed cone-opponent contrast and compared response strength across hue separations. Neural response asymmetries paralleled the behavioral ones, indicating that hue asymmetries arise at early stages of cortical color coding.
papers.authors: Jesse R. Macyczko, Osman B. Kavcar, Michael A. Crognale, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Effects of color-enhancing filters on color salience in normal trichromats
papers.abstract: Notch filters were designed to boost reddish-greenish contrast for anomalous trichromats. Here normal trichromats performed a visual search for colored targets on variegated chromatic backgrounds mimicking foraging environments, with and without such filters. The study evaluates how the filters alter color salience across target hues and contrasts.
papers.authors: Camilla Simoncelli, Donald McPherson, Kenneth Knoblauch, Michael Webster

papers.title: Warm versus cool colors and their relation to color perception
papers.abstract: Tests whether the warm-cool division of colors reflects genuine perceptual coding or learned associations. Observers rated 36 hues at three lightness levels for warmth and also located their unique and binary hues. The warm-cool axis was stable across lightness and runs from orangish-red to greenish-blue, an axis that does not match either the cone-opponent or perceptual-opponent cardinal dimensions, suggesting a distinct perceptual basis.
papers.authors: Jake Manalansan, Lorne A. Whitehead, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Color contrast adaptation and compensation in color deficiencies
papers.abstract: Anomalous trichromats have reduced L-vs-M sensitivity yet often report near-normal suprathreshold color experience. By comparing chromatic contrast adaptation aftereffects in 15 color-normal and 15 color-anomalous observers, the study probes whether sensory-level gain compensation underlies this. Results speak to where in the visual pathway compensation occurs.
papers.authors: Fatemeh Basim, Erin Goddard, Yueran Yang, Michael A. Webster

papers.title: Fundamentally different representations of color and motion revealed by individual differences in perceptual scaling
papers.abstract: Compares how people scale hue and motion direction in similar tasks. Individual differences in perceived motion direction reflect the structure of visual space (horizontal/vertical weighting), whereas hue percepts show no privileged chromatic axes or global coordinate frame. The contrast implies different representational principles for color and motion.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Kara J. Emery, Vicki J. Volbrecht, David H. Peterzell, Michael A. Webster

0457.name: Michael Arcaro
0457.bio: Arcaro is an Assistant Professor at the University of Pennsylvania whose research explores how intrinsic neural architectures and sensory experiences interact to shape the organization of the primate visual system. Using multimodal approaches including fMRI, electrophysiology, and behavioral psychophysics, Arcaro’s work characterizes the development of topographic maps and functional domains from birth through adulthood. Their research includes identifying the necessity of early visual experience for the formation of face-selective domains and analyzing the comparative evolution of cortical expansion in humans versus other primates.
0457.research_direction: Dr. Arcaro has recently been investigating the developmental, evolutionary, and anatomical foundations of the primate visual system. Their recent work explores the intrinsic functional architecture of the brain at birth, utilizing resting-state and diffusion MRI in human neonates to map innate cortical pathways, retinotopy, and cortico-pulvinar connectivity prior to postnatal visual experience. In a comparative vein, they are studying the evolution of the primate visual cortex by contrasting human and macaque retinotopic maps to determine how cortical expansion relates to conserved spatial layouts. Furthermore, their research probes the specific functional and metabolic organization of visual processing, using high-field fMRI encoding models to map feature and category representations within the subcortical pulvinar, and aligning in vivo macaque fMRI with ex vivo histology to investigate the metabolic architecture underlying category-selective networks.

papers.title: Functional organization of the human visual system at birth and across late gestation
papers.abstract: Using resting-state fMRI from 584 neonates in the Developing Human Connectome Project, the authors map the functional architecture of visual cortex within hours of birth and across the third trimester. Newborns already show three distinct pathways (ventral, lateral, dorsal), each with posterior-to-anterior hierarchy and adult-like topography, unlike the two-pathway layout seen in macaques. These features strengthen with gestational age, pointing to intrinsic developmental mechanisms rather than postnatal experience.
papers.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Metabolic organization of macaque visual cortex reflects visual field topography and perceptual specialization
papers.abstract: The authors align in vivo fMRI maps of eccentricity and category selectivity with ex vivo cytochrome oxidase histology in macaque visual cortex. The centrally biased face-selective region ML shows higher oxidative metabolism than the peripherally biased scene-selective place patch, and metabolic intensity varies with eccentricity within these regions. The results tie cortical metabolic architecture to retinotopic organization and perceptual specialization.
papers.authors: Hiroki Oishi, Vladimir K. Berezovskii, Margaret S. Livingstone, Kevin S. Weiner, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Expansion of a conserved architecture drives the evolution of the primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study compares retinotopic maps in humans and macaques to ask whether the larger human visual cortex arises from new areas or from enlarging an existing shared map layout. It finds expansion is mainly growth of a conserved set of maps, strongest in higher-order and parietal areas, and that these relative size differences are already present in human neonates. A meta-analysis links the most expanded areas to higher-level cognitive functions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Emily E. Meyer, Marcelina Martynek, Sabine Kastner, Margaret S. Livingstone, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: An intrinsic hierarchical, retinotopic organization of visual pulvinar connectivity in the human neonate
papers.abstract: Using diffusion MRI tractography in human newborns, the authors show that pulvinar-to-cortex pathways to each visual area already exist at birth. These connections show retinotopic organization within the pulvinar and hierarchical ordering across ventral, lateral and dorsal streams, largely resembling adults. Ventral-stream connectivity is the least adult-like, consistent with its slower maturation.
papers.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg, Chenjie Song, Michael J. Arcaro

papers.title: Processing of natural scenes in the human pulvinar
papers.abstract: Analyzing a 7T fMRI dataset of responses to tens of thousands of natural scenes, the authors use encoding models to characterize what the human pulvinar represents. They find organized maps for low-level features such as contrast and a region selective for bodies and faces in the contralateral field that is co-active with cortical body and face areas. The work argues that functional clustering and hierarchy also occur in subcortex, challenging cortico-centric views of object vision.
papers.authors: Daniel R. Guest, Emily J. Allen, Kendrick N. Kay, Michael J. Arcaro

0458.name: Michael Beyeler
0458.department: Department of Computer Science and Department of Psychological & Brain Sciences
0458.bio: Michael Beyeler is an Associate Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and directs the Bionic Vision Lab. Their research integrates computational neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and neuroengineering to develop visual neuroprostheses for individuals with blindness. Beyeler focuses on building biophysically grounded models of neural stimulation and using virtual reality testbeds to optimize prosthetic interfaces. This work utilizes multimodal data and machine learning to investigate and augment human visual perception.
0458.research_direction: Dr. Beyeler has recently been investigating the intersection of biological and artificial vision, focusing heavily on optimizing visual prostheses and understanding robust neural representations. Their recent work explores how to improve outcomes for retinal and cortical implant users by developing computational "virtual patients" to forecast behavioral performance, conducting psychophysical studies to test different spatial stimulation schedules, and building differentiable forward models of evoked percepts to optimize surgical electrode placement. In parallel, they are examining how to make artificial intelligence systems more biologically grounded and resilient to visual perturbations. To this end, they are developing novel distillation techniques to transfer robust representational structures between deep learning models, as well as creating open benchmarks that directly compare artificial reinforcement-learning agents against behavioral and neural recordings from mice in shared visual tasks.

papers.title: Mouse vs. AI: A Neuroethological Benchmark for Visual Robustness and Neural Alignment (NeurIPS 2026 version: Visual robustness and neural alignment in a shared foraging task: The Mouse vs. AI benchmark)
papers.abstract: The authors build an open benchmark in which reinforcement-learning agents and real mice perform the same visually guided foraging task in a 3D virtual environment. Submissions are scored on two tracks: robustness to visual perturbations and how well an agent's internal representations align with recordings from thousands of mouse visual cortex neurons. The resource links RL, computer vision and neuroscience to push toward more robust, biologically grounded visual AI.
papers.authors: Marius Schneider, Joe S. Canzano, Yuchen Hou, Jing Peng, Anjali Deepu, Utsab Karan, Phu-Hoa Pham, Tran Chi Nguyen, Dao Sy Duy Minh, Phu Quy Nguyen Lam, Trung-Kiet Huynh, Simone Azeglio, Spencer LaVere Smith, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: BIRD: Behavior Induction via Representation-structure Distillation
papers.abstract: BIRD transfers desirable behaviors such as robustness from a well-behaved teacher network to a student by matching the structure of their internal representations instead of their weights or outputs. It improves out-of-distribution robust accuracy by up to 16% over prior methods and still works when the teacher is trained on simpler data and is 25x smaller. An analysis of 400+ teacher-student pairs shows that task relevance, behavioral relevance and complementary knowledge explain most of the variance in transfer success.
papers.authors: Galen Pogoncheff, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Percept-aware surgical planning for visual cortical prostheses with vascular avoidance
papers.abstract: Electrode placement for cortical visual prostheses is cast as a constrained optimization in anatomical space, with electrode coordinates treated as learnable parameters of a differentiable forward model of evoked percepts. Optimizing directly for perceptual error, while enforcing gray-matter feasibility and keeping electrodes away from blood vessels, clearly beat coverage-based placement on reading and image-recognition tasks in realistic folded cortical geometry. Vascular safety constraints did not cost visual quality.
papers.authors: Galen Pogoncheff, Alvin Wang, Jacob Granley, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Intact early visual representations, not phosphene-adapted features, account for human perceptual behavior with retinal prostheses
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a computational virtual patient that combines anatomically grounded phosphene simulation with task-optimized deep networks to forecast what implant users can do across six visual tasks and six electrode layouts. Predicted task difficulty tracks real patient outcomes on FLORA-style assessments and psychophysics in sighted subjects viewing simulations. Frozen natural-image features explained human behavior better than features fine-tuned to phosphenes, consistent with limited adult cortical plasticity, positioning the pipeline as a pre-implantation planning tool.
papers.authors: Jonathan Skaza, Shravan Murlidaran, Apurv Varshney, Ziqi Wen, Miguel P. Eckstein, Michael Beyeler

papers.title: Simulated prosthetic vision confirms checkerboard as an effective raster pattern for epiretinal implants
papers.abstract: Sighted participants performed letter recognition and motion discrimination through an immersive, psychophysically validated simulation of epiretinal implants while electrodes were activated in horizontal, vertical, checkerboard or random sequences. Checkerboard scheduling gave higher accuracy and lower rated difficulty and matched unstructured activation while respecting safety constraints on simultaneous neighbouring electrodes. Random scheduling did worst, showing activation order matters for functional prosthetic vision.
papers.authors: Justin M. Kasowski, Apurv Varshney, Roksana Sadeghi, Michael Beyeler

0459.name: Michael Bonner
0459.bio: Michael F. Bonner is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Cognitive Science at Johns Hopkins University, where he directs the Bonner Lab. His research investigates the computational principles of the human visual system by integrating functional neuroimaging with deep neural network modeling. He focuses on characterizing the high-dimensional nature of cortical representations, challenging traditional low-dimensional theories of neural coding through advanced statistical techniques. His recent work explores the alignment between artificial and biological vision systems and the latent manifold structure that underlies individual differences in visual experience.
0459.research_direction: The Bonner Lab studies how brains and deep networks learn to represent the visual world. Combining large-scale neuroimaging with computational modeling, the lab analyzes biological and artificial systems with the same tools so they can be compared directly. Recent work shows that networks with very different architectures and training objectives converge on a common set of universal features, and that these are the features most reliably found in visual cortex. Current work asks where such representations come from: architecture and image statistics alone, extremely coarse learning objectives, or local learning rules that build a visual hierarchy without backpropagation.

papers.title: High-dimensional structure underlying individual differences in naturalistic visual experience
papers.abstract: The research investigates the neural mechanisms by which unique subjective visual experiences are constructed from shared sensory inputs by analyzing the high-dimensional geometry of the human visual hierarchy. Utilizing spectral decomposition of fMRI responses acquired during naturalistic movie viewing, the authors demonstrate that idiosyncratic neural signatures are robustly maintained across several orders of magnitude of the latent eigenspectrum. This multidimensional representation, which is not captured by standard intersubject correlation (ISC) metrics, significantly predicts individual variance in subsequent memory recall, including the semantic richness and abstraction of narrative descriptions. The findings suggest that individual perception is mediated by information integration across an expansive, high-dimensional manifold in the visual cortex.
papers.authors: Chihye Han, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Universal scale-free representations in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Utilizing the Natural Scenes Dataset, this study characterizes the large-scale population covariance of the human visual cortex to identify its fundamental organizing principles. By applying a spectral analysis to fMRI responses, the authors discovered that neural representations follow a consistent scale-free organization, with variance decaying as a power law across approximately four orders of magnitude of latent dimensions. This scale-invariant structure is highly conserved across individual subjects and across multiple regions of the visual hierarchy from V1 to V4. Furthermore, functional hyperalignment reveals that these high-dimensional dimensions are shared between brains, suggesting a universal spectrum of visual information that is systematically distributed across the entire representational manifold rather than confined to low-dimensional subspaces.
papers.authors: Raj Magesh Gauthaman, Brice Ménard, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Universal dimensions of visual representation
papers.abstract: This work addresses whether the representational alignment between deep neural networks (DNNs) and the human visual cortex is driven by specific optimization constraints, such as architecture and task objectives, or by universal features of natural image representation. By characterizing the universality of latent dimensions across an ensemble of hundreds of networks with diverse designs, the authors identified a common subspace of shared representational features. Comparative analysis with human fMRI data showed that the specific features which align most closely with cortical responses are those that are universal across artificial networks, independent of their individual task or architectural biases. This suggests that biological and artificial vision systems converge on similar high-dimensional geometries dictated by the statistical regularities of natural visual inputs.
papers.authors: Zirui Chen, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: Convolutional architectures are cortex-aligned de novo
papers.abstract: The study investigates the role of architectural inductive biases in the emergence of cortex-aligned representations in neural networks, challenging the prevailing view that massive experience-dependent training is necessary for brain-model similarity. The authors demonstrate that untrained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) exhibit significant representational alignment with the ventral visual streams of humans and macaques 'de novo,' provided they incorporate specific architectural constraints: spatial dimensionality compression via pooling and feature-channel expansion. In contrast, scaling feature dimensionality in transformers or fully connected architectures failed to generate similar brain-like representations. The results suggest that the fundamental wiring of the visual cortex is closely mimicked by the architectural constraints of CNNs, allowing for brain-aligned processing even without learning.
papers.authors: Atlas Kazemian, Eric Elmoznino, Michael F. Bonner

papers.title: High-performing neural network models of visual cortex benefit from high latent dimensionality
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the 'compression hypothesis' in visual neuroscience, which posits that neural networks should reduce image representations to low-dimensional manifolds to achieve robust semantic invariance. By quantifying the latent dimensionality of numerous DNN models of the visual system, the authors demonstrate that, conversely, models with high effective dimensionality are superior predictors of neural activity in both human fMRI and macaque electrophysiology. Furthermore, high latent dimensionality was positively correlated with improved generalization performance when learning novel object categories. These results provide evidence that the visual cortex prioritizes high-dimensional sensory codes that preserve rich perceptual detail, challenging traditional views that emphasize low-dimensional representations as the goal of cortical visual processing.
papers.authors: Eric Elmoznino, Michael F. Bonner

0460.name: Michael Gaebler
0460.institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences
0460.bio: Michael Gaebler is a cognitive and neuroscientist who leads the Mind-Body-Emotion Group at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences. Gaebler’s research focuses on the bidirectional relationship between mental states and peripheral physiology, specifically examining how brain-heart interactions influence emotional arousal, interoception, and sensory perception.
