They utilize high-density neuroimaging, including EEG and fMRI, alongside immersive virtual reality to develop naturalistic paradigms for investigating subjective experience in healthy and pathological populations. Gaebler’s work also explores the integration of digital health tools and ambulatory assessments to connect laboratory findings with real-world affective phenomena.
0460.research_direction: Dr. Gaebler has recently been investigating the interplay between neural and physiological systems, proposing theoretical frameworks that model coupled brain-heart activity as integrated "brain-body states" linked to both mental and cardiovascular health. Their recent empirical work explores these interactions during naturalistic emotional arousal, utilizing immersive virtual reality (VR) environments combined with simultaneous EEG and ECG recordings to map heartbeat-evoked potentials and directional information flow. To support this research, they are developing open-source methodological tools that allow participants to continuously rate their affective experiences in real time during dynamic VR exposure. Additionally, their research touches on visual processing in 3D environments, using time-resolved neural decoding and eye tracking to examine how the brain represents emotional facial expressions and integrates stereoscopic depth cues.

papers.title: Brain–body states as a link between cardiovascular and mental health
papers.abstract: The authors propose viewing coupled brain and cardiovascular activity as 'brain-body states' that move through a state space with attractors. These are grouped into micro-, meso- and macro-states by duration and reversibility, reflecting mechanisms from fast neural interactions to hormonal signalling and structural plasticity. Longer-lasting states constrain shorter-term ones, which they argue helps explain the shared course of cardiovascular and brain function over the lifespan and in diseases such as hypertension and depression, with clinical implications.
papers.authors: Arno Villringer, Vadim V. Nikulin, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: Using immersive VR, EEG and eye tracking, the study asked how the brain represents faces when stereoscopic depth cues are present or absent. Time-resolved decoding of EEG from 34 participants separated neutral, happy, angry and surprised expressions and also picked up a distinct signature of stereoscopic depth. Expression decoding was similar with and without depth cues, and gaze patterns did not explain the neural representations.
papers.authors: Felix Klotzsche, Ammara Nasim, Simon M. Hofmann, Arno Villringer, Vadim Nikulin, Werner Sommer, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: AffectTracker: real-time continuous rating of affective experience in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: The paper presents AffectTracker, an open tool for continuously rating valence and arousal while people watch dynamic stimuli such as 360-degree videos in VR, with grid, pulsating 'Flubber', or no visual feedback. Two two-site studies (n = 51 and n = 82) showed good user experience and low interference for the Grid and Flubber options, including during a longer 23-minute immersive experience. The tool is meant to capture moment-to-moment affect more naturally than post-hoc summary ratings.
papers.authors: Antonin Fourcade, Francesca Malandrone, Lucy Roellecke, Anthony Ciston, Jeroen de Mooij, Arno Villringer, Sara Carletto, Michael Gaebler

papers.title: Linking brain-heart interactions to emotional arousal in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: Twenty-nine adults went through a VR experience with rollercoasters while EEG and ECG were recorded, then rated their emotional arousal continuously during a video replay. Higher arousal went with smaller heartbeat-evoked potentials over left fronto-central electrodes, while heart rate variability and parieto-occipital alpha power showed weaker or no links. Directional information-flow models between brain and heart signals added further evidence that brain-heart coupling tracks emotional arousal in naturalistic conditions.
papers.authors: Antonin Fourcade, Felix Klotzsche, Simon M. Hofmann, Alessandro Mariola, Vadim V. Nikulin, Arno Villringer, Michael Gaebler

0461.name: Michael H. Herzog
0461.department: Brain Mind Institute, School of Life Sciences
0461.bio: Michael H. Herzog is a Professor of Psychophysics at EPFL's Brain Mind Institute and directs the Laboratory of Psychophysics. Herzog’s research focuses on the spatio-temporal dynamics of human vision, specifically how global context and grouping mechanisms resolve visual crowding and feature integration. Herzog employs an interdisciplinary framework of psychophysical experiments, electrophysiology, and mathematical modeling to examine feed-forward models of visual processing. Their laboratory also investigates visual perception as a potential endophenotype for psychiatric conditions, notably schizophrenia, to identify biomarkers of neural dysfunction.
0461.research_direction: Dr. Herzog's recent work explores the spatial and temporal dynamics of visual processing, with a major focus on the mechanisms of visual crowding and unconscious feature integration. Using paradigms like sequential metacontrast masking and complex flanker configurations, they have recently been investigating whether crowding and target discrimination are constrained by low-level local pooling limits or higher-order perceptual grouping over time. In parallel, their research applies vision science methods to clinical populations to understand the neural and behavioral basis of psychiatric and perceptual abnormalities. Specifically, they are using EEG to track cortical alpha-band traveling waves to probe feedforward and feedback predictive coding deficits in schizophrenia, while also deploying comprehensive psychophysical batteries to systematically characterize the subjective symptoms of visual snow syndrome.

papers.title: Failure to replicate a superiority effect in crowding
papers.abstract: Crowding is usually thought to impair recognition of a target when clutter surrounds it, but an earlier report claimed that certain flanker arrangements can actually make target discrimination better. The authors ran a set of preregistered-style replications and extensions of that paradigm and did not find the improvement, with performance behaving as classic crowding accounts predict. The paper is a cautionary test of a result that would have challenged grouping-based and pooling accounts of crowding.
papers.authors: Ayberk Ozkirli, David Pascucci, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Visual Crowding
papers.abstract: A review of what is known about how nearby clutter degrades object perception. It argues that crowding is not a fixed low-level, purely local pooling limit but depends on perceptual grouping, timing, and the layout of complex stimuli. The article surveys models and evidence, and points to open questions about the mechanisms involved.
papers.authors: Lisa Schwetlick, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Oscillatory Traveling Waves Provide Evidence for Predictive Coding Abnormalities in Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Using EEG from patients with schizophrenia and healthy controls, the authors quantified alpha-band waves travelling across the cortex in feedforward and feedback directions. Patients showed altered wave patterns consistent with disturbed top-down prediction, linking predictive-coding theory to a measurable neural signature of the disorder.
papers.authors: Andrea Alamia, Dario Gordillo, Eka Chkonia, Maya Roinishvili, Celine Cappe, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Investigating the relationship between subjective perception and unconscious feature integration
papers.abstract: The study uses a sequential metacontrast paradigm in which visual features are integrated unconsciously for a few hundred milliseconds before a percept emerges. It tests how this hidden integration relates to what observers subjectively report seeing, examining whether the two track each other across conditions.
papers.authors: Lukas Vogelsang, Maëlan Q. Menétrey, Leila Drissi-Daoudi, Michael H. Herzog

papers.title: Understanding visual perception in visual snow syndrome: a battery of psychophysical tests plus the 30-day clinical diary
papers.abstract: Twenty patients with visual snow syndrome and 17 controls completed a broad battery covering acuity, contrast sensitivity, illusions, spatiotemporal vision, motion, and attention. Patients performed like controls on nearly everything except susceptibility to the honeycomb illusion, suggesting that standard tests capture little of the subjective symptoms. The work also paired the tests with a clinical diary of symptoms.
papers.authors: Simona Garobbio, Reza Mazloum, Michael Rosio, Jeanette Popovova, Raphaela Schöpfer, Fabienne C Fierz, Leah R Disse, Konrad Peter Weber, Christoph J Schankin, Lars Michels, Michael H Herzog

0462.name: Michael J Tarr
0462.bio: Michael J. Tarr is the Kavčić-Moura Professor of Cognitive and Brain Science at Carnegie Mellon University and investigates the computational and neural architectures underlying high-level visual perception. Tarr’s research focuses on how the primate brain transforms two-dimensional retinal inputs into representations of objects, faces, and scenes, emphasizing the role of perceptual expertise and learning. They employ a multi-disciplinary approach that integrates large-scale functional neuroimaging, such as the BOLD5000 dataset, with deep learning and generative AI models to bridge the gap between biological and artificial vision systems. Tarr’s current work explores the inductive biases of the human visual system and develops NeuroAI frameworks to map cortical semantic selectivity across the ventral visual pathway.
0462.research_direction: Dr. Tarr has recently been using advanced deep learning models to map and decode visual representations in the human brain. Their recent work explores how generative frameworks, such as diffusion models and vision transformers, can be combined with fMRI to synthesize images that maximally drive specific cortical regions, ground semantic selectivity at the spatial patch level, and reconstruct dynamic motion from neural activity. Alongside these large-scale computational neuroimaging approaches, they are developing parametrically controlled, procedurally generated stimulus toolkits to systematically investigate category learning mechanisms in both humans and artificial neural networks. Additionally, Dr. Tarr is engaged in metascientific issues, recently examining the impact of editorial gatekeeping and advocating for greater equity in the journal desk-review process.

papers.title: Brain Mapping with Dense Features: Grounding Cortical Semantic Selectivity in Natural Images With Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: The authors use a vision transformer's dense, patch-level features to build a model that predicts fMRI responses and, crucially, localizes which parts of a natural image drive a given cortical voxel or region. This yields fine-grained, spatially grounded maps of semantic selectivity in higher visual cortex, including category-selective areas, and lets them probe how selectivity depends on image content beyond whole-image labels.
papers.authors: Andrew F. Luo, Jacob Yeung, Rushikesh Zawar, Shaurya Dewan, Margaret M. Henderson, Leila Wehbe, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: Reanimating Images using Neural Representations of Dynamic Stimuli
papers.abstract: This work asks whether fMRI signals recorded during video viewing can be used to recover motion information, by training decoders that map brain activity to video-model representations. The decoded motion representations are then used to animate static images with a video diffusion model, effectively reconstructing dynamic content from the brain and linking motion representations in the brain and in video models.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR, oral)
papers.authors: Jacob Yeung, Andrew F. Luo, Gabriel Sarch, Margaret M. Henderson, Deva Ramanan, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: The Oomplet dataset toolkit as a flexible and extensible system for large-scale, multi-category image generation
papers.abstract: The authors release a toolkit that procedurally generates millions of controlled cartoon-like characters (Oomplets) with parametrically specified category structure. Because features and category boundaries are fully controllable, the resource supports systematic studies of category learning in humans and in artificial neural networks.
papers.authors: John P. Kasarda, Angela Zhang, Hua Tong, Yan Tan, Rui Wang, Timothy Verstynen, Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: Gatekeeping Without Peer Review
papers.abstract: A short commentary arguing that journals and editors should improve the editorial desk-review stage, alongside efforts to make peer review itself more equitable and less biased, since desk rejection can silently gatekeep work without any peer scrutiny.
papers.authors: Michael J. Tarr

papers.title: Brain Diffusion for Visual Exploration: Cortical Discovery using Large Scale Generative Models
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to use a diffusion model steered by an fMRI-trained encoder to synthesize images that are predicted to maximally activate specific parts of visual cortex. The generated images allow data-driven discovery of fine-grained functional structure, including category-selective and within-category subregions, and were validated against held-out neural responses and behavior.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Andrew F. Luo, Margaret M. Henderson, Leila Wehbe, Michael J. Tarr

0463.name: Michael K. McBeath
0463.lab_name: PEARL Lab (Perception, Ecological Action, Robotics, and Learning Lab)
0463.bio: Michael K. McBeath is a Professor of Psychology at Arizona State University whose research explores the intersection of psychology, engineering, and perception-action. McBeath works on the Linear Optical Trajectory (LOT) model, which describes the navigational strategies used by humans and animals to intercept moving targets such as baseballs and frisbees. Their methodology utilizes computational modeling and psychophysical experiments to investigate multisensory object perception, auditory illusions like the Doppler effect, and the influence of natural regularities on empirical aesthetics.
0463.research_direction: Dr. McBeath has recently been exploring how perception is shaped by regularities in the natural world. One line of work examines the vertical attention bias, the tendency to look first at the tops of objects but the bottoms of scenes, and asks whether it reflects useful structure in real environments rather than simple image features. In audition, their recent work asks how the timbre of vowel sounds maps onto physical properties of sound, and how well listeners understand the Yoruba talking drum as a stand-in for speech, depending on their language familiarity and musical training. Across both senses, they are interested in how people pick up on the statistics of the environment to guide attention and interpretation.

papers.title: Yorùbá Speech Surrogacy with the Dùndún Talking Drum: Recognition Accuracy is a Function of Language Familiarity and Music Training
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the acoustic correspondence and perceptual intelligibility of the Nigerian dùndún talking drum as a surrogate for Yorùbá vocalizations in both speech and song. Utilizing a cross-cultural 2x2 experimental design, the study compared recognition performance across four groups: native Yorùbá versus American English speakers, further divided by musical expertise. Acoustical analyses confirmed that the dùndún precisely replicates microstructural temporal patterns, fundamental frequency (f0) contours, and intensity modulations characteristic of tonal language. Perceptual data demonstrated that while the drum maintains high surrogacy fidelity, identification accuracy is significantly moderated by linguistic familiarity and musical training. These findings support the conceptualization of drum languages as specialized cognitive platforms that exploit sound-symbolic regularities to facilitate tonal communication, highlighting the interplay between cultural expertise and universal psychoacoustic principles.
papers.authors: Kristina L. Knowles, K. Jakob Patten, Cecilia Durojaye, Babatunji O. Dada, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: Scat Singing and Vocal Winging: Vowel Phoneme Timbre Dimensions Reflect Physical Natural Regularities
papers.abstract: The study investigates the ecological grounding of vowel phoneme timbre by exploring the mapping between spectral dimensions and perceptual biases. Using multidimensional scaling of similarity ratings for fundamental frequency-matched vowel stimuli, the research identifies two primary spectral dimensions: tone height (spectral centroid) and harmonicity (alignment of overtones). Experiment 2 reveals that participants utilize phonemes at spectral extremes (e.g., /i/ for high-frequency 8 kHz signals and /Ʌ/ for low-frequency 60 Hz signals) during vocal mimicry of non-speech auditory stimuli. Analysis of scat singing and spontaneous speech further validates that vowel phonemes possess characteristic f0 values correlating with their perceived tone height. The results demonstrate that the auditory system internalizes these natural acoustic regularities as perceptual biases, serving a functional role in source tracking and segregation during auditory scene analysis.
papers.authors: K. Jakob Patten, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: When right side up is upside down: Vertical attention bias tracks interactive feature regularities in upright and inverted images
papers.abstract: This investigation examines the Vertical Attention Bias (VAB), which directs observers' attention toward the tops of objects and the bottoms of scenes, potentially reflecting the spatial distribution of behaviorally relevant affordances. Across two experiments utilizing triptych image paradigms, the study tested whether this bias is driven by low-level image features or higher-order ecological regularities. Results indicate that the VAB pattern—top-salience for objects and bottom-salience for scenes—effectively flips following stimulus inversion (180° rotation), although the effect magnitude is attenuated. These findings provide evidence that the bias is coupled to behaviorally relevant environmental invariants, such as gravity-constrained interaction zones, rather than fixed retinotopic locations. The data suggest a generic downward vantage tendency that optimizes the perceptual processing of interactive space and body-level affordances.
papers.authors: Matthew D. Langley, Madelaine T. Vu, Michael K. McBeath

papers.title: Vertical attention bias for tops of objects and bottoms of scenes
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Matthew D. Langley, Michael K. McBeath

0464.name: Michael Pratte
0464.bio: Michael S. Pratte is an Associate Professor and Associate Department Head at Mississippi State University, where they direct the Perception and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Pratte's research integrates psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and hierarchical Bayesian modeling to investigate the mechanisms of human vision and memory. They have studied visual working memory capacity, demonstrating that discrete limits exist when accounting for stimulus-specific variability, and have analyzed the sudden-death dynamics of iconic memory decay. Pratte's methodological work focuses on developing computational models and multivariate pattern analysis techniques to decode sensory representations and attentional selection from neural activity in the human visual cortex.
0464.research_direction: Dr. Pratte's recent work investigates the underlying architecture of visual working memory and the mechanisms of perceptual metacognition. Using behavioral paradigms like change-detection tasks alongside hierarchical Bayesian modeling, they have recently been exploring visual working memory limits, specifically asking whether spatial location is a mandatory feature for object binding and whether individual differences in working memory performance actually stem from earlier iconic memory bottlenecks rather than storage capacity itself. Additionally, their research examines perceptual confidence, using global-motion random-dot stimuli to test how well metacognitive judgments can access the existence versus the precision of internal discrete perceptual representations. Together, their investigations seek to disentangle how visual information is initially encoded, how its features are stored over short durations, and how accurately observers can monitor these internal states.

papers.title: Perceptual confidence has near perfect access to the existence of discrete representations, but only weak access to precision
papers.abstract: Tests whether metacognitive confidence is read out from internal perceptual representations, using global-motion random-dot stimuli. When a stimulus produced discrete all-or-none segmentation of signal from noise, confidence closely tracked whether a representation existed but not how precise it was. With stimuli producing continuous motion pooling, confidence tracked precision only weakly, suggesting poor meta-knowledge of precision.
papers.authors: Marshall L. Green, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: Features without their locations in visual working memory: Evidence from change-detection tasks
papers.abstract: Asks whether location is a mandatory feature to which other object properties are bound in visual working memory. Novel change-detection variants show that colors can be retained without their locations, with the effect surviving articulatory suppression. Location memory is sometimes merely imprecise and sometimes absent altogether, so location is not a necessary component of memory storage.
papers.authors: Conne George, Michael S. Pratte

papers.title: Systematic differences in visual working memory performance are not caused by differences in working memory storage
papers.abstract: Shows that individual and display-level differences in visual working memory performance are almost entirely accounted for by matching differences in iconic memory. Nonparametric factor analysis and hierarchical Bayesian model comparison support this across three experiments, including different paradigms. The link seems to reflect perceptual or attentional processes rather than working memory storage.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Michael S. Pratte, Marshall L. Green

0465.name: Michael S. Landy
0465.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
0465.lab_name: Landy Laboratory for Vision and Action
0465.bio: Michael S. Landy is a Professor of Psychology and Neural Science at New York University, where they investigate the computational principles underlying human perception and action. Landy’s research focuses on sensory cue integration, specifically the development of ideal-observer models that characterize how the brain combines multiple sources of sensory information. Their methodology incorporates psychophysical experimentation, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and mathematical modeling. This work addresses topics such as texture segregation, depth perception, and sensory decision-making under uncertainty.
0465.research_direction: Dr. Landy has recently been using Bayesian and ideal observer models to investigate how the human brain computes confidence and estimates uncertainty across a range of perceptual and motor tasks. Their recent work explores the specific cues underlying metacognitive judgments, asking whether visual confidence accurately tracks increasing internal sensory noise in the periphery, and whether sensorimotor confidence relies on prospective motor knowledge or retrospective proprioception during adaptation to reaching errors. Additionally, they have been examining audiovisual temporal recalibration to understand how precision-based causal inference helps the brain update its sense of timing after exposure to asynchronous sights and sounds. Finally, their research investigates the theoretical limits of visual processing by questioning whether ensemble summary statistics are computed via the subsampling of a few items or through the whole-display integration of a fixed budget of sensory resources.

papers.title: Visual confidence accurately tracks increasing internal noise with eccentricity in peripheral vision
papers.abstract: Using incentivized post-decision wagering, the study tests whether perceptual confidence follows the growing sensory noise of peripheral vision in spatial localization and orientation estimation tasks. Confidence ranges, predicted from noise estimated from the perceptual responses alone, were compared across a normative Bayesian model and several alternatives. The results support the view that confidence is derived from the Bayesian posterior and tracks internal noise across the visual field.
papers.authors: Luhe Li, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: No benefit of subsampling in ensemble coding
papers.abstract: The paper challenges the idea that the visual system computes ensemble summary statistics from a small sampled subset of items. It shows that subsampling models only work if total coding resources grow without limit with set size. Under a realistic fixed resource budget, an ideal observer integrating the whole ensemble matches accuracy with less total resource and fits existing data at least as well.
papers.authors: Long Ni, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Precision-based causal inference modulates audiovisual temporal recalibration
papers.abstract: Observers' sense of audiovisual timing shifts after exposure to a constant delay between sight and sound. The authors compare six observer models of how this recalibration is updated, and find that a causal-inference observer, which weighs the chance of a common versus separate cause and uses modality-specific timing precision, best captures the plateauing and asymmetric recalibration. The work ties temporal recalibration to Bayesian causal inference driven by sensory precision.
papers.authors: Luhe Li, Fangfang Hong, Stephanie Badde, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Sensorimotor confidence during explicit motor adaptation
papers.abstract: Participants reached to a target with an unseen hand and then set an arc size to report confidence, while visual feedback was rotated by 20 degrees mid-block. Four Bayesian models of confidence, using prospective cues, retrospective proprioceptive cues, or both, were compared. The work shows how confidence in action success evolves during explicit adaptation and which cues it relies on.
papers.authors: Marissa H. Evans, Michael S. Landy

papers.title: Feeling lucky? Prospective and retrospective cues for sensorimotor confidence
papers.abstract: People judged their confidence in reaches made without sight of the hand, setting the size of a circle that earned points only if it enclosed the true endpoint. Three Bayesian models based on prospective cues (knowledge of motor noise and past performance), retrospective cues (proprioception), or both were compared. Most participants were either ideal observers combining both cues or relied on prospective cues alone.
papers.authors: Marissa E. Fassold, Shannon M. Locke, Michael S. Landy

0467.name: Michael-Paul Schallmo
0467.bio: Michael-Paul Schallmo is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences at the University of Minnesota. Their research utilizes a multimodal neuroimaging approach, including high-field functional MRI (7T), MR spectroscopy, and EEG, combined with behavioral psychophysics to investigate how psychiatric and neurological conditions alter neural processing in the visual system. Schallmo focuses on the functional and neurochemical foundations of visual dysfunction in populations such as those with schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, and visual snow syndrome. As an investigator for the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, Schallmo's work aims to identify objective biomarkers for sensory impairments and clarify the link between brain chemistry and perceptual organization.
0467.research_direction: Dr. Schallmo has recently been investigating how basic visual processing differs in psychosis and other altered brain states. They use psychophysics, ultra-high-field 7T fMRI, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to study how neurons in early visual areas suppress their responses to surrounding context and combine fragments into contours in people with psychotic disorders. A related thread asks whether simple EEG measures of the balance between excitation and inhibition reflect the brain's glutamate levels. They also study how psilocybin changes contrast perception, and they have developed a way to quantify what people with visual snow syndrome actually see.

papers.title: Aperiodic slope reflects glutamatergic tone in the human brain
papers.abstract: Non-invasive quantification of the cortical excitation-inhibition (E:I) balance remains a fundamental challenge in human neuroscience. This research investigated whether the aperiodic (1/f) exponent of the electroencephalography (EEG) power spectrum serves as a reliable proxy for neurochemical concentrations. By integrating resting-state EEG with ultra-high field (7T) magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) in the medial occipital cortex, the study demonstrated that shallower (flatter) aperiodic slopes are significantly associated with higher concentrations of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate. Conversely, no significant relationship was found between the aperiodic slope and GABA levels. These results validate the aperiodic slope as a physiologically grounded, non-invasive metric for assessing excitatory tone in the human brain, providing a quantitative tool for investigating E:I dynamics across varying functional and clinical states.
papers.authors: Aislin A. Sheldon, Hannah R. Moser, Kamar S. Abdullahi, Karly D. Allison, Carter B. Mulder, Samantha A. Montoya, Scott R. Sponheim, Małgorzata Marjańska, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Impaired Contour Object Perception in Psychosis
papers.abstract: Contour integration—the neural synthesis of fragmented visual elements into a coherent whole—is a well-documented deficit in schizophrenia. This study utilized a transdiagnostic framework to investigate whether these impairments are specific to schizophrenia or represent a broader feature of psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). Utilizing behavioral psychophysics and ultra-high field (7T) functional MRI, the researchers found significant contour discrimination deficits in PwPP, particularly those with schizophrenia, compared to healthy controls and biological relatives. Imaging data revealed hyper-responsiveness in the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and aberrant task-based functional connectivity between primary and higher-order visual regions. These neural abnormalities were contingent on the requirement to segment contours from background noise, suggesting that impaired suppressive mechanisms and disorganized connectivity underlie visual integration failure in the psychosis spectrum.
papers.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
papers.authors: Rohit S. Kamath, Kimberly B. Weldon, Hannah R. Moser, Kamar S. Abdullahi, Philip C. Burton, Scott R. Sponheim, Cheryl A. Olman, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Center-surround processing in psychosis
papers.abstract: As part of the Psychosis Human Connectome Project, this study explored the mechanisms of altered contrast surround suppression in individuals with psychotic psychopathology (PwPP). The researchers combined psychophysical testing, 7T fMRI, and 7T MRS to measure contextual modulation in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateral occipital complex (LOC). While V1 surround suppression strength was found to be comparable across groups, individuals with psychosis and their first-degree relatives exhibited significantly reduced suppression specifically in the LOC. Furthermore, multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) indicated that the neural representations of spatial context in V1 are less reliable in PwPP. The findings suggest that while low-level gain control remains largely intact, higher-order contextual processing and the robustness of spatial coding are selectively disrupted in psychosis.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Hannah R. Moser, Rohit S. Kamath, Li Shen Chong, Andrea N. Grant, Małgorzata Marjańska, Scott R. Sponheim, Stephen A. Engel, Cheryl A. Olman, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: Enhanced visual contrast suppression during peak psilocybin effects: Psychophysical results from a pilot randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Surround suppression is a fundamental visual property where the perceived contrast of a target stimulus is attenuated by its spatial context. This pilot, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the impact of the serotonergic psychedelic psilocybin on this process. During peak drug effects (25 mg), participants performed a contrast-matching psychophysical task. The results showed that psilocybin significantly enhanced the magnitude of contrast surround suppression compared to the niacin placebo, indicating a shift toward less veridical perception. The degree of suppression enhancement positively correlated with the intensity of subjective visual alterations. These findings provide evidence for the role of serotonin (likely 5-HT2A receptor) modulation in visual contextual processing and suggest that psychedelic states involve heightened sensitivity to surrounding context during object perception.
papers.authors: Link Ray Swanson, Sophia Jungers, Ranji Varghese, Kathryn R. Cullen, Michael D. Evans, Jessica L. Nielson, Michael-Paul Schallmo

papers.title: What does visual snow look like? Quantification by matching a simulation
papers.abstract: Visual Snow Syndrome (VSS) is defined by the persistent perception of flickering, pixelated noise throughout the visual field, yet quantitative characterization of this percept has been limited. This study introduced a novel psychophysical matching paradigm in which participants with VSS (n=31) adjusted a computer simulation to reflect their internal visual experience. The results provided a standard quantitative profile: visual snow elements were exceptionally small (diameter < 2 arcmin), highly dynamic (mean temporal frequency = 18.2 Hz), and perceived at low contrast (average RMS contrast = 2.56%) with low density (2.87%). High intra-observer reliability (ICC > 0.89) validates this simulation as a precise tool for characterizing VSS phenomenology, enabling objective symptom tracking and furthering research into the syndrome's neural origins.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Carter B. Mulder, Karly D. Allison, Michael S. Lee, Stephen A. Engel, Michael-Paul Schallmo

0468.name: Michael. S. Beauchamp
0468.bio: Michael S. Beauchamp is a Professor and Vice Chair for Research in the Department of Neurosurgery at the University of Pennsylvania. Beauchamp’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of multisensory integration and visual perception, focusing on the combination of auditory and visual information during speech. Utilizing blood-oxygen-level-dependent functional magnetic resonance imaging (BOLD fMRI) and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG), Beauchamp has identified the superior temporal sulcus (STS) as a hub for integrating complex sensory signals. Their current research involves developing computational models of multisensory perception and advancing brain-mapping techniques to assist patients with language and perceptual impairments.
0468.research_direction: Dr. Beauchamp has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms of multisensory integration, with a primary focus on how the human brain combines auditory and visual speech. Their recent work explores the classic McGurk illusion across multiple levels of analysis, employing cross-linguistic behavioral paradigms to study noisy sensory encoding and testing whether prolonged exposure to mismatched audiovisual stimuli induces long-lasting perceptual recalibration. To map the precise neural circuits underlying these processes, they are leveraging human intracranial electrophysiology to capture high-resolution multisensory responses directly from integration hubs like the superior temporal sulcus. Alongside this in vivo work, Dr. Beauchamp is developing deep neural network models to computationally simulate audiovisual speech integration, as well as building open-source anatomical localization software to support advanced intracranial research pipelines.

papers.title: A deep neural network model of audiovisual speech recognition reports the McGurk effect
papers.abstract: An audiovisual speech-recognition deep network is tested on McGurk stimuli, where a mismatched face changes the heard syllable. The model reproduces the illusion and its dependence on the stimulus, providing a computational account of audiovisual integration. It connects the lab's perceptual and modeling work to modern machine-learning speech recognizers.
papers.authors: Haotian Ma, Zhengjia Wang, Xiang Zhang, John F. Magnotti, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: Stereoelectroencephalography Reveals Neural Signatures of Multisensory Integration in the Human Superior Temporal Sulcus during Audiovisual Speech Perception
papers.abstract: Using depth electrodes implanted in neurosurgical patients, the study records from the superior temporal sulcus while people watch and listen to audiovisual speech. It identifies neural response signatures showing that auditory and visual speech information are combined there. The work gives direct intracranial evidence for a multisensory hub that had mostly been inferred from fMRI.
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, John F. Magnotti, Xiang Zhang, Zhengjia Wang, Yingjia Yu, Kathryn A. Davis, Sameer A. Sheth, H. Isaac Chen, Daniel Yoshor, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: The McGurk effect is similar in native Mandarin Chinese and American English speakers
papers.abstract: McGurk susceptibility is compared across native Mandarin and American English speakers. Despite the language difference, the illusion behaves similarly and is well predicted by a common model of noisy encoding of audiovisual disparity. The finding argues against strong language-specific accounts of the effect.
papers.authors: John F. Magnotti, Debshila Basu Mallick, Gan Feng, Bo Zhou, Wen Zhou, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: Repeatedly experiencing the McGurk effect induces long-lasting changes in auditory speech perception
papers.abstract: Participants repeatedly experienced McGurk stimuli and were then tested on how they perceived auditory speech. The exposure produced lasting shifts in perception, showing that the illusion recalibrates auditory speech processing. The results are interpreted within a causal-inference framework for multisensory speech.
papers.authors: John F. Magnotti, Anastasia Lado, Yue Zhang, Arnt Maasø, Audrey Nath, Michael S. Beauchamp

papers.title: YAEL: Your Advanced Electrode Localizer
papers.abstract: Presents a software tool for localizing intracranial electrodes by aligning post-implant imaging to the patient's anatomy and visualizing contacts on the brain surface. It is part of the lab's open-source RAVE analysis ecosystem for intracranial recordings. The tool streamlines a step needed in nearly all human iEEG studies.
papers.authors: Zhengjia Wang, John F. Magnotti, Xiang Zhang, Michael S. Beauchamp

0470.name: Michele Rucci
0470.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0470.bio: Michele Rucci is a Professor of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and Neuroscience at the University of Rochester and co-directs the Active Perception Laboratory. Rucci’s research investigates the intersection of sensory processing and motor behavior, specifically examining how microscopic eye movements such as drifts and microsaccades facilitate visual perception and neural encoding. Through the use of computational modeling, psychophysics, and high-precision eye tracking, Rucci has found that these fixational movements are components for high-acuity spatial vision rather than random noise. Their work addresses the theory of active vision by proposing that the brain utilizes oculomotor dynamics as an information-processing stage to decode the visual environment.
0470.research_direction: Dr. Rucci's recent work explores how active motor behaviors—ranging from microscopic eye movements to blinks—continuously reformat retinal input, challenging the traditional camera analogy of the visual system. Using high-resolution eye tracking and gaze-contingent displays, they are investigating how the kinematics of both fixational drift and larger saccades convert static spatial scenes into dynamic temporal signals that actively filter spatial frequencies and shape contrast sensitivity. Their research has recently been examining other components of the sensorimotor cycle as well, testing whether eye blinks function as an active stage of early visual processing rather than mere interruptions. Additionally, they are probing the underlying triggers of fixational saccades, weighing spatial gaze-correction errors against temporal pacing factors to better understand why the visual system initiates these microscopic shifts.

papers.title: The visual system does not operate like a camera
papers.abstract: A perspective by leading researchers on active vision arguing against the camera analogy for the visual system. It assembles evidence from the authors' work that eye movements, including fixational drift and microsaccades, continuously reformat retinal input and are integral to encoding spatial and temporal information. The article outlines the implications for models of vision.
papers.authors: Michele Rucci, Ehud Ahissar, David C. Burr, Igor Kagan, Martina Poletti, Jonathan D. Victor

papers.title: What one sees depends on how far the eye has moved
papers.abstract: Shows that the amplitude of a saccade acts as a filter on spatial frequency: smaller saccades reduce post-saccadic sensitivity in an amplitude-dependent range of low spatial frequencies. This arises because saccade kinematics convert the scene into a spatiotemporal flow whose content within the retina's temporal bandwidth predicts visibility. Saccades thus select information by content, not only by location.
papers.authors: Y. Howard Li, Michele A. Cox, Jonathan D. Victor, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Spatial and Temporal Factors Influencing Fixational Saccades
papers.abstract: Addresses why microsaccades occur during fixation, a long-standing debate between spatial (gaze-centering) and temporal (periodic release) accounts. Using a gaze-contingent procedure to directly estimate the perceived center of the visual field, the authors show that fixational saccades correct fixation errors accurately, yet also occur with gaze centered, with latency increasing as error shrinks. Both spatial and temporal factors thus contribute.
papers.authors: Jie Z. Wang, Claudia Cherici, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Consequences of eye movements for spatial selectivity
papers.abstract: Tests the idea that spatial tuning in human vision is not fixed by retinal wiring but depends on how the eye's fixational motion shapes the temporal signals reaching the retina. Using high-resolution eye tracking and gaze-contingent displays that alter retinal stimulation, the authors show that contrast sensitivity follows the strength of luminance modulations within a narrow temporal band. Changing fixational motion therefore shifts sensitivity in opposite directions at low and high spatial frequencies, supporting a dynamic, eye-movement-dependent encoding of space.
papers.authors: Janis Intoy, Y. Howard Li, Norick R. Bowers, Jonathan D. Victor, Martina Poletti, Michele Rucci

papers.title: Eye blinks as a visual processing stage
papers.abstract: Shows that blinks, usually treated as interruptions of vision, actively contribute to visual processing. Blinks produce rapid changes in retinal input that, together with the small eye movements that accompany them, enhance sensitivity to particular spatial scales. The work reframes blinks as part of the sensorimotor cycle that structures visual input.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Bin Yang, Janis Intoy, Michele Rucci

0471.name: Michelle Greene
0471.bio: Michelle R. Greene is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Barnard College who studies how people perceive and understand natural scenes. Greene's research combines behavioral psychophysics, electroencephalography (EEG), and computational modeling, and includes the Visual Experience Dataset, a corpus of head-mounted video with eye- and head-tracking recorded from human observers.
0471.research_direction: Dr. Greene has recently been investigating how people rapidly recognize scenes and objects. Their recent work compares the roles of visual structure (image complexity) and conceptual richness in scene detection and categorization, finding that high visual complexity impairs both while semantic richness affects them differently. They have also studied how the actions a scene affords support categorization, how EEG signals prioritize the basic level of object categories, and how the everyday visual experience of observers, captured in egocentric video, relates to perceptual performance. Their recent commentary argues for a formal taxonomy of natural behavior to guide research on visual cortex organization.

papers.title: Scaling vision to the body: Height predicts visual experience and perceptual performance
papers.abstract: Shows that an observer's stature shapes what they see: in more than 200 hours of egocentric video, taller people met faces lower and hands higher in their visual field. A behavioral experiment then found that categorization of faces and hands is best in the parts of the visual field where each is typically encountered, with height modulating the effect. Perception thus tracks the embodied statistics of one's own vantage point.
papers.authors: Michelle R. Greene, Benjamin J. Balas

papers.title: The Limits of Learning from Pictures and Text: Vision-Language Models and Embodied Scene Understanding
papers.abstract: Compares 18 vision-language models with more than 2,000 human participants across 15 scene-understanding tasks. Models come close to people on general knowledge but persistently fall short on affordance-related judgments, a gap that neither prompt engineering nor newer model releases closed. The authors argue that learning from images and text alone cannot capture the action possibilities that embodied, three-dimensional experience provides.
papers.authors: Gillian Rosenberg, Skylar Stadhard, Bruce C. Hansen, Michelle R. Greene

papers.title: The brain prioritizes the basic level of object category abstraction
papers.abstract: Recorded 64-channel EEG while people viewed 1080 objects in a three-level category taxonomy and performed one-back tasks at either the basic or subordinate level. Time-resolved regression showed that basic-level category information is used from roughly 50 ms and spreads from posterior to anterior electrodes over about 300 ms. Task demands only altered the signal after about 200 ms, indicating that basic-level coding is early and largely automatic.
papers.authors: Michelle R. Greene, Alyssa Magill Rohan

papers.title: Function over form: The temporal evolution of affordance-based scene categorization
papers.abstract: Tests whether the actions a scene affords drive categorization even when materials and surface features are equally informative. Observers chose affordance-mismatched images as odd-ones-out, made more false alarms to distractors sharing affordances with the target, and EEG decoding showed weaker target-category representations when distractors were affordance-similar. Functional similarity therefore competes strongly with visual similarity during rapid scene categorization.
papers.authors: Michelle R. Greene, Bruce C. Hansen

papers.title: The visual experience dataset: Over 200 recorded hours of integrated eye movement, odometry, and egocentric video
papers.abstract: Introduces VEDB, a large open dataset of more than 240 hours of first-person video recorded together with eye and head tracking from dozens of observers spanning childhood to middle age. The paper documents how the data were collected, processed and labeled, and where bias or error may enter. The resource is meant to let researchers study real-world image statistics, improve gaze tracking, and train scene and activity recognition networks on realistic visual diets.
papers.authors: Michelle R. Greene, Benjamin J. Balas, Mark D. Lescroart, Paul R. MacNeilage, Jennifer A. Hart, Kamran Binaee, Peter A. Hausamann, Ronald Mezile, Bharath Shankar, Christian B. Sinnott, Kaylie Capurro, Savannah Halow, et al.

0473.name: Miguel Eckstein
0473.bio: Miguel Eckstein is a Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and directs the Vision and Image Understanding Laboratory. Eckstein’s research integrates psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques—including fMRI and EEG—to investigate the mechanisms of human visual search, attention, and face perception. Their work includes modeling human performance in complex tasks, such as medical image interpretation. Eckstein also develops bio-inspired computer vision systems to bridge the gap between human and machine intelligence.
0473.research_direction: Dr. Eckstein has recently been investigating how fundamental visual behaviors emerge from task optimization, using artificial neural networks to explore how human-like covert spatial attention and spatial cueing benefits arise during target detection in noise. Their work probes the specific unit-level mechanisms within these models that mediate target selection, generating testable predictions for the neural basis of attention in the primate brain. Alongside covert attention, their recent work explores overt gaze behavior in naturalistic environments, combining human eye-tracking with foveated vision-language models to test whether free-viewing fixation patterns are driven by an overarching objective to maximize semantic scene understanding rather than low-level visual saliency. Furthermore, they are applying these computational approaches to medical image perception, evaluating how deep learning model observers discount signal-like anatomical backgrounds during visual search in simulated 3D breast imaging to better model and understand clinical radiological search.

papers.title: Why We Look Where We Look: Emergent Human-like Fixations of a Foveated Visual Language Model Maximizing Scene Understanding
papers.abstract: Trains an agent with simulated foveated vision to choose fixations that maximize how well it can understand a scene. Without being fit to human gaze, the agent shows human-like free-viewing behaviour: it looks first near the scene center and then toward people, text and other semantically important regions. Variants optimized for search or classification, or given different peripheral vision, predict human fixations worse, supporting scene understanding as the driving objective.
papers.authors: Shravan Murlidaran, Ziqi Wen, Sana Shehabi, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Emergent neuronal mechanisms mediating covert attention in convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Follows up on the lab's finding that feedforward CNNs trained to detect targets in noise show human-like cueing benefits, by dissecting the individual units responsible. The authors identify distinct neuron types in the network, including units that carry cue information and units whose responses are gated by the cue, and show how these combine to implement attention-like target selection. The results offer concrete, testable predictions for the kinds of neurons that should support covert attention in the brain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, William Yang Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Eye movements during free viewing to maximize scene understanding
papers.abstract: Asks why people look where they do when freely viewing natural scenes. Combining human eye-tracking during free viewing and scene description with foveated vision-language-model based analyses, the work argues that fixation patterns are well explained as serving the goal of understanding the scene under the constraints of a foveated visual system. This links gaze behaviour to a scene-comprehension objective rather than to low-level saliency.
papers.authors: Shravan Murlidaran, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Convolutional neural network model observers discount signal-like anatomical structures during search in virtual digital breast tomosynthesis phantoms
papers.abstract: Evaluates CNN-based model observers for detecting small lesions in simulated 3D breast tomosynthesis with realistic anatomical backgrounds. The networks learn to discount background structures that resemble the signal, behaving more like a visually searching observer, and are compared with traditional model observers. The work supports the use of learned observers for evaluating imaging systems and understanding radiologist search.
papers.authors: Aditya Jonnalagadda, Bruno B. Barufaldi, Andrew D. A. Maidment, Miguel P. Eckstein

papers.title: Emergent human-like covert attention in feedforward convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Shows that standard feedforward convolutional networks trained only to detect targets in noisy displays with a spatial cue spontaneously exhibit behavioural signatures of covert attention seen in humans, such as improved accuracy and faster processing at cued locations and a cost for invalid cues. The trained networks track an ideal Bayesian observer and human data across several cueing manipulations, without any explicit attention mechanism. This suggests attention-like behaviour can arise from task optimization alone.
papers.authors: Sudhanshu Srivastava, William Yang Wang, Miguel P. Eckstein

0475.name: Miki Uetsuki
0475.department: Department of Community Studies, College of Community Studies
0475.main_research_area: cognitive and visual processing of reading
0475.bio: Miki Uetsuki is an Associate Professor in the Department of Community Studies at Aoyama Gakuin University, specializing in experimental and cognitive psychology. Uetsuki's research examines the psychophysical and cognitive mechanisms underlying reading, with a focus on visual crowding effects and the temporal characteristics of sentence processing in Japanese scripts. They utilize methodologies ranging from psychophysical behavioral measurements to event-related potentials (ERPs) to investigate how dynamic visual information processing correlates with reading proficiency. Additionally, their work explores human information processing in clinical populations and the psychological impressions of 'textual prosody' in reading.
0475.research_direction: Dr. Uetsuki has recently been studying how familiarity shapes what we can see and recognize, with a focus on reading. Their recent work examines visual crowding, the difficulty of identifying letters surrounded by other letters, and asks whether familiar letter strings suffer less from it. They test this in Japanese readers, who read text both horizontally and vertically, to see whether the benefit depends on text direction. They have also explored a different social perception question: how people match handmade dolls to their makers, and which visual cues and personality traits support that link.

papers.title: Japanese readers show a crowding reduction even in vertically oriented strings of letters
papers.abstract: Visual crowding in letter strings degrades target recognition performance, yet this perceptual degradation is significantly attenuated for familiar letter strings relative to strings composed of arbitrary symbols. Although earlier investigations in readers of Latin script have shown that this crowding reduction is strictly constrained to horizontally aligned text, this study evaluated native Japanese readers who possess extensive, bidirectional literacy across both horizontal and vertical orthographic layouts. Psychophysical assessments demonstrated that Japanese readers exhibit significant crowding attenuation for alphabetic strings presented vertically as well as horizontally, indicating that acquired reading experience directly modulates the spatial tuning and directionality of letter-specific crowding reduction. Conversely, this attenuation failed to generalize to Japanese syllabic kana characters relative to symbol strings, indicating fundamental differences in the early visual processing mechanisms engaged by alphabetic versus moraic Japanese scripts.
papers.authors: Miki Uetsuki, Kazushi Maruya

papers.title: Effect of personality traits on matching dolls and their makers
papers.abstract: Prior investigations show that individuals can accurately link personal belongings, pets, and handcrafted artifacts to their owners or creators above chance levels; however, the precise visual and psychological mechanisms mediating this association remain poorly understood. Three experimental paradigms were conducted utilizing handcrafted cloth dolls produced by novice collegiate makers and standardized photographs of the makers. In Experiment 1, masking the periocular area of the dolls slightly reduced performance compared to unmasked baselines but retained statistically significant above-chance matching accuracy (χ²(1) = 5.44, φ = 0.19, p < 0.05), demonstrating that matching relies on features beyond the eye region. In Experiment 2, participants achieved above-chance matching accuracy even when presented solely with the dorsal (rear) perspective of the dolls, confirming the diagnostic utility of non-facial physical attributes. In Experiment 3, the influence of personality trait inferences was evaluated using the Big Five framework. While facial morphology dominated matching judgments when faces were visible, inferred personality congruence significantly predicted matching accuracy when facial information was visually occluded.
papers.authors: Miki Uetsuki, Misako Kimura

0476.name: Min-Shik Kim
0476.bio: Min-Shik Kim is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at Yonsei University and the director of the Yonsei Cognition Lab. Kim’s research examines the mechanisms of attentional control and the representation of visual information using computational modeling, psychophysics, and neuroscientific techniques. Their work investigates how executive working memory capacity influences visual search efficiency and the conditions under which memory contents capture spatial attention. Kim also studies object continuity, visual imagery, and the application of cognitive science within education and marketing contexts.
0476.research_direction: Dr. Kim has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual attention and working memory, focusing on how spatiotemporal context and feature information guide visual processing. In the domain of visual working memory, their recent work explores how temporal structure is represented—specifically contrasting relative serial order with item-interval associations—and tests how overlapping spatial or temporal positions disrupt feature binding between distinct objects. Their research on visual search examines how learned spatial biases are affected by trial-to-trial variations in target templates and questions whether implicit contextual cueing can be driven by socially meaningful regularities, such as facial identities, rather than just spatial layouts. Additionally, they are investigating the attentional boost effect to determine whether memory enhancements for items paired with a detected target spread across entire objects or depend strictly on feature-based filtering.

papers.title: Feature-based filtering determines object-based selection in the attentional boost effect
papers.abstract: The attentional boost effect is the finding that items shown together with a detected target are remembered better than items shown with distractors. The authors ask whether this enhancement spreads across whole objects or depends on which features are task-relevant. Their experiments indicate that feature-based filtering of the task-defining feature governs which object parts benefit, so that object-based selection follows from feature selection rather than operating independently of it.
papers.authors: Juyeon Joe, Yoongeol Yang, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Temporal structure in visual working memory: Contributions of relative order and item-interval associations
papers.abstract: This work examines how sequences are represented in visual working memory, contrasting memory for relative serial order with memory for associations between items and the temporal intervals separating them. The experiments dissociate these two sources of temporal structure and show that both contribute to recall performance. The results refine accounts of how time is bound to content in working memory.
papers.authors: Hyeri Yoh, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Implicit learning of social information in contextual cueing
papers.abstract: Contextual cueing is usually studied with spatial layouts, and this paper asks whether socially meaningful information can also guide attention implicitly. Across three experiments with face stimuli, spatial configurations were fully randomized while different social mappings (for example, associations between target and distractor identities) served as the predictive context. Participants learned these social regularities without awareness and searched faster, showing that social information can act as a contextual cue independent of spatial layout.
papers.authors: Lijeong Hong, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Spatiotemporal position overlap disrupts feature binding in visual working memory
papers.abstract: The study tests when the features of an object are correctly bound to each other in visual working memory. When memory items share the same spatial location or the same moment in time, features from different objects become confusable and binding errors increase. The findings indicate that position, in space and time, is an important cue that keeps features of separate objects apart in memory.
papers.authors: Juyeon Joe, Min-Shik Kim

papers.title: Attenuation of spatial bias with target template variation
papers.abstract: Using a visual search task in which the target often appeared in one region, the authors tested how learned spatial biases depend on the target's identity. When the target and distractor shapes stayed fixed, attention stayed persistently biased toward the frequent location. When the target template varied unpredictably from trial to trial, the spatial bias was weakened, suggesting that the bias depends on repeated attentional shifts within a consistent search context.
papers.authors: Injae Hong, Min-Shik Kim

0477.name: Ming Meng
0477.lab_name: Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Reading and Development in Children and Adolescents
0477.bio: Ming Meng is a neuroscientist specializing in the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and mental representation. Utilizing functional MRI, psychophysical experiments, and computational modeling, Meng investigates how the brain decodes visual information both with and without conscious awareness. Their research explores the interplay between binocular rivalry and stereopsis, the lateralization of face processing, and the neural substrates of aphantasia. Meng has demonstrated that individuals lacking subjective mental imagery still exhibit stimulus-specific representations in early visual cortices, revealing a dissociation between neural encoding and conscious experience.
0477.research_direction: Dr. Meng has recently been investigating the neural and perceptual mechanisms underlying binocular vision, focusing on the dynamic interactions between visual integration and competition. Using a combination of psychophysics and fMRI multivariate decoding, their recent work explores how interocular suppression alters stereopsis and binocular disparity coding along the dorsal visual pathway. They have also been utilizing dichoptic paradigms to probe the locus of early attentional modulation, examining how contextual contrast imbalances and interocular sensory switching impact local depth perception and continuous multiple object tracking. In a distinct line of research, they are investigating top-down visual processing by mapping early visual cortex activity in individuals with aphantasia to understand how V1 representations relate to the conscious experience of mental imagery.

papers.title: Interocular suppression weakens binocular disparity integration in the dorsal visual stream
papers.abstract: Uses fMRI and multivariate decoding to ask how binocular rivalry (interocular suppression) alters the neural coding of binocular disparity. Local rivalry weakened near-far disparity decoding, increasingly along the dorsal pathway from V1 through V3A to IPS, with little loss in ventral areas. In V3A, the representation of anticorrelated stereograms was also disrupted, and suppression reduced V3A-centered informational connectivity, implicating dorsal regions in coordinating integration and suppression.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Ming Meng

papers.title: Imageless imagery in aphantasia revealed by early visual cortex decoding
papers.abstract: Compared fMRI signals in primary visual cortex between people with validated aphantasia and controls during attempts to imagine images. Imagery content could be decoded in both groups, but in aphantasia the decodable patterns were on the ipsilateral side and could not be cross-decoded from perceptual responses, and perception-evoked BOLD amplitude was lower. This suggests aphantasic V1 carries an imagery-related representation containing little or transformed sensory information, challenging the view that V1 activity necessarily yields visual qualia.
papers.authors: Shuai Chang, Xinyu Zhang, Yangjianyi Cao, Joel Pearson, Ming Meng

papers.title: Contextual Binocular Imbalance Impairs Local Stereopsis
papers.abstract: Three psychophysical experiments show that an interocularly imbalanced contrast context around a stereo target raises local stereo thresholds (about 62 to 111-115 arcsec), regardless of which eye dominates. The effect is reduced when context and target are not collinear and appears with both fusion and rivalry contexts. The authors conclude that lateral connections in V1 contribute to stereopsis, with implications for restoring binocular balance in clinical conditions.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Shuai Chang, Xin-Ping Yu, Ming Meng

papers.title: Monocular advantage for multiple object tracking
papers.abstract: Uses a dichoptic multiple-object-tracking task in which target positions swap between the eyes while perception stays constant. Interocular switching of target information lowered tracking accuracy, but switching of other stimuli or sensory confounds did not. This indicates that attentional modulation in tracking starts early, at or before V1, and may involve subcortical monocular circuitry, and suggests a method for assessing interocular deficits in strabismus and amblyopia.
papers.authors: Guiping Zheng, Rong Jiang, Ke Zhou, Shuai Chang, Xinping Yu, Liqin Zhou, Ming Meng

papers.title: Integration and suppression interact in binocular vision
papers.abstract: Psychophysics showing that binocular rivalry and stereopsis, the integrative and competitive outcomes of dichoptic input, influence each other. Rivalry raised peripheral stereo thresholds in proportion to contrast, while stereopsis with larger disparity balanced rivalry dynamics and made eye dominance more equal. The authors propose that both processes mediate one another through a shared mechanism regulating eye dominance.
papers.authors: Rong Jiang, Ming Meng

0478.name: Mingzhou Ding
0478.department: J. Crayton Pruitt Family Department of Biomedical Engineering
0478.bio: Mingzhou Ding is the J. Crayton Pruitt Family Professor at the University of Florida and utilizes engineering and computational approaches to investigate the neural foundations of cognitive functions. Ding applies Granger causality to neuroscience to provide a mathematical framework for assessing directional information flow and functional connectivity in brain networks. Their research integrates multimodal imaging techniques—including EEG, fMRI, ECoG, and local field potentials—to study visual spatial attention, emotional processing, and the dynamics of large-scale networks in healthy aging and clinical conditions such as Parkinson's disease. This work focuses on the technical development of signal processing methods and their application to understanding how the brain coordinates sensory input and top-down control.
0478.research_direction: Dr. Ding has recently been studying how the human brain directs and shapes visual attention, using fMRI and EEG to look at brain activity patterns. Their recent work explores how people internally choose where to attend versus following an external cue, how the brain samples a target and a competing emotional distractor in rhythmic alternation, and how attention control signals can be decoded across the visual hierarchy. They also examine how repeatedly seeing the same stimulus changes early visual cortex over time, and how the amygdala and neighboring regions represent pleasant versus unpleasant emotional valence.

papers.title: Neural representation of emotional valence in human amygdala and surrounding regions
papers.abstract: This study employs high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to characterize the neural encoding of affective valence within the human amygdala complex and adjacent subcortical structures. The research evaluates whether emotional valence—spanning from pleasant to unpleasant—is represented via unidimensional population codes or dissociable neural patterns. Our findings demonstrate that the amygdala represents the full spectrum of valence using distinct ensemble activity patterns that allow for robust decoding of affective categories. The representational geometry revealed a negative bias in amygdalar activity space, where aversive stimulus patterns occupied a more expansive manifold; notably, this bias was found to normalize following clinical interventions. These results establish the amygdala as a high-dimensional hub for affective evaluation, utilizing population-level neural patterns to discriminate between rewarding and threatening sensory information.
papers.authors: Ke Bo, Lihan Cui, Yujun Chen, Guanghui Zhang, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control
papers.abstract: We contrasted the neural substrates of willed (internally generated) and instructed (externally cued) visual spatial attention control using fMRI and electroencephalography (EEG). While both attention types recruited the canonical dorsal attention network (DAN), willed attention—prompted by a choice cue—uniquely engaged a frontoparietal decision network involving the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), we successfully decoded the intended direction of attention from activity within this decision network prior to stimulus presentation. Furthermore, EEG analyses revealed that the power and phase of alpha-frequency (8-12 Hz) oscillations in the period immediately preceding the choice cue predicted both the subsequent attentional decision and the level of activation in the decision network, suggesting that spontaneous attentional shifts are significantly biased by ongoing, pre-cue intrinsic brain states.
papers.authors: Changhao Xiong, Qiang Yang, Sungkean Kim, Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Jesse J. Bengson, George R. Mangun, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Rhythmic sampling and competition of target and distractor in a motion detection task
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural dynamics of rhythmic sampling and resource competition in a visual attention task using EEG and frequency tagging. Participants performed a motion detection task on a random-dot kinematogram (RDK) target flickered at 4.29 Hz, superimposed on emotional IAPS distractors flickered at 6 Hz. Moving-window multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) decoding was applied to the 6 Hz power patterns to index distractor processing, while the 4.29 Hz power tracked target processing. Results demonstrated that both target and distractor representations are sampled rhythmically at a delta frequency (~1 Hz). Critically, the relative phase between the target and distractor sampling time courses predicted behavioral performance: a phase difference near π (temporal separation within the sampling cycle) was associated with higher coherent motion detection rates, suggesting that temporal segregation of sampling cycles mitigates the detrimental effects of distraction.
papers.authors: Changhao Xiong, Nathan M. Petro, Ke Bo, Lihan Cui, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Stimulus Repetition Induces a Two-Stage Learning Process in the Primary Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the competing fatigue and sharpening models of stimulus repetition by applying moving-window MVPA decoding and weight map analysis to fMRI data from the primary visual cortex (V1). Human subjects were passively exposed to 120 repetitions of oriented Gabor patches. The analysis identified a distinct two-stage learning trajectory in V1. The initial stage (Stage 1), comprising approximately the first twelve repetitions, was characterized by univariate repetition suppression and a decline in decoding accuracy to chance levels, aligning with the fatigue model's prediction of a non-selective reduction in neural response. In contrast, the subsequent stage (Stage 2) showed a progressive increase in decoding accuracy above chance as repetitions continued, supporting the sharpening model where representations become more distinct through long-term learning and selective reduction of irrelevant neural activity.
papers.authors: Lihan Cui, Ke Bo, Changhao Xiong, Yujun Chen, Andreas Keil, Mingzhou Ding

papers.title: Decoding Visual Spatial Attention Control
papers.abstract: We utilized multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and a meta-analytic approach on two fMRI datasets to characterize the neural patterns of anticipatory spatial attention control across the visual hierarchy. The study evaluated both univariate BOLD activation and multivariate decoding accuracy in regions of interest (ROIs) during instructed and choice-based attention paradigms. Results revealed that while univariate activation increases were most pronounced in higher-order visual areas, MVPA decoding was significant across all visual cortical ROIs, with the highest decoding accuracies observed in lower-order areas like V1. Furthermore, individual differences in stimulus discrimination performance were more accurately predicted by decoding strength than by the magnitude of univariate signal changes, providing evidence that the information content of population-level neural patterns, rather than simple gain modulation, is a primary driver of attentional benefits.
papers.authors: Sreenivasan Meyyappan, Abhijit Rajan, Qiang Yang, George R. Mangun, Mingzhou Ding

0479.name: Miranda Scolari
0479.bio: Miranda Scolari is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Texas Tech University and the director of the Selective Attention & Perception Lab. Scolari’s research characterizes the neural and behavioral mechanisms that allow the human visual system to prioritize information within limited processing capacities, focusing on the functional architecture of the frontoparietal attention network. Using methodologies such as fMRI, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and pupillometry, Scolari investigates how top-down attentional gain is allocated to sensory neurons and how space- and feature-based selection mechanisms interact during perceptual decision-making. Their work further examines the representational sharpening of visual information and the intersection of selective attention with working memory and implicit learning processes.
0479.research_direction: Dr. Scolari's recent work investigates how attention, learning, and cognitive control dynamically shape visual processing and higher-order cognition. Using fMRI and inverted encoding models, they have recently been examining how rule-based category learning selectively sharpens feature representations in early visual cortex and how this sensory tuning is driven by top-down signals from the frontoparietal attention network. Their research also explores the underlying mechanisms of attentional selection and effort, modeling how spatial and feature-based cues operate across distinct sensory and decision-making stages, and using pupillometry to track how sustained attentional effort relates to self-control failure during demanding tasks. Additionally, their recent behavioral work touches on memory research by testing whether individual differences in mental imagery vividness play a role in the well-known memory advantage for animate objects.

papers.title: Individual differences in mental imagery do not moderate the animacy advantage in memory
papers.abstract: Tests whether people who report more vivid mental imagery show a larger memory benefit for animate over inanimate items. Across the reported experiments, imagery differences did not moderate the animacy advantage, arguing against imagery vividness as an explanation of that effect.
papers.authors: Michael J. Serra, Julia N. Keiner, Nicolasa C. Villalobos, Abigail Kortenhoeven, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Category Learning Selectively Enhances Representations of Boundary-Adjacent Exemplars in Early Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and an inverted encoding model, the study tracked how orientation representations in V1-V3 change while people learn to sort identical gratings by either an orientation rule or a spatial-frequency rule. Only learners for whom orientation was the relevant dimension showed enhanced reconstructed orientation representations, and the enhancement was strongest for values close to the category boundary. This supports the idea that category learning sharpens sensory populations tuned to the most diagnostic feature values during active learning.
papers.authors: Sean R. O'Bryan, Shinyoung Jung, Anto J. Mohan, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: The role of the frontoparietal attention network during rule-based categorization
papers.abstract: Follow-up fMRI study asking whether the sensory sharpening seen during category learning is driven by top-down feature-based attention from the frontoparietal control network.
