Connectivity analyses showed that intraparietal subregions (IPS0/1, IPS2/3, IPS4/5) coupled with visual cortex during category learning, and encoding models revealed enhanced orientation representations in IPS during learning, with the pattern depending on rule relevance in posterior and middle IPS.
papers.authors: Shinyoung Jung, Sean O'Bryan, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Changes in pupil size track self-control failure
papers.abstract: Participants completed a high- or low-demand attention task and then a Stroop task while pupil size was recorded. Sustained pupil dilation during the demanding task rose with demand, carried over into the Stroop task, and predicted more errors on incongruent trials, forming a serial mediation path for ego-depletion effects. A separate route ran through transient attentional effort, implicating attention as a mechanism behind self-control failure.
papers.authors: Sean R. O'Bryan, Mindi M. Price, Jessica L. Alquist, Tyler Davis, Miranda Scolari

papers.title: Space- and feature-based attention operate both independently and interactively within latent components of perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: Three experiments manipulated the reliability of spatial and feature cues in a search task and modeled the data with a decision-process framework. Space- and feature-based attention acted independently on signal enhancement, but interacted in higher-order decision components such as pre-evidence time and response conservatism, depending on the probability of the cued object. The authors conclude selection mechanisms are independent at the sensory level and interdependent only at decision level.
papers.authors: Guangsheng Liang, John E. Poquiz, Miranda Scolari

0480.name: MiYoung Kwon
0480.lab_name: The Kwon Lab for Low Vision and Brain Research
0480.bio: MiYoung Kwon is an Assistant Professor at Northeastern University whose research explores basic and clinical vision science to understand how the human brain processes visual information under degraded or atypical sensory conditions. Kwon investigates the mechanisms of visual perception and brain plasticity in the context of aging and eye diseases such as glaucoma and macular degeneration. Utilizing an approach that includes psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG), eye tracking, and computational modeling, Kwon examines how the visual system adapts to sensory loss. Their research aims to uncover principles of visual reconstruction and develop strategies for the detection of vision loss and the enhancement of functional vision for individuals with visual impairments.
0480.research_direction: Dr. Kwon has recently been investigating how age, lighting conditions, and ocular disease impact spatial vision and everyday tasks like reading. Their recent work explores the functional consequences of visual field defects and glaucomatous retinal ganglion cell damage, utilizing gaze-contingent eye-tracking and psychophysics to examine altered oculomotor strategies and central visual processing. Additionally, they are using fMRI population receptive field mapping to investigate how rod-dominant mesopic lighting alters basic spatial computations, such as summation and surround suppression, in human early visual cortex. To characterize normative sensory trajectories, they also track how contrast sensitivity, binocular summation, and reading performance change across the adult lifespan under both bright and dim lighting conditions.

papers.title: Impact of Rod-Dominant Mesopic Conditions on Spatial Summation and Surround Suppression in Early Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI population receptive field mapping, this study asked how dim, rod-dominated light changes spatial integration in human early visual cortex. Under mesopic conditions receptive-field summation areas grew and surround suppression weakened relative to bright light, mirroring retinal changes seen in animal recordings. The results suggest that cortex compensates for reduced light by trading spatial resolution for sensitivity.
papers.authors: Michaela Klimova, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Age-Related Changes in Mesopic Reading Vision Across Adulthood
papers.abstract: The authors measured reading speed and related metrics in healthy adults spanning a wide age range under both bright and dim lighting. Reading performance declined with age, and the decline was noticeably steeper in mesopic light. The findings show that everyday dim-light reading is a sensitive marker of aging vision that standard photopic testing underestimates.
papers.authors: Boris Peñaloza, Traci-Lin Goddin, David S. Friedman, Cynthia Owsley, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Significant Age-Related Visual Declines but Preserved Binocular Summation of Contrast Sensitivity and Visual Acuity Across Adulthood
papers.abstract: This study compared monocular and binocular contrast sensitivity and acuity across the adult lifespan. Both measures worsened substantially with age, yet the benefit of using two eyes over one stayed intact. Binocular combination therefore appears resilient to healthy aging even as basic visual function declines.
papers.authors: Boris Peñaloza, MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Impact of Glaucomatous Ganglion Cell Damage on Central Visual Function
papers.abstract: A sole-author review arguing that glaucoma should be understood as a disease of central as well as peripheral vision. It draws on macular imaging and psychophysics showing that retinal ganglion cell loss near the fovea is common even in early disease and that this damage alters contrast coding, reading and other pattern-vision functions. The paper frames the visual consequences of RGC loss in terms of the cell-level computations these neurons perform.
papers.authors: MiYoung Kwon

papers.title: Altered Eye Movements During Reading With Simulated Central and Peripheral Visual Field Defects
papers.abstract: Normally sighted readers viewed text through gaze-contingent simulations of central or peripheral field loss while their eye movements were tracked. Central and peripheral defects each produced distinct changes in fixation and saccade patterns, and slowed reading in different ways. The work clarifies how oculomotor strategies adapt to specific kinds of visual field loss.
papers.authors: Haojue Yu, MiYoung Kwon

0483.name: Monica D. Rosenberg
0483.lab_name: Cognition, Attention, and Brain Lab (CAB Lab)
0483.bio: Monica D. Rosenberg is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Chicago and the Principal Investigator of the Cognition, Attention, and Brain Lab. Rosenberg’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying sustained attention and individual differences in cognition using functional MRI and machine learning. They utilize connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) to identify whole-brain functional connectivity fingerprints that predict attentional states and traits from task-based and resting-state data. This work further examines the temporal dynamics of attention across the lifespan and its functional intersections with learning, memory, and clinical symptoms such as ADHD.
0483.research_direction: Dr. Rosenberg’s recent work explores the neural and cognitive dynamics of sustained attention, subjective mental states, and expectation violation across both controlled experimental tasks and naturalistic environments. Using multimodal behavioral paradigms and fMRI connectome-based predictive modeling, they have recently been investigating how continuous fluctuations in attention relate to long-term memory and whether heightened attentional states act as a selective "spotlight" or a global "floodlight" for processing concurrent sensory inputs. Their research also examines how time-resolved functional brain networks track second-to-second shifts in task engagement and momentary surprise during ecological activities like watching movies or sports. Finally, they are probing the cognitive basis of intrinsic brain organization by mapping how idiosyncratic, spontaneous streams of thought during resting-state fMRI correlate with functional connectivity patterns and predict trait-level behavioral differences. They have also investigated how attention and memory change across development and vary with experiences and environments.

papers.title: Ongoing thoughts at rest reflect functional brain organization and behaviour
papers.abstract: Participants described their spontaneous streams of thought during resting-state fMRI, and the content and dynamics of those thoughts were related to time-resolved functional connectivity. Brain-network patterns tied to particular kinds of thoughts also related to individual differences in traits and behaviour. The work links what people think about at rest to the intrinsic functional organization of the brain.
papers.authors: Jin Ke, Taylor A. Chamberlain, Hayoung Song, Anna Corriveau, Ziwei Zhang, Taysha Martinez, Laura Sams, Marvin M. Chun, Yuan Chang Leong, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Cortical reinstatement of causally related events sparks narrative insights by updating neural representation patterns
papers.abstract: During movie viewing, moments when viewers gain insight into how earlier and later events are causally related were tied to reinstatement of the earlier event's neural pattern in cortex. This reinstatement was accompanied by updating of neural representations, supporting a role for memory retrieval in narrative comprehension. Results connect episodic memory and naturalistic understanding.
papers.authors: Hayoung Song, Jin Ke, Rhea Madhogarhia, Yuan Chang Leong, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Sustained attentional state is a floodlight not a spotlight
papers.abstract: Across several experiments, fluctuations in sustained attentional state affected memory and perception of both task-relevant and task-irrelevant items. This suggests that a high attentional state boosts processing broadly, like a floodlight, rather than selectively, like a spotlight. It reframes what attentional state fluctuations do to concurrent sensory input.
papers.authors: Anna Corriveau, Anthony R. James, Megan T. deBettencourt, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Brain network dynamics predict moments of surprise across contexts
papers.abstract: Time-resolved functional connectivity was used to build models that predict moment-to-moment surprise in a controlled visual task and in naturalistic viewing of movies and sports. Models generalized across these very different contexts, suggesting a common brain-network signature of expectation violation. The study extends the lab's network-dynamics approach from sustained attention to surprise.
papers.authors: Ziwei Zhang, Monica D. Rosenberg

papers.title: Large-scale neural dynamics in a shared low-dimensional state space reflect cognitive and attentional dynamics
papers.abstract: Whole-brain fMRI activity from several tasks and rest was embedded in a common low-dimensional state space. Trajectories through this space tracked moment-to-moment attention and cognitive states and generalized across datasets. The paper offers a compact dynamical account of how large-scale brain activity relates to attention.
papers.authors: Hayoung Song, Won Mok Shim, Monica D. Rosenberg

0484.name: Moreno I. Coco
0484.bio: Moreno I. Coco is an Associate Professor at Sapienza University of Rome and a research affiliate at I.R.C.C.S. Fondazione Santa Lucia. Coco's research integrates cognitive neuroscience with computational modeling to investigate the mechanisms of vision, language, and memory across the human lifespan. Utilizing eye-tracking and co-registered electro-physiology (fixation-related potentials), they explore how semantic knowledge and contextual information guide visual attention and information encoding. Their recent work focuses on the development of diagnostic tools by identifying early cognitive markers of neurodegeneration in prodromal stages of dementia.
0484.research_direction: Dr. Coco has recently been investigating how higher-level cognitive, semantic, and linguistic factors guide visual attention and memory in naturalistic environments. Their recent work explores object-scene integration across the lifespan, utilizing eye-tracking and change-detection tasks to understand how semantic consistency and spatial layout influence visual short-term memory in healthy aging and mild cognitive impairment. In parallel, they are examining the coordination of gaze and speech production, investigating whether a universal semantic framework organizes visual scan paths across different spoken languages, and how interacting partners align their eye movements and speech during joint, goal-directed tasks. To support these distinct lines of inquiry, they have also developed a newly normed visual database designed specifically for testing how semantic and spatial object properties capture human attention.

papers.title: The Cross-Linguistic Coordination of Overt Attention and Speech Production as Evidence for a Language of Vision
papers.abstract: Tests whether an abstract, language-independent 'language of vision' organizes meaning across modalities, using eye-tracking while speakers described scenes in English, Portuguese and Japanese. Semantic similarity between sentences strongly predicted similarity of the accompanying scan patterns in all three languages, even across scenes and across languages. Syntactic constraints mattered only weakly, within language and scene, and mainly during early utterance planning, supporting a universal semantic scaffold with syntax as a local constraint.
papers.authors: Moreno I. Coco, Eunice G. Fernandes, Manabu Arai, Frank Keller

papers.title: Task goals constrain the alignment in eye-movements and speech during interpersonal coordination
papers.abstract: Examines how two people's gaze and speech become aligned during joint tasks such as route planning and search. The degree of alignment depends on the task goals, with task demands shaping how partners coordinate what they look at and say. The work links interpersonal alignment to task structure rather than treating it as a generic social tendency.
papers.authors: Alexia Galati, Rick Dale, Camila Alviar, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: Object Features Hierarchically Guide Eye-Movement and Short-Term Memory for Naturalistic Scenes with Preserved Spatial Layout Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: Younger and older adults detected identity, location or joint changes to objects in scenes, with semantic consistency manipulated and spatial layout kept intact by swapping objects. Location changes were harder to detect when layout was preserved, and semantically inconsistent objects were detected better and fixated longer, an advantage seen mainly in younger adults. The findings argue that when global structure is unchanged, visual working memory is guided by hierarchical object features with semantics playing an organising role.
papers.authors: Elena Allegretti, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: Visual short-term memory binding and attentional processes during object-scene integration are preserved in mild cognitive impairment
papers.abstract: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment and healthy controls detected changes to object identity and location in naturalistic scenes while eye movements were recorded. Binding of objects to their scene locations and the attentional effects of semantic consistency were largely preserved in MCI. The results suggest that object-scene integration could support markers of cognitive status without being lost in prodromal decline.
papers.authors: Elena Allegretti, Marika Mauti, Moreno I. Coco

papers.title: The Visual Integration of Semantic and Spatial Information of Objects in Naturalistic Scenes (VISIONS) database: attentional, conceptual, and perceptual norms
papers.abstract: Presents a normed database of naturalistic scenes in which objects vary in semantic consistency and spatial placement. Norms cover attentional, conceptual and perceptual properties collected from human raters. It is offered as a resource for studies of object-scene integration in attention and memory.
papers.authors: Elena Allegretti, Giorgia D'Innocenzo, Moreno I. Coco

0485.name: Moritz Wurm
0485.department: Department of Psychology and Cognitive Science
0485.bio: Moritz Wurm is a cognitive neuroscientist at CIMeC, University of Trento, where they investigate the neural basis of action recognition and understanding. Using fMRI and MEG combined with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), Wurm examines how the brain decodes actions across different levels of abstraction, from physical kinematics to conceptual meanings. Their work has identified roles for the lateral occipitotemporal and parietal cortices in representing the "physics of actions" and integrating action-object knowledge. Currently, Wurm focuses on characterizing the predictive mechanisms the brain uses to process dynamic visual events and social interactions.
0485.research_direction: Dr. Wurm has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying how we perceive and make sense of the actions of others. Their recent work explores how the brain represents the physical mechanics of observed events, using fMRI decoding to ask whether human actions and inanimate object interactions share a common neural code grounded in intuitive physics. Alongside this, they are using MEG, time-resolved representational similarity analysis, and computational modeling to examine the predictive processing of biological motion, testing how hierarchical priors allow the visual system to forecast unfolding naturalistic movements. Finally, their research bridges visual perception and social cognition by charting the distinct cortical stages required to transform the visual recognition of actions and objects into inferences about an actor's mental states.

papers.title: Decoding the neural stages from action and object recognition to mentalizing
papers.abstract: Using fMRI decoding, the study charts how the brain moves from recognizing what action is being performed and which objects are involved to inferring an actor's mental states. Distinct regions and processing stages were identified for perceptual action and object information versus mentalizing-related representations. The results provide a stage-wise account of how visual actions are turned into social understanding.
papers.authors: Moritz F. Wurm, Seoyoung Lee

papers.title: Hierarchical priors enable neural prediction of perceived biological motion
papers.abstract: Combining neural recordings with computational modelling, the paper examines how prior expectations at multiple levels of a hierarchy allow the brain to predict perceived biological motion. It shows that neural prediction of unfolding movement depends on hierarchical priors rather than only low-level continuation of motion. This links predictive coding theory to the representation of human movement.
papers.authors: Ingmar E. J. de Vries, Floris P. de Lange, Moritz F. Wurm

papers.title: Decoding the physics of observed actions in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with multivariate decoding, the study asks which cortical regions carry information about the physical mechanics of observed actions, such as the forces and contact involved, separately from the actor's goals. Physics-based action features could be read out from lateral occipitotemporal and parietal cortex and generalized across different kinds of actions. The findings support a stage of action understanding that is grounded in intuitive physics and precedes conceptual interpretation.
papers.authors: Moritz F. Wurm, Doruk Yiğit Erigüç

papers.title: A shared neural code for the physics of actions and object events
papers.abstract: The authors show that brain activity patterns evoked by observing actions can be used to decode the physical properties of object events, and vice versa. This cross-decoding indicates that a common representational format in visual and parietal regions captures the physical causal structure of both agents' actions and inanimate events. It suggests that action perception draws on general-purpose physical reasoning machinery.
papers.authors: Seda Karakose-Akbiyik, Alfonso Caramazza, Moritz F. Wurm

papers.title: Predictive neural representations of naturalistic dynamic input
papers.abstract: Using MEG and a time-resolved extension of representational similarity analysis with time-varying models, the work tracks how the brain represents unfolding biological motion. Neural responses reflected not only the current visual input but also future states of the stimulus, indicating that the brain generates predictions about ongoing dynamic events. The approach offers a general way of testing predictive coding with naturalistic stimuli.
papers.authors: Ingmar E. J. de Vries, Moritz F. Wurm

0490.name: Máté Lengyel
0490.department: Department of Engineering (University of Cambridge); Department of Cognitive Science (Central European University)
0490.bio: Máté Lengyel is a Professor of Computational Neuroscience who researches the mathematical and biological principles underlying learning and memory. Lengyel's work utilizes Bayesian approaches to statistical inference and reinforcement learning to characterize how the brain represents uncertainty and adapts to its environment. By combining normative theories with dynamical systems analysis of neural circuits, Lengyel connects behavioral goals with cellular and network mechanisms. They collaborate with experimentalists to validate these models using multi-unit recordings, human psychophysics, and functional neuroimaging.
0490.research_direction: Dr. Lengyel has recently been exploring how recurrent neural circuits optimally process and store information under biological constraints across various brain regions. In the prefrontal cortex, their research investigates how metabolic cost and neural noise shape the representational geometry of task-relevant versus irrelevant stimuli, and whether dynamic population codes during working memory reflect an optimal strategy for loading stimulus information. Their recent work also explores the hippocampus, examining how single-neuron properties like the activation functions of CA3 pyramidal cells might be tuned to support stable pattern recall. Additionally, they are investigating how shared recurrent dynamics can explain hallmark visual cortex phenomena like response sub-additivity and variability quenching, while simultaneously developing novel Bayesian latent variable models to automatically discover time-varying, compositional structures in complex neural recordings without predefining their dimensionality.

papers.title: The activation function of CA3 pyramidal neurons is optimal for the stable recall of memory patterns
papers.abstract: Analyzes a canonical recurrent network model of hippocampal CA3 and derives testable predictions for circuits that recall memories stably, including that neuronal activation functions should have an exponent slightly above 1. Intracellular recordings from 49 CA3 pyramidal neurons in behaving mice, plus 133 cells from earlier studies, confirm this exponent with notable cell-to-cell heterogeneity. The work suggests single-neuron properties in CA3 are tuned for reliable pattern recall.
papers.authors: Uri Cohen, Marco M. Picher, Andrea Navas-Olive, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Effects of noise and metabolic cost on cortical task representations
papers.abstract: Studies how neural noise and metabolic cost jointly shape the way circuits represent task-relevant versus task-irrelevant stimuli. Mathematical analysis and task-optimized recurrent networks show a range of representational geometries depending on these constraints. Primate prefrontal recordings across learning match the minimal strategy, in which irrelevant stimulus coding is suppressed as the task is learned.
papers.authors: Jake P. Stroud, Michal Wojcik, Kristopher T. Jensen, Makoto Kusunoki, Mikiko Kadohisa, Mark J. Buckley, John Duncan, Mark G. Stokes, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Discovering Temporally Compositional Neural Manifolds with Switching Infinite GPFA
papers.abstract: Introduces a Bayesian nonparametric extension of Gaussian process factor analysis in which the number and identity of latent factors can switch over time. The model finds compositional, time-varying latent structure in neural population recordings without fixing the dimensionality in advance, and is demonstrated on neural data.
papers.authors: Changmin Yu, Maneesh Sahani, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Response sub-additivity and variability quenching in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Reviews two hallmark phenomena of visual cortex, sub-additive summation of multiple inputs and reduced response variability at stimulus onset. It argues that both can be understood as consequences of shared recurrent circuit dynamics rather than separate mechanisms, and outlines the models and evidence supporting this view.
papers.authors: Robbe L. T. Goris, Ruben Coen-Cagli, Kenneth D. Miller, Nicholas J. Priebe, Máté Lengyel

papers.title: Optimal information loading into working memory explains dynamic coding in the prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Proposes that the dynamic (changing) population codes seen in prefrontal cortex during working memory arise from an optimal way of loading stimulus information into a recurrent network. The model explains why activity changes over time even while memory is maintained, and its predictions are tested against monkey prefrontal recordings. The result reframes dynamic coding as a signature of optimal computation rather than instability.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Jake P. Stroud, Kei Watanabe, Takafumi Suzuki, Mark G. Stokes, Máté Lengyel

0491.name: N. Apurva Ratan Murty
0491.bio: N Apurva Ratan Murty is an Assistant Professor of Cognition and Brain Science at the Georgia Institute of Technology and directs the Murty Lab. Murty’s research focuses on the intersection of biological vision and artificial intelligence to map the neural algorithms and codes associated with visual intelligence. By combining high-field functional MRI (3T/7T) and human electrophysiology with deep neural networks and generative AI, Murty develops models such as TopoNets to characterize the functional organization of the brain. Their work investigates category-selective brain regions and the neurobiological foundations of perceptual disorders, including agnosia and prosopagnosia.
0491.research_direction: Dr. Murty has recently been investigating the alignment between artificial neural networks and the human visual system, with a focus on high-level category representations like faces, scenes, and bodies. Their recent work explores the biological fidelity of ANN-based encoding models by evaluating their zero-shot generalization across distinct fMRI datasets and classic cognitive neuroscience experiments. They are also examining the nature of category-selective units in these models to determine if they truly share the tuning profiles and representational geometries of human ventral stream regions. Additionally, Dr. Murty is probing the behavioral and structural properties of artificial vision systems by subjecting them to standardized clinical tests of human face recognition and developing novel training objectives designed to induce brain-like spatial topography within network layers.

papers.title: Zero-shot evaluations expose structured generalization limits in predictive models of the brain
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a stricter way to evaluate ANN-based encoding models of human visual cortex: freeze the model after fitting, then test it on entirely new fMRI datasets and on classic cognitive-neuroscience experiments. Using fixed models of face-, scene- and body-selective regions (FFA, PPA, EBA) evaluated across 7 datasets and 31 experiments from 10 published studies, the authors show that generalization limits hidden by within-dataset cross-validation are systematic across regions and model classes. Models that predict well also tend to reproduce more classic findings, but the cognitive tests reveal where and why each model fails.
papers.authors: R. Wang, M. Deb, A. Abate, A. Dipani, K. R. Dudipala, S. Chillarege, K. Ravikanti, Y. Li, H. Al-Tahan, R. Koushik, E. Mieczkowski, H. Fung, N. Kanwisher, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: Standardized human tests show that most vision models are face-blind
papers.abstract: The authors give the standardized clinical and research tests of human face recognition ability to 53 vision models, placing each model on the human spectrum from prosopagnosia to super-recognizer. Most models (about 55%) fall in the face-blind range and even the best face-trained models do not reach the human super-recognizer threshold. Analyses of representations show that good models are more identity-selective and viewpoint-invariant, and removing a viewpoint-dependent subspace improves recognition in 49 of 53 models, with unit ablations revealing opposing roles for viewpoint-dependent and viewpoint-tolerant units.
papers.authors: K. R. Dudipala, F. Martinez-Addiego, D. Rahnev, B. C. Duchaine, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: Category selectivity observed in the human brain is distinct from category selectivity observed in artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: The study asks whether category-selective units in ANNs, found with standard fMRI localizers, express the same kind of selectivity as human face, scene and body regions. Human category-selective regions show a stable, subject-shared tuning profile across a broad image set, whereas ANN selective units diverge in univariate tuning and representational geometry, fall below the human-human ceiling, and depend heavily on the localizer used. Such units are also neither necessary nor sufficient for predicting brain responses, so the authors argue that full response tuning is a more discriminating test of brain-model alignment.
papers.authors: Alish Dipani, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

papers.title: TopoNets: High Performing Vision and Language Models with Brain-Like Topography
papers.abstract: The authors introduce TopoLoss, a simple additional training objective that pushes nearby units in a network layer to develop similar tuning, mimicking the spatial smoothness of cortical maps. Applied to convolutional networks and transformers for both vision and language (the resulting family is called TopoNets), it yields brain-like topographic organization while task accuracy is largely preserved. The resulting models produce category-selective clusters resembling ventral-stream patches and show efficiency benefits, and the approach is presented as a general recipe for building topographic models across architectures and modalities.
papers.venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025, Spotlight)
papers.authors: Mayukh Deb, Mainak Deb, N. Apurva Ratan Murty

0492.name: Nancy B. Carlisle
0492.bio: Nancy B. Carlisle is an Associate Professor at Lehigh University and the director of the Carlisle Attention and Memory (CAM) Lab. Carlisle’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of top-down attentional control, specifically focusing on how working memory representations guide visual selection. A central component of their work involves the study of negative templates to examine the cognitive and electrophysiological processes that allow for the proactive suppression of distractors. Carlisle utilizes behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, computational modeling, and event-related potentials (ERPs) to characterize the flexibility of the human attentional system.
0492.research_direction: Dr. Carlisle has recently been investigating the mechanisms of attentional control, with a particular focus on how observers use negative attentional templates to suppress visual distractors. Using behavioral metrics, eye tracking, and EEG/ERPs, their recent work explores the neural and cognitive underpinnings of these avoidance cues, specifically testing whether negative templates are deployed proactively or reactively and whether they are simply recoded into positive target search strategies. They have also been leveraging individual differences in working memory and cognitive control to understand why some observers are more efficient at utilizing these explicit distractor cues. Furthermore, their research probes the interplay between top-down goals and implicit statistical learning, investigating how current attentional templates might be required to unlock learned spatial biases and whether explicit cued suppression relies on the same underlying processes as implicitly learned suppression.

papers.title: Why Are Some Individuals Better at Using Negative Attentional Templates to Suppress Distractors? Exploration of Interindividual Differences in Cognitive Control Efficiency
papers.abstract: Participants differ widely in how much they benefit from being told which distractor colour to avoid. The authors relate this benefit to individual measures of cognitive control and working-memory-related abilities to identify who uses negative templates efficiently. The work frames negative-template use as a trait-linked control skill.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Distinct mechanisms of attentional suppression: exploration of trait factors underlying cued- and learned-suppression
papers.abstract: Suppression of distractors can come from explicit cues or from implicitly learned regularities. By examining individual-difference traits related to each, the study asks whether the two forms share a mechanism, and argues that they depend on partly distinct processes.
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Explicit attentional goals unlock implicit spatial statistical learning
papers.abstract: People learn where targets tend to appear in a display, but this study shows that such learned spatial biases are not applied automatically. They are expressed only when the observer holds an explicit goal that matches the category of the learned target, so the same statistical regularity can be used or ignored depending on the current template. This ties implicit learning to top-down goals.
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Neurophysiological Measures of Proactive and Reactive Control in Negative Template Use
papers.abstract: Using EEG/ERPs, the study asks whether knowing a distractor feature in advance lets the brain suppress it proactively or only reactively after the display appears. Electrophysiological markers of attention and suppression are compared across negative and positive cues, informing the neural mechanism of negative templates.
papers.authors: Matthieu Chidharom, Nancy B. Carlisle

papers.title: Assessing recoding accounts of negative attentional templates using behavior and eye tracking
papers.abstract: A common explanation is that negative cues work only because observers convert them into a positive target-based template. Behavioural and eye-tracking tests of this recoding account examine whether the data support it, helping to pin down what is actually stored during avoidance cues.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Ziyao Zhang, Nancy B. Carlisle

0493.name: Nancy Kanwisher
0493.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0493.bio: Nancy Kanwisher is the Walter A. Rosenblith Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at MIT and maps the functional architecture of the human brain using fMRI. Kanwisher identified and characterized specialized cortical regions, such as the Fusiform Face Area (FFA) for face processing and the Parahippocampal Place Area (PPA) for scene recognition. Her current research integrates intracranial recordings and deep neural networks to investigate the computational principles and developmental origins of these regions. This work examines the organization of the human mind into distinct, domain-specific processors for high-level perception and cognition.
0493.research_direction: Dr. Kanwisher studies the functional organization of the human brain as a window into the architecture of the mind. Her lab discovered cortical regions specialized for faces (FFA), places (PPA) and bodies (EBA), studies regions for music, language and thinking about other people, and asks what each region represents and computes, how it develops, and why the brain has such specialized regions at all. Favoring human-specific methods over animal models, the lab combines fMRI, including a new localizer that maps many visual, auditory and cognitive regions in a single session, with intracranial recordings in neurosurgery patients and deep neural networks that make precise, testable predictions about brain responses. Recent work extends this approach to an intuitive "physics engine" in frontoparietal cortex that tells rigid objects ("things") from substances ("stuff") and predicts how physical events will unfold, and to how the language network passes information to other brain systems to build a full understanding of what we hear and read.

papers.title: Apparent food selectivity reflects multiple non-food image properties
papers.abstract: Several recent reports claimed the ventral visual pathway has food-selective regions, based mainly on the Natural Scenes Dataset where food images correlate with color, object size and scene distance. The authors built new stimulus sets that vary these properties independently in food and non-food images and tested responses with fMRI. The results indicate that the apparent food selectivity is explained by a mix of non-food properties, prompting caution about category claims from correlated natural-image datasets.
papers.authors: Cyn X. Fang, Meenakshi Khosla, Moshe Poliak, Nancy G. Kanwisher

papers.title: Decoding predicted future states from the brain's "physics engine"
papers.abstract: The authors test whether frontoparietal 'physics network' regions actually run forward simulations of physical events. In a preregistered fMRI study they show these regions encode whether two objects are in contact, and that activity can be used to decode what will happen next in a physical scene, including predicted future states rather than only the current visual input. This supports the view that the network simulates the physical world to predict outcomes.
papers.authors: R. T. Pramod, Elizabeth Mieczkowski, Cyn X. Fang, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Dissociable cortical regions represent things and stuff in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study asks how the brain distinguishes rigid, countable objects ('things') from deformable or flowing materials ('stuff'). It finds separable cortical regions, including within the physics network, that carry information about each class and that differ in how they represent physical properties. This links material and object perception to the brain's physical-reasoning machinery.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Raghavendra Rao T. Pramod, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: An efficient multifunction fMRI localizer for high-level visual, auditory, and cognitive regions in humans
papers.abstract: Functional localizers are used to find category- and function-selective cortical regions in each individual, but standard ones target only one system at a time. The authors design a single short scanning session that reliably identifies many regions at once, spanning face, place, body, scene, language, music, speech and other cognitive networks. The tool lets many labs efficiently map the brain's specialized regions in the same participants.
papers.authors: Ammar I. Marvi, Sam Hutchinson, Evelina Fedorenko, Rebecca R. Saxe, Frederik S. Kamps, Tamar I. Regev, Emily M. Chen, Nancy G. Kanwisher

papers.title: Using artificial neural networks to ask 'why' questions of minds and brains
papers.abstract: This perspective argues that task-optimized deep neural networks can be used to address why the mind and brain have the properties they do, not just how they work. It lays out how networks trained on ecologically relevant tasks let researchers test whether a given brain feature arises from a computational or developmental pressure, with examples from face recognition. It offers a framework for using models as tools of scientific explanation.
papers.authors: Nancy Kanwisher, Meenakshi Khosla, Katharina Dobs

0494.name: Naseem Al-Aidroos
0494.bio: Al-Aidroos investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms that enable the brain to prioritize goal-relevant information within complex visual environments. Their research integrates behavioral measures, such as eye tracking and limb tracking, with neurophysiological techniques including EEG/ERP, pupillometry, and fMRI to study the optimization and failure of attentional control. Al-Aidroos examines how attention regulates functional communication between high-level and low-level regions of the visual cortex and the role of visual working memory in supporting these processes.
0494.research_direction: Dr. Al-Aidroos has recently been investigating how representations in visual long-term memory interact with working memory to guide attentional selection. Their recent work explores whether long-term memory directs attention directly or indirectly by reinstating both relevant and task-irrelevant object features into visual working memory search templates. To understand the dynamics of this memory-driven guidance, they are examining how stimulus repetition modulates the strength of memory-based attentional capture during visual search. Furthermore, they utilize high-temporal-resolution methods like the EEG N2pc component to track the precise time course of these processes and determine how early long-term memory control settings can influence visual selection.

papers.title: Task-dependent reinstatement of irrelevant features from long-term memory into visual working memory templates
papers.abstract: Asks whether features of a remembered object that are irrelevant to the current search are nonetheless pulled into the working-memory template used to find a target. Across experiments the authors show that such reinstatement of irrelevant long-term-memory features depends on the task demands rather than being automatic. This refines the account of how long-term memory guides attention through visual working memory.
papers.authors: Jessica M. Kespe, Rory Lippert, Naseem Al-Aidroos

papers.title: Control over attentional capture within 170 ms by long-term memory control settings: Evidence from the N2pc
papers.abstract: Uses the N2pc EEG component to time when a long-term-memory-based control setting can influence attentional capture. Items matching activated long-term memory captured attention, and this could be controlled, within roughly 170 ms of stimulus onset. The result indicates that memory-based attentional control operates at an early, fast stage of selection.
papers.authors: Lindsay Plater, Maria Giammarco, Samantha Joubran, Naseem Al-Aidroos

papers.title: Object feature reinstatement into working-memory? Separating the direct and indirect effects of long-term memory on attentional selection
papers.abstract: Tests whether long-term memory guides attention by reinstating object features into a working-memory template, separating direct effects of memory from indirect ones mediated by the template. The experiments disentangle these routes during visual search. The findings clarify how remembered object features influence selection.
papers.authors: Jessica M. Kespe, Niyatee Narkar, Naseem Al-Aidroos

papers.title: Repetition enhances the effects of activated long-term memory
papers.abstract: Examines whether repeatedly viewing an item strengthens how strongly an activated long-term-memory representation biases attention. Repetition increased the attentional effects of memory-matching items, showing that memory strength modulates attentional control settings. The work supports a direct interface between visual long-term memory and perception.
papers.authors: Lindsay Plater, Sandra Nyman, Samantha Joubran, Naseem Al-Aidroos

0498.name: Neda Nategh
0498.department: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
0498.bio: Nategh investigates the neural mechanisms and computational algorithms that enable stable visual perception during active behavior, particularly during rapid eye movements. Their research combines multi-electrode array recordings in non-human primates with statistical modeling, such as time-varying generalized linear models, to decode how the brain processes dynamic visual information. By examining perisaccadic neural dynamics in extrastriate and prefrontal areas, Nategh’s work identifies how sensory memory and response enhancements bridge discontinuities in retinal input. Their current research aims to develop biologically-plausible frameworks for describing high-dimensional neural data to provide insights into both biological vision and artificial intelligence.
0498.research_direction: Dr. Nategh has recently been studying how the visual system keeps track of space and time around rapid eye movements, when perception of where and when things happen becomes distorted. Their recent work records from populations of neurons in macaque visual areas V4 and MT while monkeys make saccades, and links those neural signals to what the animals perceive. They ask which areas account for the perceived shifts in position and time, using statistical models that let a neuron's tuning change from moment to moment. They have also worked on such time-varying models as a general tool for decoding neurons in higher visual areas, and on how inhibitory amacrine cells in the retina adjust the sensitivity and gain of the cells that send signals to the brain.

papers.title: Limits of V4 perisaccadic firing rate modulations in explaining perceptual mislocalization
papers.abstract: The degree to which distinct visual sensory structures mediate the perceived coordinates of visual targets remains unresolved. To determine whether extrastriate area V4 drives shifts in spatial localization around the time of saccadic eye movements, perisaccadic mislocalization was probed using an integrated behavioral and neurophysiological paradigm in non-human primates, mapping single-trial perceptual reports directly to population spike rates in area V4. Monkeys exhibited characteristic perisaccadic mislocalization oriented counter to saccade trajectories. Extrastriate population responses were evaluated by calculating the center of mass of firing rates across probe positions for V4 units whose receptive fields bordered the saccade target. Although perisaccadic responses displayed vector shifts oriented toward the saccade target, trial-by-trial variance in shift magnitude did not correlate with perceptual displacement. These data indicate that receptive field displacements inferred from mean firing rate modulations in area V4 are insufficient to explain single-trial behavioral mislocalization, demonstrating that higher-order neural population dynamics or alternative representational codes are necessary to account for perisaccadic spatial perception.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Kelsey Clark, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: A population readout of extrastriate activity reveals biased and smoothed temporal representations across saccades
papers.abstract: Perceived temporal intervals undergo transient compression and distortion perisaccadically, yet the circuit computations underpinning time representation during rapid gaze shifts remain poorly defined. To elucidate how perisaccadic temporal features are structured and decoded within extrastriate cortex, multi-electrode array recordings were gathered from macaque area MT and V4 populations during millisecond-precision visual probe stimulation alongside single-trial nonstationary statistical modeling. Decoded population readouts revealed that perisaccadic spikes systematically advance the decoded temporal profile of presaccadic receptive-field stimuli—biasing estimated onset times toward earlier latencies—while concurrently suppressing temporal sensitivity and degrading stimulus onset discrimination. Enforcing synthetic in silico perturbations demonstrated that the representational temporal bias directly causes the loss in temporal sensitivity. These results indicate that extrastriate ensembles adopt an adaptive encoding strategy prioritizing the most recent presaccadic input at the expense of temporal precision, highlighting a computational tradeoff between temporal resolution and perceptual continuity across saccades.
papers.authors: Adeleh Poursadegh, Maryam Zekri, Geyu Weng, Amir Akbarian, Kelsey Clark, Hossein Rabbani, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Neural correlates of perisaccadic visual mislocalization in extrastriate cortex
papers.abstract: Visual perception of spatial position exhibits significant distortion during saccades, a phenomenon known as perisaccadic mislocalization whose underlying neurophysiological mechanisms have remained elusive. By recording single-unit and multi-unit spiking activity across extrastriate cortex (areas V4 and MT) in four macaque monkeys during a visually guided saccade task with fine-grained visual probes, a statistical modeling framework was deployed to isolate time-varying spatiotemporal receptive field dynamics at millisecond resolution. Decoded model readouts successfully recapitulated behavioral spatial bias toward the saccade target and identified the precise underlying subcomponents of neuronal sensitivity. Crucially, the spatial bias was driven primarily by an emergent gain enhancement for probe stimuli positioned near the saccade target in neurons whose classical receptive fields were situated far from the target. These findings demonstrate that extrastriate networks transiently reallocate representational bandwidth toward the impending gaze endpoint, establishing that perisaccadic distortions emerge from targeted resource concentration supporting active foveation.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Amir Akbarian, Kelsey Clark, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Time-varying generalized linear models: characterizing and decoding neuronal dynamics in higher visual areas
papers.abstract: Cortical neurons in higher visual areas dynamically modulate their tuning properties in response to rapid interactions between feedforward sensory inputs and internal variables such as cognitive state, motor planning, and reward expectancy. Standard point-process generalized linear models (GLMs) offer an established framework for single-trial encoding and decoding of spike trains, but conventional formulations inherently assume temporal stationarity, rendering them incapable of capturing nonstationary receptive field shifts in higher visual circuits. This review synthesizes time-varying extensions of point-process GLMs engineered to resolve nonstationary tuning curves and multi-filter spatiotemporal sensitivity maps. We discuss how parameterizing time-varying kernels enables the decoding of transient perceptual representations, the dissection of specific physiological components driving behavioral changes, and the in silico manipulation of model filters to establish causal links between dynamic neural representations and visual behaviors.
papers.authors: Geyu Weng, Kelsey Clark, Amir Akbarian, Behrad Noudoost, Neda Nategh

papers.title: Modulation of input sensitivity and output gain by retinal amacrine cells
papers.abstract: The conventional canonical view of retinal processing relies on hierarchical, feedforward parallel pathways that sum visual features sequentially, leaving open how local inhibitory circuits implement contextual modulation across pathways. By deploying causal intracellular current injections into single amacrine cells paired with multi-electrode array recordings of ganglion cell populations in the salamander retina, an unsupervised dimensionality reduction and non-parametric modeling framework was developed to evaluate inhibitory influence on multi-dimensional visual stimulus spaces. Perturbing single amacrine cells unveiled two distinct functional classes of modulation: an input-pathway modulation that selectively adjusts the sensitivity and activation threshold of individual visual features within a ganglion cell, and an output modulation that divisively regulates the overall response gain across multiple features simultaneously. These findings establish distinct functional operations for amacrine cells in early visual processing, separating primary feature construction, contextual feature selection, and global retinal gain gating.
papers.authors: Neda Nategh, Mihai Manu, Stephen A. Baccus

0500.name: Nelson Cowan
0500.bio: Nelson Cowan proposed the 'embedded-processes model,' which defines working memory as an activated subset of long-term memory governed by a capacity-limited focus of attention. Their research focuses on quantifying the discrete limits of this focus—established as approximately three to four items in adults—and investigating how these constraints evolve throughout childhood development. Utilizing experimental psychology and neuroscientific frameworks, Cowan examines the interplay between selective attention, sensory storage, and the cognitive mechanisms underlying memory disorders. Their recent research extends into the relationship between consciousness and working memory architecture across the human lifespan.
0500.research_direction: Dr. Cowan has recently been investigating the mechanics of working memory, anchoring their research in an embedded-processes view where a capacity-limited focus of attention operates within activated long-term memory. Their recent work explores how this framework scales to broader cognitive phenomena, evaluating neuroscientific models of consciousness, the bidirectional dependency of attention and memory, and the roles of executive function and accumulated knowledge in cognitive aging. Alongside these theoretical evaluations, they are conducting behavioral experiments to test the structural capacity limits of visual working memory, examining how humans encode and chunk multiple sets of dissimilar features like colors, shapes, and locations. Furthermore, they are investigating the temporal dynamics of top-down control in cluttered visual displays, asking whether highly salient objects automatically hijack working memory prioritization or if observers can flexibly guide encoding when given sufficient time.

papers.title: Colors, characters, locations, and shapes: The capacity of working memory for multiple, dissimilar sets of items
papers.abstract: Tests how much people can recall when several sets of different item types (colors, characters, locations, shapes) are presented in one trial, finding performance beyond typical single-set limits. Results indicate that grouped sets are stored as newly formed, often incomplete chunks offloaded from the focus of attention to activated long-term memory, at some cost to earlier items. The authors propose a dual-stage account in which pointers in the focus of attention retrieve chunks from activated memory.
papers.authors: Luísa Superbia-Guimarães, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: Theories of consciousness from the perspective of an embedded processes view
papers.abstract: Surveys recent behavioral and neuroscientific work on consciousness and reconciles it with an information-processing view in which a capacity-limited focus of attention sits inside activated long-term memory. The authors propose that conscious content is formed by funneling information from sensory and frontal sources to a parietal hub, which they describe as roughly the converse of global broadcasting, and they offer recommendations for experimental psychologists.
papers.authors: Nelson Cowan, Nick I. Ahmed, Chenye Bao, Mackenzie N. Cissne, Ronald D. Yee-Flores, Roman M. Gutierrez, Braden Hayse, Madison L. Musich, Hamid Nourbakhshi, Nanan Nuraini, Emily E. Schroeder, Neyla Sfeir, Emilie Sparrow, Luísa Superbia-Guimarães

papers.title: Restoring a top-down control assumption: Salience effects in working memory are overcome with time
papers.abstract: Examines whether salient items are automatically prioritized in visual working memory. Across four experiments, the apparent salience advantage shrank greatly when participants had enough time to find all relevant objects, suggesting low-salience items are simply harder to find and encode under brief, crowded displays. The results favor flexible top-down control over automatic capture.
papers.authors: Nicholas Gaspelin, Nelson Cowan

papers.title: The Relation Between Attention and Memory
papers.abstract: A broad review of how attention and memory depend on each other, spanning working memory, long-term memory, individual differences, lifespan development, brain function and neuropsychological conditions. The authors organize this evidence around the embedded-processes view, in which a capacity-limited focus of attention operates within activated long-term memory, and they weigh it against rival theories, noting open questions.
papers.authors: Nelson Cowan, Chenye Bao, Brittney M. Bishop-Chrzanowski, Amy N. Costa, Nathaniel R. Greene, Dominic Guitard, Chenyuan Li, Madison L. Musich, Zehra E. Ünal

papers.title: The roles of attention, executive function and knowledge in cognitive ageing of working memory
papers.abstract: Reviews why working memory changes in older adulthood, weighing the contributions of attention, executive function and accumulated knowledge. The authors integrate behavioral findings on age-related decline and argue for which cognitive components account for it, and which remain preserved or compensatory.
papers.authors: Moshe Naveh-Benjamin, Nelson Cowan

0501.name: Nelson Roque
0501.department: Department of Human Development and Family Studies
0501.bio: Nelson Roque is an Assistant Professor at Pennsylvania State University specializing in the intersection of cognitive aging, vision science, and digital health technology. Roque's research employs ambulatory assessment frameworks and mobile health platforms to investigate the dynamics of visual attention and cognitive performance in real-world settings. Using computational phenotyping and passive sensing, Roque examines how environmental exposures, such as air quality, and behavioral factors, including sleep and technology use, influence the progression of cognitive decline in older adults. Their work focuses on the development of digital biomarkers for the detection of neurodegenerative conditions through remote, high-frequency smartphone assessments.
0501.research_direction: Dr. Roque has recently been investigating how interactions with digital technology shape cognitive function across the lifespan, shifting the field's focus from simple duration-based screen time to multidimensional models of digital engagement. Their recent work explores how active versus passive technology use, along with generational factors and stress, influences core cognitive mechanisms like processing speed, memory, and susceptibility to distraction in midlife and older adults. Additionally, they evaluate the methodological feasibility of mobile health research by surveying participant attitudes toward sharing active and passive sensor data via smartphones and wearables. Broadening their focus on structural health determinants, their research also leverages geospatial mapping to investigate demographic and socioeconomic disparities in national environmental resources, such as air quality monitoring networks.

papers.title: Screen time in context: Toward a theoretical model of digital engagement across the lifespan
papers.abstract: The paper argues that a single duration-based 'screen time' number is too crude to explain how digital technology affects people. Drawing on Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory, it proposes 'virtual microsystems' as a framework for the physical and digital contexts of use, and reviews how mode, purpose, timing, content and emotional tone of engagement shape cognitive and mental-health outcomes at different life stages. It closes with directions for multidimensional measurement and policy.
papers.authors: Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque

papers.title: Identifying air quality monitoring deserts in the United States
papers.abstract: The authors map which US counties have no EPA air quality monitoring station, terming them monitoring deserts, and relate this to county demographics and socioeconomics. They find that about 59% of counties, covering roughly 40% of US land and over 50 million residents, lack a monitor. Rural counties and those with larger minoritized populations are more likely to be deserts, with gaps concentrated in the Midwest and South.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Nelson A. Roque, Hailey Andrews, Alexis R. Santos-Lozada

papers.title: From screens to cognition: A scoping review of the impact of screen time on cognitive function in midlife and older adults
papers.abstract: A PRISMA-guided scoping review of 17 studies on screen use and cognition in adults aged 40 and older. Active screen use tended to go with better memory, executive function and attention, while passive use was linked to poorer verbal memory and global cognition. Education, activity, sleep and attitudes toward technology moderated the findings.
papers.authors: Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque

papers.title: Acceptability of Active and Passive Data Collection Methods for Mobile Health Research: Cross-Sectional Survey of an Online Adult Sample in the United States
papers.abstract: An online survey of about 1,500 US adults recruited through Prolific asked which kinds of active and passive digital data they would be willing to share for health research, alongside privacy concerns and technology use. The results inform how mobile and wearable studies, for example on dementia, can be designed to be acceptable to participants.
papers.authors: Nelson Roque, John Felt

papers.title: Cognitive Performance in the Digital Era
papers.abstract: Using the Mobile Monitoring of Cognitive Change symbol search task in 299 adults, the study examines how generation (Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z), perceived stress and subjective age relate to processing speed and the cost of distraction. It reports that age-related variables and stress shape susceptibility to distraction, and suggests longitudinal work on digital-era cohorts.
papers.venue: International Journal of Cyber Behavior, Psychology and Learning
papers.authors: Rinanda Rizky Amalia Shaleha, Nelson Roque

0502.name: Nestor Matthews
0502.department: Department of Psychology and Neuroscience Program
0502.bio: Nestor Matthews serves as Professor of Psychology and Chair of Neuroscience at Denison University, where they investigate the mechanisms of human sensory plasticity. Their research employs psychophysical methodologies to study perceptual learning, with a focus on how training affects sensitivity to visual motion, temporal order, and simultaneity. Matthews has documented the double dissociation of radial and rotational motion sensitivity and the ways in which global depth perception modulates local timing accuracy. Additionally, Matthews conducts comparative research on sensory expertise by examining populations such as professional drum corps performers to analyze the limits of temporal processing and cross-modal transfer between vision and audition.
0502.research_direction: Dr. Matthews has recently been studying how people perceive and extract structure from the everyday visual displays we use to communicate. Their recent work explores how observers learn to spot patterns such as main effects and interactions in simple two-by-two graphs, asking which perceptual grouping cues make those patterns easy or hard to see. They have also used signal detection methods to ask how accurately people judge the length of a sentence within a full page of text, treating reading layout as a psychophysics problem. Across both lines, the common thread is measuring how well and how quickly human observers can pick up relevant information from graphs and text.

papers.title: Learning to detect patterns in 2 × 2 graphs
papers.abstract: Effective visual communication and statistics pedagogy rely on observers' capacity to discern structured relationships within graphical displays. This investigation evaluated pattern detection in 2 × 2 graphs representing a continuous response variable across two bi-level predictor factors (Factor A on the abscissa and Factor B denoted by visual series markers). While previous research highlighted observers' verbal descriptions of main effects and interaction patterns, the perceptual grouping mechanisms underlying these judgments remained uncharacterized. In a preregistered trial-and-error classification task, 416 naive adults learned to categorize 2 × 2 line or bar graphs containing identical numeric data based on Factor A main effects, Factor B main effects, or two-way interactions. Line displays yielded significantly superior classification accuracy relative to bar charts for both interaction and Factor B configurations, whereas accuracy for Factor A main effects was uniformly poor across display formats. Additionally, participants trained on bar graphs frequently adopted an erroneous decision rule, reporting main effects only in the presence of an interaction; this classification bias was markedly reduced with line graphs. These results demonstrate that graph format and predictor assignment constrain the perceptual availability of statistical patterns through ensemble processing, informing visualization design and statistical literacy.
papers.authors: Nestor Matthews, Megan Lynn Broderick, Samantha Anne Kozlowski

papers.title: Omit needless words: Sentence length perception
papers.abstract: Textual brevity facilitates readability and information accessibility, but the psychophysical mechanisms that govern how human observers estimate sentence length remain largely uncharacterized. Applying signal detection theory paradigms, this study assessed sentence length discrimination among naive adult observers evaluating ecologically valid, full-page typographic layouts. Participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice task judging whether a bolded target sentence embedded within distractor prose contained more or fewer than 17 words. Findings indicated that observers discriminated target sentence length rapidly (median reaction times between 300 and 400 ms) and with high precision (~90% accuracy). Inverting the text array upside down yielded negligible latency penalties and minimal accuracy loss (90.7% correct for standard vs. 89.0% for flipped text), contrasting sharply with the robust inversion costs typical of orthographic reading and face recognition. Furthermore, observers systematically underestimated the length of mirror-reversed target sentences, a bias consistent with left-anchored scene syntax and left-to-right reading conventions. Error distribution analyses demonstrated that participants achieved high temporal and perceptual efficiency by employing a rapid text-line counting heuristic rather than explicit lexical enumeration, offering empirical support for line-based copy-editing strategies to reduce unnecessary phrasing.
papers.authors: Nestor Matthews, Folly Folivi

0504.name: Nicholas Gaspelin
0504.bio: Nicholas Gaspelin is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychological Sciences at the University of Missouri and the director of the Attention and Distraction Lab. Gaspelin’s research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms of selective attention, specifically the signal suppression account, which proposes that top-down inhibitory processes can prevent salient distractors from capturing attention. They utilize behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to analyze event-related potential (ERP) components such as the N2pc and distractor positivity (Pd). Gaspelin’s current work investigates how implicit learning and selection history influence attentional guidance and the efficiency of suppression in complex visual environments.
0504.research_direction: Dr. Gaspelin has recently been refining the signal suppression hypothesis, investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms by which the visual system actively inhibits salient distractors to prevent them from capturing attention. Their recent work explores how attentional control is dynamically learned, using both novel eye-tracking paradigms and massive, pooled datasets of saccadic behavior to examine whether an initial instance of distraction ultimately strengthens subsequent suppression. Additionally, they are investigating the spatial constraints of these inhibitory mechanisms, combining behavioral measures and EEG to test how distractor suppression operates within narrowly versus broadly focused attentional windows. To map the temporal and spatial dynamics of ignoring irrelevant visual information, Dr. Gaspelin frequently leverages precise oculomotor metrics alongside established neural markers of inhibitory processing, such as the distractor positivity ERP component.

papers.title: From capture to control: Initial capture increases learned suppression
papers.abstract: Proposes that a first instance of being distracted by a salient stimulus can actually strengthen later suppression of it. Using a new eye-tracking approach across three experiments with 120 college students, the authors show that initial capture precedes the onset of suppression, and that experiencing capture makes subsequent suppression more effective. The result reframes distraction as part of how attentional control is learned.
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: Ignoring salient distractors inside and outside the attentional window
papers.abstract: Tests the attentional window account, which says salient items capture attention only when attention is broadly focused. Behavioral and EEG measures show that salient distractors are suppressed even when they fall inside a narrowly or broadly focused attentional window, arguing against the idea that capture failures simply reflect a narrow window.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Steven J. Luck, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: What can a half-million saccades tell us about distractor suppression?
papers.abstract: Pools a very large body of eye-movement data from visual search experiments with salient distractors to ask what saccade behavior reveals about suppression. The analysis uses the large sample to characterize how often and when eyes are drawn to salient distractors and how this relates to the suppression account.
papers.authors: Kaitlyn N. Drennan, Nicholas Gaspelin

papers.title: Signal suppression 2.0: An updated account of attentional capture and suppression
papers.abstract: Updates the signal suppression hypothesis, the framework holding that salient stimuli generate a priority signal that can be actively inhibited so they fail to capture attention. The authors review the evidence and criticisms accumulated since the original proposal and refine the account, clarifying when capture occurs and how proactive and learned suppression operate. It serves as the current statement of the lab's central theory.
papers.authors: Nicholas Gaspelin, Xiaojin Ma, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: The Distractor Positivity Component and the Inhibition of Distracting Stimuli
papers.abstract: A collaborative review by a dozen researchers summarizing work using the distractor positivity (Pd) ERP component as a marker of inhibitory attentional processing. It evaluates what the Pd indexes, how it has been used to study whether salient stimuli automatically capture attention, and where interpretations remain contested.
papers.authors: Nicholas Gaspelin, Dominique Lamy, Howard E. Egeth, Heinrich R. Liesefeld, Dirk Kerzel, Ananya Mandal, Matthias M. Müller, Jeffrey D. Schall, Anna Schubö, Heleen A. Slagter, Brad T. Stilwell, Dirk van Moorselaar

0506.name: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti
0506.bio: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Yale University and a faculty member of the Wu Tsai Institute, where they investigate the ontogenetic origins of logical reasoning. Their research focuses on the 'logic of thought,' examining how preverbal infants and children utilize logical operations such as disjunctive syllogism and quantification to support learning and decision-making. Using methodologies including high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and behavioral paradigms, Cesana-Arlotti has provided evidence that logical concepts emerge before the acquisition of language. Their work explores the computational interface between these logical resources and adult visual perception to analyze the continuity of domain-general reasoning throughout development.
0506.research_direction: Dr. Cesana-Arlotti has recently been studying the origins of logical reasoning, asking whether infants, toddlers, and adults carry out simple deductions without language. Their recent work explores how a child or adult can rule out one option in an either-or situation and infer the other, and whether adults do this automatically while watching visual scenes. They also examine how young children and infants understand what is certain, likely, unlikely, possible, or impossible, and use that understanding to make decisions and predict what others will do. Together, this work tests whether a common logical machinery underlies reasoning about objects, agents, and word meanings early in development.

papers.title: Irresistibly Logical: Automatic Logical Inferences in Visual Scene Processing
papers.abstract: The capacity for deductive inference pervades intuitive reasoning, yet its automaticity in non-linguistic perception remains unresolved. Across five behavioral experiments, this investigation tests whether disjunctive elimination occurs spontaneously and involuntarily during visual scene processing in adults. Observers viewed animations where an ambiguous item was sampled into a cup from a two-item set, after which one candidate appeared outside the cup. Participants exhibited significantly accelerated response times when revealed outcomes matched the deductively entailed identity compared to when they violated it. This inferential advantage persisted across repeated trials, even when the logically implied target contradicted prior statistical base rates (a 2:1 sampling bias favoring the alternative outcome). Furthermore, the effect facilitated rapid object classification and dissociated from non-logical spatiotemporal object-tracking heuristics, demonstrating that deductive inferences operate automatically and imperviously to probabilistic counterevidence within visual scene perception.
papers.authors: Nathaniel Braswell, Chaz Firestone, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: Logical Concepts of (Im)possibility Guide Young Children's Decision‐Making
papers.abstract: Rational decision-making in stochastic environments depends on modal judgment: discriminating between states that are necessary, merely possible, or impossible. It has long been theorized that robust modal judgments emerge late in childhood, contingent upon mastering modal vocabulary. In two experiments, 96 children between 34 and 65 months old were tasked with assisting an agent to achieve a goal or prevent harm by interacting with apparatuses possessing distinct topological constraints. Preschoolers systematically chose the optimal course of action when options crossed qualitative, categorical modal boundaries (such as distinguishing impossible paths from possible or necessary outcomes). In contrast, children struggled when selections differed merely in continuous probability (e.g., distinguishing between 66% and 33% likelihoods). These results reveal that preschool children spontaneously deploy discrete logical modal concepts to direct instrumental decisions prior to the mastery of explicit modal language.
papers.authors: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti, Sofia Jáuregui, Peter Mazalik, Shaun Nichols, Justin Halberda

papers.title: Core Logic: Fourteen-month-olds exclude physical possibilities that would make an agent irrational
papers.abstract: Human reasoning is distinguished by the capacity to perform abstract computations that integrate information across disparate cognitive domains. This research investigates whether preverbal infants possess the logical resources to integrate physical probability with expectations of social rationality. Across three preregistered experiments, the authors demonstrate that both adults and 14-month-old infants spontaneously employ disjunctive syllogism (A or B; not A; therefore B) to resolve ambiguity in social events. Specifically, infants were shown an agent reaching for a hidden object whose identity was ambiguous between two physical possibilities. Infants exhibited increased looking times when the agent's subsequent behavior was inconsistent with a logically inferred preference, suggesting they had eliminated impossible outcomes to deduce the agent's goal. These findings provide evidence for a domain-general 'core logic' that serves as a foundation for human thought, functioning independently of natural language and specific domain-restricted representations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Zihan Wang, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: The origin of the possible: 12-month-olds' understanding of certain, likely, and unlikely events
papers.abstract: The capacity for modal cognition—representing and reasoning about potentiality and necessity—is fundamental to human planning and prediction. This study investigates the developmental origins of these abilities by examining whether 12-month-old infants can represent modal categories (e.g., certainty vs. mere possibility) before the acquisition of modal language. Using two preregistered habituation experiments, the researchers tested infants' ability to distinguish between future physical outcomes based on their probability levels. In Experiment 1, infants were presented with events having 100% vs. 66% probability, while Experiment 2 tested 66% vs. 33% probability. The results indicate that 12-month-olds can distinguish between likely and unlikely outcomes, suggesting they possess the cognitive resources to mentally represent and compare multiple possible future states. These findings challenge minimalistic views of early probabilistic intuition and suggest that a proto-modal representational system for potentiality emerges early in the ontogeny of the mind.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Şeref Can Esmer, Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti

papers.title: A Continuity in Logical Development: Domain-General Disjunctive Inference by Toddlers
papers.abstract: While preverbal infants show looking-time signatures consistent with elementary deductions, it remains contentious whether such inferences represent domain-general logic or domain-specific heuristics, and whether they persist into early childhood. In this study, 36 toddlers aged 2.3 to 3.2 years were tested across three distinct cognitive tasks: novel word-to-referent mapping, agentive preference induction, and physical race outcome prediction.
