Using high-resolution eye tracking, toddlers displayed systematic oculomotor double-checking—shifting fixation to examine and reject an alternative candidate prior to settling on the target—across all three contexts. Toddlers executed these disjunctive inferences successfully prior to formal schooling and without relying on explicit logical language, providing robust evidence for an ontogenetically continuous, domain-general logic of thought operating across diverse representational domains.
papers.authors: Nicolò Cesana-Arlotti, Justin Halberda

0507.name: Nihong Chen
0507.bio: Nihong Chen is a Professor at the School of Psychology, South China Normal University. Chen’s research investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception, focusing on how perceptual learning and attention reshape the functional architecture of the visual cortex. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysical modeling, they have characterized the cortical plasticity of areas like V3A and MT+ and explored the computational strategies the brain employs to resolve visual crowding. Chen’s current work examines how cortical population codes and multi-stage integration models facilitate object recognition in complex and ambiguous visual environments.
0507.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been studying how the human visual system combines information across space and features, and how experience reshapes it. Their recent work explores how perceptual learning changes the way working memory is stored in visual cortex, using fMRI to track whether sensory-like or more abstract memory codes are strengthened across the visual hierarchy. They also study how the brain binds features such as color and motion, how peripheral vision copes with crowding, and how focused attention shapes signal flow between visual areas. In addition, they compare how humans and deep neural networks learn the statistics of natural textures, and have written on how hierarchical and parallel processing in primate visual cortex relates to artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Perceptual learning reformats working memory codes along a reverse visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study asks how training on a visual motion discrimination task changes the way working memory contents are stored in the brain. After learning, early visual cortex (V1) held more precise sensory information during the delay period, and this gain tracked individual learning improvement, whereas mnemonic information in the intraparietal sulcus declined. The authors conclude that learning shifts memory resources from higher-order parietal areas toward high-fidelity sensory maintenance in early visual cortex.
papers.authors: Siyuan Cheng, Yiran Ge, Nihong Chen

papers.title: Hierarchical and parallel processing: From primate visual cortex to artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: This invited review surveys evidence that primate visual cortex combines serial, hierarchical stages with parallel pathways to support object recognition. It draws links between these biological organizing principles and the architectures of modern deep neural networks, discussing what each field could borrow from the other.
papers.authors: Nihong Chen, Hailin Ai, Jiewei Chen, Peng Zhang

papers.title: Learning Improves Peripheral Vision Via Enhanced Cortico-Cortical Communications
papers.abstract: The study trained observers on a peripheral visual task and used fMRI to see how the brain changed. Learning improved peripheral performance and strengthened communication between cortical areas along the visual hierarchy, rather than only altering local responses. This points to enhanced cortico-cortical interaction as a mechanism by which training can partly overcome peripheral limits such as crowding.
papers.authors: Yuwei Cui, Xincheng Lu, MiYoung Kwon, Nihong Chen

papers.title: A comparison of statistical learning of naturalistic textures between DCNNs and the human visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: Humans and deep convolutional networks were compared on learning the statistics of naturalistic textures. Human learning effects appeared along the visual hierarchy, and the paper contrasts this pattern with what different layers of DCNNs pick up. The results highlight both similarities and differences between biological and artificial visual learning.
papers.authors: Xincheng Lu, Ziqi Yuan, Yichi Zhang, Hailin Ai, Siyuan Cheng, Yiran Ge, Fang Fang, Nihong Chen

papers.title: Seeing in crowds: Averaging first, then max
papers.abstract: Crowding is thought to arise from over-integration of neighbouring items in peripheral vision. By measuring internal response distributions in an orientation crowding task, the authors found that observers' errors were better explained by picking the largest response than by simple averaging. A two-stage model with averaging followed by a signed-max operation accounts for the varied error patterns, suggesting linear and nonlinear pooling at different processing stages.
papers.authors: Xincheng Lu, Ruijie Jiang, Meng Song, Yiting Wu, Yiran Ge, Nihong Chen

0509.name: Niko A. Busch
0509.bio: Niko A. Busch is a Professor of Experimental Psychology who studies the neural mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and memory. Busch investigates how spontaneous brain oscillations, specifically in the alpha band (8–13 Hz), modulate cortical excitability and bias subjective perceptual experience prior to stimulus onset. Their methodology integrates electroencephalography (EEG) and psychophysics with a focus on open science, including leadership in the EEGManyPipelines project to assess the robustness of neuroimaging analysis. Current research in their laboratory examines rhythmic sampling in visual attention and the role of typicality in complex scene recognition.
0509.research_direction: Dr. Busch's recent work explores the temporal dynamics of visual memory across multiple timescales, investigating how spontaneous pre-stimulus fluctuations in brain states influence the initial capacity and decay of sensory traces. Using a combination of pupillometry and EEG signals like alpha-band lateralization and contralateral delay activity, they have recently been probing the effects of varying arousal and cortical excitability on iconic memory, as well as testing how spatial working memory is anchored across saccades in retinotopic versus screen-centered reference frames. Expanding this focus into higher-level visual cognition, their research also examines continuous, long-term recognition memory for natural scenes. Within this domain, they are utilizing event-related potentials and deep neural network features to disentangle parallel encoding and retrieval processes and to determine how a scene's representational distinctiveness within a visual category drives its memorability.

papers.title: Pre-stimulus pupil-linked arousal enhances initial stimulus availability and accelerates decay in iconic memory
papers.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in arousal, indexed by pupil size before a stimulus appears, are tested as a determinant of iconic memory. Fitting a model in which a brief stimulus evokes a decaying internal response, the study finds that higher pre-stimulus arousal increases how much information is initially available but makes it fade faster. The result shows that arousal shapes the time course of sensory availability, not just detection sensitivity or decision criteria.
papers.authors: Paul Justin Connor Smith, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Scene memorability reflects representational distinctiveness within visual categories
papers.abstract: Some images are remembered better than others, and this study tests whether that reflects how distinctive a scene is within its category. Across three experiments (N = 477), typical indoor scenes were categorized faster but remembered worse, with a more liberal recognition bias, than atypical ones. Distinctiveness computed from deep-network image representations accounted for these memory differences, linking subjective typicality to the underlying visual representation.
papers.authors: Charlotte Atzert, Filip Děchtěrenko, Jiří Lukavský, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Encoding and Retrieval in Parallel: ERP Correlates of Continuous Recognition Memory for Natural Scenes
papers.abstract: Participants judged a continuous stream of scene photographs from only four categories as old or new, so that encoding and retrieval happened at once on every trial. The study measures event-related potentials to separate the electrophysiological signatures of these overlapping memory processes for natural scenes. It extends the lab's work on long-term scene memory to a demanding, more realistic recognition setting.
papers.authors: Elena Cesnaite, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Spontaneous Alpha-Band Lateralization Extends Persistence of Visual Information in Iconic Memory by Modulating Cortical Excitability
papers.abstract: The authors ask why the brief sensory trace of a scene (iconic memory) lasts longer on some trials than others. Using EEG with a partial-report task, they show that spontaneous lateralization of alpha-band power before stimulus onset predicts how long information about the stimulus stays available. They interpret this as spontaneous shifts in cortical excitability that prolong the persistence of visual information.
papers.authors: Paul Justin Connor Smith, Niko A. Busch

papers.title: Contralateral delay activity and alpha lateralization reflect retinotopic and screen-centered reference frames in visual memory
papers.abstract: After an eye movement, a remembered item can be coded relative to the retina or relative to the screen. Using EEG markers of working memory (contralateral delay activity) and alpha lateralization, the authors show that these signals track both retinotopic and screen-centered reference frames. The work clarifies how spatial memory is anchored across saccades.
papers.authors: Wanja Alexander Mössing, Svea Christine Schröder, Anna Lena Biel, Niko A. Busch

0510.name: Nikolaus Kriegeskorte
0510.bio: Nikolaus Kriegeskorte is a Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Columbia University and the Director of Cognitive Imaging at the Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute. Kriegeskorte specializes in cognitive computational neuroscience, developing deep neural network models that simulate the human visual system's ability to recognize objects and scenes. They developed Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA), a methodology that characterizes neural representations through their geometry to facilitate comparisons between brain activity, behavior, and computational models. Their current research focuses on integrating feedforward and recurrent processing in brain-inspired AI to investigate the inferential nature of biological vision.
0510.research_direction: Dr. Kriegeskorte's recent work explores how deep neural networks can be optimized and rigorously evaluated to model the computations of the human visual system. They have recently been investigating top-down visual attention and high-level cortical responses by building biologically constrained, energy-efficient recurrent networks and transformer-based fMRI encoding models. To empirically distinguish between these highly flexible computational theories, their research examines optimal experimental design by synthesizing "controversial" stimuli tailored to make competing models predict fundamentally different neural responses. Additionally, they are expanding the analytical toolkits used to map neural population codes, developing advanced statistical methods to compare the geometric and topological organization of representational spaces across brains, stimuli, and artificial models.

papers.title: Making models disagree to learn how brains compute
papers.abstract: Neural network models can capture brain computations, but their huge flexibility means many different models fit experimental data equally well when tested on ordinary stimuli. This Review lays out how to design stimuli that make competing models predict different responses, so that experiments can actually tell them apart. It covers the choices involved (a prior over candidate images, a measure of model-discrimination power, and a way to select or synthesize the stimuli) and frames controversial stimuli as a bridge between naturalistic and artificial stimulus sets, tied to Bayesian optimal experimental design.
papers.authors: Tal Golan, Heiko H. Schütt, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: How attention saves energy in vision
papers.abstract: The paper builds a recurrent network, the Energy-efficient Attention Network, in which top-down multiplicative gain over features, space and time is trained under a joint objective of task accuracy and biologically grounded energy costs that include the attention-control circuitry itself. On a search task requiring identification and localization, the model concentrates energy on relevant locations and features and cuts total energy by up to 50% at matched accuracy. It also reproduces classic attention effects on firing rates, variability, noise correlations and V4-to-V1 feedback suppression, and best matches human errors when combining spatial and feature attention.
papers.authors: Eivinas Butkus, Zhuofan Ying, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: Transformer brain encoders explain human high-level visual responses
papers.abstract: Standard fMRI encoding models linearly map deep-network features to voxels, which needs many parameters and ignores the spatial structure of feature maps. The authors instead use an attention mechanism, so each voxel or region queries the image features through a learned, image-dependent read-out rather than a fixed receptive field. This transformer encoder predicts high-level visual cortex responses better than linear baselines, uses far fewer parameters, and yields interpretable maps of what each region attends to.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 38)
papers.authors: Hossein Adeli, Sun Minni, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: The topology and geometry of neural representations
papers.abstract: Beyond distances between activity patterns, the authors ask how neural population codes are organized topologically. They introduce topological representational similarity analysis (tRSA), which uses geo-topological summary statistics that are robust to noise and to distortions between individuals while remaining sensitive to how representations are arranged. Applied to simulated and real data, it separates features of representational structure that geometry alone misses.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Baihan Lin, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

papers.title: Statistical inference on representational geometries
papers.abstract: Representational geometry analyses compare brain regions and models by their pattern of distances between stimulus representations, but proper inference must generalize over both subjects and stimuli. The authors develop bootstrap and noise-ceiling based methods, including a flexible model comparison framework, that resample both subjects and conditions, and validate them on simulations and fMRI, calcium imaging and human data. The result is a principled, widely applicable toolkit for testing which models explain representational geometry.
papers.authors: Heiko H. Schütt, Alexander D. Kipnis, Jörn Diedrichsen, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

0511.name: Nikolaus Weiskopf
0511.institution: Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences
0511.bio: Nikolaus Weiskopf is the Director of the Department of Neurophysics at the Max Planck Institute for Human Cognitive and Brain Sciences and holds honorary professorships at Leipzig University and University College London. Weiskopf’s research focuses on the development of 'in vivo histology,' a technique using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) to non-invasively map the human brain's microstructure, including myelin and iron content. By integrating high-resolution MRI with biophysical modeling, Weiskopf studies cortical laminar architecture and fine-scale brain connectivity. Their work bridges the gap between macroscopic neuroimaging and microscopic anatomy to investigate the structural foundations of brain function and pathology.
0511.research_direction: Dr. Weiskopf has recently been advancing the development and application of ultra-high-field quantitative MRI to probe the fine-scale microstructure and functional architecture of the brain. Their recent work explores methodological frontiers at 7 Tesla, developing novel sequence models for sub-millimeter T2 mapping and assessing how venous vasculature impacts the spatial specificity of gradient-echo versus spin-echo BOLD signals during layer-specific fMRI in the visual cortex. Beyond sequence development, they are investigating visual connectivity by combining diffusion imaging and microscopy to map the retinotopic layout of short U-fibers linking V1 and V2. Additionally, they study the plasticity and evolution of cortical myelin, examining how long-term sensory deprivation from congenital blindness alters early visual cortex microstructure and how motor cortex lateralization differs between humans and chimpanzees.

papers.title: Congenital blindness reduces myelination in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using quantitative MRI that is sensitive to myelin, the study compares the visual cortex of people born blind with that of sighted people. It asks whether the loss of visual experience changes how heavily early visual cortex is myelinated, and reports lower myelination in the blind group. The work links long-term sensory deprivation to the microstructure of the cortex rather than only to its function.
papers.authors: Anna-Lena Stroh, Luke J. Edwards, Daniel Haenelt, Fakhereh Movahedian Attar, Kerrin J. Pine, Robert Trampel, Marcin Szwed, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Evolution of the motor cortex microstructure and its lateralization: a comparative study of chimpanzees and humans
papers.abstract: High-resolution quantitative MRI is used to compare cortical microstructure in the leg, hand and face regions of motor cortex in chimpanzees and humans. The study tests whether the strongly myelinated hand-knob and the hemispheric asymmetry linked to human right-handedness also appear in great apes. It provides an evolutionary view of how motor cortex microstructure relates to hand specialisation.
papers.authors: Maelig Chauvel, Evgeniya Kirilina, Ilona Lipp, Fabian Buettner, Carsten Jäger, Kerrin J. Pine, Luke J. Edwards, Sophia J. Ebel, Katja S. Kopp, Saskia Helbling, Peter McColgan, Diana Rose, Tobias Gräßle, Richard McElreath, Denis Chaimow, Catherine Crockford, Roman M. Wittig, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Short association fibres form topographic sheets in the human V1-V2 processing stream
papers.abstract: The authors combine high-resolution diffusion MRI with post-mortem microscopy to trace the short U-fibres linking V1 and V2. They find that these fibres are arranged in sheet-like bundles that preserve the retinotopic layout of the visual field. The result gives a fine-scale wiring picture between early visual areas that had not been available in living humans.
papers.authors: Fakhereh Movahedian Attar, Evgeniya Kirilina, Denis Chaimow, Daniel Haenelt, Christian Schneider, Luke J. Edwards, Kerrin J. Pine, Carsten Jäger, Katja Reimann, Andreas Pohlmann, João Periquito, Tobias Streubel, Robert Trampel, Siawoosh Mohammadi, Thoralf Niendorf, Markus Morawski, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: Spatial specificity of the functional gradient echo and spin echo BOLD signal across cortical depth at 7 T
papers.abstract: The paper measures how well gradient-echo and spin-echo BOLD fMRI localise neural activity across cortical layers in the human visual cortex at 7 T. It compares the two contrasts at fine spatial scale to see how much the venous vasculature blurs the signal in each. The findings guide which acquisition is better suited for laminar and columnar fMRI.
papers.authors: Daniel Haenelt, Robert Trampel, Denis Chaimow, Amir Shmuel, Martin I. Sereno, Nikolaus Weiskopf

papers.title: High-resolution quantitative T2 mapping of the human brain at 7 T using a multi-echo spin-echo sequence and dictionary-based modeling
papers.abstract: The authors build a 7 T multi-echo spin-echo sequence and a dictionary-based signal model to estimate T2 relaxation. This yields sub-millimetre whole-brain T2 maps that correct for the imperfections of the acquisition. The maps offer a quantitative tissue-property contrast for detailed anatomical and microstructural studies at ultra-high field.
papers.authors: Jochen Schmidt, Dvir Radunsky, Patrick Scheibe, Carsten Jäger, Noam Ben-Eliezer, Robert Trampel, Nikolaus Weiskopf

0513.name: Nilsu Atilgen
0513.lab_name: Reading, Eye-movements, Attention and Digital Interfaces Lab (READ-lab)
0513.bio: Nilsu Atilgen is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Bilkent University and a Scientific Consultant for The Readability Consortium. Their research examines the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of reading, specifically focusing on how sensory constraints such as visual crowding and peripheral vision influence fluency. Atilgen utilizes psychophysical methods and eye-tracking to study how typographic variables and digital display settings affect reading performance for individuals with dyslexia and low vision. This work connects vision science with human-computer interaction to address digital accessibility and inclusive information design.
0513.research_direction: Dr. Atilgen has recently been studying how people read and write, and how the visual form of text affects that process. They examine how adults pick up the statistical rules that govern which letter sequences are allowed in words, using typing as a way to see this learning through production rather than perception. They also investigate how typographic choices such as font and letter spacing change reading speed and comprehension in school-age children, including differences between individual readers.

papers.title: Statistical learning of orthotactic constraints: Evidence from typing
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the acquisition of orthotactic constraints—the statistical regularities governing letter sequences—within the motor modality of typing. Across three experiments using a typing-to-dictation paradigm, the researchers demonstrate that adult participants rapidly internalize novel first-order and complex second-order sequential rules through production. The findings reveal that while learners successfully acquire coda-based constraints, acquisition of onset constraints is less consistent, suggesting that the underlying mechanism for new sequencing rules relies on a chaining-type process rather than hierarchical representation. Critically, the study provides evidence that orthotactic learning is functionally independent of phonotactic learning, supporting the existence of domain-general incremental learning principles that operate across distinct modalities of language production.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Nilsu Atılgan, Nazbanou Nozari

papers.title: The Influence of Format Readability on Children’s Reading Speed and Comprehension
papers.abstract: This study examines how typographic variables—specifically font face and character spacing—modulate reading performance in a pediatric population (grades 3–5). Researchers manipulated eight distinct fonts (serif vs. sans serif) and three levels of character spacing (narrow, normal, wide) while measuring reading speed and comprehension through narrative text passages. Linear mixed-effects modeling revealed that passages presented in Roboto and Arial yielded significantly higher reading velocities at the group level. On an individual basis, students demonstrated substantial performance gains when matched with their personal 'best-fit' font variation, without observing a speed–comprehension trade-off. The results emphasize the importance of individualized typographic formatting in educational technology to support fluency and literacy development.
papers.authors: Stephanie L. Day, Nilsu Atılgan, Amy E. Giroux, Ben D. Sawyer

0514.name: Nitzan Censor
0514.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0514.bio: Nitzan Censor is a Professor at Tel Aviv University investigating the neurobehavioral mechanisms underlying human perceptual and motor learning. Their research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, non-invasive brain stimulation, and functional neuroimaging to examine how skill-based memories are formed, modified, and consolidated within neural representation systems. Censor studies the temporal dynamics of memory reactivation and the role of offline consolidation in learning and memory modification. Their work also addresses the interaction between visual memory representations and computational models such as convolutional neural networks to decode the dynamics of human vision over time.
0514.research_direction: Dr. Censor has recently been investigating the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning and the dynamic nature of visual memory. Their recent work explores whether brief memory reactivations can replace exhaustive repetitive training to efficiently drive visual learning and spatial generalization, using fMRI to map the neural networks supporting this process. Additionally, they are utilizing convolutional neural networks to probe how the reliance on low-level visual features versus high-level conceptual representations changes as working memory transitions into long-term memory. Beyond basic vision science, Dr. Censor is translating their memory reactivation frameworks into clinical applications, testing whether hippocampal-targeted TMS or directed forgetting of associated verbal content can successfully weaken intrusive negative visual memories in populations with PTSD.

papers.title: Brief memory reactivations enable generalization of offline visual perceptual learning mechanisms
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning in adults usually stays tied to the trained retinotopic location. Here, participants encoded a visual discrimination at one location and then received brief five-trial reactivations on separate days at that same location. Performance at an untrained location improved markedly, whereas a control without reactivations showed little transfer, suggesting reactivation promotes offline generalization and could be a more efficient route to learning.
papers.authors: Kondat T, Sasaki Y, Watanabe T, Censor N

papers.title: Hippocampal-network transcranial magnetic stimulation to target reactivated intrusive memories: A proof-of-concept study in PTSD treatment
papers.abstract: This proof-of-concept clinical study combines reactivation of traumatic memories with TMS targeted at a hippocampal network in people with PTSD. The aim was to test whether modulating a reactivated intrusive memory can be done safely and to gauge its effect on symptoms. It is the clinical translation of the lab's memory reactivation and neuromodulation research.
papers.authors: Dezachyo O, Yair N, Mendelovich N, Tik N, Pine DS, Sharon H, Tavor I, Bar-Haim Y, Censor N

papers.title: Targeting memory of embedded positive verbal content indirectly modulates negative visual memory
papers.abstract: Participants saw sequences of positive words embedded among negative pictures and were then told to remember or forget the words. Intentionally forgetting the positive words weakened memory for the negative pictures that followed them, and even without verbal retrieval, remember instructions reduced negative visual memory indirectly. The results suggest a way to weaken distressing visual memories by working through associated positive content, relevant to PTSD.
papers.authors: Kozak S, Markovits T, Hacohen N, Bar-Haim Y, Censor N

papers.title: Distinct Neural Plasticity Enhancing Visual Perception
papers.abstract: The study asks whether visual perceptual learning can be made efficient by reactivating a consolidated memory rather than repeating training. Twenty participants who received only five-trial reactivations on separate days improved about as much as a matched group given standard repetition-based training. fMRI showed that reactivation-induced learning drew more on bilateral intraparietal sulcus activity and changed temporal-parietal resting connectivity in ways that tracked behavioral gains, implying attention and control regions support this faster route to learning.
papers.authors: Kondat T, Tik N, Sharon H, Tavor I, Censor N

papers.title: Convolutional neural networks uncover the dynamics of human visual memory representations over time
papers.abstract: The authors used the layer hierarchy of a convolutional neural network to build distractors that resemble a remembered image at low or high visual feature levels, then measured how memory strength depended on each level. Working memory relied about equally on low- and high-level features, but from a few minutes to the next day, memory leaned increasingly on high-level, conceptual representations. The work links deep-network models to the time course of human visual memory.
papers.authors: Zohar E, Kozak S, Abeles D, Shahar M, Censor N

0515.name: Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana
0515.bio: Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana is an Assistant Professor of Biomedical Engineering at Columbia University and the principal investigator of the Systems Intelligence Lab. Their research investigates the neural computations and coding schemes that facilitate adaptive cognitive processes, such as flexible decision-making, memory maintenance, and contextual information processing. By integrating biologically constrained recurrent neural networks with experimental data from human intracranial recordings and functional neuroimaging, Rungratsameetaweemana characterizes the mechanisms of goal-directed information transformation across the cortical hierarchy. Their work demonstrates that early sensory regions play an active, task-dependent role in shaping neural representations to support flexible behaviors.
0515.research_direction: Dr. Rungratsameetaweemana has recently been investigating the computational and physiological mechanisms that support working memory and flexible top-down visual processing. Their recent work explores how cellular and synaptic heterogeneity shape the temporal dynamics and robustness of working memory, utilizing both artificial recurrent neural networks and human single-neuron recordings. Alongside this memory research, they are studying how shifting categorization rules and top-down feedback dynamically reshape sensory representations in the early visual cortex, combining human fMRI with hierarchical network models evaluating efficient coding and stimulus bias. To link these system-level phenomena to cortical microcircuits, they are also modeling how biologically constrained architectures, such as disinhibitory interneuron networks, gate top-down signals to enable context-dependent behavior.

papers.title: Disinhibitory signaling enables flexible coding of top-down information in cortical networks
papers.abstract: Using biologically constrained recurrent network models, the authors show that disinhibitory inhibitory-neuron circuits allow top-down signals to flexibly gate and reshape cortical representations. This supports context-dependent coding across tasks. The model makes predictions about how inhibitory interneuron subtypes support flexible behavior.
papers.authors: Tomas G. Aquino, Robert Kim, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Random noise promotes slow heterogeneous synaptic dynamics important for robust working memory computation
papers.abstract: Using recurrent neural networks trained on working-memory tasks, the study shows that injecting random noise during training pushes networks toward heterogeneous synapses with slow short-term dynamics. This synaptic diversity makes memory maintenance more robust to perturbations. The work links noise, synaptic timescales and stable working-memory computation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana, Robert Kim, Thiparat Chotibut, Terrence J. Sejnowski

papers.title: Dynamic categorization rules alter representations in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Participants categorized the same visual stimuli under changing rules while undergoing fMRI. Representations in visual cortex, including early areas, shifted with the active categorization rule, rather than simply reflecting fixed stimulus features. The results indicate that early sensory regions are actively reshaped by task demands.
papers.authors: Margaret M. Henderson, John T. Serences, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Neural heterogeneity shapes the temporal structure of human working memory
papers.abstract: Single-neuron recordings from human patients are analyzed to ask whether working memory relies on sustained firing or on transient coordinated activity. The study finds that heterogeneity across neurons shapes the temporal structure of memory representations. This links cellular diversity to working-memory dynamics in humans.
papers.authors: Daria Kussovska, Robert Kim, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

papers.title: Feedback promotes efficient-coding while attenuating bias in recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: A three-layer hierarchical continuous-time RNN was trained on biased versus unbiased stimulus distributions. The network encodes high-probability stimuli more strongly, consistent with efficient coding, and reducing top-down feedback amplifies this bias at the cost of rare stimuli. Feedback therefore protects processing of low-probability inputs.
papers.authors: Holly Kular, Robert Kim, John Serences, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana

0516.name: Oakyoon Cha
0516.lab_name: DCANT Lab (Dynamic Cognition, Attention, & Neural Timing Lab)
0516.bio: Oakyoon Cha is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Sogang University and director of the DCANT Lab, following a tenure as a faculty member at Sungshin Women's University. Cha’s research utilizes psychophysics, EEG, and computational modeling to investigate the mechanisms of visual awareness, with an emphasis on ensemble perception and perceptual rhythms. They examine how the human visual system summarizes complex information from large stimulus sets and how neural oscillations contribute to a continuous visual experience. Cha’s work also explores individual differences in object recognition and the underlying domain-general abilities involved in statistical visual processing.
0516.research_direction: Dr. Cha has recently been studying how the visual system summarizes groups of similar items, such as a crowd of faces. Their work asks whether people can judge the most common category or the number of distinct categories in a set, rather than just averages, and whether faces in these group judgments are processed as whole faces or by parts. They have also developed a statistical framework for finding rhythmic temporal structure in behavioral data, such as response times and the alternating perceptual phases seen in binocular rivalry.

papers.title: Categorical frequency judgments as effective ensemble judgments for object features
papers.abstract: Visual ensemble perception research has predominantly concentrated on univariate summary metrics, such as mean and variance, which often fail to account for the multidimensional complexity inherent in natural visual stimuli. This investigation examines whether categorical frequency statistics—specifically the mode (the most prevalent category within a set) and diversity (the number of distinct categories)—operate as viable ensemble representations for complex visual entities. In Study 1, the shared variance between mode identification and diversity discrimination across facial identities was evaluated, establishing that observers reliably track categorical distributions of facial identities. In Study 2, the evaluation of mode extraction was extended across disparate visual classes, specifically comparing facial identities with novel geometric silhouettes (blobs). The findings reveal significant shared behavioral covariance across categorical frequency tasks regardless of visual category, indicating that categorical summary statistics engage domain-general ensemble mechanisms that operate effectively across high-dimensional object features.
papers.authors: Oakyoon Cha

papers.title: Procedure for extracting temporal structure embedded within psychophysical data
papers.abstract: Although extensive neurophysiological evidence demonstrates that perceptual and cognitive processing is modulated by intrinsic neural rhythms (such as theta and alpha oscillations), isolating behavioral markers of these rhythmic dynamics from psychophysical data remains technically challenging. To resolve these methodological limitations, the authors introduce the Parametric Analysis of Temporal Structure (PATS) framework. PATS models duration data—such as response times and multistable perceptual dominance phases in binocular rivalry—by fitting a rhythmic cumulative distribution function (rCDF) that incorporates periodic sinusoidal modulations into standard cumulative distribution functions. The method quantifies the incremental variance accounted for by the oscillatory component relative to a non-rhythmic baseline and rescales fitted oscillation amplitudes accordingly. Psychophysical experiments and simulations indicate that PATS exhibits high statistical power and parameter stability even when applied to small sample sizes, establishing a robust computational pipeline for decoding discrete temporal periodicities in behavioral time courses.
papers.authors: Oakyoon Cha, Randolph Blake

papers.title: Faces are Not Processed Holistically in Ensemble Judgments
papers.abstract: Tests whether face ensembles are processed holistically by asking whether bottom halves of faces can be selectively ignored when judging the average identity of top halves. Bayesian evidence indicates selective attention to parts is preserved, with only a small configural effect.
papers.authors: Oakyoon Cha, Isabel Gauthier

0517.name: OH-SANG KWON
0517.institution: Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology
0517.bio: Oh-Sang Kwon is an Associate Professor at UNIST whose research examines the computational principles of human perception and action. Kwon utilizes Bayesian modeling and psychophysical techniques to investigate how the brain integrates sensory signals with internal models of scene statistics to form inferences. They have modeled visual illusions as products of rational inference and developed accounts for the interaction between motion and position perception. Current research focuses on the effects of sensory history on perception and the cognitive and perceptual changes associated with aging.
0517.research_direction: Dr. Kwon's recent work spans computational vision, temporal psychophysics, and sensorimotor control to investigate how the brain processes sensory and conceptual information. They have recently been exploring how the brain resolves perceptual ambiguity using probabilistic and machine learning frameworks, specifically asking how preceding scene motion biases visual-vestibular heading estimates and using generative adversarial networks to model attractive and repulsive biases in orientation perception. In the temporal domain, their research examines how predictive processing and event-termination cues dilate perceived time, as well as the psychophysical filtering mechanisms that govern brief flicker or twinkle artifacts in luminance and color displays. Additionally, they are investigating ideomotor theory by testing how the abstract conceptual meaning of a stimulus unintentionally manifests in physical movement control.

papers.title: Environmental motion presented ahead of self-motion modulates heading direction estimation
papers.abstract: The study asks how the brain judges its own direction of travel when the surrounding scene was already moving before self-motion began. Using visual and vestibular heading tasks combined with computational modeling, the authors show that motion in the environment preceding the movement systematically biases heading estimates. The results are interpreted within a probabilistic inference framework in which the brain decides whether earlier scene motion should be attributed to the world or to the self.
papers.authors: Liana Nafisa Saftari, Jongmin Moon, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Attractive and Repulsive Perceptual Biases Naturally Emerge in Generative Adversarial Inference
papers.abstract: The authors train a generative adversarial network to perform perceptual inference from noisy oriented-grating stimuli, without hand-specified likelihoods or priors. The trained network spontaneously reproduces the classic human pattern in which estimates are attracted toward prior expectations under high stimulus noise but repelled from them under low noise. This offers a single machine-learning account linking efficient coding and Bayesian inference to bias reversals.
papers.authors: Hyun-Jun Jeon, Hansol Choi, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Temporal processing underlying transient twinkle perception in luminance and chromatic stimuli
papers.abstract: The paper examines the brief flicker-like 'twinkle' percept that appears at transient changes in luminance or color. Psychophysical measurements are used to characterize the temporal filtering that governs when such twinkles are visible for luminance versus chromatic stimuli. The findings inform how display and stimulus temporal properties determine visible artifacts.
papers.authors: Chang-Yeong Han, Seonggyu Choe, Eun Cho, Hyo-sun Kim, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: An event-termination cue causes perceived time to dilate
papers.abstract: Perceived duration is shown to stretch when a cue signals that an ongoing event is about to end. Across psychophysical experiments, the authors relate this dilation to expectation about event termination. The result links time perception to predictive processing.
papers.authors: Seonggyu Choe, Oh-Sang Kwon

papers.title: Strong evidence for ideomotor theory: Unwilled manifestation of the conceptual attribute in movement control
papers.abstract: The work tests ideomotor theory, the idea that thinking of an action's concept shapes the movement itself. Experiments show that the conceptual attribute of a stimulus (for example its meaning) is unintentionally expressed in motor output. The authors argue this supports ideomotor accounts of movement control.
papers.authors: Yun Kyoung Shin, Seonggyu Choe, Oh-Sang Kwon

0518.name: Okihide Hikosaka
0518.bio: Okihide Hikosaka is an investigator at the National Eye Institute, where they head the Neuronal Networks Section within the Laboratory of Sensorimotor Research. Hikosaka’s research focuses on the neurophysiological mechanisms of the basal ganglia, specifically their role in controlling saccadic eye movements, habit formation, and reward-based decision-making. Utilizing electrophysiological recordings and optogenetic manipulations in non-human primates, Hikosaka’s work has identified parallel circuits that independently process stable long-term values versus flexible short-term reward associations. These findings regarding the lateral habenula and dopamine neuron diversity address mechanisms of motivational control and their relationship to neurological and psychiatric conditions such as Parkinson's disease and depression.
0518.research_direction: Dr. Hikosaka's recent work explores the neural circuitry underlying value-based decision making and saccadic action control in non-human primates. Using single-unit recordings and pharmacological manipulations, they have recently been investigating how basal ganglia structures traditionally viewed as motor brakes, such as the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, and substantia nigra, actively balance the facilitation and suppression of goal-directed eye movements. Their research also examines the maintenance of motivation in volatile environments, probing how the lateral habenula and periaqueductal gray dynamically encode reward prediction errors and remaining reward expectancy. Additionally, Dr. Hikosaka is utilizing retrograde optogenetics in awake macaques to dissect corticotectal pathways, questioning how mixed visual and motor signals converge from the frontal eye field to the superior colliculus to drive saccades.

papers.title: Lateral habenula and periaqueductal gray neurons signal reward prediction error and continuity of remaining reward expectancy
papers.abstract: The study contrasts phasic reward-prediction-error signals in the lateral habenula with tonic periaqueductal gray activity that tracks how much reward is still expected after negative outcomes. The balance between the two signals predicts whether animals keep seeking reward or give up after unexpected negative events. The authors propose this maintains motivational continuity in volatile environments.
papers.authors: Hyunchan Lee, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Retrograde optogenetics reveals sensorimotor convergence within a corticotectal pathway of non-human primates
papers.abstract: Using retrograde optogenetics in awake macaques, the team tested whether frontal eye field output to the superior colliculus carries pure motor commands or mixed sensory-motor signals. Activating the pathway evoked contralateral saccades and shifted reaction times, and tagged FEF-to-SC neurons proved to be a heterogeneous mix of visual, visuomotor and motor cells. The output converges on SC in a way that supports broad sensorimotor signaling.
papers.authors: Xuefei Yu, Atul Gopal, Ken-ichi Inoue, Martin O. Bohlen, Genevieve M. Kuczewski, Marc A. Sommer, Hendrikje Nienborg, Masahiko Takada, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Beyond the brake: The subthalamic nucleus predominantly facilitates action in non-human primates
papers.abstract: Across 187 STN neurons recorded while macaques made value-based sequential choices, clustering revealed three populations. About 89% of task-responsive neurons showed facilitative activity scaled by learned object value, mostly locked to the target rather than the movement, while a small group signaled negative value for unrewarded objects. The findings challenge the classic view of the STN as mainly a brake.
papers.authors: Atsushi Yoshida, Richard J. Krauzlis, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Excitatory drive to the globus pallidus external segment facilitates action initiation in non-human primates
papers.abstract: Recording single GPe neurons in macaques performing a sequential accept/reject choice task, the authors find clusters that increase firing for saccades to both good and bad objects and others selectively tied to good-object saccades or to rejection. Blocking glutamate receptors in caudal dorsal GPe lengthened saccade latencies and reduced rejection saccades. The results argue the primate GPe actively facilitates actions rather than only serving as an indirect-pathway brake.
papers.authors: Atsushi Yoshida, Okihide Hikosaka

papers.title: Contribution of glutamatergic projections to neurons in the nonhuman primate substantia nigra pars reticulata for reactive inhibition
papers.abstract: Individual SNr neurons in macaques lowered their firing when a target was chosen and raised it when a target was rejected, showing bidirectional control of saccades. Pharmacologically blocking glutamatergic input to lateral SNr disrupted saccade control and impaired suppression of reflexive saccades. This gives causal evidence that excitatory input, possibly from the subthalamic nucleus, drives SNr-mediated action suppression.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Atsushi Yoshida, Okihide Hikosaka

0520.name: Oliver Layton
0520.bio: Oliver W. Layton is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Colby College. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying human navigation and self-motion perception, combining large-scale dynamical neural modeling with psychophysical experiments to investigate how the primate brain processes optic flow. Layton developed the Competitive Dynamics model to simulate interactions between cortical areas such as MSTd, MT, and V1, exploring how these systems facilitate figure-ground segregation and world-relative object motion recovery. Their current work evaluates the efficacy of accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks in modeling the primate dorsal stream and applies bio-inspired algorithms to autonomous navigation.
0520.research_direction: Dr. Layton has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying self-motion perception and optic flow processing. Their recent work explores how well various artificial neural networks model the tuning properties of macaque area MSTd, specifically testing whether accuracy-optimized deep networks or unsupervised autoencoders better capture dorsal stream representations. Alongside this theoretical modeling, they are examining how network architectural choices, such as activation functions and sparsity constraints, influence both computational robustness and biological realism. Furthermore, their research extends into human psychophysics, investigating how the visual system parses complex optic flow to accurately judge world-relative object motion during active locomotion.

papers.title: For MSTd, Autoencoding is all you need
papers.abstract: The authors compared 54 artificial neural networks on how well their units match the optic-flow tuning of neurons in macaque area MSTd. Accuracy at estimating self-motion turned out not to predict neural alignment, whereas networks trained simply to reconstruct their motion input (autoencoders) matched MSTd best, and adding sparsity or non-negativity constraints made the match worse. This suggests the dorsal stream is organized around an unsupervised, efficient-representation objective rather than task accuracy, unlike the goal-driven picture that works for the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: What Do Deep Neural Networks Reveal About the Neural Mechanisms of Self-Motion Perception?
papers.abstract: A single-author overview that reviews what deep networks trained on self-motion tasks tell us about area MSTd. It highlights the paradox that accuracy-trained networks align weakly with MSTd while unsupervised autoencoders align much better, and proposes the brain favors efficient representation over accuracy in self-motion processing.
papers.venue: VISION (Journal of the Vision Society of Japan)
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton

papers.title: Accuracy optimized neural networks do not effectively model optic flow tuning in brain area MSTd
papers.abstract: Convolutional networks that predict neural responses well in the ventral stream were tested as models of optic-flow tuning in dorsal area MSTd and compared with a non-negative matrix factorization model that captures many MSTd properties. Although the CNNs estimated self-motion accurately, their units fit MSTd tuning poorly, even when variants were built to mimic the NNMF constraints of sparse coding and non-negative weights. The work argues that accuracy-optimized deep networks are not sufficient models of the dorsal stream.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: ReLU, Sparseness, and the Encoding of Optic Flow in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The study asks how the choice of activation function (ReLU, leaky ReLU, GELU, Mish) affects CNNs and MLPs trained to estimate self-motion from optic flow for robotic navigation. ReLU and leaky ReLU networks were more accurate on novel flow patterns and more robust under difficult conditions, plausibly because they produce sparser representations. Their units also showed optic-flow tuning more similar to that of MSTd neurons.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Siyuan Peng, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: The accuracy of object motion perception during locomotion
papers.abstract: People can judge how objects move relative to the stationary world even while moving themselves, but simulated-self-motion studies find biased judgments. Following a recent report that real walking with optic flow yields accurate judgments, the authors tested comparable conditions in a controlled setting and examined how accurately observers recover world-relative object motion. The results speak to how the visual system factors out self-motion using optic flow.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Melissa S. Parade, Brett R. Fajen

0521.name: Olivia S. Cheung
0521.bio: Cheung is an Assistant Professor who studies the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying high-level visual perception and the acquisition of perceptual expertise. They utilize a multimodal approach integrating behavioral psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to examine how visual features and conceptual knowledge interact to represent categories such as faces, objects, and musical notation. Cheung’s research focuses on the neural malleability of the ventral stream, specifically exploring how experience and learning shape category-selective brain regions. Additionally, they investigate the influence of socio-emotional factors and implicit biases on visual recognition and holistic face processing.
0521.research_direction: Dr. Cheung has recently been studying how people perceive and judge faces, and what experience and social factors shape those judgments. One line of their work asks what the different behavioral tests of holistic face processing, in which the features of a face are perceived as a unified whole, actually measure, and why these tests often disagree. They also examine how holistic processing of other-race and other-age faces relates to implicit bias and to how much contact a person has with those groups. A related thread looks at first impressions from faces, such as trustworthiness and competence, including how implicit bias and experience affect trust judgments of other-race faces and how masculinity or femininity of politicians' faces affects competence judgments and predictions of election outcomes.

papers.title: Two faces of holistic face processing: Facilitation and interference underlying part-whole and composite effects
papers.abstract: Holistic processing, characterized by the obligatory perceptual integration of disparate facial features into a unified gestalt, is widely considered a defining hallmark of face perception. Established behavioral paradigms—specifically the part-whole task, the standard partial-design composite task, and the complete composite face task—are conventionally used to quantify these holistic effects. However, empirical discrepancies and weak or absent inter-task correlations across diverse populations and experimental manipulations have challenged the construct validity and theoretical coherence of a singular holistic mechanism. Here, the distinct contributions of facilitation and interference were isolated within the complete composite paradigm to evaluate their correspondence with performance in other tasks. Generalized linear mixed-effects modeling and individual differences analyses revealed that the holistic effect observed in the part-whole task was selectively associated with facilitation rather than interference in the complete composite task. In contrast, the holistic effect in the standard composite task correlated specifically with interference and showed no relationship with facilitation. These results demonstrate that conventional paradigms probe dissociable facets of holistic processing, establishing that partitioning holistic mechanisms into distinct facilitatory and inhibitory components is critical for understanding face perception.
papers.authors: Haiyang Jin, William G. Hayward, Olivia S. Cheung

papers.title: Implicit bias and experience influence overall but not relative trustworthiness judgment of other-race faces
papers.abstract: Facial trustworthiness evaluations are generated rapidly during first impressions; however, the degree of cross-racial consistency and the determinants of individual variation remain disputed. While normative consensus is widely reported, socio-cognitive factors—specifically negative implicit racial bias and deficient intergroup contact—have been linked to depressed trustworthiness appraisals for other-race faces. In this preregistered investigation, cohorts of White (N = 338) and Black (N = 299) observers completed a 200-face trustworthiness rating task (100 Black, 100 White faces), a race Implicit Association Test (IAT), and an intergroup contact inventory. Although absolute, overall trustworthiness ratings for other-race targets were significantly modulated by both implicit racial bias and contact experience, relative trustworthiness judgments (relative differences evaluated against own-race baseline ratings) remained highly concordant across observers irrespective of bias or contact levels. These findings demonstrate an operational dissociation wherein top-down socio-cognitive attitudes alter the absolute scaling of trustworthiness impressions, whereas bottom-up morphological cues driving relative approach-versus-avoidance determinations remain invariant across racial groups.
papers.authors: Olivia S. Cheung, Nathan J. Quimpo, James Smoley

papers.title: Effects of masculinity vs. femininity on competence judgement of politician faces and election outcome prediction
papers.abstract: Rapid visual inferences of competence from candidate photographs reliably predict real-world electoral victories, yet it remains debated whether these impressions stem from intrinsic facial morphology or extraneous photographic cues such as hairstyle, apparel, and posture. Across four preregistered experiments using counterbalanced designs, observers evaluated candidate competence on individual faces and forecasted electoral outcomes for winner–runner-up pairs. In Experiments 1 and 2, assessments were performed using unedited photographic portraits and standardized computer-generated face models reconstructed exclusively from candidate facial morphology, respectively. In Experiments 3 and 4, the synthetic facial stimuli were systematically manipulated along a masculinity–femininity continuum. Across Experiments 1 through 3, electoral victors elicited significantly higher competence ratings and higher predicted win probabilities than runners-up; this predictive effect was reversed or eliminated solely in Experiment 4, where winner facial morphology was feminized and runner-up morphology was masculinized. Across all conditions, perceived competence ratings remained robustly correlated with election outcome forecasts. These results confirm that facial morphological cues alone are sufficient to drive competence inferences and predict electoral success, and that masculine features reinforce stereotypical leadership impressions.
papers.authors: Olivia S. Cheung, Davit Jintcharadze

papers.title: The role of implicit social bias on holistic processing of out-group faces
papers.abstract: While perceptual expertise facilitates robust holistic processing of in-group faces, findings regarding holistic coding for out-group categories and its underlying determinants remain equivocal. This study investigated how out-group holistic processing magnitude—assessed across two distinct social categories (other-race and other-age)—is predicted by implicit social bias, individuating intergroup contact, and baseline in-group holistic processing capacity. Although participants exhibited substantial contact with the racial out-group but limited contact with the age out-group, implicit social bias emerged as a significant positive predictor of holistic processing for both other-race and other-age facial stimuli. Moderation analyses further revealed that the relationship between implicit bias and out-group holistic processing was selectively pronounced among observers possessing superior in-group holistic perceptual ability coupled with minimal experiential familiarity with out-group members. These findings indicate that top-down social evaluative biases interact with perceptual mechanisms to shape the configural encoding of out-group facial representations.
papers.authors: Wei Chen, Mahlet T. Kassa, Olivia S. Cheung

0522.name: Olivier Collignon
0522.department: Institute for Research in Psychology (IPSY) and Institute of Neuroscience (IoNS)
0522.bio: Olivier Collignon investigates the neurobiological foundations of multisensory perception and crossmodal plasticity. Their research explores how the human brain adapts to sensory deprivation, demonstrating that visual cortical regions in blind individuals can be functionally repurposed for auditory and tactile processing. By combining psychophysical methods with neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and M/EEG, Collignon identifies the computational principles governing brain reorganization and its potential for sensory restoration. Collignon serves as a Principal Investigator at the Crossmodal Perception and Plasticity Lab and is affiliated with the School of Health Sciences at HES-SO Valais-Wallis.
0522.research_direction: Dr. Collignon has recently been investigating how sensory experience and deprivation shape the functional organization of the human brain. Their recent work explores the nature of multisensory and supramodal representations, using fMRI and multivariate decoding to ask how classically visual regions, such as hMT+/V5 and the ventral occipito-temporal cortex, encode motion direction, spoken phonemes, and object shape across visual, tactile, and auditory modalities in both sighted and early blind individuals. Additionally, they are examining the developmental timelines of sensory processing by testing how transient neonatal blindness from congenital cataracts alters sensitive periods across different stages of the visual hierarchy, and by using fast periodic EEG to probe the early emergence of voice selectivity in young infants. Through these distinct lines of inquiry, their research ultimately probes the fundamental interplay between innate cortical architecture and sensory experience.

papers.title: Aligned representation of visual and tactile motion directions in hMT+/V5 and fronto-parietal regions
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study shows that motion-selective area hMT+/V5 responds to both seen and felt motion and encodes motion directions across changes in hand posture. Tactile direction information in right hMT+/V5 is stronger when described in external space than in skin-based coordinates. Decoding across vision and touch reveals a shared motion code in right hMT+/V5 and fronto-parietal regions, provided touch is expressed in an external reference frame.
papers.authors: Iqra Shahzad, Ceren Battal, Filippo Cerpelloni, Alice Van Audenhaege, André Mouraux, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Impact of a transient neonatal visual deprivation on the development of the ventral occipito-temporal cortex in humans
papers.abstract: The authors studied people who were briefly blind from birth because of congenital cataracts and later regained sight, asking which parts of visual cortex develop normally. Early visual cortex showed lasting deficits in encoding low-level image properties, while categorical responses in ventral occipito-temporal cortex were preserved. Degrading the input of normal-sighted controls, and training a deep network on degraded images, reproduced this dissociation, pointing to different sensitive periods for different cortical stages.
papers.authors: Stefania Mattioni, Mohamed Rezk, Xiaoqing Gao, Junghyun Nam, Zhong-Xu Liu, Remi Gau, Valérie Goffaux, Andrea I. Costantino, Hans Op de Beeck, Terri Lewis, Daphne Maurer, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Phonological Representations of Auditory and Visual Speech in the Occipito-temporal Cortex and Beyond
papers.abstract: Participants underwent fMRI while perceiving spoken phonemes and silent lip movements (visemes), and functionally defined face, word-selective, scene and audiovisual speech regions were analysed with multivariate decoding. Word-selective ventral occipito-temporal cortex and the left superior temporal sulcus carried phonological information from both sound and lip-reading. The results indicate that regions traditionally considered visual take part in a multisensory phonological code for speech.
papers.authors: Alice Van Audenhaege, Stefania Mattioni, Filippo Cerpelloni, Remi Gau, Arnaud Szmalec, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Voice categorization in the four-month-old human brain
papers.abstract: The study used fast periodic auditory stimulation with scalp EEG to ask whether young infants treat voices as a distinct category. Sequences of varied non-vocal sounds with a voice inserted every third item evoked a reliable voice-selective response over temporal regions in 23 four-month-olds, detectable in most infants within minutes. The response shrank for frequency-scrambled sounds, so it is not explained by the spectral or envelope content alone.
papers.authors: Roberta P. Calce, Diane Rekow, Francesca M. Barbero, Anna Kiseleva, Siddharth Talwar, Arnaud Leleu, Olivier Collignon

papers.title: Similar object shape representation encoded in the inferolateral occipitotemporal cortex of sighted and early blind people
papers.abstract: Comparing early blind and sighted adults, the authors separated shape from conceptual knowledge of manmade objects. Inferolateral occipitotemporal cortex in both groups was more active during a shape task than a conceptual task and its activity patterns tracked object shape similarity but not conceptual association. Together with frontoparietal grasp-related areas it forms a shape-specialised circuit, supporting a supramodal shape representation that does not depend on visual experience.
papers.authors: Yangwen Xu, Lorenzo Vignali, Federica Sigismondi, Davide Crepaldi, Roberto Bottini, Olivier Collignon

0523.name: Paola Binda
0523.department: Department of Translational Research and New Technologies in Medicine and Surgery
0523.bio: Paola Binda is a neuroscientist who researches the physiological foundations of human visual perception and its interactions with cognitive and metabolic processes. Binda’s research in pupillometry demonstrates that pupil diameter serves as an index of high-level visual attention and cortical processing rather than a simple reflex. Their work utilizes ultra-high-field (7T) fMRI and psychophysics to investigate short-term ocular dominance plasticity and the role of subcortical structures like the pulvinar in visual stability. Binda leads the Pisa Vision Lab and the ERC-funded PUPILTRAITS project, which examines how individual variations in visual processing correlate with personality traits and physiological biomarkers.
0523.research_direction: Dr. Binda has recently been investigating the mechanisms of adult visual plasticity, with a primary focus on how short-term monocular deprivation and sensory discrepancies shift ocular dominance. Their recent work explores how this homeostatic plasticity is gated by behavioral states, examining whether goal-directed voluntary actions and predictive visuomotor mismatches modulate visual adaptation differently than passive viewing. To understand the neural circuitry underlying these effects, they are using high-resolution 7T fMRI to examine how thalamo-cortical functional connectivity, specifically signals relayed from the pulvinar to primary visual cortex, might regulate this plasticity. Alongside their research on cortical adaptation, Dr. Binda is also leveraging pupillometry combined with frequency-tagging paradigms to track the implicit, time-resolved statistical learning of high-level visual properties like numerosity.

papers.title: Visually guided voluntary actions boost short-term ocular dominance plasticity
papers.abstract: Participants underwent one hour of monocular deprivation while either performing a visually guided goal-directed task or passively watching a replay of their own actions, with identical visual input. The ocular dominance shift was larger after active performance. This gives direct evidence that voluntary action modulates visual plasticity.
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Giacomo Pennella, Maria Concetta Morrone, Giulio Sandini, Paola Binda

papers.title: The pulvinar regulates plasticity in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Two hours of monocular deprivation transiently shifts ocular dominance in healthy adults. Using 7T fMRI, the authors show this shift coincides with reduced directed functional connectivity from the pulvinar to primary visual cortex, and that people with stronger pulvinar-to-V1 coupling show smaller shifts. This supports a model in which adult V1 plasticity is gated by modulatory signals relayed through the pulvinar.
papers.authors: Miriam Acquafredda, Jan W. Kurzawski, Laura Biagi, Michela Tosetti, Maria Concetta Morrone, Paola Binda

papers.title: Pupillometric signature of implicit learning of statistical regularities
papers.abstract: Using a frequency-tagging design, the study shows that pupil size tracks the learning of hidden temporal pairings of numerosities, with the pupil responding at the pairing frequency after only a few minutes of passive viewing. Learning occurred even when attention was diverted from numerosity and also worked for pairs of digits. The pupil thus gives an implicit, time-resolved readout of statistical learning of global stimulus properties.
papers.authors: Paola Binda, Chiara Terzo, Marco Turi, David C. Burr

papers.title: Short-term monocular deprivation in healthy humans: a meta-analysis and new perspectives
papers.abstract: A meta-analysis of 73 studies confirms that brief monocular deprivation reliably shifts ocular dominance toward the deprived eye, with effect size depending mainly on deprivation duration and the measurement technique but not on patching design. Similar shifts arise without deprivation, for example from distorted or task-irrelevant monocular images. The authors propose a predictive-coding-inspired account of the effect.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Giacomo Pennella, Paola Binda

papers.title: Active vision gates ocular dominance plasticity in human adults
papers.abstract: The authors asked whether homeostatic ocular dominance plasticity requires degrading the monocular image, or whether a visuomotor mismatch is enough. Delaying the image in one eye while participants performed a visuomotor task shifted ocular dominance toward the delayed eye, whereas passive viewing did not. Plasticity appears to be gated by a discrepancy between seen and expected visual input during active behavior.
papers.authors: Cecilia Steinwurzel, Maria Concetta Morrone, Giulio Sandini, Paola Binda

0524.name: Pascal Mamassian
0524.institution: French National Centre for Scientific Research
0524.bio: Pascal Mamassian is a CNRS Director of Research and the director of the Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs at the École Normale Supérieure (ENS), PSL University. Mamassian’s research focuses on mid-level vision, examining the computational link between the detection of elementary image features and the conscious awareness of natural scenes. They utilize behavioral psychophysics and Bayesian probabilistic modeling to investigate 3D perception, motion, and the temporal dynamics of sensory integration. Their work centers on visual confidence and meta-perception, exploring the mechanisms through which observers evaluate the accuracy of their own perceptual decisions.
0524.research_direction: Dr. Mamassian has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual metacognition and perceptual history. Much of their recent work focuses on how perceptual confidence is formed, including developing new generative models to disentangle sensory noise from confidence-specific noise and tracking whether confidence acts as an internal teaching signal during feedback-free perceptual learning. They are also examining how confidence interacts with diverse visual processes, asking whether natural perceptual priors bias confidence differently than basic decisions, and how metacognitive evaluation differs across low- and high-level stages of the visual hierarchy when subjected to delays or backward masking. In a distinct line of research, they are exploring serial dependence, specifically investigating how stimulus uncertainty dictates whether sequential visual inputs produce attractive or repulsive orientation aftereffects.

papers.title: Perceptual learning without feedback is accompanied with systematic changes in confidence processing
papers.abstract: Asks whether confidence can serve as an internal teaching signal when perceptual learning happens without external feedback. Over five days of motion discrimination, observers who improved (learners) showed lower sensory noise but also higher confidence-specific noise and greater use of extra evidence beyond the decision, while non-learners showed no such changes. Confidence therefore appears to evolve during feedback-free learning.
papers.authors: Nadia Hosseinizaveh, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: The confidence-noise confidence-boost (CNCB) model of confidence rating data
papers.abstract: Proposes a generative model of confidence ratings with two parameters: confidence noise, which degrades confidence beyond what sensory noise does, and confidence boost, which captures whether confidence draws on the same evidence as the decision or on extra information. The model yields a theory-driven confidence-efficiency measure as an alternative to the widely used M-ratio, and extends to continuous confidence ratings without binning. A toolbox and re-analyses of earlier datasets accompany it.
papers.authors: Pascal Mamassian, Vincent de Gardelle

papers.title: Long-term perceptual priors drive confidence bias that favors prior-congruent evidence
papers.abstract: Tests whether a naturally acquired prior, the expectation that things move slowly, influences confidence in the same way as it influences perceptual decisions. Observers judged the direction of tilted moving lines, and confidence showed a bias toward evidence congruent with the prior beyond what the decision itself showed. The results argue that priors act differently at the confidence stage than at the decision stage.
papers.authors: Marika Constant, Elisa Filevich, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Attractive and repulsive visual aftereffects depend on stimulus contrast
papers.abstract: Studies how stimulus uncertainty, manipulated through contrast, shapes serial dependence effects in orientation perception. Observers viewed sequences of Gabor patches while orientation and contrast were varied, and the direction and size of aftereffects (attraction versus repulsion) changed with contrast. The work ties history effects to how the visual system weights uncertain inputs.
papers.authors: Nikos Gekas, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Metacognitive evaluation of postdecisional perceptual representations
papers.abstract: Examines whether the ability to judge one's own accuracy depends on the level of the visual hierarchy being probed. Confidence in low-level decisions deteriorated with delay and backward masking, whereas confidence in high-level decisions was immune to masking and improved with time. A model in which confidence relies on postdecisional evidence explains the pattern.
papers.authors: Tarryn Balsdon, Valentin Wyart, Pascal Mamassian

0525.name: Patrick Bennett
0525.bio: Patrick J. Bennett is a Professor and Senior Canada Research Chair in Vision Science at McMaster University and co-directs the Vision and Cognitive Neuroscience Lab. Their research utilizes psychophysics, computational modeling, and electrophysiology to study the mechanisms of visual perception, with a focus on the effects of healthy aging and perceptual learning. Bennett applies ideal observer theory to establish benchmarks for human performance in tasks involving face and object recognition. Their current investigations examine how neural noise and changes in executive control relate to age-associated declines in visual processing and decision-making strategies.
0525.research_direction: Dr. Bennett has recently been studying how vision changes with age and with practice. Their recent work asks whether older adults' poorer motion perception reflects broader tuning of the visual mechanisms that detect motion direction, testing this by measuring how well moving dots can be seen against masking motion in younger and older observers. They have also been examining how quickly perceptual learning becomes specific to the trained stimulus, following people who practice identifying textures and testing how much of the benefit persists after a day or a week.

papers.title: The effects of aging on directionally selective masking
papers.abstract: Age-related degradation of motion perception may stem from an expansion of the bandwidth of directionally selective visual mechanisms. To evaluate this hypothesis, directional masking was measured in younger and older adults across five psychophysical experiments. Experiments 1–3 quantified the contrast necessary to discriminate the direction of coherently drifting signal dots embedded within high-contrast mask dots, where the directional distribution of the mask dots was systematically manipulated using notch filters; directional selectivity was defined by the slope of the threshold-versus-notch function. Older adults exhibited elevated thresholds and reduced directional selectivity; however, scaling signal and mask contrast to multiples of each observer's unmasked motion discrimination threshold eliminated these age effects. Experiments 4 and 5 assessed direction discrimination thresholds by varying the proportion of coherently moving dots in masks composed of dots drifting in directions that differed across conditions. In these suprathreshold conditions, older observers continued to show increased discrimination thresholds and reduced directional selectivity. These findings support the hypothesis that directionally selective mechanisms become more broadly tuned during senescence.
papers.authors: Lia E. Tsotsos, Eugenie Roudaia, Allison B. Sekuler, Patrick J. Bennett

papers.title: The time course of stimulus-specific perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Perceptual task training can produce long-lasting, stimulus-specific performance enhancements. While rapid stimulus-specific learning emerging after just 105 practice trials has been observed in face identification, other visual tasks typically exhibit a much longer progression. This study investigated the acquisition dynamics and durability of stimulus-specific learning using unfamiliar, non-face texture stimuli across two sessions separated by either 24 hours (Experiment 1) or one week (Experiment 2). Observers performed a 1-of-10 texture identification task with varying amounts of Session 1 training (21, 63, 105, or 840 trials) and completed 840 trials in Session 2, where half of the participants maintained the trained textures and half transitioned to novel textures.
