In both experiments, stimulus-specific learning—operationalized as the accuracy difference between the identical and novel conditions—scaled as a linear function of the log-transformed number of Session 1 trials and achieved statistical significance after approximately 100 trials. The effect size of stimulus novelty did not vary between the 1-day and 1-week retention intervals, indicating that stimulus-specific perceptual learning for complex textures emerges continuously with practice, concurrently with task-general learning.
papers.authors: Patrick J. Bennett, Ali Hashemi, Jordan W. Lass, Allison B. Sekuler, Zahra Hussain

0526.name: Patrick Cavanagh
0526.bio: Patrick Cavanagh conducts research in visual neuroscience, specifically in the areas of visual attention, motion perception, and the intersection of art and science. Cavanagh utilizes discrepancies between perception and reality found in shadows and artistic depictions to examine how the brain reconstructs the visual world through inference processes. They identified that motion can distort the perceived position of objects, leading to theories regarding the neural representation of space. Their work also investigates 'visual language' and the mechanisms by which the brain compresses sensory information for communication with higher-order cognitive centers.
0526.research_direction: Dr. Cavanagh has recently been investigating how the visual system constructs stable, organized representations of the world despite constant changes in retinal input. Their recent work explores the mechanisms of trans-saccadic remapping and visual stability, examining theoretical network architectures that could update the early cortical feature locations of attended targets across eye movements. In addition to mapping the broader neurocognitive architecture of object-based attention, they are conducting psychophysical experiments to determine the spatial and temporal limits of how moving reference frames shift the perceived positions of flashed visual probes. Furthermore, Dr. Cavanagh uses visual illusions as tools to probe the visual hierarchy, investigating the physiological drivers of anomalous motion phenomena like the peripheral drift illusion and evaluating methods to pinpoint exactly where conscious perception emerges apart from top-down attentional feedback.

papers.title: Steerable autoencoders underlying remapping, spatiotopy, and visual stability
papers.abstract: Reviews why the visual system seems to keep world-anchored (spatiotopic) locations despite retinotopic maps, arguing that a few attended targets are tracked and remapped rather than whole maps being shifted. Proposes that each attended target's identity is linked to its feature locations in early visual cortex via a steerable autoencoder network that moves feature activity to the new location at each saccade, accounting for reports of trans-saccadic integration. Presents this as part of the overall architecture of visual processing.
papers.authors: Patrick Cavanagh, David Melcher

papers.title: Frame effects across space and time
papers.abstract: Eight experiments characterize how a moving frame shifts the perceived positions of probes flashed within it. The influence extends several degrees beyond the frame's borders and across depth planes but does not extend in time before or after the frame. The effect is driven mainly by frame displacement rather than by motion signals, and is unaffected by self-initiation or by two hours of testing.
papers.authors: Bernard Marius 't Hart, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Pupil dilation underlies the peripheral drift illusion
papers.abstract: Proposes that the peripheral drift illusion, in which static sawtooth-luminance patterns seem to move after saccades, blinks or onsets, is triggered by transient retinal luminance changes from reflexive pupil-size changes. Supports this with tests linking pupil responses to illusory motion episodes, explaining a puzzle unresolved since 1979.
papers.authors: George Mather, Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: Using Illusions to Track the Emergence of Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Defines illusions as conflicts between perception and cognition and argues they can reveal where in the visual hierarchy perception is constructed. Discusses how top-down attention signals broadcast expected properties across visual areas, obscuring where an illusion actually arises. Surveys methods that get around this obstacle to localize illusion effects.
papers.authors: Patrick Cavanagh

papers.title: The architecture of object-based attention
papers.abstract: A comprehensive review of how attention selects and operates over objects rather than locations. Draws on behavioral, neuroimaging and physiological evidence to propose an architecture in which object-level attention is implemented across a hierarchy of visual representations. Identifies open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Patrick Cavanagh, Gideon P. Caplovitz, Taissa K. Lytchenko, Marvin R. Maechler, Peter U. Tse, David L. Sheinberg

0529.name: Pawan Sinha
0529.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0529.lab_name: The Sinha Lab for Developmental Research
0529.bio: Pawan Sinha is a Professor of Vision and Computational Neuroscience at MIT who investigates the biological and computational mechanisms underlying perceptual development and object recognition. Sinha founded Project Prakash, an initiative that restores sight to congenitally blind children in India to study how the brain interprets visual information after prolonged deprivation. Their research also explores neurodevelopmental disorders, advancing the hypothesis that autism is characterized by a deficit in sensory prediction. By combining experimental data from diverse populations with computational modeling, their laboratory investigates the processes that allow the human brain to transform sensory input into mental representations.
0529.research_direction: Dr. Sinha has recently been investigating the role of early visual experience and developmental timelines in shaping the organization of the visual system. Their recent work explores the behavioral impacts of late sight onset following treatment for congenital blindness, specifically probing how early visual deprivation alters a patient's reliance on color cues during object recognition and their ability to use motion to process facial expressions. To uncover the mechanisms underlying these developmental trajectories, they employ deep neural networks to computationally model how time-limited neuronal plasticity and the staggered infant maturation of spatial acuity and color sensitivity might drive the emergence of early pathways like the parvocellular-magnocellular division. Additionally, they are theoretically examining how the brain's detection of temporal regularities may serve as a fundamental scaffolding mechanism for organizing input across multiple sensory modalities.

papers.title: The Temporal Scaffolding of Sensory Organization
papers.abstract: This review argues that detecting and exploiting temporal regularities is a common principle by which developing brains organize input across sensory modalities. It integrates neurophysiology, cognitive neuroscience and theoretical computer science, concluding that time may be the fundamental dimension of sensory organization and that ecological heuristics make the problem tractable. Implications for typical and atypical development and for modeling are discussed.
papers.authors: Pawan Sinha, Lukas Vogelsang, Marin Vogelsang, Albert Yonas, Sidney Diamond

papers.title: Potential role of developmental experience in the emergence of the parvo-magno distinction
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that the parvocellular/magnocellular division of the early visual pathway arises partly from the temporal overlap of how spatial-frequency and color sensitivity develop in infancy. Deep networks trained with developmentally inspired protocols show receptive-field properties consistent with this idea. Such training also yields a more human-like bias toward global shape, potentially driven by magno-like units.
papers.authors: Marin Vogelsang, Lukas Vogelsang, Gordon Pipa, Sidney Diamond, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Computationally Probing the Role of Time-Limited Neuronal Plasticity in Early Visual Development
papers.abstract: Using deep neural networks, the authors test whether declining plasticity, modeled as decreasing learning rates, helps preserve early-formed visual mechanisms when input quality improves over development. Across acuity and color, time-limited plasticity gives modest gains and stabilizes early representations. Further analysis suggests such gains may depend on other factors in developmental progression.
papers.authors: Marin Vogelsang, Lukas Vogelsang, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Impact of early visual experience on later usage of color cues
papers.abstract: Congenitally blind children who gained sight through surgery were tested months to years later on object recognition with and without color. Unlike normally sighted children, they were markedly hurt by color removal, indicating over-reliance on chromatic cues. The authors argue that the greater maturity of their color system at sight onset explains this, and deep network simulations support the account, suggesting that typical early color-poor vision is adaptive and may inform machine vision training.
papers.authors: Marin Vogelsang, Lukas Vogelsang, Priti Gupta, Tapan K. Gandhi, Pragya Shah, Piyush Swami, Sharon Gilad-Gutnick, Shlomit Ben-Ami, Sidney Diamond, Suma Ganesh, Pawan Sinha

papers.title: Motion's privilege in recognizing facial expressions following treatment for blindness
papers.abstract: Children treated for congenital cataracts were tested on recognizing facial expressions from static images versus dynamic video. Motion provided a special advantage for expression recognition after late sight onset, suggesting that dynamic cues are a robust route to expression understanding even without early visual experience. The work speaks to innate versus experience-dependent origins of expression recognition.
papers.authors: Sharon Gilad-Gutnick, Grace S. Kurian, Priti Gupta, Pragya Shah, Kashish Tiwari, Chetan Ralekar, Tapan Gandhi, Suma Ganesh, Umang Mathur, Pawan Sinha

0530.name: Peter Bandettini
0530.bio: Bandettini co-led the development of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) using blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) contrast and introduced correlation analysis for functional mapping. Bandettini's research focuses on advancing the spatial resolution, temporal sensitivity, and interpretability of fMRI through ultra-high-field imaging of cortical layers and the development of multi-echo pulse sequences. Their current work explores the extraction of neuronal and physiological signatures from fMRI time series data to examine individual differences in brain connectivity and visual processing. Bandettini serves as the Director of the NIH Functional MRI Facility and is the current Editor-in-Chief of Aperture Neuro, having previously served as Editor-in-Chief of NeuroImage.
0530.research_direction: Dr. Bandettini's recent work explores the methodological boundaries and neurocognitive applications of advanced functional magnetic resonance imaging. Methodologically, they have recently been investigating ways to enhance high-field laminar fMRI by mitigating scanning artifacts and reducing macrovascular draining vein biases, while also pushing temporal limits via ultra-fast acquisitions to rapidly decode visual object representations. Applying these refined techniques to sensory and cognitive phenomena, their recent research traces the conscious experience of negative afterimages from large-scale brain networks down to specific cortical layers. Additionally, they are exploring how spontaneous, unconstrained thoughts during scanning dynamically shape resting-state functional connectivity networks.

papers.title: In-scanner thoughts contribute to resting-state functional connectivity
papers.abstract: The study asks how the unconstrained thoughts people have while lying in the scanner shape resting-state fMRI connectivity. By collecting thought reports alongside scans, the authors show that thought content and its dynamics account for a meaningful share of connectivity patterns. The results suggest that what participants do during rest is a substantive source of variance in the measure, not mere noise.
papers.authors: Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Megan A. Spurney, Ka Chun Lam, Isabel S. Gephart, Francisco Pereira, Daniel A. Handwerker, Julia W. Y. Kam, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: Short-term gradient imperfections in high-resolution EPI lead to Fuzzy Ripple artifacts
papers.abstract: High-resolution EPI acquisitions used for laminar and columnar fMRI show a previously unexplained ripple-like blurring artifact. The authors trace it to short-term gradient imperfections and characterize how it degrades image sharpness. They demonstrate mitigation strategies that restore effective resolution in submillimeter fMRI.
papers.authors: Laurentius (Renzo) Huber, Rüdiger Stirnberg, A. Tyler Morgan, David A. Feinberg, Philipp Ehses, Lasse Knudsen, Omer Faruk Gulban, Kenshu Koiso, Isabel Gephart, Stephanie Swegle, Susan G. Wardle, Andrew S. Persichetti, Alexander J. S. Beckett, Tony Stöcker, Nicolas Boulant, Benedikt A. Poser, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: Rapid decoding of neural information representation from ultra-fast functional magnetic resonance imaging signals
papers.abstract: Using very fast fMRI acquisition, the study tests how quickly visual object information can be read out of the BOLD signal. Multivariate decoding shows that object category is recoverable within a couple of seconds of stimulus onset. This pushes the temporal limits of what fMRI can resolve about neural representations.
papers.authors: Yoichi Miyawaki, Kenshu Koiso, Daniel A. Handwerker, Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Laurentius Huber, Arman Khojandi, Yuhui Chai, Daniel Glen, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: The human brain mechanisms of afterimages: From networks to cortical layers
papers.abstract: Combining network-level and laminar 7T fMRI, the authors examine which brain systems and cortical layers support the conscious experience of negative afterimages. Activity is traced from large-scale networks down to layer-specific signals in visual cortex. The work links visual perception and consciousness to laminar circuit-level mechanisms.
papers.authors: Sharif Ismail Kronemer, Burak Akin, Micah Holness, A. Tyler Morgan, Laurentius Huber, Paul A. Taylor, Javier Gonzalez-Castillo, Daniel A. Handwerker, Peter A. Bandettini

papers.title: Improving laminar fMRI specificity by reducing macrovascular bias revealed by respiration effects
papers.abstract: Draining veins bias laminar fMRI toward the cortical surface. The authors use respiration-induced signal changes to reveal this macrovascular contribution and show acquisition and analysis approaches that reduce it. The result is improved layer specificity of high-field fMRI.
papers.authors: Yuhui Chai, A. Tyler Morgan, Daniel A. Handwerker, Linqing Li, Laurentius Huber, Bradley P. Sutton, Peter A. Bandettini

0531.name: Peter Bex
0531.bio: Professor Peter Bex conducts cross-disciplinary research at the intersection of basic visual neuroscience and clinical ophthalmology. Bex's laboratory utilizes computational modeling, psychophysics, and eye-tracking to examine how the human visual system processes dynamic, cluttered real-world environments compared to laboratory stimuli. A focus of their translational work is the development of objective, automated diagnostic tools—such as the Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) and Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD)—to monitor the progression and remediation of visual function loss in patients with glaucoma, amblyopia, and macular degeneration. Through these tools, Bex seeks to optimize residual vision and develop rehabilitation strategies for blinding eye diseases.
0531.research_direction: Dr. Bex has recently been developing novel, self-administered psychophysical paradigms—such as Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) and Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD)—to precisely quantify visual functions like color discrimination, stereopsis, and face perception. Through these tools, their recent work explores how to rapidly extract fine-grained sensory thresholds for both clinical and remote applications. Beyond applied visual assessments, they are also investigating the fundamental dynamics of binocular vision and sensorimotor integration. Specifically, they are using unsupervised clustering and hidden Markov models to map the diverse perceptual states and transition dynamics that emerge during multistable binocular rivalry. Additionally, they are probing the motion system by examining how first- and second-order global motion features differentially drive conscious perceptual judgments versus reflexive ocular following eye movements.

papers.title: Which perceptual categories do observers experience during multistable perception?
papers.abstract: Using data collected with the InFoRM-Rivalry method for tracking binocular rivalry, the authors let perceptual categories emerge from unsupervised clustering instead of assuming a fixed set. Around ten categories appeared on average, mostly falling in the monocular-exclusive and superimposed regions. A hidden Markov model of transitions showed that switches mostly run between monocular-exclusive and binocular-superimposed states, suggesting rivalry reflects conflict between monocular and binocular processing sites rather than only mutual inhibition.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Jan Skerswetat, Peter Bex

papers.title: Novel color vision assessment tool: AIM color detection and discrimination
papers.abstract: Introduces Angular Indication Measurement (AIM) for colour, a self-administered adaptive tablet-style test in which observers report the orientation of gaps or colour edges in cone-isolating and equiluminant stimuli. In 23 colour-normal and 15 colour-deficient observers it was validated against the HRR, FM100 and anomaloscope. The test measures detection and discrimination quickly and with fine resolution, without clinician oversight.
papers.authors: Jingyi He, Jan Skerswetat, Peter J. Bex

papers.title: Distinctive feature sensitivity of ocular following initiation during global motion perception
papers.abstract: Compares ocular following responses and perceptual judgments for global motion built from first-order carrier and second-order envelope features. Both systems respond most to envelope motion, but perceptual speed is impaired by short presentations while eye movements are not, and trial-by-trial perceptual speed is uncorrelated with ocular following speed. Direction signals do correlate with a delay, pointing to shared feedback-controlled direction processing.
papers.authors: Joonsik Moon, Peter Bex

papers.title: Comparison of Foraging Interactive D-prime and Angular Indication Measurement Stereo with different methods to assess stereopsis
papers.abstract: Tests two new self-administered stereopsis tests, FInD Stereo and AIM Stereo, against 2-AFC paradigms and clinical Titmus and Randot tests in 40 normally sighted and 5 binocularly impaired participants. The new tests were compared on agreement, repeatability and duration. They address the coarse steps, memorisation and poor repeatability of standard clinical stereotests.
papers.authors: Sonisha Neupane, Jan Skerswetat, Peter J. Bex

papers.title: A novel, rapid, quantitative method for face discrimination
papers.abstract: Combines the Foraging Interactive D-prime (FInD) paradigm with the Basel Face Model to measure face-discrimination thresholds quickly, in the lab and remotely. Observers were most sensitive to the first ten structural principal components; thresholds were similar remotely and in-lab and were lower when two components changed together than one, consistent with probability summation. Face rotation raised thresholds, showing the method is not driven by pointwise image comparison.
papers.authors: Kerri Walter, Peter Bex

0532.name: Peter J Kohler
0532.bio: Peter J. Kohler is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at York University and director of the Kohler Visual Neuroscience Lab. Kohler’s research focuses on mid-level visual processing, investigating how the human brain transforms early sensory signals into representations of symmetry, shape, and motion. Utilizing a combination of high-density steady-state EEG, functional MRI, and psychophysical modeling, Kohler characterizes the spatiotemporal dynamics of neural populations across topographically organized visual areas. Their current work explores the hierarchical organization of pattern regularity and the binocular integration mechanisms required for perceiving motion in depth.
0532.research_direction: Dr. Kohler has recently been studying how the visual system uses symmetry and regular structure to organize what we see. Their recent work asks how easily people can find a target in a cluttered display depending on the kind of symmetry involved, such as reflection versus rotation, and on how regular the repeating texture is. The aim is to understand whether these cues let the visual system process a scene in parallel or force it to inspect items one by one.

papers.title: Visual search efficiency is modulated by symmetry type and texture regularity
papers.abstract: While symmetry serves as a foundational Gestalt cue facilitating perceptual organization and scene understanding, empirical work has predominantly focused on isolated reflectional symmetry. Here, visual search paradigms were employed to investigate how search efficiency is differentially governed by symmetry class (reflection versus rotation) and spatial regularity across repeating lattice textures. Observers searched for target elements embedded within multi-element arrays across varying set sizes, allowing quantification of search slopes (ms/item) as an index of serial versus parallel attentional deployment. Search slopes were significantly shallower for targets defined by reflectional symmetry compared to rotational symmetry, indicating higher processing efficiency and greater parallel extraction for mirror symmetry. Additionally, global lattice regularity significantly facilitated target detection relative to disordered configurations, demonstrating that macro-level structural regularity interacts with micro-level symmetry processing. These results reveal that the visual system recruits distinct computational mechanisms across different symmetry classes and that spatial periodicity in wallpaper-like visual textures fundamentally modulates attentional gating and perceptual efficiency.
papers.authors: Rachel Moreau, Nihan Alp, Alasdair D. F. Clarke, Erez Freud, Peter J. Kohler

0533.name: Peter Kok
0533.department: Department of Imaging Neuroscience, Queen Square Institute of Neurology
0533.bio: Peter Kok is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience and Sir Henry Dale Fellow at the UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, where they conduct research on the neural mechanisms of predictive coding. Kok’s work examines how the brain integrates prior knowledge and sensory input to shape visual perception, utilizing ultra-high field (7T) fMRI to study laminar-specific activity in the visual cortex. They also employ magnetoencephalography (MEG) to analyze the temporal unfolding of perceptual inferences and investigate the role of the hippocampus in generating top-down expectations. This research aims to characterize the computational architecture of the visual system and its implications for understanding perceptual disorders.
0533.research_direction: Dr. Kok has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying top-down influences on visual perception, focusing on how expectations and prior knowledge shape early sensory representations. Their recent work explores the spatial architecture of perceptual inference by using 7T layer-resolved fMRI to isolate the specific cortical layers involved in routing memory-based predictions from the hippocampus, generating expectation-driven false percepts, and processing postdictive visual illusions. Concurrently, they use MEG to examine the temporal dynamics of these phenomena, asking how predictive representations evolve rhythmically at alpha frequencies in the pre-stimulus period and tracking how neural time courses diverge when comparing veridical perception to hallucination-like false percepts. Together, this research probes how the visual system integrates predictive cues with incoming—or even subsequent—sensory evidence to dynamically construct and revise our conscious visual experience.

papers.title: The post-hoc montage of perception: deep layers of primary visual cortex encode postdictive percepts
papers.abstract: Using 7T layer-specific fMRI during two audio-visual postdictive illusions, the study asked whether later sensory information rewrites the representation of earlier visual input in V1. Illusory percepts produced activity patterns resembling real percepts in the deep layers of V1, and connectivity analyses pointed to superior temporal cortex as the feedback source. This extends V1's role from prediction to post-hoc revision of perception.
papers.authors: Pieter Barkema, Christoph Koenig, Joost Haarsma, Peter Kok

papers.title: Communication of perceptual predictions from the hippocampus to the deep layers of the parahippocampal cortex
papers.abstract: Using 7T layer-resolved fMRI, the authors tested how the hippocampus conveys learned predictions about upcoming visual stimuli to visual-related cortex. Prediction-related signals in the hippocampus were accompanied by stimulus-specific activity in the deep layers of parahippocampal cortex, consistent with top-down feedback targeting deep layers. This gives a laminar account of how memory-based predictions reach perceptual regions.
papers.authors: Oliver Warrington, Nadine N. Graedel, Martina F. Callaghan, Peter Kok

papers.title: Contents of Visual Predictions Oscillate at Alpha Frequencies
papers.abstract: Using MEG and a decoding approach, the study examined how the content of a predicted visual stimulus is represented before it appears. The predicted stimulus content was decodable in the pre-stimulus period and fluctuated rhythmically at alpha frequencies, suggesting predictions are sampled periodically rather than held constantly. These fluctuations related to subsequent perception.
papers.authors: Dorottya Hetenyi, Joost Haarsma, Peter Kok

papers.title: Shared and Diverging Neural Dynamics Underlying False and Veridical Perception
papers.abstract: Using MEG, the authors compared the time course of neural representations for false percepts (hallucination-like perceptions of expected but absent stimuli) and for real stimuli. Both showed stimulus-specific activity, but their dynamics diverged, pointing to partly shared and partly distinct mechanisms. The results bear on how perceptual inference gives rise to false percepts.
papers.authors: Joost Haarsma, Dorottya Hetenyi, Peter Kok

papers.title: Expectation Cues and False Percepts Generate Stimulus-Specific Activity in Distinct Layers of the Early Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: With 7T layer-resolved fMRI, the authors compared how expectation cues and false percepts engage the layers of early visual cortex. Both produced stimulus-specific activity, but in different cortical layers, indicating distinct laminar circuits for expectation-driven feedback and for perceiving something that is not there. The work established a laminar signature of false perception.
papers.authors: Joost Haarsma, Narin Deveci, Nadege Corbin, Martina F. Callaghan, Peter Kok

0534.name: Peter Neri
0534.department: Sensory Processing and Computation Unit (Center for Human Technologies, CHT@Erzelli, Genoa)
0534.bio: Peter Neri is a CNRS Director of Research at the École Normale Supérieure (ENS) in Paris and leads the Vision team within the Laboratoire des Systèmes Perceptifs. Neri’s research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human sensory processing, focusing on how the brain extracts structural features from complex natural scenes and noisy environments. By integrating high-resolution psychophysical reverse correlation techniques with quantitative system identification models, Neri characterizes the nonlinear transformations and ‘perceptual templates’ that underlie visual detection and discrimination. Their work aims to provide physiologically plausible accounts of how diverse sensory signals are processed to drive and control behavior across both visual and auditory domains.
0534.research_direction: Dr. Neri has recently been investigating how human visual processing operates within ecologically valid contexts, exploring how the complex statistical structure of natural scenes influences near-threshold detection and sensory adaptation. Using diverse methods including augmented and virtual reality, EEG, psychophysics, and deep neural networks, their recent work examines whether slow, global environmental regularities govern local perceptual evidence formation. To support this ecological focus, they are evaluating how reverse correlation techniques can accurately map human perceptual templates amidst natural image statistics, while also proposing novel computational frameworks that treat sensory perception as geometric measurements over a manifold rather than traditional energy-extraction circuits. Broadening their inquiry into visual signaling, Dr. Neri is additionally studying multimodal communication in cephalopods by testing the behavioral function of stereotyped arm-wave displays in cuttlefish.

papers.title: Perceptual Processes as Charting Operators
papers.abstract: Neri recasts sensory operators, traditionally modeled as small circuits of energy extraction and gain control, in the language of intrinsic geometry. Perception is treated as measuring distances over a sensory manifold, and this representation is shown to reproduce a wide range of empirical effects seen in psychophysics and neurophysiology. The framework offers a unified alternative to circuit-based models and yields predictions for how perceptual templates behave.
papers.authors: Peter Neri

papers.title: Scene Structure Predicts Perceptual Decisions in Naturalistic Detection Tasks
papers.abstract: The study asks how the statistical structure of natural scenes shapes whether near-threshold targets are detected correctly. Combining psychophysics, outdoor augmented reality, deep networks, image-feature analysis and EEG, it finds that background structure alone, with no target present, predicts correct and incorrect behavioral outcomes. This points to global scene context contributing to local perceptual evidence formation.
papers.authors: Jun Yang, Tiziana Vercillo, Teresa Emma Cutrona, Simone Azeglio, Giandomenico Iannetti, Peter Neri

papers.title: Reverse correlation of natural statistics for ecologically relevant characterization of human perceptual templates
papers.abstract: Reverse correlation is the standard way to estimate receptive fields, but natural scene statistics complicate its use in behavioral experiments. The authors test contemporary techniques for handling natural statistics, developed in neuronal settings, on human observers. They show these techniques work in psychophysics but carry caveats that can lead to gross misinterpretation of perceptual templates if ignored.
papers.authors: Lorenzo Landolfi, Peter Neri

papers.title: Cuttlefish interact with multimodal "arm wave sign" displays
papers.abstract: The paper describes four previously undocumented stereotyped arm-wave displays in two cuttlefish species, Sepia officinalis and Sepia bandensis. Non-invasive behavioral experiments test whether these displays function as communication signals, examining how animals respond to them across modalities. The work extends Neri's interest in visual signaling to cephalopod communication.
papers.authors: Sophie Cohen-Bodénès, Peter Neri

papers.title: Human sensory adaptation to the ecological structure of environmental statistics
papers.abstract: This paper examines how human edge detection adapts to slow, global regularities in the environment, such as how reliable shadows are. Using virtual reality experiments, it shows that sensory processing tracks the ecological structure of environmental statistics rather than only local stimulus properties.
papers.authors: Peter Neri

0535.name: Peter U. Tse
0535.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0535.bio: Peter Ulric Tse is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Dartmouth College, where Tse investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual consciousness and volitional attention. Their research employs functional MRI, psychophysics, and neurophysiology to examine how the brain constructs subjective experience and manages top-down volitional mental operations. Tse developed the 'criterial causation' framework, which explores how informational causation is realized in physical neural circuits. Tse additionally conducts research on form-motion interactions, octopus cognition, and the neural basis of imagination.
0535.research_direction: Dr. Tse's recent work spans empirical visual neuroscience, comparative animal cognition, and theoretical philosophy of mind. In the domain of human vision, they have recently been using fMRI and multivariate decoding to investigate how the dorsal attention network manages capacity bottlenecks across hemifields during multiple-object tracking, as well as how volitional intention prospectively shapes early sensory representations to bias ambiguous apparent motion. Expanding their study of visual behavior to invertebrates, their recent work explores convergent cognition by testing whether octopuses can utilize mirrors to locate hidden targets out of direct sight. Additionally, they are investigating the evolutionary and physical foundations of thought, theorizing how open-ended human imagination might stem from premotor action-planning circuitry and critically evaluating physicalist versus substrate-independent models of consciousness.

papers.title: Octopus bimaculoides can learn to utilize a mirror to localize a reward outside the line of sight
papers.abstract: Using mirrors to find hidden objects has been shown in many vertebrates but never in an invertebrate. The authors projected a virtual crab visible only through a mirror reflection onto a tank wall and trained three octopuses to go to the projection site instead of the mirror itself. All three learned the task, suggesting that cephalopods can use mediated perception, a possible precursor to self-recognition, and adding evidence for convergent cognition in a lineage that split from ours over 500 million years ago.
papers.authors: Mary Kieseler, Marvin R. Maechler, Kelly R. Finn, Carl Harris, Jay Michael Vincelli, Zachary Hoffman, Navneet Dhanoa, Jean Fang, Scott Gies, James McHugh III, Julia Valenti, Mira Ram, John O. Fitzgerald, Madison Augusto, David Edelman, Peter U. Tse

papers.title: Seeing at Will: Shared Neural Representations of Motion Perception and Intention
papers.abstract: Twelve participants underwent fMRI while passively viewing quartet apparent-motion stimuli or intending to see a subsequent ambiguous shift as vertical or horizontal motion. Multivariate cross-decoding showed that activity during the intention period resembled patterns evoked by real and illusory motion, most strongly in dorsal and lateral visual regions (hMT+, V3AB, IPS). This indicates that volitional intention sets up prospective sensory representations that shape later perception.
papers.authors: Wentao Si, Eunhye Choe, Nathan H. Heller, Peter J. Kohler, Patrick Cavanagh, Viola S. Stoermer, Peter Tse

papers.title: The Disencapsulated Mind: A Premotor Theory of Human Imagination
papers.abstract: Proposes that human imagination is built on neural circuitry that originally evolved for planning sequences of hand and arm movements. The premotor-based machinery lets the brain assemble, rehearse and recombine mental content in a way that is not locked into perceptual or modular boundaries, which the author argues explains the open-ended, creative nature of human thought.
papers.authors: Peter U. Tse

papers.title: Hemifield Specificity of Attention Response Functions during Multiple-Object Tracking
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while people tracked varying numbers of moving targets among identical distractors, the study asks whether load-related attention responses differ between the two visual hemifields. Contralateral load affected activity in early dorsal and ventral visual areas, whereas ipsilateral load emerged later, and both drove the dorsal attention network in parietal and frontal cortex. The authors suggest hemifield-biased regions may impose the bottleneck on tracking capacity and speed.
papers.authors: Marvin R. Maechler, Eunhye Choe, Patrick Cavanagh, Peter J. Kohler, Peter U. Tse

papers.title: Ontological conceptions of information cannot account for consciousness
papers.abstract: Argues that theories treating information as an ontological, substrate-independent entity cannot explain subjective experience. The author instead favors an account in which consciousness depends on physical neural processes meeting particular criteria, consistent with his criterial-causation framework.
papers.authors: Peter U. Tse

0536.name: Petra Vetter
0536.bio: Petra Vetter is an Assistant Professor who investigates how the human brain integrates non-visual signals—such as auditory, emotional, and motor information—to shape visual perception. Vetter's work utilizes high-field fMRI with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and eye-tracking to demonstrate that the early visual cortex represents sensory content in the absence of retinal input or conscious awareness. They study neuroplasticity in congenitally blind individuals, examining how visual cortical areas are repurposed for spatial mapping through touch and audition. Vetter's research is supported by SNSF PRIMA and Consolidator grants and focuses on the mechanisms of cognitive penetration and cross-modal guidance of eye movements.
0536.research_direction: Dr. Vetter’s recent work explores how non-visual information, such as auditory and motor signals, is represented within the early visual cortex. Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis in blindfolded and congenitally blind individuals, they are investigating whether areas like V1–V3 encode semantic sound categories, cross-modal sound-symbolic mappings like the "bouba-kiki" effect, and reach directions independent of prior visual experience. They have also recently been examining the interplay between action and visual awareness, using continuous flash suppression and eye tracking to test whether executing physical movements can unconsciously guide gaze toward action-relevant images. Expanding beyond specific cross-modal interactions, their research investigates the theoretical bounds of top-down processing by establishing rigorous methodological criteria to evaluate the genuine cognitive penetrability of perception across various sensory modalities.

papers.title: Decoding the "bouba-kiki" effect in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis, the study asks whether sound symbolism, the mapping of words like 'bouba' to round shapes and 'kiki' to spiky ones, has a neural basis beyond language. In the absence of any visual input, round versus spiky sounding words produced distinguishable activity patterns in auditory and speech regions, parietal cortex and early visual cortex including V1. These patterns tracked participants' behavioural shape judgements, suggesting a route by which phonological features link to cross-modal shape representations.
papers.authors: Stefano Ioannucci, Carole Jordan, Anne-Sophie Carnet, Carolyn McGettigan, Petra Vetter

papers.title: Executing actions guides the eyes selectively towards action-related body part images suppressed from visual awareness
papers.abstract: Combines action execution with eye tracking and continuous flash suppression to test whether the eyes are drawn to images of body parts related to the action being performed, even when the images are hidden from awareness. The results indicate that motor actions can guide gaze selectively toward action-relevant body parts without visual awareness. This extends her work on how non-visual signals steer eye movements below awareness.
papers.authors: Petra Vetter, Tiago Mesquita, Stephanie Badde

papers.title: Decoding semantic sound categories in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Blindfolded participants listened to 36 natural sounds while undergoing fMRI. Multivoxel pattern analysis could tell apart animate from inanimate sounds, and human, animal, vehicle and object sounds, from activity in V1-V3, with human-made sounds the most distinct. Searchlight analyses found similar sound information in higher visual and multisensory regions, extending early visual cortex's role beyond visual feature processing.
papers.authors: Giusi Pollicina, Samuel A Müller, Polly Dalton, Petra Vetter

papers.title: Evaluating cognitive penetrability of perception across the senses
papers.abstract: This review lays out criteria for deciding whether cognition genuinely alters perception rather than attention or post-perceptual judgement, and applies them to evidence across vision, audition, touch and other senses. It argues for testing penetrability with designs that separate perceptual from decisional effects, and identifies which findings across modalities best meet those standards. It sets an agenda for cross-modal work on the top-down influence of beliefs and expectations.
papers.authors: Petra Vetter, Stephanie Badde, Elisa Raffaella Ferrè, Janina Seubert, Barbara Shinn-Cunningham

papers.title: Decoding Reach Direction in Early "Visual" Cortex of Congenitally Blind Individuals
papers.abstract: In congenitally blind participants, the direction of a reaching movement could be decoded from fMRI activity in early visual cortex, so neither visual experience nor imagery is required for this region to carry action information. Decoding was best in foveal-representing regions and fell toward the periphery, hinting at a predictive mechanism aligning action and visual space. Reach direction was also decodable in dorsal stream areas involved in action.
papers.authors: Łukasz Bola, Petra Vetter, Mohr Wenger, Amir Amedi

0537.name: Philip J. Kellman
0537.bio: Philip J. Kellman is a Distinguished Professor at UCLA and the Director of the UCLA Human Perception Laboratory, where Kellman investigates the mechanisms of visual interpolation, object formation, and cognitive development. Their research explores how human perceivers extract structure from motion and contours to achieve object unity, a framework known as unit formation. Currently, Kellman’s work examines the intersection of human vision and artificial intelligence, specifically evaluating how deep convolutional neural networks differ from biological systems in processing global shape and abstract relational properties. Kellman also develops adaptive learning technologies that apply principles of perceptual learning to the medical, aviation, and educational domains.
0537.research_direction: Dr. Kellman has recently been investigating the mechanisms of perceptual learning and the processes underlying abstract shape representation in the visual system. Their recent work explores how adaptive, comparison-based training regimens reshape perceived visual similarity and improve category learning in complex naturalistic domains, such as medical image diagnosis and face identification. In parallel, they are examining how the human visual system extracts global shape from discrete elements like dot arrays, using behavioral tasks to probe whether the processing of local contour features is mechanistically distinct from global shape representation. Furthermore, Dr. Kellman is comparing these human spatial and configural capacities with deep convolutional neural networks, testing AI architectures on relational tasks like visual enclosure and same-different judgments to identify limitations in how current models encode abstract visual information.

papers.title: Categorization-driven perceptual learning changes perceived similarity in the naturalistic domain of skin lesion diagnosis
papers.abstract: Participants with no medical training rated how alike pairs of skin lesions looked, before and after a comparison-based training program using more than 500 examples across ten categories. Training made lesions in the same category look more alike and lesions in different categories look less alike. The size of this perceptual shift predicted how well people generalized to new lesions, indicating that category learning reshapes perception in a realistic, large-category-set task.
papers.authors: Victoria L. Jacoby, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Adaptively triggered comparisons enhance perceptual category learning: evidence from face learning
papers.abstract: The authors built a training method in which errors made during interactive learning automatically trigger a side-by-side comparison of the confused categories. Applied to learning to identify faces, this adaptive comparison approach improved learning of hard-to-tell-apart categories relative to standard training. The work extends the lab's adaptive perceptual learning technology to a new domain beyond medical images.
papers.authors: Victoria L. Jacoby, Christine M. Massey, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Shape from dots: a window into abstraction processes in visual perception
papers.abstract: Using arrays of separate dots, the study asks what spatial relations make the visual system perceive a smooth contour versus a shape with vertices. Experiments show that perceived smoothness depends on the spacing and orientation relations among dots, and the results point to constraints on curvature and smoothness in forming abstract shape. The paper positions dot displays as a tool for studying abstraction in vision and for comparison with neural network models.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Configural relations in humans and deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Building on earlier findings that deep convolutional networks are insensitive to global object shape, the authors test whether this reflects a broader limitation with relations. AlexNet and ResNet-50 were trained on relational tasks such as same-different judgments of two shapes and enclosure of a dot by a closed figure amid contour noise. The networks struggled to learn and generalize these relations in ways humans do, supporting the view that abstract relational encoding is missing from current architectures.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Patrick Garrigan, Austin Phillips, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Independent mechanisms for processing local contour features and global shape
papers.abstract: The paper examines whether human perception of local contour features and of global shape rely on separable processes. Behavioral experiments dissociate the two, suggesting that global shape representations are not simply built from local contour information. The findings bear on how shape is represented in human vision and why models built on local features may fall short.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

0540.name: Philippe G. Schyns
0540.bio: Philippe G. Schyns is a Professor of Psychology and Director of the Institute of Neuroscience and Psychology at the University of Glasgow. Schyns developed the 'Bubbles' technique, a data-driven methodology designed to isolate the specific visual information—such as spatial frequency and orientation—that humans utilize for object, scene, and face categorization. Their research integrates computational modeling, psychophysics, and brain imaging (MEG and EEG) to decode the information-processing content of neural signals. Currently, their work utilizes generative models and Deep Neural Networks to examine the relationship between brain activity and cognitive computation in the representation and transmission of visual information.
0540.research_direction: Dr. Schyns has recently been investigating how the human brain dynamically selects, routes, and processes complex visual information to serve specific behavioral goals. Their recent work explores how task demands dictate visual computations, using magnetoencephalography and generative 4D stimulus models to track how dynamic facial movements for emotion and static identity features are gated and channeled through distinct neural pathways. They are also examining the top-down mechanisms of perception, specifically asking how the prefrontal cortex guides dimension-reducing transformations in the visual cortex during categorization tasks and how predictive neural representations bias perceptual decision-making. Additionally, Dr. Schyns is exploring broader computational frameworks, investigating how generative stimulus models can be deployed to explicitly test and compare visual feature utilization across both biological brains and deep neural networks.

papers.title: Task demands dynamically structure feature selection, routing, and integration in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using generative 4D face stimuli and participant-specific MEG (N=24), the study asks how task demands control visual computations. Task-relevant features are first gated in occipital cortex, then routed along separate channels (3D identity to the ventral pathway, 4D emotion to the lateral pathway), and finally combined in temporal cortex. The results give an account of how tasks shape feature selection, routing and integration in the brain.
papers.authors: Yuening Yan, Jiayu Zhan, Yaocong Duan, Oliver Garrod, Robin Ince, Changsong Zhou, Rachael Jack, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: The brain computes dynamic facial movements for emotion categorization using a third pathway
papers.abstract: Participants categorized dynamic facial expressions generated by a 4D face model while MEG was recorded. Information-theoretic analyses linking face movement features, brain activity and behavior revealed, in each participant, a pathway from occipital cortex to superior temporal gyrus that specifically carries the facial movements needed for emotion categorization. This supports a dedicated third social pathway for dynamic signals, functionally separate from the ventral route that handles identity.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Yuening Yan, Jiayu Zhan, Oliver G. B. Garrod, Robin A. A. Ince, Rachael E. Jack, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: Pre-frontal cortex guides dimension-reducing transformations in the occipito-ventral pathway for categorization behaviors
papers.abstract: Combining MEG with generative models of faces and information-theoretic tools, the authors show that occipito-ventral cortex compresses visual input into the dimensions needed for the current categorization task. Prefrontal cortex guides this dimension-reducing transformation, and the effect changes with the task, for example emotion, gender or vehicle judgments.
papers.authors: Yaocong Duan, Jiayu Zhan, Joachim Gross, Robin A.A. Ince, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: Strength of predicted information content in the brain biases decision behavior
papers.abstract: Using MEG and a design that manipulates the predicted content of stimuli, the study links the strength of brain representations of predicted category features to biases in perceptual decisions. Stronger neural representation of predicted information leads to more biased choices.
papers.authors: Yuening Yan, Jiayu Zhan, Oliver Garrod, Xuan Cui, Robin A.A. Ince, Philippe G. Schyns

papers.title: Stimulus models test hypotheses in brains and DNNs
papers.abstract: This opinion piece argues that generative stimulus models let researchers test explicit hypotheses about which stimulus features brains and deep networks use. It sets out how such models can be used to compare the information processing of biological and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Philippe G. Schyns, Lukas Snoek, Christoph Daube

0541.name: Phillip Guan
0541.bio: Phillip Guan is a research scientist at Meta Reality Labs Research, where they investigate the interface between human vision science and near-eye display architectures. Guan’s research focuses on perceptual requirements for immersive computing, specifically establishing thresholds for world-locked rendering, stereopsis, and eye-tracked distortion correction in virtual and augmented reality. Their work involves the quantification of visual discomfort through the identification of behavioral correlates and the development of adaptive psychophysical frameworks such as AEPsych. Guan received a PhD in Vision Science from the University of California, Berkeley, where their doctoral research focused on stereoscopic depth constancy and binocular vision.
0541.research_direction: Dr. Guan has recently been investigating the perceptual psychophysics and ergonomics of mixed, virtual, and augmented reality systems. Their recent work explores how system artifacts—such as latency, tracking imperfections, and head-pose jitter—impact visual comfort, utilizing both subjective time-resolved symptom tracking and objective behavioral measures like blink and eye-movement patterns. To rigorously probe these phenomena, they have developed custom ultra-low latency passthrough hardware that isolates how specific rendering and display factors affect mixed reality perception. Additionally, they are examining the perceptual thresholds required for stable world-locked rendering and investigating how stereoscopic geometry errors distort perceived distance and drive visuomotor recalibration during active reaching tasks.

papers.title: A Two-Millisecond Passthrough Headset for Perceptual Studies
papers.abstract: Describes a custom video see-through headset built as a research platform, with end-to-end passthrough latency of about two milliseconds so that real-world imagery is presented with near-negligible delay. The system is intended to let vision scientists probe how latency, rendering and display factors affect perception in mixed reality under tightly controlled conditions.
papers.authors: Eric Penner, Josephine D'Angelo, Clinton Smith, Nathan Matsuda, Navaneethan Siva, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Subthreshold Jitter in VR Can Induce Visual Discomfort
papers.abstract: Combines a psychophysical measurement of the detection threshold for sinusoidal head-pose jitter with a multi-session study in which participants played a commercial VR game on a Quest 3 with jitter set below that threshold. Even undetectable jitter produced measurable discomfort, visible only in frequent time-resolved symptom ratings and not in standard pre/post questionnaires.
papers.venue: UIST 2025 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
papers.authors: Samuel J. Levulis, Kevin W. Rio, James P. Wilmott, Pablo Ramon Soria, Charlie S. Burlingham, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Perceptual Sensitivity to Stereo Geometry Errors in Head-Mounted Displays
papers.abstract: Presents a geometric framework predicting how errors in render-camera position and viewing position in a headset distort perceived distance. Five experiments on a Quest 3 with eye tracking show that such errors cause both under- and over-estimation of distance, and that real-time visual feedback can recalibrate reaching so that reach distance becomes accurate anyway.
papers.authors: Raffles Xingqi Zhu, Charlie S. Burlingham, Olivier Mercier, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Identifying Behavioral Correlates to Visual Discomfort
papers.abstract: Searches for objective behavioral signals of visual discomfort in head-mounted displays, examining measures such as blinking and eye-movement patterns recorded while users experience conditions that induce discomfort. The work aims to replace or supplement subjective questionnaires with measurable indicators usable for evaluating displays.
papers.authors: David Tovar, James Wilmott, Xiuyun Wu, Daniel Martin, Michael Proulx, Dave Lindberg, Yang Zhao, Olivier Mercier, Phillip Guan

papers.title: Perceptual Requirements for World-Locked Rendering in AR and VR
papers.abstract: Measures how much error in the rendered position of virtual content, caused by head-motion and pose-estimation imperfections, observers can tolerate before the content stops appearing fixed in the world. The results give quantitative perceptual requirements for latency and tracking in AR and VR rendering pipelines.
papers.authors: Phillip Guan, Eric Penner, Joel Hegland, Benjamin Letham, Douglas Lanman

0542.name: Pinglei Bao
0542.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences
0542.bio: Pinglei Bao is a Principal Investigator researching the neural mechanisms of high-level visual cognition, including object recognition, scene categorization, and contour segmentation. Bao integrates large-scale electrophysiological recordings using Neuropixels, functional MRI, and micro-electrical stimulation in human and non-human primate models. Their research characterizes the primate inferotemporal (IT) cortex by identifying a systematic map of 'object space' to explain the organization of visual representations across the cortical surface. Bao's current work focuses on bridging population-level dynamics and single-neuron activity while using deep learning frameworks to model transformations in the primate visual system.
0542.research_direction: Dr. Bao has recently been investigating the neural representation of complex visual objects across different species and cognitive states. To bridge the gap between single-neuron dynamics and large-scale cortical maps, they are combining fMRI with dense Neuropixels recordings in the macaque inferotemporal cortex to examine how nonhuman primate responses to natural scenes align with human neuroimaging datasets. In parallel, their recent work explores how high-level visual representations are spatially reorganized to support different cognitive demands. Specifically, they use fMRI decoding to investigate how interhemispheric coordination and the spatial distribution of object identity codes shift when a stimulus is maintained in visual working memory versus when it is actively perceived.

papers.title: Triple-N dataset: large-scale fMRI-guided dense recordings of nonhuman primate neural responses to natural scenes
papers.abstract: The authors built a macaque counterpart to the human Natural Scenes Dataset, recording dense Neuropixels activity from inferotemporal cortex and early visual areas while monkeys viewed the same 1,000 images, with recording sites guided by fMRI-defined category-selective regions. Analyses show robust category tuning, diverse response time courses and image-dependent latency differences across units. Aligning the monkey data with human NSD fMRI reveals both correspondences and divergences in representational geometry, making the resource a bridge between single-neuron dynamics, cortical maps and cross-species comparison.
papers.authors: Yipeng Li, Xieyi Liu, Wanru Li, Jia Yang, Baoqi Gong, Wei Jin, Zhengxin Gong, Kesheng Wang, Jingqiu Luo, Zishuo Zhao, Pinglei Bao

papers.title: Spatial reorganization of object representations in high-level visual cortex distinguishes working memory from perception
papers.abstract: Using matched tasks and fMRI decoding, the study compares where object identity is represented in object-selective cortex during perception versus visual working memory. Perception keeps object information mostly in the contralateral hemisphere, whereas working memory recruits robust ipsilateral representations even for bilateral memory items, using over 90% of ipsilateral vertices. These ipsilateral codes mirror the contralateral ones and are not explained by attention span, pointing to interhemispheric coordination that lets memory flexibly reorganize high-level visual representations.
papers.authors: Wanru Li, Jia Yang, Pinglei Bao

0543.name: Po-Jang (Brown) Hsieh
0543.bio: Po-Jang Hsieh is a faculty member in the Department of Psychology at National Taiwan University and directs the Brain & Consciousness Lab. Hsieh’s research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying visual awareness, attention, and the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing. Their findings demonstrate how neural activity patterns in the visual cortex predict subjective perceptual states and decision-making behaviors. Prior to this position, Hsieh held an assistant professorship at Duke-NUS Medical School and conducted postdoctoral research at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
0543.research_direction: Dr. Hsieh's recent work explores the neural mechanisms of visual awareness and object representation using fMRI, MEG, and multivariate decoding. Specifically, they are investigating how deeply dynamic faces and scenes are processed without awareness under interocular suppression, and whether higher visual areas encode true object shapes or viewpoint-dependent perspectival shapes. They have also recently been examining spatial-boundary representations in visual memory, testing how boundary extension errors shift when scenes are recalled from first-person versus third-person perspectives. Additionally, their recent behavioral experiments probe multisensory time perception by measuring how visual and auditory information drive intentional binding, while also evaluating whether 40-Hz sensory stimulation can actually enhance visual thresholds and spatial memory in healthy observers.

papers.title: Attenuated boundary extension in observer perspective memory compared to field perspective memory
papers.abstract: Boundary extension is a memory error in which people recall seeing more of a scene than was shown. This study compares recall from an observer perspective (seeing oneself in the scene) with recall from a field perspective (the original viewpoint). Boundary extension appeared in observer-perspective memory but was weaker than in field-perspective memory, and higher cognitive load and greater viewing distance reduced it further. The results point to different spatial-boundary representations in the two memory perspectives.
papers.authors: Shao-Chi Chiu, Ying-Tung Lin, Christopher Jude McCarroll, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Decoding dynamic faces and scenes without awareness under dis-continuous flash suppression
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in 43 participants, the study asks how deeply faces are processed when interocular suppression makes them invisible. Univariate activation differences between faces and scenes vanished under suppression, but whole-brain multivariate decoding could still tell invisible faces from scenes in occipito-temporal cortex, and FFA/OFA separated dynamic invisible faces from dynamic invisible scenes. The authors argue that better stimuli, paradigms and analyses reveal in-depth unconscious processing in the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Yen-Ju Feng, Shao-Min Hung, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Visual information shows dominance in determining the magnitude of intentional binding for audiovisual outcomes
papers.abstract: Intentional binding is the compression of perceived time between a voluntary action and its outcome. Using a modified Libet clock and a dynamic collision event, two experiments (n = 42 each) show binding also occurs for audiovisual outcomes but is weaker than for auditory outcomes, regardless of audiovisual integration. Vision appears to dominate the binding magnitude, supported by Bayesian evidence that audiovisual and visual outcomes do not differ.
papers.authors: De-Wei Dai, Po-Jang (Brown) Hsieh

papers.title: Neural representations of perspectival shapes and attentional effects: Evidence from fMRI and MEG
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether higher visual areas such as lateral occipital cortex represent viewpoint-dependent (perspectival) shapes rather than only true object shape. Combining fMRI, MEG and multivariate decoding, classifiers trained on round and oval shapes labeled rotated objects by their perspectival shape in LOC starting about 200 ms after onset. Attention spread this effect from occipital to temporal cortex and made it more sustained.
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Yung-Yi Hsu, Tony Cheng, Pin-Cheng Hsiung, Chen-Wei Wu, Po-Jang Hsieh

papers.title: Forty-Hertz audiovisual stimulation does not have a promoting effect on visual threshold and visual spatial memory
papers.abstract: Motivated by mouse studies showing that 40-Hz sensory stimulation helps Alzheimer's-like pathology, the authors tested whether it boosts visual performance in healthy people. Across five experiments varying stimulus source, frequency, modality and task (visual threshold, spatial memory, spatial frequency), stimulated groups showed no benefit over controls beyond a lost practice effect. They conclude that 40-Hz stimulation does not enhance visual threshold or visual spatial memory.
papers.authors: Pin-Cheng Hsiung, Po-Jang Hsieh

0544.name: Preeti Verghese
0544.lab_name: Verghese Lab: Vision Research on Attention and Adaptation
0544.bio: Preeti Verghese is a Senior Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute whose research investigates the neural mechanisms and behavioral strategies governing visual attention, spatial perception, and oculomotor control. Verghese explores how clinical populations, particularly those with age-related macular degeneration and amblyopia, adapt to vision loss through altered eye-movement patterns and the use of peripheral retina for tasks such as stereopsis and visual search. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, eye tracking, and computational modeling, they examine the integration of binocular and monocular cues to understand depth perception and target tracking in both healthy and impaired visual systems. Recent research by Verghese focuses on the recovery of stereopsis and the development of rehabilitative interventions designed to optimize functional vision in individuals with central field loss.
0544.research_direction: Dr. Verghese's recent work has been investigating the interplay between oculomotor control and visual perception, with a strong focus on how eye movements shape depth and dynamic vision in both normal and clinical populations. Much of their research explores visual function in macular degeneration, specifically testing how reliance on the peripheral retina and deficits in smooth pursuit impact dynamic visual acuity and the ability to extrapolate target motion. They have also recently been examining depth perception mechanisms, mapping stereoacuity across the central visual field to question fovea-centric assumptions and evaluating how patients with central vision loss combine binocular disparity and motion parallax cues. Additionally, their work probes the binocular deficits of amblyopia by measuring eye vergence during stereo tasks to determine how oculomotor anomalies contribute to impaired stereopsis.

papers.title: The best stereoacuity is rarely at the fovea
papers.abstract: Stereoscopic depth sensitivity is usually assumed to peak at the fovea, but this study maps stereoacuity across the central visual field in observers with normal vision. For most observers the best depth sensitivity lay outside the fovea, at eccentric locations. The result challenges the fovea-centric view and bears directly on depth perception when central vision is lost.
papers.authors: Ângela Gomes Tomaz, Adrien Chopin, Noelia Gabriela Alcalde, Dennis M. Levi, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Cue combination for depth perception in macular degeneration: Motion parallax augments disparity
papers.abstract: The paper asks how people with macular degeneration combine binocular disparity and motion parallax to judge depth when they must rely on peripheral retina. Adding motion parallax to disparity improved depth judgments in these observers, so cue combination remains useful despite central field loss. This points to practical routes for supporting depth perception in patients.
papers.authors: Jade Guénot, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Vergence anomalies are associated with impaired stereopsis in amblyopia
papers.abstract: The study measures eye vergence during stereo tasks in people with amblyopia and links it to their stereoacuity. Observers with poorer stereopsis showed more abnormal vergence behavior, suggesting oculomotor control contributes to the deficit alongside sensory factors. The work connects binocular eye movements to depth perception in amblyopia.
papers.authors: Preeti Verghese, Adrien Chopin, Ângela Gomes-Tomaz, Noelia Gabriela Alcalde, Dennis M. Levi

papers.title: Oculomotor challenges in macular degeneration impact motion extrapolation
papers.abstract: Observers with macular degeneration tracked and predicted the path of a moving target that briefly disappeared. Unstable fixation and poor smooth pursuit when using a non-central retinal locus degraded their ability to extrapolate the motion. The results show how eye-movement problems limit dynamic vision in central field loss.
papers.authors: Jason F. Rubinstein, Noelia Gabriela Alcalde, Adrien Chopin, Preeti Verghese

papers.title: Smooth pursuit deficits impact dynamic visual acuity in macular degeneration
papers.abstract: This work tests how well people with macular degeneration see moving targets and relates it to how accurately they pursue them. Poorer smooth pursuit went with worse dynamic visual acuity, so oculomotor deficits account for part of the functional loss. It supports pursuit as a target for rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Natela M. Shanidze, Preeti Verghese

0545.name: Qasim Zaidi
0545.bio: Qasim Zaidi is a SUNY Distinguished Professor who investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception through psychophysics, computational modeling, and neurophysiology. Their research focuses on how the visual system decodes information such as color constancy, three-dimensional shape from texture, and the perception of material properties. Zaidi studies the functional architecture of the primary visual cortex and retinal ganglion cell wiring, using generative models to link neural filter transformations to perceptual phenomena like amblyopic distortions and visual illusions. Recent work by Zaidi utilizes connectomics and fMRI-guided recordings to explore color decoding and the dynamics of primate retinal circuits.
0545.research_direction: Dr. Zaidi has recently been investigating how the visual system constructs complex representations of form, motion, and 3D space from low-level sensory signals. Their recent work explores the perceptual mechanisms governing object rigidity, using psychophysics and computational modeling to test how motion energy, feature tracking, shape priors, and hardwired V1 orientation anisotropies determine whether a rotating stimulus appears rigid or deforming. In the clinical domain, they are studying generative visual anomalies in amblyopia, utilizing dichoptic matching and reverse correlation to map the altered cortical receptive fields responsible for phantom shape perception. Additionally, their research bridges high-level spatial inference and visual aesthetics by examining the implicit projective geometry humans use for 3D pose estimation, and by combining behavioral ratings with pupillometry to investigate how global shape configurations drive the perception of dynamism in art.

papers.title: Dynamism in paintings and photographs: how the power of diagonals in art overcomes the oblique effect in visual perception
papers.abstract: Diagonals convey dynamism in art although vision is less sensitive to oblique orientations. Using rhombus configurations with independently manipulated global and local orientation, ratings, pairwise comparisons and pupillometry show that global configuration orientation and shape, not local edge orientation, drives perceived dynamism, giving perceptual principles for dynamic composition.
papers.authors: Serena Castellotti, Elvio Blini, Maria Michela Del Viva, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Phantom Forms in Amblyopic Vision and what they reveal about the Generative Brain
papers.abstract: Many people with amblyopia see phantom shapes that are more complex than the simple gratings shown to their amblyopic eye. Using dichoptic displays, the authors found that nearly all such phantoms could be matched exactly by plaids shown to the fellow eye. From this matching they derived the amblyopic cortical receptive fields as linear transforms of the fellow-eye ones; the resulting model reproduces the phantoms, is validated by reverse correlation, and accounts for deficits in form detection and localization.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Bhavatharini Ramakrishnan, Farzaneh Olianezhad, Jingyun Wang, Jose-Manuel Alonso, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Anisotropy of object nonrigidity: High-level perceptual consequences of cortical anisotropy
papers.abstract: Two rigidly connected rotating rings look rigid when they rotate about a vertical axis but appear to wobble independently when the same video is turned 90 degrees. The authors explain this by decoding V1 outputs that include the known cortical anisotropies (more, and more narrowly tuned, horizontal-orientation cells) and by optic-flow gradients that align differently with rigid versus non-rigid motion. The work shows how hardwired low-level cortical properties can shape high-level failures of shape constancy and rigidity.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Perceptual transitions between object rigidity and non-rigidity: Competition and cooperation among motion energy, feature tracking, and shape-based priors
papers.abstract: Rotating objects can look rigid or deformable depending on stimulus details, and the percept can switch between the two. The authors show these transitions arise from competition and cooperation among motion-energy signals, feature-tracking signals, and priors about object shape, and they build a model that predicts human judgments across conditions.
papers.authors: Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

papers.title: Complexity of mental geometry for 3D pose perception
papers.abstract: The study asks how observers judge the 3D orientation of objects in scenes and pictures, and how hard the underlying geometric computation is. Results indicate that people rely on an implicit sense of projective geometry, with performance depending on the complexity of the required inference across poses and views.
papers.authors: Crystal Guo, Akihito Maruya, Qasim Zaidi

0546.name: Qi Chen
0546.bio: Qi Chen is a cognitive neuroscientist who uses computational modeling and multi-modal neuroimaging, including fMRI, EEG, and intracranial recordings, to study the neural mechanisms of human perception and cognition. Their research explores the dynamics of visual attention and perceptual inference, demonstrating how intrinsic alpha-band oscillations facilitate perceptual grouping and resolve ambiguity through predictive preactivation. Chen also investigates numerical cognition, reinforcement learning, and the functional organization of the frontoparietal and default mode networks in cognitive control and multisensory integration.
0546.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been using scalp and human intracranial EEG to investigate the high-resolution neural dynamics underlying perception, motor control, memory, and clinical pathology. In the perceptual and cognitive domains, their recent work explores the influence of top-down task demands on pre-stimulus alpha frequency and sensory templates during bistable apparent motion, as well as the specific thalamocortical networks engaged by auditory versus visual attentional cues. They are also investigating the temporal progression of human motor planning across the cortical hierarchy, alongside theoretical work probing how the neural representations of fear extinction contexts map onto established episodic memory taxonomies. Finally, their clinical electrophysiology research examines the reproducibility of high-frequency spectral activity and network connectivity across repeated seizures to evaluate their utility in identifying epileptogenic zones.

papers.title: Extinction memories: putting learning into context
papers.abstract: This opinion piece builds on human intracranial recordings showing that the neural representations of extinction contexts are more distinct than those formed during fear acquisition. It argues that extinction memories therefore behave like episodic, context-bound memories, and considers what this means for established taxonomies of memory systems and for understanding fear generalization.
papers.authors: Nikolai Axmacher, Daniel Pacheco-Estefan, Antoine Bouyeure, Qi Chen

papers.title: Earlier finish of motor planning in the premotor cortex predicts faster motor command in the primary motor cortex: Human intracranial EEG evidence
papers.abstract: Using intracranial EEG in patients performing a cued finger-movement task, the study tracks how high-gamma activity unfolds across premotor cortex, supplementary motor area and primary motor cortex. Activity in these regions switches on in sequence, and the faster planning-related activity in the non-primary motor areas returns to baseline, the earlier the primary motor cortex issues its command and the shorter the reaction time. Longer-lasting coherence between motor areas goes along with slower responses, revealing a temporal signature of hierarchical motor control.
papers.authors: Jing Xia, Deshan Gong, Biao Han, Qiang Guo, Yang Zhan, Gereon R. Fink, Silvia Daun, Qi Chen

papers.title: Reproducibility of temporally evolving seizure patterns and network connectivity in focal epilepsy
papers.abstract: In 14 patients with focal epilepsy recorded with stereo-EEG, the study asks whether signals, spectra and connectivity are reproducible across repeated seizures and whether this separates the epileptogenic zone from propagation and uninvolved zones. Reproducibility of high- and low-frequency activity was greater in the epileptogenic zone during seizures, and beta-band reproducibility and connectivity patterns could already discriminate the epileptogenic zone before seizure onset, suggesting a stable neuronal-population signature useful for localization.
papers.authors: Yaohong Wei, Wei Zhang, Sinclair Xingzhou Liu, Biao Han, Qi Chen

papers.title: Superior Attentional Efficiency of Auditory Cue via the Ventral Auditory-thalamic Pathway
papers.abstract: Two experiments compared informative auditory and visual cues and found that auditory cues that matched the upcoming target gave larger reaction-time benefits than matched visual cues. When the target matched the auditory cue, auditory-thalamic connectivity scaled with the behavioral benefit, while violations of the cue engaged a ventral auditory-prefrontal pathway whose coupling scaled with the behavioral cost. A dorsal frontoparietal network reacted to violations regardless of cue modality.
papers.authors: Ke Wang, Ying Fang, Qiang Guo, Lu Shen, Qi Chen

papers.title: Task demands modulate pre-stimulus alpha frequency and sensory template during bistable apparent motion perception
