papers.abstract: Using EEG with a bistable Ternus apparent-motion display, the authors manipulated sustained task demands toward temporal integration or segregation. Task demands shifted the pre-stimulus peak alpha frequency, which gates the temporal integration window, and time-resolved decoding showed that sensory templates resembling the preferred percept appear even before the stimulus evidence is sufficient. Top-down goals therefore bias ambiguous perception through both alpha frequency and pre-stimulus sensory templates.
papers.authors: Biao Han, Yanni Zhang, Lu Shen, Lei Mo, Qi Chen

0547.name: Quan Lei
0547.bio: Quan Lei is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Wichita State University and the director of the Vision and Accessibility (VISA) Lab. Lei integrates psychophysics, eye tracking, and computational modeling to investigate visual processes such as attention, perception, and short-term memory. Their research applies these principles to accessibility for individuals with visual impairments, including the development of inclusive autonomous vehicle interfaces. Lei also identified the 'weak conquer the strong' illusion in visual numerosity, which demonstrates how contrast energy modulates perceived quantities.
0547.research_direction: Dr. Lei has recently been studying how people with low vision see and get around in everyday environments. Their recent work explores how indoor lighting levels affect whether someone can spot steps and ramps, and what people with different degrees of vision loss want from autonomous vehicles in terms of safety, trust, and interface design. They are also interested in a basic perceptual question, how people judge the number of items in a display, and have been developing a model in which these estimates depend on the total contrast energy of the elements.

papers.title: The Effect of Illumination on the Visibility of Steps and Ramps for People with Low Vision
papers.abstract: In indoor environments, inadequate visibility of architectural features such as stairs and ramps introduces substantial navigational hazards for individuals with low vision. This investigation evaluated the influence of varying indoor photopic illuminance on step and ramp identification in low-vision individuals and normally sighted control observers under simulated acuity reduction. Physical full-scale step and ramp configurations were set up within an enclosed room under three overhead photopic lighting conditions: 800, 80, and 8 lux. Participants performed a five-alternative forced-choice (5-AFC) target identification task and provided subjective confidence ratings on a 5-point scale, with visual acuity and Pelli-Robson contrast sensitivity measured concurrently across each illuminance level. Objective recognition accuracy remained statistically invariant across the 8 to 800 lux photopic range in both cohorts. In contrast, ambient illuminance exerted a significant effect on subjective confidence ratings among low-vision participants, who exhibited systematically elevated certainty with increasing lighting levels. Furthermore, regression analyses revealed that objective identification accuracy was best predicted by contrast sensitivity, whereas subjective judgment confidence was primarily predicted by visual acuity. These findings demonstrate that while indoor photopic illumination shifts do not impair objective hazard identification accuracy, higher illumination levels are necessary to preserve subjective perceptual confidence during low-vision mobility.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Rachel Gage, Daniel Kersten, Gordon E. Legge

papers.title: Preferences of Individuals With Different Levels of Visual Impairment for Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: This research investigates the nexus between the magnitude of visual impairment and user expectations regarding autonomous vehicle (AV) technology. A cohort of individuals with varying degrees of vision loss provided data through a structured survey focused on perceived safety, technological trust, and human-machine interface (HMI) requirements. Analysis revealed that while there is an overarching inclination toward Level 5 full automation, participants with less severe deficits exhibited significantly higher acceptance of lower-level automation compared to those with total blindness. Furthermore, although auditory and speech-based modalities were the universally preferred interaction methods, the data indicates that individuals with residual vision retain a strong desire for redundant visual feedback. These results emphasize the necessity of adaptive, multi-modal interface designs tailored to the specific functional vision of the end-user.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Robert Beran, Yueh-Hsun Wu, Quan Lei

papers.title: Numerosity depends on normalized contrast energy: Review and square-root law model
papers.abstract: Judgments of visual numerosity for randomly distributed elements of static contrast depend systematically on the integrated contrast energy (CE) of the stimulus array. We present a computational framework demonstrating that the square root of contrast energy, √(CE), normalized by stimulus contrast amplitude, accurately fits human numerosity estimation across varied psychophysical tasks and extensive set sizes. The model shows that judged numerosity scales as a linear function of √(N) for element counts exceeding the subitization regime. This square-root dependency accounts for several well-documented perceptual phenomena: the pervasive underestimation in absolute numerosity estimation; contrast constancy (the invariance of perceived quantity across varying contrasts in segregated arrays); the 'weak outnumber strong' illusion in which higher-contrast items appear less numerous when intermingled with lower-contrast items; and psychometric discrimination thresholds and sensitivity between arrays containing N and M items. The close fit of this normalized contrast energy formulation across broad ranges, including regimes traditionally categorized under Weber's law, indicates that normalized contrast energy serves as a fundamental sensory substrate encoding visual numerosity.
papers.authors: Quan Lei, Adam Reeves

0548.name: Quoc Vuong
0548.department: School of Psychology and Biosciences Institute
0548.bio: Quoc Vuong is a Senior Lecturer at Newcastle University’s Biosciences Institute and School of Psychology. Vuong investigates the neural and cognitive mechanisms involved in multi-sensory perception, specifically how the brain integrates spatiotemporal information from vision, audition, touch, and pain for object and face recognition. They utilize a multi-modal approach combining psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye-tracking. Their work explores the development of visual expertise and the cortical networks supporting the perception of dynamic objects and communicative interactions.
0548.research_direction: Dr. Vuong has recently been investigating how humans perceive actions, bodies, and social interactions across diverse visual contexts. Their recent work explores the visual and neural mechanisms of action perception, using spatial and temporal video manipulations to isolate the minimal visual features needed to recognize first-person egocentric actions, and fMRI with point-light displays to map how we incidentally process the spatiotemporal cues of communicative interactions. Additionally, they are examining affective and multisensory processing by meta-analyzing the developmental trajectory of bodily emotion recognition in early childhood and by building standardized audiovisual stimulus databases to study emotional responses to everyday misophonia triggers. Extending these core interests in perception and affect, they are also applying cognitive models of emotion and attitude to study complex real-world decision-making, such as modeling consumer preferences for alternative fuel vehicles.

papers.title: Seeing Just Enough: The Contribution of Hands, Objects and Visual Features to Egocentric Action Recognition
papers.abstract: The authors ask which visual information humans need to recognise everyday actions in first-person video. They took easy and hard egocentric kitchen videos, had participants label them, and then progressively cropped and scrambled each clip in a large online study to find minimal recognisable configurations. Recognition broke down when the manipulated object and strong orientation signals were removed, and frame-scrambling disrupted most clips, while the acting hand mattered only marginally. The results point to a role for both mid- and high-level features in naturalistic action perception.
papers.authors: Filip Rybansky, Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Andrew Gilbert, Frank Guerin, Anya C. Hurlbert, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: SAVi-M: A Standardised Auditory-Visual Database to Investigate Affective Response to Trigger Events
papers.abstract: The paper releases a lab-made set of 250 short videos of scripted everyday sounds and actions (eating, tapping, rustling, mouth/nose, throat and neutral) for misophonia research. In an online study, 96 participants, including people with misophonia and controls, rated each video on arousal, valence and dominance. The database gives researchers a standardised, ecologically valid audiovisual stimulus set.
papers.authors: Paris Arizona Ash, Timothy Griffiths, Quoc Vuong

papers.title: Cognitive consistency and preferences for alternative fuel vehicles: A latent class model
papers.abstract: The study models vehicle fuel-type choice with a latent class discrete choice model in which attitudes and emotional appraisals from a hot-coherence (HOTCO) cognitive model shape class membership and preferences. Data came from a stated choice experiment plus an attitudinal questionnaire. Three segments emerged, potential innovators, laggards and sceptics, differing in motives and preferences, which has implications for policy design.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment
papers.authors: Cristian Domarchi, Elisabetta Cherchi, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: Incidental visual processing of spatiotemporal cues in communicative interactions: An fMRI investigation
papers.abstract: Observers viewed point-light displays of two people either interacting communicatively or acting independently while performing an unrelated brightness task, so that the body movements were processed incidentally. Communicative interactions engaged right anterior superior temporal sulcus only when the agents faced each other, and, after controlling for local motion, parietal cortex, left amygdala and brainstem/cerebellum. The work shows that spatial and temporal relations between people are picked up even outside attention.
papers.authors: Anthony P. Atkinson, Quoc C. Vuong

papers.title: The development of emotion processing of body expressions from infancy to early childhood: A meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This meta-analysis pools developmental studies that used body stimuli to test whether infants and young children discriminate and process emotions from body expressions. Across many stimulus types and paradigms, children could process body emotion, and the evidence did not show clear changes in ability with age. The authors discuss gaps in the literature and argue for more naturalistic approaches.
papers.authors: Quoc C. Vuong, Elena Geangu

0550.name: Rachel Denison
0550.bio: Rachel Denison is an Assistant Professor at Boston University whose research investigates the temporal dynamics of visual perception, attention, and decision-making. Denison uses a multi-methodological approach integrating psychophysics, eye tracking, fMRI, and MEG/EEG with computational modeling to characterize how the brain prioritizes information at specific moments in time. Their research includes the development of a dynamic normalization model of temporal attention and high-resolution functional mapping of the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways in the human lateral geniculate nucleus. Denison’s current work examines the mechanisms of voluntary temporal attention and how the brain incorporates uncertainty into perceptual choices and confidence judgments.
0550.research_direction: Dr. Denison has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms of visual attention, with a strong focus on temporal attention—how the visual system anticipates and prioritizes specific moments in time. Using a combination of MEG and psychophysics, their recent work explores the anticipatory and evoked cortical dynamics that support this temporal prioritization. They are also utilizing artificial neural networks and developing dynamic spatiotemporal normalization models to understand how attention-like behaviors and contextual effects, such as adaptation and suppression, emerge computationally. Furthermore, their collaborative behavioral research rigorously probes the intersection of attention and consciousness by examining the phenomenon of subjective inflation to test how inattention dissociates objective visual performance from subjective visibility reports.

papers.title: How attention-like behavior emerges in an artificial neural network
papers.abstract: The authors train a neural network on visual tasks and examine how attention-like behavioral effects arise without any explicit attention mechanism being built in. Analyzing the network reveals which computational ingredients give rise to signature attentional benefits, connecting biological attention findings to model mechanisms. The study offers a testbed for hypotheses about how attention could emerge from learning and normalization-style computations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Angus F. Chapman, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: A dynamic spatiotemporal normalization model captures perceptual and neural effects of spatial and temporal context
papers.abstract: The paper presents a computational model in which divisive normalization operates jointly over space and time to explain how the visual system responds to stimuli given their surrounding and preceding context. The single model reproduces a range of perceptual phenomena and neural response patterns, including those seen in temporal and spatial suppression and adaptation, that were previously handled by separate accounts. It offers a unifying framework for context effects in vision.
papers.authors: Angus F. Chapman, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: Attention robustly dissociates objective performance and subjective visibility reports (When awareness outstrips performance: critical tests of subjective inflation under inattention)
papers.abstract: A large multi-lab collaboration stress-tests the claim of subjective inflation, in which unattended peripheral stimuli seem stronger than attended ones despite matched performance. Across carefully controlled experiments the authors find that attention robustly dissociates performance from visibility reports in ways that challenge the inflation account. The results bear directly on theories of consciousness that rely on this dissociation.
papers.authors: Karen J. Tian, Brian Maniscalco, Michael L. Epstein, Angela Shen, Olenka Graham Castaneda, Taiga Kurosawa, Jennifer A. Motzer, Emil Olsson, Emily E. Russell, Michael E. Walsh, Juneau Wang, Tugral Bek Awrang Zeb, Richard Brown, Victor A. F. Lamme, Hakwan Lau, Biyu J. He, Jan W. Brascamp, Ned Block, David Chalmers, Megan A. K. Peters, Rachel N. Denison

papers.title: Anticipatory and evoked visual cortical dynamics of voluntary temporal attention
papers.abstract: Using MEG with a task that cues participants to attend to one of two brief moments in time, the study tracks how visual cortex activity changes both before a target appears and in response to it. Voluntary temporal attention produced anticipatory shifts in baseline activity and modulated the evoked responses, with gain-like effects on neural responses that tracked behavioral benefits. The work links preparatory and stimulus-driven dynamics in a single account of how the brain prioritizes moments in time.
papers.authors: Rachel N. Denison, Karen Tian, David J. Heeger, Marisa Carrasco

papers.title: Visual temporal attention from perception to computation
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes what is known about how observers prioritize moments in time in vision, spanning behavior, neural mechanisms, and computational models. It organizes the field around the distinction between anticipatory and stimulus-driven processes and identifies open questions, including how temporal attention should be modeled. It serves as a roadmap for research on temporal attention.
papers.authors: Rachel N. Denison

0551.name: Rachel Kelly
0551.bio: Rachel Kelly is a Principal Scientist at Exponent specializing in the intersection of cognitive neuroscience, perception, and human behavior. Kelly’s research focuses on human performance and safety, specifically investigating driver behavior, visibility, attention, and the neurophysiology of motor planning. They apply technical expertise in applied physiology to evaluate human interaction with complex systems, including the assessment of warning effectiveness and behavioral responses to risk communication. Kelly performs the design and execution of human subjects studies, focus groups, and usability evaluations for consumer and medical technology.
0551.research_direction: Dr. Kelly has recently been studying how immersive technology affects the visual and physical wellbeing of users. Their recent work explores what happens when children aged 10 to 12 play in virtual reality headsets for an hour a day over several days, tracking measures such as visual function, sensorimotor performance, and cognitive outcomes. The central question is whether moderate, repeated headset use is safe for developing visual systems.

papers.title: Effects of virtual reality use in children aged 10 to 12 years
papers.abstract: While immersive head-mounted displays (HMDs) are increasingly utilized by pediatric demographics for educational and gaming applications, empirical investigations regarding the safety and physiological impacts of sustained, moderate virtual reality (VR) exposure on developing populations remain limited. This study evaluated the short-term physiological, sensorimotor, and cognitive outcomes in children aged 10 to 12 years across four consecutive days of 60-minute VR gaming sessions. Standardized batteries assessed visual functioning (including monocular and binocular visual acuity, stereoacuity, accommodation, and vergence facility), visuomotor and hand-eye coordination, postural stability (center-of-pressure and sway metrics), and executive function indexed via an inhibitory control task, alongside subjective ratings of musculoskeletal discomfort and visually induced motion sickness (VIMS). Assessments administered before immersion on Day 1, immediately post-exposure on Day 4, and following a washout period on Day 5 demonstrated no clinically meaningful or statistically significant impairments in visual performance, postural control, or inhibitory capacity. Furthermore, self-reported visual and physical discomfort remained negligible throughout testing. These findings indicate that repeated moderate VR usage is well tolerated in late childhood without precipitating acute functional deficits, offering quantitative benchmarks to support pediatric ergonomics and user-safety guidelines.
papers.authors: Karol Silva, Nichole Breeland, Ashley M. Clark, Ilke Öztekin, Rachel L. Kelly

0552.name: Rachel Pye
0552.department: School of Psychology and Clinical Language Sciences
0552.bio: Rachel Pye is an Associate Professor in the School of Psychology and Clinical Language Sciences at the University of Reading and formerly served as the Head of Psychology for the University of Reading Malaysia. Pye’s research investigates the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms of literacy, focusing on dyslexia and reading development in monolingual and multilingual populations. They utilize behavioral methodologies and eye-tracking to evaluate the efficacy of visual and phonological interventions for reading difficulties and to measure individual differences in attentional speed. Pye's work also extends to pedagogical science, exploring the prevalence of neuromyths among educators and the optimization of assessment strategies in psychological education.
0552.research_direction: Dr. Pye has recently been working on how to measure cognitive abilities fairly and how people learn and are taught. Their recent work explores testing for reading difficulties in multilingual settings, using a test-teach-retest approach that separates learning potential from language proficiency, and developing a measure of how quickly individuals can deploy visual attention from the errors they make in rapid streams of items. They also examine education and mental health practice, including how common neuromyths are among educators and health students, how reducing assessment load affects undergraduate psychology courses, and how using an interpreter relates to waiting times and outcomes in NHS talking therapies.

papers.title: Clients using interpreters wait longer and have poorer outcomes in Talking Therapies for Anxiety and Depression – a retrospective cohort study on waiting times and treatment outcomes
papers.abstract: Although NHS Talking Therapies for Anxiety and Depression (TTad) delivers evidence-based cognitive behavioural interventions across England, therapeutic inequities continue to impact patients from culturally and linguistically diverse communities. This retrospective observational cohort study investigated waiting periods and clinical recovery rates for clients receiving interpreter-mediated Step 3 Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT). Utilizing national routine service audit datasets from 177,340 clients accessing care during the 2022–2023 period, treatment trajectories were contrasted between clients requiring language interpreters and non-interpreter controls. Survival and comparative analyses demonstrated that individuals requiring interpreter assistance incurred significantly prolonged referral-to-treatment intervals. Clinical outcomes also exhibited significant disparities: reliable clinical improvement was attained by only 58.5% of interpreter-assisted clients compared to 69.2% of non-interpreter clients. Concurrently, rates of reliable recovery were marked at 32.5% in the interpreter group versus 44.5% in the standard delivery cohort. The findings indicate systemic delays and diminished therapeutic efficacy in interpreter-facilitated talking therapies, underscoring the need for tailored structural and clinical adaptations.
papers.authors: Taf Kunorubwe, Natalie Meek, Rachel Emma Pye

papers.title: The Understanding, Use and Prevalence of Neuromyths among Medical Students, Health Sciences Students and Educators in Malaysia
papers.abstract: Neuromyths are pervasive misconceptions regarding neurobiology and cognitive architecture that originate from oversimplified, distorted, or ungrounded interpretations of neuroscientific evidence. Within instructional settings, such misconceptions threaten pedagogical efficacy by misdirecting institutional and instructor resources away from empirically substantiated learning methodologies. This empirical study evaluated the prevalence and endorsement of neuromyths versus established neuroscientific facts across secondary educators, university faculty, and undergraduate students pursuing medical and healthcare degrees in Malaysia. Administering an opportunity-sampled questionnaire battery across these cohorts, results demonstrated high overall rates of neuromyth endorsement concordant with international baselines. Significant cross-cohort divergence was identified: higher-education faculty endorsed significantly fewer neuromyths relative to secondary teachers and tertiary students. Neuromyths pertaining to learning styles, hemispheric dominance ('left-brain/right-brain'), and Brain Gym exhibited the highest persistence. Furthermore, a significant positive correlation emerged between accurate neurofact endorsement and myth resistance, indicating that foundational scientific and neurobiological literacy provides a protective epistemic buffer against instructional neuromyths.
papers.authors: Rachel E. Pye, Madihah Rushaidhi, Jun Jie Lim, Y. L. Soo, Paul S. Hubbard

papers.title: Measuring individual differences in the speed of attention using the distractor intrusion task
papers.abstract: Quantifying individual variability in the temporal deployment of visual attention remains challenging, as traditional visual search response times (RTs) and search slopes suffer from low test–retest reliability and confounding motor or sensory factors. Here, the post-target distractor intrusion (DI) rate in rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) is evaluated as a reliable psychometric index of attentional latency. When targets are briefly presented amidst rapid distractor streams, erroneous reports of the immediate post-target item (lag +1 intrusion) reflect delayed transient attentional facilitation, closely tied to delays in the electrophysiological N2pc component. Across three experiments and downsampling simulations, DI rates demonstrated robust within-session internal consistency (Cronbach's α > .85) and one-year test–retest stability (r > .90), achievable within approximately 50 trials (around 5 minutes of administration). Furthermore, individual DI propensities correlated systematically with attentional processing speed, while remaining dissociable from unrelated executive control indices, reading speed, and attentional blink magnitude. These findings support the DI paradigm as an efficient, highly reliable instrument for measuring individual differences in the speed of selective attention.
papers.authors: Alon Zivony, Claudia C. von Bastian, Rachel Pye

papers.title: High stakes in the assessment arms race: a mixed-methods analysis of reducing assessment in an undergraduate psychology programme
papers.abstract: Reducing programmatic assessment load is widely proposed to mitigate student stress and afford curricular space for slow scholarship and deep learning. However, both faculty and learners often resist reductions, perceiving continuous assessment as necessary for engagement or risk management. This quasi-experimental, mixed-methods investigation examined the institutional shift to a single 100% summative assessment per module across final-year optional undergraduate psychology modules at an international branch campus in Malaysia. Quantitative comparisons across four cohorts (2018/19–2021/22; two pre-reform and two post-reform) revealed no significant change in overall module academic achievement. Qualitative reflexive thematic analysis from focus groups showed heightened student anxiety regarding high-stakes, single-assessment designs, regardless of whether students had experienced the previous multi-assessment framework. Participants overwhelmingly favored a dual-assessment model on the basis of perceived procedural fairness, risk dispersion, and portfolio diversity. The study highlights that merely decreasing assessment frequency without addressing assessment design, authenticity, and student workload perceptions fails to deliver the educational benefits envisioned by slow scholarship models.
papers.authors: Rachel Pye, Lynnette K. Gnagi, Ainslie Bi Qi Chuah, Kai Li Chung

papers.title: Dynamic tests as a language-free method for assessing reading in a multilingual setting
papers.abstract: Diagnosing developmental dyslexia and evaluating reading ability in linguistically diverse environments, such as Malaysia, is complicated by simultaneous multilingualism and multiliteracy, where low performance on conventional literacy batteries may stem from limited language proficiency rather than underlying phonological or orthographic decoding deficits. This study explored the diagnostic utility of the Dynamic Testing paradigm—a test-teach-retest framework aimed at isolating learning potential from pre-existing linguistic competence. A sample of 59 multilingual Malaysian adults reading English, Bahasa Melayu, and/or Chinese completed a dynamic reading test alongside the Adult Reading History Questionnaire (ARHQ) and a lexical decision task (LDT). Dynamic test performance significantly predicted self-reported risk for reading difficulty on the ARHQ, while remaining independent of lexical processing speed on the LDT. Stratifying participants by primary script literacy into alphabetic (English/Bahasa Melayu) and morphosyllabic (Chinese) cohorts demonstrated equivalent overall performance across orthographic groups. However, dynamic test scores significantly predicted reading difficulty only among alphabetic readers. The findings indicate that while dynamic testing reduces linguistic bias in multilingual populations, orthographic typology influences its diagnostic validity.
papers.authors: Rachel E. Pye, Huey Hwa Chan

0554.name: Ralf M. Haefner
0554.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0554.bio: Ralf M. Haefner is an Associate Professor in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the computational and neural mechanisms of perceptual decision-making. Their research focuses on how the brain performs probabilistic inference, specifically exploring how population responses in the visual cortex represent internal beliefs about the external world. Utilizing normative mathematical models and machine learning, Haefner’s work tests the hypothesis that the brain implements inference through neural sampling from learned generative models. Their studies address the functional role of correlated variability and top-down feedback in shaping sensory representations during hierarchical motion perception and evidence integration.
0554.research_direction: Dr. Haefner has recently been exploring the computational principles underlying visual perception, framing both neural activity and behavior through the lens of Bayesian probabilistic models. Much of their recent work investigates how the visual system utilizes hierarchical causal inference to solve complex motion perception challenges, examining how human observers and single neurons in area MT integrate or segment moving stimuli, resolve center-surround interactions, and dynamically assign spatial reference frames. Beyond motion processing, they tested Bayesian predictions about learning in macaque visual cortex: tracking V4 population responses as monkeys learned visual discrimination tasks showed that learning increases, rather than reduces, redundancy in neural responses, consistent with generative rather than discriminative inference. To support these theoretical efforts, their recent research explores novel methodological approaches, developing encoding-agnostic techniques to rigorously evaluate competing Bayesian models against neural population data without relying on rigid assumptions about how the brain represents probability distributions.

papers.title: Task learning increases information redundancy of neural responses in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Recording V4 populations while monkeys learned a visual discrimination, the study tests a Bayesian prediction that learning should change how inference is performed rather than simply pruning noise. Contrary to discriminative accounts, learning increased redundancy of information in the population response, matching predictions of a generative, sampling-based account.
papers.authors: Shizhao Liu, Anton Pletenev, Ralf M. Haefner, Adam C. Snyder

papers.title: Bayesian causal inference unifies perceptual and neuronal processing of center-surround motion in area MT
papers.abstract: A causal inference model of center-surround motion is used to account for both human perceptual reports and the responses of MT neurons. The same computation explains why surround motion can enhance or suppress perception and neural responses depending on stimulus context, linking behavior and neurophysiology.
papers.authors: Gabor Lengyel, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Hierarchical motion perception as causal inference
papers.abstract: The authors propose that the visual system perceives motion by performing hierarchical Bayesian causal inference over how moving elements group into common reference frames. A single model with no fitted per-condition parameters explains classic phenomena such as motion integration, segmentation and induced motion, and generates new predictions verified in human psychophysics.
papers.authors: Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Causal inference predicts the transition from integration to segmentation in motion perception
papers.abstract: Human observers judged motion direction of stimuli in which the relationship between elements was varied. Behavior shifted from integrating to segmenting motion as cues changed, as predicted by a causal inference model that infers whether elements share a common cause.
papers.authors: Boris Penaloza, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Gabor Lengyel, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Ralf M. Haefner

papers.title: Bayesian encoding and decoding as distinct perspectives on neural coding
papers.abstract: The paper argues that two ideas often lumped together as 'Bayesian brain' hypotheses are actually different: Bayesian encoding (neural activity represents probability distributions over the world) and Bayesian decoding (downstream circuits read out sensory information with a Bayesian rule). The authors show these can be dissociated conceptually and empirically, and that ignoring the distinction leads to confused interpretations of neural data. They provide a framework and tests for evaluating each hypothesis separately.
papers.authors: Richard D. Lange, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Ankani Chattoraj, Ralf M. Haefner

0555.name: Ralph G. Hale
0555.bio: Ralph G. Hale is an Associate Professor of Psychological Science at the University of North Georgia and the Associate Director of the Center for Teaching, Learning, and Leadership. Hale’s research focuses on the intersection of visual perception and memory, specifically examining the watercolor illusion, color spreading, and figure-ground organization. Using psychophysical paradigms and virtual reality environments, Hale investigates how luminance, contrast, and environmental context influence spatial perception and visual long-term memory accuracy. Hale is also a co-author of a cognitive psychology textbook and mentors undergraduate researchers.
0555.research_direction: Dr. Hale has recently been investigating the mechanisms of perceptual organization, specifically examining how the watercolor illusion and luminance contrast bias figure-ground assignment and how color spreading operates across disconnected stimulus parts. Their recent work also explores higher-order visual cognition, testing whether the aesthetic appeal and familiarity of complex scenes impact the accuracy of visual long-term memory. Additionally, they are studying the role of social and contextual cues in guiding visual processing. To do this, Dr. Hale uses eye-tracking to probe how another person's gaze direction impacts visual search performance, while also investigating how surrounding situational scenarios alter the perception of emotion in facial expressions.

papers.title: Visual aesthetics and familiarity: Do they matter for visual long-term memory?
papers.abstract: Tests whether how aesthetically pleasing and how familiar a picture is affects the accuracy of visual long-term memory for it. The lab's related work used virtual reality change/no-change tasks with real-world scenes and paintings.
papers.venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
papers.authors: Ralph G. Hale, Courtney G. Nutt

papers.title: Impact of the watercolor illusion and contrast on figure-ground reversibility
papers.abstract: Examines how the watercolor illusion, in which a faint color tint spreads from a colored fringe, interacts with luminance contrast to influence how observers perceive and switch between figure and ground in ambiguous displays. The work extends the lab's line of research on how color spreading biases figure assignment.
papers.authors: Ralph G. Hale, Benjamin A. McDunn, Tanner L. Lumpkin, Hannah H. Hyman, Patsy E. Folds, Courtney G. Nutt

papers.title: Replication: Influence of Context on Emotion Perception in Facial Expressions
papers.abstract: Replicates the classic finding that surrounding context changes what emotion people read from a fear face. Participants judged the same face after a congruent, incongruent or no-context scenario, and context strongly shifted the emotion chosen.
papers.venue: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
papers.authors: Danica A. Barron, Ralph G. Hale

papers.title: Exploring watercolor illusion spreading between dissected stimulus parts
papers.abstract: Asks whether the watercolor illusion's color spreading reaches out from unenclosed ends when a stimulus is broken into disconnected parts, and how global configuration affects illusion strength. Participants rated illusion magnitude for a range of dissected stimuli. The results refine the earlier view that the illusion always spreads outward in the absence of an enclosing border.
papers.authors: Ralph G. Hale, James M. Brown

papers.title: Role of Social Gaze on Visual Search in an Eye-Tracking Paradigm
papers.abstract: Uses eye tracking to test how another person's gaze direction (toward the target, away from it, or straight ahead) shapes search times in letter arrays. It examines the interaction of gaze-cue congruency with visual search performance.
papers.venue: Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research
papers.authors: Jonathan K. Kroeger, Erin A. Conway, Ralph G. Hale

0556.name: Randi Starrfelt
0556.bio: Randi Starrfelt is a Professor of Neuropsychology who researches the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual object recognition, focusing on word and face processing. Starrfelt studies acquired and developmental disorders, such as pure alexia and prosopagnosia, to examine how specialized visual functions are organized and dissociated in the brain. Their methodological approach combines experimental psychology, clinical neuropsychology, and brain imaging to assess the effects of brain injury and neurodevelopmental conditions. Their current work explores the relationship between reading and face recognition, along with the qualitative experiences of individuals with face blindness.
0556.research_direction: Dr. Starrfelt has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural architecture of high-level visual recognition, with a focus on face and word processing in developmental and acquired disorders. In developmental prosopagnosia (DP), their recent work explores the methodological complexities of defining and diagnosing the condition, scrutinizing how psychometric cutoffs, assessment tools and task demands shape our understanding of its prevalence and core deficits, and they use carefully matched behavioral paradigms to test the degree of functional independence between face recognition, visual word recognition and fine-grained object discrimination. A second strand examines visual perceptual impairments following acquired brain injury: in a large group of patients with posterior cerebral artery stroke, they relate deficits in recognising faces, objects, words and colour to lesion volume, laterality and location, asking whether category-selective deficits are the rule or the exception.

papers.title: Definition: Simultanagnosia
papers.abstract: A definitional article in Cortex that sets out what the term simultanagnosia should and should not cover, a disorder of seeing multiple visual elements at once after brain damage. It addresses inconsistent use of the term and clarifies its relation to related visual deficits.
papers.authors: Silvia Primativo, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Disentangling developmental prosopagnosia: A scoping review of terms, tools and topics
papers.abstract: A preregistered scoping review that maps how developmental prosopagnosia has been studied in adults, covering 224 empirical papers. It examines how the condition is defined, how people are classified as having it, and which aspects of it researchers investigate. The authors find little consensus on specific definitions and diagnostic criteria, and argue for clearer, more consistent conceptualization and assessment.
papers.authors: Erling Nørkær, Silvia Regina Gobbo, Tone Roald, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Evidence for a Classical Dissociation between Face and Object Recognition in Developmental Prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: Tests whether developmental prosopagnosia is specific to faces by replicating an earlier small-sample study in a larger, independent group (N=21) and matched controls. Unlike the earlier group, these participants showed no disproportionate visual-similarity effect and performed within the control range on demanding object tasks. The authors conclude that they can demonstrate a classical dissociation between face and object recognition in this group.
papers.authors: Christian Gerlach, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Comparing word and face recognition – An insoluble conundrum?
papers.abstract: A discussion of the difficulties in comparing visual word recognition and face recognition, which are often studied as competing or cooperating specialized functions. The authors consider the methodological and conceptual obstacles to such comparisons and how to make them more meaningful.
papers.authors: Ro Julia Robotham, Randi Starrfelt

papers.title: Systematic evaluation of high-level visual deficits and lesions in posterior cerebral artery stroke
papers.abstract: Reports the Back of the Brain project, the largest and most detailed study to date of patients (N=64) with posterior cerebral artery stroke selected by lesion location rather than by behavioural symptoms. Lesion mapping and behavioural indices for word, object and face processing are analysed together to ask whether category-selective deficits are the rule or the exception. The results show how deficits in high-level vision relate to lesion location, laterality and volume.
papers.authors: Ro Julia Robotham, Grace E. Rice, Alex P. Leff, Matthew A. Lambon Ralph, Randi Starrfelt

0560.name: Reinoud Bootsma
0560.department: Institut des Sciences du Mouvement Etienne Jules Marey (ISM)
0560.bio: Reinoud J. Bootsma is a Professor of Human Movement Science at Aix-Marseille Université and a senior member of the Institut Universitaire de France. Bootsma’s research focuses on the ecological approach to perception and action, specifically investigating how visual information like time-to-collision (tau) regulates motor control in tasks such as catching, hitting, and aiming. Utilizing kinematic analysis and dynamical systems modeling, Bootsma explores the underlying principles of information-movement coupling and Fitts' law. Their current research focuses on the study of joint action and social coordination, analyzing how behavioral patterns emerge from continuous visual couplings between multiple actors.
0560.research_direction: Dr. Bootsma has recently been investigating the dynamical and informational principles that govern complex motor behaviors across both individual and multi-agent contexts. Their recent work explores how the visual system guides continuous hand movements during lateral target interception, using dynamical-systems modeling and kinematic tracking to probe counter-intuitive phenomena like initial wrong-way hand reversals and angle-of-approach effects. In addition to individual visuomotor control, they are examining interpersonal coordination through cooperative ball-and-beam paradigms to understand how motor skills transfer from solo to joint actions and how interacting partners freeze or free degrees of freedom during multi-agent learning. Finally, their research extends these motor control principles into the realm of cultural expertise, analyzing the physical shaping paths of expert potters to investigate how community-specific motor habits influence the morphological evolution of crafted artifacts.

papers.title: Toward an Operational Dynamical Model of Lateral Manual Interception Behavior
papers.abstract: The authors build a dynamical-systems model of discrete hand movements used to intercept a moving target along a lateral axis. A fixed-point attractor at the perceived arrival location, combined with a hybrid nonlinear damping term, generates realistic movement kinematics under different arrival locations and time pressures using one set of four coefficients. The model also naturally reproduces speed-accuracy trade-off behaviour.
papers.authors: Danial Borooghani, Remy Casanova, Frank T. J. M. Zaal, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Interpersonal coordination in a ball-and-beam paradigm: Transfer of skill from solo action to joint action
papers.abstract: Pairs of participants jointly tilt a beam to roll a ball between two targets, after each member had earlier practiced the task alone. Speed-related characteristics of solo performance carried over strongly to the joint task, whereas accuracy-related ones carried over only moderately. Dyads mostly settled on an anti-phase coordination with asymmetries in which the better solo performer tended to lead, showing coordination emerges from the interaction while constrained by task goals.
papers.authors: Marijn S. J. Hafkamp, Remy Casanova, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Cultural attraction in pottery practice: Group-specific shape transformations by potters from three communities
papers.abstract: Expert potters from three communities were asked to reproduce the same unfamiliar vessel shapes on the wheel. Final shapes and the underlying morphogenetic paths varied more between communities than within them, so deviations were systematic rather than random. The results support the idea that community-specific habits of working clay drive cultural alignment of artifact form.
papers.authors: Tetsushi Nonaka, Enora Gandon, John A. Endler, Thelma Coyle, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Angle-of-approach and reversal-movement effects in lateral manual interception
papers.abstract: The study tests whether two counter-intuitive effects in manual interception, the influence of target trajectory angle on hand movement and the hand first moving the wrong way before reversing, can be reliably reproduced. Using conditions that increased uncertainty about arrival location and varied target speed, both effects appeared, more strongly for slower targets. The authors argue guidance relies on information of intermediate order, a partial mix of position and velocity.
papers.authors: Simon Ledouit, Danial Borooghani, Remy Casanova, Nicolas Benguigui, Frank T. J. M. Zaal, Reinoud J. Bootsma

papers.title: Freezing and freeing of degrees of freedom in joint action learning
papers.abstract: Dyads learned a novel task in which two people each hold one end of a beam to roll a ball between targets, compared against a solo version. Dyads without prior solo practice initially coordinated sequentially, freezing whenever the partner moved, while those with solo experience moved in a more complementary way. Initial joint practice did not improve later solo performance, suggesting multi-agent learning starts by freezing then freeing degrees of freedom.
papers.authors: Marijn S. J. Hafkamp, Remy Casanova, Reinoud J. Bootsma

0561.name: Remy Allard
0561.bio: Rémy Allard is an Assistant Professor at the School of Optometry at the Université de Montréal and a researcher at the Psychophysical Laboratory of Vision. Allard's research investigates the mechanisms underlying motion and contrast perception, specifically focusing on how these processes are influenced by healthy aging and retinal pathologies such as age-related macular degeneration. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and computational modeling, they develop functional clinical tests to assess photoreceptor efficiency and improve the detection of ocular diseases. Their research also extends to the characterization of visual symptoms following traumatic brain injuries to optimize post-trauma rehabilitation strategies.
0561.research_direction: Dr. Allard has recently been working on how the retina's early stages limit what people can see, using behavioral tests to infer what happens inside the eye. Their recent work explores how efficiently rod photoreceptors, which handle vision in dim light, capture light, using a motion-discrimination task with and without added visual noise. They have also been investigating whether differences in motion perception in autism, and in their family members, track measurable changes in retinal electrical responses.

papers.title: Psychophysically measuring the efficiency of rods
papers.abstract: While equivalent input noise (EIN) paradigms using external luminance noise have successfully quantified the quantal absorption efficiency of retinal cone photoreceptors, functional psychophysical estimation of rod efficiency has remained unestablished. Here, an external noise paradigm was adapted to evaluate rod photon-detection efficiency in healthy human observers through a motion direction discrimination task. Contrast thresholds were quantified with and without spatiotemporally extended dynamic external noise across a wide continuum of luminance intensities, spatial frequencies, and temporal frequencies under monochromatic blue and red display conditions (the latter minimizing rod stimulation). Two stimulus geometries were evaluated: an eccentric Gabor patch situated at 20° eccentricity and a rotating sinusoidal annular grating at 10° eccentricity. In both configurations, within a restricted scotopic-to-mesopic luminance regime, equivalent input noise scaled inversely with background luminance—conforming to the square-root de Vries–Rose law—and exhibited spectral and temporal flatness characteristic of Poisson photon noise. Crucially, contrast sensitivity under these conditions was markedly superior for short-wavelength (blue) relative to long-wavelength (red) illumination at matched photopic luminances, confirming that contrast sensitivity was bottlenecked by quantal fluctuations within the rod photoreceptor mosaic. These results demonstrate that rod photon absorption efficiency can be isolated and measured psychophysically via motion contrast thresholds in external noise using short-wavelength stimuli within the photon-noise-limited regime.
papers.authors: Geneviève Rodrigue, Laurine Paris, Judith Renaud, Rémy Allard

papers.title: Global motion coherent deficits in individuals with autism spectrum disorder and their family members are associated with retinal function
papers.abstract: This research investigates the association between global motion perception deficits and retinal processing abnormalities in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and their biological family members. By evaluating motion coherence thresholds alongside electroretinography (ERG) metrics, the study demonstrates that both ASD probands and their parents—particularly mothers—exhibit significantly elevated motion coherence thresholds. These perceptual deficits correlate with distinct retinal response alterations, specifically reduced amplitudes of the photopic negative response (PhNR) and increased peak latencies for retinal a- and b-waves. The results provide empirical evidence that sensory processing anomalies in autism may originate at the retinal level and follow a familial inheritance pattern, suggesting a low-level biological basis for some autistic traits.
papers.authors: Irene O. L. Lee, Dennis M. Fritsch, Maximilian Kerz, Dorothy Thompson, Maryam Rezaei, Daphné Silvestre, Marko Nardini, Arthur Trognon, Michelle McKerral, David Skuse, Rémy Allard

0562.name: Renate Rutiku
0562.bio: Renate Rutiku is a Principal Investigator and Group Leader at the Institute of Psychology, Jagiellonian University, researching the neurobiological foundations of conscious perception. Rutiku's work focuses on disambiguating the neural correlates of consciousness (NCC) from their precursors and consequences, specifically examining the role of cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons in coupling the state and contents of consciousness. Utilizing a multi-modal approach including electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and psychophysics, they investigate the temporal dynamics of perceptual markers and how the brain integrates top-down predictions with sensory evidence. Rutiku currently leads a SONATA BIS project exploring integration across the perceptual hierarchy using neuroimaging and behavioral modeling.
0562.research_direction: Dr. Rutiku has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive architecture underlying visual working memory and conscious perception. In the visual domain, their recent work explores how fine-grained microstructural properties of the early visual cortex shape individual differences and visual field asymmetries in working memory, as well as whether working memory maintenance relies on dissociable conscious and unconscious representations. Beyond vision, they are also evaluating event-related EEG markers of predictive processing and active perception, such as mismatch negativity, the P3b component, and auditory figure-ground modulation. Specifically, Dr. Rutiku is testing the single-subject reliability of these neural signatures across various oddball paradigms to develop robust, non-report indices that can track active perception across altered states of consciousness, including sleep and clinical disorders.

papers.title: Visual field inhomogeneities and the architectonics of early visual cortex shape visual working memory
papers.abstract: Asks whether the fine-grained structure of primary visual cortex helps explain why people differ in visual working memory. In 292 participants, quantitative multiparametric MRI maps of cortical microstructure were related to performance on a working-memory task built to expose polar-angle asymmetries in the visual field. Vertical-meridian asymmetry in behavior tracked several V1 microstructural parameters, and cortical thickness in V3 tracked left-right asymmetry, supporting the sensory-recruitment view that early visual areas constrain working memory.
papers.authors: Julia Papiernik-Kłodzińska, Simon Hviid Del Pin, Kristian Sandberg, Michał Wierzchoń, Marisa Carrasco, Renate Rutiku

papers.title: The Two Lives of Visual Working Memory: Evidence for Distinct Conscious and Unconscious Representations
papers.abstract: Tests whether visual working memory relies on two representations: an item-specific unconscious trace and a consciously accessible, integrated ensemble-like representation. In 216 participants doing change detection with awareness ratings, manipulating item size statistics pushed subjective awareness and objective accuracy in opposite directions, and imagery vividness related only to subjective awareness and estimation bias. The authors read this dissociation as evidence that behavior can draw on both kinds of representation.
papers.authors: Aleksandra Lipińska, Kinga Ciupińska, Renate Rutiku

papers.title: Figure-ground modulation as a marker of active auditory perception across levels of consciousness
papers.abstract: Proposes an EEG response to auditory figure-ground separation as a marker that a listener is actively perceiving sound, evaluated across different levels of consciousness including sleep and disorders of consciousness. The single-author paper argues the marker could index active perception without requiring an overt behavioral report.
papers.authors: Renate Rutiku

papers.title: Assessing mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3b within-individual sensitivity - A comparison between the local-global paradigm and two specialized oddball sequences
papers.abstract: Compares the popular local-global paradigm with two dedicated oddball sequences for measuring mismatch negativity and P3b as EEG markers in single individuals. In 15 healthy participants MMN was found in all, and P3b in 13-14, with P3b correlated across paradigms but the local effect differing in timing and shape from a classic MMN. The authors caution against equating the local effect with MMN across studies and note that P3b sensitivity is lower than expected.
papers.authors: Renate Rutiku, Chiara Fiscone, Marcello Massimini, Simone Sarasso

0564.name: Richard J. Krauzlis
0564.institution: National Eye Institute, National Institutes of Health
0564.department: Laboratory of Sensorimotor Research (Visual Circuits Section)
0564.bio: Richard J. Krauzlis is a Senior Investigator at the National Eye Institute who examines the neural mechanisms underlying visual attention, perception, and oculomotor control. Krauzlis's research characterizes the superior colliculus, demonstrating its role in the internal orienting of attention and goal-directed selection independent of its motor functions. Utilizing electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling in both non-human primates and mice, their laboratory investigates how subcortical circuits, including the basal ganglia, interact with the neocortex to govern flexible visual behaviors and perceptual decision-making.
0564.research_direction: Dr. Krauzlis has recently been investigating the functional role of the superior colliculus in visual cognition and how it integrates with broader cortical and subcortical networks in both non-human primates and mice. Their recent work explores the causal mechanisms underlying covert visual attention and perceptual decision-making by deploying optogenetics, reversible inactivation, and layer-specific electrophysiology during behavioral tasks. Specifically, they are examining whether attention-related modulations in the midbrain are dynamically shaped by learned behavioral relevance rather than fixed visual inputs. Additionally, they are probing the anatomical pathways that supply visual drive to the colliculus, asking how projections from the lateral geniculate nucleus, visual cortex, and basal ganglia support everything from basic visually evoked spiking to rapid face processing.

papers.title: Neuronal features of visual attention in the mouse superior colliculus depend on learned behavioral relevance
papers.abstract: Mice were trained on different task rules that gave the same visual stimuli different behavioral meaning, while colliculus activity was recorded across layers. Attention-related modulation in superior colliculus neurons emerged and scaled with how relevant the stimuli had become to the animal, rather than being fixed by the visual input. This shows that collicular attention signals are shaped by learning.
papers.authors: Lupeng Wang, Christian Quaia, Kerry Elliott, Kara K. Cover, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: A distinct circuit for biasing visual perceptual decisions and modulating superior colliculus activity through the mouse posterior striatum
papers.abstract: Anatomical work shows the direct pathway of the posterior striatum is largely separate from that of the dorsomedial striatum. Optogenetically activating posterior-striatum D1 neurons in mice doing a visual change-detection task strongly biased perceptual choices, and altered activity in the superior colliculus. The study identifies a basal-ganglia route from visual cortex to colliculus that shapes visual decisions.
papers.authors: Kara K. Cover, Kerry Elliott, Sarah M. Preuss, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Visual activity in primate superior colliculus requires geniculostriate input
papers.abstract: Recording from macaque superior colliculus before and during reversible inactivation of the ipsilateral LGN, the authors found that visually evoked spiking was nearly abolished. This indicates that, in primates, collicular visual responses depend mainly on retinal signals routed through LGN and V1 rather than direct retinal input alone. The result revises ideas about the source of visual drive to the primate midbrain.
papers.authors: Leor N. Katz, Gongchen Yu, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Optogenetic Manipulation of Covert Attention in the Nonhuman Primate
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether brief optogenetic suppression of primate superior colliculus alters performance in a cued covert-attention change-detection task, beyond known effects on saccades. Silencing colliculus neurons at the attended location impaired detection, giving causal evidence that the SC contributes to covert attention in monkeys. It demonstrates optogenetics can probe cognitive functions in primates.
papers.authors: Leor N. Katz, Martin O. Bohlen, Gongchen Yu, Carlos Mejias-Aponte, Marc A. Sommer, Richard J. Krauzlis

papers.title: Short-latency preference for faces in primate superior colliculus depends on visual cortex
papers.abstract: Recordings in macaque superior colliculus show that neurons there respond preferentially to face images within a very short latency, earlier than many would expect for a midbrain structure. Reversibly inactivating visual cortex removed much of this face preference, indicating that it is not computed subcortically on its own but relies on cortical input. The work reframes the colliculus as part of the circuitry for rapid social-object processing.
papers.authors: Gongchen Yu, Leor N. Katz, Christian Quaia, Adam Messinger, Richard J. Krauzlis

0565.name: Richard A. Abrams
0565.bio: Richard A. Abrams is a Professor of Psychological & Brain Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis and directs the Attention & Performance Lab. Abrams's research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms governing visual attention and motor execution, specifically focusing on the coordination of eye and limb movements and the control of covert attentional shifts. Abrams has conducted work on attentional capture, inhibition of return, and the role of perceptual objects in guiding action. Their recent investigations explore the suppression of unpredictable visual distractors and how specific action-related goals modulate ensemble perception and visual search performance.
0565.research_direction: Dr. Abrams’s recent work explores the mechanisms of attentional control in visual search, specifically focusing on how the visual system proactively suppresses salient distractors to prevent attentional capture. They have recently been investigating the underlying mechanics and boundaries of this distractor avoidance, testing whether suppression is achieved through active, goal-driven control or passive spatial filtering, and whether it requires prior knowledge of a distractor's exact features. Their research also examines the broader scope and downstream consequences of ignoring salient items, probing whether proactive inhibition can prevent capture by robust dynamic stimuli like abrupt motion onsets and how suppressing a distractor might simultaneously boost attention to spatially grouped task-relevant stimuli. To cleanly assess these phenomena, Dr. Abrams is developing novel, bias-free psychophysical measures designed to separate true proactive inhibition from decision-level response biases in standard probe-based tasks.

papers.title: Distractor avoidance is achieved by active control rather than passive exclusion
papers.abstract: Tests a debate over whether people avoid salient distractors through active, goal-driven attentional control or through passive exclusion caused by a narrow attentional window in serial search. Across three experiments, the authors varied how serial the search was by changing element similarity and stimulus arrangement, and measured how much distractor avoidance depended on it. The pattern favors active control over the attentional-window account.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Avoidance of capture by motion onset
papers.abstract: Suppression of salient items has been shown almost only for color singletons. Here, motion-onset distractors first impaired search in an additional-singleton task, then had no effect when participants searched for a prespecified shape, showing that capture by abrupt motion onsets can also be prevented. This extends proactive suppression beyond color to a historically robust capture stimulus.
papers.authors: Jahnavi Nair, Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Bias-free measure of distractor avoidance in visual search
papers.abstract: Probe-based tasks used to show that salient distractors are proactively ignored can be contaminated by decision-level response biases. The authors develop a bias-free psychophysical measure of distractor processing in visual search that separates true inhibition from bias. It gives a cleaner test of whether proactive avoidance of salient distractors occurs.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Visual Distraction's "Silver Lining": Distractor Suppression Boosts Attention to Competing Stimuli
papers.abstract: Across five experiments (N = 120), a target grouped with a suppressed distractor was identified better than one in a different perceptual group. This suggests distractor suppression not only downweights undesired items but also enhances responses to task-relevant items competing with the distractor, fine-tuning the suppression.
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

papers.title: Ignoring the unknown: Attentional suppression of unpredictable visual distraction
papers.abstract: Prior work concluded that only distractors with a known color can be proactively suppressed. Using a modified search task with the most prevalent shape as the target, the authors show that salient distractors of unpredictable color still facilitate search, so they are suppressed. This implies suppression need not rely on feature-specific templates.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Xiaojin Ma, Richard A. Abrams

0567.name: Robert Allison
0567.department: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
0567.bio: Robert S. Allison is a Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a member of the Centre for Vision Research at York University. Allison’s research focuses on the psychophysics and computational modeling of stereoscopic depth perception, examining how the human visual system processes three-dimensional information in natural and virtual environments. They specialize in the measurement and analysis of eye movements, the integration of multi-modal depth cues, and the optimization of human-computer interfaces for virtual and augmented reality systems. Their work relates to the application of technologies in 3D cinema, flight simulation, and clinical vision science.
0567.research_direction: Dr. Allison has recently been investigating depth perception, self-motion processing, and the sensory conflicts that drive cybersickness in virtual environments. Their recent work explores how the visual system utilizes binocular disparity and motion parallax to estimate depth, and how these distance cues help observers parse optic flow to distinguish their own movement from moving objects in a scene. In the realm of virtual reality, they are evaluating competing theories of cybersickness by testing whether symptoms under display lag stem from physical-virtual head pose mismatches or subjective vertical conflicts, alongside analyzing how low-level visual display properties provoke motion sickness. Furthermore, their research examines sensorimotor adaptation, testing how exposure to altered visual gain during active movement impacts both perceived stationarity and visually driven postural sway.

papers.title: Reexamining the Relationship Between Stereopsis and Motion Parallax
papers.abstract: A review comparing the two main sources of depth information, binocular disparity and motion parallax, which rest on similar geometry but differ in practice. Disparity generally allows finer depth discrimination and more accurate perceived depth magnitudes, whereas motion parallax is complicated by head movements and by object and scene motion. The authors discuss how eye movements and matching ambiguity affect both cues and what this means for depth perception in natural and virtual settings.
papers.authors: Laurie M. Wilcox, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Axes of self-motion and object motion shape how we perceive world-relative motion
papers.abstract: Two experiments in a wide-field stereoscopic display examined how observers judge the direction of a moving target while simulating their own movement through a room or object cluster. Flow parsing was stronger when target motion and self-motion were orthogonal than when parallel, depending on the direction combination. The findings indicate that distance cues such as disparity and size are integrated to help separate self-motion from object motion.
papers.authors: Hongyi Guo, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Visual Factors in Cybersickness: A Literature Survey and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: A systematic review and meta-analysis of how low-level visual properties of a display influence cybersickness in virtual reality, focusing on motion-sickness-related symptoms. The authors searched several databases and pooled results across studies, excluding higher-level factors such as head-tracking latency or content. The work summarizes which visual stimulus characteristics reliably provoke or reduce sickness.
papers.authors: Robert S. Allison, Stephen Palmisano

papers.title: The effect of gain adaptation on perception and posture
papers.abstract: Participants adapted to VR in which physical self-motion was displayed at normal, reduced, or increased gain, and were then tested on perceived stationarity during active motion and on postural sway. Perceived stationarity did not shift with adaptation gain, since active movement supplies enough body feedback to offset it, but visually driven sway was altered after non-unity gain exposure. Posture did not recalibrate immediately, suggesting it operates independently of perceptual recalibration.
papers.authors: Xue Teng, Laurie M. Wilcox, Robert S. Allison

papers.title: Testing the 'differences in virtual and physical head pose' and 'subjective vertical conflict' accounts of cybersickness
papers.abstract: Thirty-two headset users made oscillating pitch or yaw head rotations while viewing a virtual room with added display lag. The study pits two theories of why lag causes cybersickness against each other: one based on mismatches between virtual and physical head pose, the other on conflict with the sensed vertical. Results are used to judge which mechanism better explains the sickness.
papers.authors: Stephen Palmisano, Lance Stephenson, Rodney G. Davies, Juno Kim, Robert S. Allison

0568.name: Robert Desimone
0568.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0568.bio: Robert Desimone serves as the Director of the McGovern Institute for Brain Research and the Doris and Don Berkey Professor at MIT, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of selective attention and executive control. Desimone’s research characterizes how the brain manages information overload by utilizing synchronous neuronal firing to amplify relevant sensory signals while suppressing background distractions. By employing electrophysiology, MEG, and optogenetics in primate models, Desimone identified circuits in the prefrontal and extrastriate cortex that coordinate top-down attentional focus. These findings inform the development of treatments for brain disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.
0568.research_direction: Dr. Desimone has recently been studying how the primate brain selects and holds onto visual information. Their recent work explores how tiny involuntary eye movements called microsaccades interact with spatial attention, and how this shapes neural responses in visual cortex and the pulvinar of monkeys. They have also asked whether attending to a visual feature and remembering it in working memory use the same neurons across motion-processing and prefrontal areas. In humans, they have mapped the large-scale functional networks of the cortex using fMRI while people watch movies, including how attention-related control networks relate to other networks.

papers.title: Stimulus representations in visual cortex shaped by spatial attention and microsaccades
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that fixational eye movements, specifically microsaccades (MSs), are fundamentally linked to the neural mechanisms of covert spatial attention in the primate visual system. Utilizing multiunit recordings from rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) across cortical areas V4 and IT, as well as the lateral pulvinar, the researchers found that the typical firing rate enhancements associated with spatial attention are only engaged following a microsaccade directed toward the attended stimulus. If the initial MS after an attentional cue is directed away from the target, the expected gain modulation is delayed until the subsequent target-directed MS occurs. Furthermore, stimulus decoding accuracy and the precision of tuning curves in V4 were significantly improved during intervals following target-directed MSs compared to those following MSs directed away from the target. These findings imply that microsaccades do not merely correlate with attention but serve to coordinate and amplify object processing in extrastriate cortex, providing a neural basis for active vision during periods of fixation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Karthik Srinivasan, Eric Lowet, Bruno Duarte Gomes, Robert Desimone

papers.title: Dissociable neuronal substrates of visual feature attention and working memory
papers.abstract: In this investigation, the authors challenge the hypothesis that visual working memory (WM) and feature-based attention rely on the same neural substrates within the primate brain. By performing simultaneous laminar recordings in macaque monkeys across a hierarchy of areas including MT, MST, LIP, and the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), they characterized the neural signatures of motion-direction WM and feature-based attention. The results reveal that while both processes recruit similar cortical regions, they are represented by distinct neuronal populations and rely on different circuit mechanisms. Specifically, whereas feature attention consistently modulates the gain of sensory-driven responses, WM representations are maintained through distinct firing patterns in different subpopulations. Optogenetic inactivation of the posterior LPFC selectively impaired attentional modulation without abolishing the underlying WM representation, demonstrating a functional dissociation between the selection of incoming sensory information and the maintenance of internal representations.
papers.authors: Diego Mendoza-Halliday, Haoran Xu, Frederico A. C. Azevedo, Robert Desimone

papers.title: Functional architecture of cerebral cortex during naturalistic movie watching
papers.abstract: This research provides a comprehensive map of the human cerebral cortex's functional organization by analyzing high-resolution fMRI data from 176 subjects during 60 minutes of naturalistic movie watching. Utilizing a data-driven clustering approach, the authors identified a stable macro-architecture consisting of 24 functional networks, each specialized for distinct sensory or cognitive processes such as language, social interactions, and visual feature extraction. The study highlights the existence of three domain-general executive control networks that exhibit a robust 'push-pull' relationship with domain-specific sensory areas; these networks were most active during transitions between movie segments and least active when feature-specific networks were highly engaged. By mapping the cortex under naturalistic conditions rather than constrained tasks, the study reveals a more unified and ecologically relevant parcellation scheme that captures the dynamic interplay of large-scale brain systems.
papers.authors: Reza Rajimehr, Haoran Xu, Asa Farahani, Simon Kornblith, John Duncan, Robert Desimone

0569.name: Robert G. Alexander
0569.bio: Robert G. Alexander is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Counseling and a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the mechanisms of human vision. Their research utilizes high-resolution eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to quantify the oculomotor signatures of perceptual expertise in professional domains such as radiology and aviation. By modeling how experts search and interpret complex visual environments, Alexander develops scalable educational tools and diagnostic biomarkers intended to reduce human error and accelerate skill acquisition. Alexander's work also explores the intersection of fixational eye movements, clinical visual impairments, and the development of deep learning tools for modeling expertise.
0569.research_direction: Dr. Alexander's recent work explores the dynamics of fixational eye movements—particularly microsaccades—and how they serve as behavioral biomarkers across applied visual tasks and clinical conditions. By employing eye tracking during medical image perception, they have been investigating the visual and cognitive factors that cause radiologists to miss pulmonary nodules, as well as testing whether specific oculomotor patterns can differentiate varying levels of radiologic expertise. In the clinical domain, their recent research examines how ophthalmic and neurologic diseases disrupt fixation stability, evaluating the potential of these eye movement metrics for disease monitoring while accounting for confounds like fatigue and arousal. Additionally, Dr. Alexander has recently been applying these eye-tracking methodologies to the study of art perception, analyzing how classical painters' pictorial manipulations of joint attention and scene composition subtly steer a viewer's gaze dynamics.

papers.title: Microsaccade Dynamics Enhance Nodule Detection and Discriminate Reader Expertise Levels During Chest Radiography
papers.abstract: Eye tracking was used while naive observers, radiology residents and attending radiologists searched 148 chest radiographs for nodules. When a nodule was correctly found, readers made more microsaccades per fixation on the nodule region than elsewhere, and this pattern disappeared on misses, even after matching fixation durations. Microsaccade measures inside the target region separated lower- from higher-accuracy readers, suggesting a largely involuntary oculomotor biomarker of radiologic expertise.
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Stephen Waite, Shawn Lyo, Ashwin Venkatakrishnan, Arkadij Grigorian, Riley Morrone, Samuel Sabzanov, Shamsul Alam, Ellis Gayles, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde

papers.title: Fixational eye movements: Implications for applied and clinical assessments
papers.abstract: Reviews how microsaccades and drift change in neurologic and ophthalmic disease and how they can serve as biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring. Covers factors such as arousal, fatigue and substance use that alter fixational measurements and could confound clinical assessments, arguing these need to be controlled for.
papers.venue: Handbook of Clinical Neurology (Retina Structure, Function, and Genetics)
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde
