papers.title: Abnormal Fixational Eye Movements in Ophthalmic Disease: Implications for Visual Function and Clinical Assessment
papers.abstract: Narrative review of how fixation stability and other oculomotor dynamics are disrupted across ophthalmic disorders, and how these changes relate to acuity, reading and binocular function. The authors argue fixational metrics could serve as research biomarkers and for treatment monitoring, contingent on normative datasets and accessible eye-tracking tools.
papers.authors: Sophia Castro, Nancy O. Mahfouz, Simrat Renu, Kathiana Jeanty, Elana Safonova, Doris Prela, Ola Abozid, Ayesha Mulla, Josey M. Spiers, Robert G. Alexander

papers.title: Missed Pulmonary Nodules on CT: Determinants and Implications for Radiologic Practice
papers.abstract: Review of why radiologists overlook lung nodules on chest CT, grouping causes into technical limitations, nodule and surrounding-anatomy characteristics, and reader factors such as bias and fatigue. Also discusses the role of AI and computer-aided detection and the medicolegal notion of 'obviousness', calling for more objective descriptions of missed nodules.
papers.authors: Stephen Waite, Talia Lilikakis, Elizabeth A. Krupinski, Jean Jeudy, Michael A. Bruno, Shawn Lyo, Robert G. Alexander

papers.title: Why did Rubens add a parrot to Titian's The Fall of Man? A pictorial manipulation of joint attention
papers.abstract: Rubens copied Titian's painting but changed characters' gaze directions and added a red parrot. The authors recorded viewers' eye movements on Titian's original, Rubens's version and a version with the parrot digitally removed. Viewers looked at Eve's face more and with more tightly clustered gaze in Rubens's painting, and the parrot altered gaze dynamics, showing that Rubens's changes measurably steer viewer attention.
papers.authors: Robert G. Alexander, Ashwin Venkatakrishnan, Jordi Chanovas, Sophie Ferguson, Stephen L. Macknik, Susana Martinez-Conde

0570.name: Robert L. Goldstone
0570.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0570.bio: Robert L. Goldstone is a Distinguished Professor and Chancellor’s Professor at Indiana University and the director of the Percepts and Concepts Lab. Goldstone’s research focuses on the bidirectional interaction between perceptual and conceptual systems, specifically exploring how mental categories reshape sensory discrimination through mechanisms like unitization and differentiation. This methodology integrates human behavioral experiments with computational modeling, including neural networks and agent-based simulations. Goldstone also investigates collective behavior, examining how individual-level cognitive rules scale to produce emergent group intelligence and social coordination.
0570.research_direction: Dr. Goldstone has recently been investigating how cognitive processes operate across both individual perception and complex social systems. At the collective level, their recent work explores the behavioral mechanisms driving the emergence of specialized roles within interacting groups and uses agent-based network simulations to model how community structure influences the spread of beliefs. On the individual level, they are studying the acquisition and inherent biases of perceptual learning, applying psychophysical methods to massive real-world datasets—such as millions of professional baseball umpire calls—to track how sensory expertise and decision biases evolve over time. Additionally, they examine the reciprocal relationship between human categorization and the scientific method, investigating how established scientific concepts systematically shape and bias the very empirical evidence used to test them.

papers.title: The Spread of Beliefs in Partially Modularized Communities
papers.abstract: Introduces a network-based framework (SBMC) in which agents on stochastic-block-model social networks adopt beliefs of differing utility by pooling evidence from neighbors. Simulations show that more cross-community connectivity does not always help, that some decision randomness can improve collective outcomes, and that summing rather than averaging evidence can help. The overall conclusion is that intermediate levels of belief exploration best spread useful beliefs, bearing on echo chambers and filter bubbles.
papers.authors: Robert L. Goldstone, Marina Dubova, Rachith Aiyappa, Andy Edinger

papers.title: Bias in perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Proposes a systematic framework for the ways perceptual learning can be biased, including cases that do not clearly benefit the learner. Argues these are compatible with perceptual learning being beneficial, but that benefits are tied to the learner's narrow interests and training environment, so changes can turn gains into (often temporary) liabilities.
papers.authors: Madeleine Ransom, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: The psychophysics of home plate umpire calls
papers.abstract: Analyzes over three million ball/strike calls by 121 MLB umpires as a real-world perceptual-expertise task. Monitoring and feedback improve accuracy over time, yet decision biases persist, suggesting bias and accuracy are separable and that reducing bias needs targeted interventions. Younger umpires improve faster than older ones.
papers.authors: Kevin S. Flannagan, Brian M. Mills, Robert L. Goldstone

papers.title: The Emergence of Specialized Roles Within Groups
papers.abstract: Notes that group coordination requires role differentiation as well as synchrony, which existing models neglect. Presents the CARMI framework (Communication, Adaptation to feedback, Repulsion, Multi-level planning, Intention modeling) and argues roles emerge as agents complement what they expect others to do. Describes three lab paradigms used to study role formation.
papers.authors: Robert L. Goldstone, Edgar J. Andrade-Lotero, Robert D. Hawkins, Michael E. Roberts

papers.title: Carving joints into nature: reengineering scientific concepts in light of concept-laden evidence
papers.abstract: Argues that efforts to revise scientific concepts based on accumulated data face a circularity, because concepts themselves shape the evidence: they bias scientists toward within-category similarity, sharpen measurement of concept-relevant dimensions, serve as units of experiment and theory, and can alter the phenomena. Scholars proposing better concepts must account for this concept-laden evidence to avoid a self-reinforcing loop.
papers.authors: Marina Dubova, Robert L. Goldstone

0571.name: Robert M. McPeek
0571.department: Department of Biological and Vision Sciences
0571.bio: Robert M. McPeek is a Professor at the SUNY College of Optometry whose research focuses on the neural mechanisms governing visual attention and the coordination of visually-guided actions, such as saccadic eye movements and reaching. McPeek investigates how the brain selects targets for action, specifically examining the functional roles of the superior colliculus and the frontal cortex in oculomotor selection and decision-making. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical studies, neurophysiological recordings, and causal interventions, their laboratory seeks to bridge the gap between neural activity and behavioral output in complex visual environments.
0571.research_direction: Dr. McPeek has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying saccade target selection, visual search, and spatial attention. Their recent work explores how populations of neurons in the monkey superior colliculus guide eye movements, specifically examining how the physical size of extended objects influences the neural build-up and timing of saccadic decisions. Additionally, they are studying how the superior colliculus implements inhibitory tagging during cluttered visual search to suppress neural activity for previously fixated items and prioritize the selection of new targets. Broadening their focus to human clinical populations, Dr. McPeek is also investigating the theoretical link between attention and oculomotor planning by measuring exogenous spatial cueing effects in patients with paralytic strabismus.

papers.title: Physiological correlates of a simple saccadic-decision task to extended objects in superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Saccade initiation is usually studied with small point targets, yet real scenes contain extended objects, and humans show longer saccade latencies for larger targets. The authors recorded from monkey superior colliculus during a simple saccadic decision task with objects of different sizes and linked the size-dependent latency effect to how collicular activity builds up across the population. The results give a neural account of how target extent shapes the timing of saccade decisions.
papers.authors: Baptiste Caziot, Bonnie Cooper, Mark R. Harwood, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: Exogenous spatial attention is functional in paralytic strabismics
papers.abstract: Absent cueing effects in patients with paralytic strabismus have been taken as evidence that attention is obligatorily tied to eye-movement planning. Two experiments with facilitating and inhibiting visual cues and a no-cue control show that these patients still exhibit exogenous attention effects on target-directed response latencies, challenging a strict premotor linkage.
papers.authors: Kevin T. Willeford, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: Inhibitory tagging both speeds and strengthens saccade target selection in the superior colliculus during visual search
papers.abstract: Extending earlier work on inhibitory tagging, this study quantifies how reduced activity for previously fixated objects changes target selection in the monkey superior colliculus during a time-limited search task. Tagging both accelerates and strengthens the selection of the next saccade target, tying the neural signal to efficient search behavior.
papers.authors: Christopher Conroy, Rakesh Nanjappa, Robert M. McPeek

papers.title: Inhibitory tagging in the superior colliculus during visual search
papers.abstract: During cluttered visual search, people avoid re-inspecting objects they have already rejected, and inhibitory tagging has been proposed as the mechanism. Recording from monkey superior colliculus during search, the authors show that collicular activity is reduced for previously fixated objects, consistent with the SC implementing this inhibition as part of saccade target selection.
papers.authors: Christopher Conroy, Rakesh Nanjappa, Robert M. McPeek

0572.name: Robert Volcic
0572.bio: Robert Volcic is an Associate Professor of Psychology at New York University Abu Dhabi exploring the mechanisms of human multisensory perception and sensorimotor integration. Their research examines how visual and haptic information are integrated to guide motor actions, such as reaching and grasping, within three-dimensional environments. By employing psychophysical experiments, movement tracking, and computational modeling, Volcic investigates the bidirectional relationship between active motor behavior and sensory processing. Current work focuses on understanding how the brain resolves sensory uncertainties using redundant cues and how physical interactions with the environment shape perceptual estimates.
0572.research_direction: Dr. Volcic has recently been investigating the computational rules and multisensory mechanisms that guide human action, focusing heavily on whether visually guided grasping and reaching movements obey Weber's law. By carefully evaluating action variability and grip aperture at the exact moment of goal attainment, they are exploring long-standing debates about whether perceptual and motor systems rely on shared or distinct metrics. Their recent work also probes haptic spatial memory and multisensory integration, specifically asking how the brain combines vision with haptic feedback from handheld tools and how body posture influences the accuracy of memory-guided reaching. In addition to this fundamental sensorimotor research, Dr. Volcic is examining practical methodological issues for vision scientists, such as how LED degradation impacts the luminance and color calibration of experimental displays.

papers.title: The impact of LED degradation on the calibration accuracy of displays and light sources
papers.abstract: The paper describes two separate ways in which LEDs degrade over time and how this undermines luminance linearity and colour fidelity in displays used for vision experiments. It presents a measurement method to identify each mechanism, tested on a low-latency wide-gamut LCD. The work gives vision scientists practical guidance for keeping stimulus calibration reliable.
papers.authors: Zoltan Derzsi, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Bimanual Postural Similarity Facilitates Haptic Memory-Guided Reaching
papers.abstract: Participants reached toward locations first encoded by touch after a memory delay. Accuracy improved when the posture of the hand used to reach resembled the posture of the hand or hands that had encoded the location. This suggests that haptic spatial memory is tied to body posture and that similarity between encoding and reaching postures supports sensorimotor transfer.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Tool-sensed object information effectively supports vision for multisensory grasping
papers.abstract: The study asks whether information about an object's size and position that is felt through a handheld tool (a grabber) can be combined with vision to guide grasping as it is with direct touch. Participants grasped objects while vision and tool-mediated haptics were varied and made conflicting. Tool-sensed information supported grasping about as effectively as direct hand haptics and was integrated with vision, showing that the brain treats tools as extensions of the senses.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Alessandro Farne, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Actions obey Weber's law when precision is evaluated at goal attainment
papers.abstract: Earlier work suggested that movement precision does not scale with target size as Weber's law predicts. The authors measure variability at the moment the goal is reached, rather than at earlier movement stages, and find that action precision does follow Weber's law. This resolves an apparent discrepancy between perception and action by tying the effect to when precision is evaluated.
papers.authors: Ivan Camponogara, Robert Volcic

papers.title: Not only perception but also grasping actions can obey Weber's law
papers.abstract: Weber's law says that perceptual noise grows in proportion to stimulus size, and grasping was long claimed to escape this rule. Using visually guided grasps of objects of different sizes, the authors show that grasp aperture precision can scale with object size when precision is assessed appropriately, so actions are not exempt from Weber's law. The result reframes the long-running debate about whether perception and action rely on different metrics.
papers.authors: Zoltan Derzsi, Robert Volcic

0573.name: Roberto Caldara
0573.bio: Roberto Caldara is a Full Professor at the University of Fribourg, where Caldara directs the Eye and Brain Mapping Laboratory (iBMLab) and holds the Chair of Visual and Social Neuroscience. Their research focuses on the 'other-race' effect and the cross-cultural variability of facial expression perception, addressing the universality of human visual cognition. Through eye-tracking, electrophysiology (EEG), and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), Caldara investigates how cultural factors modulate the neural mechanisms and oculomotor strategies used to decode social information. This work includes the development of psychophysical frameworks to isolate the diagnostic features utilized during the spatiotemporal processing of dynamic facial signals.
0573.research_direction: Dr. Caldara has recently been studying how people rapidly recognize faces and read social information such as identity, race, and emotion. Their recent work uses EEG and psychophysics to measure how quickly and from how little visual signal the brain can categorize faces, including the speed of categorizing race and the relationship between two common EEG markers of face processing. They also study a patient with prosopagnosia, a severe impairment in recognizing faces, to test which brain regions are needed for these judgments. Another thread examines where observers look when recognizing facial expressions, asking whether individual gaze strategies persist for moving faces and whether facial motion helps recognition when the image is noisy.

papers.title: Prosopagnosia and the role of face-sensitive areas in race perception
papers.abstract: This study investigates the functional necessity of core face-processing regions—specifically the right Occipital Face Area (rOFA) and left Fusiform Face Area (lFFA)—for the rapid extraction of racial information from faces. By testing patient PS, a case of pure acquired prosopagnosia with lesions in these areas, the authors examined the Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA). PS exhibited a preserved ORCA, categorizing other-race faces faster than same-race faces, comparable to healthy controls. However, psychometric function analyses revealed that PS required significantly more visual signal intensity (signal-to-noise ratio) to identify racial categories in ambiguous morphed faces. These data suggest that while basic racial categorization remains resilient to damage in the core face network, the rOFA and lFFA are indispensable for processing fine-grained, high-level racial representations.
papers.authors: Pauline Schaller, Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Justin Duncan, Peter de Lissa, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Cross-Validating the Electrophysiological Markers of Early Face Categorization
papers.abstract: The relationship between the N170 event-related potential (ERP) and the steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) generated by fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS) during face categorization remains a subject of methodological debate. This research concurrently recorded EEG signals using both transient ERP and FPVS paradigms to determine if FPVS frequency-domain responses serve as a proxy for the N170. Results demonstrated that the magnitude of the FPVS response does not directly correlate with isolated ERP components such as the P1 or N170. Instead, the FPVS frequency response was significantly predicted by peak-to-peak amplitude differences between the N170 and the subsequent P2 component. This evidence indicates that FPVS-based neural markers reflect higher-order integration across multiple processing stages rather than a singular, early face-sensitive categorization stage captured by the N170.
papers.authors: Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles, Lisa Stacchi, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Idiosyncratic Fixation Patterns generalize across Dynamic and Static Facial Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: This investigation sought to determine whether the stable, idiosyncratic oculomotor strategies observed in static face recognition—termed "fixation fingerprints"—extend to the decoding of dynamic facial expressions of emotion (FEE). Utilizing the iMap computational framework to analyze fixation distributions, the authors compared the spatial sampling patterns of observers identifying static FEEs versus dynamic sequences that capture the temporal evolution of emotional signals. Despite the increased visual complexity and temporal variance of dynamic stimuli, observers maintained highly consistent and unique fixation strategies across both formats. These findings suggest that the internal representational models used to extract diagnostic social information from faces are remarkably robust to stimulus dynamics, reflecting a stable, viewer-dependent trait in visual social cognition.
papers.authors: Anita Paparelli, Nayla Sokhn, Lisa Stacchi, Antoine Coutrot, Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: Recognizing facial expressions of emotion amid noise: A dynamic advantage
papers.abstract: To evaluate the ecological benefit of facial dynamics in social perception, this study employed a psychophysical approach to measure recognition thresholds for the six basic facial expressions under varying levels of visual signal intensity (0%–100% normalized phase and contrast). While young adults showed comparable recognition for static and dynamic expressions at full signal (except for high-dynamics expressions like happiness and surprise), a profound dynamic advantage emerged at lower signal intensities, peaking around 20%. The temporal unfolding of facial movements significantly lowered the sensory thresholds required for accurate expression decoding compared to static snapshots. These results demonstrate that the human visual system effectively integrates temporal cues to compensate for suboptimal viewing conditions, resolving the "ceiling effect" often reported in studies of dynamic emotion recognition in healthy populations.
papers.authors: Anne-Raphaëlle Richoz, Lisa Stacchi, Pauline Schaller, Junpeng Lao, Michael Papinutto, Valentina Ticcinelli, Roberto Caldara

papers.title: The speed of race
papers.abstract: The Other-Race Categorization Advantage (ORCA)—the phenomenon where observers categorize other-race faces faster than same-race faces—is hypothesized to stem from heightened sensitivity to early visual race signals. This study combined behavioral reaction-time measures with EEG to explore the neural correlates of ORCA under parametric visual degradation (random noise). Behavioral results revealed a specific threshold at low signal intensities where only other-race signals remained sufficient for categorization. Neurally, this sensitivity was reflected in early ERP components, with enhanced amplitudes for other-race stimuli observed in the P1, N170, and N250 peaks. The findings suggest that the ORCA is driven by a hierarchy of neural processes, starting with low-level perceptual saliency in the early visual stream, which facilitates the rapid categorization of faces belonging to less familiar ethnic groups.
papers.authors: Peter de Lissa, Pauline Schaller, Roberto Caldara

0574.name: Roland Fleming
0574.main_research_area: Visual perception of materials and objects
0574.bio: Roland W. Fleming holds the Kurt Koffka Professorship of Experimental Psychology at Justus Liebig University Giessen and serves as the Executive Director of the Center for Mind, Brain and Behavior, a collaborative research center involving the Universities of Marburg and Giessen and TU Darmstadt. Fleming’s research investigates how the human brain estimates physical and functional properties of objects, such as 3D shape, gloss, and material elasticity, from retinal images. To study these processes, their lab combines psychophysical experiments, computer graphics, and unsupervised deep learning to model the visual system’s method of disentangling environmental cues. Fleming’s recent work focuses on the neural representations of core material dimensions and the computational mechanisms that enable humans to predict physical events and guide motor actions.
0574.research_direction: Dr. Fleming's recent work explores how the visual system infers complex material, spatial, and dynamic properties from optical information. They have recently been investigating the computational mechanisms of material perception, utilizing large-scale behavioral data to map the latent psychological dimensions of materials and employing tiny convolutional neural networks to test whether gloss perception relies on simple, image-computable features rather than inverse optics. Their research also examines 3D shape-from-shading by analyzing how early-vision measurements like local image orientation fields might drive human surface curvature judgments and characteristic visual illusions. Furthermore, Dr. Fleming probes how observers infer dynamic physical properties, using extensive simulations of bouncing objects to isolate the specific visual cues and heuristic strategies that guide human perceptions of elasticity.

papers.title: Human gloss perception reproduced by tiny neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors show that very small convolutional networks, with only a handful of filters, account for human gloss judgments better than much larger networks trained to recover physical specular reflectance. This suggests gloss perception relies on a compact set of image-computable features rather than inverse-optics-style estimation of physical properties. It offers a parsimonious, mechanistic account of how the visual system infers surface material.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, Arash Akbarinia, Katherine R. Storrs, Jacob R. Cheeseman, Hannah E. Smithson, Karl R. Gegenfurtner, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Visual cues and strategies for perceiving elasticity
papers.abstract: The authors selected stimuli from more than 100,000 simulated movies of bouncing cubes to pit candidate cues for elasticity against one another. Simple heuristics predicted both the successes and the characteristic errors of human elasticity judgments. This shows how observers infer dynamic physical properties from limited visual information.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Florian S. Bayer, Joshua Tenenbaum, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Core dimensions of human material perception
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale, data-driven behavioral approach with thousands of material images, the study uncovers the latent dimensions people use to represent and compare materials. These dimensions are interpretable and predict human similarity judgments. The work provides a compact map of the mental space of materials.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Filipp Schmidt, Martin N. Hebart, Alexandra C. Schmid, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: Orientation fields predict human perception of 3D shape from shading
papers.abstract: By analysing millions of pixels from renderings of shaded objects, the authors find a strong statistical link between local image orientation patterns and 3D surface curvature. A simple model built on orientation fields reproduces key errors and illusions in human shape-from-shading. This ties shape perception to the kind of measurements made by early visual cortex.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Celine Aubuchon, Romain Vergne, Steven A. Cholewiak, Benjamin Kunsberg, Daniel Holtmann-Rice, Steven W. Zucker, Roland W. Fleming

0576.name: Rosanne L. Rademaker
0576.bio: Rosanne L. Rademaker is a cognitive neuroscientist and Group Leader at the Ernst Strüngmann Institute for Neuroscience, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of human perception and visual working memory. Their research employs high-field fMRI, M/EEG, psychophysics, and computational modeling to examine how the brain maintains sensory representations in the absence of direct input. Rademaker contributed to the sensory recruitment theory by demonstrating that the early visual cortex simultaneously represents incoming sensory signals and mnemonic information through flexible neural codes. Their work also explores how memory representations transition from veridical sensory formats to abstract, categorical formats along the visual hierarchy to facilitate goal-directed behavior.
0576.research_direction: Dr. Rademaker’s recent work explores the neural mechanisms and dynamic formatting of visual working memory, investigating how sensory representations are maintained and transformed to support behavior. Using techniques like fMRI and eye-tracking, they are examining how remembered orientations transition toward abstract categorical formats along the cortical hierarchy, and how features like color are flexibly recoded into spatial coordinates based on task demands. Through recurrent network modeling, their research also tests whether working memory traces in early visual cortex are primarily driven by top-down feedback from anterior regions or by local short-term synaptic plasticity. Beyond memory maintenance, they have recently been probing the fundamental spatial reference frames of human visual processing, utilizing EEG and head-tilt paradigms to dissociate retinocentric from allocentric orientation coding. Finally, they are investigating critical methodological constraints in cognitive neuroscience, evaluating how model mimicry in forward-encoding approaches limits the ability to infer single-neuron tuning properties and stimulus priors from macroscopic population signals.

papers.title: Converting color memory toward a spatial format to benefit behavior
papers.abstract: In an eye-tracking study, participants remembered a color or a spatial position and knew the color would later be reported via a location. When the color could be mapped onto space, gaze and recall showed that the memory was flexibly converted into a spatial format. Working memory thus recodes contents within the visual domain to fit anticipated goals.
papers.authors: Amit Rawal, Michael J. Wolff, Rosanne L. Rademaker

papers.title: A gradual transition toward categorical representations along the visual hierarchy during working memory, but not perception
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while people viewed or held oriented gratings in memory, the authors compared how orientation is coded across visual areas. Representations in early cortex stay close to the physical stimulus, but along the hierarchy the remembered orientations drift toward category-like, abstract formats. This shift appears only during memory and not during direct viewing, suggesting memory codes are progressively reformatted for behavior.
papers.authors: Chaipat Chunharas, Michael J Wolff, Meike D Hettwer, Rosanne L Rademaker

papers.title: Model mimicry limits conclusions about neural tuning and can mistakenly imply unlikely priors
papers.abstract: This Matters Arising piece shows that forward-encoding and related tuning models fit to EEG/fMRI data can mimic each other, so good fits do not uniquely identify single-neuron tuning properties. Simulations reveal that the approach can spuriously suggest implausible priors over stimulus space. The authors urge caution in interpreting neural tuning from population-level signals.
papers.authors: Michael J. Wolff, Rosanne L. Rademaker

papers.title: Top-down feedback can explain the existence of working memory traces in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using recurrent network modeling, the study tests whether top-down feedback from higher areas or short-term synaptic plasticity traces better explain working memory content in early visual cortex. Feedback can account for flexible selection of information and robustness of memories to distraction, two hallmarks of working memory. The results argue that feedback from anterior regions is sufficient to explain EVC memory traces.
papers.authors: N. N. Krause, A. Compte, R. L. Rademaker

papers.title: Visual representations in the human brain rely on a reference frame that is in between allocentric and retinocentric coordinates
papers.abstract: Participants tilted their heads to dissociate retinal from world-centered orientation while EEG tracked orientation representations in visual cortex. Neural coding was neither purely retinocentric nor purely allocentric but fell in between the two. This shows that early visual representations already partially compensate for the observer's body orientation.
papers.authors: Maria S. Servetnik, Michael J. Wolff, Chaipat Chunharas, Rosanne L. Rademaker

0577.name: Roy Luria
0577.bio: Roy Luria is a Professor at Tel Aviv University whose research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual working memory and executive control. Their work uses electrophysiological measures, specifically the contralateral delay activity (CDA) event-related potential, to track the maintenance and filtering of visual information in real-time. Luria examines the processes of memory updating and the "resetting" of mental representations, focusing on how individual differences in capacity relate to attentional control. By combining high-temporal resolution EEG with behavioral psychophysics, they study how the brain manages and updates internal representations when presented with competing visual input.
0577.research_direction: Dr. Luria has recently been investigating the underlying architecture of visual working memory, with a particular focus on the "pointer-system" that indexes and links remembered items to their stored visual content. Their recent work explores how these cognitive pointers are dynamically allocated and maintained under varying conditions, such as when objects are temporarily occluded or when spatial contexts change. Using behavioral metrics alongside EEG markers like contralateral delay activity, they are also examining how visual information is integrated and structured during memory maintenance. Specifically, they are testing whether multi-feature items are stored as unified objects or independent feature sets, and how distinct chunking mechanisms either group separate items together or merge the visual parts of a single object.

papers.title: Visual working memory's pointer system: Past, present, and future
papers.abstract: A synthesis of the pointer-system account of visual working memory, in which each remembered item is linked to its content through an index-like pointer. The review traces the behavioral and EEG evidence (notably the contralateral delay activity) for pointers, discusses how they are allocated and updated, and lays out open questions and future directions for the field.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Roy Luria

papers.title: Feature-based versus object-based representation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Asks whether multi-feature objects in visual working memory are stored as unified object representations or as independent feature sets, using behavioral and electrophysiological signatures of memory load. The work addresses how color and shape are combined or kept separate and bears on the long-running object-based versus feature-based debate.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Ayelet Ramaty, Roy Luria

papers.title: The effect of occlusion on the visual working memory pointer-system
papers.abstract: Tests how temporarily occluding remembered objects affects the pointers that keep them tied to their stored content. Combining EEG markers of memory maintenance with behavior, the study examines whether occlusion leads to updating an existing memory or discarding it and starting anew, with collaborators from the University of Padova.
papers.authors: Shani Friedman, Roberto Dell'Acqua, Paola Sessa, Roy Luria

papers.title: The effect of context on pointer allocation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Investigates when the brain assigns a new pointer to an incoming object versus reusing an existing one, and shows that this allocation depends on the surrounding context. The EEG evidence indicates that context flexibly shapes how pointers are allocated and hence how memory is updated.
papers.authors: Shani Friedman, Trafton Drew, Roy Luria

papers.title: Dissociable online integration processes in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Proposes that chunking in visual working memory reflects two distinct integration mechanisms: grouping, which combines several objects into one representation, and object unification, which merges the parts of a single object. Behavioral and neural evidence shows these processes dissociate, helping resolve mixed findings about how efficiently chunking compresses information.
papers.authors: Halely Balaban, Trafton Drew, Roy Luria

0578.name: Roy Mukamel
0578.bio: Roy Mukamel is a Professor at Tel Aviv University and directs the Motor Cognition Laboratory. Their research investigates the neural integration of action and perception, specifically examining how voluntary motor commands modulate activity in sensory cortices and how the brain represents intentions. Using a multi-modal methodology that includes functional MRI, EEG, virtual reality, and human intracranial electrophysiology, Mukamel addresses questions regarding motor skill learning, intermanual transfer, and the mechanisms of self-generated sensory feedback.
0578.research_direction: Dr. Mukamel has recently been investigating the bidirectional relationship between motor actions and sensory perception, focusing on how self-generated movements influence perceptual processing and action understanding. Their recent work uses EEG and behavioral methods to explore how motor efference signals and learned expectations shape the neural attenuation of self-triggered sounds, and whether the anticipated intensity of a sensory outcome alters the physical kinetics of a self-initiated action. In the visual domain, they are examining whether graphomotor practice with the dominant versus non-dominant hand improves subsequent visual discrimination of shapes, while also using fMRI to map how the human brain processes observed goal-directed hand movements across different hierarchical timescales. On the methodological front, Dr. Mukamel is developing novel, model-free fMRI analysis techniques that use randomized stimulus ordering to infer functional selectivity without relying on standard hemodynamic response assumptions.

papers.title: Sensory Experience and Motor Signals Shape Auditory Processing in an Independent Manner
papers.abstract: Sensory responses to sounds we trigger with our own actions are weaker than to identical externally produced sounds. Using EEG while participants learned to link motor or visual cues to tones, the study asks whether motor efference signals carry outcome-specific predictions or just general motor information. Auditory N100 declined with learning and was smaller after motor than visual cues, but the two factors did not interact, indicating that experience-based expectations and motor signals contribute independently to attenuation.
papers.authors: Batel Buaron, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: What the visual system can learn from the non-dominant hand: The effect of graphomotor engagement on visual discrimination
papers.abstract: Earlier work showed that writing shapes with the dominant hand improves later visual discrimination of those shapes. This study asked whether the effect holds for the non-dominant hand in 60 right-handed participants comparing graphomotor and purely visual training. Non-dominant graphomotor practice gave no extra benefit beyond visual training, suggesting the motor-to-visual facilitation depends on skilled dominant-hand pathways.
papers.authors: Shlomit Ben-Ami, Batel Buaron, Ori Yaron, Kyle Keane, Virginia H. Sun, Flip Phillips, Jason Friedman, Pawan Sinha, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: High or low expectations: Expected intensity of action outcome is embedded in action kinetics
papers.abstract: Three behavioral studies (n=120) tested how the intensity people expect an action to produce alters the way they perform the action. Participants pressed harder when they expected a weak outcome and less hard when they expected a strong one, but only for self-initiated, outcome-producing presses and not for reactive presses. Applied force did not change detection of near-threshold outcomes, so kinetics reflect expectation rather than causally shaping perception.
papers.authors: Batel Buaron, Daniel Reznik, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: A randomization-based, model-free approach to functional neuroimaging: A proof of concept
papers.abstract: The paper introduces TWISTER, a way to infer functional selectivity in fMRI from correlations between experimental runs whose stimulus order is randomized, without assuming a hemodynamic response model. A visuomotor mapping experiment serves as a proof of concept. The authors discuss where the model-free approach is useful and what its statistical limits are.
papers.authors: Matan Mazor, Roy Mukamel

papers.title: Temporal hierarchy of observed goal-directed actions
papers.abstract: Using inter-subject correlation of fMRI, the study tested whether observed goal-directed actions are processed on a hierarchy of timescales. Observers watched hand-movement sequences intact or scrambled at primitive, sub-goal and high-goal timescales. Motor and action-observation regions showed timescale-dependent sensitivity to temporal structure, extending known temporal receptive window hierarchies to action understanding.
papers.authors: Shahar Aberbach-Goodman, Roy Mukamel

0579.name: Ru-Yuan Zhang
0579.department: School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences; IDG/McGovern Institute for Brain Research
0579.lab_name: Laboratory of Cognitive Computational Neuroscience and Neuroimaging (CCNN)
0579.bio: Ru-Yuan Zhang is a computational neuroscientist who investigates the mechanisms of human perception, learning, and decision-making using fMRI, psychophysics, and deep learning models. Zhang’s research focuses on how the brain represents sensory uncertainty and how top-down processes like attention warp neural manifolds to optimize population coding in the human visual cortex. By comparing artificial neural networks with biological systems, they reverse-engineer the principles of perceptual learning and abstract visual reasoning to analyze human intelligence. Their work also includes computational psychiatry, applying Bayesian inference and reinforcement learning models to characterize cognitive deficits in individuals with anxiety and depression.
0579.research_direction: Dr. Zhang has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying visual plasticity, abstract reasoning, and temporal prediction across both biological and artificial systems. Their recent work explores how visual perceptual learning and task demands, such as attention, warp the manifold geometry of neural population responses in the visual cortex, using human fMRI and monkey neurophysiology to evaluate competing models of visual improvement. Beyond early sensory processing, they are also examining how self-supervised deep learning models can achieve human-level abstract visual concept learning—such as solving Raven-style matrices—by incorporating brain-inspired algorithms like mental bootstrapping and neural prediction errors. Furthermore, Dr. Zhang investigates the dynamics of sequential temporal anticipation, combining human EEG and recurrent neural networks to probe how brains and artificial models predict the precise timing of upcoming events.

papers.title: Task context improves population codes by warping response geometry in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using large-scale human fMRI data, the study examines how task demands such as attention reshape the population response geometry of visual cortex. Rather than simply boosting gain or reducing noise, task context warps the neural manifold so that task-relevant stimulus differences become easier to read out. The result links attention to the same geometric framework used for perceptual learning.
papers.authors: Yu-Qi You, Shurui Li, Yu-Ang Cheng, Yuanning Li, Kendrick Kay, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Mental bootstrapping enables human-level concept learning in self-supervised deep models
papers.abstract: The authors propose a self-supervised deep learning approach that iteratively bootstraps its own internal concepts, echoing how people build up abstract concepts. The resulting models reach human-level concept learning on visual abstract-reasoning tasks. It connects cognitive-neuroscience ideas about mental construction to machine-learning performance.
papers.authors: Lingxiao Yang, Muyang Lyu, Ying-Jie Wang, Xiaohua Xie, Zonglei Zhen, Jian-Huang Lai, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Neural prediction errors as a unified cue for abstract visual reasoning
papers.abstract: Human intelligence tests such as Raven-style matrices require inferring abstract rules from visual patterns. The paper shows that neural prediction errors can serve as a single cue that lets a model solve such analogical reasoning problems across task variants. It extends the group's earlier ICML work into a full TPAMI treatment linking brain-inspired prediction errors to reasoning.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
papers.authors: Lingxiao Yang, Xiaohua Xie, Wei-Shi Zheng, Fang Fang, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: A neural geometry approach comprehensively explains apparently conflicting models of visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The paper asks why competing accounts of visual perceptual learning (sharpened tuning, reweighting of readout, and others) each fit some data but disagree with one another. It describes learning as changes in the geometry of population responses and shows, with human fMRI, monkey neurophysiology and modeling, that this single view reconciles the seemingly conflicting models. It offers a common framework for predicting when and how training improves discrimination.
papers.authors: Yu-Ang Cheng, Mehdi Sanayei, Xing Chen, Ke Jia, Sheng Li, Fang Fang, Takeo Watanabe, Alexander Thiele, Ru-Yuan Zhang

papers.title: Sequential temporal anticipation characterized by neural power modulation and in recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: The study investigates how the brain anticipates when upcoming events will occur in sequences. EEG power modulations track anticipation, and recurrent neural networks trained on the same task reproduce the dynamics. This suggests a shared computational mechanism for temporal prediction in biological and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Xiangbin Teng, Ru-Yuan Zhang

0580.name: Ruben Coen-Cagli
0580.bio: Ruben Coen-Cagli is an Associate Professor who investigates the principles of neural computation and their relationship to perceptual experience. Coen-Cagli’s research integrates tools from computer vision, machine learning, and probabilistic neural coding to model how the primary visual cortex (V1) represents the statistics of natural images. Specifically, they explore how cortical population activity approximates probabilistic inferences, focusing on the role of contextual modulation and trial-to-trial response variability. Through a combination of normative computational modeling and experimental collaboration, their work aims to identify the mechanisms by which the brain resolves sensory ambiguity in complex natural environments.
0580.research_direction: Dr. Coen-Cagli has recently been investigating how the visual system parses complex natural scenes and represents sensory uncertainty at both the perceptual and neural population levels. A major focus of their recent work explores human perceptual segmentation, using new behavioral paradigms and iterative Bayesian inference models to measure how observers dynamically group visual features into objects and to quantify subjective uncertainty during this process. At the neural level, they are examining how natural image statistics drive patterns of response covariability in macaque primary visual cortex to test generative models based on the neural sampling hypothesis. Additionally, Dr. Coen-Cagli is developing computational frameworks to understand how this correlated variability interacts with communication subspaces to constrain the transfer of sensory information between different brain areas.

papers.title: Natural scene segmentation dynamics reveal iterative Bayesian inference
papers.abstract: Using a new paradigm to measure subjective human segmentation maps of natural images over time, the study finds spatiotemporal dynamics richer than existing segmentation theories predict. The authors introduce iterative Bayesian inference algorithms that repeatedly integrate visual features across the image to update segmentation estimates. These models reproduce the observed dynamics and explain how ambiguous scenes get parsed into objects.
papers.authors: Tridib K. Biswas, Jonathan Vacher, Sophie Molholm, Pascal Mamassian, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Are we ready to tackle perceptual segmentation of natural scenes?
papers.abstract: This perspective takes stock of the field of perceptual segmentation and asks what is missing for progress on natural scenes. It reviews behavioral and computational approaches, the ambiguity and subjectivity of natural-scene segmentation, and the gap between machine-vision segmenters and human perception, then outlines directions for a unified probabilistic account.
papers.authors: Ruben Coen-Cagli, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Relating natural image statistics to patterns of response covariability in macaque primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors extend a generative model of natural image statistics under the neural sampling hypothesis, so that pairwise neural covariability reflects shared uncertainty about latent image features. The theory predicts how noise correlations depend on the structure of the image in and around the receptive field. They test these predictions against macaque V1 population recordings and find that response covariability tracks the statistics of natural images as the model requires.
papers.authors: Amirhossein Farzmahdi, Adam Kohn, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Measuring stimulus information transfer between neural populations through the communication subspace
papers.abstract: Building on the idea of communication subspaces between brain areas, the authors develop a framework linking correlated variability in a source population to the sensory information a downstream population can receive. It combines linear Fisher information with a low-dimensional communication channel model. The framework shows how shared variability limits information transmitted between areas and gives a practical estimator.
papers.authors: Oren Weiss, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Measuring uncertainty in human visual segmentation
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to measure perceptual segmentation maps by collecting many pixel-wise same-different judgments and reconstructing the underlying map with a model. The reconstruction also yields a measure of the observer's uncertainty about segmentation. Human data are then used to compare candidate segmentation algorithms quantitatively.
papers.authors: Jonathan Vacher, Claire Launay, Pascal Mamassian, Ruben Coen-Cagli

0581.name: Ruggero Micheletto
0581.bio: Ruggero Micheletto is a Professor at Yokohama City University with research integrating solid-state physics, nanophotonics, and cognitive neuroscience. Micheletto's work in vision science utilizes experimental psychophysics and eye-tracking to investigate the critical fusion frequency of light stimuli and the cognitive effects of linguistic distortions on visual perception. Previously a visiting professor at the Harvard Visual Attention Laboratory, Micheletto has used scanning near-field optical microscopy (SNOM) for real-time biological imaging and developed sensory substitution systems like 'VisualSound'. Current research directions involve the mathematical modeling of neural networks and the study of spatiotemporal dynamics in optical semiconductor blinking.
0581.research_direction: Dr. Micheletto has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of light emission in semiconductor materials, focusing particularly on the phenomenon of photoluminescence blinking in InGaN/GaN quantum wells and nanostructures. By imaging the random flickering of emitted light across different spatial locations, sampling frequencies, and excitation wavelengths, their recent work explores the underlying mechanisms that drive these optical fluctuations, such as carrier trapping pathways and defect-mediated charge dynamics. They are especially interested in whether these microscopic blinking events are independent or linked, mapping how neighboring nanopillars or distinct spots on a material exhibit temporally correlated flickering to probe for collective coupling effects. In a distinct line of research, Dr. Micheletto also uses first-principles calculations to model the electronic properties of substitutional impurities in silicon carbide, seeking to characterize the defect levels relevant to advanced power devices.

papers.title: Time and Spatially Resolved Analysis of Single Quantum Well InGaN/GaN Photoluminescence Blinking at Multiple Sample Frequencies
papers.abstract: The study tracks the random on/off flickering of light emitted from small regions of a single InGaN/GaN quantum well, imaging it in both space and time at several sampling frequencies. Analysing how blinking statistics depend on the sampling rate reveals which timescales of carrier trapping and release dominate. The work supports a picture in which defect-mediated charge dynamics drive the emission fluctuations.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Mitsuru Funato, Yoichi Kawakami, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: Comparison of the Spatial and Temporal Photoluminescence Dynamics in InGaN/GaN at 365 nm and 430 nm Excitation
papers.abstract: The paper compares how photoluminescence from an InGaN/GaN quantum well fluctuates in space and time under two different excitation wavelengths, one above and one below the barrier band gap. Differences in the blinking behaviour between the two conditions help separate which carrier-generation and trapping pathways contribute to the flicker.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: The Electronic Properties of Magnesium, Zinc, Scandium Substitutional Impurities and their Complexes in 4H-SiC
papers.abstract: First-principles calculations are used to determine the electronic behaviour of Mg, Zn and Sc substituting on lattice sites in 4H silicon carbide, and of their complexes. The study characterises the defect levels these impurities introduce, relevant to doping and compensation in SiC power devices.
papers.authors: Giovanni Alfieri, Elizabeth Buitrago, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: Correlated photoluminescence blinking phenomenon on InGaN/GaN nanopillar structures
papers.abstract: Arrays of InGaN/GaN nanopillars were imaged for photoluminescence blinking, and neighbouring pillars were found to blink in a correlated manner. This suggests a coupling mechanism between adjacent nanostructures, likely mediated by carrier transfer or shared environmental factors, going beyond isolated-defect explanations.
papers.authors: Kotaro Oikawa, Koichi Okamoto, Mitsuru Funato, Yoichi Kawakami, Ruggero Micheletto

papers.title: Time-correlated luminescence blinking in InGaN single quantum wells
papers.abstract: Fluctuations in the luminescence of different spots on a single InGaN quantum well are shown to be temporally correlated rather than independent. The finding points to a collective or spatially extended mechanism behind the blinking and motivates later work on nanostructures and sampling-rate dependence.
papers.authors: Shunra Yoshida, Yusuke Fujii, Giovanni Alfieri, Ruggero Micheletto

0582.name: Ruth Rosenholtz
0582.bio: Rosenholtz is a Principal Research Scientist at NVIDIA Research and maintains an affiliation as a Principal Research Scientist at MIT’s Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and CSAIL. Rosenholtz developed the "Texture Tiling Model," which characterizes peripheral vision as an encoding scheme using summary statistics within localized pooling regions. Their research indicates that many observed attentional limits are consequences of peripheral encoding constraints. Rosenholtz's current work focuses on applying these computational models to analyze visual tasks such as driving, visual search, and the design of information visualizations.
0582.research_direction: Dr. Rosenholtz has recently been investigating the fundamental role of peripheral vision and summary-statistic encoding in shaping human perception, proposing a major theoretical shift in how the field conceptualizes visual attention. Their recent work explores whether phenomena classically attributed to capacity-limited attentional bottlenecks—such as conjunction search and change blindness—might instead be explained by the lossy, feature-pooling mechanisms of the visual periphery. Their work also bridges basic science and real-world applications, including how background clutter and heterogeneity affect visual search and saccade latencies in complex digital interfaces like video conferencing, as well as perception for driving and the role of peripheral vision in perception for action. Additionally, they have been evaluating the gap between biological and machine vision by developing new image datasets to test neural network robustness to simulated peripheral interference, while simultaneously investigating the minimal set of interpretable image statistics required to accurately model human texture perception and synthesis.

papers.title: Do action video gamers search better than non-gamers?
papers.abstract: Reports twelve experiments comparing action video game players and non-players on both efficient feature search and inefficient configuration search, using staircase and response-time methods. Examines exactly where any gamer advantage shows up and whether it reflects better visual processing or other factors. A large systematic test of a widely claimed effect.
papers.authors: Zoe (Jing) Xu, Josef Spjut, Ben Boudaoud, Simona Buetti, Alejandro Lleras, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: The effect of background clutter on visual search in video conferencing
papers.abstract: Tests how visual clutter and variability in participants' backgrounds affect how quickly people find and look at faces in video calls. Finds that cluttered backgrounds slow search and delay saccades, in line with peripheral crowding and clutter predictions. Offers practical design implications for video-conferencing interfaces.
papers.authors: Yelda Semizer, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: Visual Attention in Crisis
papers.abstract: Argues that vision science faces a crisis in how it thinks about attention, because many effects traditionally credited to attentional bottlenecks can instead be explained by information loss in peripheral vision. Reviews the key phenomena still needing extra capacity limits, finds what they have in common, and proposes a different framework for understanding where and why capacity is limited. Accompanied by peer commentary in BBS.
papers.authors: Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: COCO-Periph: Bridging the Gap Between Human and Machine Perception in the Periphery
papers.abstract: Introduces a dataset that applies a model of human peripheral encoding to COCO images at several eccentricities, so object detectors can be tested against peripheral-like degradation. Shows that networks are less robust than humans to this kind of distortion and examines how training on such images affects detection performance. Provides a benchmark linking human peripheral vision to machine vision robustness.
papers.authors: Anne Harrington, Vasha DuTell, Mark Hamilton, Ayush Tewari, Simon Stent, William T. Freeman, Ruth Rosenholtz

papers.title: Attributing Statistics to Synthesis Quality in Correlation-Based Texture Models
papers.abstract: Asks which image statistics in pyramid- and correlation-based texture models actually matter for producing perceptually convincing textures. Uses contrastive learning and human-relevant synthesis-quality evaluation to attribute performance to individual statistic groups, helping identify a smaller interpretable set of statistics. Relevant to modeling peripheral vision and texture perception.
papers.venue: NeurIPS (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems)
papers.authors: Vasha DuTell, Anne Harrington, Zeyu Yun, Mark Hamilton, Christian Koevesdi, Edward Adelson, Bill Freeman, Ruth Rosenholtz

0583.name: Ryan Ash
0583.department: Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences
0583.bio: Ryan Ash is a psychiatrist and neuroscientist who develops noninvasive neuromodulation technologies to treat disorders characterized by excessive neural circuit stability, such as autism and OCD. Ash utilizes transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) to investigate how brain states, particularly visual spatial attention, regulate neuroplasticity in the human visual cortex. Their work combines high-density EEG, steady-state visual evoked potentials (ssVEPs), and computational electrophysiology to connect fundamental circuit neuroscience with clinical interventions for behavioral inflexibility. Previously a clinical scholar at Stanford University, Ash currently directs a translational research program focused on image-guided ultrasound technologies and neuroplasticity-based therapeutics.
0583.research_direction: Dr. Ash has recently been studying whether focused ultrasound applied through the skull can be used to change activity in deep brain structures, using the visual thalamus (the lateral geniculate nucleus) as a test case. Their recent work examines how ultrasound settings such as pulse rate affect visual perception and brain electrical responses, and how to build better placebo controls, for example audible noise masks that hide the sound the device makes. They are also interested in how the human visual cortex changes with repeated stimulation, asking how attention and the day of testing shape this plasticity and how stable the cortex's contrast responses are over time. Across these projects they use EEG together with careful visual psychophysics to test whether non-invasive stimulation causally alters the brain.

papers.title: Effects of transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation to human lateral geniculate nucleus on visual perception and steady-state visual evoked potentials
papers.abstract: To determine whether transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) can causally modulate deep sensory nuclei in the human brain, this investigation examined the functional consequences of pulse repetition frequency (PRF)—a critical parameter hypothesized to govern acoustic radiation force versus mechanical displacement mechanisms—targeted to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). Neurotypical adult human participants (n = 25) underwent visual psychophysical testing coupled with scalp electroencephalography, combining contrast increment detection thresholds with steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPs) driven by frequency-tagged contrast-sweep stimuli. Sonication was targeted to the left LGN or an ipsilateral control site using an MRI-guided, depth-steerable 4-element focused ultrasound transducer (free-water ISPPA = 68 W/cm², 10% duty cycle, across multiple PRFs) with individual acoustic simulations and calibrated white-noise masking to eliminate auditory co-stimulation confounds. Despite acoustic modeling confirming focal target engagement in the majority of subjects, active LGN stimulation elicited no statistically significant shifts in SSVEP amplitude, phase delay, or contrast increment detection accuracy. These null findings provide an important cautionary benchmark regarding the effect sizes and efficacy of online neuronavigated deep-brain TUS paradigms in human sensory circuitry.
papers.authors: Martin TW Scott, Patti N Limon, Morteza Mohammadjavadi, Benjamin R. Kop, Nai-Feng Chen, Eva A Feredoes, Vladimir Vildavski, Gerald R Popelka, Anthony M. Norcia, Kim Butts Pauly, Ryan T Ash

papers.title: Psychophysical validation of calibrated white-noise and tuned-noise auditory masks for transcranial focused ultrasound
papers.abstract: Acoustic side-effects generated through bone conduction and transducer housing resonance present a significant confound in transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) experiments. To establish a rigorous framework for blinding participants during ultrasonic neuromodulation, the authors synthesized and calibrated auditory masking protocols against a highly salient sonication protocol (500 kHz fundamental frequency, 487.5 Hz pulse repetition frequency, 10% duty cycle, ISPPA = 68 W/cm²). Both wideband white noise and carrier-envelope spectrum-matched noise masks were calibrated for A-weighted decibel sound pressure levels using an artificial ear. Masking efficacy was quantified across 20 neurotypical adults using an adaptive QUEST+ staircase in a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) detection task. Masking successfully attenuated active TUS detection to chance levels (<55% accuracy) in 17 of 20 subjects for white noise and 18 of 20 subjects for tuned noise. However, effective masking required intensities near clinical occupational safety limits, and spectrum-tuned masking offered no significant statistical benefit over white noise, demonstrating that bone-conducted TUS percepts do not strictly follow conventional air-conduction acoustic spectra and highlighting the necessity of formal masking calibration in TUS clinical trials.
papers.authors: Martin TW Scott, Patti N Limon, Gerald R Popelka, Kim Butts Pauly, Anthony M Norcia, Ryan T Ash

papers.title: Spatial Attention and Session Day Independently Modulate Human Visual Cortical Plasticity
papers.abstract: This study examines the role of covert endogenous spatial attention in modulating stimulus-specific response potentiation (SSRP), a form of non-invasive cortical neuroplasticity, within the human visual system. Utilizing 128-channel high-density EEG, the researchers recorded frequency-tagged steady-state visual-evoked potentials (SSVEPs) at 6 Hz and 7.5 Hz in response to contrast-reversing checkerboard stimuli. While SSRP induction (2 Hz reversal) was localized to a single hemifield, the resulting response potentiation was observed bilaterally, challenging the paradigm of strict input or retinotopic specificity in humans. Crucially, the magnitude of potentiation was significantly higher on the second session day compared to the first, demonstrating that human SSRP effects accumulate over repeated exposures. Spatial attention was found to have a modest enhancing effect on potentiation in naïve participants during their initial session, but this modulation was occluded by the more robust plasticity effects observed during the second session.
papers.authors: Patricia Naomi Limon, Anthony M. Norcia, Ryan Thomas Ash

papers.title: Stability of steady-state visual evoked potential contrast response functions
papers.abstract: Repetitive sensory stimulation paradigms have frequently been posited to induce long-term potentiation-like neuroplasticity in primary sensory neocortex. In this study, the authors tested the capacity of repeated contrast-reversal sweep steady-state visual-evoked potential (ssVEP) stimuli to drive neuroplastic changes, while assessing the longitudinal stability of the underlying contrast-response function. Twenty healthy participants completed four 20-trial blocks daily over four consecutive testing days, fixating on 9-Hz contrast-reversing sinusoidal luminance gratings (3 cycles/degree) that swept logarithmically between 5% and 80% contrast across 10-second trials. Electrophysiological analysis at the 18-Hz second-harmonic frequency revealed no systematic or significant amplitude modulation across intra-day blocks or across successive testing days, failing to replicate sensory-induced cortical plasticity under these stimulus parameters. In contrast, individual ssVEP contrast-response profiles demonstrated remarkable consistency, with low within-subject coefficients of variation across blocks (15%–20%) and across days (22%–25%), confirming that sweep-ssVEP protocols provide an exceptionally reproducible electrophysiological biomarker for longitudinal repeated-measures interventional trials.
papers.authors: Ryan T Ash, Kerry C Nix, Anthony M Norcia

0584.name: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
0584.bio: Hansmann-Roth is an Assistant Professor at the University of Iceland who researches human visual perception using behavioral psychophysics and computational modeling. Their work investigates how the brain represents environmental statistical information through feature distribution learning (FDL) and the extraction of visual ensembles. Hansmann-Roth also explores the mechanisms of serial dependence and visual priming to determine how past experiences and internal uncertainty influence perceptual decisions. Additionally, their research addresses material perception by examining the cognitive and sensory factors involved in perceiving surface properties like gloss and lightness.
0584.research_direction: Dr. Hansmann-Roth has recently been investigating how the visual system compresses, stores, and integrates information across space and time. Their recent work explores the mechanisms driving temporal biases in visual working memory, specifically testing how environmental sequence volatility influences serial dependence and modeling whether the relative noise between competing representations dictates if memory biases are attractive or repulsive. Additionally, they are examining how the brain encodes spatial structure and summary statistics, using behavioral paradigms to probe whether peripheral redundancy masking is governed by perceptual grouping and asking how observers extract the complex statistical distributions of shapes during visual search. Finally, their research extends into material perception, utilizing psychophysical measurements to investigate how the visual system disentangles surface cues to estimate object glossiness through overlying transparent layers.

papers.title: Compression of visual information in redundancy masking follows grouping and segmentation
papers.abstract: Redundancy masking makes repeated items in the periphery appear fewer than they are. Across experiments, the authors show that the amount of compression depends on how the repeated elements are perceptually grouped and segmented rather than on their raw number or spacing. The findings support the idea that peripheral vision compresses redundant information according to perceptual organization.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Wolf M. Harmening, Bilge Sayim

papers.title: The effect of sequence stability on serial dependence
papers.abstract: Serial dependence is the tendency for current judgments to be biased toward recent stimuli. This study manipulates how stable or volatile the stimulus sequence is and shows that the strength of serial dependence depends on environmental stability. The result suggests the visual system adjusts how much it relies on the past according to the reliability of recent history.
papers.authors: Elín Kara Celin, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Noise in Competing Representations Determines the Direction of Memory Biases
papers.abstract: Remembered features can be pulled toward or pushed away from other items, and it has been unclear what decides which. The authors propose a model in which overlapping memory signals are separated, and the relative noise of the competing representations determines whether bias is attractive or repulsive. Behavioral data are used to test and support the model's predictions (reviewed preprint at eLife).
papers.authors: Andrey Chetverikov, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Perceiving gloss through transparency
papers.abstract: The study asks how observers judge the glossiness of a surface when it is seen behind a transparent layer. Psychophysical measurements show how the overlying layer alters perceived gloss and how the visual system partly compensates for it. It extends her material-perception work on how shape, reflectance and other cues combine.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Pascal Mamassian

papers.title: Extracting statistical information about shapes in the visual environment
papers.abstract: Building on feature distribution learning, this work tests whether observers learn the statistical distribution of shapes across a series of trials. Using priming-style search tasks, it shows the visual system encodes the shape of the whole distribution rather than just a summary such as the mean. It extends the framework beyond simple features like color and orientation.
papers.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth, Andrey Chetverikov, Arni Kristjansson

0585.name: Sabrina Pitzalis
0585.department: Department of Movement, Human and Health Sciences
0585.lab_name: Laboratorio di Neuroimmagini (IRCCS Fondazione Santa Lucia)
0585.bio: Pitzalis is an Associate Professor who specializes in the functional organization of the human visual system, specifically the dorsal stream and its role in self-motion perception. Using wide-field stimulation fMRI, retinotopic mapping, and high-density electrophysiology (ERPs), Pitzalis identified human homologs for macaque visual areas such as V6, V6A, and PEc. Their research examines how the brain segregates object-motion from egomotion (optic flow) and the integration of visuospatial signals for the control of locomotion and posture. Pitzalis conducts research at the Santa Lucia Foundation (IRCCS) in Rome on the neural substrates of spatial attention and multimodal sensorimotor interactions.
0585.research_direction: Dr. Pitzalis has recently been investigating how the human brain processes complex visual environments and coordinates visual cognition with varying motor demands. Using fMRI, their recent work explores the neural mechanisms of egomotion, specifically asking how cortical motion networks disentangle independent object motion from the optic flow generated by an observer's own movements. They are also utilizing EEG to study cognitive-motor trade-offs, examining how concurrent physical actions—such as walking, reaching, or stepping—alter anticipatory and stimulus-evoked brain activity during visual discrimination tasks. Finally, Dr. Pitzalis has been extending these electrophysiological methods to clinical and aging populations, investigating whether proactive event-related potentials and behavioral variability can serve as sensitive biomarkers for cognitive dysfunction in individuals with PTSD and older adults at risk for mild cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Markers of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Processing in Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
papers.abstract: Twenty-one PTSD patients and thirty matched controls performed a cognitive task while EEG captured both pre-stimulus preparatory activity (BP, pN, vN) and post-stimulus components (P1, N1, P3). Patients showed markedly reduced amplitudes of all anticipatory components and a smaller P3, but normal early perceptual and attentional responses. They also had slower, more variable responses without accuracy loss, pointing to anticipatory ERPs as candidate markers of cognitive dysfunction in PTSD.
papers.authors: Biancamaria Di Bello, Raffaele Costanzo, Natalie Ferrulli, Margherita Filosa, Maria Gabriela Bevacqua, Francesca Strappini, Valentina Sulpizio, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Behavioral variability and preparatory ERPs as neurobehavioral markers of mild cognitive impairment risk in older adults
papers.abstract: In 92 older adults doing a discriminative response task under EEG, the authors asked whether instability of proactive control marks early cognitive decline. Those in the MCI range on the MoCA showed higher intra-individual variability in response time and attenuated pre-stimulus Bereitschaftspotential and prefrontal negativity, while mean response time did not differ. Preparatory activity and response variability thus emerge as sensitive markers of MCI risk.
papers.authors: Francesco Di Russo, Merve Aydin, Valentina Bianco, Luca Boccacci, Roberta Forte, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Effects of Walking on Anticipatory Brain Processing During a Concurrent Cognitive Task
papers.abstract: EEG event-related potentials were recorded while people performed a visual discrimination task either standing still or walking on a treadmill, with or without optic flow. Walking strengthened both motor and cognitive preparation and improved speed and accuracy, consistent with multiple-resources accounts of non-interfering dual tasks. Adding optic flow further boosted motor preparation and speeded responses but lowered cognitive preparation and accuracy, likely from extra visual load.
papers.authors: BiancaMaria Di Bello, Camilla Panacci, Sveva Montesano, Raffaele Costanzo, Luca Boccacci, Merve Aydin, Andrea Casella, Stefania Lucia, Francesca Strappini, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Neural sensitivity to translational self- and object-motion velocities
papers.abstract: Detecting a moving object while you yourself are moving is hard because self-motion fills the retina with optic flow. The authors used fMRI with surface-based mapping of individual egomotion-sensitive regions while participants viewed virtual scenes combining different self-motion and object-motion velocities. Nearly all egomotion areas tracked self-motion speed, but only MT+, V6+ and V3A were also modulated by object-motion speed, suggesting these regions help separate scene-relative object motion from optic flow.
papers.authors: Valentina Sulpizio, Alessandro von Gal, Gaspare Galati, Patrizia Fattori, Claudio Galletti, Sabrina Pitzalis

papers.title: Electrophysiological indexes of the cognitive-motor trade-off associated with motor response complexity in a cognitive task
papers.abstract: Participants did the same visual cognitive task while responding with a keypress, a reach or a step, so that motor complexity increased while EEG was recorded. More complex responses enhanced early visual and attentional components (P1, N1) but shrank the late P3 tied to cognitive control, and a new late component (N750) grew with response complexity. Accuracy stayed constant, indicating the brain shifts resources toward motor control as actions get harder.
papers.authors: Bianca Maria di Bello, Andrea Casella, Merve Aydin, Stefania Lucia, Francesco Di Russo, Sabrina Pitzalis

0587.name: Sam Ling
0587.bio: Sam Ling is an Associate Professor at Boston University and the Director of the Visual Neuroscience Lab, where they investigate the mechanisms the human brain employs to prioritize information within cluttered visual environments. Ling’s research combines psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to characterize how attention modulates neural response properties. Their work focuses on divisive normalization, contrast adaptation, and the ways in which top-down and bottom-up processes alter early visual representations.
0587.research_direction: Dr. Ling has recently been using model-based fMRI to investigate how fundamental representations in early visual cortex are shaped by attention, internal states, and multisensory input. Their recent work explores the flexible mechanisms of visual attention, examining how feature-based attention alters population spatial frequency tuning and dynamically tracking the shifting size and location of the spatial attentional spotlight from cortical signals. Additionally, they are investigating core principles of spatial vision, such as testing the long-standing assumption of scale invariance between receptive field size and spatial frequency preference in human V1-V3. To understand broader modulatory influences on early vision, Dr. Ling is also measuring contrast response functions to determine how visuocortical gain is modulated by cognitive arousal and cross-modal audiovisual interactions.

papers.title: Spatial Frequency Tuning Follows Scale Invariance in the Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Long-standing theory assumes that receptive fields in early vision are scale invariant, so that preferred spatial frequency is inversely tied to receptive field size.
