Using model-based fMRI that estimates both spatial tuning and spatial frequency preference within voxels, the authors show that the ratio of peak spatial frequency to receptive field size (cycles per RF) is constant across V1-V3 in humans. This provides the first direct population-level test of the assumption.
papers.authors: Emily Wiecek, Luis D. Ramirez, Michaela Klimova, Sam Ling

papers.title: Audiovisual interactions modulate visuocortical gain
papers.abstract: The study examines how sounds change the gain of contrast responses in human visual cortex, using fMRI to measure contrast response functions with and without concurrent auditory input. It reports that audiovisual interactions modulate the gain of visual cortical responses. This extends the lab's normalization and gain framework to cross-modal influences on early vision.
papers.authors: Minsun Park, Sam Ling

papers.title: Attention alters population spatial frequency tuning
papers.abstract: Using voxel-wise population spatial frequency tuning measured with fMRI in V1-V3, the authors asked how feature-based attention to a low or high spatial frequency changes the tuning of neural populations. Attending to a spatial frequency pulled preferred frequency toward the attended value, and this shift also appeared in a task-irrelevant hemifield, reflecting the known spatial spread of feature-based attention. The work links attentional modulation to changes in tuning rather than only in gain.
papers.authors: Luis D. Ramirez, Feiyi Wang, Sam Ling

papers.title: Dynamic estimation of the attentional field from visual cortical activity
papers.abstract: The authors built an fMRI paradigm to track both the location and the size of covert spatial attention, by cueing regions of an annulus of varying width and reading out visual cortex activity. Cortical responses tracked the width of the cued region, showing that the attentional field can be flexibly broadened or narrowed. The approach yields a trial-by-trial estimate of the attentional spotlight from cortical signals.
papers.authors: Ilona M. Bloem, Leah Bakst, Joseph T. McGuire, Sam Ling

papers.title: Heterogeneous effects of cognitive arousal on the contrast response in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Participants solved easy or hard arithmetic problems to induce low or high cognitive arousal while fMRI measured contrast response functions in V1-V3. Arousal changed visuocortical gain in a person-specific way, increasing responses in some individuals and decreasing them in others. The direction of the effect was stable within a person and related to how much pupil size grew with arousal.
papers.authors: Jasmine Pan, Louis N. Vinke, Joseph T. McGuire, Sam Ling

0588.name: Sami R. Yousif
0588.bio: Sami R. Yousif is an Assistant Professor at The Ohio State University and the director of the Spatial Cognition Lab, having previously served on the faculty at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Yousif's research investigates the format of mental representations, specifically how the mind encodes visuospatial relations using polar coordinate systems and heuristics such as the 'additive-area' rule. By analyzing systematic errors in visual matching and estimation tasks, Yousif explores the latent structure of spatial thought and its development from childhood to adulthood. They earned a PhD in cognitive psychology from Yale University and completed postdoctoral training as a MindCORE Fellow at the University of Pennsylvania.
0588.research_direction: Dr. Yousif's recent work investigates the fundamental primitives underlying human spatial representation, particularly exploring whether visual perception and memory prioritize coarse topological relations—such as connectivity and holes—over precise Euclidean metrics. To examine these questions, they have recently been employing behavioral paradigms ranging from visual search and object matching to serial reproduction drawing tasks, while also theorizing how cognitive maps might function as a broader compositional medium for thought. Beyond spatial cognition, Dr. Yousif is critically re-evaluating core assumptions in visual processing, such as investigating whether the widely accepted phenomenon of numerosity adaptation might actually reflect adaptation to other visual properties rather than number itself. Finally, their recent research also extends into memory and time perception, exploring how repeated experiences might systematically distort subjective estimates of when past events originally occurred.

papers.title: Cognitive maps as a medium for thought
papers.abstract: An opinion article arguing that cognitive maps are not just for navigation but form a distinct, flexible medium for thought with compositional structure in spatial and nonspatial domains. It connects this to a language-of-thought view and to neural mechanisms such as replay and theta sequences that may convert map-like codes into sequential formats. Maps and symbolic cognition are presented as complementary.
papers.authors: Sami R. Yousif, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: Topological structure in human spatial representation revealed through drawing
papers.abstract: Tests whether spatial memory is organized around topological relations rather than Euclidean metrics, using drawings of memorized letter-like figures by adults and children. Angles drifted toward 90 degrees and line lengths compressed, yet topologically critical features such as T-junctions and holes were reliably preserved, especially under serial reproduction. The results support topology as a core organizing principle of spatial memory.
papers.authors: Mahwish Kittur, Agnes Zhang, Nessa V. Bryce, Sami R. Yousif

papers.title: Perceiving topological relations
papers.abstract: Asks whether adults automatically perceive coarse topological structure, such as the presence of holes or the connectivity of a shape, as opposed to precise Euclidean detail. Across six experiments, differences in simple topological features shaped performance in object matching, number estimation and visual search. The authors propose topological relations are a genuine visual primitive.
papers.authors: Sami R. Yousif, Elizabeth M. Brannon

papers.title: An illusion of time caused by repeated experience
papers.abstract: Shows that events experienced repeatedly are remembered as having first occurred further back in time, contrary to the idea that vivid memories feel more recent. In six online experiments the distortion reached roughly 25 percent of elapsed time, was seen in most participants, and persisted across a week. The authors suggest this may be a basic mechanism shaping how we reconstruct when things happened.
papers.authors: Brynn E. Sherman, Sami R. Yousif

papers.title: Number adaptation: A critical look
papers.abstract: Reviews the evidence for the widely accepted claim that people adapt to numerosity, which would make number a primary visual attribute. The authors lay out reasons to doubt the effect and offer an alternative account in which apparent number adaptation reflects adaptation to other properties. The paper anchors a lively debate that drew published replies and a rebuttal.
papers.authors: Sami R. Yousif, Stefan Clarke, Elizabeth M. Brannon

0589.name: Samuel McDougle
0589.bio: Samuel McDougle is an Assistant Professor at Yale University and directs the Action, Computation, and Thinking (ACT) Lab. McDougle's research investigates the cognitive and neural architectures of human learning, focusing on the intersection of high-level cognition and motor behavior. Using an approach that includes psychophysics, computational modeling, and fMRI, McDougle explores how the brain integrates explicit strategies with implicit adaptation to acquire motor skills and maintain behavioral control.
0589.research_direction: Dr. McDougle’s recent work explores the high-level cognitive and neural architectures that support motor learning, memory, and skill acquisition. They have recently been investigating how the brain structures stored action plans, asking whether learned visuomotor associations are organized as abstract "mental graphs" and how these abstract representations guide the refinement of complex physical skills like handwriting. Their research also probes the mechanisms of motor working memory and sensorimotor adaptation, including behavioral paradigms that test whether sensory prediction errors can drive speech adaptation even when overt vocalizations are withheld. Additionally, using computationally driven fMRI, Dr. McDougle is examining the broader cognitive functions of the human cerebellum to understand how it encodes temporally sensitive reinforcement learning and reward prediction error signals during non-motor tasks.

papers.title: The human cerebellum encodes temporally sensitive reinforcement learning signals
papers.abstract: Beyond supervised motor learning, the cerebellum has been implicated in reinforcement learning. Using computationally driven fMRI in a task lacking low-level sensorimotor demands, the authors find reward and reward prediction error signals in cognitive regions of the human cerebellum. These signals depend on the timing of outcomes, constraining how the cerebellum contributes to nonmotor learning.
papers.authors: Juliana E. Trach, Yiran Ou, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Motor working memory
papers.abstract: A review of how the brain briefly holds information about movements, such as targets, trajectories and motor plans. It contrasts motor working memory with visual and spatial working memory, describes its neural and representational codes, and shows how it interacts with explicit strategies and implicit learning during motor adaptation.
papers.authors: Samuel D. McDougle, Hanna Hillman

papers.title: Motor abstraction training generalizes to the refinement of specific movement patterns
papers.abstract: The study asks whether the motor system forms abstract representations that causally support skill learning. Participants learned to copy unfamiliar handwritten characters, and training on rotated versions of the characters transferred to improved reproduction of the specific movement patterns, implying that abstract motor representations contribute to refinement of skilled movements.
papers.venue: bioRxiv (in press, Nature Human Behaviour per lab site)
papers.authors: Zekun Sun, Zhiran Xie, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Audiomotor prediction errors drive speech adaptation even in the absence of overt movement
papers.abstract: Theories differ on whether speech adaptation arises from sensory prediction errors or from feedback-command integration. By having speakers prepare a word but withhold it on some trials while hearing altered feedback, the authors show that adaptation still occurs without executed speech. This supports sensory prediction error learning as a general mechanism across motor domains including speech.
papers.authors: Benjamin Parrell, Minju Bae, Chris Naber, Olivia A. Kim, Caroline A. Niziolek, Samuel D. McDougle

papers.title: Mental graphs structure the storage and retrieval of visuomotor associations
papers.abstract: People learn arbitrary mappings between visual cues and movements, such as which action goes with which stimulus. This work shows that such stored visuomotor associations are organized as an abstract graph-like structure, so that memory retrieval and action selection reflect the relational layout among items rather than only individual cue-action pairs. It extends cognitive-map ideas from conceptual and spatial domains into motor learning.
papers.authors: Juliana E. Trach, Samuel D. McDougle

0590.name: Sang Chul Chong
0590.lab_name: Vision, Cognition, and Consciousness Lab (VCC Lab)
0590.bio: Sang Chul Chong is a vision scientist at Yonsei University who investigates how the human brain processes complex visual scenes through ensemble perception and statistical representation. Chong’s research explores the intersection of focused attention and visual consciousness, utilizing binocular rivalry and psychophysical paradigms to examine how the visual system manages processing capacity. Methodologically, their work employs eye tracking, ERP, and computational modeling to study the metacognition of perceptual resolution and social perception. Chong completed doctoral studies under Anne Treisman at Princeton University and postdoctoral training with Randolph Blake at Vanderbilt University.
0590.research_direction: Dr. Chong has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms of ensemble perception alongside the limits of metacognitive awareness in visual processing. Their recent work explores how observers extract summary statistics from scenes, testing whether ensemble traits are read out from pooled neural population responses rather than explicit averaging, and investigating how the visual system computes the variability of complex, multi-feature objects. In parallel, they are using psychophysical paradigms to probe visual metacognition, specifically asking whether people can accurately monitor spatial asymmetries in their perceptual resolution across different eccentricities and polar angles, and whether anxious individuals are aware of their own attentional biases toward threat. Broadly, Dr. Chong is working to integrate these empirical lines of inquiry by exploring theoretical frameworks that conceptualize visual consciousness as a metacognitive model of internal representations tied to confidence and attentional states.

papers.title: Reappraising intuitions about consciousness
papers.abstract: Argues that intuitions linking measurable functions to conscious experience are more trustworthy than commonly held, because apparent dissociations can be explained by partial awareness. It recasts consciousness as a metacognitive model of internal representations, tying intuitions to confidence, attentional templates, attention modes and awareness of absence, and suggests how this can be tested empirically.
papers.authors: Cheongil Kim, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: How do people perceive the variability of multifeature objects?
papers.abstract: Investigates whether and how observers extract summary variability from sets of objects that differ along several feature dimensions at once. The experiments examine whether variability is computed separately per feature or jointly across features, extending ensemble perception to richer, more realistic stimuli.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Jinhyeok Jeong, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: Metacognitive monitoring of attentional bias toward threat in anxiety
papers.abstract: Tests whether anxious individuals are aware that their attention is preferentially captured by threat-related faces. The study compares behavioral attentional bias with participants' own reports of where their attention went, probing the accuracy of metacognitive monitoring of attention in anxiety.
papers.authors: Cheongil Kim, Juyoen Hur, Jeong Hyeon Park, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: A population response model of ensemble perception
papers.abstract: Proposes a computational account in which ensemble judgments (mean, variability, outliers) are read out from the pooled responses of feature-tuned neural populations rather than from explicit averaging of individual items. The model reproduces a range of known ensemble phenomena, including how outliers are handled and how perception depends on set variability, within one unified mechanism. It offers a mechanistic framework for the ensemble-perception program the lab has developed over two decades.
papers.authors: Igor S. Utochkin, Jeunghwan Choi, Sang Chul Chong

papers.title: Metacognition of perceptual resolution across and around the visual field
papers.abstract: Asks whether observers know that their visual resolution declines with eccentricity and differs across polar angle around fixation. Using psychophysical measures paired with metacognitive judgments, the authors show that people's monitoring tracks these non-uniformities in resolution to a meaningful degree. The work links classic visual-field asymmetries to the question of how rich or sparse visual experience feels.
papers.authors: Cheongil Kim, Sang Chul Chong

0591.name: Sang Wook Hong
0591.bio: Sang Wook Hong is a researcher at Florida Atlantic University's Stiles-Nicholson Brain Institute who examines the neural mechanisms underlying human visual perception and awareness. Using psychophysics and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Hong investigates how the brain constructs internal representations of color, motion, and facial expressions from sensory inputs. Their research utilizes binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression to explore the limits of visual awareness and the interaction between top-down knowledge and bottom-up sensory processing. Hong’s work also includes the study of individual differences in interocular grouping and the influence of visual working memory on perceptual experiences.
0591.research_direction: Dr. Hong has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying complex visual perception, employing a diverse toolkit of psychophysics, neuroimaging, and neuromodulation. Their recent work explores how the visual system processes visual features, using fMRI decoding to determine where form-independent motion direction selectivity emerges along the human dorsal pathway. Furthermore, they are utilizing non-invasive brain stimulation over early visual areas to probe causal mechanisms in spatial vision, testing how gamma-frequency tACS influences contour integration and how altering cortical excitability via tDCS modulates apparent contrast. Additionally, they use individual differences in binocular rivalry paradigms to interrogate the dynamics of perceptual organization, specifically asking whether interocular grouping is governed primarily by local eye-of-origin lateral connections or by top-down pattern coherence.

papers.title: Gamma frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation over the visual cortex modulates contour integration
papers.abstract: Participants detected a contour made of four collinear segments among random distractors while receiving 40 Hz gamma tACS, 7 Hz theta tACS, or sham stimulation over early visual cortex. Only the gamma group improved from the pre-stimulation to the stimulation session, giving causal evidence that gamma-band activity supports linking fragmented elements into contours.
papers.authors: Yosun Yoon, Sang Wook Hong

papers.title: Anodal tDCS Alters Contrast Appearance In Human Vision
papers.abstract: The study tested whether anodal transcranial direct current stimulation over occipital cortex changes how contrast looks. In a two-grating judgment task, anodal stimulation shifted the point of subjective equality so contralateral stimuli looked higher in contrast (with a reversal across stimulus configurations) and sham showed no effect, while psychometric slopes were unchanged. The authors conclude that induced changes in cortical excitability alter appearance through gain-like modulation rather than sensitivity.
papers.authors: Yosun Yoon, Sang Wook Hong

papers.title: Emergence of form-independent direction selectivity in human V3A and MT+
papers.abstract: Using fMRI decoding, the authors asked where in the human visual pathway motion direction signals stop depending on the form that carries them, given the aperture problem. Direction could be decoded reliably in all visual areas for a given stimulus type, but V1 and V2 failed to generalize between gratings and random dots, and V1 even confused random-dot motion with orthogonal grating motion, consistent with motion-streak responses. MT+ and V3A generalized across stimulus types and trajectories, indicating that form-invariant direction selectivity emerges along the dorsal pathway.
papers.authors: Sang Wook Hong, Frank Tong

papers.title: The role of pattern coherence in interocular grouping during binocular rivalry: Insights from individual differences
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether interocular grouping in binocular rivalry is governed mainly by eye-of-origin (local lateral connections) or by pattern coherence (top-down feedback). Observers who spent long periods in interocularly coherent percepts also had long monocular coherent percepts, and those prone to piecemeal percepts in ordinary rivalry stayed piecemeal in the coherence setting. This individual-difference pattern points to pattern coherence as the stronger driver of grouping dynamics.
papers.authors: Yosun Yoon, Sang Wook Hong

0592.name: Sang-Hun Lee
0592.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0592.bio: Lee is a Professor at Seoul National University who researches the neural mechanisms underlying human visual perception and decision-making. Lee specializes in the spatiotemporal dynamics of the visual cortex, utilizing psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling to study phenomena such as binocular rivalry and traveling waves of cortical activity. Their work explores the attractor dynamics of working memory and Bayesian accounts of belief updating, focusing on how the brain forms decision variables and how prior choices influence future perceptual estimates. Lee previously served as the chair of the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences and participated in the World Class University (WCU) initiative at SNU.
0592.research_direction: Dr. Lee has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms of visual working memory, combining psychophysics, fMRI, and neural network models to explore how memory representations drift toward discrete attractor states. Their recent work asks how the early visual cortex can maintain these mnemonic signals in low-dimensional representational subspaces without interfering with ongoing sensory processing. Beyond individual items, they are also examining how relational structures between multiple remembered stimuli implicitly constrain visual memory estimates. Additionally, they have been studying perceptual decision-making and spatial vision, investigating how the granularity of past choices biases future perceptual belief updates, and probing how topographic anisotropies in early visual maps relate to behavioral biases in spatial extent perception.

papers.title: Early Visual Cortex Represents Sensory and Mnemonic Orientations in Separate Subspaces with Preserved Geometry
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with long delays, the study asks how early visual cortex can hold working-memory content while still processing incoming input. Sensory- and memory-trained decoders generalize poorly to each other, yet the two signals sit in separable low-dimensional subspaces that keep the same representational geometry. Trial-by-trial variability in the mnemonic code predicts both discrimination choices and estimation reports.
papers.authors: Sungje Kim, Jaeseob Lim, Hyunwoo Gu, Heeseung Lee, Hyang-Jung Lee, Minjin Choe, Dong-gyu Yoo, Joonwon Lee, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Relational Structure Constrains Individual Value Estimates in Visual Working Memory
papers.abstract: Participants remembered two sequential orientations while biased post-encoding feedback was given for only one. The bias transferred to the un-fed-back item in the direction implied by the angular offset linking the two values, weakening with larger separation and working in both directions. The results indicate that visual working memory encodes relations between items that constrain individual value estimates.
papers.authors: Jaeseob Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Attractor dynamics of working memory explain a concurrent evolution of stimulus-specific and decision-consistent biases in visual estimation
papers.abstract: Remembered orientations are pulled both toward a few preferred stimulus values and toward the observer's own earlier categorical choice. The authors show, with behavior, fMRI and task-trained recurrent neural networks, that both biases arise from a single mechanism: memory drifts toward discrete attractor states, and a categorical decision steers that drift while it unfolds. This gives a unified neural-mechanistic account of stimulus-specific and decision-consistent biases in visual working memory.
papers.authors: Hyunwoo Gu, Joonwon Lee, Sungje Kim, Jaeseob Lim, Hyang-Jung Lee, Heeseung Lee, Min Jin Choe, Dong-Gyu Yoo, Jun Hwan (Joshua) Ryu, Sukbin Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Belief updating in decision-variable space: More fine-grained choices attract future ones more strongly
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that committing to a decision narrows the belief distribution over the underlying decision variable to the chosen range. This predicts that finer-grained past choices attract later judgments more strongly, a granularity effect that seven psychophysical experiments confirm. A Bayesian model unifies the effect and shows how humans reuse decision variables to adapt to their environment.
papers.authors: Heeseung Lee, Jaeseob Lim, Sang-Hun Lee

papers.title: Bounded contribution of human early visual cortex to the topographic anisotropy in spatial extent perception
papers.abstract: The study compares anisotropies in the fMRI topographic representation of space in early visual cortex with those in perceived spatial extent. Cortical anisotropy is driven mainly by radial position, whereas perceptual anisotropy is driven by co-axial orientation, yet individual differences in both are largely shared. Perception thus builds on the EVC map but needs an additional transformation of its topographic bias.
papers.authors: Juhyoung Ryu, Sang-Hun Lee

0594.name: Sarah Lamer
0594.bio: Sarah Lamer is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and the director of the Social Perception and Cognition (SPĀC) Lab. Lamer’s research focuses on how sociocultural and environmental cues, such as spatial positioning and televised nonverbal patterns, facilitate the transmission of gender and racial stereotypes. Utilizing psychophysics, eye-tracking, and diffusion modeling, they investigate the social-cognitive mechanisms that lead to group-based biases and perceptual distortions. Lamer’s work, supported by the National Science Foundation, examines the 'angry crowd bias' and the developmental precursors of social inequality.
0594.research_direction: Dr. Lamer has recently been investigating how subtle patterns in our visual and cultural environments shape social perception and bias. A major focus of their recent work explores the Cultural Snapshots approach, which pairs the quantification of real-world media patterns, such as nonverbal behaviors on television or linguistic framing in news articles, with controlled experiments to test how these ecological cues causally transmit gender stereotypes and social prejudices. Parallel to this research on cultural transmission, they are also studying the visual mechanisms underlying group evaluation. Specifically, Dr. Lamer is examining how the visual system utilizes ensemble perception to rapidly summarize the properties of natural crowds, allowing observers to make high-level social judgments about a group's cohesion and unity.

papers.title: Ensemble perception in entitativity judgments of natural crowds
papers.abstract: The study asks how observers judge whether a real-world crowd looks like a cohesive, unified group. Using photographs of natural crowds and ensemble-perception paradigms, it tests how quickly summarized visual properties of the crowd feed into perceived entitativity. The work links vision-science ensemble coding to social judgments about groups.
papers.authors: Sarah Ariel Lamer, Spencer Dobbs, Lindsay Goolsby, Timothy D. Sweeny, Max Weisbuch

papers.title: Survivors as Agents: How Linguistic Agency Impacts Support for Survivors and Perpetrators of Sexual Assault
papers.abstract: Coding 1,738 sentences from 494 news articles, the authors found that liberal outlets tend to give survivors more linguistic agency than perpetrators. Experiments then showed that this framing can shift readers' blame and support, potentially raising blame of survivors and lowering blame of perpetrators. The work illustrates the Cultural Snapshots logic applied to news language.
papers.authors: Darla Bonagura, Jenae Bluhm, Clara Bunnell, Wen Lou, Sarah Ariel Lamer

papers.title: Cultural snapshots: A method to explain cultural transmission of bias
papers.abstract: This chapter synthesizes research on how biases are socially transmitted through patterns present in everyday cultural environments. It presents the Cultural Snapshots method as a way to identify those patterns and test their causal influence on beliefs, drawing on work on race and gender.
papers.authors: Kristin Pauker, Max Weisbuch, Sarah Ariel Lamer

papers.title: Tracing Pathways From Social Ecology to the Mind: A Cultural Snapshots Approach to Understanding Gender Stereotype Socialization
papers.abstract: The paper lays out the Cultural Snapshots approach, which first measures recurring patterns in real-world shared environments such as media and then experimentally tests whether exposure to those patterns shapes beliefs. Applied to gender, it argues this two-step design allows causal claims about how subtle cues in everyday social ecologies teach gender stereotypes, which purely correlational or purely lab-based methods cannot. It reviews supporting evidence and outlines how the approach can be extended.
papers.authors: Sarah Ariel Lamer, Gillian Michelle Preston, Darla Bonagura, Megan Ruskey

papers.title: How Culturally Prevalent Patterns of Nonverbal Behavior Can Influence Discrimination Against Women Leaders
papers.abstract: An analysis of 18 popular TV shows found that interactions between women leaders and their subordinates were more negative in nonverbal emotion than those between men leaders and subordinates. In follow-up experiments, participants shown patterns favoring men leaders preferred working under men. The paper proposes that media-borne nonverbal patterns help transmit bias against women leaders.
papers.authors: Sarah Ariel Lamer, Haley B. Beck, Leanne ten Brinke, Gillian Michelle Preston

0595.name: Sarah Shomstein
0595.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0595.bio: Sarah Shomstein is the Thelma Hunt Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at The George Washington University. Shomstein's research explores the functional and neural mechanisms of attentional selection, specifically investigating how the human brain prioritizes information based on spatial and object-level representations. By integrating behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), their work identifies the computational signals that modulate sensory processing in both healthy individuals and patients with focal brain damage. Shomstein currently serves as the Editor-in-Chief of the journal Attention, Perception & Psychophysics.
0595.research_direction: Dr. Shomstein has recently been investigating how high-level meaning automatically guides visual attention, even when that semantic information is completely irrelevant to the observer's current task. Their recent work explores how attentional allocation is continuously modulated by the semantic grouping of objects, the contextual fit between objects and real-world scenes, and graded semantic mappings across sensory modalities, such as task-irrelevant sounds playing during visual search. To account for these phenomena, they are advancing theoretical frameworks that integrate crossmodal semantic relationships into models of real-world attentional selection, pushing the field beyond traditional unimodal paradigms. In a distinct line of research, they are also examining face perception, specifically investigating how an individual's habitual gaze strategies interact with attentional cues to support the recognition of masked and unmasked faces.

papers.title: Task irrelevant sounds influence visual attention through graded crossmodal semantic modulation
papers.abstract: Participants searched for visual targets while sounds that were irrelevant to the task played. The more semantically related a sound was to the target, the faster search became, and this benefit scaled continuously with degree of relatedness rather than being all-or-none. The work shows that meaning carried across the auditory and visual senses shapes attentional allocation automatically.
papers.authors: Kira Wegner-Clemens, George L. Malcolm, Dwight J. Kravitz, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Individual gaze preferences and attentional cues interact in masked and unmasked face recognition
papers.abstract: The study examines how where individuals prefer to look on a face (for example eyes versus mouth) interacts with attentional cues to affect recognition of faces both with and without masks. The results show that recognition depends jointly on a person's habitual gaze strategy and the cued attentional focus, linking attention and face perception.
papers.authors: Shira Tkacz-Domb, Erez Freud, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Task-irrelevant semantic grouping influences attentional allocation
papers.abstract: Using displays in which objects were related in meaning but the relationship was irrelevant to the task, the study asks whether attention is captured by semantic grouping of objects. The findings indicate that semantically related items are grouped and this grouping alters how attention is distributed across a display, extending the task-irrelevant semantics framework.
papers.authors: E. R. Robbins, Joseph C. Nah, Dick Dubbelde, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Task-irrelevant semantic relationship between objects and scene influence attentional allocation
papers.abstract: Across experiments, the semantic fit between an object and the scene it appears in influenced attention even when participants had no reason to use that information. Scene-object relatedness continuously modulated processing and interacted with object-object relationships. This extends earlier isolated-object findings to more realistic scene contexts.
papers.authors: Joseph C. Nah, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

papers.title: Predicting attentional allocation in real-world environments: The need to investigate crossmodal semantic guidance
papers.abstract: This review argues that real-world environments are multisensory and meaningful, yet attention research has mostly been unimodal and vision-centered. It surveys work on spatial, feature, object-based and semantic attention, and makes the case that cross-sensory semantic relationships must be incorporated into models of attentional selection.
papers.authors: Kira Wegner-Clemens, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

0596.name: Sarah Waugh
0596.department: Department of Optometry and Vision Sciences
0596.lab_name: Centre for Vision across the Life Span (CVLS)
0596.bio: Waugh is a Reader in Optometry and Vision Sciences and Co-Director of the Centre for Vision across the Life Span at the University of Huddersfield. They utilize psychophysical methodologies to investigate spatial vision and visual processing, focusing on visual crowding, Vernier acuity, and the mechanisms underlying amblyopia. Waugh’s research indicates that foveal crowding distance is a more effective predictor of reading ability in children than traditional visual acuity. They have also conducted research into the temporal frequency discrimination of central and peripheral vision and the clinical assessment of binocular vision and accommodation.
0596.research_direction: Dr. Waugh has recently been investigating the developmental trajectories of visual acuity and visual crowding in children, alongside the clinical assessment of amblyopia. Their recent work explores how crowding distance and spatial interactions evolve during childhood compared to standard acuity, utilizing varied stimuli such as luminance- and contrast-modulated optotypes. To improve clinical diagnostics, they are examining how standard visual charts, such as fixed-gap Landolt C tests, capture true crowding versus lateral masking in amblyopic patients, and whether isolated crowding tests might better predict early reading performance. In a distinct but clinically related line of research, Dr. Waugh is also studying the robustness of occupational vision screens by evaluating how imposed dioptric blur impacts performance on standardized color vision diagnostics like the Cambridge lantern and Ishihara tests.

papers.title: Development of Crowding Distance in Children Is Faster and Later Than Visual Acuity and Better Predicts Reading Performance
papers.abstract: Measured visual acuity and crowding distance in 227 healthy children (3-11 years) and 40 adults. Acuity approaches adult levels by about six years, whereas crowding distance shrinks nearly fivefold and only matures around eight. Crowding distance correlated with teacher-rated reading far better than acuity, including after removing the effect of age, suggesting crowding tests could flag children at risk of reading difficulty and be more sensitive for strabismic amblyopia.
papers.authors: Sarah J. Waugh, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Leticia Álvaro, Denis G. Pelli

papers.title: Development of visual acuity and spatial interactions for luminance- and contrast-modulated symbols, pictures and letters
papers.abstract: Tested acuity in children aged 3-16 and adults with luminance, luminance-noise and contrast-modulated optotypes, with and without surrounding boxes or letters. Acuity for isolated symbols reaches adult levels around six to seven years, and contrast-modulated optotypes are harder but not differently affected by age. Flanking letters hurt young children more, consistent with stronger crowding, and contrast-modulated stimuli do not appear likely to improve amblyopia detection.
papers.authors: Sarah J.H. Lalor, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Sarah J. Waugh

papers.title: Landolt C-Tests With "Fixed" Arcmin Separations Detect Amblyopia But Underestimate Crowding in Moderate-to-Severe Amblyopic Children and Adults
papers.abstract: Compared two Landolt C acuity tests with fixed small and large gaps in healthy, strabismic and anisometropic amblyopic children and adults. Both tests detect amblyopia, but crowding magnitudes and interocular differences fall short of true crowding in high-severity strabismic amblyopia because of lateral masking. The authors argue that separate isolated-acuity and crowding-distance tests target these functions better.
papers.authors: Sarah J. Waugh, Maria Fronius

papers.title: Impact of blur on clinical and occupational colour vision test results
papers.abstract: Examined how imposed dioptric blur alters results on Ishihara, the Cambridge lantern, and computerised colour discrimination tests in colour-normal adults. Normal observers can fail the lantern test, and blur of +1.00 D or more increases false failures on the lantern. Ishihara and the computerised tests remained robust until about +8 D, so uncorrected refractive error could cause spurious lantern failures.
papers.authors: Leticia Álvaro, Monika A. Formankiewicz, Sarah J. Waugh

0597.name: Sashank Varma
0597.department: School of Interactive Computing and School of Psychology
0597.bio: Sashank Varma is a cognitive scientist who integrates human experimentation with computational modeling to study forms of human intelligence. Varma investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying mathematical and computational thinking, including the processing of abstract geometric and topological concepts. Their research examines the 'cognitive alignment' between humans and machine learning models, utilizing computer vision and large language models to explore whether AI developmental trajectories mirror human cognitive progression. This work aims to define the neuroarchitecture of perception and reasoning while addressing the educational implications of cognitive learning principles.
0597.research_direction: Dr. Varma's recent work explores the intersection of human cognition and artificial neural networks, using both language and vision models to investigate how conceptual understanding and reasoning emerge. Specifically, they have been examining whether the training trajectories of these models parallel the developmental progression of geometric, numerical, and linguistic concepts in human children. Their research also probes the internal mechanics of artificial systems, investigating the representational geometry of number concepts across different tasks and testing whether large models allocate computational effort in a human-like, resource-rational manner as task complexity scales. Alongside this AI-driven research, Dr. Varma investigates foundational mechanisms of human visual perception, combining behavioral experiments and computational modeling to understand how people visually cluster and estimate numerosity in point arrays.

papers.title: The Representational Geometry of Number
papers.abstract: Asks whether concepts share a common representational manifold or occupy separate subspaces, using number concepts in language models as a testbed. Finds that number representations keep a stable relational structure across tasks while task-specific representations live in distinct subspaces, with features like magnitude and parity along separable linear directions. These subspaces can be mapped onto one another, reconciling shared and orthogonal accounts of concept representation.
papers.authors: Zhimin Hu, Lanhao Niu, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Are More Tokens Rational? Inference-Time Scaling in Language Models as Adaptive Resource Rationality
papers.abstract: Tests whether reasoning models spend computation the way resource-rational humans do. Using a variable attribution task that manipulates the number of candidate variables and trials, the authors compare instruction-tuned models with large reasoning models as task complexity grows. The work asks if adaptive allocation of reasoning effort emerges from scaling without any explicit cost-related reward.
papers.authors: Zhimin Hu, Riya Roshan, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Computer Vision Modeling of the Development of Geometric and Numerical Concepts in Humans
papers.abstract: Examines whether computer vision models show developmental alignment with children, not just adult-like alignment, in geometric and numerical concepts. In a detailed case study of ResNet-50, performance improvements across training are compared against developmental progressions observed in children. The results indicate that training trajectories of the vision network track human conceptual development.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2026); arXiv:2511.15029
papers.authors: Zekun Wang, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Human visual clustering of point arrays
papers.abstract: Investigates how people perceive groups in arrays of dots, a basic operation of visual perception that underlies numerosity and grouping judgments. Combines behavioral experiments with computational models of clustering to explain which point configurations are seen as clusters. Provides a model-based account of human visual clustering.
papers.authors: Vijay Marupudi, Sashank Varma

papers.title: Development of Cognitive Intelligence in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.abstract: Evaluates ten families of pre-trained language models across intermediate and final training checkpoints on tasks drawn from psychometric tests of human intelligence, covering numerical, linguistic, conceptual, and other abilities. Asks whether the training trajectory of models aligns with children's cognitive development. Argues that developmental alignment should be considered when treating language models as cognitive theories.
papers.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2024)
papers.authors: Raj Sanjay Shah, Khushi Bhardwaj, Sashank Varma

0598.name: Scott O Murray
0598.bio: Scott O Murray is a Professor of Psychology who researches the neural and computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception and attention. Utilizing high-resolution functional MRI (fMRI) and computational modeling, Murray characterizes how the visual cortex represents complex features such as shape, size, and lightness, exploring how contextual information and top-down attention modulate early sensory processing. A portion of their recent research focuses on neurodiversity, applying vision science frameworks to study altered cortical computations and excitation-inhibition balance in individuals with autism spectrum disorder. By linking large-scale brain activity patterns to perceptual behaviors, Murray’s laboratory aims to identify the principles of how the brain constructs a representation of the environment.
0598.research_direction: Dr. Murray's recent work explores two distinct areas of visual science: the neurocomputational mechanisms of spatial perspective-taking and the neural basis of sensory processing differences in autism. On the first front, they have recently been investigating how humans mentally rotate and align spatial viewpoints, utilizing fMRI and behavioral tasks to map the fronto-parietal networks involved in these spatial transformations. They are also translating these cognitive insights to artificial intelligence, testing whether embedding human-like dorsal-stream computations can help multimodal AI models overcome egocentric bias and improve their spatial reasoning. Concurrently, Dr. Murray is probing the mechanisms underlying self-reported heightened visual sensitivity in autistic adults by combining psychophysics, structural MRI, and functional measures like contrast-evoked fMRI and EEG alpha-band dynamics to evaluate whether this population exhibits fundamental alterations in neural sensory gain and gating.

papers.title: The neural mechanisms of aligning spatial perspectives
papers.abstract: An fMRI study of visual perspective-taking in which participants judged object positions from the viewpoint of an avatar or an empty chair. Both reaction time and BOLD signal grew linearly with the angular disparity between observer and reference viewpoints, and activation appeared across a broad frontal, parietal, premotor, temporal and cerebellar network. Individual differences in response time tracked activation size, and the chair reference gave comparable results, pointing to a general embodied spatial-transformation process.
papers.authors: Scott O Murray, Bridget Leonard, Kristin Woodard, John A Pyles

papers.title: Cognitively-Inspired Tokens Overcome Egocentric Bias in Multimodal Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models handle semantic vision-language tasks well but fail when they must take another agent's visual perspective, showing a persistent egocentric bias. The authors introduce 'perspective tokens', special embeddings that encode orientation either through body-keypoint cues or through a mental-rotation-style abstract code, and add them to LLaVA-1.5-13B. Accuracy on level-2 perspective-taking benchmarks improves, rotation-based tokens generalize to non-human reference agents, and analysis suggests fine-tuning strengthens orientation information already latent in the base model.
papers.authors: Bridget Leonard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Visual Responsivity in Autism: Measuring Visual Responses in Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults Using Psychophysics, fMRI, and EEG
papers.abstract: Autistic people often report heightened visual sensitivity, but neural evidence for altered sensory gain has been inconsistent. The study tested 31 autistic and 27 non-autistic adults with psychophysics, fMRI and EEG using flickering checkerboards at high and low contrast. Contrast modulated neural responses robustly in both groups, and no group difference appeared in BOLD or behavioral thresholds, with the group difference confined to a limited EEG measure, arguing against a simple hyper-responsivity account.
papers.authors: Daniela L. Seczon, Kristin M. Woodard, Tamar Kolodny, Hannah M. Rea, Mark Pettet, Sara Jane Webb, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Why Multimodal Models Struggle with Spatial Reasoning: Insights from Human Cognition
papers.abstract: Using tasks borrowed from developmental and cognitive science, this work tests where multimodal AI models fail at spatial reasoning, in particular taking another person's viewpoint. It argues that the failures reflect reliance on propositional rather than analog spatial representations, and that they parallel missing dorsal-stream-like computations such as mental rotation in humans. The paper offers a human-cognition framework for diagnosing and guiding improvements in such models.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 47th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Bridget Leonard, Kristin Woodard, Scott O. Murray

papers.title: Increased alpha power in autistic adults: Relation to sensory behaviors and cortical volume
papers.abstract: EEG recordings in 29 autistic and 23 non-autistic adults showed consistently higher alpha-band (about 10 Hz) amplitude in the autistic group, along with proportionally stronger alpha suppression at stimulus onset that correlated with sensory behaviors. Exploratory MRI analyses linked alpha power to total cortical volume and revealed a group-by-hippocampal-volume interaction. The results suggest altered alpha-based sensory gating and anatomical modulators of it in autism.
papers.authors: Scott O. Murray, Daniela L. Seczon, Mark Pettet, Hannah M. Rea, Kristin M. Woodard, Tamar Kolodny, Sara Jane Webb

0599.name: Scott Steinmetz
0599.bio: Scott T. Steinmetz is a researcher at Sandia National Laboratories within the Center for Computing Research, where their work focuses on computational neuroscience and human-machine teaming. Steinmetz investigates the capacity of accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to model the primate dorsal stream, specifically analyzing optic flow tuning and self-motion perception in brain area MSTd. At Sandia, they also develop frameworks for "Trusted AI," examining how human operators calibrate trust in autonomous systems through performance characterization and transparency. Steinmetz earned a Ph.D. in Cognitive Science from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, where they conducted research on the attentional modulation of the pupillary light response.
0599.research_direction: Dr. Steinmetz has recently been investigating how the brain's dorsal visual pathway processes motion, in particular how area MSTd encodes optic flow, the pattern of image motion that tells us how we are moving through the world. Their recent work asks which kinds of artificial neural networks, trained with which objectives, best reproduce the tuning of MSTd neurons, and compares many network types against a simple unsupervised decomposition method. They have also studied how design choices such as activation functions shape a network's accuracy, noise robustness and internal representations when estimating self-motion from optic flow, with relevance to robot navigation. Separately, they have helped develop a framework for describing and communicating how trustworthy an AI system is.

papers.title: For MSTd, Autoencoding is all you need
papers.abstract: While task-driven artificial neural networks (ANNs) have successfully modeled functional properties within the ventral visual pathway, their ability to explain representations in the dorsal visual stream remains less established. This study investigates the degree to which distinct computational objectives and architectural constraints induce neural alignment with the dorsal medial superior temporal area (MSTd), a cortical region selective for complex optic flow patterns that underpin self-motion and heading perception. Evaluating 54 ANNs alongside non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF) against empirical neurophysiological optic flow tuning metrics in MSTd reveals a marked divergence: models optimized for task accuracy in self-motion estimation fail to reproduce biological tuning distributions, developing strong biases toward backward azimuths. Conversely, unsupervised autoencoders trained to reconstruct motion inputs from middle temporal (MT)-like representations consistently exhibit superior alignment with MSTd tuning preferences. Incorporating explicit non-negativity or sparsity constraints does not enhance and often degrades biological fidelity, and relaxing bottleneck compression constraints does not impair correspondence. These findings indicate that the functional tuning properties of area MSTd are best accounted for by unsupervised, reconstruction-oriented objectives rather than supervised self-motion estimation.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: The Trust Calibration Maturity Model for Characterizing and Communicating Trustworthiness of AI Systems
papers.abstract: The rapid deployment and increasing scale of artificial intelligence models hinder access to critical information needed to evaluate their dependability, elevating the hazard of inappropriate or unsafe utilization. To establish an operational framework for communicating and evaluating AI trustworthiness, the Trust Calibration Maturity Model (TCMM) is proposed. The TCMM systematizes trustworthiness characterization across five interdependent dimensions of analytic maturity: Performance Characterization, Bias & Robustness Quantification, Transparency, Safety & Security, and Usability. Each dimension is evaluated along defined ordinal maturity levels, enabling system developers, evaluators, and stakeholders to systematically calibrate user trust, define rigorous operational requirements, monitor developmental maturity, and pinpoint domain-specific research requirements. The model is demonstrated on two distinct operational tasks: querying large language models (ChatGPT) for critical decision-making determinations in nuclear science, and employing PhaseNet deep neural network ensembles to characterize and categorize seismic event sources.
papers.authors: Scott T. Steinmetz, Asmeret Naugle, Paul Schutte, Matt Sweitzer, Alex Washburne, Lisa Linville, Daniel Krofcheck, Michal Kucer, Samuel Myren

papers.title: ReLU, Sparseness, and the Encoding of Optic Flow in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Visual optic flow provides essential sensory input for estimating self-motion kinematics in robotic navigation, particularly within GPS-denied environments. This study examines how different activation functions—specifically ReLU, leaky ReLU, GELU, and Mish—affect estimation accuracy, noise robustness, and internal representational characteristics in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) trained on three-dimensional translational and rotational optic flow fields. Network architectures using ReLU and leaky ReLU activation functions achieve superior generalization accuracy on novel flow patterns, maintaining translational errors within 5.5° mean absolute error (MAE) and rotational errors within 0.3°/s MAE, while also displaying significantly enhanced resilience against sparse input fields and moving object distractors compared to smooth activation counterparts. Analysis of unit activity distributions confirms that the bounded zero regimes of ReLU and leaky ReLU promote high population-level sparsity, demonstrating that sparse latent representations are key to robust, accurate self-motion estimation from dynamic optic flow.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Siyuan Peng, Scott T. Steinmetz

papers.title: Accuracy optimized neural networks do not effectively model optic flow tuning in brain area MSTd
papers.abstract: Although supervised, accuracy-optimized convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have emerged as primary predictive models for neural representations in the primate ventral stream, their suitability for modeling the dorsal visual hierarchy remains unverified. This work assesses how well accuracy-optimized CNNs capture empirical optic flow tuning properties observed in dorsal area MSTd compared to non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF), an unsupervised linear decomposition technique known to capture MSTd response properties. While CNNs achieve high regression accuracy when estimating 3D translation and rotation from full-field retinal flow patterns, their single-unit tuning properties diverge fundamentally from biological neurons, including an abnormal preference bias toward backward self-motion azimuths and improper coordination of translational and rotational tuning axes. Imposing NNMF-like biological constraints—specifically non-negative synaptic weights and explicit sparse coding—fails to rectify this divergence and substantially reduces self-motion estimation accuracy on compound flow patterns. These results establish that task accuracy alone is insufficient to drive biological receptive field organization in the dorsal stream, pointing to distinct organizational principles governing motion-processing cortical circuits.
papers.authors: Oliver W. Layton, Scott T. Steinmetz

0600.name: Scott Watamaniuk
0600.main_research_area: visual motion perception and smooth pursuit
0600.bio: Watamaniuk investigates the human visual system's capacity to process motion information and its role in guiding oculomotor and manual responses. Using high-resolution eye tracking and psychophysical methods, their research explores the coordination of binocular eye movements and the attentional demands associated with smooth pursuit. This work demonstrates that the brain can generate independent motor commands for each eye, which addresses classical theories of unitary conjugate eye control and provides data on the causes of strabismus. Additionally, Watamaniuk examines the impact of complex visual environments and cross-modal interactions, such as moving sounds, on perceptual and motor performance.
0600.research_direction: Dr. Watamaniuk has recently been studying how the two eyes are controlled when we track moving targets and shift gaze. Their recent work challenges the classic idea that a single command drives both eyes together, testing whether each eye can be controlled partly independently during smooth pursuit and during tracking of targets moving in depth. This has led them to a new oculomotor model that aims to explain unusual saccades made by an eye that is already aimed correctly. They have also examined the tiny involuntary eye movements that occur during fixation and how the layout of what we are looking at changes them.

papers.title: A new oculomotor model demystifies “Remarkable Saccades”
papers.abstract: Binocular motor control has long been conceptualized through Hering's law of equal innervation, which posits that binocular gaze shifts result from the linear summation of a unitary conjugate command and a unitary vergence command. However, evidence demonstrating temporal desynchronization between inter-ocular rotations during vergence tracking challenges the necessity of a unitary vergence controller, supporting Helmholtz's hypothesis of independent ocular control. Even so, strict monocular independence fails to account for 'remarkable saccades'—aberrant saccadic displacements executed by an eye that is already accurately foveating an aligned target during asymmetric vergence. To reconcile these mechanisms, the authors formulate the Hybrid Binocular Control (HBC) computational framework. HBC implements independent cortical pursuit controllers for each eye interacting with a centralized, conjugate saccade burst generator in the brainstem, entirely dispensing with a dedicated vergence drive. The architecture generates remarkable saccades as an emergent dynamical property and accounts for systematic behavioral variations when observers selectively attend to one ocular image via variable attentional gain modulation. The resulting simulations replicate the kinematic velocity and displacement trajectories of remarkable saccades and standard binocular saccade phenotypes, establishing how independent and conjugate oculomotor pathways coordinate without explicit vergence signals.
papers.authors: Stephen J. Heinen, Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk

papers.title: Misalignment of a covered eye reveals frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by multiple signals
papers.abstract: Oculomotor research on smooth pursuit traditionally presumes that a unitary command rotates both eyes synchronously for both conjugate and vergence tracking (Hering's Law). Although recent demonstrations of asynchronous inter-eye motion during vergence tracking challenged unitary vergence control, whether frontoparallel conjugate pursuit similarly involves independent ocular systems remains unclear. To address this, neurotypical observers tracked a 0.4° visual stimulus traversing a tangent screen horizontally under sinusoidal trajectories and pseudorandom step-ramp direction reversals (peak target velocities of 5°/s and 25°/s). Monocular infrared occlusion paired with high-frequency binocular eye tracking (EyeLink 1000+, 1 kHz) allowed simultaneous recording of both ocular trajectories under monocular visual feedback. During monocular fixation preceding motion onset, the occluded eye deviated in rotational position consistent with an individual's phoria. Crucially, during subsequent monocular pursuit, this static misalignment persisted, yet both the viewing and occluded eyes closely matched the target's translational velocity. These findings indicate that frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by dissociated neural control mechanisms: a global unitary conjugate motor drive that matches target velocity across both eyes, operating alongside independent monocular subsystems that maintain static ocular alignment.
papers.authors: Stephen Heinen, Devashish Singh, Caroline Ulep, Scott Watamaniuk

papers.title: Peripheral targets attenuate miniature eye movements during fixation
papers.abstract: Voluntary fixation of a visual target is continuously disrupted by miniature fixational eye movements, notably microsaccades and slow ocular drift. Although microsaccades prevent perceptual fading across static scenes, their abrupt displacements transiently perturb fine retinal-image stability. This study examined how target spatial configuration and retinal locus modulate fixational oculomotor dynamics. Healthy observers fixated three distinct stimulus geometries: an isolated central dot (0.2°), a virtual circular configuration defined by eight peripheral dots without a central foveal anchor, and a combined central-plus-peripheral array, while high-resolution eye tracking recorded eye movements. Peripheral fixation targets induced a pronounced attenuation in microsaccadic amplitude, decreasing excursion sizes by an average of 46.3% compared to isolated central fixation. In addition, peripheral targets significantly reduced drift velocity, thereby dampening overall retinal slip. Fixation stability, quantified by bivariate contour ellipse area (BCEA), did not differ significantly between central and peripheral arrays, demonstrating that peripheral visual references stabilize ocular gaze by selectively suppressing miniature intrusive eye movements without degrading spatial fixation performance.
papers.authors: Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Jeremy B. Badler, Stephen J. Heinen

0601.name: Se-Bum Paik
0601.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
0601.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
0601.bio: Se-Bum Paik is a computational neuroscientist and Associate Professor at KAIST, where they direct the Cognitive Intelligence Laboratory. Paik’s research investigates the developmental principles underlying the functional architecture of sensory systems in both biological and artificial neural networks. By integrating theoretical neuroscience, computational modeling, and psychophysical experiments, Paik explores how cognitive functions and neural topographies, such as cortical orientation maps, emerge from spontaneous activity and structural constraints. Their work has demonstrated that visual capabilities, including face and object detection, can arise in untrained deep neural networks as a result of innate biological strategies for information processing.
0601.research_direction: Dr. Paik's recent work explores how principles of biological brain development can explain innate visual functions and enhance the robustness of artificial neural networks. They have recently been investigating the role of pre-experiential, spontaneous neural noise, examining how pretraining networks on random inputs influences uncertainty calibration and biologically plausible learning rules like feedback alignment. Additionally, their research probes the functional advantages of innate architectural and developmental constraints, testing how prewiring early layers with static Gabor filters or simulating the gradual maturation of infant visual acuity impacts a model's ability to learn abstract, shape-biased, and domain-general representations. Finally, Dr. Paik uses randomly initialized feedforward networks to investigate how primitive cognitive abilities, such as the capacity to compare visual quantities, might emerge spontaneously in the developing brain prior to any sensory experience.

papers.title: Brain-inspired warm-up training with random noise for uncertainty calibration
papers.abstract: Randomly initialized networks tend to be overconfident before seeing any data, which the authors argue is a root cause of miscalibrated confidence and hallucination-like errors. Borrowing from the idea that spontaneous noise-like activity prepares developing brains, they briefly pretrain networks on random noise with random labels so initial confidence sits at chance. Networks warmed up this way are better calibrated during subsequent training and give low confidence on out-of-distribution inputs.
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Prewired static visual receptive fields for environment-agnostic perception
papers.abstract: The paper shows that fixing Gabor-like receptive fields in the early layers of deep networks, mimicking hard-wired early visual filters, lets the networks keep learning across large domain shifts. The resulting latent representations generalize across domains rather than encoding domain-specific variance, and the fixed filters reduce texture bias so behavior becomes more shape-based, as in primates. The result is offered as a biological strategy for reliable continual learning in changing environments.
papers.authors: Minjun Kang, Seungdae Baek, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Gradual sensory maturation promotes abstract representation learning
papers.abstract: Infants start with poor acuity and color sensitivity, whereas machine learning models are trained on full-fidelity inputs from the start and often learn shortcuts. Using network simulations and human psychophysics, the authors show that gradually maturing sensory input yields more abstract, bias-resistant and disentangled representations that support compositional reconstruction. Human and model behavior show similar resistance to misleading cues, suggesting immaturity is a functional advantage.
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Pretraining with Random Noise for Fast and Robust Learning without Weight Transport
papers.abstract: Inspired by spontaneous noise-like neural activity before sensory experience, the study pretrains networks with random noise under a feedback alignment rule. This aligns forward weights with backward feedback, speeding learning to near backpropagation levels without weight transport, and lowers effective weight dimensionality, which improves out-of-distribution generalization and adaptability across tasks.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Jeonghwan Cheon, Sang-Wan Lee, Se-Bum Paik

papers.title: Comparison of visual quantities in untrained neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors ask how newborn animals can compare visual quantities by proportion and difference before visual experience. In a biologically inspired randomly initialized feedforward network, units tuned to proportion or difference emerge spontaneously from random summation of monotonic nonlinear responses, with the response nonlinearity determining which measure a unit encodes. The findings suggest such quantity comparison is a primitive function arising before learning.
papers.authors: Hyeonsu Lee, Woochul Choi, Dongil Lee, Se-Bum Paik

0602.name: Sean Polyn
0602.bio: Sean Polyn is an Associate Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry at Vanderbilt University and directs the Vanderbilt Computational Memory Lab. Polyn's research investigates the neural and cognitive dynamics of human episodic memory, specifically examining the organization and retrieval of recently acquired information. They employ a multi-tiered methodology combining mathematical modeling, such as the Context Maintenance and Retrieval (CMR) model, with behavioral experiments, fMRI, and EEG to track the mental search process. Their work utilizes multi-voxel pattern analysis to decode category-specific neural activity during memory tasks and extends into clinical applications, including the study of memory dysfunction in schizophrenia.
0602.research_direction: Dr. Polyn has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms of human memory by developing and testing retrieved-context models to explain how we encode, organize, and recall information. Their recent work explores a wide breadth of memory phenomena, using these computational frameworks to probe how reward structures, retrieval practice, and semantic relationships modulate the temporal organization of free and serial recall. Additionally, they are examining whether unified long-term memory models can account for classic visual working memory signatures, such as set-size effects and short-term interference, without assuming a separate limited-capacity store. They are also extending these quantitative models to clinical domains to pinpoint the specific computational mechanisms driving episodic memory impairments in schizophrenia.

papers.title: Capacity not required: A long-term memory model that exhibits key signatures of working memory
papers.abstract: Argues that classic set-size effects, often taken as hallmarks of a limited-capacity working memory store, also emerge naturally from a contextual (retrieved-context) model of long-term memory. Adding contextual dynamics to a model of visual working memory yields new accounts of interference in short-term visual memory tasks and captures the temporal structure of visual experience. The authors call for re-examining unified models of human memory.
papers.authors: Sean M. Polyn, Geoffrey F. Woodman

papers.title: Value-based control over memory encoding and search
papers.abstract: Studies how reward structure shapes the temporal organization of free recall in mixed-value lists, whether reward is given at encoding or contingent on later recall. When rewards depend on later recall, people preferentially begin recall at the start of rewarded subsequences, producing a mid-list primacy effect. A new hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the CMR model, fit to individual recall sequences, indicates motivated memory involves both stronger context-to-item associations and strategic creation of accessible event boundaries.
papers.authors: Sven Wientjes, Clay B. Holroyd, Sean Matthew Polyn

papers.title: A computational model of the episodic memory impairment in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Applies retrieved-context modeling to the episodic memory deficits seen in schizophrenia, linking computational memory theory to a clinical population in collaboration with psychiatrist Stephan Heckers. Details of the model and findings were not verified from the full text.
papers.authors: Andrew Tornatore, Aslihan Imamoglu, Stephan Heckers, Sean Polyn

papers.title: Bridging CRU and CMR in free and serial recall: A factorial comparison of retrieved-context models
papers.abstract: Systematically compares two retrieved-context models of recall, the streamlined CRU and the richer CMR, by treating each as a variant of shared principles. Using factorial model selection, the authors add CMR-like features to CRU and test hybrids on free and serial recall data. CMR-like features markedly improve CRU's account of free recall, while CRU's item confusion and recall termination mechanisms help CMR capture serial recall.
papers.authors: Jordan B. Gunn, Sean M. Polyn

papers.title: The modulation and elimination of temporal organization in free recall
papers.abstract: Six experiments show that the temporal contiguity effect, one of the most robust findings in free recall, can be strongly reduced or eliminated by strong semantic structure, retrieval practice and long lists. Simulations with the CMR retrieved-context model show that these modulations follow lawful patterns predicted by the theory. The paper also identifies cases where CMR falls short and suggests how the theory could be developed.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Min Kyung Hong, Jordan B. Gunn, Lisa K. Fazio, Sean M. Polyn

0603.name: Sebastian M. Frank
0603.bio: Frank is an Emmy Noether Group Leader at the University of Regensburg, where they investigate the neurobiological foundations of learning and brain plasticity across the human lifespan. Their research utilizes visual perceptual learning as a model to study how sensory experiences lead to neural adaptations, combining psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS). Frank has identified developmental shifts in inhibitory (GABAergic) and excitatory (glutamatergic) signaling, specifically focusing on how these neurochemical dynamics differ between children and adults during skill acquisition. Beyond vision, their work examines cross-modal plasticity and the integration of visual-vestibular cues within the human cortex.
0603.research_direction: Dr. Frank has recently been investigating the neurochemical mechanisms that govern visual attention and perceptual learning. Using time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (fMRS), their recent work explores how excitatory and inhibitory dynamics, specifically involving glutamate and GABA in early visual and parietal cortices, regulate goal-directed object tracking and control the gating of task-irrelevant motion signals based on perceptual salience. Alongside these functional studies, they are developing novel fMRS-based real-time neurofeedback methods to test whether individuals can voluntarily modulate their own occipital neurotransmitter concentrations. Broadening their focus beyond the visual system, they are also examining the cortical mechanisms of somatosensory plasticity to understand how tactile learning generalizes across untrained body parts.

papers.title: Goal-directed visual information processing with GABAergic inhibition in parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Using time-resolved functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy, the study tracked GABA and glutamate in parietal and visual cortex while people followed a varying number of target objects among distractors. Parietal GABA and glutamate rose with the number of targets, whereas visual cortex showed a rise in glutamate only. The results point to inhibition in parietal cortex as a mechanism that keeps goal-relevant tracking robust against distractor interference.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Sinah Wiborg, Antonia Wittmann, Nina Beck, Susanna Hirschle, Dominik Aschenbrenner, Markus Becker, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Real-Time Neurofeedback Training to Modulate Glutamate-Glutamine Concentration Using Functional Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: The authors built a real-time neurofeedback procedure based on fMRS so that participants could learn to raise or lower glutamate plus glutamine (Glx) in an occipital volume. Over 30 trials, participants receiving veridical feedback modulated Glx in the intended direction, while a control group given random feedback did not. This shows neurotransmitter-level neurofeedback is feasible and could complement other neurofeedback approaches.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Savanna Babu, Nina Beck, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Suppression of task-irrelevant learning achieved through withdrawal of excitation in early sensory areas
papers.abstract: The paper asks how the brain avoids learning from visual signals that are irrelevant to the current task. Participants were repeatedly exposed to a task-irrelevant coherent motion direction that was either clearly visible or near threshold, while excitatory signalling in early visual cortex was measured with fMRS. Learning was suppressed when excitation in early visual areas was withdrawn, giving a neurochemical account of selective learning.
papers.authors: Markus Becker, Savanna Babu, Zhiyan Wang, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Excitatory signal processing in early visual areas based on task-relevance and perceptual salience modulates visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Participants were repeatedly exposed to a salient or a weak task-irrelevant motion signal while early visual excitation was measured with fMRS in the first and final sessions. Discrimination for the exposed direction improved more after near-threshold than suprathreshold exposure, and the change in excitatory processing across sessions tracked this pattern. The work links task relevance and salience to excitatory dynamics that gate visual learning.
papers.authors: Markus Becker, Savanna Babu, Zhiyan Wang, Sebastian M. Frank

papers.title: Transfer of Tactile Learning to Untrained Body Parts: Emerging Cortical Mechanisms
papers.abstract: This review covers evidence that tactile learning generalizes from trained to untrained fingers and other body parts, following a somatotopic pattern. It discusses the cortical mechanisms, particularly primary somatosensory cortex and its neighbouring representations, that could explain such transfer, and highlights open questions about how transfer relates to plasticity across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Sebastian M. Frank

0606.name: Serra Favila
0606.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0606.bio: Serra Favila is an Assistant Professor at Brown University who researches the neural and computational mechanisms of human episodic memory. Favila examines how environmental contexts, task goals, and interactions between similar memories transform mental representations and influence behavior. Their research utilizes functional neuroimaging (fMRI), intracranial recordings, eye-tracking, and computational modeling. Favila studies how hippocampal differentiation and visual cortex reactivation resolve competition during memory-guided attention.
0606.research_direction: Dr. Favila has recently been investigating the interplay between episodic memory and visual perception, alongside exploring how well artificial neural networks capture human cognitive representations. Using fMRI, receptive field modeling, and eye tracking, their recent work explores the neural mechanisms of memory-guided attention, asking how the hippocampus separates competing memories to sharpen spatial coding in the visual cortex and whether early visual areas (V1-V3) undergo spatially tuned reactivation to support one-shot episodic memory.
