Broadening their focus to artificial systems, they are also evaluating the extent to which modern deep learning models computationally align with human behavior. Specifically, they are examining whether vision and language networks naturally adhere to Shepard's universal law of generalization, and whether large language models rely on human-like, multi-step relational abstractions when navigating social networks.

papers.title: Hippocampal mechanisms underlying the resolution of competition in memory and perception
papers.abstract: Tests the idea that hippocampal computations that separate competing memories also sharpen sensory coding to guide attention. Using fMRI pattern similarity, receptive field modeling and eye tracking in a memory-guided visual search task, the authors show that more distinct hippocampal memory representations go with more accurate eye movements and lower competitor activation in visual cortex. Preparatory coding of the remembered location predicts search success, while coding of the competing location predicts interference errors.
papers.authors: Serra E. Favila, Mariam Aly

papers.title: Early Visual Cortex Supports One-Shot Episodic Memory via Spatially Tuned Reactivation
papers.abstract: Asks whether early visual cortex carries memory signals after only a single encoding event. Participants viewed objects once at one of four parafoveal locations, then did recognition and location-recall tasks; fMRI showed spatially tuned, weaker-than-encoding responses in V1-V3 matching the original location even when location was not task-relevant. These responses were stronger and more precise for remembered items.
papers.authors: Robert Woodry, Jonathan Winawer, Serra E. Favila

papers.title: Shepard's Law Reveals Which Deep Neural Networks Align with Human Representations
papers.abstract: Evaluates whether modern deep networks obey Shepard's universal law, in which generalization decays monotonically with distance in a latent space. Across many DNN families the learned embeddings recover this form and match human mental representations, with the entropy of how models spread probability over labels being the strongest predictor of adherence. Alignment depends on stimulus semantics, and language-aligned training improves it.
papers.authors: Daniel L. Carstensen, Steven M. Frankland, Serra E. Favila

papers.title: Humanlike representation of social networks in large language models
papers.abstract: Examines whether LLMs represent social networks the way humans do, via multistep abstraction that combines direct and indirect ties. In a text version of a human social-navigation task, LLM behavior mirrored human responses and was best explained by Katz communicability. The multistep signature persisted even in a task where it hurt accuracy, suggesting it is a core property of how LLMs represent relations.
papers.authors: Jae-Young Son, Daniel Carstensen, Serra Elizabeth Favila

0607.name: Shahin Nasr
0607.bio: Shahin Nasr is an Assistant Professor of Radiology at Harvard Medical School and a researcher at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging. Nasr’s research utilizes ultra-high field (7T) functional MRI, psychophysics, and electrophysiology to map the mesoscale architecture of the human visual cortex, including the columnar organization of features such as color, motion, and depth. They investigate the relationship between natural scene statistics and cortical organization, as well as the impact of developmental and neurodegenerative disorders, such as amblyopia and schizophrenia, on visual processing channels.
0607.research_direction: Dr. Nasr has recently been using ultra-high-field, high-resolution fMRI to investigate the mesoscale functional architecture of the human visual cortex. Their recent work explores how fine-scale cortical domains tuned to specific features—such as ocular dominance in V1 or motion, color, and stereopsis in the extrastriate magnocellular stream—are organized and functionally connected across cortical depths. They are specifically examining how these interdigitated networks compete for cortical territory during development and how their layout and resting-state connectivity are altered by conditions like strabismic and anisometropic amblyopia. Additionally, Dr. Nasr is investigating higher-level visual processing, using naturalistic stimuli to map previously undescribed scene-selective regions in the posterior intraparietal cortex to understand how the human brain encodes ego-motion during navigation.

papers.title: Mesoscale developmental rivalry in the human extrastriate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using high-resolution fMRI in 16 normally sighted people and 15 people with amblyopia, the study maps how columns tuned to disparity, motion and color share cortical territory in extrastriate areas. In controls, disparity columns compete with motion and color columns for space. In amblyopia, disparity columns shrink while motion and color columns expand, yet their interdigitated layout stays the same, suggesting that intact functions take over territory from impaired ones during development.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Shahin Nasr, Jan Skerswetat, Bryan Kennedy, Marianna E. Schmidt, Eric D. Gaier, Antony B. Morland, Peter Bex, David G. Hunter

papers.title: Differential Impacts of Strabismic and Anisometropic Amblyopia on the Mesoscale Functional Organization of the Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: High-resolution fMRI was used to compare ocular dominance responses across V1-V4 in amblyopic participants and controls. Amblyopes showed larger fused ocular-dominance patches spreading into downstream areas and elevated responses overall. Strabismic and anisometropic amblyopia differed in fellow-eye bias, binocular response and correlation of responses between V1 depths, giving direct human functional evidence for distinct mesoscale effects.
papers.authors: Shahin Nasr, Jan Skerswetat, Eric D. Gaier, Sarala N. Malladi, Bryan Kennedy, Roger B. H. Tootell, Peter Bex, David G. Hunter

papers.title: Unraveling the mesoscale resting-state functional connectivity of ocular dominance columns in humans using high-resolution functional MRI
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high-field, high-resolution fMRI, the study measures resting-state connectivity between human ocular dominance columns in V1 across cortical depth. Columns preferring the same eye are more strongly coupled than columns preferring opposite eyes, providing a noninvasive readout of mesoscale circuit organization.
papers.authors: Marianna E. Schmidt, Iman Aganj, Jason Stockmann, Berkin Bilgic, Yulin Chang, W. Scott Hoge, Evgeniya Kirilina, Nikolaus Weiskopf, Shahin Nasr

papers.title: A previously undescribed scene-selective site is the key to encoding ego-motion in naturalistic environments
papers.abstract: The authors identify a scene-selective region in the posterior intraparietal cortex that is not part of previously described scene areas. Using fMRI with naturalistic and optic-flow stimuli, they show this site responds preferentially to ego-motion cues during navigation-like viewing, and argue it is key for encoding self-motion in real-world environments.
papers.authors: Bryan Kennedy, Sarala N. Malladi, Roger B. H. Tootell, Shahin Nasr

papers.title: Two interdigitated fine-scale channels for encoding motion and stereopsis within the human magnocellular stream
papers.abstract: High-resolution fMRI shows that motion and stereopsis are processed in two minimally overlapping fine-scale channels in human extrastriate areas including V2 thick stripes, V3 and V3A. This separation held across random dots, gratings and natural scenes, and resting-state connectivity was stronger within than between the channels, refining animal-based models of the magnocellular stream.
papers.authors: Bryan Kennedy, Peter Bex, David G. Hunter, Shahin Nasr

0608.name: Shannon Ross-Sheehy
0608.bio: Shannon Ross-Sheehy is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Tennessee Knoxville and directs the Infant Visual Cognition Lab. Ross-Sheehy investigates the co-development of visual attention and memory systems, focusing on how neural substrates support the emergence of visual-cognitive competency in infants and adults. Utilizing high-resolution eye-tracking, pupillometry, and dynamic field modeling, Ross-Sheehy examines individual differences in scanning efficiency and attentional phenotypes. Their research aims to identify early attentional biomarkers in typical and atypical populations, such as preterm infants, to predict long-term cognitive outcomes.
0608.research_direction: Dr. Ross-Sheehy has recently been studying how visual short-term memory develops in infancy and how it relates to where infants look. Their recent work explores whether infants can hold on to what they saw at earlier fixations while their gaze moves on to new items, using an eye-tracking change-detection design that lets them estimate memory capacity in 5-month-olds and 11-month-olds and compare it directly with adults.

papers.title: Visual Short-Term Memory Persists Across Multiple Fixations: An n-Back Approach to Quantifying Capacity in Infants and Adults
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (STM) serves as a core architecture for broader cognitive functions, undergoing substantial maturation across the first postnatal year. Although overt gaze fixation is tightly linked to memory encoding, it remains unresolved whether developing infants can preserve distinct representations across sequentially fixated stimuli or encode items outside their foveal fixation history. In this study, cohorts of 5-month-olds, 11-month-olds, and adults (n = 24 per cohort) completed a passive change-detection paradigm featuring an n-back fixation-contingent design. High-resolution eye tracking recorded overt looking behavior while subjects observed multi-element arrays of colored circles, testing memory for the immediately preceding fixation (one-back), the penultimate fixation (two-back), and unfixated array elements (change-other). Across all age groups, convergent evidence showed retention for up to two sequentially fixated objects (one-back and two-back), alongside moderate preservation of nonfixated peripheral items. Temporal permutation analyses further demonstrated that change-preference metrics were not artifacts of spatial perseveration or systematic location biases.
papers.authors: Bret Eschman, Shannon Ross-Sheehy

0609.name: Shaul Hochstein
0609.department: Department of Neurobiology, Alexander Silberman Institute of Life Sciences
0609.bio: Shaul Hochstein is a Professor Emeritus at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, conducting research that ranges from the biophysics of photo-transduction to the cognitive psychology of conscious perception. Hochstein co-developed the Reverse Hierarchy Theory (RHT), which suggests that conscious perception begins at high-level cortical areas and descends to low-level representations when detailed scrutiny is required. Their research utilizes psychophysics, electrophysiology, and computational modeling to investigate ensemble perception, the mechanisms of perceptual skill learning, and the neural substrates of subjective experience.
0609.research_direction: Dr. Hochstein has recently been investigating the mechanisms and pervasiveness of ensemble perception, the visual system's ability to rapidly extract statistical summaries like the mean and variance from groups of items. Their recent work explores both the neural and cognitive dimensions of this phenomenon, using fMRI and multivariate pattern analysis to probe whether high-level cortical areas, such as the lateral occipital complex, encode ensemble features like mean orientation. Additionally, they are employing behavioral psychophysics to compare how statistical summaries are extracted explicitly versus implicitly across various stimulus dimensions and presentation formats. Their research also examines the temporal dynamics of these representations by investigating how perceptual history and serial dependence systematically bias observers' estimates of sequentially presented sets.

papers.title: Neural Patterns Reveal Lateral Occipital Complex Representation of Ensemble Mean Orientation
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study asks whether object-selective lateral occipital cortex carries information about the average orientation of a set of elements. Multivariate pattern analysis showed that activity in this region reflects the set's mean orientation, supporting a high-level cortical locus for ensemble representations.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Merav Ahissar, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: Comparing explicit and implicit ensemble perception: 3 stimulus variables and 3 presentation modes
papers.abstract: Observers judged set means either explicitly (reporting the average) or implicitly (through their effect on subsequent responses) for several stimulus features and presentation formats. The experiments compare how well each route recovers the mean, showing that ensemble information is extracted implicitly as well as explicitly across variables and modes.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Marina Pavlovskaya, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: The Pervasiveness of Ensemble Perception: Not Just Your Average Review
papers.abstract: A book-length review that gathers the evidence for ensemble perception, the visual system's ability to summarize sets of similar items by their mean and variability. It traces the phenomenon across features, object categories, faces and time, discusses the neural and computational mechanisms proposed, and argues that statistical summarization is a general, pervasive principle of vision rather than a niche effect.
papers.venue: Elements in Perception, Cambridge University Press
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Igor Utochkin, Shaul Hochstein

papers.title: Perceptual history biases in serial ensemble representation
papers.abstract: Examines how recently viewed stimuli distort the perceived mean of a serially presented set. Results show systematic biases toward previous trials' ensembles, indicating that the ensemble representation integrates perceptual history.
papers.authors: Noam Khayat, Merav Ahissar, Shaul Hochstein

0610.name: Shaun Wallace
0610.department: Department of Computer Science and Statistics
0610.bio: Shaun Wallace is an Assistant Professor at the University of Rhode Island and the director of the Human-Centered Experiential Technologies (HAX) Lab. Wallace’s research operates at the intersection of vision science, human-computer interaction (HCI), and systems, focusing on how personalized typographic formats affect digital readability for diverse populations. As the architect of the Virtual Readability Lab, they employ large-scale crowdsourcing and psychophysical methodologies to quantify the impact of font characteristics on reading speed and comprehension. Their work utilizes vision science principles to develop adaptive computational systems that tailor information presentation to an individual's visual processing capabilities.
0610.research_direction: Dr. Wallace has recently been investigating human-computer interaction with a dual focus on crowdsourced data curation and the visual optimization of digital reading. Their recent work explores the behavioral mechanisms that motivate both paid workers and unpaid volunteers to maintain and verify public tabular datasets, utilizing longitudinal field deployments to test various incentive structures and interface prompts. In parallel, they are studying the visual processing of digital text by conducting crowdsourced reading experiments to determine how table formatting choices, such as spacing and borders, impact reading speed and accuracy on mobile screens. Furthermore, their research probes the subjective perception of typography, examining how a reader's linguistic background and age influence which physical typographic attributes drive the perceived size of a font.

papers.title: Attract & Engage Visitors for Tabular Data Maintenance: a Longitudinal Naturalistic Field Study
papers.abstract: A long-running field deployment of a public, crowd-maintained tabular dataset (Drafty) tested what draws ordinary visitors into fixing and verifying data. The study compares different ways of surfacing insights and prompts to visitors and measures who contributes and how much. It shows that showing insights can attract and sustain contributions to an evolving dataset without paid workers.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW 2026)
papers.authors: Shaun Wallace, Na Kyoung Lee, Zhengyi Peng, Talie Massachi, Long Do, Surbhi Rathore, Sarah M. Brown, Jeff Huang

papers.title: Personalizing Font Size Normalization: Linguistic Background Shapes Which Font Attributes Matter
papers.abstract: The paper asks which typographic properties make a font look bigger or smaller to a reader, and whether this depends on the reader. Participants with different linguistic backgrounds and ages judged perceived font size across typefaces, and the attributes that predicted perceived size differed between groups. The authors argue that font size normalization should be personalized rather than based on a single physical measure.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 34th ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization (UMAP '26)
papers.authors: Yusra Suhail, Kushas Khadka, Borano Llana, Maedeh Hosseinpour, Shaun Wallace

papers.title: Towards Fair and Equitable Incentives to Motivate Paid and Unpaid Crowd Contributions
papers.abstract: This work compares paid crowd workers and unpaid volunteers contributing to the same online dataset, examining their motivations, contribution patterns and data quality. It explores incentive designs that treat the two groups fairly. Results inform how to combine payment and intrinsic motivation when sustaining crowd-curated data.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25)
papers.authors: Shaun Wallace, Talie Massachi, Jiaqi Su, Dave B. Miller, Jeff Huang

papers.title: Web Table Formatting Affects Readability on Mobile Devices
papers.abstract: Crowdsourced reading experiments examine how table formatting choices such as spacing, borders and alignment affect how quickly and accurately people read tables on phones. The results identify formatting features that improve or hurt mobile readability. The authors draw design guidelines for rendering web tables on small screens.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2023 (WWW '23)
papers.authors: Christopher Tensmeyer, Zoya Bylinskii, Tianyuan Cai, Dave B. Miller, Ani Nenkova, Aleena Niklaus, Shaun Wallace

0611.name: Sheng He
0611.institution: Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
0611.department: State Key Laboratory of Cognitive Science and Mental Health
0611.bio: Sheng He is a cognitive neuroscientist researching the functional and neural mechanisms of human vision, focusing on visual attention and the limits of conscious awareness. Using psychophysical methods and high-field (7T) functional MRI, they characterize how the brain processes visual information from early cortical stages to high-level representations, including responses to stimuli below the threshold of awareness. Their work examines binocular rivalry, the resolution of visual competition, and the role of feedback signals in the human visual cortex. They currently investigate the mesoscale neural circuitry of the visual system and the integration of visual features into coherent perception.
0611.research_direction: Dr. He has recently been studying how the human brain controls attention and builds conscious perception, combining psychophysics with high-resolution 7T fMRI. Their recent work explores the posterior inferotemporal cortex as a possible priority map for attention, testing it across motion, color, and shape tasks and examining how it connects the dorsal and ventral attention networks. They also investigate perceived time, asking whether adaptation to duration follows physical or subjectively perceived length and whether it carries across vision and hearing. A further thread looks at face-selective cortex, including how acquired expertise such as radiological training recruits it, and how feedback-driven information processing during face perception differs between the two hemispheres. They have also examined dynamic and integrative visual processing in people with schizophrenia compared with controls.

papers.title: Acquired visual expertise adopts and enhances face-selective cortex
papers.abstract: Studies how acquired visual expertise (radiological expertise) recruits and enhances face-selective visual cortex, using fMRI.
papers.authors: Haowen Guan, Min Guo, Siyuan Huang, Zhizheng Zhuo, Minghao Wu, Yunyun Duan, Yaou Liu, Sheng He

papers.title: Dynamic and integrative visual processing abilities in schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Examines dynamic and integrative visual processing abilities in patients with schizophrenia relative to controls.
papers.authors: MengYing Lan, Lan Wang, Bo Wang, Teng Cao, ZhiRen Wang, Kai Wang, Sheng He

papers.title: Hemispheric Asymmetry of Feedback-Driven Synergistic Information Processing During Face Perception
papers.abstract: Preprint on hemispheric asymmetry in feedback-driven synergistic information processing during face perception.
papers.authors: Sheng He, Xiaoxu Fan, Yong Jiang

papers.title: The distinct role of human PIT in attention control
papers.abstract: This study employs 7T high-resolution functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) to investigate the human posterior inferotemporal cortex (hPIT) as a candidate for a neural priority map. Utilizing spatial attention paradigms across multiple feature domains (motion, color, and shape), the research demonstrates that hPIT exhibits robust attentional modulation that is independent of stimulus category but highly sensitive to attentional demands. Functional connectivity analyses reveal that hPIT acts as an integrative hub bridging the dorsal and ventral attention networks, facilitating the orchestration of endogenous and exogenous control signals to optimize behavioral responses to complex visual environments.
papers.authors: Siyuan Huang, Lan Wang, Sheng He

papers.title: Duration adaptation depends on the perceived rather than physical duration and can be observed across sensory modalities
papers.abstract: By investigating duration adaptation effects through a series of psychophysical experiments, this study examines whether temporal adaptation is driven by objective physical duration or subjective perceptual duration. The results show that duration aftereffects from visual adapters align more closely with subjectively matched durations than with their physical lengths. Furthermore, the study identifies a cross-modal adaptation effect where adapting to a visual stimulus influences the perceived duration of a subsequent auditory stimulus, provided the subjective durations are matched. These findings suggest that duration is encoded at a modality-independent, high-level processing stage susceptible to top-down perceptual biases.
papers.authors: Hao Chen, Sheng He

0613.name: Shigeki Nakauchi
0613.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0613.bio: Shigeki Nakauchi is a Professor at Toyohashi University of Technology who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, color vision, and material recognition. Nakauchi's research utilizes a multidisciplinary approach combining psychophysical experimentation, EEG brain activity analysis, and mathematical modeling to study how the human visual system interprets environmental stimuli. Nakauchi developed specialized optical filters for Color Universal Design that simulate color vision deficiencies to facilitate inclusive design practices. Their current work focuses on 'Shitsukan' (material) perception and the application of spectral imaging to visualize information typically invisible to the human eye.
0613.research_direction: Dr. Nakauchi has recently been investigating a diverse set of questions across visual perception, human-robot interaction, and sensorimotor memory. In the visual domain, their recent work explores ensemble perception by testing for adaptation aftereffects to the statistical variance of facial expressions in crowds, and uses pupillometry to probe how the visual system processes the aesthetic naturalness of color compositions in paintings. Beyond vision, they are also studying human-robot collision avoidance, utilizing virtual reality, skin conductance, and kinematic cues like waist rotation to understand how pedestrians emotionally and physically react to approaching autonomous robots. Additionally, their research extends into auditory cognition by exploring how a listener's spontaneous motor rhythm, such as finger tapping, biases their recall and preference for music tempo.

papers.title: Subjective Emotions and Physiological Responses During Collision Avoidance with a Virtual Autonomous Mobile Robot
papers.abstract: Fifty participants walked toward a goal in a virtual reality room while avoiding an approaching mobile robot, rating arousal and valence and having skin conductance measured. Arousal and skin conductance dropped over trials, indicating habituation to the robot, and a second experiment examined how the robot's approach behavior changed emotional responses. The findings inform designing robot motion that feels comfortable to nearby pedestrians.
papers.authors: Yuta Matsubara, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Aftereffects of variance in the perception of facial expressions in crowds
papers.abstract: The study tests whether prolonged viewing of crowds of faces whose expressions vary a lot or a little changes how variable a later crowd appears. Adaptation produced aftereffects on perceived expression variance, suggesting the visual system encodes the spread of emotions across a group. This extends ensemble-perception research to the statistical structure of social scenes.
papers.authors: Moe Kudaka, Sachiyo Ueda, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Pupil dilation is driven by perceptions of naturalness of color composition in paintings.
papers.abstract: Using pupillometry, the study asks whether the eye's pupil reflects how natural the color composition of a painting appears. Viewers looked at paintings whose colors were altered to varying degrees, and pupil size tracked the perceived naturalness of the color arrangement. The result links color perception and aesthetic processing to an objective physiological signal.
papers.venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
papers.authors: Yuma Taniyama, Yuta Suzuki, Taisei Kondo, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: Waist rotation angle as indicator of probable human collision-avoidance direction for autonomous mobile robots
papers.abstract: Participants avoided an autonomous mobile robot approaching head-on, and their sidestep direction showed no strong left/right preference. Just before stepping aside, people twisted their waist toward the avoidance direction, so this angle predicts which way they will go. Robots that detected this cue with an ordinary RGB camera and yielded early made people more comfortable.
papers.authors: Tatsuto Yamauchi, Hideki Tamura, Tetsuto Minami, Shigeki Nakauchi

papers.title: How we remember music tempo: the role of spontaneous motor tempo in recall and preference
papers.abstract: Listeners adjusted music tempo in recall (with and without an 8-second delay) and preference tasks, and their spontaneous motor tempo was measured by finger tapping. Original tempo predicted adjustments in all tasks, while personal tapping tempo predicted the adjusted tempo only after the delay and in the preference task. This suggests rehearsal of remembered tempo is biased by one's own motor rhythm.
papers.authors: Kyoko Hine, Yoshitomo Wakana, Shigeki Nakauchi

0614.name: Shin'ya Nishida
0614.department: Graduate School of Informatics, Department of Intelligence Science and Technology
0614.bio: Shin'ya Nishida specializes in human vision and the mechanisms of sensory information processing. Nishida’s research explores visual motion, time perception, and the perception of material properties, or "Shitsukan," to investigate how humans interpret the physical world. They employ a methodology that integrates psychophysics and neuroscience with information engineering, including computer vision and virtual reality. Their current work focuses on developing biologically plausible, image-computable models of vision and aligning human perceptual capabilities with machine learning systems.
0614.research_direction: Dr. Nishida has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception, with a major focus on bridging the gap between biological and machine motion processing. Their recent work explores how observers estimate motion flow in naturalistic scenes, developing dense psychophysical measurement techniques and large-scale benchmarks to compare human perception directly against computer vision algorithms and brain-inspired neural networks integrating first- and second-order motion. Beyond motion, they are examining perceptual grouping by using Vision Transformer-generated textures to test how temporal correlations across features like color and luminance drive image segmentation. Additionally, they are probing the subjective richness of peripheral vision, specifically investigating how the visual system handles unreliable signal noise to generate the perception of a uniformly colored visual field.

papers.title: Inattentional noise leads to subjective color uniformity across the visual field
papers.abstract: The paper asks why the periphery looks richly coloured even though peripheral colour sensitivity is poor. Experiments indicate that the visual system fails to notice the noisy, unreliable colour signals in the periphery (inattentional noise) and therefore experiences the scene as uniform in colour, rather than filling in detail. This offers a mechanistic explanation for the subjective richness of peripheral vision.
papers.authors: Lana Okubo, Kiyofumi Miyoshi, Kazuhiko Yokosawa, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Machine learning modelling for multi-order human visual motion processing
papers.abstract: The authors build a brain-inspired neural network that handles both first-order (luminance-based) and second-order (contrast/texture-based) motion, a combination standard optical-flow algorithms miss. The model is trained on motion of objects made from non-diffusive materials and, without explicit training on second-order stimuli, comes to reproduce human percepts across many classic psychophysical results. It offers an image-computable account of how multiple motion mechanisms are integrated in human vision.
papers.authors: Zitang Sun, Yen-Ju Chen, Yung-Hao Yang, Yuan Li, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Human visual grouping based on within- and cross-area temporal correlations
papers.abstract: To test whether human perceptual grouping relies on global similarity computations like those in computer-vision segmentation, the authors use a Vision Transformer-based algorithm to generate textures in which within-area and cross-area temporal correlations of luminance, colour and phase are independently controlled. Human observers' segmentation performance on these stimuli shows how temporal similarity structure drives grouping across features. The results link temporal-correlation-based segregation to modern similarity-matrix models.
papers.authors: Yen-Ju Chen, Zitang Sun, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: HuPerFlow: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Human vs. Machine Motion Estimation Comparison
papers.abstract: HuPerFlow is a large psychophysical benchmark of human-perceived motion flow for natural video clips, allowing direct comparison with optical-flow algorithms. Comparing human and machine estimates shows where state-of-the-art computer-vision methods diverge from human perception. The dataset provides a new testbed for building vision models aligned with human motion perception.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Yung-Hao Yang, Zitang Sun, Taiki Fukiage, Shin'ya Nishida

papers.title: Psychophysical measurement of perceived motion flow of naturalistic scenes
papers.abstract: The study introduces a psychophysical method for measuring the perceived motion flow field across natural scenes, using a probe-based approach to obtain dense human estimates of direction and speed. Comparisons with optical-flow algorithms indicate that human motion perception departs systematically from ground-truth image motion. The work supplies the empirical foundation for later human-aligned motion models and benchmarks.
papers.authors: Yung-Hao Yang, Taiki Fukiage, Zitang Sun, Shin'ya Nishida

0615.name: Shinsuke Shimojo
0615.department: Division of Biology and Biological Engineering
0615.bio: Shinsuke Shimojo is the Gertrude Baltimore Professor of Experimental Psychology at Caltech and investigates the psychophysical and neural mechanisms underlying human perception and decision-making. Shimojo's research explores implicit brain functions, crossmodal integration, and the resolution of perceptual ambiguity using techniques such as fMRI, EEG, and transcranial brain stimulation. They study the 'social brain' through investigations into interpersonal synchrony and the neural correlates of 'team flow.' Their current work examines the dynamic interactions between predictive and postdictive neural processes and the influence of subliminal sensory information on conscious preference.
0615.research_direction: Dr. Shimojo has recently been investigating the computational mechanisms of crossmodal perception, applying psychophysics and Bayesian causal inference models to probe how the brain resolves sensory uncertainty using audiovisual illusions in low-vision populations and at the physiological blind spot. Their recent work also explores the role of intrinsic neural rhythms as individual cognitive fingerprints, using high-density EEG and hyperscanning to examine the oscillatory basis of spontaneous motor tempo and to map stable neural traits during real-time social cooperation, such as in the altered mental state of team flow. Additionally, they are investigating the temporal aspects of awareness and self-evaluation, testing whether (a) implicit magnetoreception interacts with vision, and (b) subjective experiences like an athlete's predictive "sixth sense" are driven by genuine foresight or by postdictive memory reconstruction.

papers.title: Did you see the sound? A Bayesian assessment on cross-modal perception in low vision
papers.abstract: Tests whether low vision makes people more prone to the sound-induced flash illusion, using 24 visual-field locations and measuring local flash-detection accuracy at each. Low-vision observers were less susceptible to the double-flash percept than sighted controls, and illusion strength followed local visual reliability more closely than eccentricity. Bayesian causal inference fits were poor across all locations but good at high-visibility locations, suggesting low-vision observers still integrate cues in a near-optimal way when the visual signal is reliable.
papers.authors: Ailene Y. C. Chan, Noelle R. B. Stiles, Carmel A. Levitan, Armand R. Tanguay Jr., Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: "Magnetic sand": Illusions of interactivity
papers.abstract: Reports a new family of illusions in which hand or finger movements near a random-noise display make the display look as if it is being altered by the action. Observers see a short-lived trace behind a slowly moving finger, or dots that seem attracted to, repelled by, or dragged along with the hand, even when the hand is hidden behind the display. The illusions hold across frame rate, contrast and dot size, pointing to a strong action-vision coupling.
papers.authors: Shinsuke Shimojo, Shengjie Zheng, Kensuke Shimojo, Eiko Shimojo, Daw-An Wu

papers.title: Bayesian Causal Inference Accounts for Multisensory Filling-In at the Blind Spot
papers.abstract: Asks whether audiovisual integration survives at the physiological blind spot, where there is no bottom-up visual input. Participants judged flashes and beeps in an audiovisual illusion presented across the blind spot or at a matched control location, and responses were fit with a Bayesian causal inference model that estimates sensory noise and priors. The results indicate that causal-inference computations remain intact and that the brain adapts its sensory uncertainty when visual input is missing.
papers.authors: Ailene Y. C. Chan, Noelle R. B. Stiles, Carmel A. Levitan, Daw-An Wu, Armand R. Tanguay Jr., Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: A hierarchical trait and state model for decoding dyadic social interactions
papers.abstract: Develops an EEG analysis pipeline that separates stable neural traits from moment-to-moment states during a cooperative team-flow game. Non-negative matrix factorization followed by linear discriminant analysis yields a seven-dimensional latent space with a trait-to-state hierarchy. Three dimensions carried most of the variation across people and task states, and representational similarity analysis linked them to skill and cognition measures of the social interaction.
papers.authors: Qianying Wu, Shigeki Nakauchi, Mohammad Shehata, Shinsuke Shimojo

papers.title: Implicit semantics gates visual awareness
papers.abstract: Uses a peripheral sound-induced flash illusion with briefly flashed Mandarin characters to test whether word meaning affects perception under impoverished peripheral vision. The auditory-dominance illusion replicated, and semantic congruence between the characters and the beeps modulated what observers reported perceiving. The work argues that implicit semantic information influences what reaches awareness even in the periphery.
papers.authors: Shao-Min Hung, Daw-An Wu, Po-Jang Hsieh, Shinsuke Shimojo

0617.name: Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg
0617.department: School of Psychological Sciences and Sagol School of Neuroscience
0617.bio: Yuval-Greenberg is an Associate Professor at Tel Aviv University investigating the relationship between the oculomotor system and cognitive processes such as visual perception, attention, and memory. Their research uses a multimodal approach, combining eye tracking with electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine eye movements as biomarkers for temporal expectation and cues for memory retrieval. Yuval-Greenberg has characterized the link between pre-stimulus oculomotor inhibition and expectation deficits in ADHD and developed methods for identifying and suppressing ocular artifacts in EEG recordings. Their current work focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual awareness and the integration of motor and visual components in episodic memory.
0617.research_direction: Dr. Yuval-Greenberg’s recent work explores the interplay between oculomotor behavior, attention, and high-level cognition. They have recently been investigating the trade-off between internal visual working memory storage and active visual sampling, testing whether the low behavioral cost of eye movements naturally encourages observers to re-examine visible scenes rather than relying on internal memory. In the domain of social vision, their research examines whether the classic gaze-cueing effect is strictly reflexive or if it can be altered by contextual cues, such as priming observers to interpret an averted gaze as inward cognitive effort rather than external spatial orienting. Additionally, their recent work explores broader cognitive dynamics by using task-evoked pupillometry to index fluctuations in sustained auditory attention and leveraging eye-tracking with computational modeling to determine how prior exposure to temporal variability influences a person's adaptation to new temporal regularities.

papers.title: Eye movements are a low-cost orienting behavior relative to key presses
papers.abstract: Observers doing visual working memory tasks often prefer to re-sample information that is still visible rather than storing it. This study tests whether the cost of sampling depends on how one orients, comparing sampling via eye movements with sampling via key presses. In two experiments people leaned on external sampling when it was done with the eyes and relied more on internal storage when a key press was required, suggesting that the natural fit of eye movements to behavior makes them a cheap way to gather information.
papers.authors: Rania Qais, Robert T. Knight, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: When exploration replaces storage: how eye movements shape visual working memory
papers.abstract: Standard visual working memory research restricts eye movements, whereas natural vision constantly resamples the scene. In two experiments (N=40) participants searched for a common target across two item sets and could either memorize items or switch back and forth between sets. When switching was done with the eyes, they resampled visually and used less working memory; with manual switching they stored more, even when peripheral input was matched. The results challenge fixation-based approaches to working memory.
papers.authors: Rania Qais, Robert T. Knight, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: Keeping an eye on attentive listening: Task-evoked pupil size unveils fluctuations in auditory sustained attention
papers.abstract: Across two experiments (N=54), participants performed a prolonged auditory continuous-performance task while pupil size was recorded. Smaller task-evoked pupil dilation went with more consistent reaction times, i.e. better sustained attention, and dilation also tracked self-reported ADHD symptoms beyond behavioral performance. Baseline pupil size was a less consistent marker, failing to replicate across experiments.
papers.authors: Yarden Dankner, Lilach Shalev, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: When a look means nothing: contextual interpretation abolishes the Gaze Cueing Effect
papers.abstract: Gaze cueing is usually thought to be reflexive, but gaze shifts can also signal inward, effortful thinking rather than external attention. In two preregistered experiments (N=110), one group was primed to read gaze shifts as reflecting cognitive effort while another had no such context. The gaze cueing effect shrank or vanished when the gaze was interpreted as thinking, showing that observers use context to decode others' eye movements.
papers.authors: Amit Zehngut, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

papers.title: Exposure to temporal variability promotes subsequent adaptation to new temporal regularities
papers.abstract: Participants saw visual targets at either random or fixed timing and were then tested on a new nearly-fixed timing routine. The random-exposure group adapted faster and performed better, supported by eye-tracking and computational modeling. The authors argue that temporal noise reduces overfitting and promotes generalizable temporal expectations.
papers.authors: Orit Shdeour, Noam Tal-Perry, Moshe Glickman, Shlomit Yuval-Greenberg

0618.name: Shruti Japee
0618.institution: National Institute of Mental Health, National Institutes of Health
0618.department: Laboratory of Brain and Cognition, Section on Learning and Plasticity
0618.bio: Shruti Japee is a Senior Associate Scientist in the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition at the National Institute of Mental Health. Japee’s research examines the neural mechanisms of emotion processing, with a focus on how the brain perceives and responds to facial and body expressions. By employing neuroimaging modalities such as fMRI and MEG alongside behavioral tasks, Japee investigates the functional connectivity between visual areas like the superior temporal sulcus and subcortical structures like the amygdala. Their work aims to characterize the neural correlates of emotional attention and the individual differences that modulate social and affective perception.
0618.research_direction: Dr. Japee has recently been studying how the brain reads facial expressions and how much that depends on the ability to move one's own face. Their recent work compares people with Moebius syndrome, who cannot move their faces from birth, to controls on tasks that measure sensitivity to emotional expressions, and reviews the theories linking facial movement to expression perception. They also use fMRI in macaques to ask how inferior temporal cortex responds to naturalistic expressions, including whether it tracks the social context of a face or its specific muscle configuration, and how identity and expression are coded compared with task-trained neural networks.

papers.title: On the Role of Sensorimotor Experience in Facial Expression Perception
papers.abstract: Visual perception of conspecific facial expressions operates rapidly and with high fidelity, yet the extent to which this faculty depends causally on sensorimotor embodiment remains contentious. This article examines three theoretical frameworks linking facial motor execution to visual expression decoding: motor simulation theory, the facial feedback hypothesis, and clinical models of facial paralysis. Motor simulation posits that visual categorization is mediated by covert recruitment of premotor and somatosensory circuits, whereas the facial feedback hypothesis argues that afferent proprioceptive signaling from facial musculature dynamically modulates affective experience. Evaluating empirical psychophysical evidence from individuals with Moebius syndrome (MBS), who present with congenital bilateral facial palsy, reveals elevated perceptual detection thresholds specifically across happy, fearful, and angry facial displays despite intact performance on non-affective visual control tasks. Integrating these psychophysical outcomes with functional neuroimaging data showing altered engagement of the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and amygdala, the author argues that facial sensorimotor experience developmentally calibrates sensitivity within cortical and subcortical face-processing pathways.
papers.authors: Shruti Japee

papers.title: Real Face Value: The Processing of Naturalistic Facial Expressions in the Macaque Inferior Temporal Cortex
papers.abstract: While canonical fearful facial expressions reliably drive blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) valence effects in primate inferior temporal (IT) cortex under laboratory conditions, rhesus macaques exhibit 'fear grins' across varied socio-emotional settings, questioning whether IT cortex is tuned to morphological facial action units or to contextual communicative signals. Awake macaques were scanned using monocrystalline iron oxide nanoparticle (MION) contrast-enhanced high-field fMRI at 4.7T while viewing conspecific expressions defined either by contextual affect (calm vs. threatening contexts) or by specific featural action units (neutral vs. prototypical fear grins), alongside human facial displays. Voxel-wise regression demonstrated that conspecific expressions defined by socio-emotional context drove significantly stronger valence modulation in IT cortex than stimuli selected strictly by morphological action units, whereas human expressions elicited minimal valence effects. A two-alternative forced-choice behavioral task corroborated that fear grins systematically differ in perceived pleasantness across communicative settings. These results demonstrate that macaque IT cortex represents emergent socio-emotional meaning rather than isolated geometric facial features.
papers.authors: Jessica Taubert, Shruti Japee

papers.title: Inability to move one's face dampens facial expression perception
papers.abstract: Embodied simulation models propose that recognizing the emotional expressions of others relies on covert motor mimicry and somatic feedback. To investigate whether congenital inability to execute facial movements impairs perceptual sensitivity to emotional expressions, a battery of psychophysical tasks was administered to individuals with Moebius syndrome (MBS)—a rare congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder characterized by sixth and seventh cranial nerve paralysis—and demographically matched neurotypical controls. Participants performed threshold detection tasks across static and dynamic facial and bodily expressions alongside non-emotional visual control tasks. While MBS individuals demonstrated preserved capacity to detect basic facial feature transformations (e.g., mouth aperture), they exhibited significantly elevated 50% detection thresholds for happy, fearful, and angry facial expressions. MBS participants further showed selective impairments in facial motion processing, while whole-body motion perception remained intact despite dampened extraction of affective information from body movements. Exploratory fMRI during expression matching demonstrated blunted activation within the posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and attenuated amygdala reactivity in MBS participants relative to controls, indicating that congenital facial immobility selectively impairs visual sensitivity to emotional expressions and alters corresponding affective neural networks.
papers.authors: Shruti Japee, Jessica Jordan, Judith Licht, Savannah Lokey, Moebius Syndrome Research Consortium, Gang Chen, Joseph Snow, Ethylin Wang Jabs, Bryn D. Webb, Elizabeth C. Engle, Irini Manoli, Chris Baker, Leslie G. Ungerleider

papers.title: Equivalent processing of facial expression and identity by macaque visual system and task-optimized neural network
papers.abstract: Dual-stream neurobiological models of face perception hypothesize anatomical and functional segregation between invariant identity recognition (traditionally mapped to the ventral stream) and changeable expression processing (attributed to the superior temporal sulcus). To characterize the representational architecture underlying identity and expression coding, awake rhesus macaques were imaged using high-field fMRI during exposure to a extensive database of conspecific faces systematically varying in facial identity and expression category (neutral, fearful, aggressive, and appeasing), alongside task-optimized deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Representational similarity analysis (RSA) and cross-validated multivariate pattern decoding revealed that facial identity and expression signals are jointly encoded across macaque face patches (including middle and anterior fundal/lateral face areas) rather than strictly segregating into separate anatomical routes. Furthermore, deep neural networks concurrently optimized for identity and expression categorization recapitulated the representational geometry and hierarchical layer progression observed across the macaque ventral face system, demonstrating convergent computational principles between primate visual cortex and task-constrained artificial networks.
papers.authors: Hui Zhang, Xuetong Ding, Ning Liu, Rachel Nolan, Leslie G. Ungerleider, Shruti Japee

0620.name: Shui'er Han
0620.institution: Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR)
0620.department: Institute for Infocomm Research (I2R) and Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR)
0620.bio: Shui'er Han is a vision scientist and researcher at the Institute for Infocomm Research (I2R) within Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR). Han’s research focuses on the mechanisms of binocular vision and the impact of prior experience on sensory perception, specifically regarding dichoptic stimulation and continuous flash suppression (CFS). They have characterized the temporal frequency tuning of visual suppression and utilize techniques such as psychophysical modeling and Virtual Reality to examine visual awareness. Han's work involves translating vision science into applications, including vision multiplexing configurations for augmented reality devices and assistive technologies for the visually impaired.
0620.research_direction: Dr. Han's recent work explores the phenomenon of binocular rivalry by shifting it from traditional laboratory paradigms into naturalistic, three-dimensional contexts. They have recently been using virtual reality environments to investigate whether interocular conflict naturally arises from real-world occlusion geometries, manipulating the plausibility of 3D spatial layouts using both static and moving stimuli. In more applied domains, their research examines how visual rivalry induced by peripheral head-mounted displays and smart glasses affects user mobility and target detection in augmented reality. By comparing unilateral and bilateral display configurations across varying target eccentricities, depths, and gaze movements, Dr. Han is evaluating the practical implications of vision multiplexing on human visual performance.

papers.title: Binocular rivalry under naturalistic geometry: Evidence from worlds simulated in virtual reality
papers.abstract: Binocular rivalry is normally studied with two incompatible images placed at the same physical location, a situation that almost never arises in everyday vision. The authors built a 3D virtual-reality corridor in which rival images appeared in implausible, semi-plausible, or plausible layouts, using both static and moving stimuli. Canonical rivalry alternations occurred in every layout, including ones that mimic real occlusion geometry, and a 3D modeling analysis showed that occlusion-driven interocular conflict is common in multi-object scenes. The results argue that rivalry is not just a laboratory artifact.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Randolph Blake, Celine Aubuchon, Duje Tadin

papers.title: The effect of visual rivalry in peripheral head-mounted displays on mobility
papers.abstract: Head-mounted displays and smart glasses that overlay augmented information on the natural view can cause visual rivalry between the two views. The study compared unilateral opaque, unilateral see-through and bilateral see-through peripheral configurations while manipulating target eccentricity, depth and gaze movement. Target detection was consistently poorer with unilateral configurations than with bilateral ones, pointing to binocular rivalry, though the effect weakened under more naturalistic conditions. The paper gives design recommendations for vision multiplexing devices.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Sujin Kim, Jae-Hyun Jung

0621.name: Shuo Wang
0621.bio: Shuo Wang is an Associate Professor of Radiology and Neurological Surgery who investigates the neural mechanisms of social attention, face processing, and decision-making. Wang’s research utilizes a multimodal approach, integrating human single-neuron recordings, eye tracking, fMRI, and computational modeling to examine how the brain processes socially relevant stimuli. Their work characterizes atypical neural encoding and visual saliency in individuals with autism spectrum disorder to facilitate clinical interventions.
0621.research_direction: Dr. Wang has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms that bridge high-level visual perception, attention, and memory. Using single-neuron recordings and intracranial EEG in human neurosurgical patients, their recent work explores how dense, axis-based visual feature codes in the ventral temporal cortex are transformed into sparse object and face representations in the medial temporal lobe. In a distinct line of research, they have been examining goal-directed visual attention in macaques by tracking large-scale population dynamics across visual and prefrontal cortices during free-gaze search tasks. Ultimately, Dr. Wang is probing how visual representations are dynamically reshaped by attentional states and structurally formatted to support declarative memory.

papers.title: Computational single-neuron mechanisms of visual object coding in the human temporal lobe
papers.abstract: Combining intracranial EEG from ventral temporal cortex and medial temporal lobe with medial temporal single-neuron recordings, the paper shows that VTC uses axis-based feature coding and that MTL neurons carry receptive fields within the VTC-derived feature space. This explains how dense feature representations become sparse, high-level object representations, supported by VTC-MTL interactions. Findings were validated on an independent dataset with different stimuli.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Jie Zhang, Jie Zheng, Yue Wang, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, Shuo Wang

papers.title: Computational neural dynamics of goal-directed visual attention in macaques
papers.abstract: Large-scale recordings from V4, IT, OFC and LPFC in macaques during free-gaze visual search show that population dynamics encode target categories, hold cue information across delays, and separate attentional states during search. Cue-related activity predicts later search efficiency, and foveal attention reshapes the representational geometry of peripheral stimuli. V4 and IT also preserve the spatial layout of the search array.
papers.authors: Jie Zhang, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana, Shuo Wang

papers.title: A neuronal code for object representation and memory in the human amygdala and hippocampus
papers.abstract: Recording 3173 single neurons in the human amygdala and hippocampus across four experiments, the authors show that neurons carry receptive fields in a high-level visual feature space, forming a region-based feature code for general objects. This code generalizes to new stimuli, accounts for classic category selectivity, and predicts memory performance and image memorability. The work links perceptual object coding to memory in the human medial temporal lobe.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Peter Brunner, Puneeth N. Chakravarthula, Krista L. Wahlstrom, Cory Inman, Elliot H. Smith, Xin Li, Adam N. Mamelak, Nicholas J. Brandmeir, Ueli Rutishauser, Jon T. Willie, Shuo Wang

papers.title: Feature-based encoding of face identity by single neurons in the human amygdala and hippocampus
papers.abstract: Across four experiments with 3,581 neurons from 19 neurosurgical patients, the study reveals a class of amygdala and hippocampal neurons that encode faces by shared visual features rather than by identity, semantic category or familiarity. Their receptive fields predict responses to novel faces. This bridges perceptual face representations and the identity-based semantic codes thought to support declarative memory.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Jinge Wang, Chujun Lin, Emanuela De Falco, Alina Peter, Hernan G. Rey, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, James J. DiCarlo, Alexander Todorov, Ueli Rutishauser, Xin Li, Nicholas J. Brandmeir, Shuo Wang

papers.title: A neural computational framework for face processing in the human temporal lobe
papers.abstract: Using iEEG in ventral temporal cortex and medial temporal lobe plus MTL single neurons (with macaque validation), the study shows that fusiform-centered axis-based feature codes are converted into sparse identity representations in the MTL through receptive fields in VTC feature space. Inter-areal VTC-MTL interactions provide the physiological basis for this transformation.
papers.authors: Runnan Cao, Jie Zhang, Jie Zheng, Yue Wang, Peter Brunner, Jon T. Willie, Shuo Wang

0622.name: Simona Buetti
0622.bio: Simona Buetti is a Research Associate Professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and co-directs the Vision Lab. Their research investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual attention and perception using behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and computational modeling. Buetti’s research on parallel visual processing demonstrates that visual search efficiency is often governed by logarithmic reaction time functions rather than purely serial mechanisms. Their current work examines how target-distractor distinctiveness across multiple feature dimensions—such as color, shape, and texture—is integrated to guide attentional prioritization and how background complexity influences distractor rejection times.
0622.research_direction: Dr. Buetti has recently been investigating the perceptual mechanisms and computational models underlying efficient, parallel visual search. Their recent work explores how distinct target features—such as color, shape, and texture—combine to form a unified guidance signal, and how quantitative distances in perceptual color spaces relate to behavioral search slopes across various tasks. Furthermore, they are using eye-tracking and instructional manipulations to examine the dynamic interplay between top-down goals and bottom-up salience, asking how prior task knowledge might shift attentional weighting across different stimulus dimensions. Finally, they are studying how environmental factors impact these mechanisms, specifically investigating how complex visual backgrounds modulate the local interitem distractor interactions that typically facilitate parallel processing.

papers.title: Toward a Better Understanding of Target Distinctiveness in Visual Search: How Color, Shape, and Texture Information Combine to Guide Search
papers.abstract: Real searches usually involve targets that differ from distractors along several features at once. This work measures how distinctiveness in color, shape, and texture each contribute to search efficiency, and tests quantitative models of how those dimensions are combined into a single guidance signal. It extends the lab's log-RT framework of parallel, efficient search from single features to multi-dimensional targets.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Evaluating the contributions of top-down and bottom-up processing on eye movements during parallel visual search
papers.abstract: Using efficient-search displays with color-defined targets and a highly salient distractor, the study tracks eye movements to separate goal-driven guidance from capture by salient items. Instruction conditions, including a free-viewing condition, show how top-down goals and bottom-up salience jointly shape where the first saccades land and how similarity to the target affects gaze.
papers.authors: Howard Jia He Tan, Alejandro Lleras, Zoe Jing Xu, Yifan Ding, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Quantifying the relationship between search efficiency and perceptual similarity in color space across different efficient search tasks
papers.abstract: Across several efficient search tasks, the authors relate search efficiency to distances between target and distractor colors in perceptual color space. The results show a systematic, quantifiable mapping from perceptual similarity to search slopes, generalizing across tasks and supporting a shared similarity-based guidance mechanism.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Alejandro Lleras, Zoe Jing Xu, Howard Jia He Tan, Yujie Shao, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Top-down instructions influence the attentional weight on color and shape dimensions during bidimensional search
papers.abstract: When targets differ from distractors in both color and shape, this study asks whether instructions can change how much attention each dimension receives. Manipulating what participants are told about the distractors shifts the relative weighting of color and shape in search efficiency, showing that top-down knowledge modulates otherwise stimulus-driven feature guidance.
papers.authors: Zoe Jing Xu, Alejandro Lleras, Zixu Gavin Gong, Simona Buetti

papers.title: Complex background information slows down parallel search efficiency by reducing the strength of interitem interactions
papers.abstract: Searches in scenes with complex backgrounds are slower even when the display items are simple. The study shows that background complexity weakens the interactions between neighboring distractors that normally yield efficient, logarithmic search, thereby explaining the slowdown within the lab's parallel-processing model.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Andrea Yaoyun Cui, Alejandro Lleras, Gavin Jun Peng Ng, Simona Buetti

0624.name: Simona Monaco
0624.bio: Monaco is a researcher at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC) at the University of Trento and directs the MonACo Action and Cognition Lab. Their research examines the neural mechanisms involved in integrating multisensory information, such as visual, haptic, and auditory cues, to plan and execute goal-directed motor actions. Using high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral measurements, Monaco investigates how action-specific intentions influence processing within the early visual cortex and parieto-frontal networks. Their methodology includes multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and graph theory to decode cortical representations of object features and motor strategies across the dorsal and ventral visual streams.
0624.research_direction: Dr. Monaco has recently been investigating how the human cortex processes object features for sensorimotor control across different task demands and sensory modalities. Their recent work explores the cross-modal recruitment of early visual areas, using fMRI multivoxel pattern analysis to ask whether the primary visual cortex actively encodes haptic object size or if this activity merely reflects visual imagery. Furthermore, they are investigating how the intention to perform specific motor behaviors, such as grasping versus manual alignment, dynamically modulates visual feature processing across V1 and the broader dorsal stream via top-down connectivity. To complement these empirical neuroimaging studies, their research also synthesizes large-scale fMRI and PET data to map how the presence or absence of visual feedback reshapes the frontoparietal and occipitotemporal networks driving reaching and grasping actions.

papers.title: Decoding haptic and imagined stimulus size in the human cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with blindfolded participants who either felt or imagined the size of rings, the study asks whether early visual cortex carries haptic size information and whether that is just visual imagery. Multivoxel decoding shows V1 and occipital pole represent size during touch but not imagery, ruling out imagery as the explanation. Frontal, parietal and LOtv regions decode size in both tasks, and V1 shows stronger connectivity with ventral and dorsal stream areas during touch.
papers.authors: Samantha Sartin, Federica Danaj, Fabio Del Giudice, Juan Chen, Dietrich Samuel Schwarzkopf, Irene Sperandio, Simona Monaco

papers.title: Action-specific feature processing in the human cortex: An fMRI study
papers.abstract: An fMRI cue-separation paradigm tested whether the intended action (grasping versus manual alignment) changes visual processing of oriented objects. Action-specific effects appeared only once the object was shown, as early as primary visual cortex and extending along the dorsal stream to motor and premotor areas. Task-dependent connectivity of aIPS and V1 with frontal, parietal and temporal regions supports reentrant top-down modulation of vision for action.
papers.authors: Simona Monaco, Nicholas Menghi, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Cortical areas involved in grasping and reaching actions with and without visual information: An ALE meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies
papers.abstract: A coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis of 53 fMRI and PET studies of grasping and reaching, contrasting movements made with and without vision. Frontal-parietal areas were consistently engaged regardless of visual availability, whereas occipito-temporal regions were more likely active with vision, and reach and grasp did not differ there. The results are discussed against the Goodale-Milner dual-stream model.
papers.authors: Samantha Sartin, Marco Ranzini, Cristina Scarpazza, Simona Monaco

0627.name: Soojin Park
0627.bio: Soojin Park is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms of high-level visual scene representation and its role in human navigation. Their research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics to explore how the brain's scene-selective network, including the parahippocampal place area (PPA) and occipital place area (OPA), encodes spatial boundaries and environmental navigability. Park’s work characterizes scene perception as a process that integrates visual features with the functional and spatial constraints of an observer's environment. Formerly an assistant professor at Johns Hopkins University, Park currently leads the Visual Cognitive Neuroscience Lab at Yonsei University.
0627.research_direction: Dr. Park has recently been investigating how the human brain represents spatial environments within scene-selective visual cortices like the parahippocampal and occipital place areas. Using fMRI and virtual reality paradigms, their recent work explores how our visual processing of a scene is shaped by navigational affordances, asking how the brain integrates physical obstacles, path directions, and even invisible barriers learned from past experience. Additionally, they are probing the fundamental visual cues that define spatial layout, testing whether distinct scene regions build boundaries based on continuous extended surfaces or sparse geometric features. Finally, Dr. Park is expanding this research beyond vision to examine multisensory spatial cognition, looking for shared neural codes that represent environmental properties like room size across both visual and auditory domains.

papers.title: A Scene with an Invisible Wall—Navigational Experience Shapes Visual Scene Representation
papers.abstract: Participants first navigated virtual environments either freely or while being blocked by invisible barriers, then judged the visual similarity of scene pairs and were scanned with fMRI. Scenes that differed in prior navigational experience were rated as more visually different, even when their images were matched. Activity patterns in the parahippocampal place area tracked this learned navigability beyond visual features, showing that experience reshapes scene representation.
papers.authors: Shi Pui Donald Li, Jiayu Shao, Zhengang Lu, Michael McCloskey, Soojin Park

papers.title: Dissociating the Neural Representation of Scene Boundary and Extended Surfaces in Human Visual Scene Processing
papers.abstract: Using tightly controlled artificial scenes built from poles and surfaces, the study asks whether the brain codes environmental boundaries by geometry or by continuous surface. A few isolated poles marking the corners of a 3D space were enough to evoke a wall-like response in the parahippocampal place area, whereas the occipital place area followed continuous surface properties. The two scene regions therefore handle non-wall boundaries differently.
papers.authors: Annie Cheng, Ga In Shin, Katrina Ferrara, Sang Ah Lee, Soojin Park

papers.title: Obstacle coding in scene-selective cortices
papers.abstract: This fMRI study examines how obstacles that block movement through a scene are represented in scene-selective visual cortex. It extends the lab's work on navigational affordances by asking whether regions such as the PPA and OPA encode the presence of obstacles.
papers.authors: Dongheon Kham, Yoonjung Lee, Soojin Park

papers.title: Multi-modal Representation of the Size of Space in the Human Brain
papers.abstract: The study asks how the size of a room is represented across vision and hearing, using both visual and auditory stimuli in fMRI. It looks for brain regions that carry a code for room size shared across the two senses rather than tied to one modality.
papers.authors: Jaeeun Lee, Soojin Park

papers.title: Combined representation of visual features in the scene-selective cortex
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether scene-selective regions treat layout features such as path direction and distance separately or as an integrated whole. fMRI multivariate patterns indicated that these features are represented in combination in scene cortex rather than as independent dimensions.
papers.authors: Jisu Kang, Soojin Park

0628.name: Sophia Vinci-Booher
0628.department: Department of Psychology and Human Development
0628.bio: Vinci-Booher is an Assistant Professor of Educational Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University who investigates the neural mechanisms mediating the relationship between action and perception across the lifespan. Their research examines how manual communication tasks, such as handwriting and drawing, facilitate the development of brain systems for literacy and symbol recognition. Utilizing functional and diffusion MRI, Vinci-Booher characterizes functional and structural brain changes, including white matter tract development, that occur during intensive learning periods. This work aims to identify how sensorimotor experiences drive neural reorganization and impact long-term educational outcomes.
0628.research_direction: Dr. Vinci-Booher has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms of sensorimotor learning and foundational cognitive development, particularly focusing on how motor actions like handwriting shape visual and academic skills. Their recent work explores how structural brain connectivity relates to these processes, using diffusion MRI to examine whether existing white matter microstructure predicts an adult's ability to draw novel symbols, and how dorsal and ventral pathways physically change alongside reading and math acquisition in early childhood. Concurrently, they are studying the behavioral dynamics of early visual-motor development by tracking how preschoolers' baseline phonological and literacy skills influence their ability to learn to write numbers and letters. To accurately capture these rapid, nonlinear periods of human development, Dr. Vinci-Booher has also been formalizing and advocating for dense longitudinal neuroimaging methodologies that sample individual brains frequently over short time windows.

papers.title: Short-Term Developmental Trajectories of Dorsal-Ventral Pathways and Their Relationships with First-Grade Learning
papers.abstract: In a pre-registered study, children were scanned monthly with diffusion MRI and given monthly reading and math assessments across the first-grade year. Behavioral learning followed a sigmoid course for reading and an inverted-U for math, and white matter microstructure of dorsal and ventral pathways changed over months in ways that related to individual differences in learning. The work shows that within-year brain change tracks foundational academic learning.
papers.authors: Xueying Ren, James R. Booth, Gabriele Amorosino, Franco Pestilli, Sophia Vinci-Booher

papers.title: Practical considerations for dense longitudinal neuroimaging: Ten simple rules for frequent scanning over short time periods
papers.abstract: A practical guide to designing and running dense longitudinal neuroimaging studies, especially with children and others who tolerate scanning poorly. It covers study design, measurement choices, recruitment and retention, and compliance, distilled into ten simple rules for research teams.
papers.authors: E. Cross, A. B. Compton, A. Vess, James R. Booth, Kendrick N. Kay, Sophia Vinci-Booher

papers.title: Dense longitudinal neuroimaging reveals individual brain change trajectories
papers.abstract: A review arguing for dense longitudinal neuroimaging, in which the same individuals are scanned many times across a short window of rapid change rather than sparsely over long spans. Such sampling yields precise, individual-level estimates of nonlinear brain change and supports mechanistic accounts of development and learning. The authors highlight recent findings, including the role of the motor system in shaping visual development and learning.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Xueying Ren, Kendrick N. Kay, Chen Yu, Franco Pestilli, James R. Booth

papers.title: Associative white matter tracts selectively predict sensorimotor learning
papers.abstract: Sixty adults practiced drawing 40 unfamiliar symbols on a digital tablet after diffusion tractography measured the microstructure of major white matter tracts. A machine-learning model-selection framework showed that pre-existing tract microstructure, particularly in associative tracts, selectively predicted how much drawing speed improved with practice. The result links existing white matter properties to individual differences in future sensorimotor learning.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Daniel J. McDonald, Elizabeth Berquist, Franco Pestilli

papers.title: Learning to write letters and digits by hand in preschool
papers.abstract: Thirty-seven preschoolers completed standard assessments and then six weeks of practice producing letters or digits, with each production scored for legibility and confusability. Some symbols (such as E, H, O, T, 1, 0) were produced well at the start while Z was worst, and H, R, S, Y and Z improved most. Visual-motor, literacy and phonological skills interacted to predict production learning, each helping only when the others were low.
papers.authors: Sophia Vinci-Booher, Deborah Zemlock, Susie Ju, Karin James

0629.name: Stefan Pollmann
0629.department: Institute of Psychology, Chair of General Psychology
0629.bio: Stefan Pollmann is a Professor of Experimental Psychology who investigates the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual attention and perception. Pollmann’s research focuses on contextual cueing in visual search, exploring how spatial configurations facilitate target detection through implicit learning and memory-guided saccades. Utilizing high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), eye-tracking, and event-related potentials (ERP), they examine the plasticity of the visual system and compensatory strategies such as saccadic re-referencing in cases of central vision loss. This research addresses how top-down attentional weighting and bottom-up saliency signals interact within the human visual cortex to guide environmental exploration.
0629.research_direction: Dr. Pollmann has recently been investigating the neural networks that govern visual attention, eye movements, and exploratory decision-making. Their recent work explores how the brain controls and encodes gaze in naturalistic and social settings, using fMRI to reveal how non-classic areas like the orbitofrontal cortex guide eye movements toward faces and how the ventral visual pathway represents category-specific fixation sequences. In the realm of classic visual attention, they are examining the role of the prefrontal cortex in attentional reweighting, specifically how target-dimension changes are processed differently in sparse versus crowded search displays. Furthermore, they are studying the behavioral and neural mechanisms of probabilistic foraging, comparing exploit-versus-explore patch-leaving decisions across species and mapping individual human tendencies for exploration to signaling in the frontopolar cortex.

papers.title: The orbitofrontal-anterior temporal network complements the attention network for where to look in social situations
papers.abstract: During free viewing of movies, gaze decisions were tied not only to the classic dorsal and ventral attention networks but also to orbitofrontal and anterior temporal regions that had not been linked to human eye-movement control before.
