This extra network appeared to be driven mostly by looking at socially relevant content such as faces. The authors argue that classic artificial-stimulus paradigms miss the semantic and social systems that guide gaze in natural environments.
papers.authors: Nico Marek, Radha Nila Meghanathan, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Temporal order-dependent and -independent cortical representation of gaze sequences
papers.abstract: Participants tracked dots that replayed fixation sequences recorded while others viewed faces or houses, with images absent, and were scanned with fMRI. Multivariate pattern analyses separated regions whose activity depended on the order of the gaze sequence (parietal cortex) from ventral occipitotemporal regions that carried category-specific spatial fixation patterns regardless of order. This clarifies what the ventral visual pathway actually encodes about gaze paths.
papers.authors: Radha Nila Meghanathan, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Prefrontal dimension change-related activation differs for visual search in sparse and dense displays
papers.abstract: Using fMRI during visual search, the study examined how frontal cortex, including the frontopolar region, responds when the target-defining feature dimension changes between trials. The activation pattern depended on whether displays were sparse or dense, suggesting that attentional reweighting engages prefrontal areas differently with display crowding.
papers.authors: Nico Marek, Ninja K. Horr, Dragan Rangelov, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Differential patch-leaving behavior during probabilistic foraging in humans and gerbils
papers.abstract: Humans and gerbils performed comparable probabilistic foraging tasks to test when each species decides to leave a depleting patch for a new one. The two species showed different patch-leaving strategies, which helps map how exploit-versus-explore decisions generalize across species.
papers.authors: Lasse Güldener, Parthiban Saravanakumar, Max F. K. Happel, Frank W. Ohl, Maike Vollmer, Stefan Pollmann

papers.title: Behavioral Bias for Exploration Is Associated with Enhanced Signaling in the Lateral and Medial Frontopolar Cortex
papers.abstract: Individuals differ in how strongly they favor exploring over exploiting during foraging-style decisions. fMRI showed that people with a stronger exploration bias had enhanced signaling in lateral and medial frontopolar cortex, tying individual decision tendencies to frontopolar activity.
papers.authors: Lasse Güldener, Stefan Pollmann

0630.name: Stefan Van der Stigchel
0630.bio: Stefan van der Stigchel is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology and the principal investigator of the AttentionLab, where their research examines the mechanisms of visual attention, eye movement control, and working memory. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging techniques, they explore how the brain filters sensory information to construct a coherent awareness of the environment. Their work extends to clinical populations, investigating attentional deficits such as hemispatial neglect and hemianopia to improve neurorehabilitation strategies. Currently supported by an ERC Consolidator Grant and an NWO Vici grant, Van der Stigchel is a science communicator and author of several books on concentration and focus.
0630.research_direction: Dr. Van der Stigchel has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying visual search, spatial attention, and working memory. Their recent work explores how the human brain constructs spatial priority maps, utilizing EEG decoding and inverted encoding models to examine whether past and present search goals are represented concurrently, and to determine how large-scale neural activity differentiates the preparation of overt eye movements from covert shifts of attention. Additionally, they are studying how observers balance internal cognitive resources with external visual information, using psychophysics and eye tracking to test whether multi-target search operates concurrently or sequentially, and to investigate what drives observers to continuously resample the external world instead of relying on available information in visual working memory. Finally, their recent methodological work evaluates the integrity of online behavioral experiments by analyzing reaction-time distributions in classic cueing paradigms to identify simulated or bot-like participant profiles.

papers.title: Past and present goals are represented concurrently during visual search
papers.abstract: The authors used EEG decoding to track, at the same time, how the target location from the previous trial (history-driven selection) and the current search goal shape spatial priority during visual search. Neural signals for the previous target location were reliably decodable, and were distinct from and concurrent with goal-driven signals. This suggests that history and goals are held in parallel, rather than one replacing the other, and informs models of how priority maps are built.
papers.authors: Damian Koevoet, Dirk van Moorselaar, Edward Awh, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Multitarget Visual Search Flexibly Switches Between Concurrent and Sequential Search Modes
papers.abstract: People can hold several targets in working memory, but it is debated whether they search for them concurrently or one at a time. Across three experiments using manual and eye-movement data with trial-level modeling, participants used both concurrent and sequential search as distinct modes and switched between them flexibly. The work reframes the debate away from fixed capacity limits toward flexible strategy use.
papers.authors: Alex J. Hoogerbrugge, Christoph Strauch, Noa Hoevers, Christian N. L. Olivers, Tanja C. W. Nijboer, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Will online behavioral research follow the fate of online survey research?
papers.abstract: This letter analyses reaction-time data from an online Posner cueing study and finds participant profiles that resemble simulated bot responses rather than human ones: near-perfect normality, no mean-variance relation and almost no trial-to-trial autocorrelation. The authors urge routine statistical screening of such data and warn that advancing AI may require verifying real human participation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Stefan Van der Stigchel, Christoph Strauch, Bart de Zwart, Leendert Van Maanen

papers.title: Population-Level Activity Dissociates Preparatory Overt from Covert Attention
papers.abstract: Using human EEG with decoding and inverted encoding models, the study asks whether large-scale neural activity separates preparing an eye movement from covertly shifting attention. Overt preparation showed earlier and sharper spatial tuning than covert attention, and cross-decoding revealed an additional frontal spatially selective process during overt preparation. Thus the two forms of attention overlap but diverge quickly at the population level.
papers.authors: Damian Koevoet, Vicky Voet, Henry M. Jones, Edward Awh, Christoph Strauch, Stefan Van der Stigchel

papers.title: Mountains of memory in a sea of uncertainty: Sampling the external world despite useful information in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Earlier work found people load only one or two items into visual working memory before looking again at the outside world. This study tests whether that reflects resampling before memory is depleted, by varying uncertainty and available memory information. Observers kept sampling the external world even when memory held useful information, showing a strong bias toward external sampling rather than a simple capacity limit.
papers.authors: Andre Sahakian, Surya Gayet, Chris L. E. Paffen, Stefan Van der Stigchel

0631.name: Stefania Bracci
0631.bio: Stefania Bracci is an Associate Professor at the University of Trento and a researcher within the Object Vision Group at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC). Bracci’s research investigates the organizational principles of object representations in the human visual cortex, examining the interplay between visual features, conceptual categories, and action-related properties. Utilizing functional MRI, representational similarity analysis, and computational modeling with deep neural networks, they study the topographic mapping of tool and hand representations in the occipitotemporal cortex. Their work further explores how task context and experience shape neural representational spaces, comparing biological visual processing with artificial intelligence models.
0631.research_direction: Dr. Bracci has recently been investigating how the human visual cortex represents objects within a multidimensional space driven by diverse behavioral goals and action affordances. Their recent work explores the functional dissociation between the lateral and ventral occipitotemporal cortices by mapping the specific feature dimensions that organize neural responses to categories like tools, hands, bodies, and food. To probe this fine-grained functional topography, they utilize dense fMRI sampling combined with multivariate analyses and neural-network encoding models. Additionally, they are examining the alignment between biological and artificial vision by testing whether modern topographic deep neural networks capture the same action-based spatial organization observed in the human brain.

papers.title: Encoding models uncover fine-grained feature selectivity for bodies, hands and tools
papers.abstract: Densely sampled image-level fMRI in three participants was combined with neural-network encoding models to probe category-selective areas in ventral and lateral occipitotemporal cortex. Area-specific models predicted responses to millions of new images while preserving category preferences, and comparing models from same-category areas revealed different feature sensitivities tied to location and hemisphere. This shows finer-grained specialization than broad category tuning suggests.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Martin N. Hebart, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Object dimensions underlying food representations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Two fMRI experiments in the same participants test what drives food-selective responses in lateral and ventral occipitotemporal cortex. In lateral cortex, food responses track action-related properties shared with other graspable objects, while in ventral cortex they track surface properties such as colour and ensemble configuration. The dissociation suggests the two food areas reflect different computational constraints.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Giulia Orlandi, Lotte van Campenhout, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Investigating action topography in visual cortex and deep artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with images of body parts and objects that differ in how much they afford action, the study finds a gradient in left lateral occipitotemporal cortex in which bodies, hands, tools and manipulable objects overlap along a posterior-dorsal to anterior-ventral axis. Multivariate analyses show action properties are a key organizing dimension in this region, whereas shape and animacy dominate ventral cortex. Topographic deep networks show no comparable action-based organization, exposing a gap between brain and model.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Nhut Truong, Hans Op de Beeck, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Tool Representations in Human Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: A review of neuroimaging work on how tools and other action-relevant objects are represented in visual cortex. Lateral occipitotemporal cortex encodes both shape and action-related properties, separating end-effectors such as tools and hands from other graspable objects, while ventral cortex mostly encodes surface properties like material and texture. The review also considers what artificial neural networks can and cannot capture of these dimensions.
papers.authors: Davide Cortinovis, Marius V. Peelen, Stefania Bracci

papers.title: Understanding Human Object Vision: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Representations
papers.abstract: This review argues that object vision is better understood through the full range of behavioral goals humans pursue than through object recognition alone. It surveys advances in behavioral, neuroscientific and computational work revealing a multidimensional representational space, and suggests that core object recognition may be less central than traditionally assumed.
papers.authors: Stefania Bracci, Hans P. Op de Beeck

0632.name: Stella F. Lourenco
0632.lab_name: Lourenco Lab: Vision, Cognition, and Development
0632.bio: Lourenco investigates the ontogenetic origins and computational mechanisms underlying spatial and numerical representation in humans. Their research explores how the brain processes general magnitudes—such as area, number, and time—and the extent to which these systems share a common magnitude-based framework or remain perceptually independent. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms, eye tracking, and fMRI, Lourenco maps the developmental trajectories of spatial reasoning and investigates how early visuospatial competencies support the acquisition of symbolic mathematical concepts. Additionally, their work examines the influence of evolutionary-based fears and social categories on perceptual calibration and spatial biases.
0632.research_direction: Dr. Lourenco has recently been investigating how humans extract complex spatial, physical, and social information from visual inputs across development. Their recent work explores the developmental trajectory of high-level vision, testing how young children utilize global shape to achieve robust object recognition compared to deep neural networks, and examining how perceptual boundaries for intersectional race and gender categories are calibrated from childhood to adulthood. In parallel, they are studying the visual mechanisms underlying magnitude and physical reasoning by modeling how numerosity perception relies on continuous visual properties rather than abstract modules, and how observers use geometric heuristics rather than mental simulations to make intuitive physics judgments about object stability. Finally, they are investigating spatial cognition and decision-making, employing drift diffusion modeling to understand how shifting evidence accumulation and response caution impact gender differences in mental rotation tasks under time pressure.

papers.title: Time pressure amplifies gender differences in mental rotation through shifts in evidence accumulation and response caution
papers.abstract: Using drift diffusion modeling, the study examined why men tend to outperform women on mental rotation, particularly when speed is emphasized. Time pressure increased the gender gap, and the modeling attributes this to differences in how evidence is accumulated and how cautious responding is, rather than to a single fixed spatial ability difference. The findings tie a classic spatial gender difference to malleable decision processes.
papers.authors: Yaxin Liu, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Perceptual Calibration in Intersectional Race and Gender Categorization Across Development
papers.abstract: This preprint studies how children and adults perceptually categorize faces that vary jointly in race and gender, and how the boundaries of these categories are calibrated over development. It reports systematic developmental changes and biases in how intersecting social categories are read from faces. The work extends the lab's social perception line into a developmental perceptual-calibration framework.
papers.authors: Nikita Agarwal, Maia Mast, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Fast and robust visual object recognition in young children
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether young children can recognize objects from sparse or degraded views as quickly and robustly as adults, and compared them with deep neural networks. Children showed rapid, resilient recognition, relying on global shape information, whereas standard vision networks failed under the same degradations even when trained on far more data. The work argues that early-developing shape-based representations underpin efficient human object recognition.
papers.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg, Sukran Bahar Sener, Kylee Novick, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: Object geometry serves humans' intuitive physics of stability
papers.abstract: Rather than running mental physics simulations, people appear to judge whether a stacked or balanced structure will fall using simple geometric cues about the objects. Across experiments, manipulating object shape and geometry predicted stability judgments better than simulation-style accounts. The results indicate that intuitive physics of stability can rely on visually available geometric heuristics.
papers.authors: Yaxin Liu, Vladislav Ayzenberg, Stella F. Lourenco

papers.title: A theory of perceptual number encoding
papers.abstract: This theoretical paper proposes that the perception of numerosity is built on the encoding of continuous visual properties such as area, density and contour, rather than on a dedicated abstract number module. It lays out a multichannel, magnitude-based account and shows how it explains a range of behavioral findings on number perception and interference from non-numerical cues. The framework became the basis for the lab's later interdependence-of-magnitudes work.
papers.authors: Stella F. Lourenco, Lauren S. Aulet

0633.name: Stephen Adamo
0633.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Radiology & Imaging Sciences
0633.lab_name: Attention Detection And Medical Observation (ADAMO) Lab
0633.main_research_area: visual attention and medical image perception
0633.bio: Adamo is an Assistant Professor at the University of Arizona with joint appointments in the Departments of Psychology and Radiology & Imaging Sciences. Adamo directs the Attention Detection And Medical Observation (ADAMO) Lab, where their research investigates the mechanisms of visual search and cognitive errors in medical imaging contexts. Their work examines phenomena such as 'subsequent search misses' and 'satisfaction of search' to determine how expertise, artificial intelligence, and 3D imaging technology affect detection accuracy. Adamo utilizes behavioral testing, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to connect basic vision science with applied clinical outcomes.
0633.research_direction:
Stephen's research examines how attention and other cognitive processes guide visual search, particularly in situations where observers must find rare or multiple targets in complex visual environments. His work combines cognitive science, eye tracking, EEG, medical imaging, and artificial intelligence to understand why important targets are missed and how search performance can be improved.

A major focus of his recent work applies these questions to cancer detection in medical images. This research examines how observers detect, or fail to detect, multiple abnormalities in traditional 2D mammography and 3D digital breast tomosynthesis. Using breast images, eye tracking, EEG, and measures of search performance, his lab investigates how factors such as target similarity, image complexity, and AI-based decision support influence detection. His work also examines how expertise, ranging from visually untrained novices (i.e., undergraduates) to radiographers, residents, and radiologists, influences susceptibility to search errors and reliance on AI-based decision support.

papers.title: Comparing the subsequent search miss effect between mammography and tomosynthesis
papers.abstract: Subsequent search misses occur when finding one target lowers the chance of detecting a second one. This study compares how large that effect is when observers search 2D mammograms versus 3D digital breast tomosynthesis images. It tests whether the added depth of tomosynthesis changes this multiple-target error.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 13928, Medical Imaging 2026: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Brandon Eich, Lyndon Rakusen, Miguel Lago, Claudia Mello-Thoms, Stephen H. Adamo

papers.title: Comparing multiple-target search performance and the satisfaction of search effect between 2D and segmented-3D search
papers.abstract: The paper examines how accurately observers find several targets in either a 2D display or a segmented-3D display of the kind used in tomosynthesis. It measures the satisfaction of search effect, in which finding one target reduces detection of others. It tests whether 3D viewing changes that error pattern.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 12929, Medical Imaging 2024: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Rachel Brem, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Comparing experts to novices: reduced satisfaction of search when searching with virtual breast tomosynthesis
papers.abstract: This proceedings paper compares expert and novice observers searching virtual breast tomosynthesis images for multiple targets. It asks whether expertise or 3D viewing reduces satisfaction of search errors. Results show a reduced effect under some search conditions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of SPIE 12467, Medical Imaging 2023: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Bruno Barufaldi, Miguel A. Lago

0634.name: Stephen Engel
0634.bio: Stephen Engel is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Minnesota who researches the neural mechanisms of visual perception and cortical plasticity. Engel utilizes functional MRI (fMRI) to map retinotopic organization and color tuning in the human primary visual cortex. Their current research program employs psychophysics, EEG, and immersive virtual reality systems to study how the adult visual system adapts to environmental changes. This work aims to develop therapeutic interventions for clinical conditions such as macular degeneration and amblyopia.
0634.research_direction: Dr. Engel's recent work explores a diverse range of clinical and fundamental visual phenomena using psychophysical and electrophysiological methods. They have recently been investigating visual snow syndrome, utilizing sensory adaptation techniques like dynamic noise and motion aftereffects to probe the cortical origins of this spontaneous visual activity. Another major line of their research focuses on low vision rehabilitation, testing how customizing the spatial remapping of text into the intact visual field might improve reading performance in the presence of simulated central scotomata. Additionally, they are examining the neural mechanisms underlying binocular rivalry, using frequency-tagged steady-state EEG to track the gradual accumulation of sensory signals that precede perceptual switches.

papers.title: Spatial remapping improves reading with simulated central field loss
papers.abstract: Typically sighted readers with simulated central scotomata read sentences under six strategies that shift text away from the blind region into intact visual field. At least one remapping condition beat no remapping in every participant, with an average reading-speed gain of about 24%. The best strategy depended on the shape of the scotoma, supporting customization, and the authors argue remapping should be evaluated in patients with central field loss.
papers.authors: Colin S. Flowers, Arda Fidanci, Gordon E. Legge, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Visual Snow Is Susceptible to the Motion Aftereffect
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether the spontaneous activity that produces visual snow reaches motion-selective visual areas such as V5/MT. After adapting to opposite-direction drifting gratings, most participants with visual snow (10 of 11) saw their snow drift in the opposite direction, as a classic motion aftereffect predicts, and longer adaptation produced longer-lasting illusions with a log-log linear relationship. The result suggests snow-generating activity is present at least up to motion-processing stages of cortex.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Anna J. Hillstrom, Karly D. Allison, Carter B. Mulder, Hannah R. Moser, Michael S. Lee, Michael-Paul Schallmo, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Customizing spatial remapping of letters to aid reading in the presence of a simulated central field loss
papers.abstract: The authors introduce a method for building and testing letter-remapping strategies tailored to different shapes of central field loss. Letter-recognition maps around central vision guided the design of remappings, which were then tested with word recognition in simulated scotomata. A horizontal-gap remapping performed best overall, and the benefit of each strategy depended on scotoma shape, supporting customization.
papers.authors: Colin S. Flowers, Gordon E. Legge, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: Adapting to Visual Noise Alleviates Visual Snow
papers.abstract: People with visual snow syndrome see persistent flickering specks across the visual field, and no effective treatment exists. The authors had participants with visual snow view high-contrast dynamic noise, then rated the strength of their symptom. Adaptation temporarily made the snow disappear for most observers, and its duration grew with exposure time and was specific to dynamic noise, as for normal adaptation. This indicates that spontaneous visual-system activity causally underlies the snow percept and points toward adaptation-based interventions.
papers.authors: Samantha A. Montoya, Carter B. Mulder, Michael S. Lee, Michael-Paul Schallmo, Stephen A. Engel

papers.title: An Accumulating Neural Signal Underlying Binocular Rivalry Dynamics
papers.abstract: Models of binocular rivalry propose that neural signals for the two eyes' images change gradually until a threshold triggers a perceptual switch, but direct evidence was lacking. Using steady-state EEG responses in 84 people viewing frequency-tagged orthogonal gratings, the authors found the suppressed stimulus signal rose and the dominant signal fell over each percept, more slowly for longer percepts. Signals changed rapidly at the end of every percept, matching the predictions of accumulator models of rivalry.
papers.authors: Shaozhi Nie, Sucharit Katyal, Stephen A. Engel

0635.name: Stephen Heinen
0635.bio: Stephen Heinen is a Senior Scientist at the Smith-Kettlewell Eye Research Institute, where they investigate the neural circuitry governing smooth pursuit, fixation, and saccadic eye movements. Heinen’s research utilizes oculomotor behavior as a non-invasive probe into human cognitive processes, including decision-making and attention allocation. They have provided evidence for independent ocular control during binocular viewing, which challenges classical oculomotor theories such as Hering’s Law. This work aims to translate basic neuroscience into clinical applications for diagnosing and treating conditions like strabismus, macular degeneration, and various psychiatric disorders.
0635.research_direction: Dr. Heinen has recently been questioning a classic idea in eye-movement research: that the two eyes are driven by a single shared command. Their recent work records both eyes at high temporal resolution during steady fixation, smooth tracking of moving targets, and shifts in depth, often with one eye covered, to see whether each eye is controlled independently. They have also been developing an oculomotor model to explain unusual saccades that occur when the eyes change depth, and studying how peripheral visual cues can steady gaze and reduce tiny fixational eye movements.

papers.title: A new oculomotor model demystifies “Remarkable Saccades”
papers.abstract: Oculomotor research and strabismus management have long been guided by Hering's Law of equal innervation, which states that binocular control relies on the linear summation of unitary conjugate and vergence commands. However, observations of interocular temporal asynchrony during midline vergence challenge the necessity of a unitary vergence signal, favoring independent monocular control. Yet, independent control cannot account for 'Remarkable Saccades'—paradoxical saccadic displacements executed by an eye already aligned on target during asymmetric vergence steps. To resolve this discrepancy, the Hybrid Binocular Control (HBC) computational model was developed. HBC integrates independent monocular pursuit controllers that interact directly with a unitary brainstem conjugate saccadic generator. Without invoking an explicit vergence command, HBC generates Remarkable Saccades as an emergent property. Incorporating a variable attentional gain further captures idiosyncratic behavioral variations occurring when observers direct attention to one eye's image. The model closely reproduces kinematic profiles across saccadic classes, providing empirical predictions regarding cortical-brainstem interactions and asymmetric oculomotor dynamics.
papers.authors: Stephen J. Heinen, Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk

papers.title: Misalignment of a covered eye reveals frontoparallel smooth pursuit is driven by multiple signals
papers.abstract: Traditional frameworks of ocular tracking postulate that a single unitary motor signal rotates both eyes conjugately according to Hering's Law. Although asynchronous dynamics under monocular occlusion during vergence have disputed unitary vergence commands, the role of independent control during frontoparallel tracking remains less clear. Binocular eye movements were recorded at 1000 Hz using an infrared-pass occluder while neurotypical human observers tracked a 0.4° dot translating horizontally across a tangent screen under predictable sinusoidal and pseudorandom motion regimes (peak velocities of 5°/s and 25°/s). During monocular tracking, the covered eye maintained a steady positional offset (phoria) that originated during initial fixation. Crucially, despite this persistent misalignment, the occluded eye matched the instantaneous target velocity of the viewing eye throughout pursuit. These findings indicate that while an overarching conjugate motor command drives tracking velocity, independent monocular controllers regulate binocular positional alignment via visual feedback.
papers.authors: Stephen Heinen, Devashish Singh, Caroline Ulep, Scott Watamaniuk

papers.title: Asymmetric eye movements during fixation challenge Hering's Law of a unitary neural command
papers.abstract: Binocular coordination during visual fixation is widely presumed to follow Hering's Law of equal innervation, largely because classical studies recorded from only a single eye. To determine whether fixational eye movements (FEMs) are yoked or uncoupled, binocular fixation was recorded during both binocular viewing and monocular occlusion in neurotypical subjects. Fixational stability quantified via bivariate contour ellipse area (BCEA) demonstrated interocular asymmetry even during binocular viewing, demonstrating independent oculomotor control. Under monocular occlusion, BCEAs were significantly greater in covered eyes than in viewing eyes, and eyes with larger BCEAs displayed elevated slow drift velocity. In contrast to drift disconjugacy, microsaccades were consistently binocular; however, microsaccadic amplitudes were selectively increased in viewing eyes with larger BCEAs to remediate drift errors. These findings demonstrate that while microsaccades rely on a unitary conjugate mechanism, fixational slow drift is governed by independent monocular control channels.
papers.authors: Arvind Chandna, Devashish Singh, Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Stephen Heinen

papers.title: Peripheral targets attenuate miniature eye movements during fixation
papers.abstract: Fixating an isolated central point is standard practice for stabilizing gaze in visual psychophysics and ophthalmic imaging; however, small foveated targets provoke microsaccades and slow ocular drift that perturb retinal image stability and divert attentional resources. To investigate whether peripheral boundaries can stabilize gaze without triggering foveally mediated saccadic intrusions, human fixational stability was evaluated using central targets, peripheral circular rings of varying radii, and combinations thereof. Isolating gaze control to peripheral contours substantially decreased microsaccade rates and diminished drift dispersion relative to foveal spot fixation, while maintaining central alignment accuracy. The suppression of fixational intrusions confirms that small foveal points compel unnecessary foveation commands that elicit miniature catch-up saccades. Utilizing peripheral spatial references optimizes retinal image stabilization by circumventing foveal saccadic recruitment.
papers.authors: Scott N. J. Watamaniuk, Jeremy B. Badler, Stephen J. Heinen

0636.name: Stephen Mitroff
0636.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0636.bio: Stephen Mitroff is a visual cognition researcher whose work focuses on the individual differences and malleability of visual search, perception, and memory. Mitroff’s research program leverages large-scale datasets from mobile applications and applied performance tools to analyze human variability in complex visual tasks. By investigating cohorts including radiologists, airport security officers, and elite athletes, Mitroff explores how cognitive factors like fatigue and personality moderate performance in high-stakes environments. Their current work emphasizes identifying the underlying mechanisms of expert performance and developing training regimens to enhance visual-attentional capabilities.
0636.research_direction: Dr. Mitroff's recent work explores the underlying dynamics of visual search, its applied clinical extensions, and the methodological rigor of cognitive psychology experiments. Using large-scale datasets, they have recently been investigating trial-by-trial response time patterns to determine if continuous pre- and post-error behavioral dynamics can be used to forecast upcoming search errors. Their applied research extends these visual search principles to medical radiology, comparing how the satisfaction-of-search phenomenon—where finding one target hinders the detection of another—operates across conventional 2D versus segmented-3D displays. Additionally, they are evaluating standard experimental practices, investigating how repetitive task designs and strict performance-based exclusion rules might inadvertently introduce systematic "shadow" biases that filter specific demographics, such as neurodivergent individuals, out of cognitive science samples.

papers.title: Predicting errors before they occur using trial-by-trial dynamics of pre-error and post-error behavior
papers.abstract: Using large trial-by-trial visual search datasets, the study characterizes how response behavior speeds up before an error and slows down after it, treating both as one continuous time course rather than separate effects. The authors show that these pre-error and post-error dynamics carry enough signal to forecast when an error is about to happen. This reframes error monitoring as something predictable from moment-to-moment performance patterns.
papers.authors: Sarah B. Malykke, Audrey Siqi-Liu, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

papers.title: Comparing multiple-target search performance and the satisfaction of search effect between 2D and segmented-3D search
papers.abstract: The study compares how well observers find multiple targets in conventional 2D displays versus segmented-3D (slice-based) displays, modeled on medical imaging such as breast tomosynthesis. It examines the satisfaction-of-search effect, where finding one target reduces detection of a second, under each format. The work links basic visual search research to radiology practice.
papers.venue: Medical Imaging 2024: Image Perception, Observer Performance, and Technology Assessment (SPIE)
papers.authors: Stephen H. Adamo, Rachel Brem, Stephen Mitroff

papers.title: Standard experimental paradigm designs and data exclusion practices in cognitive psychology can inadvertently introduce systematic "shadow" biases in participant samples
papers.abstract: The paper argues that common features of cognitive experiments, such as long, repetitive tasks and performance-based exclusion rules, can quietly filter who ends up in the final sample. For example, people higher in certain neurodivergent traits may avoid or drop out of such studies, or be excluded by accuracy and attention-check criteria. Analyses of participant data show these hidden selection effects, cautioning that findings may generalize less well than assumed.
papers.authors: Emma M. Siritzky, Patrick H. Cox, Sydni M. Nadler, Justin N. Grady, Dwight J. Kravitz, Stephen R. Mitroff

0637.name: Steven Dakin
0637.bio: Steven Dakin is a visual neuroscientist who researches the neural mechanisms of human perception and the development of diagnostic technologies for vision disorders. Dakin utilizes psychophysical techniques, computational modeling, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study the integration of local features into global visual structures, particularly in peripheral vision and under conditions of visual crowding. Their work focuses on the clinical application of these methods, including the creation of eye-tracking tools and pediatric vision tests like the Auckland Optotypes to assess neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions such as autism and schizophrenia. Formerly a Professor at University College London’s Institute of Ophthalmology, Dakin directs research initiatives in New Zealand aimed at improving eye-health equity through digital screening technologies.
0637.research_direction: Dr. Dakin’s recent work spans fundamental visual psychophysics and the development of accessible clinical tools. In basic vision science, they have recently been using equivalent-noise paradigms to dissociate local precision from global pooling stages in motion processing, while also investigating the mechanisms of visual crowding by testing how flicker adaptation influences letter acuity. On the clinical side, their research explores novel therapeutic approaches, such as evaluating home-based dichoptic treatments for childhood amblyopia using customized contrast-balanced binocular viewing. Additionally, Dr. Dakin is assessing the utility and limitations of consumer technology in vision research, specifically testing whether built-in iPad eye-tracking can reliably measure basic gaze dynamics or track reflexive eye movements to drifting patterns as a hardware-free way to diagnose color vision deficiencies.

papers.title: Dissociable effects of element-lifetime and stimulus-duration on local and global motion processing: An equivalent noise study
papers.abstract: Using an equivalent-noise paradigm, the study separates local direction precision from global pooling (how many samples are effectively averaged) in motion perception. Varying how long individual dots live improved local directional precision but not global integration, whereas varying overall stimulus duration mainly changed the number of samples pooled. The results support a two-stage model of motion processing with temporally dissociable local and global stages.
papers.authors: Balaje Vivekanandan, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Diagnosing Colour Vision Deficiencies Using Eye Movements (Without Dedicated Eye-Tracking Hardware)
papers.abstract: The authors test a new colour-vision screening test that runs on an unmodified iPad Pro, using its built-in eye tracking to record reflexive eye movements to drifting coloured patterns. From these movements they estimate each person's red-green equiluminant point and equivalent luminance contrast. In 33 participants (controls, deuteranopes and protanopes, confirmed by anomaloscope) the approach classified colour-vision status with about 90% sensitivity and 91% specificity, suggesting a practical hardware-free clinical test.
papers.authors: Aryaman Taore, Gabriel Lobo, Philip R. K. Turnbull, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Feasibility of a new 'balanced binocular viewing' treatment for unilateral amblyopia in children aged 3-8 years (BALANCE): results of a phase 2a randomised controlled feasibility trial
papers.abstract: A phase 2a randomised trial in 32 children with unilateral amblyopia tested a home-based dichoptic treatment in which each eye views contrast-balanced movies customised to the interocular acuity difference, compared with standard patching or atropine. The study assessed safety, adherence, retention, trial methodology and clinical vision measures over 16 weeks. It supports feasibility of the balanced binocular viewing approach and informs the design of a larger definitive trial.
papers.authors: Annegret Hella Dahlmann-Noor, John A Greenwood, Andrew Skilton, Daniel Baker, Mohamed Abbas, Emma Clay, Payal Khandelwal, Denise Dunham, Siobhan Ludden, Amanda Davis, Hakim-Moulay Dehbi, Steven C Dakin

papers.title: (The limits of) eye-tracking with iPads
papers.abstract: The paper compares gaze estimates from an iPad Pro's built-in head- and eye-tracking with a dedicated Tobii 4c tracker in 28 observers across fixation, saccade and smooth-pursuit tasks. The iPad was considerably less accurate and precise (about 3.2 deg vs 0.75 deg error) though fixation stability and saccade measures were moderately correlated across devices. It also failed catastrophically in 5-20% of observers, so the authors caution researchers to inspect iPad eye-tracking data carefully.
papers.authors: Aryaman Taore, Michelle Tiang, Steven C. Dakin

papers.title: Flicker adaptation improves acuity for briefly presented stimuli by reducing crowding
papers.abstract: Following earlier work showing that adapting to flickering noise sharpens acuity for brief stimuli, the authors ask whether this reflects better detail vision itself, altered fixational eye movements or pupil size, or reduced crowding. Acuity improved by roughly 8% after adaptation only for flanked (crowded) letters, not isolated ones, and the gain scaled with each person's susceptibility to crowding but not with fixation stability or pupil size. The improvement therefore appears to come from reduced crowding.
papers.authors: Selassie Tagoh, Lisa M. Hamm, Dietrich S. Schwarzkopf, Steven C. Dakin

0638.name: Steven J. Luck
0638.bio: Steven J. Luck is a Distinguished Professor at UC Davis specializing in the neurocognitive architecture of visual attention and working memory. Luck's research integrates behavioral psychophysics, eye tracking, and electrophysiological recordings to characterize the capacity limits of human cognition and the translational impacts of cognitive dysfunction in disorders such as schizophrenia. Luck authored a guide to event-related potential (ERP) techniques and developed the open-source ERPLAB Toolbox to standardize brain activity analysis. Luck's work extends to global training initiatives, including workshops designed to promote experimental standards in cognitive neuroscience.
0638.research_direction: Dr. Luck has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual attention and working memory, heavily utilizing behavioral measures and electroencephalography (EEG). Their recent work explores how the visual system learns to actively suppress salient distractors to prevent attentional capture, and they are developing formal population vector models to test how complex, photograph-like scenes are stored in visual working memory. Dr. Luck is also extending these experimental paradigms into clinical research, measuring trial-by-trial EEG and behavioral markers to evaluate attentional control and sensory precision across a transdiagnostic sample of patients with psychotic and mood disorders. Concurrently, they have been advancing neuroimaging methodology by investigating how multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) can be repurposed to score traditional event-related potential (ERP) components and boost statistical power in human electrophysiology studies.

papers.title: A population vector model of visual working memory for real-world scenes
papers.abstract: Existing quantitative working memory models assume simple, discrete objects, so it has been unclear how photograph-like scenes could be stored. The authors propose that a scene is held as a noisy vector of firing rates across ventral-pathway areas, estimated with a deep neural network. The model accounts for both behavioral performance and EEG activity patterns in scene working memory tasks, pointing toward formal models of natural-scene storage.
papers.authors: John E. Kiat, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Signal suppression 2.0: An updated account of attentional capture and suppression
papers.abstract: This paper revises the signal suppression hypothesis, which holds that salient stimuli generate a priority signal that can be actively suppressed before it captures attention. The authors integrate evidence gathered since the original proposal, address competing accounts such as the attentional-window view, and clarify how suppression is learned and applied. They lay out an updated framework and identify the open questions that most need experimental work.
papers.authors: Nicholas Gaspelin, Xiaojin Ma, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Assessing trial-by-trial EEG and behavioral markers of attentional control and sensory precision in psychotic and mood disorders
papers.abstract: Using a multi-site sample of people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, and healthy controls, the study measured single-trial EEG and behavioral indices of attentional control and sensory precision. It asks which neural markers of attention distinguish diagnostic groups and how they relate to symptoms. The work is part of a large transdiagnostic project on cognitive control and working memory in serious mental illness.
papers.authors: Megan A. Boudewyn, Molly A. Erickson, Kurt Winsler, Deanna M. Barch, Cameron S. Carter, Michael J. Frank, James M. Gold, Angus W. MacDonald III, J. Daniel Ragland, Steven M. Silverstein, Andrew P. Yonelinas, Steven J. Luck

papers.title: Using multivariate pattern analysis to increase effect sizes for event-related potential analyses
papers.abstract: Decoding methods are usually used to ask whether information is present in EEG; here they are repurposed as a way of scoring conventional ERP effects. Across several component paradigms, MVPA-based decoding accuracy yielded larger effect sizes than traditional mean-amplitude or peak measures. The authors argue this can boost statistical power in ERP studies.
papers.authors: Carlos Daniel Carrasco, Brett Bahle, Aaron Matthew Simmons, Steven J. Luck

0639.name: Steven K Shevell
0639.department: Departments of Psychology and Ophthalmology & Visual Science
0639.bio: Steven K. Shevell is the Eliakim Hastings Moore Distinguished Service Professor at the University of Chicago, where they investigate the neural and psychophysical mechanisms underlying human color and brightness perception. Their research focuses on how the visual system resolves ambiguity in complex scenes, utilizing paradigms such as chromatic interocular-switch rivalry to dissociate retinal stimulation from perceived color experience. By combining psychophysical methods with neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG, Shevell has demonstrated that perceptual color representations emerge in higher cortical areas, such as V4, rather than being determined solely by early retinal signals. Their recent work explores divisive normalization as a canonical computation for explaining context-dependent sensory processing and the perceptual grouping of ambiguous neural representations.
0639.research_direction: Dr. Shevell has recently been investigating how the visual system settles on a single interpretation when the input from the two eyes is ambiguous or conflicting. Their recent work explores color perception when different regions of a scene could be seen in competing ways, and why those regions sometimes take on the same color and sometimes on maximally different colors. They approach this with a model in which neural populations compete through divisive normalization, aiming to explain both outcomes within one framework.

papers.title: Perceptual resolution of ambiguity: A divisive normalization account for both interocular color grouping and difference enhancement
papers.abstract: Visual perception typically constructs an unambiguous, coherent representation of the environment, even when retinal inputs admit multiple conflicting interpretations that induce competition among neural populations. In such bistable or multistable scenarios, spatial and temporal contextual cues bias perceptual selection. While previous work has demonstrated that multiple chromatically ambiguous regions can resolve synchronously to yield identical percepts (interocular similarity grouping) or maximally distinct percepts (difference enhancement), traditional rivalry models based on fixed stimulus strength cannot readily account for these divergent outcomes, particularly given the nonlinearities inherent to chromatic processing. This work demonstrates that a feature-tuned divisive normalization framework, wherein neural responses are pooled across the stimulus space to dynamically reweight competing chromatic signals, accounts for both interocular grouping and difference enhancement. Computational simulations and psychophysical measurements in interocular-switch rivalry confirm that divisive normalization provides a parsimonious, unifying mechanism governing opposite perceptual resolutions of chromatic ambiguity.
papers.authors: Jaelyn R. Peiso, Stephanie E. Palmer, Steven K. Shevell

0641.name: Suk Won Han
0641.bio: Suk Won Han is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at Chungnam National University and directs the Cognitive Neuroscience Unit. Han’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of visual attention, working memory, and cognitive control through functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics. Their work examines the functional fractionation of stimulus-driven attention networks, the impact of working memory contents on attentional capture, and the neural bottlenecks that lead to dual-task limitations. Han previously conducted research as a postdoctoral scholar at Vanderbilt University and as a research professor at Chungbuk National University.
0641.research_direction: Dr. Han's recent work explores the mechanisms of visual search and attentional capture, particularly investigating how the size of a viewer's attentional window and their reliance on serial versus parallel processing influence distractibility. They have recently been examining how both bottom-up salient stimuli, like color singletons and abrupt onsets, and top-down working-memory-matching distractors compete for attention under these varying search modes. Additionally, their research asks at what specific cognitive stages these distractors disrupt performance and how task-irrelevant visual heterogeneity among non-targets impacts overall search efficiency. Finally, Dr. Han is investigating the broader behavioral implications of these foundational cognitive processes by testing how basic spatial attentional orienting relates to everyday social functioning and maladaptive behaviors in adults.

papers.title: Conditional automaticity of memory-driven attention: Dissociable effects on reaction time and accuracy
papers.abstract: Asks at which processing stage working-memory-matching distractors affect search. Across two visual search tasks, such distractors reliably slowed responses, showing a strong priority signal from memory, but did not reduce target-report accuracy beyond non-matching distractors. The authors infer the cost arises at a later, post-encoding stage rather than as uniform perceptual interference.
papers.authors: Sohyun Kim, Jonga Kwon, Seonbeom Heo, Suk Won Han

papers.title: The impact of task-irrelevant heterogeneity on visual search efficiency and attentional capture
papers.abstract: Examines how variability in features that are irrelevant to the task, such as spatial frequency or colour of non-targets, affects visual search. Greater irrelevant heterogeneity made search less efficient and weakened attentional capture, though the effects depended on which feature varied and on task conditions.
papers.authors: Myo-Hee Chang, Suk Won Han

papers.title: Investigation of the functional interaction between problematic behaviors, social interaction, and attentional orienting
papers.abstract: Tests whether attentional orienting relates to social functioning in typically developing adults. In 50 participants performing a spatial cueing task alongside self-report behavior and social measures, larger cueing benefits were associated with fewer self-reported maladaptive behaviors, linking basic attention to everyday social adjustment.
papers.authors: Seonmi Yun, Cheolhwan Kim, Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

papers.title: Color singletons are suppressed under serial search, but not abrupt onsets
papers.abstract: Compares two classic attention-grabbing stimuli, salient colour singletons and abrupt onsets, in visual search that is more or less serial. When many items are processed in parallel within a wide attentional window, the singleton captures attention; when search becomes serial the singleton is suppressed. Abrupt onsets capture attention regardless of search mode, indicating separable mechanisms and underscoring the role of attentional window size.
papers.authors: Hae Chan Jeong, Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

papers.title: The degree of parallel/serial processing affects stimulus-driven and memory-driven attentional capture: Evidence for the attentional window account
papers.abstract: Revisits the long-running debate over whether salient stimuli automatically capture attention, arguing earlier tests misestimated attentional window size. Using a newer paradigm that verifies whether items are processed in parallel or serially, the study finds capture by salient distractors (both stimulus-driven and memory-driven) only under parallel processing with a wide window, and none under serial shifting. The authors conclude the attentional window account offers a useful resolution of the debate.
papers.authors: Cheolhwan Kim, Nahyeon Lee, Koeun Jung, Suk Won Han

0642.name: Summer Sheremata
0642.bio: Summer Sheremata is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates how the human brain processes and maintains visual information through the coordination of attention and short-term memory. Currently an Assistant Teaching Professor at Northeastern University and formerly an Assistant Professor at Florida Atlantic University, Sheremata utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics to map visuotopic representations in the parietal and visual cortices. Their research focuses on the neural architecture of cognitive systems and how these mechanisms are impacted by aging and neuropsychiatric conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and hemispatial neglect. By examining hemispheric asymmetries and sensory mapping, Sheremata aims to identify the specific brain networks that support daily visual interactions and their potential for clinical decline.
0642.research_direction: Dr. Sheremata has recently been investigating the limits of visual short-term memory and why they differ between people. Their recent work explores whether people with lower memory capacity fail because they cannot filter out irrelevant items, and how this affects the precision of what is remembered. They also ask how spatial biases in memory relate to the way the visual system maps the world, testing whether they follow the eyes' retinotopic coordinates or coordinates fixed in the external world.

papers.title: When remembering less is more: Unfiltered items are associated with reduced memory fidelity in visual short-term memory
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (VSTM) exhibits capacity constraints that vary significantly across individuals and correlate with general cognitive metrics. This study investigated whether low-memory individuals' performance deficits stem from an inability to selectively encode only goal-relevant items, particularly when stimuli numbers exceed capacity. By varying set sizes in a change-detection paradigm and a continuous report task, the authors demonstrated that performance between low- and high-memory groups diverges specifically when memory limits are exceeded, even with task difficulty controlled. Mnemonic fidelity, as measured by the precision of representations in the continuous report task, was significantly reduced in low-capacity individuals under high load. These findings suggest that failing to filter irrelevant information leads to the storage of 'unfiltered' items, which subsequently degrades the quality and precision of the items maintained in memory.
papers.authors: Young Seon Shin, Summer L. Sheremata

papers.title: Behavioral asymmetries in visual short-term memory occur in retinotopic coordinates
papers.abstract: Visual short-term memory (VSTM) acts as a crucial buffer bridging perceptual discontinuities across interrupted sensory inputs, yet it remains severely capacity-limited due to architectural bottlenecks in underlying cortical networks. VSTM performance exhibits characteristic spatial biases that mirror neural hemispheric asymmetries associated with the visual field locus of remembered targets. Because sensory representations across early visual cortex are organized retinotopically, we examined whether spatial biases in memory performance are similarly locked to a retinotopic frame of reference rather than spatiotopic coordinates. Memory fidelity was assessed using a whole-display color change-detection paradigm across visual field quadrants while observers maintained either central fixation or eccentric fixation to displace retinal coordinates relative to monitor space. VSTM performance biases systematically tracked the retinal locus of the visual stimuli regardless of absolute screen coordinate positioning. These results indicate that spatial asymmetries governing VSTM retention operate in retinotopic coordinates, demonstrating an intrinsic dependence of behavioral visual working memory limits on retinotopically organized visual representations.
papers.authors: Summer Sheremata, George L. Malcolm, Sarah Shomstein

0643.name: Surya Gayet
0643.bio: Gayet is an Assistant Professor in Experimental Psychology at Utrecht University and the principal investigator of the CAP-Lab. Their research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms by which sensory input is transformed into conscious experience, focusing on the interplay between visual perception, attention, and working memory. Utilizing a multimodal approach including psychophysics, fMRI, and EEG, Gayet applies Rapid Invisible Frequency Tagging (RIFT) to track covert visuo-spatial attention. Their work explores how internal states—such as task goals, statistical learning, and mnemonic content—modulate neural responses to sensory information.
0643.research_direction: Dr. Gayet has recently been investigating how cognitive expectations—ranging from statistical regularities to anticipated task relevance—dynamically modulate early visual processing and conscious access. Using techniques like continuous flash suppression, EEG, and rapid invisible frequency tagging, their recent work explores how learned contextual probabilities influence which stimuli win the competition for awareness, and how the brain proactively prepares visual areas for memory-guided target selection. They are also examining the foundational mechanisms of attentional guidance, questioning whether commonly used spatial attention markers like alpha lateralization and gaze bias actually index the same underlying subprocesses, and testing whether visual search templates adaptively incorporate real-world viewing distances rather than strictly relying on retinal size. Additionally, their research extends into multisensory perception, using maximum-likelihood models to investigate how observers weigh, integrate, and prioritize auditory and visual information to track and localize moving targets during sensory occlusion.

papers.title: Independent Markers of Attentional Shifts
papers.abstract: In an EEG plus eye-tracking task (n = 23), the authors measured several proactive and reactive signatures of attending to a location: RIFT-based cortical excitability, alpha lateralization, gaze bias, probe-evoked ERPs and behavior. All markers tracked the attention manipulation, yet they did not correlate with one another, and only gaze bias predicted later behavior. Commonly used attention markers therefore are not interchangeable and likely index separable subprocesses.
papers.authors: Kabir Arora, Stefan Van der Stigchel, J. Leon Kenemans, Samson Chota, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Anticipated Relevance Prepares Visual Processing for Efficient Memory-Guided Selection
papers.abstract: Using EEG and rapid invisible frequency tagging, participants held an oriented grating in memory and then judged which of two sequential probes, cued as relevant, matched it. Relevant probes evoked stronger and more discriminable responses, and, crucially, visual responses at the empty probe location were already boosted before a relevant probe appeared. Predictable changes in relevance thus produce both proactive and reactive changes in visual processing that prepare the system for memory-guided selection.
papers.authors: Lasse Dietz, Christoph Strauch, Kabir Arora, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Samson Chota, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Using hearing and vision for motion prediction, motion perception, and localization
papers.abstract: Four experiments compared localization of auditory, visual and audiovisual moving targets to maximum-likelihood predictions. When targets were occluded, observers relied only on the modality not disrupted by the occluder and showed no multisensory precision gain for moving targets. A substantial benefit appeared for static audiovisual targets, showing near-optimal integration, so observers flexibly prioritize one sense in anticipation of modality-specific interference.
papers.authors: Yichen Yuan, Nathan Van der Stoep, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Statistical Learning Facilitates Access to Awareness
papers.abstract: Across several experiments (N = 153) using breaking continuous flash suppression and masking, objects that were statistically probable in a given context reached awareness faster and were localized more accurately than improbable ones. A preregistered accuracy-based version ruled out post-perceptual criterion shifts as an explanation. The results indicate that learned regularities change the competition for conscious access itself, tying statistical learning to the gating of consciousness.
papers.authors: Luzi Xu, Chris L. E. Paffen, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Surya Gayet

papers.title: Searching near and far: The attentional template incorporates viewing distance
papers.abstract: This study asks whether the template that guides visual search adapts to the expected viewing distance of the target, since an object's retinal size depends on how far away it is. Results indicate that search templates incorporate viewing distance rather than only fixed retinal size, so attentional guidance reflects the real-world scale of objects in depth.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Surya Gayet, Elisa Battistoni, Sushrut Thorat, Marius V. Peelen

0644.name: Susana T. L Chung
0644.bio: Chung’s research investigates the mechanisms of visual perception in individuals with normal and impaired vision, focusing on conditions such as age-related macular degeneration and amblyopia. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods, including signal detection theory and reversed-correlation, as well as neuroimaging techniques like functional MRI and Scanning Laser Ophthalmoscopy. By exploring the neural and optical limits of vision, Chung examines how the brain adapts to central vision loss through cortical plasticity. Their research aims to develop rehabilitative strategies, such as perceptual learning and oculomotor training, to improve reading speed and functional independence for patients with visual impairments.
0644.research_direction: Dr. Chung has recently been investigating the structural and functional mechanisms underlying visual impairments, with a strong clinical focus on amblyopia and central vision loss. Their recent work explores the behavioral limits of reading by testing whether healthy peripheral vision serves as a valid experimental model for patients with central scotomas. In the realm of amblyopia, they are examining the condition from multiple angles by quantifying retinal vasculature using deep-learning OCT segmentation and evaluating how abnormal eye movements impact visual performance. To better link structural and functional assessments across diverse eye disorders, they are developing automated multi-modal imaging pipelines that precisely co-register optical coherence tomography structural scans with microperimetry sensitivity maps. Additionally, their research extends into basic visual neuroscience, using EEG to isolate the frontoparietal connectivity and temporal-cortex dynamics that govern contour integration.

papers.title: Altered retinal vasculature in amblyopia
papers.abstract: Deep-learning segmentation of OCT fundus images was used to quantify retinal vessel area, fractal dimension, skeleton length and bifurcations in 23 adults with amblyopia and 40 controls. Amblyopic and fellow eyes did not differ from one another, but both showed altered vasculature relative to controls. The result challenges the view that amblyopia is purely cortical.
papers.authors: Rijul Saurabh Soans, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Is the Normal Periphery in Young Adults a Good Model for Reading in the Presence of Central Vision Loss?
papers.abstract: The study tests whether peripheral vision in healthy young adults is a valid stand-in for reading with central vision loss, a common assumption in the field. Reading speed versus print size was measured in 28 people with bilateral central vision loss and compared with matched-eccentricity normal peripheral data. Patients needed much larger print and read far slower (about 168 vs 397 words per minute), so normal periphery substantially underestimates their reading limits.
papers.authors: Susana T. L. Chung, Gordon E. Legge

papers.title: The impact of eye movements on amblyopic vision: A mini-review
papers.abstract: This review covers the kinds of abnormal eye movements seen in people with amblyopia and how they are measured. It discusses how these movements degrade visual performance, and whether they respond to amblyopia treatment or could serve as diagnostic markers.
papers.authors: Dennis M. Levi, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Unifying Structure and Function Towards a Comprehensive Macular Evaluation in Eye Disorders: A Multi-Modal Approach Using Microperimetry and Optical Coherence Tomography
papers.abstract: The paper presents an automated pipeline that registers microperimetry and OCT scanning-laser images so retinal layer thickness can be read out at the exact locations where visual sensitivity was tested. It combines feature-based and elastic registration with tracking-based quality checks, and was validated in adults with albinism, amblyopia, macular disease and healthy vision with excellent reliability.
papers.authors: Rijul Saurabh Soans, Benjamin E. Smith, Susana T. L. Chung

papers.title: Cortical Dynamics during Contour Integration
papers.abstract: EEG was recorded while contour onset time and contour fidelity were varied, separating grouping activity from generic visual evoked responses. A temporal-cortex N300 tracked contour integration, preceded by interhemispheric frontal-parietal connectivity linked to bottom-up attention and later medial frontal-parietal coupling tied to top-down processing.
papers.authors: Dongcheng He, Angeline Yang, Daniel R. Coates, Haluk Ogmen, Susana TL Chung

0645.name: Susanne Ferber
0645.bio: Susanne Ferber investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms mediating human visual awareness and the transition between perception and action. Their research employs a multimodal approach, integrating behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and EEG, alongside neuropsychological studies of patients with spatial neglect and simultanagnosia. Ferber's work examines the limits of visual working memory, the role of attentional templates in search, and the neural representation of visual cognition. Formerly the chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto, Ferber currently serves as the head of the Department of Psychology at Carnegie Mellon University.
0645.research_direction: Dr. Ferber has recently been studying what gets a visual stimulus into conscious awareness and how the details of what we see are held in mind. One line of their work uses a technique that hides an image from one eye, to test how quickly faces break into awareness depending on where the face is looking, including slightly downward gaze that has been little studied. Another line asks how memory for objects works during visual search, in particular whether people keep exemplar-specific details of the target or fall back on a shared category description when repeatedly searching for members of the same category.

papers.title: Object Details Persist in Visual Working Memory Regardless of Category Sufficiency for Search
papers.abstract: Examines whether the target representations used for visual search retain exemplar-specific details or shift to a shared category-based format when searching repeatedly for exemplars of the same category. Tests whether object details persist in visual working memory even when a category-level representation would suffice for the search task.
papers.authors: Ryan Williams, Joseph M. Saito, Keisuke Fukuda, Susanne Ferber

papers.title: Enhanced awareness of faces with slight downwards gaze in the breaking continuous flash suppression paradigm
papers.abstract: This study utilized the breaking continuous flash suppression (b-CFS) technique to investigate how vertical and horizontal gaze orientations influence the transition of facial stimuli from non-conscious processing into conscious visual awareness. While previous research has established a privileged status for direct gazes over horizontal averted gazes, vertical gaze deviations have remained largely unexplored. Participants performed a detection task followed by a gaze discrimination task for faces with downward, upward, leftward, rightward, and direct gazes rendered initially invisible through interocular suppression. The results demonstrated that detection times were significantly shorter for faces with downward gazes compared to all other gaze types, including direct gaze. Notably, while downward gazes were detected most rapidly, they were associated with lower discrimination accuracy relative to other orientations. These findings indicate that downward-tilted gazes enjoy prioritised access to conscious awareness, though this enhanced detectability does not translate to superior feature-level discrimination during pre-conscious processing.
papers.authors: Mayuna Ishida, Masaki Mori, Yingying Huang, Susanne Ferber

0647.name: T Rowan Candy
0647.bio: T. Rowan Candy is a Professor of Optometry and Vision Science at Indiana University who researches the mechanisms of typical and atypical visual development in human infants. Candy’s work focuses on how the developing brain coordinates visual experience with oculomotor responses to inform the management of conditions such as amblyopia and strabismus. Using optical modeling, neuroscience, and experimental psychology, Candy investigates the interaction between sensory input and motor output during the critical period of development. Recently, their lab has used egocentric imaging to characterize the visual statistics of naturalistic infant environments to identify the inputs that drive neural plasticity.
0647.research_direction: Dr. Candy has recently been investigating how the human visual system maintains binocular alignment and focus, particularly when challenged by sensory or optical degradation in children and adults. Using eye tracking and computationally simulated deficits, their recent work explores how reflex vergence is impacted by conditions like asymmetric blur, central scotomas, and restricted visual fields during the viewing of naturalistic scenes. Furthermore, they are examining the clinical dynamics of pediatric vision disorders to understand how specific conditions alter fundamental oculomotor responses. Through techniques like dynamic retinoscopy and simultaneous photorefraction, they assess accommodative accuracy during unilateral amblyopia therapy and investigate the neural coupling strategies used by patients to control intermittent exotropia.

papers.title: The Impact of Simulated Anisometropia and Bilateral Defocus on Reflex Vergence Responses of Children and Adults
papers.abstract: Computationally simulated blur was used to test how uncorrected anisometropia or monovision-style defocus affects the reflex vergence eye movements that keep the two eyes aligned, in adults and 4-8 year-old children. Vergence amplitude to disparity steps and tracking of random-walk disparity both declined with defocus, and unequal blur between the eyes was far more damaging than equal blur. In some participants the blurred eye was effectively ignored, so tracking was carried by the focused eye alone.
papers.authors: Clara Mestre, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: The Limitations on Vergence Responses to Naturalistic Images Resulting From Simulated Central Scotomas and Defocused Peripheral Retina
papers.abstract: Adults viewed natural images with simulated central scotomas of increasing radius, with or without added bilateral or unilateral defocus, while reflex vergence to disparity steps was recorded. Scotomas of about 10 degrees radius or larger reduced open-loop vergence amplitude, and unilateral defocus reduced it further while bilateral defocus did not. The data define how well the peripheral retina can drive eye alignment when central vision is lost or suppressed.
papers.authors: Bhagya L. Marella, Sonisha Neupane, Clara Mestre, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: Reflex maintenance of vergence eye alignment to small natural images is at risk for adults and young children
papers.abstract: Adults and 6-8 year-old children viewed dichoptic natural scenes whose radius ranged from 1 to 16 degrees, with disparity either stepping or drifting continuously. Continuous tracking held up until images shrank below about 3 degrees, whereas step-response amplitude and the range of disparities that drove a reflex response fell as images got smaller. When the disparity exceeded the reflex range, eyes drifted toward their dissociated heterophoria position, which suggests patients with peripheral field loss may struggle to realign the eyes.
papers.authors: Alyssa Bentz, Clara Mestre, Bhagya L. Marella, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: The repeatability of accommodative accuracy in childhood unilateral amblyopia
papers.abstract: Children with and without unilateral amblyopia had their monocular accommodation measured repeatedly within and across visits using dynamic retinoscopy while viewing naturalistic images at 25, 33 and 50 cm. Accommodative lag grew with stimulus demand, especially in amblyopic eyes with worse acuity, but the spread across repeated measures was under about 0.75 D and stable across visits. The result suggests children with amblyopia experience a consistent pattern of defocus during monocular amblyopia therapy.
papers.authors: Kristine Huang, Angela M. Chen, T. Rowan Candy

papers.title: Vergence and accommodation responses in the control of intermittent exotropia
papers.abstract: Simultaneous eye tracking and photorefraction were used to compare accommodation and vergence in children and young adults with different types of intermittent exotropia and in age-matched controls. Accommodation was similar between groups when eyes were aligned, and changed by less than 0.5 D when the eye deviated in most exotropes. Vergence-to-accommodation ratios were larger in exotropia, especially in some subtypes, indicating that patients use neural coupling between the two systems differently to keep the eyes aligned.
papers.authors: Clara Mestre, Sonisha Neupane, Vivian Manh, Kristina Tarczy-Hornoch, T. Rowan Candy

0648.name: T Scott Murdison
0648.bio: T. Scott Murdison is a Research Scientist at Meta Reality Labs Research studying the intersection of neuroscience, psychophysics, and immersive display technology. Their research examines oculomotor control, including smooth pursuit and saccadic eye movements, and how display properties such as temporal refresh rates and depth cues influence these behaviors. Murdison develops computational models to optimize gaze-based interaction and predict user performance based on eye-tracker specifications and environmental demands. Their work addresses perception-action dissociations in digital environments to inform the development of interfaces for augmented and virtual reality.
0648.research_direction: Dr. Murdison has recently been working on how human vision can guide the design of augmented reality displays. Their recent work explores how the eye's uneven sensitivity across the visual field can be used to dim virtual content in the periphery, saving power without hurting perceived image quality. They test this with psychophysical experiments on a stereoscopic setup, where virtual imagery is blended with real-world backgrounds at different contrast levels.

papers.title: Stereoscopic Brightness Roll‐Off in Augmented Reality
papers.abstract: The study investigates the perceptual and energy-saving efficacy of Brightness Roll-Off (BRO), a technique leveraging the human visual system's non-uniform contrast sensitivity across the visual field. Using stereoscopic AR simulations, researchers applied luminance reduction profiles to virtual foreground layers composited with real-world backgrounds across various additive contrast ratios (3:1, 6:1, and 9:1). Psychophysical evaluation using a haploscope demonstrated that peripheral brightness reduction has a negligible impact on perceived image quality and sensitivity, often performing better than predictions from established computational metrics. Analytical modeling suggests that implementing optimized BRO profiles can reduce display power consumption by 20% to 34% for microLED and LCoS display architectures, providing a viable strategy for enhancing battery efficiency in next-generation head-mounted displays without compromising the stereoscopic user experience.
papers.venue: Journal of the Society for Information Display
papers.authors: Domenic Au, Xiuyun Wu, Nava Aghdasi, Yuta Asano, T. Scott Murdison

0650.name: Taiki Fukiage
0650.department: Human Information Science Laboratory, Sensory Representation Research Group
0650.main_research_area: human visual perception and media technology
0650.bio: Taiki Fukiage is a Senior Research Scientist at NTT Communication Science Laboratories specializing in vision science and media engineering.
