Fukiage earned a Ph.D. from the University of Tokyo in 2015 and develops mathematical models of human visual information processing to optimize artificial displays, including AR and VR technologies. Their research includes visibility-based rendering techniques, the 'Deformation Lamps' projection system, and comparative analyses between human depth perception and deep neural network representations. Currently, Fukiage investigates how to align machine vision models with human perceptual biases to improve image naturalness and visual comfort.
0650.research_direction: Dr. Fukiage has recently been investigating the computational and ecological mechanisms of human depth perception by directly comparing human psychophysical data against deep neural networks. Their recent work explores whether state-of-the-art AI models inherently replicate human-like monocular depth biases, such as distance compression and lower-visual-field preferences, and probes whether algorithmic metric accuracy aligns with or diverges from human visual processing. In addition to computational benchmarking, they are also bridging basic visual psychophysics with applied display engineering. Specifically, their applied research examines how rendering subtle oculomotor cues like ocular parallax influences depth perception in virtual reality, and how the visual system's mechanisms of perceptual transparency can be leveraged to optimize image blending and mask physical screen boundaries in novel 3D monitor arrays.

papers.title: Accuracy Does Not Guarantee Human-Likeness: Cross-Domain Human-Centered Benchmark in Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: This work builds a behavioral benchmark for monocular depth estimation using human absolute-distance judgments on hundreds of KITTI outdoor and NYU indoor scenes, and evaluates 69 deep networks against it. Highly accurate models converged on similar residual error structures that stayed distinct from human ones, so metric accuracy and human-likeness turn out to be complementary, domain-sensitive properties. Human error patterns were consistent across observers while most models aligned with them less than expected.
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (v2, Aug 2026; earlier version titled 'Accuracy Does Not Guarantee Human-Likeness in Monocular Depth Estimators')
papers.authors: Yuki Kubota, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: Human-like monocular depth biases in deep neural networks
papers.abstract: The authors collected absolute depth judgments from people viewing natural indoor photographs and decomposed the errors into depth compression, per-image affine distortions and residual error. Humans showed consistent biases, such as compressed depth and treating the lower visual field as nearer. Deep networks with higher accuracy partly reproduced these biases, suggesting that such apparently suboptimal human errors may reflect efficient, ecologically adapted depth inference.
papers.authors: Yuki Kubota, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: BrickDisplay: Large, Protruding 3D Image Presentation From Multiple Non-Aligned Monitors With Perceptual Transparency
papers.abstract: BrickDisplay presents large 3D images that appear to protrude from a set of monitors that are not aligned with one another, by exploiting perceptual transparency so the physical screen boundaries and mismatches are less noticeable. It is an emerging-technology demonstration of perception-informed display design.
papers.authors: Yuri Mikawa, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: Low-Latency Ocular Parallax Rendering and Investigation of Its Effect on Depth Perception in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: The paper presents a very low-latency VR rendering pipeline that reproduces the small image shifts caused by eye rotation (ocular parallax). Using it, the authors test whether this cue actually affects perceived depth in virtual reality, linking display engineering with basic depth perception.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Yuri Mikawa, Taiki Fukiage

papers.title: A Content-adaptive Visibility Predictor for Perceptually Optimized Image Blending
papers.abstract: The visibility of one image semi-transparently overlaid on another depends strongly on both images' content. The authors developed a perceptual model that predicts the visibility of blended images with a content-adaptive weighting of spatial-frequency and colour features, trained on a large psychophysical experiment. They also use it to optimize opacity so viewers get a target visibility level, tested under practical conditions.
papers.authors: Taiki Fukiage, Takeshi Oishi

0651.name: Takeo Watanabe
0651.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0651.lab_name: Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning
0651.bio: Takeo Watanabe is the Fred M. Seed Professor of Cognitive and Linguistic Sciences at Brown University and conducts research on the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning (VPL). Watanabe documented task-irrelevant perceptual learning, showing that the human brain undergoes sensory plasticity through exposure to subliminal or unattended stimuli. Utilizing methodologies such as fMRI, real-time neurofeedback, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, their research investigates the roles of reinforcement signals, attention, and sleep in the consolidation and stabilization of visual memories. Watanabe examines how excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter balances within the visual cortex affect the window of brain plasticity and its susceptibility to interference.
0651.research_direction: Dr. Watanabe has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive mechanisms underlying visual perceptual learning (VPL) across a variety of internal states and clinical conditions. Their recent work explores how fundamental learning phenomena, such as top-down attentional suppression and retrograde interference, are influenced by whether a visual feature is a task-irrelevant natural scene or presented below conscious awareness. Using a combination of behavioral psychophysics, fMRI, EEG, and pupillometry, they are also examining how physiological factors—specifically hunger and varying reward values—alter error-sensitive neural networks and arousal responses during visual training. Furthermore, Dr. Watanabe is extending these plasticity inquiries into clinical vision science by mapping the divergent functional connectivity mechanisms that subserve identical face-processing training in healthy individuals versus patients with body dysmorphic disorder.

papers.title: Unsupervised visual learning is revealed for task-irrelevant natural scenes due to reduced attentional suppression effects in visual areas
papers.abstract: Shows that simply being exposed to task-irrelevant natural-scene images produces robust visual perceptual learning, whereas artificial images lacking the higher-order statistics of natural scenes do not. Behavior and fMRI indicate that unsupervised learning is normally suppressed by top-down attention, but natural-scene statistics escape this suppression, possibly because they reach visual areas outside the optimal window for attentional gating. The work reframes the long-running debate over whether passive exposure can drive VPL.
papers.authors: Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki, Tomoki Zama, Jonathan R. Matthews, Daiki Ogawa, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: Motivational state determines error-sensitive learning modes in visual perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study compares fasted and non-fasted participants performing an orientation discrimination task with identical reward contingencies. Both groups learned, but only fasted participants showed heightened accuracy after errors, tied to different neural signatures: reduced ventral striatal prediction-error activity under fasting versus reduced dorsolateral prefrontal engagement under satiety. Error-related responses in dorsal anterior cingulate and V1 tracked individual improvement, showing that internal state shapes how perceptual learning is expressed.
papers.authors: Dongho Kim, Zhiyan Wang, Masamichi Sakagami, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Reward evokes value-independent arousal and value-dependent reinforcement processing as dissociable physiological consequences
papers.abstract: Reward is often assumed to drive value-dependent reinforcement, but it may only raise arousal. By varying thirst to change reward value while separately inducing arousal with sound, the authors recorded pupil size and EEG. Pupil dilation was equal for high- and low-value rewards, indicating value-independent arousal, whereas only high-value reward produced an anterior-to-posterior progression of alpha power, showing that reward has two dissociable physiological consequences.
papers.authors: Yuki Nakashima, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Conscious awareness determines whether a second learning session disrupts or facilitates earlier learning
papers.abstract: Retrograde interference, where a second training session degrades a just-acquired skill, is usually treated as a universal feature of learning. The authors find that when the trained visual feature is subthreshold and thus outside awareness, the second session does not disrupt but instead facilitates the earlier learning. Conscious awareness of the trained feature therefore decides whether interactions between successive learning episodes are destructive or beneficial.
papers.authors: Patrick Bruns, Kazuhisa Shibata, Takeo Watanabe

papers.title: Learning of the same task subserved by substantially different mechanisms between patients with body dysmorphic disorder and healthy individuals
papers.abstract: Patients with body dysmorphic disorder and healthy controls were trained on detecting low-spatial-frequency faces while undergoing fMRI before and after training. Both groups improved similarly, yet fusiform face area responses rose after training in patients but fell in controls, and interhemispheric FFA connectivity moved in opposite directions. The same behavioral learning thus rests on fundamentally different neural mechanisms in this psychiatric population.
papers.authors: Zhiyan Wang, Qingleng Tan, Sebastian M. Frank, Yuka Sasaki, David Sheinberg, Katharine A. Phillips, Takeo Watanabe

0653.name: Talia Konkle
0653.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Brain Science
0653.main_research_area: cognitive and neural organization of vision
0653.bio: Talia Konkle is a Professor of Psychology at Harvard University and an associate faculty member at the Kempner Institute, specializing in the functional architecture of the human visual system. Konkle’s research uses behavioral psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling to map the representational geometry of high-level visual experiences onto the cortical surface. Their work investigates the large-scale topographic organization of object knowledge, specifically the roles of real-world size and animacy in shaping neural responses. Konkle also bridges biological and artificial intelligence by using deep neural networks to study the computational pressures that drive representation learning and cortical specialization.
0653.research_direction: Dr. Konkle has recently been investigating the computational principles that shape high-level visual representation across biological brains and artificial networks. Their recent work explores how different inductive biases—such as self-supervised contrastive objectives and dataset richness—might drive the emergence of brain-like feature spaces and category-selective topographical modules in vision models. To push beyond standard encoding metrics, they are testing these models by generating precisely parameterized stimuli for closed-loop macaque experiments to observe how well different network axes can actively control neural firing. Additionally, their research spans both advanced machine learning interpretability, where they are developing archetypal sparse autoencoders to extract stable concept dictionaries from large models, and novel human neuroimaging paradigms that examine how ultra-wide-angle, immersive displays alter cortical scene processing.

papers.title: Parametric neural control differentiates top neural network models of primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Top encoding models predict macaque visual cortex about equally well on natural images, so the paper tests whether they parameterize image space alike. Each model's fitted encoding axis is converted into graded stimulus perturbations (axis-aligned feature accentuation), and over 27,500 such stimuli are shown to five macaques in closed-loop experiments. Models differ strongly in controlling neural firing, adversarially trained ones do best, and control is better predicted by the spatial-frequency structure of input gradients than by robustness.
papers.authors: Jacob S. Prince, Binxu Wang, Thomas Fel, Akshay V. Jagadeesh, Parisa A. Vaziri, George A. Alvarez, Margaret S. Livingstone, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders used to interpret vision models are shown to be unstable, with near-identical training setups yielding different concept dictionaries. The authors constrain dictionary atoms to lie within the convex hull of the data, an archetypal-analysis approach, which greatly improves stability across seeds while preserving reconstruction quality and concept interpretability. They also introduce evaluation benchmarks for concept-extraction quality.
papers.authors: Thomas Fel, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Jacob S. Prince, Matthew Kowal, Victor Boutin, Isabel Papadimitriou, Binxu Wang, Martin Wattenberg, Demba E. Ba, Talia Konkle

papers.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
papers.abstract: The authors run controlled comparisons across 224 vision models to test how architecture, training objective and dataset shape how well model representations predict human visual cortex responses. Architecture (CNN vs transformer) and model size matter little, whereas the task objective and the richness of the training data matter substantially, with contrastive and language-aligned objectives doing well. The work provides a large-scale map of which inductive biases drive brain alignment in high-level visual cortex.
papers.authors: Colin Conwell, Jacob S. Prince, Kendrick N. Kay, George A. Alvarez, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Contrastive learning explains the emergence and function of visual category-selective regions
papers.abstract: The paper proposes contrastive coding as a way to reconcile modular and distributed accounts of category-selective regions in ventral visual cortex. In networks trained with self-supervised contrastive objectives on natural images, units selective for faces, bodies, scenes and words emerge, cluster spatially when topography is imposed, and match human fMRI selectivity. Lesioning these units yields specialized deficits, tying selectivity to functional relevance.
papers.authors: Jacob S. Prince, George A. Alvarez, Talia Konkle

papers.title: Immersive scene representation in human visual cortex with ultra-wide-angle neuroimaging
papers.abstract: The study introduces an fMRI setup using angled mirrors and a curved screen to show scenes spanning 175 degrees of visual field, far beyond the usual 10-15 degrees. Immersive wide-field scenes engage medial cortex with far-peripheral preference and scene-selective regions in ways not seen with standard-size displays. The results show that the scale and immersiveness of viewing changes cortical scene representation.
papers.authors: Jeongho Park, Edward Soucy, Jennifer Segawa, Ross Mair, Talia Konkle

0654.name: Tao Gao
0654.department: Department of Statistics and Department of Communication
0654.bio: Tao Gao is an Associate Professor at UCLA whose research focuses on the mechanisms of human intuitive social commonsense. By integrating psychophysical experiments with computational modeling, Gao investigates how humans perceive social concepts such as animacy, intentionality, and agency from sparse visual stimuli. Their work extends into the development of communicative artificial intelligence and robotics, aiming to implement human-like social reasoning to facilitate human-machine collaboration. Before this appointment, Gao completed a PhD in cognitive psychology at Yale University and a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT’s Center for Brains, Minds and Machines.
0654.research_direction: Dr. Gao has recently been investigating the cognitive and computational mechanisms underlying intention, commitment, and communication during complex social interactions. Using interactive behavioral paradigms and Bayesian theory-of-mind modeling, their recent work explores how people sustain commitment to specific goals—both individually when navigating conflicting momentary desires, and collectively when groups must coordinate on a shared target like hunting prey. They are also actively studying intention inference in non-verbal and sparse communication, asking how observers distinguish communicative pantomimes from purely instrumental actions, and how cooperating individuals decide what information is most relevant to share in real time with human or AI partners. By comparing human psychophysical data against reinforcement learning agents and large language models, Dr. Gao seeks to formally define the complex, shared mental states that enable spontaneous human coordination.

papers.title: Spontaneous coordination with self-commitment: How the presence of others alters the strength, goal and timing of commitment
papers.abstract: Asks why people commit firmly to a chosen goal, and shows that social context shapes this even in individual tasks. Across four game-like experiments (alone, beside an RL agent, beside another human, or with a passive observer), any social presence increased commitment, and people spontaneously inferred a co-actor's goal and avoided it. Bayesian theory-of-mind modelling suggests people delay revealing their intentions when a potential partner is present, rather than being affected by mere presence.
papers.authors: Shaozhe Cheng, Jingyin Zhu, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Tao Gao

papers.title: Joint commitment in human cooperative hunting through an 'imagined we'
papers.abstract: Tests how groups keep a shared commitment to one target when several goals are available, using a multi-player hunting game with psychophysics and computational modelling. An 'imagined we' model, in which each agent infers the intention of a supra-individual agent controlling the whole team, is compared with a reward-sharing model. Humans and the imagined-we model, but not reward sharing, sustained high performance by jointly committing to one prey, supporting a shared-agency account of cooperation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Ning Tang, Siyi Gong, Minglu Zhao, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Tao Gao

papers.title: Communicating Through Acting: Affording Communicative Intention in Pantomimes
papers.abstract: Examines how observers recognize a communicative gesture (pantomime) even though it looks kinematically like an instrumental action on an object. Two hypotheses are contrasted, that instrumental and communicative intention compete versus that instrumental intention is nested inside communicative intention, using a video dataset of action-object pairs of varying corpus frequency. Results and modelling favor the nested account, linking pantomime to how people infer intentions in communication.
papers.authors: Siyi Gong, Kaiwen Jiang, Jessica G. Li, Mireille Karadanaian, Ziyi Meng, Tao Gao

papers.title: A relevance model of human sparse communication in cooperation
papers.abstract: Proposes a model of how people pick the few pieces of information worth communicating in real time, based on 'relevance' from decision theory combined with theory of mind. In a navigation task where humans and an AI agent help each other avoid traps, the model accurately predicts which trap humans choose to warn about and outperforms GPT-4 playing the same role.
papers.authors: Kaiwen Jiang, Boxuan Jiang, Anahita Sadaghdar, Rebekah Limb, Tao Gao

papers.title: Intention beyond desire: Spontaneous intentional commitment regulates conflicting desires
papers.abstract: Investigates how people stick to a partially specified plan instead of following whichever desire is momentarily strongest. In sequential decision tasks with conflicting goals, participants spontaneously formed an intentional commitment that regulated competing desires, a pattern that purely reward-driven agents do not capture. The work positions commitment as a distinct mental state separate from desire.
papers.authors: Shaozhe Cheng, Minglu Zhao, Ning Tang, Yang Zhao, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Tao Gao

0655.name: Taosheng Liu
0655.lab_name: Neuroimaging of Perception and Attention Laboratory (NPAL)
0655.bio: Liu investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of visual selective attention, working memory, and perceptual decision-making. Their research employs a multimodal approach, integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) with behavioral psychophysics. A primary focus of Liu’s work involves examining how the brain prioritizes task-relevant information during sensory competition and how these selection processes guide subsequent actions and memory consolidation.
0655.research_direction: Dr. Liu has recently been studying how attention prepares the brain to select particular visual features such as a color or a direction of motion. Their recent work uses EEG, including frequency-tagged flickering stimuli and decoding of brain signals, to ask whether preparing to attend to a feature boosts responses across the whole visual field before anything appears, and how costly it is to hold several color targets in mind at once. They have also examined how strongly stored sensory templates guide selection during sustained attention, and how attention selects simple objects based on shape similarity. Another thread asks how visual attention biases decisions between options, using computational choice models.

papers.title: Preparatory attention to visual features spreads globally
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the global spread of feature-based attention (FBA) — which enhances neural responses to attended features across the entire visual field — occurs during the preparatory period before stimulus onset. Using EEG and frequency-tagging via flickering dot fields, the researchers measured frequency-specific visual-evoked responses in participants cued to attend to specific colors or motion patterns. Results demonstrated that preparatory attention to a specific feature significantly facilitated responses at task-irrelevant locations, even in conditions where the attended-side stimulus onset was delayed. These findings suggest that the global spread of FBA is an endogenous mechanism that biases feature processing in anticipation of incoming sensory inputs, supporting its functional role in guided visual search.
papers.authors: Melisa Menceloglu, Søren K. Andersen, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: Shape-similarity gain: A selection profile for simple objects
papers.abstract: Proposes and tests a shape-similarity gain profile describing how object-based attention selects simple objects.
papers.authors: Brendan Valentine, Xiaoli Zhang, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: Cost of maintaining attentional templates for multiple colors revealed by EEG decoding
papers.abstract: The research examines the behavioral and neurophysiological constraints of maintaining multiple feature-based attentional templates. Participants performed a color-coherence detection task with varying numbers of color cues (one, two, or three) while EEG was recorded. Multivariate decoding of target colors from posterior electrode signals revealed that decoding accuracy was significantly reduced when multiple colors were attended compared to a single color. Behavioral performance showed parallel declines in accuracy and reaction time for multi-cue trials. The robust correlation between neural decoding deficits and behavioral performance suggests that maintaining multiple active attentional templates incurs a significant capacity cost, effectively limiting the brain's ability to enhance sensory representations of multiple features simultaneously.
papers.authors: Melisa Menceloglu, Sari Sadiya, Susan M. Ravizza, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: The guiding strength of sensory templates during preparatory stage of sustained feature-based attention
papers.abstract: Examines how strongly sensory templates guide selection during the preparatory period of sustained feature-based attention.
papers.authors: Xiaoli Zhang, Taosheng Liu

papers.title: Attention biases preferential choice by enhancing an option's value
papers.abstract: Tests whether visual attention shifts preferential choice by increasing the subjective value of the attended option, using attention manipulations combined with computational choice modeling.
papers.authors: Timothy J. Pleskac, Shuli Yu, Sergej Grunevski, Taosheng Liu

0656.name: Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil
0656.institution: Baruch College, City University of New York
0656.bio: Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil investigates the cognitive and neural mechanisms of human vision, focusing on the interactions between attention, awareness, and memory. Emmanouil’s research integrates behavioral psychophysics with neuroimaging and neurostimulation methods, such as fMRI, EEG, and TMS, to study how visual information is summarized and stored. Their work includes research on ensemble coding—the statistical representation of visual groups—and investigations into visual processing occurring outside the focus of conscious awareness. Emmanouil also examines the neural substrates of visual working memory and the functional roles of the primary visual cortex and posterior parietal cortex in perception.
0656.research_direction: Dr. Emmanouil has recently been studying how people form quick first impressions of trustworthiness from faces and voices, particularly for virtual and conversational agents. Their recent work explores how visual cues, such as facial appearance, and auditory cues, such as tone of voice and spoken language, are combined, and how much weight each carries when they agree or conflict. The aim is to understand which nonverbal and linguistic signals lead people to trust an artificial agent, with implications for designing conversational interfaces.

papers.title: Beyond Face Value: Visual and Auditory Signals in Human and Machine Trust Judgments
papers.abstract: This study explores how bimodal visual and auditory cues interact to shape rapid human judgments of trustworthiness in the context of conversational agents. Using a behavioral experiment with 150 participants, the researchers manipulated face and voice stimuli across four trust congruence conditions to determine the relative weighting of each modality. Findings indicate that while both facial and vocal signals contribute significantly to first impressions, their integration is mandatory and resistant to instructions to ignore a specific channel. The paper analyzes the specific acoustic-prosodic and visual features that correlate with perceived trustworthiness and discusses the implications for designing multimodal virtual agents.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 7th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI 2025)
papers.authors: Natalia Tyulina, Yuwen Yu, Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil, Sarah Ita Levitan

papers.title: Understanding Linguistic and Visual Factors that Affect Human Trust Perception of Virtual Agents
papers.abstract: The authors investigate the interdisciplinary relationship between spoken linguistic cues and visual facial signals in the formation of trust toward virtual agents. Through a crowdsourced perception study, the research analyzes how users evaluate agent trustworthiness when presented with multimodal audio-visual pairs. The study identifies specific nonverbal behaviors and auditory signals that serve as indicators of trust, highlighting the importance of cross-modal consistency in interface design. The results suggest that multimodal factors interact in complex ways to influence user engagement and satisfaction, with implications for assistive robotics and psychological assessment tools.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 6th ACM Conference on Conversational User Interfaces (CUI 2024)
papers.authors: Natalia Tyulina, Tatiana Aloi Emmanouil, Sarah Ita Levitan

0657.name: Teng Leng Ooi
0657.bio: Teng Leng Ooi is a Professor in the College of Optometry at The Ohio State University, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying binocular vision and 3D space perception. Ooi’s research focuses on how the brain integrates sensory visual information with cognitive factors and motor signals to guide actions in natural, virtual, and augmented reality environments. Ooi developed the 'Push-Pull' perceptual learning protocol and video game-based therapies aimed at reducing sensory eye dominance and restoring stereopsis in individuals with amblyopia and strabismus. Their work utilizes psychophysical methods and optical imaging to explore the neural circuitry of binocular rivalry and suppression.
0657.research_direction: Dr. Ooi has recently been investigating the mechanisms of human space perception alongside the clinical assessment of amblyopia. In the realm of depth perception, their recent work explores how the visual system computes absolute distance at intermediate ranges and during self-motion, examining how cues like angular declination, binocular disparity, and temporal sampling interact with the brain's internal model of the ground surface. Parallel to this psychophysical research, they are investigating objective, quantitative methods to characterize binocular dysfunction in clinical populations. Specifically, they are using optical coherence tomography to measure how foveal fixation error relates to visual acuity loss, and they are adapting clinical tools like the Synoptophore to precisely quantify the depth of interocular suppression in amblyopic eyes.

papers.title: Absolute Distance Discrimination in the Intermediate Distance Mediated by Angular Declination/Elevation and Binocular Disparity Cues
papers.abstract: Tests how well observers can tell apart the absolute distances of targets lying a few to tens of meters away, a range where most depth cues are weak. The study identifies angular declination (or elevation) relative to the horizon and binocular disparity as the cues that carry this discrimination, and shows how they combine. It extends the lab's ground-surface-based model of egocentric distance to a natural-environment range that is rarely studied.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Perception of distance during self-motion depends on the brain's internal model of the terrain
papers.abstract: Examines how people judge how far away a target is while they are walking. Results indicate that the brain relies on an internal representation of the ground surface as a reference frame during self-motion, so distance judgments shift when that terrain model is altered or unreliable. The work links self-motion signals to the ground-based distance-coding scheme the group has developed.
papers.authors: Liu Zhou, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Determining fixation accuracy with optical coherence tomography and its implication on visual acuity in amblyopia
papers.abstract: Uses optical coherence tomography imaging to measure where the fovea is aligned relative to the fixation target in amblyopic and normal eyes, giving an objective estimate of fixation accuracy. Fixation error is then related to the reduced visual acuity seen in amblyopia. The result suggests eccentric or unstable fixation contributes to acuity loss and offers a clinically usable measurement approach.
papers.authors: Maureen D. Plaumann, Wei Wei, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Factors Affecting Stimulus Duration Threshold for Depth Discrimination of Asynchronous Targets in the Intermediate Distance Range
papers.abstract: Measures how long a pair of targets must be viewed, when shown one after the other in a real environment, before their depth order at a few to tens of meters can be discriminated. Viewing-duration thresholds depend on the available ground texture and cues, revealing how much sampling time the visual system needs to build a ground-based distance representation.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Refining Clinical Quantification of Depth of Suppression in Amblyopia through Synoptophore Measurement
papers.abstract: Extends the clinical Synoptophore, normally used for qualitative assessment, into a quantitative tool by systematically manipulating illumination to find the balance at which the two eyes fuse. In previously treated adult amblyopes, the protocol yields a numerical measure of how deeply the weaker eye is suppressed, which can be tracked across treatment. It provides a practical bridge between basic binocular-suppression research and clinical care.
papers.authors: Maureen D. Plaumann, Krista L. Roberts, Wei Wei, Chao Han, Teng Leng Ooi

0658.name: Tessa Dekker
0658.department: Institute of Ophthalmology and Experimental Psychology
0658.bio: Tessa Dekker is a Professor of Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience who researches how the human brain learns to perceive and interact with the world during development. Dekker's work explores the intersection of genetics, neural plasticity, and environmental experience to understand typical visual development and the impact of eye disease. By combining behavioral psychophysics with functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, Dekker characterizes sensory-motor integration. Their research evaluates mechanisms of sight recovery and neural adaptation following treatments such as gene therapy for inherited retinal diseases.
0658.research_direction: Dr. Dekker's recent work explores visual plasticity, developmental trajectories, and clinical assessment across the lifespan. They have recently been using fMRI and population receptive field mapping to investigate how the visual cortex adapts to congenital sight impairments like achromatopsia, alongside developing novel, fixation-independent neuroimaging methods to map contrast sensitivity in patients with severe vision loss. In parallel, their developmental research tracks the slow fine-tuning of spatial vision, measuring how foveal acuity, crowding, and the ability to use stored prior knowledge to decipher ambiguous images mature from childhood into adulthood. Finally, they are examining how sensory signals and prior expectations interact in older age by testing lifespan changes in susceptibility to flicker-induced complex visual hallucinations.

papers.title: Hierarchical cortical plasticity in congenital sight impairment
papers.abstract: The authors compare the rod-only visual system of people with congenital achromatopsia to the rod system of typically sighted people to ask which parts of visual cortex adapt to lifelong altered input and which stay fixed. Early visual cortex (V1) showed stability, with no retinotopic remapping and structural signs of deprivation. Plasticity instead appeared in how higher-order cortex reads out these inputs, in a pattern that could offset the lower resolution and missing foveal input of a rod-only system.
papers.authors: Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Mahtab Farahbakhsh, Nicholas Hedger, Andrew T. Rider, Elaine J. Anderson, Geraint Rees, Tomas Knapen, Michel Michaelides, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Mapping Visual Contrast Sensitivity and Vision Loss Across the Visual Field with Model-Based fMRI
papers.abstract: The paper introduces an fMRI method that estimates contrast sensitivity across the whole visual field without needing precise fixation, which is hard for patients with severe sight loss. It combines large-field stimuli varying in spatial frequency and contrast with population receptive field mapping or an anatomical retinotopic atlas, and models sensitivity in visual cortex. The approach recovers vision loss in patients and offers a fixation-independent objective measure of visual function.
papers.authors: Hugo T. Chow-Wing-Bom, Matteo Lisi, Noah C. Benson, Freya Lygo-Frett, Patrick Yu-Wai-Man, Frederic Dick, Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: The development of visual acuity and crowding reveals the slow fine-tuning of foveal vision
papers.abstract: The study tracks how fine spatial resolution (acuity) and sensitivity to clutter (crowding) develop across childhood into adulthood. Both continue to refine well past early childhood, indicating slow fine-tuning of foveal vision rather than early maturation. The results link the development of these measures and constrain accounts of what limits children's spatial vision.
papers.authors: John A. Greenwood, Marilia Kyprianou, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Reduced susceptibility to experimentally-induced complex visual hallucinations with age
papers.abstract: Using a flicker-induced (Ganzflicker) hallucination paradigm, the authors measured how readily younger and older adults experience complex visual hallucinations. Contrary to the idea that ageing increases such experiences, older adults reported them less often. The work bears on how prior knowledge and sensory signals combine across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Oris Shenyan, Laura Haye, Georgia A. Milne, Matteo Lisi, John A. Greenwood, Jeremy I. Skipper, Tessa M. Dekker

papers.title: Perceptual reorganization from prior knowledge emerges late in childhood
papers.abstract: Children of different ages viewed degraded two-tone images before and after seeing the original photographs, to test how prior knowledge changes recognition. The boost in recognition after cueing developed late, emerging only in later childhood. The work shows that using stored knowledge to reinterpret ambiguous input is a slowly maturing capacity.
papers.authors: Georgia A. Milne, Matteo Lisi, Aisha McLean, Rosie Zheng, Iris I.A. Groen, Tessa M. Dekker

0661.name: Thomas C. Sprague
0661.lab_name: Perception, Cognition, and Action Lab (PCA Lab)
0661.main_research_area: computational neuroimaging of vision and attention
0661.bio: Thomas C. Sprague is an Assistant Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the Principal Investigator of the Perception, Cognition, and Action (PCA) Lab. Sprague’s research investigates how top-down behavioral goals, such as visual attention and working memory, transform neural representations of sensory information across cortical networks. Using functional MRI, EEG, and computational techniques like inverted encoding models, they reconstruct and quantify the fidelity of these representations. Their work examines the neural architecture of priority maps and how the brain maintains stable information about the environment to support goal-directed actions.
0661.research_direction: Dr. Sprague has recently been investigating how the human visual system prioritizes and maintains information during spatial attention and working memory tasks. Using fMRI combined with computational approaches like inverted encoding models, their recent work explores the neural architecture of priority maps in retinotopic cortex, specifically asking how they encode multiple simultaneously attended locations and whether these spatial maps are feature-specific for dimensions like color and motion. They are also examining how top-down task goals dynamically reweight these feature representations to guide attention across the visual field. Additionally, their research probes the mechanics of visual working memory, asking how frontoparietal and visual regions allocate limited neural resources to items based on behavioral priority and testing whether sustained spatial memory codes are vulnerable to disruption from task-irrelevant visual distractors.

papers.title: Retinotopic Spatial Working Memory Representations Are Not Affected by Task-irrelevant Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: The study asks whether a brief, irrelevant visual input during a spatial working memory delay disrupts the stored representation. Using fMRI and an inverted encoding model, the authors found that an interrupting stimulus did not measurably degrade memory representations in retinotopic cortex, nor behavioral performance, indicating that sustained WM codes are robust to intervening visual events.
papers.authors: Kelvin Vu-Cheung, Edward F. Ester, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Neural priority maps encode behavioral relevance independently across multiple attended locations
papers.abstract: fMRI participants monitored zero, one, or two peripheral locations while retinotopic priority maps were reconstructed with an inverted encoding model. Relevance-related enhancement at each attended location was the same whether one or two locations were cued, with no attenuation when more locations were relevant, and modulations were spatially focal. This supports a categorical, independent encoding of behavioral relevance in priority maps rather than a shared-capacity account.
papers.authors: Amelia H. Harrison, Daniel D. Thayer, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Neural mechanisms of resource allocation in working memory
papers.abstract: Working memory capacity is limited, so the brain must decide how much resource to give each remembered item depending on its priority. Combining fMRI with computational modeling, the study shows that the strength and precision of item representations in retinotopic visual and frontoparietal cortex scale with an item's behavioral priority, with the strongest prioritization signals in prefrontal and parietal cortex. The results link a normative resource-allocation account to specific cortical population codes.
papers.authors: Hsin-Hung Li, Thomas C. Sprague, Aspen H. Yoo, Wei Ji Ma, Clayton E. Curtis

papers.title: Attention Modulates Stimulus Representations in Neural Feature Dimension Maps
papers.abstract: The authors test whether feature-responsive visual cortex forms spatial 'feature dimension maps' that are reweighted by task goals. Participants attended to either the color or the motion of a peripheral stimulus during fMRI; the stimulus representation was enhanced in color-selective regions when color was attended and in motion-selective regions when motion was attended. Enhancement was spatially local in color regions but more global in motion regions, supporting dynamic reweighting of feature maps to guide attention.
papers.authors: Daniel D. Thayer, Thomas C. Sprague

papers.title: Feature-Specific Salience Maps in Human Cortex
papers.abstract: Human visual cortex is known to contain spatial maps of stimulus salience, but it was unclear whether these maps are feature-specific. Using fMRI and an inverted encoding model, the authors reconstructed spatial maps from retinotopic regions preferring different features (color, motion) while people viewed stimuli that varied in salience along those features. Color-selective and motion-selective regions each tracked the salience of their preferred feature, supporting a set of feature-specific maps that could be combined into overall priority.
papers.authors: Daniel D. Thayer, Thomas C. Sprague

0662.name: Thomas M. Spalek
0662.lab_name: Spalek Laboratory of Attention, Memory and Perception
0662.bio: Thomas M. Spalek is a Professor of Psychology at Simon Fraser University and the director of the Spalek Laboratory of Attention, Memory and Perception. Spalek’s research examines the cognitive mechanisms of visual attention and memory, specifically investigating phenomena such as the attentional blink and inhibition of return. Using electroencephalography (EEG), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and high-fidelity driving simulators, Spalek addresses theoretical models of human information processing and their practical applications in real-world contexts. Their work includes collaborative research on re-entrant visual pathways and their role in conscious perception.
0662.research_direction: Dr. Spalek has recently been studying how emotional faces affect attention and perception, with a focus on separating emotional meaning from low-level visual features. Using simple schematic faces, their recent experiments test whether effects of emotion on reaction times, ratings, and the breadth of attention come from arousal, valence, or plain perceptual differences such as eyebrow shape. They have also been thinking about theory, arguing that models of visual processing need repeated feedback between processing levels rather than a single feedforward sweep.

papers.title: Arousal and Valence Have Dissociable Effects on Responses to Schematic Emotional Faces
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether the observed behavioral asymmetries in response to emotional faces are driven by affective meaning or by differences in perceptual complexity. Using schematic faces in a flanker paradigm, the researchers manipulated stimulus-driven arousal (e.g., presence of eyebrows) and emotional valence. The experiments reveal that arousal and valence produce dissociable effects on reaction times and subjective evaluative ratings. High-arousal features like v-shaped eyebrows facilitate rapid detection but do not necessarily modulate flanker interference patterns, suggesting that perceptual saliency and emotional meaning affect face processing at distinct stages of evaluation and structural encoding.
papers.venue: Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology / Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale
papers.authors: Regard M. Booy, Nadja Jankovic, Thomas M. Spalek

papers.title: Need for cross-level iterative re-entry in models of visual processing
papers.authors: Thomas M. Spalek, Unnikrishnan, Vincent Di Lollo

papers.title: Dissociating affective and perceptual effects of schematic faces on attentional scope
papers.abstract: Experiments testing whether emotional schematic faces alter attentional scope through affective content versus low-level perceptual features. Aims to separate affective from perceptual contributions.
papers.venue: Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology / Revue canadienne de psychologie expérimentale
papers.authors: Regard M. Booy, Anna J. Maslany, Kristen M. Thompson, Thomas M. Spalek

0663.name: Thérèse Collins
0663.bio: Collins is a Professor at Université Paris Cité and a researcher at the Integrative Neuroscience and Cognition Center (INCC). Their research investigates the mechanisms of visual perception and motor control, focusing on how the brain maintains a stable visual experience despite constant eye movements. Using psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG), Collins explores topics such as trans-saccadic integration, serial dependence, and the impact of motor planning on perceptual processing. Their work provides technical analysis of how sensory information is transformed into stable internal representations of objects and scenes.
0663.research_direction: Dr. Collins has recently been investigating the mechanisms that underlie visual stability, focusing heavily on how perceptual history and serial dependence shape current perception. Using behavioral psychophysics, EEG, and representational similarity analysis, their recent work explores whether temporal carry-over effects operate on low-level physical properties or abstract categorical representations, as well as what drives past stimuli to either attract or repel current perceptual estimates. Beyond temporal dynamics, they are developing innovative methods to map representational geometry, using eye-movement scanpaths during visual search as an implicit measure of how observers structure object similarity. Furthermore, their lab has extended these neural decoding and representational techniques beyond low-level vision into social cognition, investigating how the brain encodes abstract stereotype dimensions like warmth and competence.

papers.title: Serial Dependence operates on categorical rather than physical representations: evidence from behavior and EEG
papers.abstract: Serial dependence is the pull of current perception toward what was seen a moment ago. This work asks whether the carried-over signal reflects physical stimulus properties or abstract categories, by combining behavioral tests with EEG. The results indicate that the history effect operates mainly on categorical representations rather than on the physical stimulus, refining what the visual system carries across time to stabilize perception.
papers.authors: Pierre Costa, Thérèse Collins

papers.title: Eye movements reveal representational geometry
papers.abstract: The paper develops scanpaths in visual search as an implicit measure of how similar observers find objects, avoiding explicit similarity judgments and dual-task interference. Fixations on distractors are validated with representational similarity analysis against an odd-one-out task and against independent similarity ratings, and geometries agree across tasks. A generative model also predicts first fixations in new data, opening a route to test how representations vary with task demands.
papers.authors: Thérèse Collins

papers.title: Attractive and repulsive history effects in categorical and continuous estimates of orientation perception
papers.abstract: Recent stimuli can attract or repel current judgments, and the direction of the bias depends on how the observer reports. This study compares categorical and continuous orientation estimates, varying the task to show when attraction versus repulsion arises. The findings help reconcile conflicting results in the serial dependence literature by tying the sign of history effects to the type of response.
papers.authors: Mert Can, Thérèse Collins

papers.title: The neural representation of stereotype content
papers.abstract: This EEG study examines how the brain represents the social dimensions of warmth and competence used in stereotypes. It decodes stereotype content from neural activity while participants judge social groups. The work extends the lab's perceptual-representation methods to social cognition.
papers.authors: Thérèse Collins, Emilie Zhu, Patrick Rateau

papers.title: The Representational Similarity between Visual Perception and Recent Perceptual History
papers.abstract: The study uses representational similarity analysis to ask whether the way the brain represents a current stimulus resembles how it represents the recent stimulus history that biases it. Behavior and neural patterns show that perception and perceptual history share representational structure. This links serial dependence to the perceptual representations it acts on.
papers.authors: Junlian Luo, Thérèse Collins

0664.name: Tijl Grootswagers
0664.department: MARCS Institute for Brain, Behaviour and Development; School of Computer, Data and Mathematical Sciences
0664.bio: Tijl Grootswagers is an ARC DECRA Senior Research Fellow focusing on the temporal dynamics of visual object recognition and the neural mechanisms of human perception. Grootswagers utilizes multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and machine learning to decode information from time-series neuroimaging data, specifically EEG, MEG, and fMRI. Their research investigates how the brain transforms sensory inputs into conceptual representations and examines the relationship between neural coding and behavioral decision-making. Recently, their work has expanded to include the neural representation of AI-generated content and the development of open-source methodologies for neuroimaging analysis.
0664.research_direction: Dr. Grootswagers has recently been using time-resolved EEG decoding to investigate the millisecond-by-millisecond temporal dynamics of visual object recognition and feature integration. Their recent work explores how and when the brain constructs coherent percepts, often using rapid visual streams to track the exact latencies at which fundamental visual features, higher-level object dimensions like animacy and size, and targets hidden by real or illusory occluders become neurally decodable. Beyond standard object vision, they are investigating how quickly the visual system extracts cross-modal tactile information when observers watch social touch interactions. To connect these precise neural timelines to active decision-making, Dr. Grootswagers is also examining how continuous behavioral measures, such as mouse-movement trajectories during categorization tasks, track alongside the emergence of neural representations.

papers.title: The neural processes of illusory occlusion in object recognition
papers.abstract: Participants viewed objects partly hidden by real or illusory occluders while EEG was recorded. Decoding shows how object information emerges when the occluder is only implied by illusory contours, with signs of feedback-driven completion. The results clarify the time course of recognising partly hidden objects.
papers.authors: Almudena Ramírez-Haro, Denise Moerel, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Rapid visual engagement in neural processing of detailed touch interactions
papers.abstract: The authors recorded EEG while people watched videos of hands touching, and decoded the touch information from brain activity. Information about touch type and context appeared within a few hundred milliseconds. This suggests the visual system engages quickly with the tactile content of seen interactions.
papers.authors: Sophie Smit, Almudena Ramírez-Haro, Genevieve L. Quek, Manuel Varlet, Denise Moerel, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Mapping object space dimensions: new insights from temporal dynamics
papers.abstract: The study examines how the dimensions thought to structure object representations, such as animacy and size, emerge over time in EEG responses to rapid object streams. Different dimensions become decodable at different latencies, with a systematic temporal ordering. The findings refine models of object space by adding time.
papers.authors: Alexis Kidder, Genevieve L. Quek, Tijl Grootswagers

papers.title: Mapping the Dynamics of Visual Feature Coding: Insights into Perception and Integration
papers.abstract: Using EEG decoding on rapid streams of objects, the authors track when different visual features such as colour, shape and location become decodable in the brain and how they are combined. Feature information emerges in a staggered order and its coding is shaped by the task and by the other features present. The work gives a temporal account of how the brain builds integrated object percepts from separable features.
papers.authors: Tijl Grootswagers, Amanda K. Robinson, Sophia M. Shatek, Thomas A. Carlson

papers.title: Movement trajectories as a window into the dynamics of emerging neural representations
papers.abstract: The study links continuous mouse-movement trajectories during a categorisation task to time-resolved neural representations measured with EEG. Trajectories show when category information becomes available to guide action, and the behavioural dynamics track the neural emergence of those representations. This offers a cheap behavioural readout of the timing of neural coding.
papers.authors: Roger Koenig-Robert, Genevieve L. Quek, Tijl Grootswagers, Manuel Varlet

0665.name: Timothy Brady
0665.bio: Timothy F. Brady is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at UC San Diego and directs the Vision and Memory Lab. Their research explores how the visual system encodes and maintains information, focusing on the capacity and fidelity of visual working memory and long-term memory. Brady’s work indicates that visual memory capacity is not strictly fixed but scales with the meaningfulness of stimuli and examines how ensemble statistics facilitate the representation of complex scenes. Utilizing psychophysics, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG, Brady investigates memory limits and structural representations in the human brain.
0665.research_direction: Dr. Brady's recent work explores the computational principles underlying human visual memory, investigating how the visual system represents, compresses, and structures information across different timescales. Specifically, they have recently been examining whether items in working memory are stored independently or if they are instead shaped by ensemble perception, chunking, and hierarchical priors that produce systematic biases like mutual attraction and repulsion. To probe these questions, their research uses a priori measures of representational geometry—derived from both human similarity judgments and pretrained deep neural networks—to model and predict working memory errors for both simple features and complex stimuli like faces. Ultimately, they are working toward a unified account of visual cognition, testing how observers manage uncertainty, exploit environmental regularities, and utilize noisy feature-space activations to optimize limited capacity in both working and long-term memory.

papers.title: Chunking, attraction, repulsion and ensemble effects are ubiquitous in visual working memory
papers.abstract: Reanalyzes eleven existing datasets (about 138,000 trials) to show that items in working memory are not stored independently: displays are compressed into clusters and gist, producing chunking and mutual attraction and repulsion between items. A similarity-based model accounts for these systematic biases. The authors argue this requires a paradigm shift from item-based to cluster/gist-based theories of working memory.
papers.authors: Chaipat Chunharas, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Predicting visual working memory errors with a priori measures of representational geometry from human and artificial systems
papers.abstract: Shows that the representational geometry of stimuli, measured independently of any memory task via human similarity judgments and pretrained deep networks, predicts the full distribution of working memory errors with a single-parameter decision rule and no fitting to memory data. The pipeline transfers to thirty new face sets and to simple features such as color, orientation, shape and location, outperforming standard mixture and tuning models with fewer parameters.
papers.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson

papers.title: Representation and computation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: A review of recent computational work on human visual working memory. It argues that memories are not simple noisy copies of stimuli, since observers hold information about uncertainty and exploit environmental regularities to use limited resources well. It surveys how models at different levels converge on shared principles linking capacity to variability and uncertainty, along with proposed neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Paul M. Bays, Sebastian Schneegans, Wei Ji Ma, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: Noisy and hierarchical visual memory across timescales
papers.abstract: Reviews how contemporary theories treat visual memory as noisy, continuously varying in strength rather than a store of held items. It integrates work on working memory and long-term memory, arguing that noisy representations at multiple levels of the visual hierarchy and the priors that structure them support both. It outlines directions for a unified account of memory.
papers.authors: Timothy F. Brady, Maria M. Robinson, Jamal R. Williams

papers.title: A quantitative model of ensemble perception as summed activation in feature space
papers.abstract: Presents a formal model in which an ensemble summary of a display is the global sum of activation signals from each individual item, tying memory for single items to judgments about the group. Compared against alternative models in five experiments, the approach predicts between- and within-person differences in ensemble reports with no free parameters, using performance on single-item memory tasks. It unifies models of item memory and ensemble perception.
papers.authors: Maria M. Robinson, Timothy F. Brady

0666.name: Timothy D. Sweeny
0666.bio: Timothy D. Sweeny is an Associate Professor at the University of Denver, directing the Visual Perception, Emotion, & Cognition (VPEC) Lab and the Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience Program. Sweeny’s research utilizes psychophysics to investigate how neural and cognitive mechanisms shape visual perception, focusing on ensemble coding—the process by which the brain compresses complex social information, such as crowd gaze and emotional expressions, into summary statistics. They examine how these perceptual processes influence social behavior and consciousness, collaborating with clinical psychologists to study visual processing in populations with anxiety and autism spectrum disorder. This work connects low-level vision and high-level social-emotional cognition to analyze how humans interpret collective social cues and navigate complex environments.
0666.research_direction: Dr. Sweeny studies how people form quick visual impressions, especially of faces and emotions. Their recent work examines why observers tend to read ambiguous facial expressions negatively, and whether that bias shifts when angry faces become more or less common. They have also been asking how motion shared between objects pulls perceived shape, such as aspect ratio, toward each other through perceptual grouping. Alongside this, they have been analyzing the latent space of face-generating neural networks to understand and control which expressions these models produce.

papers.title: Biased judgments of emotion are resistant to changes in the prevalence of anger
papers.abstract: Evaluations of emotional facial expressions are inherently subject to uncertainty due to the subtlety and nuance of affective cues. Previous work showed that observers exhibit a systematic bias toward interpreting expressions negatively—a tendency that is particularly amplified in group or crowd settings. While this flexible negativity bias is hypothesized to serve an adaptive, protective function rooted in long-term statistical learning of crowd-related threat, the degree to which it recalibrates in response to short-term shifts in threat prevalence remains uncharacterized. To investigate this, observers evaluated either individual isolated faces or four-face ensembles, categorizing expressions along a happiness–anger dimension across three experiments where anger prevalence was experimentally manipulated (75% versus 25% of trials). Replicating prior findings, participants displayed a robust anger bias that was selectively enhanced when judging crowds. However, anger bias magnitudes remained invariant across prevalence regimes, irrespective of whether statistical prevalence was acquired implicitly through exposure or explicitly instructed a priori. These findings indicate that while visual emotion interpretation biases are dynamically sensitive to contextual visual factors such as crowd context, they are remarkably resilient to short-term statistical alterations in affective base rates.
papers.authors: Delaney McDonagh, Timothy Sweeny

papers.title: Similarity in motion binds and bends judgments of aspect ratio
papers.abstract: While perceptual grouping based on Gestalt similarity of features is widely recognized to bind visual objects, whether emergent grouping conversely distorts the perceived visual properties of individual constituents dynamically on a single-trial timescale is less established. This study investigated whether common motion vectors dynamically induce attraction or repulsion in perceived geometric aspect ratio on a trial-by-trial basis. Observers were briefly presented with pairs of elliptical stimuli defined by coherent random-dot kinematograms embedded in dynamic noise displays, differing in their horizontal-to-vertical aspect ratios. Following stimulus offset, an arrow retro-cue indicated which target ellipse's aspect ratio observers were to reconstruct. Coherent dot motion within the two stimuli was manipulated to be either shared (promoting grouping by common fate) or opposing/dissimilar (disrupting grouping). When shapes shared identical motion trajectories, aspect ratio reproductions of the probed shape were systematically attracted toward the aspect ratio of the unprobed item. Conversely, when motion trajectories diverged, a repulsive perceptual shift was observed. These findings demonstrate that motion-based grouping dynamically modulates perceived shape geometry within brief temporal windows, revealing that the visual system rapidly imposes perceptual assimilation or contrast in accordance with momentary perceptual organization cues.
papers.authors: Görkem Er, Timothy D. Sweeny

papers.title: GANalyzer: Analysis and Manipulation of GANs Latent Space for Controllable Face Synthesis
papers.abstract: Although state-of-the-art Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) synthesize high-fidelity facial imagery, latent representations lack direct interpretability regarding the relationship between input noise vectors and resulting facial semantics. Furthermore, models like StyleGAN3 trained on uncurated, imbalanced corpora display severe sample skew—for example, synthesizing over 77% happy expressions versus approximately 3% angry expressions across 100,000 unconstrained generations, with intersections such as angry women or happy Black individuals comprising under 1% and 2% respectively. To resolve these limitations and facilitate fine-grained facial attribute control, this paper introduces GANalyzer, a framework designed to analyze and steer the latent manifold of pre-trained GANs. GANalyzer develops specific transformation mappings to disentangle and independently modulate targeted demographic and affective attributes, including facial expression, age, perceived gender, and race. By isolating entangled directional vectors within the latent space, the framework enables both identity-preserving facial attribute editing and feature-guided synthesis. The authors validate the approach across diverse facial modifications and release an open-source balanced photo-realistic facial benchmark dataset to address demographic and expressive representation deficits.
papers.authors: Ali Pourramezan Fard, Mohammad H. Mahoor, Sarah Ariel Lamer, Timothy Sweeny

0667.name: Timothy J. Andrews
0667.bio: Timothy J. Andrews is a Professor of Psychology whose research investigates the neural mechanisms through which the human brain transforms low-level retinal signals into high-level visual perceptions of objects, faces, and scenes. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and computational modeling, Andrews’s work examines the functional organization of the visual cortex, specifically addressing the debate between modular and distributed representations of category-selective information. Their research includes studies on the holistic representation of facial identity, the neural correlates of binocular rivalry, and how structural and functional connectivity within the temporal lobes support the recognition of natural images. Furthermore, Andrews explores how idiosyncratic eye movements and neural responses correlate with individual differences in visual cognition.
0667.research_direction: Dr. Andrews has recently been investigating the neural organization and temporal dynamics of high-level visual cognition using data-driven encoding models and multimodal neuroimaging. Their recent work explores how the perceptual dimensions of natural objects are mapped spatially across the visual cortex in fMRI and how these representations unfold over time in EEG and MEG. Additionally, they are examining the processing of faces and scenes during naturalistic movie-watching to understand how prior familiarity and top-down conceptual knowledge influence neural responses. To link these sensory and cognitive domains, Dr. Andrews maps the structural and functional connectivity between core category-selective visual areas and extended non-visual networks, probing the broader integration of visual perception and memory.

papers.title: Statistically efficient neural encoding of natural object variability shapes the temporal dynamics of visual processing
papers.abstract: Extending the data-driven THINGS framework to time-resolved EEG and MEG, the study used behaviourally derived object dimensions to build encoding models of evoked responses. A few latent components captured the temporal dynamics consistently across modalities and matched the earlier MRI analysis. The authors argue that object representations reflect statistical efficiency in capturing feature co-occurrence in natural objects.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Richard Aveyard, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: A data-driven analysis of the perceptual and neural responses to natural objects reveals organizing principles of human visual cognition
papers.abstract: Using THINGS images, the authors combined perceptual similarity judgments with whole-brain fMRI responses and used partial least squares regression to predict neural activity from a handful of perceptual components. The components gave smooth, graded topographies across visual cortex, similar in both hemispheres, that captured animacy, real-world size and category. They did not map neatly onto existing theories of object perception, arguing for a data-driven view of cortical organisation.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Conceptual knowledge shapes the neural representations of learned faces in non-visual regions of the brain
papers.abstract: Participants learned faces from a movie shown in either its original or a scrambled order, giving equal visual exposure but different conceptual understanding. Core face-selective regions did not differ between groups, but a network of person-knowledge regions did, and it could also discriminate the identities of the main characters. Conceptual knowledge, more than visual experience, shapes neural face representations outside visual cortex.
papers.authors: Kira N. Noad, David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Familiarity enhances functional connectivity between visual and nonvisual regions of the brain during natural viewing
papers.abstract: Participants who knew or did not know a TV series watched a clip in the scanner. Familiar viewers showed higher inter-subject correlation in semantic, episodic and affective regions, and stronger connectivity between face/scene regions and a familiarity network. This effect was reduced in people with developmental prosopagnosia, implicating visual-nonvisual connectivity in recognising people and places.
papers.authors: Kira N. Noad, David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

papers.title: Mapping the functional and structural connectivity of the scene network
papers.abstract: Using resting-state and movie-watching fMRI plus diffusion tractography, the paper charts how scene-selective regions connect to each other and to the rest of the brain. Posterior scene regions (OPA, posterior PPA) link with visual and dorsal attention networks, while anterior PPA and retrosplenial cortex link with default-mode, control networks and hippocampus. This supports a perceptual-to-mnemonic gradient in scene processing.
papers.authors: David M. Watson, Timothy J. Andrews

0668.name: Timothy Vickery
0668.bio: Timothy Vickery is an Associate Professor at the University of Delaware whose research examines the functional and neural architecture of human visual cognition. Vickery’s work focuses on the interactions between visual perception, selective attention, and memory systems, utilizing behavioral psychophysics and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Research topics include visual statistical learning and the distortion of spatial perception by objects and grouping. They also investigate the shared representational mechanisms between working memory and attentional control.
0668.research_direction: Dr. Vickery has recently been investigating a broad array of topics spanning visual perception, memory architecture, and cognitive modeling. Their recent work explores the interplay between memory systems, using continuous-report paradigms to test whether retrieving information from long-term memory draws upon the limited capacity of visual working memory, while also examining how the visual similarity of paired items impacts incidental visual statistical learning. In the realm of perceptual organization, they are studying how object structure and boundary contours systematically warp visual perception by expanding or compressing perceived space. Additionally, Dr. Vickery employs computational modeling to investigate strategic decision-making, specifically asking how human players utilize heuristic strategies and build adaptive opponent models during simple zero-sum games.

papers.title: Retrieval from long-term memory does not bypass working memory
papers.abstract: Tests whether retrieving an item from long-term memory can happen without drawing on visual working memory. Using continuous-report measures, retrieving an LTM item lowered the fidelity of concurrently held working-memory contents, and a near-capacity working-memory load lowered the fidelity of the retrieved LTM report. The authors conclude that LTM retrieval does not bypass working memory but shares its limited resources.
papers.authors: Michael K. P. Mugno, Timothy J. Vickery

papers.title: Opponent Models and Heuristic Strategies for Simple Games
papers.abstract: Studies how people play simple zero-sum games by building models of their opponent and using heuristic strategies. Behavioral data are fit with computational models to show how players move beyond equilibrium-style play toward adaptive strategies that exploit opponent patterns.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 46th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society
papers.authors: Timothy J. Vickery

papers.title: Expansion and compression of space within and beyond the boundaries of an object
papers.abstract: Examines how the visual system distorts perceived space around objects, finding that spatial extent is perceptually stretched or compressed depending on whether it lies inside an object's boundary or outside it. The experiments bear on how object structure and grouping warp spatial perception.
papers.authors: Anton Lebed, Catherine Scanlon, Timothy J. Vickery

papers.title: Similarity Benefits Visual Statistical Learning
papers.abstract: Asks whether the similarity of items within a pair affects incidental visual statistical learning. Participants viewed streams of feature-defined creatures containing similar or dissimilar temporal pairs; across three experiments, similar pairs were recognized more often than dissimilar ones, indicating that inter-item similarity shapes what is learned from co-occurrence.
papers.authors: Alyssa P. Levy, Timothy J. Vickery

0669.name: Tina Plank
0669.bio: Tina Plank is a vision science researcher at the University of Regensburg who examines the mechanisms of neuroplasticity in the adult visual system, specifically in response to retinopathologies such as macular degeneration. Plank uses functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), population receptive field (pRF) mapping, and psychophysical methods to study cortical reorganization and the development of preferred retinal loci in patients with central vision loss. Their research investigates how targeted perceptual learning and eccentric vision training modulate neural properties in the visual cortex to influence clinical outcomes like reading speed and visual acuity. Additionally, Plank explores multisensory integration and the effects of olfactory and auditory cues on visual perception.
0669.research_direction: Dr. Plank studies how practice reshapes the visual system in adults. Their recent work has been testing whether training people to discriminate small shapes in peripheral vision changes how neurons in early visual cortex sample space, measured as population receptive fields with fMRI. They connect these cortical changes to crowding, the difficulty of recognizing objects when clutter surrounds them in the periphery.

papers.title: Training-induced changes in population receptive field properties in visual cortex: Impact of eccentric vision training on population receptive field properties and the crowding effect
papers.abstract: This study evaluated whether practice-dependent visual perceptual learning on an eccentric vision task alters population receptive field (pRF) properties in early retinotopic cortex. Fifteen healthy adult participants underwent 3-Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) before and after completing a four-day behavioral perceptual learning protocol. The training task required gap orientation discrimination (up, down, left, right) of a Landolt C optotype presented at 6.5° eccentricity in the upper right visual field flanked by ring distractors arranged in radial or tangential configurations. Flanker distance was varied using an adaptive staircase to quantify critical spacing and radial-tangential crowding anisotropy. PRF parameters were mapped across eccentricities from 0.5° to 9° using drifting bar stimuli within dorsal and ventral subdivisions of V1 and V2, including the trained region of interest (tROI). Psychophysical results showed significant post-training reductions in critical spacing and crowding anisotropy indices (p = 0.009, Cohen's d = 0.79). PRF analyses revealed an overall 21% reduction in pRF size in the tROI (p = 0.005). Significant pRF size decreases were localized to both ventral V2 (contracting from 1.47° to 1.20°, p < 0.0000001) and dorsal V2 (contracting from 1.15° to 1.04°, p = 0.009), most prominently at eccentricities matching the trained visual field location (p < 0.001). Conversely, pRF estimates remained statistically unaltered in ventral V1 (p = 0.181) and dorsal V1 (p = 0.055). These outcomes demonstrate that visual perceptual learning of a crowding task selectively refines spatial tuning in extrastriate cortex (V2), underscoring training-induced adult neuroplasticity.
papers.authors: Maka Malania, Yih-Shiuan Lin, Charlotte Hörmandinger, John S. Werner, Mark W. Greenlee, Tina Plank

0670.name: Todd Zickler
0670.department: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences
0670.bio: Todd Zickler is the William and Ami Kuan Danoff Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at Harvard University. Their research focuses on the mathematical and physical modeling of light-material interactions to extract structural and radiometric scene information from visual measurements. By integrating computer vision, applied optics, and human perception, Zickler develops imaging systems for applications in robotics, augmented reality, and generative AI. Zickler's work includes techniques in reflectance modeling, Helmholtz stereopsis, and the design of bio-inspired sensors that emulate the vision systems of organisms.
0670.research_direction: Dr. Zickler has recently been investigating how advanced generative models and computational optics can extract rich geometric and physical information from ambiguous or highly compressed visual inputs.
