Their recent work explores mid-level and high-level scene understanding, utilizing diffusion architectures to decompose scenes into occlusion-ordered layers of amodally completed objects and to resolve 3D shape and material ambiguities from subtle motion cues. In parallel, they are examining perceptual grouping by developing bottom-up, geometry-aware attention mechanisms to infer continuous sub-pixel boundaries, corners, and junctions. Additionally, Dr. Zickler's research in computational photography investigates hardware-software co-design, such as optimizing birefringent metasurfaces for polarization-controlled imaging and pairing diffractive lenses with patch-based diffusion models to reconstruct full hyperspectral scenes from single grayscale snapshots.

papers.title: Generative Perception of Shape and Material from Differential Motion
papers.abstract: Inspired by how people resolve shape and material ambiguity by moving their head or turning an object, the authors train a compact pixel-space conditional diffusion model that takes a short video of a slightly moving object and generates samples of shape and material maps. Trained on a modest set of synthetic videos, it yields diverse, multimodal predictions for static views and sharpens toward a single confident answer as motion cues accumulate, mirroring human perceptual behavior.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 38)
papers.authors: Xinran Nicole Han, Ko Nishino, Todd Zickler

papers.title: CObL: Toward Zero-Shot Ordinal Layering without User Prompting
papers.abstract: The paper represents a scene as an occlusion-ordered stack of layers, each holding one amodally completed object. A diffusion architecture generates all layers in parallel using Stable Diffusion as a prior plus inference-time guidance so the layers recomposite to the input image. Trained on a few thousand synthetic tabletop scenes, it generalizes zero-shot to real photographs with varying numbers of unseen objects.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
papers.authors: Aneel Damaraju, Dean Hazineh, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Boundary Attention: Learning curves, corners, junctions and grouping
papers.abstract: A lightweight network infers boundaries and grouping bottom-up, predicting curves, corners and junctions with sub-pixel precision. A geometry-aware local attention operation is applied densely and repeatedly to refine per-patch boundary variables, giving a rich unrasterized representation rather than a binary edge map. The model handles noise and generalizes despite being trained on simple synthetic data.
papers.authors: Mia Gaia Polansky, Charles Herrmann, Junhwa Hur, Deqing Sun, Dor Verbin, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Filterless Snapshot Hyperspectral Imaging using Guided Patch Diffusion
papers.abstract: The work reconstructs a full 31-band hyperspectral image from a single grayscale snapshot taken through only a diffractive lens and a panchromatic sensor. A shift-invariant conditional patch diffusion model is trained on limited data and its per-patch predictions are reconciled at inference using guidance from the optical point spread function. Local optical cues turn out to carry most spectral information, and multiple samples give per-pixel uncertainty estimates.
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CV), v3; earlier title 'Grayscale to Hyperspectral at Any Resolution Using a Phase-Only Lens'
papers.authors: Dean Hazineh, Luca Sacchi, Davide Cassara, Federico Capasso, Todd Zickler

papers.title: Polarization Multi-Image Synthesis with Birefringent Metasurfaces
papers.abstract: The authors show how a birefringent metasurface can encode several images that are selectively revealed by different polarization states, and present an optimization framework (built on the DFlat differentiable metasurface toolkit) to design such optics. They demonstrate polarization-controlled multi-image synthesis and discuss uses in computational imaging and displays.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Computational Photography (ICCP)
papers.authors: Dean Hazineh, Soon Wei Daniel Lim, Qi Guo, Federico Capasso, Todd Zickler

0671.name: Tom P. Franken
0671.bio: Tom P. Franken is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Neuroscience at Washington University School of Medicine, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of sensory inference. Franken’s research focuses on how the brain resolves sensory ambiguities to represent objects, with an emphasis on border ownership assignment in the visual cortex and sound localization circuits in the brainstem. Using a combination of multielectrode electrophysiology, computational modeling, and behavioral assays, their work aims to characterize the cortical and subcortical computations that support stable perception. Franken has described how feedback signals organize into columns in the primate visual cortex and how artificial neural networks replicate brain-like grouping signals to predict dynamic visual scenes.
0671.research_direction: Dr. Franken studies how the brain organizes what it sees and hears into coherent objects and events. Their recent work centers on border ownership in primate visual cortex, the way neurons signal which side of an edge is the foreground object, and on grouping signals that may feed back to establish it and keep it stable across eye movements. They have also been asking whether similar signals arise on their own in artificial networks trained only to predict upcoming video frames. In separate work on hearing, they have been recording from and characterizing distinct neuron types in the gerbil auditory brainstem region that responds to the ends of sounds.

papers.title: Grouping signals in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Visual scene perception remains remarkably stable despite frequent saccadic displacements of the retinal image. This perceptual continuity is thought to rely in part on border ownership (BOS) neurons in cortical area V2, which signal foreground surface assignment for hundreds of milliseconds after contextual cues are extinguished and transfer this assignment across saccades. Theoretical models propose that upstream BOS selectivity is established via feedback from downstream grouping cells that maintain persistent proto-object representations with short latencies, centripetal ownership preferences directed toward the receptive field center, and de novo remapping after saccades. Utilizing laminar multielectrode arrays in area V4 of awake, behaving macaques (Macaca mulatta), the authors identified a prominent population of neurons exhibiting these functional hallmark properties across all laminar compartments. These V4 units fired with response latencies sufficiently rapid to drive V2 BOS tuning via corticocortical feedback. Furthermore, these grouping cells displayed substantially weaker tuning for luminance contrast polarity than canonical BOS neurons, suggesting a functional dissociation wherein grouping units maintain the spatiotemporal continuity of segmented visual surfaces while BOS neurons integrate this spatial assignment with local surface feature properties.
papers.authors: Tom P. Franken, John H. Reynolds

papers.title: Brain-like border ownership signals support prediction of natural videos
papers.abstract: To parse visual scenes into structured objects, the primate visual cortex assigns borders to foreground surfaces via border ownership (BOS) selective neurons. Here, the authors investigated whether functional BOS signals can spontaneously emerge in an artificial neural network trained solely on self-supervised future-frame video prediction without explicit segmentation objectives or object annotations. Analyzing units within PredNet trained on natural video sequences from the KITTI dataset, responses were evaluated for classical receptive fields exposed to isolated luminance edges belonging to figures on opposing sides while manipulating edge orientation, spatial position, and contrast polarity. Both representation (R) and error (E) units in PredNet demonstrated pronounced BOS selectivity that was invariant to luminance contrast polarity and tolerant across contour orientations, reproducing key neurophysiological phenomena observed in primate V2 and V4. The proportion and amplitude of BOS units scaled progressively across the network hierarchy (L3 > L2 > L1 > L0). These results demonstrate that the objective of predicting natural visual dynamics provides sufficient computational pressure for the emergence of brain-like border ownership representations.
papers.authors: Zeyuan Ye, Ralf Wessel, Tom P. Franken

papers.title: Distinct cell classes in the superior paraolivary nucleus (SPN) region in the gerbil auditory brainstem revealed by in vivo physiological and anatomical characterization
papers.abstract: The superior paraolivary nucleus (SPN/SPON) of the mammalian superior olivary complex exhibits characteristic sound-offset responses driven by acoustic-evoked glycinergic inhibition, though in vivo synaptic dynamics and cellular heterogeneity have remained unresolved. Performing in vivo patch-clamp intracellular recordings and biocytin labeling in Mongolian gerbils (Meriones unguiculatus), 12 morphologically reconstructed neurons within and bordering the SPN were characterized across ultrastructure, intrinsic membrane properties, and responses to intracellular current injections and acoustic stimuli. The neurons segregated into three distinct physiological and anatomical classes: fast cells, which fired exclusively at the onset of depolarizing current steps, produced short-latency post-inhibitory rebound action potentials to hyperpolarizing current or sound offset, and showed dense somatic synaptic coverage; slow cells, which exhibited sustained firing during depolarizing steps, prolonged hyperpolarizing inhibitory decays, and sparse synaptic coverage; and uninhibited cells, which lacked prominent sound-evoked hyperpolarization and post-inhibitory rebound spiking. The findings indicate functional segregation where fast cells convey temporally precise offset timing to the inferior colliculus, whereas slow cells provide sustained inhibitory modulation to the cochlear nucleus.
papers.authors: Tom P. Franken, Philip X. Joris, Philip H. Smith

0672.name: Tomoyasu Horikawa
0672.bio: Tomoyasu Horikawa is a researcher at NTT Communication Science Laboratories specializing in the intersection of computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Horikawa’s work focuses on developing brain decoding methodologies that utilize deep neural networks to translate human brain activity, primarily from fMRI, into visual and linguistic representations. Their research includes 'mind captioning' and hierarchical image reconstruction, which aim to decode the content of dreams, mental imagery, and subjective perceptions into descriptive text and images.
0672.research_direction: Dr. Horikawa develops ways to read out what a person sees or imagines from their brain activity. Their recent work uses fMRI together with deep neural networks to decode mid-level visual features, such as those underlying how materials and surface qualities look. They have also been building a method that turns brain activity into descriptive sentences, using language models to generate text that reflects the meaning of a person's mental content.

papers.title: Decoding Shitsukan in the Brain
papers.abstract: Characterizing Shitsukan—the multidimensional perception of material properties, surface texture, and realistic qualities of objects—requires representational frameworks beyond simple low-level image statistics or discrete verbal labels. This work presents a brain decoding framework centered on mid-level hierarchical visual features shared between the primate visual pathway and deep neural networks (DNNs). By establishing regression models that translate functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals into DNN feature spaces, brain activity is converted into intermediate computational representations. Pairing these decoded neural representations with deep generative models enables the continuous, high-fidelity reconstruction of visual imagery, illusory percepts, and material appearances directly from cortical activity patterns. This paradigm clarifies how population codes within ventral and higher visual cortex represent subjective material qualities and provides a quantitative computational basis for materializing internal visual experiences.
papers.venue: Shitsukan: Understanding and Manipulating Material and Quality Perception (Springer Nature)
papers.authors: Yukiyasu Kamitani, Misato Tanaka, Tomoyasu Horikawa

papers.title: Mind captioning: Evolving descriptive text of mental content from human brain activity
papers.abstract: While significant progress has been achieved in decoding language representations from human cortical activity, generating coherent, syntactically structured linguistic descriptions of complex mental content rooted in visual semantics remains an unresolved challenge. A generative decoding framework termed mind captioning is demonstrated to iteratively synthesize descriptive text reflecting neural semantic representations via latent feature vectors derived from deep language models (LMs). Linear regularized regression decoders were trained on human blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data acquired during passive viewing of dynamic, soundless video clips to predict the contextualized semantic representations of reference video annotations. Candidate text sequences were subsequently evolved and optimized through masked language model (MLM)-guided word replacement and interpolation to minimize discrepancy with brain-decoded semantic vectors. The optimization progressively produced well-structured descriptive captions accurately depicting perceived dynamic scenes, persisting even when the canonical fronto-temporal language network was systematically excluded from the decoder features. Crucially, the approach generalized to verbalizing internally recalled memory content during visual imagery tasks, illustrating an interpretive bridge between nonverbal cortical representations and structured natural language.
papers.authors: Tomoyasu Horikawa

0673.name: Tony Pansell
0673.lab_name: Eye movements and vision – Tony Pansell's research group
0673.bio: Tony Pansell is a Professor of Optometry at Karolinska Institutet whose research investigates the physiological mechanisms of eye movement control and visual function, with a focus on acquired brain injuries. Their work utilizes high-resolution eye-tracking and psychophysical methods to characterize binocular vision disorders, visuo-vestibular integration, and visual motion hypersensitivity in clinical populations. Pansell identifies objective biomarkers for neurological conditions, such as post-concussive syndrome and Parkinson's disease, while evaluating the efficacy of neuro-rehabilitative interventions like color filters and vision training.
0673.research_direction: Dr. Pansell has recently been investigating the multisensory mechanisms underlying gaze stabilization and the clinical phenomenon of visual motion hypersensitivity, particularly following mild traumatic brain injury. Their recent work explores the sensory deficits driving post-concussion dizziness, utilizing psychophysical tasks like critical flicker fusion threshold mapping and oculomotor measures of vertical vergence and ocular torsion during optokinetic stimulation to probe altered perceptual noise and oculomotor gain. Alongside this clinical focus, they are developing novel eye-tracking protocols and passive-rotation paradigms to tease apart how visual, vestibular, and neck proprioceptive inputs interact to drive compensatory ocular torsion in the roll plane. Additionally, their research includes broad systematic reviews to map the clinical characteristics and risk factors of abnormal visual motion processing across a wide spectrum of neurological and vestibular disorders.

papers.title: Temporal visual processing deficits in post concussion syndrome
papers.abstract: Fifteen patients with lingering post-concussion symptoms and fifteen matched controls had their critical flicker fusion thresholds measured across several visual-field eccentricities, as a psychophysical window on the motion hypersensitivity often reported after mild brain injury. Trial-to-trial variability in the flicker measure raised thresholds more strongly in patients, pointing to increased perceptual noise rather than a shift in eccentricity dependence. Variability shrank with time since injury, suggesting gradual compensation of temporal sensitivity.
papers.authors: Davide Frattini, Mariagrazia Benassi, Tobias Wibble, Mattias Nilsson, Roberto Bolzani, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Using Eye-tracking to Assess the Relative Importance of Visual and Vestibular Input to Subcortical Motion Processing in the Roll Plane
papers.abstract: A methods protocol for separating visual and vestibular contributions to gaze stabilization in the roll plane. Participants receive optokinetic rotation, whole-body rotation in darkness, or combined visuovestibular stimulation while a head-mounted eye tracker records ocular torsion and head motion in six dimensions. The article details slow-phase velocity and nystagmus analysis, artefact rejection and repeat-trial handling.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Human proprioceptive gaze stabilization during passive body rotations underneath a fixed head
papers.abstract: Thirteen healthy volunteers were tilted on a sled underneath a stationary, upright head while torsional eye position was recorded. When a visual background was present, neck flexion produced ocular torsion opposite to the neck extension, as if the eyes were compensating for a head tilt that would straighten the head over the body. No such response occurred in darkness, indicating that neck proprioception drives torsional gaze stabilization through interaction with vision.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Concussed patients with visually induced dizziness exhibit increased ocular torsion and vertical vergence during optokinetic gaze-stabilization
papers.abstract: Nine post-concussion patients with visually induced dizziness and nine matched controls viewed optokinetic stimuli in which central and peripheral regions moved coherently, incoherently or randomly, while torsional and vergence eye movements were recorded. Patients showed higher oculomotor gain, and the responses tracked symptom severity. Eye movements favored the direction of central-field motion, with coherent motion eliciting the strongest torsion.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Davide Frattini, Mariagrazia Benassi, Roberto Bolzani, Tony Pansell

papers.title: Clinical characteristics of visual motion hypersensitivity: a systematic review
papers.abstract: A systematic review of 54 studies (from 586 screened) on groups showing abnormal responses to visual motion, covering age, migraine, concussion, vestibular disorders, psychiatric conditions and Parkinson's disease. It synthesizes the evidence per risk factor and provides a reference framework for future work on visual motion hypersensitivity.
papers.authors: Tobias Wibble, Tony Pansell

0678.name: Valerie Goffaux
0678.bio: Valerie Goffaux is an F.R.S.-F.N.R.S. Research Associate whose work characterizes the neuro-computational mechanisms underlying human face perception. Goffaux’s research indicates that face recognition is tuned to horizontal orientations and relies on specific spatial frequency integration, which challenges traditional hierarchical models of vision. Using psychophysics, high-density EEG (frequency tagging), and fMRI, they investigate how the brain leverages natural contrast statistics and visual field anisotropies to achieve face categorization. Their current projects explore the functional link between early visual cortex selectivity and high-level face-selective regions, focusing on how radial biases and contextual modulations influence perceptual resolution.
0678.research_direction: Dr. Goffaux has recently been investigating how the human visual system leverages low-level spatial orientation statistics—particularly horizontal image structure—to support robust face recognition. Using behavioral paradigms with orientation-filtered images, their recent work explores the precise mechanisms underlying this horizontal tuning, asking what specific shape or surface cues it provides and whether it operates within a retina- or face-centered reference frame. They are also examining how these orientation bands enable view-tolerant identity recognition across different head rotations. Beyond foveal vision, their research investigates face processing in the visual periphery, seeking to determine how early retinotopic phenomena like radial bias interact with fast saccadic orienting and high-level face identification mechanisms.

papers.title: The view tolerance of human identity recognition depends on horizontal face information
papers.abstract: Participants recognized famous-face identities across a range of head rotations while the images were filtered to keep only narrow orientation bands. Recognition relied on horizontal information at every viewpoint. Model observers showed why: within a single view the diagnostic cues shift from horizontal (frontal) to vertical (profile), but across views horizontal content is the most stable and best predicts a face's average appearance. This suggests view-tolerant face representations are learned from the stable statistics carried by horizontal information.
papers.authors: Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Helene Dumont, Vincent Bremhorst, Christianne Jacobs, Valerie Goffaux

papers.title: Dissociating retina- and face-centered reference frames of human face recognition
papers.abstract: Forty-two adults recognized famous faces filtered to narrow orientation bands and shown upright or rotated by 45 or 90 degrees. Recognition stayed tuned to the horizontal range of the face image regardless of rotation, though the horizontal advantage weakened at 90 degrees. The data show that the information driving face-specialized identity recognition is defined in a face-centered reference frame, with only a modest retinotopic contribution.
papers.authors: Helene Dumont, Valerie Goffaux

papers.title: Does radial bias contribute to fast saccades toward faces in the periphery?
papers.abstract: Fifty participants made saccades toward faces or vehicles at 15 degrees eccentricity along horizontal and vertical meridians. Faces drew faster, more accurate saccades and horizontal-meridian targets were faster, but the face advantage did not differ between meridians. Still, individual horizontal tuning for face identity predicted the vertical-meridian face advantage, and radial bias predicted saccade latency to faces, linking low-level orientation biases to fast face orienting.
papers.authors: Marius Grandjean, Louise Kauffmann, Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Valerie Goffaux

papers.title: Horizontal face information is the main gateway to the shape and surface cues to familiar face identity
papers.abstract: Humans lean on horizontal image structure to recognize faces, and the reason is unclear. The authors filtered familiar actors' faces into orientation bands and measured how picture-plane inversion (which disrupts shape and surface cues) and contrast negation (which disrupts surface cues) changed recognition across orientations. Both effects were concentrated in the horizontal range, indicating that horizontal information carries both the shape and the surface reflectance cues to identity.
papers.authors: Helene Dumont, Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Valerie Goffaux

papers.title: Radial bias in face identification
papers.abstract: Peripheral vision is most accurate for stimuli oriented toward the fovea, a radial bias thought to arise at early visual stages. Using face identity recognition, which depends on horizontal information, the authors show that face-selective mechanisms are more sensitive on the horizontal than the vertical meridian, where horizontal facial cues align with the radial bias. The radial bias therefore persists at high-level recognition stages.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Alexia Roux-Sibilon, Carole Peyrin, John A. Greenwood, Valerie Goffaux

0681.name: Victoria Plaza
0681.department: Department of Basic Psychology (Departamento de Psicología Básica)
0681.bio: Victoria Plaza is a Professor in the Department of Basic Psychology at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and a member of the Cognition, Attention, and Learning Lab. Plaza’s research examines the cognitive mechanisms of associative learning, focusing on the application of the differential outcomes procedure to memory and discriminative learning in clinical populations such as those with Alzheimer’s disease and Down syndrome. They also utilize eye-tracking methodologies to investigate active vision, exploring how stimulus relevance and cognitive load influence fixation durations and strategic behavior during visual search tasks.
0681.research_direction: Dr. Plaza's recent work explores the oculomotor mechanisms underlying visual search, particularly how our scanning behavior adapts when searching the same environments repeatedly. Using eye-tracking paradigms with dense, multi-item displays, they have recently been investigating the dynamic control of eye movements to understand how people adjust fixation durations, saccade amplitudes, and landing positions when encountering targets versus distractors. Additionally, their research seeks to isolate the specific drivers of performance gains in repeated search tasks by manipulating the appearance timing of critical items. Through this approach, Dr. Plaza aims to disentangle how various concurrent processes, such as peripheral target detection and prior incidental fixations, act together to optimize visual search over time.

papers.title: Hold it there! Dynamic adjustment of fixation duration in visual search tasks
papers.abstract: Across three eye-tracking experiments with different visual search tasks, the authors show that people adjust how long they fixate depending on whether a fixated item is the target or a distractor. As the same displays are searched repeatedly, fewer fixations are needed to find the target, search fixations lengthen while target fixations shorten, and saccades shrink while landing positions move closer to the target. The results point to strategic, dynamic control of oculomotor scanning during search, and the article is written as a tribute to Eileen Kowler's work.
papers.authors: M. Pilar Aivar, Laura Cepero Amores, Elena Sanz, Miguel A. Vadillo, Victoria Plaza

papers.title: What drives performance gains in repeated visual search?
papers.abstract: Participants searched for 12 target letters a total of 6 times each in unique 72-item coloured-letter displays while their eye movements were recorded, and the timing of a critical item's first appearance was manipulated. Response times and fixation counts fell with repetition, the fixation just before the target was longer and closer to it (suggesting peripheral target detection), and earlier incidental fixations on the critical item did not help. The authors conclude that several processes act at once to improve search performance.
papers.authors: M. Pilar Aivar, Elena Sanz, Victoria Plaza

0684.name: Viola Stoermer
0684.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0684.bio: Stoermer is an Associate Professor at Dartmouth College where they direct the BrainStörmer Lab, focusing on the cognitive and neural architectures of human perception, attention, and memory. Their research employs a multimodal approach—including psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI—to investigate how the brain selectively prioritizes sensory information and the mechanisms by which attention shapes subjective visual experience. Stoermer examines the representational structures of feature-based and object-based attention, the capacity limits of visual working memory, and the cross-modal integration of auditory and visual signals.
0684.research_direction: Dr. Stoermer has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms that govern visual attention and working memory capacity. Using behavioral paradigms and EEG, their recent work explores how early visual cortex dynamically tunes to task-relevant features, probing both how attention flexibly adjusts to narrow versus broad feature ranges and how incidental learning reshapes early sensory prioritization. They are also examining the architecture of visual working memory, specifically testing whether classic capacity limits for simple features change when those features are scaffolded by meaningful, real-world objects. Broadly, Dr. Stoermer's research seeks to unify diverse attentional phenomena, ranging from cross-modal paradigms that ask whether auditory spatial attention recruits early visual-cortical machinery to theoretical frameworks based on the underlying structure of perceptual representations.

papers.title: Listening shapes seeing: Sustained auditory spatial attention enhances early visual-cortical processing
papers.abstract: Asks whether directing attention to a sound location recruits the same cortical machinery as visual spatial attention. In a dichotic listening task with EEG, attending to one side of space showed behavioral and early visual-cortical signatures of spatial attention. This supports a supramodal cortical account over a purely subcortical one.
papers.authors: Yong Min Choi, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Zooming In and Out: Selective Attention Modulates Color Signals in Early Visual Cortex for Narrow and Broad Ranges of Task-Relevant Features
papers.abstract: Using EEG frequency tagging, the study tracks how early visual cortex responds when observers attend to a narrow versus a wide range of colors. Neural color signals were enhanced for the attended range and adapted flexibly to its breadth, like a zoom lens in feature space. This links behavioral evidence for flexible feature tuning to early sensory gain.
papers.authors: Mert Özkan, Angus F. Chapman, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Early Cortical Sensitivity and Speeded Target Selection Underlie Incidentally Learned Prioritization of Visual Features
papers.abstract: Observers who repeatedly meet a target feature, without being told about it, come to prioritize that feature. EEG shows this learned prioritization boosts early visual cortical responses and speeds target selection. The results indicate that incidental experience reshapes attention at early perceptual stages.
papers.authors: Kevin Ortego, Douglas A. Addleman, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: Representational structures as a unifying framework for attention
papers.abstract: This review argues that many seemingly separate attention phenomena, from feature-based to object-based selection, can be explained by the structure of the representations that attention operates over. Similarity relations among features and objects determine how efficiently selection works and how it distorts perception. The framework organizes past findings and points to testable predictions.
papers.authors: Angus F. Chapman, Viola S. Störmer

papers.title: No Fixed Limit for Storing Simple Visual Features: Realistic Objects Provide an Efficient Scaffold for Holding Features in Mind
papers.abstract: Working memory for simple features such as colors is usually thought to hit a hard ceiling of a few items. The authors show that when the same colors are embedded in meaningful, real-world objects, people hold far more of them in mind, and capacity is no longer fixed at the classic limit. Meaningful objects act as a scaffold that lets features be stored efficiently, which challenges accounts based on a fixed number of slots.
papers.authors: Yong Hoon Chung, Timothy F. Brady, Viola S. Störmer

0686.name: Vivian C. Paulun
0686.bio: Vivian C. Paulun is an Assistant Professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and directs the Paulun Lab. Paulun’s research investigates the computational and neural foundations of high-level vision, specifically how the brain infers physical properties of materials—such as stiffness, mass, and elasticity—from visual information. To explore these mechanisms, they employ a combination of psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and computational modeling that incorporates physics-based simulations and generative engines. Previously, Paulun completed postdoctoral training at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, working jointly with Nancy Kanwisher and Josh Tenenbaum in the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences.
0686.research_direction: Dr. Paulun has recently been investigating how the visual system and brain perceive the physical properties of diverse materials and objects. Their recent work explores the fundamental cognitive and neural distinction between cohesive solids and non-solid substances like liquids or sand, using fMRI to map substance-specific representations in the visual cortex and infant studies to trace when this dichotomy emerges during development. Additionally, they are examining how observers infer hidden material traits from dynamic scenes, utilizing physics simulations to test which motion and shape cues inform human judgments of elasticity. Finally, Dr. Paulun is extending the study of intuitive physics beyond isolated items by modeling the visual strategies and physical reasoning people use to estimate the ensemble mass of interacting groups of objects.

papers.title: Visual cues and strategies for perceiving elasticity
papers.abstract: The paper asks which visual signals people use to judge how bouncy or stiff an object is from moving images. Using physics simulations of bouncing objects, the authors identify motion and shape cues that carry elasticity information and test whether observers rely on them, finding that people flexibly combine cues in ways that depend on the scene. The work advances understanding of how vision infers hidden material properties.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Florian S. Bayer, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Roland W. Fleming

papers.title: The Emergence of a Distinction between Things and Stuff
papers.abstract: This developmental preprint asks when the distinction between cohesive solid objects and non-solid substances emerges. It tests infants' expectations about how solids versus substances like sand or liquid should move, spread and divide. The results bear on whether the things/stuff distinction is present early in life, linking her adult neuroimaging work to development.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Sanghee Song, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Dissociable cortical regions represent things and stuff in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the authors show that the visual cortex contains distinct regions that respond preferentially to solid objects (things) versus non-solid substances such as liquids, sand and goo (stuff). Multivariate analyses indicate these regions encode different kinds of physical information, with the stuff-selective areas tracking material behavior and flow rather than shape. The results suggest the brain has dedicated machinery for perceiving and predicting the physics of substances, complementing object-focused systems.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Raghavendra Rao T. Pramod, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Nancy Kanwisher

papers.title: Ensemble Physics: Perceiving the Mass of Groups of Objects is More Than the Sum of Its Parts
papers.abstract: The study examines how people judge the total mass of groups of objects rather than single items. Observers' judgments of group mass depart from a simple sum of individual masses, and the authors model this with physics-based reasoning about how objects in a group interact. It extends intuitive physics from single objects to ensembles.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci)
papers.authors: Vicente Vivanco, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Vivian C. Paulun, Kevin A. Smith

0687.name: Vivian M Ciaramitaro
0687.bio: Vivian M. Ciaramitaro is an Associate Professor whose research examines the development and mechanisms of multisensory integration, focusing on how visual and auditory information are processed from infancy through adulthood. Ciaramitaro’s work utilizes psychophysical techniques, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG) to investigate how attention and plasticity influence sensory perception and neural responses. They explore cross-modal correspondences, the impact of emotional states like social anxiety on perceptual biases, and the role of experience in shaping sensory thresholds. By quantifying behavioral changes alongside brain activity, their research aims to elucidate the cognitive and neural foundations of how humans navigate complex sensory environments across the lifespan.
0687.research_direction: Dr. Ciaramitaro has recently been investigating how internal states and stimulus properties bias facial emotion perception, alongside a distinct focus on how multisensory associations develop in childhood. Their recent work explores how traits like social anxiety, current mood, and the sex of a face shift how observers categorize ambiguous expressions along angry-happy morph continua across the lifespan. Furthermore, they are probing the perceptual mechanisms driving these affective biases by testing whether social anxiety alters visual adaptation to negative versus positive faces. In a separate line of research, Dr. Ciaramitaro studies crossmodal correspondences in early development, examining how the extent of prior visual exposure shapes audio-tactile sound-shape matching and haptic exploration strategies in young children.

papers.title: The emotion perceived in a face depends on the sex of the face and varies across the lifespan
papers.abstract: Studies 539 participants aged 6 to 64 on how the sex of a face shapes perceived emotion in faces morphed between angry and happy. Male faces looked angrier than female faces only in 6- to 9-year-olds, and the gap between sexes shrank with age, mainly because the angry-male bias declined. This contradicts the expectation that the bias grows early in development.
papers.authors: Erinda Morina, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

papers.title: Biases in Perceiving Positive Versus Negative Emotions: The Influence of Social Anxiety and State Affect
papers.abstract: Tests whether social anxiety biases people to judge ambiguous faces as angrier than happy, measuring the point of subjective equality along an angry-happy morph continuum. High social anxiety produced a stronger negative bias, but only among people who also reported more negative mood, so trait anxiety and state affect interact. The authors argue that control-group choice and mood must be considered when studying perceptual biases in social anxiety.
papers.authors: Vivian M. Ciaramitaro, Erinda Morina, Jenny L. Wu, Daniel A. Harris, Sarah A. Hayes-Skelton

papers.title: Four Trials Is Not Enough: The Amount of Prior Audio-Visual Exposure Determines the Strength of Audio-Tactile Crossmodal Correspondence Early in Development
papers.abstract: Asks how much visual exposure to bouba/kiki shapes is needed before 6- to 8-year-olds show audio-tactile sound-shape matching. Sixty-one children saw four or eight audio-visual trials and then felt hidden shapes, matching them to sounds. Eight but not four exposure trials strengthened the audio-tactile association, so the quantity of prior experience matters for crossmodal development.
papers.authors: Shibo Cao, Rong Tan, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

papers.title: Altered mechanisms of adaptation in social anxiety: differences in adapting to positive versus negative emotional faces
papers.abstract: Examines whether negative perceptual bias in social anxiety stems from altered adaptation to emotional faces. Adaptation to angry faces was weaker than to happy faces in high-social-anxiety participants, with no such difference in low-anxiety participants or for sad versus happy faces. The findings point to weakened adaptation to negative emotion as a mechanism maintaining negative biases.
papers.authors: Erinda Morina, Daniel A. Harris, Sarah A. Hayes-Skelton, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

papers.title: Prior visual experience increases children's use of effective haptic exploration strategies in audio-tactile sound-shape correspondences
papers.abstract: Analyzes video recordings of 6- to 8-year-olds feeling abstract shapes to see how visual experience changes haptic exploration. Children with prior visual exposure mostly used effective strategies such as poking, while those without relied on ineffective or uncategorizable strategies. This suggests visual experience improves audio-tactile matching by making touch exploration more efficient.
papers.authors: Shibo Cao, Julia Kelly, Cuong Nguyen, Hiu Mei Chow, Brianna Leonardo, Aleksandra Sabov, Vivian M. Ciaramitaro

0688.name: Walter Scheirer
0688.department: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
0688.lab_name: Notre Dame Computer Vision Research Lab
0688.bio: Walter Scheirer is the Dennis O. Doughty Collegiate Professor of Engineering at the University of Notre Dame, where they investigate recognition across vision and language. Scheirer applies extreme value theory to visual recognition and develops formal theories for open set recognition to address the identification of unknown classes in unconstrained environments. Their methodology integrates visual psychophysics to bridge human and machine perception, aiming to increase the robustness of neural networks against novel or occluded stimuli. Additionally, Scheirer’s work involves media forensics and the study of biologically-inspired learning algorithms to create adaptive and ethically grounded artificial intelligence systems.
0688.research_direction: Dr. Scheirer has recently been bridging human visual cognition and machine perception, investigating how human psychophysical measurements—such as reaction times and behavioral error patterns—can serve as principled supervision to improve the robustness of computer vision systems. They are exploring the practical utility of this approach by using human difficulty ratings to guide drone-based detection of heavily occluded targets, while concurrently testing whether human visual category boundaries are better modeled by extreme value theory rather than central prototypes or exemplars. Beyond empirical vision science, their recent work explores the mathematical foundations of open-world learning by developing information-theoretic frameworks to handle uncertain and entirely novel observations. Additionally, Dr. Scheirer has been examining the ethical dimensions of human-computer interaction, investigating how virtue ethics can be translated into concrete software design patterns that foster human flourishing rather than engagement maximization.

papers.title: Identifying Information From Observations With Uncertainty and Novelty
papers.abstract: Develops a formal information-theoretic treatment of what it means to identify information in observations when the data are uncertain and may contain novel, previously unseen elements. The framework provides definitions and results that underpin evaluation and reasoning about open-world learning systems.
papers.authors: Derek S. Prijatelj, Timothy J. Ireland, Walter J. Scheirer

papers.title: Psych-Occlusion: Using Visual Psychophysics for Aerial Detection of Occluded Persons During Search and Rescue
papers.abstract: Presents a drone-imagery dataset and training approach for finding partially hidden people in search and rescue, where human observers were tested psychophysically to quantify how difficult each occluded target is. Using these human difficulty measures to guide detector training and evaluation improves detection of heavily occluded people compared with standard approaches.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
papers.authors: Arturo Miguel Russell Bernal, Jane Cleland-Huang, Walter Scheirer

papers.title: Extreme Value Theory for Modeling Category Decision Boundaries in Visual Recognition
papers.abstract: Tests whether human category boundaries are better captured by models of the extremes of a stimulus distribution than by central-tendency prototypes or exemplars. In two experiments (line lengths and morphed 2D faces), a Weibull fit from extreme value theory predicted how people assign in-between stimuli to categories when reference sampling changed, suggesting the brain may encode discriminative information via extrema.
papers.authors: Jin Huang, Deeksha Arun, Terrance Boult, Walter Scheirer

papers.title: Design Patterns for the Common Good: Building Better Technologies Using the Wisdom of Virtue Ethics
papers.abstract: Draws on virtue ethics to derive design patterns meant to steer software and interface design toward human flourishing rather than engagement-maximization. The authors translate ethical principles into concrete, reusable patterns and show how designers can apply them to everyday technologies.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
papers.authors: Louisa Conwill, Megan K. Levis, Karla Badillo-Urquiola, Walter J. Scheirer

papers.title: Informing Machine Perception With Psychophysics
papers.abstract: A Point of View piece arguing that human psychophysical measurements can serve as a principled source of supervision and evaluation for machine perception systems. It surveys how behavioral signals such as reaction time and error patterns have been used to improve robustness and open-set behavior, and lays out a research agenda for tying computer vision more closely to human visual processing.
papers.authors: Justin Dulay, Sonia Poltoratski, Till S. Hartmann, Samuel E. Anthony, Walter J. Scheirer

0689.name: Ward van der Tempel
0689.bio: Ward van der Tempel is the CTO and co-founder of VoxelSensors, where they oversee the development of neuromorphic-inspired 3D perception systems. They earned a PhD in Electrical Engineering from Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), with research at the ETRO department focusing on Current-Assisted Photonic Demodulators (CAPD) and Time-of-Flight (ToF) imaging. Van der Tempel's current work involves the Single Photon Active Event Sensor (SPAES), which utilizes attention-based selective data gathering for low-power, low-latency spatial awareness and gaze tracking in wearable AI. They also participate in the SPECTRE program, a collaboration between VoxelSensors and VUB focused on 3D sensing for robotics and human-device interaction.
0689.research_direction: Dr. van der Tempel's recent work has been exploring advanced optical and event-driven sensing architectures for lightweight extended reality hardware. Specifically, their research investigates how to adapt dual Purkinje image eye tracking, traditionally a bulky but high-precision laboratory method, into miniaturized, low-power systems suitable for head-worn devices. Additionally, they have recently been developing attention-based, event-driven sensing methods designed to overcome the latency and power constraints of always-on 3D spatial perception. By rethinking how sensors capture high-fidelity gaze and spatial information, their work aims to determine how selective, application-driven data readout can efficiently support seamless user interaction in augmented and mixed reality.

papers.title: The next generation of DPI eye trackers for lightweight XR
papers.abstract: Presents an eye-tracking approach based on dual Purkinje image measurement, adapted so it fits in lightweight wearable XR hardware. It argues that this optical method can deliver high-precision gaze data at low power and small size, in contrast to bulkier laboratory DPI trackers.
papers.venue: Proc. SPIE 13414, Optical Architectures for Displays and Sensing in AR/VR/MR VI (SPIE AR|VR|MR 2025)
papers.authors: Boris Greenberg, Ward van der Tempel

papers.title: Low-power, low-latency perception for XR
papers.abstract: Argues that always-on perception for wearable augmented and mixed reality is limited by power and latency, and presents an event-driven sensing approach that reads out only the information the application needs. It outlines the sensor concept behind VoxelSensors' attention-based 3D perception and gaze tracking for head-worn devices.
papers.venue: Proc. SPIE 12449, Optical Architectures for Displays and Sensing in AR/VR/MR IV
papers.authors: Ward van der Tempel, Robert Collier, Kostas Pataridis, Ségolène Rogge, Arman Alaie, Jean-Sébastien Staelens, Mahmoud Shahin, Johannes Peeters, André Miodezky, Christian Mourad

0691.name: Weina Zhu
0691.bio: Weina Zhu is a Professor in the School of Information Science at Yunnan University, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual perception. Zhu’s research investigates how the human brain processes sensory information within and outside of conscious awareness, utilizing continuous flash suppression (CFS) paradigms and psychophysical modeling. They employ methodologies including high-density electroencephalography (EEG/ERP), eye-tracking, and image processing to examine the temporal dynamics of vision, the 'closure-superiority effect,' and the role of neural oscillations in defining temporal integration windows. This work connects computational mathematics and vision science to characterize mechanisms underlying rapid object recognition and visual attention.
0691.research_direction: Dr. Zhu has recently been bridging cognitive vision science and neural engineering by investigating both unconscious visual processing and advanced EEG decoding for brain-computer interfaces. In their vision research, their recent work explores how and when background scene context facilitates object recognition, using continuous flash suppression to ask whether object-scene congruency effects persist outside of conscious awareness. They are also examining the psychophysical mechanics of continuous flash suppression itself, testing how specific spatial and color features of masking stimuli interact with target images to dictate the duration of visual suppression. Concurrently, Dr. Zhu is developing novel deep-learning architectures, including multi-scale attention networks and Mamba-based state-space models, designed to extract informative spatial and temporal features from motor-imagery EEG signals to improve classification accuracy.

papers.title: TMSA-Net: A novel attention mechanism for improved motor imagery EEG signal processing
papers.abstract: Proposes an EEG decoding network for motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces that uses a new multi-scale attention mechanism to weight informative temporal and spatial features in the recorded signals. The model is benchmarked on standard motor-imagery datasets and reports gains over competing deep-learning decoders. It is the most widely cited output of the lab's recent shift toward neural signal decoding.
papers.authors: Qian Zhao, Weina Zhu

papers.title: Effects of object-scene congruency with and without awareness
papers.abstract: Tests whether an object that fits its background scene is recognized more readily, and whether that benefit survives when the object is rendered invisible with continuous flash suppression. Combines behavioral measures of object categorization with manipulations of scene consistency and visibility. The results speak to how much scene context can influence object processing outside conscious awareness.
papers.authors: Weina Zhu, Jan Drewes

papers.title: MIFNet: a Mamba-based interactive frequency convolutional neural network for motor imagery decoding
papers.abstract: Introduces a motor-imagery EEG decoder that splits signals into frequency bands, processes them with convolutional branches that exchange information, and uses a Mamba state-space module to model temporal dependencies efficiently. Evaluated on public motor-imagery benchmarks, it improves classification accuracy while keeping computation modest.
papers.authors: Luoqian Yang, Weina Zhu

papers.title: The role of scene context in object recognition: Timing and mechanisms
papers.abstract: Examines how quickly a consistent scene background starts to help object recognition and through what mechanisms, including whether the benefit persists when the object is not consciously perceived. Uses timed behavioral paradigms to separate early from later contextual contributions.
papers.authors: Mingjie Gao, Jan Drewes, Weina Zhu

papers.title: Feature-based interaction between masks and target in continuous flash suppression
papers.abstract: Investigates how the visual features of the flashing mask (such as spatial and color/frequency properties) interact with those of the target to determine how long the target stays suppressed under continuous flash suppression. Shows that suppression depends on feature-specific match between mask and target rather than mask strength alone, informing the design of CFS experiments on unconscious processing.
papers.authors: Jan Drewes, Christoph Witzel, Weina Zhu

0692.name: Weiwei Zhang
0692.lab_name: Cognitive Neuroscience of Perception, Attention, & Memory (COMPAM) Lab
0692.bio: Weiwei Zhang is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of California, Riverside, and directs the COMPAM Lab. Zhang’s research focuses on the functional and neural mechanisms of visual working memory, specifically the discrete capacity and mnemonic precision of visual representations. This work includes the fixed-resolution model of working memory, which posits that visual information is stored in a limited number of discrete slots. Their current research utilizes Bayesian cognitive modeling, psychophysics, EEG, and fMRI to explore how factors such as top-down attention, emotional states, and physical exertion modulate the quality and retention of visual information.
0692.research_direction: Dr. Zhang’s recent work explores the functional dynamics, neural substrates, and mental costs of visual working memory. They have recently been investigating how actively maintained memory contents continuously steer perception, attention, and decision-making over time, utilizing dynamic behavioral measures like mouse-trajectory tracking to capture these interactions. Additionally, their research probes the intersection of cognitive and physical effort, using hand dynamometer tasks to quantify the energetic cost of visual memory load and to test competing theories about why physical exertion impacts cognitive control. Finally, they are mapping the neural architecture of short-term retention, employing high-resolution fMRI to determine whether medial temporal lobe pathways traditionally known for episodic pattern separation also support the precise feature representations of visual working memory.

papers.title: Working Memory Guides Perceptual Decisions Through Fast Capture and Slow Drift
papers.abstract: Uses a task in which people hold colors in working memory while making a perceptual judgment to ask how remembered content steers what we perceive and choose. The results indicate a two-stage pattern: memory content rapidly captures attention/early perceptual processing, then more slowly pulls the evolving decision toward the remembered item. The authors describe this with a fast-capture, slow-drift account that ties together attention, memory and decision-making.
papers.authors: Hyung-Bum Park, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: Mental cost of simple(st) physical exertion
papers.abstract: Even a simple hand grip can degrade attention, memory and decision-making, and this paper asks why. It contrasts a resource-sharing account, in which action and cognition draw on a common pool so gripping shrinks working-memory retention, with a control-cost account, in which exertion mainly adds to the demands on control processes. Working-memory experiments under handgrip effort are used to adjudicate between these accounts of the action-cognition trade-off.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Yoojeong Choo, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: The dynamics of attentional guidance by working memory contents
papers.abstract: Memory contents can pull attention toward matching sensory input, but it is debated whether only one prioritized item or several items can do so. This study inserts a continuous perceptual-matching task with mouse-trajectory analysis into the retention interval of a working-memory task with one or two colors. Trajectories were robustly biased toward remembered colors, showing that the guidance dynamics extend to multiple memory items with limits.
papers.authors: Hyung-Bum Park, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: The entorhinal-DG/CA3 pathway in the medial temporal lobe retains visual working memory of a simple surface feature
papers.abstract: Working memory and long-term memory are usually treated as separate systems, yet both need to keep similar representations distinct. The study combines an orientation working-memory task with high-resolution fMRI to test whether the entorhinal-dentate gyrus/CA3 pathway of the medial temporal lobe, known for pattern separation in episodic memory, also supports precise item-specific working memory. It finds that this pathway carries the precision of the retained visual feature, linking hippocampal circuitry to short-term memory quality.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Marcus Cappiello, Michael A Yassa, Edward Ester, Kareem A Zaghloul, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: Effortfulness of visual working memory: Gauged by physical exertion
papers.abstract: Holding information in working memory is effortful, but how much effort it costs is poorly understood. Participants freely chose between remembering a number of colors and holding a hand dynamometer at a required percentage of maximal contraction to earn a fixed reward, letting the authors express memory effort in the same currency as physical exertion. Working-memory effort was discounted much like physical effort, providing a model of cognitive effort cost.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Weiwei Zhang

0693.name: Weizhen Xie
0693.bio: Weizhen Xie is an Assistant Professor at the University of Maryland and a researcher affiliated with the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) at the NIH. Xie directs the Integrated Cognitive Neuroscience (ICON) Lab, where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying human visual memory and cognitive control across different timescales. Their work utilizes techniques including intracranial EEG, fMRI, and behavioral modeling to explore the role of the medial temporal lobe in memory precision and consolidation. Additionally, Xie examines how cognitive representations are modulated by physiological and psychological factors such as sleep, emotion, and physical exertion.
0693.research_direction: Dr. Xie has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms that support visual memory, utilizing a combination of human intracranial recordings and lesion studies in epilepsy patients. Their recent work explores whether the medial temporal lobe and parahippocampal cortex play a direct role in maintaining the high-fidelity precision of visual short-term memories and consolidating naturalistic scenes over time. At a more granular level, they are also examining whether the temporal structure of cortical population bursts—specifically, the ordered sequences of single-neuron spiking—acts as a fundamental code for memorized content. Finally, broadening their focus on the resource demands of working memory, Dr. Xie has been probing how even minimal, continuous physical exertion might impose an overlapping mental cost on general cognitive performance.

papers.title: Mental cost of simple(st) physical exertion
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether even minimal physical effort imposes a cognitive cost. Across experiments, participants performed cognitive tasks while holding light physical exertion, and performance and effort measures were compared to no-exertion conditions. Results indicate that simple exertion taxes mental resources, extending his work on the effortfulness of working memory.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Yoojeong Choo, Weiwei Zhang

papers.title: Medial temporal lobe lesions reduce visual working memory precision
papers.abstract: The study tests whether the medial temporal lobe is needed to hold visual information over short delays by testing epilepsy patients after MTL resection. Patients with lesions showed lower precision in working memory recall than controls, while the number of remembered items was less affected. The findings support a causal role of the hippocampal-MTL system in the fidelity of short-term visual memories.
papers.authors: Yoojeong Choo, Sanikaa P. Thakurdesai, Asbah Qadri, Oceane E. Fruchet, Samantha N. Jackson, Radhika Chatterjee, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul, Weizhen Xie

papers.title: The role of the parahippocampal cortex in memory consolidation for scenes
papers.abstract: The authors follow patients who had part of the medial temporal lobe removed, testing how the parahippocampal cortex contributes to remembering complex scenes over time. Damage to this region impaired consolidation of scene memories, which is consistent with a specialized role in scene processing. It extends his lesion work to naturalistic visual memory.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Susan G. Wardle, Jonathan Langbein, Oceane Fruchet, Madeline Baumhauer, Anthony Phan, Adam P. Tong, Shruti Japee, Sara K. Inati, Chris I. Baker, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Neuronal sequences in population bursts encode information in human cortex
papers.abstract: Using intracranial recordings of single neurons from human cortex in patients performing a memory task, the authors show that brief population bursts contain ordered sequences of neuron firing. The order of spikes within these bursts carries information about the memorized content and is more informative than firing rate alone. The work suggests that sequential spiking within bursts is a code for information in the human cortex, linking memory to temporally structured population activity.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, John H. Wittig Jr., Julio I. Chapeton, Mohamad El-Kalliny, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: The medial temporal lobe supports the quality of visual short-term memory representation
papers.abstract: Combining intracranial EEG recordings in epilepsy patients with a precision-based visual short-term memory task, the paper shows that medial temporal lobe activity tracks how precisely a feature is remembered. Neural activity patterns during encoding and maintenance predicted the quality of the stored representation. This challenges the view that short-term memory is independent of MTL and links hippocampal circuits to memory fidelity.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, Julio I. Chapeton, Srijan Bhasin, Chris Zawora, John H. Wittig Jr., Sara K. Inati, Weiwei Zhang, Kareem A. Zaghloul

0694.name: William G. Hayward
0694.bio: William G. Hayward serves as Chair Professor of Psychology and Dean of Social Sciences at Lingnan University, focusing on cognitive psychology and neuroscience. Hayward’s research examines how the brain processes visual information for object and face recognition, alongside the mechanisms of visual attention. By utilizing behavioral techniques, eye-tracking, EEG/ERP, and fMRI, Hayward investigates individual differences in facial scanning and the cross-cultural factors that impact visual expertise. Their current work explores the development of face familiarity and the stability of perceptual scanning patterns over time.
0694.research_direction: Dr. Hayward has recently been investigating the cognitive and visual mechanisms of face perception, focusing heavily on how individual facial features are integrated and processed holistically. Their recent work explores the underlying dynamics of holistic processing by dissecting composite face tasks into independent facilitation and interference components, and by probing perceptual feature binding through the lens of facial illusory conjunctions. Additionally, they are investigating how idiosyncratic eye-movement strategies—quantified using hidden Markov models—correlate with classic behavioral markers of holistic processing like the face inversion effect. Broadening their scope to high-level social perception, Dr. Hayward also studies how emotional expressions modulate facial age estimation, specifically examining how these perceptual interactions are influenced by both the age and race of the observer.

papers.title: The effect of emotional expression on age estimates is modulated by face age and participant age
papers.abstract: Young Asian observers, and in a second experiment young and older Asian observers, estimated the ages of young, middle-aged and older White and Asian faces showing neutral, happy or angry expressions. Happy and angry expressions made young faces look older, and this effect grew with observer age and was stronger for other-race (White) than own-race (Asian) faces. For older faces the pattern differed, indicating that expression effects on perceived age depend on both face age and observer age.
papers.authors: Luyan Ji, Senrong Liao, William G. Hayward

papers.title: Facilitation and interference are asymmetric in holistic face processing
papers.abstract: Holistic processing is treated as a hallmark of faces, yet the part-whole and composite tasks that measure it barely correlate. The authors split the effect into facilitation (congruent trials) and interference (incongruent trials) within one complete composite task. They show these two components respond differently to the location and cueing probability of the target half of the face, suggesting they are partly independent, and argue that separating them can reconcile conflicting findings across holistic-processing paradigms.
papers.authors: Haiyang Jin, Luyan Ji, Olivia S. Cheung, William G. Hayward

papers.title: Illusory Conjunction in the Face
papers.abstract: This preprint studies illusory conjunctions for faces, that is, errors in which features from different faces are wrongly combined into a single percept, as a window on how facial features are bound during perception. It continues the lab's line of work on how face parts are integrated. (Abstract could not be retrieved; summary is inferred from the title and the related VSS 2023 abstract by the same authors.)
papers.authors: Herrick Fung, Tim Chuk, William Gordon Hayward

papers.title: Association of idiosyncratic eye-movement patterns with holistic processing of faces as measured by the composite face effect and the face inversion effect
papers.abstract: Participants completed a face inversion task and a top-cued or bottom-cued composite task while their eye movements were recorded and clustered using hidden Markov models into upper-focused (eye region) and lower-focused (face centre) groups. The groups showed no difference in inversion effect, but in the composite task the upper-focused group showed a stronger composite effect for the upper halves of faces than lower halves, while the lower-focused group did not. Individual scanning strategies are thus linked to how holistically faces are processed.
papers.authors: Nianzeng Zhong, Janet H. Hsiao, Guomei Zhou, William G. Hayward

0695.name: William H. Warren
0695.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic and Psychological Sciences
0695.bio: William H. Warren is the Chancellor’s Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences at Brown University and the director of the Virtual Environment Navigation Lab (VENLab). Warren’s research utilizes immersive virtual reality to investigate how visual information, such as optic flow and affordances, regulates human locomotion, spatial navigation, and collective crowd dynamics. By applying a dynamical systems framework, Warren models the emergence of complex social behaviors such as flocking and pedestrian interactions from local visual-motor rules. Recipient of the 2023 Ken Nakayama Medal in Vision Science, Warren integrates experimental psychology and computational modeling to study the ecological coupling between an organism and its environment.
0695.research_direction: Dr. Warren has recently been investigating how local visual information guides human spatial behavior, from individual navigation to the collective dynamics of crowds. To understand pedestrian group behavior, they utilize virtual reality and experiments with real walkers to model crowds as networks of visual-motor couplings, probing whether individuals interact with their neighbors based on physical metric distance, topological proximity, or specific visual field cues. Their recent work also explores how these social visual influences compete with environmental signage to drive human route choices and decision-making during high-pressure evacuation scenarios. Additionally, they have been examining the underlying structures of spatial memory, using non-Euclidean virtual mazes to test whether human navigators construct globally consistent Euclidean cognitive maps or rely on looser, place-to-place local graphs.

papers.title: Visual influence networks in walking crowds
papers.abstract: Uses experiments with real walking crowds to map which neighbors each pedestrian is visually influenced by and how strongly. It builds a network model of these visual influences and tests how it predicts the spread of heading changes and the effect of leaders through a group.
papers.venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface
papers.authors: Kei Yoshida, Mario di Bernardo, William H. Warren

papers.title: Navigators learn a local graph, not a global map
papers.abstract: Tests whether people build a globally consistent Euclidean map or a looser network of place-to-place links, using virtual mazes with non-Euclidean geometry. Behavior across the mazes supports learning of a local graph of routes rather than a metric global map.
papers.authors: Marianne Strickrodt, Tobias Meilinger, Heinrich H. Bülthoff, William H. Warren

papers.title: Modeling competing guidance on evacuation choices under time pressure using virtual reality and machine learning
papers.abstract: Immersive VR evacuation experiments pit conflicting social cues and signage against each other under time pressure, and machine learning models are fitted to predict which exit people choose. The work quantifies how competing guidance shapes route decisions and supports evacuation prediction.
papers.authors: Yuxin Zhang, Max Kinateder, Xinyan Huang, William H. Warren

papers.title: Human Crowds as Social Networks: Collective Dynamics of Consensus and Polarization
papers.abstract: Reviews Warren's program in which crowd behavior is modeled as a network of pairwise visual influences between walkers. It shows how simple local visual-motor coupling rules can produce global patterns such as consensus in heading and polarization, and links pedestrian data to the broader science of social networks and collective dynamics.
papers.authors: William H. Warren, J. Benjamin Falandays, Kei Yoshida, Trenton D. Wirth, Brian A. Free

papers.title: Is the neighborhood of interaction in human crowds metric, topological, or visual?
papers.abstract: Contrasts three accounts of which neighbors a walker responds to in a crowd: those within a fixed distance, the nearest few, or those determined by what is visible. Experiments with virtual crowds indicate that the interaction neighborhood is best described by visual information, with implications for models of collective motion.
papers.authors: Trenton D. Wirth, Gregory C. Dachner, Kevin W. Rio, William H. Warren

0696.name: William S. Tuten
0696.department: Herbert Wertheim School of Optometry and Vision Science
0696.bio: Tuten is an Assistant Professor who researches cellular-level mechanisms of human vision through optical engineering and psychophysical methods. They utilize adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to correct for ocular aberrations, enabling the stimulation of individual photoreceptors in living subjects. Their research examines the relationship between retinal structure and function in healthy eyes and those with degenerative diseases. Tuten investigates how spatial and color perception are shaped by photoreceptor topography and post-receptoral circuitry.
0696.research_direction: Dr. Tuten has recently been investigating the cellular basis of human color vision and the structure-function relationships of inherited retinal diseases using high-resolution adaptive optics and psychophysics. Their recent work explores how color appearance at the very limits of spatial resolution is shaped by both spatiotemporal stimulus properties and the local ratio of L- and M-cones within the foveal mosaic. By delivering precisely targeted micro-stimuli to individually mapped photoreceptors, they are probing how the visual system pools cone-opponent signals to generate perceived hue. Additionally, they have been examining how abnormal photoreceptor topographies affect visual performance, specifically testing how the dramatically elevated cellular density of S-cones in patients with Enhanced S-cone Syndrome impacts visual acuity within that specific pathway.

papers.title: Local variations in L/M ratio influence the detection and color naming of small spots
papers.abstract: Using adaptive optics to deliver tiny flashes to single cones whose L, M or S identity had been mapped, the authors asked how the local mix of L and M cones around a target cone shapes what an observer sees. Detection and hue reports for small spots depended on the local L/M ratio, showing that color appearance at this scale is tied to the underlying cone mosaic rather than being fixed by the stimulus wavelength. The findings constrain models of how the visual system pools cone signals across the fovea.
papers.authors: Maxwell J. Greene, Vimal P. Pandiyan, Ramkumar Sabesan, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Unique yellow shifts for small and brief stimuli in the central retina
papers.abstract: The wavelength that appears neither reddish nor greenish (unique yellow) was measured in the central retina using small, brief stimuli. Perceived hue for such stimuli shifted relative to large, long-duration fields, suggesting that spatial and temporal properties of the stimulus alter the cone-opponent signals that support color naming. The work reveals how retinal spatial sampling and post-receptoral processing jointly determine hue at the limits of resolution.
papers.authors: Maxwell J. Greene, Alexandra E. Boehm, John E. Vanston, Vimal P. Pandiyan, Ramkumar Sabesan, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Enhanced S-Cone Syndrome: Elevated Cone Counts Confer Supernormal Visual Acuity in the S-Cone Pathway
papers.abstract: Adaptive optics imaging and psychophysics were used in patients with Enhanced S-cone Syndrome to count cones and test acuity through the S-cone pathway. Patients had far more S cones than normal and showed acuity in that pathway that exceeded the normal range, consistent with the higher cellular sampling density. The study links retinal disease structure to visual function at cellular resolution.
papers.authors: Yiyi Wang, Jessica Wong, Jacque L. Duncan, Austin Roorda, William S. Tuten

papers.title: Enhanced S-cone Syndrome, a Mini-review
papers.abstract: A short review of the clinical features, genetics and retinal structure of Enhanced S-cone Syndrome, an inherited disease with an excess of S cones. It draws on high-resolution imaging of affected retinas to summarize what is known about cone topography and function in the condition.
papers.venue: Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology (Retinal Degenerative Diseases XIX)
papers.authors: Yiyi Wang, Jessica Wong, Jacque L. Duncan, Austin Roorda, William S. Tuten

0697.name: Wilma A Bainbridge
0697.bio: Wilma A. Bainbridge is an Associate Professor of Psychology at the University of Chicago and the director of the Brain Bridge Lab. Bainbridge's research investigates the relationship between perception and memory, specifically focusing on 'memorability' as an intrinsic stimulus attribute that influences memory performance across individuals. They utilize methodologies including functional MRI, computer vision, and deep learning models to predict memory retention and identify the neural signatures of visual representations. Their work also explores cognitive phenomena such as the Mandela Effect and the impact of aphantasia on mental imagery and recall.
0697.research_direction: Dr. Bainbridge's recent work explores the phenomenon of intrinsic memorability, investigating why certain stimuli are consistently remembered or forgotten across different observers. Using massive-scale behavioral datasets encompassing millions of recognition trials, they have recently been modeling the complex interplay of perceptual, semantic, and individual-level factors to predict memory for naturalistic object images. Their research extends this framework beyond standard visual objects to examine the specific features that drive the memorability of abstract, everyday symbols and even auditory stimuli like human voices. To unpack the cognitive mechanisms behind these stimulus-driven memory effects, Dr. Bainbridge leverages novel methodologies—such as using generative AI to reverse-engineer and manipulate the memorability of visual symbols—while continuing to investigate how processing efficiency governs what the brain ultimately retains.

papers.title: What divides and unites our memories: Multifactor trial-wise predictions of memory across 6+ million trials
papers.abstract: Memory research usually isolates one or a few influences on remembering, so this paper instead pits many factors against each other at once. Analyzing over six million recognition decisions from nearly 14,000 people viewing 26,107 object images, it compares participant-level, item-level (memorability, typicality) and environmental factors. The individual participant and the memorability of the image emerge as the strongest predictors of hits, while other factors add comparatively little, giving a unified account of what determines whether something is remembered.
papers.authors: Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: Reverse engineering what makes a symbol memorable
papers.abstract: Everyday symbols such as ! or @ are pervasive but little is known about how they are stored in memory. The authors had participants sort symbols by visual and conceptual properties, used the sorting data to isolate the features that predict memory, and then used generative AI to amplify or suppress those features in newly created symbols. Symbols designed to be memorable were recognized better, and also helped people recall the abstract words paired with them, showing that memory can be engineered through design.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Brady R. T. Roberts, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: The memorability of voices is predictable and consistent across listeners
papers.abstract: Memorability has been shown for images, but this study extends it to sound. Over 3,000 participants heard clips of different speakers saying the same sentence in a recognition task, and they tended to remember and forget the same voices, including the same speakers across different utterances.
