Regression models using low-level acoustic properties (such as fundamental frequency) and high-level traits (such as dialect) predicted memorability out of sample, establishing an intrinsic memorability of voices.
papers.authors: Cambria Revsine, Esther Goldberg, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: Memorability of visual stimuli and the role of processing efficiency
papers.abstract: This review surveys what is known about why some visual stimuli are consistently more memorable than others across observers. It covers how memorability is measured and predicted, its behavioral and neural correlates, and how it relates to typicality, distinctiveness and attention. The authors argue that processing efficiency in the visual system is a unifying account for why memorable items are remembered.
papers.authors: Wilma A. Bainbridge, Dirk B. Walther, Keisuke Fukuda, Lore Goetschalckx

papers.title: The features underlying the memorability of objects
papers.abstract: Using more than one million memory ratings for a naturalistic set of 26,107 object images built to sample concrete objects comprehensively, the study builds a feature model that predicts which objects will be remembered. Semantic features prove more influential than perceptual ones, and the relationship between memorability and typicality is more complex than a simple positive or negative association.
papers.authors: Max A. Kramer, Martin N. Hebart, Chris I. Baker, Wilma A. Bainbridge

0698.name: Wilson Geisler
0698.bio: Wilson Geisler is a vision scientist specializing in the application of ideal observer theory and natural scene statistics to model human visual perception and behavior. Geisler’s research characterizes the limits of visual performance by combining psychophysical experiments with neurophysiological recordings from the primate visual cortex and computational modeling. Their work includes the study of statistical properties of natural images, eye movement strategies during visual search, and the development of normalization models for cortical neuron responses. Geisler currently holds the David Wechsler Regents Chair in Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and is a member of the National Academy of Sciences.
0698.research_direction: Dr. Geisler has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying texture segmentation, visual search, and target detection in complex naturalistic environments. Their recent work explores how the visual system groups and segments natural textures without explicit feedback, developing hierarchical Bayesian observer models to test whether spatial proximity can serve as an unsupervised learning signal for these mechanisms. In parallel, they are examining human covert visual search and target identification under high levels of stimulus uncertainty by comparing human behavioral performance against ideal Bayesian observers, heuristic decision rules, and deep convolutional neural networks. Across these domains, their research seeks to understand how fundamental biological constraints—such as intrinsic position uncertainty, divisive normalization, and spatially correlated neural noise—account for established psychophysical phenomena like phase-dependent pattern masking and search efficiency across the visual field.

papers.title: Principles of Local and Global Grouping that Underlie Segmentation of Natural Texture Images
papers.abstract: Proposes a five-stage hierarchical Bayesian observer for texture segmentation that needs no prior experience: local similarity grouping with normalization, mutual-similarity grouping, transitive grouping, confidence grouping and region grouping. Local similarity grouping trained for accuracy predicts human texture discrimination, and the full model segments images with randomly shaped natural-texture regions, handles textures slanted in depth, and copes with illumination changes. Large deep networks often fail on the same stimuli.
papers.authors: Wilson S. Geisler, Abhranil Das

papers.title: Proximity as a Ground-Truth Proxy for Training Texture Discrimination and Segmentation
papers.abstract: Shows that spatial proximity of image patches can stand in for same/different ground truth, because near-versus-far discrimination and same-versus-different texture discrimination share mathematically identical decision bounds when built on the same features. This lets accurate decision variables and bounds be learned from arbitrary natural images with no feedback and then tuned to the current scene. The trained stages serve as the front end of a hierarchical Bayesian segmentation model, and the idea suggests a plausible developmental learning mechanism.
papers.authors: Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Optimal visual search with highly heuristic decision rules
papers.abstract: Compares human covert visual search over briefly shown displays against a Bayesian-optimal observer assuming independent information at each location. Humans slightly outperformed the optimal model despite poor foveal sensitivity. Three factors explain this: simple fixed heuristic decision rules already approach optimal search, foveal neglect mainly affects the central location, and spatially correlated neural noise can raise performance above the independent-noise prediction.
papers.authors: Anqi Zhang, Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Target identification under high levels of amplitude, size, orientation and background uncertainty
papers.abstract: Formulates target detection with heavy stimulus uncertainty as identification among exhaustive target categories and derives the optimal rule plus a simulation method. For wavelet targets in noise with five uncertain dimensions, a normalized heuristic MAX observer approximates the ideal observer, whereas a trained convolutional network falls short of it. Human data match the ideal and normalized-MAX observers, and the smaller-than-predicted uncertainty effect is largely explained by intrinsic position uncertainty.
papers.authors: Can Oluk, Wilson S. Geisler

papers.title: Phase-dependent asymmetry of pattern masking in natural images explained by intrinsic position uncertainty
papers.abstract: Measures how detection thresholds for targets in natural backgrounds depend on the phase-dependent similarity between target and background. Thresholds fall monotonically with this similarity, whereas a simple template-matching observer with divisive normalization predicts a U-shape. Adding a small, independently measured amount of intrinsic position uncertainty to the observer accounts for the observed pattern.
papers.authors: Anqi Zhang, Eric S. Seemiller, Wilson S. Geisler

0699.name: Winrich Freiwald
0699.bio: Winrich Freiwald is a neuroscientist who investigates the neural circuitry underlying face recognition, social cognition, and attention. By integrating functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with single-cell electrophysiology, Freiwald co-discovered the primate 'face patch' system, a network of brain regions dedicated to processing facial identity and expression. Their work characterizes how these regions transform sensory inputs into invariant object representations and how they interface with circuits for memory and emotional processing. Currently, their research explores the computational principles of the visual system and the mechanisms by which the brain exerts attentional control over social and non-social stimuli.
0699.research_direction: Dr. Freiwald has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying high-level social cognition, communication, and complex motor control. Using large-scale electrophysiology in non-human primates, their recent work explores how the cortex generates socially meaningful facial gestures through hierarchical coding and network synchrony, and how the brain encodes sequential action primitives as discrete, language-like symbols. In parallel, their human fMRI research probes the functional organization of the association cortex to understand how parallel networks segregate social from spatial information streams. Additionally, they are examining the intersection of high-level vision and memory by mapping specialized cortical regions in the temporal pole dedicated to processing familiar faces and individual person knowledge.

papers.title: Neural representation of action symbols in primate frontal cortex
papers.abstract: Recordings from frontal cortex of monkeys performing a drawing task show that neurons encode individual action primitives as discrete, reusable symbols rather than as continuous movement parameters. These symbol-like codes are combined in sequences that follow compositional structure, suggesting a neural basis for building complex behaviour from a vocabulary of elementary actions. The work links motor control to symbolic, language-like computation and was done with computational collaborators.
papers.authors: Lucas Y. Tian, Kedar Garzón Gupta, Daniel J. Hanuska, Adam G. Rouse, Mark A. G. Eldridge, Marc H. Schieber, Xiao-Jing Wang, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Facial gestures are enacted through a cortical hierarchy of dynamic and stable codes
papers.abstract: Using large-scale neural recordings across facial motor, premotor and cingulate cortex in macaques, the study asks how the brain produces socially meaningful facial gestures. It finds a hierarchy in which some areas carry dynamic, time-varying codes while others carry stable codes of the intended gesture. This reveals how cortical areas divide labour to generate communicative facial movements.
papers.authors: Geena R. Ianni, Yuriria Vázquez, Adam G. Rouse, Marc H. Schieber, Yifat Prut, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Neural synchrony links sensorimotor cortices in a network for facial motor control
papers.abstract: Simultaneous recordings across several cortical facial-motor areas reveal that coordinated, synchronized activity binds sensorimotor regions into a functional network. The findings indicate that communication between these areas, and not just their individual firing, supports the control of facial movements. It complements the companion Science paper on the coding hierarchy.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Yuriria Vázquez, Geena R. Ianni, Elie Rassi, Adam G. Rouse, Marc H. Schieber, Faraz Yazdani, Yifat Prut, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Parallel systems for social and spatial cognition reaching the cortical apex
papers.abstract: Individual-specific fMRI in humans shows that high-level association cortex contains separate, side-by-side systems, one preferring social content and another spatial content. The parallel organization extends to the top of the cortical hierarchy, refining ideas on how association cortex is organized by content domain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: A familiar face and person processing area in the human temporal pole
papers.abstract: Functional MRI localizes a region in the human anterior temporal pole that responds selectively to familiar faces and people, as opposed to unfamiliar ones. This connects face-patch research to memory and person knowledge, and parallels findings in monkeys.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Gazi Husain, Winrich A. Freiwald

0700.name: Woon Ju Park
0700.bio: Woon Ju Park is an Assistant Professor in the School of Psychology at the Georgia Institute of Technology and directs the Cortical Resilience Lab. Park’s research examines the mechanisms of sensory processing and brain plasticity in typical and atypical populations, including individuals with autism spectrum disorder and visual impairments. They utilize behavioral psychophysics, computational modeling, and multimodal neuroimaging techniques, such as functional and quantitative MRI, to investigate how the brain adapts to varied sensory environments. Their work specifically explores how developmental experiences and sensory deprivation influence the neural encoding of visual and auditory information.
0700.research_direction: Dr. Park has recently been investigating experience-driven neuroplasticity and the mechanistic limits of perceptual and cognitive performance across multiple sensory modalities. In the auditory domain, their recent work explores how profound sensory experience—such as early blindness or musical training—might alter auditory cortex morphology, pitch discrimination, and the spatiotemporal filters underlying auditory motion perception. To do this, they employ psychophysical reverse correlation, structural MRI, and computational modeling to determine whether these behavioral differences stem from reduced internal neural noise or sharper peripheral tuning, while theoretically framing cross-modal plasticity as a form of general skill acquisition. Additionally, Dr. Park is examining whether low-level visual sensory noise acts as a primary bottleneck for working memory precision, utilizing non-invasive brain stimulation and behavioral models to probe these limits in both neurotypical individuals and those with schizophrenia.

papers.title: Blindness reveals that Heschl's gyrus folding is not altered by auditory experience
papers.abstract: Greater duplication of Heschl's gyrus in musicians has been read as experience-driven change or as a predisposition toward music. Manual and surface-based analyses of T1 MRI from 100 blind and sighted participants found that extensive auditory experience in blindness did not increase folding. The results suggest that Heschl's gyrus morphology is largely predetermined.
papers.authors: Amy Poole, Kelly H. Chang, Feiyi Wang, Ione Fine, Woon Ju Park

papers.title: Enhanced pitch perception in early blind individuals and musicians is due to reduced internal noise
papers.abstract: Early blind and sighted listeners with matched musical training did equally well on a notched-noise detection task tapping peripheral frequency selectivity, but blind listeners were better at a cortically mediated pitch discrimination task. Modeling attributed the advantage to lower internal noise rather than sharper frequency tuning, and both blindness and musical training predicted reduced noise. Internal noise is thus proposed as a common route for experience-driven auditory plasticity.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Jasmine Awad, Ione Fine

papers.title: Sensory Neural Noise as a Limiting Factor in Visual Working Memory Precision in Neurotypicals and Individuals with Schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Individual differences in internal sensory noise during visual perception predict visual working memory capacity, challenging the view that prefrontal circuits are the main limit. Elevated visual sensory noise accounts for working memory deficits in schizophrenia, and tDCS over visual cortex that changed noise produced matching changes in memory precision. A computational model shows the same noise can limit precision during maintenance.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Megan Ichinose, Gengshi Hu, Geoffrey F. Woodman, Duje Tadin, Sohee Park

papers.title: A unified model for cross-modal plasticity and skill acquisition
papers.abstract: The paper argues that cross-modal plasticity after early blindness is better understood as skill acquisition than as a consequence of visual deprivation alone. Drawing on the cortical recycling and metamodal theories, it proposes a single hypothesis of cortical specialization in which shared functional, algorithmic and structural constraints govern both kinds of plasticity.
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

papers.title: The perception of auditory motion in sighted and early blind individuals
papers.abstract: Using psychophysical reverse correlation with spatiotemporal noise, the study asks whether the filters that support auditory motion direction discrimination behave like continuous motion-energy detectors (as in vision) or infer motion from discrete sound positions over time. Both sighted and early blind listeners turned out to use spatiotemporally separable filters. Early blind participants were nonetheless more sensitive, less affected by noise, and had filters that better captured motion onset.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Woon Ju Park, Ione Fine

0701.name: Xiaolan Fu
0701.bio: Xiaolan Fu is the Founding Dean and a Professor at the School of Psychology, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and previously served as the Director of the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Fu's research focuses on the neural and computational mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and emotion, specifically in the areas of affective computing and micro-expression recognition. They led the development of the CASME (Chinese Academy of Sciences Micro-expression) databases and developed methodologies for decoding masked facial expressions using electromyography (EMG) and deep learning. Fu’s current research integrates cognitive psychology and neuroscience to address challenges in mental health and human-computer interaction.
0701.research_direction: Dr. Fu has recently been investigating the objective measurement and automated recognition of fleeting facial micro-expressions. Their recent work explores how to quantify the physiological intensity and duration of these micro-expressions using facial electromyography, while also developing computational methods to infer key video frames and correct subjective human annotation biases in affective computing datasets. In parallel, they are studying the neural mechanisms that govern how the brain modulates sensory processing based on internal cognitive and motor states. Specifically, Dr. Fu uses neuroimaging meta-analyses and neural phase dynamics to examine how the brain attenuates sensory responses to self-generated actions, as well as how task demands influence the degree to which mind-wandering disrupts neural entrainment to external sensory and motor events.

papers.title: Evaluating and Correcting Human Annotation Bias in Dynamic Micro-Expression Recognition
papers.abstract: Examines how subjective human labeling of dynamic micro-expressions introduces bias into datasets and hence into models trained on them. The work proposes ways to evaluate label quality and correct annotation bias, aiming at more trustworthy benchmarks for micro-expression recognition.
papers.authors: Feng Liu, Bingyu Nan, Xuezhong Qian, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Task difficulty modulates the effect of mind wandering on phase dynamics
papers.abstract: Using thought probes during visual and motor tasks of varying difficulty, the study shows that mind wandering reduces neural entrainment to external events (intertrial phase coherence) only when tasks are easy, not when they are demanding. The authors argue that task difficulty tips the balance between internally and externally directed cognition, with phase coherence serving as a shared neural mechanism for both sensory input and motor output processing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Zhengkun Long, Georg Northoff, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Could Micro-Expressions Be Quantified? Electromyography Gives Affirmative Evidence
papers.abstract: The paper records facial muscle activity with electromyography during elicited micro-expressions to test whether their intensity and duration can be measured objectively. It reports that micro-expressions have quantifiable EMG signatures, giving a physiological ground truth that can complement human coding and support computational recognition.
papers.authors: Jingting Li, Shaoyuan Lu, Yan Wang, Zizhao Dong, Su-Jing Wang, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: Micro-Expression Key Frame Inference
papers.abstract: Addresses the problem of locating the onset, apex and offset frames of micro-expressions in video, which is normally done by laborious manual annotation. The authors propose an inference approach for key frames and evaluate it on micro-expression datasets, supporting more reliable data annotation and downstream recognition.
papers.authors: Su-Jing Wang, Yu-Han Miao, Jingting Li, Ling Zhou, Zizhao Dong, Mengyi Sun, Xiaolan Fu

papers.title: The neural network of sensory attenuation: A neuroimaging meta-analysis
papers.abstract: A coordinate-based fMRI meta-analysis of how the brain dampens the sensory consequences of self-generated actions. The authors identify a consistent network of regions supporting sensory attenuation, linking predictive motor signals to reduced sensory responses and informing accounts of the sense of agency.
papers.authors: Jingjin Gu, Tatia Buidze, Ke Zhao, Jan Gläscher, Xiaolan Fu

0702.name: Xiaoqing Gao
0702.bio: Gao is an Associate Professor at the Center for Psychological Sciences at Zhejiang University, specializing in the neural and behavioral development of visual functions. Gao's research investigates how early visual experiences, such as congenital cataracts, shape the processing of socially relevant information like facial identity and expressions. Utilizing neuroimaging techniques including fMRI frequency tagging, EEG, and fNIRS, Gao explores the development of face-space representations and the neural mechanisms of visual object categorization. Their work characterizes both typical development and the effects of early visual deprivation to elucidate the plasticity of the human visual system.
0702.research_direction: Dr. Gao has recently been investigating the neural and temporal architecture of familiar person perception alongside the resting-state dynamics of the human brain. To understand how we process familiarity, their recent work uses frequency-tagging EEG and fMRI to map modality-specific and multisensory recognition networks, probing the timeline of early perceptual and later evaluative stages of familiar face processing. They are also utilizing behavioral paradigms to test how real-world face familiarity influences downstream social cognition, such as perspective-taking in children. In a parallel line of research, their recent work explores time-varying brain entropy and its relationship to functional connectivity using large-scale resting-state fMRI datasets. By tracking temporal fluctuations in brain complexity, they are examining how recurring entropy states map onto network integration, network segregation, and domain-general executive functions like processing speed and cognitive flexibility.

papers.title: Neural Architecture of Familiar Person Perception: Contributions of Unimodal and Multimodal Brain Regions
papers.abstract: The authors built a frequency-tagging fMRI paradigm to ask where the brain signals that a face or a voice belongs to a familiar person. Familiarity from faces engaged posterior superior temporal cortex, while voices engaged anterior superior temporal cortex. Overlapping multisensory responses appeared in posterior STS and inferior frontal cortex, pointing to both modality-specific and shared networks for recognizing familiar people.
papers.authors: Tianxing Zheng, Stefania Mattioni, Olivier Collignon, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: How the Percept of Face Familiarity Unfolds Over Time
papers.abstract: Using frequency-tagging EEG with personally familiar faces inserted periodically into streams of unfamiliar faces at several presentation rates, the study shows that familiarity is discriminated even at 50 msec per face. An N170 that grows with presentation time and a P300 that appears only at slower rates indicate two temporally distinct stages of familiar-face processing: an early perceptual stage and a later evaluative one.
papers.authors: Mengdan Sun, Menglei Yao, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: The dynamic interplay between brain entropy and functional connectivity
papers.abstract: Using 812 resting-state fMRI scans, the study links recurring brain-entropy states to whole-brain connectivity patterns. Low-entropy states were segregated and negatively related to cognition, high-entropy states highly integrated, and two intermediate states balanced integration and segregation. Entropy-connectivity correlations were negative and state-dependent, positioning entropy as a marker of dynamic functional organization.
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xin, Jiaqian Yu, Cuiping Wang, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: Familiar faces facilitate perspective-taking in children
papers.abstract: Children aged 9 to 11 completed a Director Task in which the director's face was a familiar peer or a stranger. Perspective-taking was better with a familiar peer, and faces made familiar through real social interaction, but not through learning facts about the person, boosted later perspective-taking. The authors propose that face familiarity quickly sets the mind into a socially prepared state.
papers.authors: Xuan Wu, Minjie Wen, Jie He, Xiaoqing Gao

papers.title: The brain entropy dynamics in resting state
papers.abstract: Applying a sliding-window analysis to resting-state fMRI from 812 Human Connectome Project adults, the authors tracked time-varying brain entropy and clustered it into four recurring states. Dwell time in a very-low-entropy state related negatively to cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control and processing speed, while an intermediate state related positively. The work offers a framework for studying dynamic brain complexity in health and disease.
papers.authors: Xiaoyang Xin, Jiaqian Yu, Xiaoqing Gao

0703.name: Xuexin Wei
0703.bio: Xuexin Wei is a computational and theoretical neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying adaptive and intelligent behavior. By integrating normative modeling with bottom-up analysis of large-scale experimental data, Wei develops theories on sensory adaptation, perceptual biases, and neural manifold geometry. Wei's research applies the principle of efficient computation to understand how environmental structures and task demands shape neural representations in the domains of vision and navigation. Currently, Wei's lab focuses on bridging biological neural coding with deep learning to explore generalization and probabilistic inference in both brain and artificial systems.
0703.research_direction: Dr. Wei has recently been developing computational and theoretical frameworks to link neural population activity, Bayesian inference, and observed behavior. Their recent work explores how the combination of efficient sensory coding and Bayesian decoding might unify seemingly contradictory attraction and repulsion biases in perceptual estimation, and investigates how the geometric properties of neural manifolds shape the peculiar error distributions seen in working memory tasks. Methodologically, they are probing the limits of standard analytical tools by assessing whether the priors and noise components of Bayesian observer models can be uniquely identified from behavioral data, alongside developing novel split-trial statistical methods to more accurately quantify the information capacity of noisy neural population codes. Furthermore, their research touches on artificial intelligence and spatial navigation, investigating whether neural networks trained purely to predict continuous visual input can spontaneously develop hippocampal-style cognitive maps containing grid and place representations.

papers.title: Identifiability of Bayesian models of perception
papers.abstract: Bayesian observer models are widely fit to behavior to infer the brain's priors, sensory noise and loss functions, but it is rarely asked whether those components can be uniquely recovered. This work analyses when such model components are identifiable from behavioral data, showing that many are not without extra constraints, and demonstrates the consequences with simulations and analyses of standard perceptual tasks. It offers guidance on experimental design and model interpretation.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Michael Hahn, Entang Wang, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Split-trial analysis reveals the information capacity of neural population codes
papers.abstract: Estimating how much information a neural population carries about a stimulus is hard because noise and limited trials bias standard estimators. The authors introduce an approach that splits repeated trials to separate signal from noise and obtain an estimate of a population's information capacity. They validate it on simulations and neural recordings and use it to compare coding across populations.
papers.authors: Dylan Le, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Representational geometry explains puzzling error distributions in behavioral tasks
papers.abstract: Errors in tasks such as reporting a remembered orientation or color have peculiar, stimulus-dependent, non-Gaussian distributions that are hard to explain with standard noise models. The authors show that these patterns follow from the geometry of the underlying neural population representation, in which the neural manifold's curvature and the variable Fisher information shape how noise translates into behavioral errors. The account ties efficient-coding style population models to observed behavior.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Xue-Xin Wei, Michael Woodford

papers.title: A unifying theory explains seemingly contradictory biases in perceptual estimation
papers.abstract: Perceptual estimates are systematically biased, sometimes toward previously experienced or expected values (attraction) and sometimes away from them (repulsion), and these two effects have been treated as separate phenomena. The authors combine an efficient-coding account of how a stimulus is encoded with Bayesian decoding, and show that a single framework yields both attraction and repulsion depending on the noise and prior structure. The theory makes quantitative predictions about how bias relates to variability that they confirm across several published psychophysical datasets.
papers.authors: Michael Hahn, Xue-Xin Wei

papers.title: Cognitive maps from predictive vision
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether spatial cognitive maps can arise from vision alone. Neural networks trained to predict upcoming visual input while an agent moves through simulated environments develop internal spatial representations, including grid-like and place-like tuning. This suggests predictive learning on visual experience is a sufficient route to hippocampal-entorhinal-style codes.
papers.authors: Margaret C. von Ebers, Xue-Xin Wei

0704.name: Yaffa Yeshurun
0704.department: Department of Psychology and the Institute of Information Processing and Decision Making (IIPDM)
0704.bio: Yaffa Yeshurun is a Full Professor at the University of Haifa who researches the spatial and temporal dynamics of visual attention. Yeshurun investigates transient, stimulus-driven attention, specifically demonstrating its capacity to enhance spatial resolution and its impact on perceptual performance. Their research methodology utilizes psychophysical tasks to examine the trade-offs between integration and segregation processes, as well as the effects of perceptual load and crowding on visual processing. Yeshurun's recent studies apply these findings to real-world scenarios, including attentional selection during driving and individual variability in internal noise.
0704.research_direction: Dr. Yeshurun has recently been investigating the underlying mechanisms of visual attention, exploring both the facilitatory and inhibitory components of spatial cuing as well as whether object-based attention spreads automatically or strategically. To probe these attentional dynamics, their recent work employs diverse approaches, ranging from large-scale behavioral assessments of individual variability to utilizing the pupillary light response as a continuous, response-free readout of attentional allocation. In addition to spatial processing, they are also examining temporal interference in visual representations, specifically seeking to dissociate short-interval visual masking from longer-interval temporal crowding. Using sequential orientation-estimation tasks and computational mixture modeling, they explore how these temporal bottlenecks operate across foveal and peripheral vision, asking whether sequential items primarily degrade encoding precision or lower the overall signal-to-noise ratio.

papers.title: Large-scale examination of the benefit and cost of spatial attention and their individual variability
papers.abstract: Using a large sample of 662 participants across four experiments, the authors measured how much performance improves when a cue is valid and how much it worsens when it is invalid, relative to a neutral baseline, in an acuity task. Separating benefit from cost lets them tease apart facilitatory from inhibitory attentional mechanisms. The work also quantifies how strongly these effects vary from person to person, which small-sample studies could not resolve.
papers.authors: Felipe Luzardo, Yaffa Yeshurun

papers.title: Temporal Crowding With Central Vision Reveals the Fragility of Visual Representations
papers.abstract: Temporal crowding, the difficulty of identifying an object flanked in time by other items, had been considered mainly a peripheral phenomenon. Using sequences of three oriented items and an orientation-estimation task with mixture modeling, this study shows clear temporal crowding at the fovea, even at 400 ms intervals, and of similar magnitude to peripheral crowding. The characteristic signature is a loss of encoding precision, pointing to involvement of higher visual areas and to interference that is not simply response competition.
papers.authors: Tomer Sahar, Yaffa Yeshurun

papers.title: Interference across time: dissociating short from long temporal interference
papers.abstract: Identifying an object is often disrupted by items shown just before or after it. Using the same three-item orientation sequences and computational models, the study compares short intervals (visual masking, under 150 ms) with long intervals (temporal crowding, 175-475 ms) and varies inter-item similarity. Long-interval interference mainly reduces encoding precision, while short-interval interference mainly lowers the signal-to-noise ratio, showing they are qualitatively different phenomena.
papers.authors: Ilanit Hochmitz, Ahmad Abu-Akel, Yaffa Yeshurun

papers.title: Attention does not spread automatically along objects: Evidence from the pupillary light response
papers.abstract: Object-based attention effects are usually explained by attention spreading automatically along a cued object. To test this, the authors used a continuous, response-free readout of attentional allocation based on modulation of the pupillary light response. When the task did not encourage spreading, no automatic spread along the object appeared; when the target distribution encouraged it, spreading emerged, suggesting the classic object effect is strategic rather than automatic.
papers.authors: Felipe Luzardo, Wolfgang Einhauser, Monique Michl, Yaffa Yeshurun

0705.name: Yalda Mohsenzadeh
0705.bio: Mohsenzadeh is an Assistant Professor at Western University and a faculty member at the Vector Institute, focusing on the intersection of human visual cognition and artificial intelligence. Their research employs multi-modal neuroimaging techniques, including fMRI, MEG, and EEG, alongside deep learning architectures to decode the spatiotemporal dynamics of the human brain during visual processing and memory formation. By examining the computational principles of biological vision, such as image memorability and robust perception, Mohsenzadeh aims to develop machines that emulate human-level performance and resilience.
0705.research_direction: Dr. Mohsenzadeh has recently been investigating the neural and computational mechanisms underlying complex visual perception and image memorability. Using techniques like EEG-fMRI fusion and representational similarity analysis, their recent work explores how the brain processes naturalistic inputs, mapping out the spatiotemporal dynamics of audiovisual integration and tracking how human action representations transition from visual features to modality-invariant concepts. Additionally, they are examining the temporal signatures of conscious access during rapid object recognition by linking neural time courses to the hierarchical representations of deep neural networks. Parallel to this neuroimaging research, Dr. Mohsenzadeh is probing the computational basis of visual memory using artificial intelligence. By designing biologically inspired autoencoders and face-specific deep models, they are investigating the distinct visual characteristics that dictate why certain scenes, objects, and faces are intrinsically more memorable than others.

papers.title: Distinct perceptual and conceptual representations of natural actions along the lateral and dorsal visual streams: an EEG-fMRI fusion study
papers.abstract: The study recorded EEG and fMRI while people watched short videos and read sentences describing everyday actions, then used representational similarity analysis and EEG-fMRI fusion. Along the lateral occipitotemporal pathway representations shifted from perceptual to modality-invariant conceptual features, and the target of an action (object, person, or self) explained the most unique variance. Lateral occipitotemporal cortex and posterior STS specifically encoded action targets, with dorsal and ventral streams showing distinct conceptual codes.
papers.authors: Diana C. Dima, Jody C. Culham, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Modeling visual memorability assessment with autoencoders reveals characteristics of memorable images
papers.abstract: The authors train a CNN autoencoder in a single-epoch regime that mirrors one-exposure human memory experiments, and ask what makes an image memorable. Reconstruction error correlates with memorability scores, and latent-space distinctiveness and an MLP readout predict memorability robustly. Interpretability analysis then highlights the visual characteristics that push images toward being remembered.
papers.authors: Elham Bagheri, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Neural processing of naturalistic audiovisual events in space and time
papers.abstract: Participants viewed naturalistic videos with sound while fMRI and EEG were recorded, allowing the authors to trace where and when visual and acoustic information are processed. Cross-modal interaction was asymmetric and early: acoustic information appeared in early visual as well as auditory cortex, whereas visual information stayed in visual cortex. Categorical and semantic content emerged later in multimodal association areas, and comparison with a two-branch deep network suggested that early fusion is needed for a biologically plausible model of audiovisual perception.
papers.authors: Yu Hu, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Unveiling the neural dynamics of conscious perception in rapid object recognition
papers.abstract: Using EEG during rapid serial visual presentation of natural object images, the study asks when neural activity distinguishes consciously perceived from missed targets. Multivariate decoding and representational analysis with deep neural network features reveal a time course of visual feature processing linked to whether the object reaches awareness. It links the timing of conscious access to the hierarchy of visual representations.
papers.authors: Saba Charmi Motlagh, Marc Joanisse, Boyu Wang, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

papers.title: Predicting memorability of face photographs with deep neural networks
papers.abstract: The paper shows that generic image-memorability networks trained on scenes and objects do poorly on human face photographs, and explains why. It then proposes face-specific deep models that predict face memorability far better, using features tuned to face attributes. The work highlights how memorability depends on image category and provides a practical tool for face images.
papers.authors: Mohammad Younesi, Yalda Mohsenzadeh

0706.name: Yang Sun
0706.bio: Yang Sun is an Associate Professor at the College of Educational Sciences, Shenyang Normal University, specializing in the cognitive neuroscience of visual perception. Their research investigates the 'self-prioritization effect' and how social-referential information modulates sensory processing using psychophysical paradigms, event-related potentials (ERP), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Sun has researched neural compensatory mechanisms in the medial prefrontal cortex that preserve self-bias in aging populations and examined the modulation of early visual cortex activity by social significance. Their current work employs computational modeling to delineate the interactions between social cognition, attention, and sensory perception.
0706.research_direction: Dr. Sun has recently been investigating the intersection of unconscious visual processing, attention, and cognitive control. Their recent work explores whether spatial cues that are rendered consciously invisible through visual masking can still modulate cognitive conflict in Stroop-type tasks. By utilizing event-related potentials, they examine the electrophysiological signatures of these phenomena to determine how unconscious spatial information shapes attentional allocation. Ultimately, Dr. Sun seeks to uncover the neural dynamics that allow unseen visual information to influence conflict resolution without conscious awareness.

papers.title: Masked invisible cue could modulate Stroop effect in spatial cueing paradigm: evidence from an event-related potentials study
papers.abstract: An ERP study asking whether a masked, consciously invisible cue can still shape attentional processing in a spatial cueing task that involves Stroop-type conflict. The work examines electrophysiological signatures to test whether unconscious cue information modulates conflict effects. It sits in the PI's line on unconscious processing and attention.
papers.venue: 2023 17th International Conference on Complex Medical Engineering (CME)
papers.authors: Yufeng He, Xiaoyu Tang, Ming Zhang, Jinglong Wu, Yang Sun

0707.name: Yaoda Xu
0707.bio: Xu investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object representation and the adaptive nature of visual information processing in the human brain. Their research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to explore the functional roles of the posterior parietal and occipito-temporal cortices in visual working memory and decision-making. Xu examines how the brain manages capacity-limited visual processing and evaluates the similarities and divergences between primate vision and convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
0707.research_direction: Dr. Xu has recently been using fMRI decoding techniques to investigate the neural architecture of visual working memory, focusing specifically on the division of labor between the occipito-temporal and posterior parietal cortices. Their recent work explores whether memory representations in ventral visual areas are merely lingering sensory codes or if they are actively reformatted from perceptual inputs and driven by top-down parietal signals. To understand how the visual system handles capacity limits, they are investigating how neural responses to single objects scale to multi-item memory arrays under varying demands of attention and cognitive load. Furthermore, they are examining the multivoxel representational geometry within the posterior parietal cortex to determine how this region can simultaneously maintain multiple concurrent streams of information without interference.

papers.title: Using fMRI Representations of Single Objects to Predict Multiple Objects in Working Memory in Human Occipitotemporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: The study tests whether brain responses to individual objects can be used to predict responses when several objects are held in working memory together. It examines this across occipito-temporal and posterior parietal cortices to see how multi-item memory patterns relate to single-item ones. The results speak to how capacity-limited memory content is composed in these regions.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin Chun

papers.title: Representing Visual Objects, Attention, and Load in Human Occipito-temporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, this paper compares how occipito-temporal and posterior parietal cortices represent object identity while attention and memory load are varied. It characterizes how these regions differ in encoding attended objects and in their sensitivity to load. The findings refine the division of labor between ventral and parietal visual regions during capacity-limited processing.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu, Marvin Chun

papers.title: Transformed Visual Working Memory Representations in Human Occipitotemporal and Posterior Parietal Cortices
papers.abstract: This fMRI paper asks whether working-memory representations in visual cortex are a replay of perceptual ones or are transformed into a different format. It reports that memory codes in occipito-temporal and parietal cortices differ from perceptual codes. The work bears on how the brain re-formats sensory information for maintenance.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu

papers.title: The human posterior parietal cortices orthogonalize the representation of different streams of information concurrently coded in visual working memory
papers.abstract: This fMRI study examines how posterior parietal cortex keeps several kinds of information in working memory at once. The multivoxel patterns show that different information streams are coded in largely orthogonal formats, which would let them coexist without interfering. The work supplies a representational mechanism for how the parietal cortex handles concurrent memory content.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu

papers.title: Parietal-driven visual working memory representation in occipito-temporal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI decoding, this single-author study asks how information held in visual working memory is represented in occipito-temporal cortex versus posterior parietal cortex. It shows that working-memory representations in occipito-temporal areas are shaped by, and depend on, those in parietal cortex rather than being a simple continuation of sensory coding. The result argues for a parietal-driven account of how the ventral stream maintains object information.
papers.authors: Yaoda Xu

0708.name: Yi Jiang
0708.institution: Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
0708.department: State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science / Vision and Attention Lab
0708.bio: Yi Jiang is a Professor and Principal Investigator at the Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, directing the Vision and Attention Lab. Jiang utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI, and high-temporal-resolution EEG to study the neural mechanisms of visual perception, selective attention, and the boundaries of conscious awareness. Their research includes investigations into the subconscious processing of social signals, specifically how biological motion and facial expressions are encoded without explicit awareness. Jiang's current work examines the rhythmic nature of attentional sampling and the cross-modal integration of visual, vestibular, and olfactory cues in human perception.
0708.research_direction: Dr. Jiang's recent work explores the neural architectures underlying social vision, particularly how the primate brain processes biological motion and allocates attention. Using comparative fMRI and EEG, they have recently been investigating the cortical and subcortical pathways—such as the superior colliculus-MT-STS route—that track the hierarchical rhythms and point-light kinematics of moving agents across humans and macaques. Additionally, their research utilizes critical flicker fusion to separate conscious from unconscious visual processing, asking how visual awareness alters the temporal pacing of rhythmic attentional sampling in frontoparietal networks. Finally, they are examining how these mechanisms, specifically unconscious gaze following and higher-order audiovisual integration, develop in children and track with clinical traits of autism.

papers.title: Visual awareness sharpens and accelerates attentional sampling through enhancing inhibitory neural modulation in the attention network
papers.abstract: By making attentional cues invisible with chromatic flicker fusion, the authors test whether awareness of a cue changes rhythmic attentional sampling. Both visible and invisible cues produced rhythmic behavioral sampling and reset frontal to right occipito-parietal connectivity. Visible cues additionally drove stronger alpha activity and inhibition and a faster sampling rhythm (about 8 Hz versus 4 Hz), showing that awareness tunes the pace of attentional sampling in the frontoparietal network.
papers.authors: Yang F, Yuan P, Shen L, Zhou K, He S, Jiang Y

papers.title: Shared and Unique Neural Codes for Biological Motion Perception in Humans and Macaque Monkeys
papers.abstract: Human and macaque brains were compared while passively viewing upright and inverted human and monkey point-light motion. Human hMT+ and monkey MT responded to biological motion from both species, whereas right human pSTS was selective for human motion, supported by increased feedforward hMT+ to pSTS connectivity. Monkeys showed no comparable conspecific-specific STS subregion, suggesting upstream areas are evolutionarily conserved while downstream areas specialized.
papers.authors: Cheng Y, Xin Y, Lu X, Yang T, Ma X, Yuan X, Liu N, Jiang Y

papers.title: Cortical tracking of hierarchical rhythms orchestrates the multisensory processing of biological motion
papers.abstract: EEG recordings show that cortical rhythms track the hierarchical temporal structure of audiovisually congruent walking and footstep sounds. At the shorter step-cycle scale integration is additive, while at the longer gait-cycle scale it is super-additive. Only the higher-order effect is specific to biological motion and correlates with autistic traits, pointing to a possible neural marker.
papers.authors: Shen L, Li S, Tian Y, Wang Y, Jiang Y

papers.title: Detecting biological motion signals in human and monkey superior colliculus: a subcortical-cortical pathway for biological motion perception
papers.abstract: Using 3T and 7T fMRI in humans and macaques, the study shows that the superior colliculus, particularly its superficial layers, responds selectively to scrambled point-light walkers that retain local biological kinematics. Dynamic causal modeling indicates a route carrying these signals from the colliculus through area MT to the posterior superior temporal sulcus. This points to a cross-species subcortical mechanism that detects life-motion cues at an early stage of visual processing.
papers.authors: Lu X, Hu Z, Xin Y, Yang T, Wang Y, Zhang P, Liu N, Jiang Y

papers.title: Unconscious and Conscious Gaze-Triggered Attentional Orienting: Distinguishing Innate and Acquired Components of Social Attention in Children and Adults with Autistic Traits and Autism Spectrum Disorders
papers.abstract: Gaze cues were rendered invisible with critical flicker fusion to separate innate from consciously acquired components of social attention. Both visible and invisible gaze cues triggered attentional orienting in typical adults and children, but only responses to invisible cues tracked autistic traits and were markedly reduced in adults with autism and in children with high traits. The work marks a developmental and clinical dissociation between unconscious and conscious gaze following.
papers.authors: Yang F, Tian J, Yuan P, Liu C, Zhang X, Yang L, Jiang Y

0709.name: Ying-zi Xiong
0709.department: Department of Ophthalmology, School of Medicine
0709.bio: Ying-zi Xiong is an Assistant Professor of Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute and the Principal Investigator of the XYZ Sensory Lab. Xiong’s research examines the mechanisms through which the human brain adapts to sensory impairments, focusing on how visual and auditory deficits affect spatial localization and daily functioning. Using psychophysical methods and multisensory modeling, they develop translational tools to improve digital accessibility and clinical assessment for individuals with low vision and dual sensory loss. Xiong’s current work includes the Vision Accessibility Initiative, which integrates computer vision and human-computer interaction to create assistive technologies for reading and independent navigation.
0709.research_direction: Dr. Xiong's recent work explores the intersection of vision and hearing loss, focusing on how dual sensory impairments affect spatial perception, clinical rehabilitation, and everyday accessibility. They have recently been investigating spatial localization and audiovisual distance judgments, utilizing newly developed psychometric questionnaires and behavioral walking tasks to understand whether spatial hearing can effectively compensate for reduced vision. In the clinical domain, their research examines how concurrent hearing impairment influences functional outcomes following standard low-vision rehabilitation. Additionally, Dr. Xiong is developing objective tools to assess text accessibility by simulating visual acuity and contrast sensitivity loss in images, testing how well optical character recognition and vision-language models can estimate low-vision legibility.

papers.title: Hearing Impairment and Visual Rehabilitation Outcomes
papers.abstract: Uses data from the multicenter Low Vision Rehabilitation Outcomes Study (611 adults with vision impairment and self-reported hearing status) to test whether hearing impairment changes the chance of achieving a meaningful functional gain after vision rehabilitation. It is one of the first clinical-outcome analyses of dual sensory impairment in a conventional rehab setting.
papers.authors: Anas Obaideen, Judith E. Goldstein, Chris Bradley, Robert W. Massof, Kyoko Fujiwara, Pradeep Y. Ramulu, Yingzi Xiong

papers.title: Distance judgement in individuals with vision and hearing loss
papers.abstract: Compares visual, auditory and audiovisual distance judgement in 50 adults (controls, vision loss, and dual sensory loss) using both verbal estimates and walking to remembered targets in a normal room. It examines how well hearing compensates for reduced vision and whether added hearing loss undermines that compensation.
papers.authors: Rui Jin, Diamond Brunt, Don Fletcher, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Yingzi Xiong

papers.title: Perceived sound localization abilities in blind individuals
papers.abstract: Fifty-eight adults with total or near-total blindness (28 with normal hearing, 30 hard of hearing) completed the DS-SLQ to rate how well they localize sounds in everyday tasks. The study checks the questionnaire's measurement properties in this population and shows how hearing status shapes perceived spatial hearing, a key driver of confidence in independent travel.
papers.authors: Prachi Agrawal, Haley Cihunka, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Walter Wittich, Chris Bradley, Yingzi Xiong

papers.title: VI-OCR: "Visually Impaired" optical character recognition pipeline for text accessibility assessment
papers.abstract: Builds a pipeline that degrades images according to a chosen level of acuity and contrast-sensitivity loss and then runs OCR and vision-language models, to estimate whether text of a given size would be legible to a low-vision reader. The authors benchmark specialized OCR models and VLMs on how closely they reproduce human text recognition across three reading tasks. The result is a candidate objective tool for judging text accessibility in products and environments.
papers.authors: Qingying Gao, Roberto Manduchi, Pradeep Y. Ramulu, Gordon E. Legge, Yingzi Xiong

papers.title: Development and validation of a questionnaire for assessing visual and auditory spatial localization abilities in dual sensory impairment
papers.abstract: Introduces the Dual Sensory Spatial Localization Questionnaire (DS-SLQ), a 35-item tool that asks people how hard everyday spatial tasks are using only vision or only hearing, and which sense they lean on. In 104 participants with varied vision and hearing status, Rasch analysis supported its validity and allowed vision and hearing abilities to be compared on one scale. Vision and hearing impairment each lowered the corresponding spatial ability, and the gap between the two predicted which sense people relied on.
papers.authors: Yingzi Xiong, Joseph Paul Nemargut, Chris Bradley, Walter Wittich, Gordon E. Legge

0711.name: YiZhong Wang
0711.bio: YiZhong Wang is a visual physiologist and the Director of the Macular Function Laboratory at the Retina Foundation of the Southwest, and an Adjunct Assistant Professor in Ophthalmology at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Wang's research focuses on characterizing human shape perception, contour integration, and perceptual organization across the lifespan and in various ocular pathologies. They specialize in the development of functional biomarkers for diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and amblyopia, recently integrating deep learning frameworks to automate the segmentation and analysis of retinal structures in optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging.
0711.research_direction: Dr. Wang has recently been investigating how to improve clinical trial endpoints for inherited retinal degenerations by using deep learning pipelines to extract structural biomarkers from OCT scans. Their recent work explores longitudinal changes in photoreceptor ellipsoid zone area and outer segment volume, evaluating how these automated metrics track disease progression in X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. Alongside this structural imaging research, they are also evaluating remote digital health technologies for functional vision monitoring in patients with maculopathies. Specifically, Dr. Wang is examining the feasibility and validity of smartphone-based self-tests—such as shape discrimination hyperacuity—to see how well at-home apps can continuously track visual function and disease activity outside the traditional clinic setting.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Assisted Measurements of Photoreceptor Ellipsoid Zone Area and Outer Segment Volume as Biomarkers for Retinitis Pigmentosa
papers.abstract: Compares a deep-learning segmentation model with manual correction against fully manual grading of OCT volume scans from 48 patients with RPGR-associated X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. The corrected deep-learning output gave measurements of ellipsoid zone area and outer segment volume that agreed closely with expert graders while greatly cutting grading effort, supporting it as a new reference standard for retinal-layer biomarkers in inherited retinal degeneration trials.
papers.authors: Yi-Zhong Wang, Katherine Juroch, David Geoffrey Birch

papers.title: Deep Learning-Facilitated Study of the Rate of Change in Photoreceptor Outer Segment Metrics in RPGR-Related X-Linked Retinitis Pigmentosa
papers.abstract: Uses a deep-learning-assisted pipeline to follow the ellipsoid zone and photoreceptor outer segment metrics over time in patients with RPGR-related X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. It estimates how quickly these structural measures decline and shows they change in a measurable, consistent way, making them candidate endpoints for natural-history studies and gene-therapy trials.
papers.authors: Yi-Zhong Wang, Katherine Juroch, Yineng Chen, Gui-Shuang Ying, David G. Birch

papers.title: Home vision monitoring in patients with maculopathy: current and future options for digital technologies
papers.abstract: Reviews visual function tests that could be used at home by patients with macular disease such as AMD and diabetic macular oedema, and how well they detect disease activity and progression. It then surveys clinical evidence for app-based monitoring tools from development through validation and real-world use, arguing that remote testing can reduce clinic burden and give clinicians continuous data.
papers.authors: Konstantinos Balaskas, Faye Drawnel, Arshad M. Khanani, Paul C. Knox, George Mavromaras, Yi-Zhong Wang

papers.title: Remote Monitoring of Visual Function in Patients with Maculopathy: The Aphelion Study
papers.abstract: Reports a study in which patients with macular disease used a smartphone-based self-test of shape discrimination hyperacuity at home over an extended period. It assesses feasibility, adherence, and how well the app-derived measures track disease status compared with clinic-based visual function testing, supporting remote monitoring of maculopathy.
papers.authors: Anthony Joseph, Mark Bullimore, Faye Drawnel, Marco Miranda, Zoe Morgan, Yi-Zhong Wang

0712.name: Yonggang Shi
0712.department: Department of Neurology, Keck School of Medicine; Department of Biomedical Engineering; Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
0712.bio: Yonggang Shi is a Professor at the University of Southern California and directs the Neuro Image Computing Research (NICR) group at the Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute. Shi’s work centers on developing computational solutions for brain mapping, specifically utilizing diffusion MRI and 3D shape analysis to model connectomes and structural connectivity. Their research includes the development of algorithms for reconstructing retinofugal visual pathways and investigating neuroanatomical biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease and visual restoration. Shi holds multiple appointments across neurology and engineering, applying methodologies such as Riemannian metric optimization and Laplace-Beltrami spectral analysis to characterize the human brain in health and disease.
0712.research_direction: Dr. Shi has recently been developing advanced computational neuroimaging methods to map brain connectivity and model the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Their recent work explores new geometric and deep learning frameworks for diffusion MRI, utilizing Wasserstein space and diffusion generative models to accurately represent, compare, and restore complex white matter fiber orientations from degraded signals. They are also investigating cortical topography by designing surface-based probabilistic tractography algorithms to trace short-range superficial U-fibers that standard imaging methods traditionally struggle to capture. In parallel, Dr. Shi has been studying Alzheimer's disease by building topological graph models of tau pathology from PET scans to uncover distinct phenotypic subtypes independent of disease severity, while also developing multistage machine learning pipelines that fuse diverse clinical and imaging modalities to improve diagnostic staging.

papers.title: Graphical modeling of cortical tau pathology topography for its subtyping in Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to discover subtypes of tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease from tau PET scans. Each person's salient tau pattern on the cortical surface is summarized as a Reeb graph, and a population-level graphical model built from cross-sectional data links these patterns across disease stages. This separates real phenotypic differences from differences in disease severity, so subtypes generalize to cohorts with different severity distributions. It is tested on synthetic data and on ADNI and A4 tau PET data.
papers.authors: Jiaxin Yue, Xinkai Wang, John Ringman, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: A Wasserstein-Space-Based Framework for Processing Fiber Orientation Geometry in Diffusion MRI
papers.abstract: Fiber orientation distributions from diffusion MRI are treated as probability measures and processed in Wasserstein space, giving a geometry-aware way to interpolate, average and compare them. The framework aims to preserve fiber structure better than conventional linear or spherical-harmonic operations and supports downstream connectome analysis.
papers.authors: Xinyu Nie, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Diffusion-based generative fiber orientation restoration from severe signal loss in diffusion-weighted MRI
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI scans can suffer severe signal loss or distortion that corrupts estimated fiber orientation distributions. This work trains a diffusion generative model to restore the fiber orientation field directly, recovering plausible white-matter structure in affected regions. It extends the authors' earlier conference version with broader validation.
papers.authors: Shuo Huang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Multistage Alignment and Fusion for Multimodal Multiclass Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a machine-learning pipeline to diagnose Alzheimer's disease stage from several imaging and clinical modalities. It aligns representations across modalities in stages before fusing them, which handles the multiclass setting (normal, mild impairment, dementia) better than simple concatenation. It is evaluated on large public cohorts.
papers.authors: Shuo Huang, Lujia Zhong, Yonggang Shi

papers.title: Surface-Based Probabilistic Fiber Tracking in Superficial White Matter
papers.abstract: Superficial white matter U-fibers just beneath the cortex are hard to track with standard tractography. This work develops a probabilistic tracking approach that operates on the cortical surface and uses surface geometry and fiber orientation information to trace short-range connections while respecting cortical topography. It is evaluated for reproducibility and used to examine superficial white matter connectivity in aging and Alzheimer's-related cohorts.
papers.authors: Xinyu Nie, Jialiang Ruan, Maria Concepción Garcia Otaduy, Lea Tenenholz Grinberg, John Ringman, Yonggang Shi

0713.name: Yoshifumi Kitamura
0713.bio: Yoshifumi Kitamura is a Professor and Deputy Director at the Research Institute of Electrical Communication at Tohoku University and the Director of the Interdisciplinary ICT Research Center for Cyber and Real Spaces. Kitamura’s research investigates the technical and psychological dimensions of interactive content design, focusing on 3D user interfaces, virtual reality, and the transmission of non-verbal information. They have coordinated interdisciplinary projects, including the development of the DIEM-A database for analyzing cultural variations in emotional bodily expressions through motion capture and computer vision. Their work integrates sensory feedback and social neuroscience to develop technologies for remote human communication and spatial awareness.
0713.research_direction: Dr. Kitamura has recently been developing novel interaction and ergonomic techniques for extended reality (XR) environments. Their recent work explores how subtle behavioral and visual cues can improve XR interfaces, such as using thumb-motion kinematics to infer intended keystrokes on small virtual keyboards and tracking fingertip blanching via headset cameras to detect tactile contact on flat surfaces. They are also investigating how to physicalize and sustain virtual experiences by designing mobile inflatable robots that provide large-scale haptic feedback in room-scale VR, as well as testing systems that seamlessly integrate guided eye exercises into virtual workspaces. Expanding beyond spatial computing interfaces, Dr. Kitamura has also been compiling and validating a new motion-capture database of Asian performers to study how cultural differences shape the bodily expression and visual perception of emotion.

papers.title: EyeXRciser: Guiding Eye Exercises without Task Interruption in Virtual Workspaces
papers.abstract: Prolonged work in XR headsets strains the eyes, but dedicated eye-exercise breaks interrupt the task at hand. This work builds a system that folds guided eye exercises into ongoing virtual-workspace activity so users can train their eyes without stopping work. The authors evaluate it with user studies on how well it supports exercise while keeping task performance intact.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
papers.authors: Hongyue Xu, Kazuyuki Fujita, Yi Li, Benjamin Tag, Guanghan Zhao, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: FanType: Intention-Inferring Fan-Shaped Thumb Interface for Text Entry on Small XR Keyboards
papers.abstract: Typing on a small virtual or handheld XR keyboard with the thumb is slow and error-prone. FanType uses a fan-shaped thumb-reach interface that infers which key the user intends from thumb motion. The paper describes the design and shows improved text-entry performance in user evaluations.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
papers.authors: Guanghan Zhao, Louis Teys, Gyeonghwan Yang, Shengdong Zhao, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: BlanchTouch: Bringing Fingertip Blanch Detection into Mixed Reality for Touch Input on Flat Surfaces
papers.abstract: Detecting when a fingertip touches a surface is hard in mixed reality using headset cameras alone. BlanchTouch exploits the brief blanching (whitening) of the fingertip on contact to detect touch on ordinary flat surfaces. The authors show this visual cue can support touch input without extra hardware.
papers.venue: 2026 IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces (VR)
papers.authors: Guanghan Zhao, Yangyang Cai, Kazuyuki Fujita, Robert W. Lindeman, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: InflatableBots: Inflatable Shape-Changing Mobile Robots for Large-Scale Encountered-Type Haptics in VR
papers.abstract: Providing physical feedback for large virtual objects in room-scale VR normally needs bulky props. InflatableBots uses mobile robots carrying inflatable structures that change shape and are positioned where the user reaches. This yields large-scale encountered-type haptics with a compact, safe hardware footprint.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24)
papers.authors: Ryota Gomi, Ryo Suzuki, Kazuki Takashima, Kazuyuki Fujita, Yoshifumi Kitamura

papers.title: Toward an Asian-based bodily movement database for emotional communication
papers.abstract: Most emotional body-movement databases draw on Western performers, limiting cross-cultural study. The authors built a motion-capture database of emotional expressions by Asian performers and validated it with perceptual ratings. It provides a resource for research on how culture shapes the expression and perception of emotion through movement.
papers.authors: Miao Cheng, Chia-huei Tseng, Ken Fujiwara, Shoi Higashiyama, Abby Weng, Yoshifumi Kitamura

0714.name: Yoshiyuki Ueda
0714.department: Institute for the Future of Human Society
0714.bio: Yoshiyuki Ueda is an Associate Professor at Kyoto University's Institute for the Future of Human Society, where they investigate the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying human attention, emotion, and social interaction. Ueda's research utilizes behavioral experiments, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging to examine how cultural contexts influence visual search and perceptual processes. Their research includes ensemble perception, facial expression adaptation, and the development of facial expression databases for psychological research. Their current work also encompasses the study of human-robot interaction and the psychological markers of social exclusion.
0714.research_direction: Dr. Ueda has recently been investigating a diverse range of topics spanning visual cognition, human-robot interaction, and social psychology. In the visual domain, their recent work explores the boundary conditions of implicit visuospatial memory, specifically testing how sequential focal attention—rather than simultaneous processing—facilitates the Hebb repetition learning effect for spatial arrays. Beyond basic cognitive processing, they are studying human-robot interaction through scenario-based experiments to determine how an android's appearance, conversational politeness, and task performance feed into multi-stage cognitive models of user acceptance. Additionally, their recent work explores the behavioral consequences of social stressors, using experimental paradigms like the Cyberball task to examine how interpersonal conflict and social exclusion trigger binge eating, and how an individual's dispositional need to belong moderates this eating-based coping response.

papers.title: Sequential model based on human cognitive processing to robot acceptance
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a three-stage model of robot acceptance (first contact, interaction, decision) that follows the order in which people form impressions and carries earlier impressions forward to later stages. A scenario-based experiment varying robot appearance and conversational behavior tests how each stage feeds into the final decision to accept the robot.
papers.authors: Waka Saeki, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Impact of politeness and performance quality of android robots on future interaction decisions: a conversational design perspective
papers.abstract: Two scenario experiments varied how politely a robot spoke and whether it completed a task perfectly or slightly failed. Politeness improved impressions and raised expectations for future task outcomes, for robots and humans alike, although its effect on preference was weaker for robots. The results inform conversational design for social robots.
papers.authors: Waka Saeki, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Sequential processing facilitates Hebb repetition learning in visuospatial domains
papers.abstract: Hebb repetition learning shows that unnoticed repeated sequences are remembered better, but it has been hard to obtain in visuospatial arrays. The authors show that the learning appears when items in the array are attended one after another, so that spatial layouts are processed sequentially rather than all at once. This identifies sequential focal attention as a boundary condition for implicit visuospatial sequence learning.
papers.authors: Yoshiyuki Ueda, Tsung-Ren Huang, Zixin Shen, Chifumi Sakata, Su-Ling Yeh, Satoru Saito

papers.title: Effect of interpersonal conflicts and the moderating effect of the dispositional need to belong on binge eating
papers.abstract: The study asks whether everyday interpersonal conflict promotes binge eating and whether a person's dispositional need to belong changes that link. Conflict was associated with more binge eating, with the strength of the relationship depending on the need to belong.
papers.authors: Michihiro Kaneko, Yoshiyuki Ueda

papers.title: Dispositional need to belong and increased eating after social exclusion
papers.abstract: Ninety-seven Japanese university students played Cyberball games in which they were either excluded or included and then freely ate cookies. Those with a higher (or lower) dispositional need to belong differed in how much they ate after exclusion, indicating that the need to belong moderates eating as a coping response to social exclusion.
papers.authors: Michihiro Kaneko, Yoshiyuki Ueda

0715.name: Yuanning Li
0715.lab_name: Computational Cognitive and Translational Neuroscience Lab (CCTN Lab)
0715.bio: Yuanning Li is an Assistant Professor at ShanghaiTech University who researches the neural mechanisms of high-level cognitive processes, including speech, language, and vision. Li's work uses intracranial electrophysiology (ECoG/iEEG) and functional neuroimaging to investigate how sensory and semantic information is represented across neural populations. By integrating statistical machine learning and deep neural networks, they develop computational models for neural encoding and decoding to support brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. Li completed a postdoctoral fellowship at UCSF focused on speech neurophysiology and a doctoral dissertation at Carnegie Mellon University concerning the human ventral visual pathway.
0715.research_direction: Dr. Li has recently been developing advanced brain-computer interfaces to decode and reconstruct naturalistic speech from human cortical recordings, exploring how to capture both complex linguistic content and acoustic nuances like prosody and tonal structures. Alongside this neuroprosthetic research, their recent work uses deep neural networks as encoding models to dissect the computational architecture of sensory systems, mapping how artificial network layers align with hierarchical processing in the auditory pathway. Bridging into visual neuroscience, they are investigating how the human brain processes naturalistic images and movies by integrating multi-level deep learning features with known cortical network structures. Furthermore, Dr. Li is exploring the cross-modal integration of vision and language, using large fMRI datasets to examine how semantic information from one modality drives predictive coding mechanisms and prediction-error signatures in the early visual cortex.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Neural Speech Reconstruction through an Efficient Acoustic-Linguistic Dual-Pathway Framework
papers.abstract: A speech-from-brain decoder is presented that runs an acoustic path and a linguistic path in parallel from cortical (ECoG) signals and merges them by voice cloning. The acoustic route recovers pitch and prosody with a recurrent decoder and a neural vocoder, while the linguistic route recovers words with a transformer adaptor and text-to-speech. With only about 20 minutes of data per participant, the combined output is both intelligible and natural sounding, addressing a long-standing trade-off in speech neuroprostheses.
papers.authors: Jiawei Li, Chunxu Guo, Chao Zhang, Edward F. Chang, Yuanning Li

papers.title: Predictive vision-language integration in the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using a large new fMRI dataset and modern AI encoding models, this work asks how language and visual information are combined in the brain. Prior information in one modality modulates responses to the other even in early visual cortex, with responses following prediction-error signatures consistent with predictive coding. Distinct populations show enhancement or suppression to semantically matched cross-modal input, with the suppressed population carrying denser semantic information.
papers.authors: Shurui Li, Zheyu Jin, Ru-Yuan Zhang, Shi Gu, Yuanning Li

papers.title: A brain-to-text framework for decoding natural tonal sentences
papers.abstract: A pipeline is described for decoding natural Mandarin sentences from cortical recordings, handling the tonal structure that most speech decoders ignore. It combines neural-network decoding of syllables and tones with a language model to output text, and works on continuous sentences in patients undergoing surgery. The work shows that tonal-language speech BCIs are feasible and points to how they could be scaled.
papers.authors: Daohan Zhang, Zhenjie Wang, Youkun Qian, Zehao Zhao, Yan Liu, Xiaotao Hao, Wanxin Li, Shuo Lu, Honglin Zhu, Luyao Chen, Kunyu Xu, Yuanning Li, Junfeng Lu

papers.title: Enhancing neural encoding models for naturalistic perception with a multi-level integration of deep neural networks and cortical networks
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an encoding model for fMRI responses to natural movies and images that combines features from several depths of a deep network with cortical network structure. Integrating information across levels and networks predicts brain activity better than standard single-layer models. The results give a route to more accurate and interpretable models of visual perception.
papers.authors: Yuanning Li, Huzheng Yang, Shi Gu
