papers.title: Dissecting neural computations of the human auditory pathway using deep neural networks for speech
papers.abstract: Recordings of cortical activity from human neurosurgical patients listening to speech were compared against several self-supervised speech deep networks. Layers of the networks aligned with a hierarchy of auditory regions, from early acoustic-like responses in primary auditory cortex to phonetic and lexical selectivity in higher areas, and with distinct temporal windows of integration. The study also showed that networks trained on speech match brain responses better than those trained on other sounds, giving a model-based account of the human auditory pathway.
papers.authors: Yuanning Li, Gopala K. Anumanchipalli, Abdelrahman Mohamed, Peili Chen, Laurel H. Carney, Junfeng Lu, Jinsong Wu, Edward F. Chang

0717.name: Yuka Sasaki
0717.department: Department of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences
0717.lab_name: Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning
0717.bio: Yuka Sasaki is a Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences (Research) at Brown University and the sub-director of the Laboratory for Cognitive and Perceptual Learning. Sasaki investigates the neural mechanisms of human brain plasticity and the role sleep plays in the consolidation and stabilization of visual learning. Using an approach that combines psychophysics with polysomnography, fMRI, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, they examine how excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitter concentrations modulate learning during NREM and REM sleep. Sasaki's research describes how sleep stabilizes new perceptual skills against retrograde interference and explores the 'first-night effect' in human sleep architecture.
0717.research_direction: Dr. Sasaki has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms underlying visual perceptual learning and memory consolidation, focusing on how the brain navigates the trade-off between plasticity and stability during post-training wakefulness and sleep. Their recent work explores how the cortical excitatory-to-inhibitory (E/I) balance governs these states, utilizing concurrent EEG, polysomnography, and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track glutamate and GABA dynamics in vivo. Specifically, they are examining how shifting E/I ratios across the early visual cortex and distinct prefrontal pathways during NREM and REM sleep mediate both skill improvement and resistance to sensory interference. Additionally, they are probing how prefrontal excitation influences sleep onset latency, while also evaluating whether rapid, non-invasive EEG metrics can reliably serve as proxies for these underlying neurochemical states.

papers.title: Concurrent Multimodal Imaging Demonstrates That EEG-Based Excitation/Inhibition Balance Reflects Glutamate and GABA Balance
papers.abstract: Using simultaneous EEG and magnetic resonance spectroscopy in sleeping participants, the study asks whether cheap, fast EEG measures of excitation/inhibition balance track the neurochemical glutamate-to-GABA ratio in early visual cortex. Ten candidate EEG indices from four algorithms were compared with the MRS ratio, separating between-person from within-person variation. All indices correlated positively with MRS, most reliably in the alpha band, supporting EEG as a practical stand-in for neurochemical E/I.
papers.authors: Aaron Cochrane, Luke Rosedahl, Masako Tamaki, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Prefrontal Glx reduction during the sleep transition is associated with sleep onset latency
papers.abstract: Twenty adults took two afternoon naps inside an MR scanner with polysomnography, exploiting the first-night effect to make sleep onset slower in the first session. Excitatory Glx in medial prefrontal cortex fell when people fell asleep in the second session but not the first, and larger drops tracked faster sleep onset. GABA did not change, suggesting that failing to lower excitation, rather than altered inhibition, hinders falling asleep.
papers.authors: Takashi Yamada, Aaron Cochrane, Theodore LaBonte-Clark, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Different Learning Stabilization Processes between Wakefulness and Sleep
papers.abstract: Newly trained visual perceptual learning is fragile and must be stabilized. Recording EEG during post-training wake rest in two studies, the authors find that when learning is still vulnerable, a higher EEG-based E/I balance predicts more interference from a competing task, while lower E/I predicts stabilization, mirroring what happens in REM sleep. Once learning is fully stabilized, the relation reverses, and theta power behaves differently across wake and sleep.
papers.authors: Aaron Cochrane, Kiley Haberkorn, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Unconscious switching of dorsal and medial pathways for plasticity and stability during NREM and REM sleep
papers.abstract: Combining MR spectroscopy with polysomnography during sleep after visual training, the study shows that dorsolateral prefrontal cortex raises its E/I balance during NREM sleep in step with performance gains, whereas medial prefrontal cortex lowers it during REM sleep in step with resistance to interference. Early visual area connectivity with each prefrontal region switches with sleep stage, pointing to alternating dorsal and medial pathways for improving and stabilizing learning.
papers.authors: Takashi Yamada, Theodore LaBonte-Clark, Nitzan Censor, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

papers.title: Plasticity-stability dynamics during post-training processing of learning
papers.abstract: This review argues that learning continues after training ends and that the brain alternates between plastic and stable states during both wake and sleep. It uses the excitatory-to-inhibitory ratio as a common measure to unify behavioral and neurochemical findings on procedural learning, showing cycles that consolidate new skills and shield them from interference from later learning.
papers.authors: Takashi Yamada, Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki

0718.name: Kareem Zaghloul
0718.bio: Zaghloul serves as the Chief of the Surgical Neurology Branch and directs the Functional and Restorative Neurosurgery Unit at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. Their research utilizes intracranial electrical recordings, including electrocorticography and single-unit microelectrode arrays, to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying human episodic memory, decision-making, and visual working memory. By utilizing clinical neurosurgical procedures such as epilepsy monitoring and deep brain stimulation, Zaghloul’s laboratory characterizes the spatiotemporal patterns of neural activity and neuronal spiking sequences involved in memory encoding and retrieval. Their work integrates computational modeling and signal processing to decode the functional organization of human cortical and subcortical networks and identifies how specific neural patterns are reinstated during recall and how the basal ganglia modulate cognitive circuits.
0718.research_direction: Dr. Zaghloul has recently been investigating the precise electrophysiological mechanisms underlying human memory formation and retrieval using intracranial and single-unit recordings in neurosurgical patients. Their research explores how fine-scale temporal dynamics—specifically the reproducible sequences of single-neuron spiking within population bursts and high-frequency ripples—encode specific memory content, and how these precise temporal codes are modulated by top-down attention. At the network level, they are also examining how broader spatial dynamics support memory recall by tracking sub-second changes in transient functional connectivity and the reinstatement of macroscopic traveling waves across the cortex during associative learning tasks. Through these parallel lines of inquiry, their recent work seeks to bridge the gap between micro-scale temporal spiking codes and large-scale cortical dynamics to understand the neural architecture of human episodic memory.

papers.title: Cortical traveling wave pattern reinstatement supports successful associative memory formation and retrieval in humans
papers.abstract: Analyzing intracranial recordings during an associative memory task, this work finds that patterns of traveling waves across the cortex are reinstated when a previously learned association is successfully retrieved. Traveling-wave dynamics thus appear to be a mechanism supporting the formation and recall of episodic memories.
papers.authors: Uma Mohan, Molly Baumhauer, Kareem Zaghloul

papers.title: Attention to memory content enhances single-unit spike sequence fidelity in the human anterior temporal lobe
papers.abstract: Using microelectrode array recordings in neurosurgical patients, the study examines how neurons in the anterior temporal lobe fire in sequences while people view or read items and hold them in memory. Directing attention to the content of memory makes these spike sequences more reliable and more informative about the item. The findings tie attentional selection directly to the precision of temporal spiking codes in human cortex.
papers.authors: Kelsey K. Sundby, Alex P. Vaz, John H. Wittig Jr, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Ripple contributions to human memory: making the spiking content count
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes evidence on hippocampal and cortical ripples in human memory, arguing that the spiking content within ripples, not just their occurrence, determines their contribution to memory. It connects human single-neuron recordings with rodent replay literature and outlines open questions.
papers.authors: Joel Reithler, Kelsey K. Sundby, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Neuronal sequences in population bursts encode information in human cortex
papers.abstract: Recording spiking activity from many single neurons in the human cortex, the authors show that brief population bursts contain reproducible orderings of neuronal firing. The order in which neurons fire within a burst carries information about the content of the memory being processed, beyond what firing rates alone convey. This supports the idea that sequence-based spiking codes underlie how human cortex represents and retrieves information.
papers.authors: Weizhen Xie, John H. Wittig Jr, Julio I. Chapeton, Mostafa El-Kalliny, Samantha N. Jackson, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

papers.title: Dynamic patterns of functional connectivity in the human brain underlie individual memory formation
papers.abstract: Using intracranial EEG from 20 participants performing a paired-associates task, the authors track sub-second changes in functional connectivity between neocortical sites. Successful encoding involves connectivity dynamics specific to each word pair, and these same patterns are reinstated during successful retrieval, linking specific network dynamics to individual memories.
papers.authors: Audrey T. Phan, Weizhen Xie, Julio I. Chapeton, Sara K. Inati, Kareem A. Zaghloul

0719.name: Zaifeng Gao
0719.department: Department of Psychology and Behavioral Sciences
0719.main_research_area: visual working memory and biological motion
0719.bio: Gao is a Professor of Psychology and Human Factors at Zhejiang University and investigates the cognitive and neural architectures of visual working memory. Their research focuses on the encoding and retention mechanisms of visual information, emphasizing complex dynamic events such as biological motion and object-based attention. Utilizing behavioral experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and electroencephalography (EEG), Gao examines how attention and memory load interact during visual processing. Additionally, their work extends into human factors and human-AI interaction, exploring trust calibration and situational awareness in automated driving systems.
0719.research_direction: Dr. Gao's recent work explores the complex architecture of working memory, specifically investigating how the brain encodes and maintains dynamic, real-world information beyond simple static objects. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics and fMRI, they have recently been examining whether temporal events are held in a dedicated storage system distinct from object memory, while also mapping the neural and behavioral subdivisions of social working memory. This social cognitive research uses dynamic action stimuli to probe how multiple agents' physical and communicative interactions are involuntarily chunked together, and tests whether holding facial expressions in mind relies on different mechanisms than tracking personality traits. Broadening this cognitive focus into applied human-computer interaction, their research additionally investigates how to structure effective human-AI teaming through the lens of joint cognitive systems and proposes new theoretical models to evaluate user experience in gestural interfaces.

papers.title: PATE Model: A 30-Year Review and Analysis of Gestural Interaction Research
papers.abstract: The authors propose a Person-Action-Target-Environment model of gestural interaction and use it to guide a PRISMA systematic review of 197 articles. Research has moved from functionality to performance to user experience, four measurement dimensions recur (efficiency, ease of use, subjective experience, tolerance), and roughly forty factors in ten categories shape interaction quality.
papers.authors: Xiaojiao Chen, Jiayi Zhang, Yuanxiu Zhao, Qi Chen, Bolin Chen, Nan Xu, Entong Jin, Yi Shen, Yu Tian, Mowei Shen, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Event cache: An independent component in working memory
papers.abstract: The study argues that holding events in mind relies on a storage system separate from the one used for objects. Combining factor analysis, psychophysics and resting-state plus task fMRI, it shows that event and object memory dissociate behaviourally and neurally. The cerebellar network, especially left Crus I, is most critical for encoding and maintaining events, which challenges current working-memory models.
papers.authors: Hui Zhou, Jinglan Wu, Jiaofeng Li, Zhihe Pan, Jinying Lu, Mowei Shen, Tengfei Wang, Yuzheng Hu, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Dissecting Social Working Memory: Neural and Behavioral Evidence for Externally and Internally Oriented Components
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that social working memory splits into an externally oriented part (holding facial expressions) and an internally oriented part (holding personality traits). In an fMRI study the two tasks recruited different regions, including sensorimotor cortex versus precuneus and posterior cingulate, with distinct multivariate patterns in dorsal medial prefrontal cortex. Brain activity for each component related to affective and cognitive empathy respectively.
papers.authors: Hanxi Pan, Zefeng Chen, Nan Xu, Bolong Wang, Yuzheng Hu, Hui Zhou, Anat Perry, Xiang-Zhen Kong, Mowei Shen, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Dual routes of chunking social interaction: Insights from grouping two agent actions in working memory
papers.abstract: Using dynamic action stimuli, the authors test how two people's actions get involuntarily grouped into one chunk in working memory. Physical-contingency and communicative-contingency interactions both produced chunking, but inversion and facing direction only mattered for communicative interactions. The results point to two routes: a domain-general physical-regularity route and a domain-specific social-relationship route.
papers.authors: Jinglan Wu, Yang Guo, Zhiyun Chen, Mowei Shen, Zaifeng Gao

papers.title: Applying HCAI in Developing Effective Human-AI Teaming: A Perspective from Human-AI Joint Cognitive Systems
papers.abstract: A perspective piece arguing that effective human-AI teaming should be designed by treating human and AI as a joint cognitive system within a human-centered AI approach. It draws on cognitive-systems thinking to frame how teams of people and intelligent agents should be structured and evaluated.
papers.authors: Wei Xu, Zaifeng Gao

0721.name: Zeynep M. Saygin
0721.bio: Saygin investigates the neuroanatomical foundations of cognitive specialization, focusing on how structural connectivity fingerprints determine the functional organization of the cortex during early development. Their research employs multimodal neuroimaging techniques, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and functional MRI, combined with longitudinal assessments and computational modeling. Saygin developed methods to predict the emergence of category-selective visual areas and linguistic networks in children using pre-existing structural markers. Their current research program focuses on developing predictive models for clinical outcomes and understanding brain plasticity following adverse experiences or neonatal brain trauma.
0721.research_direction: Dr. Saygin has recently been investigating the development and functional organization of high-level visual and cognitive networks using precision, individual-level fMRI. Their recent work explores the true functional nature of the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA), probing its diverse visual and non-visual response properties in adults while also mapping how literacy acquisition and functional connectivity drive its initial emergence in young children. Additionally, they are examining the early functional dissociation of specialized cortical networks, testing how the language system separates from adjacent regions governing spatial working memory and theory of mind during early development. Through both cross-sectional and longitudinal approaches, their research investigates how the maturation and selectivity of these distinct brain networks relate to individual differences in cognitive performance across childhood and adulthood.

papers.title: Functional dissociation of language and theory of mind in the developing superior temporal lobe
papers.abstract: Focusing on the temporal lobe, this work uses individual-level fMRI in children to test whether language and theory-of-mind processing are separable early in development. Adjacent superior temporal regions show distinct functional profiles for the two domains, extending the group's evidence for early domain specialization in higher-level cognition.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, David E. Osher, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Literacy acquisition and functional connectivity drive the emergence and continued development of the visual word form area
papers.abstract: Combining cross-sectional and longitudinal fMRI in children aged 3 to 9, the study shows that, after controlling for age, learning to read increases word selectivity in the VWFA but not selectivity for other visual categories. The precursor of the VWFA at the earlier time point shows no preference for any visual category, and longitudinal changes in the region track changes in its connectivity to high-level language regions, pointing to experience-dependent connectivity as a driver of VWFA emergence.
papers.authors: Jin Li, Kelly J. Hiersche, Nii-Ayi Aryeetey, Anna Quatrale, Patricia Resnick, Zeynep Saygin

papers.title: Demystifying visual word form area visual and nonvisual response properties with precision fMRI
papers.abstract: Using precision fMRI in individual adults, the study asks what the visual word form area actually responds to. Individually defined VWFA regions respond strongly to words but also to other visual categories and to non-visual language input and attention demands, showing the region is not narrowly visual or orthographic. The results argue for a richer, multi-property account of this hallmark reading region within ventral temporal cortex.
papers.authors: Jin Li, Kelly J. Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Functional dissociation of the language network and other cognition in early childhood
papers.abstract: Young children (about 3 to 9 years) were scanned with precision fMRI using an auditory language localizer, a spatial working-memory task and resting state. Individually defined language regions were selective for language and left-lateralized, and adjacent multiple-demand regions were selective for cognitive load but not language. The two networks showed distinct functional connectivity that was stable across ages while language responses grew with age, indicating an early double dissociation.
papers.authors: Kelly J. Hiersche, Eliana Schettini, Jin Li, Zeynep M. Saygin

papers.title: Individual Variability in Performance Reflects Selectivity of the Multiple Demand Network among Children and Adults
papers.abstract: The paper compares the multiple demand network in 37 children and 44 adults using subject-specific functional regions. Children show bilateral MD activation that is distinct from language cortex and connectionally separate, with lower activation than adults. In both groups stronger MD activation tracks better working-memory performance, especially in right-hemisphere regions, including longitudinally.
papers.authors: Elana Schettini, Kelly J. Hiersche, Zeynep M. Saygin

0723.name: Zhong-Lin Lu
0723.department: Neuroscience (also Global Network Professor, Center for Neural Science, NYU)
0723.lab_name: NYU-ECNU Institute of Brain and Cognitive Science
0723.bio: Zhong-Lin Lu is a Professor of Neuroscience at NYU Shanghai whose research integrates psychophysical experimentation, functional brain imaging, and computational modeling to investigate human perception and cognition. Lu developed the three-system theory of visual motion perception and the incremental reweighting model of perceptual learning. Their current work focuses on applying hierarchical Bayesian models to develop adaptive testing methods, such as the quick Contrast Sensitivity Function (qCSF), for diagnosing visual deficits in clinical settings. Lu also examines the neural mechanisms of attention and the rehabilitation of sensory impairments in individuals with amblyopia, myopia, and dyslexia.
0723.research_direction: Dr. Lu has recently been developing advanced Bayesian and computational frameworks to radically accelerate and refine the measurement of visual and behavioral functions. Their recent work explores how hierarchical and multiresolution Bayesian models can extract high-resolution trajectories from sparse data, specifically investigating the micro-dynamics of perceptual learning to separate general learning from short-term forgetting and within-session deterioration. Beyond behavioral tracking, they are also investigating ways to optimize clinical psychophysics by creating generative "digital twins" to rapidly predict individual contrast sensitivity functions with minimal trials. Furthermore, their methodological research extends to neuroimaging, where they are designing highly optimized tree-search algorithms to speed up population receptive field mapping in fMRI retinotopy by orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Pyramid-based Bayesian modeling for high-resolution behavioral analysis
papers.abstract: Proposes a multiresolution Bayesian framework that estimates behavioral functions from very sparse data by modeling covariance only at the coarsest layer of a parameter pyramid and refining finer scales with a difference pyramid. Implemented in PyMC, the best variant (PyramidHBMc) cut error and variability by up to about 74% and 78% relative to independent Bayesian estimation across four temporal and spatial datasets. It offers a scalable, interpretable route to high-resolution estimates of perceptual and cognitive functions.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian augmented Hebbian reweighting model of perceptual learning
papers.abstract: Builds a hierarchical Bayesian version of the augmented Hebbian reweighting model so that learning curves of each participant and of the whole population are fitted within a single framework. A feature-engineering plus linear-regression approximation to the model likelihood makes estimation about 20,000 times faster, which is what makes hierarchical inference at population, subject and test levels practical. The approach is presented as general for perceptual-learning data and for other stochastic models without analytic likelihoods.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu, Shanglin Yang, Barbara Anne Dosher

papers.title: qPRF: A system to accelerate population receptive field modeling
papers.abstract: Presents qPRF, a system that speeds up population receptive field fitting to fMRI data by more than 1,000-fold by precomputing a tree-like lookup structure and searching it during fitting. On the Human Connectome Project retinotopy data (181 subjects, over 10 million vertices) it matched the goodness of fit of a standard package and finished in under 13 hours on an ordinary CPU. Additional search strategies allow unconstrained models and guarantee optimality with little extra cost.
papers.authors: Sebastian Waz, Yalin Wang, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Enabling identification of component processes in perceptual learning with nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian modeling
papers.abstract: Shows that a nonparametric hierarchical Bayesian model can recover learning curves at very fine temporal resolution (blocks as small as 10 trials), where conventional threshold estimates blur together the components of learning. Applied to a 1920-trial Gabor orientation training study, it produced unbiased, more precise estimates than independent per-block inference and let the authors separate general learning from between-session forgetting and within-session relearning or deterioration.
papers.authors: Yukai Zhao, Jiajuan Liu, Barbara Anne Dosher, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Predicting contrast sensitivity functions with digital twins
papers.abstract: Develops digital twins of the contrast sensitivity function using a hierarchical Bayesian generative model, evaluated on 12 prediction tasks that combine historical data, new subjects and missing conditions. Predictions were accurate at group and individual levels and could serve as informative priors, cutting qCSF data-collection burden by more than half at 25 trials. The work points to a route for more efficient, personalized vision assessment.
papers.authors: Yukai Zhao, Luis Andres Lesmes, Michael Dorr, Zhong-Lin Lu

0724.name: Zhou Tiangang
0724.institution: Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
0724.department: State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science
0724.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science
0724.bio: Zhou is a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Science, Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, where they investigate the neural mechanisms of visual cognition. Their work centers on the "global-first" theory of topological perception, which posits that the human visual system extracts global topological properties, such as the number of holes, as the primary units of object representation before processing local features. Using psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Zhou examines the subcortical and cortical pathways involved in visual attention, object-based working memory, and the development of brain-inspired neural networks. Their research includes applying cognitive models to artificial intelligence and diagnosing mental disorders through dual-pathway fusion perceptual networks.
0724.research_direction: Dr. Zhou has recently been investigating the intersection of human visual cognition and advanced deep learning architectures. Their recent work explores the fundamental mechanisms of visual working memory, using behavioral experiments to determine which specific visual features act as cognitive pointers to bind and update object representations. Drawing inspiration from human global and local visual processing, they are also developing brain-inspired hybrid CNN-transformer networks that utilize top-down modulation to improve general image classification. Furthermore, they have been adapting these dual-pathway and attention-based neural networks for clinical applications, designing deep learning models to reconstruct undersampled MRI scans, segment multi-organ medical images, and fuse fMRI connectivity data to identify brain regions associated with psychiatric conditions like autism and schizophrenia.

papers.title: Unravelling the object-based nature of visual working memory: insight from pointers
papers.abstract: Working memory is thought to bind features to objects via some kind of index or pointer, but which feature acts as that pointer is unresolved. Using behavioral experiments in which an object's information is updated, the study tests whether location, color or shape serves as the cue that ties a memory to its object. The results bear on how object-based representations are maintained and updated in visual working memory.
papers.authors: Ning Wei, Jintao Song, Hongyi Zhang, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: Brain Cognition-Inspired Dual-Pathway CNN Architecture for Image Classification
papers.abstract: Drawing on how the human visual system handles global and local information, the authors design CogNet, a CNN in which a convolutional local pathway extracts fine detail while a transformer-based global pathway captures overall structure. A learnable top-down modulator lets the global signal reshape the local features, and the pair is packaged into a stackable global-local block. CogNets reach state-of-the-art accuracy on six image-classification benchmarks and are more resistant to texture bias and semantic confusion.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.authors: Songlin Dong, Yihong Gong, Jingang Shi, Miao Shang, Xiaoyu Tao, Xing Wei, Xiaopeng Hong, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: Bimodality Approach to Mental Disorder Diagnosis via Dual-pathway Fusion Perceptual Network
papers.abstract: The authors build a dual-pathway fusion network that takes fMRI time courses and functional-connectivity matrices as two inputs, using self-attention and a coarse perception module to fuse their complementary information. It separates patients from healthy controls with 87.6% accuracy for schizophrenia (COBRE) and 71.1% for autism (ABIDE). Gradient-based attribution highlights disorder-related regions such as the paracentral lobe and angular gyrus.
papers.venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
papers.authors: Ruipeng Xu, Shuoqiu Gan, Feng Zhao, Zhentao Zuo, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: KDI-Net: dual-domain mapping network for undersampled magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction
papers.abstract: KDI-Net is a deep network for reconstructing MR images from undersampled k-space data by mapping jointly between the frequency (k-space) and image domains. It aims to recover high-quality images from fewer measurements, which would shorten scan times.
papers.venue: International Conference on Image, Signal Processing, and Pattern Recognition (ISPP 2024)
papers.authors: Haiyang Guo, Zhentao Zuo, Dengdi Sun, Tiangang Zhou

papers.title: Hybrid attention mechanism of feature fusion for medical image segmentation
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a segmentation network for multi-organ medical images that combines a CNN, which extracts multi-scale features, with a transformer that models long-range dependencies. A channel attention enhancement module emphasizes target organs, decoder features are fused with these through skip connections, and a refinement module sharpens same-organ consistency and between-organ discrimination. It outperforms comparison methods on the Synapse and cardiac diagnosis challenge datasets.
papers.authors: Shanshan Tong, Zhentao Zuo, Zu-Xiang Liu, Dengdi Sun, Tiangang Zhou

0725.name: Ziad M. Hafed
0725.department: Werner Reichardt Centre for Integrative Neuroscience (CIN)
0725.bio: Ziad M. Hafed is the Professor of Active Perception at the University of Tübingen and leads the Physiology of Active Vision Laboratory. Hafed’s research examines the neural mechanisms through which visual perception and motor control interact, focusing on the generation and functional impact of microsaccades and other fixational eye movements. By employing high-resolution electrophysiology, reversible neural perturbations, and computational modeling in primate models, Hafed has analyzed the role of the superior colliculus in active vision and established that phenomena like saccadic suppression can originate as early as the retina. Their work connects sensory processing and oculomotor behavior to understand how the brain maintains stable visual representations during self-motion.
0725.research_direction: Dr. Hafed's recent work investigates the deeply intertwined neural mechanisms of vision and oculomotor control, focusing on how eye movements actively shape visual processing. Using electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates, they have recently been exploring the role of the superior colliculus, examining whether traditional oculomotor bursts carry rich sensory representations of target features and how foveal neurons might compute trans-saccadic prediction errors to support perceptual stability. Their research also probes the specific neural pathways driving visually guided behavior, utilizing focal inactivation and trial-by-trial analyses to compare how the primary visual cortex and superior colliculus distinctively govern reflexive saccadic inhibition and foveation timing. Additionally, Dr. Hafed combines macaque neurophysiology with human psychophysics and retinal image stabilization to test whether the generation of fixational microsaccades actively drives shifts in peripheral visual sensitivity independent of covert attentional demands.

papers.title: Microsaccadic eye movement generation is sufficient to enhance peripheral visual sensitivity
papers.abstract: Debates persist over whether tiny fixational eye movements merely reflect shifts of covert attention or actively cause changes in peripheral sensitivity. Using real-time retinal image stabilization, superior colliculus recordings in macaques and human psychophysics, the authors show that generating a microsaccade is by itself enough to raise sensitivity far into the periphery, even without attentional demands. The effect operates through the classic pre- and post-saccadic visual processing changes, tying subliminal eye movements to cognitive processes such as attention.
papers.authors: Tong Zhang, Xiaoguang Tian, Tatiana Malevich, Matthias P. Baumann, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Much higher covariation with foveation timing by superior colliculus than primary visual cortical neuronal activity
papers.abstract: Using the same monkeys and stimuli, the study compared how trial-by-trial variability in superior colliculus and primary visual cortex visual responses relates to eye movement timing. V1 covariation with behavior was nearly absent whereas SC visual-motor neuron response strength was the strongest predictor. The authors conclude that the SC reformats sensory inputs to directly support visually driven orienting, while V1 mainly helps start the sensing process.
papers.authors: Carlotta Trottenberg, Yue Yu, Tong Zhang, Matthias P. Baumann, Tatiana Malevich, Shweta Prasad, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Transient focal inactivation of the primary visual cortex abolishes saccadic inhibition
papers.abstract: Reflexive inhibition of eye movements following sudden visual stimuli could in principle travel through many pathways. Here, brief focal inactivation of primary visual cortex eliminated visually driven saccadic inhibition, indicating dominance of the geniculostriate pathway. Chronic lesion data, modeling and detailed eye-movement analyses show that signals bypassing this pathway exist but appear less central than assumed, recasting classic views of visual-motor reflexes.
papers.authors: Tatiana Malevich, Yue Yu, Matthias P. Baumann, Xiaoxia Yu, Tong Zhang, Masatoshi Yoshida, Tadashi Isa, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Foveal neurons of the monkey superior colliculus signal trans-saccadic prediction errors
papers.abstract: The authors recorded foveal superior colliculus neurons while a target was changed during a saccade, so that the neurons never directly saw the pre-saccadic features. Post-saccadic responses were nonetheless elevated in proportion to the size of the feature discrepancy, and this did not occur without a saccade. This suggests foveal SC neurons signal a trans-saccadic prediction error, a possible mechanism for perceptual stability.
papers.authors: Tong Zhang, Amarender R. Bogadhi, Ziad M. Hafed

papers.title: Sensory tuning in neuronal movement commands
papers.abstract: The paper shows that the motor bursts of superior colliculus neurons, long thought to be pure oculomotor commands, carry a robust representation of the visual appearance of the saccade target. Similar saccades toward different images produce different bursts, with the effect strongest in deeper-layer motor neurons and stronger in feature discrimination than in visual responses. The results argue that collicular movement commands serve a fundamentally sensory function.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Matthias P. Baumann, Amarender R. Bogadhi, Anna F. Denninger, Ziad M. Hafed

0726.name: Zijiang He
0726.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
0726.main_research_area: visual space perception and binocular vision
0726.bio: Zijiang He is a Professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Louisville, specializing in the mechanisms of three-dimensional space perception and visual cognition. Their research explores the ground-based spatial coding scheme and the visual system's "intrinsic bias," an internal model used for distance representation in environments with limited visual cues. Utilizing psychophysics, virtual reality, and the blind walking-gesturing paradigm, He investigates how the brain integrates surface information through the sequential surface integration process (SSIP) and manages path integration during self-motion. Additionally, their work on binocular rivalry and sensory eye dominance has resulted in the development of "push-pull" perceptual learning protocols for treating visual impairments like amblyopia.
0726.research_direction: Dr. He has recently been investigating how the human visual system computes distance and depth in intermediate space, emphasizing the critical role of the brain's internal model of the ground surface. Their recent work explores spatial updating during self-motion, using walking tasks in cue-poor environments to determine whether the brain anchors its spatial representation to a moving body-centered frame or an allocentric starting point. Concurrently, they are examining the mechanisms of depth discrimination for midair targets by manipulating variables like stimulus duration, binocular disparity, and angular declination. Across these distinct experimental paradigms, Dr. He asks how internal spatial biases are fused with external visual cues, such as visible floor textures and continuous backgrounds, to build a stable reference frame for navigation and perception.

papers.title: Absolute Distance Discrimination in the Intermediate Distance Mediated by Angular Declination/Elevation and Binocular Disparity Cues
papers.abstract: In a large light-tight room, observers judged which of two midair targets was nearer or lower under different viewing and background conditions. Binocular disparity and angular declination/elevation both contributed, with weighted integration between them; the angular cue was weaker when a visible surface was present and could produce errors that disparity corrected. Both cues depend on a well-represented background surface.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: Perception of distance during self-motion depends on the brain's internal model of the terrain
papers.abstract: Extending the allocentric-odometer idea, observers walked short distances in a cue-poor room and then localized dim targets. The intrinsic bias stayed at the starting point, causing distance underestimation, and when floor texture was visible the perceived floor appeared slanted toward the start location. The results suggest the brain fuses the allocentric internal ground model with external depth cues to build a ground reference frame during self-motion.
papers.authors: Liu Zhou, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

papers.title: An allocentric human odometer for perceiving distances on the ground plane
papers.abstract: Walking observers in the dark keep judging target distance relative to the spot where they started, not where they are now. This shows that the brain's built-in model of the ground surface (the intrinsic bias) is anchored in world-based coordinates rather than moving with the body. Path integration turns out to be asymmetric: distance along the ground plane is updated during movement, while the vertical component is not, in line with a terrestrial ground-based spatial code.
papers.authors: Liu Zhou, Wei Wei, Teng Leng Ooi, Zijiang J. He

papers.title: Factors Affecting Stimulus Duration Threshold for Depth Discrimination of Asynchronous Targets in the Intermediate Distance Range
papers.abstract: The study asks whether depth discrimination improves with stimulus duration at intermediate distances (about 2-25 m) as it does in near space. Discrimination improved with longer target duration, binocular viewing and a visible texture background, and was near chance monocularly. A continuously visible background helped further, underscoring the role of ground-surface representation in spatial coding.
papers.authors: Yiya Chen, Zijiang J. He, Teng Leng Ooi

0728.name: Árni Kristjánsson
0728.bio: Kristjánsson is a Professor of Vision Science at the University of Iceland. Their research characterizes the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual attention, search, and memory. They investigate attentional priming, visual foraging, and how the human brain learns and represents the statistical distributions of features in the environment. Their methodology integrates traditional psychophysics and eye-tracking with electroencephalography (EEG) and computational modeling. Current research directions include investigating serial dependence in perception and exploring sensory substitution through haptic feedback systems for prosthetic applications.
0728.research_direction: Dr. Kristjánsson has recently been investigating how the visual system integrates information across space and time, focusing on how spatiotemporal routines and serial dependence create a sense of perceptual continuity from moment to moment. Their recent work explores ensemble perception and statistical learning, using novel paradigms like Feature Frequency Reports to ask whether observers can consciously access the fine-grained shape of environmental feature distributions rather than just compressed summary statistics. Additionally, they are examining how this learned statistical information guides active, goal-directed visuomotor behavior. To this end, they study how learned color distributions influence saccadic eye movements during visual search, while also mapping the cognitive mechanisms of multi-target visual foraging to understand how observers decide to select, maintain, or switch between target types in complex scenes.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal routines in visual perception
papers.abstract: A review-style synthesis arguing that visual perception depends on routines that operate jointly across space and time, rather than on isolated snapshots of the scene. It brings together work on how the visual system uses recent history, expectations and stable regularities to organise what we see from moment to moment. The authors outline a framework linking these processes and point to open questions for the field.
papers.authors: David Pascucci, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Explicit access to detailed representations of feature distributions
papers.abstract: Prior work held that conscious access to ensemble information is limited to summary statistics such as the mean and variance. Using a new Feature Frequency Report paradigm, in which observers view many colored disks and report how often specific features occurred, the authors show that observers can explicitly report fine-grained shape of the feature distribution. This challenges the view that only compressed summaries are available to awareness.
papers.authors: Vladislav Khvostov, Árni Gunnar Ásgeirsson, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: How does color distribution learning affect goal-directed visuomotor behavior?
papers.abstract: Environmental feature distributions are relatively stable, and observers can learn surprising details of color distributions even for ignored distractors in visual search. Here the authors test whether such learning influences orienting, measured with saccadic eye movements in odd-one-out search tasks. The results indicate that learned distributions shape where the eyes go, linking distribution learning to visuomotor behavior and not only to attention.
papers.authors: Léa Entzmann, Árni Gunnar Ásgeirsson, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Understanding human visual foraging: a review
papers.abstract: A review of research on human visual foraging, in which observers collect multiple targets in sequence in a scene instead of finding a single one. It covers how people decide what to pick up next, when to stay with one target type or switch, and how these choices relate to foraging theory from ecology. The authors discuss the methods developed and remaining questions.
papers.authors: Tómas Kristjánsson, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Serial dependence in visual perception: A review
papers.abstract: The paper asks how the visual system creates a sense of continuity in constantly changing input, given the finding that what was seen a moment ago biases current perception. It reviews the behavioral and neural evidence for serial dependence, compares the leading theoretical accounts, and discusses the conditions under which it arises. The authors also identify methodological pitfalls and outstanding questions for the field.
papers.authors: David Pascucci, Ömer Dağlar Tanrıkulu, Ayberk Ozkirli, Christian Houborg, Gizay Ceylan, Paul Zerr, Mohsen Rafiei, Árni Kristjánsson

0730.name: Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu
0730.bio: Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of New Hampshire and directs the UNH Vision Lab. Tanrikulu’s research explores the computational foundations of visual perception, focusing on how the visual system organizes sensory input through perceptual grouping and depth perception. By integrating psychophysical methods with virtual reality simulations, they investigate the interaction between contour geometry and dynamic motion cues like texture accretion and deletion. Tanrikulu also examines the philosophical underpinnings of cognitive science, specifically regarding the probabilistic and Bayesian nature of mental representations in visual processing.
0730.research_direction: Dr. Tanrikulu's recent work explores the complexity of mental representations in visual perception and attention, particularly investigating whether the visual system relies on full probability distributions or adopts simpler shortcuts governed by task demands and resource rationality. They have recently been examining this probabilistic framework across multiple domains, from synthesizing neurophysiological evidence on how recent trial history updates attentional templates during visual search, to using large language models to analyze whether researchers view Bayesian models of cognition as literal neural mechanisms or simply useful mathematical tools. Alongside these theoretical and metascientific pursuits, their experimental work investigates 3D vision and depth perception using psychophysics and virtual reality. In this area, they are probing how serial dependence biases operate on realistic 3D object representations across different spatial planes, and how geometric figure-ground cues interact with optic flow to resolve the relative depth of surfaces.

papers.title: Priming of probabilistic attentional templates II: Evidence from neuroscience
papers.abstract: This follow-up theory paper reviews neural evidence bearing on the idea that attentional templates in visual search are probability distributions over target features, updated by recent trial history. It synthesizes findings from neuroimaging and electrophysiology and considers how they support or challenge a probabilistic-template account of priming.
papers.authors: Árni Kristjánsson, Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu

papers.title: LLM-Assisted Stance Detection in Scientific Discourse: A Test Case in Bayesian Cognitive Science
papers.abstract: The study asks whether authors treat Bayesian models of the mind as literal descriptions of mental mechanisms (realism) or as useful mathematical tools (instrumentalism). The team builds a theory-driven codebook and optimizes a shared zero-shot prompt validated against expert annotations, then has three frontier LLMs code thousands of quotes from hundreds of articles with high reliability. Stance was mostly weakly realist, and low-level perception and motor papers leaned more realist than high-level cognition papers.
papers.authors: Eyup Engin Kucuk, Tarik Kelestemur, Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu

papers.title: Beyond Suboptimality: Resource-Rationality and Task Demands Shape the Complexity of Perceptual Representations
papers.abstract: The paper takes on the claim that frequent suboptimality in perceptual decisions shows the brain cannot represent full probability distributions. The authors argue instead that people adopt resource-rational shortcuts whenever a task can be solved with little attention, and those shortcuts look like simple representations. Across three experiments that progressively made shortcuts ineffective, model fits shifted from simple to complex representations, indicating that representational complexity depends on task demands and that resource-rationality should be treated as a design constraint.
papers.authors: Andrew Jun Lee, Daniel Turek, Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu

papers.title: Stronger serial dependence in the depth plane than the fronto-parallel plane between realistic objects: Evidence from virtual reality
papers.abstract: Using virtual reality with realistic everyday objects, the authors measured how the perceived 3D orientation of an object is biased toward the one seen just before. Serial dependence was stronger for rotations in depth than for rotations in the image plane. The result suggests that these history effects operate on 3D object representations rather than only on 2D image features.
papers.authors: Ömer Dağlar Tanrikulu, David Pascucci, Árni Kristjánsson

papers.title: Interaction of contour geometry and optic flow in determining relative depth of surfaces
papers.abstract: The paper studies how occluding-contour shape and dynamic texture accretion/deletion jointly determine which of two adjoining surfaces looks nearer. Using psychophysics, the authors show that geometric figure-ground cues can override the standard depth-from-accretion/deletion cue, and characterize how the two cues combine.
papers.authors: Ömer Dağlar Tanrıkulu, Vicky Froyen, Jacob Feldman, Manish Singh

E001.name: Fred Rieke
E001.bio: Rieke researches the biophysical mechanisms of sensory signal processing, focusing on the operation of the visual system at the physical limits of photon detection. Their work combines quantitative electrophysiological experiments and computational modeling to examine the transduction of light by rod and cone photoreceptors and the processing of these signals by retinal circuits. Current projects in Rieke’s laboratory address the origins of biological noise in photoreceptors, the integration of rod and cone signals under mesopic conditions, and the parallel pathways that transmit visual information from the eye to the brain.
E001.research_direction: Dr. Rieke has recently been investigating how specific cellular mechanisms and synaptic dynamics shape the flow of visual information through parallel pathways in the retina. Their recent work explores the origins of early nonlinearities in the primate outer retina, examining how horizontal cell integration and photoreceptor light adaptation influence downstream receptive-field surrounds and natural texture processing. Alongside this research, they are studying how circuit-level features—such as spatially local inhibition, synaptic depression, and bipolar cell vesicle pool dynamics—diverge to create distinct kinetic and spatial properties in mouse retinal ganglion cells. To bridge these cellular mechanisms with broader visual computation, Dr. Rieke employs a diverse toolkit that includes patch-clamp electrophysiology, glutamate imaging, 3D electron microscopy, computational modeling, and predictive stimulus designs.

papers.title: Horizontal cell nonlinearities create asymmetric texture processing in ON and OFF primate retinal outputs
papers.abstract: Examines how the receptive-field surround shapes texture responses in the major primate retinal output pathways. Spatial structure in the surround boosts ON parasol and ON midget ganglion cells but suppresses their OFF counterparts, so ON pathways act as spatial integrators and OFF pathways as differentiators. The asymmetry traces back to nonlinear spatial integration in horizontal cells, which are usually treated as linear, and natural image structure engages them so that they modulate ON and OFF bipolar cells differently.
papers.authors: Arthur Hong, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Spatially local inhibition and synaptic plasticity together enable dynamic, context-dependent integration of parallel sensory pathways
papers.abstract: Mouse Off-transient alpha ganglion cells respond strongly to uniform stimulation but are suppressed by spatial structure, fitting neither classic ganglion cell category. Two circuit mechanisms explain this: inhibition is tuned to finer spatial scales than excitation, so the excitation-inhibition balance depends on spatial scale, and excitatory synapses undergo strong depression that presynaptic inhibition modulates, amplifying responses to transitions from structured to uniform input. A spatiotemporal model with these features reproduces the recorded responses.
papers.authors: Qiang Chen, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Origin and functional impact of early nonlinearities in primate retina
papers.abstract: Standard linear receptive-field models miss nonlinear stimulus dependence, and nonlinear alternatives are mostly empirical and hard to tie to cellular mechanisms. This work shows that two nonlinear mechanisms in the primate outer retina shape neural responses and contribute substantially to responses to natural stimuli and to retinal output. Building these outer-retinal nonlinearities into visual models should help trace features of downstream responses to specific mechanisms.
papers.authors: Vyom Raval, Rachel Oaks-Leaf, Qiang Chen, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Cone bipolar cell synapses generate transient versus sustained signals in parallel ON pathways of the mouse retina
papers.abstract: Combining patch-clamp recording, glutamate imaging and 3D electron microscopy, the study asks how transient and sustained ON alpha ganglion cells get different kinetics from shared cone input. Presynaptic bipolar cell types (5i, 6, 7) respond almost identically to light, yet glutamate release and postsynaptic currents onto the two ganglion cell types differ in kinetics. Differences in ribbon-associated vesicle pools at bipolar terminals may explain this, placing the divergence of the pathways at the bipolar cell synapse.
papers.authors: Sidney P. Kuo, Wan-Qing Yu, Prerna Srivastava, Haruhisa Okawa, Luca Della Santina, David M. Berson, Gautam B. Awatramani, Rachel O. L. Wong, Fred Rieke

papers.title: Predictably manipulating photoreceptor light responses to reveal their role in downstream visual responses
papers.abstract: Introduces a tool that designs light stimuli to produce predictable rod and cone phototransduction currents, including stimuli that compensate for nonlinearities such as light adaptation. Built on established phototransduction cascade models, it separates nonlinearities arising in phototransduction from those in downstream circuits. This allows direct tests of how photoreceptor adaptation shapes downstream visual signals and perception.
papers.authors: Qiang Chen, Norianne T. Ingram, Jacob Baudin, Juan M. Angueyra, Raunak Sinha, Fred Rieke

E002.name: Stephen Baccus
E002.bio: Stephen Baccus investigates the circuit mechanisms through which the retina encodes and adapts to natural visual environments. By integrating large-scale multielectrode recordings with biophysically-inspired deep learning models, their lab characterizes the nonlinear transformations performed by retinal interneurons during processes like contrast adaptation and motion sensitivity. Baccus also explores ultrasonic neuromodulation as a high-resolution, non-invasive method for stimulating neural tissue. Their work focuses on identifying principles of neural computation that explain how the visual system compresses information while maintaining ethological relevance.
E002.research_direction: Dr. Baccus has recently been investigating how retinal circuits process natural scenes by combining deep learning encoding models with electrophysiological recordings. Their recent work explores how AI interpretability methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can map the hidden units of convolutional networks onto biological interneurons to uncover the computational mechanisms behind dynamic receptive fields and contrast adaptation. They are also utilizing stochastic population models and information geometry to examine how adaptation and correlated neural variability shape the discriminability of naturalistic stimuli. Furthermore, their research extends along the visual pathway, using matched multielectrode recordings in both the retina and visual cortex to determine how complex features like object motion are sequentially constructed across different stages of the visual hierarchy.

papers.title: Causal Interpretation of Neural Network Computations with Contribution Decomposition (CODEC)
papers.abstract: CODEC uses sparse autoencoders to decompose how hidden units contribute to a network's output, rather than only looking at activations. Contributions become sparser and more separated into positive and negative effects across layers, and the resulting modes can be used to manipulate outputs and visualize image components in classifiers. Applied to retinal models, it reveals interneuron interactions and the sources of dynamic receptive fields.
papers.authors: Joshua Brendan Melander, Zaki Alaoui, Shenghua Liu, Surya Ganguli, Stephen A. Baccus

papers.title: Parallel construction of object motion from retina to cortex
papers.abstract: Using matched multielectrode recordings in mouse retina and visual cortex plus computational modeling, the study tests whether cortex simply inherits retinal object-motion sensitivity. It finds that retina and cortex have different tuning, with retina preferring fine jitter and cortex preferring coarse drift, so cortex recomputes object motion. The authors argue for parallel construction of object motion across the two stages.
papers.authors: Javier C. Weddington, David D. Au, Joshua B Melander, Youssef Faragalla, Zaki Alaoui, Stephen A. Baccus

papers.title: Adaptation of retinal discriminability to natural scenes
papers.abstract: The work builds a retinal population model that captures both mean responses and correlated variability under natural scenes, and uses it to compute how well the population can discriminate stimuli. It shows that adaptation tunes discriminability to the statistics of natural scenes, with correlated variability playing a role. This addresses whether the visual system is optimized for natural stimuli.
papers.authors: Xuehao Ding, Dongsoo Lee, Joshua B. Melander, Surya Ganguli, Stephen A. Baccus

papers.title: Interpreting the retinal neural code for natural scenes: From computations to neurons
papers.abstract: The authors show that a three-layer convolutional network can predict retinal ganglion cell responses to natural scenes with accuracy close to experimental limits. Using interpretability methods, they map the model's hidden units onto identifiable retinal interneurons (bipolar and amacrine cells) and recover known circuit mechanisms such as contrast adaptation, motion sensitivity and feature selectivity. It is presented as a general approach for relating deep-network computations to biological neurons.
papers.authors: Niru Maheswaranathan, Lane T. McIntosh, Hidenori Tanaka, Satchel Grant, David B. Kastner, Joshua B. Melander, Aran Nayebi, Luke E. Brezovec, Julia H. Wang, Surya Ganguli, Stephen A. Baccus

papers.title: Information Geometry of the Retinal Representation Manifold
papers.abstract: The authors build a stochastic CNN encoding model of salamander retinal ganglion cell populations that reproduces mean responses and second-order statistics to natural scenes. Applying information geometry, they quantify how well retinal representations let downstream areas discriminate stimuli and which stimulus directions are best encoded. The framework links model-derived geometry to visual discrimination.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Xuehao Ding, Dongsoo Lee, Joshua Melander, George Sivulka, Surya Ganguli, Stephen Baccus

E003.name: Botond Roska
E003.institution: Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel
E003.department: Faculty of Medicine and Faculty of Science
E003.lab_name: Human Retinal and Central Visual Circuits Group
E003.bio: Botond Roska is a neurobiologist who investigates the functional organization of retinal circuits and the development of optogenetic therapies to restore sight. Roska's research group maps the interactions of approximately 100 retinal cell types using viral-mediated circuit tracing, electrophysiology, and computational modeling. They developed cell-type-targeted optogenetic strategies to reactivate light sensitivity in blind retinas, which resulted in clinical applications of this technology in humans. Their current research explores human retinal architecture and the integration of sensory signals within central visual pathways to advance translational treatments for hereditary blindness.
E003.research_direction: Dr. Roska has recently been investigating novel therapeutic strategies for retinal degeneration, exploring approaches like cell-type-targeted mitochondrial transplantation and running small-molecule screens in human retinal organoids to find pharmacological routes that prevent cone photoreceptor death. Parallel to these translational efforts, their recent work explores fundamental mechanisms of visual processing across distinct anatomical stages. Specifically, they are examining how horizontal cells regulate feedback to photoreceptors at the first visual synapse via bicarbonate transport, and how individual inhibitory interneurons in the mouse visual thalamus are functionally specialized to tune specific visual features en route to the cortex. Broadening their focus to general neurodevelopment, they are also probing how pyramidal neurons assemble into transient, multilayered circuits during early neocortical development and how these nascent networks are disrupted by autism-associated mutations.

papers.title: Cell-type-targeted mitochondrial transplantation rescues cell degeneration
papers.abstract: The study develops a way to deliver healthy mitochondria selectively into a chosen cell type and shows that this restores function in cells whose own mitochondria are failing. Applied to degenerating retinal cells, the transplanted organelles rescued cells that would otherwise die, pointing to a general organelle-replacement strategy for degenerative disease.
papers.authors: Temurkhan Ayupov, Verónica Moreno-Juan, Serena Curtoni, Alex Fratzl, Upnishad Sharma, Susana Posada-Céspedes, Ramona Ratiu, Rei Morikawa, Alexandra Graff Meyer, Margherita Pezzoli, Glenn Bantug, Morgan Chevalier, Yanyan Hou, Sarah A. Nadeau, Álvaro Herrero-Navarro, Vikram Ayinampudi, Elizabeth Kastanaki, Natasha Whitehead, Rebecca A. Siwicki, Mariana M. Ribeiro, Ji Hoon Han, Annalisa Bucci, Christoph Hess, Simone Picelli, Magdalena Renner, Daniel J. Müller, Cameron S. Cowan, Simon Hansen, Botond Roska

papers.title: Cell-type-focused compound screen in human organoids reveals CK1 inhibition protects cone photoreceptors from death
papers.abstract: Using human retinal organoids, the authors ran a small-molecule screen that read out survival of specific retinal cell types, focusing on cone photoreceptors. They identified inhibition of casein kinase 1 as protective against cone death, offering a pharmacological route to slow vision loss in hereditary retinal degeneration.
papers.authors: Stefan E. Spirig, Álvaro Herrero-Navarro, Larissa Utz, Valeria J. Arteaga-Moreta, Zoltan Raics, Susana Posada-Céspedes, Stephanie Chreng, Olaf Galuba, Inga Galuba, Isabelle Claerr, Steffen Renner, Miklos Boldogkoi, Verónica Moreno-Juan, P. Timo Kleindienst, Adrienn Volak, Jannick Imbach, Svitlana Malysheva, Rebecca A. Siwicki, Vincent Hahaut, Yanyan Hou, Tiago M. Rodrigues, Simone Picelli, Marco Cattaneo, Josephine Jüttner, Cameron S. Cowan, Myriam Duckely, Daniel K. Baeschlin, Magdalena Renner, Vincent Unterreiner, Botond Roska

papers.title: The sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter Slc4a5 mediates feedback at the first synapse of vision
papers.abstract: The paper addresses how horizontal cells send feedback to photoreceptors at the first synapse of vision. It identifies the transporter Slc4a5 as a key mediator, linking pH and bicarbonate handling at the synapse to the feedback signal that shapes early visual processing.
papers.authors: Rei Morikawa, Tiago M. Rodrigues, Helene Marianne Schreyer, Cameron S. Cowan, Sarah Nadeau, Alexandra Graff-Meyer, Claudia P. Patino-Alvarez, Mohammad Hossein Khani, Josephine Jüttner, Botond Roska

papers.title: Individual thalamic inhibitory interneurons are functionally specialized toward distinct visual features
papers.abstract: Recording from inhibitory interneurons in the visual thalamus of mice, the study shows that individual cells are not generic but each is tuned to particular visual features, and that they pick up specific retinal inputs. This implies that inhibition in the thalamus is feature-specific and part of how visual signals are shaped en route to cortex.
papers.authors: Fiona E. Müllner, Botond Roska

papers.title: Pyramidal neurons form active, transient, multilayered circuits perturbed by autism-associated mutations at the inception of neocortex
papers.abstract: The authors examine how excitatory pyramidal neurons connect and fire in the earliest stages of mouse neocortical development, finding transient multilayered active circuits. They show that autism-associated mutations disrupt these early circuits, suggesting a developmental origin of the disorder.
papers.authors: Martin Munz, Arjun Bharioke, Georg Kosche, Verónica Moreno-Juan, Alexandra Brignall, Tiago M. Rodrigues, Alexandra Graff-Meyer, Talia Ulmer, Stephanie Haeuselmann, Dinko Pavlinic, Nicole Ledergerber, Brigitte Gross-Scherf, Balázs Rózsa, Jacek Krol, Simone Picelli, Cameron S. Cowan, Botond Roska

E005.name: Thomas Euler
E005.bio: Thomas Euler is a Professor for Ophthalmic Research at the University of Tübingen, where Euler investigates the functional organization and computational principles of retinal microcircuits. Their research utilizes two-photon calcium imaging and electrophysiology to record light-evoked population activity in mouse and zebrafish models. Euler has characterized the functional diversity of retinal bipolar and ganglion cells and applies natural scene statistics to probe early visual processing. Additionally, their laboratory develops open-source scientific tools and investigates how retinal circuits are altered during neurodegeneration.
E005.research_direction: Dr. Euler has recently been investigating how the mouse retina turns light into the many parallel signals sent to the brain. Their recent work asks how retinal ganglion cells, the eye's output neurons, differ in their sensitivity to contrast, color, and visual context, and how factors like nitric oxide or position on the retina tune those responses. They combine two-photon calcium imaging with deep neural network models of natural-movie responses to predict and then test what individual cell types detect. They have also been building a large shared dataset of ganglion cell responses and studying how these cell types are affected as photoreceptors degenerate in disease.

papers.title: A large-scale dataset of functional mouse ganglion cell layer responses
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the ALL-GCL dataset, a high-throughput functional imaging resource containing two-photon calcium recordings from over 80,000 neurons in the mouse retinal ganglion cell layer (GCL). The dataset aggregates data from 139 experimental sessions collected over nine years using a standardized battery of visual stimuli, including full-field chirps and moving bars, to enable the probabilistic classification of neurons into 46 functional groups. The work quantifies the impact of experimental metadata, such as fluorescent indicator kinetics and recording configurations, on response consistency, providing a standardized benchmarking platform for system identification and convolutional neural network (CNN) modeling of retinal computation.
papers.authors: Dominic Gonschorek, Jonathan Oesterle, Thomas Zenkel, Federico D'Agostino, Chenchen Cai, Nadine Dyszkant, Klaudia P. Szatko, Florentyna Deja, Tom Schwerd-Kleine, Ryan Arlinghaus, Katrin Franke, Zhijian Zhao, Timm Schubert, Philipp Berens, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Photoreceptor degeneration has heterogeneous effects on functional retinal ganglion cell types
papers.abstract: This longitudinal study characterizes the functional impact of progressive rod and cone degeneration on the physiological output of the mouse retina using the rd10 mutant model. By employing large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and functional clustering, the authors assessed the light-evoked responsiveness of specific retinal ganglion cell (RGC) types as the disease progressed from early rod loss (P45) to near-complete photoreceptor depletion (P180). The findings reveal significant heterogeneity in functional resilience across RGC channels; On-pathway and specific orientation-selective RGCs displayed relative functional stability, whereas Off-pathway and direction-selective circuits demonstrated early physiological deterioration. These results indicate that retinal circuits undergo type-specific functional remodeling, which may inform the temporal window for neuroprotective interventions.
papers.authors: Nadine Dyszkant, Jonathan Oesterle, Yongrong Qiu, Merle Harrer, Timm Schubert, Dominic Gonschorek, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Task-specific regional circuit adaptations in distinct mouse retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: This paper explores the existence of regional microcircuit specializations across the nasotemporal axis of the mouse retina, focusing on sustained ON alpha (sONα) retinal ganglion cells. Utilizing dendritic calcium imaging and presynaptic glutamate sensors, the researchers identified a functional asymmetry where temporal sONα RGCs exhibit markedly stronger surround suppression and unique temporal kinetics compared to their nasal counterparts. Computational population models using an encoder-decoder framework demonstrate that these localized circuit adaptations are optimized for the detection of small, dark, high-velocity stimuli, effectively tuning the retinal output to support ethologically relevant behaviors such as prey capture (e.g., cricket hunting).
papers.authors: Jonathan Oesterle, Yanli Ran, Paul Stahr, Jason N. D. Kerr, Timm Schubert, Philipp Berens, Thomas Euler

papers.title: Nitric oxide modulates contrast suppression in a subset of mouse retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: The study investigates the neuromodulatory influence of nitric oxide (NO) on the visual feature representations encoded by mouse retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Through a combination of two-photon calcium imaging and multi-electrode array (MEA) recordings, the authors found that NO selectively targets a subset of suppressed-by-contrast RGC types, significantly attenuating their temporal suppression and accelerating response kinetics while leaving spatial receptive field properties unaffected. Additionally, the study characterizes a significant baseline adaptational response change in approximately one-third of RGC types during prolonged ex vivo experiments, necessitating the use of a sequential-recording paradigm to isolate drug-induced neuromodulation from intrinsic physiological adaptation.
papers.authors: Dominic Gonschorek, Matías A Goldin, Jonathan Oesterle, Tom Schwerd-Kleine, Ryan Arlinghaus, Zhijian Zhao, Timm Schubert, Olivier Marre, Thomas Euler

papers.title: A chromatic feature detector in the retina signals visual context changes
papers.abstract: The authors identify a novel chromatic feature detection mechanism in the mouse retina that signals transitions in visual context, such as ground-to-sky shifts. By training deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on large-scale RGC responses to natural movies and performing model-guided in silico stimulus optimization (Maximally Exciting Inputs, MEIs), the study predicted a specific chromatic selectivity in transient Suppressed-by-Contrast (tSbC) RGCs. Experimental verification confirmed that tSbCs are selectively activated by full-field switches between green and ultraviolet illumination, matching the chromatic statistics of natural horizon transitions. The results suggest that these cells provide a contextual reference signal to higher brain regions to facilitate state-dependent visual processing.
papers.authors: Larissa Höfling, Klaudia P. Szatko, Christian Behrens, Yuyao Deng, Yongrong Qiu, David A. Klindt, Zachary Jessen, Gregory W. Schwartz, Matthias Bethge, Philipp Berens, Katrin Franke, Alexander S. Ecker, Thomas Euler

E006.name: Greg Field
E006.main_research_area: retinal neural coding and circuit function
E006.bio: Greg D. Field is an Associate Professor in the Department of Ophthalmology at UCLA and holds the Joan and Jerome Snyder Chair in Vision Sciences. Field’s research focuses on the neural coding of the retina, specifically investigating how populations of retinal ganglion cells transform visual scenes into electrical signals transmitted to the brain. Utilizing high-density multi-electrode arrays, computational modeling, and mouse genetics, their lab characterizes the functional connectivity and signal processing of diverse retinal cell types. This approach aims to understand the principles of sensory processing and inform the development of therapies for vision restoration in degenerative conditions such as glaucoma and retinitis pigmentosa.
E006.research_direction: Dr. Field’s recent work investigates the functional organization, circuitry, and therapeutic rescue of retinal ganglion cells. To study large populations of these neurons, they have recently been developing high-throughput physiological techniques, including 1-photon light-sheet microscopy and retrograde viral phototagging approaches that link a cell's light responses on a multi-electrode array to its specific downstream brain targets. With these tools, their research explores how retinal circuits process visual information, examining phenomena such as the systematic asymmetries between ON and OFF pathways and how GABAergic inhibition regulates the sensitivity and receptive field size of direction-selective cells near the absolute threshold of vision. Furthermore, they are investigating translational questions in retinal degeneration, specifically probing how the developmental timing of gene therapy interventions impacts the ultimate recovery of retinal ganglion cell output in models of retinitis pigmentosa.

papers.title: Projection targeting with phototagging to study the structure and function of retinal ganglion cells
papers.abstract: The authors present a method that links what a retinal ganglion cell projects to, how it looks, and how it responds to light, all within the same cell. Retrogradely delivered virus is used to tag cells that project to a chosen brain target, and these are then found on a large multi-electrode array. Because it needs no transgenic animals, it should be usable across species. In rats, they show that several ganglion cell types project to the superior colliculus, in line with earlier mouse work.
papers.authors: Martin O. Bohlen, Andra M. Rudzite, Tierney B. Daw, Genevieve M. Kuczewski, Ergi Spiro, Cassie Hammond, Darienne R. Rogers, Alejandro Gallego-Ortega, Michael B. Manookin, Suva Roy, Kimberly Ritola, Marc A. Sommer, Greg D. Field

papers.title: Retinal ganglion cell function: ON and OFF pathways
papers.abstract: A review of how the retina splits visual signals into ON and OFF channels, from photoreceptor-bipolar synapses through to paired ganglion cell types. It discusses the systematic asymmetries between ON and OFF cell types in receptive field size, dynamics and contrast sensitivity, and how these pathways differ in disease and matter for optogenetic and prosthetic therapies.
papers.authors: Greg D. Field

papers.title: GABAergic Inhibition Controls Receptive Field Size, Sensitivity, and Contrast Preference of Direction Selective Retinal Ganglion Cells Near the Threshold of Vision
papers.abstract: With large-scale multi-electrode recordings, the study shows that superior-preferring ON-OFF direction-selective ganglion cells are about ten times more sensitive to dim flashes than other ON-OFF DS cells, and also have larger receptive fields. Removing GABAergic signaling by conditional knockout changes their receptive field size, sensitivity and contrast preference near visual threshold. Inhibition therefore shapes how these cells balance detection against direction coding in dim light.
papers.authors: Suva Roy, Xiaoyang Yao, Jay Rathinavelu, Greg D. Field

papers.title: Late gene therapy limits the restoration of retinal function in a mouse model of retinitis pigmentosa
papers.abstract: Using a mouse model of retinitis pigmentosa in which the disease gene can be genetically rescued, the study asks how retinal function depends on when treatment begins. Rescue at early and mid stages of rod loss restores retinal ganglion cell output to near normal. Rescue at a late stage (70% rod loss) leaves sensitivity and signal fidelity still declining, with persistent abnormalities. The work sets a best-case benchmark for the timing of gene therapy.
papers.authors: Miranda L. Scalabrino, Mishek Thapa, Tian Wang, Alapakkam P. Sampath, Jeannie Chen, Greg D. Field

papers.title: Large-scale interrogation of retinal cell functions by 1-photon light-sheet microscopy
papers.abstract: This methods paper describes a light-sheet microscopy approach for optically recording the activity of many retinal cells at once. It extends the lab's electrophysiology toolkit with large-scale imaging of cell function in the retina, enabling many cells to be interrogated in a single preparation.
