papers.authors: Suva Roy, Depeng Wang, Andra M. Rudzite, Benjamin Perry, Miranda L. Scalabrino, Mishek Thapa, Yiyang Gong, Alexander Sher, Greg D. Field

E007.name: Sheila Nirenberg
E007.bio: Sheila Nirenberg is a neuroscientist who works on the retina's neural code, the mathematical language used to transmit visual information to the brain. Their research involves implementing these codes into optogenetic-based prosthetic systems to bypass damaged photoreceptor cells and restore sight in patients with degenerative retinal diseases. By integrating computational modeling, gene therapy, and wearable computerized devices, Nirenberg developed a platform that stimulates ganglion cells with specific spatiotemporal patterns. Nirenberg is also adapting these biological coding principles to the development of machine vision algorithms and robotic sensory processing.
E007.research_direction: Dr. Nirenberg has recently been working on restoring sight in people who have lost their photoreceptors to inherited retinal degeneration. Their recent work develops an optogenetic gene therapy that makes retinal ganglion cells, the eye's output neurons, respond directly to light, and tests its safety and effectiveness in mouse models. They have also been building the hardware and software needed to bring this therapy into the clinic, including a high-intensity light stimulator and tools for testing and training patients. The common thread is turning a laboratory understanding of neural coding in the retina into a practical treatment for blindness.

papers.title: A clinically viable approach to restoring visual function using optogenetic gene therapy
papers.abstract: The researchers present preclinical safety and efficacy data for a novel optogenetic gene therapy (BS01) aimed at restoring vision in patients with advanced-stage retinitis pigmentosa (RP). The therapy utilizes an adeno-associated virus (AAV2) vector to express the high-speed, light-sensitive opsin ChronosFP in retinal ganglion cells. Efficacy was validated in rd1 mice using dose-dependent electroretinogram (ERG) responses and multi-electrode array recordings, demonstrating that the treated retinas could produce high-fidelity spike patterns matching the natural retinal code. Safety profiles were established in rats, non-human primates, and mice through long-term immunohistochemical analysis, cell counts, and ocular toxicology assays. The study found that ChronosFP-expressing vectors were well-tolerated and remained efficacious over a broad range of vector doses and stimulating light intensities without causing significant anatomical or electrophysiological damage to the inner retina, supporting the transition to human clinical trials (NCT04278131).
papers.authors: Boyuan Yan, Suresh Viswanathan, Scott E. Brodie, Wen-Tao Deng, Kirsten E. Coleman, William W. Hauswirth, Sheila Nirenberg

papers.title: An Engineering Platform for Clinical Application of Optogenetic Therapy in Retinal Degenerative Diseases
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a comprehensive hardware and software platform designed for the clinical testing, training, and rehabilitation of patients undergoing optogenetic gene therapy for blindness. The system addresses the limitations of standard ophthalmic equipment by integrating a high-intensity DLP-based light stimulator with real-time neural computation units. Key features include a specialized software application capable of generating diverse visual stimuli (e.g., gratings, moving objects, and natural scenes) and converting them into precise spatiotemporal light patterns that mimic the normal retinal output. Crucially, the platform incorporates adjustable geometrical mapping functions to account for the radial displacement between foveal cones and their corresponding ganglion cells. Experimental validation demonstrated the system's ability to achieve millisecond temporal resolution and spatial resolution up to 0.05°, sufficient for cellular-level stimulation in the central retina. This engineering platform provides the infrastructure necessary for customizing prosthetic parameters and assessing visual acuity, motion detection, and object recognition in a clinical setting.
papers.venue: IEEE Journal of Translational Engineering in Health and Medicine
papers.authors: Boyuan Yan, Sheila Nirenberg

E009.name: Dario Ringach
E009.bio: Dario Ringach is a Professor of Neurobiology and Psychology at UCLA. Their research focuses on the functional organization and computational principles of the primary visual cortex. Ringach developed reverse-correlation techniques to map the receptive fields of visual neurons and conducted studies on the temporal dynamics of orientation selectivity and population coding. Their recent work utilizes large-scale two-photon calcium imaging and theoretical modeling to investigate energy-efficient coding, the development of binocular circuitry, and the relationship between spontaneous and stimulus-driven cortical activity.
E009.research_direction: Dr. Ringach has recently been investigating the computational principles and temporal dynamics of population coding in the primary visual cortex, focusing on how these networks adapt to the statistics of their sensory environments. Using techniques like two-photon imaging in mice, their recent work explores how neural populations balance information transmission with metabolic cost to achieve energy-efficient coding following stimulus onset. Specifically, they are studying the mathematical rules governing visual adaptation, examining how population response magnitudes scale with stimulus probability and intensity, and testing whether pattern and contrast adaptation are driven by a shared, low-dimensional gain control mechanism. In addition to adaptation, they have recently been developing efficient reverse-correlation methods to map receptive fields during natural free-viewing, utilizing translation properties of basis functions to quickly correct for eye movements without the need for complex networks.

papers.title: Contrast and pattern adaptation in visual cortex share a common gain control mechanism
papers.abstract: Contrast adaptation and pattern adaptation have usually been treated as separate phenomena. At the level of V1 population response distributions, the authors show both produce the same low-dimensional change: coordinated shifts in sparsity and mean activity with log-variance preserved. Responses across all conditions collapse onto a one-dimensional manifold, pointing to a single shared gain variable.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Elaine Tring, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: Subspace reverse-correlation estimation of receptive fields during free viewing
papers.abstract: Mapping receptive fields during natural viewing requires correcting for eye movements, which usually means costly shifter networks. The authors exploit the translation properties of Hartley basis functions so that eye position acts as a simple phase shift, giving closed-form gradients and fast optimization. On high-density mouse V1 recordings the method sharpens receptive fields by about 56 percent versus naive estimates and runs in minutes on a desktop.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Elaine Tring, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: Dynamics of energy-efficient coding in visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study follows how V1 population activity evolves in time after stimulus onset. Early responses are broad and carry a lot of information, then competition sharpens the population code, raising sparseness while keeping mutual information roughly constant. The result is a steady, time-dependent improvement in coding efficiency, balancing information against metabolic cost.
papers.authors: S. Amin Moosavi, Antonia Pastor, Alfredo G. Ornelas, Elaine Tring, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: On the contrast response function of adapted neural populations
papers.abstract: In mouse V1, the magnitude of the population response depends both on stimulus intensity and on how probable that stimulus is in the environment. The authors show that the vector magnitude of the population response is captured by a separable power law that factors intensity and probability, giving a compact description of contrast responses after adaptation.
papers.authors: Elaine Tring, Mario Dipoppa, Dario L. Ringach

papers.title: A power law describes the magnitude of adaptation in neural populations of primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using two-photon imaging in mouse V1, the authors exposed animals to different stimulus environments defined by how often each oriented grating appeared. They found that the size of a population's response to a stimulus scales as a power law of that stimulus's probability, while the direction of the response vector stays essentially unchanged. This simple rule lets one predict how the cortex will respond after adapting to a new environment, and the authors show how it supports efficient coding of the environment.
papers.authors: Elaine Tring, Mario Dipoppa, Dario L. Ringach

E010.name: Matteo Carandini
E010.bio: Carandini is a Professor of Visual Neuroscience researching the principles of neural computation and how populations of neurons represent sensory information. Carandini developed the divisive normalization model, which describes a computation used by the brain to regulate neuronal activity. Their research utilizes technologies such as high-density Neuropixels probes and widefield calcium imaging to map brain-wide activity during behavior, specifically investigating how non-visual signals like locomotion and arousal influence visual processing. As a co-director of the Cortexlab and a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory, Carandini coordinates the integration of experimental data with computational models to study the neural basis of perception and decision-making.
E010.research_direction: Dr. Carandini has recently been investigating large-scale neural population dynamics while concurrently advancing the neurotechnologies required to measure them. Their recent work explores methodological innovations for chronic in vivo recording, including the development of Neuropixels probes integrated with depth-addressable optogenetics and new computational tools to track the functional stability of individual neurons across weeks of learning. Using these high-density electrophysiology techniques alongside functional ultrasound, they are examining brain-wide activity patterns, investigating how opposing neural populations drive neurovascular coupling and probing the structure of persistent, millisecond-scale firing sequences in the visual cortex and other regions. Additionally, their recent theoretical work explores perceptual decision-making, investigating how diverse sensory and multisensory influences might be integrated by the brain through a framework of logistic classification.

papers.title: Brainwide blood volume reflects opposing neural populations
papers.abstract: The authors measured neuronal firing and blood volume together across the mouse brain, using functional ultrasound imaging alongside Neuropixels recordings. They found that neurons whose activity rises with whisking (an arousal marker) and neurons whose activity falls have different haemodynamic response functions. Summing their contributions predicts blood volume across brain states, and both populations coexist in every region. This explains apparent regional differences in neurovascular coupling.
papers.authors: Agnès Landemard, Michael Krumin, Kenneth D. Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Neuropixels Opto: combining high-resolution electrophysiology and optogenetics
papers.abstract: This paper presents prototype Neuropixels Opto probes that put 960 recording sites and two sets of 14 blue and red light emitters on a single thin shank. In mouse cortex the probes gave good recordings with depth-addressable optogenetic activation and silencing. In striatum and other deep structures they allowed efficient optotagging of two cell types in parallel.
papers.authors: Anna A. Lakunina, Karolina Z. Socha, Alexander E. Ladd, Anna J. Bowen, Susu Chen, Jennifer Colonell, Anjal Doshi, Bill Karsh, Michael Krumin, Pavel Kulik, Anna J. Li, Pieter Neutens, John O'Callaghan, Meghan Olsen, Jan Putzeys, Charu Bai Reddy, Harrie A. C. Tilmans, Sara Vargas, Marleen Welkenhuysen, Zhiwen Ye, Michael Häusser, Christof Koch, Jonathan T. Ting, Barundeb Dutta, Timothy D. Harris, Nicholas A. Steinmetz, Karel Svoboda, Joshua H. Siegle, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Invariant activity sequences across the mouse brain
papers.abstract: The study shows that the millisecond-scale firing sequences seen in cortex, where neurons fire in a fixed order with characteristic delays, are found in every brain region examined. In visual cortex the sequences appear both in stimulus responses and in spontaneous activity, and each neuron's coupling strength and delay to the population stays stable for weeks. This points to a canonical, persistent scaffold for population activity.
papers.authors: Célian Bimbard, Kenneth D. Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Tracking neurons across days with high-density probes
papers.abstract: The authors introduce UnitMatch, a post-spike-sorting method that matches neurons across recording sessions using only their average waveforms. Applied to chronic Neuropixels recordings in mouse, it tracked neurons for weeks, showing stable inter-spike-interval structure, correlations and visual selectivity in visual cortex, while striatal responses changed as animals learned a task.
papers.authors: Enny H. van Beest, Célian Bimbard, Julie M. J. Fabre, Sam W. Dodgson, Flóra Takács, Philip Coen, Anna Lebedeva, Kenneth D. Harris, Matteo Carandini

papers.title: Sensory choices as logistic classification
papers.abstract: A single-author perspective arguing that perceptual decisions can be described as logistic classification: weight each factor, sum them, and use the sum as the log odds of a choice. It reviews evidence that this covers sensory, multisensory and non-sensory influences and the effects of local inactivations, and suggests the brain implements it via thresholded stochastic inputs, using it as a near-optimal heuristic.
papers.authors: Matteo Carandini

E011.name: Kenneth Harris
E011.department: UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology
E011.bio: Kenneth Harris is a Professor of Quantitative Neuroscience at University College London and co-directs the Cortical Processing Laboratory. Harris researches how large-scale populations of neurons in the cerebral cortex integrate sensory information with internal brain states to guide perceptual decisions. Their work in neurotechnology and data analysis includes the development of Neuropixels probes and Kilosort spike-sorting software. These tools are used for the high-density recording and characterization of thousands of individual neurons across multiple brain regions.
E011.research_direction: Dr. Harris has recently been investigating the computational geometry of neuronal population codes and the neural circuits underlying complex decision-making in mice. In the visual domain, their recent work explores the mathematical rules governing high-dimensional V1 representations, utilizing nonlinear latent-variable models and AI-driven equation discovery to understand single-cell tuning and population-level dynamics. They are also examining how these visual cortical codes are transformed by visuomotor task training to become more sparse and orthogonal. Beyond sensory encoding, they utilize large-scale Neuropixels recordings and optogenetics to probe frontal cortical regions, specifically investigating how the secondary motor cortex integrates additive multisensory evidence and drives perseverative behaviors during dynamic reward-learning tasks.

papers.title: Dorsal prefrontal cortex drives perseverative behavior in mice
papers.abstract: Mice in a dynamic reward-learning task often repeat an action even when the alternative pays more, and repeated choices are made faster. Neuropixels recordings found neurons in anterior secondary motor cortex (MOs) whose activity tracked perseveration and predicted fast reactions. Optogenetically silencing this region at choice time reduced perseveration and slowed responses, whereas silencing medial prefrontal cortex only mattered after reward delivery, for learning.
papers.authors: Anna Lebedeva, Yifan Wang, Lorenzo Funnell, Bex Terry, Yeon Jae Oh, Kenneth Miller, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: AI-discovered tuning laws explain neuronal population code geometry
papers.abstract: Measured visual cortical population codes are high-dimensional, yet standard single-neuron tuning models predict low-dimensional codes. The authors built an AI-science system in which LLMs evolve candidate equations, written as short programs, guided by graphical diagnostics of the fits. The resulting equation fits single-cell orientation tuning better, reproduces the high-dimensional geometry of the population code, and has a smoothness parameter that also accounts for head-direction cells. It also suggests a circuit mechanism for high-dimensional coding.
papers.authors: Reilly Tilbury, Dabin Kwon, Ali Haydaroğlu, Jack Ratliff, Valentin Schmutz, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth Miller, Kimberly Stachenfeld, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: Visual experience orthogonalizes visual cortical stimulus responses via population code transformation
papers.abstract: The authors imaged about 4,000 mouse V1 neurons before and after visuomotor task training. Complex changes in single-cell tuning curves turned out to follow one simple rule, a convex transformation that suppresses responses to task stimuli in mid-level cells, and its strength varies from trial to trial. The result is sparser, more orthogonal population codes for task stimuli, which helps a suboptimal downstream decoder but not an optimal one.
papers.authors: Samuel W. Failor, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: High-dimensional neuronal activity from low-dimensional latent dynamics: a solvable model
papers.abstract: The paper shows that a recurrent network whose dynamics reduce exactly to a low-dimensional system can still generate high-dimensional activity. The authors develop a nonlinear latent-variable method, the Neural Cross-Encoder, and apply it to mouse visual cortex recordings. They find that responses to drifting gratings need high-dimensional latents rather than a few latent dimensions.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025, Oral)
papers.authors: Valentin Schmutz, Ali Haydaroğlu, Shuqi Wang, Yixiao Feng, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

papers.title: Mouse frontal cortex mediates additive multisensory decisions
papers.abstract: The authors trained mice to localize audiovisual stimuli and showed that frontal cortex, unlike visual or parietal cortex, is needed to respond to either sensory modality. Recordings from over 14,000 neurons showed that anterior MOs additively encodes visual and auditory evidence after learning, matching the behavior. An accumulator model applied to these signals reproduced the choices and reaction times.
papers.authors: Philip Coen, Timothy P.H. Sit, Miles J. Wells, Matteo Carandini, Kenneth D. Harris

E013.name: David Heeger
E013.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Neural Science
E013.bio: David Heeger is a Silver Professor at New York University who investigates the computations of neural circuits. Heeger developed the normalization model, a theory of neural processing that explains how neurons integrate and scale signals within the visual cortex. Their research focuses on establishing a theoretical framework for cortical function. Heeger utilizes methodologies including functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling of neural dynamics.
E013.research_direction: Dr. Heeger has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying both biological and artificial visual systems, with a prominent focus on the circuit-level dynamics of divisive normalization. Their recent theoretical work explores how normalization mechanisms can stabilize strongly recurrent neural networks and mediate hierarchical, inter-areal communication spaces between visual areas like V1 and V2. In parallel, they are developing biologically motivated architectures for machine learning, examining how continuous-time recurrent networks can overcome signal delays through prospective coding and how contrastive representation learning can be reframed using physical models of manifold packing. On the behavioral side, Dr. Heeger is also studying the limits of visual attention and inattentional blindness, specifically testing how dynamic features like object speed, rather than static physical salience, determine whether unexpected events capture our awareness during focused visual tracking tasks.

papers.title: Stabilization of recurrent neural networks through divisive normalization
papers.abstract: Shows that a recurrent network can stay stable even with a spectral radius above 1 as long as it uses divisive normalization, which damps individual neuron responses. As recurrent weights get stronger the network passes through critical slowing down before it goes unstable, and this onset coincides with the breakdown of normalization, which the authors predict analytically from synaptic strength and input magnitude. The result suggests normalization is widespread in cortex partly because it secures stability under strong recurrent interactions.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Flaviano Morone, Shivang Rawat, David J. Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: Hierarchical Neural Circuit Theory of Normalization and Inter-areal Communication
papers.abstract: Builds a hierarchical circuit model in which feedback connections implement divisive normalization across cortical areas, instantiated for V1 and V2. The theory yields analytic power and coherence spectra that match observed shifts with stimulus contrast, and it accounts for low-dimensional communication subspaces between areas. It also predicts how feedback strength trades off inter-areal against within-area communication.
papers.authors: Asit Pal, Shivang Rawat, David J. Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
papers.abstract: Addresses the way stacked continuous-time recurrent layers delay bottom-up signals and weaken top-down error signals. The authors introduce Recursive Quadrature Filters, biologically motivated complex-valued band-pass filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models, and add a parameter-free two-tap prospective input correction. Prospective variants match or beat their controls across RQFs, S5 and ORGaNICs, with a small six-layer RQF reaching 96% on raw-audio Speech Commands.
papers.authors: Shivang Rawat, Mirko Morello, Flaviano Morone, David J. Heeger

papers.title: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning As Neural Manifold Packing
papers.abstract: Recasts contrastive representation learning as packing of neural manifolds, using a loss modeled on short-range repulsive particle systems from the physics of liquids and jammed packings. Each image class is a set of sub-manifolds of augmented views whose sizes and positions are optimized by the packing loss. The method reaches competitive linear-evaluation accuracy and yields class manifolds that separate naturally, linking physics, neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 38)
papers.authors: Guanming Zhang, David J. Heeger, Stefano Martiniani

papers.title: The visible gorilla: Unexpected fast—not physically salient—objects are noticeable
papers.abstract: Revisits inattentional blindness by testing whether a moving unexpected object is noticed while people are absorbed in a tracking task. Speed, rather than physical salience such as contrast or size, determined whether the object was noticed. The authors argue that observers hedge between task focus and readiness for unexpected, potentially important events, so inattentional blindness is not simply an inevitable deficit.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Pascal Wallisch, Wayne E. Mackey, Michael W. Karlovich, David J. Heeger

E016.name: Serge Dumoulin
E016.department: Computational Cognitive Neuroscience & Neuroimaging group; Director, Spinoza Centre for Neuroimaging
E016.bio: Serge Dumoulin is the Director of the Spinoza Centre for Neuroimaging and holds professorships at Utrecht University and VU Amsterdam. Dumoulin’s research characterizes the functional architecture of the human visual system using ultra-high field (7T) fMRI, psychophysics, and biologically-inspired computational models. They developed the population receptive field (pRF) mapping technique to quantify the spatial response properties of neural populations non-invasively. Dumoulin’s recent work applies these computational approaches to the topographic representation of higher-order cognitive functions, such as numerosity, and the plasticity of visual maps in response to neurological and ophthalmological disorders.
E016.research_direction: Dr. Dumoulin has recently been investigating the computational and neurochemical architecture of the human visual system by combining high-resolution 7T fMRI and MEG with population receptive field modeling. Their recent work explores how canonical visual computations, such as divisive normalization and surround suppression, map onto underlying neurotransmitter receptor distributions and are altered by serotonergic psychedelics like psilocybin. In addition to these mechanistic links, they are examining the broader spatiotemporal dynamics of the visual pathway to non-invasively estimate temporal integration windows across different cortical areas. Furthermore, their research investigates how early areas like V1 process perceptually meaningful object borders in natural scenes, while also extending topographic mapping to higher-order cognitive dimensions to uncover how human neural populations and artificial networks encode ordinal sequence position.

papers.title: Non-invasive mapping of the temporal processing hierarchy in the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study combines MEG with pRF modeling to estimate when different visual areas respond and how long their responses integrate information over time. The resulting maps reveal a hierarchy in which temporal windows lengthen and latencies increase along the visual pathway, mirroring the known spatial hierarchy. The method offers a non-invasive route to characterizing temporal dynamics across human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Katharina Eickhoff, Arjan Hillebrand, Tomas Knapen, Maartje C. de Jong, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Neural Tuning for Ordinal Processing: Convergent Patterns in Human Brains and Artificial Networks
papers.abstract: Building on the lab's numerosity mapping work, this paper examines how neural populations are tuned to ordinal position in a sequence, using 7T fMRI in humans alongside artificial neural networks. Similar tuning patterns are found in the brain and in the networks, suggesting a shared solution for representing order. It extends the topographic-maps-of-quantity program to ordinal information.
papers.authors: Shir Hofstetter, Marcus Daghlian, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Psilocybin alters visual contextual computations
papers.abstract: The authors combined 7T fMRI in humans with a population receptive field model that captures surround suppression to test how psilocybin changes visual processing. Under the drug, the way cortical populations integrate stimulus context was altered, with modeled changes to the balance of center and surround interactions across visual cortex. The work links a serotonergic perturbation to specific computational parameters of early vision, offering a mechanistic account of psychedelic visual effects.
papers.authors: Marco Aqil, Gilles de Hollander, Nina Vreugdenhil, Tomas Knapen, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: Computational model links normalization to chemoarchitecture in the human visual system
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a pRF-style model with divisive normalization whose parameters are fit to 7T fMRI responses and then compared with post-mortem maps of neurotransmitter receptor density. Variation in normalization across the visual hierarchy tracks the distribution of specific receptor types, tying a canonical neural computation to cortical chemoarchitecture. It provides a bridge between functional imaging models and underlying neurochemistry.
papers.authors: Marco Aqil, Tomas Knapen, Serge O. Dumoulin

papers.title: V1 neurons are tuned to perceptual borders in natural scenes
papers.abstract: Using human fMRI, macaque V1 recordings and modeling, the study asks how primary visual cortex responds to object borders in natural images. V1 responses were found to be enhanced at borders that observers perceive as separating objects, beyond what local image features predict. This indicates that early visual cortex encodes perceptually meaningful border information, with feedback from later stages implicated.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Wietske Zuiderbaan, Rob R. M. Teeuwen, Amparo Gilhuis, Matthew W. Self, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Serge O. Dumoulin

E017.name: Kendrick Kay
E017.bio: Kendrick Kay is an Associate Professor at the University of Minnesota’s Center for Magnetic Resonance Research (CMRR) specializing in the intersection of computational modeling and high-resolution functional MRI. Kay's research focuses on developing predictive encoding models to characterize how the human visual cortex represents naturalistic stimuli and facilitates perceptual decision-making. They have developed neuroimaging resources, such as the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), and statistical tools like GLMsingle for fMRI response estimates. Kay's current investigations use ultra-high-field (7T and 10.5T) imaging to resolve functional architectures across cortical layers and columns.
E017.research_direction: Dr. Kay's recent work explores the computational and physiological foundations of human visual processing, heavily leveraging ultra-high-field 7T fMRI and massive neuroimaging datasets. They have recently been investigating the nature of visual encoding by testing how well various computational frameworks—ranging from large language models to models probed with synthetic, out-of-distribution images—can predict complex scene representations across the visual cortex. Beyond stimulus-driven encoding, their research also examines how top-down cognitive tasks alter neural activity and how these behavioral states can be formally integrated into models of vision. Concurrently, Dr. Kay is advancing the broader methodological toolkit for neuroimaging, developing generative statistical methods to disentangle signal from noise in neural recordings and pioneering fast 7T MRI techniques to map the mesoscopic venous networks that underlie hemodynamic signals.

papers.title: A 7T fMRI dataset of synthetic images for out-of-distribution modeling of vision
papers.abstract: This paper releases a companion to the Natural Scenes Dataset in which subjects viewed controlled synthetic images at 7T, designed to probe how visual encoding models behave outside the natural-image distribution. Analyses show how the data can be used to test models of visual representation and reveal where current models fail to generalize out of distribution.
papers.authors: Alessandro T. Gifford, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick Kay

papers.title: Whole-brain meso-vein imaging in living humans using fast 7-T MRI
papers.abstract: Using recent MR sequence and image-processing advances, the study shows that detailed mesoscopic images of the whole-brain venous vasculature can be acquired quickly in living humans at 7T. This enables tracking of cerebrovascular disease and offers a better handle on the vascular basis of hemodynamic brain signals.
papers.authors: Omer Faruk Gulban, Rudiger Stirnberg, Desmond Ho Yan Tse, Alessandra Pizzuti, Kenshu Koiso, Mario Eduardo Archila-Melendez, Laurentius (Renzo) Huber, Saskia Bollmann, Rainer Goebel, Kendrick Kay, Dimo Ivanov

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether the contextual knowledge held in large language models can help explain the complex scene information encoded in visual cortex. Embeddings of scene captions turn out to predict 7T fMRI responses to natural scenes in the Natural Scenes Dataset well, with the mapping extending across high-level visual cortex. Such caption embeddings match or beat other model families, suggesting the brain's high-level visual code carries rich, language-like relational and semantic structure.
papers.authors: Adrien Doerig, Tim C. Kietzmann, Emily J. Allen, Yihan Wu, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick Kay, Ian Charest

papers.title: Disentangling signal and noise in neural responses through generative modeling
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a simple generative approach that estimates the distributions of signal and noise underlying repeated neural measurements. The recovered signal and noise structure improves principal components analysis and dimensionality estimates, and the framework is demonstrated on large neural datasets including NSD.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Jacob S. Prince, Thomas Gebhart, Greta Tuckute, Jingyang Zhou, Thomas Naselaris, Heiko H. Schutt

papers.title: Tasks and their role in visual neuroscience
papers.abstract: This review argues that visual neuroscience has emphasized stimulus control while underplaying the observer's task. It surveys how tasks alter neural activity across the visual system and sketches a formal framework for incorporating tasks into models of vision.
papers.authors: Kendrick Kay, Kathryn Bonnen, Rachel N. Denison, Mike J. Arcaro, David L. Barack

E018.name: Nicholas Priebe
E018.bio: Nicholas Priebe is a Professor of Neuroscience at the University of Texas at Austin where they investigate the circuit-level mechanisms and computations underlying sensory transformations in the mammalian visual cortex. Using in vivo whole-cell electrophysiology, two-photon imaging, and computational modeling, Priebe explores how neurons integrate thalamic and cortical inputs to generate selectivity for features such as orientation, motion, and depth. Their research examines contrast-invariant tuning, cross-orientation suppression, and the impact of behavioral states, such as locomotion and arousal, on cortical representation. Current projects focus on how these sensory representations are modulated by internal goals and integrated across different visual areas to guide behavior.
E018.research_direction: Dr. Priebe’s recent work investigates the network dynamics and subthreshold mechanisms that shape primary visual cortex responses in both mouse and non-human primate models. Using a combination of large-scale population recordings, in vivo whole-cell membrane potential tracking, and optogenetics, they are exploring how excitation-inhibition balance and synchronous network inputs govern irregular cortical spiking and sensory signal amplification. Their research also probes the precise nature of thalamocortical drive, testing whether average thalamic input or brief coincident fluctuations are responsible for establishing cortical feature selectivity. Furthermore, Dr. Priebe has recently been examining how visual circuits maintain invariant feature encoding across shifting luminance levels, as well as how fluctuating subthreshold internal states mediate the link between early visual activity and behavioral reaction times.

papers.title: Synchrony timescales underlie irregular neocortical spiking
papers.abstract: The paper asks why cortical neurons fire so irregularly and tests whether weakly synchronous network input, rather than intrinsic cell properties, is responsible. Dynamic-clamp experiments show intrinsic properties contribute little, while large-scale in vivo recordings reveal synchrony timescales of roughly 25 to 200 ms that shift faster during sensory drive. This shift naturally reduces response variability across cortical areas, while individual neurons keep distinct, stable responses.
papers.authors: Jagruti J. Pattadkal, Ronan T. O'Shea, David Hansel, Thibaud Taillefumier, Darrin H. Brager, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: Fluctuating internal states mediate neural-behavioral covariations in V1
papers.abstract: Whole-cell membrane potential recordings from single V1 neurons in macaques performing a reaction-time detection task show that most cells slowly depolarize in preparation for target onset, and the size of this buildup tracks reaction time. Post-onset membrane-potential fluctuations also covary with choice, depending on target location and contrast. A simple model with a fluctuating multiplicative gain reproduces these effects, implicating internal-state modulation at or before V1.
papers.authors: Baowang Li, Jason M. Samonds, Yuzhi Chen, Thibaud Taillefumier, Nicholas J. Priebe, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Luminance invariant encoding in mouse primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors measured thalamic (LGN) and cortical population activity across light levels to see how the visual system copes with the retina's changing code between night and day. Although retinal-driven LGN responses change with luminance, orientation and spatial-frequency selectivity in V1 stays largely constant. They argue that convergence of parallel thalamocortical pathways lets cortex keep stable selectivity while still supporting luminance sensitivity.
papers.authors: Ronan T. O'Shea, Ian Nauhaus, Xue-Xin Wei, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: The fluctuation-based regime of thalamocortical circuitry
papers.abstract: Using in vivo whole-cell recordings in mouse V1 with optogenetic cortical silencing, the study compares isolated thalamic input to the current threshold needed to evoke spikes. Average thalamic drive falls short of threshold, so thalamic input alone cannot explain cortical selectivity for orientation, direction and disparity. Instead, brief coincident fluctuations in sparse thalamic input can push cells over threshold, defining a fluctuation-based operating regime.
papers.authors: Liam Jennings, David Hansel, Nicholas J. Priebe

papers.title: Primate neocortex performs balanced sensory amplification
papers.abstract: Recording many single neurons at once in awake marmoset visual cortex, the authors compared driven and spontaneous network activity against circuit models. The data point to a regime of non-normal balanced amplification, in which strong recurrent feedback transiently boosts incoming signals by briefly disrupting excitation-inhibition balance. Rapid inhibition then quenches the response, allowing the network to track stimuli that change quickly over time.
papers.authors: Jagruti J. Pattadkal, Boris V. Zemelman, Ila Fiete, Nicholas J. Priebe

E024.name: Daniel Yamins
E024.department: Departments of Psychology and Computer Science
E024.bio: Daniel Yamins is an Associate Professor of Psychology and Computer Science at Stanford University whose research focuses on the intersection of artificial intelligence and neuroscience. Yamins develops performance-optimized deep neural networks that serve as models of primate visual and auditory systems, showing that task-optimized architectures can predict neural response patterns. Their research uses high-throughput neurophysiology, functional brain imaging, and large-scale data analysis to model the algorithms of the human brain. Yamins currently investigates how self-supervised learning and 3D scene understanding contribute to the functional organization of sensory pathways and works on methodologies for model-brain comparisons.
E024.research_direction: Dr. Yamins has recently been investigating the computational principles that drive the functional organization of the primate visual system, developing self-supervised neural networks constrained by spatial smoothness to model the emergence of topographic maps across the early and higher ventral stream. Their recent work also explores how predictive video models can learn physical structure without explicit labels, constructing probabilistic world models that capture properties like optical flow, depth, and object motion through counterfactual reasoning. By treating diverse 3D vision tasks—such as novel view synthesis and object manipulation—as different inference paths through a unified graphical model, they are examining how generalized physical understanding can be extracted zero-shot from large-scale video data. Additionally, they have been exploring the theoretical foundations of representation alignment, probing the mathematical conditions under which artificial and biological networks solving complex tasks are likely to undergo convergent evolution.

papers.title: Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling
papers.abstract: Proposes 3WM, a physical world model expressed as a probabilistic graphical model over scene elements like RGB, optical flow and camera pose, so that many 3D tasks become different inference paths through the same model. Novel view synthesis, object manipulation and depth estimation all emerge zero-shot from prompting, without task-specific training. It matches or beats specialist baselines and supports composed operations such as moving an object while navigating.
papers.authors: Wanhee Lee, Klemen Kotar, Rahul Mysore Venkatesh, Jared Watrous, Honglin Chen, Khai Loong Aw, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: Contravariance Theory: Strong Alignment for Minimal Solutions to Hard Tasks
papers.abstract: A theoretical result showing that for any two minimal deep network solutions to a sufficiently hard task, affine (weak) alignment of representations implies alignment of privileged axes (strong alignment), and this alignment propagates up the network hierarchy. It formalizes the contravariance principle, argues that model-brain comparison metrics matter less when tasks are strong, and suggests convergent evolution between artificial and biological networks is likely.
papers.authors: Daniel L. K. Yamins, Aran Nayebi

papers.title: World Modeling with Probabilistic Structure Integration
papers.abstract: Introduces Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI), a recipe for building controllable, promptable world models. A random-access autoregressive sequence model of video is probed causally to zero-shot extract structures such as optical flow, depth and object segments, and these structures are fed back as new token types so the model improves and gains new control handles. Trained on about 1.4 trillion tokens of internet video, it delivers strong flow, depth and segmentation and improved video prediction.
papers.authors: Klemen Kotar, Wanhee Lee, Rahul Venkatesh, Honglin Chen, Daniel Bear, Jared Watrous, Simon Kim, Khai Loong Aw, Lilian Naing Chen, Stefan Stojanov, Kevin Feigelis, Imran Thobani, Alex Durango, Khaled Jedoui, Atlas Kazemian, Dan Yamins

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Motion Concepts by Optimizing Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: Presents a method that estimates motion and optical flow from video without labels by optimizing counterfactual perturbations with a pretrained video prediction model. Motion concepts are discovered by asking how a small change to a frame would change the predicted future, and the approach yields state-of-the-art unsupervised flow and motion segmentation on real-world benchmarks. It highlights how predictive video models implicitly encode motion structure.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025, Spotlight)
papers.authors: Stefan Stojanov, David Wendt, Seungwoo Kim, Rahul Mysore Venkatesh, Kevin Feigelis, Klemen Kotar, Khai Loong Aw, Jiajun Wu, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: A unifying framework for functional organization in early and higher ventral visual cortex
papers.abstract: The paper shows that a single deep network objective, combining self-supervised object learning with a spatial smoothness constraint on a 2D cortical sheet, can reproduce the topographic organization of both early and higher ventral visual cortex. Orientation pinwheels, face and other category-selective patches, and their relative layout all emerge from one principle instead of separate area-specific models. The resulting models predict neural responses and offer a unified account of how cortical maps arise.
papers.authors: Eshed Margalit, Hyodong Lee, Dawn Finzi, James J. DiCarlo, Kalanit Grill-Spector, Daniel L.K. Yamins

E026.name: SueYeon Chung
E026.lab_name: NeuroAI and Geometric Data Analysis (NAIGDA) group
E026.bio: SueYeon Chung is a theoretical neuroscientist who researches geometric and physical principles underlying neural representations in biological and artificial systems. Chung develops mathematical frameworks using high-dimensional geometry and statistical physics to analyze how neural population structures facilitate information processing and task execution. Their work focuses on characterizing neural manifolds to understand transformations of representations across processing stages, relating brain science to artificial intelligence. Formerly an Assistant Professor at New York University’s Center for Neural Science, Chung leads a research program that constructs neurally-plausible network models and biologically-inspired learning rules.
E026.research_direction: Dr. Chung has recently been investigating how the geometric structure of neural population activity supports flexible and efficient computation in both biological brains and artificial networks. Their recent work explores how representational manifolds systematically untangle across cortical hierarchies and learning stages, as well as how single-neuron tuning diversity in early vision shapes population geometry to improve stimulus separability. They are also developing analytical theories that link these mesoscopic manifold properties to a network's ability to generalize across tasks with shared latent structures. Furthermore, Dr. Chung has been translating these neuroscience-derived metrics into machine learning, using manifold capacity to track feature-learning dynamics during artificial network training and to design new objective functions for self-supervised image representation.

papers.title: Neural population geometry and optimal coding of tasks with shared latent structure
papers.abstract: Develops an analytical theory that ties the mesoscopic statistics of a neural population, such as its manifold geometry and correlations, to how well it generalizes across multiple related tasks that share latent structure. The theory identifies which aspects of population activity matter for flexible, generalizable coding and yields predictions about optimal representations that the authors test on data. It is a flagship statement of the group's geometry-based approach to neural coding.
papers.authors: Albert J. Wakhloo, Will Slatton, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Feature Learning beyond the Lazy-Rich Dichotomy: Insights from Representational Geometry
papers.abstract: Argues that the lazy versus rich picture of network learning is too coarse and proposes tracking how task-relevant representational manifolds change during training. Using theory and experiments, the paper shows that manifolds progressively untangle, and that their geometry reveals distinct learning stages and strategies across algorithms, architectures and data. It links representational geometry to feature-learning dynamics in artificial networks.
papers.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Spotlight
papers.authors: Chi-Ning Chou, Hang Le, Yichen Wang, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Representational geometry reveals how neuronal diversity supports perceptual performance
papers.abstract: Asks why visual neurons show such varied tuning by relating the distribution of tuning amplitude and bandwidth to population information capacity. With theory, simulations and macaque V1 recordings, it shows that amplitude diversity spreads representation centers apart while bandwidth diversity decorrelates them, both improving stimulus separability. This links single-neuron heterogeneity to population geometry in early vision.
papers.authors: Sonica Saraf, J. Anthony Movshon, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Geometry Linked to Untangling Efficiency Reveals Structure and Computation in Neural Populations
papers.abstract: Introduces GLUE, a data-driven analysis framework that connects geometric descriptors of neural activity with manifold capacity to measure how well task-relevant representations are untangled. Applied to more than seven datasets across species, tasks and recording methods, it finds untangling along cortical hierarchies, with learning and over intrinsic dynamics. It offers a general tool for reading computation from population geometry.
papers.authors: Chi-Ning Chou, Royoung Kim, Luke A Arend, Yao-Yuan Yang, Brett D Mensh, Won Mok Shim, Matthew G Perich, SueYeon Chung

papers.title: Learning Efficient Coding of Natural Images with Maximum Manifold Capacity Representations
papers.abstract: Recasts self-supervised image representation learning as an efficient-coding problem by using manifold capacity as the objective to maximize. The resulting MMCR method avoids collapse without explicit constraints and learns representations that perform well on standard benchmarks while showing links to information-theoretic and neural-coding principles. It ties a theoretical measure from neuroscience to practical visual SSL.
papers.authors: Thomas Yerxa, Yilun Kuang, Eero Simoncelli, SueYeon Chung

E028.name: Surya Ganguli
E028.bio: Ganguli is an Associate Professor of Applied Physics at Stanford University and directs the Neural Dynamics and Computation Lab. Their research integrates principles from physics, machine learning, and neurobiology to examine how cognitive functions such as sensory perception, memory, and motor control result from the collective dynamics of neural circuits. In vision science, Ganguli developed deep learning frameworks to model retinal responses to natural scenes and investigated the mechanisms of core object recognition in the ventral visual stream. Their current work focuses on 'NeuroAI,' aiming to establish a theoretical foundation for artificial intelligence by drawing insights from biological neural networks and the statistical mechanics of learning.
E028.research_direction: Dr. Ganguli has recently been developing exact analytical theories to uncover the mathematical foundations of learning, generalization, and perception in deep neural networks. Their recent work explores the mechanisms by which architectural inductive biases and information constraints determine whether image-generating diffusion models memorize finite training data or successfully generalize to synthesize novel outputs. They are also investigating the broader dynamics of network training, from probing how pretraining task diversity influences the emergence of in-context learning in transformers to modeling how specific initialization scales dictate a model's transition into rich feature-learning regimes. Furthermore, they are studying the geometric misalignment between human and machine vision, analyzing the massive dimensionality of network perceptual manifolds to understand why artificial systems remain vulnerable to adversarial examples.

papers.title: Solving adversarial examples requires solving exponential misalignment
papers.abstract: The authors define a network's perceptual manifold as all inputs it confidently assigns to a class, and find that its dimensionality is orders of magnitude higher than that of human concepts. This implies exponentially many inputs are labeled confidently by machines but not by humans, which offers a geometric account of adversarial examples. The work links robustness to how well machine and human perceptual concepts align.
papers.authors: Alessandro Salvatore, Stanislav Fort, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: An exact information theory of generalization phase transitions in Bayesian diffusion models
papers.abstract: The paper introduces analytically tractable Bayesian information-restricted diffusion (BIRD) models that explain how diffusion models generalize instead of memorizing from finite data. Spatially local BIRD models closely match trained diffusion models early in training across UNet and DiT architectures. The authors also characterize a phase transition in generalization that follows from the information restriction.
papers.authors: Henry Hunt, Mason Kamb, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models
papers.abstract: The paper explains why diffusion image generators produce novel images instead of memorizing their training data. The authors show that two inductive biases of convolutional networks, locality and equivariance, prevent the ideal score-matching solution and give rise to a form of combinatorial creativity. They turn this into fully analytic local-score machines that predict the outputs of trained ResNet and UNet diffusion models with high accuracy.
papers.authors: Mason Kamb, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
papers.abstract: The paper gives exact solutions to a minimal model that moves between lazy and rich (feature-learning) training regimes. It shows that layer-specific initialization scales and learning rates set the regime through conserved quantities that constrain how learning trajectories move in parameter and function space. The analysis is extended to multi-neuron, multi-layer linear models and to shallow nonlinear networks.
papers.authors: Daniel Kunin, Allan Raventós, Clémentine Dominé, Feng Chen, David Klindt, Andrew Saxe, Surya Ganguli

papers.title: Pretraining task diversity and the emergence of non-Bayesian in-context learning for regression
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether transformers can do in-context learning on tasks unlike those seen in pretraining. Varying the number of distinct regression tasks in pretraining, they find a diversity threshold. Below it the model acts like a Bayesian estimator tied to the pretraining prior, and above it the model generalizes to unseen tasks and behaves like ridge regression.
papers.authors: Allan Raventós, Mansheej Paul, Feng Chen, Surya Ganguli

E032.name: Thomas Naselaris
E032.bio: Thomas Naselaris is an Associate Professor in the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Minnesota and a member of the Medical Discovery Team on Optical Imaging and Brain Science. Naselaris's research focuses on the generative capabilities of the human visual system, employing high-field fMRI and voxel-wise encoding models to investigate how the brain represents natural scenes and mental imagery. They have developed mathematical frameworks for reconstructing visual experiences from human brain activity through neural decoding. Currently, Naselaris's work integrates deep learning with functional neuroimaging to examine the transformations between perceptual and mnemonic representations in the visual cortex.
E032.research_direction: Dr. Naselaris has recently been investigating the neural relationship between visual perception and mental imagery, as well as the geometric and computational structure of representations in the human visual cortex. Using high-resolution 7T fMRI, their recent work explores how neural population activity transforms—such as through dimensionality shifts and subspace reorientations—when a person transitions from seeing an image to actively imagining it. To computationally ground this relationship, they are developing new fMRI benchmark datasets and multimodal diffusion-based decoding models to test how well image reconstructions trained on visual perception can generalize to mental imagery. Additionally, Dr. Naselaris is probing the broader architecture of visual processing by analyzing the geometry of concept manifolds across brain areas and deep neural networks (DNNs), and testing whether brain-optimized DNNs of early visual cortex actually require strictly hierarchical architectures to predict neural responses.

papers.title: MIRAGE: Robust multi-modal architectures translate fMRI-to-image models from vision to mental imagery
papers.abstract: Builds on the NSD-Imagery benchmark to develop MIRAGE, a decoder trained on seen-image fMRI data that generalizes to mental images. It combines a linear backbone with multimodal text and image features feeding a diffusion model, and it sets state of the art on NSD-Imagery by feature metrics and human ratings. Ablations show that low-dimensional image features plus text and high/low-level guidance work best, supporting use of existing vision datasets to train imagery decoders.
papers.authors: Reese Kneeland, Cesar Kadir Torrico Villanueva, Tong Chen, Jordyn Ojeda, Shubh Khanna, Jonathan Xu, Paul S. Scotti, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: Variation in the geometry of concept manifolds across human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Uses a large 7T fMRI dataset to estimate the geometry of 'concept manifolds' (sets of activity patterns for images of one concept) and links it to few-shot linear classification accuracy. Across human visual cortex, accuracy differences are driven mainly by the separation between manifold centers, whereas across DNN layers they are driven by manifold dimensionality. Signal and dimensionality trade off strongly in both systems, suggesting different routes to the same classification ability.
papers.authors: Ghislain St-Yves, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: A transformation from vision to imagery in the human brain
papers.abstract: Introduces the 'imagery transformation', a mapping from activity evoked when seeing an image to activity when imagining it, and estimates it in two 7T fMRI datasets. Imagery is not simply weakened vision: in early visual cortex the transformation roughly halves the number of active dimensions and reorients them into a distinct subspace. The reoriented dimensions still coarsely carry the same features as vision.
papers.authors: Tiasha Saha Roy, Jesse Breedlove, Ghislain St-Yves, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: NSD-Imagery: A Benchmark Dataset for Extending fMRI Vision Decoding Methods to Mental Imagery
papers.abstract: Releases a benchmark of fMRI activity paired with mental images that complements the Natural Scenes Dataset. Evaluating several NSD-trained decoders (MindEye1/2, Brain Diffuser, and others) shows that performance on seen-image reconstruction is largely decoupled from performance on imagined images. Simple linear, multimodal-feature decoders generalize best to imagery, while complex architectures tend to overfit to vision data.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Reese Kneeland, Paul S. Scotti, Ghislain St-Yves, Jesse L. Breedlove, Kendrick N. Kay, Thomas Naselaris

papers.title: Brain-optimized deep neural network models of human visual areas learn non-hierarchical representations
papers.abstract: Trains DNNs directly to predict fMRI responses in V1-V4, comparing a single-branch network for all areas with a multi-branch network for each area independently. Only the single-branch network learned a layer hierarchy even though the multi-branch one could have. Hence hierarchical representations are not required to predict human visual-area activity, and brain-like DNNs may take varied architectures.
papers.authors: Ghislain St-Yves, Emily J. Allen, Yihan Wu, Kendrick Kay, Thomas Naselaris

E033.name: Ian Charest
E033.bio: Ian Charest is an associate professor and Courtois chairholder in cognitive and computational neuroscience who investigates how the human brain processes high-level visual and auditory information. Charest’s research utilizes a multi-methodological approach that combines functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magneto-electroencephalography (M-EEG) with computational modeling, including representational similarity analysis (RSA) and artificial neural networks. A focus of their work involves characterizing individual representational idiosyncrasies and understanding the interaction between vision and semantics during the recognition of natural scenes.
E033.research_direction: Dr. Charest has recently been studying how the human brain turns visual input into high-level meaning, and how well modern AI models capture that process. Their recent work explores whether the brain's representations of natural scenes line up with the embeddings of large language models, and whether vision and language converge on a shared space of perceived similarity. They also use time-resolved EEG to study face recognition, comparing typical observers, exceptionally skilled super-recognizers, and a patient with prosopagnosia, and they ask which computations, such as low-level visual features or semantic information, differ across these groups.

papers.title: Representations in vision and language converge in a shared, multidimensional space of perceived similarities
papers.abstract: The research explores the hypothesis that human sensory systems transform inputs into a shared, modality-agnostic representational space where visual and linguistic information converge. Participants performed behavioral similarity judgments on natural scene images and their corresponding textual captions from the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD). Representational similarity analysis (RSA) revealed that both visual and linguistic similarity structures not only converged at the behavioral level but also accurately predicted fMRI responses in a consistent network of mid-to-high-level visual brain regions. Furthermore, computational models trained to align images with LLM-based embeddings outperformed standard category-trained networks in capturing this shared behavioral similarity structure. These findings suggest that conceptual representations are grounded in a commonRelational code that reflects the stable structure of the environment, transcending the specific sensory modality of input.
papers.authors: Katerina Marie Simkova, Adrien Doerig, Clayton Hickey, Ian Charest

papers.title: High-level visual representations in the human brain are aligned with large language models
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether the complex visual information extracted by the human brain from natural scenes—including object interrelations and environmental context—is effectively modeled by the representational format of large language models (LLMs). Utilizing the 7T fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), the authors demonstrate that LLM embeddings derived from scene captions successfully characterize neural activity across an extensive network of brain regions. Through controlled model comparisons, they show that the alignment between brain and model representations arises from the LLMs' capacity to integrate relational information beyond the sum of individual words. Furthermore, deep neural networks (DNNs) trained to map visual inputs into this caption-based semantic space exhibit greater brain-model similarity than traditional object-recognition models, suggesting that visuo-semantic transformation constitutes a fundamental objective of the human visual system.
papers.authors: Adrien Doerig, Tim C. Kietzmann, Emily Allen, Yihan Wu, Thomas Naselaris, Kendrick Kay, Ian Charest

papers.title: Neural computations in prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: This investigation identifies the computational deficits underlying the loss of face identification ability in brain-lesioned patient PS, a classic case of acquired pure prosopagnosia. By collecting a large-scale dataset of high-density electroencephalography (EEG) and applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), the authors compared time-resolved brain representations against various computational models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DNNs) and semantic embeddings. The study revealed that PS's neural representations exhibited excessive generalization of early visual patterns, remaining more similar to early layers of visual DNNs than those of neurotypical controls. Crucially, PS showed significant representational deficits in high-level visual and semantic computations, particularly during the N170 and P300 processing windows. These results provide mechanistic evidence that impaired face recognition is linked to a failure in constructing abstract, high-level representational geometries within the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Simon Faghel-Soubeyrand, Anne-Raphaelle Richoz, Delphine Waeber, Jessica Woodhams, Roberto Caldara, Frédéric Gosselin, Ian Charest

papers.title: Decoding face recognition abilities in the human brain
papers.abstract: This study employs a data-driven approach to characterize the neuro-computational variations across the face recognition spectrum, ranging from typical recognizers to 'super-recognizers' (individuals with exceptional face identification skills). Using high-density EEG and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA), the authors successfully decoded individual face recognition ability scores from just one second of brain activity with high accuracy. Comparisons with DNN models of vision and semantics indicated that super-recognizers exhibit enhanced mid-level visual computations at early latencies and richer semantic representations at later latencies (approx. 600–700 ms). These findings provide the first direct empirical evidence linking high-level semantic brain computations to individual differences in face recognition ability, suggesting that superior performance is supported by more robust integration of visual and conceptual features.
papers.authors: Simon Faghel-Soubeyrand, Meike Ramon, Eva Bamps, Matteo Zoia, Jessica Woodhams, Anne-Raphaelle Richoz, Roberto Caldara, Frédéric Gosselin, Ian Charest

E035.name: Tim Kietzmann
E035.bio: Tim C. Kietzmann is a Professor of Machine Learning at the University of Osnabrück's Institute of Cognitive Science. Their research integrates deep learning and cognitive neuroscience to characterize the neuro-computational principles of human vision, focusing on how recurrent neural networks model the dynamic transformation of sensory signals in the brain. By combining neuroimaging techniques like MEG, EEG, and fMRI with neuro-inspired artificial intelligence, Kietzmann investigates how biological systems derive representations from environmental regularities. Kietzmann previously held positions at the Donders Institute and the University of Cambridge, where they used connectionist models to explain cortical dynamics.
E035.research_direction: Dr. Kietzmann has recently been advancing a neuroconnectionist framework that utilizes artificial neural networks as a computational language to generate falsifiable theories of human visual processing. Their recent work explores how biologically grounded constraints, such as incorporating human-like developmental trajectories of visual acuity or employing topographic architectures without weight sharing, shape the emergence of cortical maps and robust, shape-based object recognition. Beyond spatial architectures, they are also investigating the temporal dynamics of active vision by training self-supervised recurrent models to integrate and predict upcoming visual features along natural scanpaths. Furthermore, they are examining the cognitive and neural drivers of this active sampling behavior, leveraging large-scale MEG and eye-tracking datasets to disentangle whether fixation durations during scene viewing primarily reflect perceptual processing demands or ongoing memory encoding.

papers.title: Adopting a human developmental visual diet yields robust and shape-based AI vision
papers.abstract: Trains vision networks with a curriculum that mimics human visual development, gradually improving acuity, contrast sensitivity and colour. Models trained this way rely more on object shape than texture, recognise abstract shapes better, and resist image corruptions and adversarial attacks better than standard models. The results suggest robustness can come from how a model learns rather than only how much data it sees.
papers.authors: Zejin Lu, Sushrut Thorat, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Fixation duration on natural scenes is explained by memory encoding not processing demand
papers.abstract: Uses a large MEG and eye-tracking dataset of 4,080 natural scenes viewed by five participants, plus neural-network modelling, to ask why some fixations last longer. Longer fixations did not track prolonged visual processing or classification difficulty. They tracked how memorable a scene patch was and showed increased theta-gamma coupling in frontal and hippocampal regions, pointing to memory encoding as the main driver of fixation timing.
papers.authors: Philip Sulewski, Carmen Amme, Martin N. Hebart, Peter König, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: Predicting upcoming visual features during eye movements yields scene representations aligned with human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Proposes Glimpse Prediction Networks, recurrent models trained in a self-supervised way to predict the embedding of the next glimpse along human-like scanpaths. The networks pick up object co-occurrences and spatial layouts and integrate information across fixations. Their representations align strongly with human fMRI responses in mid- and high-level visual cortex, matching or beating other leading models.
papers.authors: Sushrut Thorat, Adrien Doerig, Alexander Kroner, Carmen Amme, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: End-to-end topographic networks as models of cortical map formation and human visual behaviour
papers.abstract: Introduces all-topographic neural networks (All-TNNs), vision models without weight sharing in which every unit has its own local receptive field and neighbouring units are encouraged to be similar. These networks spontaneously develop smooth orientation and category selectivity maps like those seen in primate visual cortex, and do so on a lower energy budget. A new dataset of human spatial biases in object recognition is better predicted by All-TNNs than by control models.
papers.authors: Zejin Lu, Adrien Doerig, Victoria Bosch, Bas Krahmer, Daniel Kaiser, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Tim C. Kietzmann

papers.title: The neuroconnectionist research programme
papers.abstract: Perspective arguing that artificial neural networks should be judged as a computational language for stating falsifiable theories of brain computation, not as one fixed model. Drawing on Lakatos's philosophy of science, it lays out the core, framework and tools of the neuroconnectionist programme. It reviews past and current projects and argues the programme is progressive because it keeps producing new insights into the brain.
papers.authors: Adrien Doerig, Rowan P. Sommers, Katja Seeliger, Blake Richards, Jenann Ismael, Grace W. Lindsay, Konrad P. Kording, Talia Konkle, Marcel A. J. van Gerven, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Tim C. Kietzmann

E037.name: Samuel Nastase
E037.department: Department of Psychology (also Center for Computational Language Sciences)
E037.bio: Samuel Nastase investigates the neural mechanisms underlying human communication and shared cognition using naturalistic stimuli such as narratives and cinema. Nastase employs computational techniques, including hyperalignment and intersubject correlation, to map high-dimensional representational spaces shared across individual brains. Their recent work focuses on integrating large language models with neuroimaging data to understand how linguistic structures facilitate the transmission of information during social interaction.
E037.research_direction: Dr. Nastase has recently been exploring how the human brain encodes complex information during naturalistic communication and observation. Much of their recent work investigates the intersection of human language and large language models, probing how distributed neural populations unify linguistic structures and examining whether internal transformer computations map onto functionally specialized cortical regions. They are also investigating how neural representations align across individuals, utilizing intracranial recordings to test whether conversational speakers and listeners rely on a shared linguistic code and developing functional alignment techniques to project highly variable patient data into a common representational space. Beyond language, their recent work explores the cortical representational geometry of natural vision, using fMRI to investigate how the meaning and social content of observed actions are organized across the brain.

papers.title: Unifying the structures of language in a neural population code
papers.abstract: A synthesis paper arguing that the many structural levels of language, from words through syntax to discourse, can be described within a single population-coding framework in cortex. It builds on recent work relating large language model representations to neural activity during natural language use. It sets out a unified account of how distributed neural populations may encode linguistic structure. (Summary based on title and lab description; full abstract could not be retrieved.)
papers.authors: Samuel A. Nastase, Zaid Zada, Adele Goldberg, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Behaviorally-relevant features of observed actions dominate cortical representational geometry in natural vision
papers.abstract: Participants viewed 90 naturalistic video clips of social and nonsocial actions during fMRI. Behavioral arrangement tasks yielded models of action meaning (transitive purpose and social content) and of visual content, which were compared against semantic word-embedding and low-level visual models. Action-meaning models explained the most cortical variance, extending beyond the classic action observation network into ventral temporal cortex.
papers.authors: Jane Han, Vassiki Chauhan, Rebecca Philip, Morgan K. Taylor, Heejung Jung, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: Aligning brains into a shared space improves their alignment with large language models
papers.abstract: Intracranial recordings from different patients have electrodes in different places, which limits population-level analyses. The authors align individual brains into a common representational space using a functional alignment approach. This yields improved prediction of neural responses from large language model embeddings and better generalization across subjects.
papers.authors: Arnab Bhattacharjee, Zaid Zada, Haocheng Wang, Bobbi Aubrey, Werner Doyle, Patricia Dugan, Daniel Friedman, Orrin Devinsky, Adeen Flinker, Peter J. Ramadge, Uri Hasson, Ariel Goldstein, Samuel A. Nastase

papers.title: A shared model-based linguistic space for transmitting our thoughts from brain to brain in natural conversations
papers.abstract: Using intracranial recordings from pairs of people having spontaneous conversations, the study represents each word with contextual embeddings from a large language model. It shows that the same embedding space predicts neural activity in the speaker before a word is produced and in the listener after it is heard. The findings indicate that brains of speaker and listener share a common linguistic code that supports communication.
papers.authors: Zaid Zada, Ariel Goldstein, Sebastian Michelmann, Erez Simony, Amy Price, Liat Hasenfratz, Emily Barham, Asieh Zadbood, Werner Doyle, Daniel Friedman, Patricia Dugan, Lucia Melloni, Sasha Devore, Adeen Flinker, Orrin Devinsky, Samuel A. Nastase, Uri Hasson

papers.title: Shared functional specialization in transformer-based language models and the human brain
papers.abstract: Rather than comparing the final embeddings of transformer language models to brain activity, this work analyzes the internal attention-head computations that build those embeddings. It finds that different computational operations in the transformer map onto distinct, functionally specialized cortical regions during story listening. The results suggest similar functional specialization in models and the brain.
papers.authors: Sreejan Kumar, Theodore R. Sumers, Takateru Yamakoshi, Ariel Goldstein, Uri Hasson, Kenneth A. Norman, Thomas L. Griffiths, Robert D. Hawkins, Samuel A. Nastase

E038.name: Haim Sompolinsky
E038.department: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology and Department of Physics
E038.bio: Sompolinsky works in computational neuroscience, applying principles from statistical physics and nonlinear dynamics to study the mechanisms of neural circuit function. They developed attractor network models for associative memory and the balanced state theory of neural networks, which provides a framework for understanding the variability of neuronal activity. Their research methodologies integrate statistical mechanics and disordered systems theory to investigate neural population coding, learning, and the dynamics of brain circuits. Currently, Sompolinsky focuses on the intersection of biological and artificial intelligence, employing geometric methods to study information processing in vision and language within deep neural networks.
E038.research_direction: Dr. Sompolinsky has recently been investigating the fundamental principles of learning, representation, and memory across biological and artificial neural networks by applying analytical frameworks from statistical mechanics. In artificial systems, their recent work explores the physics of deep learning, seeking to understand how network nonlinearities shape emergent coding schemes and how the geometry of neural manifolds dictates interference and phase transitions during continual learning. Within biological circuits, they are analyzing heterogeneous recurrent networks using dynamical mean-field theory to understand how robust continuous attractors—such as those underlying head-direction and grid-cell representations—can emerge despite massive synaptic disorder. Additionally, Dr. Sompolinsky is utilizing large language models to test neuro-inspired cognitive architectures, investigating how hippocampus-like sparse gating and replay mechanisms might facilitate the continuous consolidation of naturalistic episodic memories without catastrophic forgetting.

papers.title: Order parameters and phase transitions of continual learning in deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Develops an analytically tractable statistical-mechanics theory of how deep, wide networks learn a sequence of tasks. A small set of order parameters describing task and rule similarity predicts forgetting and interference on standard benchmarks, and greater depth reduces interference. For task-specific readouts, the theory reveals a phase transition in which too-dissimilar tasks produce catastrophic anterograde interference, where old tasks are kept but new ones cannot be learned.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Haozhe Shan, Qianyi Li, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: A complementary learning system for continual episodic memory in large language models
papers.abstract: Uses an LLM as a model system for continual episodic memory in a complementary-learning-systems framework.
