A hippocampus-like module assigns each episode an extremely sparse low-rank adapter selected by competitive gating, retaining recall across streams of up to 1,000 episodes, while slow consolidation is modelled by replay fine-tuning of base weights. This yields a network that stores, recalls and consolidates naturalistic memories.
papers.authors: Xu Pan, Ely Hahami, Roy Siegelmann, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Coding schemes in neural networks learning classification tasks
papers.abstract: Studies wide fully connected networks trained on classification with a Bayesian framework in the feature-learning regime. Learning produces strong class-dominated representations, termed coding schemes, whose form depends on the neuronal nonlinearity: analog in linear networks, and redundant or sparse via spontaneous symmetry breaking in nonlinear ones. Shows that weight scaling and nonlinearity fundamentally shape emergent representations.
papers.authors: Alexander van Meegen, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Symmetries and Continuous Attractors in Disordered Neural Circuits
papers.abstract: Reconciles classic continuous-attractor theory with heterogeneous mouse head-direction data by building recurrent networks directly from measured tuning curves. Dynamical mean-field analysis shows these disordered networks are equivalent to ring attractors with Mexican-hat interactions and spontaneously broken continuous symmetry, with the symmetry visible as eigenvalue degeneracies in the weights. The framework extends to two-dimensional grid-cell toroidal attractors.
papers.authors: David G. Clark, L. F. Abbott, Haim Sompolinsky

papers.title: Representations and generalization in artificial and brain neural networks
papers.abstract: A perspective arguing that the geometry of neural manifolds (their dimension and radius) for objects, words and concepts acts as an order parameter linking neural representations to generalization. It also argues that the theory of learning in very wide networks explains how weight regularization, architecture and hyperparameters shape those geometries. The piece additionally touches on representational drift and unifies neuroscience, machine learning and cognitive science views.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Qianyi Li, Ben Sorscher, Haim Sompolinsky

E039.name: Martin Schrimpf
E039.department: School of Life Sciences and School of Computer and Communication Sciences
E039.bio: Martin Schrimpf is a Tenure-Track Assistant Professor at EPFL and head of the NeuroAI Lab, where their research integrates machine learning, neuroscience, and cognitive science. Schrimpf is an architect of the Brain-Score platform, an initiative designed to benchmark artificial neural networks against large-scale neural and behavioral datasets to identify brain-like computational architectures. Their work focuses on developing predictive models of the primate visual ventral stream and the human language network to identify the functional principles of natural intelligence. Currently, Schrimpf investigates the use of these brain models for clinical applications, including the development of visual prosthetics and diagnostic tools for neurological disorders.
E039.research_direction: Dr. Schrimpf has recently been investigating the computational alignment between artificial neural networks and biological brains across both visual and linguistic domains. In vision, their recent work explores how deep learning models capture representations within the primate ventral stream, examining the scaling laws of neural alignment and probing human-like perceptual mechanisms such as contour integration. They are also utilizing topographic neural-network frameworks to guide targeted electrical microstimulation in primate high-level visual cortex, investigating how to predictably steer perceptual choices for next-generation visual prosthetics. Broadening this comparative approach, Dr. Schrimpf is applying functional localizer paradigms from cognitive neuroscience to large language models, mapping how causally task-relevant language and reasoning units emerge during training and tracking their ongoing alignment with the human brain's language network.

papers.title: Model-Guided Microstimulation Steers Primate Visual Behavior
papers.abstract: The authors build a computational framework for predicting where and how to electrically stimulate high-level visual cortex. It combines a module that turns stimulation parameters into changes in neural activity, topographic neural-network models that mimic cortical spatial layout, and a procedure that maps model-chosen sites onto monkey cortex. In two macaques doing a recognition task, stimulation experiments prototyped in the model produced significant, site-by-site predictable shifts in perceptual choices, and in-silico stimulation of face-selective sites yielded images resembling a patient's reported facephenes. This is a proof of principle for model-guided next-generation visual prosthetics.
papers.authors: Johannes Mehrer, Ben Lonnqvist, Anna Mitola, Abdulkadir Gokce, Paolo Papale, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: Scaling Laws for Task-Optimized Models of the Primate Visual Ventral Stream
papers.abstract: Evaluating more than 600 vision models trained under controlled scaling of compute, model size and data, the paper asks how scale affects alignment with V1, V2, V4, IT and behavior. Behavioral alignment keeps improving with scale, but neural alignment saturates across architectures and datasets, with higher visual areas benefiting most from scaling. The result argues that simply scaling current architectures will not produce better models of the ventral stream and that new strategies are needed.
papers.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML, spotlight)
papers.authors: Abdulkadir Gokce, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.abstract: Using the functional-localizer approach from human neuroscience, the authors identify language-selective units in 18 large language models. Ablating these units, but not random ones, causes severe deficits on language tasks, and the units align better with human language-network recordings than random units. The paper also finds specialized reasoning and social-cognition units in some, but not all, models.
papers.authors: Badr AlKhamissi, Greta Tuckute, Antoine Bosselut, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: From Language to Cognition: How LLMs Outgrow the Human Language Network
papers.abstract: The study tracks 34 training checkpoints across eight model sizes to see how alignment with the human language network evolves during training. Brain alignment follows the development of formal linguistic competence more closely than functional competence such as reasoning and world knowledge, and it fades once models exceed human-level language proficiency. Model size alone does not predict alignment once feature size is controlled, and existing neural language benchmarks are not yet saturated.
papers.authors: Badr AlKhamissi, Greta Tuckute, Yingtian Tang, Taha Binhuraib, Antoine Bosselut, Martin Schrimpf

papers.title: Contour Integration Underlies Human-Like Vision
papers.abstract: The paper tests how well over 1,000 vision models recognize objects made of progressively fewer contour fragments, compared with 50 human observers. Humans remain accurate with sparse contours, whereas most models are near chance, approaching human performance only at very large training-set scale (about 5B images). Humans show an integration bias favoring directional fragments; models that share it perform better, and training for contour integration raises shape bias.
papers.authors: Ben Lonnqvist, Elsa Scialom, Abdulkadir Gokce, Zehra Merchant, Michael H. Herzog, Martin Schrimpf

E040.name: Andreas Tolias
E040.bio: Tolias is a Professor of Ophthalmology at Stanford University and directs a research program focused on the intersection of systems neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Their work utilizes large-scale neural recordings and machine learning to investigate the network-level principles of perceptual inference and decision-making. Tolias led the MICrONS project, which produced a functional connectomics dataset, and developed 'digital twins' to simulate biological brain computation. Their current research focuses on reverse-engineering biological algorithms to design AI systems that are interpretable, robust, and efficient.
E040.research_direction: Dr. Tolias has recently been exploring the functional properties and structural wiring of the mammalian visual cortex by combining large-scale physiological recordings with artificial intelligence and nanometer-scale electron microscopy. Their recent work uses deep learning-driven inception loops—training predictive models to synthesize stimuli that optimally drive individual neurons—to investigate complex feature tuning, such as bipartite invariance in mouse primary visual cortex, topological organization in primate V4, and how neurons use opposing excitatory and suppressive receptive fields for bidirectional coding. In parallel, they are investigating the physical circuitry underlying these functional responses by mapping two-photon calcium imaging onto dense connectomic reconstructions to uncover general synaptic wiring rules. To unify these diverse scales of cortical computation, they are also developing foundational AI models of neural activity designed to predict sensory responses to novel visual stimuli while capturing shared principles of cellular and anatomical organization.

papers.title: Functional bipartite invariance in mouse primary visual cortex receptive fields
papers.abstract: Using an inception-loop approach that cycles between large-scale recordings, predictive models, in silico image synthesis and in vivo testing, the authors synthesize diverse images that all drive a given V1 neuron. These reveal a bipartite invariance in which one part of the receptive field tolerates shifts of a high-frequency texture while the other encodes a fixed low-frequency pattern. This organization matches object boundaries defined by spatial-frequency differences and is supported by connectomic analysis, hinting at a role in segmentation.
papers.authors: Zhuokun Ding, Dat Tran, Kayla Ponder, Zhiwei Ding, Rachel Froebe, Lydia Ntanavara, Paul G. Fahey, Erick Cobos, Luca Baroni, Maria Diamantaki, Eric Y. Wang, Andersen Chang, Stelios Papadopoulos, Jiakun Fu, Taliah Muhammad, Christos Papadopoulos, Santiago A. Cadena, Alexandros Evangelou, Konstantin Willeke, Fabio Anselmi, Sophia Sanborn, Jan Antolik, Emmanouil Froudarakis, Saumil Patel, Edgar Y. Walker, Jacob Reimer, Fabian H. Sinz, Alexander S. Ecker, Katrin Franke, Xaq Pitkow, Andreas S. Tolias

papers.title: Deep learning-driven characterization of single cell tuning in primate visual area V4 supports topological organization
papers.abstract: The study fits deep neural network models to macaque V4 responses and uses them to synthesize the images that best drive individual neurons. The resulting preferred features are complex and vary along the cortical surface, and neurons that lie near each other tend to prefer similar features. This supports a topographic organization of tuning in V4 that was not evident from simple stimuli.
papers.authors: Konstantin F. Willeke, Kelli Restivo, Katrin Franke, Arne F. Nix, Santiago A. Cadena, Tori Shinn, Cate Nealley, Gabrielle Rodriguez, Saumil Patel, Alexander S. Ecker, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas S. Tolias

papers.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
papers.abstract: Model-based image synthesis shows that neurons in mouse and macaque visual cortex are tuned to two distinct features: one that excites them and another that suppresses them. This dual selectivity lets a neuron signal changes in either direction relative to its baseline, giving a bidirectional code. The result reframes single-neuron tuning as encoding a contrast between two features rather than one preferred stimulus.
papers.authors: Katrin Franke, Nikos Karantzas, Konstantin Willeke, Maria Diamantaki, Kandan Ramakrishnan, Hasan Atakan Bedel, Pavithra Elumalai, Kelli Restivo, Paul Fahey, Cate Nealley, Tori Shinn, Gabrielle Garcia, Saumil Patel, Alexander Ecker, Edgar Y. Walker, Emmanouil Froudarakis, Sophia Sanborn, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas Tolias

papers.title: Foundation model of neural activity predicts response to new stimulus types
papers.abstract: The authors train one large predictive model on recordings from many mice viewing a wide range of movies and images, so that it captures shared principles of visual cortex. With little extra data, the model accurately predicts neural responses to stimulus types it was never trained on, such as new video and image classes. It also carries information about cell type and anatomical features and links to connectomic data from the MICrONS volume.
papers.authors: Eric Y. Wang, Paul G. Fahey, Zhuokun Ding, Stelios Papadopoulos, Kayla Ponder, Marissa A. Weis, Andersen Chang, Taliah Muhammad, Saumil Patel, Zhiwei Ding, Dat Tran, Jiakun Fu, Casey M. Schneider-Mizell, R. Clay Reid, Forrest Collman, Nuno Maçarico da Costa, Katrin Franke, Alexander S. Ecker, Jacob Reimer, Xaq Pitkow, Fabian H. Sinz, Andreas S. Tolias

papers.title: Functional connectomics reveals general wiring rule in mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Combining in vivo two-photon recordings with nanometer-scale electron microscopy of the same tissue, the study links the functional tuning of thousands of neurons to their synaptic connectivity. Excitatory neurons preferentially form synapses with partners that have similar response tuning and correlated activity, a rule that holds across cell types and visual areas. The finding gives a concrete circuit-level principle for how cortical connectivity relates to function.
papers.authors: Zhuokun Ding, Paul G. Fahey, Stelios Papadopoulos, Eric Y. Wang, Brendan Celii, Christos Papadopoulos, Andersen Chang, Alexander B. Kunin, Dat Tran, Jiakun Fu, Zhiwei Ding, Saumil Patel, Lydia Ntanavara, Rachel Froebe, Kayla Ponder, Taliah Muhammad, J. Alexander Bae, Agnes L. Bodor, Derrick Brittain, JoAnn Buchanan, Daniel J. Bumbarger, Manuel A. Castro, Erick Cobos, Sven Dorkenwald, Leila Elabbady, Akhilesh Halageri, Zhen Jia, Chris Jordan, Dan Kapner, Nico Kemnitz, Sam Kinn, Kisuk Lee, Kai Li, Ran Lu, Thomas Macrina, Gayathri Mahalingam, Eric Mitchell, Shanka Subhra Mondal, Shang Mu, Barak Nehoran, Sergiy Popovych, Casey M. Schneider-Mizell, William Silversmith, Marc Takeno, Russel Torres, Nicholas L. Turner, William Wong, Jingpeng Wu, Wenjing Yin, Szi-Chieh Yu, Dimitri Yatsenko, Emmanouil Froudarakis, Fabian Sinz, Krešimir Josić, Robert Rosenbaum, H. Sebastian Seung, Forrest Collman, Nuno Maçarico da Costa, R. Clay Reid, Edgar Y. Walker, Xaq Pitkow, Jacob Reimer, Andreas S. Tolias

E041.name: Matthias Bethge
E041.bio: Matthias Bethge is a Professor for Computational Neuroscience and Machine Learning at the University of Tübingen and the Director of the Tübingen AI Center. Their research integrates statistical inference, deep learning, and psychophysics to investigate principles of perceptual inference in both biological and artificial systems. Bethge’s work includes neural style transfer, saliency modeling with DeepGaze, and the development of the DeepLabCut framework for pose estimation. Currently, their laboratory focuses on the robustness of visual representations and the study of neural decision-making through the lens of lifelong learning.
E041.research_direction: Dr. Bethge has recently been exploring the intersection of biological vision and artificial intelligence, investigating how computational models represent information compared to the human brain. Within visual neuroscience, their recent work examines dataset-specific biases in human gaze prediction and develops new fMRI-based benchmarks to test whether deep vision models truly replicate the complex representational relationships across different regions of the visual cortex. Beyond biological vision, they are rigorously interrogating the evaluation metrics of large foundation models to uncover the underlying drivers of artificial performance. Specifically, Dr. Bethge is investigating how pretraining data frequencies influence apparent zero-shot generalization in multimodal networks and probing the methodological pitfalls that compromise reproducibility in language model reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Only Brains Align with Brains: Cross-Region Alignment Patterns Expose Limits of Normative Models
papers.abstract: The paper argues that today's model-brain alignment benchmarks cannot tell apart very different vision models, so high scores say little about whether a model is computationally similar to visual cortex. The authors propose alignment pattern analysis, which checks whether a model reproduces the characteristic profile of how each brain region relates to all others. On video fMRI (BOLD Moments), these patterns are stable across subjects, yet even top-ranked models often fail to reproduce them.
papers.venue: ICLR 2026 (Fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations)
papers.authors: Larissa Höfling, Matthias Tangemann, Lotta Piefke, Susanne Keller, Katrin Franke, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: A Sober Look at Progress in Language Model Reasoning: Pitfalls and Paths to Reproducibility
papers.abstract: The authors show that reported gains on mathematical reasoning benchmarks depend heavily on implementation details such as decoding settings, seeds, prompt format and hardware. They propose a standardized, statistically grounded evaluation framework and re-assess recent methods with it. Most reinforcement-learning approaches give only modest improvements and overfit small benchmarks like AIME'24, while supervised finetuning generalizes more consistently.
papers.authors: Andreas Hochlehnert, Hardik Bhatnagar, Vishaal Udandarao, Samuel Albanie, Ameya Prabhu, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: Modeling Saliency Dataset Bias
papers.abstract: Saliency models trained on one eye-movement dataset lose about 40% of their performance on another, and most of this gap comes from dataset-specific biases rather than a lack of diversity. The paper introduces an architecture with a mostly shared encoder-decoder and fewer than 20 dataset-specific parameters controlling interpretable factors such as multi-scale structure, center bias and fixation spread. Adapting only those parameters closes most of the gap and yields state of the art on the MIT/Tuebingen Saliency Benchmark datasets.
papers.authors: Matthias Kümmerer, Harneet Singh Khanuja, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: No "Zero-Shot" Without Exponential Data: Pretraining Concept Frequency Determines Multimodal Model Performance
papers.abstract: The study measures how often downstream concepts occur in web-scale image-text pretraining sets and relates that to CLIP-style and diffusion model performance across 34 models and five datasets. Performance improves only log-linearly with concept frequency, meaning exponentially more data is needed for linear gains, so 'zero-shot' generalization is largely an artifact of data coverage. The authors also release a long-tail benchmark, Let it Wag!, on which models do poorly.
papers.authors: Vishaal Udandarao, Ameya Prabhu, Adhiraj Ghosh, Yash Sharma, Philip H. S. Torr, Adel Bibi, Samuel Albanie, Matthias Bethge

papers.title: Predicting Visual Fixations
papers.abstract: This Annual Review surveys how computational models of where people look have evolved, from hand-designed saliency features to deep-learning-based fixation predictors such as the DeepGaze family. It discusses how models are evaluated with probabilistic metrics and benchmarks, what they reveal about the role of image content, scene structure and task in guiding gaze, and where remaining gaps lie.
papers.authors: Matthias Kümmerer, Matthias Bethge

E042.name: Thomas Serre
E042.department: Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences; Computer Science
E042.bio: Thomas Serre is a Professor of Cognitive, Linguistic, and Psychological Sciences and Computer Science at Brown University. Serre conducts research at the intersection of biological and artificial vision, focusing on the computational principles of the visual cortex. Their work investigates how recurrent and feedback circuitry support visual reasoning and perception. By developing brain-inspired deep learning architectures and cognitive benchmarks, Serre aims to quantify the alignment between human and machine vision to advance neuroscience and artificial intelligence.
E042.research_direction: Dr. Serre has recently been investigating the complex intersection between artificial intelligence and biological vision, critically examining whether the push for highly predictive, internet-scale foundation models actually yields better theoretical models of the primate brain. Their recent work explores the behavioral and mechanistic gaps between humans and machines by designing targeted benchmarks to probe advanced spatial cognition, such as 3D visual perspective taking. To help bridge these biological and artificial gaps, they are also developing brain-inspired network architectures, investigating mechanisms like neural phase synchrony for tracking objects that dynamically change in appearance and location. Additionally, they are tackling the challenge of black-box model interpretability by building unified theoretical frameworks to extract and evaluate human-understandable visual concepts from deep neural networks.

papers.title: Better artificial intelligence does not mean better models of biology
papers.abstract: The authors show, on three benchmarks, that the once-rising agreement between deep neural networks and primate vision or neural responses has stopped improving, and in places gets worse, as models reach human-level or superhuman accuracy. They suggest models are drifting toward visual strategies that primates do not use. The piece argues that progress in AI should not be assumed to translate into better neuroscience models, and that vision science should build biologically grounded algorithms instead of chasing internet-scale benchmarks.
papers.authors: Drew Linsley, Pinyuan Feng, Thomas Serre

papers.title: From prediction to understanding: Will AI foundation models transform brain science?
papers.abstract: This Neuron perspective asks whether large foundation models, which excel at predicting neural and behavioral data, will actually deepen scientific understanding of the brain. The authors weigh predictive accuracy against explanation and interpretability, and lay out what would be needed for such models to become genuine tools for theory in neuroscience rather than just powerful black-box predictors.
papers.authors: Thomas Serre, Ellie Pavlick

papers.title: The 3D-PC: a benchmark for visual perspective taking in humans and machines
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a benchmark of three natural-image tasks (depth ordering, basic perspective taking and a strategy-controlled version) that probes whether deep networks can take another viewpoint in a 3D scene. Testing 33 people and over 300 networks, it finds that humans do this easily while networks that handle depth still fail at perspective taking, and that scale barely helps. The results suggest current architectures lack the mechanisms needed for this social-cognitive skill.
papers.authors: Drew Linsley, Peisen Zhou, Alekh Karkada Ashok, Akash Nagaraj, Gaurav Gaonkar, Francis E. Lewis, Zygmunt Pizlo, Thomas Serre

papers.title: Tracking objects that change in appearance with phase synchrony
papers.abstract: The authors propose a complex-valued recurrent network that uses neural synchrony to control attention to features independently of their locations, a mechanism long proposed in neuroscience for binding and tracking. They test it on FeatureTracker, a large benchmark where objects change appearance and position in controlled ways. Humans and the synchrony model track well while standard deep networks struggle, supporting synchrony as a computational route to object tracking.
papers.authors: Sabine Muzellec, Drew Linsley, Alekh K. Ashok, Ennio Mingolla, Girik Malik, Rufin VanRullen, Thomas Serre

papers.title: A Holistic Approach to Unifying Automatic Concept Extraction and Concept Importance Estimation
papers.abstract: Concept-based explainability methods first extract human-interpretable visual concepts from a network's activations and then estimate how important each is. This paper gives a single theoretical framework that defines both steps, shows that existing extraction methods are variants of dictionary learning or matrix factorization, and proposes new evaluation metrics for comparing them. It also extends attribution methods to concept importance and provides optimality guarantees, with experiments showing improved explanations.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Thomas Fel, Victor Boutin, Mazda Moayeri, Rémi Cadène, Louis Béthune, Léo Andéol, Mathieu Chalvidal, Thomas Serre

E043.name: Yukiyasu Kamitani
E043.bio: Kamitani researches brain decoding, developing methodologies to translate functional MRI signals into specific contents of human perception and mental imagery. Their work utilizes deep neural networks and machine learning to map hierarchical neural representations onto visual features, facilitating the reconstruction of seen images, dreams, and subjective illusory experiences. Currently, Kamitani focuses on generative brain decoding and the development of brain-machine interfaces that combine computational neuroscience with artificial intelligence to study human cognition.
E043.research_direction: Dr. Kamitani has recently been investigating how to decode and reconstruct subjective perceptual experiences from human fMRI activity using deep neural networks. Their recent work explores whether brain-to-image reconstruction can visualize purely subjective states, such as visual illusions, rather than just physical retinal inputs, while also extending these feature-decoding approaches into the auditory domain to reconstruct natural sounds. To overcome practical barriers in large-scale neuroimaging, they are testing computational methods to align neural codes across different individuals and scanning sites without requiring shared calibration stimuli. Furthermore, they are critically examining the validity of modern brain-decoding methods by investigating how to distinguish genuine visual detail from spurious diffusion-model priors, alongside exploring theoretical frameworks that redefine neural representations based on input recoverability rather than traditional feature tuning.

papers.title: Readout Representation: Redefining Neural Codes by Input Recovery
papers.abstract: Proposes defining what a neural code represents by the information that can be recovered from it, rather than by tuning to features. It tests this by reconstructing inputs from heavily altered internal features of deep networks, showing that recoverable information can be preserved in unexpected ways. This reframes how representations in brains and models are compared.
papers.authors: Shunsuke Onoo, Yoshihiro Nagano, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Inter-individual and inter-site neural code conversion without shared stimuli
papers.abstract: Presents a method that aligns brain activity across different people and scanners without requiring them to view the same stimuli, by matching the representations through the features of a deep neural network. Converted signals can be fed into decoders trained on another individual, enabling decoding and image reconstruction across subjects and sites. This removes a major practical barrier to pooling neuroimaging data for brain decoding.
papers.authors: Haibao Wang, Jun Kai Ho, Fan L. Cheng, Shuntaro C. Aoki, Yusuke Muraki, Misato Tanaka, Jong-Yun Park, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Spurious reconstruction from brain activity
papers.abstract: Critically examines recent diffusion-model-based image reconstruction from brain activity, showing that apparently impressive outputs can come from generic category-level priors and text or classification information rather than genuine stimulus detail. It proposes controls and analyses to separate true reconstruction from classification and retrieval. The paper sets out standards for credible brain-to-image reconstruction claims.
papers.authors: Ken Shirakawa, Yoshihiro Nagano, Misato Tanaka, Shuntaro C. Aoki, Kei Majima, Yusuke Muraki, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Natural sounds can be reconstructed from human neuroimaging data using deep neural network representation
papers.abstract: Reconstructs natural sounds heard by participants from fMRI by decoding the features of a deep auditory network and synthesizing audio from them. Reconstruction quality varies across auditory cortex and follows the hierarchy of network layers. It extends the lab's feature-decoding approach from vision to audition.
papers.authors: Jong-Yun Park, Mitsuaki Tsukamoto, Misato Tanaka, Yukiyasu Kamitani

papers.title: Reconstructing visual illusory experiences from human brain activity
papers.abstract: Shows that deep-network-based reconstruction trained on real images can visualize illusory percepts from fMRI, including illusory colors and shapes that differ from the physical stimulus. The reconstructions track what participants subjectively perceived rather than the retinal input. This supports the idea that perceived content is decodable from visual cortical representations.
papers.authors: Fan L. Cheng, Tomoyasu Horikawa, Kei Majima, Misato Tanaka, Mohamed Abdelhack, Shuntaro C. Aoki, Jin Hirano, Yukiyasu Kamitani

E044.name: Grace Lindsay
E044.department: Department of Psychology and Center for Data Science
E044.bio: Grace Lindsay is an Assistant Professor at New York University who utilizes computational neuroscience, psychology, and machine learning to study neural information processing. Their research employs artificial neural networks as functional models of the visual system to investigate how attentional mechanisms modulate sensory processing and task performance. Lindsay evaluates the validity of analytical tools in systems neuroscience and develops computer vision applications for climate change mitigation, such as analyzing satellite imagery to track environmental transitions. They are also the author of 'Models of the Mind,' a book detailing the mathematical history and theoretical foundations of brain research.
E044.research_direction: Dr. Lindsay's recent work explores the bidirectional intersection of artificial neural networks and biological brains across vision, cognition, and motor control. In the visual domain, they have recently been investigating temporal dynamics by developing biologically plausible recurrent convolutional networks to model time-dependent phenomena like adaptation, delayed normalization, and robustness to noise. Beyond early vision, their recent work explores how reward prediction errors might act to modulate feature-based attention during value learning, as well as how embedding mammalian neural-circuit priors into AI agents can efficiently guide quadruped locomotion. Concurrently, they are investigating multi-level interpretability by deploying cognitive and neuroscience frameworks to understand large AI models, while using those artificial networks as ground-truth testbeds to validate standard neuroscience analysis tools.

papers.title: Modeling Dynamical Vision with Biologically Plausible Recurrent Convolutional Networks
papers.abstract: Introduces DynVision, an open-source toolbox for building and comparing recurrent convolutional networks that include cortically motivated recurrence and heterogeneous conduction delays, solved with ODE integrators. Systematic sweeps show that temporal phenomena such as adaptation and delayed normalization depend strongly on often-implicit modeling choices like where recurrence is applied and which time window the loss covers. Continuous-time recurrence can produce cortical-like dynamics without explicit divisive normalization, while another configuration yields near-human robustness to noise.
papers.authors: Robin Gutzen, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Modulation of feature attention by reward prediction error explains value learning behavior
papers.abstract: Builds a reinforcement-learning model with a perceptual front end to test how reward prediction errors could set the gain of feature-based attention. Five candidate transfer functions are compared against macaque behavior in a shifting-reward color task. The best account is a single-focus model in which attention flips away from the top-valued feature after a negative prediction error, and prefrontal, FEF and LIP neurons carry the previous-trial error signal.
papers.authors: Ming-Ze Leukos (李铭泽), Alex Liang, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Multilevel interpretability of artificial neural networks: leveraging framework and methods from neuroscience
papers.abstract: Argues that understanding large neural networks, like understanding brains, requires analysis at several levels rather than one. Analysis tools from neuroscience and cognitive science are organized under Marr's computational, algorithmic and implementation levels. The paper proposes this as a shared framework and research agenda for people studying biological and artificial systems.
papers.authors: Zhonghao He, Jascha Achterberg, Katie Collins, Kevin K. Nejad, Danyal Akarca, Yinzhu Yang, Wes Gurnee, Ilia Sucholutsky, Yuhan Tang, Rebeca Ianov, George Ogden, Chole Li, Kai J. Sandbrink, Stephen Casper, Anna Ivanova, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Quadruped Locomotion
papers.abstract: Replaces the generic MLP policy in learned quadruped locomotion with a network wired like mammalian limb and spinal-cord circuits. The bio-inspired architecture starts out with decent performance, matches final MLP performance with far less data and orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and generalizes better to task changes. It can be deployed on a physical robot without standard sim-to-real tricks.
papers.authors: Nikhil X. Bhattasali, Venkatesh Pattabiraman, Lerrel Pinto, Grace W. Lindsay

papers.title: Testing methods of neural systems understanding
papers.abstract: Notes that neuroscience analysis tools are rarely validated against systems whose mechanisms are known. Proposes applying those tools to artificial neural networks as a ground-truth testbed, which would also promote a joint field of neural systems understanding spanning brains and AI. Reviews common neuroscience methods, prior applications to ANNs, and related interpretable-AI efforts.
papers.authors: Grace W. Lindsay, David Bau

E045.name: Wieland Brendel
E045.department: AI Research Group (Brendel Lab); also independent Group Leader at Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems
E045.bio: Wieland Brendel is an independent Group Leader at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and a Hector-endowed Fellow at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen. Their research operates at the intersection of computational neuroscience and machine learning, with a focus on human and artificial perception through robust and interpretable models. Brendel identified the texture bias in ImageNet-trained convolutional neural networks and works on causal representation learning to increase model generalizability. They were awarded the 2023 German Pattern Recognition Award for work in the field of computer vision.
E045.research_direction: Dr. Brendel's recent work explores the fundamental mechanisms of generalization, representation learning, and reasoning across large-scale AI models. They have recently been investigating whether generative architectures are strictly necessary for data-efficient compositional perception in vision, while also probing whether generating intermediate visual imagery helps multimodal models solve complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. On a theoretical level, their research examines how realistic data augmentations impact the latent spaces of contrastive learning algorithms. Furthermore, they are studying the profound influence of pretraining data distributions on model performance, both by evaluating how data curation shapes downstream scaling laws in language models and by rigorously testing whether the apparent out-of-domain robustness of vision models like CLIP stems from true domain generalization or simply overlapping training data.

papers.title: Is Generation Required for Data-Efficient Perception?
papers.abstract: Asks whether generative models are needed for human-like data efficiency in vision, focusing on compositional generalization. Theory shows that the inductive biases an encoder would need are complex and hard to impose through architecture, whereas decoder-side biases are simple and enforceable. Experiments agree: non-generative models often fail to generalize compositionally unless pretrained at scale, while generative approaches generalize without extra data.
papers.authors: Jack Brady, Bernhard Schölkopf, Thomas Kipf, Simon Buchholz, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: MentisOculi: Revealing the Limits of Reasoning with Mental Imagery
papers.abstract: Introduces a procedurally generated, stratified suite of multi-step reasoning problems that can in principle be solved visually, tuned to be hard for frontier models. Tests whether unified multimodal models benefit from generating intermediate images while reasoning. They mostly do not: generation errors compound, and models fail to exploit even ground-truth visualizations.
papers.authors: Jana Zeller, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Fanfei Li, Thomas Klein, Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Matthias Bethge, Felix Wichmann, Ryan Cotterell, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: LLMs on the Line: Data Determines Loss-to-Loss Scaling Laws
papers.abstract: Studies how the relationship between pretraining loss and downstream loss changes across language models. Finds that loss-to-loss scaling is driven mainly by the pretraining data distribution, with tokenizer and architecture playing minor roles. This suggests that curating data is the main lever for shaping how models transfer to downstream tasks.
papers.authors: Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Sayak Mallick, Matthias Bethge, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: InfoNCE: Identifying the Gap Between Theory and Practice
papers.abstract: Contrastive learning theory usually assumes augmentations sample the latent factors independently, but real augmentations such as cropping do not behave that way. The authors extend the theory to augmentation-defined latent variation and show when InfoNCE-based representation learning recovers the true factors and when it does not. Experiments back the theory on controlled and real data.
papers.venue: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS 2025)
papers.authors: Evgenia Rusak, Patrik Reizinger, Attila Juhos, Oliver Bringmann, Roland S. Zimmermann, Wieland Brendel

papers.title: In Search of Forgotten Domain Generalization
papers.abstract: Builds large LAION-derived datasets that differ in style from ImageNet and DomainNet test sets (natural and rendition images) and trains CLIP models on them. Much of CLIP's apparent out-of-domain robustness turns out to come from in-domain-like training examples rather than true domain generalization. The paper also studies how mixing natural and rendition data affects generalization.
papers.authors: Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Roland S. Zimmermann, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Evgenia Rusak, Attila Juhos, Matthias Bethge, Wieland Brendel

E046.name: Felix Wichmann
E046.bio: Felix Wichmann is a Professor of Neural Information Processing at the University of Tübingen, where they investigate human perception through psychophysical experimentation and computational modeling. Wichmann’s work includes the statistical analysis of psychometric functions and the evaluation of deep neural networks as behavioral models of human vision. Their research integrates machine learning, Bayesian inference, and signal detection theory to study the connection between early spatial vision and high-level object recognition. Current projects in Wichmann's laboratory focus on "shortcut learning" in artificial systems, the role of shape versus texture in recognition, and the perceptual mechanisms underlying the detection of causality.
E046.research_direction: Dr. Wichmann's recent work explores the computational mechanisms underlying human visual perception by rigorously comparing behavioral data against both traditional psychophysical models and modern deep neural networks. A major focus of their research investigates whether these networks serve as adequate models of human core object recognition, utilizing image distortions and developmental data from children and adults to probe human-machine gaps in out-of-distribution robustness. To further dissect these discrepancies, they have recently been using carefully controlled psychophysical tasks to determine exactly where along the visual processing hierarchy the behavioral divergences between humans and algorithms first arise. Alongside this comparative work, their recent research also investigates the low-level mechanics of early spatial vision, developing computational frameworks to separate early visual noise from late decision noise and exploring how biophysical mechanisms like dendritic nonlinearities might explain classic psychophysical puzzles such as plaid masking.

papers.title: Behavioral differences between humans and machines arise early in visual processing
papers.abstract: Compares human observers with deep networks on carefully controlled psychophysical tasks to locate where behavioral divergences first show up along the visual processing hierarchy. The results indicate that differences between people and models are already present at early stages of visual processing, rather than emerging only in high-level object recognition. This challenges the assumption that human-machine gaps are primarily a late-stage phenomenon.
papers.authors: Thomas Klein, Wieland Brendel, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Estimating the contribution of early and late noise in vision from psychophysical data
papers.abstract: Presents a psychophysical method and model framework to separate how much of the variability in human visual performance stems from noise early in the visual pathway versus noise at the decision stage, using only behavioral measurements. The approach is validated against data and gives a principled way to quantify the two noise sources, which matters for interpreting contrast-detection and masking results.
papers.authors: Jesús Malo, José Juan Esteve-Taboada, Guillermo Aguilar, Marianne Maertens, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Plaid masking explained with input-dependent dendritic nonlinearities
papers.abstract: Argues that the standard model of early spatial vision fails to predict plaid masking because it oversimplifies single-neuron computation. A spatial vision model that includes input-dependent dendritic nonlinearities, meaning nonlinear summation of inputs, is shown to have the potential to account for plaid masking data, tying a long-standing psychophysical puzzle to dendritic biophysics.
papers.authors: Marcelo Bertalmío, Alexia Durán Vizcaíno, Jesús Malo, Felix A. Wichmann

papers.title: Are Deep Neural Networks Adequate Behavioral Models of Human Visual Perception?
papers.abstract: A review of the evidence on whether current deep networks are adequate behavioral models of human core object recognition. The authors argue for separating statistical tools from computational models, and assess network quality by image computability, prediction, and explanation. They discuss where DNNs succeed and fail, including texture bias, shortcut learning and out-of-distribution robustness, and what would be needed for better models.
papers.authors: Felix A. Wichmann, Robert Geirhos

papers.title: The developmental trajectory of object recognition robustness: Children are like small adults but unlike big deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Tests children of several ages, adults and a range of deep networks on object recognition with distorted images to see how robustness develops. Children's robustness resembles that of adults, already at a young age, and their error patterns look adult-like, whereas even large networks trained on far more data remain less robust and behave differently. The findings show that data quantity alone does not explain human-level robustness.
papers.authors: Lukas S. Huber, Robert Geirhos, Felix A. Wichmann

E055.name: Pieter Roelfsema
E055.bio: Pieter Roelfsema is a neuroscientist specializing in the cortical mechanisms of visual perception, attention, and conscious experience. Their research utilizes primate electrophysiology, human neuroimaging, and computational modeling to investigate the function of the early visual cortex as a 'cognitive blackboard' during tasks such as perceptual grouping. A focus of their current work involves developing high-channel-count cortical neuroprostheses intended to restore rudimentary vision in blind individuals via electrical stimulation. Roelfsema's research group examines how feedback and lateral connections modulate neuronal activity to represent task-relevant features and facilitate object-background segregation.
E055.research_direction: Dr. Roelfsema has recently been investigating the functional architecture of the visual hierarchy, exploring how object representations are constructed across the ventral stream using large-scale spiking datasets from non-human primates. Their recent theoretical and empirical work examines the neural mechanisms of perceptual grouping and attention, investigating whether feature binding is driven by enhanced firing rates rather than neural synchrony, and evaluating how feedforward and feedback signals interact across cortical layers to test alternatives to predictive coding. In the translational realm, they are developing calibration methods for visual neuroprostheses, testing how correlations in spontaneous cortical activity can be used to accurately map artificial percepts without relying on verbal reports. Furthermore, their research extends into human cognition, utilizing single-unit recordings in the hippocampus to explore how concept cells reactivate to link stored memories with language elements during reading.

papers.title: Large-scale mapping of artificial perceptions for neuroprostheses using spontaneous neuronal activity in macaque and human visual cortex
papers.abstract: To place artificial percepts (phosphenes) correctly in the visual field, a prosthesis needs to know the receptive-field locations of its electrodes. The authors show that correlations in spontaneous activity across electrodes can be used to map phosphene locations at large scale, validating the approach in macaques and human visual cortex. This offers a way to calibrate visual prostheses without requiring subjects' verbal reports.
papers.authors: Antonio Lozano, Xing Chen, Mike La Grouw, Bingshuo Li, Feng Wang, Maureen van der Grinten, Cristina Soto-Sanchez, Aitor Morales-Gregorio, Eduardo Fernandez, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Hierarchical interactions between sensory cortices defy predictive coding
papers.abstract: This opinion article reviews recent laminar and areal recordings showing how feedforward and feedback signals interact across the visual hierarchy. The authors argue that the observed patterns of modulation and response enhancement conflict with the core assumptions of predictive coding. They propose alternative accounts in which feedback carries task- and attention-related information.
papers.authors: Jacob A. Westerberg, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: An extensive dataset of spiking activity to reveal the syntax of the ventral stream
papers.abstract: The authors recorded spiking activity from large numbers of neurons across macaque ventral-stream areas V1, V4 and IT while animals viewed tens of thousands of natural images, creating a shared resource for the field. They show how the dataset can be used to probe representational structure and test deep-network models of the visual hierarchy, and document how tuning and dynamics change along the stream. The resource is intended to let others study how object information is built up across areas.
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Feng Wang, Matthew W. Self, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Pronouns reactivate conceptual representations in human hippocampal neurons
papers.abstract: Single-neuron recordings from epilepsy patients show that hippocampal neurons that respond to a specific concept during reading are reactivated when a later pronoun refers back to that concept. This reactivation occurs even though the pronoun itself carries no lexical information about the referent, suggesting the hippocampus supports linking of language elements to stored concepts. The work connects concept cells to the resolution of anaphoric references in language.
papers.authors: D. E. Dijksterhuis, M. W. Self, J. K. Possel, J. C. Peters, E. C. W. van Straaten, S. Idema, J. C. Baaijen, S. M. A. van der Salm, E. J. Aarnoutse, N. C. E. van Klink, P. van Eijsden, S. Hanslmayr, R. Chelvarajah, F. Roux, L. D. Kolibius, V. Sawlani, D. T. Rollings, S. Dehaene, P. R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Solving the binding problem: Assemblies form when neurons enhance their firing rate - they don't need to oscillate or synchronize
papers.abstract: This theoretical perspective argues that the brain binds features into objects through enhanced firing rates of neurons that code for attended features, spreading along horizontal and feedback connections, rather than through synchrony or oscillations. It reviews neurophysiological evidence for such rate-based assemblies and shows how the idea is consistent with recent deep-learning models of vision. The piece frames a competing account of how perceptual grouping and attention create coherent object representations.
papers.authors: Pieter R. Roelfsema

E056.name: Caspar Schwiedrzik
E056.main_research_area: cognitive neurobiology of learning and perception
E056.bio: Caspar M. Schwiedrzik is a Professor of Cognitive Neurobiology at Ruhr University Bochum, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying learning and cognitive flexibility. Schwiedrzik utilizes a comparative approach that integrates electrophysiological recordings and functional neuroimaging in both humans and non-human primates to examine the interplay of feedforward and feedback signals within the visual hierarchy. Their research explores how the brain generates sensory predictions and how these top-down signals facilitate the learning of abstract models and identity recognition. By combining empirical data with computational modeling, Schwiedrzik seeks to identify the principles that allow cortical circuits to adapt to environmental changes and generalize across novel situations.
E056.research_direction: Dr. Schwiedrzik has recently been investigating how visual representations are dynamically shaped by task demands, learning, and hierarchical processing. Using human intracranial recordings and macaque fMRI, their recent work explores how top-down signals—such as shifting task instructions or contextual predictions—dynamically alter neural representational geometry in areas ranging from the ventral temporal cortex to the face-processing hierarchy. They are also studying the mechanisms of visual perceptual learning, combining behavioral modeling and human neuroimaging to understand how introducing task-irrelevant stimulus variability during training affects network-level functional connectivity and enables behavioral generalization. Additionally, they employ whole-brain macaque fMRI and deep neural networks to examine how sensory information is distributed across the visual stream, specifically investigating the functional role of low-level features like orientation re-emerging within high-level hubs like inferotemporal cortex.

papers.title: Multiple task-demands flexibly optimize neural geometry in human ventral temporal cortex
papers.abstract: Using intracranial recordings from epilepsy patients who switched trial by trial between individuating, categorizing and conceptualizing the same images, the study asks how the brain implements instantly instructed task flexibility. Task-appropriate representational geometries did not appear right after the cue but built up over successive stimulus repetitions within a trial. Ventral temporal cortex was the only region that adjusted its geometry for all three tasks, dynamically reshaping within- and between-category distances to fit the current demand.
papers.authors: Tarana Nigam, Andrea F. Campos-Pérez, Pierre Mégevand, Juan R. Vidal, Marcela Perrone-Bertolotti, Philippe Kahane, Thomas Thesen, Orrin Devinsky, Lucia Melloni, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Re-emergence of orientation coding in primate IT cortex and deep networks reveals functional hubs for visual processing
papers.abstract: Efficient-coding theories predict that basic features like orientation, already encoded early, should not be redundantly represented in high-level areas. Macaque whole-visual-stream fMRI with multivoxel decoding instead revealed robust orientation information from V1 all the way to inferotemporal cortex, distributed in both cortical and representational space and strongest in IT. Comparable re-emergence in deep networks points to functional hubs that reuse low-level information for high-level visual processing.
papers.authors: Behnam Karami, Tarana Nigam, Sandrin S. Plewe, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: The Sweet Spot of Plasticity in Perceptual Learning Depends on Training Variability
papers.abstract: Human fMRI during orientation-discrimination training with low or high task-irrelevant variability in spatial frequency showed that only high-variability training transferred to a new location. Early visual orientation representations changed similarly in both groups, whereas functional connectivity differed: low variability strengthened intraparietal sulcus-V2 coupling, high variability altered coupling with hV4. This supports a sweet-spot model in which variability reconfigures network-level readout instead of local sensory representations.
papers.authors: Giorgio L. Manenti, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Predictions enable top-down pattern separation in the macaque face-processing hierarchy
papers.abstract: Macaque fMRI of the three-level face-processing hierarchy showed that when contextual predictions are available, early stages develop well-separated, high-dimensional neural geometries resembling those at the top of the hierarchy. Tuning properties shifted systematically from higher to lower areas, giving lower areas invariant, higher-order representations rather than purely feedforward tuning. The work argues that top-down predictions separate neural patterns to improve identity recognition.
papers.authors: Tarana Nigam, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

papers.title: Variability in training unlocks generalization in visual perceptual learning through invariant representations
papers.abstract: The paper shows that varying task-irrelevant stimulus features during training lets perceptual learning transfer to new conditions. Behavioral experiments and modeling link this generalization to invariant representations at higher stages of visual processing that abstract away the varied dimension. It provides a mechanistic account of when perceptual learning stays specific versus generalizes.
papers.authors: Giorgio L. Manenti, Aslan S. Dizaji, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik

E057.name: Jason Fischer
E057.department: Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences
E057.bio: Fischer’s research investigates the cognitive and neural architectures used to navigate and predict the behavior of physical environments, a capability termed intuitive physics. Using functional MRI, psychophysics, and computational modeling, Fischer characterized a "physics engine" in the brain located within action-planning regions such as the premotor cortex. Their findings demonstrate that physical simulations occur in real-time to support survival-critical interactions and can operate independently of vivid visual imagery. Additionally, Fischer’s work examines serial dependence, describing how the brain integrates past and present visual information to maintain a stable and continuous perceptual experience.
E057.research_direction: Dr. Fischer’s recent work explores the cognitive and perceptual mechanisms underlying intuitive physics, investigating how the human brain represents and anticipates the mechanics of the everyday visual world. Using behavioral paradigms, they have recently been examining whether humans possess a dedicated mental capacity for physical reasoning that operates independently of general-purpose working memory. Their research also probes how observers compute and integrate hidden physical variables to guide action, asking whether people rely on internal estimates of a center of mass for real-world balancing tasks and whether biases in collision judgments stem from a noisy, yet fundamentally sound, internal Newtonian model. Additionally, they are investigating the close interaction between physical inference and visual processing by exploring how the brain uses forward simulation to predict upcoming object trajectories, as well as examining novel perceptual illusions where an object's apparent mass systematically distorts its perceived velocity.

papers.title: Center of mass computations underlie real-world balance judgements
papers.abstract: The study uses a hands-on task in which people must remove one block so that a board with several blocks stays balanced. Participants picked the best block reliably, and their errors were better predicted by an internal estimate of the center of mass than by simple visual heuristics. Because the center of mass cannot be seen directly, the work shows that observers compute this hidden property and use it spontaneously in a novel physical scenario.
papers.authors: Giuliana Bucci Mansilla, Jason Fischer

papers.title: Velocity-Not Perceived as Such: The Role of Object Mass in Velocity Estimation
papers.abstract: The authors report a mass-speed illusion in which objects that look heavier are judged to move more slowly than lighter-looking ones, even when retinal speed and size are identical. Across three experiments with 176 participants, the bias held across very different stimulus manipulations and was strikingly consistent across observers. This challenges the assumption that mass and velocity are encoded independently, suggesting perception internalises everyday mass-velocity relations.
papers.authors: Abdul-Rahim Deeb, Jason Fischer

papers.title: Visual simulation: Catching a glimpse of what's to come
papers.abstract: This Current Biology Dispatch discusses recent findings on how the brain simulates upcoming visual events. It frames visual simulation as a predictive process that lets us anticipate where objects will go before they get there, and relates it to the intuitive-physics framework. The piece highlights open questions about the neural mechanisms behind such forward simulation.
papers.authors: Jason Fischer

papers.title: A dedicated mental resource for intuitive physics
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether reasoning about physical events draws on a specialised pool of mental capacity rather than on general-purpose working memory. Using dual-task behavioural experiments, the authors show that physical prediction and other physics-related judgements interfere with each other in ways that comparable non-physical tasks do not. The results argue that intuitive physics relies on a resource of its own, consistent with a dedicated system in the brain.
papers.authors: Alex Mitko, Ana Navarro-Cebrian, Sarah Cormiea, Jason Fischer

papers.title: Do striking biases in mass inference reflect a flawed mental model of physics?
papers.abstract: People systematically misjudge the masses of objects that collide, and this has been taken as evidence that our mental physics is flawed. The authors test whether such biases instead come from a noisy but otherwise sensible internal model of Newtonian mechanics. Their experiments and modelling suggest that the apparent errors can be explained by how observers weigh and integrate the available evidence, not by a fundamentally wrong physical theory.
papers.authors: Alex Mitko, Jason Fischer

E060.name: Rufin VanRullen
E060.institution: French National Centre for Scientific Research
E060.department: Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo)
E060.bio: Rufin VanRullen is a CNRS Research Director at the Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo) whose work spans computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence. VanRullen investigates the rhythmic nature of human vision, specifically examining how alpha and theta brain oscillations produce discrete "perceptual cycles" in attention and perception. Their current research, supported by an ERC Advanced Grant, focuses on developing brain-inspired AI architectures that incorporate the Global Workspace Theory and predictive coding principles. By combining psychophysical experiments with deep learning and EEG analysis, VanRullen seeks to characterize the neural dynamics that enable flexible and robust cognition.
E060.research_direction: Dr. VanRullen has recently been investigating multimodal neural representations and oscillatory dynamics by bridging cognitive neuroscience with advanced artificial intelligence. Their recent fMRI work explores how the brain encodes complex visual and linguistic information, utilizing generative latent diffusion models to reconstruct natural scenes and testing whether cortical embeddings exhibit compositional, algebraic structures. Alongside this decoding work, they are developing bio-inspired artificial neural networks based on Global Workspace theory to align modalities like images and text within a shared latent space. In a distinct line of electrophysiological research, they are using EEG to probe the mechanisms of spatial visual attention, specifically investigating how forward and backward propagating alpha-band traveling waves might coordinate bottom-up and top-down cortical processing.

papers.title: Modality-agnostic decoding of vision and language from fMRI
papers.abstract: The study trains decoders on fMRI responses to images and to captions, so that a single model can read out what a person is seeing or reading regardless of input modality. Modality-agnostic decoders match or beat modality-specific ones and generalize to imagined content, pointing to shared multimodal representations in cortex.
papers.authors: Mitja Nikolaus, Milad Mozafari, Isabelle Berry, Nicholas Asher, Leila Reddy, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Evidence for compositionality in fMRI visual representations via Brain Algebra
papers.abstract: The authors show that arithmetic-like operations on fMRI-derived embeddings (adding or subtracting concept representations) yield vectors that correspond to the composed concepts. This suggests brain visual representations of scenes have a compositional, vector-algebra structure similar to that seen in deep networks.
papers.authors: Matteo Ferrante, Tommaso Boccato, Nicola Toschi, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Semi-Supervised Multimodal Representation Learning Through a Global Workspace
papers.abstract: The paper builds a global-workspace-inspired network that aligns several modalities (e.g. images and text) in a shared latent space using only a small amount of paired data plus cycle-consistency and translation objectives. It achieves strong cross-modal translation and matching with far less supervision than standard approaches.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
papers.authors: Benjamin Devillers, Léopold Maytié, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Natural scene reconstruction from fMRI signals using generative latent diffusion
papers.abstract: The authors reconstruct the photographs a person is viewing from their fMRI activity by mapping brain signals onto the latent space of a Stable Diffusion-style model, including a semantic text-like pathway and a low-level visual pathway. The pipeline produces high-fidelity images and beats earlier reconstruction methods on standard metrics, while also letting the authors probe which brain regions carry which kinds of information.
papers.authors: Furkan Ozcelik, Rufin VanRullen

papers.title: Distinct roles of forward and backward alpha-band waves in spatial visual attention
papers.abstract: Using EEG, the authors show that alpha-band traveling waves propagating forward and backward across the cortical hierarchy carry different functional signatures during spatial attention. Backward waves relate to top-down attentional and predictive processing, while forward waves relate to bottom-up stimulus-driven processing.
papers.authors: Andrea Alamia, Lucie Terral, Malo Renaud D'ambra, Rufin VanRullen

E061.name: Jan Brascamp
E061.bio: Jan Brascamp is an Associate Professor at Michigan State University who investigates the neural mechanisms of interpretation and selection that transform sensory input into conscious visual experience. Brascamp uses psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling to explore phenomena such as binocular rivalry and perceptual bistability. Their research indicates that the visual cortex can independently perform decision-making tasks during perceptual switches, which addresses traditional models of cortical hierarchy. Brascamp also examines pupillary responses and visual prediction anomalies as potential biomarkers for psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia.
E061.research_direction: Dr. Brascamp has recently been investigating the interplay between physiological ocular signals, visual perception, and memory. Their recent work explores how pupil dynamics and fixational saccades serve as windows into underlying neural mechanisms, probing whether pupillary responses are driven by perceptual switches during bistability, task relevance, cortical processing of isoluminant stimuli, or internal motor preparation. Additionally, they are examining the phenomenon of slow change blindness by developing new semi-automated pipelines to generate gradually shifting visual stimuli. Using these novel methods, Dr. Brascamp is interrogating the precision and decay of visual memory traces to understand how and why observers fail to notice continuous feature changes.

papers.title: The pupil response to perceptual switches: What happens when you ignore them
papers.abstract: Pupil dilations after perceptual switches in bistable displays have been taken to implicate norepinephrine in causing the switches, but switches were usually also task-relevant. Using a rotating structure-from-motion sphere and eye-movement-based inference of when switches occurred, the authors compared reported switches with task-irrelevant ones. Dilations followed only the task-relevant switches, suggesting pupil-linked neuromodulation is tied to task relevance rather than to bistability itself, matching their earlier binocular-rivalry result.
papers.authors: Bobicheng Zhang, Vasilii Marshev, Jan W. Brascamp

papers.title: No evidence for a cortical origin of pupil constriction responses to isoluminant stimuli
papers.abstract: The pupil constricts to patterns that change local luminance without altering net luminance, and this has been used as an index of visual processing of unclear origin. The authors reduced cortical responses through contrast adaptation and asked whether the constriction shrank across three experiments. It did not, and Bayesian analyses favored no effect, arguing against a cortical origin of the response.
papers.authors: Vasilii Marshev, Haley G. Frey, Jan Brascamp

papers.title: Fixational saccade inhibition and pupil dilation during self-paced limb movement preparation
papers.abstract: The study tracked fixational saccades while people made self-paced hand and foot movements, without any sensory cue. Saccade rate fell steadily before each movement and rebounded afterward, and this drop covaried trial by trial with the pre-movement pupil dilation. The timing indicates the pupil change was not a consequence of the saccade change, pointing to a shared neural factor behind both signals.
papers.authors: Jan W. Brascamp, Bobicheng Zhang, Vasilii Marshev

papers.title: Memory representations during slow change blindness
papers.abstract: Slow change blindness occurs when a feature drifts gradually without any visual disruption. Across three experiments, observers who never noticed the change nonetheless held two memory traces of the display: a precise but short-lived one for recent states, and a longer-lasting but coarse one. This suggests failure to compare stored representations, rather than loss of them, may underlie missing slow changes.
papers.authors: Haley G. Frey, Lua Koenig, Ned Block, Biyu J. He, Jan W. Brascamp

papers.title: A novel, semi-automatic procedure for generating slow change blindness stimuli
papers.abstract: Slow change blindness has been little studied partly because few stimuli exist and single-trial responses tend to contaminate later trials. The authors present a semi-automatic pipeline that quickly produces many slow-change images designed to allow trial-by-trial assessment. Three validation experiments show the stimuli reliably induce slow change blindness and are suitable for systematic studies.
papers.authors: Haley G. Frey, Lua Koenig, Biyu J. He, Jan W. Brascamp

E062.name: Matthew Self
E062.bio: Matthew Self is a neuroscientist and Senior Lecturer at the University of Glasgow’s School of Psychology and Neuroscience, where they direct research into the neural mechanisms of visual perception and memory formation. Self's work focuses on the functional significance of top-down feedback and recurrent connections between the visual cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus. Using a cross-species approach, they employ high-density electrophysiology, such as Neuropixels in mice and intracranial recordings in neurosurgical patients, to investigate how the brain integrates contextual information and experience-based predictions. Self has recorded from the human lateral geniculate nucleus and characterized the laminar-specific effects of attention and figure-ground segregation in the primary visual cortex.
E062.research_direction: Dr. Self has recently been investigating how early visual circuits process contextual information and resolve scene structure across multiple stages of the visual hierarchy. Their recent work explores the neural mechanisms of figure-ground organization, using macaque electrophysiology and human fMRI to ask how V4-to-V1 feedback connectivity is organized around border-ownership and how V1 represents occluded regions of natural images. They are also examining the perceptual consequences of these contextual signals, employing psychophysics to test how inferred 3D surfaces modulate orientation-tuned surround suppression and how border-ownership dynamics influence metacontrast masking. Finally, alongside this cortical and behavioral research, their work probes the foundational properties of the human visual system by utilizing rare intracranial recordings to map receptive fields in the lateral geniculate nucleus and investigate how eye closure affects subcortical spiking activity.

papers.title: Border-ownership reversals determine the strength of metacontrast masking
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that the time a target keeps ownership of its borders determines whether it is perceived under metacontrast masking. When a mask reverses the border-ownership direction, the target is more strongly suppressed. The behavioural experiments link a neural figure-ground signal to a classic masking phenomenon.
papers.authors: Doris E. Dijksterhuis, Nina Vreugdenhil, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

papers.title: Effects of eye closure on the spiking activity of human lateral geniculate neurons
papers.abstract: The authors recorded spiking activity from the lateral geniculate nucleus of two epilepsy patients with implanted electrodes. Human LGN cells showed bursting responses to strong stimulation, and their receptive fields resembled those in monkeys, including ON/OFF circular subfields, red-green opponency in dorsal layers and a preference for high temporal frequencies in ventral layers. Closing one eye reduced spontaneous activity of broad-spiking neurons preferring that eye and raised the activity of other cells.
papers.authors: Matthew W. Self, Osvaldo Vilela-Filho, Sergio Neuenschwander, Hélio F. Silva-Filho, Lissa C. Goulart, Pieter R. Roelfsema

papers.title: Orientation-tuned surround-suppression is strongest within perceived 3D surfaces
papers.abstract: The study tests how the perceived 3D layout of a scene changes surround suppression of contrast. Suppression tuned to orientation was strongest when centre and surround appeared to lie on the same 3D surface. This suggests that context-dependent suppression in early vision depends on inferred scene structure.
papers.authors: Jessy K. Possel, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

papers.title: Border-ownership tuning determines the connectivity between V4 and V1 in the macaque visual system
papers.abstract: The authors examined how area V4 feeds back to V1 depending on which side of an edge an object lies. They found that V4 neurons tuned to a border-ownership side preferentially influence V1 neurons with matching tuning, so feedback connectivity is organised by border-ownership preference. This links figure-ground computation to specific feedback circuits.
papers.authors: Danique Jeurissen, Anne F. van Ham, Amparo Gilhuis, Paolo Papale, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

papers.title: The representation of occluded image regions in area V1 of monkeys and humans
papers.abstract: The study asks how primary visual cortex represents parts of a natural image that are hidden behind an occluder. Using recordings in monkeys and fMRI in humans, the authors show that V1 carries information about the occluded region, consistent with feedback from higher areas filling in the missing content. This supports a role for contextual feedback in early visual cortex.
papers.authors: Paolo Papale, Feng Wang, A. Tyler Morgan, Xing Chen, Amparo Gilhuis, Lucy S. Petro, Lars Muckli, Pieter R. Roelfsema, Matthew W. Self

E063.name: Mauro Manassi
E063.bio: Mauro Manassi is a vision scientist whose research focuses on how the human brain organizes and stabilizes visual information to create a coherent perception of the world. Manassi examines serial dependence and 'continuity fields,' exploring how the visual system biases current perception toward the recent past to maintain temporal stability. Utilizing psychophysical paradigms and visual illusions, their research addresses fundamental mechanisms like visual crowding as well as applied domains such as medical image perception. Their current work investigates the spatiotemporal integration processes that allow the brain to smooth over discontinuous retinal inputs and manage environmental clutter.
E063.research_direction: Dr. Manassi's work examines how the visual system organizes information over space and time to create a coherent perception of a cluttered world. A long-standing line of research studies visual crowding and its release (uncrowding), showing that crowding depends on how the whole stimulus is grouped and segmented rather than on target-flanker distance alone. Their recent work in this area asks whether surface completion can support uncrowding and measures the fine-grained time course of vision, showing that the recurrent grouping mechanisms that overcome crowding take longer than crowding itself to unfold. A second line explores how temporal context shapes perception, investigating the boundary conditions that determine whether recent visual stimuli produce attractive serial dependence or repulsive negative aftereffects. They map these sequential biases across domains, from testing the integrity of perceptual priors in schizophrenia using low-level orientation adjustment tasks to exploring how adaptation and serial biases modulate high-level trait impressions such as facial trustworthiness.

papers.title: Time, space and feature similarity determine attractive and repulsive serial biases in trustworthiness impressions
papers.abstract: Uses a trustworthiness rating task to show that first impressions of faces are shaped by preceding faces in two opposite ways, attraction toward and repulsion away from the past. The direction and size of the bias depend on exposure duration, feature similarity and spatial proximity to previous faces. The results extend serial biases from low-level vision to social perception.
papers.authors: Fiammetta Marini, Clare A. M. Sutherland, Linda Jeffery, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Dynamics of vision: Grouping takes longer than crowding
papers.abstract: Measures the fine time course of visual crowding and uncrowding to test whether they unfold at the same speed. Grouping-based release from crowding takes longer to emerge than crowding itself, consistent with recurrent processing that organizes the whole stimulus. The findings support computational models in which grouping operates over time to resolve clutter.
papers.authors: Martina Morea, Michael H. Herzog, Gregory Francis, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Continuity fields enhance visual perception through positive serial dependence
papers.abstract: Argues that the visual system stabilizes perception by pulling the current percept toward recent inputs, a process termed continuity fields. The piece reviews evidence that this positive serial dependence smooths noisy, discontinuous retinal input and improves accuracy in a changing environment. It frames continuity as an active mechanism for a stable perceptual experience.
papers.authors: Mauro Manassi, David Whitney

papers.title: Intact Serial Dependence in Schizophrenia: Evidence from an Orientation Adjustment Task
papers.abstract: Tests the idea that schizophrenia reduces reliance on prior information by measuring serial dependence in 26 patients and 27 controls with a classic orientation adjustment task. Both groups show a comparable attractive bias to the previous stimulus, contradicting the account of a general deficit in perceptual priors. The paper argues that earlier reports of reduced serial dependence depend on the specific paradigm.
papers.authors: David Pascucci, Maya Roinishvili, Eka Chkonia, Andreas Brand, David Whitney, Michael H. Herzog, Mauro Manassi

papers.title: Serial dependence in visual perception: A meta-analysis and review
papers.abstract: Pools results from many published serial dependence studies to quantify how reliable and large the attractive bias toward past stimuli is. The analysis tests how factors such as stimulus type, task, timing and spatial and feature similarity modulate the effect, and identifies gaps for future work. It serves as a quantitative reference for the field.
papers.authors: Mauro Manassi, Yuki Murai, David Whitney

E064.name: Heiko Neumann
E064.department: Institute of Neural Information Processing (Institut fuer Neuroinformatik); Senior Professor
