E064.bio: Heiko Neumann is a Senior Professor at the Institute of Neural Information Processing at Ulm University and leads the Vision and Perception Science group. Neumann's research uses neural modeling to investigate the computational principles of visual information processing in biological systems and artificial architectures. They study the dynamics of motion perception, object recognition, and visual attention, focusing on how hierarchical neural circuits integrate contextual information for task-relevant behavior. Neumann's theoretical findings are applied to domains including autonomous robotics, medical image analysis, and human-computer interaction.
E064.research_direction: Dr. Neumann has recently been investigating the intersection of biological neural circuits and artificial computer vision systems. Their recent work explores mechanistic models of cortical visual processing, simulating how thalamo-cortical loops support incremental attentional binding during mental contour tracing and how pyramidal cell microcircuits integrate contextual visual information. In parallel, they are examining the functional gaps between primate and machine vision, probing why deep neural networks are biased toward color and texture rather than shape and advocating for the inclusion of recurrent cortical motifs in artificial architectures. Applying computational principles to engineering challenges, their research also involves developing novel fusion modules that combine convolutional and transformer networks for multi-modal tasks like gesture recognition.

papers.title: Coherence from Context - Two-Point Neuron Models for Contextual Integration in Visual Information Processing
papers.abstract: This preprint builds a mechanistic model of cortical pyramidal cells as two-point neurons that combine driving input at basal dendrites with modulating context at apical dendrites. The model is extended with local PV, SOM and VIP interneuron circuits so that feedforward-feedback interaction, contextual feedback and pooled inhibition amplify coherent signals selectively. It is then validated on visual integration phenomena.
papers.authors: Daniel Schmid, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: A model of thalamo-cortical interaction for incremental binding in mental contour-tracing
papers.abstract: The paper presents a neural dynamical model of how attention spreads across an object to bind its parts step by step, as when mentally tracing a contour. It gives a mechanistic account of why binding speed depends on distractor layout and is scale invariant (the growth-cone hypothesis). The circuit uses thalamo-cortical loops in which higher-order thalamic and cortical stages exchange modulatory feedback under attentional control, and simulations reproduce known behavioral findings.
papers.authors: Daniel Schmid, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Teaching deep networks to see shape: Lessons from a simplified visual world
papers.abstract: The study asks why deep networks rely on color and texture whereas primate vision depends strongly on shape. Using simple synthetic datasets in which shape, color and texture can each predict the class, the authors train networks from scratch and show that some architectures cannot use shape at all while others can but are biased toward other features. They explain the bias through training dynamics and show how it can be countered.
papers.authors: Christian Jarvers, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Canonical circuit computations for computer vision
papers.abstract: This perspective argues that computer vision can draw on structural and functional principles of cortical circuits that engineering-driven, benchmark-focused systems have overlooked. It surveys recurrent feedforward, lateral and feedback interactions as computational motifs and shows how they can be turned into design principles for machine vision mechanisms and models.
papers.authors: Daniel Schmid, Christian Jarvers, Heiko Neumann

papers.title: Convolutional Transformer Fusion Blocks for Multi-Modal Gesture Recognition
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a self-attention fusion module that adds convolutions to the attention function and can be inserted at several levels of two-stream CNNs to combine modalities such as RGB and depth. It also compares multi-level fusion pathways to study how information flows between streams. The method reaches state-of-the-art or competitive accuracy on IsoGD, NVGesture and IPN Hand while being resource efficient.
papers.authors: Basavaraj Hampiholi, Christian Jarvers, Wolfgang Mader, Heiko Neumann

E065.name: Philipp Sterzer
E065.bio: Philipp Sterzer is a neuroscientist and psychiatrist whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and their disruption in psychiatric conditions. Sterzer uses functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), psychophysics, and computational modeling to investigate how the brain processes ambiguous sensory information and integrates prior expectations through predictive coding. Their work analyzes the pathogenesis of delusions and hallucinations in psychosis, framing these symptoms as alterations in hierarchical belief updating. Formerly the head of the Visual Perception Lab at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Sterzer currently heads the Translational Psychiatry Lab at the University of Basel and maintains a clinical fellowship with the Berlin Institute of Health.
E065.research_direction: Dr. Sterzer's recent work has been investigating the computational mechanisms of perceptual inference, with a strong focus on how predictive processing is altered in psychosis and schizophrenia. To understand how the brain balances prior expectations against incoming sensory evidence, their recent research explores perceptual dynamics in both auditory and visual decision-making tasks, utilizing phenomena like bistable perception and serial dependence. They have been examining these belief-updating processes across multiple levels, from characterizing how perception naturally fluctuates between internally and externally driven modes in humans and mice, to testing how pharmacological challenges like ketamine disrupt the weighting of perceptual priors. Additionally, Dr. Sterzer has recently been working to ground these computational markers in neurobiology, mapping prediction-error signals onto specific cortical circuits and proposing hierarchical models to explain complex clinical puzzles such as the delusion paradox.

papers.title: N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor hypofunction causes recurrent and transient failures of perceptual inference
papers.abstract: Using a pharmacological challenge in healthy volunteers, the study tests whether blocking NMDA receptors with ketamine disrupts how the brain balances prior expectations against sensory evidence during a bistable-perception task. Modelling of perceptual dynamics shows that ketamine produces brief, recurring lapses in which perceptual inference fails, resembling the instability of belief updating proposed in psychosis. The work links a specific receptor-level manipulation to computational markers of aberrant inference.
papers.authors: Veith Weilnhammer, Marcus Rothkirch, Deniz Yilmaz, Merve Fritsch, Lena Esther Ptasczynski, Katrin Reichenbach, Lukas Roediger, Philip Corlett, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Reduced weighting of short-term perceptual priors during auditory perceptual decision-making in psychosis-prone individuals
papers.abstract: Participants with varying levels of psychosis proneness performed an auditory perceptual decision task in which recent stimulus history could bias choices. Individuals higher in psychosis proneness relied less on short-term priors from the recent past, in line with altered belief-updating. The results extend earlier visual findings to audition and support a general prior-weighting alteration along the psychosis continuum.
papers.authors: Anna-Chiara Schaub, Anna-Lena Eckert, Stijn A. Nuiten, Veith Weilnhammer, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Predictive Processing: A Circuit Approach to Psychosis
papers.abstract: This review asks how predictive-processing accounts of hallucinations and delusions can be grounded in cortical circuitry. It maps prediction-error and prediction signals onto specific cortical layers and interneuron classes, and considers how disturbed excitation-inhibition balance or neuromodulation could shift the weighting of priors and sensory input. The authors outline testable circuit-level hypotheses for psychosis.
papers.authors: Georg B. Keller, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Sensory processing in humans and mice fluctuates between external and internal modes
papers.abstract: The authors show that perception in both humans and mice alternates over time between a mode dominated by current sensory input and a mode dominated by prior internal information. Using serial-dependence analyses in cross-species datasets, they characterise how these modes fluctuate and how they relate to behaviour. The findings offer a general account of how perceptual inference switches between stimulus-driven and history-driven states.
papers.authors: Veith Weilnhammer, Heiner Stuke, Kai Standvoss, Philipp Sterzer

papers.title: Resolving the Delusion Paradox
papers.abstract: Delusional patients often hold beliefs with great conviction yet fail to act on them as expected, a puzzle known as the delusion paradox. The paper proposes a predictive-processing account in which delusions reflect altered precision and belief-updating across hierarchical levels, explaining both strong conviction and weak behavioural consequences. It offers a unifying framework and points to empirical tests.
papers.authors: Predrag Petrovic, Philipp Sterzer

E066.name: Duje Tadin
E066.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E066.bio: Duje Tadin is a Professor and Chair of the Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences at the University of Rochester and serves as the Interim Dean of the School of Arts & Sciences. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of visual perception, focusing on motion processing, spatial suppression, and the limits of sensory integration. Tadin utilizes human psychophysics, computational modeling, and non-invasive brain stimulation to study how these processes are altered in clinical populations, including individuals with schizophrenia and autism. Tadin’s laboratory also develops neuro-rehabilitative strategies, such as virtual reality-based training, to improve visual function and recovery following cortical damage.
E066.research_direction: Dr. Tadin studies how the visual system balances sensitivity and suppression, and how this balance varies across individuals and clinical conditions. His lab showed that center–surround suppression in MT/V5 enables rapid segmentation of moving objects. In autism, the lab linked atypical perception to high internal noise, larger receptive fields and atypical motion prediction. In schizophrenia, it showed that sensory noise limits working memory. With Krystel Huxlin, he showed that training vision soon after occipital stroke recovers it much faster, while identifying limits such as contrast sensitivity. His lab has also shown that adults adapt to their own optics, which shapes contrast sensitivity and stereovision. Increasingly, the lab uses virtual reality to connect laboratory and real-world vision, studying binocular rivalry in realistic 3D scenes, steering after cortical blindness, and reaching after stroke.

papers.title: Binocular rivalry under naturalistic geometry: Evidence from worlds simulated in virtual reality
papers.abstract: Binocular rivalry is typically studied by presenting two irreconcilable images separately to the two eyes, an artificial geometric arrangement in which two distinct objects appear to occupy the same physical location—a configuration rarely, if ever, encountered in everyday vision. This raises doubts about whether laboratory rivalry findings generalize to naturalistic binocular viewing. The authors used a head-mounted virtual reality system to embed classic rivalry stimuli within a geometrically plausible, cue-rich 3D corridor environment, parametrically varying the spatial plausibility of the rival images (e.g., placing them at congruent versus incongruent depths and locations within the simulated scene). They found that rivalry dynamics—including dominance durations and switching rates—were systematically modulated by the naturalistic geometric plausibility of the rival images, indicating that the visual system's resolution of interocular conflict is sensitive to whether the conflicting inputs are consistent with a coherent 3D scene, and supporting the external validity of binocular rivalry as a tool for studying everyday binocular vision.
papers.authors: Shui'er Han, Randolph Blake, Celine Aubuchon, Duje Tadin

E069.name: James Elder
E069.department: Department of Electrical Engineering & Computer Science and Department of Psychology
E069.bio: James Elder is the York Research Chair in Human and Computer Vision and the Director of the Centre for AI & Society at York University. Elder's research integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling to study the principles of biological vision for the development of machine vision systems. Their technical focus includes natural scene statistics, perceptual organization, and contour processing. Recent applications of this work include 3D urban awareness, socially-aware robotics, and intelligent systems for sustainable mobility.
E069.research_direction: Dr. Elder has recently been developing applied computer vision systems for dynamic multi-object tracking, focusing on domains like sports video and urban traffic monitoring. Their recent work explores long-term tracking challenges by integrating hierarchical graph-based models with domain-specific cues such as scene-text jersey recognition, as well as correcting perspective distortion in traffic cameras via real-world metric ground-plane projections. Alongside these applied tracking systems, they are investigating the fundamental computational gaps between biological and artificial vision, using spectral analysis to probe how humans and deep neural networks differ in their sensitivity to local contour frequencies versus global configural shape. Additionally, Dr. Elder has been expanding their vision research into socially aware assistive robotics by designing sensing and control frameworks for autonomous wheelchair convoys navigating cluttered environments.

papers.title: Spectral Analysis Reveals Fundamental Differences between Human and Deep Neural Network Shape Representations
papers.abstract: Humans are sensitive to global, configural shape whereas ImageNet-trained deep networks seem to rely on local features, but the exact nature of the gap has been hard to pin down. The authors use a shape-frequency analysis to measure human and network sensitivity across the spectrum of contour frequencies and to test amplitude versus phase information. Humans turn out to be tuned to much lower shape frequencies than networks, so the models cannot account for most of the variance in human shape judgements, and recent curriculum-based fixes mainly damp high frequencies rather than sharpening low-frequency tuning.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, John Wilder, James H. Elder

papers.title: Towards Long-Term Player Tracking with Graph Hierarchies and Domain-Specific Features
papers.abstract: Following players through a whole game is hard because teammates look alike and are often occluded or out of view for long periods. The paper introduces SportsSUSHI, a hierarchical graph-based tracker that stitches tracklets together using domain cues such as jersey numbers, team identity and field coordinates. It performs strongly on SoccerNet and on a new hockey dataset with long sequences filmed from a fixed camera that covers the whole rink.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW)
papers.authors: Maria Koshkina, James H. Elder

papers.title: A General Framework for Jersey Number Recognition in Sports Video
papers.abstract: Jersey numbers are a key cue for following individual players over long stretches of sports video, and reading them can be treated as a scene-text-recognition problem. The authors release a new hockey jersey-number dataset and adapt scene-text recognition models to it, handling heavy occlusion and testing transfer from hockey to soccer. They also show how frame-level predictions can be aggregated into a single number per tracklet, reaching about 91% accuracy on hockey images and 87% on soccer tracklets.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) Workshops
papers.authors: Maria Koshkina, James H. Elder

papers.title: Ground Plane Projection for Improved Traffic Analytics at Intersections
papers.abstract: Traffic analytics from intersection cameras is hampered by perspective distortion in the raw image view. The authors project detected vehicles onto the ground plane so that tracking and movement analysis are done in real-world metric coordinates rather than image coordinates. This yields more accurate vehicle counting and movement analysis at urban intersections.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
papers.authors: Sajjad Pakdamansavoji, Kumar Vaibhav Jha, Baher Abdulhai, James H. Elder

papers.title: Robot Wheelchair Convoys for Assistive Human Transportation
papers.abstract: The paper describes a robotic system in which several wheelchairs autonomously follow a lead guide, so that one caregiver can transport multiple people with mobility impairments. It covers the sensing and control design needed for reliable following in cluttered, dynamic environments. The work is part of the lab's socially aware assistive robotics effort.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Smart Mobility (SM)
papers.authors: Helio Perroni Filho, Jenny Ren, Mohammad Akhavan, Yuqian Hou, Walleed Khan, Arian Haghparast, Julian Forsyth, Kimia Rajaeifar, Michael Jenkin, James H. Elder

E075.name: Frederick Kingdom
E075.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Department of Psychology
E075.bio: Kingdom's research explores the computational and psychological mechanisms linking early-stage feature detection, such as edge and orientation sensing, to intermediate-level visual processing of contours, textures, and surfaces. Their investigations encompass domains including color vision, stereopsis, and the perception of transparency and lightness, frequently utilizing natural scene analysis to examine environmental constraints on vision. Kingdom integrates psychophysical experimentation with mathematical modeling and image processing to map the underlying architecture of human visual perception. Additionally, they are a co-developer of the Palamedes toolbox, a software resource for the analysis of psychophysical data.
E075.research_direction: Dr. Kingdom has recently been investigating the mechanisms of binocular vision, specifically focusing on how the visual system integrates signals from the two eyes via binocular sum and difference channels. Their recent work explores this framework across both luminance and chromatic domains, using psychophysical tasks like surround masking and the detection of interocular-anti-phase stimuli to probe how these channels mediate interocular suppression and stimulus identification. Beyond binocular integration, they are also examining motion perception by testing whether observers exhibit gravity-related perceptual biases when judging the acceleration of simulated falling objects. Additionally, their research spans texture processing, utilizing complex Gabor arrays to determine whether the cognitive demands of a given task—such as detection versus discrimination—dictate if the visual system relies on edge-based or region-based mechanisms.

papers.title: Detection and identification of monocular, binocular, and dichoptic stimuli are mediated by binocular sum and difference channels
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether the visual system encodes signals from the two eyes in binocular sum and difference channels, and whether these channels underlie both detecting and identifying stimuli shown to one eye, both eyes, or in opposite phase to the two eyes. Psychophysical detection and identification results are compared against the predictions of a sum-and-difference (adding and differencing) channel model. It extends the group's long-running binocular channel framework to a full account of stimulus identification.
papers.authors: Mark A. Georgeson, Hiromi Sato, Ronald Chang, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: When two eyes are worse than one: Binocular summation for chromatic, interocular-anti-phase stimuli
papers.abstract: Normally two eyes detect a stimulus better than one, but the study shows that for colour-defined (chromatic) gratings presented in opposite phase to the two eyes, binocular detection can be worse than monocular detection. The finding is interpreted through binocular summing and differencing channels for chromatic vision. It extends the sum/difference account from luminance to colour, Kingdom's core specialty.
papers.authors: Frederick A. A. Kingdom, Xingao (Clara) Wang, Huayun Li, Yoel Yakobi

papers.title: Surround masking reveals binocular adding and differencing channels
papers.abstract: The study uses surround masking, where a surrounding pattern reduces sensitivity to a central target, to probe how binocular signals are combined. Masking depended on whether the surround and target matched in ways predicted by separate adding (sum) and differencing (difference) binocular channels. The results give independent support for these channels and bear on how interocular suppression is organized.
papers.authors: Rinku Sarkar, Kiana Zanetti, Alexandre Reynaud, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: A visual bias for falling objects
papers.abstract: Following Aristotle's belief that falling objects move at constant velocity, the authors asked whether visual judgements of motion acceleration are biased. Observers judged whether a ball in a naturalistic simulated scene accelerated or decelerated while moving in different directions. More acceleration was needed for a downward-falling ball to look constant-velocity than for an upward-moving one, with no direction differences in sensitivity, suggesting a perceptual bias tied to gravity-related motion.
papers.authors: Mai Huong Phan, Björn Jörges, Laurence R. Harris, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

papers.title: Task-dependent contribution to edge-based versus region-based texture perception
papers.abstract: Texture studies suggest some textures are processed by edge-based and others by region-based mechanisms, but detection and segregation tasks have given conflicting evidence. Using Gabor texture arrays with orientation, luminance, contrast, and variance modulations and sine, square and cusp waveforms with sharp edges, the authors compared detection with discrimination tasks. The results address whether the task itself determines which mechanism is engaged.
papers.authors: Elena Gheorghiu, Cassandra Diggiss, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

E076.name: Anitha Pasupathy
E076.bio: Pasupathy investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual object recognition and scene perception, focusing on the intermediate cortical area V4. Their research addresses boundary curvature as a basis for shape encoding in the primate brain, extending earlier edge-detection models to explain complex form representation. Utilizing multi-contact electrode recordings, reversible cortical inactivation, and computational modeling, Pasupathy's lab examines how the ventral visual stream processes partially occluded objects and encodes form and texture. Their work aims to bridge biological vision and deep convolutional neural networks to determine how the brain achieves scene segmentation and understanding.
E076.research_direction: Dr. Pasupathy has recently been investigating the functional architecture and computational roles of the primate ventral visual stream, focusing heavily on mid-level areas V2 and V4. Utilizing advanced high-density electrophysiology methods like Neuropixels in awake macaques, their recent work explores how neurons tuned to shape, texture, and motion are spatially organized across cortical layers and whether they form traditional columnar structures. Beyond functional mapping, they are actively examining the neural mechanisms of visual crowding by testing how V4 shape selectivity is impacted by the spatial arrangement and pooling of targets and distractors. Additionally, their research expands the traditional functional divide of visual pathways by investigating the ventral stream's capacity to compute long-range object motion and exploring how this complements motion processing in the dorsal stream.

papers.title: Functional Clusters for Shape, Texture, and Motion Encoding in Macaque V2
papers.abstract: Using high-density Neuropixels recordings in three macaques, the authors map how V2 neurons are organized while viewing shape, texture, grating and motion stimuli. They find dense clusters of similarly tuned neurons spanning roughly half a millimetre, resembling columns. V2 responses are largely explained by local image statistics and orientation filters, in contrast to V4, supporting a progression from columnar organization to sparse clusters along the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Taekjun Kim, Rohit Kamath, Gaku Hatanaka, Tomoyuki Namima, Celeste Dylla, Wyeth Bair, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: High-Density Recording Reveals Sparse Clusters (But Not Columns) for Shape and Texture Encoding in Macaque V4
papers.abstract: Neuropixels probes were used in awake monkeys to record dozens of V4 neurons simultaneously across cortical layers while they viewed shape and texture stimuli. Only about a fifth of neurons shared tuning with their neighbours, and these clusters were confined to a few layers rather than forming columns. The authors argue that V4 organization is coarse and non-columnar, reflecting the diversity of inputs feeding V4 tuning.
papers.authors: Tomoyuki Namima, Erin Kempkes, Polina Zamarashkina, Natalia Owen, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Crowding in Macaque Area V4
papers.abstract: The authors recorded single V4 neurons while monkeys viewed crowded displays and texture-matched metamers, testing whether crowding stems from pooled encoding of target and distractor features. V4 shape selectivity changed with the number, distance and position of distractors in ways that parallel human psychophysics, and salient targets could escape crowding. Pooling alone could not explain the data, so they propose V4 preferentially encodes salient stimuli.
papers.authors: Taekjun Kim, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Inserting a Neuropixels probe into awake monkey cortex: two probes, two methods
papers.abstract: The paper describes hardware and surgical procedures for inserting two kinds of Neuropixels probe into the awake macaque cortex through thick primate dura. A dural-eyelet method allows repeated insertion of the fine rodent probe without breakage, and an artificial-dura system supports the thicker NHP probe. Recordings across three animals and seven chambers yielded stable results over months.
papers.authors: Tomoyuki Namima, Erin Kempkes, Bob Smith, Lydia Smith, Amy L. Orsborn, Anitha Pasupathy

papers.title: Dissociation in neuronal encoding of object versus surface motion in the primate brain
papers.abstract: Dorsal-stream neurons often fail to signal long-range motion jumps, yet such motion is perceptually salient. The paper shows that ventral-stream area V4 contains neurons whose direction selectivity persists for long-range object motion, even with conflicting local motion, but not for surface motion behind apertures. Motion direction can be decoded from a few V4 neurons, revealing a ventral-stream motion computation complementary to the dorsal pathway.
papers.authors: Anthony Bigelow, Taekjun Kim, Tomoyuki Namima, Wyeth Bair, Anitha Pasupathy

E080.name: Stella Yu
E080.bio: Stella X. Yu is a Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the University of Michigan, conducting research at the intersection of computer vision, machine learning, and human perception. Yu’s work focuses on actionable representation learning, utilizing unsupervised and self-supervised methodologies to identify mid-level visual structures and hierarchical groupings from unlabeled data. By integrating structural inductive biases such as symmetry and geometric priors into deep learning architectures, Yu aims to develop artificial sensing systems modeled after biological vision. Their research extends to interdisciplinary applications in medical imaging, robotics, and data-driven scientific discovery.
E080.research_direction: Dr. Yu has recently been working at the intersection of hierarchical visual representation learning and embodied AI for humanoid robots. In the computer vision domain, their recent work explores novel learning paradigms, investigating how foundational vision models can be trained via next-embedding prediction of image patches and how part-to-whole image segmentation can emerge intrinsically from high-level recognition objectives rather than explicit dense supervision. They are also examining hierarchical classification under real-world constraints, specifically how models can learn from and predict "free-grained" taxonomy labels of mixed semantic depth using text-attribute supervision. Concurrently in the robotics space, their research investigates integrative skill development, asking how hierarchical reinforcement learning, temporal vision models, and human demonstrations can be combined to teach humanoids complex, end-to-end behaviors like autonomous trail hiking and unified fall-and-recovery sequences.

papers.title: Unified Humanoid Fall-Safety Policy from a Few Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Instead of treating fall avoidance, impact reduction and standing back up as separate problems, this work learns a single humanoid policy covering the whole fall-and-recovery process. It fuses a few human demonstrations with reinforcement learning and an adaptive diffusion-based memory of safe reactions. Experiments in simulation and on a Unitree G1 robot show robust sim-to-real transfer.
papers.venue: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
papers.authors: Zhengjie Xu, Ye Li, Kwan-Yee Lin, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Free-Grained Hierarchical Recognition
papers.abstract: Hierarchical classifiers usually assume every training image is labeled along its full taxonomy path, but real labels come at mixed granularity (a distant bird is just 'bird'). The paper introduces free-grain training with new benchmarks and shows existing methods degrade sharply. It proposes text-based attribute supervision and a semi-supervised treatment of missing labels, and studies free-grained inference where the model picks how deep to predict.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Seulki Park, Zilin Wang, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Next-Embedding Prediction Makes Strong Vision Learners
papers.abstract: Borrowing the generative-pretraining recipe from language models, the paper trains a plain Transformer to predict the embedding of the next image patch given earlier ones (causal masking with stop-gradient), with no pixel reconstruction, tokenizer, or contrastive loss. This shifts the goal from learning features to learning a predictive model. The simple ImageNet-1k pretraining reaches strong classification accuracy and transfers to other tasks such as segmentation.
papers.authors: Sihan Xu, Ziqiao Ma, Wenhao Chai, Xuweiyi Chen, Weiyang Jin, Joyce Chai, Saining Xie, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Let Humanoids Hike! Integrative Skill Development on Complex Trails
papers.abstract: The authors argue that humanoid research is fragmented across locomotion and semantic navigation, and propose teaching a vision-equipped humanoid to hike complex trails so that perception, decision making and motor control develop together. Their LEGO-H framework uses a temporal vision transformer inside hierarchical reinforcement learning to anticipate local goals, plus latent joint-movement representations with hierarchical metric learning. The result is autonomous hiking over unpredictable terrain.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Kwan-Yee Lin, Stella X. Yu

papers.title: Learning Hierarchical Image Segmentation For Recognition and By Recognition
papers.abstract: The paper treats segmentation as an internal process that emerges with recognition rather than a separately supervised task. A ViT with adaptive segment tokens and graph pooling learns hierarchical part-to-whole segmentation using only image-level recognition objectives. This yields segmentations that in turn improve recognition.
papers.authors: Tsung-Wei Ke, Sangwoo Mo, Stella X. Yu

E081.name: Nicholas Baker
E081.bio: Nicholas Baker is an Assistant Professor of Neuroscience in the Department of Psychology at Loyola University Chicago and directs the Human Perception Lab. Baker’s research examines the information processing systems that transform local visual contours into abstract shape representations, building upon Gestalt principles. Using psychophysical methodologies and computational modeling, Baker investigates the nature of shape abstraction in human vision and compares these processes to the mechanisms of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Their work identifies discrepancies between biological vision and artificial intelligence, specifically regarding the sensitivity of deep networks to global object configuration.
E081.research_direction: Dr. Baker has recently been investigating the computational and cognitive mechanisms underlying shape perception, frequently comparing human visual processing with that of deep neural networks. Their recent work explores the fundamental differences in how these systems extract form, using novel "shape frequency" analyses to probe sensitivities to coarse versus fine features and manipulating 3D cues like shading and internal contours to test object recognition across diverse viewpoints. They are also testing the capacity of artificial systems to learn abstract configural relations, evaluating whether convolutional networks can extract concepts like topological enclosure or simple "same-different" pairings. Alongside this comparative research, Dr. Baker uses psychophysical paradigms to study shape abstraction in human observers, employing sparse dot arrays to ask how discrete elements are organized into continuous contours and examining whether local contour details and global object shape are handled by independent visual pathways.

papers.title: Spectral Analysis Reveals Fundamental Differences between Human and Deep Neural Network Shape Representations
papers.abstract: Introduces a 'shape frequency' analysis to probe how sensitive humans and ImageNet-trained networks are to shape components across a spectrum from coarse to fine. Humans are tuned to much lower shape frequencies than networks, and the two differ in how they respond to the amplitude and phase of shape components. Curriculum tweaks meant to make networks more human-like mostly dampen high-frequency sensitivity rather than sharpening low-frequency tuning, so the models cannot explain most of the variance in human shape judgements.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, John Wilder, James H. Elder

papers.title: Three-dimensional shape cues affect human and artificial recognition systems differently
papers.abstract: Tests whether humans and neural networks can classify texture-substituted objects by shape when 3D cues such as shading, attached shadows and internal contours are present or removed. Using 120,000 ShapeNet-based images from many viewpoints, humans were far better than any network at recognising shape, though some cue manipulations narrowed the gap. The results show networks depend on different shape information than people, especially for non-canonical views.
papers.authors: Mikayla Cutler, Luke Baumel, Joseph Tocco, William Friebel, George K. Thiruvathukal, Nicholas Baker

papers.title: Shape from dots: A window into abstraction processes in visual perception
papers.abstract: Uses sparse dot arrays to ask what spatial relations let the visual system organise discrete elements into smooth contours versus vertices, and then into whole shapes. Perceived smoothness depended on relations among dots beyond the three defining an angle, with a firm boundary near 90 degrees. Further experiments extend these findings to how dot arrays are grouped into abstract shape representations.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Configural relations in humans and deep convolutional neural networks
papers.abstract: Building on earlier findings that convolutional networks are insensitive to global object shape, this paper asks whether the limitation extends to relational judgements. AlexNet and ResNet-50 were trained and tested on same-different, enclosure (dot inside or outside a closed figure) and related relations. The networks struggled to learn and generalise these abstract relations, unlike human observers.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Patrick Garrigan, Austin Phillips, Philip J. Kellman

papers.title: Independent mechanisms for processing local contour features and global shape
papers.abstract: Examines whether the visual system handles fine local contour features and overall global shape through separate mechanisms. Psychophysical experiments manipulating each kind of information indicate they are processed independently rather than by a single pathway. This helps explain why global form can be perceived even when local detail is degraded or altered.
papers.authors: Nicholas Baker, Philip J. Kellman

E082.name: Zoe Kourtzi
E082.bio: Zoe Kourtzi is a Professor of Experimental Psychology and Computational Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge and the head of the Adaptive Brain Lab. Kourtzi’s research integrates multimodal neuroimaging, including 7T fMRI, EEG, and MRS, with machine learning to investigate the neural mechanisms of brain plasticity and lifelong learning. They examine how humans translate sensory experiences into adaptive decisions and develop predictive AI-guided models for the early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases and mental health disorders. This work connects systems neuroscience with translational neuroinformatics in the study of vision science and clinical diagnostics.
E082.research_direction: Dr. Kourtzi’s recent work explores the neural mechanisms of adult brain plasticity alongside the development of translational clinical tools for neurodegeneration. In the realm of vision and cognition, they have recently been investigating how perceptual learning and decision-making are supported by cortical plasticity, using 7T MR spectroscopy, fMRI, and brain stimulation to probe how GABAergic inhibition and large-scale network connectivity refine visual templates. Concurrently, their research applies interpretable machine learning to structural MRI and behavioral data to predict early dementia and Alzheimer's disease trajectory, aiming to improve patient stratification in clinical trials and real-world memory clinics. Additionally, they are investigating how personalized cognitive flexibility training can be optimized to transfer beyond laboratory tasks to support everyday functioning and mental health across the lifespan.

papers.title: AI-guided patient stratification improves outcomes and efficiency in the AMARANTH Alzheimer's Disease clinical trial
papers.abstract: The AMARANTH trial of lanabecestat for early Alzheimer's disease failed to show a benefit in the overall population. The authors trained a machine-learning model on baseline cognitive and imaging data to predict individual patients' rates of decline and used it to split participants into slow and fast progressors. Stratifying this way revealed treatment effects hidden in the pooled data and showed that trials could reach the same power with fewer participants, arguing for AI-guided enrichment in dementia trial design.
papers.authors: Delshad Vaghari, Gayathri Mohankumar, Keith Tan, Andrew Lowe, Craig Shering, Peter Tino, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Neurogenetic phenotypes of learning-dependent plasticity for improved perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: The paper asks how genes shape the brain changes that support perceptual learning in adults. Brain-wide gene expression maps were related to training-dependent changes in cortical microstructure and functional connectivity in visual and fronto-parietal networks. Brain stimulation of visual cortex during training boosted learning and altered connectivity between these networks rather than local microstructure, revealing neurogenetic signatures of plasticity.
papers.authors: Liz Yuanxi Lee, Joseph J. Ziminski, Polytimi Frangou, Vasilis M. Karlaftis, Yezhou Wang, Boris Bernhardt, Varun Warrier, Richard A. I. Bethlehem, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Robust and interpretable AI-guided marker for early dementia prediction in real-world clinical settings
papers.abstract: Memory clinics need a practical way to tell which patients will go on to develop dementia. The team built an interpretable machine-learning marker from routine cognitive tests and structural MRI, trained on research cohorts and validated in independent memory-clinic data from the UK and Singapore. It predicted conversion to dementia more accurately than standard clinical measures and stayed reliable across sites and with missing data.
papers.authors: Liz Yuanxi Lee, Delshad Vaghari, Michael C. Burkhart, Peter Tino, Marcella Montagnese, Zhuoyu Li, Katharina Zuhlsdorff, Joseph Giorgio, Guy Williams, Eddie Chong, Christopher Chen, Benjamin R. Underwood, Timothy Rittman, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Recurrent inhibition refines mental templates to optimize perceptual decisions
papers.abstract: Using 7T MR spectroscopy and fMRI, the study followed how people learn to discriminate visual orientations under noise. Training-related gains in performance were linked to changes in GABA-mediated inhibition in early visual cortex, which sharpened the internal templates used to read out sensory evidence. The findings tie inhibitory circuit plasticity to more efficient perceptual decisions in the adult brain.
papers.authors: Ke Jia, Mengxin Wang, Cecilia Steinwurzel, Joseph J. Ziminski, Yinghua Xi, Uzay Emir, Zoe Kourtzi

papers.title: Cognitive flexibility training for impact in real-world settings
papers.abstract: This review looks at whether training cognitive flexibility can improve everyday functioning rather than just lab task scores. It surveys behavioral, neuroimaging and computational evidence on how flexibility develops and adapts across the lifespan, and discusses what makes training transfer to real-world settings. The authors outline how personalized, data-driven training could support learning and mental health.
papers.authors: Liz Y. Lee, Mairead P. Healy, Nastassja L. Fischer, Ke Tong, Annabel S. H. Chen, Barbara J. Sahakian, Zoe Kourtzi

E083.name: Benoit Cottereau
E083.department: Centre de Recherche Cerveau et Cognition (CerCo)
E083.lab_name: SV3M (Spatial Vision in Man, Monkey and Machine)
E083.bio: Benoit Cottereau is a CNRS Research Director at the CerCo laboratory in Toulouse and the IPAL laboratory in Singapore, specializing in the mechanisms of spatial vision and 3D scene understanding. His research combines human and non-human primate neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG, MEG) with psychophysical experiments and computational modeling. Cottereau focuses on the development of bio-inspired artificial vision systems, utilizing event-based cameras and spiking neural networks to model biological processes such as optic flow, binocular disparity, and symmetry perception. This work encompasses fundamental neuroscience, clinical applications for rehabilitating visual pathologies like macular degeneration, and the design of energy-efficient artificial intelligence for robotic navigation.
E083.research_direction: Dr. Cottereau’s research focuses on visual perception and processing, with a particular interest in motion perception, spatial vision, and the adaptation of visual cortical networks to changes in visual input. His work combines behavioral experiments, neuroimaging, and computational modeling to study visual processing in humans and non-human primates. A major focus of his recent research is understanding how the visual system adapts to central vision loss in macular degeneration, and how residual vision can be enhanced through perceptual learning. He also develops bio-inspired and neuromorphic models of vision, including spiking neural networks (SNNs) that process information from event-based cameras, using principles of biological visual processing to better understand vision and build more efficient artificial systems.

papers.title: Event-driven neuromorphic vision enables energy-efficient visual place recognition
papers.abstract: The authors present SpikeVPR, a bio-inspired system that pairs event cameras with spiking neural networks to learn compact place descriptors from few exemplars. It is trained end to end with surrogate gradients and uses an EventDilation augmentation to cope with changes in speed and timing. On three benchmarks it matches leading deep networks while being about 50 times smaller and using an estimated 30 to 250 times less energy.
papers.authors: Geoffroy Keime, Nicolas Cuperlier, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: SpikeCLR: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning for Few-Shot Event-Based Vision using Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: SpikeCLR adapts contrastive self-supervised learning to spiking neural networks so they can learn visual representations from unlabeled event-camera data. The authors adapt frame-based augmentations to the spiking domain and train with surrogate gradients. This eases the shortage of labeled event datasets and supports few-shot classification on neuromorphic-ready hardware.
papers.authors: Maxime Vaillant, Axel Carlier, Lai Xing Ng, Christophe Hurter, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: Motion processing in visual cortex of maculopathy patients
papers.abstract: Using fMRI with random-dot motion stimuli, the authors compared patients with age-related macular degeneration or Stargardt disease against controls viewing gaze-matched artificial scotomas. Translational motion drove robust responses in hMT+, V3A, V6 and peripheral-representing parts of early visual cortex in the patients. The same pattern appeared in the controls, which argues against large-scale reorganization of the motion network after central vision loss and indicates the network is preserved.
papers.authors: Célia Michaud, Jade Guénot, Cynthia Faurite, Mathilde Gallice, Christophe Chiquet, Nathalie Vayssière, Isabelle Berry, Yves Trotter, Vincent Soler, Carole Peyrin, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: Talk2Event: Grounded Understanding of Dynamic Scenes from Event Cameras
papers.abstract: The paper introduces the first large-scale benchmark for language-driven object grounding in event-camera data, built from real driving scenes with over 30,000 validated referring expressions. Each expression carries appearance, status, and viewer- and object-relation attributes. The authors also propose EventRefer, a grounding model that fuses these attributes with a mixture of event-attribute experts, and it beats baselines with event-only, frame-only and event-frame input.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Lingdong Kong, Dongyue Lu, Ao Liang, Rong Li, Yuhao Dong, Tianshuai Hu, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi, Benoit R. Cottereau

papers.title: EventFly: Event Camera Perception from Ground to the Sky
papers.abstract: EventFly tackles cross-platform adaptation for event-camera dense perception, for example moving from cars to drones or quadrupeds with different motion, viewpoint and class statistics. It combines an activation prior that targets confident regions in the new domain, a blending scheme that mixes source and target event voxel grids, and a dual-discriminator matching step for domain-invariant features. The approach gives clear gains over prior adaptation methods across platforms.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Lingdong Kong, Dongyue Lu, Xiang Xu, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi, Benoit R. Cottereau

E086.name: Elena Gheorghiu
E086.bio: Gheorghiu is an Associate Professor at the University of Stirling whose research examines the hierarchical mechanisms of human visual processing and the integration of features into representations like contours, textures, and 3D shapes. Their work investigates binocular vision, stereopsis, and symmetry perception, with a focus on how contextual modulation enhances contour detection through the suppression of surround textures. Using psychophysics, EEG/ERP, and computational modelling, Gheorghiu maps the relationship between initial feature extraction and higher-order perceptual organization. Gheorghiu was a co-winner of the 2007 Best Visual Illusion of the Year contest for the discovery of the 'Leaning Tower Illusion.'
E086.research_direction: Dr. Gheorghiu has recently been studying how the human visual system organizes simple patterns into structure. Their recent work looks at visual symmetry, testing how the brain's electrical response to symmetric dot patterns changes when light and dark elements are grouped in different ways across the symmetry axis. They are also asking how texture perception depends on the task, exploring whether people rely on edges between textured regions or on the overall properties of the regions themselves when segmenting versus detecting patterns.

papers.title: The interaction between luminance polarity grouping and symmetry axes on the ERP responses to symmetry
papers.abstract: While visual symmetry constitutes a salient ecological cue, its perceptual processing is susceptible to ambient illumination such as shading cast across its symmetry axis. This study evaluated the functional interplay between symmetry detection and luminance-polarity grouping and assessed how this interaction modulates the Sustained Posterior Negativity (SPN) component of Event-Related Potentials (ERPs). Stimuli comprised dot patterns displaying reflection, rotation, translation, or quasi-random noise configurations, with luminance polarity segregated across a grouping axis into bright and dark dot regions. Relative angular offsets between symmetry axes and polarity-grouping axes were varied at 0°, 30°, 60°, and 90°. Psychophysical measurement using a two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) detection task showed that co-axial alignment (0° offset) yielded higher accuracy than single-polarity displays for rotational and translational regularity (though not reflection) and significantly outperformed all misaligned angular separations across all symmetry classes. Electrophysiologically, the SPN dissociated topographically into an early parieto-occipital subcomponent tuned to luminance-polarity grouping and a subsequent late component over central electrode sites sensitive to pattern regularity. Increasing relative axis disparities revealed systematic distinctions between cardinal (0°, 90°) and oblique (30°, 60°) angular separations. Moreover, a polarity-grouping effect emerged in the SPN interval for pure noise arrays contingent on symmetry condition, highlighting top-down task set influences. These results demonstrate that luminance-polarity grouping facilitates regularity detection when symmetry is less immediately salient, but misaligned grouping axes concurrently impose behavioral and neural processing costs.
papers.authors: Benjamin Dering, Damien Wright, Elena Gheorghiu

papers.title: Task-dependent contribution to edge-based versus region-based texture perception
papers.abstract: Texture segregation experiments suggest that specific texture types are processed via edge-based mechanisms while others recruit region-based mechanisms; however, nominally edge-based textures recruit region-based encoding when the perceptual demand involves detection rather than segregation. This study investigated whether the nature of the behavioral task governs the recruitment of edge-based versus region-based mechanisms in human texture vision. Stimuli were dense arrays of pseudo-randomly positioned Gabor micropatterns featuring five distinct modulation classes—orientation modulation, orientation variance modulation, luminance modulation, contrast modulation, and contrast variance modulation (CVM)—tested at modulation spatial frequencies of 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8 cpd. Waveform profiles included square-wave (SQ), sine-wave (SN), and a compound missing-fundamental (CS) waveform generated by subtracting a fundamental sinewave from an equal-amplitude square-wave. In a detection task, threshold modulation amplitudes obeyed the ordering SQ < SN < CS across all spatial frequencies, consistent with integration of overall stimulus modulation energy by region-based mechanisms. In contrast, for the orientation discrimination task at low modulation spatial frequencies and for CVM textures across all spatial frequencies, thresholds exhibited the ordering CS ≤ SQ < SN, diagnostic of localized edge-based boundary processing. Computational modeling using Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filter responses confirmed lower peak amplitude responses for detection than discrimination across all stimuli except CVM textures, establishing that behavioral task demands dictate whether texture processing relies on boundary edges or spatial regions.
papers.authors: Elena Gheorghiu, Cassandra Diggiss, Frederick A. A. Kingdom

E089.name: Doris Tsao
E089.department: Department of Molecular & Cell Biology; Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute
E089.bio: Doris Tsao is a neuroscientist who researches the primate visual system, specifically the mechanisms underlying object and facial recognition. Tsao identified the macaque 'face patch system,' a series of cortical regions dedicated to face processing, using fMRI-guided single-unit recordings. Their work characterized the neural code for facial identity as a linear projection onto specific shape and appearance axes to describe how high-level visual features are represented. Currently, Tsao’s research at UC Berkeley extends to 3D vision and the global organization of object space, employing a methodology that combines electrophysiology, functional imaging, and computational modeling.
E089.research_direction: Dr. Tsao has recently been investigating the neural computations underlying high-level visual perception, using single-neuron and Neuropixels recordings across humans, macaques, and tree shrews to map the functional organization of the ventral stream. Their recent work explores how neural populations in the inferotemporal cortex dynamically multiplex information over time, examining how these networks might transition from general face detection to fine individual discrimination and how they separate perceptual signals from memory codes for familiar faces. They are also investigating the mechanisms of visual imagery by recording from the human ventral temporal cortex to test whether imagined and perceived objects share a common generative axis code. Additionally, Dr. Tsao probes the broader evolutionary and architectural rules of the visual system by studying fMRI-targeted modules for figure-ground segmentation in macaque intermediate cortex and testing the universality of the primate form-processing hierarchy in tree shrews.

papers.title: A shared code for perceiving and imagining objects in human ventral temporal cortex
papers.abstract: Recording from single neurons in the human ventral temporal cortex of epilepsy patients, the authors show that most visually responsive cells represent objects through a distributed axis code. That code allowed them to reconstruct viewed objects and design optimal synthetic images. When subjects then imagined objects, roughly 40 percent of axis-tuned neurons re-used the same code, providing single-neuron evidence for a generative model in human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Varun S. Wadia, Chrystal M. Reed, Jeffrey M. Chung, Leah M. Bateman, Adam N. Mamelak, Ueli Rutishauser, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: Rapid concerted switching of the neural code in the inferotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Face-selective cells in macaque inferotemporal cortex first use a general code suited to detecting faces, then within about 20 ms the whole population switches to a face-specific code that supports fine discrimination of individuals. Tuning gradients along detection dimensions reverse and new high-dimensional tuning emerges, and this happens only for faces, not other objects. This challenges the view of fixed tuning functions and helps settle the debate over category-specific versus general codes in IT.
papers.authors: Yuelin Shi, Dasheng Bi, Janis K. Hesse, Frank F. Lanfranchi, Shi Chen, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: A compressed hierarchy for visual form processing in the tree shrew
papers.abstract: Neuropixels recordings across cortical and thalamic areas of awake tree shrews, a close relative of primates, reveal a primate-like hierarchy in receptive field size, latency and texture selectivity. However, area V2 already carries a full high-level object space and supports the best object decoding and reconstruction, indicating a compressed hierarchy. The work tests how universal primate-style ventral stream organization is.
papers.authors: Frank F. Lanfranchi, Joseph Wekselblatt, Daniel A. Wagenaar, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: Temporal multiplexing of perception and memory codes in IT cortex
papers.abstract: In macaque face patches AM and perirhinal cortex, the encoding axis for familiar faces is rotated relative to unfamiliar faces at long latency, while the initial response stays the same. Response magnitude alone is not a reliable familiarity signal, and the change appears to arise within IT cortex itself. Memory and perception are thus multiplexed in time within the same population, which a network model explains.
papers.authors: Liang She, Marcus K. Benna, Yuelin Shi, Stefano Fusi, Doris Y. Tsao

papers.title: Functional modules for visual scene segmentation in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI to locate patches in V2, V3, V3A, V4 and V4A that respond to figures versus ground across texture, motion, luminance and disparity cues, the authors targeted them for single-unit recording. Cells within these patches were more consistently tuned to figure-ground and borders than cells elsewhere. This indicates dedicated modules for segmentation in intermediate visual cortex.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Janis K. Hesse, Doris Y. Tsao

E090.name: Radoslaw Martin Cichy
E090.lab_name: Neural Dynamics of Visual Cognition Group
E090.bio: Radoslaw Martin Cichy investigates the neural basis of human visual cognition, specifically the transformation of retinal signals into object representations. Cichy utilizes a framework that combines fMRI, M/EEG, and behavioral data with deep neural network modeling to resolve cortical dynamics in space and time. They developed representational similarity analysis and fusion techniques to map the hierarchical correspondence between biological and artificial vision systems. Cichy’s current work examines the interaction of vision with language and attention, as well as the development of visual representations in early childhood.
E090.research_direction: Dr. Cichy's recent work investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics and computational principles of human visual processing by tightly coupling large-scale neuroimaging with artificial neural networks. Using multivariate EEG and backward masking, they are exploring how the brain transitions from early sensory representations to high-level semantic meaning, specifically mapping the time course of recurrent processing and fusing vision and large language models to predict neural responses. Their research also probes the spatial organization of the ventral stream, using self-supervised networks to test whether category-selective regions like the FFA and PPA can emerge from domain-general learning, and deploying in silico encoding models to discover how representational content is shared or isolated across the visual hierarchy. Additionally, Dr. Cichy has recently been characterizing how the visual system processes dynamic, naturalistic events by leveraging massive video-fMRI datasets to capture second-scale neural responses to real-world visual scenes.

papers.title: Self-supervised learning yields representational signatures of category-selective cortex
papers.abstract: The study asks whether face- and scene-selective regions like FFA and PPA can arise from a general visual learning mechanism. Applying a functional-localizer approach to both human fMRI and self-supervised networks, the authors identify selective units and compare them across a broad set of classic signatures such as curvature, animacy, size, mid-level features and spatial layout. Self-supervised models reproduce many of these signatures, supporting domain-general accounts of category selectivity.
papers.authors: Daniel Janini, Radoslaw Cichy

papers.title: In silico discovery of representational relationships across visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors introduce 'relational neural control', which uses encoding models to generate large numbers of synthetic fMRI responses in silico and then searches for images that make two visual cortical areas respond alike or differently. Exploring these controlling images reveals which visual areas share representational content and which carry unique content, yielding a network-level map of relationships across the visual hierarchy. The approach is a general way to turn brain-encoding models into hypothesis-generating tools.
papers.authors: Alessandro T. Gifford, Maya A. Jastrzębowska, Johannes J. D. Singer, Radoslaw M. Cichy

papers.title: Recurrence affects the geometry of visual representations across the ventral visual stream in the human brain
papers.abstract: Combining backward masking with multivariate analysis of EEG and fMRI, the study isolates recurrent processing in object vision. Recurrence reshapes representations from about 100 ms in early visual cortex, with additional phases near 175 and 300 ms in lateral occipital cortex, adding persistent rather than transient dynamics. Comparison with convolutional networks indicates that recurrence changes representational geometry in ways feedforward models do not capture.
papers.authors: Siying Xie, Johannes Singer, Bati Yilmaz, Daniel Kaiser, Radoslaw M. Cichy

papers.title: The time course of visuo-semantic representations in the human brain is captured by combining vision and language models
papers.abstract: Using a large EEG dataset recorded while people viewed object images, the authors build encoding models from a vision network, a large language model, and a fusion of both. The fusion model predicts EEG better than either alone or than earlier approaches, and the two model types explain complementary parts of the signal. Vision networks account for early responses while language models add later, meaning-related variance, tracing the transition from visual to semantic representation.
papers.authors: Boyan Rong, Alessandro Thomas Gifford, Emrah Düzel, Radoslaw Martin Cichy

papers.title: Modeling short visual events through the BOLD moments video fMRI dataset and metadata
papers.abstract: This paper releases the BOLD Moments Dataset, whole-brain fMRI from ten people who each viewed over a thousand 3-second naturalistic video clips, along with rich metadata. The authors show that the brain reflects word- and sentence-level descriptions of events, find memorability correlates reaching into parietal cortex, and show a hierarchical match between cortical regions and video-based neural networks. Time-resolved analyses demonstrate that the data capture second-scale dynamics of visual events.
papers.authors: Benjamin Lahner, Kshitij Dwivedi, Polina Iamshchinina, Monika Graumann, Alex Lascelles, Gemma Roig, Alessandro Thomas Gifford, Bowen Pan, SouYoung Jin, N. Apurva Ratan Murty, Kendrick Kay, Aude Oliva, Radoslaw Cichy

E093.name: Kalanit Grill-Spector
E093.bio: Kalanit Grill-Spector is a professor of psychology whose research examines the neural mechanisms of visual perception and their maturation throughout the human lifespan. Grill-Spector developed the fMRI-adaptation technique to probe the functional properties of cortical neurons and conducted studies on the ventral temporal cortex's role in face and object recognition. Their laboratory employs multimodal neuroimaging and computational modeling, including deep neural networks, to investigate how structural connectivity and visual experience drive the development of specialized brain regions. This research focuses on the relationship between cortical organization and the behavioral improvement of recognition abilities from infancy to adulthood.
E093.research_direction: Dr. Grill-Spector has recently been investigating the functional organization and development of higher-level visual cortex. Their recent work explores the origins of category-selective representations for stimuli like faces, places, and bodies, using infant fMRI, EEG, and diffusion MRI to track the early maturation of cortical responses and their underlying white matter scaffolding. In parallel, they have been employing topographic deep artificial neural networks to test whether single unified learning objectives, when constrained by spatial smoothness and wiring length, can successfully model the spatial layout of distinct processing streams across the human brain. Additionally, their research probes basic visual encoding mechanisms by fitting compressive spatiotemporal population receptive field (pRF) models to fMRI data to investigate whether nonlinear summation over space and time can explain phenomena like simultaneous suppression.

papers.title: A single computational objective can produce specialization of streams in visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether the separation of visual cortex into distinct processing streams needs separate objectives for each stream. Using topographic deep neural networks trained with a single unified objective, they show that stream-like specialization (e.g., for faces, bodies, places and scenes) emerges together with the spatial layout of responses seen in the human ventral, lateral and dorsal visual cortex. This supports a single-objective account of how functional organization in high-level vision arises.
papers.authors: Dawn Finzi, Eshed Margalit, Kendrick Kay, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: White matter connections of human ventral temporal cortex are organized by cytoarchitecture, eccentricity, and category-selectivity from birth
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI in newborn infants is used to map the white matter tracts connecting ventral temporal cortex to the rest of the brain. Already at birth, the connectivity of face-, place-, word- and limb-selective regions is distinguishable and tracks cortical cytoarchitecture and eccentricity. The result implies that the wiring that scaffolds category-selective cortex is present before extensive visual experience.
papers.authors: Emily Kubota, Xiaoqian Yan, Sarah Tung, Bella Fascendini, Christina Tyagi, Sophie Duhameau, Danya Ortiz, Mareike Grotheer, Vaidehi S. Natu, Boris Keil, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: A unifying framework for functional organization in early and higher ventral visual cortex
papers.abstract: The paper introduces the topographic deep artificial neural network (TDANN), which predicts the spatial organization of several ventral visual areas in primates. The model balances learning a general sensory representation against making responses spatially smooth on the cortical sheet, and the resulting representations are more brain-like than those of unconstrained models. It also suggests this balance trades task performance against wiring length between areas.
papers.authors: Eshed Margalit, Hyodong Lee, Dawn Finzi, James J. DiCarlo, Kalanit Grill-Spector, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: The emergence of visual category representations in infants' brains
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and EEG in infants during the first months of life, the study tracks when category-selective responses to faces, limbs and places appear. Category representations are weak in the youngest infants and become more distinct across the first year, with the greatest development in regions such as face-selective cortex. This challenges the idea that category selectivity is present at full strength from birth.
papers.authors: Xiaoqian Yan, Sarah Shi Tung, Bella Fascendini, Yulan Diana Chen, Anthony M Norcia, Kalanit Grill-Spector

papers.title: Rethinking simultaneous suppression in visual cortex via compressive spatiotemporal population receptive fields
papers.abstract: Simultaneously presented stimuli evoke smaller responses than the same stimuli shown one at a time. Rather than attributing this to attentional or competitive mechanisms, the authors fit a compressive spatiotemporal pRF model to fMRI responses and show that nonlinear summation over space and time accounts for the suppression across visual areas. The model provides a unified, image-computable explanation.
papers.authors: Eline R. Kupers, Insub Kim, Kalanit Grill-Spector

E096.name: James Haxby
E096.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
E096.bio: James V. Haxby works in cognitive neuroscience and introduced multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) to functional neuroimaging to decode high-level visual representations. Haxby’s research challenged modular theories of brain organization by demonstrating that faces and objects are represented by distributed, overlapping patterns of activity in the ventral temporal cortex. Recently, their work has focused on the development of "hyperalignment," a computational framework that maps idiosyncratic individual brain topographies into a common high-dimensional representational space. This methodology utilizes naturalistic stimuli, such as movies, to model the shared functional architecture of the human brain and investigate individual differences in neural tuning.
E096.research_direction: Dr. Haxby has recently been working on tools for mapping how the brain's functional organization differs and generalizes across individuals. Their recent work includes a model that describes the fine-grained tuning of each point on an individual's cortex, capturing both what a region responds to and how those responses are laid out across the cortical surface, while still generalizing across stimuli and tasks. They have also helped build a new cortical surface template from over a thousand brain scans, aimed at better aligning and comparing fMRI data across people. They have also written a historical account of the early brain imaging work that mapped object and spatial vision pathways at the NIMH.

papers.title: The Laboratory of Brain and Cognition: A Lab Is Born
papers.abstract: In this invited historical essay, Haxby recounts the founding of the Laboratory of Brain and Cognition (LBC) at the National Institute of Mental Health, describing how he, Cheryl Grady, and Barry Horwitz approached Leslie Ungerleider in the late 1980s with a proposal to use PET measurements of regional cerebral blood flow to map the ventral 'object vision' and dorsal 'spatial vision' pathways in the human brain. The piece traces the intellectual and institutional circumstances that led to LBC's founding, situates the lab's early PET studies within the broader emergence of functional neuroimaging as a tool for testing psychological theories of visual cortical organization, and reflects on how those foundational studies shaped the subsequent trajectory of research on the functional architecture of human visual and object perception.
papers.authors: James V. Haxby

papers.title: A cortical surface template for human neuroscience
papers.abstract: Existing cortical surface templates used for aligning and comparing fMRI and other neuroimaging data across individuals are typically built from a few dozen structural brain scans, limiting how well they represent population variability in cortical folding and surface area. The authors introduce 'onavg,' a new cortical surface template constructed from openly available high-quality structural MRI scans of 1,031 individual brains—roughly 25 times more brains than prior standard templates—yielding more uniform vertex sampling of the cortical surface and better representation of anatomical variability. They show that surface-based analyses (including functional alignment and group-level statistical mapping) performed using the onavg template achieve improved anatomical correspondence and downstream analytic accuracy compared with commonly used legacy templates, and they release onavg as an open resource for the human neuroimaging community.
papers.authors: Ma Feilong, Guo Jiahui, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby

papers.title: The individualized neural tuning model: Precise and generalizable cartography of functional architecture in individual brains
papers.abstract: The authors introduce the Individualized Neural Tuning (INT) model, a fine-grained model of cortical functional organization designed to capture idiosyncratic neural tuning at the level of individual cortical vertices while remaining generalizable across stimuli and tasks. Unlike coarser parcellation- or network-level approaches, INT jointly models representational content (what features a cortical location responds to) and topographic organization (how those response profiles are arranged across the cortical sheet) at fine spatial grain. Using naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI data, the authors show that INT-derived individual tuning maps generalize across independent stimulus sets and outperform standard hyperalignment and anatomical-alignment approaches at predicting held-out neural responses, demonstrating that INT provides a precise and generalizable cartography of idiosyncratic functional brain architecture.
papers.authors: Ma Feilong, Samuel A. Nastase, Guo Jiahui, Yaroslav O. Halchenko, M. Ida Gobbini, James V. Haxby

E099.name: Alexander Todorov
E099.bio: Alexander Todorov investigates social perception, focusing on the cognitive and neural mechanisms involved in forming impressions from facial appearance. Their lab employs data-driven computational methods and generative adversarial networks to visualize the perceptual structures underlying social judgments. By synthesizing behavioral experiments with functional neuroimaging, Todorov’s research characterizes systematic biases inherent in human face evaluation and analyzes their impact on real-world outcomes such as electoral success and judicial decisions.
E099.research_direction: Dr. Todorov has recently been investigating how human observers form complex social judgments and spontaneous impressions from faces, shifting focus from group-level averages to highly idiosyncratic individual differences. Their recent work explores how people mentally represent specific social traits—such as trustworthiness—as well as broader concepts like the "typical" face, utilizing generative AI models and reverse-correlation techniques to visualize an individual observer's unique, context-sensitive mental templates. Additionally, they are examining the cognitive mechanisms driving false facial stereotypes, specifically testing whether observers rapidly extract statistical regularities from very few exemplars and subsequently under-sample new information. Finally, Dr. Todorov is mapping the spontaneous content of facial evaluations by applying natural language processing to large-scale free-response descriptions, aiming to build a comprehensive taxonomy of the social, moral, and physical dimensions people use to judge naturalistic faces.

papers.title: A consistent but highly varied androcentric bias in the visual representation of "typical" faces
papers.abstract: Prior work found that mental images of a typical face look more female than male, at odds with the broader androcentrism literature. Using generative reverse correlation across two studies, the authors show that at the group level people equate a typical person with a man. They also find large individual differences in both typical-person imagery and typicality judgments, which complicates conclusions from aggregate data.
papers.authors: Daniel N. Albohn, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Individualized models of social judgments and context-dependent representations
papers.abstract: Most work on perception and judgment infers from group averages, yet for complex judgments like trustworthiness most of the meaningful variance is specific to the individual. The paper presents a data-driven reverse-correlation approach, built on generative image models, that visualizes an individual's own mental image of a social trait. The resulting photorealistic representations are reliable, psychologically valid, and sensitive to context (e.g., a person trusted to babysit versus one trusted to fix a car).
papers.authors: Daniel N. Albohn, Stefan Uddenberg, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Face evaluation: Findings, methods, and challenges
papers.abstract: A review of two decades of research on how people judge faces. It summarizes early emergence, cross-cultural consistency, links between trustworthiness and valence and resemblance to emotional expressions, and the role of data-driven computational models. It argues that most variance in complex judgments is idiosyncratic and describes a method for modeling individual observers.
papers.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Alexander Todorov, DongWon Oh, Stefan Uddenberg, Daniel N. Albohn

papers.title: Learning too much from too little: False face stereotypes emerge from a few exemplars and persist via insufficient sampling
papers.abstract: The paper proposes 'Insta-learn', a mechanism by which people quickly extract statistical regularities from very few examples and then stop sampling too early. Six experiments (N = 1,565) with computer-generated faces paired with behaviors, where the true face-behavior relationship was zero, showed that participants learned novel stereotypes from as few as three exemplars and under-sampled when free to choose. This offers an account of how false face stereotypes arise and persist.
papers.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
papers.authors: Xuechunzi Bai, Stefan Uddenberg, Brandon P. Labbree, Alexander Todorov

papers.title: Spontaneous content of impressions of naturalistic face photographs
papers.abstract: Two studies (N = 4,526) analyzed thousands of free-response descriptions of computer-generated naturalistic faces using AI-based text analysis to build a taxonomy of spontaneous impressions. Nearly all content fell into categories such as appearance, sociability, morality, ability, emotion, social group and status, with dimensions like uniqueness and health also common. The taxonomy improved prediction of overall face evaluations and hypothetical decisions.
