papers.authors: Gandalf Nicolas, Stefan Uddenberg, Alexander Todorov

E105.name: Jason Barton
E105.department: Departments of Medicine (Neurology), Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences, and Psychology
E105.lab_name: Human Vision and Eye Movement Laboratory
E105.main_research_area: higher visual and ocular motor function
E105.bio: Jason J. S. Barton is a Professor and Canada Research Chair at the University of British Columbia specializing in the neurology of visual perception and ocular motor control. Barton’s research investigates higher-level cortical processing using psychophysics, functional MRI, and studies of clinical populations with neurological deficits such as prosopagnosia and hemianopic dyslexia. Barton examines the mechanisms of face and word recognition, navigational orientation, and the volitional control of saccadic eye movements. Their current work also focuses on perceptual learning and rehabilitative programs designed to improve perceptual functions and reading plasticity in patients with cerebral lesions.
E105.research_direction: Dr. Barton has recently been investigating high-level visual processing and visual expertise, with a primary focus on how the brain recognizes faces and words. Their recent work explores the behavioral and structural variants of prosopagnosia, combining decades of patient data to map how distinct lesion profiles differentially impact face perception versus facial imagery. They are also utilizing modern computational tools to identify behavioral biomarkers, specifically applying deep learning to eye-tracking scanpaths to characterize gaze strategies in both developmental and acquired prosopagnosia. Furthermore, Dr. Barton investigates general mechanisms of visual expertise in healthy observers, designing novel tasks to directly compare face and word superiority effects and testing how linguistic versus purely visual task demands drive hemifield asymmetries during text processing.

papers.title: Imagery and perception in acquired prosopagnosia: Functional variants and their relation to structure
papers.abstract: Drawing on 25 years of testing, the study compares face-shape perception and imagery for famous faces in 23 patients with acquired prosopagnosia. Occipitotemporal lesions produced an apperceptive profile (poor perception, spared imagery), while severe imagery loss (amnestic profile) required right anterior temporal damage, often combined with other lesions. The results support a family of prosopagnosia variants tied to distinct lesion sites.
papers.authors: Jason J. S. Barton, Brad Duchaine, Andrea Albonico

papers.title: Face and word superiority effects: Parallel effects of visual expertise
papers.abstract: The authors built a face-superiority task modeled on the classic word-superiority test so the two categories could be compared directly in the same 40 participants. Real, pseudo and non-stimuli produced parallel accuracy and latency patterns for faces and words, and reaction times correlated across the tasks. This supports shared expert-processing mechanisms for faces and words.
papers.authors: Marko Chi-Wei Tien, Andrea Albonico, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: Scanning faces: a deep learning approach to studying eye movements in prosopagnosia
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks were trained on scanpath images to distinguish prosopagnosic from control face-viewing fixations. Only four fixations were enough to separate acquired prosopagnosia from controls (AUC about 80%), with biases toward the lower face and right eye, whereas developmental prosopagnosia looked more like degraded normal scanning. It demonstrates deep learning as a way to find behavioral markers in a disorder of face processing.
papers.authors: Atlas Kazemian, Ipek Oruc, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: Reading words versus seeing font or handwriting style: a study of hemifield processing
papers.abstract: Twenty-three subjects saw five-letter words in computer font or handwriting in a tachistoscopic task, matching either word identity or text style. A right-field advantage appeared only when reading the word, not when judging style, and text type had no effect. The field advantage for text thus reflects the linguistic task rather than stimulus style.
papers.authors: Helena Ghorbani, Gülcenur Özturan, Andrea Albonico, Jason J. S. Barton

papers.title: The 2024 Richardson Lecture: Prosopagnosia - A Classic Neurologic Deficit Meets the Modern Era
papers.abstract: This invited lecture review distills three decades of work into five observations about acquired prosopagnosia: distinct apperceptive and amnestic variants, clustering with other perceptual syndromes, additional deficits for expert object categories, selective sparing of some facial information such as expression, and modest improvement through training. It frames prosopagnosia as a window on expert-level visual processing.
papers.authors: Jason J. S. Barton

E107.name: Russell Epstein
E107.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of vision and navigation
E107.bio: Russell Epstein is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, where they direct the Epstein Lab and serve as the Director of Graduate Studies for the Department of Psychology. Epstein’s research characterizes the neural mechanisms supporting human scene perception, spatial navigation, and the formation of cognitive maps using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and behavioral psychophysics. Epstein identified the parahippocampal place area (PPA), and their ongoing work investigates how the brain integrates visual information with spatial memory to represent environmental landmarks and guide wayfinding across both physical and abstract domains.
E107.research_direction: Dr. Epstein has recently been investigating how the human brain constructs and utilizes spatial representations during naturalistic navigation. Using fMRI and virtual reality paradigms, their recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying our sense of orientation and place, probing how the cortex forms a neural compass for heading direction and how it integrates distinct visual perspectives into coherent scene representations. They are also studying the structural format of cognitive maps, specifically examining how these mental models adapt to different environmental layouts and how the brain encodes hierarchical, nested spaces. Broadening the scope of spatial cognition, Dr. Epstein is additionally asking whether these map-like spatial representations might serve as a more general cognitive medium for abstract thought and reasoning.

papers.title: Cognitive maps as a medium for thought
papers.abstract: This Trends in Cognitive Sciences article considers cognitive maps not only as devices for spatial navigation but as a format that the mind may use for thinking and reasoning more broadly. It brings together work on spatial and abstract map-like representations to argue for their general role in cognition.
papers.authors: Sami R. Yousif, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: A neural compass in the human brain during naturalistic virtual navigation
papers.abstract: Participants freely navigated a virtual-reality city while undergoing fMRI, and encoding-model analyses revealed voxel clusters in retrosplenial complex and superior parietal lobule that were tuned to the direction the person was facing. These directional tunings generalized across perceptually different versions of the city, across spatially separate locations, and across sessions, and a 7T dataset replicated the effect. The findings identify a candidate human neural compass that supports a stable sense of orientation during real-world-like wayfinding.
papers.authors: Zhengang Lu, Joshua B. Julian, Geoffrey K. Aguirre, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: Distinct Mechanisms for Panoramic and Landmark-Based View Integration in Human Place-Selective Cortex
papers.abstract: Navigators must combine different views into a coherent representation of a place. Participants learned a route through a virtual city in which storefronts were linked either by facing each other across a street (panoramic association) or by being views of the same distal landmark from different vantage points. fMRI showed that these two kinds of viewpoint integration engage different place-selective regions, indicating separable mechanisms for building place representations.
papers.authors: Linfeng Tony Han, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: Cognitive maps for hierarchical spaces in the human brain
papers.abstract: Everyday environments are often nested, with spaces inside other spaces. Participants learned a virtual courtyard containing a building and were scanned with fMRI while judging spatial relationships within and across the subspaces; integrating across subspaces cost accuracy and time behaviorally. Neural results indicated that the brain represents such hierarchical layouts with structure sensitive to the nesting of the subspaces.
papers.authors: Michael Peer, Russell A. Epstein

papers.title: The format of the cognitive map depends on the structure of the environment
papers.abstract: Across several experiments, participants learned virtual environments differing in structure and were tested on the spatial relationships between locations. The results show that the format of the resulting cognitive map is not fixed but depends on the layout and structure of the environment being learned, challenging one-size-fits-all accounts of spatial memory.
papers.authors: Michael Peer, Catherine Nadar, Russell A. Epstein

E109.name: Monica Castelhano
E109.bio: Castelhano is a Professor at Queen's University whose research investigates the cognitive mechanisms underlying visual attention, memory, and perception within real-world environments. They utilize eye-tracking and behavioral measures to analyze how initial scene representations, or "gist," facilitate eye-movement guidance during complex visual search tasks. Castelhano’s work on the surface guidance framework examines how spatial layout and object functional properties interact with semantic information to shape human visual cognition. Their recent studies integrate Virtual Reality to investigate these processes in three-dimensional, naturalistic spaces.
E109.research_direction: Dr. Castelhano has recently been investigating how prior knowledge and spatial structure guide visual attention and navigation in complex environments. Their recent work explores the mechanics of visual search in natural scenes by examining how human attention is driven by object spatial predictability—quantified through a novel Object Spatial Certainty Index—and semantic consistency. In addition to scene context, they are investigating how search operates across depth planes, specifically probing a "foreground bias" that prioritizes near-space targets and testing how scene priors might dynamically modulate this depth-based attention. Broadening their methodological scope, Dr. Castelhano is also utilizing Large Language Models to computationally model human scene expectations, while separately employing 3D virtual environments to study how self-motion and visual cues independently contribute to directional decision-making during spatial navigation.

papers.title: Modulating the Foreground Bias: How Scene Knowledge and Depth Structure Guide Visual Search
papers.abstract: Attention across depth is uneven, with near-space (foreground) information favored. Across two experiments using normal and mismatched 'chimera' scenes, targets in the foreground were found faster and with fewer fixations, and this was not explained by target size. A brief scene preview reduced the bias selectively in chimera scenes, so the foreground bias appears to be a strong default that scene knowledge can flexibly adjust.
papers.authors: Louisa Lok Yee Man, Hannah Lum Smith, Karolina Krzys, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: Where do I go from here?: Contribution of idiothetic and allothetic representations to directional decisions when switching environments
papers.abstract: Participants walked through a rendered 3D city street, entered an indoor space of low or high path complexity to induce disorientation, and then exited with the street view sometimes mirror-reversed. This dissociated self-motion-based (idiothetic) representations from visual-cue-based (allothetic) ones. The study tests how each contributes to directional decisions when moving between environments.
papers.authors: Karolina J. Krzyś, Piotr Francuz, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: Object spatial certainty as a measure of spatial variability and its influence on attention
papers.abstract: The authors introduce an Object Spatial Certainty Index that ranks 150 everyday objects by how consistently people expect them to appear in one region of a scene, from very predictable (boots) to very variable (plant). Using this index, two visual search experiments show that scene context helps search more for high-certainty targets than for low-certainty ones. Spatial variability of object locations is therefore a key determinant of how strongly scene knowledge guides attention.
papers.authors: Karolina J. Krzyś, Carmel Avitzur, Carrick C. Williams, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: A Framework for Leveraging LLMs for Scene Analysis and Cognitive Processing
papers.abstract: Building on the observation that people use prior knowledge of where objects usually appear to search efficiently, this paper proposes an annotation pipeline. It extracts a knowledge graph from automatically labeled objects in an image and feeds it to large language models to predict likely target locations. The approach is presented as a first use of LLMs to capture scene priors and link human scene understanding with computational models.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques
papers.authors: Catarina Moreira, Jeffrey Cockburn, Monica S. Castelhano

papers.title: Foreground bias: Semantic consistency effects modulated when searching across depth
papers.abstract: The study examines how the depth position of a target (foreground or background) interacts with whether the scene is semantically consistent during visual search. Foreground targets were found more efficiently, and this advantage changed with semantic consistency. Depth is therefore an important factor in how scene meaning guides search.
papers.authors: Karolina J. Krzyś, Louisa L. Y. Man, Jeffrey D. Wammes, Monica S. Castelhano

E110.name: Edward Silson
E110.department: School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences
E110.bio: Edward Silson is a Lecturer in Visual Perception and Cognition who investigates the neural mechanisms of human visual perception and its integration with memory systems. Silson utilizes high-resolution fMRI, population receptive field (pRF) modeling, and TMS to map the functional architecture of the visual cortex, focusing on scene-selective regions and the medial parietal cortex. They explore how cortical specializations for categories such as faces and places interact with long-term memory and how brain damage or retinal disease impacts these systems. Recently, Silson’s lab has employed EEG-fMRI fusion to characterize the top-down dynamics of mental imagery and the role of opponent visuospatial coding as an organizing principle of brain integration.
E110.research_direction: Dr. Silson has recently been investigating the functional architecture bridging visual perception, memory, and scene processing. Using fMRI and population receptive field modeling, their recent work explores how retinotopic coding acts as a spatial scaffold for perception-memory interactions, specifically examining opponent visuospatial codes in high-level cortical regions during both external viewing and internal recall. In parallel, they are examining the spatiotemporal dynamics of scene understanding and visual imagery, combining fMRI, MEG, and EEG to determine precisely when and where the visual system decodes mentally visualized categories and extracts navigational affordances from a given environment. Furthermore, they are interrogating the internal structural organization of established scene-selective networks, probing how fine-grained retinotopic map divisions drive the varied visual responses traditionally attributed to unitary regions like the occipital place area.

papers.title: Early spatiotemporal dynamics of navigational affordance coding in the dorsal visual cortex
papers.abstract: Combining fMRI, MEG and behaviour, this study asks where and when the brain extracts which routes through a scene are navigable. Affordance information appeared earliest in dorsal early visual cortex, about 110 ms after stimulus onset, before scene-selective regions, though the occipital place area's involvement was replicated. Affordance signals were weak for 33-66 ms presentations and became robust beyond about 132 ms, challenging accounts that place the key locus in higher-level scene areas.
papers.authors: Elisa Zamboni, Rebecca Lowndes, Richard Aveyard, Catriona L. Scrivener, Jessica A. Teed, Yumeng Ma, Antony B. Morland, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Opponent visuospatial coding structures responses during memory recall and visual perception in medial parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and population receptive field modelling, the study finds positive and negative pRFs within medial parietal cortex memory areas. The more different the timecourses of a positive/negative pRF pair, the more different their responses during both memory recall and visual perception, tasks with very different demands. This supports opponent visuospatial coding as an organizing principle linking internally and externally oriented processing.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: Visual imagery of familiar people and places in category selective cortex
papers.abstract: Participants formed mental images of personally familiar people and places in separate EEG and fMRI sessions. Category selectivity for imagery appeared in medial parietal, ventral temporal and other regions, and individual items could be decoded from fMRI and EEG. EEG-fMRI fusion indicated similar timing in medial parietal and ventral temporal cortex, with early place-selective fusion in ventral temporal cortex.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Jessica A. Teed, Edward H. Silson

papers.title: A retinotopic code structures the interaction between perception and memory systems
papers.abstract: The authors show that memory-related regions at the top of the cortical hierarchy, which are usually thought to use an abstract non-spatial code, carry inverted (negative) retinotopic maps that mirror the positive maps of category-selective perceptual areas. Paired perceptual and memory populations respond in a spatially specific, opponent fashion during both viewing and recall, suggesting mutual inhibition. Retinotopic coding is thereby proposed as a scaffold for perception-memory interaction.
papers.authors: Adam Steel, Edward H. Silson, Brenda D. Garcia, Caroline E. Robertson

papers.title: Retinotopy drives the variation in scene responses across visual field map divisions of the occipital place area
papers.abstract: Combining pRF modelling with representational similarity analysis, the study shows that the visual field maps overlapping the occipital place area respond differently to complex scenes. Seven candidate models based on scene properties, visual features and navigational affordances did not explain this, but differences in retinotopic profile across maps did. The OPA may therefore not be best treated as a single scene-selective region.
papers.authors: Catriona L. Scrivener, Elisa Zamboni, Antony B. Morland, Edward H. Silson

E111.name: Christopher Baldassano
E111.bio: Christopher Baldassano is an Associate Professor at Columbia University where they direct the Dynamic Perception and Memory Lab. Their research utilizes functional MRI, behavioral experiments, and machine learning to investigate how the human brain segments continuous experiences, such as narratives and films, into discrete event representations. Baldassano examines the computational mechanisms by which prior knowledge and schematic scripts influence the encoding and retrieval of information to connect high-level vision and episodic memory. Their work uses naturalistic stimuli and data analysis to characterize the processes by which the brain constructs and updates internal models of the world.
E111.research_direction: Dr. Baldassano has recently been investigating how the human brain structures continuous experiences into discrete events and leverages spatial contexts to build episodic memories. Their recent work explores the neural mechanisms of event segmentation, using fMRI and naturalistic stimuli like films and audio narratives to examine how repeated viewing and top-down attention dynamically shift the timescales and boundaries of perceived events. Additionally, they are studying how spatial schemas scaffold memory formation, measuring how neural pattern reliability in virtual reality memory palaces and longitudinal training in the Method of Loci support the conjunctive binding and cortical reinstatement of specific objects. Finally, Dr. Baldassano is probing how the hippocampus and higher-order visual regions hierarchically map temporal structures when individuals anticipate multi-step past and future events within learned sequences.

papers.title: Spatial contexts with reliable neural representations support reinstatement of subsequently placed objects
papers.abstract: Participants learned a 23-room virtual-reality memory palace, then watched videos of the rooms during fMRI so the reliability of each room's neural pattern could be measured. Rooms with more reliable patterns before encoding predicted stronger cortical reinstatement of objects later placed in them during recall. The effect was not explained by better retrieval of the rooms themselves and held for both group-level and idiosyncratic reliability.
papers.authors: Rolando Masís-Obando, Kenneth A. Norman, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Binding items to contexts through conjunctive neural representations with the Method of Loci
papers.abstract: Participants underwent a month-long Method of Loci training course and were scanned longitudinally as they memorized word lists by linking items to imagined loci. Neural patterns were captured for loci and items alone, for their integrated combination at encoding, and at retrieval, with participant descriptions of the associations. Default mode network regions carried conjunctive item-locus representations, giving a neural account of how schemas scaffold new episodic memories.
papers.authors: Jiawen Huang, Akshay Manglik, Nick Dutra, Hannah Tarder-Stoll, Taylor Chamberlain, Robert Ajemian, Qiong Zhang, Kenneth A. Norman, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: Repeated Viewing of a Film Clip Changes Event Timescales in The Brain
papers.abstract: Thirty participants watched three 90-second clips from a film six times each during fMRI. Hidden Markov models and pattern-similarity searchlights measured the strength of event structure at slow and fast timescales on each viewing. Most regions were stable, but some became finer or coarser in their event representations with repetition, showing that familiarity flexibly reshapes how experience is segmented.
papers.authors: Narjes Al-Zahli, Mariam Aly, Christopher Baldassano

papers.title: The brain hierarchically represents the past and future during multistep anticipation
papers.abstract: Participants learned sequences of virtual-reality environments and, during fMRI, anticipated environments several steps ahead in a given sequence. The hippocampus and higher-order visual regions coded temporal structure in both directions, with graded representations of past and future events. Farther events were represented in progressively more anterior regions, and hippocampal codes were sequence-specific and tied to anticipation response-time costs.
papers.authors: Hannah Tarder-Stoll, Christopher Baldassano, Mariam Aly

papers.title: Top-down attention shifts behavioral and neural event boundaries in narratives with overlapping event scripts
papers.abstract: The authors built 16 audio narratives that each combine a location script (e.g., restaurant, airport) with a social script (e.g., breakup, proposal). fMRI showed angular gyrus, parahippocampal cortex and medial prefrontal regions tracking scripts from both domains. Directing attention to one script shifted where listeners perceived event boundaries and moved neural boundaries in those regions.
papers.authors: Alexandra De Soares, Tony Kim, Franck Mugisho, Elen Zhu, Allison Lin, Chen Zheng, Christopher Baldassano

E112.name: Iris Groen
E112.bio: Groen is an Associate Professor and MacGillavry Fellow at the University of Amsterdam’s Informatics Institute, specializing in the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and computer vision. Their research examines the neural representation of real-world scenes and videos by employing human brain imaging techniques, including fMRI, EEG, and ECoG, alongside deep neural networks. Groen investigates how the human brain processes natural image statistics and extracts action affordances from the environment to understand the principles of biological vision. Through this interdisciplinary approach, they aim to develop bio-inspired models of perception and align artificial intelligence with human neural processing.
E112.research_direction: Dr. Groen has recently been investigating the spatiotemporal dynamics of naturalistic vision by combining neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and intracranial EEG with large-scale computational modeling. Much of their recent work explores dynamic video understanding, benchmarking hundreds of deep neural networks against brain data to determine which architectural and task-related factors best predict human neural responses over time. Additionally, they are examining how specific biological constraints—such as retina-like foveal sampling and short-term neural adaptation—shape the temporal profiles of visual processing across the cortical hierarchy. Finally, their research probes higher-level scene perception, using behavioral and neural measures to ask how the human visual system and artificial models encode locomotive action affordances in complex environments.

papers.title: The Human Brain as a Dynamic Mixture of Expert Models in Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Benchmarks more than 100 video and image models against time-resolved EEG responses to short natural videos. The results indicate that the brain does not match one single model. Instead, different models best explain different moments and stages of the response, in line with a dynamic mixture of experts, with implications for how video models are designed and evaluated.
papers.authors: Christina Sartzetaki, Anne W. Zonneveld, Pablo Oyarzo, Alessandro T. Gifford, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Pascal Mettes, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: Linking retinal sampling in neural encoding models to temporal profiles of visual processing in humans
papers.abstract: Adds retina-like spatial sampling (foveal versus peripheral) to CNN-based encoding models of human neural responses. Doing so reveals different temporal profiles for processing central and peripheral information. This ties the retinotopic organization of visual cortex to the timing of visual processing and improves model-brain predictions.
papers.authors: Niklas Müller, Hong-Ye Chen, Sofie Wahlberg, H. Steven Scholte, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: Representation of locomotive action affordances in human behavior, brains, and deep neural networks
papers.abstract: Asks how people perceive which locomotive actions (walking, swimming, climbing and so on) a scene affords. Combining behavioral ratings, fMRI and deep neural networks, it shows that scene-selective visual cortex carries affordance information that is not explained by objects, materials or scene category. Standard scene-trained DNNs capture this only in part, so affordance perception is not just a by-product of recognition.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Clemens G. Bartnik, Christina Sartzetaki, Abel Puigseslloses Sanchez, Elijah Molenkamp, Steven Bommer, Nikolina Vukšić, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: One Hundred Neural Networks and Brains Watching Videos: Lessons from Alignment
papers.abstract: A large comparison of 100 video and image networks against fMRI responses to natural videos. It examines which factors, such as temporal modeling, training task and architecture, drive alignment with different brain areas. The work gives practical lessons on what makes a model resemble the brain during dynamic vision.
papers.authors: Christina Sartzetaki, Gemma Roig, Cees G. M. Snoek, Iris I. A. Groen

papers.title: Temporal dynamics of short-term neural adaptation across human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Uses intracranial EEG recorded while patients viewed naturalistic images at varying durations and repeat intervals. Adaptation is slower and lasts longer in ventral and lateral occipitotemporal cortex than in early visual cortex V1-V3. A computational account of the response dynamics is supplied.
papers.authors: Amber Marijn Brands, Sasha Devore, Orrin Devinsky, Werner Doyle, Adeen Flinker, Daniel Friedman, Patricia Dugan, Jonathan Winawer, Iris I. A. Groen

E113.name: Hugo Spiers
E113.bio: Hugo Spiers is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at UCL whose research investigates how the brain constructs neural representations of space to support navigation, memory, and future planning. Spiers co-led the 'Sea Hero Quest' project, which utilized a mobile game to collect navigation data from millions of people worldwide to benchmark cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s risk. Their experimental methodology integrates high-resolution neuroimaging, virtual reality, and computational modeling to map the functional roles of the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex in complex spatial tasks. Current research directions involve environmental neuroscience and neuroarchitecture, focusing on how built environments and urban design influence human spatial behavior and neural dynamics.
E113.research_direction: Dr. Spiers's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying human spatial navigation and real-world behavior. They have recently been leveraging massive mobile gaming datasets to investigate how demographic and experiential factors, such as education and lifespan development, drive individual differences in wayfinding ability on a global scale. Their research also examines extreme spatial expertise by tracking how London taxi drivers allocate cognitive resources to plan routes across vast street networks, testing formal models of hierarchical decision-making. Furthermore, Dr. Spiers is investigating how regions like the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex process the spatial complexity and aesthetics of architectural spaces during naturalistic viewing, which aligns with their broader methodological push to integrate rigorous lab-based neuroimaging with ecologically valid human cognition.

papers.title: Determinants of individual navigation ability
papers.abstract: A Nature Reviews Psychology synthesis of why people differ so much in how well they find their way. It draws together evidence on cognitive, neural, developmental, demographic and experiential contributors to navigation skill, including findings from large-scale game-based and virtual-reality testing. It frames the current state of the field and points to open questions for explaining individual differences.
papers.authors: Emre Yavuz, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Brain Dynamics during Architectural Experience: Prefrontal and Hippocampal Regions Track Aesthetics and Spatial Complexity
papers.abstract: Participants in an fMRI scanner watched first-person films of journeys through buildings and cities and judged either spatial layout complexity or how pleasant the space was. Prefrontal valence-related regions tracked aesthetic quality, while hippocampal and prefrontal areas tracked spatial complexity, and later memorability was also assessed. The results link the neuroscience of navigation with the experience of architecture.
papers.authors: Lara Gregorians, Zita Patai, Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Fiona E. Zisch, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Expert navigators deploy rational complexity-based decision precaching for large-scale real-world planning
papers.abstract: The study tracks how London taxi drivers plan routes street by street across a network of more than 26,000 streets. Drivers appear to decide early on the hard, high-complexity junctions and leave simpler ones for later, in line with a rational resource-allocation account of planning. The work links real-world expertise to formal theories of planning and hierarchical decision-making.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Pablo Fernandez Velasco, Eva-Maria Griesbauer, Iva K. Brunec, Jeremy Morley, Daniel C. McNamee, Ed Manley, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Education Is Positively and Causally Linked With Spatial Navigation Ability Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: Using data from a navigation task built into the mobile game Sea Hero Quest, the authors measured wayfinding in nearly 400,000 people from 38 countries. Higher education was associated with better navigation, with the gap larger in some countries, and causal analyses (including a genetic approach) supported an effect of education on navigation ability. The scale of the dataset makes it a landmark for individual-differences research on spatial cognition.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Antoine Coutrot, Rogier A. Kievit, Stuart J. Ritchie, Ed Manley, Jan M. Wiener, Christof Hölscher, Ruth C. Dalton, Michael Hornberger, Hugo J. Spiers

papers.title: Ecological brain: reframing the study of human behaviour and cognition
papers.abstract: This paper argues for studying cognition in real-world settings while keeping the rigour of the lab. It proposes a cyclic framework that alternates between bringing the lab into the real world (wearables, mobile recording) and bringing real-world complexity into the lab (VR, naturalistic stimuli), combining exploratory and confirmatory research. It reviews the methods that make this feasible and lays out an interdisciplinary agenda.
papers.authors: Gabriella Vigliocco, Laura Convertino, Sara De Felice, Lara Gregorians, Viktor Kewenig, Marie A. E. Mueller, Sebastijan Veselic, Mirco Musolesi, Andrew Hudson-Smith, Nicholas Tyler, Eirini Flouri, Hugo J. Spiers

E114.name: Thomas Wolbers
E114.bio: Thomas Wolbers investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms of spatial navigation and their vulnerability to aging and neurodegeneration. Utilizing immersive virtual reality, high-field functional MRI, and computational modeling, Wolbers’ laboratory has identified age-related declines in entorhinal grid cell representations and head-direction signals in the human thalamus. Their research extends from the mapping of the brain's navigation circuit to the development of VR-based diagnostic markers and behavioral interventions. These applications are designed to enhance memory consolidation and address cognitive decline in clinical populations.
E114.research_direction: Dr. Wolbers has recently been investigating how spatial navigation networks degrade during healthy human aging and the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. Using immersive virtual reality paired with fMRI and PET imaging, their recent work explores how disruptions in specific spatial computations, such as entorhinal grid-cell-like coding and the neural representation of environmental boundaries, might mechanically link tau pathology to episodic memory decline. They are also utilizing biologically inspired computational models, including ring-attractor networks, to understand how small-scale neuronal loss and synaptic noise could drive age-related behavioral deficits in head-direction tracking. Furthermore, Dr. Wolbers is examining the fundamental cognitive architecture of spatial perception by combining eye-tracking and neuroimaging to disentangle the distinct neural mechanisms involved in updating one's own position versus updating the locations of external objects during self-motion.

papers.title: Entorhinal grid coding as a functional link between tau accumulation and episodic memory in human aging
papers.abstract: Cognitively normal older adults performed a virtual-reality navigation task during fMRI and also underwent tau PET and a delayed word-list recall test. Weaker grid-cell-like signal in the left entorhinal cortex was associated with poorer episodic memory, and higher entorhinal tau burden went along with weaker grid-like coding. The findings position entorhinal grid coding as a mechanistic bridge between early tau pathology and individual differences in memory aging.
papers.authors: Vladislava Segen, Tugce Belge Bernard, Gerard Callau Navarro, Philip Bahrd, Nina Behrenbruch, Bernd Schumann-Werner, Stephanie Schwarck, Berta Garcia-Garcia, Henryk Barthel, Osama Sabri, Michael Kreissl, Emrah Duzel, Anne Maass, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Path Integration and Spatial Updating Recruit Distinct Cognitive-Neural Mechanisms in Humans
papers.abstract: Combining an eye-tracking experiment with an fMRI study, the authors compared path integration (updating one's own start location) with spatial updating (updating other locations) from identical self-motion input. Participants showed different fixation patterns and faster responses in spatial updating, challenging the idea that path integration is the fundamental building block. Precuneus and dorsal premotor cortex were more active for spatial updating, indicating partly distinct neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Xiaoli Chen, Jan Wiener, Mary Hegarty, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Path integration impairments reveal early cognitive changes in subjective cognitive decline
papers.abstract: Using an immersive virtual-reality path integration task, the study compared people with subjective cognitive decline (a risk group for Alzheimer's disease) with healthy controls. A Bayesian model split path integration error into separate sources and showed that the group difference was driven mainly by increased memory leak, while velocity gain and sensory or reporting noise were unaffected. The authors propose that memory leak in path integration, which relies on the entorhinal grid system, could serve as an early behavioral marker of Alzheimer's-related change.
papers.authors: Vladislava Segen, Md Rysul Kabir, Adam Streck, Jakub Slavik, Wenzel Glanz, Michaela Butryn, Ehren Newman, Zoran Tiganj, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: How human aging disrupts the head direction network: evidence from VR experiments and mechanistic models
papers.abstract: The authors built an immersive VR paradigm that gives direct behavioral read-outs of the head-direction signal, together with a biologically inspired ring-attractor model. Older adults showed larger angular errors and greater heading uncertainty after a brief delay than younger adults. Adding synaptic noise and small-scale neuronal loss to the model reproduced the magnitude and dynamics of these age-related deficits.
papers.authors: Matthieu Bernard, Jonathan Shine, Andrej Bicanski, Thomas Wolbers

papers.title: Altered Coding of Environmental Boundaries in Human Aging: An fMRI Study
papers.abstract: Young and older adults performed a virtual object-location memory task in a square arena while undergoing fMRI. Both groups remembered objects near boundaries more accurately, but older adults' precision fell off more steeply with distance from boundaries. The neural coding of boundary distance in entorhinal cortex and subiculum was altered with age, linking boundary processing to age-related spatial memory decline.
papers.authors: Vladislava Segen, Matthias Stangl, Jonathan Shine, Thomas Wolbers

E119.name: Janice Chen
E119.bio: Janice Chen is an Assistant Professor at Johns Hopkins University who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the construction and retrieval of complex, real-world episodic memories. Their research utilizes naturalistic stimuli such as movies and narratives combined with functional neuroimaging and pattern analysis techniques to characterize how mnemonic and sensory systems interact. Chen has conducted studies on neural reinstatement and shared neural representations across individuals during the processing of continuous, semantically rich information.
E119.research_direction: Dr. Chen has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying how we process, segment, and remember naturalistic continuous experiences. Their recent work explores how the brain responds to event boundaries across the cortical hierarchy during movie viewing, as well as how a person's active agency within interactive stories shapes the personalization and temporal integration of their episodic memory. Using fMRI and continuous spoken recall paradigms, they are also examining the shared spatial codes and neural states within the posterior medial cortex that support the reactivation of complex social and action-oriented memories. Furthermore, Dr. Chen's research encompasses broader theoretical and methodological efforts, including formalizing the computational value of narratives for causal inference and creating highly granular, time-aligned neuroimaging datasets to propel the study of naturalistic memory retrieval.

papers.title: Interactive narratives reveal the personalizing effect of agency on episodic memory
papers.abstract: Participants read choose-your-own-adventure stories in which they had full, partial, or no control over what happened next. Across all conditions, causally and semantically central events were remembered best, but people with full control recalled more idiosyncratic sets of events and were less well predicted by generic sentence embeddings. Agency also made consecutive events more likely to be remembered or forgotten together, indicating that choice makes memory more personal and strengthens local temporal integration.
papers.authors: Xian Li, Nicole Kim Ni, Savannah J. Born, Ria J. Gualano, Iris Lee, Buddhika Bellana, Janice Chen

papers.title: A core set of neural states underlying memory reactivation of naturalistic events in the posterior medial cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI from people encoding and then freely recalling naturalistic movies, the authors identify a small set of stimulus-locked neural states in posterior medial cortex that have a spatial organization shared across individuals. Just 16 states reproduce the reactivation seen with standard methods, and the states relate to actions and social-affective features of the movie events. The work points to a common, spatially organized code in the posterior default mode network during natural recollection.
papers.authors: Yoonjung Lee, Hongmi Lee, Janice Chen

papers.title: The causal structure and computational value of narratives
papers.abstract: This review argues that narratives are valuable to the mind because they encode causal structure among events. The authors connect work on event memory, causal inference and reinforcement-learning-style computation to explain how stories support memory, prediction and decision making, and they lay out open questions for studying narrative as a cognitive tool.
papers.authors: Janice Chen, Aaron M. Bornstein

papers.title: The Relationship between Event Boundary Strength and Pattern Shifts across the Cortical Hierarchy during Naturalistic Movie-viewing
papers.abstract: The authors measured transient multivoxel pattern shifts at event boundaries of weak, moderate and strong salience during movie viewing. Auditory cortex showed clearly graded shifts with boundary strength, while long-timescale default-mode regions showed weaker, individual-level modulation. Stronger boundaries also produced better temporal alignment of shifts across the cortical hierarchy and greater hippocampal activity.
papers.authors: Yoonjung Lee, Janice Chen

papers.title: Word-timestamped transcripts of two spoken narrative recall functional neuroimaging datasets
papers.abstract: This data paper releases word-level timestamped transcripts of participants' spoken recall for two fMRI naturalistic movie-and-recall datasets. The transcripts allow recall speech to be aligned in time with brain activity and the original stimuli, making the datasets usable for fine-grained analyses of memory retrieval.
papers.authors: Savannah J. Born, Kathy Shi, Haemy Lee Masson, Hongmi Lee, Yoonjung Lee, Janice Chen

E121.name: Moshe Bar
E121.bio: Moshe Bar is a cognitive neuroscientist and former director of the Gonda Multidisciplinary Brain Research Center at Bar-Ilan University and the Cognitive Neuroscience Laboratory at Harvard Medical School. Bar’s research focuses on the "proactive brain" framework, exploring how the brain utilizes memory and contextual associations to generate top-down predictions that facilitate visual recognition and guide behavior. Utilizing neuroimaging methods such as fMRI and MEG, Bar investigates the neural substrates of scene perception, mind-wandering, and creativity. Their current work applies these cognitive principles to clinical neuroscience by examining how thought progression and predictive mechanisms are altered in mood disorders like depression.
E121.research_direction: Dr. Bar has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural dynamics of spontaneous thought, exploring how mind-wandering, curiosity, and creativity function as mental "play" and expressions of a unified novelty-seeking drive within the default mode network. Their recent work applies these insights to mood disorders by proposing a "thought progression" framework, which investigates whether depression is better characterized by the structural dynamics of thought—such as reduced speed, breadth, and flexibility—rather than just negative content. To test this mechanistic account of rumination and deep attractor states, they are conducting randomized controlled trials using gamified mobile apps designed to train fast, semantically broad associative thinking. Through these digital behavioral interventions, Dr. Bar is actively examining whether accelerating thought progression can successfully alleviate depressive symptoms and identifying the specific cognitive changes that mediate these clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Facilitating Thought Progression: A Neurocognitive Framework Linking Thought Dynamics and Mood Disorders
papers.abstract: Bar and Baror propose that depression is best understood as a disorder of thought dynamics rather than thought content. They describe five parameters (breadth, speed, flexibility, novelty and scope) that set how fluently thought progresses. Diminished progression, seen as repetitive, slow and narrow thinking, is tied to excess inhibition, reduced plasticity, blunted reward signalling and overly deep attractor states. The framework offers a testable mechanistic account and motivates interventions that expand associative thinking.
papers.authors: Moshe Bar, Shira Baror

papers.title: Facilitating Thought Progression via a Gamified Mobile Application for Depression: Possible Mediators of Outcomes
papers.abstract: This follow-up analysis of the gamified thought-progression app examines which psychological and cognitive changes might mediate its antidepressant effect. It probes how changes in thought dynamics relate to symptom improvement, helping to specify the mechanism of the intervention.
papers.authors: Paola Pedrelli, Joshua Curtiss, Sydney DeCaro, Isabella Henneman, Miranda Zea, Minna Behnan, Shira Baror, Bar Sofer, Shai-Lee Yatziv, Moshe Bar

papers.title: Spontaneous thought as play: the value of fictional goals in the default mode network
papers.abstract: The paper suggests that mind-wandering in the default mode network functions like play. The brain simulates fictional goals and scenarios at low cost, which sharpens prediction and can spark new ideas. It links this view to work on curiosity, creativity and the value of imagined outcomes.
papers.authors: Gaia Molinaro, Moshe Bar

papers.title: Facilitating Thought Progression to Reduce Depressive Symptoms: Randomized Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: The study tested a gamified mobile app that trains fast, semantically broad and creative associative thinking as a way to counter rumination. Participants using the app for 8 weeks (n=74) were compared with a waitlist control group (n=27). The app group showed reductions in depressive symptoms relative to controls, supporting thought progression as a treatment target.
papers.authors: Shai-Lee Yatziv, Paola Pedrelli, Shira Baror, Sydney Ann DeCaro, Noam Shachar, Bar Sofer, Sunday Hull, Joshua Curtiss, Moshe Bar

papers.title: A shared novelty-seeking basis for creativity and curiosity
papers.abstract: The authors argue that curiosity and creativity are two expressions of a single underlying drive to seek novelty. They show that both draw on the same cognitive faculties (memory, cognitive control, attention, reward) and the same interplay among the default mode, salience and executive control networks. They then propose a novelty-seeking framework that unifies the two and yields predictions for how the drive develops and is affected in health and disease.
papers.authors: Tal Ivancovsky, Shira Baror, Moshe Bar

E122.name: Elissa Aminoff
E122.bio: Elissa Aminoff is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Fordham University and the director of the Vision and Memory (VAM) Lab. Aminoff’s research investigates the psychological and neural mechanisms of high-level visual perception, specifically how it interacts with memory and contextual associations. They employ a multi-method approach combining neuroimaging (fMRI, EEG, MEG), computational modeling, and psychophysics to explore scene understanding and object processing. This research characterizes scene-selective brain regions and the involvement of these areas in processing the associations evoked by complex visual environments.
E122.research_direction: Dr. Aminoff has recently been studying how the brain represents scenes and how those representations relate to objects and memory. Their work uses large fMRI datasets to ask how the objects inside a natural scene shape activity in scene-selective brain regions, questioning the traditional split between scene and object processing. They have also been examining how self-perceived age relates to cognitive performance, and which factors such as mood and health might mediate that link. More broadly, they have contributed to philosophical and cognitive-science discussions of what it means to understand, and whether the world models in AI systems count as understanding.

papers.title: Levels of understanding, world models, and artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: A philosophy and cognitive-science paper on what it means to understand, and whether AI systems' world models amount to understanding. Written with Fordham philosophers.
papers.authors: Stephen R. Grimm, Joseph Vukov, Elissa Aminoff

papers.title: Examining Mediators of the Relationship Between Subjective Age and Cognition
papers.abstract: Although empirical work has established robust associations linking subjective age—the self-perceived age that an individual experiences relative to chronological age—to cognitive functioning, the intermediary pathways mediating this relationship remain largely undercharacterized. This investigation evaluated the predictive utility of subjective age on both objective cognitive performance and subjective cognitive assessments, specifically testing depressive symptomatology and self-rated health (SRH) as potential statistical mediators. Leveraging cross-sectional secondary survey data collected from a cohort of 247 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older, hierarchical linear regression analyses and formal mediation models were estimated. An older subjective age was significantly associated with decrements across subjective cognition metrics, with depressive symptoms and self-rated health operating as significant partial mediators of these associations. Given the clinical malleability of depressive affect and perceived health status, these factors provide tractable behavioral targets for interventions designed to preserve perceived cognitive vitality in aging adults.
papers.venue: GeroPsych: The Journal of Gerontopsychology and Geriatric Psychiatry
papers.authors: Karen L. Siedlecki, Veronika Kobrinsky, Elissa Aminoff

papers.title: Scene-selective brain regions respond to embedded objects of a scene
papers.abstract: Visual scenes are structurally defined by their embedded objects and associated affordances, yet high-level cortical processing of scenes has historically been conceptualized in functional opposition to object processing. Utilizing human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from the large-scale BOLD5000 dataset, this study examined whether constituent objects predict neural representational geometry across 1,179 unique natural scene exemplars distributed across 18 semantic scene categories. Representational similarity analyses of embedded object composition were conducted both across distinct semantic categories and among exemplars within identical scene categories. Neural response patterns across both scene-selective and object-selective visual cortex were significantly predicted by embedded object identities, with this effect manifesting as equally or more pronounced within scene-preferring regions. In particular, object composition explained significantly more variance when evaluating scenes within the same semantic category than across categories. These results indicate that the computational profile of scene-selective cortex directly encompasses the encoding of constituent objects, suggesting that functional specialization in higher visual cortex reflects processing demands deployed during interaction with stimulus arrays rather than categorical segregation by stimulus class.
papers.authors: Elissa M. Aminoff, Tess Durham

E125.name: Miriam Spering
E125.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
E125.bio: Miriam Spering is an Associate Professor at the University of British Columbia and director of the UBC EyeLab, specializing in the neural mechanisms of visual-motor control. Their research utilizes eye movements as a model system to investigate how the human brain transforms sensory signals into coordinated motor responses. By integrating visual psychophysics with high-resolution eye tracking and motion capture, Spering examines the intersection of perception and action in healthy populations, athletes, and clinical groups. Their investigations focus on identifying the sensorimotor signals underlying decision-making and developing ocular biomarkers for neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions, such as Parkinson's disease.
E125.research_direction: Dr. Spering has recently been investigating how the visual system turns motion signals into fast eye and hand movements. Their recent work explores how uncertainty in motion information, such as a target being shown briefly or hidden behind an occluder, affects the accuracy of catching or intercepting a moving object and the smooth pursuit eye movements that go with it. They also ask how eye movements and motion perception share mechanisms, how sounds can help the eyes stop tracking a target, and how the gap between what people report seeing and how their eyes respond can inform studies of consciousness. A related strand looks at eye-movement changes in Parkinson's disease as a window into basal ganglia circuits and as a possible diagnostic tool.

papers.title: Visual factors that determine sensory uncertainty in rapid interceptive hand movements
papers.abstract: Human manual interception and the accompanying smooth pursuit eye movements are fundamentally constrained by the reliability of visual motion signals, determined here through independent manipulations of presentation and occlusion durations. Using a simulated flyball paradigm, this study demonstrates that truncated target presentation durations lead to a significant center-of-distribution bias in hand interception endpoints, indicative of increased reliance on internal priors under conditions of high sensory uncertainty. Conversely, while long occlusions also degrade performance, short occlusion durations effectively resolve the center bias, provided that sufficient initial motion evidence was accumulated. Trial-by-trial correlations between oculomotor tracking accuracy and interception spatial/timing errors suggest that predictive mechanisms for both eye and hand movements operate on a unified readout of target motion information from the motion integration system.
papers.authors: Abibat A. Akande, Philipp Kreyenmeier, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Perception-action dissociations as a window into consciousness
papers.abstract: Experimental paradigms that reveal qualitative dissociations between perceptual reports and motor actions offer a robust methodology for identifying the neural correlates of conscious and unconscious processing. This perspectives article synthesizes evidence showing that human eye movements, particularly smooth pursuit, can accurately track stimulus motion even when the observer lacks conscious awareness of the motion direction due to binocular rivalry or flash suppression. Such dissociations demonstrate that the oculomotor system possesses a lower sensitivity threshold for certain motion signals than the perceptual system, accessing information that remains subliminal to phenomenal awareness. These findings highlight the functional autonomy of specific sensorimotor pathways and suggest that oculomotor responses provide a more nuanced indicator of visual processing than report-based measures alone.
papers.authors: Marisa Carrasco, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Shared Mechanisms Drive Ocular Following and Motion Perception
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the dynamics of neural motion integration in humans by comparing perceptual direction estimates with short-latency ocular following responses (OFR) to complex moving plaid stimuli. By systematically varying the contrast ratio between the two component gratings, the authors demonstrate that both eye movements and perceptual judgments exhibit an initial bias toward the high-contrast component direction before transitioning to pattern-based motion tracking as integration progresses. This temporal evolution of behavioral responses parallels the physiological shift from component- to pattern-tuning observed in direction-selective neurons within primate area MT. The presence of significant trial-by-trial correlations between tracking performance and perceptual reports further suggests that perception and the OFR utilize a common motion integration stage, establishing the OFR as a reliable behavioral proxy for neural integration dynamics.
papers.authors: Philipp Kreyenmeier, Romesh Kumbhani, J. Anthony Movshon, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Smooth pursuit inhibition reveals audiovisual enhancement of fast movement control
papers.abstract: Rapid sensorimotor control, such as the inhibition of ongoing smooth pursuit eye movements during target interception, utilizes multisensory signals to optimize performance in dynamic environments. Observers were tasked with suppressing pursuit as a target reached a hit zone, while congruency and timing of auditory motion cues were varied. The results indicate that auditory motion signals congruent with the visual target significantly improve both the latency and spatial precision of pursuit inhibition, reducing stop-signal delays and spatial variability. This cross-modal enhancement suggests that the low-level oculomotor circuitry responsible for fast motor decisions integrates auditory and visual information to enhance movement stability, confirming that multisensory integration facilitates the execution of high-speed motor control and reactive inhibitory processes.
papers.authors: Philipp Kreyenmeier, Israt Bhuiyan, Megan Gian, Hiu Mei Chow, Miriam Spering

papers.title: Eye movements in Parkinson's disease: from neurophysiological mechanisms to diagnostic tools
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) provides a critical clinical model for investigating the role of basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuitry in oculomotor regulation. This review delineates how dysfunction in the hyperdirect, direct, and indirect pathways manifests as hallmark oculomotor deficits, including prolonged saccadic latencies, reduced gain, and impaired smooth pursuit maintenance. The authors synthesize recent advances in utilizing these eye movement metrics as objective, non-invasive digital biomarkers for phenotyping disease progression and monitoring response to therapeutic interventions such as dopaminergic medication and deep brain stimulation. While current evidence suggests that eye movements lack the specificity required for standalone diagnosis, their integration into high-dimensional longitudinal datasets alongside other clinical indicators represents a promising avenue for precision neurology in movement disorders.
papers.authors: Chrystalina A. Antoniades, Miriam Spering

E129.name: John M. Henderson
E129.bio: John M. Henderson is a Professor of Psychology at UC Davis whose research examines the acquisition and manipulation of visual information from complex environments to guide behavior. Utilizing a multimodal approach including eye-tracking, fMRI, and computational simulations, Henderson investigates the cognitive processes underlying scene perception, reading, and visual memory. Their current research focuses on the role of semantics in gaze control, specifically through the development of 'meaning maps' to quantify how knowledge-based importance drives visual attention. Henderson also studies the neural correlates of fixation durations and the interaction between vision and language during naturalistic tasks.
E129.research_direction: Dr. Henderson has recently been studying how people decide where to look in real-world scenes and how the meaning of a scene guides attention. Their recent work explores how a quick impression of a scene's gist creates expectations about which objects belong, and how turning a scene upside down weakens those expectations. They use meaning maps and a vision-language transformer model to estimate which image regions carry the most semantic information, and test whether this predicts how quickly changes are noticed. They also examine how meaning guides looking in infants, and how older adults use schema knowledge, meaning what they expect to find in a scene, to help or mislead their memory.

papers.title: Scene inversion impairs activation of scene-object semantic bias
papers.abstract: This study examines the top-down mechanisms of gist-activated scene-object semantic bias in parsing complex naturalistic environments. Utilizing a brief presentation paradigm with upright and inverted scenes, the researchers assessed how global semantic structure modulates the activation of expectations for semantically consistent versus inconsistent objects. Findings reveal that scene inversion significantly attenuates and delays the activation of these biases. Furthermore, the results highlight a hierarchical processing advantage, where superordinate-level semantic biases are activated earlier and exhibit greater robustness than basic-level biases, providing evidence for the functional priority of global scene gist in driving local semantic associations.
papers.authors: Alan Z. Lu, John M. Henderson

papers.title: DeepMeaning: Estimating and Interpreting Scene Meaning for Attention Using a Vision-Language Transformer
papers.abstract: The authors introduce DeepMeaning, a computational framework leveraging the Contrastive Captioner (CoCa) vision-language transformer to quantify local scene semantics and their influence on attentional guidance. By mapping image-text embeddings from a model trained on large-scale datasets, the framework estimates patch-level meaning and decomposes these representations into four primary semantic dimensions: object density, figure-ground organization, interaction potential, and local context consistency. Results indicate that these dimensions collectively account for over 50% of the explainable variance in human meaning ratings and fixation density, demonstrating that multimodal transformers can effectively serve as interpretable models for scene-based cognitive guidance.
papers.authors: Taylor R. Hayes, John M. Henderson

papers.title: Meaning maps predict reaction time in change detection
papers.abstract: Investigating the role of high-level semantic representations in visual change detection, this research employs a data-driven meaning-map methodology within a classic flicker paradigm. Across two experiments, the authors demonstrate that changes occurring in regions of high semantic informativeness (local meaning) are detected significantly faster than those in low-meaning regions, an effect that persists after statistically controlling for low-level image saliency. The observed semantic advantage was markedly reduced under scene inversion, suggesting that the visual system prioritizes the comparison of semantic features maintained in working memory for detecting environmental modifications.
papers.authors: Alan Z. Lu, Aditya Upadhyayula, John M. Henderson

papers.title: How schema knowledge influences memory in older adults: Filling in the gaps, or leading memory astray?
papers.abstract: This investigation explores the complex dynamics of schema-congruency effects on episodic memory in the context of cognitive aging. Using a spatial recall task for target objects in congruent or incongruent scene locations, the authors contrast compensatory and impairment-based accounts of age-related schema reliance. The findings demonstrate that increased schematic influences on spatial memory in older adults are statistically mediated by declines in recollection-based memory processes. The data suggest that schema knowledge serves as a compensatory scaffold when precise episodic details are unavailable, with recollection acting as a primary mechanism capable of overriding schematic bias in both young and older populations.
papers.authors: Michelle M. Ramey, Andrew P. Yonelinas, John M. Henderson

papers.title: The role of local meaning in infants' fixations of natural scenes
papers.abstract: The study characterizes the developmental trajectory of semantic influences on visual attention by evaluating the impact of local meaning on the fixation patterns of infants aged 4 to 12 months. Controlling for physical saliency and center bias through meaning-map and saliency-map comparisons, the researchers found that infants increasingly prioritize semantically informative scene regions for fixation as they mature. This provides the first empirical evidence for an age-related shift from predominantly feature-driven (bottom-up) attentional control to more meaning-driven (top-down) guidance during the first year of life, aligning infant scene-viewing behavior with adult-like cognitive priorities.
papers.authors: Lisa M. Oakes, Taylor R. Hayes, Shannon M. Klotz, Katherine I. Pomaranski, John M. Henderson

E131.name: Doug Munoz
E131.department: Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Psychology, and Medicine
E131.bio: Douglas P. Munoz is a Professor at Queen’s University and the founding director of the Queen’s Centre for Neuroscience Studies. Munoz's research investigates the neural circuitry governing saccadic eye movements, pupillary responses, and blinking, with a focus on the roles of the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and superior colliculus. By integrating behavioral neurophysiology, neuroimaging, and high-resolution eye-tracking, their laboratory develops quantitative metrics to evaluate sensory, motor, and cognitive brain functions. Their work focuses on translating these findings into clinical applications, specifically establishing eye-tracking biomarkers for the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of neurological and psychiatric disorders, including Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease.
E131.research_direction: Dr. Munoz's recent work explores the behavioral and neural dynamics of the oculomotor system, bridging basic neurophysiology with clinical biomarker development. In fundamental vision science, they have recently been investigating how midbrain saliency computations in the macaque superior colliculus drive fixation durations during the free viewing of dynamic natural scenes. Their human behavioral research also characterizes basic physiological mechanisms, examining the nonlinear dynamics of luminance-evoked pupil responses and mapping how the strategic timing of blinks during cognitive tasks adapts across the human lifespan. Clinically, they are investigating how performance on pro- and anti-saccade tasks can serve as a scalable, non-invasive biomarker for Parkinson's disease, utilizing longitudinal data and machine learning to predict future motor deficits like freezing of gait and to classify stages of cognitive decline.

papers.title: Learning to Blink Strategically Is Crucial to Performance in a Predictable Saccade Task and Varies Across the Lifespan
papers.abstract: In 703 healthy participants aged 5-91 performing an interleaved pro/anti-saccade task, the study examined how people learn to time blinks around task-relevant stimuli. Participants rapidly suppressed blinks when they would compromise antisaccade execution and blinked more when visual input mattered less. Better blink-timing adaptation related to better performance, and the pattern changed across the lifespan.
papers.authors: Isabell C. Pitigoi, Donald C. Brien, Heidi C. Riek, Blake K. Noyes, Rachel Yep, Olivia G. Calancie, Ryan H. Kirkpatrick, Brian C. Coe, Michele Morningstar, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Saliency Response in Superior Colliculus at the Future Saccade Goal Predicts Fixation Duration during Free Viewing of Dynamic Scenes
papers.abstract: Macaques freely viewed natural videos while neurons were recorded in the superficial and intermediate superior colliculus, and a computational saliency model was used to quantify saliency at each upcoming saccade goal. Higher saliency at the goal, especially from motion and edge features, went with shorter fixations before the saccade. Colliculus visual saliency responses at the goal also predicted fixation duration, tying midbrain saliency coding to the timing of natural gaze behavior.
papers.authors: Jessica Heeman, Brian J. White, Stefan Van der Stigchel, Jan Theeuwes, Laurent Itti, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: The relation of eye movements to the occurrence of freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Using longitudinal data from the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative, the study asked whether baseline eye-movement abnormalities predict who will later develop freezing of gait in Parkinson's disease. Slower anti-saccade reaction times and higher error rates, together with upper-limb rigidity, predicted freezing of gait within two years. The authors argue that oculomotor deficits mark a prodromal phase of freezing pathogenesis.
papers.authors: Juan Fernandez-Ruiz, Heidi C. Riek, Donald C. Brien, Brian C. Coe, David A. Grimes, Anthony E. Lang, Connie Marras, Mario Masellis, Richard H. Swartz, Brian Tan, Malcolm A. Binns, Stephen R. Arnott, the ONDRI Investigators, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Main Sequence of Human Luminance-evoked Pupil Dynamics
papers.abstract: Pupil responses to luminance changes were measured in young adults to characterize nonlinearities and inter-individual variability. Final diameter is linear in log-luminance, while constriction (but not dilation) peak change and velocity are nonlinear in log-luminance. Across participants, overall pupil size correlates with pupil gain, yielding a stereotyped main-sequence-like relationship that aids interpretation of pupil data.
papers.authors: Jonathan D. Coutinho, Jeff Huang, Philippe Lefèvre, Gunnar Blohm, Douglas P. Munoz

papers.title: Classification and staging of Parkinson's disease using video-based eye tracking
papers.abstract: Video-based eye tracking during an interleaved pro/anti-saccade task was combined with machine learning to build a simple, non-invasive classifier for Parkinson's disease and its cognitive stages (mild cognitive impairment, dementia). The classifier reached an AUC of 0.88 overall and about 0.95 for dementia, with confidence scores tracking disease severity. This supports oculomotor measures as scalable biomarkers.
papers.authors: Donald C. Brien, Heidi C. Riek, Rachel Yep, Jeff Huang, Brian Coe, Christopher Areshenkoff, David Grimes, Mandar Jog, Anthony Lang, Connie Marras, Mario Masellis, Paula McLaughlin, Angela Roberts, Brian Tan, Derek Beaton, Wenlu Lou, Richard Swartz, the ONDRI Investigators, Douglas P. Munoz

E136.name: Tirin Moore
E136.bio: Tirin Moore is the Ben Barres Professor of Neurobiology at Stanford University and an Investigator of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Moore’s research investigates the neural circuits integrating visual perception with motor control, particularly the mechanisms of selective attention and gaze control in primates. This work identifies a causal link between prefrontal cortical activity in the frontal eye fields and the modulation of visual signals in the extrastriate cortex. Moore’s laboratory uses neurophysiological methods, including large-scale, high-density electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological perturbations, to examine the circuit-level logic of cognitive functions.
E136.research_direction: Dr. Moore's recent work explores how large-scale cortical populations in macaques encode complex visual features, maintain working memory, and map sensory inputs to motor responses. Using high-density recordings across multiple visual areas, they have recently been investigating the microcircuitry underlying contextual visual processing, such as how interlaminar signal flow in V1 computes border ownership, how area MT organizes pattern and component motion cells to compute object motion, and how extrastriate neuronal ensembles track objects hidden behind occluders. Additionally, their research examines the prefrontal mechanisms of spatial working memory, looking beyond persistent firing models to explore how intermittent neural bursts and cue-specific network states maintain information over a delay. Finally, they are probing the influence of top-down cognitive control, testing how feedback from the frontal eye field shapes activity in area V4 to reflect rule-dependent motor preparation rather than purely spatial representations.

papers.title: A modular neural circuit for computing the motion of objects
papers.abstract: Using high-density probes in macaque area MT, the study shows that neurons tuned to component motion and neurons tuned to pattern motion are distinct cell types in a hierarchical circuit, with pattern cells pooling inputs from component cells. The two populations are also spatially segregated into modules across cortical columns that map motion direction. The organization matches a classic theoretical solution for computing object motion.
papers.authors: Ethan Trepka, Chenyi Yue, Ruobing Xia, Shude Zhu, Sharif Saleki, Danielle A. Lopes, Stephen Nino Cital, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Dependence of contextual modulation in macaque V1 on interlaminar signal flow
papers.abstract: Neuropixels recordings across layers of macaque V1 measured border-ownership modulation, a signal that depends on context beyond the classical receptive field. Neurons within a column preferred the same side of an object, and interlaminar cross-correlations differed for stimulation outside versus inside the receptive field. Stronger border-ownership modulation accompanied more signal flow from feedback and horizontal layers to input layers.
papers.authors: Shude Zhu, Yu Jin Oh, Ethan B. Trepka, Xiaomo Chen, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Ensemble Coding of Hidden Objects in Visual Cortex
papers.abstract: Macaques tracked objects that passed behind an occluder while large populations in dorsal extrastriate cortex were recorded. Firing rates carried the hidden object's trajectory but lost its identity before the trial ended, yet pairwise correlations between neurons still depended on which object was hidden. Thus visual cortex retains information about occluded objects in coordinated ensemble activity rather than in single-neuron rates.
papers.authors: Shude Zhu, Danielle A. Lopes, Stephen Nino Cital, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Robust encoding of stimulus-response mapping by neurons in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Monkeys alternated between two tasks that used different rules to map a remembered cue location onto an eye movement. Delay-period activity in area V4 signaled the cue location only in a way that depended on the rule, indicating that it reflects preparation of the appropriate motor response rather than spatial working memory alone. Inactivating the frontal eye field reduced this motor-related activity.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Donatas Jonikaitis, Ruobing Xia, Tirin Moore

papers.title: Intermittent rate coding and cue-specific ensembles support working memory
papers.abstract: Recordings from large populations of prefrontal neurons in monkeys performing a spatial working-memory task show that memories are not held by steady, persistent firing. Instead, information is carried by brief bursts of activity together with ensembles of neurons that are specific to the remembered cue, and these patterns explain how a memory is maintained across a delay. The work reframes how prefrontal circuits store information over time.
papers.authors: Matthew F. Panichello, Donatas Jonikaitis, Yu Jin Oh, Shude Zhu, Ethan B. Trepka, Tirin Moore

E140.name: Eckart Zimmermann
E140.bio: Eckart Zimmermann is a Professor of Perceptual Psychology at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, where they investigate the mechanisms underlying visual stability and spatial perception. Zimmermann’s research focuses on how the brain maintains a representation of the environment during retinal shifts caused by saccadic eye movements. Utilizing psychophysical methods, eye-tracking, and fMRI adaptation, they study spatiotopic coding, the role of efference copies in sensory attenuation, and the repulsive aftereffects of visual adaptation. Their work also addresses numerosity perception and the processes by which motor actions, such as walking, calibrate the visual perception of distance.
E140.research_direction: Dr. Zimmermann's recent work explores how the brain uses internal models to predict the sensory consequences of self-generated actions, framing movements as perceptual experiments that continuously calibrate spatial and temporal processing. They have recently been investigating visual stability phenomena like saccadic omission and serial dependence, asking whether our failure to perceive motion blur during eye movements stems from learned sensorimotor contingencies rather than dedicated suppression mechanisms.
