Their research also examines how these internal predictions are updated via sensory feedback, utilizing immersive virtual reality paradigms to test whether disrupted efference-copy mechanisms can explain atypical sensorimotor behaviors in individuals with high autistic traits. Broadening this predictive framework beyond vision, they are also probing the somatosensory system by matching active and passive movement kinematics to understand how motor prediction influences tactile sensitivity and sensory gating.

papers.title: Actions as perceptual experiments
papers.abstract: A review of how actions serve as experiments that test and recalibrate internal spatial and temporal hypotheses. It covers post-saccadic errors that induce serial dependencies, comparisons of expected and sensed motion during eye-head gaze shifts, and prediction-driven changes in sensory attenuation. The authors argue these findings converge on a single error-driven calibration principle.
papers.authors: Eckart Zimmermann, Antonella Pomè

papers.title: Reduced prediction updating shapes serial dependence in autistic traits
papers.abstract: Using an immersive virtual-reality penalty-kick task, the study examines whether serial dependence reflects feedback-based updating of internal models. Participants with higher autistic traits updated their predictions less after feedback, producing altered serial dependence. This suggests that reduced model updating underlies atypical sensorimotor behaviour in autism.
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Michael Wiesing, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Movement enhances tactile sensitivity through prediction
papers.abstract: Touch is normally dampened during movement. By matching kinematics precisely between active and passive movements, the study shows that sensitivity is reduced in both, but that predicting the movement's consequences can enhance tactile sensitivity. The results challenge accounts that attribute sensory gating purely to motor execution.
papers.authors: Pierangelo Nicolas D'Onofrio Pacheco, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Disrupted sensorimotor predictions in high autistic characteristics
papers.abstract: People with high autistic traits were tested on saccadic omission, the normal failure to notice the self-generated visual motion produced by rapid eye movements. Their omission was weaker, consistent with a reduced ability to predict the visual consequences of their own saccades. The study ties the sensory symptoms of autism to impaired efference-copy-based prediction.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Eckart Zimmermann

papers.title: Prediction of sensorimotor contingencies generates saccadic omission
papers.abstract: The authors ask why we do not see the blur caused by our own saccades. Rather than a dedicated suppression mechanism, they show that the visual system learns the expected sensory consequences of saccades and habituates to them, so the predicted motion is omitted from awareness. Manipulating those contingencies changes what is omitted.
papers.authors: Antonella Pomè, Nadine Schlichting, Clara Fritz, Eckart Zimmermann

E141.name: Melvyn A. Goodale
E141.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Physiology and Pharmacology
E141.bio: Melvyn A. Goodale is a Distinguished University Professor Emeritus at Western University and co-proposed the "two-visual-systems" hypothesis, which dissociates the ventral stream for object perception from the dorsal stream for the visual control of action. Goodale’s research utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and kinematic behavioral analysis to investigate the neural pathways underlying visual processing in both healthy individuals and patients with neurological damage. Their work demonstrates how the brain separates conscious visual experience from the unconscious motor programming required for interacting with the physical world.
E141.research_direction: Dr. Goodale's recent work continues to explore the functional architecture of the visual system, with a strong focus on the perception-action dissociation and the respective roles of the dorsal and ventral streams. To test the boundaries of these pathways, they are investigating whether the dorsal stream is involved in global shape perception using data from neuropsychological patients, as well as examining how pictorial size illusions influence grasping behavior across left- and right-handed individuals. In the broader context of motor control, their research also probes how evolutionarily older subcortical visual circuits interact with newer cortical networks to regulate rapid, visually guided actions. Additionally, Dr. Goodale has recently been bridging biological and machine vision by evaluating facial age estimation in human observers and artificial intelligence, developing analytical frameworks that decompose overall estimation errors into systematic bias and random noise.

papers.title: A new framework for facial age estimation in humans and AIs
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a way to evaluate age estimates made from faces by splitting the overall error into random noise and systematic bias. Applying this to both human observers and AI age-estimation systems, it shows that comparing them on raw accuracy alone hides important differences in how each one goes wrong. The framework gives a cleaner basis for judging and improving face-based age estimation.
papers.authors: Tzvi Ganel, Yarden Mazuz, Daniel Algom, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: Linking past and present worlds in the visual control of behavior
papers.abstract: An open peer commentary arguing that evolutionarily old subcortical visual pathways remain functional in humans alongside newer cortical networks. The authors suggest cortex presets these subcortical circuits to allow or suppress very fast actions when needed. This offers a layered rather than replacement view of how vision evolved to control behavior.
papers.authors: Melvyn A. Goodale, Brian D. Corneil

papers.title: Revisiting the effect of visual illusions on grasping in left and right handers
papers.abstract: This study re-examines whether pictorial size illusions influence grasping differently in left- and right-handed people, a claim that bears on the perception-action dissociation. It tests grasp and perceptual responses in both handedness groups to see whether the motor system is equally resistant to the illusions. The results speak to how robust the two-visual-systems account is across individuals.
papers.authors: Tzvi Ganel, Melvyn A. Goodale

papers.title: Shape perception does not require dorsal stream processing
papers.abstract: Responding to recent claims that the dorsal visual stream is needed to perceive object shape, the authors argue the evidence does not support that conclusion. They point to neuropsychological findings and the wider literature indicating that ventral-stream processing is sufficient for shape perception, while the dorsal stream serves action control. The piece defends the perception-action division of labor.
papers.authors: Melvyn A. Goodale, A. David Milner

papers.title: Patients with dorsal-stream lesions can perceive global shape
papers.abstract: A follow-up reply arguing that patients with damage to the dorsal stream still show intact perception of global object shape. The authors use this patient evidence to support the view that conscious shape perception depends on the ventral stream rather than dorsal regions. It reinforces their case against dorsal involvement in shape perception.
papers.authors: Melvyn A. Goodale, A. David Milner

E143.name: J. Randall Flanagan
E143.department: Department of Psychology and Centre for Neuroscience Studies
E143.bio: Flanagan’s research examines the cognitive, computational, and neural mechanisms involved in the planning, control, and learning of human actions, specifically object manipulation. Using methodologies such as robotic interfaces, eye-tracking, and functional magnetic resonance imaging, Flanagan analyzes how the brain integrates sensory feedback with internal models to predict and adapt to environmental dynamics. Their work addresses eye-hand coordination and the predictive nature of gaze behavior during tool use and manual interaction. Current research investigates the whole-brain dynamics of sensorimotor adaptation and the manifold structures within the cerebellar-cortical network that underlie motor reinforcement learning.
E143.research_direction: Dr. Flanagan has recently been investigating the intricate coordination of eye and hand movements during goal-directed actions, focusing on how the brain allocates gaze and integrates sensory feedback to guide movement. Their recent work explores how various oculomotor behaviors, ranging from involuntary microsaccades and gaze anchoring to smooth pursuit, interact with reach execution, specifically asking how vision is shared between guiding the hands and monitoring the broader environment. By employing robotic manipulanda, visual perturbations, and altered haptic conditions, they examine how tactile feedback modulates visual fixation demands and how peripheral vision enables rapid visuomotor corrections even when the eyes are engaged in moving tracking tasks. Additionally, they are utilizing hybrid reinforcement learning models to understand how humans learn to navigate reachable space, probing how state familiarity, effector costs, and haptic feedback drive the shift between model-based and model-free motor control strategies.

papers.title: Managing Gaze Competition during Simultaneous Manual Action Control and Environment Monitoring
papers.abstract: People often manipulate objects while also watching the environment for events that require central vision, so gaze must be shared between the two tasks. Participants grasped and placed balls while detecting probabilistic visual events. They kept action-task fixations brief and used them to direct the hand, relying on touch to finish grasping and placing, but fixated longer to guide the hand when a tool reduced tactile feedback. They also timed gaze and hand movements around the statistics of the monitoring events to reduce conflicts.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Roland S. Johansson, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Adaptive integration of model-based and model-free strategies in human reinforcement learning of reachable space
papers.abstract: Using a robotic maze task in which people learn to move a handle around obstacles within reachable space, the study fits hybrid reinforcement-learning models to reach trajectories. Participants gradually shift from model-based to model-free control, more so for familiar states, states far from the goal, and with haptic-only feedback, and greater model-free reliance goes with faster movements. Compared with a matched virtual navigation task, reachable space showed stronger model-free reliance, suggesting a shared computational architecture tuned to effector costs.
papers.authors: Tianyao Zhu, Rohaan Syan, Shrika Vejandla, Jason P. Gallivan, Daniel M. Wolpert, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Rapid responses to reach errors are equally strong during fixation and visual pursuit
papers.abstract: Rapid visuomotor corrections of reaching depend on peripheral vision of the hand. This study asked whether these corrections are disrupted when the eyes are smoothly pursuing a moving target rather than fixating. Corrective gain after visual perturbation of the hand was unchanged by gaze task, though pursuit performance dipped slightly during reaching, indicating that pursuit and reach-related visuomotor processing run largely independently.
papers.authors: Renato Moraes, Jolande Fooken, Jason P. Gallivan, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Microsaccadic modulation in goal-directed reaching
papers.abstract: The study examines how small involuntary eye movements called microsaccades change while people fixate during reaching movements. Microsaccade behavior was modulated by the demands and timing of goal-directed reaching, linking oculomotor fixation control to action planning and execution.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Renato Moraes, Allison M. Scott, J. Randall Flanagan

papers.title: Gaze-related functions driving gaze anchoring in reaching
papers.abstract: When reaching to a target, gaze typically stays anchored on it even if a competing saccade target appears. The authors compared visual targets with visual-haptic targets that give force feedback on contact, and found anchoring in both, but limited to the initial directing phase of the reach when touch confirms attainment. In bimanual reaching, the non-reaching left hand started moving before the eyes, so anchoring did not extend to it, tying eye-hand timing to the function of fixations.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Nethmi H. Illamperuma, Jason P. Gallivan, J. Randall Flanagan

E144.name: Eli Brenner
E144.bio: Eli Brenner is a researcher at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam whose work focuses on the intersection of visual perception and motor control. Brenner investigates how the brain utilizes distinct visual cues, such as position and velocity, to guide goal-directed movements like grasping, reaching, and hitting moving targets. Their methodology combines laboratory psychophysics with naturalistic studies to examine human interaction with dynamic environments. Currently, Brenner’s research explores the mechanisms of sensorimotor adaptation, the role of eye movements in locomotion, and the impact of sensory uncertainty on human action.
E144.research_direction: Dr. Brenner has recently been investigating the continuous visual guidance of motor actions across both reaching tasks and natural locomotion. Their recent work explores how people cope with sensory and motor uncertainty through moment-by-moment online corrections, utilizing kinematic modeling and reaching paradigms with jittering targets or briefly occluded hands to test whether these rapid visuomotor adjustments are adaptive or automatic. Additionally, they are studying gaze behavior in real-world environments by recording eye movements as individuals navigate familiar staircases. Through these naturalistic locomotion studies, Dr. Brenner examines how task instructions, explicit expectations, and the physical demands of ascending versus descending shape exactly where and how far ahead people look to safely guide their steps.

papers.title: Very briefly hiding the hand impedes goal-directed arm movements
papers.abstract: Asks whether the latest visual information about the hand guides movements moment by moment. Delaying that information by a few milliseconds through brief hiding of the hand lengthened the time needed to reach the target, consistent with continuous visual guidance.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Guiding Movements by Constantly Reconsidering One's Actions: A Kinematic Approach
papers.abstract: Reviews how people cope with sensory and motor uncertainty by continuously re-evaluating their movement plan rather than committing to it in advance. The authors present a simple kinematic model built on the principle that smooth movement is always beneficial, and show it can account for many published findings on online corrections, including diverting a movement to a different target.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Do people only adjust ongoing movements vigorously when it is advantageous to do so?
papers.abstract: Tests whether the strong online adjustments seen in reaching toward a jittering target reflect an adaptive strategy. Participants responded to targets that either followed a random walk or fluctuated around a fixed position, where vigorous updating is pointless; most participants kept adjusting vigorously in both cases, suggesting a largely automatic mechanism.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Myrthe L. Vlasblom, Iris Rap, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Methods matter: Exploring how expectations influence common actions
papers.abstract: Examines gaze while people walk up and down a staircase and shows that task instructions shape behavior in natural settings. Participants fixated more steps and looked around less when told to navigate the staircase than when told to walk outside, even though the physical demands were identical.
papers.authors: Andrea Ghiani, David Mann, Eli Brenner

papers.title: Where do people look when walking up and down familiar staircases?
papers.abstract: Records gaze of people using staircases in their own homes without telling them stairs were the focus. Gaze was often sequential but included fixations back to earlier steps and skipping ahead, covering about half the steps and reaching further ahead when ascending than descending.
papers.authors: Andrea Ghiani, Lieke R. Van Hout, Josephine G. Driessen, Eli Brenner

E145.name: Jeroen Smeets
E145.bio: Jeroen Smeets is a Professor of Human Movement Sciences at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, specializing in the computational and experimental analysis of sensorimotor control. Their research focuses on the integration of visual information for goal-directed actions, specifically within the domains of interception, prehension, and the influence of perceptual illusions on motor performance. Smeets developed mathematical models of grasping and investigated the distinctions between perceptual and motor processing pathways. Their work examines how humans manage neural delays through continuous online corrections and the flexible use of sensory cues in dynamic environments.
E145.research_direction: Dr. Smeets has recently been investigating the mechanisms of online visuomotor control, motor adaptation, and spatial perception. Their recent work explores how the motor system integrates continuous visual feedback during goal-directed actions, using methods like brief visual occlusions and stochastic target perturbations to measure visual processing latencies and the strategic scaling of mid-flight corrective vigor. Beyond real-time movement control, they are studying reward-based motor learning across the lifespan to understand how differing success rates and binary feedback frequencies shape motor adaptation. Additionally, they are examining the interplay between multisensory signals and expectations in, for instance, the size-weight illusion and motion sickness.

papers.title: Enforcing a high success percentage interferes with reward-based motor learning
papers.abstract: Reward-based motor learning was tested when task difficulty was adjusted to enforce a high success rate. The results show that keeping success rates artificially high, which reduces informative failures, hampers learning compared with letting success rates vary, with implications for how games and training tasks should dose difficulty.
papers.authors: Katinka van der Kooij, Nina M. van Mastrigt, Moira van Leeuwen, Maaike R. van der Horst, Joyce E. Burger, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Guiding Movements by Constantly Reconsidering One's Actions: A Kinematic Approach
papers.abstract: This review argues that people cope with sensory and motor uncertainty by continuously re-evaluating their movement plan rather than committing to it in advance. The authors present a simple kinematic model built on the principle that smooth movement is always beneficial, and show that it accounts for a wide range of findings on small online adjustments and even complete changes of target during a movement.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Do people only adjust ongoing movements vigorously when it is advantageous to do so?
papers.abstract: Participants reached toward targets that either followed a random walk or varied randomly around a fixed position, where vigorous adjustments to the latest position are only useful in the former case. Most participants still responded vigorously in both cases, suggesting that the vigour of online adjustments is a fairly automatic feature of visuomotor control rather than a strategic choice.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Melissa L. Vlasblom, Ivo Rap, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Anticipatory cues can mitigate car sickness on the road
papers.abstract: On-road experiments examined whether giving passengers advance cues about upcoming vehicle motion reduces motion sickness. Anticipatory cues lowered sickness symptoms during real driving, indicating a practical countermeasure for motion sickness in cars and automated vehicles.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Part F: Traffic Psychology and Behaviour
papers.authors: A. J. C. Reuten, I. Yunus, J. E. Bos, M. H. Martens, J. B. J. Smeets

papers.title: Continuous use of visual information about the position of the moving hand
papers.abstract: By adding jitter to a cursor that follows the finger, the study shows that people continuously use visual information about their own moving hand, responding to cursor jitter much as they do to target jitter. Responses grow more vigorous late in movement, when little time remains, though they are weaker for the cursor, presumably because of jitter-free kinaesthetic information.
papers.authors: Eli Brenner, Jeroen B. J. Smeets

E147.name: Stéphanie Rossit
E147.bio: Rossit is an Associate Professor at the University of East Anglia who researches the neural mechanisms of human perception, motor control, and spatial attention. Their work focuses on how these processes are affected by stroke and brain injury, specifically visual neglect. Rossit uses functional MRI (fMRI), lesion-symptom mapping, and eye-tracking to develop and test interventions such as the c-SIGHT and EyeFocus neurorehabilitation trials. This research program relates cognitive neuroscience and clinical practice to study recovery outcomes for survivors of brain disease.
E147.research_direction: Dr. Rossit has recently been investigating how the visual system processes spatial and object information to guide action, blending behavioral, neuroimaging, and neuropsychological methods. Their recent work explores the neural and spatial mechanisms of object affordances, using fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis to ask whether viewing familiar tools evokes specific action representations in the occipitotemporal cortex that share a neural format with actual motor pantomiming. Behaviorally, they are testing whether these affordance-driven motor responses are preferentially triggered in the lower visual field, corresponding to the typical space of manual interactions. Beyond tool use, Dr. Rossit is also studying spatial attention and visuomotor control, examining how stroke survivors with visual neglect and extinction coordinate peripheral and bimanual reaching, and mapping how far-space visual attention shifts across the healthy aging lifespan.

papers.title: Human see, human do? Viewing tool pictures evokes tool-use action information in hand-selective occipitotemporal cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and multivoxel pattern analysis, the study asks whether viewing pictures of familiar tools evokes information about the specific action each tool affords (rotate vs squeeze, matched for grip) and whether that information shares a format with actually pantomiming the action. Action information was decodable in lateral occipitotemporal, parietal and even somatosensory cortex, and hand-selective LOTC was the only region where action decoding beat tool-identity decoding in both viewing and pantomime. Cross-task decoding was not reliable, suggesting perception and production carry action information in task-dependent rather than shared formats.
papers.authors: Annie Warman, Diana Tonin, Fraser Smith, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Is there a lower visual field advantage for object affordances? A registered report
papers.abstract: A registered report testing whether pictures of graspable objects speed responses through affordances rather than spatial compatibility. In 68 participants the handle-compatibility effect failed to replicate once spatial compatibility was controlled, but in a further 68 participants a handle compatibility effect emerged when objects appeared in the lower, and not the upper, visual field. The authors suggest a lower-field advantage for affordances, consistent with the lower field being where hand actions typically occur.
papers.authors: Annie Warman, Allan Clark, George L. Malcolm, Maximillian Havekost, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Peripheral and bimanual reaching in a stroke survivor with left visual neglect and extinction
papers.abstract: A single-case study of a stroke survivor with left neglect and extinction but without hemiparesis or hemianopia, allowing reaching to be tested without motor confounds. Her reaching to peripheral targets in the neglected left field was inaccurate regardless of hand (an optic-ataxia-like field effect), and she showed a larger bimanual cost when the two hands reached to incongruent locations. The visuomotor profile resembles optic ataxia, indicating that attentional deficits co-occur with visuomotor deficits in the affected field.
papers.authors: Ethan Knights, Robert D. McIntosh, Catherine Ford, Gavin Buckingham, Stéphanie Rossit

papers.title: Aging effects on extrapersonal (far-space) attention: cancellation and line bisection performance from 179 healthy adults
papers.abstract: Cancellation and line bisection were presented on a large screen in far space to 179 healthy adults aged 18-94, yielding preliminary age-graded norms for far-space visuospatial attention. Ageing slowed both tasks and reduced search quality but did not change line bisection error, and the two tasks were related through search speed and quality. Participants showed a leftward pseudoneglect bias and males searched faster than females.
papers.authors: Helen Morse, Amy A. Jolly, Hannah Browning, Allan Clark, Valerie Pomeroy, Stéphanie Rossit

E149.name: Stephen H. Scott
E149.department: Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences
E149.bio: Stephen H. Scott is a Canadian neuroscientist and engineer specializing in the neural and computational foundations of voluntary motor control. Scott developed the Kinarm robotic system, a tool used to investigate transcortical feedback pathways and quantify sensorimotor impairments in clinical populations. Their research methodology integrates primate neurophysiology and human behavioral experiments, utilizing optimal feedback control (OFC) theory to interpret how the brain processes sensory information to manage limb biomechanics. Scott's current work focuses on the intersection of robotics and brain-machine interfaces to facilitate the assessment and rehabilitation of neurological disorders such as stroke.
E149.research_direction: Dr. Scott's recent work explores the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying rapid sensorimotor control and goal-directed movement corrections. Using both human and non-human primate models, they have recently been investigating how the primary motor cortex and spinal circuits integrate visual and proprioceptive feedback to adjust reaching movements in real-time when faced with spatial or mechanical perturbations. Their research also probes the behavioral dynamics of these fast responses, examining how agonist-antagonist muscle co-contraction impacts limb control and how contextual factors like urgency and predictability differentially modulate eye-hand coordination during target interception. Additionally, Dr. Scott translates these kinematic methodologies into clinical applications by developing uncertainty-aware deep learning models to analyze robotic exoskeleton data, aiming to improve the automated detection of subtle motor impairments in stroke patients.

papers.title: Agonist-antagonist muscular co-contraction improves rapid corrective responses
papers.abstract: Human participants recaptured a target after a mechanical perturbation while their arm muscles were pre-activated to different degrees. Even small amounts of co-contraction improved corrective performance relative to a relaxed state or single-muscle activation. The benefit was partly explained by neural mechanisms, since both muscle groups contributed to limb control via reflex responses, beyond simple mechanical stiffness.
papers.authors: Daniel P. Armstrong, Kevin J. Deluzio, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Optimizing Stroke Detection Using Evidential Networks and Uncertainty-Based Refinement
papers.abstract: Kinematic data from 337 stroke patients and 368 healthy controls on three Kinarm exoskeleton tasks were analysed with an evidential deep-learning network that outputs prediction uncertainty. Retraining on the least uncertain samples and excluding the most uncertain test cases raised sensitivity for subtle impairment in patients scoring normal on clinical scales from 0.55 to 0.75. The model also detected transient ischemic attack with accuracy rising from 0.86 to 0.92.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering
papers.authors: Faranak Akbarifar, Sean P. Dukelow, Albert Jin, Parvin Mousavi, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Parallel feedback processing for voluntary control: knowledge of spinal feedback in motor cortex
papers.abstract: The study asks how spinal reflexes and cortical feedback pathways cooperate to produce goal-directed corrections. In monkeys, experimentally increasing spinal reflex gain to applied loads produced a reciprocal drop in the primary motor cortex response. A neural network model shows how knowledge of lower-level reflex processing can be built into parallel feedback pathways to generate goal-directed corrections.
papers.authors: Hui Guang, Joseph Y. Nashed, J. Andrew Pruszynski, Hari T. Kalidindi, Frederic Crevecoeur, Kevin P. Cross, Gunnar Blohm, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Rapid Online Corrections for Proprioceptive and Visual Perturbations Recruit Similar Circuits in Primary Motor Cortex
papers.abstract: Monkeys reached to targets while goal jumps, cursor jumps, or mechanical loads perturbed the task on random trials. About 73% of recorded primary motor cortex neurons responded to at least one perturbation, with highly correlated response ranges across the two visual perturbations and substantial correlation between visual and proprioceptive ones. Population subspace analysis showed overlapping structure, indicating that vision and proprioception recruit shared M1 circuits for fast corrections.
papers.authors: Kevin P. Cross, Douglas J. Cook, Stephen H. Scott

papers.title: Rapid eye and hand responses in an interception task are differentially modulated by context-dependent predictability
papers.abstract: Participants intercepted a moving target with a virtual paddle while the target sometimes jumped sideways, with certainty and response urgency manipulated. Certainty sped both eye and hand responses, while urgency shortened hand reaction times and raised hand vigor but did not scale eye vigor. Eye and hand responses correlated only weakly, suggesting shared early sensorimotor processing with separately modulated rapid responses.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Parsa Balalaie, Kayne Park, J. Randall Flanagan, Stephen H. Scott

E150.name: Bijan Pesaran
E150.bio: Bijan Pesaran is the Robert A. Groff Professor of Neurosurgery at the University of Pennsylvania, where Pesaran investigates the neural mechanisms of multiregional communication and decision-making. Their research employs large-scale electrophysiological recordings and computational modeling to understand how distributed brain networks coordinate behaviors such as eye-hand movements. Transitioning from a background in theoretical physics to systems neuroscience, Pesaran developed techniques for decoding local field potentials and spiking activity to create brain-machine interfaces. Pesaran's current work focuses on engineering neurotechnologies and therapies for neurological disorders by mapping and controlling large-scale brain circuits.
E150.research_direction: Dr. Pesaran has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics that support multiregional brain communication in primates, with a particular focus on how oscillatory coherence orchestrates complex behaviors. Their recent work explores the role of specific network frequency bands—such as prefrontal beta rhythms and mesolimbic theta rhythms—in mediating top-down attentional control and routing information between sender and receiver networks. They are also studying how distributed populations of specific cell types guide behavioral state transitions during unconstrained, naturalistic eye-hand coordination. To support these physiological investigations, Dr. Pesaran is developing advanced neurotechnologies, including computer-vision pipelines and fluorescence microscopy setups for cellular-resolution, real-time structural tracking of the primate cortex across multiple days.

papers.title: Neural signatures of behavioral transitions during naturalistic eye-hand coordination
papers.abstract: Recordings from macaque parietal and premotor cortex during free, naturalistic eye-hand behavior identify neural signatures that mark transitions between behavioral states. The work extends the lab's multiregional eye-hand coordination program from constrained tasks to unconstrained movement, showing how distributed populations shift between states as behavior unfolds.
papers.authors: Robert A. Shewcraft, Shaoyu Qiao, Isabel C. Garwood, Bijan Pesaran

papers.title: Cellular-Resolution Image-Guided Localization in the Primate Brain
papers.abstract: A fluorescence microscope on a parallel-kinematic stage can be positioned over the dorsal cortical surface of a macaque. A computer-vision pipeline registers new images to earlier imaging sessions, giving real-time (10-20 s) localization at 10-20 micrometre accuracy across days.
papers.venue: 2024 46th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC)
papers.authors: Jacob Stefanowicz, John S. Choi, Katie E. Wingel, Jarl Haggerty, Adam S. Charles, Bijan Pesaran

papers.title: Top-down control of exogenous attentional selection is mediated by beta coherence in prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Two rhesus monkeys performed a free-choice, two-target task in which a salient luminance cue competed with reward value. Visual-movement neurons in lateral prefrontal cortex carried both exogenous and endogenous selection signals. Beta-frequency coherence in the prefrontal network specifically shaped exogenous selection during conflict, suggesting that beta-band coherence gates sensory communication channels to implement top-down attentional control.
papers.authors: Agrita Dubey, David A. Markowitz, Bijan Pesaran

papers.title: Putative cell-type-specific multiregional mode in posterior parietal cortex during coordinated visual behavior
papers.abstract: In macaque posterior parietal reach and saccade regions, communication depends on spike timing relative to beta-band LFP, known as dual coherence. The authors model dual coherence as shared multiregional excitability and identify a latent multiregional mode across parietal populations. The mode's power is tied to spiking of putative pyramidal neurons rather than interneurons, implicating pyramidal cells in multiregional communication.
papers.authors: Mohammad Farhan Khazali, Yan T. Wong, Heather L. Dean, Maureen A. Hagan, Margaret M. Fabiszak, Bijan Pesaran

papers.title: Causal evidence of coherent theta rhythms in the modulation of multiregional brain communication
papers.abstract: By stimulating sender sites while recording at receiver sites in the mesolimbic mood network, the study finds dynamic multiregional communication carried by theta-coherent dynamics across sender, receiver and modulator sites. Modulator sites are highly theta-coherent with the receiver and site specific. The results support theta coherence as a target for neuromodulation in neuropsychiatric disorders.
papers.authors: Gino Del Ferraro, Shaoyu Qiao, Joshua I. Sedillo, Bijan Pesaran

E151.name: Richard A. Andersen
E151.department: Division of Biology and Biological Engineering
E151.bio: Richard A. Andersen studies the neural mechanisms of sensory-motor integration and movement planning within the posterior parietal cortex (PPC). Andersen identified "gain fields," a computational principle that allows the brain to transform visual information into various coordinate systems by integrating sensory stimuli with eye and body position signals. Their laboratory develops cognitive-based brain-machine interfaces that decode intentional signals from the PPC of paralyzed patients to control robotic limbs and computer cursors. Andersen currently utilizes machine learning and neuroimaging techniques to develop neural prosthetics for the restoration of functions such as speech and coordinated reaching.
E151.research_direction: Dr. Andersen has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of motor intention and cognitive planning to develop advanced brain-machine interfaces. Using intracortical microelectrode recordings in individuals with tetraplegia, they are exploring how the posterior parietal and motor cortices hierarchically encode intended versus merely observed hand actions, while also examining single-neuron representations of internal, silent speech in the supramarginal gyrus. In parallel primate models, their recent work explores the use of minimally invasive, closed-loop functional ultrasound imaging to decode planned actions and to map the mesoscopic spatial organization of saccades in the lateral intraparietal area. Furthermore, they are testing the limits of these neural decoders in applied, real-world contexts, investigating whether intracortical signals can enable human users to achieve fast, precise control over complex machinery like commercial electric vehicles.

papers.title: Hierarchical and context-dependent encoding of actions in human posterior parietal and motor cortex
papers.abstract: Using Utah arrays in motor cortex and superior parietal lobule of two tetraplegic participants, the authors compared neural responses when hand actions were intended versus merely observed. Motor cortex mainly carried intention-specific codes, whereas superior parietal lobule held shared codes for intended and observed actions down to single units. When instructed and observed actions conflicted, parietal cortex represented the observed action only if it was behaviorally relevant, suggesting a context-dependent gating and a hierarchy from parietal to motor cortex.
papers.authors: Vasiliki Bougou, Jorge Gamez, Emily R. Rosario, Charles Liu, Kelsie Pejsa, Ausaf Bari, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Functional ultrasound neuroimaging reveals mesoscopic organization of saccades in the lateral intraparietal area
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging was used to map the lateral intraparietal area of macaques during saccade tasks at mesoscopic resolution across cortical depth and areas. The maps reveal spatially organized responses related to saccade direction and planning within LIP, and the signals support decoding of eye-movement variables. The work links classic parietal eye-movement physiology to a scalable whole-region imaging method.
papers.authors: Whitney S. Griggs, Sumner L. Norman, Mickael Tanter, Charles Liu, Vasileios Christopoulos, Mikhail G. Shapiro, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Control of a commercially available vehicle by a tetraplegic human using a brain-computer interface
papers.abstract: A person with tetraplegia, implanted with arrays in posterior parietal and hand-area motor cortex, drove a commercial electric car using bimanual cursor-and-click brain control for steering, speed and braking. Performance in simulated town driving and obstacle courses matched that of able-bodied controls, and the participant also operated the real vehicle remotely across the country. The work shows that intracortical BCIs can deliver fast, precise control of complex real-world machines.
papers.authors: Xinyun Zou, Jorge Gamez, Meghna Menon, Phillip Ring, Chadwick Boulay, Likhith Chitneni, Jackson Brennecke, Shana R. Melby, Gracy Kureel, Kelsie Pejsa, Emily R. Rosario, Ausaf A. Bari, Aniruddh Ravindran, Tyson Aflalo, Spencer S. Kellis, Dimitar Filev, Florian Solzbacher, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Decoding motor plans using a closed-loop ultrasonic brain-machine interface
papers.abstract: The study builds a real-time brain-machine interface based on functional ultrasound imaging rather than electrodes, recording from posterior parietal cortex of macaques. Single-trial ultrasound signals were decoded online to predict planned eye and hand movement directions, letting animals steer a cursor in closed loop. It shows that minimally invasive, large-field-of-view ultrasound neuroimaging can support movement-intention decoding, and that the decoder can be trained with limited data and updated across sessions.
papers.authors: Whitney S. Griggs, Sumner L. Norman, Thomas Deffieux, Florian Segura, Bruno-Felix Osmanski, Geeling Chau, Vasileios Christopoulos, Charles Liu, Mickael Tanter, Mikhail G. Shapiro, Richard A. Andersen

papers.title: Representation of internal speech by single neurons in human supramarginal gyrus
papers.abstract: Recording from the supramarginal gyrus of tetraplegic participants implanted with microelectrode arrays, the authors examined neural activity during silent, internally spoken and vocalized words. Single neurons and populations in this parietal area carried information about the words, and internal speech could be decoded from them with above-chance accuracy, including via a real-time decoder. The findings point to the supramarginal gyrus as a site for speech-related representations and as a candidate for speech neuroprostheses.
papers.authors: Sarah K. Wandelt, David A. Bjanes, Kelsie Pejsa, Brian Lee, Charles Liu, Richard A. Andersen

E152.name: Tamar Makin
E152.department: Medical Research Council Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit
E152.bio: Tamar Makin is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Cambridge and the leader of the Plasticity Lab at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit. Their research investigates the neural mechanisms of brain plasticity, specifically how the brain represents the body and adapts to changes such as limb loss or the integration of augmentative technologies. Using neuroimaging, psychophysics, and bioengineering, Makin has demonstrated the persistence of latent limb representations in the brain following amputation. Their current work focuses on motor augmentation, exploring how the human brain can be harnessed to control and embody artificial body parts to enhance physical capabilities.
E152.research_direction: Dr. Makin has recently been investigating the limits of sensorimotor plasticity, focusing on how the adult brain adapts to both the loss of a limb and the addition of robotic body parts. Their recent work explores the fundamental stability of the brain's functional architecture, using longitudinal fMRI to track whether somatosensory cortical body maps actually undergo large-scale reorganization following arm amputation. In parallel, they are examining the cognitive and behavioral mechanisms of motor augmentation by testing how individuals learn to control artificial appendages, such as bionic hands and wearable extra digits. By deploying devices like the robotic Third Thumb across diverse populations and controlled laboratory experiments, they investigate how different control mappings affect prosthetic skill acquisition and whether users can flexibly generalize these newly learned motor abilities to entirely untrained tasks.

papers.title: Broad skill generalization with an extra robotic body part
papers.abstract: Participants trained for several days to use the Third Thumb, a wearable extra robotic digit, and were then tested on many untrained tasks. Skill learned on the device transferred widely to new movements and objects rather than staying specific to trained tasks. This suggests the brain can build a flexible control strategy for a body-part augmentation, informing the design of motor augmentation technology.
papers.authors: Maria Molina-Sanchez, Lucy Dowdall, Giulia Dominijanni, Viktorija Pavalkyte, Clara Gallay, Edmund da Silva, Dani Clode, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Stable cortical body maps before and after arm amputation
papers.abstract: Using longitudinal fMRI in people scheduled for arm amputation, the study scanned participants before and after surgery and tracked how the hand and other body-part representations in somatosensory cortex changed. The cortical map of the missing hand stayed remarkably stable, and neighbouring body-part representations did not invade it. The results challenge the classic view that deprivation drives large-scale cortical remapping after limb loss.
papers.authors: Hunter R. Schone, Roni O. Maimon-Mor, Mathew Kollamkulam, Malgorzata A. Szymanska, Craig Gerrand, Alexander Woollard, Norbert V. Kang, Chris I. Baker, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Evaluating initial usability of a hand augmentation device across a large and diverse sample
papers.abstract: The Third Thumb, an extra robotic thumb worn on the hand, was tested with about 600 people of widely different ages, genders and backgrounds at a public science exhibition. Nearly everyone learned to use it and complete tasks within a minute of instruction, with no strong dependence on demographic factors. The work makes the case for inclusive testing of augmentation technology.
papers.authors: Dani Clode, Lucy Dowdall, Edmund da Silva, Klara Selen, Dorothy Cowie, Giulia Dominijanni, Tamar R. Makin

papers.title: Biomimetic versus arbitrary motor control strategies for bionic hand skill learning
papers.abstract: Able-bodied participants learned to operate a prosthetic-like bionic hand using either a control scheme mimicking natural hand movements or an arbitrary mapping. The biomimetic strategy yielded faster learning and better performance in some respects, though arbitrary control showed its own advantages. The results bear on how prosthesis controllers should be designed around how people learn.
papers.authors: Hunter R. Schone, Malcolm Udeozor, Mae Moninghoff, Beth Rispoli, James Vandersea, Blair Lock, Levi Hargrove, Tamar R. Makin, Chris I. Baker

papers.title: Against cortical reorganisation
papers.abstract: This influential review argues that the widely cited evidence for large-scale cortical reorganisation after amputation, deafferentation or sensory loss is better explained by unmasking and preserved latent representations. The authors re-examine classic findings and propose that the adult brain's functional architecture is far more stable than textbooks suggest, and outline how future studies should test this.
papers.authors: Tamar R. Makin, John W. Krakauer

E153.name: J. Douglas Crawford
E153.bio: J. Douglas Crawford is a Research Professor and Canada Research Chair in Visuomotor Neuroscience at York University. Crawford’s research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visuospatial memory and sensorimotor transformations for coordinated eye, head, and hand movements in three-dimensional space. Utilizing a multimodal approach that includes fMRI, MEG, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and neurophysiological recordings, their work explores how the brain updates internal representations of visual goals during self-motion. Crawford examines the 3D geometry of the gaze system and the role of the posterior parietal cortex in integrating target and effector information for reach planning.
E153.research_direction: Dr. Crawford has recently been investigating the neural networks and computations that underlie goal-directed motor behaviors like reaching, grasping, and eye movements. Their recent work explores how the brain integrates diverse streams of information—such as egocentric and allocentric spatial reference frames—to dynamically plan these complex actions. To map these visuomotor transformations, they employ human fMRI coupled with graph theory analysis, alongside non-human primate neurophysiology and computational modeling. Recently, they have examined how large-scale cortical networks functionally reorganize to support transsaccadic spatial constancy, and how distinct neural recording scales in the frontal eye fields capture the nuanced spatial and cognitive signals required for gaze control. Currently, the Crawford lab is focused on the cortico-cerebellar mechanisms for eye-hand coordination during visually-aimed reach and placement movements.

papers.title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Differentiates Egocentric vs. Allocentric Network Hubs for Memory-Guided Reach
papers.abstract: Sixteen participants reached to a remembered target while a landmark shifted during a memory delay, following either an egocentric (ignore landmark) or allocentric (use landmark) rule. TMS over superior occipital cortex degraded both kinds of reach, whereas inferior occipital TMS impaired only allocentric reach. Network analyses showed the stimulation altered network-behaviour relations in a site- and task-specific way, providing causal evidence for a dorsal egocentric default and a ventral role for landmark-based actions.
papers.authors: Lina Musa, Gaelle N. Luabeya, Brando Sheldrick, Ali Rezaei, Saihong Sun, Xiaogang Yan, Michael Vesia, John Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Beyond Reach I: Neuroimaging Reveals Different Cortico-cerebellar Networks for Grasp vs. Object Placement
papers.abstract: Twenty participants alternately grasped an object and placed it onto templates during event-related fMRI, and whole-brain activation plus graph-theoretical connectivity were analysed across planning and execution. Both tasks shared prefrontal planning and sensorimotor execution activity, but placement recruited more cerebellar and action-related planning activation and allowed the tasks to be decoded. Both networks split into the same three modules with task-specific modularity differences, indicating shared circuitry with differences tied to intentionality and sensory feedback.
papers.authors: Gaelle N. Luabeya, Erez Freud, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Neural integration of egocentric and allocentric visual cues in the gaze system
papers.abstract: This review lays out how prefrontal neurons in the frontal and supplementary eye fields combine eye-centred target information with landmark-centred information to guide gaze. It summarizes human whole-brain and behavioural evidence for ego/allocentric integration and the primate egocentric gaze-coding literature. It then explains how single-neuron visual and motor responses multiplex target and landmark signals in intermediate reference frames to optimize gaze behaviour.
papers.authors: Vishal Bharmauria, Serah Seo, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Saccades influence functional modularity in the human cortical vision network
papers.abstract: Using graph-theory analysis of fMRI from 50 vision-related cortical nodes, the study asks how functional modules emerge when people judge object shape or orientation with or without an intervening saccade. During fixation, a parietofrontal module and two lateralized occipitotemporal modules appeared; saccades across hemifields raised connectivity and merged the two ventral modules into one bilateral sub-network with hubs in lateral intraparietal and dorsomedial occipital cortex. The results show that saccades reorganize modular cortical networks for transsaccadic integration.
papers.authors: George Tomou, Bianca R. Baltaretu, Amirhossein Ghaderi, J. Douglas Crawford

papers.title: Perceptual-Cognitive Integration for Goal-Directed Action in Naturalistic Environments
papers.abstract: This review argues that real-world actions require combining bottom-up sensory input with top-down cognitive and motor signals, which demands cutting across traditional neuroscience silos. It surveys how neuroimaging, virtual reality and motion tracking now allow such studies in natural settings for both healthy and clinical populations. Six topics are covered where naturalistic approaches have advanced understanding of perception, cognition and action.
papers.authors: Jolande Fooken, Bianca R. Baltaretu, Deborah A. Barany, Gabriel Diaz, Jennifer A. Semrau, Tarkeshwar Singh, J. Douglas Crawford

E154.name: Paul Gribble
E154.bio: Paul Gribble is a Professor at Western University whose research examines the neural and computational mechanisms of human motor control and learning. Gribble investigates how the brain coordinates multi-joint movements and the role of sensory plasticity within the somatosensory cortex in acquiring motor skills. Their work includes studies on motor learning through visual observation, specifically how the brain maps observed actions onto its own motor system. This research employs a combination of human behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and peripheral nerve stimulation.
E154.research_direction: Dr. Gribble has recently been investigating the computational and behavioral mechanisms underlying human sensorimotor control and motor learning. Their recent work explores how the motor system adapts to physical perturbations, probing phenomena such as the temporal durability of observational motor learning and the computational rules that drive "savings," or the faster relearning of previously experienced motor tasks. They are also examining how fast sensorimotor feedback loops operate during reaching movements, specifically testing whether these rapid, reflexive responses to mechanical disruptions can be dynamically modulated by task rewards. To support these mechanistic investigations, Dr. Gribble builds open-source computational and community resources, most notably developing a Python-based deep-learning framework that trains recurrent neural networks to control differentiable, biomechanically realistic models of human limbs.

papers.title: A Context-Free Model of Savings in Motor Learning
papers.abstract: Savings is the faster relearning of a movement perturbation that was experienced before. This paper proposes a computational account of savings that does not need an explicit representation of context or of separate memory modules. A single model with learning-rate changes driven by experienced errors reproduces a range of classic savings findings across adaptation paradigms.
papers.authors: Mahdiyar Shahbazi, Olivier Codol, Jonathan A. Michaels, Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: How to design your academic website
papers.abstract: A practical guide to building an effective academic or lab website, covering what content to include, how to organize it, and technical choices for creating and hosting it. Written as a career-oriented how-to piece for researchers.
papers.authors: Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: MotorNet: a Python toolbox for controlling differentiable biomechanical effectors with artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: MotorNet is an open-source Python package for training recurrent neural networks to control biomechanically realistic, differentiable models of the arm and other effectors. It lets researchers study sensorimotor control with neural network models in a framework built on modern deep-learning tooling. The paper shows example uses and the toolbox is documented and freely available.
papers.authors: Olivier Codol, Jonathan A. Michaels, Mehrdad Kashefi, J. Andrew Pruszynski, Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: Durability of Motor Learning by Observing
papers.abstract: This work asks how long motor learning acquired by watching another person lasts. Participants who learned a movement perturbation by observation were retested after delays, and the learning was retained over time, comparable to the retention seen after physical practice. It extends the lab's research on observational motor learning and its somatosensory basis.
papers.authors: Natalia Mangos, Christopher J. Forgaard, Paul L. Gribble

papers.title: Sensorimotor feedback loops are selectively sensitive to reward
papers.abstract: The study tests whether reward changes the gain of fast feedback responses to mechanical perturbations during reaching. Human participants showed reward-dependent modulation of the feedback response, and this was selective for aspects of the response relevant to the task. The results suggest that reward shapes even rapid sensorimotor feedback loops, not just voluntary movement planning.
papers.authors: Olivier Codol, Mehrdad Kashefi, Christopher J. Forgaard, Joseph M. Galea, J. Andrew Pruszynski, Paul L. Gribble

E155.name: Constanze Hesse
E155.bio: Constanze Hesse is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Aberdeen and leads the Grasper Lab investigating the cognitive and sensory mechanisms underlying human motor control. Hesse’s research utilizes psychophysical experimentation and motion tracking to examine how visual information, material properties, and environmental constraints influence the planning and execution of reaching and grasping movements. Their work addresses the dorsal and ventral visual streams through studies on multisensory perception and clinical neuropsychology, including research with patients possessing visual agnosia. Hesse is currently exploring natural behavior in virtual reality environments and investigating how the affective or emotional properties of objects modulate motor avoidance strategies.
E155.research_direction: Dr. Hesse's recent work explores the visuomotor control of action across a diverse range of behaviors, investigating how both physical constraints and perceptual evaluations shape movement. They have recently been examining how maximum grip aperture scales when grasping exceptionally tiny objects near the limits of sensorimotor precision, and identifying which visual depth cues are necessary to elicit naturalistic obstacle avoidance during reaching in virtual reality environments. Their research also extends motor avoidance beyond purely spatial dimensions by testing how affective surface properties, such as perceived danger or unpleasantness, alter foot trajectories during stepping. Additionally, Dr. Hesse is investigating broader links between visual perception, action, and expertise, testing how manipulating the color saturation of food images influences implicit approach biases, and whether athletic motor expertise fine-tunes the general perceptual discrimination of human kinematics.

papers.title: Fading appetite: Desaturation of food images reduces cravings but not approach biases
papers.abstract: Colour saturation is a visual feature that may signal how ripe or appealing food is. The authors manipulated saturation in food images and measured both self-reported cravings and implicit approach tendencies. Desaturating the images lowered cravings, yet approach biases toward the foods stayed the same, suggesting that these two responses are dissociable.
papers.authors: Daniela Ruseva, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: Obstacle avoidance of physical, stereoscopic, and pictorial objects
papers.abstract: Virtual and augmented reality are increasingly used to study and train motor actions, but it is unclear whether behaviour there matches behaviour in the real world. The authors compared how people reach around real obstacles with how they reach around closely matched 2D and stereoscopic 3D images of the same obstacles. The results identify which visual cues are needed for hand movements in simulated environments to look naturalistic.
papers.authors: Martin Giesel, Daniela Ruseva, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: From discomfort to danger: Exploring how affective obstacle properties influence avoidance in stepping
papers.abstract: Stepping over obstacles means adjusting foot trajectory to avoid surfaces that may be hazardous or unpleasant. Participants stepped over obstacles covered in stones of varying size and density, and rated them for danger, unpleasantness and painfulness. The study links these affective evaluations to changes in stepping strategy, extending motor avoidance research from physical constraints to perceived affective properties.
papers.authors: Zhong Jian Chee, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: Grasping tiny objects
papers.abstract: Maximum grip aperture is the standard readout of how the visuomotor system represents object size, but safety, comfort and efficiency demands can distort how it scales with size. The authors extend the classic grasping literature to very small objects (under 5 mm), a range never tested before, and examine how hand opening scales when targets approach the limits of visual resolution and motor precision. The work speaks to what grip aperture actually reveals about size perception in action.
papers.authors: Martin Giesel, Federico De Filippi, Constanze Hesse

papers.title: Action Perception in Athletes: Expertise Facilitates Perceptual Discrimination
papers.abstract: Athletes are known to be better than non-athletes at anticipating sport-related actions. Across two experiments, sprinters and non-experts judged whether pairs of videos of walking or sprinting were identical, without any need to anticipate. Sprinters were more accurate, and the advantage carried over to non-sport actions, indicating that motor expertise tunes perceptual discrimination more broadly.
papers.authors: Róisín E. Harrison, Martin Giesel, Constanze Hesse

E156.name: Volker Franz
E156.department: Wilhelm Schickard Institute for Computer Science
E156.bio: Volker Franz is a Professor of Experimental Cognitive Science at the University of Tübingen and leads the Experimental Cognitive Science research group. Their research examines human visual information processing, focusing on the interaction between sensory input and motor control in tasks such as grasping and object recognition. Franz conducts empirical evaluations of the 'two visual systems' hypothesis by using visual illusions to test functional similarities between perception and action pathways. Additionally, Franz works on neuroscientific methodology, specializing in statistical rigor, confidence interval estimation, and the development of software such as the Optotrak Toolbox for kinematic analysis.
E156.research_direction: Dr. Franz has recently been investigating how the human brain processes environmental regularities, while also critically re-evaluating several classic models in visual cognition. Their recent work explores modality-general surprise mechanisms by tracking pupillary dynamics in response to sudden structural shifts in both auditory and visual sequences, aiming to understand how the perceptual system updates its internal models. Additionally, they are rigorously testing established behavioral dissociations in vision science, such as probing the two-visual-systems hypothesis via Garner interference in grasping versus estimation tasks, and analyzing whether contextual cueing paradigms truly capture unconscious learning. Rounding out this methodological breadth, Dr. Franz is also investigating metacognitive confidence through an information-theoretic lens, developing new mathematical bounds to evaluate how well observers can pool their confidence during group decision-making.

papers.title: Modality-general sensitivity of pupil responses to regularity violations
papers.abstract: Using sequences of visual dots and of auditory tones, the study asks whether pupil responses to broken regularities are specific to one sense. Regular-to-random and regular-to-regular transitions triggered pupil dilations in vision, replicating the earlier auditory pattern, while random-to-regular transitions did not reliably do so. A direct cross-modal comparison showed strongly similar pupil responses across modalities, pointing to a modality-general surprise mechanism.
papers.authors: Hamit Basgol, Florian Raab, Peter Dayan, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Measures of Metacognition: Bounds and Relation to Group Performance
papers.abstract: Metacognition, or Type 2 performance, is usually quantified with signal-detection measures that assume a particular (truncated normal) noise distribution behind confidence ratings. The authors instead build on information theory and derive upper and lower bounds on the information a classifier's confidence can transmit at a given accuracy, showing that normal noise is only an intermediate case between binary and uniform noise. From these bounds they propose a new measure, relative metainformation (RMI), and link it to how well groups of observers can pool their confidence to make better decisions.
papers.authors: Sascha Meyen, Frieder Göppert, Carina Schrenk, Ulrike von Luxburg, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Violation of auditory regularities is reflected in pupil dynamics
papers.abstract: Participants listened to tone sequences that switched between regular and random patterns while pupil size was recorded. Switches from regular to random, and from one regular pattern to another, produced pupil dilations, consistent with the brain discarding and resetting its internal model, whereas random-to-regular switches did not, consistent with gradual model updating. The authors also fitted pupil response functions to show that pupil activity tracks trial-by-trial changes in the information content of the sequences.
papers.authors: Hamit Basgol, Peter Dayan, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: Reviewing evidence for the perception-action model from Garner interference
papers.abstract: The two-visual-systems view predicts that perceptual tasks suffer Garner interference while visuomotor tasks such as grasping are immune to it. The authors ran two improved replications comparing manual size estimation with grasping, finding smaller Garner effects in estimation than earlier reports, and then tested whether manipulating response timing changes the effect. A literature review of all relevant studies concludes that the evidence for the dissociation is weaker than commonly assumed.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Kriti Bhatia, Angela Osenberg, Markus Janczyk, Volker H. Franz

papers.title: No evidence for contextual cueing beyond explicit recognition
papers.abstract: Contextual cueing studies often claim unconscious learning of visual regularities because response-time benefits coexist with near-chance explicit recognition. The authors argue this reasoning is flawed because the sensitivity underlying the RT effect is never actually computed, and they apply a proper sensitivity comparison in a reanalysis of 20 studies. Not a single study showed convincing evidence that RT effects exceed explicit recognition, so implicit-recognition claims are not supported.
papers.authors: Sascha Meyen, Miguel A. Vadillo, Ulrike von Luxburg, Volker H. Franz

E157.name: Heiner Deubel
E157.department: Department of Psychology, Chair of General and Experimental Psychology
E157.bio: Deubel is an emeritus professor of psychology whose research focuses on the functional relationship between visual attention, perception, and the control of motor actions such as saccades and reaching. Deubel demonstrated the obligatory coupling of attentional selection to the goal of upcoming eye movements, a finding that supports the 'selection-for-action' framework of cognitive control. Their methodologies involve behavioral psychophysics and eye-tracking to investigate how the brain maintains visual stability and spatial constancy despite frequent eye movements. Additionally, their work explores transsaccadic memory, predictive remapping, and the mechanisms by which perceptual learning generalizes across different retinal locations through active exploration.
E157.research_direction: Dr. Deubel has recently been studying how vision stays stable and useful while the eyes make rapid jumps between fixation points. Their recent work asks what people can learn about visual features when a target is viewed across a saccade, and whether that learning depends on where the target lands on the retina or only on what the target looks like. They have also been developing a new way to measure visual attention that uses dynamic noise as the background, so that the test signals do not create sudden onsets or landmarks that would themselves pull attention around.

papers.title: Perceptual learning across saccades: Feature but not location specific
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is conventionally characterized by tight retinotopic and feature specificity, traditionally assessed while observers maintain steady central fixation. However, natural visual exploration relies on rapid saccadic eye movements that project target objects across differing retinal coordinates. Here, human observers were trained to saccade to a peripheral oriented grating and discriminate an intraduration orientation change occurring during the eye movement. Training induced robust transsaccadic perceptual learning that was strictly feature-tuned, showing no transfer to an untrained orientation. In contrast to fixation-based learning, orientation training transferred entirely to an untrained visual hemifield location. Three control experiments confirmed that this cross-location generalization is contingent upon active saccade execution, as training without saccades eliminated the transfer. Furthermore, learning at the trained location generalized to an untrained fixation task, whereas transfer to the untrained location did not. These findings demonstrate that transsaccadic perceptual learning operates via a dual mechanism involving a location-specific presaccadic component and an active, saccade-driven mechanism that provides flexible spatial generalization.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Lukasz Grzeczkowski, Zhuanghua Shi, Martin Rolfs, Heiner Deubel

papers.title: A dynamic 1/f noise protocol to assess visual attention without biasing perceptual processing
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical investigations of visual attention deploy discrete, localized test items to quantify perceptual sensitivity across space and time. However, the transient presentation of these localized probes introduces luminance transients and structural landmarks that inevitably bias the spatial and temporal distribution of attention. To resolve this methodological confound, this work introduces a novel psychophysical protocol that embeds orientation-filtered test signals directly into a seamless, full-screen dynamic 1/f ('pink') noise background. Because probe signals are integrated into the continuous texture without introducing distinct object boundaries or temporal onset transients, observer expectations and perceptual allocation remain uncontaminated. The utility and sensitivity of the protocol were verified across both covert spatial attention and presaccadic attention tasks, demonstrating that it reliably captures the spatial distribution, temporal dynamics, and performance costs and benefits of visual attention across the visual field.
papers.authors: Nina M. Hanning, Heiner Deubel

E158.name: Daniel Wolpert
E158.bio: Daniel Wolpert is a Professor of Neuroscience and Vice-Chair of the Department of Neuroscience at Columbia University's Zuckerman Institute. Wolpert’s research explores the computational principles governing how the brain plans and controls movement through Bayesian decision theory and internal models. Their work examines how the central nervous system integrates sensory signals with prior knowledge to compensate for biological noise and uncertainty. Wolpert's current research focuses on the 'COIN' (COntextual INference) model, investigating how the brain uses contextual cues to segment, store, and retrieve a repertoire of motor memories.
E158.research_direction: Dr. Wolpert has recently been investigating the computational principles of sensorimotor control, particularly how practice schedules and contextual inference govern multitask learning and memory consolidation. Their recent work also explores the intersection of movement and cognitive development, using functional neuroimaging and behavioral metrics to examine the relationship between early sensorimotor variability and cognitive trajectories in young children with autism spectrum disorder. Furthermore, to overcome the limitations of traditional lab-based studies, they are developing open-source virtual reality platforms that utilize precise kinematic tracking to conduct remote, ecologically valid behavioral experiments. By integrating theoretical modeling with pediatric fMRI pipelines and modern WebXR technologies, Dr. Wolpert aims to build a comprehensive picture of how human motor systems adapt and function in both typical and atypical populations.

papers.title: Implicit vs. explicit choice promotes the combination vs. selection of sensorimotor memories under contextual uncertainty
papers.abstract: Participants learned to reach in two opposing force fields cued by the direction of random-dot motion of varying coherence, testing whether uncertain context leads to blending or picking of motor memories. When they moved before reporting the dot direction, adaptation scaled with coherence and Bayesian models favoured belief-weighted combination. When they had to report their choice first, adaptation ignored coherence and models favoured categorical selection, so how memories are expressed depends on whether contextual inference is implicit or explicit.
papers.authors: Anvesh S. Naik, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Carlos A. Velázquez-Vargas, James N. Ingram, Máté Lengyel, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Curriculum effects in multitask learning through the lens of contextual inference
papers.abstract: This review examines how the structure of practice affects multitask learning, including the speed-versus-retention trade-off seen in blocked versus interleaved motor training and catastrophic forgetting in machine learning. It argues that contextual inference, which weighs task transition dynamics, contextual cues and observation noise, unifies these effects. The authors suggest the framework could inspire ways to reduce catastrophic interference in artificial systems.
papers.authors: Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Máté Lengyel, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Ouvrai opens access to remote virtual reality studies of human behavioural neuroscience
papers.abstract: Ouvrai is a free, open-source toolkit that lets researchers run behavioural experiments remotely in consumer VR headsets through the browser using WebXR. It provides JavaScript templates and a component library and integrates with Firebase, Prolific and Mechanical Turk, and it also supports desktop and touchscreen studies. Three motor learning experiments demonstrate that it yields usable high-resolution kinematic data outside the lab.
papers.authors: Evan Cesanek, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, James N. Ingram, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Sensorimotor variability distinguishes early features of cognition in toddlers with autism
papers.abstract: The study analysed quantitative and observational movement measures in more than 1,000 toddlers with autism across IQ levels. Lower-IQ autistic toddlers showed clearly altered sensorimotor features, whereas higher-IQ autistic toddlers were indistinguishable from typically developing controls. The authors suggest that atypical movement may affect sensorimotor learning and thereby core autistic behaviours in lower-IQ children.
papers.authors: Kristina Denisova, Daniel M. Wolpert

papers.title: Contextual inference in learning and memory
papers.abstract: The paper builds a common vocabulary for how context shapes learning and memory across conditioning, episodic memory, economic choice and motor learning. It proposes a Bayesian model in which context is a hidden variable that must be inferred, and this inference governs how memories are created, expressed and updated. The framework separates proper learning (building and updating memories) from apparent learning (shifts in which memory is expressed), and reviews extensions to more complex settings.
papers.authors: James B. Heald, Máté Lengyel, Daniel M. Wolpert

E159.name: Andrew Pruszynski
E159.bio: Andrew Pruszynski is an Associate Professor at Western University and holds the Canada Research Chair in Sensorimotor Neuroscience. Their research examines the neural computations underlying motor control and sensory perception, focusing on how the nervous system integrates tactile and proprioceptive feedback to facilitate skilled reaching and object manipulation. Pruszynski has shown that rapid motor reflexes exhibit goal-dependent characteristics previously attributed to voluntary control, and that peripheral tactile neurons process geometric features like edge orientation. Pruszynski’s laboratory utilizes high-density electrophysiology, robotic Kinarm perturbations, and computational modeling to map the population dynamics of motor circuits during active behavior.
E159.research_direction: Dr. Pruszynski has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms underlying flexible motor control, sequential action planning, and active tactile perception. Using electrophysiological recordings in non-human primates, their recent work explores how motor and premotor cortices utilize population-level neural dynamics to coordinate posture and anticipate incoming mechanical disturbances during skilled reaching. At the human behavioral level, they are studying how rapid movement sequences are planned and learned, using reaching paradigms to test how cognitive representations of multiple future actions interact and whether sequence learning relies on better target prediction or trajectory optimization. Finally, their research also probes active sensory processing, investigating how movement parameters like fingertip scanning speed influence the sensory system's ability to extract and discriminate tactile features such as edge orientation.

papers.title: Speed-dependent modulation of tactile edge orientation discrimination
papers.abstract: During active exploration with the fingertip, the authors tested how scanning speed affects the ability to judge the orientation of an edge. Performance varied with speed and was best at very slow speeds. The result links to the lab's tactile neuroscience work on how edge geometry is extracted from fingertip signals during movement.
papers.authors: Vaishnavi Sukumar, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Sensory expectations shape neural population dynamics in motor circuits
papers.abstract: Recording from populations of neurons in monkey motor circuits while the animals reached, the authors manipulated what mechanical disturbances the arm should expect. Expectations changed the state of the population before any disturbance arrived, and this preparatory shift reshaped how the circuit responded to the feedback that followed. The work shows that anticipation of sensory input is built into motor-cortical dynamics and helps explain flexible, context-dependent feedback control.
papers.authors: Jonathan A. Michaels, Mehrdad Kashefi, Jack Zheng, Olivier Codol, Jeffrey Weiler, Rhonda Kersten, Jonathan C. Lau, Paul L. Gribble, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Compositional neural dynamics during reaching
papers.abstract: Because arm mechanics make reaching depend on posture, the authors used a task in which the same targets serve as start points on some trials and end points on others, separating direction from final posture.
