In monkey primary motor and dorsal premotor cortex, population activity had three parts: a posture subspace with fixed points, rotational dynamics moving between those points so that similar rotations give similar movements, and a condition-independent shift tracking trial progress. This gives a population-level account of how motor cortex supports posture-dependent skilled reaching.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Kashefi, Jonathan A. Michaels, Rhonda Kersten, Jonathan C. Lau, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Motor Sequence Learning Involves Better Prediction of the Next Action and Optimization of Movement Trajectories
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether sequence learning comes from faster execution of single movements, better anticipation of which target comes next, or sequence-specific optimization of how movements are performed. Behavioral experiments with sequential reaching separate these accounts. Learning was explained mainly by improved prediction of the upcoming action and by smoother, more optimal movement trajectories within the sequence.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Kashefi, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

papers.title: Future movement plans interact in sequential arm movements
papers.abstract: Rapid action sequences require planning upcoming movements while the current one is still being executed. Using a new sequential reaching paradigm that varies how many future reaches can be previewed while holding execution of the ongoing reach constant, the authors show that people plan at least two future reaches at once. These future plans are not independent of each other, indicating interacting representations of upcoming movements.
papers.authors: Mehrdad Kashefi, Sasha Reschechtko, Giacomo Ariani, Mahdiyar Shahbazi, Alice Tan, Jörn Diedrichsen, J. Andrew Pruszynski

E161.name: Sabine Kastner
E161.department: Department of Psychology and Princeton Neuroscience Institute
E161.bio: Kastner investigates the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception, attention, and awareness through a comparative translational framework involving humans and non-human primates. Their research utilizes a multi-modal approach that integrates functional neuroimaging, diffusion tensor imaging, and intracranial electrophysiology to map large-scale cognitive networks. A significant focus of this work involves elucidating the role of the thalamus in regulating cortical communication and exploring the rhythmic temporal dynamics of attentional selection. Additionally, Kastner examines the development of these cognitive functions in children and characterizes their disruption following focal brain lesions.
E161.research_direction: Dr. Kastner has recently been investigating the large-scale neural dynamics that support visual spatial attention across both human and non-human primate models. Their recent work explores how rapid spiking bursts in higher-order thalamic structures like the pulvinar, along with cortical alpha-band oscillations, interact to route information and gate visual processing. To study these phenomena, they utilize diverse methods including macaque electrophysiology with microstimulation, human intracranial recordings from epilepsy patients, and cross-frequency network analyses. Broadening their focus on population coding, they are also developing novel computational methods and biophysical models to examine spatial filtering through ephaptic coupling and to advance geometry-free automated spike sorting for high-density neural data.

papers.title: Higher-order thalamic bursts are drivers of attention control
papers.abstract: Records pulvinar and parietal cortex in macaques performing an attention task and finds that bursts of rapid spiking in the pulvinar are modulated by attention and predict whether a target is detected. Pulvinar bursts also reshape how cortical populations encode spatial location. Electrical microstimulation that evokes pulvinar bursts improves detection and synchronizes cortical spiking, establishing bursts as a causal thalamic mechanism for attention control.
papers.authors: Rober Boshra, Michael Harris, Kacie Dougherty, Melissa Berg, Britney M. Morea, Henry J. Alitto, Mario C. Rodriguez, W. Martin Usrey, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: KIASORT: Knowledge-Integrated Automated Spike Sorting for Geometry-Free Neuron Tracking
papers.abstract: Introduces a spike-sorting method that builds channel-specific models and tracks each neuron independently, without assuming a particular probe geometry or a single global drift model. In simulations and ground-truth benchmarks with neuron-specific drift it recovers more high-quality units than Kilosort4 while running in real time on CPUs, and it works on primate and mouse data. The software includes a graphical interface for curation.
papers.authors: Kianoush Banaie Boroujeni, Thilo Womelsdorf, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: Ephaptic coupling improves the neural population code
papers.abstract: Builds matched spiking network models with and without a self-generated extracellular field to test the functional role of ephaptic coupling. A network's own field decorrelates the population, raises dimensionality and improves decoding, whereas the same field imposed externally synchronizes and harms coding. A theory frames the field as a spatial filter, and multi-patch recordings show a matching distance-dependent trace in neighbors.
papers.authors: Kianoush Banaie Boroujeni, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: High-frequency bursts facilitate fast communication for human spatial attention
papers.abstract: Combines human intracranial recordings from epilepsy patients with spiking network models during spatial cueing tasks. Brief high-frequency activity bursts, coupled to slow rhythms, mark windows of elevated population firing, and their strength and decoupling from slow rhythms predict accuracy. Bursts synchronize across brain-wide subnetworks with lead-lag structure, suggesting they route information during attention.
papers.authors: Kianoush Banaie Boroujeni, Randolph F. Helfrich, Ian C. Fiebelkorn, J. Nicole Bentley, Peter Brunner, Jack J. Lin, Robert T. Knight, Sabine Kastner

papers.title: Differential neural mechanisms underlie cortical gating of visual spatial attention mediated by alpha-band oscillations
papers.abstract: Analyzes electrocorticography from eight epilepsy patients doing a spatial attention task. Alpha desynchronization in contralateral dorsal parietal areas is dissociated from alpha synchronization in ipsilateral ventrolateral extrastriate areas, mapping to enhancement versus suppression. Cross-frequency analyses suggest alpha phase in early visual areas gates high-frequency activity downstream.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Xiaofang Yang, Ian C. Fiebelkorn, Ole Jensen, Robert T. Knight, Sabine Kastner

E167.name: Stefan Treue
E167.institution: German Primate Center (Leibniz Institute for Primate Research)
E167.bio: Stefan Treue investigates the physiological mechanisms of visual perception and attention in the primate brain. Utilizing extracellular recordings in macaque monkeys and human psychophysical experiments, Treue examines how top-down cognitive signals modulate sensory processing in cortical areas such as the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) regions. Treue proposed the feature-similarity gain model, which describes how attention multiplicatively increases the gain of neurons selective for attended visual features across the entire visual field. Their research was recognized with the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, and Treue currently serves as the Director of the German Primate Center, where they advocate for transparency and ethics in animal research.
E167.research_direction: Dr. Treue has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of visual attention as well as the behavioral dynamics of social perceptual decision-making. In the domain of visual processing, their recent work explores the functional anatomy of top-down selective attention, using pathway-selective optogenetics in macaques to dissect how frontal eye field (FEF) projections modulate firing rates versus oscillatory phase-locking in motion area MT. Beyond single-agent perception, they are examining how real-time social information influences continuous decision-making, comparing how human and macaque dyads integrate social cues, share confidence, and coordinate competitive or cooperative strategies during shared behavioral games. Additionally, their research probes the temporal dynamics of human vision, using dense-sampling psychophysics and computational modeling to investigate whether observed perceptual behavioral rhythms reflect continuous internal oscillations or discrete, phase-aligned performance peaks across trials.

papers.title: Perceptual rhythms by phase-aligned perceptual performance peaks across trials
papers.abstract: Dense-sampling psychophysics often reports rhythmic fluctuations in perceptual performance after a reset event. The authors propose that each trial may contain only a single efficiency peak, locked to one peak of an ongoing internal oscillation, so that rhythmicity emerges only when averaging across trials. Simulations and reanalysis of three published datasets support the possibility of such phase-aligned peaks.
papers.authors: Tobias Schoeberl, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Confidence over competence: Real-time integration of social information in human continuous perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: Pairs of people performed a continuous perceptual report task with wagering, alone and together, to see how real-time social information changes judgments about noisy motion stimuli. Partners in a dyad became more confident, but accuracy on average did not improve. Partners' accuracy and confidence converged toward each other, helping the weaker partner at the cost of the stronger one.
papers.authors: Felix Schneider, Antonino Calapai, Roger Mundry, Raymundo Báez-Mendoza, Alexander Gail, Igor Kagan, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Pathway-selective optogenetics reveals the functional anatomy of top-down attentional modulation in the macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors used optogenetics in macaques performing a spatial attention task to silence the direct projection from the frontal eye field (FEF) to motion area MT. Inhibiting this pathway reduced attentional modulation in MT by roughly one third while leaving the neurons' basic sensory responses intact. The direct FEF-to-MT pathway contributed both to enhancement of attended targets and suppression of distractors, showing FEF shapes MT firing rates through its direct axons.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Janina Hüer, Pankhuri Saxena, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Dissecting attention: Rate modulation vs. phase locking
papers.abstract: This Neuron commentary discusses a study reporting direct top-down modulation of neuronal firing rates underlying selective visual attention. The authors place it in the debate between rate-based and oscillatory phase-locking accounts of attentional modulation, arguing the findings support rate modulation.
papers.authors: Moein Esghaei, Julio Martinez-Trujillo, Stefan Treue

papers.title: Human and macaque pairs employ different coordination strategies in a transparent decision game
papers.abstract: Two agents sat face to face at a shared transparent touchscreen to play a Bach-or-Stravinsky coordination game. Most human pairs developed dynamic turn-taking that equalized payoffs, whereas all macaque pairs settled into simpler static coordination. Two monkeys learned dynamic coordination after training with a human confederate, using a competitive turn-taking strategy explained by visibility of the partner's action.
papers.authors: Sebastian Möller, Alexander M. Unakafov, Julia Fischer, Alexander Gail, Stefan Treue, Igor Kagan

E168.name: Nilli Lavie
E168.department: Department of Psychology and the Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience
E168.bio: Lavie is a professor of cognitive neuroscience who developed the 'Load Theory of Attention and Cognitive Control' to address the early versus late selection debate. Their research utilizes a combination of psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to investigate the neural mechanisms of information processing capacity. Lavie's work demonstrates how perceptual load and executive control determine the extent of distractor interference, impacting visual awareness and task performance. Currently, their research extends these frameworks to individual differences in attention and the application of cognitive load principles to real-world environments such as driving and clinical disorders.
E168.research_direction: Dr. Lavie's recent work has been investigating the mechanisms of sustained selective attention and distractibility, specifically examining how perceptual load modulates neural and behavioral focus. Using EEG techniques such as frequency-tagging and aperiodic 1/f slope analysis, they are exploring the neural oscillatory dynamics that govern moment-to-moment fluctuations between focused and lapsed states over time. Their recent research applies these theoretical frameworks to diverse populations, measuring how attention control develops during adolescence to predict real-world classroom inattention, and testing whether impaired distractor filtering under varying perceptual loads explains attention deficits in stroke survivors with chronic fatigue. Additionally, they have recently been expanding into applied visual attention by utilizing unsupervised clustering and information theory to model and monitor driver gaze distributions during naturalistic driving scenarios.

papers.title: Sustained attention under load: Neurophysiological mechanisms and behavioural consequences
papers.abstract: Sustained attention declines with time on task, while perceptual load is known to improve task focus by directing neural resources to task-relevant processing. This preprint asks how perceptual load changes the neurophysiological signatures of sustained attention decline over time. It examines EEG measures including the aperiodic 1/f slope, a proposed index of excitation-inhibition balance, alongside behavioural outcomes.
papers.authors: Louise Catheryne Barne, Xuran Fu, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Effects of Perceptual Load on Sustained Attention States
papers.abstract: Sustained attention fluctuates between effective focus and error-prone lapses. Using EEG during a gradual-onset continuous performance task, this line of work characterises the neural oscillatory dynamics that distinguish in-the-zone from out-of-the-zone states and tests how perceptual load shapes them. It links load theory to the moment-to-moment neural basis of attention lapses.
papers.authors: Rodolfo Solís-Vivanco, Louise Barne, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Increased neural responsiveness to distractors irrespective of perceptual load explains attention deficit in post-stroke fatigue
papers.abstract: Thirty-two chronic stroke survivors did a selective attention task at low, medium or high perceptual load while frequency-tagged EEG tracked neural responses to targets and to task-irrelevant flickering distractors. Higher fatigue was tied to stronger distractor responses that did not shrink with load. The findings show that attention deficits in post-stroke fatigue stem from impaired distractor filtering, applying load theory to a clinical population.
papers.authors: Annapoorna Kuppuswamy, Anthony Harris, William De Doncker, Adrian Alexander, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Applying Information Theory Divergence to Unsupervised Clustering of Driving Gaze Distribution
papers.abstract: The paper builds a 'vocabulary' of driver gaze patterns from naturalistic driving. An information-theoretic unsupervised clustering approach, starting from Gaussian mixture representations of gaze segments, captures mutual information between driving scenarios such as approaching junctions and the resulting gaze clusters. It offers a data-driven way to monitor driver visual attention.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
papers.authors: Ron M. Hecht, Omer Tsimhoni, Andrea Braunshtain, Ariel Telpaz, Yael Shmueli Friedland, Gershon Celniker, Nilli Lavie

papers.title: Sustained selective attention in adolescence: Cognitive development and predictors of distractibility at school
papers.abstract: Adolescents and adults performed a sustained selective-attention task, and the study also tracked distractibility in real school lessons. The work charts how attention control and susceptibility to distraction develop across adolescence. It also identifies which individual factors predict inattention in the classroom, linking laboratory measures of attention to everyday educational outcomes.
papers.authors: Michael H. Hobbiss, Nilli Lavie

E170.name: John Duncan
E170.department: MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit
E170.lab_name: Brain mechanisms of attention and control
E170.bio: John Duncan is a cognitive neuroscientist who researches the neural mechanisms of selective attention and fluid intelligence. Duncan co-developed the biased competition framework of visual attention and identified the multiple-demand (MD) system, a frontoparietal network involved in organizing goal-directed thought. Their research integrates functional neuroimaging, neuropsychology, and single-cell electrophysiology to analyze how the brain partitions complex cognitive tasks into structured attentional episodes. Duncan’s recent work explores the relationship between these cortical control systems and the processes of human reasoning and problem-solving.
E170.research_direction: Dr. Duncan’s recent work explores the functional architecture and representational coding of the frontoparietal cognitive control system, broadly known as the multiple-demand network. Using high-resolution human fMRI, they have recently been investigating how this domain-general system maps onto fine-grained cortical topography and how its regions encode abstract task operations compared to specific stimulus identities. To bridge species and spatial scales, their research also utilizes comparative human-macaque fMRI and primate electrophysiology to examine the evolutionary homology of these control networks and to probe how attentional selection drives the exchange of task information across the lateral prefrontal cortex. Ultimately, they are developing unifying theoretical frameworks to explore whether these distributed frontoparietal regions support cognition by constructing structured mental models to guide goal-directed behavior.

papers.title: Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
papers.abstract: The authors scanned humans and two macaques with fMRI during a multi-step saccadic maze task, contrasted with a control needing similar moves but no goal-based decisions. The human data closely matched the canonical multiple-demand network and extended into much of the dorsal attention network. The monkeys showed matching activity in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal and posterior temporal cortex, with a less clear lateral frontal correspondence, giving the first direct human-macaque comparison of the system.
papers.authors: Valentina Mione, Freja Holm Prins, Moataz Assem, Urs Schüffelgen, Søren Kyllingsbæk, Mark J. Buckley, Daniel J. Mitchell, John Duncan

papers.title: Attentional selection drives information convergence within macaque lateral prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Recording population activity in dorsal and ventral lateral prefrontal cortex of monkeys performing an attentional selection task, the study measures directed mutual information about several task features between the two regions. Information about multiple features converges in both directions, specifically after the selection of the target from the visual display. This suggests attention is a coherent state that emerges through inter-regional exchange in prefrontal cortex.
papers.authors: Daniel J Mitchell, Mikiko Kadohisa, Makoto Kusunoki, Cheshta Bhatia, Mark J Buckley, John Duncan

papers.title: Construction and use of mental models: Organizing principles for the science of brain and mind
papers.abstract: A theoretical synthesis arguing that cognition is organised around building and using mental models: structured internal representations that bind together the entities, roles and relations relevant to current behaviour. The paper explains how frontoparietal control regions could implement these models and proposes that this idea gives the science of brain and mind a set of unifying organising principles.
papers.authors: John Duncan

papers.title: Basis of executive functions in fine-grained architecture of cortical and subcortical human brain networks
papers.abstract: Using Human Connectome Project-style high-resolution fMRI in individual participants, the authors mapped three classic executive tasks (n-back, rule switching, stop signal). Activations from all tasks converge in nine domain-general territories across frontal, parietal and temporal cortex, and each task also shows its own fine-grained topography around and between these territories. The work links the domain-general multiple-demand system to task-specific specialisation at a much finer anatomical scale than earlier studies.
papers.authors: Moataz Assem, Sneha Shashidhara, Matthew F Glasser, John Duncan

papers.title: Task and stimulus coding in the multiple-demand network
papers.abstract: Using HCP-style fMRI with a 360-parcel cortical parcellation, the authors compared multivertex activity patterns for every combination of three tasks and two stimulus classes (faces, buildings) in each region. Multiple-demand regions carried strong task-related patterns, with stimulus identity encoded only as a smaller variation on them. This mirrors what has been seen in monkey prefrontal neurons and indicates that these regions organise activity around the operation being performed.
papers.authors: Sneha Shashidhara, Moataz Assem, Matthew F Glasser, John Duncan

E174.name: Laurent Itti
E174.department: Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science
E174.bio: Laurent Itti is a Professor of Computer Science, Psychology, and Neuroscience at the University of Southern California and the director of the iLab. Itti developed computational frameworks for visual saliency and bottom-up attention that simulate the neural mechanisms biological systems use to prioritize visual stimuli. Their research connects computational neuroscience and machine vision, focusing on scene understanding, eye-movement control, and the role of Bayesian surprise in perception. Itti’s recent work applies neuromorphic algorithms to real-time gaze prediction and uses eye-tracking behavior as a diagnostic tool for identifying neurological disorders.
E174.research_direction: Dr. Itti's recent work explores a diverse intersection of embodied artificial intelligence, biologically inspired neural architectures, and the security of generative machine learning models. In the domain of embodied AI, they have recently been investigating how to leverage multimodal vision-and-language models for zero-shot agent navigation, alongside developing self-supervised pretraining schemes and reward-generation methods that allow robots to learn complex policies from minimal or imperfect demonstrations. Their research also delves into neuroscience-inspired computing by designing artificial dendrite-like nodes that model biological nonlinear error prediction to compress and improve artificial neural networks. Furthermore, they are examining the Riemannian-geometric fingerprints of generative models, utilizing non-Euclidean manifold distances to trace the provenance of synthetic media and safeguard intellectual property.

papers.title: Three-Step Nav: A Hierarchical Global-Local Planner for Zero-Shot Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Addresses the failures of multimodal-LLM agents in zero-shot vision-and-language navigation with a three-stage protocol that needs no fine-tuning. The agent first looks ahead to spot landmarks and draft a plan, then checks the current view to refine direction, and finally reviews its whole path history to remove accumulated errors. It is competitive on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks and code is released.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), PMLR
papers.authors: Wanrong Zheng, Yunhao Ge, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Value Explicit Pretraining for Learning Transferable Representations
papers.abstract: Introduces a self-supervised contrastive pretraining scheme that uses Monte Carlo value estimates from imperfect, unlabeled demonstrations to build encoders whose representations vary smoothly with task progress. Transfer to unseen tasks in Ant locomotion, navigation and Atari yields up to 2x higher reward and 3x better sample efficiency than prior pretraining methods.
papers.authors: Kiran Lekkala, Henghui Bao, Sumedh A. Sontakke, Erdem Biyik, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Riemannian-Geometric Fingerprints of Generative Models
papers.abstract: Formalizes the idea that each generative model leaves a characteristic fingerprint, and defines it using geodesic distances on a non-Euclidean manifold rather than Euclidean distances. A gradient-based algorithm built on this theory separates a large set of models (27 architectures, two resolutions, vision and vision-language) better than prior methods and generalizes to unseen datasets and model types, with uses in IP protection and detecting synthetic training data.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV 2025, Highlight)
papers.authors: Hae Jin Song, Laurent Itti

papers.title: Perforated Backpropagation: A Neuroscience Inspired Extension to Artificial Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Motivated by the fact that biological dendrites perform nonlinear computation, this work adds dendrite-like nodes to trained networks that learn to predict the remaining error. These nodes are then frozen and the original neurons retrained with the extra signal, and the cycle can repeat. The method improves accuracy across several PyTorch architectures and allows substantial model compression.
papers.authors: Rorry Brenner, Laurent Itti

papers.title: RoboCLIP: One Demonstration is Enough to Learn Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Proposes using a pretrained video-language model to turn a single demonstration, either a video (even of a human) or a text description, into a reward signal for reinforcement learning, so no hand-designed reward or large demonstration set is needed. Agents trained on this reward reach roughly two to three times the zero-shot performance of competing imitation-learning baselines on manipulation tasks.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Sumedh A. Sontakke, Jesse Zhang, Sebastien M. R. Arnold, Karl Pertsch, Erdem Biyik, Dorsa Sadigh, Chelsea Finn, Laurent Itti

E175.name: Eyal Seidemann
E175.department: Department of Neuroscience and Department of Psychology
E175.bio: Eyal Seidemann is a Professor of Neuroscience and Psychology at the University of Texas at Austin and directs the Seidemann Lab. Seidemann's research investigates the neural basis of visual perception and decision-making by combining widefield optical imaging with electrophysiology and optogenetics in alert macaque monkeys. Their work involves characterizing spatiotemporal population dynamics in the primary visual cortex and developing computational decoding models to predict psychophysical performance from neural signals. Seidemann's current research focuses on the real-time monitoring and manipulation of cortical circuits to elucidate the causal relationship between population-level activity and visual behavior.
E175.research_direction: Dr. Seidemann has recently been investigating the population dynamics and internal states of the primary visual cortex (V1), utilizing advanced techniques in awake macaques ranging from whole-cell membrane potential recordings to pioneering the use of genetically-encoded voltage indicators. Their recent work explores how V1 populations process fundamental stimulus features, examining neural responses to diverse temporal waveforms and investigating how visual contrast is encoded over the exceptionally wide dynamic ranges found in natural scenes. Additionally, they are actively examining the links between early neural signals and visual behavior to understand how fluctuating internal states mediate reaction times and how delayed divisive normalization mechanisms might drive perceptual similarity masking. To tie these findings together, Dr. Seidemann is also working to reconcile disparate nonlinear dynamics observed across different measurement modalities and species, using computational modeling to bridge subthreshold voltage signals, calcium transients, and human neuroimaging data.

papers.title: Fluctuating internal states mediate neural-behavioral covariations in V1
papers.abstract: Whole-cell membrane potential recordings from single V1 neurons in macaques doing a reaction-time detection task show that most cells slowly depolarize before target onset, and the size of this buildup tracks reaction time. After the target appears, membrane-potential fluctuations covary with choice, with strength depending on target location and contrast. A model with a fluctuating multiplicative gain reproduces the effects, implying internal-state-driven nonlinear modulation at or before V1.
papers.authors: Baowang Li, Jason M. Samonds, Yuzhi Chen, Thibaud Taillefumier, Nicholas J. Priebe, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Wide dynamic range of contrast-encoding in neural responses in macaque V1
papers.abstract: Contrast coding in V1 is usually studied up to 100% Weber contrast, yet natural scenes contain many locations far above that. Using single-neuron electrophysiology and population calcium imaging in fixating macaques with Gaussian stimuli up to 900% Weber contrast, responses kept rising above 100% and only a minority of neurons saturated early. V1 contrast encoding is therefore broader than previously assumed.
papers.authors: Hiroichi Yoshida, Yuzhi Chen, Wilson S. Geisler, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Fast neural population dynamics in primate V1 captured by a genetically-encoded voltage indicator
papers.abstract: The authors express a genetically encoded voltage indicator in excitatory V1 neurons of macaques for the first time and image population responses to stimuli with varied temporal waveforms and contrasts. Compared with a calcium indicator, the voltage signal shows faster dynamics, follows higher temporal frequencies and responds to lower contrasts. A simple nonlinear model predicts responses to arbitrary temporal waveforms and contrasts, supporting the view that the signal reflects locally summed membrane potential.
papers.authors: Jingyang Zhou, Yuzhi Chen, Matt Whitmire, Pin Kwang Tan, Jimin Wu, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Jacob T. Robinson, Wilson S. Geisler, Vincent A. Pieribone, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Neural correlates of perceptual similarity masking in primate V1
papers.abstract: Voltage-sensitive dye imaging of V1 in macaques detecting targets against backgrounds of varying similarity shows that early target responses are paradoxically enhanced by similarity, then reverse in a later phase to match the behavioral masking effect. A delayed divisive normalization model qualitatively accounts for the pattern, supporting a V1 gain-control contribution to similarity masking.
papers.authors: Spencer Chin-Yu Chen, Yuzhi Chen, Wilson S. Geisler, Eyal Seidemann

papers.title: Disparate nonlinear neural dynamics measured with different techniques in macaque and human V1
papers.abstract: Widefield voltage-sensitive dye and GCaMP imaging in macaque V1 with stimuli of varied temporal waveforms yield near-additive temporal dynamics, unlike the strongly sub-additive dynamics reported for human fMRI and ECoG. The discrepancy therefore does not stem from sub- versus supra-threshold signals. A delayed normalization model with different parameters fits all the measurements.
papers.authors: Jingyang Zhou, Matt Whitmire, Yuzhi Chen, Eyal Seidemann

E177.name: Klaus Oberauer
E177.bio: Klaus Oberauer is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology at the University of Zurich, specializing in the computational and functional architecture of human cognitive capacity. Oberauer proposed a three-level framework of working memory that distinguishes between the focus of attention, a region of direct access for maintaining ad-hoc bindings, and activated long-term memory. Their research utilizes a synthesis of behavioral experiments, eye-tracking, and formal computational modeling—specifically interference-based and Bayesian models—to investigate the mechanisms of information binding and retrieval. Current work by Oberauer explores the interactions between working memory and long-term memory, the nature of visual working memory representations, and the advancement of formal theory development in psychological science.
E177.research_direction: Dr. Oberauer's recent work explores the cognitive and computational mechanisms underlying working memory and its relationship to long-term learning. They have recently been developing formal mathematical models to investigate how item-context bindings are maintained, how semantic meaning influences verbal recall, and how visual and verbal information interfere with one another to cause forgetting. Beyond working memory maintenance, their research investigates how temporary representations transition into long-term memory, using repetition paradigms to test whether learning occurs gradually and implicitly or requires discrete, conscious awareness. Finally, Dr. Oberauer is also investigating the broader theoretical foundations of executive function, conducting conceptual analyses to rigorously define "attention control" so that researchers can better measure individual differences in overarching cognitive abilities.

papers.title: Semantic representations in working memory: A computational model.
papers.abstract: Presents a computational model that adds semantic representations to a mechanistic account of verbal working memory, so that meaning-based similarity and association influence how lists of words are encoded and retrieved. The model is tested against the patterns of semantic effects on recall found in earlier work. It links working memory to long-term semantic knowledge within one formal framework.
papers.authors: Benjamin Kowialiewski, Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: A multinomial model-based analysis of bindings in working memory.
papers.abstract: Develops a multinomial processing-tree model that separates the contributions of different kinds of information (items, their bindings, and guessing) to recall in tasks that require remembering which item goes with which context. Applying it to data lets the authors test competing accounts of how bindings are formed and maintained in working memory. It offers a practical measurement tool for a central theoretical question in the field.
papers.authors: Suaad Said Al Hadhrami, Lea M. Bartsch, Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: The meaning of attention control.
papers.abstract: A single-author theoretical analysis of what researchers actually mean by attention control, a construct central to individual-differences work on working memory and executive function. It lays out the distinct functions and mechanisms that get lumped under the term and argues the concept needs clearer definition before it can be measured or related to other abilities. The paper is a conceptual reference point for current debates on how to measure attentional control.
papers.authors: Klaus Oberauer

papers.title: An interference model for visual and verbal working memory.
papers.abstract: Extends an interference-based computational model of working memory to cover both visual and verbal materials with one set of mechanisms. Forgetting and errors arise from interference among bound representations rather than from a fixed number of slots or decay. The model reproduces a broad set of benchmark findings across the two domains.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Klaus Oberauer, Hsuan-Yu Lin

papers.title: Repetition learning is neither a continuous nor an implicit process
papers.abstract: Uses the Hebb repetition paradigm, in which a repeated memory list is gradually recalled better, to test whether learning accumulates continuously and without awareness. The experiments indicate that repetition learning appears to be discrete rather than gradual and depends on participants noticing the repetition. This challenges a widely held view of how long-term memory traces are built up from repeated exposure.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Philipp Musfeld, Alessandra S. Souza, Klaus Oberauer

E178.name: Bradley Postle
E178.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Psychiatry
E178.bio: Bradley Postle is a Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who investigates the cognitive and neural foundations of human visual cognition, focusing on working memory, attention, and consciousness. Postle proposes that working memory is an emergent property of the brain, resulting from the coordinated recruitment of sensory and motor systems rather than a distinct storage buffer. Their laboratory utilizes a multi-methodological approach—including fMRI, EEG, and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), often in simultaneous combinations—alongside multivariate computational modeling to examine the dynamic representation and prioritization of information in the mind.
E178.research_direction: Dr. Postle has recently been investigating the dynamic mechanisms of visual working memory, focusing on how information is prioritized, shielded from interference, and actively removed. Their recent work explores the neural signatures of these flexible states by pairing retrocuing tasks with EEG to track beta-band oscillations, and by using transcranial magnetic stimulation to probe whether deprioritized memory items are maintained in latent, activity-silent states. They are also investigating how cognitive control resolves processing conflicts between active working memory representations and incoming visual perception, as well as the distinct neural mechanisms required to actively purge no-longer-relevant items from memory. To complement these human neuroimaging and perturbation experiments, Dr. Postle leverages recurrent neural network simulations to model how the brain might segregate stable trial context and shifting priority demands into distinct, orthogonal neural subspaces.

papers.title: Prioritization in working memory reduces interference via beta band-linked stimulus transformations
papers.abstract: Participants held two items in working memory and used a two-step retrocue in which the item left uncued by the first cue could still be prioritized by the second. Behavioral recall oscillated at about 15 Hz under prioritization versus about 20 Hz under neutral cues, and the prioritized item was shielded from bias by the other item and by the previous trial. In an EEG experiment, the prioritization cue triggered a low-beta phase reset and spectral peak that burst analyses could not explain, pointing to sustained beta-band dynamics that transform stimulus representations.
papers.authors: Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Effects of TMS on the Decoding and Electrophysiology of Priority in Working Memory
papers.abstract: Using double-serial retrocuing with simultaneous EEG, the authors delivered single TMS pulses to right intraparietal sulcus and asked how this alters representations of unprioritized versus irrelevant memory items. Pulses restored decodability of the unprioritized item during stimulation and of the irrelevant item some time later, an effect tied to a specific EEG signature. The results support the view that deprioritized information is held in a latent, activity-silent-like state that can be reactivated by perturbation.
papers.authors: Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: EEG Correlates of Active Removal from Working Memory
papers.abstract: Removing no-longer-relevant information from working memory can happen passively, by withdrawing attention, or actively. Using an ABC-retrocuing task with EEG, the authors tested a hijacked-adaptation account in which active removal works by top-down down-weighting of the sensory gain tuned to the to-be-removed content. The EEG evidence supported neural signatures distinguishing active removal from simple attentional withdrawal.
papers.authors: Jiangang Shan, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Temporal Dynamics and Representational Consequences of the Control of Processing Conflict between Visual Working Memory and Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Participants performed a dual task combining orientation working memory with a tilt discrimination during the delay, with congruity between the two manipulated, while EEG was recorded. Behavior was fit with a reinforcement-learning model of cognitive control to obtain trial-wise estimates of preparatory and reflexive control demand. These estimates tracked distinct EEG signatures and shaped how the memory representation was affected by the conflicting percept.
papers.authors: Chunyue Teng, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Mattia Pietrelli, Jiefeng Jiang, Bradley R. Postle

papers.title: Representing context and priority in working memory
papers.abstract: The authors simulated the double serial retrocuing task with recurrent neural networks and used dimensionality reduction to examine how trial context and priority are represented. Ordinal context, stable across the trial, was implemented by segregating items into orthogonal subspaces, whereas priority, which changes several times per trial, relied on a different mechanism. The model reproduces and generates predictions for the lab's human EEG/fMRI findings on prioritization.
papers.authors: Quan Wan, Adel Ardalan, Jacqueline M. Fulvio, Bradley R. Postle

E180.name: Paul Bays
E180.bio: Paul Bays is a Professor of Computation and Cognition at the University of Cambridge, where they direct the Computational Cognition Group. Bays's research utilizes visual psychophysics, mathematical modeling, and eye-tracking to investigate how the brain constructs and maintains internal representations for goal-directed behavior. This work focuses on the resource-based limits of visual working memory, arguing that memory fidelity is constrained by neural noise rather than discrete storage slots. Additionally, their research characterizes the computational principles of feature binding, Bayesian efficient coding, and the predictive attenuation of self-generated sensory inputs.
E180.research_direction: Dr Bays' lab has recently been investigating the computational principles governing how the human brain encodes sensory information and allocates limited cognitive resources across modalities. Their recent work explores the dynamics of visual working memory, utilizing continuous analogue report tasks to isolate internal representational noise from motor execution errors and to examine how memory precision is impacted by varying set sizes, temporal delays, and intrinsic motivational states. Beyond visual cognition, they are also probing sensorimotor predictions and haptic perception, applying Bayesian efficient coding and probabilistic frameworks to investigate classical phenomena like the size-weight illusion and the mechanisms of sensory attenuation during self-touch.

papers.title: Dynamics of variability and bias in working memory
papers.abstract: Studies disagree on whether higher memory load speeds up the deterioration of stored information during a delay, and whether recall drifts toward canonical values over time. Using large, carefully analysed datasets that separate response variability from stimulus-specific bias, the authors test predictions of resource and attractor models. The results constrain how memory representations evolve during maintenance.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Sebastian Schneegans, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Intrinsic rewards guide visual resource allocation via reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Observers prioritise encoding of stimuli tied to internal rewards such as a sense of competence. By manipulating confidence via deceptive feedback or real differences in reliability, the authors show that resources shift toward stimuli estimated well and away from those estimated poorly, harming overall accuracy. A normalization model of resource allocation plus a simple reinforcement-learning rule reproduces the data quantitatively.
papers.venue: Nature Human Behaviour (in press; bioRxiv preprint 2025)
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Rodrigo Raimundo, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Bayesian efficient coding as a theory of perception: progress, controversies, and prospects
papers.abstract: A review of Bayesian efficient coding, which merges efficient coding and Bayesian inference by treating natural stimulus statistics as shaping both encoding and perceptual interpretation. It explains how the framework accounts for counterintuitive biases and lawful relations between bias and variability, surveys empirical support and disputes, and outlines future directions.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Máté Lengyel, Paul M. Bays

papers.title: Representation and computation in visual working memory
papers.abstract: A review of how visual working memory stores and manipulates information, weighing resource-based accounts (neural population codes with limited fidelity) against slot and other discrete accounts. It covers how memories are encoded, maintained, bound and read out, and how these mechanisms support computation over remembered items. The authors identify the open questions the field must resolve.
papers.authors: Paul M. Bays, Sebastian Schneegans, Wei Ji Ma, Timothy F. Brady

papers.title: A dynamic neural resource model bridges sensory and working memory
papers.abstract: Recall fidelity drops sharply between a few hundred milliseconds and a second after a display vanishes, traditionally attributed to separate iconic and working memory systems. The authors add a temporal dimension to a neural population model, with fast stimulus-driven activity build-up and slower accumulation of internal error that makes memories drift. This single model quantitatively explains memory fidelity across both timescales and predicts new behavioural effects.
papers.authors: Ivan Tomić, Paul M. Bays

E181.name: Wei Ji Ma
E181.department: Department of Psychology and the Center for Neural Science
E181.main_research_area: Bayesian models of perception and working memory
E181.bio: Wei Ji Ma is a Professor of Neural Science and Psychology whose research investigates the computational principles underlying human decision-making, perception, and memory. Ma developed Bayesian models of sensory processing and introduced the concept of probabilistic population codes to describe how the brain represents uncertainty. Their current work utilizes human behavioral experiments and mathematical modeling to explore resource rationality in visual working memory and the mechanics of multi-step planning in complex environments. Ma’s methodology integrates computational cognitive science with neuroimaging and electrophysiology to connect algorithmic theories with their biological implementations.
E181.research_direction: Dr. Ma's work centers on how the brain represents and uses uncertainty, with visual perception and visual working memory as the main testbeds. They introduced probabilistic population codes, a proposal for how neural populations can carry probability distributions so that Bayesian inference is neurally implementable, and have tested Bayesian ideal-observer models against human behavior in tasks such as visual search, and against neural data from visual cortex. A second theme is resource-based accounts of visual working memory, in which variability in encoding precision, rather than a fixed number of slots, limits memory, and, more recently, the neural mechanisms by which limited memory resources are allocated across items. A third theme is confidence and attention-dependent uncertainty, where observers appear to incorporate the reliability of their own sensory evidence into decisions. More recently their group has extended this normative approach to higher-level cognition, including human planning, temporal discounting and procrastination, and to how dopaminergic neurons encode reward.

papers.title: Environmental stochasticity reduces human planning effort
papers.abstract: Participants planned in tasks where outcomes of actions were either deterministic or partly random. Behavior and modeling showed that when the environment is stochastic, people invest less planning effort, because deep look-ahead is less valuable when the future is uncertain. The results tie resource-rational accounts of planning to the amount of uncertainty in the world.
papers.authors: Jordan Lei, Jeroen Olieslagers, Nastaran Arfaei, Daisy Xinlei Lin, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: A computational model of backward reasoning in human problem solving
papers.abstract: The authors model how people solve problems by reasoning backward from a goal, decomposing it into subgoals as in AND/OR trees, rather than only searching forward. The model captures human choices and search patterns in a behavioral task. It extends the lab's work on planning to problem solving and goal pursuit.
papers.authors: Jeroen Olieslagers, Zahy Bnaya, Daisy Xinlei Lin, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Decision reversals in sequential decision-making
papers.abstract: The study examines when and why people reverse an earlier decision partway through a sequence of choices. Behavioral experiments and computational models are used to characterize the conditions that produce reversals and what they reveal about how people plan and update. It adds to the lab's account of sequential decision-making beyond single-shot planning.
papers.authors: Sherry Dongqi Bao, Dongjae Kim, Qi Xiu Fu, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Reward prediction error neurons implement an efficient code for reward
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that dopamine reward prediction error neurons are tuned to encode reward in an efficient way, with response functions matched to the distribution of rewards the animal experiences. Using this efficient-coding framework, the authors reproduce features of the diversity of dopamine neuron responses and show the account agrees with recorded data. It links a normative theory of neural coding to reinforcement-learning signals.
papers.authors: Heiko H. Schütt, Dongjae Kim, Wei Ji Ma

papers.title: Expertise increases planning depth in human gameplay
papers.abstract: The authors collected a large set of moves from people of different skill levels playing a simple board game (four-in-a-row) and fit a resource-rational planning model to the choices. Stronger players were best explained by a model that searches deeper and considers more candidate moves, while also evaluating positions more accurately. The work gives a mechanistic account of how expertise changes the computations behind multi-step planning.
papers.authors: Bas van Opheusden, Ionatan Kuperwajs, Gianni Galbiati, Zahy Bnaya, Yunqi Li, Wei Ji Ma

E186.name: Earl Miller
E186.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E186.bio: Earl K. Miller is the Picower Professor of Neuroscience at MIT, where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying executive brain functions such as attention, working memory, and rule learning. Miller developed the integrative theory of prefrontal cortex function and identified mixed selectivity in neurons, which allows for multifunctional neural representations. Their laboratory uses multi-electrode neurophysiology and computational modeling to study how oscillatory dynamics, specifically interactions between gamma and beta frequencies, coordinate top-down control across cortical networks. Currently, this research explores how large-scale neural dynamics enable the organization of thought and action in both healthy and disordered brains.
E186.research_direction: Dr. Miller has recently been investigating how macroscopic cortical oscillations, such as theta, alpha, and beta rhythms, orchestrate cognitive functions like working memory and spatial attention. Using multi-electrode recordings in the prefrontal cortex and frontal eye fields of behaving macaques, their recent work explores whether these rhythmic electric fields act as spatial scans or inhibitory stencils that dictate precisely where and when sensory-related spiking occurs across the cortex. In parallel, they are studying the neural dynamics of consciousness by using novel time-series methods to examine how different anesthetics, including propofol and ketamine, alter the stability and large-scale phase alignment of cortical networks. Across both empirical and theoretical lines of research, Dr. Miller seeks to understand how goal-directed cognition and conscious awareness emerge from the continuous, bidirectional interactions between mesoscale brain waves and discrete neuronal spiking.

papers.title: Working memory readout varies with frontal theta rhythms
papers.abstract: Recording in the frontal eye field of monkeys performing a change-detection working memory task, the authors show that the phase of 3-6 Hz theta at test-array onset predicts behavioral performance, and does so differently for targets at different vertical locations. This is consistent with theta acting like a scan that sweeps across the FEF and thus across visual space. Theta was coupled on opposing phases to spiking and to beta, which a travelling-wave account can explain. The work links rhythmic attention to how remembered content is read out.
papers.authors: Hio-Been Han, Scott L. Brincat, Timothy J. Buschman, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Oscillatory control of cortical space as a computational dimension
papers.abstract: This paper tests the spatial computing framework with multi-electrode prefrontal recordings in monkeys doing object working memory, sequence working memory and categorization tasks. Alpha/beta oscillations carried task information, formed spatial patterns that changed with task conditions, and were inversely related to where sensory-related spiking was expressed, acting like inhibitory stencils. The oscillation patterns also tracked the animals' misattributions of the task and their trial-by-trial decisions. Together the findings show oscillations shape where in cortex content is represented, not only when.
papers.authors: Zhen Chen, Scott L. Brincat, Mikael Lundqvist, Roman F. Loonis, Melissa R. Warden, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Analog Cognition and Consciousness
papers.abstract: A perspective proposing that cognition and consciousness arise from two-way interactions between neuronal spiking and rhythmic electric field activity, i.e. brain waves. Brain waves can exert mesoscale control over excitability, route and organize signals and support analog computation. The authors argue that goal-directed thought, action and unified consciousness emerge from cortex-wide wave dynamics that both reflect and reshape spiking into coherent brain states.
papers.authors: Earl K. Miller, Scott L. Brincat, Jefferson E. Roy

papers.title: Convergent effects of different anesthetics on changes in phase alignment of cortical oscillations
papers.abstract: Ketamine and dexmedetomidine were given at anesthetic doses to nonhuman primates while prefrontal oscillations were recorded. Both drugs increased phase locking within and across hemispheres, but the pattern differed: subregions within a hemisphere became more anti-phase, consistent with large travelling waves, whereas homologous areas across hemispheres became more in-phase. The results suggest different anesthetics converge on strong cortical phase alignment that may underlie loss of responsiveness.
papers.authors: Alexandra G. Bardon, Jesus J. Ballesteros, Scott L. Brincat, Jefferson E. Roy, Meredith K. Mahnke, Yumiko Ishizawa, Emery N. Brown, Earl K. Miller

papers.title: Propofol anesthesia destabilizes neural dynamics across cortex
papers.abstract: The authors introduce DeLASE, a method that estimates how stable the population dynamics of a complex system are from recorded time series. Applied to macaque cortical field potentials across the transition from wakefulness to propofol unconsciousness, it shows that dynamics become less stable under anesthesia, in line with predictions from destabilized linear systems. Simulated networks with increased inhibitory tone reproduced the effect. The results suggest that dynamic stability is required for consciousness.
papers.authors: Adam J. Eisen, Leo Kozachkov, André M. Bastos, Jacob A. Donoghue, Meredith K. Mahnke, Scott L. Brincat, Sarthak Chandra, John Tauber, Emery N. Brown, Ila R. Fiete, Earl K. Miller

E187.name: Timothy Buschman
E187.department: Department of Psychology, Princeton Neuroscience Institute
E187.bio: Timothy Buschman is an Associate Professor at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute where their research investigates the neural mechanisms underlying cognitive control, attention, and working memory. Buschman utilizes a multi-species approach integrating large-scale electrophysiology in non-human primates with optical imaging and optogenetics in rodents to examine how cognition emerges from the dynamic interaction of neural networks. Their findings characterize the divergent roles of prefrontal and parietal regions in top-down and bottom-up attention, as well as the low-dimensional subspaces that route information to guide flexible behavior. This work aims to develop computational models of brain function and provide insights into the dysfunction associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders.
E187.research_direction: Dr. Buschman has recently been studying how the brain flexibly reconfigures itself to do different tasks with the same neural hardware. Their recent work explores how populations of neurons in prefrontal, parietal, and striatal areas reuse shared low-dimensional activity patterns to build new tasks from familiar sensory and motor components, and how the brain routes information between regions through overlapping activity subspaces. They have also been investigating how animals learn and update internal templates of what to look for during visual search, how these templates are organized in neural population codes, and how the brain represents abstract task structure. In parallel, they have been asking how cortex-wide activity patterns in mice differ across individuals with different behavioral tendencies.

papers.title: Building compositional tasks with shared neural subspaces
papers.abstract: This study demonstrates that cognitive flexibility is achieved through the reuse of low-dimensional 'neural subspaces' that represent sensory features and motor actions across different behavioral contexts. Monkeys were trained to alternate between three tasks with overlapping categorical and motor requirements. Population-level recordings from the lateral prefrontal cortex, parietal cortex, and striatum revealed that task-relevant variables (e.g., color, shape, and response direction) are encoded within stable subspaces that are shared across tasks. During task performance, neural activity transforms representations from a sensory-specific subspace into a common motor subspace. Flexibility arises as animals iteratively update internal task beliefs based on reward feedback, which then selectively gates the engagement of the appropriate shared subspaces. These results suggest a compositional neural architecture where complex behaviors are assembled from modular representational components.
papers.authors: Sina Tafazoli, Flora M. Bouchacourt, Adel Ardalan, Nikola T. Markov, Motoaki Uchimura, Marcelo G. Mattar, Nathaniel D. Daw, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Multiplexed subspaces route neural activity across brain-wide networks
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which the brain dynamically routes information across distributed networks to support cognitive flexibility are explored using mesoscale calcium imaging and high-density electrophysiology (Neuropixels) in mice. The researchers identified that brain regions interact through 'multiplexed subspace networks,' where distinct dimensions of neural activity within a single area are functionally coupled to different, overlapping sets of other regions. Information routing is controlled by the alignment of local population activity with these specific subspace dimensions; shifting the geometry of a representation within a region's high-dimensional activity space selectively engages different brain-wide networks. This geometric mechanism allows the brain to reconfigure communication channels on a moment-to-moment basis without structural rewiring.
papers.authors: Camden J. MacDowell, Alexandra Libby, Caroline I. Jahn, Sina Tafazoli, Adel Ardalan, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Cognitive neuroscience: How the brain navigates abstract task spaces
papers.abstract: This peer-reviewed dispatch analyzes how biological systems utilize abstract task representations to facilitate rapid generalization to novel environments. It discusses recent empirical findings regarding the neural construction of abstract task spaces, focusing on how the brain maps sensory inputs and behavioral goals onto structured internal manifolds. The commentary evaluates the role of the prefrontal cortex in representing relational structures and suggests that such abstract representations are essential for overcoming the limitations of trial-and-error learning, thereby supporting complex decision-making and cognitive flexibility in both humans and non-human primates.
papers.authors: Sina Tafazoli, Adel Ardalan, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Differences in the expression of cortex-wide neural dynamics are related to behavioral phenotype
papers.abstract: This research investigates the neural basis of individual differences in behavior by analyzing cortex-wide spatiotemporal motifs of activity in mice using widefield calcium imaging. The study found that while a small set of approximately 14-16 motifs explains the majority of variance in neural activity across all individuals (both 'typical' and 'atypical' neurotypes), individuals differ significantly in the frequency with which they express specific motifs. These variations in the sampling of low-dimensional dynamics explain a substantial portion of the variance in global functional connectivity and specific behavioral phenotypes. These findings suggest that behavioral diversity and neuropsychiatric symptoms may result from changes in the control processes that select and express specific large-scale neural patterns over time.
papers.authors: Camden J. MacDowell, Brandy A. Briones, Michael J. Lenzi, Morgan L. Gustison, Timothy J. Buschman

papers.title: Learning attentional templates for value-based decision-making
papers.abstract: Attentional templates—internal representations of task-relevant features—are critical for filtering sensory input. To investigate how these templates are learned and updated, monkeys were trained on a visual search task requiring the repeated acquisition of new templates. Recordings from the prefrontal and parietal cortex revealed that templates are represented in a structured geometric manner, where perceptually similar templates exhibit similar neural population codes. Learning occurs through an incremental shift in the neural representation toward rewarded features. Crucially, the attentional template transforms diverse stimulus features into a common value representation, allowing a unified decision-making mechanism to deploy attention regardless of the specific template identity. This work defines the neural mechanisms for the flexible control and reward-based learning of attention.
papers.authors: Caroline I. Jahn, Nikola T. Markov, Britney Morea, Nathaniel D. Daw, R. Becket Ebitz, Timothy J. Buschman

E191.name: Masud Husain
E191.department: Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences and Department of Experimental Psychology
E191.bio: Masud Husain is a Professor of Neurology and Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Oxford, where their work bridges the Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences and the Department of Experimental Psychology. Husain’s research integrates clinical neurology with experimental neuroscience to investigate the mechanisms governing human attention, working memory, and motivated decision-making. By employing brain imaging and behavioral paradigms, they examine how these cognitive processes are impaired in conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and stroke. Their research has challenged static models of working memory capacity, demonstrating instead that it is a resource that can be dynamically allocated based on task demands.
E191.research_direction: Dr. Husain's recent work explores the mechanisms underlying visual cognition, decision-making, and motivation across both healthy populations and diverse neurological conditions. They have recently been investigating transsaccadic working memory, using eye-tracking and computational modeling to determine how spatial and color information are maintained and updated across eye movements in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. In the realm of motivation and action, their research probes how patients with focal hippocampal damage weigh complex decision-making trade-offs involving reward, physical effort, and uncertainty. Additionally, they are evaluating large-scale cognitive and behavioral phenotyping methods, utilizing rapid web-based tasks to quantify cognitive slowing in Long COVID while analyzing extensive clinical datasets to isolate distinct behavioral and social dimensions of apathy across various dementias and brain disorders.

papers.title: Transsaccadic working memory in healthy ageing and neurodegenerative disease
papers.abstract: An eye-tracking paradigm combined with computational modelling examined how spatial and colour information are carried across saccades. Saccades harmed spatial but not colour memory, and the model indicated spatial content is held in an eye-centred frame updated by a noisy memory of the saccade. In Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, failures of initial encoding and faster memory decay, rather than the saccadic update itself, explained the spatial deficits.
papers.authors: Sijia Zhao, Thomas Parr, Rob Udale, Verena Klar, Gabriel Davis Jones, Anna Scholcz, Sofia Toniolo, Sanjay G Manohar, Masud Husain

papers.title: The social dimension of apathy: evidence for a distinct domain from 11,243 individuals across health and neurocognitive disorders
papers.abstract: Item-level apathy data from over 11,000 people, including patients with Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, frontotemporal dementia, autoimmune encephalitis and small vessel disease, plus depressed and healthy adults, were analysed. Factor analyses, symptom networks and lifespan analyses all identified social apathy as a coherent, separable dimension across groups and ages. This supports treating social motivation as its own target for assessment and treatment.
papers.authors: Sijia Zhao, Rong Ye, Qian-Yuan Tang, Bahaaeddin Attaallah, Sofia Toniolo, Youssuf Saleh, Matthew A Rouse, Peter Garrard, M John Broulidakis, Sian Thompson, Sanjay G Manohar, Sarosh R Irani, Yuen-Siang Ang, Patricia Lockwood, Matthew A J Apps, Panpan Hu, Kai Wang, James B Rowe, Campbell Le Heron, Masud Husain

papers.title: Self- versus caregiver-reported apathy across neurological disorders
papers.abstract: In 335 patients across dementia, Parkinson's, cerebrovascular and autoimmune encephalitis diagnoses, caregiver ratings of apathy exceeded self-ratings in every condition, and self-report explained only about 14% of the variance in caregiver ratings. The gap was largest where insight is impaired, such as behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, and related to memory and fluency deficits. The authors argue for combining patient and caregiver views in clinical apathy assessment.
papers.authors: Sijia Zhao, Anna Scholcz, Matthew A Rouse, Verena S Klar, Akke Ganse-Dumrath, Sofia Toniolo, M John Broulidakis, Matthew A Lambon Ralph, James B Rowe, Peter Garrard, Sian Thompson, Sarosh R Irani, Sanjay G Manohar, Masud Husain

papers.title: The role of the human hippocampus in decision-making under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Patients with acute autoimmune limbic encephalitis, who have focal hippocampal damage, were tested on trade-offs between reward, uncertainty and physical effort across four experiments. They showed blunted sensitivity to reward and effort only when uncertainty was involved, while valuation on uncertainty-free tasks and uncertainty sensitivity itself were intact. The reduction tracked the severity of hippocampal damage, indicating a context-specific role for the hippocampus in value-based decisions.
papers.authors: Bahaaeddin Attaallah, Pierre Petitet, Rhea Zambellas, Sofia Toniolo, Maria Raquel Maio, Akke Ganse-Dumrath, Sarosh R Irani, Sanjay G Manohar, Masud Husain

papers.title: Long COVID is associated with severe cognitive slowing: a multicentre cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Two short web-based tasks (simple reaction time and number vigilance) were given to 270 people with post-COVID condition in the UK and Germany and compared with recovered and uninfected controls. Patients were about three standard deviations slower on a 30-second reaction time task, and over half fell beyond two standard deviations of control performance. The finding replicated across both clinics and offers a simple objective marker of cognitive slowing.
papers.authors: Sijia Zhao, Eva Maria Martin, Philipp A Reuken, Anna Scholcz, Akke Ganse-Dumrath, Annie Srowig, Isabelle Utech, Valeska Kozik, Monique Radscheidt, Stefan Brodoehl, Andreas Stallmach, Matthias Schwab, Emily Fraser, Kathrin Finke, Masud Husain

E196.name: Igor Utochkin
E196.bio: Igor S. Utochkin is a Staff Research Scientist at the University of Chicago’s Institute for Mind and Biology and a member of the Awh-Vogel Lab. Utochkin’s research examines the cognitive and neural mechanisms of ensemble perception, focusing on how the visual system summarizes statistical information from groups of objects. They have developed computational models, such as the population response model, to explain the interaction between summary statistics and individual item representations in visual working memory. Their work utilizes behavioral psychophysics and signal-detection analysis to investigate how attention, feature similarity, and task requirements affect visual search and memory capacity.
E196.research_direction: Dr. Utochkin has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying ensemble perception, visual attention, and object recognition memory. Their recent work explores how the visual system compresses crowded scenes into summary statistics, utilizing both computational population response models and EEG to determine how single-item representations interact with ensemble gist and whether these computations require focal attention. Alongside this, they are mapping the psychological structure of visual recognition memory using signal-detection analysis to understand whether object confusion spaces remain invariant across retrieval contexts and how intrinsic item memorability might drive asymmetric recognition errors between targets and foils. Furthermore, Dr. Utochkin uses lateralized ERP components to examine the neural dynamics of visual selection, testing how prior memory history and current task goals compete to guide spatial attention and working memory.

papers.title: Recognition-memory asymmetries predicted by individual item memorability
papers.abstract: Examines why confusability between objects in recognition memory is often asymmetric, using item-level memorability measures alongside signal-detection modeling. Shows that individual item memorability predicts which item is more likely to be mistaken for the other. Links the memorability literature with models of the structure of recognition memory.
papers.authors: Igor Utochkin, Nicholas Chiang, Wilma A. Bainbridge

papers.title: Competition between memory and goals shapes the neural dynamics of attention, working memory, and recognition
papers.abstract: Uses EEG in a two-alternative forced-choice task in which an old and a new object appear in opposite hemifields and participants report the location of either. Separating memory history from goal relevance reveals a sustained lateralized ERP component, termed retrieval-related contralateral delay activity, that tracks how attention and working memory are allocated between competing options. The findings show memory and current goals jointly shape selection during recognition.
papers.authors: Igor Utochkin, Edward K. Vogel

papers.title: Invariant Recognition Memory Spaces for Real-World Objects Revealed With Signal-Detection Analysis
papers.abstract: Tests whether the psychological space that governs confusion between remembered targets and foils stays stable when other foils are added or when target memory strength changes. Using signal-detection modeling on data from over 1,300 adults, distances (d') from each foil to a target linearly predict confusion in more complex retrieval contexts. The recognition space is therefore largely invariant across contexts and memory strengths.
papers.authors: Igor Utochkin, Daniil Azarov, Daniil Grigorev

papers.title: The role of attention in basic ensemble statistics processing
papers.abstract: Uses EEG to test whether the visual system can compute basic ensemble statistics such as average orientation without focal attention, by comparing neural responses to attended versus unattended stimulus arrays. The results indicate that ensemble processing depends more on attention than is often assumed. This informs whether summary statistics are truly automatic.
papers.authors: Anton Lukashevich, Heida Maria Sigurdardottir, Nikita Kudriavtsev, Igor Utochkin

papers.title: A population response model of ensemble perception
papers.abstract: Proposes a model in which both the summary statistics of a group of objects and the representation of individual items are read out from the same population of feature-tuned neuronal responses. The model reproduces classic ensemble effects, such as averaging and range or variance estimates, and predicts how ensemble and single-item judgments interact and trade off. It is presented as a unified account of how the visual system compresses crowded scenes into gist.
papers.authors: Igor S. Utochkin, Jeunghwan Choi, Sang Chul Chong

E197.name: Jennifer E. Corbett
E197.department: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); also affiliated with Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES)
E197.bio: Jennifer E. Corbett is a vision scientist specializing in the cognitive and neural mechanisms of ensemble representation and visual averaging. Corbett’s research examines how the visual system extracts statistical summaries, such as the mean and variance of features, to represent complex scenes and support perception across eye movements. They have investigated the functional role of these summary statistics in visual search, their influence on visually guided action, and differences in ensemble processing in clinical populations. Recent work by Corbett includes a synthesis of the pervasiveness of ensemble perception and the development of frameworks to optimize user performance in 3D environments.
E197.research_direction: Dr. Corbett has recently been investigating how the visual system processes complex, naturalistic environments, bridging fundamental perceptual mechanisms with applied human-computer interactions. Their recent work explores ensemble perception as a pervasive strategy for extracting summary statistics to overcome severe capacity limits in attention and memory. To study visual cognition in highly ecological settings, they have been leveraging commercial video games and 3D interfaces as ready-made laboratories, utilizing behavioral timing and eye tracking to probe phenomena like sensorimotor compatibility and spatial navigation strategies. Additionally, they are developing psychophysics-informed AI pipelines to synthesize semantically ambiguous stimuli, allowing them to probe category boundaries and compare perceptual alignment between human observers and machine vision models.

papers.title: A Framework for Generating Semantically Ambiguous Images to Probe Human and Machine Perception
papers.abstract: Using the duck-rabbit illusion as inspiration, the authors build a psychophysics-informed pipeline that interpolates between two concepts in CLIP embedding space to synthesize continuous spectra of ambiguous images. Human observers and machine classifiers then report where they place the category boundary; classifiers lean toward 'rabbit' while humans track the synthesis embedding more closely, and guidance scale affects humans more than classifiers. The approach is proposed as an interpretability probe for human-model alignment.
papers.authors: Yuqi Hu, Vasha DuTell, Ahna R. Girshick, Jennifer E. Corbett

papers.title: Prêt-à-Jouer: commercial videogames as ready-made human perception labs
papers.abstract: The authors argue that commercial videogames are demanding, motivating, and consistent enough across players to serve as ecologically valid testbeds for perception, attention, and executive function. They lay out a minimal toolkit based on screen recording, eye tracking, and behavioral timing, and explain how to choose games and derive testable hypotheses from a game's affordances without developer cooperation. They also delineate which ecological questions the approach can and cannot answer.
papers.authors: Jaap Munneke, Brian Anthony, Jennifer E. Corbett

papers.title: Why axis inversion? Optimizing interactions between users, interfaces, and visual displays in 3D environments
papers.abstract: The paper asks why many gamers invert the vertical axis on their controllers and uses that puzzle to study how control schemes affect performance in settings from video games to laparoscopic surgery. It synthesizes fragmented findings across disciplines, reports a study linking behavioral and cognitive factors to y-axis inversion preference in experienced third-person gamers, and proposes a general framework for predicting sensorimotor compatibility effects, illustrated with a laparoscopic procedure.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Jaap Munneke

papers.title: The Pervasiveness of Ensemble Perception: Not Just Your Average Review
papers.abstract: This Cambridge Elements review argues that summary-statistical representation of feature sets (means, variances) is a pervasive, general strategy of the visual system rather than a niche phenomenon. It integrates evidence across features, modalities, and populations and discusses the role of ensemble coding in overcoming capacity limits in perception, attention, and memory.
papers.authors: Jennifer E. Corbett, Igor S. Utochkin, Shaul Hochstein

E198.name: Andrey Chetverikov
