E198.lab_name: Bergen Laboratory for the Study of Decision, Intuition, Consciousness, and Emotion (DICE)
E198.bio: Andrey Chetverikov is an Associate Professor of Cognitive Psychology at the University of Bergen, where they investigate the computational and neural foundations of visual perception. Chetverikov's research explores how the brain represents environmental variability and uncertainty, using "feature distribution learning" to analyze how observers approximate internal probability distributions of stimulus ensembles. By integrating Bayesian modeling with psychophysics and functional MRI, they examine the mechanisms behind perceptual and mnemonic biases, specifically how the visual system decodes noisy sensory signals. Their current work focuses on refining normative models of inter-item biases and the representation of motion and orientation features in the human visual cortex.
E198.research_direction: Dr. Chetverikov has recently been investigating how the visual system encodes uncertainty and resolves overlapping sensory signals across both perception and working memory. Their recent work explores the nature of probabilistic neural representations, using fMRI pattern decoding and Bayesian modeling to examine how the visual cortex estimates motion direction by integrating velocity with spatial "streaks." Alongside this research into feature encoding, they are also studying the computational principles that drive inter-item and serial biases. By combining psychophysical tasks, such as color-memory and spatial pointing paradigms, with normative "demixing" models, Dr. Chetverikov seeks to understand how the relative sensory noise and similarity of competing stimuli determine whether mental representations attract or repel one another over time.

papers.title: Noise in Competing Representations Determines the Direction of Memory Biases
papers.abstract: Argues that attraction or repulsion between memorized items is an inevitable outcome of the brain disentangling overlapping memory signals, so bias direction should depend on the relative noise of the items rather than absolute noise. Four color-memory experiments with independently manipulated noise confirmed that identical absolute noise can yield either attraction or repulsion. A model with only noise levels as free parameters also reproduces nonlinear bias patterns in existing data.
papers.authors: Andrey Chetverikov, Sabrina Hansmann-Roth

papers.title: Between repulsion and attraction in serial biases: Replication of Chen and Bae (2024)
papers.abstract: A student-led replication of a recent report of repulsive serial bias in a pointing task, asking when perception is drawn toward versus pushed away from the past. The study tests how robust the earlier finding is and how bias sign depends on task conditions.
papers.authors: Juni B. Akselberg, Sara B. Cardona, Mikkel Dybvad, Lise Martine Karlstad, Malin Langemyr, Ingrid A. Mellingsaeter-Jokic, Mats K. K. Moe, Amalie C. Solvang, Andrey Chetverikov

papers.title: Motion direction is represented as a bimodal probability distribution in the human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Tests the idea that the brain infers motion direction from both velocity and the spatial orientation 'streak' left by moving objects. A Bayesian model predicts that decoded probability distributions from visual cortex activity should be bimodal, with peaks at the motion direction and its opposite, which is what fMRI pattern-based decoding and psychophysics showed. The work provides direct neural evidence for probabilistic (uncertainty-carrying) representations in human visual cortex.
papers.authors: Andrey Chetverikov, Janneke F. M. Jehee

papers.title: Demixing model: A normative explanation for inter-item biases in memory and perception
papers.abstract: Proposes a normative model in which biases between similar items in memory and perception arise for any optimal observer inferring multiple objects from a mixture of sensory observations. The model predicts how bias strength and direction depend on item similarity and noise, and accounts for both attraction and repulsion patterns reported across paradigms.
papers.authors: Andrey Chetverikov

E202.name: Michael A. Cohen
E202.department: Department of Psychology and Program in Neuroscience
E202.bio: Michael A. Cohen is an Assistant Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Amherst College and a Research Scientist at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research at MIT. Cohen’s research investigates the cognitive and neural limitations determining which environmental information reaches conscious awareness, examining the functional architecture of the visual system as a bottleneck for information processing. By combining psychophysics with neuroimaging methods such as fMRI and EEG, Cohen characterizes the bandwidth of perceptual experience and the distinctions between neural correlates of awareness and post-perceptual processes. Cohen received the 2024 Vision Sciences Society Young Investigator Award for research on how prior knowledge and neural representation shape the capacity of human vision.
E202.research_direction: Dr. Cohen has recently been investigating the limits and underlying nature of conscious visual awareness, asking whether perceptual experience is fundamentally rich or sparse and if it manifests along a graded continuum rather than as an all-or-none phenomenon. Their recent work also explores the cognitive penetrability of vision, using ambiguous stimuli and virtual reality to test how top-down knowledge and environmental familiarity might expand the bandwidth of what observers actually perceive. To probe these questions, they employ behavioral paradigms like continuous reproduction, crowding, and inattentional blindness, as well as EEG-based no-report masking tasks. Through these diverse methods, Dr. Cohen aims to isolate the genuine neural and cognitive signatures of visual experience, carefully separating true conscious awareness from structural sensory bottlenecks and downstream task-reporting demands.

papers.title: Conscious Awareness Across the Visual Field
papers.abstract: A review of why visual experience feels rich and seamless even though observers notice surprisingly little, tracing the limits imposed by retinal sampling, cortical organization and attentional selection. It uses inattentional blindness and crowding to show the consequences of these bottlenecks. It argues that the historical split between rich-phenomenology and sparse-access theories has narrowed and may reduce to smaller, resolvable differences.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen

papers.title: Top-down knowledge can affect perception when the input is ambiguous
papers.abstract: Tests whether prior knowledge can change what people actually perceive, rather than only their judgments, by using stimuli that are ambiguous in appearance. Across experiments, top-down knowledge shifted perceptual reports when the sensory input was underdetermined but not when it was clear. The work speaks to the long-running debate over cognitive penetrability of vision.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Mabel Shanahan, Katherine Besch, Andrew Rios, Esther Min, Rosa Lafer-Sousa

papers.title: Neural signatures of visual awareness independent of postperceptual processing
papers.abstract: Uses EEG with a no-report masking paradigm to separate neural activity tied to conscious visual experience from activity tied to reporting or post-perceptual processing. The results identify signals of awareness that persist when observers do not need to report. This supports the idea that awareness-related neural correlates are not merely consequences of task demands.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Cole Dembski, Kevin Ortego, Clay Steinhibler, Michael Pitts

papers.title: Familiarity Alters the Bandwidth of Perceptual Awareness
papers.abstract: Investigates whether familiar scenes let observers consciously perceive more, using inattentional-blindness style measures including virtual reality. Familiarity with the environment increased how much information reached awareness, suggesting that prior knowledge expands the bandwidth of perceptual experience.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Skyler Sung, Zaki Alaoui

papers.title: Perceptual Awareness Occurs Along a Graded Continuum: No Evidence of All-or-None Failures in Continuous Reproduction Tasks
papers.abstract: Asks whether awareness of a stimulus is all-or-none or graded by using continuous reproduction tasks and modeling of response distributions. Across paradigms such as masking and attentional-blink-style tasks, the data showed no evidence of discrete guessing failures and instead favored graded awareness. The paper challenges a widely used inference for all-or-none perception.
papers.authors: Michael A. Cohen, Jonathan Keefe, Timothy F. Brady

E203.name: Jason Haberman
E203.bio: Jason Haberman is an Associate Professor of Psychology at Rhodes College who researches ensemble perception, a heuristic that allows the visual system to represent information via summary statistics. Haberman’s work uses psychophysical methods to examine how the brain extracts average features—such as orientation, size, or facial expression—from groups of objects. Their current research investigates the intersection of vision science and social cognition, specifically examining the perception of social status and self-representation. Haberman previously held a postdoctoral position at Harvard University and completed their doctoral studies at the University of California, Davis.
E203.research_direction: Dr. Haberman has recently been studying how our everyday visual experience shapes the way we judge faces. Their recent work explores what happens when people see their own face mirror-reversed, as it appears in selfie cameras and video calls, versus the way others actually see it. They ask how adapting to one version or the other changes how much a face looks like oneself and how attractive it seems.

papers.title: A reflection on faces seen under mirror reversal
papers.abstract: A substantial portion of visual exposure to human faces, particularly one's own, is mediated by digital technologies that often present a mirror-reversed perspective relative to direct physical viewing. To investigate how disparities in visual diet modulate subjective evaluative judgments, observers were presented with photographs of their own facial likeness that were either horizontally flipped (mirror-reversed) or displayed in true orientation (non-reversed). Using a 2 × 2 factorial design, perceptual adaptation to reversed versus non-reversed stimuli was systematically manipulated alongside image orientation. Participants evaluated both perceived self-resemblance and aesthetic appeal (pleasantness), subsequently completing the identical task using photographic likenesses of familiar close peers. Results demonstrated that non-reversed self-portraits were judged as significantly less representative of self-identity and elicited lower pleasantness ratings than mirror-reversed depictions. Conversely, this effect was absent when evaluating close peers, for whom non-reversed depictions constitute the canonically familiar orientation, and perceptual adaptation elicited asymmetric evaluative shifts. Experiment 1A was independently replicated seven years later. These findings indicate that technological exposure constructs an internalized yet adaptable visual self-representation that becomes disrupted when unfamiliar vantage points accentuate intrinsic facial asymmetries.
papers.authors: Jordan Suchow, Malerie McDowell, Jessica Huang, Jason Haberman

E210.name: Joshua A. Solomon
E210.institution: City St George's, University of London
E210.department: Centre for Applied Vision Research (School of Health & Medical Sciences)
E210.bio: Joshua A. Solomon is a Professor of Visual Psychophysics at City, University of London, where they investigate the mechanisms of human visual perception through technical psychophysical and computational methods. Solomon’s work focuses on ensemble perception and summary statistics, specifically characterizing how the visual system extracts global features from crowded or noisy stimulus arrays. Their research employs signal detection theory and stochastic observer models to analyze texture segregation, motion detection, and the role of attention in visual sensitivity. Currently, Solomon examines numerosity and motion adaptation, visual search asymmetries, and spatial summation for motion detection.
E210.research_direction: Dr. Solomon's recent research uses psychophysics and computational observer models to identify the basic mechanisms of human spatial and motion vision. Their recent work tests whether numerosity adaptation is truly bidirectional, using a comparison-of-comparisons paradigm that separates perceptual aftereffects from decisional biases, and finds only downward shifts consistent with monotonic neural coding. They also use visual search asymmetries to ask whether plaids carry a basic feature, such as intrinsic two-dimensionality, that is absent from their component gratings, and use spatial summation with velocity noise to model motion detection as sparse sampling by difference-of-Gaussians templates. Alongside this, their work applies a signal-detection framework to show how monocular and binocular mechanisms detect modulations of dot density and dot contrast.

papers.title: No consistent bidirectional aftereffect from numerosity adaptation
papers.abstract: Some studies say perceived numerosity shifts in both directions after adaptation, as expected for population coding by tuned mechanisms, while others find only downward shifts. The authors use a four-quadrant comparison-of-comparisons design in which simple decisional biases cannot mimic perceptual ones. Six observers adapted to sparse or dense dot clouds showed only downward aftereffects, largest after 100-dot adaptors and none upward, which fits monotonic neural coding and suggests earlier bidirectional reports reflected non-perceptual bias.
papers.authors: Kristina Zeljic, Michael J. Morgan, Joshua A. Solomon

papers.title: A visual search asymmetry for plaids
papers.abstract: Search asymmetries are a classic test for whether a stimulus carries a basic visual feature. The authors superimpose two perpendicular Gabor patterns to form plaids and find that search for a Gabor among plaids depends strongly on set size, whereas finding a 2 or 4 c/deg plaid among its component Gabors is much more efficient. This suggests plaids carry a basic feature such as intrinsic two-dimensionality that the components lack, while mixed-frequency plaids do not pop out.
papers.authors: Joshua A. Solomon, Michael J. Morgan, Charles F. Chubb

papers.title: Spatial summation for motion detection
papers.abstract: The paper asks how the visual system pools motion signals over space when detecting coherent motion in noisy displays. Using spatial summation measurements with velocity noise, the authors model detection as sparse sampling by difference-of-Gaussians templates. The results constrain the size and structure of the mechanisms that integrate local motion.
papers.authors: Joshua A. Solomon, Fintan Nagle, Christopher W. Tyler

papers.title: Monocular and binocular mechanisms detect modulations of dot density and dot contrast
papers.abstract: Observers detected modulations of dot density and dot contrast in random-dot displays presented to one or both eyes. Applying a signal-detection framework, the authors compare monocular and binocular sensitivity to work out how the two eyes' signals are combined. The results support separate mechanisms for density and contrast, with binocular combination differing between them.
papers.authors: Kristina Zeljic, Michael J. Morgan, Joshua A. Solomon

papers.title: Illusory Radial Displacement in Two-Flash Displays
papers.abstract: While piloting a localization experiment, the author noticed that the second of two brief flashes appeared closer to fixation even when it was not. Using a comparison-of-comparisons paradigm, he measured the size of this bias relative to performance-limiting noise, finding an average bias-to-noise ratio around 0.5. No obvious link to fixation behaviour emerged, and no explanation is offered yet.
papers.authors: Joshua A. Solomon

E214.name: Barbara Anne Dosher
E214.bio: Barbara Anne Dosher is a cognitive scientist specializing in the mathematical modeling of human information processing, focusing on visual perception, attention, and memory. Dosher develops formal models such as the Perceptual Template Model (PTM) and the Integrated Reweighting Theory (IRT) to quantify how the brain filters external noise and enhances signal quality during task performance. As a Fellow of the National Academy of Sciences, Dosher investigates the mechanisms of perceptual learning and experience-dependent plasticity. Their research explores how training optimizes the decoding of visual information from early representations to decision-making units.
E214.research_direction: Dr. Dosher has recently been investigating how the visual system gets better with practice, a process called perceptual learning. Their recent work asks how learning depends on the kind of feedback observers receive, including full feedback, only right-or-wrong signals, or none, and when learning on one feature such as orientation carries over to another such as spatial frequency. They interpret these effects using models in which learning re-weights how sensory signals are read out, and they have extended those models with hierarchical Bayesian methods that track individual observers trial by trial. A related thread applies similar Bayesian modeling to separate the mechanisms by which spatial attention improves visual performance.

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian augmented Hebbian reweighting model of perceptual learning
papers.abstract: The augmented Hebbian reweighting model (AHRM) has been widely applied to account for collective observer behavior in perceptual learning paradigms, but characterizing individual trial-by-trial learning dynamics within a unified statistical framework has historically been limited by severe computational tractability issues. To address this, the authors introduce the hierarchical Bayesian augmented Hebbian reweighting model (HB-AHRM), which jointly infers hyperparameter and parameter posterior distributions across population, observer, and testing tiers. To circumvent the prohibitive burden of simulation-based parameter estimation, an approximated likelihood approach was implemented via feature engineering and linear regression alongside PyTensor GPU acceleration, accelerating parameter estimation by roughly 20,000-fold relative to conventional simulation methods. Compared against an unpooled Bayesian inference procedure (BIP), the HB-AHRM achieved substantially reduced parameter posterior uncertainty and superior out-of-sample predictive accuracy for individual empirical learning curves across distinct training accuracy and feedback regimens.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu, Shanglin Yang, Barbara Anne Dosher

papers.title: Transfer of visual perceptual learning over a task-irrelevant feature through feature-invariant representations: Behavioral experiments and model simulations
papers.abstract: Perceptual learning is traditionally characterized by sharp specificity to trained stimulus attributes, but the degree to which learning generalizes across variation in task-irrelevant dimensions remains unresolved. Observers completed multi-session training in eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) identification paradigms using Gabor stimuli with response feedback under high external noise and zero-noise conditions: either orientation identification across multiple task-irrelevant spatial frequencies or spatial-frequency identification across multiple task-irrelevant orientations. Training on orientation identification with a single spatial frequency yielded broad transfer across untrained spatial frequencies (with mild specificity emerging only at the highest frequency), whereas spatial-frequency training transferred completely across all orientations. To explain these generalization patterns, the authors extended the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT) into an expanded model (eI-IRT) that incorporates feature-invariant representations alongside feature-tuned representations. Simulations confirmed that Hebbian reweighting of feedforward readouts from both feature-tuned and feature-invariant channels to decision units quantitatively accounts for the empirical cross-feature transfer.
papers.authors: Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Dosher

papers.title: Informational feedback accelerates learning in multi-alternative perceptual judgements of orientation
papers.abstract: The vast majority of visual perceptual learning studies have evaluated two-alternative forced-choice paradigms, leaving open the degree to which performance gains in higher-dimensional tasks depend on the informational specificity of external supervision. Observers were trained on an eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) peripheral orientation identification task with Gabor stimuli across three contrast levels in high external noise under three feedback protocols: response feedback (RF; indicating the true stimulus class), accuracy feedback (AF; indicating only binary correctness), or no feedback (NF). While modest unsupervised learning emerged even under NF, the rate and magnitude of learning scaled systematically with informational content: RF accelerated threshold reduction, providing an additional benefit of approximately 2 standard deviations relative to unsupervised training. The full trajectory of proportion-correct learning curves and evolving identification confusion matrices were quantitatively captured by the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT), demonstrating that augmented Hebbian reweighting rules flexibly exploit graded supervisory feedback signals during multi-alternative visual decision-making.
papers.authors: Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Anne Dosher

papers.title: Learning spatial frequency identification through reweighted decoding
papers.abstract: Although perceptual learning has been extensively documented in spatial orientation and contrast discrimination, evidence for plasticity in spatial-frequency judgments remains sparse, particularly in absolute multi-alternative identification. Observers were trained over multiple sessions on an eight-alternative forced-choice (8AFC) spatial-frequency identification task in peripheral vision using Gabor targets presented at low, medium, and high contrasts embedded in external noise, followed by noiseless transfer assessments. Training with full response feedback yielded significant improvements across all contrast levels (mean accuracy rose from 31.16% to 38.72%) and systematic contrast threshold reductions at both trained retinal locations. To model the underlying computational architecture, the authors introduced the identification integrated reweighting theory (I-IRT), combining an early sensory representation module with tuned spatial frequency and orientation filters feeding into competitive decision units. Model fits demonstrated that learning in absolute spatial-frequency identification reflects the optimized reweighting of feedforward readout connections to decision mechanisms rather than alterations in early sensory channel tuning.
papers.authors: Barbara Dosher, Jiajuan Liu, Zhong-Lin Lu

papers.title: Hierarchical Bayesian perceptual template modeling of mechanisms of spatial attention in central and peripheral cuing
papers.abstract: The perceptual template model (PTM) and external noise paradigm isolate three core mechanisms of visual attention: stimulus enhancement, external noise exclusion, and multiplicative noise reduction. Traditionally, PTM parameters are estimated independently per subject using maximum likelihood or separate Bayesian methods, which lack population-level pooling and require high trial counts. The authors formulated a three-level hierarchical Bayesian perceptual template model (HBPTM) that unifies trial-by-trial data across population hyperparameters, individual subject parameters, and experimental cuing conditions. Applied to psychophysical data from endogenous (central) and exogenous (peripheral) spatial precuing tasks in four-alternative pseudo-character identification, HBPTM accurately dissociated attentional mechanisms while dramatically reducing posterior parameter variance through shrinkage. Extensive simulation studies across varying participant sample sizes and trial budgets demonstrated that HBPTM consistently outperforms unpooled Bayesian inference, offering superior estimation accuracy and parameter stability in low-trial psychophysical regimes.
papers.authors: Zhong-Lin Lu, Barbara Anne Dosher

E216.name: Kazuhisa Shibata
E216.department: Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning
E216.lab_name: Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning
E216.bio: Shibata serves as the Team Leader of the Laboratory for Human Cognition and Learning at the RIKEN Center for Brain Science. Their research focuses on the neural mechanisms of visual perception, learning, and decision-making through a combination of psychophysics, functional MRI, and computational modeling. Shibata has used decoded fMRI neurofeedback (DecNef) to demonstrate that inducing specific activity patterns in the early visual cortex can drive perceptual learning without external stimuli. Their recent investigations explore the neurochemical factors, such as the ratio of excitatory to inhibitory neurotransmitters, that facilitate the stabilization and consolidation of newly acquired visual skills.
E216.research_direction: Dr. Shibata has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying human learning, memory, and decision-making across perceptual, metacognitive, and motor domains. In vision science, their recent work explores the boundaries of unsupervised perceptual learning, using fMRI to examine how the higher-order statistics of natural scenes might allow task-irrelevant stimuli to bypass top-down attentional suppression. They are also probing the nature of metacognition, employing signal-detection modeling and behavioral paradigms to determine whether confidence judgments inherently demand cognitive effort and how the methodological timing of these reports impacts self-evaluation. Furthermore, they are studying how memory representations shape other complex behaviors, testing whether implicit memory integration drives logical reasoning fallacies and whether passive somatosensory feedback from a robotic exoskeleton is sufficient to independently update motor skill memories.

papers.title: Unsupervised visual learning is revealed for task-irrelevant natural scenes due to reduced attentional suppression effects in visual areas
papers.abstract: The authors show that simply exposing people to natural-scene images they are not attending to produces robust visual perceptual learning, whereas artificial images lacking the higher-order statistics of natural scenes do not. Behavior and fMRI suggest that unsupervised learning is normally suppressed by top-down attention. Higher-order natural-image structure appears to escape this suppression, likely because it is processed beyond V1 outside the window in which attention can gate it.
papers.authors: Takeo Watanabe, Yuka Sasaki, Takuro Zama, Julian R. Matthews, Daiki Ogawa, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: Metacognition is mentally demanding
papers.abstract: Challenging the view that confidence judgments come for free with decisions, this work shows that people will give up monetary reward to make self-evaluation easier, indicating metacognition is effortful. Paying people to self-evaluate reduces the well-known confidence-leak bias, suggesting some metacognitive inefficiency reflects rational effort avoidance. A signal-detection simulation shows that stability of confidence criteria can account for these effort trade-offs.
papers.authors: Julian Matthews, Atsushi Kikumoto, Kentaro Miyamoto, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: Somatosensory information drives modification of a motor memory
papers.abstract: Using a hand-exoskeleton robot that replays a person's learned finger sequence without voluntary movement, the authors test whether afferent somatosensory input alone can modify a motor memory. A brief passive exoskeleton reinstatement produced performance gains comparable to voluntary practice, and controls ruled out visual replay, mental rehearsal, arousal and warm-up. Partially matching sequences helped only in the passive condition, suggesting somatosensory input broadly activates skill memory while voluntary execution acts in a sequence-specific way.
papers.authors: Hiroki Ohashi, Hayato Nishioka, Yuki Ogasawara, Keitaro Murakami, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: The order of task decisions and confidence ratings has little effect on metacognition
papers.abstract: Using a preregistered Registered Report with a perception experiment (n=75) and a memory experiment (n=50), the study tested whether the order in which people report a decision and a confidence rating changes metacognitive efficiency. Even with report time and motor preparation experimentally controlled, order had little effect. The result implies that existing metacognition studies need not be constrained or discounted by the choice of report order.
papers.authors: Julian R. Matthews, Narumi Sugihara, Sofia Nagisa, Hiroki Ohashi, Kazuhisa Shibata

papers.title: The role of memory in affirming-the-consequent fallacy
papers.abstract: The paper questions the standard view that the affirming-the-consequent fallacy, accepting a reversed transitive relation as true, arises from explicit reasoning at the moment of judgment. Using an implicit memory paradigm with behavior and fMRI, it supports a two-stage memory account: a reversed-sequence memory forms at encoding and then gets integrated with the forward memory over time, strengthening the fallacy. The fallacy may therefore begin unwittingly when a relation is memorized.
papers.authors: Yoko Higuchi, Ethan Oblak, Hiroko Nakamura, Makiko Yamada, Kazuhisa Shibata

E217.name: C. Shawn Green
E217.bio: C. Shawn Green is the Mark and Ilene Laufman Family Professor and Chair of the Department of Psychology at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where they direct the Learning and Transfer Lab. Green’s research investigates the computational and neural mechanisms of human learning, with a focus on how experience with complex environments, such as action video games, can drive improvements in perception and attention. They utilize psychophysical testing, cognitive training paradigms, and modern media to study the factors that determine the rate of learning and the extent to which acquired skills generalize to novel tasks. Green also serves as the Editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Cognitive Enhancement and applies their findings to domains including motor learning and educational practice.
E217.research_direction: Dr. Green's recent work explores the mechanisms and optimization of cognitive training, with a particular focus on how video game mechanics influence learning, skill transfer, and executive function. They have recently been investigating the broad cognitive benefits of action video games, questioning how enhanced attentional control might facilitate a generalized ability to extract environmental statistics and learn novel tasks. Additionally, their research critically evaluates the psychometric validity of traditional planning metrics, such as the Tower of London, and tests whether custom-designed mini-games can provide a more cohesive stealth assessment of goal-directed behavior. To understand what drives learning over time, they are also applying expectancy-value theory to sustain motivation in cognitive training, and modeling perceptual learning as a continuous function of time-on-task to increase theoretical specificity and statistical power.

papers.title: Rethinking planning metrics: An analysis of common measurements of planning abilities
papers.abstract: Examines whether widely used planning tasks such as the Tower of London actually measure a coherent planning ability. Analyses of the psychometric properties across common measures call into question their validity and suggest that planning is assessed less cleanly than typically assumed.
papers.authors: Emma G. Cunningham, Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Evaluating planning through play: Exploring the use of mini games to assess planning abilities
papers.abstract: Tests whether custom-designed mini-games can serve as a more cohesive, engaging stealth assessment of planning than traditional lab tasks. The results explore how well game-based measures capture planning ability and how they relate to conventional metrics.
papers.authors: Emma G. Cunningham, Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: No Expectancy Effect on Visual Attention Performance After a Single Session of Playing Sudoku: A Failed Replication of Tiraboschi et al. (2019)
papers.abstract: Attempts to replicate a report that expecting cognitive benefits from a brief game session boosts subsequent visual attention performance. The replication found no expectancy effect, bearing on how placebo and expectation confounds are handled in cognitive-training and video-game research.
papers.authors: Freya Joessel, Emma G. Cunningham, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Learning and Transfer: A Perspective From Action Video Game Play
papers.abstract: Reviews what action video game play reveals about how people learn and when learning carries over to new tasks. The authors argue that gamers appear to acquire a generalized ability to learn (extracting statistical regularities and controlling attention) rather than merely narrow task-specific skills, and lay out implications for training design and future research.
papers.authors: Daphne Bavelier, C. Shawn Green

papers.title: Modeling Perceptual Learning as a Continuous Function of Time-on-Task Increases Theoretical Specificity and Statistical Power
papers.abstract: Proposes analyzing perceptual learning as a continuous function of time spent on the task instead of collapsing data into discrete sessions or blocks. Using modeling and reanalysis of learning data, the authors show this yields more specific theoretical claims and greater statistical power for detecting learning effects.
papers.authors: Aaron Cochrane, Zhong-Lin Lu, C. Shawn Green

E225.name: Maria Concetta Morrone
E225.department: Department of Translational Research on New Technologies in Medicine and Surgery
E225.bio: Morrone is a Professor of Physiology who investigates the functional architecture and plasticity of the mammalian visual system. Their work combines psychophysics, ultra-high field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI), and electrophysiology to explore mechanisms of motion perception, visual stability across saccades, and multisensory integration. Morrone has researched how the brain maintains a stable spatial representation during eye movements and the role of the pulvinar in gating adult cortical plasticity. Their current research focuses on the development of the human visual system and the application of neuroimaging to study metabolic and physiological markers of cortical excitability.
E225.research_direction: Dr. Morrone's recent work explores the neural mechanisms underlying perceptual stability, particularly investigating how short-term priors and serial dependence shape visual perception across saccades. Using EEG and behavioral tracking, they have recently been examining how alpha and beta oscillations carry memory traces of previous stimuli—ranging from simple oriented gratings to complex face genders—to continuously update current perceptual judgments. Beyond temporal integration, their research also investigates cross-modal sensory networks, using high-resolution fMRI and dynamic causal modeling to map how the primary visual cortex is recruited during auditory spatial localization. Additionally, they are studying the early functional development of the human visual system by employing fMRI in young infants to track the maturation and resting-state connectivity of motion-sensitive cortical networks.

papers.title: Saccade-synchronized alpha rhythms predict strength of memory trace of stimulus orientation
papers.abstract: EEG was recorded while observers made visually driven saccades and reproduced the orientation of a brief Gabor patch. Both alpha and beta oscillations were synchronized to the saccades. Only the strength of pre-saccadic alpha, especially over right parietal cortex, tracked how strongly the previous stimulus biased the current response. This suggests alpha carries information across saccades to support perceptual stability.
papers.authors: Chiara Terzo, David C. Burr, Xin-Yu Xie, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Primary visual cortex BOLD responses to relative localization of sounds at 7T
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and dynamic causal modeling, ten participants judged the position of a sound relative to two spatial landmarks. Primary visual cortex, primary auditory cortex and intraparietal sulcus were all activated. Effective connectivity from auditory cortex to IPS and from IPS to V1 increased during the task, suggesting V1 is recruited for high-level auditory spatial computation via parietal feedback.
papers.authors: Monica Riberto, Maria Bianca Amadeo, Alessandro Inuggi, Mauro Costagli, Claudio Campus, Monica Gori, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Recent, but not long-term, priors induce behavioral oscillations in peri-saccadic vision
papers.abstract: Participants made 16-degree saccades while judging the orientation of brief Gabor probes presented around saccade onset. Judgments were biased toward both a pre-saccadic inducer and the previous trial, and this bias oscillated at alpha frequency (about 9.5 Hz) locked to the saccade. The bias toward the mean orientation stayed constant over time. The authors conclude that alpha rhythms carry short-term perceptual memory across saccades, while long-term priors rely on different circuitry.
papers.authors: Xin-Yu Xie, David C. Burr, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Serial dependence in face-gender classification revealed in low-beta frequency EEG
papers.abstract: Observers judged the gender of intermingled male, female and androgynous faces while EEG was recorded. Judgments of ambiguous faces were pulled toward the previous face, and the strength of this pull oscillated in the beta range (about 14 Hz after female faces, 18 Hz after male faces). Decoding of the previous stimulus from EEG worked best in those bands and correlated with the size of the behavioral bias across individuals.
papers.authors: Giacomo Ranieri, David C. Burr, Jason Bell, Maria Concetta Morrone

papers.title: Development of BOLD Response to Motion in Human Infants
papers.abstract: The authors scanned 5-week-old infants with fMRI using coherent-flow motion stimuli and compared them with earlier 8-week-old data. Motion areas MT+ and PIVC responded similarly at both ages, whereas V6 responses were weaker at 5 weeks and the cuneus motion area could not yet be identified. V1 showed rapid maturation between 5 and 8 weeks. Resting-state connectivity was adult-like among motion areas but not between V1 and temporo-occipital cortex.
papers.authors: Laura Biagi, Michela Tosetti, Sofia Allegra Crespi, Maria Concetta Morrone

E226.name: Merav Ahissar
E226.department: Department of Psychology and the Edmond & Lily Safra Center for Brain Sciences
E226.bio: Ahissar developed the Reverse Hierarchy Theory of perception and learning, which posits that perceptual learning is a top-down driven process proceeding from high-level generalizations to low-level sensory details. Ahissar's research utilizes behavioral psychophysics, Bayesian computational modeling, ERP, and fMRI to investigate mechanisms of skill acquisition and the neural basis of individual differences. They developed the 'poor-anchoring' theory of dyslexia, which suggests that reading disabilities stem from the rapid decay of perceptual memory traces rather than sensory deficits alone. Their current research, supported by an ERC Advanced Grant, examines the computational and neural constraints affecting the acquisition of communicative skills in populations with dyslexia and autism.
E226.research_direction:
Dr. Ahissar’s research examines how perception emerges from the interaction between immediate sensory traces and accumulated knowledge about the environment. Her lab studies these processes across audition and vision, using auditory frequency discrimination, visual grating discrimination, and face-discrimination tasks. Behavioral paradigms are combined with electroencephalography (EEG) and Bayesian modeling to investigate how information acquired over different timescales shapes perceptual expectations, decisions, and learning.

The lab uses two-tone frequency discrimination as a particularly sensitive window into learning: although the task is simple, perceptual judgments systematically reveal the influence of recent stimuli and longer-term environmental statistics. The lab traces the dynamics of analogous perceptual biases in grating and face discrimination and compares them with those observed in audition. These cross-modal comparisons test whether individuals have characteristic timescales for integrating information and updating perceptual representations across different sensory and stimulus domains.

A central hypothesis is that neurodevelopmental conditions involve distinct temporal dynamics of internal representations. In dyslexia, perceptual traces appear to decay unusually rapidly, reducing the influence of recent experience. In autism, accumulated representations may be updated too slowly when environmental conditions change. Recent work also examines neural responses to performance feedback, including feedback-related negativity, to characterize reduced sensitivity to immediate feedback and recent experience in autism. Together, these studies seek general principles that explain how perceptual priors are learned, maintained, and revised—and why these dynamics differ consistently across individuals.

papers.title: Rapid decay of perceptual memory in dyslexia
papers.abstract: The mechanistic underpinnings of developmental dyslexia are re-examined through the lens of perceptual learning and expertise acquisition. Integrating behavioral, electrophysiological (neural adaptation), and computational modeling evidence, the authors propose that dyslexia is fundamentally characterized by an accelerated decay of perceptual memory traces for both speech and non-speech regularities. This rapid trace decay prevents the efficient accumulation of environmental statistics, leading to reduced complexity in the formation of perceptual categories and a diminished learning slope for linguistic expertise. Paradoxically, this deficit causes the performance gap between dyslexic and neurotypical individuals to widen as cumulative exposure to stimulus regularities increases.
papers.authors: Ayelet Gertsovski, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Digital–Analog Perceptual Duality
papers.abstract: This work formalizes a mapping between the classic mind-body duality and the distinction between 'brain-world' (BW) and 'brain-brain' (BB) interaction domains. BW interactions are defined as analog, continuous motor-sensory loops where neural systems interface with physical substances. Conversely, BB interactions represent inter-individual mental communication, which is inherently digital and discrete, relying on categorization to overcome bandwidth limitations. The authors provide a review of neural architectures, such as neuronal phase-locked loops (NPLLs), that perform the non-invertible transformations between analog sensory input and digital mental representation. They conclude that the perceived gap between physical and mental processes emerges from these unidirectional transformations within neural hierarchies.
papers.authors: Ehud Ahissar, Daniel Polani, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: The different roles of learning recent and accumulative statistics
papers.abstract: This review examines how humans integrate immediate temporal regularities (recent statistics) with long-term distributional knowledge (accumulative statistics) during perceptual inference. Utilizing Bayesian frameworks, the authors characterize the weighting of these information sources across neurodevelopmental conditions. Neurotypical perception is characterized by a flexible balance: fast updating of internal models in response to recent changes and stable reliance on accumulative statistics in invariant environments. In contrast, dyslexia is marked by an overweighting of the immediate past due to fast prior decay, while autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with an overweighting of accumulative statistics, leading to slower updating of expectations and reduced social interactive flexibility.
papers.authors: Aviel Sulem, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Reduced perceptual error monitoring is a biomarker of autism
papers.abstract: This study utilizes electroencephalography (EEG) and behavioral modeling to evaluate performance monitoring and feedback sensitivity in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Using a two-tone pitch discrimination task with choice-contingent feedback, the researchers tracked the feedback-related negativity (FRN), an ERP component localized to the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Results revealed that a clear FRN was absent in more than half of the ASD cohort, while present in nearly all neurotypical controls. Behaviorally, ASD participants exhibited diminished post-error response slowing and reduced online adjustment based on task difficulty. These findings suggest that impaired ACC-mediated monitoring of internal and external feedback is a robust biomarker for the reduced behavioral flexibility characteristic of autism.
papers.authors: Nathaniel J. Zuk, Nadezhda Slobodskoy-Plusnin, Yarden Weiss, Sivasankari Sampath, Katharina Düsterwald, Athena Akrami, Merav Ahissar

papers.title: Frequency-Specific Contributions to Auditory Perceptual Priors: Testing the Predictive-Coding Hypothesis
papers.abstract: This investigation tests the computational architecture of auditory perceptual priors by adjudicating between top-down predictive coding and bottom-up memory-based integration. By analyzing recency biases in a high-trial-count frequency discrimination task, the authors demonstrated that perceptual priors are frequency-specific and persistent across intervening task-irrelevant stimuli. Crucially, the bias was independent of the subjective percept of the preceding trial, indicating that priors are constructed from low-level sensory traces rather than being generated via high-level top-down predictions. These results support a bottom-up model of statistical learning where the brain's internal priors emerge directly from the temporal integration of recent sensory inputs.
papers.authors: Itay Lieder, Aviel Sulem, Merav Ahissar

E227.name: Dov Sagi
E227.bio: Dov Sagi is a Professor in the Department of Brain Sciences at the Weizmann Institute of Science, specializing in the psychophysics of human vision and the plasticity of sensory systems. Sagi developed the texture discrimination task (TDT), which demonstrated that adult visual performance can be enhanced through practice. Their research utilizes psychophysical methodologies and computational models, such as signal detection theory and the drift-diffusion model, to investigate lateral interactions in the visual cortex, spatial integration, and the role of context in orientation estimation. Currently, Sagi examines how sensory adaptation interacts with learning generalization and investigates the mechanisms of serial dependence in perceptual decision-making.
E227.research_direction: Dr. Sagi has recently been studying the dynamics of visual awareness, in particular why a clearly visible object can intermittently vanish from perception when surrounded by moving patterns, a phenomenon called motion-induced blindness. Their recent work tests whether these disappearances behave like a noisy excitable system, one that switches abruptly and then recovers on its own after a perturbation. The aim is to link the timing of what people consciously see to simple network-level dynamics in the visual system.

papers.title: Motion-induced blindness as a noisy excitable system
papers.abstract: In motion-induced blindness (MIB), salient visual stimuli intermittently vanish from visual awareness when surrounded by a moving mask pattern, though the precise temporal and network mechanics remain incompletely characterized. This study investigated whether the temporal dynamics of MIB exhibit the canonical properties of a noisy excitable system, which is defined by abrupt state transitions triggered by suprathreshold perturbations, autonomous stimulus-independent trajectory completions, and obligatory recovery phases. Psychophysical experiments tested observers with dynamic masks consisting of rotating radial bars configured with a central gap around a parafoveal luminous target, delivering periodic spatiotemporal perturbations to the target perimeter. The sweep of mask elements adjacent to the target locus frequently triggered abrupt perceptual suppression, confirming spatial locality. Consistent with excitable state kinetics, the duration of perceptual invisibility was decoupled from subsequent bar sweeps traversing the field during the suppressed epoch and demonstrated negligible dependence on global mask configuration. Following perceptual reappearance, a robust refractory interval spanning 0.5 to 2 seconds was observed during which further suppressive events could not be triggered. These findings indicate that MIB reflects the behavior of an excitable neural circuit where the mask acts as a perturbing trigger while subsequent perceptual suppression and recovery trajectories are governed by intrinsic network states.
papers.authors: Mikhail Katkov, Alexander Cooperman, Noya Meital-Kfir, Dov Sagi

E228.name: Uri Polat
E228.department: School of Optometry and Vision Science, Faculty of Life Sciences
E228.bio: Uri Polat is a Professor at Bar-Ilan University and Head of the School of Optometry and Vision Science, specializing in the mechanisms of visual perception and neuroplasticity. Polat conducted research on perceptual learning, demonstrating that targeted training with Gabor stimuli and lateral masking can improve visual function in adults with amblyopia. Their research investigates spatial interactions, visual crowding, and the temporal properties of visual processing to develop non-invasive clinical interventions for conditions such as presbyopia. Polat's work integrates psychophysical methodologies with clinical applications to explore the brain's capacity to compensate for blurred retinal input through cortical reorganization.
E228.research_direction: Dr. Polat's recent work has primarily been investigating the temporal and spatial constraints of early visual processing, particularly focusing on how foveal crowding impacts both object identity and color under severely limited viewing durations. Their research explores how these time-limited perceptual mechanisms operate across different populations, testing how visual processing speed, spatial integration, and contrast sensitivity are altered in normal aging and in adults with ADHD. They have also recently been examining the neural conditions required for generalization in perceptual learning, using visual adaptation and masking to determine when training on texture discrimination transfers to untrained contrast detection tasks. Additionally, Dr. Polat is probing the contextual factors that shape binocular summation, utilizing flanked Gabor targets and interleaved stereoscopic displays to test how spatial spacing, exposure time, and observer awareness influence early visual integration.

papers.title: Early visual processing in adults with ADHD: evidence from contrast sensitivity, spatial integration, and external noise
papers.abstract: Compares 21 adults with ADHD and 24 controls on foveal contrast sensitivity at brief durations, the benefit of enlarging the stimulus, and tolerance to external noise. The ADHD group had overall lower contrast sensitivity and less benefit from larger stimuli at 40 ms, while noise exclusion was similar between groups. The authors argue that ADHD involves selective early visual differences, mainly when high-spatial-frequency information must be integrated quickly.
papers.authors: Hani Ifrah-Tsruya, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: Foveal crowding modifies a target's properties under a brief presentation time
papers.abstract: Tests whether visual crowding at the fovea also degrades a target's colour, not only its identity, using a dual identification-plus-chromaticity task at 20-120 ms exposures. Both identity and colour discrimination were impaired at 20-40 ms and recovered with longer exposure, and adding backward masking made the deficit larger. The authors conclude that crowding under brief presentation behaves like masking and arises at a later processing stage after an initial masking stage.
papers.authors: Ziv Siman-Tov, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: Foveal crowding increases with age under limited viewing conditions
papers.abstract: Thirty-three observers aged 20-89 did a letter recognition task with varied target-flanker spacing under unlimited and brief viewing. Crowding at the fovea was negligible with unlimited viewing across all ages, but under brief presentation older adults showed markedly stronger crowding and worse acuity, with reaction times also rising with age. The pattern points to slowed processing speed rather than a spatial deficit and argues for time-limited testing in older adults.
papers.authors: Noah Rappeport, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

papers.title: Generalization in perceptual learning across stimuli and tasks
papers.abstract: Examines when perceptual learning on the texture discrimination task transfers to contrast detection of Gabor targets, alone or backward-masked, with and without visual adaptation. Transfer depended on adaptation and target location: at the peripheral target site it appeared only under adaptation, whereas at the central site it appeared in both conditions. The results support the idea that transfer occurs when trained and untrained tasks share overlapping neural processes, likely involving inhibitory interactions.
papers.authors: Ravit Kahalani-Hodedany, Maria Lev, Dov Sagi, Uri Polat

papers.title: What Factors Affect Binocular Summation?
papers.abstract: Revisits binocular summation using stereoscopic glasses with randomly interleaved monocular and binocular trials, so observers cannot know which condition is running. Using Gabor targets with collinear or orthogonal flankers at several separations and durations, the authors examine how spacing, exposure time and awareness of the tested eye shape summation. The work frames binocular vision as a model system for awareness and shows summation depends on stimulus and presentation context.
papers.authors: Marzouk Yassin, Maria Lev, Uri Polat

E229.name: Ladan Shams
E229.bio: Ladan Shams is a Professor of Psychology, BioEngineering, and Neuroscience at UCLA and directs the Multisensory Processing Lab. Their research investigates the computational principles and neural mechanisms of multisensory perception, examining how the brain integrates sensory modalities to form representations and facilitate learning. Shams has conducted work on the sound-induced flash illusion and the application of Bayesian Causal Inference models to explain sensory integration and recalibration. Their current research includes investigating top-down cognitive influences on perception and developing behavioral methods for assessing and remediating cognitive decline.
E229.research_direction: Dr. Shams has recently been investigating multisensory perception through the lens of Bayesian causal inference, exploring how the brain determines whether sights and sounds share a common underlying source. Their recent work expands these computational models to evaluate multiple stimulus dimensions simultaneously, examining phenomena like the sound-induced flash illusion across varying gaps in both time and numerosity. A major focus of their methodological research involves developing open-source modeling tools and simulation pipelines to help scientists mathematically disentangle true multisensory binding from unisensory precision and prior expectations. Beyond immediate perception, they are also exploring the broader cognitive impacts of these mechanisms by investigating how crossmodal interactions between the senses shape human perceptual learning and memory encoding.

papers.title: Crossmodal interaction of flashes and beeps across time and number follows Bayesian causal inference
papers.abstract: Extends the Bayesian causal inference model of multisensory perception from a single stimulus dimension to two at once, using the sound-induced flash illusion with sounds and flashes that differ in both timing and count. The probability that observers bind the two signals falls as the timing gap grows. The expanded model captures behavior well, which suggests the brain infers a common cause jointly across several cues rather than one dimension at a time.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Yiyang Zhang, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: Analyzing multisensory integration: do's and dont's
papers.abstract: Argues that common behavioral measures of multisensory integration, such as illusion magnitude and the width of the temporal binding window, mix together unisensory precision, priors and the binding process, so they cannot be read as integration strength on their own. Simulations in a Bayesian causal inference framework show that the same behavior can come from very different causes, which leads to misattributed group differences. The paper reviews other computational frameworks and proposes a model-based analysis pipeline for separating sensory fidelity, priors and integrative tendency.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: The overlooked role of unisensory precision in multisensory research
papers.abstract: A commentary in Current Biology on findings that football goalkeepers show weaker multisensory illusions than outfield players or non-athletes. It shows that the goalkeepers' better unisensory precision alone can explain the weaker illusion, without any change in integration. The point is that unisensory precision has to be controlled before differences in multisensory integration are inferred.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: BCI Toolbox: An open-source python package for the Bayesian causal inference model
papers.abstract: Presents an open-source Python package for fitting the Bayesian causal inference model to behavioral data. It describes the model's algorithm and tests reliability with parameter-recovery simulations. The toolbox is meant both as a working analysis tool and as a teaching aid for the model.
papers.authors: Haocheng Zhu, Ulrik Beierholm, Ladan Shams

papers.title: Crossmodal interactions in human learning and memory
papers.abstract: Reviews evidence that human perceptual learning and memory are shaped by interactions between the senses, especially vision and audition, and not just by unisensory experience. It argues that the nervous system encodes memory traces according to how the senses relate to each other. It proposes possible neural mechanisms and lays out open questions for future work.
papers.authors: Carolyn A. Murray, Ladan Shams

E230.name: Marc Ernst
E230.bio: Marc O. Ernst is the Chair of Applied Cognitive Psychology at Ulm University, where they investigate the computational principles underlying how the human brain integrates information from sensory modalities like vision, touch, and audition. Ernst’s research demonstrates that humans combine sensory cues in a statistically optimal, Bayesian fashion to minimize perceptual uncertainty. Their work utilizes psychophysical experiments, virtual reality, and mathematical modeling to explore perception-action loops, the role of prior knowledge in sensory processing, and the development of multisensory integration. Before joining Ulm, Ernst held positions at Bielefeld University and the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics.
E230.research_direction: Dr. Ernst has recently been investigating the role of early visual experience in sensorimotor development by studying individuals who have gained vision after treatment for congenital bilateral cataracts. Their recent work explores how this delayed visual input affects visually guided grasping, postural stability in response to optic flow, and whether targeted multisensory training can facilitate the acquisition of spatial cognition. In parallel, they study the fundamental mechanisms of multisensory processing, using psychophysical experiments and biologically inspired computational modeling to ask whether the brain relies on transient or sustained channels to compute audiovisual timing and near-optimal cue integration. Additionally, they are examining spatial navigation, employing homing tasks to determine how navigators track the spatio-temporal stability of environmental landmarks and whether they dynamically weight these cues according to Bayesian principles.

papers.title: Multisensory integration operates on correlated input from unimodal transient channels
papers.abstract: The authors ask whether the brain combines audio and visual signals using sustained (intensity over time) or transient (change-detecting) channels. Two psychophysical experiments show that transient channels drive audiovisual integration. They then propose a biologically inspired 'multisensory correlation detector' model that correlates transient unimodal inputs and, tested against many published datasets, jointly explains perceived audiovisual timing, detection facilitation, causality judgments and near-optimal cue integration.
papers.authors: Cesare V. Parise, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Postural stability and optic flow sensitivity following sight restoration from congenital bilateral cataracts
papers.abstract: Individuals treated for congenital cataracts years after birth were tested on how well vision stabilises their stance and how they respond to radial and translational optic flow. They swayed more than controls and gained less from opening their eyes, though those tested longer after surgery swayed less, suggesting partial learning. Optic flow also induced weaker illusory self-motion in them, pointing to lasting deficits in sensorimotor use of vision.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Irene Senna, Priscilla Balestrucci, Sophia Piller, Dennis Wiebusch, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Multisensory training improves the development of spatial cognition after sight restoration from congenital cataracts
papers.abstract: The study tests whether a brief multisensory training can help spatial abilities develop in people whose sight was restored after congenital cataracts. Participants who received the multisensory training showed improved spatial cognition compared with those who received alternative training. The results indicate that cross-sensory experience can partially compensate for missing early visual input.
papers.authors: Irene Senna, Sophia Piller, Chiara Martolini, Elena Cocchi, Monica Gori, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Grasping behavior does not recover after sight restoration from congenital blindness
papers.abstract: People who regained sight after being born with dense bilateral cataracts were tested on visually guided reach-to-grasp tasks and compared with typically sighted controls. Despite vision being restored years earlier, their grasping remained atypical, and it did not improve with time since surgery. The finding suggests that visuomotor skills for grasping depend on early visual experience and are not readily acquired later in life.
papers.authors: Sophia Piller, Irene Senna, Dennis Wiebusch, Itay Ben-Zion, Marc O. Ernst

papers.title: Did it move? Humans use spatio-temporal landmark permanency efficiently for navigation
papers.abstract: Using a homing task with three landmarks, one of which was secretly moved during learning, the authors show that people quickly learn how permanent each landmark is and weight it accordingly when navigating home. Short-term learned statistics dominated over long-term prior knowledge of object permanency. The behavior is consistent with a Bayesian account of navigation.
papers.authors: Charlotte Roy, Dennis Wiebusch, Mario Botsch, Marc O. Ernst

E232.name: Uta Noppeney
E232.department: Donders Centre for Neuroscience, Biophysics Department
E232.lab_name: Multisensory Perception, Learning and Attention Group
E232.bio: Uta Noppeney is a Professor of Systems Neuroscience who investigates how the human brain integrates sensory inputs to form perceptions and guide behavior. They apply normative Bayesian frameworks to model multisensory causal inference and reliability-weighted cue integration across cortical hierarchies. Noppeney combines psychophysics and computational modeling with neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI, MEG, and EEG to characterize the neural dynamics of decision-making, learning, and attention. Their work explores these multisensory computational principles in healthy individuals across the lifespan and in clinical populations, such as those with neuropsychiatric disorders.
E232.research_direction: Dr. Noppeney's recent work explores the neural and computational mechanisms underlying multisensory integration, investigating how the human brain combines or segregates signals across different modalities. Using psychophysics, Bayesian modeling, EEG, and fMRI, they have recently been examining how audiovisual spatial localization and causal inference operate across diverse populations, including healthy older adults and individuals with schizophrenia. Their research also probes the boundary conditions of cross-sensory interactions, testing whether conscious awareness—manipulated via continuous flash suppression—is necessary for visual stimuli to bias auditory spatial coding, and investigating how vibrotactile signals merge with hearing to process temporal structures like musical beats. Additionally, they have been critically evaluating foundational theories in perceptual neuroscience, specifically assessing the evidence and methodologies used to link alpha oscillations to the temporal binding windows of perception.

papers.title: Invisible flashes bias spatial coding in the auditory system
papers.abstract: The study combines spatial ventriloquism with dynamic continuous flash suppression and EEG to test whether awareness is needed for cross-sensory integration. Flashes that observers could not see, even when mislocalised, still shifted perceived sound location. Multivariate decoding showed the invisible flash location is encoded early and then fades, yet progressively biases neural encoding of sound location at 300-600 ms, challenging all-or-none accounts of consciousness.
papers.authors: Pierre Delong, Chloe Pleche, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Feeling the music: Audiotactile encoding of temporal structure in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using psychophysics, fMRI and time-resolved EEG decoding, this work examines how vibrotactile signals combine with auditory music to encode beat and envelope. Touch improved detection of targets in music, and beat information from hearing and touch converged in planum temporale and parietal operculum via distinct dynamics. Tactile input sharpened and amplified auditory envelope coding in primary auditory cortex and helped segregate coherent streams in polyphonic music.
papers.authors: Gianluca Degano, Alessandro Ferrari, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Multisensory perceptual and causal inference is largely preserved in medicated post-acute individuals with schizophrenia
papers.abstract: Combining psychophysics, Bayesian modelling and EEG, the study asked whether audiovisual causal inference is disrupted in medicated individuals with schizophrenia with limited psychotic symptoms. Both patients and controls balanced integration and segregation of flash-beep sequences in line with Bayesian causal inference, and weighted causal-structure priors similarly. EEG showed the same dynamic cascade of unisensory-then-combined numerosity estimates in both groups, arguing that core multisensory computations are largely intact in this population.
papers.authors: Tim Rohe, Klaus Hesse, Ann-Christine Ehlis, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Older adults preserve audiovisual integration through enhanced cortical activations, not by recruiting new regions
papers.abstract: Using fMRI and multivariate Bayesian decoding, the authors compared how younger and older adults combine auditory and visual spatial cues when localising sounds. Older adults kept localisation accuracy and used the same dorsal pathways as younger adults but showed stronger activations across a wide frontal-temporal-parietal network. Those extra activations carried additional stimulus information, but the information gain did not track individual behavioural benefit, so ageing preserves integration by amplifying existing rather than recruiting new circuitry.
papers.authors: Samuel A. Jones, Uta Noppeney

papers.title: Alpha Oscillations and Temporal Binding Windows in Perception - A Critical Review and Best Practice Guidelines
papers.abstract: The review examines the alpha temporal resolution hypothesis, which proposes that sensory signals within one alpha cycle are fused while those in separate cycles are segregated. It scrutinises experimental designs, psychophysics and neurophysiological analyses used to test it and evaluates between-subject, within-subject and causal perturbation evidence. The authors highlight interpretational ambiguities and offer guidelines for future studies.
papers.authors: Jan-Mathijs Schoffelen, Ugo Giulio Pesci, Uta Noppeney

E234.name: Christoph Kayser
E234.department: Department for Cognitive Neuroscience, Faculty of Biology
E234.bio: Christoph Kayser is a Professor and Chair for Cognitive Neuroscience at Bielefeld University, where they investigate the neural mechanisms underlying multisensory integration and perceptual decision-making. Their research utilizes magnetoencephalography (MEG), electrophysiology, and computational modeling to determine how the brain combines information from different sensory modalities, such as vision and audition, to enhance perception in complex environments. Kayser’s work explores the functional role of neural oscillations in sensory tracking and the contribution of motor-auditory interactions to speech intelligibility. Additionally, their recent studies examine the alignment of physiological processes like respiration and oculomotor behavior with cognitive and sensory-motor events.
E234.research_direction: Dr. Kayser has recently been investigating how internal physiological rhythms and motor actions interact with sensory encoding and behavioral performance. A major branch of their recent work explores the link between respiration and cognition, using EEG decoding and behavioral tracking to examine whether the phase of the breathing cycle modulates task-specific visual representations, response speeds, and the anticipation of effort. In a distinct line of research, they are also examining auditory-motor integration by testing how active eye movements might alter hearing. Specifically, they are using near-threshold detection and spatial discrimination tasks to determine if saccades and their associated eye movement-related eardrum oscillations (EMREOs) influence an observer's ability to detect and lateralize sounds.

papers.title: The alignment of respiration to sensory-motor events is shaped by expected effort
papers.abstract: The study examines how people time their breathing around upcoming sensory-motor events and finds that this alignment depends on how much effort the anticipated task is expected to require. Respiration is thus treated as an adaptive tool for allocating physiological resources, not a fixed rhythm. It extends the lab's respiration work into the effort and anticipation domain.
papers.authors: Christoph Kayser, Lena Hehemann, Lisa Stetza

papers.title: Sound lateralization ability is affected by saccade direction but not eye movement-related eardrum oscillations (EMREOs)
papers.abstract: The authors tested whether EMREOs actually reflect the eardrum movements that would affect hearing by comparing sound lateralization in spatial discrimination tasks. Performance changed with saccade direction, but not with the magnitude or sign of the EMREO deflection. This suggests the EMREO signal is not a direct readout of functionally relevant eardrum displacement.
papers.authors: Nancy Sotero Silva, Felix Bröhl, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Evidence That Respiratory Phase May Modulate Task-Related Neural Representations of Visual Stimuli
papers.abstract: Using EEG and single-trial decoding in two visual categorization tasks, the authors asked whether the phase of the breathing cycle changes how strongly the brain encodes task-relevant stimulus information, rather than just overall brain state. They report that stimulus-related neural representations vary with respiratory phase, with evidence that this modulation is task-specific. The work links bodily rhythms to the quality of visual perceptual encoding.
papers.authors: Lisa Stetza, Lena Hehemann, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Respiration shapes response speed and accuracy with a systematic time lag
papers.abstract: Two known phenomena, that people align their breathing to expected events and that the respiratory phase on a given trial predicts behaviour, are shown here to co-exist in the same data. Both the average breathing phase of an individual relative to task events and trial-to-trial phase variations explain response speed and accuracy, with a consistent time lag between respiration and behaviour. The study reconciles two strands of respiration-cognition research.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Cosima Harting, Lena Hehemann, Lisa Stetza, Christoph Kayser

papers.title: Detection of Spatially Localized Sounds Is Robust to Saccades and Concurrent Eye Movement-Related Eardrum Oscillations (EMREOs)
papers.abstract: Saccadic eye movements induce small eardrum movements known as EMREOs, raising the question of whether they alter hearing. Across three experiments on near-threshold click detection, sound detection was unaffected by timing relative to saccade onset, saccade amplitude or direction, and by concurrent EMREOs. The results argue that active hearing during eye movements is robust to these ear-level signals.
papers.authors: Felix Bröhl, Christoph Kayser

E235.name: Henrik Ehrsson
E235.bio: Ehrsson is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at Karolinska Institutet, focusing on the multisensory processes that underpin the perception of the bodily self. Their research characterizes the neural mechanisms and computational principles by which the brain integrates visual, tactile, and proprioceptive signals to produce the experience of body ownership and self-location. Utilizing experimental paradigms such as the rubber hand illusion and virtual reality, Ehrsson employs functional neuroimaging and psychophysics to map the cortical networks responsible for bodily awareness. Their work investigates the relationship between multisensory integration and consciousness, with applications in neuroprosthetics and the treatment of psychiatric disorders.
E235.research_direction: Dr. Ehrsson has recently been investigating the multisensory and computational mechanisms underlying bodily self-perception and body ownership. Their recent work explores how the brain integrates visual, tactile, and proprioceptive signals to construct a sense of the bodily self, using experimental paradigms like the rubber hand illusion and delayed self-touch. A major focus of their research examines whether specific neural oscillations, such as parietal alpha rhythms for visuotactile processing and beta frequencies for purely somatosensory integration, act as internal clocks that determine the temporal binding windows necessary for body ownership. Furthermore, they use fMRI and computational approaches—including drift-diffusion and Bayesian causal-inference modeling—to probe how proprioceptive uncertainty, sensory evidence accumulation, and temporal recalibration dynamically influence our conscious awareness of the body.

papers.title: Parietal alpha frequency shapes own-body perception by modulating the temporal integration of bodily signals
papers.abstract: Tests whether the speed of individual alpha-band rhythms in parietal cortex determines how long a window the brain uses to bind visual and tactile signals into a sense of body ownership. Faster alpha frequency narrowed the temporal binding window and sharpened sensitivity, and stimulation that shifted alpha frequency changed these windows, indicating a causal role. A causal-inference model linked alpha frequency to the uncertainty about asynchrony between the senses.
papers.authors: Mariano D'Angelo, Renzo C. Lanfranco, Marie Chancel, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Beta oscillations support somatosensory temporal integration for body ownership
papers.abstract: Extends the alpha-frequency account of body ownership to purely somatosensory situations such as self-touch. Individual beta frequency, not alpha, predicted the temporal window within which two touches were judged simultaneous and within which illusory self-touch ownership arose, while it did not predict visuotactile integration. The work suggests different oscillatory clocks for different sensory combinations of the bodily self.
papers.authors: Mariano D'Angelo, Renzo C. Lanfranco, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Conscious awareness, sensory integration, and evidence accumulation in bodily self-perception
papers.abstract: Asks how the feeling of owning a body relates to conscious awareness by building a psychophysical rubber-hand paradigm that separately quantifies multisensory integration, awareness and metacognition. Using signal-detection analysis, metacognitive modeling and drift-diffusion modeling, it shows how ownership judgments emerge from accumulating sensory evidence and how they relate to conscious report.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Renzo C. Lanfranco, Sucharit Katyal, August Hägerdal, Xiaole Luan, Victoria Nos, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Dynamic changes in somatosensory and cerebellar activity mediate temporal recalibration of self-touch
papers.abstract: Combines psychophysics and fMRI to study how the brain updates its expected timing of self-generated touch. After repeated exposure to delayed self-touches, attenuation of the sensation weakened and somatosensory cortex stopped distinguishing delayed from non-delayed touches, while the ipsilateral anterior cerebellum showed increased activity and cingulate responses grew, consistent with conflict as adaptation proceeded.
papers.authors: Konstantina Kilteni, H. Henrik Ehrsson

papers.title: Proprioceptive uncertainty promotes the rubber hand illusion
