papers.abstract: Uses tendon vibration to add noise to proprioception while participants judged whether a rubber hand felt like their own under varying visuotactile asynchrony. Illusion probability rose with proprioceptive noise, and a Bayesian causal-inference model fitted this best as a change in the prior probability of a common cause for vision and touch. It shows how the reliability of body-position signals shapes ownership.
papers.authors: Marie Chancel, H. Henrik Ehrsson

E236.name: Charles Spence
E236.bio: Spence heads the Crossmodal Research Laboratory at the University of Oxford, investigating how the human brain integrates information across various sensory modalities to form perceptual experiences. Their research utilizes psychophysical methodologies to explore the role of attention in multisensory processing, including a study on how auditory cues modulate the perceived freshness of food that received an Ig Nobel Prize. Spence’s current work focuses on gastrophysics—the science of multisensory food design—and the application of crossmodal insights to human-computer interaction, automotive safety signals, and environmental well-being through "sensehacking."
E236.research_direction: Dr. Spence has recently been investigating the theoretical boundaries and cognitive mechanisms of multisensory perception and crossmodal associations. Their recent work explores how semantic congruency across the senses—such as matching a sound to a visual stimulus—impacts short-term and episodic memory, and whether auditory-conceptual mappings, like associating specific musical motifs with visual characters, are conserved across different cultures. In addition to clarifying foundational concepts in the field, such as what constitutes an "amodal" sensory dimension, they are testing whether temporal structures like rhythm and beat can be perceived crossmodally or even through the chemical senses. Finally, expanding into applied visual perception, Dr. Spence is evaluating the specific visual features that drive perceived deliciousness by comparing human aesthetic responses to real versus AI-generated food imagery.

papers.title: Crossmodal semantics in memory: Scoping review and meta-analyses of multisensory effects in short-term and episodic memory systems
papers.abstract: Reviews three decades of research on whether events whose features are semantically congruent across the senses (e.g., a dog's image and its bark) are remembered better. Combining a systematic scoping review with meta-analyses across short-term and episodic memory, the authors find broad support for a memory benefit of crossmodal congruency, with some exceptions. They also lay out the competing theoretical accounts and the open questions that remain.
papers.authors: Salvador Soto-Faraco, Charles Spence

papers.title: Perceiving temporal structure within and between the senses: A multisensory/crossmodal perspective
papers.abstract: Reviews how people perceive rhythm, beat and metre in sequences of sounds, touches and visual events, and asks whether this ability extends to crossmodal patterns and to the chemical senses. The evidence points to similar behaviour across audition, vision and touch, but is thin or unconvincing for crossmodal and chemosensory cases, which challenges the idea of a single amodal temporal processor.
papers.authors: Nicola Di Stefano, Charles Spence

papers.title: Assessing the visual appeal of real/AI-generated food images
papers.abstract: Compares how appealing people find real photographs of food versus AI-generated images of the same kinds of dishes. The work asks what visual features drive perceived deliciousness and whether synthetic food imagery can match or beat photographs, with implications for food marketing and consumer expectations.
papers.authors: Giovanbattista Califano, Charles Spence

papers.title: What, if anything, can be considered an amodal sensory dimension?
papers.abstract: Examines how the term 'amodal' is used differently by developmental scientists, cognitive neuroscientists and perception researchers (e.g., amodal completion). The authors sort out these usages and argue about which perceptual dimensions can legitimately be called amodal, offering a conceptual framework for the multisensory field.
papers.authors: Charles Spence, Nicola Di Stefano

papers.title: Prokofiev was (almost) right: A cross-cultural investigation of auditory-conceptual associations in Peter and the Wolf
papers.abstract: Tests whether music excerpts from Peter and the Wolf are matched with the characters they depict (bird, duck, wolf, cat, grandfather) in images and words, using participants from many countries. Listeners reliably matched the wolf and bird excerpts regardless of culture or musical training, and these matches were mediated by shared emotional profiles.
papers.authors: Nicola Di Stefano, Alessandro Ansani, Andrea Schiavio, Charles Spence

E238.name: Monica Gori
E238.bio: Monica Gori is a Senior Scientist and Principal Investigator of the Unit for Visually Impaired People (U-VIP) at the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia. Gori’s research integrates psychophysics, computational modeling, and engineering to investigate the development of multisensory integration and spatial cognition in sighted and visually impaired individuals. Gori formulated the 'cross-sensory calibration' hypothesis, which proposes that vision is used to calibrate other senses like hearing and touch for spatial tasks. Their work has led to the development of assistive technologies, including the ABBI (Audio Bracelet for Blind Interaction), and has been supported by an ERC Starting Grant (MySpace) and ERC Proof of Concept grant.
E238.research_direction: Dr. Gori has recently been investigating how visual experience shapes the development of multisensory spatial perception. By comparing sighted infants, children, and adults with those who are congenitally blind or visually impaired, their recent work explores whether vision acts as a necessary calibration reference for organizing touch, hearing, and embodied spatial maps. Using behavioral paradigms, EEG, and neural network modeling, they examine phenomena such as the neural remapping of tactile coordinates during crossed-hand postures, the developmental emergence of statistically optimal audio-tactile spatial integration, and how spatial layouts influence cross-modal temporal order judgments. Additionally, their research spans broader audiovisual interactions, testing how auditory inputs can drive border assignment and figure-ground segregation during the processing of ambiguous visual images.

papers.title: The development of spatial perception with and without visual experience
papers.abstract: A review of how the sense of space is built up across development, contrasting people who grow up sighted with those born blind or visually impaired. It argues that vision acts as the reference that calibrates and organizes touch, hearing and body-based spatial coding, and shows how its absence reshapes spatial abilities and their neural basis. The authors also point to implications for early intervention and assistive technology.
papers.authors: Monica Gori, Maria Bianca Amadeo, Andrew J. Bremner

papers.title: Space Impacts Temporal Processing via a Visual-Dependent Spatially Organized Neural Architecture
papers.abstract: Sighted children and adults and early blind participants judged the temporal order of sounds and touches delivered to the same or different hands, close together or far apart. In sighted people, timing precision was influenced by spatial layout, consistent with implicit causal inference, but early blind participants did not show this spatial effect. A neural network model was used to argue that spatially organized sensory maps that depend on visual experience underlie the space-time interaction.
papers.authors: Maria Bianca Amadeo, Cristiano Cuppini, Alessia Tonelli, Carolina Tammurello, Walter Setti, Claudio Campus, Sabrina Signorini, Elena Cocchi, Margherita Bonino, Francesca Tinelli, Paola Camicione, Massimiliano Serafino, Monica Gori

papers.title: The Development of Audio-Tactile Spatial Integration: Unraveling Vision's Contribution
papers.abstract: Sighted and blind children of different ages localized auditory, tactile and combined audio-tactile stimuli. In sighted children, touch stabilizes before hearing and statistically optimal audio-tactile integration only appears after about 12 years, while blind children show more precise single-sense performance early but little multisensory improvement with age. The work suggests vision shapes how multisensory spatial integration matures.
papers.authors: Alessia Tonelli, Irene Senna, Maria Bianca Amadeo, Walter Setti, Nicola Domenici, Sabrina Signorini, Elena Cocchi, Giuseppina Giammari, Sandra Strazzer, Francesca Tinelli, Paola Camicione, Massimiliano Serafino, Monica Gori

papers.title: Vision drives the neural construction of a two-stage hierarchy of spatial processing in infancy
papers.abstract: Using EEG in sighted and severely visually impaired infants, the study tracked how touches are first coded on the skin and later remapped into external space when the hands are crossed. Sighted infants showed the later remapping stage, tied to orienting errors toward the wrong hand, whereas visually impaired infants kept a purely skin-based response across both stages. The results indicate that early visual experience builds the neural machinery for embodied spatial coding.
papers.authors: Monica Gori, Helene Vitali, Andrew J. Bremner, Alessia Tonelli, Maria Bianca Amadeo, Walter Setti, Carolina Tammurello, Sabrina Signorini, Elena Cocchi, Giuseppina Giammari, Sandra Strazzer, Francesca Tinelli, Massimiliano Serafino, Paola Camicione, Claudio Campus

papers.title: Disambiguating vision with sound
papers.abstract: Shows that a sound can decide which region of an ambiguous figure-ground image is perceived as the object, an influence much stronger than voluntary intention. The finding demonstrates that auditory input can directly shape how the visual system assigns borders and segregates objects from background.
papers.authors: Monica Gori, David Burr, Claudio Campus

E239.name: Mark Wallace
E239.department: Department of Psychology; Department of Hearing and Speech Sciences
E239.bio: Mark T. Wallace is a neuroscientist and the Louise B. McGavock Chair of Neuroscience at Vanderbilt University, where they investigate how the brain synthesizes information across sensory modalities such as vision, hearing, and touch. Wallace’s research employs a multidisciplinary approach involving animal neurophysiology, human psychophysics, and neuroimaging techniques like fMRI and EEG to map the neural substrates of multisensory processing. Their work focuses on the development and plasticity of multisensory circuits and how these processes are altered in clinical conditions, including autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Wallace has characterized the multisensory temporal binding window and its role in shaping perception and behavior across the lifespan.
E239.research_direction: Dr. Wallace has recently been investigating the mechanisms of multisensory integration, using behavioral paradigms and reliability-weighted models to explore how the brain combines visual and auditory motion cues. Their research applies these multisensory frameworks to neurodevelopmental conditions, probing whether spatial localization and temporal processing differ in autistic children and examining predictive coding accounts of emotion dysregulation across autism and ADHD. Additionally, they are exploring translational interventions to enhance sensory processing, testing whether perceptual training to narrow the multisensory temporal binding window can improve speech-in-noise comprehension. Their recent work also investigates neuropharmacological approaches to perception, reviewing how cholinergic modulation might be leveraged to promote cross-sensory plasticity and aid recovery from sensory loss.

papers.title: Behavioral evidence for visually dominant audiovisual motion integration
papers.abstract: Sixty participants judged the direction of moving sounds, moving visual stimuli, and combined audiovisual motion while being cued to attend to one or both senses. Visual direction estimates were more reliable than auditory ones and bimodal estimates beat either single sense, and when directions conflicted the visual signal dominated. Reliability-weighted cue-combination models captured the pattern, indicating that audiovisual motion is integrated in a statistically sensible but visually weighted way.
papers.authors: Adam J. Tiesman, Kalina Stoyanova, Ramnarayan Ramachandran, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Prediction Gone Awry: A Computational Framework for Emotion Dysregulation Across Autism and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a predictive-coding account of emotion dysregulation in which regulation depends on predicting bodily and environmental signals and on how much precision is assigned to prediction errors. Autism is hypothesized to involve overweighted surprising inputs plus slow updating of expectations, whereas ADHD involves weak priors and unstable gain control. The authors suggest physiological markers such as heart-rate variability, pupil variability and mismatch negativity to test these ideas.
papers.venue: Journal of Child and Adolescent Psychopharmacology
papers.authors: Hari Srinivasan, Carissa J. Cascio, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Effects of multisensory simultaneity judgment training on the comprehension and cortical processing of speech in noise: a randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Adults were randomly assigned to three days of audiovisual simultaneity-judgment training or to testing only, to see whether narrowing the temporal binding window improves speech-in-noise understanding. Trained participants showed a significantly narrower binding window, and those with the largest narrowing improved most in auditory word recognition in noise, though group-level word scores did not change. The work is a translational test of whether multisensory temporal training can be used as a hearing intervention.
papers.authors: Ansley J. Kunnath, Hannah S. Bertisch, Andrew S. Kim, René H. Gifford, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Intact Audiovisual Spatial Integration in Autistic Children
papers.abstract: Autistic and non-autistic children aged 7-17 completed a free-response audiovisual spatial localization task to test whether cross-modal integration in space, rather than time, differs in autism. The two groups did not differ in how they integrated sight and sound spatially, and performance was related to clinical features only in limited ways. The result contrasts with the well-documented temporal differences and helps delimit which aspects of multisensory processing are altered in autism.
papers.venue: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
papers.authors: Sarah G. Vassall, Ingrid Shragge, Hari Srinivasan, William J. Quackenbush, Mark T. Wallace

papers.title: Cholinergic modulation of sensory perception and plasticity
papers.abstract: This review examines how acetylcholine shapes plasticity in visual and auditory systems, including the reorganization that follows sensory loss and the recovery that follows restoration. It surveys evidence that cholinergic drugs can improve human visual and auditory perception and cross-sensory integration. The authors argue that targeting plasticity pharmacologically is a promising, so far untapped route to treating sensory loss.
papers.authors: Ansley J. Kunnath, René H. Gifford, Mark T. Wallace

E240.name: Jean Vroomen
E240.bio: Jean Vroomen is a Professor and Head of the Department of Cognitive Neuropsychology at Tilburg University. Vroomen's research focuses on multisensory perception, specifically regarding the integration of auditory and visual signals during speech processing and temporal recalibration. Utilizing behavioral experiments and electroencephalography (EEG), they investigate these mechanisms across various populations, including infants, children, and clinical groups such as individuals with autism or schizophrenia. Vroomen’s work also examines the neural correlates of affective salience and the electrophysiological markers of predictive coding in sensory integration.
E240.research_direction: Dr. Vroomen's recent work explores the behavioral and neural mechanisms underlying audiovisual speech perception and multisensory integration. They have recently been using EEG and behavioral paradigms to investigate how visual information, such as a talker's head viewing angle or lip movements, modulates auditory event-related potentials and helps listeners adapt to degraded speech, including in populations with developmental dyslexia. Additionally, their recent research examines the phenomenon of selective speech adaptation, probing both the ear-specificity and the electrophysiological correlates of how repeated exposure to a phoneme alters the categorization of subsequent ambiguous sounds. Beyond phonetic processing, they are also investigating multisensory social cognition by testing how visual face shape, vocal pitch, and semantic spoken content interact to shape human judgments of trustworthiness.

papers.title: A behavioral and electrophysiological investigation of the effect of horizontal head viewing angle on audiovisual speech integration
papers.abstract: The study asks how much a talker's head rotation (frontal to side-back views) affects the benefit listeners get from seeing the face during speech. Behaviourally, the lip-reading gain in noise shrank as the head turned away, though only for certain consonants. In EEG, the visually induced suppression of the auditory N1 was largest at an oblique 45-degree view and reduced at profile and back views, while P2 suppression stayed constant, suggesting temporal prediction is more viewpoint-sensitive than phonetic integration.
papers.authors: Jeroen J. Stekelenburg, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Ear-specific selective speech adaptation
papers.abstract: This paper continues the group's work on selective speech adaptation, in which repeated exposure to a speech sound shifts how later ambiguous sounds are categorised. As the title indicates, it tests whether the adaptation effect is specific to the ear that received the adapting sounds. (Summary inferred from title and the authors' related work; no abstract was retrievable.)
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Martijn Baart, Isar H. J. Syed, Jeroen J. Stekelenburg, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Electrophysiological correlates of selective speech adaptation
papers.abstract: Listeners were repeatedly exposed to a Dutch vowel (/e/ or /o-slash/) and then categorised ambiguous vowels lying between them, which were heard as the opposite phoneme in over 90% of trials. EEG showed that this contrastive perceptual shift was accompanied by late deviations beginning around 575 ms, localised mainly to left superior temporal gyrus. The authors interpret this as a higher-level cortical stage that resolves perceptual ambiguity.
papers.authors: Jeroen J. Stekelenburg, Jakob Limpens, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: The Multimodal Trust Effects of Face, Voice, and Sentence Content
papers.abstract: Twenty-six female participants rated the trustworthiness of voices speaking neutral or romantic sentences while viewing faces. Voice pitch and the face width-to-height ratio were systematically varied. The work brings social trust cues (face, voice and message content) into a multisensory framework and finds that the spoken content carried a clear influence on trust judgements.
papers.authors: Isar Syed, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

papers.title: Perceptual Adaptation to Noise-Vocoded Speech by Lip-Read Information: No Difference between Dyslexic and Typical Readers
papers.abstract: Adults with developmental dyslexia and typical readers heard acoustically degraded (noise-vocoded) Dutch words in audiovisual training blocks interleaved with audio-only tests. Seeing the speaker improved word recognition in both groups, and both groups showed comparable lip-read-driven adaptation to the distorted speech that carried over to audio-only trials. The results argue against reduced use of lip-read information in dyslexia for this kind of learning.
papers.authors: Faezeh Pourhashemi, Martijn Baart, Jean Vroomen

E241.name: Fiona Newell
E241.department: School of Psychology and Trinity College Institute of Neuroscience (TCIN)
E241.bio: Newell is a Professor of Experimental Psychology at Trinity College Dublin whose research explores the behavioral and neural principles of multisensory integration. They examine how the human brain processes information from sensory modalities, such as vision, audition, and haptics, to facilitate object recognition, scene perception, and social interactions. Using psychophysical experiments and neuroimaging techniques including fMRI and EEG, Newell investigates perceptual changes across the lifespan and the mechanisms underlying conditions like synaesthesia. Their recent projects leverage virtual reality and neuroaesthetics to study human preferences and develop interventions for age-related cognitive decline.
E241.research_direction: Dr. Newell has recently been investigating how multisensory perception shapes the formation of object categories across the lifespan. Their recent work explores whether combining visual information with tactile motion, auditory spatial cues, or natural crossmodal correspondences (such as pitch and size) influences how humans learn rule-based categories and generalize to unseen exemplars. Beyond foundational category learning, they are also applying multisensory psychophysics to aging research, specifically examining whether the temporal precision of audiovisual integration—measured via the sound-induced flash illusion—can serve as a predictive marker for longitudinal fall risk in older adults.

papers.title: Visual and tactile motion cues enhance the categorisation of novel object shapes
papers.abstract: Participants learned to categorise novel object shapes while the objects' motion was conveyed through vision, touch, or both. Adding motion cues in either modality improved category learning, showing that dynamic information helps form object categories and that the senses can complement each other. The work extends multisensory categorisation beyond static shape.
papers.authors: Martina A. Seveso, Rebecca J. Hirst, Alan O'Dowd, Ivan Camponogara, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Crossmodal correspondences influence adaptation during rule-based category learning of objects
papers.abstract: Examined whether natural mappings between sensory features, such as pitch and size, affect how learners adapt during rule-based category learning of objects. Correspondence between modalities shaped how quickly and flexibly participants adapted to new category rules. It links crossmodal correspondence research to category learning.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Rebecca J. Hirst, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Generalisation to novel exemplars of learned shape categories based on visual and auditory spatial cues does not benefit from multisensory information
papers.abstract: Tested whether learning shape categories from combined visual and auditory spatial cues helps people generalise to unseen exemplars better than a single sense. Multisensory training did not confer an advantage in generalisation over unisensory training. The result qualifies the assumption that more senses always yield better category learning.
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Rebecca J. Hirst, Martina A. Seveso, Eimear M. McKenna, Fiona N. Newell

papers.title: Multisensory perception constrains the formation of object categories: a review of evidence from sensory-driven and predictive processes on categorical decisions
papers.abstract: Reviews behavioural and neural evidence that object categories are shaped by information from several senses rather than vision alone. The authors argue that both bottom-up sensory input and top-down predictive processes govern how multisensory cues are combined during categorical decisions, and that this changes across the lifespan. The paper sets out the theoretical framing for the lab's later category-learning experiments.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Fiona N. Newell, Eimear McKenna, Martina A. Seveso, Isla Devine, Fahad Alahmad, Rebecca J. Hirst, Alan O'Dowd

papers.title: The temporal precision of audio-visual integration is associated with longitudinal fall incidents but not sensorimotor fall risk in older adults
papers.abstract: Used a large longitudinal cohort of older adults (TILDA) to relate the temporal precision of audiovisual integration, measured with the sound-induced flash illusion, to later falls. Less precise integration was linked to more falls over time, though not to sensorimotor measures of fall risk. It positions multisensory timing as a marker of ageing and functional decline.
papers.authors: Alan O'Dowd, Rebecca J. Hirst, Annalisa Setti, Orna A. Donoghue, Rose Anne Kenny, Fiona N. Newell

E242.name: Virginie van Wassenhove
E242.bio: Van Wassenhove is a Director of Research at CEA and heads the Cognition & Brain Dynamics lab within the Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit at NeuroSpin. Their research investigates the neurobiological underpinnings of temporal cognition and multisensory integration, focusing on how the brain encodes durations and sequences to construct experiences of time. Van Wassenhove utilizes neuroimaging techniques, including magnetoencephalography (MEG) and electroencephalography (EEG), to analyze the role of neural oscillations in predictive coding and information parsing. Their work characterizes the influence of alpha oscillations on perceptual priors and explores the impact of environmental factors, such as isolation, on subjective temporal maps. Current investigations integrate behavioral psychophysics with computational models to define the functional brain dynamics involved in timing and postdiction.
E242.research_direction: Dr. van Wassenhove's recent work explores the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying how humans perceive, remember, and represent time. They have recently been using MEG and EEG to investigate the neural geometry of temporal durations, asking whether time is encoded along a simple linear timeline or a more complex multidimensional space, and how working memory load for these abstract intervals is tracked by alpha and beta oscillations. Their research also examines the episodic memory of "when," using virtual environments to uncover how the hierarchical nesting of information within events drives the temporal compression of retrospective memory. Finally, they are investigating the broader subjective experience of elapsed time, comparing prospective and retrospective timing contexts to probe how cognitive load, environmental factors like social isolation, and spontaneous resting-state neural dynamics influence our sense of how long events last and how fast time seems to pass.

papers.title: Alpha power indexes working memory load for durations
papers.abstract: Using MEG during an n-item delayed duration reproduction task, the authors asked how sequences of time intervals are held in working memory. The number of durations in a sequence, not their total length, reduced recall precision, and this number could be decoded from alpha and beta activity during retention. Alpha power emerges as a general marker of working memory load that mediates recall precision even for an abstract feature such as duration.
papers.authors: Sophie K. Herbst, Izem Mangione, Charbel-Raphaël Segerie, Richard Höchenberger, Tadeusz Kononowicz, Alexandre Gramfort, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Uncovering the representational geometry of durations
papers.abstract: The study asks whether a simple linear mental timeline is enough to explain how durations are represented. Behavioural similarity judgments were best explained by three latent dimensions (magnitude, contextual encoding relative to the set mean, and a periodic component) consistent with a helical model, whose parameters related to individual resting oscillations. EEG showed the neural geometry of durations unfolding in two stages, first logarithmic and then spring-like.
papers.authors: Camille L. Grasso, Ladislas Nalborczyk, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Nested contextual change and the temporal compression of episodic memory
papers.abstract: Participants moved through virtual rooms containing images and later reported what, when, and where for each item. Memory for when showed strong temporal compression at both item and event levels, and events made of fewer items were compressed more than events with more items. The results indicate that memory for time depends on how information is nested within events.
papers.authors: Matthew Logie, Camille Grasso, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Cognitive effects on experienced duration and speed of time, prospectively, retrospectively, in and out of lockdown
papers.abstract: Using online data gathered during the Covid-19 pandemic, participants performed an n-back task and after each trial judged its duration and how fast time seemed to pass. Cognitive load pushed duration estimates in opposite directions depending on prospective versus retrospective timing, short durations felt fast, and social isolation affected duration and speed judgments differently.
papers.authors: Cyril Nicolaï, Maximilien Chaumon, Virginie van Wassenhove

papers.title: Spontaneous α Brain Dynamics Track the Episodic "When"
papers.abstract: Participants sat quietly in an MEG scanner without knowing they would later be asked how long the recording lasted. The relative duration of spontaneous alpha bursts linearly predicted their retrospective duration estimates, better than alpha power or amplitude, but did not predict prospective timing. The finding gives a neural signature of the conscious sense of elapsed time over minutes.
papers.authors: Leila Azizi, Ignacio Polti, Virginie van Wassenhove

E243.name: David Burr
E243.department: Department of Neuroscience, Psychology, Drug Research and Child Health
E243.bio: David Burr is Professor Emeritus of Physiological Psychology at the University of Florence, focusing on human vision and multisensory neuroscience. Burr's research investigates visual stability, specifically regarding saccadic suppression and the compression of space and time during eye movements. Burr also identified a specialized 'number sense' for non-symbolic numerosity perception across various sensory modalities and actions. Their work utilizes Bayesian frameworks to model perceptual processes, including theories on the 'hypo-priors' characteristic of autistic perception.
E243.research_direction: Dr. Burr's recent work explores the spatial and temporal integration mechanisms that optimize visual processing, alongside a sustained investigation into numerosity as a fundamental perceptual attribute. They have recently been examining how contextual history and spatial surroundings shape current perception, using Bayesian frameworks to probe phenomena like serial dependence and color crowding. A key focus of their research is determining whether these adaptive effects, as well as visual adaptation to dot arrays, operate at early sensory levels or reflect later decisional biases, which they investigate using continuous behavioral metrics like confidence ratings and reaction times. Furthermore, they are exploring novel methodological approaches, utilizing frequency-tagged pupillometry to track the implicit statistical learning of numerical regularities during passive viewing.

papers.title: Adaptation acts directly on the sensory representation of numerosity
papers.abstract: Adaptation to sparse dot fields produces smaller effects than adaptation to dense fields, leaving open whether it reflects response bias rather than a change in perception. By measuring confidence and reaction times alongside numerosity estimates, the authors show that both dense and sparse adaptation shift confidence and response-time profiles in step with the perceptual shift, so maximum uncertainty falls at the subjective point of equality. This indicates adaptation acts on the sensory representation before decision stages, supporting numerosity as a primary perceptual attribute.
papers.authors: Alessandro Benedetto, Giovanni Anobile, Roberto Arrighi, Egle Casavecchia, David C. Burr

papers.title: Is number a primary perceptual attribute?
papers.abstract: A single-author review of two decades of evidence that number should be considered a primary perceptual attribute, focusing on adaptation studies and supporting psychophysical, pupillometric, EEG and imaging results. It addresses the main challenges to this view, and to adaptation itself, and speculates on the functional role of numerosity adaptation and open research directions.
papers.authors: David Burr

papers.title: Pupillometric signature of implicit learning of statistical regularities
papers.abstract: Using frequency-tagged pupil recordings, the study shows that the pupil responds to the repetition rate of numerosity pairings in a sequence of dot arrays even though participants never notice the pairings. Learning became detectable within about three minutes of passive viewing and persisted when attention was directed away from numerosity, though it was modulated. Pupillometry is thus offered as a sensitive, non-invasive readout of implicit statistical learning.
papers.authors: Paola Binda, Chiara Terzo, Marco Turi, David C. Burr

papers.title: Serial Dependence in Perception
papers.abstract: A review of the evidence that perception is systematically pulled toward recently seen similar stimuli, an effect that touches almost every aspect of vision and often produces large distortions for weak or ambiguous input. The authors argue, drawing on Bayesian modelling and predictive-coding ideas, that the effect is on balance beneficial because it stabilizes and improves efficiency of perception, and that the relevant priors are generated at high cortical levels and fed back to sensory areas.
papers.authors: Guido Marco Cicchini, Kyriaki Mikellidou, David Charles Burr

papers.title: Color crowding considered as adaptive spatial integration
papers.abstract: The paper tests the proposal that crowding reflects efficient exploitation of spatial redundancy in natural scenes rather than a processing bottleneck. Measuring color discrimination for targets flanked by variably colored stimuli, it confirms that crowding is stronger for less salient targets and that flanker interference can coincide with higher precision. Reaction-time analyses place the integration at the sensory rather than the decisional level.
papers.authors: Guido Marco Cicchini, Giovanni D'Errico, David Charles Burr

E244.name: John Foxe
E244.lab_name: Frederick J. and Marion A. Schindler Cognitive Neurophysiology Laboratory
E244.bio: John J. Foxe is a translational neuroscientist serving as the Chair of the Department of Neuroscience and Director of the Del Monte Institute for Neuroscience at the University of Rochester. Foxe’s research focuses on identifying endophenotypic biomarkers for neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders, with a primary emphasis on autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia. Utilizing high-density electrophysiology (EEG), structural and functional neuroimaging (fMRI), and psychophysical methods, Foxe investigates how the brain processes and integrates multisensory information. Their work aims to link these neural markers to underlying genotypes to better understand the biological mechanisms of disease and inform the development of targeted therapeutic interventions.
E244.research_direction: Dr. Foxe has recently been investigating how sensory processing, multisensory integration, and sensorimotor coupling differ in individuals on the autism spectrum across the lifespan. Their recent work explores visual predictive coding via EEG, using illusory contours to test whether weakened top-down feedback shapes autistic perception, alongside advanced diffusion MRI to map in vivo microstructural differences in gray matter and neurite architecture. They are also examining integration across other modalities, using fMRI to measure how audiovisual speech-in-noise perception tracks with symptom severity, and combining high-density EEG with virtual reality to probe how the autistic brain handles self-generated versus externally triggered touch. Finally, to understand these sensory and cognitive systems under naturalistic demands, they employ mobile brain-body imaging to study the dynamic interplay of neural responses, visual optic flow, and gait during complex, multi-domain walking tasks.

papers.title: Associations between symptom severity in autism and functional neuroimaging measures of audiovisual speech perception
papers.abstract: Examines whether multisensory speech deficits scale with autism symptom severity, using a speech-in-noise behavioral task (n=32) and an fMRI study (n=37). Higher calibrated severity scores tracked poorer audiovisual but not auditory-only performance, and lower multisensory gain in dorsal speech and language regions. Exploratory analyses suggest that speech-motor regions may be engaged differently in autism.
papers.authors: Lars A. Ross, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

papers.title: A symphony of functioning: exploring the interplay of cognition, movement, and visual demands in adolescents on the autism spectrum using mobile brain-body imaging (MoBI)
papers.abstract: Uses mobile brain-body imaging, recording 64-channel EEG, motion tracking and response-inhibition performance, in adolescents with and without ASD while standing or walking on a treadmill, with or without optic flow and a cognitive task. Typically developing teens became more accurate when walking, whereas the ASD group did not, and their N200/P300 modulations were similar in direction but weaker. The authors propose coupled neural-gait responses under multi-domain demands as a marker of altered cross-domain integration in ASD.
papers.authors: Paige R. Nicklas, Lisa N. Cruz, Carol Terilli, Erin K. Bojanek, Pierfilippo De Sanctis, Edward G. Freedman, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

papers.title: Adults on the autism spectrum differ from neurotypical peers when self-generating but not passively-experiencing somatosensation: a high-density electrophysiological (EEG) mapping and virtual reality study
papers.abstract: Combines high-density EEG with virtual reality to compare vibrotactile responses in 30 autistic and 30 neurotypical adults when touch was self-triggered versus externally triggered. Autistic adults showed smaller N1 to passive but not active touch and larger P300 overall, while mismatch responses to duration deviants were comparable between groups. The results suggest subtle differences in handling self-generated versus external somatosensory input.
papers.authors: Emily L. Isenstein, Edward G. Freedman, Grace A. Rico, Zakilya Brown, Duje Tadin, John J. Foxe

papers.title: Autism is associated with in vivo changes in gray matter neurite architecture
papers.abstract: Applies restriction spectrum imaging to diffusion MRI from the ABCD cohort, comparing 142 autistic adolescents with about 9,000 controls, to probe cortical and cerebellar microstructure in vivo. Autism was linked to reduced total neurite density in right cerebellar cortex and to diffuse shifts in restricted isotropic and directional diffusion across the brain, which held against a psychiatric comparison group. The work offers a scalable in vivo route to the cytoarchitectural differences previously seen only in postmortem tissue.
papers.authors: Zachary P. Christensen, Edward G. Freedman, John J. Foxe

papers.title: Severely Attenuated Visual Feedback Processing in Children on the Autism Spectrum
papers.abstract: Tests the idea that autism involves weakened top-down feedback to early visual cortex by recording EEG while 29 autistic and 31 neurotypical children (7-17 years) passively viewed Kanizsa illusory-contour stimuli. Autistic children showed markedly reduced automatic contour-integration responses over lateral occipital cortex. The authors interpret this as evidence that weakened predictive feedback (weak priors) contributes to altered visual perception in autism.
papers.authors: Emily J. Knight, Edward G. Freedman, Evan J. Myers, Alaina S. Berruti, Leona A. Oakes, Cody Zhewei Cao, Sophie Molholm, John J. Foxe

E245.name: Salvador Soto-Faraco
E245.department: Departament de Tecnologies de la Informació i les Comunicacions
E245.bio: Soto-Faraco is an ICREA Research Professor who heads the Multisensory Research Group at Universitat Pompeu Fabra’s Center for Brain and Cognition. Soto-Faraco's research examines the cognitive and neural principles governing how the brain integrates information across sensory modalities, including vision, audition, and somatosensation. Using a combination of psychophysics, neuroimaging techniques such as EEG and fMRI, and non-invasive brain stimulation, they investigate the interplay between top-down attention and multisensory binding. Their current work explores perception in naturalistic, real-world environments to connect laboratory-based findings with ecological validity.
E245.research_direction: Dr. Soto-Faraco has recently been investigating how the brain integrates multisensory information and how this crossmodal processing shapes broader cognitive functions. Their recent work explores whether semantically congruent audiovisual stimuli, such as an object paired with a matching sound, interact with factors like event rarity to influence encoding in both short-term and episodic memory. In the realm of speech perception, they are using EEG to examine how neurotypical and autistic adults combine auditory speech and visual gestures in noisy, naturalistic social scenes by tracking alpha-band neural oscillations. Additionally, they are studying potential avenues for cognitive enhancement by testing whether rhythmic visual or auditory sensory stimulation at specific brain-matched frequencies can elevate visual working memory capacity.

papers.title: Crossmodal semantics in memory: Scoping review and meta-analyses of multisensory effects in short-term and episodic memory
papers.abstract: Reviews thirty years of studies asking whether events whose sights, sounds and other senses match semantically are remembered better, covering both short-term and episodic memory. Combines a systematic scoping review with meta-analyses, then lays out the inconsistencies across methods and the competing theoretical accounts. Concludes with the open empirical questions the field still needs to settle.
papers.authors: Salvador Soto-Faraco, Charles Spence

papers.title: Multisensory Integration of Naturalistic Speech and Gestures in Autistic Adults
papers.abstract: Compares autistic and neurotypical adults on audio-visual speech-in-noise perception within a multi-speaker social scene while recording EEG. Neurotypical adults showed a non-linear audio-visual effect in alpha oscillations whereas autistic adults showed only additive processing, yet both groups gained similar behavioural benefit from seeing the speaker. Suggests different neural routes to comparable multisensory benefits in autism.
papers.authors: Magdalena Matyjek, Sotaro Kita, Mireia Torralba Cuello, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Crossmodal semantic congruence and rarity improve episodic memory
papers.abstract: Across four experiments (N = 232) uses a dual-process signal-detection approach to show that hearing a sound that matches an object during incidental encoding boosts both recollection and familiarity 48 hours later. The benefit appears in older adults too and persists even when congruent events are much rarer or commoner than incongruent ones, although rare events are generally more memorable. Rarity and crossmodal congruence thus contribute independently to long-term memory.
papers.authors: Pau Alexander Packard, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Multisensory integration of speech and gestures in a naturalistic paradigm
papers.abstract: Tests how adults combine seeing and hearing a speaker, including iconic gestures, in a realistic social scene with noisy speech. Audio-visual trials gave better word recognition and stronger alpha-power suppression than unimodal ones, and the EEG effect exceeded the sum of the unimodal responses, pointing to genuinely non-linear integration. Argues for studying multisensory speech with naturalistic stimuli rather than idealised ones.
papers.authors: Magdalena Matyjek, Sotaro Kita, Mireia Torralba Cuello, Salvador Soto-Faraco

papers.title: Sensory stimulation enhances visual working memory capacity
papers.abstract: Six behavioural experiments (N = 209) tested whether rhythmic visual or auditory stimulation at 4 or 7 Hz can raise visual working memory capacity, mirroring earlier theta-tACS findings. Stimulation at either frequency improved capacity, with slightly larger gains at 7 Hz, and the benefit was concentrated in low-capacity individuals. Attention-network and pupillometry follow-ups did not attribute the effect to arousal changes.
papers.authors: Indre Pileckyte, Salvador Soto-Faraco

E246.name: Michael N. Shadlen
E246.bio: Michael N. Shadlen investigates the neurobiological underpinnings of decision-making as a framework to understand cognitive processes such as reasoning and planning. Their research focuses on how the brain accumulates and integrates sensory evidence to reach a categorical commitment, emphasizing the role of the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) and the computational principles of the speed-accuracy tradeoff. Utilizing single-neuron electrophysiology in non-human primates, behavioral psychophysics, and computational modeling, Shadlen identifies how neural circuits transform visual signals into volitional actions. Their current work explores the scalability of these decision mechanisms to address complex cognitive operations, including memory-based choices and the neural basis of confidence.
E246.research_direction: Dr. Shadlen has recently been investigating the precise neural circuit dynamics underlying perceptual decision-making, focusing on how the brain accumulates evidence and commits to a choice. Using high-density electrophysiology in the primate parietal cortex, their recent work explores how populations of neurons track drift-diffusion dynamics during a single trial, how specific circuits implement decision bounds to terminate deliberation, and how these networks encode subjective decision confidence prior to receiving feedback. They are also extending this decision framework to flexible cognition in mice, using two-photon imaging to examine how motor cortex circuits dynamically reconfigure to support context-dependent stimulus-response mappings. More broadly, Dr. Shadlen is exploring how these well-defined computational mechanisms of evidence accumulation can provide a theoretical framework for investigating the neural boundaries between conscious and nonconscious thought.

papers.title: Anterior lateral motor cortex enables contextual decision-making via dynamic reconfiguration of local circuits
papers.abstract: Mice must map the same stimulus onto different actions depending on context. Two-photon imaging of anterior lateral motor cortex shows that local circuits are dynamically reconfigured with the context, so the same population supports flexible stimulus-response mapping. This extends the lab's decision framework to mouse motor cortex and flexible cognition.
papers.authors: Jia Shen, Nuttida Rungratsameetaweemana, Prayshita Sharma, Darcy S. Peterka, Herbert Zheng Wu, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: Conscious and nonconscious thought: Insights from the neuroscience of decision-making
papers.abstract: This perspective argues that conscious thought need not be a special class of neural processing. Drawing on decision-making studies of evidence accumulation, it reasons that the same mechanisms can operate with and without awareness. It offers a framework for relating deliberate, conscious cognition to the underlying neural computations.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: A population representation of the confidence in a decision in the parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Confidence is the belief that a choice is correct, formed before any feedback. The study analyzes populations of parietal neurons in monkeys performing a race between competing accumulators and shows that the population state encodes the confidence associated with the decision. It links the neural representation to how evidence for the alternatives is combined and to the behavioral report of confidence.
papers.authors: Ariel Zylberberg, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: Direct observation of the neural computations underlying a single decision
papers.abstract: Using Neuropixels recordings of many parietal neurons at once, the authors track the evolution of a single decision as it happens rather than averaging over trials. Population activity reveals the accumulation of evidence trial by trial, together with the moments when the process ends, and this activity predicts the choice and its timing. The results show that the drift-diffusion-like dynamics long inferred from averages are visible in individual decisions.
papers.authors: Natalie Steinemann, Gabriel M. Stine, Eric M. Trautmann, Ariel Zylberberg, Daniel M. Wolpert, Michael N. Shadlen

papers.title: A neural mechanism for terminating decisions
papers.abstract: Recorded from parietal area LIP in monkeys with high-density probes, the study asks how accumulated evidence is converted into a commitment to stop deliberating. It finds a distinct population of neurons whose activity registers the termination event, separate from the neurons that carry the accumulating evidence, and shows that this signal is consistent with a threshold-crossing mechanism. The work supplies a concrete circuit-level account of how a decision bound is implemented.
papers.authors: Gabriel M. Stine, Eric M. Trautmann, Danique Jeurissen, Michael N. Shadlen

E247.name: Joshua I. Gold
E247.department: Department of Neuroscience, Perelman School of Medicine
E247.bio: Joshua I. Gold is a Professor of Neuroscience at the University of Pennsylvania, where Gold directs the Gold Lab and co-directs the Computational Neuroscience Initiative. Gold's research investigates the neural mechanisms of decision-making, specifically focusing on how the brain integrates uncertain sensory evidence with prior experience through inference and learning processes. To explore these functions, their laboratory employs a multidisciplinary approach that combines human psychophysics and pupillometry with non-human primate electrophysiology and computational modeling. This work aims to characterize the biological principles of belief updating and cognitive arousal to identify how adaptive behaviors are optimized within dynamic and complex environments.
E247.research_direction: Dr. Gold has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making and evidence accumulation under uncertainty. Using techniques ranging from MT neuron recordings and pupillometry in non-human primates to human visual psychophysics, their recent work explores how evidence weighting is dynamically shaped by early sensory adaptation, neuromodulation, and temporally correlated environments. They are also examining the flexible decision rules that govern speed-accuracy trade-offs, testing how individuals adaptively terminate evidence accumulation to maximize reward rates across changing task conditions. Furthermore, Dr. Gold is studying broader principles of suboptimal human inference, utilizing information-bottleneck frameworks to parse limits in cognitive capacity and formal Bayesian model-selection theories to understand how people apply Occam's razor to evaluate competing explanations.

papers.title: Suboptimal human inference reflects an efficient and flexible information bottleneck
papers.abstract: Proposes that variability in human suboptimal inference reflects limits on information processing. Applies a task-general information-bottleneck framework that separates how much information individuals use (capacity) from how well they use it (efficiency), and applies it to choice behavior on two different inference tasks. Individual differences in performance are explained by these two quantities.
papers.authors: Jacob A. Parker, Alexandre L. S. Filipowicz, Kristen Li, Vijay Balasubramanian, Joseph W. Kable, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Human decision-makers terminate evidence accumulation using flexible decision rules
papers.abstract: Examines when people stop accumulating evidence and commit, a rule that sets the trade-off between speed and accuracy. A novel task shows people adapt their stopping rules to changing conditions in ways that follow reward-rate-maximizing normative predictions rather than a single fixed bound.
papers.authors: I. Kalburge, A. Dallstream, K. Josic, ZP Kilpatrick, L. Ding, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Sensory adaptation supports flexible evidence accumulation during perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: Recorded MT neurons and pupil-linked arousal in monkeys performing a random-dot direction task preceded by adapting stimuli of varying temporal stability. Investigates whether flexibility in evidence accumulation arises from adaptation at the stage of sensory encoding and from arousal-related neuromodulation rather than only from the accumulator itself.
papers.authors: Kara D. McGaughey, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: How Occam's razor guides human decision-making
papers.abstract: Tests whether people prefer simpler explanations when interpreting uncertain data, using preregistered behavioral experiments. Preferences match the predictions of formal model-selection theory that penalizes excessive model flexibility. The work links a classic philosophical principle to Bayesian model selection and to how people actually weigh explanations during decisions.
papers.authors: Eugenio Piasini, Shuze Liu, Pratik Chaudhari, Vijay Balasubramanian, Joshua I. Gold

papers.title: Normative evidence weighing and accumulation in correlated environments
papers.abstract: Extends normative theory of evidence accumulation to observations that are correlated, which changes how much each observation should count. Online participants performing a visual discrimination task with uncued, trial-by-trial changes in correlation adjusted their weighting and accumulation accordingly, close to normative predictions.
papers.authors: Nathan Tardiff, Jiwon Kang, Joshua I. Gold

E249.name: Stephen M. Fleming
E249.department: Department of Experimental Psychology and Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience
E249.bio: Stephen M. Fleming is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at University College London and leads the MetaLab, where their research focuses on the computational and neural basis of self-awareness and conscious experience. By integrating psychophysics, functional neuroimaging (fMRI/MEG), and Bayesian modeling, Fleming has developed frameworks for understanding how the brain monitors and evaluates its own cognitive processes. Their work examines the mechanisms of metacognition and confidence across domains such as visual perception and decision-making, while also investigating the clinical implications of metacognitive distortions in psychiatric and neurological conditions.
E249.research_direction: Dr. Fleming has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of metacognition, reality monitoring, and conscious awareness. In the visual domain, their recent work explores how the human brain distinguishes vivid mental imagery from actual perception using fMRI, and evaluates theoretical predictions regarding the evolutionary role of conscious vision in offline, model-based planning. Beyond basic sensory processing, they are examining how individuals form global beliefs about their own performance, modeling how local trial-level confidence signals are updated and learned to better understand transdiagnostic underconfidence in conditions like anxiety and depression. Additionally, their research extends these questions of mind perception to human-AI interactions, testing how human attributions of emotional or conscious states to large language models influence users' trust and reliance on artificial intelligence.

papers.title: A neural basis for distinguishing imagination from reality
papers.abstract: Asks how the brain keeps vivid imagery apart from real perception. Using fMRI while people imagined or perceived faint visual patterns, the authors found that a single region of fusiform cortex tracks how strong the sensory signal is, and that the strength of this signal predicts the reality judgment. Frontal regions then read out this signal, suggesting a shared perception-imagery pathway with a downstream reality-monitoring computation.
papers.authors: Nadine Dijkstra, Thomas von Rein, Peter Kok, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: Sensory horizons and the functions of conscious vision
papers.abstract: Argues that conscious vision is too slow to guide immediate actions and instead evolved to support offline, model-based planning once animals moved onto land and gained longer sensory horizons. The authors link this to reality monitoring, the ability to tell external signals from internally generated ones. They derive predictions for comparative work on which species should have conscious vision.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Fleming, Matthias Michel

papers.title: Distorted learning from local metacognition supports transdiagnostic underconfidence
papers.abstract: Anxious and depressed individuals tend to be persistently underconfident, which is puzzling because performance feedback should let them calibrate. In two large general-population samples, the authors measured both local, trial-level confidence and global self-beliefs. Underconfidence was explained by distorted learning of global confidence from local metacognitive signals rather than by impaired local metacognition itself.
papers.authors: Sucharit Katyal, Quentin J. M. Huys, Raymond J. Dolan, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: The influence of mental state attributions on trust in large language models
papers.abstract: People often attribute experiences such as emotions and consciousness to LLMs, and these folk-psychological attributions differ from views of an AI's intelligence. Across experiments, the authors tested whether such mental state attributions change how much users trust and follow an LLM's advice. Attributing mental states shaped trust beyond attributions of intelligence, linking beliefs about AI minds to reliance on it.
papers.authors: Clara Colombatto, Jonathan Birch, Stephen M. Fleming

papers.title: Metacognition and Confidence: A Review and Synthesis
papers.abstract: A single-author review that proposes a road map linking neuroscience of uncertainty in sensory and motor systems with personal-level metacognitive beliefs about one's own performance. It focuses on propositional confidence computations and lays out how they might be modelled and implemented in the brain. It also covers how confidence is learned and how it relates to psychiatric symptoms.
papers.authors: Stephen M. Fleming

E251.name: Jan Drugowitsch
E251.bio: Jan Drugowitsch is an Associate Professor of Neurobiology at Harvard Medical School who investigates the mathematical and biological foundations of neural computation and decision-making. Their laboratory employs machine learning, statistical physics, and normative modeling to study how the nervous system represents and processes information in the presence of environmental uncertainty. Drugowitsch’s research has addressed the mechanisms of near-optimal speed-accuracy trade-offs and the hierarchical parsing of visual motion. They are currently working to generalize these computational theories to multi-timescale structure inference and value-sensitive foraging behavior.
E251.research_direction: Dr. Drugowitsch has recently been developing mathematical theories of how the brain infers hidden causes from noisy sensory signals and uses that information to decide and navigate. Their recent work explores how the visual system breaks a complex moving scene into nested components, such as object motion versus self-motion, and how humans and monkeys make that attribution while steering. They also study how populations of neurons, including ring attractor circuits and hippocampal place cells, can represent uncertainty and why varied receptive field sizes help. In addition, they argue that difficult real-world decisions are limited more by retrieving memories and computing values than by neural noise.

papers.title: Hierarchical Vector Analysis of Visual Motion Perception
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes a body of theoretical and behavioral work on how the visual system parses complex, layered motion scenes into simpler, meaningful components—a problem the authors term motion parsing. They present a hierarchical vector-analysis framework in which observers infer a small number of motion 'vectors' organized hierarchically (e.g., object motion nested within scene-level or observer-level motion) via approximate online Bayesian inference, rather than estimating a single global flow field. The review discusses psychophysical evidence that human motion perception exhibits signatures of this hierarchical decomposition, including biases and illusions that are naturally explained when motion is inferred relative to a structured hierarchy of reference frames, and outlines how this framework unifies previously disparate phenomena in motion perception under a common computational account.
papers.authors: Samuel J. Gershman, Johannes Bill, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: A unifying theory of receptive field heterogeneity predicts hippocampal spatial tuning
papers.abstract: Neural populations encoding continuous variables, such as hippocampal place cells encoding allocentric position, typically show substantial heterogeneity in receptive field size and shape rather than uniform tuning. This paper develops a normative, information-theoretic framework that unifies and extends prior theories of receptive field heterogeneity, showing analytically that heterogeneity in receptive field properties generally increases the Fisher information (and thus decoding precision) carried by a population's activity. For populations encoding multi-dimensional variables, such as 2D spatial position, the theory predicts that heterogeneity in both receptive field size and shape (not size alone) is required to yield an information gain over a homogeneous population. Applying this framework to recorded hippocampal place-cell data, the authors find that empirical place fields exhibit strong size and shape heterogeneity consistent with the theory's normative predictions, suggesting that hippocampal spatial coding is shaped by pressure to maximize information through diverse receptive field geometry.
papers.authors: Zoe Cohen, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: Major sources of computational complexity in complex decision-making
papers.abstract: This perspective challenges the widespread assumption in systems neuroscience that neuronal noise is the primary bottleneck limiting decision-making performance. The authors argue that for the kinds of complex, real-world decisions supported by large vertebrate memories, the dominant computational bottlenecks are instead algorithmic: retrieving relevant information from memory and computing the values of candidate choice options. They contend that even a perfectly noiseless neural circuit would face substantial computational complexity in searching large memory stores or propagating value estimates through large Bayesian or associative networks, and that these algorithmic costs—rather than noise averaging—are likely the major rate-limiting steps in complex, naturalistic decision-making, calling for decision-making theories that explicitly model memory search and value computation as computational resources.
papers.authors: Jan Drugowitsch, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Causal inference during closed-loop navigation: parsing of self- and object-motion
papers.abstract: Building internal models of a dynamic environment requires the brain to correctly attribute retinal motion to its underlying causes—self-motion, object motion, or both—a form of Bayesian causal inference. This study examines how humans and monkeys perform this attribution during closed-loop navigation, in which the observer actively steers through a virtual environment containing a independently moving object, so that retinal flow reflects a mixture of self-generated and object-generated motion that must be disambiguated online. Using a combination of psychophysical steering tasks and computational modeling, the authors show that behavior during closed-loop navigation is well described by a causal-inference model that dynamically infers whether observed retinal motion arises from self-motion, object-motion, or both, and that this inference process shapes online steering corrections, extending causal-inference accounts of multisensory perception to the closed-loop, active-navigation setting.
papers.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Johannes Bill, Haoran Ding, Jacob Vastola, Gregory C. DeAngelis, Dora Angelaki, Jan Drugowitsch

papers.title: Bayesian inference in ring attractor networks
papers.abstract: Ring attractor networks are a canonical circuit motif thought to maintain continuous variables such as head direction in working memory, but conventional ring attractor models do not represent the uncertainty associated with the stored estimate, limiting their ability to appropriately weight new sensory evidence against existing memory. The authors develop a normative benchmark—a circular Kalman filter—for how a ring attractor network should combine prior belief and incoming evidence about a circular variable while tracking uncertainty, and then show that the recurrent connectivity of a conventional ring attractor can be retuned so that its dynamics approximate this Bayesian benchmark. Applying the model to the fly head-direction system, the authors demonstrate that a retuned ring attractor can implement near-optimal Bayesian updating of a circular estimate, providing a mechanistic account of how uncertainty-sensitive inference could be realized in biological ring attractor circuits.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Anna Kutschireiter, Melanie A. Basnak, Rachel I. Wilson, Jan Drugowitsch

E252.name: Roozbeh Kiani
E252.department: Center for Neural Science; Department of Psychology
E252.bio: Roozbeh Kiani investigates the neurobiological principles governing decision-making, focusing on how the brain integrates sensory evidence to guide commitment to an action. Kiani’s laboratory employs large-scale neural recordings, causal perturbations, and computational modeling to identify the circuit-level dynamics within the frontoparietal network that support choice selection and decision confidence. Their research includes characterizing the neural signatures of choice certainty, the mechanisms underlying 'changes of mind,' and the development of internal models for flexible behavior. Kiani’s current research explores how multiscale integration processes interact across brain regions to adaptively regulate strategies in complex environments.
E252.research_direction: Dr. Kiani's recent work explores the distributed neural mechanisms underlying flexible perceptual decision-making, combining computational modeling with single-neuron and population recordings in both non-human primates and humans. They have recently been investigating how evidence accumulation is represented outside classical decision-making circuits, probing how high-level ventral stream regions like the anterior inferotemporal cortex integrate task-relevant evidence during categorization tasks. Their research also examines how sensory choices adapt to shifting rules and rewards, analyzing population geometry in the monkey prefrontal cortex during learning and recording from the human basal ganglia-thalamic circuit to understand how perceptual decisions and confidence are dynamically bound to motor actions. Additionally, they are developing new analytical approaches to determine how the complex, non-linear spiking statistics of individual neurons reflect the connectivity and goal-directed functions of the broader neural networks in which they reside.

papers.title: The geometry of context-dependent biased decisions during learning
papers.abstract: Large populations of lateral prefrontal neurons were recorded as monkeys learned a direction-discrimination task in which reward contingencies flipped between left and right. Reward context was encoded as shifts in the geometry of curvilinear decision manifolds along the decision-variable axis, so a fixed linear readout yields context-dependent biases. Across learning, transitions between manifolds became faster, paralleling one-trial behavioral generalization, and recurrent networks reproduced the behavior and geometry.
papers.authors: Ramon Nogueira, Saleh Esteki, Stefano Fusi, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: Hierarchical binding of cognition to action in the human basal ganglia-thalamic circuit
papers.abstract: Single-neuron recordings were made across the human pallidothalamic circuit (GPe, GPi, STN, motor thalamus) during perceptual decisions reported with confidence-weighted reaching. Choice and confidence were encoded before, during and after movement, with dynamic upstream codes becoming stable and low-dimensional in motor thalamus. Motor thalamus also combined confidence and outcome into a signal resembling unsigned reward prediction error, recasting the circuit as an interface binding decision, action and evaluation.
papers.authors: Dennis London, Morgane Soula, L. Pan, Michael Pourfar, Alon Mogilner, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: Anterior inferotemporal cortex represents decision formation and termination without ramps
papers.abstract: Recording from anterior inferotemporal cortex (TEa) in macaques doing face categorization, the authors find that neurons carry an accumulated decision variable as a running average of task-relevant evidence rather than a ramping signal. This code boosts category signal-to-noise, allows flexible weighting of relevant features, and loses sensitivity to new evidence once a choice is made. Its timing matches or slightly precedes simultaneously recorded LIP, arguing against feedback inheritance, and a simple subunit model reproduces it. The work recasts ventral visual cortex as a decision-aware hub.
papers.authors: Gouki Okazawa, Roozbeh Kiani

papers.title: Spiking dynamics of individual neurons reflect changes in the structure and function of neuronal networks
papers.abstract: Using multifractal analysis of interspike intervals, the study characterizes the non-linear, non-stationary spiking of single neurons and shows this signature is sensitive to network connectivity yet fairly stable across stimuli and unaffected by unobserved ensembles. Spiking networks trained on different goal-directed tasks could be told apart with the same measure, linking single-neuron firing statistics to network structure and function.
papers.authors: Ruochen Yang, Heng Ping, Xiongye Xiao, Roozbeh Kiani, Paul Bogdan

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms That Make Perceptual Decisions Flexible
papers.abstract: This review surveys how the brain adjusts perceptual decision processes to changing rules, goals and contexts, drawing on evidence for context-dependent activity in parietal, sensory, motor, subcortical and prefrontal regions. The authors argue that flexibility arises from a distributed network and outline experimental and theoretical directions for studying it.
papers.authors: Gouki Okazawa, Roozbeh Kiani

E253.name: Valentin Wyart
E253.bio: Valentin Wyart is an Inserm Research Director at the École Normale Supérieure, where they lead the Cognitive Variability research group within the Laboratoire de Neurosciences Cognitives (LNC2). Wyart’s research examines the computational and neural mechanisms of human learning and decision-making under conditions of environmental uncertainty and volatility. By integrating Bayesian behavioral modeling with multimodal functional neuroimaging techniques such as MEG and fMRI, Wyart investigates the origins and functional implications of internal computation noise. Their work addresses how limited computational precision contributes to human cognitive variability and characterizes its potential adaptive benefits for stabilizing statistical inference.
E253.research_direction: Dr. Wyart has recently been investigating the computational and neurobiological mechanisms underlying human decision-making, learning, and inference under uncertainty. Their recent work explores how sensory evidence integration interacts with higher-level rule discovery during temporal prediction, frequently leveraging artificial neural networks to examine how computational noise might functionally help cognitive systems adapt to novel environments. They are also studying the distinct cognitive pressures that drive human exploration by designing behavioral tasks that isolate exploratory behavior from standard explore-exploit dilemmas. Additionally, Dr. Wyart is examining how specific biological and psychiatric factors influence reinforcement learning, using computational modeling to untangle whether pharmacological interventions like dopamine or clinical traits like compulsivity primarily alter the underlying value-updating process or the variability of subsequent choices.

papers.title: Sensory integration, temporal prediction, and rule discovery reflect interdependent inference processes
papers.abstract: Humans were shown rhythmic sequences of ten stimuli, some governed by a hidden rule that shifts the stimulus statistics after the fifth item, and had to predict the tenth from partial sequences. How long a person integrates sensory evidence predicted how quickly they found the rule, and finding the rule in turn changed how they integrated evidence. Disrupting rhythm hurt rule discovery but not integration accuracy, and recurrent neural networks trained on the task and selectively perturbed reproduced these specific dependencies.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Lucas Benjamin, Benjamin Morillon, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Competing cognitive pressures on human exploration in the absence of trade-off with exploitation
papers.abstract: The authors designed a sequential sampling task in which exploration can be studied both with and without an explicit explore-exploit trade-off. Model-based analyses of behaviour showed that people's exploration is shaped by competing pressures, rather than by the trade-off alone. This separates the behavioural signatures of exploration from those of the reward-maximisation dilemma with which they are usually confounded.
papers.authors: Clemence Almeras, Valerian Chambon, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Compulsivity is linked to suboptimal choice variability but unaltered reinforcement learning under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Compulsivity has been tied to variable behaviour under uncertainty, but that variability can come from stochastic choice selection or from noise in value updating. Using a model that separates these two sources across two independent datasets, the authors find that higher compulsivity is associated with increased suboptimal choice variability, while reinforcement learning itself is unaltered. This reframes compulsive behaviour as a choice-stage rather than a learning-stage difference.
papers.authors: Junseok K. Lee, Marion Rouault, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Dopamine drives a positive reward bias on human reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, healthy volunteers given the dopamine precursor L-DOPA performed a volatile two-armed bandit task. L-DOPA reduced switching after below-average rewards, and reinforcement learning models indicated changes to both learning rate and learning precision. Using recurrent neural networks as implementational models, the authors explain both effects through one mechanism, a positive reward bias at the input of the recurrent layer.
papers.authors: Arnaud Zalta, Vasilisa Skvortsova, Samuel R. C. Hewitt, Michael Moutoussis, Matthew M. Nour, Raymond J. Dolan, Charles Findling, Tobias U. Hauser, Valentin Wyart

papers.title: Computation noise promotes zero-shot adaptation to uncertainty during decision-making in artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Noise in information processing is usually viewed as harmful, yet humans adapt well to uncertain conditions despite noisy neural activity. The authors show that moderate computation noise in artificial neural networks enables zero-shot generalisation to new uncertain decision problems. Noise-free networks fail to do this, whereas noisy networks behave like human participants tested in the same conditions, suggesting a functional role for computation noise.
papers.authors: Charles Findling, Valentin Wyart

E254.name: Tobias H. Donner
E254.bio: Tobias H. Donner is a Professor of Integrative Neuroscience and Director of the Department of Neurophysiology and Pathophysiology at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf. Donner’s research explores the neural basis of perceptual decision-making, specifically investigating how sensory evidence is accumulated and transformed into actions through large-scale cortical interactions. Using neuroimaging techniques such as MEG, EEG, and high-field fMRI, Donner characterizes the role of neuromodulatory systems, including the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine system, in regulating brain states and decision biases. Their work identifies how internal factors like arousal and choice history modulate neural circuit activity to support adaptive behavior in uncertain environments.
E254.research_direction: Dr. Donner has recently been investigating the large-scale cortical dynamics and neuromodulatory mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making and belief updating. Using source-level MEG and computational modeling, their recent work explores how sensory evidence is accumulated and read out across distributed cortical networks to form subjective confidence, track hidden behavioral rules, and drive confirmation bias. They are also probing the role of catecholaminergic arousal in shaping these computations, specifically testing how pharmacological interventions alter choice history biases during perceptual tasks. Furthermore, Dr. Donner is extending these approaches to clinical populations by mapping how intrinsic cortical dynamics are altered in early-stage psychosis, aiming to link large-scale network disruptions with underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor profiles.

papers.title: Cortex-wide Dynamics of Internal Decisions About Behavioral Context
