papers.abstract: The paper studies decisions that select a rule rather than an action: participants tracked a hidden, unpredictably switching stimulus-response mapping by accumulating ambiguous cues. Model-based decoding of source-level MEG revealed belief about the active rule in many cortical areas, including occipital cortex, with profiles matching normative predictions and those seen in frontal action areas during overt decisions. This suggests a widely distributed network implements evidence accumulation for internal decisions.
papers.authors: Joshua Calder-Travis, Ruud L. van den Brink, Saanchi Thawani, Lars Schwabe, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Confirmation bias through selective readout of information encoded in human parietal cortex
papers.abstract: The authors asked whether confirmation bias arises from distorted encoding of new evidence or from how encoded evidence is used. Participants estimated the source of a stream of visual-spatial samples while MEG tracked cortical activity, with a mid-stream category judgment. Evidence in parietal cortex was encoded accurately even when it contradicted the earlier choice, but it contributed less to the final report, indicating that belief-inconsistent information is selectively under-read rather than under-encoded.
papers.authors: Hame Park, Ayelet Arazi, Bharath Chandra Talluri, Marco Celotto, Stefano Panzeri, Alan A. Stocker, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Catecholamines reduce choice history biases in perceptual decision making
papers.abstract: The study tests causally whether the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor atomoxetine changes the influence of past choices on perceptual decisions. Choice history biases were idiosyncratic (repetition in some people, alternation in others), and atomoxetine reduced both kinds. Modeling attributed the reduction to a weaker bias in evidence accumulation rather than in the starting point, and the effect related to pupil-linked arousal.
papers.authors: Jan Willem de Gee, Niels A. Kloosterman, Anke Braun, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Multi-area Decision Dynamics Across Human Cortex Shape Confidence
papers.abstract: Using source-level MEG while people made difficult decisions, the authors tracked choice-selective signals across many cortical areas at once. Premotor cortex showed competition between signals favoring the chosen and the alternative option, each contributing oppositely to confidence. In addition, the number and strength of associative-area signals supporting the chosen option contributed further, suggesting confidence reflects consensus across distributed local decision modules.
papers.authors: Alessandro Toso, Ayelet Arazi, Jaime de la Rocha, Konstantinos Tsetsos, Tobias H. Donner

papers.title: Large-scale maps of altered cortical dynamics in early-stage psychosis are related to GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission
papers.abstract: MEG source imaging was used to map psychosis-related changes in intrinsic cortical population dynamics in first-episode and clinical-high-risk individuals. The cortex-wide alteration patterns followed the anatomical hierarchy and resembled maps of GABA-A receptor density and of pharmacological GABA-A and NMDA effects in healthy people. Individual-patient similarity to GABA-A effects tracked positive symptoms and similarity to NMDA effects tracked negative symptoms.
papers.authors: Ayelet Arazi, Alessandro Toso, Tineke Grent-'t-Jong, Peter J. Uhlhaas, Tobias H. Donner

E255.name: Anne E. Urai
E255.bio: Anne E. Urai is an Assistant Professor at Leiden University who researches the neural mechanisms underlying perceptual decision-making and choice history biases. Utilizing a cross-species approach, their work integrates psychophysics and computational modeling with high-density electrophysiological recordings in both humans and rodents. Urai investigates how trial-by-trial variability and internal states, such as decision uncertainty and pupil-linked arousal, influence the process of evidence accumulation. They are a founding member of the International Brain Laboratory and have expanded their research into the cognitive foundations of social tipping points and climate action.
E255.research_direction: Dr. Urai has recently been investigating the computational and neural mechanisms that drive trial-to-trial variability in perceptual decision-making. Using standardized visual tasks across species, their recent work explores how choices are continuously shaped by internal states, such as choice history biases, fluctuations in pupil-linked arousal, and the physiological impacts of aging. To uncover the structured, temporal nature of this behavioral noise, they employ latent-state analyses, diffusion decision models, and large-scale electrophysiology to map how dynamic brain states and past experiences alter the evidence accumulation process. Beyond their core cognitive neuroscience research, Dr. Urai is also examining the intersection of academic practice and the climate crisis, proposing new frameworks for how universities and scientists can reshape institutional norms to drive environmental action.

papers.title: Age-related changes in behavioural and neural variability in a decision-making task
papers.abstract: The authors recorded from more than 18,000 neurons across 16 brain regions in younger and older mice performing the International Brain Laboratory visual decision task. Older mice had more variable response times, as is seen in human ageing. Ageing raised firing rates and post-stimulus neural variability and weakened the drop in variability at stimulus onset, most strongly in visual and motor cortex, striatum and thalamus, giving a region-specific account of age-related decline.
papers.authors: Fenying Zang, Anup Khanal, Sonja Förster, International Brain Laboratory, Anne K. Churchland, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Structure uncovered: understanding temporal variability in perceptual decision-making
papers.abstract: This review argues that trial-to-trial variability in perceptual decisions is not just noise but has temporal structure, unfolding over several timescales. It brings together evidence from humans and animals on history biases, fluctuations in engagement and arousal, and latent-state models, and outlines how such structure should be modelled and linked to neural mechanisms.
papers.authors: Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Choice history biases evidence accumulation: a cross-species comparison from humans to mice
papers.abstract: The study fits diffusion decision models to choices from 62 mice doing the standardized IBL task to test whether the human finding of history-biased evidence accumulation carries over to mice. Individual differences in choice repetition were explained by a bias in the drift rate, not the starting point, matching the human result and suggesting a shared cross-species strategy.
papers.authors: Kianté Fernandez, Alexander Fengler, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: A dynamical systems model of arousal-driven behavioural state transitions
papers.abstract: Using a hidden Markov model of response times, the authors label mice as engaged or disengaged in a visual decision task and show that intermediate baseline pupil size goes with engagement. Changes in the mean and variability of pupil-linked arousal predict state switches, which they explain with a double-well attractor model in which arousal reshapes the landscape of population activity.
papers.authors: Philippa A. Johnson, Sander Nieuwenhuis, Jorge Mejías, Anne E. Urai

papers.title: Rethinking academia in a time of climate crisis
papers.abstract: Drawing on the Doughnut Economics framework, the authors argue that universities are well placed to lead climate action but mostly do not, while scientists are hampered by bureaucracy and hypercompetition. They propose seven principles for reshaping scientific norms and a call to action for academics.
papers.authors: Anne E. Urai, Clare Kelly

E259.name: Alexandre Pouget
E259.bio: Alexandre Pouget is a computational neuroscientist who researches how neural circuits represent and compute with probability distributions. Pouget's research introduced the concept of probabilistic population codes, demonstrating how neurons can implement Bayesian inference to handle uncertainty in tasks such as multisensory integration and perceptual decision-making. Pouget co-founded the International Brain Laboratory and the COSYNE conference to facilitate large-scale collaborations mapping brain-wide activity. Currently, their work explores the neural basis of compositional thinking and general intelligence, aiming to link low-level neural representations and high-level cognitive reasoning.
E259.research_direction: Dr. Pouget has recently been investigating the computational principles underlying flexible cognition, with a major focus on how neural networks leverage compositional representations to generalize to novel situations. Their recent work explores this by combining recurrent neural networks, language models, and Bayesian inference to model how the brain might translate linguistic instructions into new sensorimotor rules or rapidly infer tasks from reusable computational modules. In parallel, they are examining the neural architecture of perceptual decision-making, utilizing brain-wide Neuropixels recordings in mice to map how and where prior expectations about upcoming stimuli are distributed across sensory and frontal regions. Additionally, Dr. Pouget is investigating multi-timescale reinforcement learning, recording from dopamine populations to test whether the mammalian brain tracks delayed rewards using a heterogeneous spectrum of discount factors.

papers.title: The compositionality continuum as a principle for studying the neural basis of intelligence
papers.abstract: This perspective argues that compositionality should be seen as a graded continuum rather than a binary property of cognition and neural computation. The authors review how neural circuits and artificial networks can build flexible behavior from reusable components, and propose the continuum as a guiding principle for linking low-level neural representations to high-level reasoning. They outline experimental and modelling directions that follow from this view.
papers.authors: Reidar Riveland, Alexandre Pouget, Laura Driscoll

papers.title: Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making
papers.abstract: Using Neuropixels recordings from the International Brain Laboratory's brain-wide dataset, the study asks where in the mouse brain the animal's expectation about upcoming stimulus side is represented. Prior information is found to be encoded widely across the brain, including in sensory areas, not only in frontal or decision-related regions. The result challenges purely hierarchical views of Bayesian inference and supports a distributed view of how priors shape perception and choice.
papers.authors: Charles Findling, Felix Hubert, International Brain Laboratory, Luigi Acerbi, Brandon Benson, Julius Benson, Daniel Birman, Niccolo Bonacchi, E. Kelly Buchanan, Sebastian Bruijns, Matteo Carandini, Joana A. Catarino, Gaelle A. Chapuis, Anne K. Churchland, Yang Dan, Felicia Davatolhagh, Eric E. J. DeWitt, Tatiana A. Engel, Michele Fabbri, Mayo A. Faulkner, Ila Rani Fiete, et al., Anthony Zador, Yizi Zhang, Peter Dayan, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Multi-timescale reinforcement learning in the brain
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether dopamine neurons collectively represent rewards with a spectrum of discount timescales, as predicted by multi-timescale (distributional-in-time) reinforcement learning. Recordings from mouse dopamine neurons during tasks with varying reward delays show neuron-to-neuron variation in discounting that matches the theory. This heterogeneity lets the brain estimate reward timing and adapt learning to task structure, offering a richer account than a single discount factor.
papers.authors: Paul Masset, Pablo Tano, HyungGoo R. Kim, Athar N. Malik, Pierre Bech, Alexandre Pouget, Naoshige Uchida

papers.title: Compositional meta-learning through probabilistic task inference
papers.abstract: The paper proposes a meta-learning framework in which tasks are represented as structured combinations of reusable computational modules. Learning a new task then becomes probabilistic inference over which modules to combine rather than gradient-based parameter updates. In rule-learning and motor-learning settings the model recovers the underlying components and can learn a new task from a single example, combining neural-network expressivity with the data efficiency of Bayesian inference.
papers.authors: Jacob J. W. Bakermans, Pablo Tano, Reidar Riveland, Charles Findling, Alexandre Pouget

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.abstract: The authors build a recurrent neural network model in which a pretrained language model encodes written task instructions, and show it can then carry out sensorimotor tasks it has never been trained on. The resulting network reveals structured, compositional representations across tasks, and the model can also produce a linguistic description of a task it has learned so another network can perform it. The work also yields testable predictions about how the human brain might link language and motor rule-following.
papers.authors: Reidar Riveland, Alexandre Pouget

E260.name: Christopher Summerfield
E260.bio: Christopher Summerfield is a Professor of Cognitive Neuroscience at the University of Oxford and a Research Director at the UK AI Safety Institute. Summerfield's research investigates the computational principles and neural mechanisms that govern human learning, perception, and decision-making by drawing parallels between biological cognition and artificial intelligence. By combining behavioral testing, functional neuroimaging, and deep neural network modeling, they study how humans acquire structured knowledge and navigate complex environments. Summerfield’s work examines how the brain represents tasks and categories, alongside the use of AI as both a model for and an assistant to human cognition.
E260.research_direction: Dr. Summerfield has recently been investigating the intersection of human cognition and artificial intelligence, focusing on learning dynamics, neural representations, and the societal impact of large language models. Their recent work explores how both humans and artificial neural networks handle continual rule learning and varied data distributions, specifically examining phenomena like catastrophic interference, transfer, and the balance between in-context generalization and memory recall. In parallel cognitive neuroscience studies, they are using fMRI to probe how distinct brain regions, such as the hippocampus and visual cortex, support symbolic compositional generalization when humans combine elementary visual attributes to make novel spatial inferences. Furthermore, their research evaluates how conversational AI interacts with human beliefs at scale, investigating the computational strategies that drive political persuasion as well as whether AI mediators can successfully facilitate consensus-building among individuals with divergent viewpoints.

papers.title: Distinct roles of hippocampus and neocortex in symbolic compositional generalization
papers.abstract: Participants combined a shape and a colour to make a novel spatial inference while undergoing fMRI. The hippocampus represented elementary visual attributes in a high-dimensional, parallel format that allows flexible individuation of items. In vmPFC, parietal cortex and V1, activity for novel composites was predictable as a linear combination of activity for familiar elements, with vmPFC doing so in a high-dimensional format and PPC/V1 in a low-dimensional, response-aligned frame.
papers.authors: Zilu Liang, Leonie Glitz, Matthias Nau, Michelle B. Hefner, Denis C.L. Lan, Miriam C. Klein-Flugge, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: The levers of political persuasion with conversational artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Roughly 77,000 UK participants held conversations with 19 different language models on hundreds of political issues, letting the authors test what actually drives AI persuasion. Post-training and prompting strategies that encourage information-dense arguments boosted persuasiveness far more than sheer model scale or personalisation. The same techniques that made models more persuasive also made them less accurate, raising concerns about the trade-off between influence and truthfulness.
papers.authors: Kobi Hackenburg, Ben M. Tappin, Luke Hewitt, Ed Saunders, Sid Black, Hause Lin, Catherine Fist, Helen Margetts, David G. Rand, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: Humans and neural networks show similar patterns of transfer and interference during continual learning
papers.abstract: People and neural networks learned sequential rule-based tasks in an A-B-A design. Both benefited more from prior knowledge when tasks were similar but also suffered more interference when retested on the first task, contradicting the idea that humans escape catastrophic interference. Humans split into 'lumpers' (more transfer, more interference) and 'splitters' (the reverse), mirroring networks trained in rich versus lazy regimes.
papers.authors: Eleanor Holton, Lukas Braun, Jessica A. F. Thompson, Jan Grohn, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: Shared sensitivity to data distribution during learning in humans and transformer networks
papers.abstract: Humans (n=530) and transformer networks were trained on a rule-learning task with manipulated diversity and redundancy of training examples, then tested for in-context generalisation and in-weights recall. In both learners, diversity favours in-context learning while redundancy favours in-weights memory, and a balanced mix supports both. Unlike transformers, humans additionally benefit from curricula that place diverse examples early.
papers.authors: Jacques Pesnot Lerousseau, Christopher Summerfield

papers.title: AI can help humans find common ground in democratic deliberation
papers.abstract: The authors trained a language-model 'mediator' that writes group statements from participants' differing opinions on contested issues. In experiments with thousands of UK participants, these AI-generated statements were preferred over those written by human mediators and drew broader endorsement across viewpoints. The work suggests AI can support consensus-building in deliberative settings.
papers.authors: Michael Henry Tessler, Michiel A. Bakker, Daniel Jarrett, Hannah Sheahan, Martin J. Chadwick, Raphael Koster, Georgina Evans, Lucy Campbell-Gillingham, Tantum Collins, David C. Parkes, Matthew Botvinick, Christopher Summerfield

E262.name: Timothy D. Hanks
E262.department: Department of Neurology, Center for Neuroscience
E262.bio: Timothy D. Hanks investigates the neural substrates of decision-making and executive function using behavioral, computational, and physiological approaches. Their research employs high-throughput automated training in rodents and comparative studies in non-human primates to dissect circuit-level computations involved in evidence accumulation and commitment. Utilizing tools such as optogenetics and high-density neural recordings, Hanks characterizes the dynamical structure of corticostriatal and parietal circuits to study how the brain evaluates sensory information and tracks elapsed time. This research aims to establish principles of neural computation to inform future treatments for neuropsychiatric and neurological disorders.
E262.research_direction: Dr. Hanks has recently been studying how the brain turns a stream of sensory evidence into a timed decision. Their recent work explores how populations of neurons in the rat frontal orienting field, anterior striatum, and posterior parietal cortex evaluate evidence, keep track of elapsed time, and commit to a choice. Using large-scale Neuropixels recordings while rats detect changes in an auditory stimulus, they ask how these circuits share the work and how the window over which evidence is weighed adapts when the environment changes over time.

papers.title: Population-level temporal decoding and dynamical structure in frontostriatal circuits during decision making
papers.abstract: Perceptual decisions unfold across time, requiring distributed neural networks to evaluate sensory evidence, maintain an internal representation of elapsed time, and commit to an action. To determine how these computational operations are distributed across corticostriatal nodes, large-scale neural population activity was recorded using Neuropixels probes in the rat frontal orienting field (FOF) and anterior dorsal striatum (ADS) during a free-response auditory change-detection paradigm. Both brain regions exhibited low-dimensional, highly dynamic population trajectories during task execution. Single-trial decoding revealed that FOF and ADS populations robustly track both retrospective time elapsed from stimulus onset and prospective time preceding decision report. A dynamical motif decomposition of the temporal decoding space demonstrated two primary population modes: monotonic ramping trajectories and transient bump-like patterns. While both motifs were similarly engaged during the initial evidence evaluation epoch across both areas, FOF manifested pronounced movement-aligned state transitions near decision report. Population geometry analyses confirmed that stable low-dimensional subspaces present during evidence deliberation undergo reconfiguration at commitment, with substantially greater subspace restructuring observed in FOF than ADS, identifying specialized frontal cortical reorganization at decision commitment within a shared frontostriatal dynamical architecture.
papers.authors: Adam B. Goldring, Anandita De, Tanner Stevenson, Kendall Stewart, Aya Akhmetzhanova, Rishidev Chaudhuri, Timothy D. Hanks

papers.title: Time-adaptive modulation of evidence evaluation in rat posterior parietal cortex
papers.abstract: Effective perceptual decision making demands dynamic calibration of the temporal window over which sensory evidence is integrated, as transient changes in non-stationary environments favor recency-weighted evaluation rather than lossless linear accumulation. Spiking activity was recorded using Neuropixels probes in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of rats performing a free-response auditory change detection task requiring short-timescale evidence evaluation. PPC neurons exhibited evidence-dependent firing rate modulation, choice selectivity, and functionally opponent subpopulations displaying positive versus negative rate modulations. In sharp contrast to tasks involving persistent second-long temporal integration, PPC single units displayed transient responses to discrete evidence pulses, with impact decaying over a timeframe directly corresponding to behavioral evaluation timescales. Additionally, PPC demonstrated time-dependent gain modulations in evidence sensitivity that paralleled behavioral urgency shifts. Targeted reversible inactivation established that PPC causally influences auditory change detection, altering choice accuracy and shifting the temporal window of sensory integration. These results demonstrate that PPC adaptively tailors evidence evaluation timescales and response gains to meet task-specific temporal demands.
papers.authors: Preetham Ganupuru, Adam B. Goldring, Tanner Stevenson, Kendall Stewart, Rishidev Chaudhuri, Timothy D. Hanks

E263.name: Marius Usher
E263.bio: Marius Usher is a Professor in the School of Psychological Sciences at Tel Aviv University, where they investigate the computational and neural mechanisms of human decision-making and visual perception. Their research includes the development of the Leaky Competing Accumulator (LCA) model, a framework for how the brain integrates noisy evidence to reach categorical choices. Usher’s work connects cognitive neuroscience and philosophy of mind, specifically exploring preference formation, phenomenal consciousness, and the role of attention in perceptual experience. By combining psychophysical experimentation with computational modeling, Usher investigates the algorithmic basis of rationality, memory, and agency.
E263.research_direction: Dr. Usher’s recent work explores the cognitive and perceptual dynamics underlying preferential decision-making and conscious visual experience. They have recently been investigating the computational strategies people use in complex, multi-attribute choices, combining behavioral data with formal modeling to test whether individuals rely on holistic evaluations, within-attribute comparisons, or fast probabilistic heuristics. To capture the real-time mechanisms of these decisions, their research extends drift-diffusion models to account for value certainty and utilizes eye-tracking to examine how information variability and accessibility guide gaze allocation. Additionally, their work extends into visual affect, using Garner-style interference paradigms with faces and scenes to ask whether the emotional pleasantness of a stimulus and low-level perceptual features like brightness are processed as integrated dimensions.

papers.title: Within-Alternative Processing Supports Transitivity of Preferences in Multiattribute Choice
papers.abstract: People often violate transitivity when choosing among multi-attribute options, which has been taken as evidence for within-attribute comparison heuristics. The authors compare within-attribute and within-alternative processing accounts using formal tests of transitivity and modelling. They find that choices are best explained by integrating attributes within each alternative, which supports transitive preferences, and that apparent violations arise from noise and context rather than intransitive rules.
papers.authors: Gilad Pessach, Konstantinos Tsetsos, Michel Regenwetter, Marius Usher

papers.title: Contrasting holistic-compensatory with probabilistic heuristic strategies in multi-attribute decisions
papers.abstract: Recent work disputes the idea that people under time pressure rely on simple heuristics such as Take the Best. The authors test a probabilistic extension of Take the Best, in which each attribute is sampled by importance, against holistic compensatory integration. Behavioural data and model comparison are used to see which strategy better describes fast multi-attribute choice.
papers.authors: Gal Atun, Vincent de Gardelle, Marius Usher

papers.title: Variability and Accessibility of Information Guide Gaze Dynamics in Decision Making
papers.abstract: Using eye tracking in multi-option choice tasks where attribute information was revealed selectively, the study asks how people decide where to look. Gaze was guided by how variable and how accessible each piece of information was, not simply by value. The authors argue that attention allocation and choice form a coupled dynamic process that models of decision making need to capture.
papers.authors: Douglas G. Lee, Konstantinos Tsetsos, Giovanni Pezzulo, Nitzan Shahar, Marius Usher

papers.title: Valence in perception: Are affective valence and visual brightness integral dimensions in visual experience?
papers.abstract: The paper asks whether the pleasantness of a visual stimulus is processed separately from its perceptual properties or interacts with them. Using Garner-style interference and related paradigms with faces and scenes, the authors test whether affective valence and brightness are integral dimensions. The results bear on how emotion and perception are entangled in conscious visual experience.
papers.authors: Hilla Jacobson, Zohar Ongil, Daniel Algom, Marius Usher

papers.title: Value certainty in drift-diffusion models of preferential choice
papers.abstract: Standard drift-diffusion models of preference treat the value difference between options as the driver of choice, but people also differ in how certain they are about each option's value. This paper extends the model so that value certainty modulates the drift and shows that the extension explains choice, confidence and response-time patterns in preferential decisions that value alone cannot capture.
papers.authors: Douglas G. Lee, Marius Usher

E264.name: Floris P. de Lange
E264.department: Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour
E264.bio: Floris P. de Lange is a Professor of Perception and Cognition whose research examines how internal brain states, including prior expectations and attentional goals, shape visual perception and decision-making. De Lange utilizes the predictive coding framework, using high-resolution laminar fMRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG) to map the flow of top-down and bottom-up signals in the human cortex. Their methodologies combine psychophysical experiments with computational modeling to study how the brain functions as a predictive machine to encode sensory information. De Lange’s recent work focuses on the neural implementation of surprise and the mechanisms by which expectations facilitate or sharpen sensory representations.
E264.research_direction: Dr. de Lange has recently been investigating how predictive processing shapes perception, examining how scene context, learned regularities, and object knowledge modulate neural activity across the visual hierarchy. Their recent work explores the specific nature of prediction errors in early visual cortex, using human fMRI, large-scale mouse recordings, and deep neural networks to ask whether areas like V1 primarily flag low-level sensory mismatches or violations of abstract, higher-level features in natural scenes. Beyond spatial and contextual expectations, they are also probing how the brain anticipates temporal sequences. By tracking responses to learned visual series, their research examines whether the visual cortex and hippocampus utilize successor-like predictive maps to coordinate spatial and temporal expectations for future events.

papers.title: Higher-level spatial prediction in natural vision across mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: The study uses deep generative models to estimate how predictable image patches are from their spatial surroundings in natural images, and relates this to large-scale Allen Brain Observatory recordings in mouse visual cortex. More predictable patches evoke weaker responses, neurons in primary visual areas are mostly sensitive to predictability of higher-level features, the effect is strongest in superficial layers of V1, and it does not depend on recent experience, suggesting reliance on long-term priors.
papers.authors: Micha Heilbron, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: High-level visual prediction errors in early visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while people viewed expected and unexpected images, together with deep neural network features to separate low- from high-level image properties, the authors ask what kind of surprise early visual cortex signals. They find that prediction-error responses in V1-V3 track violations of high-level, abstract features rather than only local low-level mismatches. This challenges the view that early sensory prediction errors reflect purely low-level redundancy reduction.
papers.authors: David Richter, Tim C. Kietzmann, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Predictive processing of scenes and objects
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes evidence for how predictions derived from scene context, learned regularities and object knowledge shape perception of scenes and objects. It covers the neural mechanisms and behavioural consequences of such predictions across the visual hierarchy and points to open questions for the field.
papers.authors: Marius V. Peelen, Eva Berlot, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Successor-like representation guides the prediction of future events in human visual cortex and hippocampus
papers.abstract: After participants learned an arbitrary four-item visual sequence, fMRI showed that presenting a single item reactivated V1 patterns at the successor positions of the sequence but not the predecessor positions, in line with a successor representation. The hippocampus showed similar future-skewed activity and also encoded temporal distance in sequence space, whereas V1 tracked spatial distance in stimulus space. The results support predictive-map style coding in both visual cortex and hippocampus.
papers.authors: Matthias Ekman, Sarah Kusch, Floris P. de Lange

E266.name: Richard Aslin
E266.department: Child Study Center, Yale School of Medicine
E266.bio: Richard Aslin is a Senior Research Scientist and Clinical Professor at the Yale Child Study Center who researches infant language acquisition and visual perception. Aslin formalized the concept of statistical learning, demonstrating that infants extract structural regularities from environmental input through implicit exposure. Their current research employs a multimodal approach—incorporating eye-tracking, fNIRS, EEG, and fMRI—to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying infant attention and the computational constraints of developmental learning. A member of the National Academy of Sciences, Aslin studies how infants transition from processing raw sensory statistics to forming complex cognitive representations and categories.
E266.research_direction: Dr. Aslin has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of statistical learning across various stages of development. Their recent work explores how humans extract structural regularities from their environment, utilizing visual search paradigms to measure how long-term orthographic knowledge impacts reading skills and testing whether sequence learning transfers between auditory and visual modalities. They are also actively advancing the methodological toolkit for developmental neuroscience, evaluating the practical challenges of using non-invasive recording tools like fMRI and MEG in awake, behaving infants. Expanding beyond individual cognition, their research proposes using simultaneous caregiver-child neural hyperscanning to investigate how early social interactions and attentional disruptions shape the longitudinal development of working memory and executive function.

papers.title: Cross-Modal Transfer of Statistical Learning: Evidence from auditory and visual sequence learning
papers.abstract: Adults were exposed to spoken and written linguistic regularities in sequence, with transfer direction, exposure order and task demands manipulated. Learning transferred symmetrically across modalities in both recognition and recall, though recall showed more modality sensitivity, supporting a hybrid account with modality-general representations plus modality-specific retrieval constraints.
papers.authors: Claudia Ruzza, Erin Isbilen, Richard Aslin

papers.title: Statistical learning: A core mechanism in a developmental hierarchy
papers.abstract: Reviews three decades of work showing that humans and other animals extract structure from mere exposure to input, tracing its roots in psychology and linguistics and its later connection to computational and cognitive neuroscience. Argues that statistical learning is shaped by evolutionary and learning biases, breaks it into component processes and their possible neural implementations, and makes the case that studying it in early development is especially revealing because immature neural systems expose its underlying mechanisms.
papers.authors: Richard N. Aslin, Jenny R. Saffran

papers.title: Finding words in a sea of text: Word search as a measure of sensitivity to statistical regularities in reading
papers.abstract: Tests whether the letter statistics people absorb from natural text explain individual differences in reading, rather than relying on short training with novel artificial stimuli. Adults searched for high- versus low-probability letter strings embedded in text, and their search performance served as a measure of long-term orthographic statistical learning linked to reading skill.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Erin S. Isbilen, Abigail Laver, Noam Siegelman, James S. Magnuson, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Neural hyperscanning in caregiver-child dyads: A paradigm for studying the long-term effects of facilitated vs. disrupted attention on working memory and executive functioning in young children
papers.abstract: Proposes a research paradigm using simultaneous neural recording from caregiver and child to ask how caregiver behavior that supports or disrupts a child's attention affects later working memory and executive function. Explains how under-engaged or intrusive caregiving may change children's learning, and lays out how hyperscanning could track these dynamics longitudinally.
papers.authors: Maya L. Rosen, Annabelle Li, Catherine A. Mikkelsen, Richard N. Aslin

papers.title: Infant neuroscience: how to measure brain activity in the youngest minds
papers.abstract: Catalogs the noninvasive tools now available for recording brain activity in human infants, including EEG, MEG, near-infrared spectroscopy, optically pumped magnetometers and fMRI in awake infants performing cognitive tasks. Discusses the practical challenges of each and what they could contribute to understanding the infant mind.
papers.authors: Nicholas B. Turk-Browne, Richard N. Aslin

E267.name: Eileen Birch
E267.lab_name: Crystal Charity Ball Pediatric Vision Laboratory
E267.bio: Birch is the Director of the Crystal Charity Ball Pediatric Vision Laboratory at the Retina Foundation of the Southwest and holds an adjunct professorship in Ophthalmology at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Their research characterizes the neurodevelopmental mechanisms of amblyopia and identifies critical periods for visual development in children affected by strabismus and congenital cataracts. Utilizing a combination of psychophysical testing and randomized clinical trials, Birch demonstrated the efficacy of early dietary docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) on retinal development and established binocular treatment protocols for amblyopia. Current investigations by Birch utilize deep phenotyping to refine therapeutic interventions aimed at reducing interocular suppression and restoring functional stereoacuity.
E267.research_direction: Dr. Birch’s recent work explores the treatment and broader neurodevelopmental consequences of childhood binocular vision disorders. They have recently been investigating novel dichoptic therapies—such as contrast-rebalanced training and at-home 3D movies—in clinical trials to improve stereoacuity and deviation control in patients with amblyopia and intermittent exotropia. Beyond testing these behavioral interventions, their research examines how manipulating underlying neural plasticity mechanisms, like the excitation/inhibition balance, might help extend therapeutic critical periods into older childhood and adulthood. Additionally, Dr. Birch aims to understand the "whole child" impact of early discordant binocular experience by assessing how these visual deficits influence systemic, real-world outcomes like motor skills, physical activity, and self-perceived athletic competence.

papers.title: Self-reported physical activity in school age children with amblyopia
papers.abstract: A cross-sectional study of 132 children aged 8-13 (amblyopic, formerly amblyopic or strabismic, and controls) asked whether motor-skill difficulties in amblyopia reduce physical activity. Overall activity and BMI did not differ across groups, and all reported light to moderate activity. Children with amblyopia did show deficits in motor skills and self-perceived athletic competence.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
papers.authors: Brooke A. Koritala, Reed M. Jost, Christina Cheng-Patel, Cynthia Beauchamp, Prashanthi Giridhar, Becky Luu, Eileen E. Birch

papers.title: Baseline and outcome stereoacuity of children with anisometropic amblyopia undergoing dichoptic amblyopia treatment
papers.abstract: Pools data from 185 children aged 3-12 with anisometropic amblyopia across eight single-site trials of contrast-rebalanced dichoptic treatment. Better baseline and post-treatment stereoacuity and binocular function tracked with better baseline acuity, less suppression and less anisometropia, and with the amount of visual acuity gain. Young children who fully recovered acuity often also recovered stereoacuity.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
papers.authors: Eileen E. Birch, Reed M. Jost, Krista R. Kelly

papers.title: A pilot, randomized clinical trial of dichoptic 3D movies versus dichoptic 2D movies for treatment of childhood intermittent exotropia
papers.abstract: A masked pilot randomized trial in 41 children with intermittent exotropia compared at-home dichoptic 3D animated movies with 2D sham movies over four weeks. Control of the deviation improved significantly in the 3D group but not the sham group, and the between-group difference was modest but significant. Near control, alignment and stereoacuity did not change, so larger trials are needed.
papers.venue: Journal of American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
papers.authors: Reed M. Jost, Kartik Kumar, Lori M. Dao, Becky Luu, Anastasia A. Alex, Brooke A. Koritala, Krista R. Kelly, Yi-Zhong Wang, Eileen E. Birch

papers.title: Leveraging neural plasticity for the treatment of amblyopia
papers.abstract: Reviews how conventional patching and newer binocular therapies improve acuity yet leave residual amblyopia, with frequent recurrence and little benefit at older ages. Draws on animal work on plasticity regulation, such as shifting the excitation/inhibition balance, removing molecular brakes on plasticity and metaplasticity, to describe emerging treatments. Considers how these approaches could extend recovery to older children and adults.
papers.authors: Eileen E. Birch, Kevin R. Duffy

papers.title: Amblyopia and the whole child
papers.abstract: A review arguing that amblyopia is a neurodevelopmental disorder arising from discordant binocular experience in early childhood, and that its consequences reach well beyond visual acuity. It contends that the wide variability in response to treatment should be met with deep phenotyping of each child's deficits to select therapies. It also surveys the knock-on effects on visually guided skills, self-perception and quality of life, and calls for a whole-person approach to care.
papers.venue: Progress in Retinal and Eye Research
papers.authors: Eileen E. Birch, Krista R. Kelly

E268.name: James A. Bourne
E268.department: Section on Cellular and Cognitive Neurodevelopment (Systems Neurodevelopment Laboratory)
E268.lab_name: Section on Cellular and Cognitive Neurodevelopment
E268.bio: James A. Bourne is a Senior Investigator and Chief of the Section on Cellular and Cognitive Neurodevelopment at the National Institute of Mental Health. Bourne's research characterizes the maturation and plasticity of the primate visual system using a multidisciplinary cell-to-system approach that integrates anatomy, in vivo imaging, and behavioral tasks. A primary focus of their work is the role of thalamocortical circuits, particularly the pulvinar nuclei, in establishing functional brain systems and their vulnerability to developmental perturbations. By examining these circuits, Bourne aims to elucidate the neurodevelopmental substrates of disorders such as schizophrenia and autism, building on their previous work regarding the hierarchical development of cortical areas like the middle temporal area.
E268.research_direction: Dr. Bourne has recently been investigating the postnatal development and organization of corticothalamic and visual networks, primarily using the marmoset model. Their recent work explores how inhibitory interneuron circuits mature in the primate prefrontal cortex and examines the impact of early-life medial pulvinar disruptions on working memory and schizophrenia-relevant cortical physiology. To advance these cognitive and electrophysiological investigations, they are developing open-source, in-cage touchscreen testing platforms that allow for autonomous behavioral assessment in freely moving nonhuman primates. Furthermore, Dr. Bourne is mapping widespread corticothalamic inputs using retrograde tracing to understand the inferior pulvinar's function within spatial and visuomotor networks, while also probing the broader, dynamic, network-level stages of higher-order visual maturation.

papers.title: Early-life medial pulvinar disruption drives schizophrenia-relevant prefrontal inhibitory and cognitive deficits in primates
papers.abstract: Neonatal bilateral lesions of the medial pulvinar in marmosets changed how the prefrontal cortex matured through adolescence and led to adult working-memory deficits, whereas similar lesions made in adulthood did not. Lesioned animals had weaker thalamic input onto layer 3 parvalbumin interneurons, reduced prefrontal gamma power and lower parvalbumin expression, with fast-spiking cells retaining an immature physiology. The work argues that thalamic input during a developmental window shapes prefrontal inhibitory maturation, so some psychiatric-disease dysfunction may originate in thalamic inputs rather than cortex.
papers.authors: Jack T. Scott, Sara Fin, Adam P. Caccavano, Maxwell Walker, Diego Szczupak, Jordan Jontz, Jihane Homman-Ludiye, William C. Kwan, Kevin Marche, Gordon Fishell, Afonso C. Silva, Kenneth A. Pelkey, Chris J. McBain, James A. Bourne

papers.title: Widespread Corticothalamic Connectivity Identifies the Inferior Pulvinar as a Central Node in Visual Network Architecture
papers.abstract: Using MRI-guided retrograde tracer injections restricted to the medial inferior pulvinar in marmosets, the study mapped the cortical sources of input to this nucleus. Labeled layer V neurons were spread across occipital, temporal, parietal and cingulate cortex, with the MT complex and occipital areas supplying about 60% of input and parietal cortex about 20%. The pattern positions the inferior pulvinar as an integrative hub for motion, spatial and visuomotor networks rather than a simple relay.
papers.authors: William C. Kwan, Angela Y. Fan, Andrea J. Romanowski, Inaki-Carril Mundinano, Mitchell J. de Souza, James A. Bourne

papers.title: Developmental dynamics of marmoset prefrontal cortical SST and PV interneuron networks highlight primate-specific features
papers.abstract: The authors mapped postnatal expression of PV, SST, KCC2, Kv3.1b and Nav1.1 across six prefrontal areas in marmosets. PV interneurons matured slowly into adolescence while gaining ion channels that support fast firing, whereas SST interneuron density declined after birth, unlike the rodent pattern. This gives a primate-specific framework for how inhibitory circuit refinement may relate to neurodevelopmental disorder vulnerability.
papers.authors: Nafiseh S. Hosseini Fin, Adrian Yip, Jack T. Scott, Leon Teo, Jihane Homman-Ludiye, James A. Bourne

papers.title: CalliCog is an open-source cognitive neuroscience toolkit for freely behaving nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: CalliCog is an open-source, modular in-cage operant platform that lets small primates such as marmosets do touchscreen cognitive tasks autonomously in their home cages. Naive marmosets reached touchscreen proficiency within about two weeks at two independent facilities and completed behavioral flexibility and working-memory tasks. The system also synchronizes behavior with ECoG recordings in freely moving animals, aiming to democratize cognitive testing in small nonhuman primates.
papers.authors: Jack T. Scott, Bruno L. Mendivez Vasquez, Brian J. Stewart, Dylan D. Panacheril, Darren K. J. Rajit, Angela Y. Fan, James A. Bourne

papers.title: Development of Higher-Level Vision: A Network Perspective
papers.abstract: This review argues that development of visual areas beyond V1 does not simply follow the sequence of the adult hierarchy, but passes through distinct network configurations at each stage. It highlights major gaps in knowledge about higher-level visual development and calls for network-level studies to understand normal maturation, vulnerabilities to developmental disorders, and eventual treatments.
papers.authors: James A. Bourne, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Lynne Kiorpes, Maria Concetta Morrone, Michael J. Arcaro, Kristina J. Nielsen

E270.name: Angela Chen
E270.bio: Angela M. Chen is a Professor at the Southern California College of Optometry at Marshall B. Ketchum University, specializing in the diagnosis and management of pediatric vision disorders. Their research focuses on binocular vision anomalies, including strabismus, amblyopia, and accommodative insufficiency, through the use of multi-center randomized clinical trials. Chen serves as a primary clinical investigator for National Eye Institute-supported studies within the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group (PEDIG) and the Convergence Insufficiency Treatment Trial (CITT-ART). Their work evaluates the effectiveness of vision therapy, optical interventions such as overminus lenses, and the repeatability of accommodative accuracy in children with unilateral amblyopia.
E270.research_direction: Dr. Chen's recent work broadly explores the clinical assessment and management of binocular vision and ocular motor disorders across diverse patient populations. They have recently been investigating the efficacy of various therapeutic strategies, evaluating the evidence base for interventions like vestibular rehabilitation and vision therapy in patients with mild traumatic brain injury, as well as exploring how gross convergence therapy can be adapted for sensory exotropia in individuals with severe vision loss. Additionally, their research examines the methodological rigor of standard clinical vision tests, specifically using Bland-Altman analysis to determine the longitudinal test-retest reliability of accommodative amplitude and facility measurements in adolescents. As an active voice in pediatric optometry, they are also curating broader scientific discussions on emerging clinical practices surrounding amblyopia, strabismus, and accommodative function.

papers.title: Test-retest reliability of clinical accommodative measures in adolescents
papers.abstract: In 93 adolescents aged 12 to under 17.5 with normal accommodation, the team measured accommodative amplitude (push-up) and facility (flippers) at baseline and again about 90 days later. Bland-Altman analysis was used to quantify how much the measures vary within a person over three months. The work provides reliability benchmarks needed to judge whether changes in accommodative function after treatment are real; it comes from the EPICC study group.
papers.authors: Angela M. Chen, Chris Koutures, Loraine T. Sinnott, Ann Morrison, Carissa Wu, Caitlyn Lew, Matthew Vaughn, Emily K. Wiecek, Mitchell Scheiman, Lisa A. Jordan, Tawna L. Roberts, for the EPICC Study Group

papers.title: Guest editorial: Advances in Pediatrics and Binocular Vision Feature Issue
papers.abstract: An editorial introducing a themed issue of Optometry and Vision Science on pediatric and binocular vision research. It highlights recent progress in areas such as amblyopia, strabismus and accommodation, and orients readers to the contributed articles.
papers.authors: Angela M. Chen, Susan A. Cotter, the Advances in Pediatrics and Binocular Vision Feature Issue Editorial Team

papers.title: Scoping review: Intervention for ocular motor disorders in children and adults with mild traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: The authors systematically mapped English-language intervention studies from 2003 to 2024 in which people with mild traumatic brain injury had ocular motor function assessed before treatment. They compared strategies such as watchful waiting, vestibular rehabilitation, vision therapy and optical interventions across disciplines. The evidence base turned out to be thin and inconsistent, and they argue for randomized trials with standardized testing and diagnostic criteria.
papers.authors: Angela M. Chen, Aaron D. Salzano, Allegra P. Burgher, Lynn D. Greenspan, Tiong Peng Yap, Jacqueline Theis, Su-Hsun Liu, Mitchell Scheiman, Tawna L. Roberts

papers.title: Case Report: Gross Convergence Therapy for the Treatment of Sensory Exotropia in a Patient with Severe Vision Loss
papers.abstract: A clinical case report describing the use of gross convergence therapy to manage sensory exotropia in a patient with severe vision loss. It illustrates how binocular vision therapy principles can be adapted for patients with very low vision, where standard therapy is hard to apply.
papers.authors: Angela M. Chen, Susan A. Cotter

E271.name: Ben Deen
E271.bio: Ben Deen is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at Tulane University and a Faculty Associate of the Tulane Brain Institute. Deen's research utilizes high-resolution fMRI, intracranial recordings, and behavioral psychophysics to map the functional organization of the human brain, specifically regarding social perception and memory. By employing awake infant fMRI techniques, Deen identified that category-selective regions in the visual cortex are functional by four months of age. Their current investigations focus on the neural networks of the superior temporal sulcus and the parallel systems for social and spatial reasoning within the brain's association cortex.
E271.research_direction: Dr. Deen has recently been using precision, individual-participant fMRI to map the large-scale organization of high-level vision and social cognition. Their recent work explores how the primate brain segregates processing for people, places, and objects, specifically investigating whether distinct, parallel networks for social and spatial cognition extend up the cortical hierarchy into association areas and the default mode network. They are also examining category selectivity at the apex of the ventral visual stream, questioning how anterior temporal lobe regions process personally familiar faces to bridge the gap between pure visual perception and social memory. To support this mapping of memory and high-level perception, Dr. Deen has been developing new methodological resources, including surface-based probabilistic atlases of the medial temporal lobe designed to overcome traditional signal dropout challenges in these complex cortical regions.

papers.title: Three distinct profiles of visual category preference within the anterior temporal lobe
papers.abstract: Analyzing Human Connectome Project fMRI data from 830 people with a region-of-interest approach that copes with signal dropout, the study characterizes category responses in the temporal pole and perirhinal cortex. It reports three replicable profiles, including a face-preferring perirhinal subregion and an object-preferring one, with a patchy spatial arrangement. Functional connectivity shows these subregions couple with regions of matching category preference, extending category selectivity to the apex of the ventral visual stream.
papers.authors: Chencheng Shen, Ben Deen

papers.title: Parallel systems for social and spatial cognition reaching the cortical apex
papers.abstract: Using precision fMRI in individual participants, the authors compare how the brain handles people, places, and objects across visual, semantic, and episodic tasks. They find person-preferring and place-preferring regions that sit side by side throughout frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortex within the default mode network. The two sets of regions have domain-specific response profiles and connect preferentially to like-preferring regions, indicating parallel social and spatial networks at the top of the cortical hierarchy.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: The MTL200: a surface-based, probabilistic atlas of the medial temporal lobe
papers.abstract: The paper presents a surface-based probabilistic atlas of the temporopolar, entorhinal, perirhinal, and parahippocampal cortices, built from hand-drawn boundaries in anatomical MRI of 200 people. It fills gaps left by earlier atlases, which are volumetric, small-sample, or omit temporopolar cortex. The resource supports surface-based analyses of memory and high-level perception regions.
papers.authors: Ian Faul, Adya Agarwal, Stephen Graziose, Andrew Nwacha, Janis Park, Anisah Sahibul, Katie Tong, Ben Deen

papers.title: A familiar face and person processing area in the human temporal pole
papers.abstract: High-resolution individual-participant fMRI identifies a region in the human temporal pole that responds preferentially to personally familiar faces and other cues to familiar people. The area is distinct from neighboring face-selective regions in the ventral visual stream and is tied to person memory rather than face perception per se. The work extends the monkey anterior face-area literature to humans and links visual face processing to social memory.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Gazi Husain, Winrich A. Freiwald

papers.title: Specialized Networks for Social Cognition in the Primate Brain
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes evidence from human and macaque neuroimaging on how the primate brain is organized for social cognition. It covers networks for face processing, social interaction perception, and mental-state reasoning, and considers how they interact and how they compare across species. The authors argue for domain-specific, interconnected systems and outline open questions.
papers.authors: Ben Deen, Caspar M. Schwiedrzik, Julia Sliwa, Winrich A. Freiwald

E272.name: Takao Hensch
E272.department: Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology
E272.bio: Takao Hensch identifies the biological mechanisms governing critical periods of brain development, specifically within the visual system. Their research integrates molecular, cellular, and systems neuroscience to demonstrate how specific inhibitory GABAergic circuits trigger the onset of these plastic windows, while molecular factors like perineuronal nets close them. Using mouse models and in vivo electrophysiology, Hensch’s laboratory investigates how early sensory experiences shape neural architecture and how these processes are altered in neurodevelopmental disorders. Their current work examines the potential to reopen plasticity in the adult brain to treat conditions such as amblyopia, autism, and mental illness.
E272.research_direction: Dr. Hensch has recently been investigating critical periods, the developmental windows when sensory circuits are especially easy to reshape, with the visual cortex as the main model system. Their recent work explores how inhibitory neurons and gamma-frequency brain rhythms mark when these windows open in mice, and how much plasticity remains in the adult visual cortex. They have also asked whether general anesthesia in human infants shifts the timing of visual cortex development, which could be a clinical way of nudging a critical period. A further thread links early-life adversity, sleep, and dopamine signaling to later attention problems, and another looks at how electromagnetic stimulation changes brain metabolic state during stroke recovery.

papers.title: Frequency-specific electromagnetic modulation of brain redox state precedes cortical activity in stroke recovery
papers.abstract: The rehabilitation of neural function following ischemic stroke is contingent upon the restoration of metabolic homeostasis and circuit excitability within perilesional tissue. This study evaluates the efficacy of frequency-specific electromagnetic field (EMF) stimulation in modulating cortical states in a rodent model of cerebral ischemia. Utilizing real-time optical monitoring of NADH/NAD+ ratios alongside electrophysiological recordings, the authors demonstrate that EMF-induced shifts in the brain's redox potential occur significantly earlier than the recovery of stimulus-evoked cortical responses. These results establish that metabolic and redox rebalancing is a primary mechanism driving the neuroplastic effects of electromagnetic interventions, suggesting that redox-state dynamics serve as a predictive biomarker for functional recovery and therapeutic efficacy in stroke rehabilitation.
papers.authors: Henry Hing Cheong Lee, Shira Reznik Balter, Nathaniel W. Hodgson, Ana Parabucki, Batsheva Weisinger, Yaron Segal, Glen M. Doniger, Esther Shohami, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: General anesthesia in early infancy accelerates visual cortical development
papers.abstract: Postnatal maturation of GABAergic inhibitory circuits is known to trigger the onset of critical periods for cortical plasticity in mammalian models. This investigation assesses whether exogenous potentiation of the GABA system via clinical general anesthesia (GA) alters the pace of human neurodevelopment. Through longitudinal visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings in a cohort of 93 infants, the study reveals that prolonged or repeated GA exposure (primarily sevoflurane and propofol) in the first six months of life leads to a premature maturation of VEP waveforms. This acceleration suggests that early exposure to GABA-active anesthetics may serve as an artificial trigger for critical period onset, potentially disrupting the typical windows of sensory plasticity and impacting the lifelong establishment of excitatory-inhibitory circuit balance in the human brain.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Laurel J. Gabard-Durnam, Sarah A. McCormick, Ellen Underwood, Alice Tao, Isabelle Kim, Siobhan Coffman, Lindsay Benster, Maria Graziano, Charles A. Nelson, Charles B. Berde, Laura Cornelissen, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: Rapid and cumulative adult plasticity in the mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Experience-dependent remodeling of the mature visual system can be elicited by repetitive sensory stimulation, yet the temporal constraints and consolidation mechanisms of adult plasticity remain poorly defined. This study utilizes flash-evoked visual potentials (VEPs) to characterize the induction and stabilization of response potentiation in the adult mouse primary visual cortex (V1). The researchers identified two distinct temporal phases: a rapid, within-session increase in VEP magnitude and a cumulative, multi-session potentiation across days. Mechanistic analysis indicates that while both phases require NMDA receptor-mediated signaling, the consolidation of cumulative plasticity is specifically dependent on NREM sleep. These findings provide a robust framework for understanding how sensory experience and sleep-dependent offline processing interact to regulate the boundaries of adult brain plasticity.
papers.authors: Hiroyuki Miyamoto, Emi Mazaki, Yuichi Makino, Q. Fang, T. Hamada, Youichi Handa, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: Sleep-sensitive dopamine receptor expression in male mice underlies attention deficits after a critical period of early adversity
papers.abstract: Early life stress (ELS) is associated with long-term cognitive and emotional deficits, yet the circuit-level mechanisms remain largely unknown. This study identifies a neonatal critical period (P2–P9) in mice where fragmented maternal care induces a persistent imbalance in dopamine receptor expression within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Adult male offspring exhibited significantly elevated D2R and suppressed D4R expression, which correlated with impaired performance in visual attention tasks and disrupted sleep architecture, including heightened NREM fragmentation and elevated hypothalamic orexin. These attention deficits were acutely rescued in adulthood by pharmacological restoration of D2/D4 signaling in the ACC. The findings establish a sleep-sensitive dopaminergic pathway as a critical mediator of the sex-specific cognitive consequences of early adversity.
papers.authors: Yuichi Makino, Nathaniel W. Hodgson, Emma Doenier, Anna Victoria Serbin, Koya Osada, Pietro Artoni, Matthew J. Smith, Dennis M. Twomey, Susan B. Mierau, Charles A. Nelson, Michela Fagiolini, Takao K. Hensch

papers.title: Rapid synaptic and gamma rhythm signature of mouse critical period plasticity
papers.abstract: The transition into windows of heightened neural plasticity, known as critical periods (CPs), is fundamental for the refinement of sensory circuits. This study demonstrates that a transient peak in gamma-band (40 Hz) EEG power serves as a robust biomarker for the open CP state in the primary visual cortex of mice. This oscillatory signature is acutely induced by sensory deprivation and is contingent upon the maturation of parvalbumin-positive (PV+) inhibitory interneurons, which facilitate the E-I circuit balance necessary for plastic rewiring. The identification of this gamma-band signal provides a non-invasive tool for monitoring the onset and closure of sensitive periods in brain development and may assist in the early detection of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by deviant plasticity timing.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Kathleen B. Quast, Rebecca K. Reh, Maddalena D. Caiati, Nancy Kopell, Michelle M. McCarthy, Takao K. Hensch

E273.name: Robert Hess
E273.bio: Robert Hess is a Professor of Ophthalmology at McGill University and Director of the McGill Vision Research Unit, focusing on the neurobiology of human vision and cortical plasticity. Their research integrates psychophysical experiments with computational modeling and multimodal neuroimaging, including fMRI and MEG, to investigate mechanisms of spatial, temporal, and motion perception. Hess has conducted research on binocular suppression and contour integration, resulting in the development of dichoptic digital therapeutics for amblyopia. Their current work explores the modulation of the adult visual cortex through non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to assist functional recovery in patients with visual impairments.
E273.research_direction: Dr. Hess has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of visual neuroplasticity and amblyopia to guide the development of more principled, binocular-focused clinical treatments for adult patients. Their recent work explores the cortical dynamics of interocular suppression and ocular dominance plasticity, using paradigms like brief monocular deprivation and steady-state VEPs to probe whether these processes share neural substrates with general contrast adaptation and how they might recruit nonvisual extrastriate brain networks. Furthermore, they are studying depth perception anomalies in the general population, specifically comparing tasks that require simple disparity detection against those requiring depth-sign discrimination to better understand the mechanisms and true prevalence of stereo-anomaly.

papers.title: Changing views on visual neuroplasticity lead to novel treatments for adults with amblyopia
papers.abstract: A 2026 review by Hess and Thompson on how the view that the adult visual cortex is fixed has given way to evidence for substantial plasticity, and how this has opened new treatment routes for adults with amblyopia. (Summary inferred from the title and authors' known work; full abstract was not retrievable.)
papers.authors: Robert F. Hess, Benjamin Thompson

papers.title: Towards a principled and efficacious approach to the treatment of amblyopia. A review.
papers.abstract: Surveys the now-wide menu of amblyopia treatments, from traditional patching (penalization) through visual training and non-invasive brain stimulation aimed at the weak eye, to newer methods that target binocular function directly. Argues that a half-century of progress in understanding visual function and the origin of the amblyopic deficit means treatment choices (how, when and why to treat) should now follow a more principled framework.
papers.authors: Robert F. Hess

papers.title: Stereo-anomaly is found more frequently in tasks that require discrimination between depths
papers.abstract: Measures stereoacuity with a digital tool in 228 people with normal vision, comparing tasks that need only detecting a disparity with tasks that need judging its sign (near versus far). Nearly everyone could detect disparity, but roughly a third struggled to tell the direction of depth, and about half of those could not do it at all. This helps explain the wildly different stereo-anomaly prevalence figures in the literature and implies direction discrimination needs extra processing beyond detection.
papers.authors: Alex S. Baldwin, Seung Hyun Min, Sara Alarcon Carrillo, Zili Wang, Ziyun Cheng, Jiawei Zhou, Robert F. Hess

papers.title: Flash Suppression Reveals an Additional Nonvisual Extrastriate Contribution for Amblyopic Suppression
papers.abstract: Uses a flash-suppression paradigm with steady-state VEPs in 13 adult amblyopes and 13 controls to probe interocular suppression at different suppressor contrasts. Suppression from the fellow eye was stronger than from the amblyopic eye, consistent with chronic suppression of the amblyopic eye. EEG showed similar occipital effects across groups but a difference over frontal regions, suggesting amblyopic suppression also involves nonvisual extrastriate areas.
papers.authors: Dave Saint-Amour, Laura Lefebvre, Clémence Bertrand Pilon, Robert F. Hess

papers.title: Is ocular dominance plasticity a special case of contrast adaptation?
papers.abstract: Asks whether the ocular dominance shifts seen after a brief period of monocular deprivation are simply an instance of ordinary contrast adaptation, both being contrast-gain adjustments. Re-analysing previously published results, the paper concludes that the two processes are dissociable and do not share a common neural substrate.
papers.authors: Robert F. Hess, Seung Hyun Min

E274.name: Zsuzsa Kaldy
E274.bio: Zsuzsa Kaldy is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston and the director of the Early Minds Lab. Kaldy’s research investigates the developmental trajectory of visual attention and visual working memory, specifically how infants and young children encode and maintain object representations. Using eye-tracking and pupillometric methodologies, they examine the intersection of cognitive effort and attentional focus in early learning processes. Their work integrates behavioral paradigms with developmental neuroscience to characterize typical development and the cognitive profiles of individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder.
E274.research_direction: Dr. Kaldy's recent work explores the development of visual working memory and cognitive control, with a major focus on how young children navigate the "sampling-remembering trade-off." Using gamified touchscreen paradigms where the temporal cost of accessing hidden visual information is manipulated, they have recently been investigating how children flexibly balance the use of internal working memory against the external sampling of their visual environment. Their research also examines the underlying mechanisms of memory control, specifically charting how vulnerability to proactive interference in visual working memory changes across early and middle childhood. Additionally, they are investigating the broader developmental drivers of these cognitive skills, employing meta-analytic techniques to disentangle how formal schooling, as opposed to natural maturation, shapes children's core executive functions.

papers.title: How Much Do You Remember When It's up to You? Measuring Memory Use Without Response Bias in Young Children
papers.abstract: Using a gamified Shopping Game, the authors tested the sampling-remembering trade-off in preschoolers in two preregistered experiments with 157 children aged 4.5 to 7. Children chose items from a virtual store using a list they could toggle to, with the cost of accessing the list manipulated. The forced-choice measure avoids response bias and shows that even young preschoolers shift between looking and remembering according to cost.
papers.authors: Candice Koolhaas, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: School changes minds: A meta-analysis shows that schooling modestly improves children's executive functions
papers.abstract: A meta-analysis pooling studies that compare children just above and below school-entry cutoffs to separate the effect of schooling from that of age. Schooling produced a modest but reliable improvement in executive functions. The work speaks to how formal education shapes core cognitive control skills.
papers.authors: Jamie Donenfeld, Mahita Mudundi, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: The Extended Mind in Young Children: Cost-Dependent Trade-Off Between External and Internal Memory
papers.abstract: Children played a touchscreen shopping game in which the shopping list and the store could not be viewed at once, and the delay before the list reappeared was varied. Across three preregistered experiments in the US and China (141 children aged 5 to 8), children checked the list less often, studied it longer and remembered more when re-checking was costly. They also judged the no-delay condition to be easier, showing that young children adaptively balance external resources against working memory.
papers.authors: Yibiao Liang, Erik Blaser, Jia Ying Yi, Liyang Sai, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: How attention and working memory work together in the pursuit of goals: The development of the sampling-remembering trade-off
papers.abstract: This theoretical review argues that goal-directed behavior depends on a dynamic trade-off between sampling the environment through attention and remembering in working memory. The authors lay out how this balance is shaped by the cost of each option and how it changes across development. They use the framework to organize existing findings and to point to open questions in children's cognition.
papers.authors: Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

papers.title: Can't get it out of my head: Proactive interference in the visual working memory of 3- to 8-year-old children
papers.abstract: The study asks how earlier memory contents interfere with new visual working memory contents in children aged 3 to 8. Using a child-friendly task, it charts how vulnerability to proactive interference changes across early and middle childhood. The results bear on the development of memory control.
papers.authors: Mollie Hamilton, Tessyia Roper, Erik Blaser, Zsuzsa Kaldy

E275.name: Lynne Kiorpes
E275.department: Center for Neural Science and Department of Psychology
E275.bio: Lynne Kiorpes is a Professor of Neural Science and Psychology at New York University and the Dean of the Graduate School of Arts and Science. Kiorpes investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the postnatal development of visual function and the pathophysiology of amblyopia using macaque monkey models. By integrating quantitative psychophysical methods with physiological and anatomical techniques, Kiorpes explores how early abnormal visual experience disrupts the maturation of visual pathways, particularly in extrastriate cortical areas. Their research characterizes the relationship between behavioral immaturities and neural responses with the goal of informing therapeutic interventions for developmental vision disorders.
E275.research_direction: Dr. Kiorpes has recently been studying how vision matures in young macaque monkeys, combining behavioral testing with recordings from neurons across the visual cortex. Their recent work explores how the ability to see global shapes and naturalistic textures develops over the first year, and whether the delay in behavior reflects immature responses in mid-level visual areas such as V2 and V4 or something later in the pathway. They have also been examining amblyopia, a developmental disorder of vision, by recording from motion-sensitive cortex in monkeys raised with an induced form of the condition. This work asks how abnormal early visual experience alters the way neurons respond to the two eyes and to moving stimuli.

papers.title: Neural Sensitivity to Radial Frequency Patterns in the Visual Cortex of Developing Macaques
papers.abstract: This study investigates the neural substrates of global form perception development by recording neuronal population activity in areas V1, V2, V4, and the posterior inferotemporal cortex (PIT) of young macaque monkeys (19–54 weeks) and an adult control. Using radial frequency stimuli—circular patterns with sinusoidal radial modulations—the researchers employed population decoding to evaluate whether improvements in behavioral sensitivity observed in early life are limited by the maturity of extrastriate representations. Findings reveal that while V1 neurons lack sensitivity to these global form patterns, populations in area V4 encode radial frequency stimuli maturely by 4–6 months of age. Because behavioral performance continues to refine long after these neural representations have stabilized, the results suggest that the primary bottlenecks for the development of shape perception reside in processing stages downstream of V4 rather than in the mid-level visual cortex itself.
papers.authors: Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Gerick M. Lee, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Developmentally stable representations of naturalistic image structure in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: To determine whether postnatal improvements in form vision derive from developmental changes in mid-level visual cortical areas, this study analyzed neuronal and behavioral responses to synthetic texture stimuli containing naturalistic higher-order statistics versus spectrally matched noise. Longitudinal psychophysical testing showed that behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic structure reaches half-maximum at approximately 25 weeks of age. In contrast, multiunit neural sensitivity in areas V2 and V4 remained remarkably stable from the earliest recording point (20 weeks) through 56 weeks and into adulthood. Neural sensitivity was highest in V4 and significantly lower in V1. The observed dissociation between stable neural representations in the ventral stream and protracted behavioral maturation suggests that the limiting factors for texture perception development lie in the capacity of downstream circuits to effectively read out or integrate these stable sensory signals.
papers.authors: Gerick M. Lee, Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Development of radial frequency pattern perception in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: This behavioral study characterizes the developmental trajectory of global shape sensitivity in macaque monkeys (aged 2 months to 10 years) using radial frequency (RF) stimuli. Utilizing a novel four-choice oddity task alongside traditional two-alternative forced-choice paradigms, the researchers measured discrimination thresholds for circular targets with sinusoidal radius modulations. Results indicate that RF pattern perception is present as early as 2 months postnatal, with sensitivity steadily improving well beyond the first year of life. Macaques exhibited higher sensitivity for patterns with higher radial frequencies (higher concentrations of curvature and orientation cues), matching the hyperacuity maturation patterns seen in humans.
