The study establishes a comprehensive behavioral benchmark for the protracted maturation of contour integration and global form processing in primates.
papers.authors: Charlie L. Rodríguez Deliz, Gerick M. Lee, Brittany N. Bushnell, Najib J. Majaj, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

papers.title: Responses to visual motion of neurons in the extrastriate visual cortex of macaque monkeys with experimental amblyopia
papers.abstract: Researchers characterized the representation of visual motion in the dorsal stream by recording single-unit responses in area MT and adjacent extrastriate regions of awake, fixating macaque monkeys with experimental strabismic amblyopia. Behavioral assessments confirmed substantial contrast and motion sensitivity deficits in these subjects. Neurophysiological results demonstrated a severe reduction in binocularity and a significant decrease in the number of neurons driven by the amblyopic eye compared to the fellow eye. While neurons driven by the amblyopic eye maintained qualitatively normal receptive field structures, they exhibited higher response variance and reduced evidence of temporal integration of upstream motion signals. The findings suggest that the primary driver of motion perception deficits in amblyopia is the reduction in the total number and strength of neuronal signals transmitted through the amblyopic eye to the extrastriate cortex.
papers.authors: Tom J. Van Grootel, Ramanujan T. Raghavan, Jenna G. Kelly, J. Anthony Movshon, Lynne Kiorpes

E276.name: Kang Lee
E276.department: Department of Applied Psychology and Human Development
E276.bio: Lee is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair specializing in the developmental neuroscience of social cognition, specifically the mechanisms of face processing and the emergence of moral behaviors such as deception. Their research utilizes behavioral paradigms, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging techniques including fMRI, fNIRS, and EEG to examine how children perceive social categories and develop honesty. Lee is the co-inventor of Transdermal Optical Imaging (TOI), a contactless technology that employs machine learning to extract physiological data from facial blood flow patterns. Their work in vision science contributed to legal reforms in Canada regarding the standards for child witness testimony.
E276.research_direction: Dr. Lee has recently been investigating the psychological mechanisms driving moral development in young children, alongside a distinct line of applied clinical research. Their recent work explores the behavioral levers that influence honesty and cheating during early childhood, using behavioral experiments to test how factors like being entrusted with a task, anticipating an adult's emotional reactions, and performing specific embodied physical actions shape children's moral choices. They are also examining the familial dynamics of deception by formalizing theoretical frameworks to understand why parents lie to their children and how this practice impacts development. In a separate applied track, their recent work uses machine learning and feature selection to optimize psychiatric questionnaires, aiming to build highly concise, scalable online screening instruments for anxiety disorders.

papers.title: Physical actions shape moral choices: Environment-directed movements reduce cheating in young children
papers.abstract: Five preregistered studies with 330 preschoolers tested whether the kind of physical action a child performs changes their honesty. Children were more honest after acting on the external environment (e.g., pulling a screen down over a box) than after performing the same movement on themselves (e.g., pulling a blindfold over their own face). The results support an embodied account in which moral decisions are causally shaped by action.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Xinxin Huang, Yuanyuan Lu, Haiying Mao, Fang Fang, Kang Lee

papers.title: Telling young children an adult's emotional reactions to their future honest or dishonest behavior causes them to cheat less
papers.abstract: In five preregistered studies with 480 children aged 3-6, the researchers told children how a familiar adult (teacher or mother) would react emotionally if they were later honest or dishonest on a hard test. Warning 5- to 6-year-olds of negative reactions to dishonesty reduced cheating, and 3- to 4-year-olds cheated less when told of their mother's pleasure at honesty or displeasure at dishonesty. Anticipated adult emotion is thus an effective lever for promoting honesty.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Weihao Yan, Paul L. Harris, Kang Lee

papers.title: Concise multi-class anxiety disorder risk assessment: A novel advanced machine learning approach
papers.abstract: Using machine learning and feature selection on the 42-item DASS scale, the authors built a much shorter scale that still predicts anxiety risk levels with high validity. The reduced tool is deployed as an online self-screening instrument aimed at faster, scalable early detection, especially for underserved groups.
papers.authors: Haochong Yang, Yuan Hong Sun, Kang Lee

papers.title: Trusting young children to help causes them to cheat less
papers.abstract: Across five experiments with 328 kindergartners, the authors asked whether being trusted makes children more honest. Children whom an adult entrusted with helping on a task cheated less in a later temptation test than children who were not trusted. The work gives causal evidence that trust promotes honesty and suggests a practical way for adults to foster honest behaviour in children.
papers.authors: Li Zhao, Haiying Mao, Paul L. Harris, Kang Lee

papers.title: Parenting by Lying
papers.abstract: This review describes the emerging research on parents lying to children to steer their emotions or behaviour. It lays out theoretical and methodological difficulties in studying the practice and proposes a framework for understanding its causes and consequences to guide future work.
papers.authors: Peipei Setoh, Petrina Hui Xian Low, Gail D. Heyman, Kang Lee

E279.name: Glen Prusky
E279.lab_name: Laboratory for Visual Disease and Therapy
E279.bio: Glen Prusky is a neuroscientist whose research investigates the mechanisms of adaptive change and experience-dependent plasticity within the visual system. Prusky developed OptoMotry, a standardized virtual reality-based methodology that utilizes the optokinetic reflex to quantify visual thresholds in non-verbal subjects, ranging from rodent models to children with cerebral visual impairment. Their work integrates cellular, electrophysiological, and behavioral techniques to develop therapeutic interventions, including cell-based retinal transplantations and rehabilitative visual experiences for brain injury and stroke recovery. Currently, Prusky focuses on translating these psychophysical assessments into clinical tools to monitor and stimulate visual recovery in pediatric populations with neurological disorders.
E279.research_direction: Dr. Prusky has recently been developing ways to measure vision objectively in young children who cannot reliably report what they see. Their recent work builds gamified, eye-tracking-based tests that estimate how faint a pattern a child can detect (contrast sensitivity) by following where the child looks, using an adaptive statistical procedure to make testing fast and reliable. They also apply a gaze-based interactive tool to hospitalized children with brain injury, tracking eye movements, visual field symmetry, and contrast sensitivity over time to identify patterns of visual impairment and how vision recovers.

papers.title: A Novel Eye Tracking–Based Gamified Assessment of Contrast Sensitivity Function in Children: Prospective Development and Reliability Study
papers.abstract: Traditional psychophysical assessment of the contrast sensitivity function (CSF) in pediatric populations is constrained by the subjective nature of standard behavioral reports and the limited attentional capacity of young children. We developed an Eye Tracking–Based Gamified Contrast Sensitivity Function (ETGCSF) tool that utilizes automated gaze-contingent detection coupled with an adaptive Bayesian algorithm to objectively estimate contrast thresholds. In a prospective study of preschool-aged children, the ETGCSF demonstrated high test-retest reliability and significantly improved testing efficiency compared to standard methods. Our findings suggest that integrating eye-tracking with gamified reinforcement enables high-resolution spatial vision profiling in previously untestable or non-verbal pediatric populations, providing a scalable diagnostic tool for early detection of ocular and neurological visual pathologies.
papers.authors: Yunsi He, Yijing Zhuang, Lei Feng, Xuanyu Xu, Ying Deng, Moruomi Li, Yangfei Pang, Ying Yao, Wentong Yu, Zixuan Xu, Yusong Zhou, Yudan Zhong, Qiuying Li, Qingqing Ye, Junpeng Yuan, Yun Wen, Jinrong Li, Scott W. J. Mooney, Nazia M. Alam, Glen Prusky

papers.title: Quantitative patterns of visual impairment and recovery in children with brain injury
papers.abstract: Pediatric brain injury results in complex visual deficits that are often poorly quantified due to comorbid cognitive and communicative impairments. We utilized the 'Visual Ladder,' a gaze-based interactive software program, to longitudinally measure eye movement kinematics, visual field symmetries, and contrast sensitivity in a cohort of hospitalized children with diverse brain injuries. Our analysis identifies distinct diagnostic clusters of visual impairment based on objective psychophysical metrics and characterizes specific trajectories of functional recovery over time. These findings indicate that automated, high-resolution eye-tracking assessments can overcome the limitations of subjective clinical evaluations, providing a robust evidence base for the prognosis and management of pediatric cortical visual impairment.
papers.authors: Scott W. J. Mooney, Nazia M. Alam, Matthew J. Sciarabba, Kieran R. Sheldon, Glen T. Prusky

E280.name: Karthik Shekhar
E280.department: Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering
E280.bio: Shekhar is the John F. Heil Jr. Professor at UC Berkeley, directing a research program at the intersection of neuroscience, genomics, and biophysics. Their work employs high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics and statistical machine learning to characterize the molecular diversity of neuronal types in the retina and visual cortex. Shekhar investigates how neural circuits develop and evolve across vertebrate species, and how sensory experience and electrical activity refine neuronal identity. Additionally, the Shekhar lab develops theoretical models to understand the electrochemical dynamics and diffuse charge transport at biological membrane interfaces.
E280.research_direction: Dr. Shekhar has recently been investigating the evolutionary origins and molecular identities of diverse neuronal cell types using large-scale single-cell transcriptomics. A major focus of their recent work explores the evolutionary history of the vertebrate visual system by comparing single-cell atlases across dozens of species to trace the conservation and diversification of specific retinal neurons, including ancestral photoreceptors and highly diverse amacrine cells. Beyond evolutionary vision science, they are also examining how early sensory experience and deprivation shape the developmental gene expression of distinct neuronal classes in the mammalian somatosensory cortex. Additionally, their research extends into fundamental membrane biophysics, using theoretical simulations to model the spatiotemporal dynamics of ion gradients and electrochemical signal propagation near excitable cell membranes.

papers.title: The Extreme Diversity Of Retinal Amacrine Cells Has Deep Evolutionary Roots
papers.abstract: Integrating transcriptomic atlases from 24 vertebrate species, the study reconstructs the evolutionary history of amacrine cells, the most diverse inhibitory neuron class in the retina. It defines 42 orthologous amacrine cell types, most matching one-to-one across amniotes and often across vertebrates, while abundance and gene expression vary with visual ecology. The results argue that the extreme diversity of these cells was established early in vertebrate evolution.
papers.authors: Dario Tommasini, Aboozar Monavarfeshani, Vishruth Dinesh, Joshua Hahn, Jared Tangeman, Olivier Marre, Seth Blackshaw, Teresa Puthussery, Joshua R. Sanes, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic insights into the evolution of vertebrate photoreceptor types
papers.abstract: Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases from zebrafish, chicken, lizard, opossum, ground squirrel and human were compared to find conserved molecular signatures of the five ancestral photoreceptor types (red, green, blue and UV cones, and rods). The analysis identified and validated markers for the two members of the tetrapod double cone, and suggests the principal member descends from ancestral red cones while the accessory member's origin is less clear. It clarifies how photoreceptor types are related across vertebrates.
papers.authors: Dario Tommasini, Takeshi Yoshimatsu, Teresa Puthussery, Tom Baden, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Molecular states underlying neuronal cell type development and plasticity in the postnatal whisker cortex
papers.abstract: The study assembled a developmental transcriptomic atlas of mouse whisker somatosensory cortex with 45 neuronal types, and tracked how gene expression changes between the onset of whisking and the close of the critical period. Roughly 250 genes were regulated in a subclass-specific manner by sensory experience, and whisker trimming altered these programs. The work shows how experience shapes molecular identity of cortical neuron types.
papers.authors: Salwan Butrus, Hannah R. Monday, Christopher J. Yoo, Daniel E. Feldman, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of ionic reorganization near biological membrane interfaces
papers.abstract: Using theory and simulation, the authors model localized ion pumping across a lipid membrane and show how the resulting ionic gradients and electric fields relax in space and time, both in and out of the membrane plane. This goes beyond the standard equivalent-circuit picture of capacitors and resistors. The results bear on how electrochemical signals propagate near excitable cell membranes.
papers.authors: Hyeongjoo Row, Joshua B. Fernandes, Kranthi K. Mandadapu, Karthik Shekhar

papers.title: Evolution of neuronal cell classes and types in the vertebrate retina
papers.abstract: The authors built and integrated single-cell transcriptomic atlases of the retina from 17 vertebrate species spanning mammals, a bird, a reptile, a teleost and a lamprey. The six retinal cell classes are strongly conserved, while neuronal types diverge more, with retinal ganglion cells and amacrine cells changing the most and some types being species-specific. The work establishes a comparative molecular framework for tracing how visual circuits evolved and how cell types relate across species.
papers.authors: Joshua Hahn, Aboozar Monavarfeshani, Mu Qiao, Allison H. Kao, Yvonne Kölsch, Ayush Kumar, Vincent P. Kunze, Ashley M. Rasys, Rose Richardson, Joseph B. Wekselblatt, Herwig Baier, Robert J. Lucas, Wei Li, Markus Meister, Joshua T. Trachtenberg, Wenjun Yan, Yi-Rong Peng, Joshua R. Sanes, Karthik Shekhar

E281.name: Elizabeth Spelke
E281.bio: Elizabeth Spelke is a researcher in cognitive development who formulated the core knowledge theory, which posits that infants possess innate systems for representing objects, agents, and number. Their methodology utilizes behavioral tasks, such as habituation and looking-time paradigms, to map the cognitive foundations of human knowledge. Spelke’s current research focuses on how these systems interact with language and symbolic thought to facilitate capacities for formal mathematics and abstract reasoning.
E281.research_direction: Dr. Spelke studies the core knowledge systems that infants bring to learning, and how they support children's later mastery of mathematics and other abstract knowledge. Building on the work summarized in What Babies Know, the lab now carries developmental cognitive science into field settings in low- and middle-income countries. One line of work develops an open battery of laboratory-based cognitive tests for children aged 1 to 7, validated with more than 1,400 children in Ghana, with numeracy and spatial reasoning tasks proving especially reliable. Another designs and tests, in large randomized experiments, classroom math games that link children's intuitive sense of number and geometry to school mathematics, aimed at children at high risk of falling behind. Related work in India shows that arithmetic skills children learn in markets and in school do not transfer from one setting to the other.

papers.title: Scaling cognitive science with classroom games for learning mathematics
papers.abstract: Two large randomized trials in low-income Delhi neighborhoods tested math games that tie children's intuitive number and geometry concepts to the language and symbols of school mathematics. In NGO-run preschools (1,986 children) the games improved math mastery immediately and a year later; in government schools (2,828 children) they stayed effective when regular teachers ran them with larger groups. The work shows how basic research on core intuitions can yield interventions that are ready to scale.
papers.authors: Joshua T. Dean, Moira R. Dillon, Esther Duflo, Harini Kannan, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Developing an Open Multi-Domain Assessment Battery Using Laboratory Tasks for Children in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
papers.abstract: The authors adapted experimental paradigms from developmental cognitive science into an open battery of tasks that can be run in noisy outdoor field settings for children in low- and middle-income countries. Administered to 1,435 children in Ghana, the battery tapped abilities that emerge across cultures and predict later skills, with numeracy and spatial reasoning tasks proving especially reliable. It offers a tool for measuring early-childhood intervention impacts.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Joseph R. Coffey, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: The Emergence of a Distinction between Things and Stuff
papers.abstract: Infants aged 4-6 and 13-15 months watched solid objects or sand fall onto a wedge and then either split apart or stay together. Both age groups looked longer when a solid object unexpectedly split, showing robust cohesion expectations for objects. For sand, infants showed no preference either way, suggesting expectations for objects and non-solid substances develop along different trajectories.
papers.authors: Vivian C. Paulun, Sanghee Song, Elizabeth Spelke

papers.title: Children's arithmetic skills do not transfer between applied and academic mathematics
papers.abstract: Surveying about 1,400 working children in markets in Kolkata and Delhi, the authors found that nearly all use complex mental arithmetic fluently at work and can solve concrete market-style problems. Yet the same children largely fail to solve equivalent formal school arithmetic problems, and conversely school-taught skills do not carry over to market settings. The results indicate that skills learned in applied and academic contexts remain largely separate, with implications for how math is taught to at-risk children.
papers.authors: Abhijit V. Banerjee, Swati Bhattacharjee, Raghabendra Chattopadhyay, Esther Duflo, Alejandro J. Ganimian, Kailash Rajah, Elizabeth S. Spelke

papers.title: Toddlers Prefer Agents Who Help Those Facing Harder Tasks
papers.abstract: Across three experiments with 94 sixteen-month-olds, toddlers saw two agents attempt tasks and then help. Toddlers preferentially looked at and reached toward the agent who helped the person in greater need, whether the need stemmed from a more effortful task or a harder-to-achieve goal. This suggests early social evaluation takes the cost of another's task into account.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Brandon Woo, Shari Liu, Hyowon Gweon, Elizabeth S. Spelke

E283.name: John-Dylan Haynes
E283.department: Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience Berlin and Berlin Center for Advanced Neuroimaging
E283.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience and mental state decoding
E283.bio: John-Dylan Haynes is a Professor at the Bernstein Center for Computational Neuroscience Berlin and Director of the Berlin Center for Advanced Neuroimaging. Haynes's research focuses on decoding mental states from human brain activity using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA). Their work on the neural prediction of volitional decisions demonstrates that intentions can be decoded from brain signals several seconds before reaching conscious awareness. Haynes's current research explores the boundaries of brain-reading technology, the neural correlates of consciousness, and the ethical implications of neurotechnology.
E283.research_direction: Dr. Haynes has recently been investigating the neural representations of visual working memory, focusing on how memory formats in the visual cortex differ from those used during active perception. Using fMRI and multivariate decoding, their recent work explores whether early visual areas maintain information in strictly sensory-like formats, or if these neural codes dynamically transform and become categorical during memory delays. They are also testing how the brain protects memory contents from incoming sensory distractors by mapping how perception and memory occupy distinct neural subspaces. Additionally, their research investigates the broader boundaries of visual memory by modeling behavioral readout latency during the rapid decay of iconic memory and probing whether early visual working memory signals actually depend on vivid phenomenal imagery by studying individuals with aphantasia.

papers.title: Visual working memory representations of naturalistic images in early visual cortex are not sensory-like
papers.abstract: Tests the sensory recruitment account of working memory by comparing how early visual cortex encodes naturalistic object scenes during perception versus during memory delays. Memory contents remain decodable throughout the delay. But in the later delay the code no longer matches the format used during perception. The result suggests that early sensory areas hold memory information in a transformed, not strictly sensory-like, format.
papers.authors: Leonardo Pettini, Carsten Bogler, Karla Matic, Kai Gorgen, Christian F. Doeller, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Neural dynamics of visual working memory representation during sensory distraction
papers.abstract: Reanalyses fMRI data in which people held orientations in memory while distractors appeared. Memory codes in visual cortex shift over time and sit in subspaces distinct from those carrying the distractors. Trials where the distractor impaired recall show more overlap between memory and sensory subspaces, supporting a mix of dynamic and stable coding that lets the brain keep perception and memory apart.
papers.authors: Jonas Karolis Degutis, Simon Weber, Joram Soch, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Temporal dynamics and readout latency in perception and iconic memory
papers.abstract: Uses closely spaced readout cues together with a model of information availability to study the transition from perception into iconic memory. Reportable information already begins to decay when a cue arrives 10 to 30 ms before stimulus offset. The authors attribute this to a cue-processing latency delaying readout, not to early loss of sensory encoding. They also show that spatial proximity of items affects the representation during encoding and early decay.
papers.authors: Karla Matic, Issam Tafech, Peter Konig, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Working memory signals in early visual cortex are present in weak and strong imagers
papers.abstract: Compares people with strong and weak visual imagery on a delayed-recall task, decoding remembered images from early visual cortex. Reconstruction quality was just as good in weak imagers, including aphantasic participants, and tracked behavioural precision in both groups. This indicates that early visual working memory signals do not depend on vivid phenomenal imagery.
papers.authors: Simon Weber, Thomas Christophel, Kai Gorgen, Joram Soch, John-Dylan Haynes

papers.title: Categorical working memory codes in human visual cortex
papers.abstract: Uses fMRI and multivariate encoding models to show that color is stored categorically in extrastriate areas V4 and VO1 during working memory, even when observers are not prompted to categorize. The categorical code appears in memory but not in perception. This supports the view that visual working memory relies partly on abstracted representations.
papers.authors: Chang Yan, Thomas B. Christophel, Carsten Allefeld, John-Dylan Haynes

E284.name: Marius Peelen
E284.bio: Marius Peelen is a Professor of Visual and Cognitive Neuroscience and a Principal Investigator at the Donders Institute. Peelen investigates the neural mechanisms that enable efficient object and scene perception in naturalistic environments, bridging the gap between low-level visual processing and higher-order cognitive functions. Utilizing multivariate neuroimaging techniques such as fMRI and MEG alongside behavioral psychophysics, Peelen examines how top-down factors—including attention, expectations, and episodic memory—shape cortical representations. Recent work by Peelen focuses on the predictive nature of the visual system and the competitive interactions between external sensory input and internal cognitive processes like visual imagery.
E284.research_direction: Dr. Peelen’s recent work explores how real-world context and learned associations guide human visual perception and attention. Using fMRI, eye-tracking, and multivariate pattern analysis, they have recently been investigating how the visual cortex uses 3D scene structure and object co-occurrence to generate predictions that dynamically update object representations, even during full occlusion. Their research also examines how attention operates in naturalistic settings by probing how the brain balances flexible, goal-driven search templates with stable, experience-based spatial priors and anchor objects. Furthermore, Dr. Peelen is advancing the methodological rigor of the field by establishing frameworks for using multivariate neuroimaging data to explicitly test cognitive theories of high-level vision rather than merely demonstrating information decodability.

papers.title: Dynamic context-based updating of object representations in the visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using two fMRI studies, the paper shows that visual cortex updates object representations using predictions from the surrounding 3D scene. Object representations were stronger when an object rotated consistently with the scene, and the inferred orientation of a fully occluded object could be decoded from cortical activity.
papers.authors: Giacomo Aldegheri, Surya Gayet, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: Attention in the wild: balancing flexibility and stability
papers.abstract: A review of how attention operates in naturalistic settings, where searches are guided by scene context, associated objects and learned regularities. It discusses how flexible, goal-driven attentional templates are balanced against stable, experience-based priors.
papers.authors: Maëlle Lerebourg, Surya Gayet, Floris P. de Lange, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: Predictive processing of scenes and objects
papers.abstract: Reviews how the visual system uses knowledge about scene structure and object co-occurrence to generate predictions that shape perception. It covers evidence for predictive signals in visual cortex, their role in facilitating recognition and search, and points to open questions about the neural implementation of context-based prediction.
papers.authors: Marius V. Peelen, Eva Berlot, Floris P. de Lange

papers.title: Attentional guidance through object associations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: In an fMRI and eye-tracking context-guided search task, participants searched for targets that were paired with associated anchor objects. First fixations were guided by the anchor, and preparatory activity in visual cortex reflected the anchor object as well as the target, showing that context-associated objects shape attentional templates.
papers.authors: Maëlle Lerebourg, Floris P. de Lange, Marius V. Peelen

papers.title: Testing cognitive theories with multivariate pattern analysis of neuroimaging data
papers.abstract: Argues that multivariate pattern analysis of fMRI/MEG/EEG should be used to test explicit predictions of cognitive theories rather than only to show that information is decodable. The authors lay out how to link theory-derived hypotheses to pattern-based measures, using examples from object, scene and body perception, and discuss common pitfalls in interpretation.
papers.authors: Marius V. Peelen, Paul E. Downing

E286.name: Shinji Nishimoto
E286.bio: Nishimoto is a Professor at Osaka University and a Principal Investigator at the Center for Information and Neural Networks (CiNet). Their research focuses on the quantitative modeling of human brain activity evoked by naturalistic stimuli to investigate the neural basis of perceptual and cognitive functions. Nishimoto has worked on reconstructing dynamic visual experiences from fMRI signals and developing brain-decoding techniques using deep learning and generative models. Their current projects involve building high-dimensional encoding models to examine how the brain represents information across diverse modalities, timescales, and internal states.
E286.research_direction: Dr. Nishimoto has recently been leveraging state-of-the-art generative AI to decode and map complex, naturalistic experiences from human brain activity. Their recent work explores high-fidelity sensory reconstruction, utilizing latent diffusion models to recreate viewed images and text-to-music architectures to decode auditory semantics directly from fMRI signals. Beyond sensory decoding, they are investigating how the cortex organizes higher-level cognitive representations, such as the hierarchical timescales of spontaneous conversation modeled via large language models. Additionally, their broader neuroimaging program evaluates the representational geometry of subject-specific cognitive states across diverse tasks and systematically benchmarks the limits of visual information decoding across fMRI, MEG, and EEG.

papers.title: A Quantitative Benchmark of Visual Information in Human Brain Recordings Across fMRI, MEG, and EEG
papers.abstract: This preprint builds a unified decoding framework to compare fMRI, MEG and EEG under matched conditions using the same naturalistic THINGS stimuli. fMRI gives by far the best object-category decoding, MEG is intermediate, and single-subject EEG is lower, with analyses of how much visual information each modality retains. It provides a quantitative reference for choosing noninvasive recording methods in visual decoding.
papers.authors: Taisei Hara, Yoshito Masai, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Text-to-music generation models capture musical semantic representations in the human brain
papers.abstract: Using fMRI while people listened to music, the study reconstructs the music either by retrieval or by conditioning Google's MusicLM on brain activity, producing audio that matches the heard music in genre, instrument and mood. Encoding analyses show that internal representations of the text-to-music model predict auditory cortex activity, and reveal that musical text descriptions are represented in distinct cortical areas.
papers.authors: Timo I. Denk, Yu Takagi, Takuya Matsuyama, Andrea Agostinelli, Tomoya Nakai, Christian Frank, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Conversational content is organized across multiple timescales in the brain
papers.abstract: Participants underwent fMRI during hours of spontaneous two-person conversation, and neural responses were modelled with GPT contextual embeddings computed over different timescales. Representations of produced and perceived speech overlap in some regions and differ in others, with longer timescales tied to higher-level cortical areas. The work shows how the brain integrates conversation into hierarchical discourse structure.
papers.authors: Masahiro Yamashita, Rieko Kubo, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: Cortical representational geometry of diverse tasks reveals subject-specific and subject-invariant cognitive structures
papers.abstract: Using fMRI across 25 cognitive tasks, the study combines inter-subject correlation, representational similarity analysis and vertex-wise encoding models to quantify individual differences in task-relation structure. Individuals can be identified with perfect accuracy from as few as 14 tasks, and association cortex shows more subject-specific structure than sensorimotor cortex, while some structure is shared across people.
papers.authors: Tomoya Nakai, Rieko Kubo, Shinji Nishimoto

papers.title: High-resolution image reconstruction with latent diffusion models from human brain activity
papers.abstract: The authors reconstruct images a person viewed from their fMRI activity by mapping brain signals onto the latent space and text conditioning of Stable Diffusion, with no training or fine-tuning of the generative model itself. The approach yields high-fidelity, semantically faithful reconstructions and, as a by-product, lets them ask which brain regions carry image layout versus semantic information. It became a landmark demonstration of diffusion-based brain decoding.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
papers.authors: Yu Takagi, Shinji Nishimoto

E287.name: Umut Güçlü
E287.bio: Umut Güçlü is a Principal Investigator at the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, focusing on the integration of neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Güçlü’s research utilizes deep learning and in silico connectionism to develop computational frameworks for neural encoding and decoding, often referred to as 'brain reading' and 'brain writing.' They have worked on the reconstruction of perceived natural images from brain activity using generative adversarial networks and the characterization of feature complexity gradients in the human visual system. As an ELLIS Scholar, Güçlü’s work involves simulating and emulating in vivo neural computation to investigate the synergy between biological and machine intelligence.
E287.research_direction: Dr. Güçlü has recently been working on reconstructing what a person or animal sees from recorded brain activity, using deep learning. Their recent work builds decoders that turn fMRI signals in humans and multi-electrode recordings in macaque visual cortex into images and video, with attention mechanisms that decide which brain regions matter for each part of the reconstruction. They build these models around known brain organization, such as the spatial map of the visual field across cortex, and also make encoding models that predict neural responses from images. They have also compared how the macaque visual cortex aligns with the internal features of image-generating networks like GANs and diffusion models.

papers.title: Neural encoding with affine feature response transforms
papers.abstract: This study introduces Affine Feature Response Transforms (AFRT), a methodology designed to integrate neuroscientifically grounded spatial priors into linearizing encoding models that characterize the mapping from sensory stimuli to neural activity. Standard encoding frameworks often overlook the intrinsic retinotopic organization of the brain, which can compromise model efficiency and the biological interpretability of the learned feature mappings. AFRT addresses this by formalizing the feature response through affine transformations that respect the spatial topology of the cortex. When applied to high-dimensional neuroimaging datasets, AFRT demonstrates improved predictive performance for voxel-level responses and provides more coherent representations of receptive field characteristics, thereby enhancing the functional alignment between artificial feature spaces and biological neural hierarchies.
papers.authors: Lynn Lê, Nils Kimman, Thirza Dado, Katja Seeliger, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Pieter Roelfsema, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: Inverse receptive field attention for naturalistic image reconstruction from the brain
papers.abstract: This research presents a novel neural decoding paradigm for the high-fidelity reconstruction of naturalistic images and videos from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data by leveraging the functional organization of neuronal receptive fields. The proposed Inverse Receptive Field Attention mechanism explicitly exploits spatial priors derived from retinotopic mapping to constrain the latent representations of image-to-image transformation networks. By integrating these spatial mappings into a generative modeling pipeline, the framework significantly improves the structural and semantic accuracy of visual reconstructions compared to baseline models. The approach demonstrates that incorporating biologically inspired spatial attention allows for the recovery of complex, dynamic visual experiences from large-scale, single-participant neuroimaging datasets with unprecedented detail.
papers.authors: Lynn Lê, Thirza Dado, Katja Seeliger, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Pieter Roelfsema, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Marcel van Gerven, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: MonkeySee: Space-time-resolved reconstructions of natural images from macaque multi-unit activity
papers.abstract: This paper presents a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based decoder architecture designed to reconstruct naturalistic images from multi-unit activity (MUA) recorded via Utah arrays in macaque cortical areas V1, V4, and IT. The authors investigate the differentiation of neural readout characteristics across the visual hierarchy, demonstrating that the CNN-based technique effectively captures region-specific representations. A key contribution is the development of a space-time-resolved decoding framework that leverages the high temporal resolution of MUA to capture the dynamics of visual processing. Additionally, the introduction of a Learned Receptive Field (LRF) layer allows the model to dynamically organize neural inputs into 2D spatial representations during training, significantly enhancing both the fidelity of the reconstructions and the structural interpretability of the decoding process.
papers.authors: Lynn Le, Paolo Papale, Katja Seeliger, Antonio Lozano, Thirza Dado, Feng Wang, Pieter Roelfsema, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: PAM: Predictive attention mechanism for neural decoding of visual perception
papers.abstract: This work introduces Predictive Attention Mechanisms (PAMs), a novel task-driven architectural component for neural decoding that optimizes the integration of neural signals across the cortical hierarchy. Unlike standard self-attention mechanisms that compute input-input relationships, PAMs learn optimized 'output queries' during training that specifically target neural responses most relevant for reconstructing the latent features of generative models. This approach facilitates the dynamic allocation of attention across diverse brain regions based on their functional relevance to the reconstruction task. Validated on both macaque multi-unit activity and human fMRI datasets, PAM-enhanced decoders demonstrate superior performance in mapping brain activity to the latent spaces of generative adversarial networks and diffusion models, yielding high-precision reconstructions of perceived naturalistic stimuli.
papers.authors: Thirza Dado, Lynn Le, Marcel van Gerven, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

papers.title: Brain2GAN: Feature-disentangled neural encoding and decoding of visual perception in the primate brain
papers.abstract: This study characterizes the alignment between high-level neural representations in the macaque visual cortex and the feature-disentangled latent spaces of contemporary generative adversarial networks (GANs) and diffusion models. By analyzing multi-unit activity (MUA) recorded during a passive fixation task involving naturalistic images and faces, the authors compare the neural encoding efficacy of StyleGAN's z- and w-latents alongside language-contrastive CLIP representations. Mass univariate encoding analyses reveal that disentangled w-latent features significantly outperform conventional latents in predicting cortical responses, particularly in higher-level visual areas. Leveraging these feature-disentangled representations, the authors implement a multivariate decoding pipeline that achieves state-of-the-art spatiotemporal reconstructions of visual perception, underscoring the critical role of disentanglement in modeling biological visual processing.
papers.authors: Thirza Dado, Paolo Papale, Antonio Lozano, Lynn Le, Feng Wang, Marcel van Gerven, Pieter Roelfsema, Yağmur Güçlütürk, Umut Güçlü

E289.name: Gemma Roig
E289.lab_name: Computational Vision and Artificial Intelligence (CVAI) Lab
E289.bio: Gemma Roig is a Full Professor at Goethe University Frankfurt and leads the Computational Vision and Artificial Intelligence lab. Roig’s research integrates computer vision with cognitive neuroscience to develop brain-inspired AI architectures and uses deep neural networks as models for predicting human brain activity and behavior. They investigate representational alignment, multimodal learning, and invariant object recognition, utilizing data from MRI and EEG to benchmark machine intelligence against human perception. Before joining Goethe University, Roig held research and faculty positions at the Singapore University of Technology and Design and the MIT Center for Brains, Minds and Machines.
E289.research_direction: Dr. Roig's recent work explores the inner workings of deep neural networks by integrating conceptual tools and analytical techniques from cognitive neuroscience. They have recently been investigating the mechanistic interpretability of vision transformers and vision-language models, using methods like causal mediation, attention knockout, and representation projection to understand how these architectures route information to build category decisions and localize objects. Additionally, their research examines model robustness, seeking to identify and mitigate unsupervised shortcut learning by probing the behavior of specific attention heads when models rely on spurious visual cues. To further bridge artificial and biological vision, they are also developing open-source neuroinformatics frameworks that enable researchers to directly benchmark the internal representations of artificial vision models against human fMRI and electrophysiological data.

papers.title: Mechanisms of Object Localization in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Using ablations, attention knockout and causal mediation on LLaVA-1.5 and InternVL-3.5, the paper dissects how vision-language models figure out where an object is. Localization turns out to rely on object-aligned tokens that mark the object's spatial extent, with the arrangement of tokens inside that region mattering little. A very small set of attention heads carries the causal effect for both classification and localization, though the two tasks mostly rely on distinct specialized heads.
papers.authors: Timothy Schaumlöffel, Martina G. Vilas, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Efficient Unsupervised Shortcut Learning Detection and Mitigation in Transformers
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a way to find shortcut features (spurious cues a model exploits instead of the true signal) in transformers without needing any labels for those cues. By inspecting how attention heads and representations behave, it flags shortcut-reliant behavior and then reduces it with a lightweight mitigation step. Experiments on standard shortcut benchmarks show the approach is efficient and competitive with methods that require supervision.
papers.venue: IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
papers.authors: Lukas Kuhn, Sari Saba-Sadiya, Jörg Schlötterer, Florian Buettner, Christin Seifert, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Net2Brain: a toolbox to compare artificial vision models with human brain responses
papers.abstract: Net2Brain is an open-source Python toolbox that lets researchers extract features from hundreds of pretrained vision networks and compare them directly with human brain data. It bundles standard representational similarity analysis and encoding-style comparisons, along with ready-to-use fMRI and MEG/EEG datasets, so that model-brain benchmarking takes a few lines of code. The paper documents the design and demonstrates it on several worked examples.
papers.authors: Domenic Bersch, Martina G. Vilas, Sari Saba-Sadiya, Timothy Schaumlöffel, Kshitij Dwivedi, Christina Sartzetaki, Radoslaw M. Cichy, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Position: An Inner Interpretability Framework for AI Inspired by Lessons from Cognitive Neuroscience
papers.abstract: This ICML position paper argues that current 'inner interpretability' work on neural networks can borrow mature conceptual tools from cognitive neuroscience. It organizes methods into a framework distinguishing what a model represents from how it computes, and shows how neuroscience-style approaches (lesion, decoding, causal manipulation) map onto AI systems. It also points out shortcomings of present practice and proposes directions for more principled analysis.
papers.authors: Martina G. Vilas, Federico Adolfi, David Poeppel, Gemma Roig

papers.title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space
papers.abstract: The authors project the internal token representations of vision transformers into the space of the classifier's class embeddings, letting them read out which classes each layer and token are already 'voting' for. This reveals how class-specific evidence is gradually built up across layers and how it is routed through attention, and they use it to trace back which image regions and earlier tokens produce a given prediction. The approach offers a concrete mechanistic account of how ViTs turn patches into category decisions.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS)
papers.authors: Martina G. Vilas, Timothy Schaumlöffel, Gemma Roig

E290.name: Hee-Yeon Im
E290.bio: Hee-Yeon Im is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of British Columbia and the Principal Investigator of the Interactive Mind and Movement Lab. Im’s research investigates the neurocognitive mechanisms mediating the interaction between visual perception and goal-directed motor actions across typical and atypical development. Utilizing multimodal neuroimaging techniques such as magnetoencephalography (MEG) and functional MRI alongside psychophysics, they examine how the brain organizes visual inputs to guide task-relevant behaviors in various social and physical environments.
E290.research_direction: Dr. Im has recently been studying how children learn to adjust their movements when what they see no longer matches what they do, as in visuomotor adaptation with a rotated cursor. Their recent work compares school-age children with adults, looking at how quickly and accurately they reach and how that behavior changes as they develop. They also use magnetoencephalography to track brain oscillations during these reaches, asking how the brain's feedforward and feedback-related processes mature at different rates.

papers.title: Developmental changes in MEG oscillatory activity during visuomotor adaptation: Differential maturation of feedforward and feedback-related mechanisms
papers.abstract: Visuomotor adaptation—the sensorimotor recalibration of reach trajectories using visual discrepancy signals—matures continuously throughout childhood, yet the precise electrophysiological dynamics governing this ontogeny remain insufficiently elucidated. Whole-head magnetoencephalography (MEG) was recorded in children (6–12 years) and adults executing reaching movements toward targets under an abrupt 45° cursor rotation. Cortical oscillatory power was segregated into two distinct kinematic phases: the pre-peak velocity interval (dominated by feedforward predictive control) and the post-peak velocity deceleration interval (dominated by online feedback-driven correction). While both cohorts successfully adapted reaching trajectories, adult participants demonstrated superior accuracy, higher velocity, and decreased temporal variance. During the feedforward phase, children exhibited reduced pre-movement beta synchronization and attenuated post-stimulus beta desynchronization across motor, parietal, and occipital cortices compared to adults, reflecting immature predictive internal modeling. Concurrently, children showed prolonged, elevated prefrontal theta power following target display, consistent with enhanced reliance on executive supervisory mechanisms. In contrast, oscillatory divergences between age cohorts narrowed substantially during the deceleration window, suggesting that feedback-mediated trajectory correction matures closer to adult levels earlier than feedforward motor preparation. Stronger brain-behavior coupling between cortical oscillations and adaptation metrics in children highlights ongoing neurodevelopmental specialization.
papers.authors: Minsu Song, Alexander J. Cook, Advitya Hajela, Deborah E. Giaschi, Hee-Yeon Im

papers.title: Speed and Accuracy of Movement During Visuomotor Adaptation Are Still Developing in School-Age Children
papers.abstract: Visuomotor adaptation serves as a fundamental mechanism for acquiring and refining motor competencies during development. Although children as young as age five can compensate for rotational visual perturbations, the kinematic and temporal characteristics distinguishing pediatric adaptation from mature performance remain incompletely specified. Kinematic parameters—including onset latency, movement duration, velocity profiles, and directional error curves—were contrasted between adults (19–45 years) and school-aged children stratified into younger (6–8 years) and older (9–12 years) groups during reaching tasks under visual rotation. Adults and older children exhibited exponential reductions in angular error characteristic of cognitive feedforward re-aiming integrated with implicit calibration, whereas younger children demonstrated a linear error reduction profile with prolonged onset latencies, reflecting heavier dependence on slower feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, while terminal endpoint accuracy asymptotically approached adult levels by the end of training blocks across all cohorts, movement velocity and temporal stability remained immature in school-age children, indicating divergent developmental timetables for speed versus spatial accuracy optimization in sensorimotor recalibration.
papers.authors: Alexander J. Cook, Deborah E. Giaschi, Hee Yeon Im

E291.name: Nicole Rust
E291.bio: Rust is a Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, focusing on the neural and computational mechanisms of visual object recognition and memory. Their research group combines behavioral experiments, large-scale neural recordings, and machine learning to examine how neurons in the inferotemporal cortex encode image memorability and familiarity. As a Simons Foundation Pivot Fellow, Rust applies systems neuroscience to investigate the biological basis of human emotion and mood. Rust also works on applying complex-systems frameworks to brain research, specifically regarding the challenges of treating psychiatric and neurological disorders.
E291.research_direction: Dr. Rust has recently been investigating how the primate brain transforms visual inputs into signals of memory and familiarity, using macaque electrophysiology across the inferotemporal cortex and medial temporal lobe to probe phenomena like single-exposure memorability and visual pattern separation. Their recent work also explores the methodological challenge of translating between animal spiking and human-proxy local field potentials, testing how representations coded by population response magnitudes, such as novelty and recency, align differently across recording scales compared to distributed categorical codes. Beyond visual cognition, they have been examining the neural basis of emotion by modeling subjective mood fluctuations during gambling tasks to isolate persistent affective signals in the primate anterior insula. Additionally, their scholarship tackles broader theoretical challenges in neuroscience, analyzing how the ways researchers define core functions like memory, attention, and emotion shape experimental design and interpretation.

papers.title: Sharpened Visual Memory Representations Are Reflected in Inferotemporal Cortex
papers.abstract: Monkeys reliably judged whether images were repeats even when similar lures were present, and their memory performance was sharper than expected from the visual representation in inferotemporal cortex alone. Recordings from both hippocampus and ITC showed neural correlates of this behavioral sharpening. The results indicate that pattern-separation-like computations are not unique to the hippocampus but are also reflected in ITC.
papers.authors: Barnes G. L. Jannuzi, Catrina M. Hacker, Simon Bohn, Travis Meyer, Madison L. Hay, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: Neural representations of visual memory in inferotemporal cortex reveal a generalizable framework for translating between spikes and field potentials
papers.abstract: Spiking and high-gamma LFP activity align in macaque ITC for variables coded as population response magnitude (novelty, recency, memorability) but not for variables coded as distributed patterns (category). Re-analysis of prior studies shows the same principle explains earlier successes and failures. The paper offers a framework for translating between animal spiking and human LFP.
papers.authors: Catrina M. Hacker, Simon Bohn, Brett L. Foster, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: A two-stage algorithm underlies the transformation from vision to familiarity in the primate brain
papers.abstract: Using image memorability as a probe, the authors compared ITC and hippocampal responses while macaques performed a single-exposure familiarity task. ITC mixes memorability and familiarity signals (repetition suppression stronger for memorable images) but the mixture is linearly decodable, whereas the medial temporal lobe extracts a cleaner familiarity signal with little memorability modulation. This supports a two-stage transformation from visual representation to familiarity.
papers.authors: Simon Bohn, Catrina M. Hacker, Barnes G. L. Jannuzi, Travis Meyer, Madison L. Hay, Nicole C. Rust

papers.title: The representation of mood in primate anterior insular cortex
papers.abstract: The authors built a human mood model predicting fluctuations in subjective happiness during a gambling task, then applied the same task to monkeys. Persistent responses of anterior insular units matched the model's signatures, including its integration timescale, while dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reflected them only weakly. This points to recurrent integration of events in insula as a neural basis of mood.
papers.authors: Nicole C. Rust, You-Ping C. Yang, Catrina M. Hacker, Veit Stuphorn

papers.title: The tricky business of defining brain functions
papers.abstract: This opinion piece argues that the ways neuroscientists define functions such as memory, attention, or emotion are often ambiguous and can mislead research. The authors, from different theoretical camps, discuss how differing definitions of a function cause conflicting conclusions and suggest ways to improve conceptual clarity.
papers.authors: Nicole C. Rust, Joseph E. LeDoux

E292.name: Christopher Niell
E292.department: Department of Biology and Institute of Neuroscience
E292.bio: Christopher Niell is a Professor at the University of Oregon who investigates the neural circuits underlying visual perception and behavior. Niell's research group utilizes methodologies including two-photon calcium imaging and high-density extracellular recordings to analyze the functional organization of the visual system. Their research established that behavioral states, such as locomotion, modulate sensory processing in the primary visual cortex. Niell’s current research explores visual processing during naturalistic ethological tasks and examines the neural architecture of the octopus brain to study the evolution of visual systems.
E292.research_direction: Dr. Niell has recently been investigating how the visual system operates under natural, ecologically relevant conditions, with a major focus on active vision in freely moving animals. Their recent work explores the role of gaze shifts—coordinated head and eye movements—as discrete sampling events to understand how these behaviors initiate temporally structured visual processing sequences in the primary visual cortex and the superior colliculus. By combining high-density electrophysiology and behavioral tracking in species like mice and marmosets, they are examining how movement dynamics and newly sampled visual inputs shape neural responses outside of traditional head-fixed paradigms. Expanding the comparative breadth of their research, Dr. Niell is also utilizing calcium imaging to map the functional architecture of the octopus optic lobe, probing the retinotopic organization and feature tuning of the cephalopod visual system.

papers.title: Temporally organized activity in mouse V1 encodes newly sampled visual content during free movement
papers.abstract: Building on the gaze-shift sequence in V1, the authors show that the size of the visual change caused by each gaze shift scales response amplitude, whereas movement magnitude alone does not in darkness. Head-fixed receptive-field filters predict response timing during free movement, and population decoding moves toward the newly sampled scene. Gaze shifts therefore act as sampling events after which V1 encodes visual information in a temporally ordered way.
papers.authors: Jhoseph Shin, Elliott T. T. Abe, Philip R. L. Parker, Dylan M. Martins, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: Ecological Visual Processing in the Mouse
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes what is known about how the mouse visual system supports natural behaviors such as prey capture, threat detection and navigation. It argues that studying vision in ecologically relevant, freely moving contexts reveals computations that are missed with passive stimuli in head-fixed animals. It also outlines open questions for linking circuits to behavior.
papers.authors: Cristopher M. Niell, Michael Beyeler, Michael J. Goard, Spencer LaVere Smith

papers.title: Neural dynamics in superior colliculus of freely moving mice
papers.abstract: The authors recorded from the superficial and deep layers of the superior colliculus with high-density probes while mice moved freely and explored their environment, tracking head and eye movements. Activity in the two layers was shaped differently by gaze shifts and by the visual input each movement brought in. The work extends the study of colliculus function from head-fixed screens to natural active vision.
papers.authors: Shelby L. Sharp, Jhoseph Shin, Dylan M. Martins, Keaton Jones, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: A dynamic sequence of visual processing initiated by gaze shifts
papers.abstract: Recording V1 in freely moving mice and freely gazing marmosets, the study shows that neurons respond mainly to gaze shifts, where head movement is paired with compensatory eye movement. Responses unfold as a temporal sequence in which new visual input is processed from coarse to fine. This reframes movement-related V1 activity as an organized sampling sequence conserved across species.
papers.authors: Philip R. L. Parker, Dylan M. Martins, Emmalyn S. P. Leonard, Nathan M. Casey, Shelby L. Sharp, Elliott T. T. Abe, Matthew C. Smear, Jacob L. Yates, Jude F. Mitchell, Cristopher M. Niell

papers.title: Functional organization of visual responses in the octopus optic lobe
papers.abstract: Using calcium imaging in the octopus optic lobe, the authors mapped how neurons respond to visual stimuli across the region. They found retinotopic organization and neurons tuned to features such as spatial structure and motion, with a layered functional architecture. This provides some of the first physiological evidence of visual processing in a cephalopod brain.
papers.authors: Judit R. Pungor, V. Angelique Allen, Jeremea O. Songco-Casey, Cristopher M. Niell

E294.name: Andrea Benucci
E294.department: School of Biological and Behavioural Sciences
E294.lab_name: Laboratory for Neural Circuits and Behavior
E294.bio: Andrea Benucci is a neuroscientist who investigates the computational principles of sensory processing and visual perception. Benucci's research integrates large-scale neural recordings, such as two-photon imaging and high-density electrophysiology, with patterned optogenetic manipulations and artificial neural network modeling. They developed automated, high-throughput behavioral platforms that standardize mouse training for complex visual tasks to facilitate the study of population-level neural dynamics. Their recent work focuses on the plasticity of cortical representations and how non-visual signals, including motor-related inputs, are integrated within the visual hierarchy to support perceptual stability and decision-making.
E294.research_direction: Dr. Benucci has recently been studying how the mouse visual cortex encodes natural scenes and combines vision with the animal's own movements and internal state. Their recent work asks how visual areas represent natural textures, and whether this reflects efficient coding of image statistics. They also model how eye movements and other behavioral signals interact in cortex, and how these interactions shift with arousal. A further line uses widefield calcium imaging in mice performing a visual discrimination task to map how choice-related signals are distributed across posterior cortex.

papers.title: Regularizing hyperparameters of interacting neural signals in the mouse cortex reflect states of arousal
papers.abstract: Cortical networks concurrently represent and nonlinearly integrate pervasive movement-related signals alongside sensory inputs, yet regularizing the spatiotemporal interaction kernels between such multifaceted behavioral signals poses significant inferential challenges. Applying an Automatic Locality Determination (ALD) Bayesian regularization framework to widefield calcium recordings in GCaMP6s mice, we modeled the second-order, quadratic interaction kernels between saccadic eye movements and body movements across the posterior cortex during a visual discrimination task. We observed that the estimated ALD hyperparameters governing kernel smoothness, scale, and spatial locality systematically vary across individual animals in proportion to the magnitude of signal interactions, the variability of visual responses, and overall trial-to-trial variance. These hyperparameter fluctuations strongly track internal cognitive states, demonstrating significant positive correlations with pupil diameter variations as a physiological metric of arousal and attentional engagement. Consequently, regularizing hyperparameters inferred from generalized linear models serve as an objective readout of behavioral and cognitive states shaping cortical population dynamics.
papers.authors: Dmitry R. Lyamzin, Andrea Alamia, Mohammad Abdolrahmani, Ryo Aoki, Andrea Benucci

papers.title: Efficient coding of natural images in the mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: The computational mechanisms by which ventral visual areas extract and encode naturalistic texture statistics to drive perception remain insufficiently understood. Using psychophysical paradigms in mice, we demonstrate that rodents can accurately discriminate natural textures from spectrally matched synthesized noise scrambles as well as differentiate across distinct texture families. Widefield calcium imaging across the visual cortex in untrained mice revealed that the secondary visual area (LM) demonstrates markedly greater selectivity for natural textures than primary visual cortex (V1), driven by higher-order statistical features parameterized via the Portilla–Simoncelli model. Textures are embedded in distinct low-dimensional neural subspaces whose distances correlate directly with stimulus statistical divergence and behavioral discriminability. These neural manifolds are significantly more compact in LM than in V1, yielding enhanced linear decoding performance. These findings identify texture perception in mice and provide an empirical link connecting natural image statistics, cortical subspace geometry, and perceptual discriminability in accordance with efficient coding principles.
papers.authors: Federico Bolaños, Javier G. Orlandi, Ryo Aoki, Akshay V. Jagadeesh, Justin L. Gardner, Andrea Benucci

papers.title: Distributed context-dependent choice information in mouse posterior cortex
papers.abstract: Choice signals across posterior cortical networks are commonly intertwined with concurrent sensory and motor activations, limiting understanding of their functional role in decision computations. We conducted mesoscale calcium imaging across the posterior cortex of mice performing an invariant visual orientation discrimination task designed to minimize mnemonic, motor, and novel sensory confounds. Choice signals defined an independent decision variable distributed across multi-area networks, with substantial representation along the ventral visual stream. This choice subspace remained nearly orthogonal to co-occurring sensory and motor representation dimensions and was systematically modulated by discrimination difficulty and attentional engagement. Training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) directly on empirical choice behavior yielded an equivalent decision variable whose low-dimensional trajectories matched the context-dependent dynamics of the cortical data. These findings reveal a distributed, context-dependent decision variable in the posterior cortex suited for flexible inference computations during dynamic task engagement.
papers.authors: Javier G. Orlandi, Mohammad Abdolrahmani, Ryo Aoki, Dmitry R. Lyamzin, Andrea Benucci

E295.name: Alessandra Angelucci
E295.bio: Angelucci investigates the anatomical organization and functional properties of neuronal circuits within the visual cerebral cortex to understand the mechanisms of visual perception. Their research employs optical imaging, array electrophysiology, optogenetics, and neuroanatomical tracing to map the connectivity of feedforward and feedback pathways. Angelucci’s work examines how these circuits integrate contextual information and modulate parallel processing streams between cortical areas such as V1 and V2. Their laboratory also develops computational neural network models to simulate cortical computations and explores the role of inhibitory interneuron subtypes in sensory processing.
E295.research_direction: Dr. Angelucci has recently been investigating the laminar microcircuitry of the primate primary visual cortex (V1) alongside the development of advanced neurotechnologies to probe these networks. Their recent work explores how specific cortical layers and inhibitory cell types, such as parvalbumin-expressing interneurons, govern fundamental computations like orientation tuning and the spatial surround modulation of neural response variability. To enable precise mechanistic studies in non-human primates, they are evaluating viral-mediated strategies for the selective genetic targeting of these GABAergic populations. Furthermore, they are validating the functional efficacy and acute tissue biocompatibility of the Utah Optrode Array, aiming to optimize this high-density penetrating device for large-scale, depth-resolved optogenetic stimulation. She also investigates the anatomical organization and function of corticocortical feedback projections using viral technology and optogenetics in the marmoset monkey.

papers.title: Size tuning of neural response variability in laminar circuits of macaque primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Recordings across cortical layers of macaque V1 with laminar probes were used to ask how trial-to-trial variability depends on stimulus size. Variability is quenched more strongly by stimuli that engage the surround, and this effect differs across layers and neuron types, pointing to feedback and lateral connections as a source. The results tie the circuit mechanisms of surround suppression to changes in the reliability of neural responses.
papers.authors: Lauri Nurminen, Maryam Bijanzadeh, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Laminar-specific control of response gain and orientation-tuning by parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Viral vectors restricted to GABAergic cells were used to express opsins in parvalbumin interneurons of macaque V1, and activity was recorded across layers while these cells were manipulated. The perturbations changed response gain and orientation tuning in ways that depended on cortical layer. This gives causal evidence for how a defined inhibitory class shapes basic V1 computations in the primate.
papers.authors: Amin Vafaei, Andrew M Clark, Alireza Khadir, Weifeng Dai, Frederick Federer, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: An Optrode Array for Spatiotemporally Precise Large-Scale Optogenetic Stimulation of Deep Cortical Layers in Non-human Primates
papers.abstract: The paper introduces the Utah Optrode Array, a grid of penetrating light emitters that delivers patterned light to deep cortical layers over a large volume of tissue. In macaque cortex, it drives optogenetic responses with high spatial and temporal precision, which surface illumination cannot achieve in primates. The device makes circuit-level optogenetic experiments feasible in large primate brains.
papers.authors: Andrew M. Clark, Andrew Ingold, Christopher F. Reiche, David Cundy, Julie L. Balsor, Frederick Federer, Niall McAlinden, Yiyuan Cheng, John D. Rolston, Lars Rieth, Martin D. Dawson, Keith Mathieson, Steve Blair, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Primate V2 Receptive Fields Derived from Anatomically Identified Large-Scale V1 Inputs
papers.abstract: Combining anatomical tracing of the V1 neurons that project to a given V2 site with receptive-field mapping in V1, the study reconstructs the inputs that each V2 location receives. The pooled V1 inputs are then used to predict V2 receptive-field properties. It links large-scale feedforward anatomy to the emergence of more complex selectivity along the ventral stream.
papers.authors: Mahlega S. Hassanpour, Sam Merlin, Frederick Federer, Qasim Zaidi, Alessandra Angelucci

papers.title: Laminar specificity and coverage of viral-mediated gene expression restricted to GABAergic interneurons and their parvalbumin subclass in marmoset primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: The authors evaluate AAV vectors with enhancers targeting GABAergic interneurons and the parvalbumin subclass in marmoset V1. They quantify how specifically and how completely each vector labels the intended cells in each cortical layer. The results give practical guidance for cell-type-specific circuit manipulation in nonhuman primates.
papers.authors: Frederick Federer, Julie Balsor, Andrew Ingold, David P. Babcock, Jordane Dimidschstein, Alessandra Angelucci

E296.name: Marlene Cohen
E296.bio: Marlene R. Cohen is a Professor of Neurobiology at the University of Chicago, investigating how neuronal populations encode sensory information to guide behavior. Cohen’s research examines visual attention, specifically how it modulates noise correlations between neurons to affect the fidelity of the population code. Using high-density multi-electrode electrophysiology and computational modeling, their lab characterizes the relationship between large-scale neural dynamics and perceptual decisions. Their current work focuses on identifying the neural principles of cognitive flexibility and exploring translational applications related to attention disorders and neurodegeneration.
E296.research_direction: Dr. Cohen has recently been investigating how visual and cognitive information is dynamically formatted across neuronal populations to support flexible behavior. Using multi-area recordings, microstimulation, and computational modeling in primates and humans, their recent work explores how task uncertainty and shifting goals alter population codes and downstream readouts in visual and prefrontal cortices. They are also examining the computational role of correlated trial-to-trial variability, asking how the structural geometry of shared neural activity tracks task-relevant features and distinguishes the functional roles of different brain areas. Furthermore, Dr. Cohen is applying these systems-level approaches to neurodegeneration, tracking how the breakdown of coordinated cortical activity relates to early visually guided behavioral deficits in a primate model of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Feature interference underlies a neuronal basis for the behavioral cost of task uncertainty
papers.abstract: Humans and monkeys make less accurate perceptual decisions when they are unsure which of two tasks they must perform, unlike a neural network trained to be optimal. Comparing that network with one fit to the participants' choices suggested that the cost arises from interference between task features, which strengthens irrelevant feature representations and entangles feature codes in neuronal populations. Behavioral, physiological and causal experiments in monkeys and people supported this account of the price of cognitive flexibility.
papers.authors: Cheng Xue, Sol K. Markman, Ruoyi Chen, Lily E. Kramer, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: The structure of correlated variability reflects task-relevant information in sensory neurons
papers.abstract: Shared trial-to-trial variability across sensory neurons falls when perception improves, yet because it is low-dimensional an optimal readout could ignore it, so why does it track behavior so reliably? The authors propose that shared variability reflects circuit structure and reveals the information passed downstream. A circuit model plus population recordings across several areas and tasks show the dominant variability axis aligns with task-relevant stimulus features and action plans, and that microstimulation effects on behavior are predicted by projection onto this axis.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Ramanujan Srinath, Yunlong Xu, Douglas A. Ruff, Amy M. Ni, Brent Doiron, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Stable readout of visual representations mediates flexible generalization
papers.abstract: Using multi-area recordings in V1 and mid-level area V4 while monkeys flexibly reported different visual features, the study tests how task-dependent response modulations enable flexible behavior. Modulations in V4, but not V1, are coordinated across the population so that downstream neurons can keep a fixed, stable readout and still get the right information for the current task, without changes to information coding or synaptic weights. This proposes a new computational role for task-dependent modulation.
papers.authors: Ramanujan Srinath, Martyna M. Czarnik, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Loss of neuronal population organization links pathology to behavior in a model of Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: In a macaque model of early-stage Alzheimer's disease, the authors tracked behavior and neuronal population activity longitudinally alongside fluid and histological biomarkers. Visually guided exploration became more disorganized while performance on simple tasks stayed intact, and coordinated activity within and between visual and parietal populations declined even though single-neuron tuning was preserved. The changes tracked biomarker progression and appeared while pathology was largely confined to regions feeding back to visual cortex.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Douglas A. Ruff, Drew E. G. Sheets, Ramanujan Srinath, Giovanne B. Diniz, Devon J. Griggs, Danielle Beckman, Sean Ott, Kayla Schwartz, Carissa T. Erices, Scott Muller, Jeffrey H. Kordower, John H. Morrison, Marlene R. Cohen

papers.title: Linking neural population formatting to function
papers.abstract: Every behavior-relevant variable can usually be decoded from almost any brain area, so what distinguishes areas? Comparing motion area MT and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex while monkeys made decisions from motion and reward information, both areas carried both signals, but MT encoded them separably while dlPFC combined them jointly. The authors argue that an area's function is determined by how information types are formatted together in its population code rather than by mere presence of information.
papers.authors: Douglas A. Ruff, Sol K. Markman, Jason Z. Kim, Marlene R. Cohen

E297.name: Adam Kohn
E297.department: Dominick P. Purpura Department of Neuroscience
E297.bio: Adam Kohn is Professor and Chair of the Dominick P. Purpura Department of Neuroscience at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine, with additional appointments in the departments of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences and Systems & Computational Biology. Kohn’s research examines the mechanisms by which cortical neuronal populations encode visual information and the processes governing communication between distinct brain areas. Using multielectrode array recordings, computational modeling, and psychophysics, their laboratory investigates how sensory adaptation and correlated variability influence neural representations and perceptual outcomes. Kohn defined the 'communication subspace' that mediates inter-areal signaling and explored the role of rhythmic synchronization in the visual hierarchy.
E297.research_direction: Dr. Kohn has recently been investigating how early visual circuits process naturalistic stimuli and route information in the macaque brain. Their recent work explores the transformation of naturalistic textures from V1 to V2, using population recordings to examine how representational geometry, perceptual salience, and sensory adaptation evolve along the early ventral stream. Beyond stimulus representation, they are investigating the theoretical origins of shared neural variability, testing whether noise correlations in primary visual cortex reflect joint uncertainty about latent natural image statistics. Additionally, their research maps the broader communication architecture of these networks by probing whether the pulvinar acts as a diffuse broadcaster or a specific feedforward relay for population signals traveling between cortical areas.

papers.title: Role of the pulvinar in early visual cortical signaling in the macaque
