papers.abstract: The authors recorded population spiking at the same time in V1, V2 and the pulvinar of anesthetized macaques to ask whether the pulvinar broadcasts shared signals to cortex or relays activity between cortical areas. Cortico-pulvinar and cortico-cortical interactions used distinct patterns of population activity, which fits a relay role. Signaling was biased in the feedforward direction, with V1 leading pulvinar and pulvinar leading V2, suggesting the pulvinar mainly carries signals from lower to higher visual cortex.
papers.authors: Alison Xu, Anna I. Jasper, Adam Kohn

papers.title: The representational geometry of naturalistic textures in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: Population recordings in macaque V1 and V2 were used to characterize the geometry of the neural representation of naturalistic textures. The analysis examines how that geometry is transformed between the two areas, providing a population-level account of how texture information is reformatted along the early ventral stream.
papers.authors: Abhimanyu Pavuluri, Adam Kohn

papers.title: Adaptation with Naturalistic Textures in Macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: This study measured how prolonged exposure to naturalistic textures changes responsivity and tuning in macaque V1 and V2. Both areas respond to textures, but V2 neurons are sensitive to higher-order image statistics that V1 largely ignores. The effects of adaptation on the two areas were compared to determine how much of the change in V2 is inherited from V1 versus produced locally.
papers.authors: Aida Davila, Adam Kohn

papers.title: Relating natural image statistics to patterns of response covariability in macaque primary visual cortex
papers.abstract: Building on a generative model of natural image statistics and the neural sampling hypothesis, the paper proposes that shared variability between neurons reflects joint uncertainty about latent image features. The model predicts that enlarging an image lowers correlations for pairs with overlapping receptive fields and raises them for offset pairs. Recordings from macaque V1 confirmed this prediction, tying noise correlations to natural scene statistics.
papers.authors: Amirhossein Farzmahdi, Adam Kohn, Ruben Coen-Cagli

papers.title: Assessing neuronal correlates of salience and their adaptability with naturalistic textures in macaque V1 and V2
papers.abstract: Perceptual salience, the pop-out of a stimulus that differs from its surroundings, is often thought to be encoded in V1 through differences in responsivity to simple features. This preprint tests whether V1 and V2 signal salience of naturalistic textures among distractors and whether prior adaptation to textures changes that signal.
papers.authors: Aida Davila, Adam Kohn

E299.name: Edward Callaway
E299.main_research_area: neural circuit mapping and visual processing
E299.bio: Edward Callaway is a neuroscientist at the Salk Institute who developed the monosynaptic rabies virus tracing technique for mapping direct synaptic connections between specific cell types. Callaway's research focuses on the organization and function of neocortical circuits, specifically investigating how neuronal populations in the visual cortex process and integrate sensory information. By integrating viral tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and in vivo physiological recordings, their lab identifies the circuit-level mechanisms underlying visual perception and cortical computation. This work describes the architectural principles of the brain and investigates how circuit disruptions contribute to conditions such as autism and schizophrenia.
E299.research_direction: Dr. Callaway has recently been investigating the precise structural, molecular, and functional organization of visual circuits across different animal models. Their recent work explores how advanced single-cell omics can be combined with viral tracing—such as developing the START method and utilizing epi-retro-seq—to map the fine transcriptomic and epigenomic identities of both local primary visual cortex presynaptic inputs and brain-wide long-range projections. In parallel, they are mapping the complex anatomy of higher-order visual pathways, investigating how driver and modulator cortico-thalamo-cortical loops are organized through the mouse pulvinar. Furthermore, they are advancing primate electrophysiology by developing analytical approaches to precisely assign high-density Neuropixels recordings to specific fine sublayers within macaque primary visual cortex based on physiological signatures.

papers.title: Protocol for mapping neural circuit connectivity with START: Single transcriptome assisted rabies tracing
papers.abstract: Step-by-step protocol for START, covering Cre-dependent helper virus delivery, EnvA-pseudotyped rabies infection, microdissection and nuclei sorting, followed by library preparation and computational annotation of nuclei. It lets other labs identify which transcriptomic cell types provide input to a chosen neuronal population in mouse cortex.
papers.authors: Maribel Patiño, Sai Krishna Bhamidipati, Christian Cazares, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Complementary Organization of Mouse Driver and Modulator Cortico-thalamo-cortical Circuits
papers.abstract: Maps how the mouse pulvinar relays signals between higher visual cortical areas by tracing the inputs and outputs of pulvinar neurons that project to five different higher visual areas. The work finds that driver-type and modulator-type transthalamic loops are organized in complementary, systematic ways rather than intermingled at random.
papers.authors: Rachel M. Cassidy, Angel V. Macias, Willian N. Lagos, Chiamaka Ugorji, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Transcriptomic Cell Type Specificity of Local Cortical Circuits
papers.abstract: Introduces START, which pairs monosynaptic rabies tracing with single-nucleus RNA-seq so the transcriptomic identity of presynaptic neurons can be read out for defined postsynaptic populations. Applied to five layer-specific excitatory populations in mouse V1, it shows that inhibitory inputs follow connection rules at the level of fine transcriptomic subtypes, beyond what subclass-level analyses had revealed.
papers.authors: Maribel Patiño, Marley A. Rossa, Willian Nuñez Lagos, Neelakshi S. Patne, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: High-Resolution Laminar Identification in Macaque Primary Visual Cortex Using Neuropixels Probes
papers.abstract: Shows that high-density Neuropixels recordings in macaque V1 can be used to assign recorded neurons to fine cortical layers, including sublayers of layer 4, using electrophysiological signatures. The method gives a practical way to place primate V1 recordings in laminar context at much higher resolution than earlier approaches.
papers.authors: Li A. Zhang, Peichao Li, Edward M. Callaway

papers.title: Brain-wide correspondence of neuronal epigenomics and distant projections
papers.abstract: Uses epi-retro-seq to link single-cell epigenomes to long-range projection targets for tens of thousands of mouse neurons across 32 source regions and 24 targets. The resulting atlas shows how projection identity relates to epigenomic and transcriptomic cell types and supports genetic access to projection-defined populations.
papers.authors: Jingtian Zhou, Zhuzhu Zhang, Minh Wu, Hanqing Liu, Yan Pang, Anna Bartlett, Zihao Peng, Wubin Ding, Angeline Rivkin, Willian N. Lagos, Elora Williams, Cheng-Ta Lee, Paula Assakura Miyazaki, Andrew Aldridge, Qiurui Zeng, Jackson L. A. Salinda, Naomi Claffey, Michelle Liem, Conor Fitzpatrick, Lara Boggeman, Zizhen Yao, Kimberly A. Smith, Bosiljka Tasic, Joseph Altshul, Mia A. Kenworthy, Cynthia Valadon, Joseph R. Nery, Rosa G. Castanon, Neelakshi S. Patne, Minh Vu, Mohammad Rashid, Matthew Jacobs, Tony Ito, Julia Osteen, Nora Emerson, Jasper Lee, Silvia Cho, Jon Rink, Hsiang-Hsuan Huang, Antonio Pinto-Duartec, Bertha Dominguez, Jared B. Smith, Carolyn O'Connor, Hongkui Zeng, Shengbo Chen, Kuo-Fen Lee, Eran A. Mukamel, Xin Jin, M. Margarita Behrens, Joseph R. Ecker, Edward M. Callaway

E300.name: Marla Feller
E300.department: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology; Department of Neuroscience
E300.bio: Feller investigates mechanisms governing the assembly and functional organization of neural circuits within the developing retina. Their research focuses on retinal waves, which are patterned spontaneous activity bursts in immature retinas that facilitate the wiring of connections to the central visual system. Using two-photon excitation microscopy, electrophysiology, and anatomical techniques, Feller’s lab explores how these activity patterns shape direction-selective circuits and the morphology of glial cells. Current projects also examine the role of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells and the impact of early light-driven signals on nascent retinal networks.
E300.research_direction: Dr. Feller's research is best known for retinal waves, the spontaneous bursts of activity in the developing retina, including the cellular mechanisms that generate them and their role in visual system development. Their recent work increasingly investigates the developmental mechanisms that establish precise connectivity in early visual circuits, focusing heavily on the assembly of direction-selective networks in the retina. They have recently been exploring how structured spontaneous activity, specifically early retinal waves, guides both the morphological outgrowth of starburst amacrine cells and the axis-specific synaptic wiring of direction-selective ganglion cells. To disentangle the interplay between activity-dependent and hardwired developmental programs, their research incorporates two-photon calcium imaging, dual whole-cell recordings, and subtype-specific transcriptomic screening to hunt for molecular cues that instruct asymmetric synaptogenesis. Furthermore, their recent work explores methodological advancements in functional imaging, including the engineering of a combined two-photon and single-photon microscopy platform to simultaneously track calcium transients and near-infrared neurotransmitter sensors.

papers.title: Retinal waves shape starburst amacrine cell dendrite development through a direction-selective dendritic computation
papers.abstract: Shows that before eye opening, the nasally biased propagation of spontaneous retinal waves, which resembles forward optic flow, is converted by starburst amacrine cells into asymmetric dendrite growth. The conversion relies on direction-selective computations within the dendrites themselves. This links a specific spatiotemporal activity pattern directly to the structural development of a motion-detection neuron.
papers.authors: Miah N. Pitcher, Aanica S.B. Gonzales, Raul Habib, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Müller Glia-Vasculature Interactions in the Developing Retina
papers.abstract: Tests whether retinal waves influence angiogenesis and finds vascular growth is normal without wave activity. Müller glial processes contact endothelial tip cells and form Aquaporin-4-rich endfeet from the earliest stages of vessel growth. Glial endfeet show compartmentalized calcium transients that are largely uncorrelated with retinal waves, defining how neurons, glia and vasculature interact during development.
papers.authors: Samira Monshietehadi, Angel J. Garcia, Benjamin E. Smith, Matthew Tarchick, Kiara Abhayaratne, Aileen Conley, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Activity-dependent development of synaptic circuits mediates direction selectivity in an axis-specific manner
papers.abstract: Mice lacking cholinergic retinal waves lose horizontal but not vertical direction selectivity, and the study shows this also abolishes the horizontal optokinetic reflex. Paired recordings reveal that the loss stems from weakened GABAergic asymmetric inhibition onto horizontal-preferring direction-selective ganglion cells. Spontaneous activity before vision therefore shapes wiring for one axis of motion selectively.
papers.authors: Karina Bistrong, Rachana Deven Somaiya, Eugene Y. Liang, Benjamin E. Smith, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Differential Expression Analysis Identifies Candidate Synaptogenic Molecules for Wiring Direction-Selective Circuits in the Retina
papers.abstract: Paired recordings identify postnatal day 10 as when asymmetric SAC-to-DSGC synapses form. RNA sequencing of nasal- versus ventral-tuned ON-OFF DSGCs at that age yields candidate molecules for direction-specific wiring. Conditional deletion of the synaptic organizer Cbln4 produced only a small tuning deficit in ventral-preferring cells, indicating it is not a primary cell-autonomous wiring cue.
papers.authors: Joshua M. Tworig, Robert D. Morrie, Karina Bistrong, Rachana D. Somaiya, S. Hsu, J. Liang, K. G. Cornejo, Marla B. Feller

papers.title: Mapping the Retina onto the Brain
papers.abstract: A review of how the many retinal ganglion cell types project to their central targets and how the resulting visual maps are organized. It covers the developmental mechanisms, including molecular cues and spontaneous activity, that establish retinotopic and eye-specific organization. It serves as a reference synthesis for the field.
papers.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology
papers.authors: Daniel Kerschensteiner, Marla B. Feller

E301.name: John Maunsell
E301.bio: John Maunsell studies the physiological mechanisms underlying visual perception and attention. Maunsell's research utilizes electrophysiological recordings from single neurons in behaving primates and mice to determine how cognitive factors modulate sensory representations in the visual cortex. This work indicates that attention increases the gain of neuronal responses without altering stimulus selectivity, enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio for attended information. Maunsell’s laboratory currently employs optogenetic tools and computational analysis to investigate how specific cortical layers and cell classes contribute to perceptual sensitivity and behavioral decision-making.
E301.research_direction: Dr. Maunsell's recent work explores the neural circuits underlying visual perception and spatial attention, investigating how cortical, subcortical, and neuromodulatory systems contribute to visually guided behavior. Using electrophysiology and optogenetics in non-human primates, they have recently been examining how structures like the locus coeruleus and superior colliculus support selective attention, specifically probing how these regions isolate perceptual sensitivity from internal decision or motor criteria. Their research also leverages reverse-correlation optogenetics in mice to tease apart the division of labor between V1 and the midbrain during the detection of distinct stimulus features, such as luminance versus contrast. Additionally, they investigate the computational rules of sensory encoding and cortical readout by modeling how neuronal normalization operates across receptive field locations in macaque area MT and by using human psychophysics to test perceptual asymmetries in the detection of dynamic motion coherence.

papers.title: Attention-related modulation in the superior colliculus encodes perceptual sensitivity, but not perceptual choice
papers.abstract: Monkeys performed a spatial attention task in which sensitivity, perceptual decision criterion and motor criterion were manipulated independently, allowing the authors to separate what superior colliculus activity represents. SC responses tracked behavioral sensitivity and motor selection of a saccade target, but stayed unchanged when decision criterion shifted without motor bias, and did not predict trial-by-trial accuracy. The SC therefore supports the sensitivity and response-selection components of attention, not the internal decision criterion.
papers.authors: Supriya Ghosh, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Neuronal normalization in monkey MT is an intensity-weighted average
papers.abstract: Recording in macaque area MT, the authors examine how normalization depends on where stimuli fall within neurons' receptive fields. Standard normalization models fit poorly for stimuli at arbitrary locations, whereas a model in which each stimulus's weight is its contrast times a location-specific receptive-field weight explains the data closely. The same intensity-weighted account also explains a systematic rise in contrast sensitivity at sites nearer the RF center.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Chery Cherian, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Locus coeruleus norepinephrine contributes to visual-spatial attention by selectively enhancing perceptual sensitivity
papers.abstract: Recording from norepinephrine neurons in the monkey locus coeruleus, the study shows they fire to attended stimuli in the contralateral hemifield, and that this firing tracks improved discrimination sensitivity rather than motor factors and is absent on error trials. Optogenetic activation of these neurons selectively improves detection of contralateral stimuli without changing response criteria, indicating a causal, spatially specific role for NE in selective attention.
papers.authors: Supriya Ghosh, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Stimulus-dependent differences in cortical versus subcortical contributions to visual detection in mice
papers.abstract: Mice detected changes in contrast or luminance while white-noise optogenetic stimulation was delivered to inhibitory neurons in V1 or the superior colliculus. Reverse correlation of the optogenetic patterns gave a neuronal-behavioral kernel for each area. Early SC activity was critical for detecting both luminance and contrast changes, whereas V1 mattered mainly for contrast, revealing stimulus-dependent division of labor between cortex and midbrain.
papers.authors: Jackson J. Cone, Autumn O. Mitchell, Rachel K. Parker, John H. R. Maunsell

papers.title: Increments in visual motion coherence are more readily detected than decrements
papers.abstract: Motivated by findings that mice detect optogenetic increases in V1 spiking better than decreases, the authors tested whether humans show a similar asymmetry using dynamic random-dot motion. Observers were more sensitive to increments in motion coherence than to matched decrements, consistent with the fact that increments on average raise MT firing rates. The result supports the idea that cortical readout preferentially relies on increases in spiking.
papers.authors: Lai Wei, Autumn O. Mitchell, John H. R. Maunsell

E302.name: Greg Horwitz
E302.bio: Gregory Horwitz investigates the neural mechanisms of visual perception and decision-making, focusing on the cortical processing of color and spatial vision. Horwitz’s research integrates high-density electrophysiological recordings using microfabricated electrode arrays with viral gene delivery and optogenetic techniques to manipulate cell types in the primate visual system. By combining these neurophysiological approaches with psychophysical threshold measurements and computational modeling, the Horwitz Lab examines the relationship between retinal signaling and behavioral perception. Their research specifically addresses how chromatic and spatial contrast are integrated within the primary visual cortex (V1).
E302.research_direction: Dr. Horwitz has recently been studying how the primate brain processes visual features such as color and luminance, and developing tools to manipulate specific neuron types. Their recent work explores how complex cells in macaque V1 combine color and brightness edges, and how that compares with the units of deep neural networks trained to recognize objects. They have also been testing viral vectors that target particular classes of cortical neurons in the primate brain, so that those cells can be identified and controlled. In a separate line of work, they use closed-loop optogenetic stimulation of the cerebellum to test whether it holds an internal model that helps guide rapid eye movements.

papers.title: Preferential transduction of parvalbumin-expressing cortical neurons by AAV-mDLX5/6 vectors
papers.abstract: Viral vectors bearing cell type-specific cis-regulatory elements provide a critical methodology for targeting and functionally interrogating neuronal subclasses in the non-human primate brain. In this study, the cellular tropism of adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors expressing fluorophore reporters under the regulation of an 862-bp murine Dlx5/6 intergenic enhancer-promoter construct was evaluated in adult cortex. Vectors were administered via intracortical microinjections into the primary and extrastriate visual cortex of two macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta), the prefrontal cortex of two additional macaques, and the sensorimotor cortex of three rats. Quantitative post-mortem fluorescence immunohistochemistry revealed that transgene expression was predominantly restricted to GABAergic interneurons, exhibiting high selectivity for parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) interneurons across cortical layers and species. Conversely, calretinin-positive (CR+) cortical interneurons demonstrated minimal to negligible transduction. These findings indicate that AAV-mDLX5/6 vectors exhibit substantial subclass bias rather than unbiased pan-GABAergic tropism, likely reflecting the differential activity of distal-less homeobox transcriptional regulatory machinery across distinct interneuron developmental lineages.
papers.authors: Padideh Yazdan-Shahmorad, Shane Gibson, Joanne C. Lee, Gregory D. Horwitz

papers.title: Closed-Loop Optogenetic Perturbation of Macaque Oculomotor Cerebellum: Evidence for an Internal Saccade Model
papers.abstract: Accurate execution of rapid saccadic eye movements is widely thought to require an internal forward model encoded in the cerebellum that estimates oculomotor plant dynamics and compares instantaneous eye displacement against target command in real time. To probe the causal role and temporal operating regime of this putative feedback loop, closed-loop optogenetic excitation was delivered to Purkinje cells (P-cells) within the oculomotor vermis (OMV, lobules VIc/VII) of rhesus macaques during horizontal saccades. Brief laser pulses (10–30 ms) were triggered contingent on online saccade detection at discrete delays (0, 10, 20, or 30 ms after initiation) in animals transduced with AAV-L7-ChR2. Optical stimulation induced dysmetria whose magnitude, trajectory curvature, and deceleration profile were systematically contingent upon stimulus onset timing, saccade duration, and initial eye velocity. Perturbations applied early in long-duration saccades produced substantial hypometria or hypermetria depending on target vector and hemifield, whereas identical pulses delivered near saccade termination yielded negligible endpoint errors. Computational simulations of an internal feedback loop incorporating a local cerebellar integrator successfully accounted for these parametric kinematic alterations, providing empirical support that the primate oculomotor vermis computes an internal feedback signal that shapes ongoing saccade trajectories on a millisecond timescale.
papers.authors: Robijanto Soetedjo, Gregory D. Horwitz

papers.title: Color and luminance processing in V1 complex cells and artificial neural networks
papers.abstract: Visual object boundary segmentation relies heavily on the spatial concurrence of luminance gradients and chromatic transitions in natural scenes. To elucidate how cortical receptive fields represent multi-attribute spatial contrast, the tuning of phase-invariant complex cells in macaque primary visual cortex (V1) was compared to corresponding spatial-phase-invariant convolutional units in deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on ImageNet categorization. In awake macaques, single-unit V1 responses to drifting luminance and cone-contrast gratings were characterized using automated closed-loop isoresponse measurements and multidimensional quadratic receptive field modeling. The observed isoresponse surfaces revealed a dichotomy: complex cells were either tuned purely along luminance/achromatic axes or exhibited ellipsoidal/hyperbolic isoresponse geometries indicating joint, nonlinear sensitivity to both luminance and chromatic contrast, while units selective solely to chromatic contrast were exceptionally rare. An analogous non-uniform distribution of spatiochromatic selectivity emerged among phase-invariant pooling units in the second layer of feedforward CNNs. These comparative results indicate that the selective representation of joint chromatic-luminance boundaries without an isolated chromatic-only complex representation provides an optimal computational basis for illumination- and contrast-polarity-invariant object recognition.
papers.authors: Luke M. Bun, Gregory D. Horwitz

E304.name: Gregory C. DeAngelis
E304.department: Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences
E304.bio: Gregory C. DeAngelis is the George Eastman Professor at the University of Rochester, where they investigate the cortical circuits mediating 3D vision, motion perception, and multisensory integration. DeAngelis employs a multidisciplinary approach combining primate neurophysiology, psychophysics, and computational modeling to study how the brain processes binocular disparity and optic flow for navigation. Their research identifies the functional roles of the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas in depth perception and self-motion. Currently, DeAngelis explores how the brain utilizes causal inference and eye-movement signals to distinguish object motion from self-motion in complex environments.
E304.research_direction: Dr. DeAngelis's recent work explores how the primate visual system computes object motion and 3D depth during observer self-motion. They have recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of optic flow parsing in macaque visual areas MT and MSTd, examining how these circuits use background flow and dynamic perspective cues to distinguish moving objects from the observer's own body and eye movements. To connect these neural recordings with perception, their research integrates human psychophysics and computational modeling to ask how the brain flexibly infers viewing geometry from visual cues. Additionally, they are developing innovative behavioral methodologies, such as an online Bayesian technique designed to reward animal subjects based on their subjective trial-by-trial percepts, enabling the study of natural perceptual biases without distorting them through objective reward contingencies.

papers.title: Flexible computation of object motion and depth based on viewing geometry inferred from optic flow
papers.abstract: The paper proposes that the brain infers the viewing geometry (how the observer is moving relative to the scene) from optic flow and then uses it to jointly interpret object motion and depth. A computational model based on this idea captures human perceptual biases across tasks, showing that a single flexible inference process can account for effects previously explained by separate mechanisms.
papers.authors: Zhe-Xin Xu, Jiayi Pang, Akiyuki Anzai, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Seeing a Three-Dimensional World in Motion: How the Brain Computes Object Motion and Depth During Self-Motion
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes how the brain perceives object motion and depth while the observer moves. It links computational accounts, human psychophysics, and neural recordings on optic flow parsing, motion parallax, and coordinate transformations into a unified framework.
papers.authors: Zhe-Xin Xu, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Rewarding animals based on their subjective percepts is enabled by online Bayesian estimation of perceptual biases
papers.abstract: Rewarding animals for correct choices is problematic when perception is biased, since rewards can distort the very biases being studied. The authors develop an online Bayesian method that estimates the animal's subjective percept trial by trial and delivers rewards according to it, and demonstrate it in a motion perception task with monkeys.
papers.authors: Yelin Dong, Gabor Lengyel, Sabyasachi Shivkumar, Akiyuki Anzai, Grace F. DiRisio, Ralf M. Haefner, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: A neural mechanism for optic flow parsing in macaque visual cortex
papers.abstract: Recordings in macaque visual cortex examine how neurons help separate the image motion caused by moving objects from that caused by the observer's own movement. The authors identify a mechanism in area MT, based on surround interactions tuned to background flow, that subtracts the self-motion component, and relate it to responses in MSTd.
papers.authors: Nicole E. Peltier, Akiyuki Anzai, Rubén Moreno-Bote, Gregory C. DeAngelis

papers.title: Neurons in Primate Area MSTd Signal Eye Movement Direction Inferred from Dynamic Perspective Cues in Optic Flow
papers.abstract: MSTd neurons are tested with visual stimuli that simulate eye rotation through dynamic perspective cues in optic flow, in the absence of real eye movements. Many neurons signal the inferred direction of the eye movement, suggesting that MSTd uses visual cues to help compensate for eye movements during self-motion perception.
papers.authors: Grace F. DiRisio, Yongsoo Ra, Yinghui Qiu, Akiyuki Anzai, Gregory C. DeAngelis

E305.name: Dora E. Angelaki
E305.department: Center for Neural Science; Tandon School of Engineering (Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering)
E305.bio: Dora E. Angelaki is a neuroscientist who investigates how the brain integrates multisensory signals, such as visual and vestibular cues, to support spatial orientation, navigation, and decision-making. Angelaki’s work utilizes engineering-inspired computational frameworks, including Kalman filters and Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP), to model how neural populations represent latent variables and update internal beliefs during naturalistic foraging tasks. They also explore the breakdown of these neural computations in conditions such as autism, focusing on the interplay between sensory evidence and internal model-driven behavior. A member of the National Academy of Sciences, Angelaki has conducted research on heading perception and the representation of inertial motion within cortical and subcortical circuits.
E305.research_direction: Dr. Angelaki's recent work explores the computational and neural mechanisms underlying spatial navigation, internal belief updating, and strategic decision-making across humans, macaques, and rodents. Combining virtual reality with reinforcement learning and recurrent network models, they have recently been investigating how modular neural architectures influence long-term reward optimization during navigation, and how humans might use eye movements to actively embody internal beliefs during memory-guided steering. In rodent models, their research probes the neural dynamics of spatial orientation, specifically examining how active locomotion and motor predictions influence thalamic head-direction attractor networks under conditions of vestibular conflict. Additionally, they are using brain-wide recordings in genetically distinct mouse models of autism to investigate potential shared circuit-level anomalies in how sensory and frontal cortices encode and flexibly update statistical priors during decision-making.

papers.title: Neural and computational correlates of strategic aborting and long-run policy optimization in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
papers.abstract: Macaques freely navigating in virtual reality sometimes abort offers, giving up immediate reward to maximise returns across a whole session. Reinforcement-learning models suggest this is supported by modular actor-critic networks in which a policy module optimises long-term value. Consistent with model predictions, dorsolateral prefrontal units and population dynamics, but not parietal area 7a or MSTd, reflected the eventual abort decision already at offer presentation.
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Ruiyi Zhang, Xaq Pitkow, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: Active locomotion predictively rescues head direction attractor dynamics in head-fixed mice
papers.abstract: Head-fixation, the standard preparation for mouse physiology, creates vestibular conflict that disrupts head-direction coding in the anterodorsal thalamus at the unit and population level. Attractor dynamics are perturbed during immobility but recover a few hundred milliseconds before locomotion begins, implying that an efference copy or predicted reafference is needed to sustain the network. A ring-attractor model with perturbed lateral connectivity reproduces the effects.
papers.authors: Alexandr Pak, Janna Aarse, Heng Wei Zhu, Jean-Paul Noel, Simon Carrillo Segura, Andre A. Fenton, Dora Angelaki

papers.title: A common computational and neural anomaly across mouse models of autism
papers.abstract: Mice carrying autism-linked mutations (Fmr1, Cntnap2, Shank3B) were tested on a decision task in which they must update expectations about stimulus statistics. All three genotypes showed blunted, inflexible updating of priors, mirroring the computational-psychiatry account of autism in humans. Brain-wide recordings showed that in inflexible mice, prior encoding shifted from sensory toward frontal cortex, and frontal areas carried more units signalling deviations from the long-run prior. The results point to a shared computational and neural signature across distinct genetic causes.
papers.authors: Jean-Paul Noel, Edoardo Balzani, Luigi Acerbi, Julius Benson, The International Brain Laboratory, Cristina Savin, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: Belief embodiment through eye movements facilitates memory-guided navigation
papers.abstract: Humans steering with a joystick toward a briefly flashed target in a virtual world track the hidden target with their gaze even without optic flow, suggesting eye movements externalise the internal belief about goal position. A recurrent network model with tuned coupling between oculomotor and evidence-integrating frontoparietal circuits reproduces the behaviour and predicts that gaze-related signals improve navigation. Disrupting or constraining gaze impairs performance, supporting eye movements as a cognitive resource for memory-guided navigation.
papers.authors: Akis Stavropoulos, Kaushik J. Lakshminarasimhan, Dora E. Angelaki

papers.title: Inductive biases of neural network modularity in spatial navigation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents with different architectures were trained on a naturalistic navigation task to ask why the brain is modular. An agent that separates state representation, value and action into specialised modules learned faster and generalised better. Its internal state estimate combined prediction and observation weighted by uncertainty, akin to recursive Bayesian estimation, and its behaviour resembled that of macaques more than other architectures.
papers.authors: Ruiyi Zhang, Xaq Pitkow, Dora E. Angelaki

E307.name: Christopher C. Pack
E307.bio: Christopher C. Pack is a Professor at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital, where their research focuses on the neural mechanisms underlying visual perception and sensorimotor integration. Pack’s laboratory utilizes microelectrode recordings and computational modeling to investigate how the cerebral cortex encodes visual motion, particularly within cortical areas such as MT and V4. Pack's work examines the role of traveling waves in integrating sensory and motor signals during eye movements, as well as the impact of brain plasticity and non-invasive electrical stimulation on neural circuit function. This research aims to establish a quantitative understanding of the neural code to develop therapeutic interventions for neurological disorders affecting vision.
E307.research_direction: Dr. Pack's recent work explores the mechanistic physiological effects of non-invasive brain stimulation, using single-neuron recordings in macaques to investigate how techniques like temporal interference and transcranial alternating current stimulation influence spike timing and entrain long-range projection neurons. They are also investigating the origins of decision-related activity in the visual cortex, utilizing microelectrode recordings and targeted inactivation to parse whether choice probabilities in areas like MT and V4 reflect causal sensory drive, saccade preparation, or non-causal top-down feedback across distinct local field potential bands. Additionally, their research examines the neural basis of visual plasticity, leveraging reversible cortical inactivation to understand how intermediate areas supply the inductive biases that constrain perceptual learning and generalization.

papers.title: Distinct sources of decision-related signals in visual cortex are represented in different local field potential bands
papers.abstract: Correlations between single-neuron activity and perceptual choices are often read as causal, but can have other origins. The authors recorded LFPs in macaque MT and V4 during two decision tasks, with and without spiking inactivation. High-gamma choice signals vanished when spikes were silenced, consistent with a causal role, whereas lower-gamma signals persisted, implying non-causal input, and low-frequency signals carried information about the previous trial's outcome.
papers.authors: Yueyue Sapphire Hou, Pooya Laamerad, Liu D. Liu, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Brain stimulation preferentially influences long-range projections in primates
papers.abstract: The authors recorded single units in macaques receiving transcranial alternating current stimulation and identified putative long-range projection neurons. These cells were entrained more strongly than other neurons and accounted for the most extreme entrainment events. This suggests stimulation acts mainly on the edges of neural networks rather than on the nodes, which should change how stimulation protocols are designed.
papers.authors: Pedro G. Vieira, Matthew R. Krause, Pooya Laamerad, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Inactivation of primate cortex reveals inductive biases in visual learning
papers.abstract: This study combines reversible inactivation of macaque visual cortex (area V4) with perceptual learning tasks to ask what cortical circuits contribute to learning shapes and discriminations. The results indicate that V4 supplies inductive biases that constrain how visual learning proceeds, rather than being needed only for basic perception. It links cortical computation to learning-related generalization.
papers.authors: Pooya Laamerad, Matthew R. Krause, Daniel Guitton, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Temporal interference stimulation disrupts spike timing in the primate brain
papers.abstract: Using single-neuron recordings in macaques, the authors tested whether temporal interference (TI) stimulation, proposed as a non-invasive way to reach deep brain targets, actually affects neurons. TI reliably altered when neurons fired but not how often, but the approach demands high carrier frequencies, multiple electrodes and amplitude-modulated waveforms that together make it roughly 80% weaker than other non-invasive stimulation. The results suggest TI is poorly suited to broad entrainment but might help disrupt pathological oscillations.
papers.authors: Pedro G. Vieira, Matthew R. Krause, Christopher C. Pack

papers.title: Decision-related activity and movement selection in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Choice probability in sensory neurons is often interpreted as evidence that they causally drive decisions. The authors show that in a standard motion discrimination task, MT neurons respond more when the monkey will make a saccade toward their receptive field, and this movement-related activity explains much of the measured choice probability. It emerges with training, and MT inactivation biased choices away from the affected visual field locations.
papers.authors: Pooya Laamerad, Liu D. Liu, Christopher C. Pack

E308.name: Nikolaus F. Troje
E308.bio: Nikolaus F. Troje is a Professor at York University and holds the Canada Research Chair in Reality Research, where they direct the BioMotion Lab. Troje’s research investigates how the brain transforms sensory input into perceptual representations, focusing on biological motion and the extraction of social information from human movement. Utilizing 3D motion capture, computational modeling, and virtual reality, Troje explores the mechanisms of multi-sensory integration and the psychophysics of person perception. This work connects biology, psychology, and computer science to study how humans recognize identity, intent, and emotion through visual and kinematic cues.
E308.research_direction: Dr. Troje has recently been investigating how the human visual system relies on depth and kinematic cues to interpret social signals and the spatial structure of the world. Their recent work explores the relationship between real visual space and two-dimensional pictorial space, using virtual reality and infant behavioral paradigms to examine how the brain integrates binocular disparity and motion parallax to judge object distance, direction, and flatness. In an applied extension of this spatial research, they are investigating the perceptual mechanisms that cause flat monitors to disrupt natural eye contact during video calls, exploring technological solutions based on restoring accurate head parallax. Additionally, Dr. Troje continues to study biological motion processing, reviewing developmental and evolutionary frameworks to understand how the visual system uses local kinematic cues from point-light displays to rapidly detect animacy and living entities.

papers.title: Motion parallax allows 7-8-month-old infants to distinguish pictures from their referents
papers.abstract: Tests whether infants use motion parallax to tell that a picture is a flat depiction rather than the real object. Seven- to eight-month-olds responded differently to depicted versus real referents when parallax information was available, suggesting that parallax helps young infants separate pictures from the things they show.
papers.authors: Nikolaus F. Troje, Lucie Preißler, Gudrun Schwarzer

papers.title: Relating visual and pictorial space: Integration of binocular disparity and motion parallax
papers.abstract: Follow-up experiments examine how the visual system integrates binocular disparity and motion parallax when both are available for judging depth in pictures and real scenes. The results show how the cues are weighted and combined, extending the earlier geometric account of the relation between visual and pictorial space.
papers.authors: Xiaoye Michael Wang, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Zoom disrupts eye contact behaviour: problems and solutions
papers.abstract: Argues that video calls break natural eye contact because the image of a person on a flat screen lacks the depth cues, especially motion parallax, that make gaze direction depend on where the viewer is. Shows why the gaze of a person on screen appears to follow or miss the viewer inconsistently, and proposes technical solutions based on restoring consistent parallax to the displayed head.
papers.authors: Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Relating visual and pictorial space: Binocular disparity for distance, motion parallax for direction
papers.abstract: Using virtual reality, the study asks how depth cues combine to determine how far and in which direction objects in a picture seem to lie relative to real space. It finds that binocular disparity mostly informs perceived distance while motion parallax mostly informs perceived direction, and a geometric model relates real visual space to the distorted space seen in pictures.
papers.authors: Xiaoye Michael Wang, Nikolaus F. Troje

papers.title: Life Detection From Biological Motion
papers.abstract: A review of how the visual system detects living things from the way they move, covering the local, feet-first cues in point-light walkers that signal animacy and the role of this mechanism as an early-warning system. It connects the work to development, evolution, and clinical questions, and outlines open problems for the field.
papers.authors: Nikolaus F. Troje, Dorita H. F. Chang

E309.name: Deborah Giaschi
E309.department: Department of Ophthalmology and Visual Sciences
E309.bio: Deborah Giaschi is a Professor at the University of British Columbia and a principal investigator at the BC Children's Hospital Research Institute. Giaschi's research program investigates the neural mechanisms underlying the typical and atypical development of motion perception, stereopsis, and visuomotor coordination. Utilizing a multimodal approach that includes child-friendly psychophysics, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and magnetoencephalography (MEG), they characterize how cortical maturation is disrupted in disorders such as amblyopia and developmental dyslexia. Their current work focuses on translating these neuroscientific insights into binocular treatment strategies, including the use of customized video games and virtual reality to improve visual outcomes.
E309.research_direction: Dr. Giaschi has recently been investigating the mechanisms of typical and atypical visual development, with a primary focus on extra-striate processing in amblyopia. Their recent work explores how global motion and motion-defined form perception are impaired in both the amblyopic and fellow eyes across different clinical profiles, such as those with deprivation cataracts. To better understand these impairments, they are examining whether such perceptual deficits stem from low-level issues like fixation instability, and assessing whether novel dichoptic video-game treatments can successfully restore binocular vision and motion processing. Broadening their scope beyond amblyopia, their research also tracks the typical maturation of the contrast sensitivity function across spatial frequencies from early childhood into adulthood. Additionally, they have recently been evaluating neuroimaging evidence to determine whether a unified, large-scale functional brain network supports visual attention across various search, cueing, and divided-attention tasks.

papers.title: Evaluation of motion perception and binocular vision following dichoptic treatment for amblyopia
papers.abstract: Twenty-one people aged 6 to 56 with amblyopia were tested before and after roughly eight weeks of video-game-based binocular (dichoptic) training delivered through an optometry practice. The study asked whether this treatment restores binocular function and the motion perception deficits that occlusion therapy typically leaves unresolved, in both amblyopic and fellow eyes. It links a clinical intervention to the lab's long-standing motion-perception markers of amblyopia.
papers.authors: Akosua Kesewah Asare, Cindy S. Ho, Hee Yeon Im, Deborah Eileen Giaschi

papers.title: The Development of the Contrast Sensitivity Function From Childhood to Early Adulthood
papers.abstract: Contrast thresholds for orientation discrimination were measured at seven spatial frequencies from 0.5 to 30 cycles per degree in 103 participants aged 4 to 27. Model fits assessed when the contrast sensitivity function becomes adult-like and whether maturation is uniform across spatial frequencies, addressing inconsistent earlier findings that used different methods and age groups.
papers.authors: Frédéric Gosselin, Jessica Tardif, Laveniya Kugathasan, Deborah Eileen Giaschi

papers.title: Poor fixation stability does not account for motion perception deficits in amblyopia
papers.abstract: Adults with amblyopia have elevated global motion coherence thresholds at slow speeds, and also fixate less stably. The authors measured both together and found that fixation instability was raised across all motion conditions rather than selectively where perceptual deficits appeared. Unstable fixation therefore does not explain the motion deficit, pointing to genuine differences in cortical motion processing.
papers.authors: Kimberly Meier, Simon Warner, Miriam Spering, Deborah Giaschi

papers.title: Large-scale functional networks underlying visual attention
papers.abstract: This review compares neuroimaging evidence (fMRI, EEG, MEG) across visual cueing, visual search and divided-attention tasks to ask whether a unified attention system exists independent of other cognitive and sensory networks. It evaluates the Attention Network Task's alerting, orienting and executive-control framework against the broader literature.
papers.authors: Alexander J. Cook, Hee Yeon Im, Deborah E. Giaschi

papers.title: Motion-Defined Form Perception in Deprivation Amblyopia
papers.abstract: Motion-defined form coherence thresholds were measured in 30 children with unilateral-cataract deprivation amblyopia and 59 controls, alongside acuity, stereoacuity, fusion and suppression. Nearly all children were impaired with the amblyopic eye and a substantial minority with the fellow eye, with similar deficits for congenital and later-onset cataracts. The work extends her extra-striate motion/form processing account to deprivation amblyopia.
papers.authors: Deborah E. Giaschi, Akosua K. Asare, Reed M. Jost, Krista R. Kelly, Eileen E. Birch

E312.name: Ari Rosenberg
E312.bio: Rosenberg’s research examines the hierarchical neural circuits and computations through which the brain reconstructs three-dimensional object representations from two-dimensional retinal inputs. Their lab integrates high-density neuronal recordings in non-human primates, human psychophysical experiments, and computational modeling to quantify 3D orientation selectivity and sensorimotor transformations. Investigations focus on the integration of monocular and binocular cues, multisensory processing for spatial constancy, and the characterization of canonical neural computations, such as divisive normalization, to study the neurodevelopmental basis of autism.
E312.research_direction: Dr. Rosenberg's recent work explores how the mammalian visual system transforms ambiguous 2D retinal images into rich representations of a dynamic 3D world. Utilizing macaque electrophysiology and computational modeling, they have recently been investigating the hierarchical computations that convert 2D motion cues into 3D motion selectivity, particularly focusing on the pathway from area MT to FST. Their research also probes how visual feature selectivity, decision-making, and saccade-related signals are spatially clustered and integrated within dorsal stream areas like V3A and CIP to support sensorimotor synthesis. Additionally, they are mapping parallel 3D-processing channels across the dorsal and ventral streams using cross-species physiological and imaging data, asking how distinct neural codes support binocular disparity, 3D object perception, and visually guided behavior.

papers.title: Primate area FST: A nexus for synthesizing a world in motion
papers.abstract: A forthcoming Trends in Neurosciences review that examines area FST as a hub where motion, depth and other signals are combined to build representations of a dynamic 3D world. It draws on macaque physiology and human imaging to synthesize what is known about FST's functions and highlights open questions.
papers.authors: Rachel Ezzo, Zikang Zhu, Lowell W Thompson, Bas Rokers, Ari Rosenberg

papers.title: The Richness of Vision in the Mammalian Brain: Neural Codes for Visual Perception and Behavior in Three Dimensions
papers.abstract: A cross-species review of how visual systems cope with a 3D world. It covers binocular-disparity coding in primate visual cortex and, more recently, tree shrews and mice, noninvasive disparity mapping in humans, geometric-part coding of 3D objects in the ventral stream, and dorsal-stream codes for 3D position and orientation that stay stable across gaze. The synthesis offers a new framing of the neural basis of rich 3D visual experience.
papers.authors: Ari Rosenberg, Holly Bridge, Charles E Connor, Jason M Samonds, Seiji Tanabe, Kristine Krug

papers.title: Differential clustering of visual and choice- and saccade-related activity in macaque V3A and CIP
papers.abstract: Using simultaneously recorded, well-isolated neurons in macaque V3A and CIP, the paper measures how visual-feature selectivity, choice-related activity and saccade-related activity are each spatially clustered. All three show significant clustering in both areas, but visual and saccade signals cluster more strongly in V3A while choice signals cluster more strongly in CIP. This suggests V3A favors within-domain processing and CIP favors cross-domain sensorimotor synthesis.
papers.authors: Zikang Zhu, Byounghoon Kim, Raymond Doudlah, Ting-Yu Chang, Ari Rosenberg

papers.title: Hierarchical computation of 3D motion across macaque areas MT and FST
papers.abstract: Recording from macaque area MT and its downstream target FST during a motion-discrimination task with multiple motion cues, the study asks where the brain converts 2D retinal motion into 3D motion. Many FST neurons but few MT neurons carry cue-invariant 3D motion selectivity, revealing a hierarchical transformation along the pathway. A model shows that such FST tuning can arise by selectively pooling the outputs of 2D-motion-selective MT neurons.
papers.authors: Lowell W Thompson, Byounghoon Kim, Bas Rokers, Ari Rosenberg

papers.title: Neuronal Representations Supporting Three-Dimensional Vision in Nonhuman Primates
papers.abstract: This review synthesizes how the primate dorsal and ventral pathways reconstruct the 3D world from ambiguous 2D retinal images through parallel channels tuned to shape, orientation, motion and scene structure. It argues that area V3A is a likely branchpoint for several 3D-processing channels and speculates that its expansion in humans supports advanced 3D spatial reasoning. Future directions for studying 3D information transmission are outlined.
papers.authors: Ari Rosenberg, Lowell W Thompson, Raymond Doudlah, Ting-Yu Chang

E319.name: Anya Hurlbert
E319.bio: Anya Hurlbert is a Professor of Visual Neuroscience who researches the physiological and computational mechanisms of human color perception, specifically color constancy. Their work employs psychophysical experimentation, computational modeling, and neuroimaging to investigate how the brain stabilizes object color across varying illuminants and the impact of individual differences on these processes. Hurlbert's current research also includes developing lighting technologies for health and applying machine learning to retinal OCT imaging for the early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases. They hold degrees in physics, physiology, and medicine, and co-founded the Institute of Neuroscience at Newcastle University.
E319.research_direction: Dr. Hurlbert has recently been investigating the perception of illumination, treating the visual system's ability to sense and discriminate lighting as a fundamental process in its own right rather than solely a mechanism for color constancy. Their recent work explores the spectral and temporal dynamics of natural daylight, pairing large-scale physical light-field measurements with psychophysical tests of human sensitivity to these environmental fluctuations. They are also studying how illumination cues shape complex visual judgments, asking how near-metameric lighting changes alter the perceived ripeness of real food and how viewers use image statistics to infer the time of day depicted in paintings. Additionally, Dr. Hurlbert is examining the photoreceptor basis of these abilities by measuring how color constancy under daylight changes is affected by varying cone class distributions in anomalous trichromats and dichromats.

papers.title: Seeing the Light: Perception and Discrimination of Illumination Color
papers.abstract: Reviews how the visual system separates the contributions of surface reflectance and illumination in the light reaching the eye, tracing the historical debate on lightness and colour constancy. Draws on modern physical measurements of the spatial, spectral and temporal structure of natural light and on studies of how well observers discriminate and perceive illumination changes. Argues for treating illumination perception as a topic in its own right rather than only a byproduct of colour constancy.
papers.authors: Anya Hurlbert, Cehao Yu

papers.title: Near-metameric illumination changes affect visually perceived food attributes
papers.abstract: Observers judged real fruit viewed in a spectrally tunable lightroom under illuminations that were nearly metameric, i.e. matched in chromaticity but different in spectral power distribution. Even these small spectral changes altered perceived attributes such as ripeness, quality and naturalness. The results show that spectral composition of light, and not only its colour temperature, matters for how food looks.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: I. Cebioglu, M. Mistry, R. Vasey, A. Hurlbert

papers.title: Physical and perceptual measurements of temporal dynamics in natural daylight
papers.abstract: Reports a large set of directional daylight spectra (thousands of measurements, hundreds of complete light-field samples) recorded across several days, two sites and varied weather. The study quantifies how chromaticity and illuminance change over time and pairs this with perceptual measurements of how sensitively observers notice such changes. It gives an empirical basis for modelling natural illumination dynamics.
papers.authors: Cehao Yu, Ruben Pastilha, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Time-of-day perception in paintings
papers.abstract: Tested whether viewers can infer the time of day depicted in paintings and which image statistics support this. Observers' judgements were related to chromatic and luminance properties of the artworks. The findings suggest that people rely on learned regularities of natural illumination when interpreting depicted light.
papers.authors: Cehao Yu, Mitchell J. P. Van Zuijlen, Cristina Spoiala, Sylvia C. Pont, Maarten W. A. Wijntjes, Anya Hurlbert

papers.title: Color constancy for daylight illumination changes in anomalous trichromats and dichromats
papers.abstract: Compared colour constancy for illumination changes along the daylight locus in observers with anomalous trichromacy and dichromacy against normal trichromats. The work asks how much colour constancy depends on the number and type of functioning cone classes. It shows that colour-deficient observers retain a substantial degree of constancy.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Stacey Aston, Gabriele Jordan, Anya Hurlbert

E321.name: Hannah Smithson
E321.main_research_area: human visual perception and neural mechanisms
E321.bio: Hannah Smithson investigates the neural and perceptual mechanisms of human vision, focusing on color and material perception. Smithson’s research utilizes high-resolution retinal imaging via adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (AOSLO) to link individual photoreceptor activity with visual performance in the living eye. By combining psychophysical experimentation with computer-rendered stimuli, they examine how the visual system achieves perceptual constancy and processes properties such as gloss, roughness, and translucency. Smithson also directs interdisciplinary initiatives that apply computational and optical analysis to historical medieval scientific texts regarding color and light.
E321.research_direction: Dr. Smithson has recently been studying how the human visual system deals with the physics of light and the biology of the retina to perceive colour. Their recent work asks how people estimate the colour of a light source from specular highlights, how much natural lighting helps us tell surface colours apart, and how spectral sensitivity of L cones varies across individuals and genetic backgrounds. They also characterize the mix of daylight and artificial light in indoor spaces in terms of the human photoreceptor classes, and are developing adaptive optics imaging to view the living retina over long sessions without dilating the pupil.

papers.title: Investigating ethnicity-related variability in the human L-cone spectral sensitivity function
papers.abstract: This study quantifies inter-individual and inter-ethnic variances in the spectral sensitivity of long-wavelength-sensitive (L) cones. By integrating psychophysical measurements with genetic profiling of the OPN1LW gene, specifically the Ser180Ala polymorphism, the researchers evaluated how demographic and ethnic factors influence peak spectral sensitivity (lambda_max). The investigation aims to refine standard cone fundamentals to better represent the natural diversity of retinal photopigments across diverse human populations.
papers.authors: Allie C. Schneider, Takuma Morimoto, Michelle E. McClements, Robert E. MacLaren, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: When the brightest is not the best: illuminant estimation from the geometry of specular highlights
papers.abstract: This research evaluates the 'brightest is white' heuristic in human color constancy, which posits that the visual system estimates illuminant chromaticity based on the highest luminance pixel in a scene. Utilizing computer-rendered stimuli with controlled surface textures and varying specularity, the authors demonstrate that operational color constancy remains robust even when specular highlights fall on dark textural regions and do not constitute the brightest elements. The results suggest the visual system utilizes the spatial geometry and structural regularities of highlights—specifically their alignment with surface curvature—to disentangle material reflectance from illumination spectra.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, Robert J. Lee, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: Quantifying CIE alpha-opic signals in the indoor built environment
papers.abstract: The study provides a comprehensive spectral and chromatic characterization of mixed-illuminant indoor 'built' environments, where artificial lighting and natural daylight interact. Using hyperspectral imaging, the authors calculate alpha-opic signals for the five human photoreceptor classes (L, M, S cones, rods, and melanopsin ipRGCs) across a typical office setting. Findings indicate that indoor environments exhibit statistical regularities in chromatic variation similar to those found in naturalistic scenes, primarily driven by daylight ingress, which may support both short-term and seasonal adaptational processes.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Samuel Ponting, Ruth Kelly Waskett, Manuel Spitschan, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: How many surfaces can you distinguish by color? Real environmental lighting increases discriminability of surface colors
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how directional variations in natural environmental illumination influence chromatic discriminability. By applying computer-graphics simulations to measured hyperspectral illumination maps, the authors quantify the resolution of illuminant metamerism for trichromatic and dichromatic observers. The results show that the directional complexity of real-world light allows for the disambiguation of over 80% of metameric surface pairs simply through changes in surface tilt, thereby effectively increasing the volume of distinguishable surface colors relative to uniform illumination conditions.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento, Hannah E. Smithson

papers.title: Extended-period AOSLO imaging in the living human retina without pupil dilation: a feasibility study
papers.abstract: This study assesses the feasibility of longitudinal high-resolution retinal imaging using an adaptive optics scanning laser ophthalmoscope (AOSLO) without pharmacological mydriasis. By monitoring six participants over 1.5-hour sessions with concurrent visual stimulation, the authors modeled the dynamic relationship between natural pupil diameter and image metrics such as sharpness and contrast-to-noise ratio. The findings demonstrate that cellular-scale resolution of the photoreceptor mosaic is reproducible and stable across extended sessions, validating the use of AOSLO in scenarios where pupil dilation is contraindicated or undesirable.
papers.authors: Jiahe Cui, Maria Villamil, Allie C. Schneider, Penelope F. Lawton, Laura K. Young, Martin J. Booth, Hannah E. Smithson

E322.name: Christoph Witzel
E322.bio: Christoph Witzel is an Associate Professor at the University of Southampton and directs the Soton Colour Lab. Witzel’s research employs psychophysics, behavioral experiments, and mathematical modeling to investigate the subjective reality of color, focusing on mechanisms of color constancy, categorical perception, and the evolution of color naming across languages. They have published findings on the memory color effect and evidence challenging color-opponent theories of afterimages in favor of cone-adaptation models. Witzel’s work also explores multisensory integration through geomagnetic sensory augmentation and examines the cognitive impacts of generative artificial intelligence.
E322.research_direction: Dr. Witzel has recently been investigating the mechanisms underlying both foundational and applied color perception, utilizing precise behavioral color-matching tasks to determine whether complementary color afterimages originate from early cone adaptation, subcortical color-opponent neurons, or later cortical processing. Their recent work explores the perceptual mechanics of color constancy, using hyperspectral imaging to examine how human observers expect surface colors to shift under varying naturalistic and artificial illumination. Alongside this, they are testing whether simplified computational matrix models can efficiently approximate full spectral renderings of these lighting changes without observers detecting a difference. Furthermore, their research extends into the applied psychological impacts of illumination, examining how the specific properties of colored lighting influence emotional and atmospheric impressions in physical spaces.

papers.title: Coloured Lighting and Perceived Atmosphere
papers.abstract: This book chapter reviews how the colour of lighting shapes the atmosphere people perceive in a space. It draws on colour perception research to link lighting properties to emotional and atmospheric impressions, with relevance to design, marketing and retail settings. The chapter reflects the Perceived Atmosphere theme of the Southampton colour lab.
papers.authors: Giulio Palma, Christoph Witzel

papers.title: The non-opponent nature of colour afterimages
papers.abstract: Complementary colour afterimages have shaped colour science for centuries, yet it has remained unclear whether they arise from adaptation in cone photoreceptors, colour-opponent subcortical neurons, or cortical mechanisms. Across several experiments, observers matched the exact colours of afterimages for inducers spanning many hues and saturations. The measured afterimage colours were not colour-opponent as commonly assumed. They followed a quantitative model of cone adaptation closely. This locates the origin of afterimages at the first stage of colour processing and offers a behavioural way to probe those mechanisms.
papers.authors: Christoph Witzel

papers.title: Colour expectations across illumination changes
papers.abstract: The study asks what observers expect a surface's colour to do when the lighting changes, a question central to colour constancy and to lighting and design applications. Using hyperspectral images of natural scenes, observers judged which rendered colour change looked plausible for naturalistic versus artificial illuminant and reflectance spectra. They favoured naturalistic changes only modestly when the whole scene was manipulated, but identified naturalistic reflectances much more reliably when a single object was altered. The results point to relational colour constancy and prior knowledge about surface colour shifts as what allows observers to recognise surfaces across illuminants.
papers.authors: Hamed Karimipour, Christoph Witzel

papers.title: Sensory representation of surface reflectances: assessments with hyperspectral images
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether a simple 3x3 matrix can summarise how a surface reflectance changes the sensory colour signal across illuminants. Observers tried to tell approximate matrix-based renderings from full spectral renderings of hyperspectral images. Discrimination was possible under narrowband illuminants but almost never under naturalistic broadband ones. The matrix model therefore captures the relevant sensory information for realistic lighting at lower computational cost than spectral rendering.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Hamed Karimipour, J. Kevin O'Regan, Christoph Witzel

E323.name: Takehiro Nagai
E323.department: Department of Information and Communications Engineering, School of Engineering
E323.bio: Takehiro Nagai is an Associate Professor at the Institute of Science Tokyo, where their research examines the psychological and computational mechanisms of human color and material perception. Nagai investigates how the visual system interprets surface qualities such as glossiness, translucency, and texture through psychophysical experimentation and image analysis. Their work addresses higher-level chromatic mechanisms and the top-down cognitive factors that influence material recognition in diverse environments. Previously, Nagai conducted postdoctoral research at the University of California, San Diego, and held faculty positions at Toyohashi University of Technology and Yamagata University.
E323.research_direction: Dr. Nagai's recent work explores how the human visual system processes complex color and material properties in naturalistic and virtual environments. They have recently been investigating whether internal representations of physical color gamuts—such as optimal colors and real-world spectral libraries—guide high-level judgments of scene realism and luminosity thresholds. Their research also utilizes head-mounted displays to examine how factors like wide fields of view and scene complexity influence color constancy. Additionally, they are probing both the plasticity of color vision by studying how repeated discrimination training distorts perceptual color spaces, and the mechanisms of material perception by measuring how motion, binocular disparity, and top-down cognitive factors modulate perceived translucency.

papers.title: The perception of realism is correlated with physical gamuts
papers.abstract: Tests whether how real a natural scene looks depends on how plausible its colors are given the physically possible surface colors. Observers rated realism of scenes whose target regions were shifted across the CIE chromaticity space, and ratings tracked a theoretical gamut built from optimal colors, except for saturated greens. A gamut modelled from real-world spectral libraries (USGS, ECOSTRESS) fit even better, supporting the idea that the visual system uses an empirically learned internal reference of natural colors.
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Optimal colors can predict luminosity thresholds in natural scenes
papers.abstract: Examines the boundary at which a surface stops looking illuminated and starts looking self-luminous. Earlier work showed that optimal colors, the theoretical limit of surface reflectances, predict this threshold for abstract stimuli; here the authors show it also holds in naturalistic scenes. The results suggest luminosity and naturalness judgments share one internal reference, a physical gamut of all colors possible for a non-emitting object.
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Impact of field of view on color constancy in virtual reality
papers.abstract: Uses a head-mounted display to ask whether VR's wide field of view and scene complexity affect color constancy. Observers judged the color of patches under different illuminants and conditions. A wider field of view strongly improved constancy, whereas scene complexity made little difference, showing VR's promise as a tool for color-constancy research.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Killian Duay, Takehiro Nagai

papers.title: Top-down effects on translucency perception in relation to shape cues
papers.abstract: Measures how motion and binocular disparity contribute to perceived translucency of objects. These cues raised perceived translucency mainly when shape information from shading was weak. The effect also depended on the order of experimental conditions, pointing to top-down, shape-related cognitive factors modulating translucency judgments.
papers.authors: Takehiro Nagai, Hiroaki Kiyokawa, Juno Kim

papers.title: Color discrimination repetition distorts color representations
papers.abstract: Investigates perceptual learning in color vision by having participants train on color discrimination at one base color over five days. Thresholds declined as expected, and unique hues, color category boundaries and color appearance near the trained color all shifted toward it. This indicates that short-term repetition can reshape the visual system's color representation.
papers.authors: Suzuha Horiuchi, Takehiro Nagai

E324.name: Maria Olkkonen
E324.bio: Olkkonen is a docent of cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki who investigates the computational and neural mechanisms underlying perceptual constancy. Their research examines how the human visual system constructs stable representations of color and material properties by integrating sensory signals with prior knowledge and memory. Olkkonen utilizes psychophysics, functional MRI (fMRI), and Bayesian computational modeling to characterize how the brain resolves internal noise and environmental variation. They also serve as a principal color scientist at Microsoft Finland, focusing on color perception in applied contexts such as augmented reality.
E324.research_direction: Dr. Olkkonen has recently been investigating how the visual system aggregates and contextualizes complex information, with a strong focus on color and ensemble perception. Their recent work explores how observers compute average colors when hue, lightness, and chroma vary simultaneously, and whether segmenting colored targets from distractors relies on low-level perceptual similarity rather than higher-level categorical boundaries. Beyond ensemble coding, they are examining spatial and temporal biases in vision by using adjustment and delayed-matching tasks to tease apart short-term serial dependence from long-term central tendency biases, and by testing whether background colors genuinely modulate the perception of facial expressions. Finally, they are translating these basic perceptual insights into applied display design by developing VR-based simulator tools that replicate the optical limitations and color distortions of augmented reality environments for rapid user research.

papers.title: Complex interactions between lightness, chroma, and hue in color ensemble perception
papers.abstract: The paper asks how people form a single perceived average color from a spatially varied set of patches when lightness, chroma and hue all vary at once and may be correlated. Using comparison and adjustment tasks with baselines from discrimination thresholds, it finds a consistent bias toward higher-than-average chroma, but little sign of a lightness bias. Perceived average hue is sometimes pulled toward hues that go with higher chroma or lightness, so color averaging is not a simple colorimetric mean.
papers.authors: Lari S. Virtanen, Toni P. Saarela, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: Does background color influence the perception of facial expression? Adjustment to neutral expression by Caucasian and Japanese participants
papers.abstract: The study tests whether a red background makes faces look angrier, using a task where participants adjust an expression to look neutral so that neither color nor emotion has to be named explicitly. Neutral points did not shift with background color or with participant ethnicity. This suggests earlier reports of red-enhanced anger perception may reflect response bias rather than a genuine perceptual effect.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Tarja Peromaa, Kaisa Tiippana, Kun Qian, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: Ensemble percepts of colored targets among distractors are influenced by hue similarity, not categorical identity
papers.abstract: Observers judged the mean hue of a target set of colored elements presented among distractor hues. They could selectively report the target mean, but distractors added noise and biased the estimates, more so when distractor hues were close to the targets. A color category boundary between targets and distractors gave no benefit, suggesting segmentation of ensembles depends on hue similarity rather than color names.
papers.authors: Lari S. Virtanen, Toni P. Saarela, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: AR-in-VR simulator: A toolbox for rapid augmented reality simulation and user research
papers.abstract: The authors present a toolbox that reproduces the optical limitations of augmented reality headsets, such as limited transparency and color distortions, inside a virtual reality headset. This lets researchers prototype and test perception and user experience for AR designs quickly without dedicated AR hardware. It links basic color perception knowledge to applied display design.
papers.authors: Jacob Hadnett-Hunter, Benjamin Lundell, Ian Ellison-Taylor, Michaela Porubanova, Tapani Alasaarela, Maria Olkkonen

papers.title: Independent short- and long-term dependencies in perception
papers.abstract: Perception is biased both by the immediately preceding stimulus (serial dependence) and by the long-run average of stimuli (central tendency bias), but these are usually studied separately. Using hue and line-length judgments in delayed matching tasks with psychometric and mixed-model analyses, the authors show both biases are present and independent, and that omitting one distorts estimates of the other. The number of intervening stimuli mattered more than elapsed time for serial dependence.
papers.authors: Toni P. Saarela, Saija M. Niemi, Maria Olkkonen

E325.name: Sophie Wuerger
E325.bio: Sophie Wuerger was a visual neuroscientist who researched the neural mechanisms underlying human color perception and the geometry of color space models. Utilizing a combination of psychophysics, electroencephalography (EEG), and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), Wuerger investigated how chromatic signals from the retina are translated in the brain and how color constancy is maintained across the human lifespan. Their research addressed fundamental vision science and applied fields, including the development of computational appearance models, multisensory integration, and 3D skin-printing technologies.
E325.research_direction: Dr. Wuerger has recently worked on measuring and modeling how humans see color and contrast. Their recent work explores a unified model that predicts contrast sensitivity from color, size, speed, brightness and position in the visual field, and how color-opponent signals in the thalamus and visual cortex are altered in glaucoma and related eye disease.
