They have also built a large multicultural archive of skin reflectance spectra, which serves as a reference for how skin color varies across people. A further thread asks how the brain keeps sight and sound aligned in time, and how the timing judgment shifts with the intensity of the preceding stimulus.

papers.title: The International Skin Spectra Archive (ISSA): a multicultural human skin phenotype and colour spectra collection
papers.abstract: This paper introduces the International Skin Spectra Archive (ISSA), a comprehensive multicultural resource comprising 15,256 spectral and colorimetric records derived from 2,113 subjects across eight countries. The archive utilizes a standardized measurement protocol for human skin phenotype data collected between 2012 and 2024, facilitating the systematic study of biological, cultural, and environmental influences on skin color variability. The dataset provides high-resolution spectral reflectance data (360–780 nm) alongside CIE colorimetric parameters, structured by ethnicity, age, gender, and anatomical body location to support advanced research in computer vision, dermatology, and anthropological science.
papers.authors: Yan Lu, Kaida Xiao, Michael Pointer, Ruili He, Sicong Zhou, Ahmed Nasseraldin, Suchitra Sueeprasan, Cheng Gao, Changjun Li, Ali Sohaib, Yuanyuan He, Yoko Mizokami, Mengmeng Wang, Esther Perales Romero, Faraedon Zardawi, Lesley Gill, Ningfang Liao, Sophie Wuerger

papers.title: Analysis of the BOLD signal along colour-opponent pathways in LGN and V1 and Microstructural Alterations of the Optic Radiation in POAG and OHT Patients
papers.abstract: This study employs functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) to investigate neural processing alterations in patients with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and ocular hypertension (OHT). By analyzing the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and primary visual cortex (V1) in response to cone-opponent chromatic stimuli, the authors identify specific functional deficits within the geniculostriate pathway. Additionally, diffusion tractography revealed microstructural alterations in the white matter of the optic radiation, which significantly correlated with clinical indicators of visual field loss and light sensitivity thresholds.
papers.authors: Joanne L. Powell, Laura M Parkes, Anshoo Choudhary, Sophie M Wuerger

papers.title: castleCSF — A contrast sensitivity function of color, area, spatiotemporal frequency, luminance and eccentricity
papers.abstract: The authors present castleCSF, a unified analytical model of the human contrast sensitivity function (CSF) that incorporates spatial frequency, temporal frequency, chromatic modulation direction, background luminance, eccentricity, and stimulus area. The model was trained and validated using a consolidated database from 18 psychophysical studies, achieving a high level of predictive accuracy (3.59 dB error) across a broad parameter space. By isolating and characterizing the achromatic and chromatic mechanisms within a post-receptoral framework, castleCSF provides a robust tool for predicting visual performance and perceptual quality in display engineering and image processing applications.
papers.authors: Maliha Ashraf, Rafał K Mantiuk, Alexandre Chapiro, Sophie Wuerger

papers.title: Perceived Audio-Visual Simultaneity Is Recalibrated by the Visual Intensity of the Preceding Trial
papers.abstract: This study examines the rapid recalibration of audio-visual simultaneity perception as a function of stimulus intensity. Through a series of temporal-order judgment (TOJ), simultaneity judgment (SJ), and simple reaction-time (RT) tasks, the authors demonstrate that the point of subjective simultaneity (PSS) shifts based on the visual intensity of the stimulus in the preceding trial. These findings suggest that the human visual system dynamically recalibrates its perception of timing to compensate for intensity-dependent processing latencies in central arrival times, although the effect is task-contingent and appears more robust in TOJ paradigms than in SJ tasks.
papers.authors: Ryan Horsfall, Neil R Harrison, Georg F Meyer, Sophie M Wuerger

E326.name: Andrew Stockman
E326.bio: Stockman is the Steers Chair of Investigative Eye Research at the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology and directs the Colour & Vision Research Laboratories. Their research focuses on the psychophysical and physiological foundations of human color vision, specifically cone spectral sensitivities, temporal sensitivity, and light adaptation mechanisms. Stockman developed standardized physiologically-based color-matching functions and the CVRL database. Their work integrates visual psychophysics with molecular genetics to investigate how specific genetic defects affect visual processing speeds and sensitivity in normal and clinical populations.
E326.research_direction: Dr. Stockman’s recent work explores the physiological basis of individual differences in human color vision, specifically focusing on modeling variations in cone spectral sensitivities. They have recently been using multi-LED visual trichromators and color matching tasks to measure how factors such as lens thickness, macular pigment density, and L- and M-cone opsin peak shifts vary across observers of different ages. Furthermore, their research investigates the practical consequences of this physiological variability, examining how narrow-band primaries in modern wide-gamut displays amplify observer metamerism and cause screen colors to appear differently across color-normal individuals. To address these mismatches, they are developing closed-form formulae and extended physiological observer models to predict individual cone sensitivities and facilitate personalized colorimetry.

papers.title: Why the colours of modern displays can look so different to different observers
papers.abstract: Examines how narrow-band primaries in modern wide-gamut displays amplify observer metamerism, so the same screen colour looks different across people with normal colour vision. Links the effect to individual differences in cone spectral sensitivities and shows how the mismatches arise and might be predicted or corrected.
papers.authors: Andrew Rider, John Frith, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Importance of individual differences in cone spectral sensitivities and color matching functions and how to correct for them: tutorial
papers.abstract: A tutorial on standard cone spectral sensitivities and colour matching functions and on how observers differ. It explains that differences stem from genetically determined shifts in L- and M-cone pigment curves and variability in lens, macular pigment and photopigment optical densities, and why these matter for narrow-band displays and lighting. It describes ways to correct for them through individualised colorimetry.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Andrew T. Rider, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Individual differences in color matches and cone spectral sensitivities in 51 young adults
papers.abstract: Forty-six young adults, plus five from an earlier study, made colour matches to a 7500 K white using a new multi-LED visual trichromator at 2 and 10 degree fields. A more intuitive CIELAB-based matching procedure lowered inter- and intra-observer variability. The matches were then fitted with a physiological observer model to estimate each person's cone spectral sensitivities.
papers.authors: Keyu Shi, Ming Ronnier Luo, Andrew T. Rider, Siyuan Song, Tingwei Huang, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Individual color matches and cone spectral sensitivities in 100 observers of varying age
papers.abstract: Extends earlier LED-trichromator measurements with 70 additional observers aged 8 to 80. The colour matches were fitted with an extended CIE physiological observer model allowing lens and macular pigment density, photopigment density and L/M cone peak positions to vary. The fits reveal how these parameters change with age relative to the standard observer.
papers.authors: Keyu Shi, Ming Ronnier Luo, Andrew T. Rider, Siyuan Song, Tingwei Huang, Andrew Stockman

papers.title: Formulae for generating standard and individual human cone spectral sensitivities
papers.abstract: Provides closed-form formulae and tables for the standard CIE-sanctioned LMS cone spectral sensitivities of Stockman and Sharpe, so they can be computed at any wavelength step. Extends the same framework so that individual cone sensitivities can be generated by varying lens and macular pigment density, photopigment optical density and L/M opsin peak position. It is a practical reference for colorimetry and personalised colour specification.
papers.authors: Andrew Stockman, Andrew T. Rider

E328.name: Yoko Mizokami
E328.bio: Mizokami is a Professor at Chiba University's Graduate School of Informatics and directs the Vision Science Laboratory. Their research employs psychophysical techniques and image statistics to investigate human visual information processing, specifically color constancy and visual adaptation to natural environments. Mizokami has published on the perception of material properties (shitsukan), including the relationship between lighting and the visual appearance of skin color and texture. Their work applies these findings to color engineering, universal design for color vision diversity, and the evaluation of lighting environments.
E328.research_direction: Dr. Mizokami's recent work explores the visual mechanisms underlying how we perceive complex surfaces, with a primary focus on human skin color and material gloss. In their face perception research, they are investigating how specific pigment modulations—such as varying melanin and hemoglobin—and distinct color-axis shifts influence cross-cultural judgments of facial brightness, healthiness, and overall impression. By comparing observer color matches of holistic faces against isolated skin patches, they are probing how face-specific visual processing and observer ethnicity cause perceived skin color to systematically deviate from raw colorimetric averages. In a distinct line of material appearance research, Dr. Mizokami has recently been examining the spatial and angular properties of specular reflections on varied physical objects. By utilizing high-resolution goniometry and surface normal vectors, their work aims to mathematically quantify, model, and digitally archive "gloss unevenness" and the bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDF) of diverse materials.

papers.title: Facial Brightness Perception Is Influenced by Hemoglobin and Melanin Modulation
papers.abstract: The study asks how the two main skin pigments shape how bright a face looks. Using face images in which hemoglobin (redness) or melanin was simulated to rise or fall, Japanese observers judged brighter faces when hemoglobin increased or melanin decreased. The same colour changes applied to uniform patches did not produce this effect, pointing to a face-specific perceptual compensation for skin pigmentation.
papers.authors: Yuanyuan He, Takahisa Kitano, Hiromi Sato, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Quantifying Skin Color Appearance in Human Faces and Textured Skin Patches
papers.abstract: Seventy-six Caucasian and Chinese observers matched the overall colour appearance of face images or textured skin patches in CIELAB space, using 80 Caucasian and 80 Chinese faces. Perceived colour systematically departed from the colorimetric average: matches to faces were lighter and less chromatic, while matches to skin patches were slightly lighter and more chromatic. The deviations depended on stimulus type and ethnicity, informing how skin colour should be measured.
papers.authors: Yan Lu, Kaida Xiao, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Gloss Archiving with Normal Vectors
papers.abstract: The paper proposes recording the gloss of a material through surface normal-vector information so that glossy appearance can be archived and reproduced digitally. It connects the lab's gloss measurement work to practical digital archiving of material appearance.
papers.authors: Shinichi Inoue, Yoshinori Igarashi, Shota Tsuneyasu, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Cross-cultural comparison of the influence of skin-color change on facial impressions
papers.abstract: Face images of three ethnic groups were shifted along the red-yellow axis and rated by Japanese, Chinese, Thai and Caucasian observers on healthiness, preference, brightness, whiteness, transparency and skin tone. Cultures differed in which skin colours carried positive impressions: East Asian observers linked reddish skin with positive traits, while Caucasian observers more often linked yellowish skin with them.
papers.authors: Yuanyuan He, Hiromi Sato, Yoko Mizokami

papers.title: Analysis of Gloss Unevenness and Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function in Specular Reflection
papers.abstract: The authors built a goniometric apparatus with 0.02 degree angular resolution to measure gloss unevenness, the intensity variation within a highlight. Measuring mirrors, plastics and glossy papers, they found unevenness peaks at angles slightly off the centre of specular reflection. They relate this to the BRDF and propose a physical definition of gloss unevenness.
papers.authors: So Nakamura, Shinichi Inoue, Yoshinori Igarashi, Hiromi Sato, Yoko Mizokami

E329.name: Sérgio Nascimento
E329.bio: Sérgio Miguel Cardoso Nascimento is an Associate Professor in the Physics Department at the University of Minho, where they conduct research within the Colour Science Laboratory. Nascimento’s work explores the intersection of human visual perception and the physical properties of light, focusing on color constancy, spectral imaging, and the statistical properties of colors in natural and artistic scenes. They have used hyperspectral imaging to quantify visual information and have integrated neural network architectures to develop automated diagnostic tools for color vision deficiencies and virtual restoration of historical paintings. Nascimento’s current research investigates how atmospheric scattering and natural lighting variations modulate color discrimination and aesthetic preferences in human observers.
E329.research_direction: Dr. Nascimento has recently been investigating how human color vision operates within the statistical structure of natural environments. Their recent work explores the interaction between eye movements and color perception, specifically using gaze tracking and hyperspectral imaging to understand how individual cone photoreceptors sample global scene color statistics to maximize surface information and facilitate retinal adaptation. Additionally, they have been examining red-green color vision deficiencies, combining computational models to estimate real-world visual information loss with neural network-assisted color-naming tasks to develop rapid diagnostic tools. They are also probing the computational limits of relational color constancy, investigating how natural deviations in cone-excitation ratios influence an observer's ability to accurately distinguish illuminant changes from material surface changes.

papers.title: Eye movements efficiently expose single cone photoreceptors to global scene color statistics
papers.abstract: Observers' gaze was recorded while they freely viewed natural scenes outdoors and, indoors, hyperspectral renderings of the same scenes. Accumulating local histograms of long-, medium- and short-wavelength cone excitations over time, the authors show that despite very uneven gaze patterns, individual cones are exposed to the full scene's global color statistics within a few seconds. This sampling should let local retinal adaptation discount changes in the illuminant.
papers.authors: Takuma Morimoto, Luna Wang, Kinjiro Amano, David H. Foster, Sérgio M.C. Nascimento

papers.title: Directing gaze to maximize surface color information from natural scenes
papers.abstract: Using two sets of gaze recordings on natural scenes (target search and free viewing), the study estimates how much surface-color information cone photoreceptors gather at fixations. Information acquired approached the possible maximum, matched a deep-network model, rose with scene color diversity (color entropy), and fell with fewer cone classes as in some color deficiencies. The authors argue gaze is directed to maximize elementary surface-color information.
papers.authors: David H. Foster, Kinjiro Amano, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: Rapid test for detecting red–green color vision deficiencies using a neural network-assisted color-naming task
papers.abstract: Fifty-six observers (normal trichromats, dichromats and anomalous trichromats) named 182 natural-scene colors with 11 basic terms, and a neural network classified each person. Screening reached about 97-99% sensitivity and specificity, and a 20-color subset sufficed, so a test could take under two minutes. Color naming thus offers a fast, accurate digital screen for red-green deficiency.
papers.authors: José A. R. Monteiro, Dora N. Marques, João M. M. Linhares, Sérgio M. C. Nascimento

papers.title: Little information loss with red-green color deficient vision in natural environments
papers.abstract: Computationally estimating the information available about colored surfaces in sets of 50 and 100 hyperspectral natural scenes, the study finds red-green color deficient observers lose only a little relative to normal trichromats. Large lightness variation, small redness-greenness variation and uneven frequencies of surface colors explain this. Although deficiency hampers some tasks, it has much less impact on gaining information from natural environments.
papers.authors: David H. Foster, Sérgio M.C. Nascimento

papers.title: Misidentifying illuminant changes in natural scenes due to failures in relational colour constancy
papers.abstract: Observers can usually tell illuminant changes from surface changes, which is often attributed to preserved cone-excitation ratios between surfaces. This work shows that natural deviations in those ratios can cause illuminant changes to be misidentified. It shows the limits of relational color constancy in natural scenes.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
papers.authors: Sérgio M. C. Nascimento, David H. Foster

E330.name: Paul Martin
E330.main_research_area: Primate color vision and retinal circuitry
E330.bio: Paul R. Martin is a Professor of Experimental Ophthalmology who researches the functional architecture of the primate visual system, focusing on the retinal and subcortical pathways mediating color, form, and motion perception. Martin’s work utilizes high-resolution neuroanatomical tracing, electrophysiology, and connectomic reconstruction to identify specific visual channels, including investigations into the role of 'thorny' and 'tufted' retinal ganglion cells. Martin has characterized the koniocellular pathway and the physiological mechanisms of chromatic sensitivity in the lateral geniculate nucleus. Their current research involves the connectomic mapping of the human fovea and the study of retinal circuit resilience to transsynaptic degeneration following cortical lesions.
E330.research_direction: Dr. Martin has recently been investigating the anatomical organization, developmental vulnerabilities, and metabolic constraints of specific parallel visual pathways in primate models. Their recent experimental work explores how lesions to the primary visual cortex at various developmental stages in marmosets induce retrograde transsynaptic degeneration, using targeted immunohistochemistry to assess the relative vulnerability of midget versus parasol retinal ganglion cells and the lateral geniculate nucleus. In parallel, they are mapping the fundamental spatial limits of the magnocellular pathway by employing selective antibody markers and dye injections to quantify the topographical distribution of ON and OFF parasol cells across varying eccentricities in the macaque retina. Finally, their recent theoretical writings examine the broader principles of visual processing, focusing on how distinct populations of retinal neurons divide signaling burdens and metabolic demands to adapt to changing environmental light levels.

papers.title: Transsynaptic Degeneration of Retinal Ganglion Cells Following Lesions to Primary Visual Cortex in Marmosets
papers.abstract: Marmosets were given a unilateral lesion of primary visual cortex either as infants or as a young adult, and about two years later retinal ganglion cell (RGC) density and LGN volume were measured. RGC loss near the fovea was roughly twice as large after lesions in the first two postnatal weeks as after lesions at 4 or 6 weeks, and was negligible after an adult lesion, and RGC loss tracked LGN shrinkage. Widefield/parasol-type cells labelled by CaMKII or GABA-A receptor antibodies were largely spared, indicating that the midget pathway is the most vulnerable to retrograde transneuronal degeneration.
papers.authors: Tanin Sepehrisadr, Nafiseh Atapour, Alyssa K. Baldicano, Marcello G. P. Rosa, Ulrike Grünert, Paul R. Martin

papers.title: Contribution of parasol-magnocellular pathway ganglion cells to foveal retina in macaque monkey
papers.abstract: Using CA8 antibodies, which the authors show selectively mark OFF parasol cells, together with GABA-A receptor labelling and dye injections, they counted ON and OFF parasol ganglion cells across macaque retina. Each polarity makes up about 6% of ganglion cells in central retina and about 10% in the far periphery, so parasol density near the fovea is higher and declines more gently with eccentricity than earlier estimates. The parasol array's sampling limit falls well short of behavioural grating acuity, implying that other pathways set high-acuity vision.
papers.authors: Ivy C. K. Ma, Sara Nasir-Ahmad, Sammy C. S. Lee, Ulrike Grünert, Paul R. Martin

papers.title: Neurons share an intense load
papers.abstract: A Science Perspective on work showing that cells in the eye which detect time of day adjust their responses to light intensity in a customised way. It frames how neurons in the visual system divide up the burden of signalling and metabolic demand.
papers.authors: Paul R. Martin

E331.name: Maureen Neitz
E331.bio: Neitz is a Professor and the Ray H. Hill Endowed Chair in Ophthalmology at the University of Washington, where they specialize in the molecular genetics and neurobiology of the visual system. Neitz’s research identifies genetic variants in human cone photopigments that contribute to color vision deficiencies, nearsightedness, and age-related macular degeneration. This work includes research in gene therapy and the use of viral vectors to treat color blindness in adult non-human primates. Neitz's current work focuses on applying genomic techniques, such as long-read sequencing and droplet digital PCR, to develop diagnostic tools for early risk detection and therapeutic interventions for inherited retinal disorders.
E331.research_direction: Dr. Neitz has recently been investigating the biological mechanisms underlying refractive development and inherited color vision anomalies. A major focus of their recent work explores the contrast theory of myopia, probing how peripheral retinal contrast signals—processed via ON and OFF retinal pathways—modulate eye elongation. They are actively translating these mechanistic models into clinical applications by evaluating how light-scattering spectacle lenses can reduce retinal contrast to slow myopia progression in children. Additionally, their research continues to examine the molecular genetics of color vision disorders, mapping variations in X-linked opsin gene arrays to specific clinical phenotypes and exploring the potential for targeted gene therapies in primate models.

papers.title: The Predictive and Explanatory Power of the Contrast Theory of Myopia
papers.abstract: Lays out the contrast theory of myopia, which holds that the eye elongates in response to the strength of contrast signals in the peripheral retina, with ON and OFF signaling pathways acting as the detector. The authors argue that the theory accounts for many otherwise puzzling observations about how myopia develops and responds to optical interventions. They also use it to make testable predictions about which treatments should and should not slow progression.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: Color Vision Defects
papers.abstract: Book chapter reviewing the genetics and molecular basis of inherited color vision deficiencies. It covers the opsin gene arrays on the X chromosome, how gene rearrangements and variants produce different deficiencies, and the implications for diagnosis and counseling. It also touches on gene therapy prospects.
papers.venue: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics and Genomics
papers.authors: Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Disorders of Color Vision
papers.abstract: Book chapter in a genetic eye disease text summarizing the inherited and acquired disorders of color vision. It describes the underlying photopigment genetics, clinical presentation and testing, and current directions for treatment including gene therapy in primate models.
papers.venue: Genetic Diseases of the Eye (Oxford University Press)
papers.authors: Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT): A Myopia Control Spectacle Lens Based on Contrast Theory
papers.abstract: Describes a spectacle lens that scatters light slightly to lower retinal image contrast, designed directly from contrast theory to slow myopia progression in children. The paper explains the optical design, how it reduces contrast signals without a large loss of visual acuity, and summarizes supporting clinical evidence. It links a mechanistic hypothesis about eye growth to a deployable treatment.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: Clarification on the understanding of contrast theory in relation to the article "ON and OFF receptive field processing in the presence of optical scattering": comment
papers.abstract: A short comment responding to another paper on how optical scattering affects ON and OFF retinal receptive fields. The authors clarify what contrast theory of myopia actually claims and correct a misreading of how scattering lenses are supposed to act on retinal contrast.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

E332.name: Jay Neitz
E332.bio: Neitz is the Bishop Professor of Ophthalmology at the University of Washington and co-director of the Neitz Lab. Their research integrates molecular genetics with primate psychophysics to investigate the biological mechanisms underlying color perception and retinal disease. Neitz demonstrated the restoration of trichromatic vision in adult monkeys via gene therapy, a study concerning neural plasticity in the adult visual system. Currently, their work focuses on the 'contrast theory' of myopia and the development of spectacle lens technologies designed to mitigate the progression of nearsightedness.
E332.research_direction: Dr. Neitz's recent work explores the mechanistic foundations of both refractive error and color vision, spanning theoretical modeling, retinal connectomics, and translational clinical tools. They have recently been investigating the contrast theory of myopia, evaluating whether lowering retinal image contrast via specialized diffusion spectacles can slow eye elongation and account for broader epidemiological trends. In parallel, their research on color processing examines how cone signals combine to produce unique hues and maps the precise synaptic inputs to OFF midget ganglion cells in the macaque retina using serial block-face electron microscopy. Additionally, they are developing accessible diagnostic methods, most notably by testing a smartphone-based anomaloscope against opsin genotyping to provide accurate, widely available screening for red-green color deficiency.

papers.title: The Predictive and Explanatory Power of the Contrast Theory of Myopia
papers.abstract: Argues that the contrast theory of myopia accounts for a broad range of experimental and epidemiological findings, from animal lens-treatment results to why some environments promote myopia. The authors use it to make testable predictions and to compare it with competing explanations.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: Amacrine cell inputs to OFF midget ganglion cells in macaque retina
papers.abstract: Uses serial block-face electron microscopy of macaque retina to identify which amacrine and bipolar cells synapse onto OFF midget ganglion cells, the cells behind fine acuity and part of the colour pathway. The reconstruction gives a wiring diagram that helps explain how these cells get their light responses.
papers.authors: David W. Marshak, Andrea S. Bordt, Emma R. Yang, Joel N. Yearick, Marcus Mazzaferri, James A. Kuchenbecker, Judith Mosinger Ogilvie, Sara S. Patterson, Jay Neitz

papers.title: iPhone-based anomaloscope for accessible, accurate color vision testing
papers.abstract: Presents a smartphone version of the classic anomaloscope for diagnosing red-green colour deficiency, meant to reproduce the lab instrument's accuracy on a widely available device. It is checked against opsin gene genotyping.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Dragos Rezeanu, James A. Kuchenbecker, Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

papers.title: Diffusion Optics Technology (DOT): A Myopia Control Spectacle Lens Based on Contrast Theory
papers.abstract: Describes a spectacle lens that scatters light slightly to lower retinal image contrast, on the premise that reduced contrast slows eye elongation. The paper sets out the contrast-theory rationale behind the design and how the lens works optically. It is the theoretical and design basis for a commercial myopia-control lens.
papers.authors: Jay Neitz, Maureen Neitz

papers.title: From cones to color vision: a neurobiological model that explains the unique hues
papers.abstract: Proposes a physiologically grounded model of how cone signals are combined to produce the four unique hues, meant to avoid the post hoc adjustments earlier models needed to place unique red and green. It also addresses the nonlinearity of the blue/yellow system.
papers.venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America A
papers.authors: Dragos Rezeanu, Maureen Neitz, Jay Neitz

E333.name: Mark Fairchild
E333.department: Integrated Sciences Academy, College of Science
E333.bio: Mark D. Fairchild is a Professor whose research focuses on the psychophysical modeling of color appearance and the human visual system's response to high-dynamic-range (HDR) imagery. They developed the iCAM image appearance framework, contributed to the CIECAM02 color appearance model, and authored the textbook 'Color Appearance Models.' Fairchild’s technical work investigates chromatic adaptation, observer metamerism, and the development of LMS-based fundamental lightness and brightness scales. Currently, their research explores individual differences in color perception and the application of colorimetric measurement to complex natural stimuli, including vegetation and viticulture sensory evaluation.
E333.research_direction: Dr. Fairchild has recently been investigating the computational modeling of color appearance and the various environmental and physiological factors that shape human color perception. Their recent work explores fundamental color spaces by deriving hue scales directly from cone responses and modeling the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect to better predict the perceived brightness of chromatic stimuli. They are also examining individual differences in visual systems by using cross-media metameric matching experiments to estimate observer-specific color matching functions. Furthermore, Dr. Fairchild studies how spatial and ambient contexts influence perception on modern emissive displays, utilizing psychophysical methods to quantify how stimulus size alters perceived lightness and how surrounding illumination drives chromatic adaptation.

papers.title: Derivation and evaluation of fundamental hue scales
papers.abstract: Builds on an earlier fundamental hue model that computes hue directly from cone (LMS) responses. Cone signals are converted to opponent axes and then rotated, using either five principal hues (a hue-discrimination scale) or four unique hues (a hue-appearance scale). The refined model is tested against the Munsell, NCS, Hung-Berns and Ebner-Fairchild datasets and against three new experiments, examining linearity, spacing and hue quadrature.
papers.authors: Saeedeh Abasi, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Changes in Displayed Brightness/Lightness with Stimulus Size
papers.abstract: Studies how the perceived brightness and lightness of an emissive display stimulus change as its size changes. Uses psychophysical measurements on a high-dynamic-range display to quantify the effect, since standard appearance models do not account for stimulus size in this regime.
papers.venue: Journal of Imaging Science and Technology
papers.authors: Saeedeh Abasi, Luke Hellwig, Dale Stolitzka, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Chromatic Adaptation in Displays: The Influence of Ambient Environment
papers.abstract: Uses a series of psychophysical experiments to test how surround light, background properties and stimulus luminance affect chromatic adaptation to a display. Finds a significant interaction between background and surround conditions, and proposes two frameworks for the mixed adaptation mechanism that predict observer responses across ambient conditions.
papers.authors: Eddie Pei, Susan P. Farnand, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: Individual color matching functions from cross-media color-matching experiment
papers.abstract: Presents a cross-media matching experiment in which physical pigment samples are matched against a digital display to estimate individual observers' color matching functions. Kubelka-Munk theory is used to synthesize broadband pigments and design metameric pairs that separate categorical observers. Individual functions predicted matches better than the CIE 1931 2-degree standard observer, and the paper discusses how higher bit depth, narrower-band displays and more repetitions could improve accuracy.
papers.authors: Che Shen, Mark D. Fairchild

papers.title: The brightness of chromatic stimuli
papers.abstract: Reports three brightness-matching experiments that constrain the chroma difference between matched stimulus pairs. This refinement enables a calculus-based model of the brightness of chromatic stimuli and of the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect, formulated to be compatible with CIECAM16 and CIELAB. The CIECAM16-based model predicts four newer datasets best but overpredicts the weaker effect seen in three older studies, and the authors discuss possible experimental reasons for the split.
papers.authors: Luke Hellwig, Dale Stolitzka, Mark D. Fairchild

E337.name: Trafton Drew
E337.main_research_area: visual attention and medical image perception
E337.bio: Drew investigates the neural underpinnings and practical consequences of human attentional and memory limitations within the domain of medical image perception. Their research utilizes a multimodal approach combining electroencephalography (EEG), eye-tracking, and behavioral metrics to analyze how experts such as radiologists navigate complex visual information. Drew has demonstrated inattentional blindness in expert observers, showing that specialists can miss salient anomalies when engaged in focused search tasks. Their work currently focuses on developing interventional methods to reduce diagnostic errors and mapping the electrophysiological correlates of hybrid search processes involving both visual space and memory.
E337.research_direction: Dr. Drew has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying complex visual search, particularly how working and long-term memory systems interact during hybrid search tasks. Using techniques like EEG and incidental recognition paradigms, their recent work explores how attentional allocation, distractor encoding, and premature search termination are influenced by factors such as categorical target-distractor similarity and the reliability of predictive cues. In addition to basic search mechanisms, they are examining real-world visual expertise among professionals like pathologists, radiologists, and architects. By leveraging eye-tracking and pupillometry, Dr. Drew investigates how holistic viewing strategies, diagnostic difficulty, and experience levels manifest in oculomotor behavior, and whether these expert perceptual strategies can transfer across different visual domains.

papers.title: Electrophysiological Correlates of Visual Memory Search
papers.abstract: In hybrid search, observers look through a scene for any of several items held in memory. Using EEG across three experiments, the authors tracked a marker of long-term memory recognition (FN400) and one of working-memory load (CDA) as the number of remembered targets grew. Both signals scaled with memory set size even when the set exceeded working-memory capacity, and both were modulated by how similar targets and distractors were, showing that the two memory systems work together during memory search.
papers.authors: Lauren H. Williams, Iris Wiegand, Mark Lavelle, Jeremy M. Wolfe, Keisuke Fukuda, Marius V. Peelen, Trafton Drew

papers.title: Cue relevance drives early quitting in visual search
papers.abstract: Salient distractors are known to make people quit searching early. This study asks whether a task-relevant cue that sometimes fails to mark the target does the same. When a highly predictive red-circle cue was a false positive, observers ended search sooner and missed more targets than in a no-cue control, whereas a poorly predictive cue produced no such effect, indicating that trust in a cue drives premature stopping.
papers.authors: Jeff Moher, Anna Delos Reyes, Trafton Drew

papers.title: Pathologist pupil dilation reflects experience level and difficulty in diagnosing medical images
papers.abstract: Pathologists' eye movements and pupil diameter were recorded while they viewed digital whole-slide breast biopsy images. Pupil size tracked how hard a case was, judged by diagnostic disagreement among experts, and differed with the pathologist's experience level. The results suggest pupillometry could help flag difficult cases and gauge competence during training.
papers.authors: Trafton Drew, Catherine E. Konold, Mark Lavelle, Tad T. Brunyé, Kathleen F. Kerr, Hannah Shucard, Donald L. Weaver, Joann G. Elmore

papers.title: Visual expertise is more than meets the eye: an examination of holistic visual processing in radiologists and architects
papers.abstract: Holistic visual processing, in which experts take in a wider region of the image while fixating more selectively, was compared in radiologists, architects and novices using eye tracking. Expertise proved domain specific, yet the holistic viewing strategy itself transferred across domains. Despite this, the strategy did not translate into faster or more accurate search outside the expert's own field.
papers.authors: Spencer Ivy, Taren Rohovit, Jeanine Stefanucci, Dustin Stokes, Megan Mills, Trafton Drew

papers.title: Incidental recognition reveals attentional tradeoffs shaped by categorical similarity
papers.abstract: Using an incidental memory test after search, the authors probed what observers attend to and encode during hybrid-style visual search. Recognition patterns reveal tradeoffs in attentional allocation that depend on how similar items are to the target category, linking search behavior to memory for distractors.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Mark Lavelle, Roy Luria, Trafton Drew

E339.name: Christian Olivers
E339.department: Department of Experimental and Applied Psychology, Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences
E339.bio: Christian Olivers is a Full Professor of Visual Cognition whose research examines the functional and neural interactions between visual attention, working memory, and multisensory perception. Olivers investigates the 'attentional template,' specifically how representations stored in working memory guide selective vision and prioritize task-relevant environmental stimuli. Their work includes the development of the 'Boost and Bounce' theory of temporal attention and studies on the attentional blink and visual search using behavioral psychophysics, eye-tracking, and EEG. Currently, Olivers focuses on the dynamics of target representations in complex, multi-target search environments and the role of retinal eccentricity in selection biases.
E339.research_direction: Dr. Olivers has recently been investigating how cognitive mechanisms like selective attention and working memory operate across different regions of the visual field, treating retinal eccentricity as a fundamental variable in visual processing. Their recent papers examine how distance from the fovea alters attentional priority when simultaneous stimuli compete, and whether perceptual biases like serial dependence vary between central and peripheral vision. Using methods such as EEG decoding, they are also exploring the spatial dynamics of visual working memory, specifically testing how peripherally encoded memories generalize across locations before being selected for report. Additionally, their research probes the interaction between working memory and motor plans, investigating how the intent to act upon a memorized object influences its capacity to bias visual selection.

papers.title: Spatial generalization of peripherally encoded memories emerges before selection for report
papers.abstract: Uses EEG decoding to follow how a memory item presented in the periphery is represented over time. Memories encoded in the periphery spread to other spatial locations early on, before observers select the item for report, indicating that peripheral memory content is not tied to its original location.
papers.authors: Güven Kandemir, Christian Olivers

papers.title: Serial dependence is stronger for peripheral than for central vision
papers.abstract: Tests whether the tendency for current perception to be pulled toward recently seen stimuli varies across the visual field. Serial dependence turns out stronger in the periphery than at the center of gaze, consistent with the periphery relying more on prior information when sensory evidence is noisier.
papers.authors: Guven Kandemir, Christian N. L. Olivers

papers.title: Selective attention and eccentricity: A comprehensive review
papers.abstract: Reviews the literature on how attentional selection changes with distance from the fovea. It argues that stimuli nearer fixation are favored across search, capture and memory tasks, and that this cannot be reduced to a simple fixation bias or to visual acuity limits. It sets out an agenda for treating eccentricity as a core variable in theories of attention.
papers.authors: Christian N.L. Olivers

papers.title: Eccentricity determines the competition for attention
papers.abstract: Examines how competition between simultaneously present stimuli is resolved as a function of where they fall in the visual field. The work shows that retinal eccentricity shapes which stimulus wins selection, positioning eccentricity as a determinant of attentional priority alongside salience and relevance.
papers.authors: Christian N. L. Olivers, Güven Kandemir, Elle van Heusden

papers.title: Visual working memory representations bias attention more when they are the target of an action plan
papers.abstract: Shows that a memorized object guides attention more strongly when participants plan to act on it than when they only need to remember it. This supports the idea that action relevance prioritizes working memory content and boosts its influence on visual selection.
papers.authors: Caterina Trentin, Heleen A. Slagter, Christian N.L. Olivers

E341.name: Melissa Võ
E341.bio: Melissa Võ investigates "scene grammar," the semantic and syntactic rules governing the organization of objects in real-world environments. Using eye-tracking, EEG, and immersive virtual reality, they examine how these internal representations guide attention and affect the efficiency of visual search. Võ's work addresses how "anchor objects" provide spatial context for locating smaller targets and how the brain processes inconsistencies in scene structure. Currently, their lab focuses on the developmental trajectories of scene knowledge and the implementation of these cognitive constraints into computational models of vision.
E341.research_direction: Dr. Võ has recently been investigating the mechanisms of rapid scene understanding and object memory, focusing on how the visual system exploits structural and functional regularities known as scene grammar. Their recent work explores how observers flexibly utilize distinct visual cues—such as action-structuring anchor objects, category-predictive diagnostic objects, and global texture statistics—to evaluate scene realism, categorize environments, and extract functional meaning from scenes. To probe these questions, they leverage a diverse methodological toolkit that includes GAN-generated scene manipulations, lexical priming, eye-tracking, and EEG. Furthermore, they are investigating the neural and behavioral differences in how objects are recollected during active visual search compared to intentional memorization, while also mapping the broader developmental trajectory of scene and object representations in children.

papers.title: Flexible usage of object and global scene information during human scene categorization
papers.abstract: Examines how observers combine information from individual objects and global scene texture statistics to extract scene gist and categorize scenes. Using manipulated and generated scenes, the study shows that people flexibly shift their reliance between these information sources depending on what is available. This refines accounts of how objects contribute to rapid scene understanding.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Sandro L. Wiesmann, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: The development of object representations in children
papers.abstract: Studies how children's mental representations of objects, including their scene-based structure, develop across childhood. The paper extends the lab's scene-grammar framework to a developmental population, which is a growing focus of the group.
papers.authors: Dilara Deniz Türk, Jacopo Turini Volonghi, Melissa Le-Hoa Võ

papers.title: The role of anchor objects in scene function understanding
papers.abstract: Proposes that scenes are structured hierarchically by actions, with anchor objects marking functionally distinct phrases, and tests whether anchor objects inform understanding of scene function. Removing action-related anchors impaired matching to action words and weakened priming in a lexical decision task, more than removing unrelated anchors or random objects. Scene context alone did not always suffice for understanding function.
papers.authors: Lea Alexandra Müller Karoza, Sandro L. Wiesmann, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: Incidental Encoding of Objects during Search Is Stronger Than Intentional Memorization due to Increased Recollection Rather Than Familiarity
papers.abstract: Asks whether the memory advantage for objects found during visual search reflects stronger memory overall or a difference in recollection versus familiarity. In a preregistered study combining remember-know judgments, ROC analyses, EEG (FN400, LPC) and eye tracking, searched-for targets were more often recollected than intentionally memorized objects, with no familiarity difference. The neural signatures only partly matched this behavioral dissociation.
papers.authors: Jason Helbing, Dejan Draschkow, Melissa L.-H. Võ

papers.title: Anchor objects drive realism while diagnostic objects drive categorization in GAN generated scenes
papers.abstract: Tests which object properties underlie scene understanding by using GAN-generated scenes that naturally vary in realism and categorizability. Anchor objects, together with high-level features from pretrained deep networks, drove how realistic scenes looked, while diagnostic objects (predictive of scene category) mainly determined categorization, regardless of realism. The work supports the view that the visual system exploits reliable object co-occurrence statistics.
papers.authors: Aylin Kallmayer, Melissa L.-H. Võ

E342.name: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño
E342.department: Departamento de Psicología Social y Metodología
E342.lab_name: Atención Visual y Memoria de Trabajo a lo largo de la Vida (Visual Attention & WM Lifespan Lab)
E342.bio: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño is a Professor at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid who researches the functional interactions between visual attention and working memory. Their work utilizes experimental psychophysics, eye-tracking, and fMRI to investigate cognitive mechanisms in tasks such as hybrid visual foraging and rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP). Gil-Gómez de Liaño studies the development of these systems across the lifespan, including typical and atypical trajectories in children and clinical populations such as patients with traumatic brain injuries. Their recent projects, including the ForageKid and Hyperfocus initiatives, model the cognitive architectures underlying search behavior to develop interventions for attentional improvement.
E342.research_direction: Dr. Gil-Gómez de Liaño has recently been studying how people search a display for many targets and decide when to move on, a process called visual foraging. Their recent work explores how the spatial pattern of a person's target selections can predict when they will quit a patch, which matters for tasks like radiological screening or baggage inspection. They also follow how these search strategies unfold over time and change across the lifespan. A related thread uses a search task with children, teens, and young adults to ask how developing attention and executive control affect whether people notice an unexpected object, a lapse known as inattentional blindness.

papers.title: One factor to bind them all: visual foraging organization to predict patch leaving behavior with ROC curves
papers.abstract: Determining quitting thresholds represents a fundamental problem in visual search paradigms such as radiological screening and security baggage inspection. This investigation evaluates the predictive capacity of spatial organization indices—specifically the best-r metric, mean intertarget distance (mean ITD), proximity to the nearest adjacent target (PAO), and intersection rate (IR)—as optimal criteria governing patch-leaving decisions during multi-target visual foraging amidst distractors. In a cohort of 29 adults tested across static and dynamic foraging tasks, combined with secondary analyses of diverse lifespan foraging datasets, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve modeling demonstrated that spatial organization indices consistently outperform conventional animal-derived intake rate metrics in classifying human quitting behavior. Crucially, combining spatial organization metrics and classical intake rates within a single unitary latent factor yielded maximal predictive power, establishing scanpath organization as a critical determinant in modeling optimal patch departure decisions.
papers.authors: Marcos Bella-Fernández, Manuel Suero Suñé, Alicia Ferrer-Mendieta, Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño

papers.title: The time course of visual foraging in the lifespan: Spatial scanning, organization search, and target processing
papers.abstract: In non-exhaustive visual foraging, observers search a display for an undetermined subset of targets among distractors before choosing to leave the patch. While spatial scanning and organization metrics have been established in exhaustive cancellation paradigms, their temporal evolution in non-exhaustive dynamic foraging across development remains poorly characterized. Here, spatial organization metrics—including best-r, mean intertarget distance (mean ITD), PAO, intersection rates, and Bayesian spatial parameters—were applied to evaluate foraging dynamics in a cross-sectional cohort of 279 observers aged 4 to 25 years during feature and conjunction foraging under free giving-up time. The analyses demonstrate that younger observers deploy significantly less organized scanpaths, and feature foraging exhibits greater organization than conjunction foraging. Furthermore, organization decreases as display set size increases and degrades systematically across the duration of search within a patch, indicating that impending search termination is indexed by an organization decline that signals patch-leaving rules.
papers.authors: Marcos Bella-Fernández, Manuel Suero Suñé, Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño

papers.title: Attentional development can help us understand the inattentional blindness effect in visual search
papers.abstract: Inattentional blindness (IB) occurs when an observer fails to notice a salient, unexpected visual event while engaged in an attentionally demanding primary task. To determine how developmental differences in attentional and executive mechanisms modulate IB, an unexpected critical stimulus was embedded within an ongoing visual search protocol administered to 277 participants aged 4 to 25 years. Participants were assessed with the Continuous Performance Test (CPT/K-CPT) for attentional functioning, the Reynolds Intellectual Screening Test (RIST) for general cognitive capacity, and classic visual search metrics (hit rate, reaction times, search slopes, and intercepts). A robust developmental effect was identified: younger children aged 4 to 8–9 years demonstrated substantially heightened IB rates (spanning 60% to over 90%) relative to older cohorts, whereas IQ proxies and basic task performance did not predict IB susceptibility. These findings indicate that the ontogeny of visual attention and executive control networks directly governs susceptibility to inattentional blindness.
papers.authors: Beatriz Gil-Gómez de Liaño, Chiara Castelletti, Elena Perez-Hernandez, María Quirós-Godoy, Jeremy M. Wolfe

E343.name: Todd Horowitz
E343.department: Behavioral Research Program, Division of Cancer Control and Population Sciences
E343.bio: Todd S. Horowitz is a cognitive psychologist and Program Director at the National Cancer Institute, managing research portfolios at the intersection of cognitive neuroscience and cancer control. Previously an Assistant Professor at Harvard Medical School and Associate Director of the Visual Attention Laboratory at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Horowitz conducts research on visual search, multiple object tracking, and attentional mechanisms. Their work focuses on applying vision science to medical image interpretation and developing neuroscience-based approaches to cancer-related cognitive impairment. Horowitz utilizes psychophysical and experimental paradigms to investigate how human perceptual and cognitive limitations impact diagnostic performance in clinical settings.
E343.research_direction: Dr. Horowitz has recently been working on how people find things in cluttered visual scenes. Their recent work traces the history of visual search research and questions the classic idea of a fast parallel stage followed by a slow serial one. It also covers newer multi-target foraging tasks, where observers must decide how long to keep searching. A separate line of work applies large-scale genetics to attentional control and other executive functions, asking how genetic differences relate to psychopathology.

papers.title: Molecular genetic influences on attentional control and other executive processes and their links with psychopathology in the AFFECT study
papers.abstract: Attentional control (AC) is an essential component of executive functioning, yet its genetic architecture and relationship with psychopathology remain poorly understood. This study performed a large-scale multivariate genomic characterization of AC and general executive function using data from over 20,000 individuals. We identified two dissociable latent genetic factors: a broad factor influencing Common Executive Function (CEF) and a narrow factor specific to Attentional Control. While both factors showed significant heritability, they exhibited distinct patterns of genetic overlap with cognitive and clinical outcomes. AC was uniquely linked to polygenic liability for specific psychiatric conditions, such as ADHD, independent of general executive function. These results suggest that attentional control is influenced by a specialized shared polygenic architecture, emphasizing the need for more granular cognitive phenotyping in neuropsychiatric research.
papers.authors: Justin D. Tubbs, Travis T. Mallard, Maria Dalby, Yunxuan Jiang, Younga H. Lee, Karmel W. Choi, Tian Ge, Niels Plath, Lene Hammer-Helmich, Julie M. Granka, 23andMe Research Group, Andrew D. Grotzinger, David Hinds, Jordan W. Smoller, Joshua W. Buckholtz, Todd S. Horowitz

papers.title: From Features to Foraging: Current Developments in Visual Search by Human Observers
papers.abstract: This major theoretical review synthesizes over a century of visual search research, tracing the transition from single-target feature searches to complex multi-target foraging paradigms. It provides a critical analysis of the 'two-stage assumption'—the dichotomy between preattentive parallel processing and attentive serial processing—arguing that standard reaction time (RT) slopes of set size often fail to capture the nuances of attentional deployment. The review examines the impact of target prevalence on detection errors and decision criteria, the mechanics of hybrid search involving both visual and working memory components, and the influence of individual variability. By integrating findings from medical image perception and professional screening tasks, the paper advocates for search models that better account for the continuous, interactive nature of real-world visual behavior.
papers.authors: Todd S. Horowitz

E344.name: Carly Leonard
E344.bio: Carly J. Leonard is an Associate Professor at the University of Colorado Denver and directs the Laboratory for Integrative Vision. Leonard’s research characterizes the interactions between perceptual and attentional mechanisms to understand how internal goals and prior experiences shape visual behavior. Using psychophysics, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological techniques (EEG/ERP), they investigate individual differences in oculomotor control and the neural mechanisms of visual selection. Leonard also examines cognitive dysfunction in schizophrenia, focusing on how attentional filtering and inhibitory mechanisms contribute to hyperfocusing and working memory deficits.
E344.research_direction: Dr. Leonard has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral mechanisms that govern oculomotor timing during visual search, particularly how the visual system utilizes perceptual grouping to plan eye movements. Their recent work explores whether early sensory evidence accumulation or later attentional selection, tracked via posterior EEG components like the P1 and N1, best explain the latency of a participant's first saccade toward a contour-integration target. They are also examining how stable individual differences in these initial saccade latencies relate to broader patterns of overt search behavior. Additionally, Dr. Leonard's broader cognitive research investigates the psychology and neuroscience of mental and physical effort, recently co-editing a special issue to synthesize emerging frameworks across cognitive and affective neuroscience.

papers.title: Trying in the 21st century: An introduction to the special issue on effort
papers.abstract: This editorial introduces a special issue on the psychology and neuroscience of mental and physical effort, co-edited by Leonard, Salamone and Treadway. It frames why effort has become a central concept across cognitive, affective and behavioral neuroscience and previews the contributions in the issue.
papers.authors: Carly J. Leonard, John D. Salamone, Michael T. Treadway

papers.title: Early visual modulation and selection predict saccadic timing during visual search: An ERP study
papers.abstract: Participants searched for a contour-integration target while EEG tracked posterior activity between display onset and the first eye movement. Trials were split by saccade speed to test whether early evidence accumulation (P1) or selection strength (N1) explains timing. Slow saccades showed a weaker N1 but a larger P1 than middle-speed ones, suggesting delays arise when the visual system is swamped with input and takes longer to commit to a saccade. The results help reconcile accounts of eye-movement timing that stress either information accrual or selection.
papers.authors: Ryan V. Ringer, Carly J. Leonard

papers.title: Individual differences in first saccade latency predict overt behaviour during search for a contour integration target
papers.abstract: This single-author study asks whether stable individual differences in how quickly people launch their first saccade during visual search carry over to other aspects of overt search behaviour. It uses a contour-integration search target built from aligned elements, connecting basic perceptual grouping to oculomotor control. The work extends the lab's line on why observers differ in the speed and pattern of their eye movements.
papers.authors: Carly J. Leonard

E347.name: Stanislas Dehaene
E347.main_research_area: Cognitive neuroscience of consciousness and literacy
E347.bio: Stanislas Dehaene investigates the neural architecture underlying high-level human functions, particularly reading, mathematics, and consciousness. Dehaene characterized the 'visual word form area' in the ventral visual stream and identified the 'number sense' in the intraparietal sulcus, illustrating how education repurposes evolutionarily older cortical circuits. Using functional neuroimaging (fMRI, M/EEG), experimental psychology, and computational modeling, their research explores the transition from subliminal to conscious processing. This work currently focuses on the Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and the neural codes governing hierarchical symbolic representations in the human brain.
E347.research_direction: Dr. Dehaene has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural foundations of human symbolic thought, spanning reading, mathematics, and high-level language. Their recent work explores how the ventral visual stream transforms retinotopic inputs into abstract, position-invariant codes during visual word recognition, and probes how the brain processes geometric shape regularity using fMRI, MEG, and comparisons to feedforward artificial neural networks. Beyond visual perception, they are examining the broader architecture of cognition by mapping the distinct, amodal neural networks used to comprehend domains like syntax, arithmetic, geometry, and social knowledge. To further understand the developmental and theoretical origins of these capacities, their research uses large-scale educational datasets to track the early emergence of mathematical gender gaps in primary school, and asks whether numerical and geometric reasoning ultimately stem from a shared, compositional "language of thought" built from basic mental primitives.

papers.title: A geometric shape regularity effect in the human brain
papers.abstract: The authors show that humans process regular geometric shapes (squares, rectangles, symmetric forms) more efficiently than irregular ones, and that this regularity effect is reflected in fMRI and MEG responses. The effect engages dorsal and ventral visual regions plus areas used for mathematical thinking, and is not captured by standard feedforward vision networks. This supports the idea that geometric shape perception recruits a symbolic, math-related code beyond ordinary visual features.
papers.authors: Mathias Sablé-Meyer, Lucas Benjamin, Cassandra Potier Watkins, Chenxi He, Maxence Pajot, Théo Morfoisse, Fosca Al Roumi, Stanislas Dehaene

papers.title: Rapid emergence of a maths gender gap in first grade
papers.abstract: Using a large national dataset of French first graders followed from the very start of school, the authors show that boys and girls perform equally on entry but that a gap in mathematics appears within the first months of schooling and grows over the year, while no comparable gap appears in reading. The effect is seen across socio-economic backgrounds and suggests that early classroom experiences, rather than innate ability, drive the emergence of the disparity. The findings point to early primary school as a critical window for intervention.
papers.authors: P. Martinot, B. Colnet, T. Breda, J. Sultan, L. Touitou, P. Huguet, E. Spelke, G. Dehaene-Lambertz, P. Bressoux, S. Dehaene

papers.title: Origins of numbers: a shared language-of-thought for arithmetic and geometry?
papers.abstract: This opinion piece argues that number concepts and geometric concepts may derive from a common compositional mental language built from a small set of primitives (such as repetition, symmetry and recursion) combined by syntactic rules. The authors review behavioural and brain-imaging evidence from humans, children, and other primates that supports such a program-like code, and outline how it could explain why humans, but not other species, develop rich mathematics.
papers.authors: Stanislas Dehaene, Mathias Sablé-Meyer, Lorenzo Ciccione

papers.title: From retinotopic to ordinal coding: Dissecting the cortical stages of visual word recognition
papers.abstract: Combining fMRI analyses with a neural network model of reading, this work traces how a written word is transformed from a retinotopic letter map into position-invariant codes for letter identity and order across the ventral visual hierarchy. It identifies stages at which letter position is progressively replaced by an ordinal code and links these stages to the visual word form area. The model makes testable predictions about how reading acquisition retunes visual cortex.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)
papers.authors: Aakash Agrawal, Stanislas Dehaene

papers.title: Languages of the brain: fMRI dissection of the amodal networks for language, mathematics, and social knowledge
papers.abstract: Adults and adolescents judged the truth of meaningful and meaningless written and spoken statements spanning several knowledge domains, in a systematic fMRI design. Distinct cortical regions were selective for syntax versus semantics, math versus non-math knowledge, geometry versus arithmetic, and social knowledge, and each responded essentially identically for written and spoken input. The results indicate that the brain hosts separate amodal networks for composing different types of thought.
papers.authors: Antonio Moreno, Marie Amalric, Manon Pietrantoni, Séverine Becuwe, Bertrand Thirion, Christophe Pallier, Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz, Stanislas Dehaene

E348.name: Laurent Cohen
E348.bio: Laurent Cohen is a Professor of Neurology at Sorbonne University and a clinical neurologist at the Pitié-Salpêtrière University Hospital. Cohen co-directs the PICNIC Lab at the Paris Brain Institute, where their research investigates the neural architecture underlying high-level cognitive functions such as language, reading, and calculation. Cohen identified the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) and co-developed the Triple-Code model of numerical cognition with Stanislas Dehaene. Their current research utilizes functional neuroimaging and neuropsychological methods to explore cortical plasticity and the reorganization of the visual system in response to sensory deprivation and the acquisition of expertise.
E348.research_direction: Dr. Cohen has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral intersections of visual perception, reading, and spoken language. Using ultra-high-field fMRI, their recent work explores the fine-grained functional organization of the visual word form area to understand how the brain accommodates vastly different written scripts in bilingual readers. They are also examining how auditory and visual systems interact during atypical language processing, utilizing both functional and diffusion MRI to map the cortical networks and white matter pathways underlying ticker-tape synaesthesia, a phenomenon where heard speech triggers a vivid stream of mental text. Additionally, they employ fMRI and eye-tracking to study the cross-modal mechanisms of Cued Speech, investigating how deaf and hearing individuals distribute their gaze and recruit cortical language regions to decode linguistic content from combined lip movements and hand shapes.

papers.title: Gaze dynamics of cued speech perception
papers.abstract: Eye tracking was used to examine how deaf and hearing cued speech users distribute their gaze between the speaker's face and hand while perceiving cued speech. The paper characterizes the timing and strategy of gaze shifts during decoding. It shows how viewers coordinate lip and manual cues to extract linguistic information.
papers.authors: Annahita Sarré, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Seeing speech: Neural mechanisms of cued speech perception in prelingually deaf and hearing users
papers.abstract: This fMRI study asked how deaf and hearing users of Cued Speech, a system combining lip movements with hand shapes, process this visual form of spoken language. It maps the cortical regions engaged when decoding cued speech and compares how the networks differ by hearing status and language history. The results clarify how visual and auditory language systems can be recruited for the same linguistic content.
papers.authors: Annahita Sarré, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Bridging speech and sight: white matter anatomy in ticker-tape synaesthesia
papers.abstract: Using diffusion MRI tractography, this work tests whether ticker-tape synaesthetes differ from controls in the white matter pathways linking auditory-language and visual reading regions. It reports anatomical differences in these connections. The results provide structural support for the functional account of how speech evokes visual text.
papers.authors: Romain Delsanti, Fabien Hauw, Romain Lahbari, Florence Bouhali, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Subtitled speech: the neural mechanisms of ticker-tape synaesthesia
papers.abstract: The study investigates ticker-tape synaesthesia, in which heard speech triggers a vivid mental stream of written text. Using fMRI in synaesthetes and controls, it identifies the brain regions that show altered activity while listening to speech. It proposes a neural account in which speech-processing areas engage the visual word form system.
papers.authors: Fabien Hauw, Benoit Beranger, Laurent Cohen

papers.title: Does the visual word form area split in bilingual readers? A millimeter-scale 7-T fMRI study
papers.abstract: Using ultra-high-field 7T fMRI at sub-millimeter resolution, the authors examined whether reading in two very different scripts, Chinese and French, recruits distinct patches of the left ventral occipitotemporal cortex in bilingual readers. They found that the two scripts activate largely overlapping but partially separable subregions of the visual word form area. This supports a single specialized reading region with fine-grained functional organization, rather than fully separate systems per writing system.
papers.authors: Minye Zhan, Christophe Pallier, Aakash Agrawal, Stanislas Dehaene, Laurent Cohen

E349.name: Jonathan Grainger
E349.department: Laboratoire de Psychologie Cognitive (LPC, UMR 7290), CNRS
E349.main_research_area: Visual word recognition and orthographic processing
E349.bio: Jonathan Grainger is a CNRS Research Director at Aix-Marseille University who researches the cognitive and computational foundations of visual word recognition and orthographic processing. Grainger developed the Multiple Read-Out Model (MROM) and conducted research on letter-position coding and the open-bigram representation of printed words. Utilizing behavioral priming, eye-tracking, and electrophysiological techniques, their work maps the transition from low-level visual features to complex linguistic structures. Grainger's recent projects examine the application of these mechanisms to sentence-level reading and investigate the cross-species evolutionary foundations of sequential memory and orthographic-like processing.
E349.research_direction: Dr. Grainger has recently been developing a comprehensive cognitive and computational framework for how the brain reads, focusing on how visual information is integrated from individual letters up to complete sentences. Their recent work heavily explores the hypothesis of parallel word processing, using electrophysiology and co-registered eye-tracking to investigate whether the neural signatures of upcoming words are extracted simultaneously before they are directly fixated. To understand how the visual system keeps track of sequence and syntax, they are measuring how rapidly the brain extracts grammatical structure from briefly presented word arrays by investigating phenomena like the "sentence superiority" and "transposed-word" effects. Additionally, their research broadens this inquiry by comparing reading with speech perception, asking whether the way the brain handles the order of phonetic sounds in spoken sentences mimics the spatial order-encoding mechanisms observed in visual word recognition.

papers.title: The transposed-word effect under serial presentation revisited: a replication study and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This paper re-tests whether readers show a transposed-word effect when words are shown one at a time, and pools earlier work in a meta-analysis. The effect is found to hold up under serial presentation, though its size differs from parallel presentation. The findings speak to how much word-order information depends on simultaneous access to several words.
papers.authors: Yun Wen, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Are Transposed-Phoneme Effects Observed When Listening to Sentences?
papers.abstract: The study asks whether transposed-phoneme effects, known from isolated nonwords, carry over when such nonwords are placed inside spoken sentences. Across four experiments using nonword detection and correct/incorrect decisions, no such effect appeared. The result points to a difference in how order information is handled in speech and in reading.
papers.authors: Sophie Dufour, Jonathan Mirault, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Letters, Words, Sentences, and Reading
papers.abstract: A single-author synthesis that lays out a cognitive and computational account of reading, from letter identification through word recognition to sentence-level processing. It argues that orthographic processing is organized around parallel processing of multiple words and highlights recent evidence on how readers handle word order. It functions as a programmatic statement of the author's current framework.
papers.authors: Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Sentence superiority in the reading brain
papers.abstract: Using MEG/EEG-style electrophysiology, the study compares brain responses to briefly presented word sequences that are grammatical versus scrambled. Grammatical sequences produced distinct neural signatures early in processing, indicating that syntactic-like structure is extracted rapidly and in parallel across words. This links the behavioral sentence superiority effect to a specific neural time course.
papers.authors: Stéphane Dufau, Jeremy Yeaton, Jean-Michel Badier, Sophie Chen, Phillip J. Holcomb, Jonathan Grainger

papers.title: Parallel word reading revealed by fixation-related brain potentials
papers.abstract: Participants read word sequences while eye movements and EEG were recorded, and brain responses were time-locked to fixations. The upcoming word to the right influenced the neural response before it was fixated, and it did so in a way that depended on whether it fit the sentence. These results support the view that several words are processed at once during reading rather than strictly one after another.
papers.authors: Joshua Snell, Jeremy Yeaton, Jonathan Mirault, Jonathan Grainger

E350.name: Marc Brysbaert
E350.department: Department of General and Applied Psychology
E350.bio: Marc Brysbaert is a Professor of Psychology at Ghent University whose research centers on the cognitive and neural mechanisms of visual word recognition and reading. Brysbaert developed the SUBTLEX word frequency norms and examines hemispheric lateralization in language processing, including the split-fovea theory. Their research utilizes a combination of behavioral megastudies, eye-tracking, and neuroimaging to investigate how lexical variables influence language acquisition and bilingualism. Brysbaert currently focuses on integrating big data and open science methodologies to improve the reliability and reproducibility of psycholinguistic benchmarks.
E350.research_direction: Dr. Brysbaert's recent work explores how large language models can be leveraged to scale up and modernize psycholinguistic research. They have recently been investigating whether AI can generate reliable, large-scale estimates for critical word properties—such as familiarity, concreteness, and emotional valence—across multiple languages to serve as alternatives to traditional human ratings and corpus frequency counts. Furthermore, their research tests the viability of an "LLM-as-participant" framework by attempting to simulate human behavioral response times in lexical decision tasks, probing whether computational models can supplement costly behavioral megastudies. Alongside this AI-driven research, they are also developing statistical methodology for the cognitive sciences, providing practical tutorials on running linear mixed-effects models and calculating standardized effect sizes for experimental designs involving both participant and item variance.

papers.title: Updating the German Psycholinguistic Word Toolbox with AI-Generated Estimates of Concreteness, Valence, Arousal, Age of Acquisition, and Familiarity
papers.abstract: Builds AI-generated word norms for German covering concreteness, valence, arousal, age of acquisition and familiarity, and compares them with existing human norms. The estimates agree well with human ratings and greatly expand vocabulary coverage. The resulting resource updates the German psycholinguistic toolbox for researchers.
papers.authors: Javier Conde, Gonzalo Martínez, María Grandury, Carlos Arriaga, Juan Haro, Sascha Schroeder, Florian Hintz, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert

papers.title: Simulating lexical decision times with large language models to supplement megastudies and crowdsourcing
papers.abstract: Examines whether large language models can be used to simulate how long people take to recognise words in lexical decision tasks. Model-simulated decision times track those from human megastudies, suggesting they can supplement or partly replace costly data collection. The work extends the LLM-as-participant idea from word ratings to behavioural response times.
papers.authors: Gonzalo Martínez, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert
