papers.title: How to Run Linear Mixed Effects Analysis for Pairwise Comparisons? A Tutorial and a Proposal for the Calculation of Standardized Effect Sizes
papers.abstract: A practical tutorial on running linear mixed-effects models for pairwise condition comparisons in experiments with participants and items. It also proposes a way to compute standardized effect sizes from such models so results can be compared and used in power analysis. Worked examples show how to implement the approach.
papers.authors: Marc Brysbaert, Dries Debeer

papers.title: Moving beyond word frequency based on tally counting: AI-generated familiarity estimates of words and phrases are an interesting additional index of language knowledge
papers.abstract: Argues that familiarity ratings produced by GPT-style language models can serve as a richer index of how well people know words and phrases than raw corpus frequency counts. The AI-derived estimates predict human word-processing and word-knowledge measures as well as or better than frequency norms, and extend to multiword expressions. The paper proposes AI familiarity as a new standard predictor for psycholinguistic research.
papers.authors: Marc Brysbaert, Gonzalo Martínez, Pedro Reviriego

papers.title: AI-generated estimates of familiarity, concreteness, valence, and arousal for over 100,000 Spanish words
papers.abstract: Tests whether GPT-4o can generate useful estimates of familiarity, concreteness, valence and arousal for Spanish words, replicating earlier English findings. The AI estimates correlate strongly with human ratings and in validity checks sometimes outperform traditional measures. The authors release lists covering over 100,000 Spanish words for free use in research and teaching.
papers.authors: Gonzalo Martínez, Javier Conde, Pedro Reviriego, Marc Brysbaert

E351.name: Elizabeth Schotter
E351.lab_name: Eye Movements and Cognition Lab (EMaC Lab)
E351.bio: Elizabeth Schotter is an Associate Professor at the University of South Florida who researches the neuro-cognitive mechanisms of language comprehension and production. Schotter utilizes eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and co-registration techniques to study how visual perception and linguistic experience influence word recognition and oculomotor control. Their research explores parafoveal processing, the sign superiority effect in deaf signers, and the computational modeling of lexical identification during natural reading. Schotter's current work links saccadic behavior to cognitive-linguistic processing through the coupled analysis of eye movements and neural language signals.
E351.research_direction: Dr. Schotter has recently been investigating the cognitive and neural mechanisms of reading by examining the precise coupling between visual, oculomotor, and linguistic systems. Their recent work explores how much information readers extract from the periphery before moving their eyes, using co-registered eye tracking and EEG to measure fixation-related potentials during parafoveal preview, word skipping, and semantic integration. Alongside this neurophysiological research, they are comparing the perceptual and word-identification spans of deaf and hearing individuals to understand the distinct visual factors that drive reading efficiency across different populations. To advance the field's methodological toolkit, they have also been developing practical guides and theoretical frameworks that encourage researchers to look beyond traditional fixation durations to more dynamically capture the eye-brain interface.

papers.title: Looking inside and beyond eye fixations in reading
papers.abstract: A Trends in Cognitive Sciences review arguing that fixation durations alone are too coarse a window on reading. It surveys how combining eye tracking with neural measures such as fixation-related potentials, and looking at what happens between and around fixations, reveals the timing of word recognition and the coupling of language and oculomotor systems.
papers.authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter, Brennan R. Payne

papers.title: Understanding the Eye-Brain Interface During Reading: Connecting Word Skipping and Comprehension Using Behavior-Contingent Fixation-Related Potentials
papers.abstract: Uses co-registered eye movements and EEG during sentence reading to sort fixations by whether the upcoming word was later skipped or fixated. The parafoveal N400 signal shows that skipped words are processed more deeply than expected in the periphery, linking saccade decisions to comprehension.
papers.authors: Sara Milligan, Elizabeth R. Schotter

papers.title: A beginner's guide to eye tracking for psycholinguistic studies of reading
papers.abstract: A practical tutorial on designing, running and analyzing eye-tracking experiments on reading. It covers hardware, stimulus and design choices, data cleaning, measures and statistical analysis, aimed at newcomers to psycholinguistics.
papers.authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter, Brian Dillon

papers.title: The role of perceptual and word identification spans in reading efficiency: Evidence from hearing and deaf readers
papers.abstract: Compares skilled deaf signers and hearing readers to ask which visual and linguistic spans make reading efficient. Deaf readers show larger perceptual and word-identification spans that account for their faster reading without loss of comprehension.
papers.authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter, Casey Stringer, Emily Saunders, Frances G. Cooley, Grace Sinclair, Karen Emmorey

papers.title: Event-related potentials show that parafoveal vision is insufficient for semantic integration
papers.abstract: Presents ERP experiments testing whether readers can integrate the meaning of a word into sentence context before fixating it. Semantic anomaly effects appear only after the word is directly viewed, so parafoveal preview supports word identification but not full semantic integration.
papers.authors: Elizabeth R. Schotter, Sara Milligan, Victoria M. Estevez

E352.name: Jason Yeatman
E352.department: Graduate School of Education; Department of Psychology; Division of Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics
E352.bio: Jason Yeatman is an Associate Professor at Stanford University with joint appointments in the Graduate School of Education, the Department of Psychology, and the School of Medicine. Yeatman’s research integrates vision science, computational neuroscience, and education to investigate how the brain's reading circuitry—specifically the Visual Word Form Area and white matter connections—develops in response to learning. As director of the Brain Development and Education Lab, Yeatman utilizes neuroimaging and the Rapid Online Assessment of Reading (ROAR) platform to study brain plasticity in typically developing children and those with dyslexia. Their current research focuses on how targeted behavioral interventions reshape neural circuits to design personalized literacy programs for diverse learners.
E352.research_direction: Dr. Yeatman has recently been investigating the neural and behavioral foundations of reading development and dyslexia. Their recent work explores the structural and functional circuitry of literacy, using longitudinal fMRI and diffusion MRI to ask how the visual word form area and white matter tracts like the arcuate fasciculus reorganize, or remain stable, during intensive reading interventions. Alongside these developmental questions, they are examining how top-down task demands and attention selectively modulate neural responses within specialized reading regions of the visual cortex. To translate these foundational insights into broader educational applications, their group is also developing scalable behavioral tools, including rapid computerized adaptive testing and language-agnostic visual processing measures designed to screen diverse populations for early reading difficulties.

papers.title: Visual processing is a language-agnostic window into heterogeneity in early reading development
papers.abstract: The study examines whether simple, language-independent visual processing measures can flag differences in how young children's reading develops. Working with a diverse sample of early readers, it links performance on rapid visual tasks to reading outcomes across children with different language backgrounds. The results position visual processing as a scalable, fair complement to language-based screening for early reading difficulty.
papers.authors: Mahalakshmi Ramamurthy, Klint Kanopka, Julian M. Siebert, Lucy Yan, Carrie Townley-Flores, Monica Zegers, Francesca Pei, Phaedra Bell, Hugh Catts, Maria Luisa Gorno-Tempini, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: The balance between stability and plasticity of the visual word form area in dyslexia
papers.abstract: The authors tracked the visual word form area, a ventral temporal region specialized for written words, in children with dyslexia before and after intensive reading intervention and compared them with typical readers. The region is small or hard to detect in many children with dyslexia, and it stays largely stable in location and selectivity even as reading improves. Together the findings argue that VWFA differences are a durable trait of dyslexia while still allowing limited plasticity, with implications for how intervention shapes the reading circuit.
papers.authors: Jamie L. Mitchell, Maya Yablonski, Hannah L. Stone, Mia Jimenez, Megumi E. Takada, Kenny A. Tang, Jasmine E. Tran, Clementine Chou, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: ROAR-CAT: Rapid Online Assessment of Reading ability with Computerized Adaptive Testing
papers.abstract: The paper builds an adaptive-testing version of the lab's browser-based ROAR reading assessment using item response theory. The adaptive version reaches comparable measurement precision to the full test in far fewer items, cutting testing time so it can be deployed at scale in schools. It validates the approach against standard measures of reading ability across many students.
papers.authors: Wanjing Anya Ma, Adam Richie-Halford, Amy K. Burkhardt, Klint Kanopka, Clementine Chou, Benjamin W. Domingue, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Development of the arcuate fasciculus is linked to learning gains in reading
papers.abstract: Using longitudinal diffusion MRI in children during a period of reading instruction, the authors relate development of the left arcuate fasciculus, a white matter tract linking language regions, to gains in reading skill. Changes in tract properties track learning rather than simply age. The work supports a dynamic view of how white matter and literacy co-develop.
papers.authors: Ethan Roy, Emily M. Harriott, Tin Q. Nguyen, Adam Richie-Halford, Ariel Rokem, Laurie E. Cutting, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Engaging in word recognition elicits highly specific modulations in visual cortex
papers.abstract: Using fMRI in adults performing tasks with words, the study shows that engaging in word recognition changes responses in visual cortex in a highly selective way, concentrated in word-selective regions rather than broadly across visual areas. It indicates that task demands strongly modulate the visual word form system. This clarifies how attention and task shape the cortical circuitry for reading.
papers.authors: Alex L. White, Kendrick Kay, Kenny A. Tang, Jason D. Yeatman

E353.name: Kathleen Rastle
E353.bio: Kathleen Rastle is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology who investigates the mental and neural processes underlying reading acquisition and skilled word recognition. Rastle’s work employs a multi-methodological approach, including behavioral experiments, neuroimaging, and computational modeling, to understand how the brain extracts and represents orthographic, phonological, and morphological information. This research includes contributions to the development of the Dual-Route Cascaded model and analysis of how the statistical regularities of writing systems influence the neural pathways involved in literacy.
E353.research_direction: Dr. Rastle's recent work explores the cognitive and environmental factors that drive how children acquire reading and literacy skills. They have recently been developing large-scale lexical databases of children's literature to precisely quantify the word frequencies and morphological structures that young readers are naturally exposed to. Using these corpora alongside computational models, their research investigates how readers learn meaningful word parts, like prefixes and suffixes, from the inherently noisy statistical distributions of natural text. Beyond printed books, Dr. Rastle also uses eye-tracking to examine how children visually attend to same-language subtitles in videos, probing how reading skill and content influence gaze behavior. Furthermore, their work addresses global educational challenges by investigating the critical role of foundational decoding skills for literacy development in low- and middle-income countries.

papers.title: Morphemes in the wild: Modelling affix learning from the noisy landscape of natural text
papers.abstract: Uses a computational model trained on large-scale natural text to ask how readers could learn prefixes and suffixes from experience, given that many letter strings that look like affixes are not (e.g. the -er in corner). The model shows that noisy, misleading distributional evidence still supports learning of affix meaning and function. The work links morphological learning to the statistical structure of real text.
papers.authors: Maria Korochkina, Marco Marelli, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Morphology in children's books, and what it means for learning
papers.abstract: Analyses the morphological structure of a large corpus of books read by UK children to establish which affixes and morphological patterns young readers are actually exposed to. The results show how much of children's text supports learning of meaningful word parts and where the input is uninformative, with implications for teaching and text selection.
papers.authors: Maria Korochkina, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Where Do Children Look When Watching Videos With Same-Language Subtitles?
papers.abstract: Children's eye movements were recorded while they watched videos with same-language subtitles to test whether they actually read the captions. The study characterises how much attention subtitles attract and how gaze depends on reading skill and content, informing claims that subtitled video can support literacy.
papers.authors: Anastasiya Lopukhina, Walter J. B. van Heuven, Rebecca Crowley, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: Inadequate foundational decoding skills constrain global literacy goals for pupils in low- and middle-income countries
papers.abstract: Reviews evidence on the foundational decoding skills of pupils in low- and middle-income countries and argues that weak decoding, rather than later comprehension alone, limits progress towards global literacy targets. It calls for systematic, evidence-based decoding instruction and better measurement of these skills.
papers.authors: Michael Crawford, Neha Raheel, Maria Korochkina, Kathleen Rastle

papers.title: The Children and Young People's Books Lexicon (CYP-LEX): A large-scale lexical database of books read by children and young people in the United Kingdom
papers.abstract: Presents a lexical database built from a large collection of books read by UK children and young people, giving word frequencies and other statistics by age band. It provides a resource for modelling children's text experience and for testing theories of vocabulary and reading development.
papers.authors: Maria Korochkina, Marco Marelli, Marc Brysbaert, Kathleen Rastle

E354.name: Manuel Carreiras
E354.institution: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language
E354.bio: Manuel Carreiras is the Scientific Director of the Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language (BCBL) and an Ikerbasque Research Professor. Their research utilizes neuroimaging methodologies, including fMRI, MEG, and EEG/ERPs, to examine the cognitive and neural foundations of language processing. Carreiras focuses on the mechanisms of visual word recognition, sentence comprehension, and the neuroplasticity associated with bilingualism and literacy. Their current work explores the cortical rhythms involved in language perception and the clinical applications of neuroimaging in studying language-related neurodegeneration and brain gliomas.
E354.research_direction: Dr. Carreiras has recently been investigating the neural, cognitive, and genetic foundations of language comprehension, including how structural brain variations and genetics relate to individual differences in reading performance. Their recent work uses multivariate fMRI to map how the brain's reading network transitions from perceiving visual letter strings to accessing word meaning, while also examining the alternative orthographic strategies used by skilled deaf readers who cannot rely on auditory phonology. Expanding beyond written text, they are studying visual language processing by measuring how cortical rhythms track different physical articulators—like hands and faces—during sign language, asking how a viewer's linguistic knowledge shapes this neural synchronization. Additionally, their lab is compiling massive neuroimaging and linguistic datasets of hundreds of adults to unravel how bilingual and multilingual experiences shape brain organization.

papers.title: Alternative strategies of orthographic processing: the case of skilled deaf readers
papers.abstract: The study examines how skilled deaf readers recognize letters and words when they cannot rely on sound-based codes. It tests whether orthographic processing in this group follows the same route as in hearing readers or uses different strategies. The findings inform general theories of reading by showing what visual word recognition looks like without auditory phonology.
papers.authors: Sendy Caffarra, Brendan Costello, Noemi Fariña, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Unraveling the Complexity of Multilingual Comprehension: Neuroimaging and Linguistic Profiling in 700+ Adults
papers.abstract: This data descriptor presents a large open resource combining brain imaging with detailed linguistic and cognitive profiling of more than 700 adult multilingual speakers. It documents how the sample was collected and what data are available. The dataset is intended to let researchers study how bilingual and multilingual experience relates to brain organization and comprehension.
papers.authors: Ileana Quiñones, Amaia Carrión-Castillo, Iñigo Diez-Zabala, Laura de Frutos-Sagastuy, Brendan Costello, David Carcedo, Lucía Manso-Ortega, Maksim Slivka, Abraham Sánchez, Anique Schüller, César Caballero-Gaudes, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Cortical tracking of sign language: The role of language knowledge in tracking of different articulators
papers.abstract: Brain activity of deaf signers and of hearing non-signers was compared while they watched sign language, to see how cortical rhythms follow the movements of different body parts such as the hands and the face. The results show that tracking of the articulators depends on whether the viewer knows the language, so language knowledge shapes how the brain follows visual linguistic signals. This extends work on neural tracking from speech to signed language.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.authors: Chiara L. Rivolta, Mikel Lizarazu, Brendan Costello, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: From perceiving words to reading: Neural multivariate representations of sublexical vs. lexico-semantic processing during word-reading
papers.abstract: Using multivariate fMRI analyses, the paper separates the brain patterns that support form-based (sublexical) processing of written words from those supporting lexical and meaning-based processing. It maps how these representations differ across the reading network. The result clarifies how the brain moves from perceiving letter strings to accessing word meaning.
papers.authors: Abraham Sánchez, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Manuel Carreiras

papers.title: Brain structure, phenotypic and genetic correlates of reading performance
papers.abstract: Using a large population sample, the study relates individual differences in reading ability to variation in brain anatomy and to genetic influences. It links structural measures of the brain with reading-related phenotypes and asks how much of the association is shared with genetics. The work helps pin down which neural and genetic factors underlie why some people read better than others.
papers.authors: Amaia Carrión-Castillo, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso, Manuel Carreiras

E356.name: Victor Kuperman
E356.bio: Victor Kuperman is a Professor and Canada Research Chair in Psycholinguistics at McMaster University and holds an associate membership in the Department of Psychology, Neuroscience & Behaviour. Their research integrates oculomotor monitoring, behavioral experimentation, and computational modeling to investigate the cognitive processes underlying visual word recognition and sentence comprehension. Kuperman examines the impact of morphological complexity, individual differences in literacy, and the effects of aging on linguistic processing. By utilizing large-scale eye-tracking corpora and norming studies, Kuperman develops probabilistic models of visual comprehension to analyze how reader-level and text-level variables interact during naturalistic reading.
E356.research_direction: Dr. Kuperman has recently been investigating the visuo-oculomotor mechanics of reading by analyzing naturalistic eye-tracking data across dozens of distinct languages and scripts. Their recent work explores whether fundamental reading behaviors, such as the influence of word length and frequency on fixation durations, are universal across different orthographies or language-specific. Using large-scale shared datasets like the Multilingual Eye-Movement Corpus, they are also examining the precise spatial and temporal metrics of eye movements, probing where the eyes land during backward regressive saccades and how they navigate return sweeps between lines of text. Furthermore, Dr. Kuperman is studying second-language reading to understand how the linguistic distance between a reader's native language and English impacts their reading fluency, oculomotor patterns, and overall comprehension.

papers.title: Universal patterns in eye movements across lines of text
papers.abstract: Using MECO data from 28 language samples spanning 22 languages and several scripts, the paper examines where the eyes land and how long they dwell around return sweeps to the next line. Roughly 80% of each line is covered by extreme fixations, and fixation durations follow the same positional pattern everywhere, shorter at line ends and longer at line starts. Script, language properties and reading direction have little influence, pointing to a largely visuo-oculomotor, universal signature of reading.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
papers.authors: Victor Kuperman, Yaqian (Borogjoon) Bao

papers.title: Wave 2 of the Multilingual Eye-Movement Corpus (MECO): New text reading data across languages
papers.abstract: This data descriptor presents the second wave of MECO, a large multi-lab collaboration that collected eye movements during passage reading, along with reading-related skills, from participants reading in their first language and in English as a second language. The release extends coverage to many more languages and participant groups and documents the materials, preprocessing and quality checks. It provides a shared resource for comparing reading behavior across writing systems and proficiency levels.
papers.authors: Noam Siegelman, Sascha Schroeder, Yaqian Borogjoon Bao, Cengiz Acartürk, Niket Agrawal, Lena S. Bolliger, Jan Brasser, César Campos-Rojas, Denis Drieghe, Dušica Filipović Đurđević, Sofya Goldina, Romualdo Ibáñez Orellana, Lena A. Jäger, Ómar I. Jóhannesson, Anurag Khare, Nik Kharlamov, Hanne B. M. Sá, Andrea Santana-Covarrubias, Irina Sekerina, Heida M. Sigurdardottir, Anna Smirnova, Priyanka Srivastava, Elisangela N. Teixeira, Ivana Ugrinic, Kerem Alp Usal, Karolina Vakulya, Ark Verma, João M. M. Vieira, Denise H. Wu, Jin Xue, Sunčica Zdravković, Junjing Zhuo, Laoura Ziaka, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: The metrics of regressive saccades during reading in 13 written languages
papers.abstract: Drawing on eye-tracking data from 589 native readers of 13 languages, the study characterizes where regressive saccades land compared with forward saccades. Forward saccades show the familiar launch-distance dependent undershoot and overshoot, whereas inter-word regressions land near word centre regardless of launch distance or word length. Intra-word regressions behave like forward saccades, and the pattern holds across all languages, supporting universal oculomotor control in reading.
papers.authors: Laura Schwalm, Ralph Radach, Victor Kuperman

papers.title: How does language distance affect reading fluency and comprehension in English as second language?
papers.abstract: Using MECO data from advanced English L2 readers with 18 different first languages, this single-author study tests whether the distance between a reader's L1 and English acts directly, through component reading skills, or both. Mediation analyses show both a direct and an indirect effect on reading fluency and eye movements, but no effect on comprehension. The work specifies a mechanism by which L1-L2 distance shapes L2 reading acquisition.
papers.authors: Victor Kuperman

papers.title: Word length and frequency effects on text reading are highly similar in 12 alphabetic languages
papers.abstract: Using eye-tracking data from native readers of 12 alphabetic languages in the MECO project, the study asks whether the two classic word-level predictors, length and frequency, shape reading in the same way across languages. Effects on skipping, fixation durations and total reading time turn out to be strikingly similar in size and direction, despite large differences in orthography and morphology. The results argue for largely language-general word-recognition and oculomotor processes in alphabetic reading.
papers.authors: Victor Kuperman, Sascha Schroeder, Daniil Gnetov

E357.name: Johannes Ziegler
E357.department: Centre de Recherche en Psychologie et Neurosciences (CRPN)
E357.bio: Johannes Ziegler is a Research Director at the CNRS and head of the Laboratoire de Psychologie Cognitive at Aix-Marseille University, specializing in the cognitive and neural substrates of literacy acquisition. Ziegler co-developed the Psycholinguistic Grain Size Theory, a framework for understanding cross-linguistic differences in reading development and dyslexia. Their research utilizes large-scale computational modeling, such as the Dual Route Cascaded (DRC) and CDP+ architectures, to simulate visual word recognition and the effects of orthographic depth on phonological decoding. Currently, Ziegler’s work focuses on integrating neuroimaging with digital pedagogical interventions to enhance reading fluency and support children with learning disabilities.
E357.research_direction: Dr. Ziegler has recently been investigating the cognitive, neural, and computational mechanisms of reading and word recognition, with a major focus on developmental dyslexia. Their recent work explores the brain networks of adults with dyslexia using fMRI and representational similarity analysis to test whether the reading disorder stems from domain-general statistical learning deficits or involves atypical, semantically driven compensatory strategies. On an applied front, they are testing the efficacy of home-based, multi-component digital interventions designed to remediate the specific visual-attentional, auditory, and cross-modal processes that support reading in children. Beyond dyslexia, they are conducting behavioral experiments to determine whether abstract word meanings are grounded in emotional and social experiences, while also employing parameter optimization techniques to better evaluate complex connectionist models of reading aloud.

papers.title: Back on track: remediating developmental dyslexia with a home-based multi-component program
papers.abstract: In a pre-registered multiple single-case study, 144 children aged 8-13 with dyslexia completed home-based digital training aimed at visual-attentional, auditory-phonological and cross-modal processes, with parents supervising. Each training type improved its own targeted skill, and the full three-stage program produced cumulative gains in reading fluency, spelling and comprehension beyond those from conventional remediation alone. The work supports a componential, computer-assisted approach to dyslexia remediation.
papers.authors: Karine Louna Harrar-Eskinazi, Ambre Denis-Noël, Bruno De Cara, Gilles Leloup, Julie Nothelier, Hervé Caci, Sylvane Faure, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: The role of social and emotional experience in representing abstract words
papers.abstract: Seven experiments in French and English tested whether emotional valence and socialness ground the meaning of abstract words, using lexical decision, semantic categorization and priming. Concreteness reliably sped word recognition and valence helped abstract words, but mainly when the task called for valence judgments. Socialness effects were inconsistent across languages and not boosted by social primes, so emotion appears to play a strategic role while social experience does not.
papers.authors: Daria Goriachun, Kristof Strijkers, Núria Gala, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: Neural Networks for Semantic and Syntactic Prediction and Visual-Motor Statistical Learning in Adult Readers With and Without Dyslexia
papers.abstract: Using fMRI, the study asked whether linguistic prediction during reading and domain-general statistical learning share neural substrates, and whether they differ in adults with dyslexia. It compares brain networks for semantic and syntactic prediction with those recruited in a visual-motor statistical learning task in typical and dyslexic readers. The results bear on claims that a statistical-learning deficit underlies dyslexia.
papers.authors: Elisa Gavard, Valérie Chanoine, Franziska Geringswald, Jean-Luc Anton, Eddy Cavalli, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: Atypical hemispheric re-organization of the reading network in high-functioning adults with dyslexia: Evidence from representational similarity analysis
papers.abstract: Representational similarity analysis of fMRI data tested whether university students with dyslexia compensate by encoding words more by meaning than by spelling. Contrary to that reorganization hypothesis, dyslexic adults showed weaker, not stronger, semantic sensitivity in left posterior fusiform cortex, and lacked orthographic sensitivity in left inferior frontal gyrus seen in typical readers. The pattern points to atypical hemispheric organization of the reading network.
papers.authors: Eddy Cavalli, Valérie Chanoine, Yang Tan, Jean-Luc Anton, Bruno L. Giordano, Felipe Pegado, Johannes C. Ziegler

papers.title: Understanding the complexity of computational models through optimization and sloppy parameter analyses: The case of the Connectionist Dual-Process Model
papers.abstract: The authors optimized the parameters of the Connectionist Dual-Process (CDP) model of reading aloud against large empirical datasets and found it then predicted independent datasets well. Sloppy-parameter analysis showed that only a few parameter combinations strongly constrain the model's behavior, clarifying how complex cognitive models can be understood and tested. The paper is a methodological advance for computational modeling of reading.
papers.authors: Conrad Perry, Rick Evertz, Marco Zorzi, Johannes C. Ziegler

E358.name: Erik Reichle
E358.bio: Erik Reichle is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology at Macquarie University specializing in the computational modeling of the cognitive, perceptual, and motor processes underlying skilled reading. Reichle developed the E-Z Reader model, a serial-attention framework that simulates eye-movement control by integrating word identification, visual attention, and saccadic programming. Their research methodology combines computer simulations with eye-tracking and neuroimaging data to investigate how reading processes vary across different writing systems and digital formats. Reichle’s current research extends these models to examine the "eye-mind link" and the neurocognitive mechanisms involved in complex visual information processing.
E358.research_direction: Dr. Reichle has recently been investigating the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms of reading, utilizing eye-tracking and computational frameworks like the E-Z Reader model to understand how text is processed in real time. A major focus of their recent work explores how eye-movement control and saccade targeting operate in unspaced, non-alphabetic scripts like Chinese, specifically examining the roles of character versus word predictability during text segmentation. They are also examining how visual attention adapts to modern reading environments, studying the effects of dynamic digital displays like scrolling and subtitles on cognitive processing. Additionally, their research investigates higher-level comprehension and learning through the lens of eye movements, mapping the real-time processing effort involved in acquiring novel words and evaluating corrections to misinformation.

papers.title: Examining the effects of character and word predictability in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: Applies a cloze-task analysis approach to Chinese sentence reading, comparing predictability measures defined over characters against those defined over words. Both kinds of measure explained the facilitation of eye movements by predictability about equally well, and the results are discussed in relation to how Chinese readers segment text without explicit word boundaries. The findings inform models of eye-movement control in Chinese.
papers.authors: Jin Tian, Lili Yu, Roslyn Wong, Aaron Veldre, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Real-time processing of misinformation and its correction: Insights from eye movements during reading
papers.abstract: Recorded the eye movements of 74 adults reading pairs of news-style articles in which a key causal claim was either retracted or not. Retractions raised processing effort when the correction was read and reduced re-reading of non-causal details, while reminders of the original claim sped reading. Reading proficiency and verbal working memory predicted lower susceptibility to the continued influence of misinformation.
papers.authors: Roslyn Wong, Lili Yu, Aaron Veldre, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Eye Tracking and Simulating the Spacing Effect During Orthographic Learning
papers.abstract: Eighty adults read sentences containing novel words four times, with repetitions either spaced or massed, while their eye movements were recorded. Spaced items were read longer during learning and gave better orthographic post-test performance, and longer fixations during learning predicted later accuracy. Simulations with the E-Z Reader model, given a processing deadline, reproduced the pattern and suggested massed items received less attentional processing.
papers.authors: Signy Wegener, Anne Castles, Elisabeth Beyersmann, Kate Nation, Hua-Chen Wang, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Towards a model of eye-movement control in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: Proposes a computational account of how readers of Chinese, a script with no spaces between words, decide where and when to move their eyes. The authors review the key eye-movement findings for Chinese and lay out what a model of saccade targeting and word or character identification would need to explain, drawing on the E-Z Reader framework as a starting point. The paper sets an agenda for extending models of reading beyond alphabetic scripts.
papers.authors: Yanping Liu, Lili Yu, Erik D. Reichle

papers.title: Dynamic reading in a digital age: new insights on cognition
papers.abstract: Reviews how reading on screens and with dynamic text presentation, such as scrolling, subtitles, and rapid serial presentation, changes the underlying cognitive processes compared with static print. It connects eye-tracking evidence to models of reading and discusses consequences for comprehension and for designing digital reading formats. The authors identify open questions about how attention and eye-movement control adapt to dynamic displays.
papers.authors: Sixin Liao, Lili Yu, Jan-Louis Kruger, Erik D. Reichle

E359.name: Simon Liversedge
E359.lab_name: Perception, Cognition and Neuroscience Research Group
E359.bio: Simon Liversedge is a Professor of Cognitive Psychology whose research utilizes eye-tracking and psychophysiological methodologies to examine the cognitive processes involved in reading and visual cognition. Liversedge investigates parafoveal processing and the effects of linguistic properties on oculomotor control across alphabetic and non-alphabetic scripts, such as Chinese. Their recent work employs the co-registration of eye movements and fixation-related potentials to integrate behavioral and neural data for the study of lexical identification.
E359.research_direction: Dr. Liversedge has recently been investigating the visual and cognitive mechanisms underlying reading, relying heavily on eye-tracking and gaze-contingent display methods. Their recent work explores parafoveal processing to understand how readers extract orthographic, phonological, and semantic information from upcoming text before directly fixating on it, and how this preview span is modulated by the cognitive load of the currently viewed word. By focusing largely on the visual complexity of Chinese text, they are examining how sub-lexical components like semantic radicals facilitate novel word learning and whether multi-character idioms are processed as single holistic units rather than sequential sequences. Additionally, they have been exploring the developmental trajectory of these perceptual reading skills in children, alongside large-scale cross-linguistic comparisons to distinguish universal reading mechanisms from language-specific visual behaviors.

papers.title: Sublexical semantic decoding during incidental novel word learning in natural Chinese reading
papers.abstract: Chinese readers encountered invented semantic-phonetic pseudo-characters whose semantic radicals either fit or clashed with a strongly constraining sentence context, while their eye movements were recorded across repeated exposures. Words with transparent radicals were read faster than opaque ones, and this advantage shrank with repeated exposure, indicating learning. Faster readers gained more from radical meaning, and the results are discussed with respect to radical-processing models and the self-teaching hypothesis.
papers.authors: Feifei Liang, Ying Xiang, Linlin Feng, Xuejun Bai, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Exploring effects of foveal load and preview restrictions for single and multiple parafoveal words in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: Using gaze-contingent preview manipulations, this study asked how much upcoming text Chinese readers process when the currently fixated word is easy or hard, and whether restricting preview to one versus several upcoming words changes this. It bears on whether parafoveal processing is distributed across multiple words or serial in Chinese reading, and how it is modulated by foveal processing difficulty.
papers.authors: Manman Zhang, Zhichao Zhang, Fang Li, Xuejun Bai, Chuanli Zang, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Development of orthographic, phonological and semantic parafoveal processing in Chinese reading
papers.abstract: Three boundary-paradigm eye-movement experiments tested Grade 2-5 children (n=366) and adults (n=90) reading Chinese, manipulating whether the preview was identical, related or unrelated in orthography, phonology or semantics. Orthographic parafoveal processing was effective in every group, whereas phonological and semantic parafoveal effects emerged later, from around grades 3-4 to adulthood. The authors argue that orthographic processing takes developmental precedence because sound and meaning are reached via the character's form.
papers.authors: Min Liu, Sainan Li, Zhu Meng, Yongsheng Wang, Chuanli Zang, Guoli Yan, Simon P. Liversedge

papers.title: Universality in eye movements and reading: A replication with increased power
papers.abstract: A large-sample replication of a 2016 cross-language study comparing eye movements while reading Chinese, Finnish and English, using at least 80 new readers per language and formal cross-language mixed-effects models that include a measure of visual complexity. Fine-grained eye-movement differences between languages replicated, but Chinese readers now read sentences faster than Finnish and English readers, which the authors attribute to cultural change over the intervening decade. They argue the overall pattern still supports universal aspects of reading and rebut the earlier criticism that the original work was underpowered.
papers.authors: Simon P. Liversedge, Henri Olkoniemi, Chuanli Zang, Xin Li, Guoli Yan, Xuejun Bai, Jukka Hyönä

papers.title: Parafoveal processing of Chinese four-character idioms and phrases in reading: Evidence for multi-constituent unit hypothesis
papers.abstract: Boundary-paradigm eye-tracking experiments compared preview benefits for four-character idioms and matched phrases in Chinese sentences. Readers extracted upcoming information from idioms as a whole unit, in a way not seen for ordinary phrases, supporting the view that familiar multi-character expressions are represented and processed as single multi-constituent units.
papers.authors: Chuanli Zang, Shuangshuang Wang, Xuejun Bai, Guoli Yan, Simon P. Liversedge

E360.name: Adrian Staub
E360.department: Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
E360.bio: Adrian Staub is a Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and directs the UMass Eyetracking Lab. Staub's research investigates the real-time cognitive mechanisms of language comprehension, focusing on how word recognition and syntactic parsing operate during reading. Using eye-tracking and EEG co-registration, Staub explores how lexical predictability, word frequency, and grammatical structures influence oculomotor control and neural processing. Additionally, their work examines the role of visual attention and perceptual inference in the detection of linguistic errors, such as word transpositions and function word omissions.
E360.research_direction: Dr. Staub's work explores the cognitive and oculomotor mechanisms underlying reading, primarily using experiments in which readers' eye movements are monitored. He investigates both syntactic processing and lexical processing in sentence context. His recent work has been focused on understanding the interaction between top-down and bottom-up processes underlying the common failure to notice seemingly obvious errors in text, such as the repetition of a word, the omission of a word, or the transposition of two words. He has also used eye movement data to investigate the nature and sources of predictability effects in reading, the phenomenon of agreement attraction, and the sources of difficulty in processing complex syntactic structures.

papers.title: Predictability effects in natural reading are logarithmic: Evidence from an eye-movement replication of Brothers and Kuperberg (2021)
papers.abstract: Replicates a prior study to test the shape of the relation between word predictability and reading time. Eye-movement data from natural reading show that reading times rise linearly with the logarithm of a word's probability, as surprisal theory predicts. The result bears directly on the debate over how prediction shapes reading.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Ryan Buggy, Stephanie Cho, Cory Shain, Adrian Staub

papers.title: Predictability in Language Comprehension: Prospects and Problems for Surprisal
papers.abstract: A critical review of surprisal theory, the view that the difficulty of processing a word tracks how improbable it is given its context. The article weighs the empirical evidence from reading and other measures for and against this account, and lays out conceptual problems in equating predictability with processing cost. It sets out what a more adequate theory of predictability effects would need to explain.
papers.authors: Adrian Staub

papers.title: The 'Sentence Superiority Effect' is due to guessing
papers.abstract: Words in grammatical sentences are reported better than words in scrambled strings even under very brief presentation, which had been taken as evidence for parallel word processing. Four experiments argue that the effect arises because participants guess the missing words from context, not from parallel processing of several words. This challenges a prominent argument for parallel lexical processing in reading.
papers.authors: Adrian Staub, Ellie Deutsch, John Greene, Jillian Hammond

papers.title: Perceptual inference corrects function word errors in reading: Errors that are not noticed do not disrupt eye movements
papers.abstract: Readers often fail to notice function word errors such as omitted or repeated words. Using eye tracking, the study shows that when an error goes unnoticed it leaves no trace in eye movements, whereas noticed errors do. This supports the view that readers silently correct the input through perceptual inference that combines the visual signal with expectations.
papers.authors: Adrian Staub, Harper McMurray, Anthony Wickett

papers.title: The function/content word distinction and eye movements in reading
papers.abstract: Examines whether function words are processed differently from content words during reading, drawing on eye-movement measures such as skipping and fixation durations. The article re-examines the standard characterization of these word classes and argues that the observed differences reflect properties such as length and predictability more than a categorical distinction. It bears on models of eye-movement control in reading.
papers.venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
papers.authors: Adrian Staub

E361.name: Jon Andoni Duñabeitia
E361.bio: Jon Andoni Duñabeitia is a Full Professor and Director of the Nebrija Research Center on Cognition (CINC). Duñabeitia's research investigates the neurobiological and cognitive substrates of multilingualism, literacy, and visual word recognition across the human life cycle. Using experimental paradigms involving eye-tracking, virtual reality simulations, and behavioral psycholinguistic tasks, Duñabeitia examines how environmental factors and cognitive load modulate linguistic processing and executive control. Their current research integrates digital health technologies to develop predictive biomarkers for cognitive health and early neurodevelopmental interventions.
E361.research_direction: Dr. Duñabeitia has recently been investigating visual cognition and language processing in increasingly naturalistic environments, shifting traditional psycholinguistics into immersive setups. Their recent work explores how classic reading phenomena operate in virtual reality, testing word recognition both in standard lexical decision tasks and during simulated driving paradigms under varying conditions of perceptual disfluency, such as simulated rain. They are also utilizing eye-tracking to study how bilingual viewers distribute their visual attention across dynamic scenes, examining gaze shifts between a speaker's face and dual-language subtitles, while separately evaluating the minimum eye-tracker sampling rates required to reliably capture natural reading behavior. In a distinct line of behavioral research, they are exploring acoustic analysis, investigating how physiological states like acute stress and cognitive load manifest as measurable vocal biomarkers during non-lexical singing tasks.

papers.title: Hearing once, reading twice: How dual subtitles shape visual attention in bilingual viewing
papers.abstract: Spanish-English bilinguals watched instructional videos while their eye movements were tracked, first without subtitles and then with dual subtitles (captions plus translation). Without subtitles, first-language audio drew gaze to the speaker's eyes while second-language audio split it between eyes and mouth; with dual subtitles gaze moved strongly to the text, favoring the top line and the line matching the audio. Comprehension improved for second-language audio with subtitles.
papers.authors: Inka Romero-Ortells, Manuel Perea, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: Singing reveals vocal biomarkers of stress and cognitive load
papers.abstract: Fourteen Spanish speakers sang non-lexical syllable melodies under acute-stress versus neutral conditions and under immediate versus delayed reproduction. Stress raised pitch and shifted formants and spectral energy toward a noisier signal, while cognitive load shortened singing duration and increased pitch, jitter and shimmer. The work argues singing is a low-burden, language-independent source of vocal biomarkers.
papers.authors: Irene Rodrigo-Herrero, Sergio Navas-León, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: Transforming language research from classic desktops to virtual environments
papers.abstract: The authors ran the same lexical decision task on a standard PC monitor and in a virtual reality headset, matching stimulus size and visual angle and collecting responses with VR controllers in both. Classic effects such as the word versus nonword advantage were replicated in VR, showing that basic word-recognition findings carry over. The paper establishes VR as a valid and reliable platform for studying language processing in more naturalistic settings.
papers.authors: Francisco Rocabado, Laís Muntini, Omar Fahmi Jubran, Thomas Lachmann, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: How low can you go? Tracking eye movements during reading at different sampling rates
papers.abstract: Readers' eye movements were recorded at several sampling rates from 250 to 2000 Hz, and the classic word-frequency effect on fixation durations was recovered across all of them. Simulations then downsampled the data further to find where the effect breaks down. The results show that cheaper, lower-rate eye trackers can support many reading experiments.
papers.authors: Bernhard Angele, Zeynep Gunes Ozkan, Marina Serrano-Carot, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

papers.title: Word recognition during movement under simulated weather conditions
papers.abstract: Participants drove through a realistic virtual environment and identified and named words shown on road signs under sunny or rainy weather. High-frequency words were recognized better than low-frequency ones even while moving, and rain slowed responses relative to sun. The study shows how perceptual disfluency from adverse conditions affects reading in dynamic, real-world-like scenes.
papers.authors: Francisco Rocabado, Natasha Alonso-Bernal, Jon Andoni Duñabeitia

E362.name: Julie Fiez
E362.department: Department of Psychology and Department of Neuroscience
E362.main_research_area: cognitive neuroscience of language and learning
E362.bio: Julie A. Fiez is a cognitive neuroscientist who investigates the neural mechanisms underlying speech, reading, and learning. Utilizing multimodal techniques such as functional neuroimaging (fMRI/PET), intracranial recordings, and behavioral testing, Fiez explores how the brain processes orthographic and phonological information during visual word recognition and working memory. Fiez's research examines the non-motor roles of the cerebellum and basal ganglia, specifically their contributions to error-correction and reinforcement learning systems. Currently, they work to bridge basic neuroscience and education by developing interventions that aim to optimize the acquisition of reading and mathematical skills.
E362.research_direction: Dr. Fiez has recently been investigating the neural and cognitive architectures supporting reading, language, and numeracy. Their recent work explores the earliest stages of reading acquisition by training adults on artificial alphabets, using fMRI to examine how brain network engagement shifts between domain-general executive systems and specialized language regions as reading expertise develops. Additionally, they are using these novel artificial scripts and pseudowords to probe the specific cognitive bottlenecks—such as decoding accuracy versus fluency—that drive long-standing reading difficulties in adults. Furthermore, they are studying chronic stroke survivors to investigate both the cerebellum's non-motor contributions to sound-based decoding in reading, and to map how precisely precise versus approximate numerical abilities anatomically overlap with language networks and aphasia symptoms.

papers.title: Phonological decoding and orthographic learning in poor and typical adult readers
papers.abstract: Adults with long-standing reading difficulties and matched typical readers learned letter-sound mappings in English pseudowords and in an artificial writing system. Poor readers reached near-ceiling accuracy on new mappings but stayed slower, and their orthographic learning was comparable to controls given equal exposure. The authors conclude fluency, not decoding accuracy, is the main bottleneck, with heterogeneous profiles among poor readers.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Kailee Lear, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Contributions of the multiple demand network to emergent and skilled reading
papers.abstract: Adults were trained on an artificial alphabet and then scanned with fMRI while reading in it, to see which brain networks support the earliest stage of reading. Emergent reading recruited the domain-general multiple demand network far more than the language network, and overlapped only partly with the skilled reading network. The results suggest that as reading expertise grows, engagement shifts from general executive systems toward language regions.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Kailee Lear, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Established and Emergent Reading Skills in Adults with Cerebellar Stroke: Evidence of Phonological Alexia
papers.abstract: Adults with chronic cerebellar stroke were tested on reading skills they already had and on learning to read a new artificial script. The work asks whether cerebellar damage selectively impairs sound-based decoding, pointing to a phonological alexia pattern. It ties into her long-standing argument for non-motor cerebellar roles in language.
papers.authors: Anna Chrabaszcz, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Lesion-symptom mapping reveals differential relationships between language and precise versus approximate numeracy
papers.abstract: Using support vector regression lesion-symptom mapping in 104 chronic left-hemisphere stroke survivors, the study compares damage patterns for approximate versus precise numeracy. Approximate numeracy was linked to intraparietal sulcus damage and unrelated to aphasia, whereas precise numeracy overlapped with language regions and tracked aphasia severity.
papers.authors: Erin Duricy, Corrine Durisko, Julie A. Fiez

papers.title: Small but Mighty: Ten Myths and Misunderstandings About the Cerebellum
papers.abstract: Written as the editors' introduction to a special issue on the cerebellum and language, this piece lists ten common myths that keep the cerebellum out of cognitive accounts of language. It argues that modern evidence supports cerebellar contributions to comprehension and production beyond articulatory coordination.
papers.authors: Julie A. Fiez, Catherine J. Stoodley

E363.name: Ken Pugh
E363.department: Department of Psychological Sciences (also President & Director of Research, Haskins Laboratories, New Haven; Associate Professor, Yale Child Study Center)
E363.bio: Kenneth Pugh is a cognitive neuroscientist specializing in the neurobiological foundations of language and literacy development. Pugh utilizes functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and other multimodal neuroimaging techniques to delineate the cortical networks involved in typical reading and developmental dyslexia. Their research examines the functional connectivity and neuroplasticity of the literate brain, investigating how pedagogical interventions and environmental factors modulate circuitry for word recognition and phonological processing. As the Director of the Yale Reading Center and President of Haskins Laboratories, Pugh integrates genetic, behavioral, and neuroimaging data to develop models of reading disabilities and individual differences in learning.
E363.research_direction: Dr. Pugh has recently been examining how the brain changes when children get better at reading after targeted instruction. Their recent work pulls together neuroimaging studies of reading interventions to ask which parts of the left-hemisphere reading circuitry become more typical, and where other regions step in to compensate. The broader question is how behavioral gains in reading show up as measurable shifts in brain activity and connectivity.

papers.title: Electrophysiological indices of reading intervention response: A systematic review
papers.abstract: This comprehensive review synthesizes 39 neuroimaging investigations to elucidate the relationship between behavioral improvements following reading interventions and concurrent neuroplastic changes. The analysis reveals evidence of altered neural activation, structural connectivity, and functional architecture within the canonical left-hemisphere reading circuitry, as well as compensatory recruitment of right-hemisphere, frontal, and subcortical regions. While individualized studies demonstrate specific patterns of normalization or compensation—such as increased left inferior frontal gyrus engagement or enhanced white matter integrity—a formal meta-analysis of longitudinal activation changes across a subset of eight studies failed to yield statistically significant global effects, highlighting the high degree of heterogeneity in neural response patterns across different pediatric and adult cohorts.
papers.venue: Advances in Child Development and Behavior
papers.authors: Brittany Lee, Nicole Landi, Kenneth R. Pugh

E364.name: Bruce McCandliss
E364.bio: Bruce McCandliss is a researcher in developmental cognitive neuroscience who investigates how educational experiences in literacy and mathematics transform the human brain. McCandliss’s research focuses on the neural mechanisms of reading acquisition and mathematical cognition, utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and high-density EEG to track experience-dependent plasticity. They examine the development of the visual word form area and use steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP) to study the temporal dynamics of visual word recognition. Currently, McCandliss directs the Educational Neuroscience Initiative at Stanford, where they conduct longitudinal studies and school-based interventions to connect laboratory findings with classroom practice.
E364.research_direction: Dr. McCandliss has recently been investigating the neural mechanisms of reading and academic development by deploying frequency-tagged EEG directly within real-world elementary classrooms. A major focus of their recent work explores how the developing visual cortex tunes to printed words, specifically examining how cortical latency and steady-state responses to novel letter combinations evolve during everyday instruction to support reading fluency. In addition to visual word recognition, they are studying selective attention during naturalistic learning by measuring how students neurally track a teacher's speech in bustling school environments. Broadening their scope beyond literacy, their recent projects also investigate the developmental trajectory of math cognition from childhood to adolescence using scalable, tablet-based assessments of arithmetic fluency.

papers.title: Cortical latency predicts reading fluency from late childhood to early adolescence
papers.abstract: Using frequency-tagged EEG, the study measures how quickly the cortex responds to printed words in students across late childhood and early adolescence. Faster cortical timing to words tracked reading fluency, and this held across ages and beyond simple response size. The work points to processing speed in the visual word pathway as a marker of reading skill development.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Quynh Trang H. Nguyen, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Bringing Attention to Education: Revisiting the Neural Mechanisms of Selective Attention in Naturalistic Learning
papers.abstract: Fifth- and sixth-graders learned new material from their own teacher while researchers manipulated whether they attended to or ignored the teacher's speech, with EEG recorded at school. Attention changed cortical speech tracking at about 170 ms rather than at early sensory stages, and students who boosted tracking more when the speech was relevant learned more from it. The same late-stage marker also distinguished students their teacher rated as good attenders.
papers.authors: Adi Korisky, Radhika S. Gosavi, Sarah Whittet, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Vaibhav Dewan, Blair Kaneshiro, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Steady-state EEG captures how elementary classroom instruction drives plasticity for novel visual words
papers.abstract: Children in an elementary school were taught new written words by their own teachers during regular class time, while frequency-tagged EEG recorded from the students tracked how their visual cortex responded to those words. Neural responses to the taught letter combinations grew within weeks of classroom instruction, showing that everyday teaching produces measurable, word-specific tuning in the reading circuitry. It establishes school-based EEG as a practical way to watch learning unfold in real classrooms.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Blair Kaneshiro, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Tablet-based arithmetic fluency assessment reveals developments in math cognition and math achievement from childhood to adolescence
papers.abstract: A brief tablet-based mental arithmetic task was given to a large sample of students spanning childhood into adolescence. Performance fluency showed clear developmental gains and was closely related to standardized math achievement, indicating that the task indexes real growth in math cognition. The measure offers a scalable way to assess arithmetic development in schools and research.
papers.authors: Ethan Roy, Mathieu Guillaume, Amandine Van Rinsveld, Project iLead Consortium, Joaquin A. Anguera, Silvia A. Bunge, Adam Gazzaley, Fumiko Hoeft, Jyoti Mishra, Miriam Rosenberg-Lee, Melina R. Uncapher, Bruce D. McCandliss

papers.title: Progress in elementary school reading linked to growth of cortical responses to familiar letter combinations within visual word forms
papers.abstract: Elementary school children were followed with steady-state EEG while their reading developed. Cortical responses to familiar letter combinations inside words grew as reading progressed, and this growth tracked gains in reading skill. The results link visual word form tuning to real-world reading progress in school-age children.
papers.authors: Fang Wang, Blair Kaneshiro, Elizabeth Y. Toomarian, Radhika S. Gosavi, Lindsey R. Hasak, Suanna Moron, Quynh Trang H. Nguyen, Anthony M. Norcia, Bruce D. McCandliss

E365.name: Guinevere Eden
E365.lab_name: Center for the Study of Learning
E365.bio: Eden is a Professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Georgetown University and the Director of the Center for the Study of Learning. They use structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying reading development and developmental dyslexia. Eden applied fMRI to the study of dyslexia, focusing on how the brain's visual and auditory systems support literacy acquisition. Their research examines the impact of sensory experience on brain plasticity and identifies neurobiological markers of reading remediation in children and adults.
E365.research_direction: Dr. Eden's recent work explores the structural and functional neuroanatomy underlying neurodevelopmental differences, particularly focusing on reading disability and early bilingualism. Using large-scale pediatric datasets, they have recently been investigating whether classic neural signatures of dyslexia, such as altered gray matter volume and cerebello-cortical functional connectivity during reading and math tasks, are robust and reproducible phenomena. Their research also examines how early bilingual experience shapes cortical thickness and volume, and tests whether established brain-based models of reading disability hold true across both bilingual and monolingual children. Furthermore, they are rigorously evaluating structural neuroimaging methodologies by assessing how analytic choices, such as the use of different processing pipelines or variations in atlas granularity, impact the reliability of cortical measurements.

papers.title: A Discovery and Replication Study of Dyslexia Does Not Reveal Reproducible Gray Matter Volume Differences
papers.abstract: Using ABCD Study data from 262 children, the authors ran a discovery and a replication analysis of gray matter volume differences in reading disability. The group differences did not replicate across samples, whether using voxel-based or surface-based morphometry. Follow-up reproducibility analyses showed that the divergence depends largely on whether total gray matter volume is controlled, calling into question the long-cited left perisylvian anatomical signature of dyslexia.
papers.authors: Alison K. Schug, Iria S. Gutierrez-Schieferl, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Role of Bilingualism in the Neuroanatomical Differences in Children With Reading Disability (dyslexia)
papers.abstract: The study asks whether brain-based models of dyslexia hold in bilingual children, using a factorial design on 268 early Spanish-English bilingual and monolingual 9-10 year-olds from the ABCD Study. Both dyslexia and bilingualism were associated with gray matter volume and thickness differences, with stronger effects for bilingualism. The absence of an interaction indicates the dyslexia signature is not compounded by bilingual experience.
papers.authors: Alison K. Schug, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Neuroanatomical differences in early bilingual and monolingual children
papers.abstract: In a large ABCD sample of 1,209 matched Spanish-English early bilingual and English monolingual children, the authors mapped gray matter volume and cortical thickness differences using voxel-wise, vertex-wise and parcel-wise approaches. Bilinguals showed widespread regions of both greater and lesser volume and thickness. Parcel-wise findings agreed with vertex-wise results only when a fine-grained atlas was used, highlighting the influence of analytic choices.
papers.authors: Mia R. Coutinho, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Agreement between FreeSurfer and CAT12 Cortical Thickness Measurements: A Discovery and a Replication Study in Children/Adolescents
papers.abstract: The paper compares cortical thickness estimates from two widely used pipelines in separate discovery and replication samples of children and adolescents aged 6-16. The two tools correlate strongly at whole-cortex and regional levels, but FreeSurfer gives systematically lower values than CAT12 in nearly all regions. Age, image quality and scanner manufacturer influenced how well the programs agreed.
papers.authors: Cameron C. McKay, Marissa Laws, Gabrielle-Ann A. Torre, Ashley S. VanMeter, Guinevere F. Eden

papers.title: Activation and functional connectivity of cerebellum during reading and during arithmetic in children with combined reading and math disabilities
papers.abstract: The study tested whether children with co-occurring reading and math disabilities show altered cerebellar activation or cerebello-cortical connectivity during reading and arithmetic tasks. Control and combined-disability groups did not differ on activation, background connectivity or task-dependent connectivity. The results do not support cerebellar accounts of deficits in reading and math.
papers.authors: Sarah M. Ashburn, Anna A. Matejko, Guinevere F. Eden

E366.name: Marco Marelli
E366.bio: Marco Marelli is a Full Professor at the University of Milano-Bicocca’s Department of Psychology, specializing in the cognitive and computational mechanisms of language processing. Marelli's research focuses on the representation of meaning in the semantic system, exploring how linguistic information interacts with perceptual and motor domains through multimodal models. Utilizing vector space modeling, eye-tracking, and behavioral experiments, they investigate word recognition and the acquisition of novel word meanings. Marelli directs the ERC-funded project 'BraveNewWord,' which applies computational linguistics to study semantic learning in adult speakers.
E366.research_direction: Dr. Marelli has recently been investigating semantic representation and word processing by comparing human behavioral data with computational models. Their recent work explores how humans interpret novel concepts, producing large-scale behavioral benchmarks for pseudoword processing and probing how orthographic similarities shape our explicit intuitions about meaning. They are also examining the cognitive capacities of large language models, specifically testing whether these networks can extract implicit relations within compound words and evaluating how their analogical reasoning abilities compare to human performance across various task formats. Additionally, Dr. Marelli is exploring how concepts are grounded in the physical world, developing distributional models to test whether the spatial organization of objects in visual scenes provides semantic information that complements traditional text-based learning.

papers.title: The English Pseudoword Lexicon Project (EPLeP): A resource for investigating pseudoword processing
papers.abstract: This paper presents a large-scale resource of behavioral data and norms for English pseudowords, collected to support research on how readers process letter strings that are not real words. It is intended as a shared benchmark for testing models of pseudoword and novel-word processing.
papers.authors: Fabio Marson, Rolando Bonandrini, Iva Šaban, Simona Amenta, Marco Marelli

papers.title: High variability in LLMs' analogical reasoning
papers.abstract: The authors test whether large language models reason by analogy like humans, using a range of analogy problems and comparing model accuracy with human performance. Model performance turns out to be highly variable across task formats and problem types, and it depends heavily on how the problems are presented. The work argues against treating LLM analogical ability as a single stable capacity.
papers.authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Chiara Saponaro, Marco Marelli

papers.title: A distributional model of concepts grounded in the spatial organization of objects
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a concept-representation model that learns from how objects are positioned relative to one another in annotated real-world scenes, rather than from text alone. The resulting vectors predict human relatedness ratings and word-recognition behavior, showing that scene-level spatial structure carries semantic information that complements language-based models.
papers.authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Marco A. Petilli, Marco Marelli

papers.title: Conceptual Combination in Large Language Models: Uncovering Implicit Relational Interpretations in Compound Words With Contextualized Word Embeddings
papers.abstract: The study examines whether contextual embeddings from large language models capture the implicit relations that people infer when interpreting compound words (for example what links the two parts). The models recover these relational interpretations and their patterns line up with human intuitions, supporting their use as tools for modeling conceptual combination.
papers.authors: Marco Ciapparelli, Calogero Zarbo, Marco Marelli

papers.title: On humans' (explicit) intuitions about the meaning of novel words
papers.abstract: Participants were asked to explicitly judge the meaning of words they had never seen, and their judgments were compared with predictions from distributional semantic models built on the form of the novel word. The results show that people hold systematic, shared intuitions about pseudoword meaning that can be traced to sub-lexical and orthographic similarity with known words.
papers.authors: Daniele Gatti, Francesca Rodio, Luca Rinaldi, Marco Marelli

E367.name: Binxu Wang
E367.department: Kempner Institute for the Study of Natural and Artificial Intelligence
E367.bio: Binxu Wang investigates neural representation along the primate ventral visual stream and the computational mechanisms governing deep generative architectures. By combining closed-loop electrophysiology with generative models and differential geometry, Wang developed optimization frameworks to synthesize maximally activating stimuli and map tuning manifolds across the visual hierarchy. Their ongoing research focuses on mechanistic interpretability and the theoretical physics of learning dynamics in diffusion models and vision transformers. Through these approaches, their work bridges systems neuroscience and machine learning to examine shared principles of biological perception and artificial generation.
E367.research_direction: Dr. Wang's recent work explores both the representational coding strategies of the primate visual system and the mathematical foundations of generative image models. In biological vision, they have recently been using closed-loop optimization to investigate how single neurons across the macaque ventral stream dynamically tune their responses to distinct texture and object manifolds. On the computational side, their research investigates the learning dynamics of diffusion models, applying spectral analysis and random matrix theory to probe the temporal trajectories of how different spatial frequencies are learned and to examine the statistical consistency of generative outputs. Additionally, they are applying mechanistic interpretability techniques to diffusion transformers to map the internal cross-attention circuitry that dictates how these networks construct specific spatial relationships between synthesized objects.

papers.title: Neuronal tuning aligns dynamically with object and texture manifolds across the visual hierarchy
papers.abstract: Uses closed-loop optimization in which single neurons in macaque V1, V4 and posterior inferotemporal cortex steer two families of generative image models, one texture-like and one object-like, to synthesize their preferred images. Early areas align better with texture-based spaces, whereas many PIT neurons respond equally well to both, favoring shared local motifs over whole-object templates. Alignment with object structure appears only later in the response, clarifying coding principles across the ventral stream and the limits of current vision models.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Carlos R. Ponce

papers.title: A Random Matrix Theory Perspective on the Consistency of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Explains why diffusion models trained on disjoint data subsets generate nearly identical images from the same noise, using random matrix theory on the shared Gaussian statistics of the data. Sampling variability acts like a renormalization of the noise level, and cross-split disagreement depends on eigenmode anisotropy, input inhomogeneity and dataset size. Predictions are checked on linear models, UNets and DiTs outside the memorization regime.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth, Cengiz Pehlevan

papers.title: Circuit Mechanisms for Spatial Relation Generation in Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Applies mechanistic interpretability to diffusion transformers to find how they place objects in a requested spatial relation. With random text embeddings the model uses a two-stage circuit in which separate cross-attention heads read the relation and the object attributes. With a pretrained T5 encoder it instead fuses both kinds of information within individual tokens, and the two solutions differ in robustness to out-of-domain prompts.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Jingxuan Fan, Xu Pan

papers.title: An Analytical Theory of Spectral Bias in the Learning Dynamics of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Derives closed-form learning dynamics for diffusion denoisers, showing that the time for each eigen- or Fourier mode to reach its target variance scales inversely with its data-covariance eigenvalue. Coarse, high-variance structure is therefore learned much earlier than fine detail. The theory covers linear, convolutional and deep denoisers, and shows how weight sharing and locality change the learning dynamics.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, Cengiz Pehlevan

papers.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Gaussian Score Approximation for Diffusion Models and its Applications
papers.abstract: Shows that at moderate to high noise levels the learned score of a diffusion model is dominated by its linear, Gaussian approximation, and that networks learn this Gaussian component early in training. At lower noise a coarse Gaussian-mixture picture becomes more relevant. The authors use this to build an analytical teleportation trick that skips early sampling steps, cutting 15-30% of steps with quality intact and working with existing fast samplers.
papers.authors: Binxu Wang, John J. Vastola

E368.name: Bria Long
E368.bio: Bria Long is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at the University of California, San Diego, who investigates how humans learn to extract semantic meaning from visual experience across development. Their research program integrates behavioral studies with infants, children, and adults alongside computational modeling and machine learning analyses of large, naturalistic datasets. Long's work includes characterizing the role of mid-level visual features in high-level object representation, tracking changes in visual concept acquisition through children's drawings, and quantifying early visual input using egocentric infant cameras. Their current work focuses on building ecological, computationally grounded accounts of visual concept learning and understanding how everyday environments shape early cognitive representation.
E368.research_direction: Dr. Long has recently been investigating the development of visual concept knowledge from infancy through late childhood by combining large-scale behavioral paradigms with the analysis of naturalistic first-person video. Their recent work explores the statistical structure of early visual environments, using object detectors and multimodal AI models on egocentric video to quantify the everyday objects infants encounter and to assess the alignment between these visual scenes and concurrent spoken language.
