Additionally, they are studying the evolving precision of visual representations across development by leveraging extensive, gamified datasets from museums and online platforms. Through drawing production and word-picture matching tasks, their research tracks how children's ability to recognize sketches, depict visual concepts, and differentiate between semantically and visually similar items matures over time.

papers.title: Characterizing the visual representation of objects from the child's view
papers.abstract: Using object detectors on about 3 million frames of BabyView first-person video from children aged 5 to 36 months, the study measures what objects young children actually see. Exposure is highly skewed toward a few categories and objects often appear partially hidden, cluttered or as pictures, yet detected categories still cluster strongly by superordinate category, more so than in canonical photo datasets. The authors argue that models of visual category learning must exploit this structure despite non-canonical, sparse input.
papers.authors: Jane Yang, Tarun Sepuri, Alvin Wei Ming Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Michael C. Frank, Bria Long

papers.title: Assessing the alignment between infants' visual and linguistic experience using multimodal language models
papers.abstract: The team used CLIP-style multimodal models to automatically score how well what infants see matches what they hear in home egocentric video. Idealized moments where a word is spoken while its referent is visible turn out to be much rarer than in machine learning datasets, and alignment varies considerably across children. This limits simple accounts of early word learning and offers a scalable alternative to manual coding.
papers.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan, Jane Yang, Tarun Sepuri, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Zi Yin, Virginia A. Marchman, Michael C. Frank, Bria Long

papers.title: Developmental changes in the precision of visual concept knowledge
papers.abstract: In a word-picture matching game with 3,575 children aged 3 to 14 and 211 adults, the authors examined the kinds of errors people make. Younger children more often choose unrelated images when wrong, whereas older children choose more visually or semantically similar foils. The results indicate that children's visual concept representations become progressively more fine-grained with age.
papers.authors: Bria Long, Wanjing Anya Ma, Alvin Wei Ming Tan, Rebecca Silverman, Michael C. Frank, Jason D. Yeatman

papers.title: Parallel developmental changes in children's production and recognition of line drawings of visual concepts
papers.abstract: The authors combined a large museum-kiosk drawing game with a recognition task to study how children's drawings and their ability to recognize sketches change with age. Drawings become more recognizable as children grow older, and recognition of others' drawings improves in parallel, and both are linked to how much detail children include. Together the results tie the growth of visual production to the growth of visual concept knowledge.
papers.authors: Bria Long, Judith E. Fan, Holly Huey, Zixian Chai, Michael C. Frank

E369.name: Carsen Stringer
E369.main_research_area: large-scale neural computation in visual cortex
E369.bio: Carsen Stringer is a Group Leader at HHMI Janelia Research Campus, where Stringer co-leads the Pachitariu + Stringer lab with Marius Pachitariu. The lab develops algorithms for understanding large-scale neural activity, combining machine learning with two-photon imaging of tens of thousands of neurons at once to study sensory representations and plasticity rules in mouse visual cortex. It also builds widely used open-source tools for the neuroscience community, including Cellpose for cellular segmentation, Suite2p, Kilosort, Facemap and Rastermap, and shares all of the data it generates.
E369.research_direction: Dr. Stringer’s recent work explores the computational principles underlying large-scale neural populations, spanning visual processing, brain-wide dynamics, and foundational software development. In the visual system, they have recently been investigating unsupervised plasticity during early learning and fitting interpretable convolutional minimodels to massive in vivo datasets to study how V1 neurons achieve stimulus invariance. Beyond the visual cortex, their research examines the eigenvalue spectra of brain-wide recordings to determine how biological network initialization states might confer computational advantages to artificial networks performing working memory tasks. Concurrently, they continue to develop critical computational tools for the neuroscience community, designing advanced graph-based spike-sorting algorithms for high-density electrophysiology and deep learning pipelines optimized for cellular segmentation and image restoration in microscopy.

papers.title: A critical initialization for biological neural networks
papers.abstract: The paper shows that the eigenvalue spectrum and dynamics of brainwide neural recordings in mice resemble linear dynamics from a critically normalized random symmetric matrix, with hippocampal CA1 as an exception that behaves like an efficient decorrelated code. Artificial networks initialized this way develop high-dimensional global activity modes that survive sparse, clustered or spatial connectivity and help on time-dependent tasks such as zero-shot working memory. The authors argue that initialization conditions of connected neural populations can confer computational advantages.
papers.authors: Marius Pachitariu, Lin Zhong, Alexa Gracias, Amanda Minisi, Crystall Lopez, Carsen Stringer

papers.title: Unsupervised pretraining in biological neural networks
papers.abstract: Recording up to 90,000 neurons in mouse V1 and higher visual areas while animals learned tasks or were merely exposed to the same stimuli, the authors found that most learning-related neural changes also appeared without reward, pointing to unsupervised plasticity. The changes were strongest in medial higher visual areas and followed visual rather than spatial rules, while a ramping reward-prediction signal appeared only in task mice in anterior areas. The work predicts, and behavioral experiments confirm, that unsupervised exposure speeds later task learning.
papers.authors: Lin Zhong, Scott Baptista, Rachel Gattoni, Jon Arnold, Daniel Flickinger, Carsen Stringer, Marius Pachitariu

papers.title: A simplified minimodel of visual cortical neurons
papers.abstract: Using a new dataset of over 29,000 mouse V1 neurons responding to up to 65,000 natural images, the authors show that two-convolutional-layer networks with a small first layer predict over 70% of response variance. Fitting a small per-neuron second stage yields interpretable 'minimodels', and similar simplifications hold for monkey V1. The minimodels are used to examine how stimulus invariance arises in single neurons.
papers.authors: Fengtong Du, Miguel Angel Núñez-Ochoa, Marius Pachitariu, Carsen Stringer

papers.title: Cellpose3: one-click image restoration for improved cellular segmentation
papers.abstract: Cellpose3 adds a set of restoration networks that denoise, deblur and upsample microscopy images before segmentation, trained by optimizing for segmentation quality rather than pixel fidelity. This markedly improves segmentation of degraded images across many modalities and generalizes to unseen data, and is offered as a one-click option in the Cellpose software. It also ships an updated general segmentation model.
papers.authors: Carsen Stringer, Marius Pachitariu

papers.title: Spike sorting with Kilosort4
papers.abstract: Kilosort4 is a redesigned spike-sorting algorithm for high-density extracellular probes that replaces earlier template-matching with graph-based clustering and improved drift correction. It matches or beats existing sorters on simulations and real Neuropixels data at high speed and with little manual curation. The software is widely used across electrophysiology labs.
papers.authors: Marius Pachitariu, Shashwat Sridhar, Jacob Pennington, Carsen Stringer

E370.name: Ashley J. Thomas
E370.bio: Ashley J. Thomas is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at Harvard University, where Thomas directs the Thomas Lab within the Harvard Laboratory for Developmental Studies. The lab studies how infants and children make sense of the social world, including how they learn about social relationships, social hierarchies and networks, and how demographics shape their understanding of these concepts. Thomas has proposed that humans have core knowledge of social relationships, allowing even infants to recognize different kinds of relationships and judge how strong they are.
E370.research_direction: Dr. Thomas has recently been investigating the developmental origins of social cognition, specifically exploring how infants and young children construct intuitive theories about the relationships between other people. Their recent work asks whether preverbal infants possess a core knowledge of distinct social categories, using behavioral experiments to test how babies use observable visual cues—such as saliva-sharing, behavioral imitation, and asymmetrical caregiving—to infer intimacy and future affiliation between individuals. Beyond infancy, they are also examining how older children link this relational knowledge to their theory of mind, investigating whether kids assume that individuals who display physical closeness also possess accurate knowledge of one another's mental states. Ultimately, Dr. Thomas is seeking to map how early humans develop cognitive representations of their social environments, testing whether children evaluate social bonds not just as individual dispositions, but as abstract, observable networks of obligation and care.

papers.title: Four- to 6-month-old infants use saliva-sharing interactions to infer social intimacy
papers.abstract: Extends the lab's earlier finding that older infants and children treat saliva sharing as a marker of close relationships down to 4- to 6-month-olds. Young infants watched interactions involving saliva sharing versus other contact and showed expectations consistent with inferring that the participants were socially intimate. The results suggest that sensitivity to cues of thick relationships appears very early, before infants have much experience or explicit teaching.
papers.authors: Brandon M. Woo, Elizabeth S. Spelke, Rebecca Saxe, Ashley J. Thomas

papers.title: Developing Intuitions That Close Friends Know the Content of Each Other's Minds
papers.abstract: Asks whether children treat accurate mental-state reasoning as a sign of closeness. In three experiments, 5- to 9-year-olds, but not 4-year-olds, inferred that characters who engage in affective touch or otherwise appear close are more likely to know what the other is thinking. The work links children's theory of mind to their theory of relationships and marks a developmental shift in how they connect the two.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Brandon M. Woo, Emma Yu, Megan Richardson, Ashley J. Thomas

papers.title: How Do Infants Experience Caregiving?
papers.abstract: An essay arguing that infants may represent caregiving through an abstract intuitive theory with its own structure, distinct from other social relationships. It reviews methods and findings on how infants understand people and relationships, and proposes that caregiving is understood as intimate, altruistic and asymmetric even before language. It sets out open questions for research on infants' experience of care.
papers.authors: Ashley J. Thomas, Christina M. Steele, Alison Gopnik, Rebecca R. Saxe

papers.title: Cognitive representations of social relationships and their developmental origins
papers.abstract: Proposes that humans possess core knowledge of social relationships. Drawing on infant studies, the target article argues that even preverbal infants sort relationships into relational-model categories such as communal sharing, authority ranking and equality matching, and gauge how strong each relationship is from cues like expected future interaction, obligation and commitment. It evaluates the evidence and alternative explanations, and was published with a set of open peer commentaries.
papers.authors: Ashley J. Thomas

papers.title: Infants Infer Social Relationships Between Individuals Who Engage in Imitative Social Interactions
papers.abstract: Tested whether infants read social interactions in terms of relationships rather than only individual dispositions. Twelve-month-olds and 16- to 18-month-olds who saw one character imitate another expected the imitator and its target to respond to each other's distress and to affiliate. Findings support the idea that imitation is used as a cue that two individuals share a social relationship.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Vanessa Kudrnova, Elizabeth S. Spelke, Ashley J. Thomas

E371.name: Moira R. Dillon
E371.main_research_area: development of geometric and spatial cognition
E371.bio: Moira R. Dillon is an Assistant Professor of Psychology at New York University, where Dillon directs the Lab for the Developing Mind. The lab uses cognitive, developmental and computational approaches to study the origin and development of uniquely human cognition, from the basic sensitivities of infants to children's untutored use of symbols and language to the high-level concepts of adults. Current areas of investigation include early knowledge about objects, people and places; symbolic and abstract reasoning about geometry; pictorial and linguistic production; and the relation between human and machine intelligence, pursued with partners including the National Museum of Mathematics, Lookit and J-PAL.
E371.research_direction: Dr. Dillon has recently been investigating the cognitive and developmental origins of human spatial intelligence, specifically asking whether abstract geometric intuitions are grounded in ancient spatial navigation systems rather than a dedicated language of thought. Their recent work explores this hypothesis by testing how adults extrapolate minimal lines and points in visual tasks, analyzing whether these spatial judgments implicitly track a navigating agent's path or rely instead on object-shape completion mechanisms. In related developmental research, they are examining how humans parse visual environments, using infant looking-time paradigms and behavioral tasks with young children to probe how global spatial layouts, local objects, and verbal labels interact to drive the categorization of places. Furthermore, their research extends beyond spatial cognition by comparing preverbal infants and state-of-the-art neural networks on benchmark visual tasks designed to probe how both humans and machines predict the goal-directed actions and efficiencies of other agents.

papers.title: The cognitive origins of geometry
papers.abstract: A single-author synthesis that challenges the view that geometry rests on a dedicated, modular language of thought. Dillon proposes the Wanderers Hypothesis: human geometry is grounded in navigation-like processes shared with other animals that approximate Euclidean geometry, and people gain flexible access to them through natural language. The argument draws together infant studies, cross-cultural work and cognitive modeling.
papers.authors: Moira R. Dillon

papers.title: Scene and Heard: Spatial layout and verbal labels support young infants' categorization of places
papers.abstract: Three looking-time experiments with pre-crawling 6-month-olds (N = 96) tested whether infants can form categories of places such as fields versus canyons. With a shared novel label, infants preferred a novel place category at test, showing sensitivity to spatial layout; scrambling the layout or removing the label eliminated evidence of categorization. Young infants thus learn place categories before exploring on their own, especially when labels are present.
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Agata Bochynska, Daniel D. Dilks, Moira R. Dillon

papers.title: We are wanderers: Abstract geometry reflects spatial navigation
papers.abstract: Across two preregistered experiments, adults watched minimal videos of two points and line segments described with slightly different language, and were asked where an open figure would continue. Their responses tracked a navigating agent's path when the context was framed as navigation or abstract surface, and did not follow object-shape completion. This supports the idea that abstract geometric intuitions reuse the spatial navigation system.
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Moira R. Dillon

papers.title: Seeing the Forest but Naming the Trees: An Object-Over-Place Bias in Learning Noun Labels
papers.abstract: Across six experiments, adults and 3- to 4-year-olds extended novel nouns to scenes containing a room-like place and an object, or matched controls with figure-ground structure but no place information. Adults showed a specific object-over-place bias in extending noun labels, mirroring the priority of object shape over place information in drawings. Children's pattern differed, indicating that the bias develops and is tied to language.
papers.venue: Open Mind: Discoveries in Cognitive Science
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Moira R. Dillon

papers.title: Commonsense psychology in human infants and machines
papers.abstract: The authors test 11-month-old infants and state-of-the-art neural-network models on the Baby Intuitions Benchmark, tasks probing predictions about why agents act. Infants expected agents to act toward objects rather than locations and to act efficiently toward goals, whereas the models failed to capture these expectations. The work offers a framework for comparing infant and machine commonsense psychology.
papers.authors: Gala Stojnić, Kanishk Gandhi, Shannon Yasuda, Brenden M. Lake, Moira R. Dillon

E372.name: S. P. Arun
E372.main_research_area: high-level object vision and shape perception
E372.bio: S. P. Arun is a Professor at the Centre for Neuroscience, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bangalore, where they direct Visionlab@IISc. Their research aims to crack the code by which the brain represents objects, asking whether the vast space of shapes we see can be described by a small set of features and rules, much as color perception is three-dimensional. The lab combines visual search and other behavioral experiments in humans, fMRI, single-neuron recordings in monkey inferotemporal cortex, and comparisons with deep networks to study object and shape perception, reading, and face recognition. Arun trained in electrical engineering at IIT Bombay and Johns Hopkins University and was a postdoctoral fellow at Carnegie Mellon University.
E372.research_direction: Dr. Arun's recent work explores high-level visual and sensorimotor processing across both controlled and naturalistic contexts, utilizing wireless neural recordings in freely moving macaques to investigate how the brain encodes natural actions and complex social variables like grooming reciprocity. They have also recently been mapping the qualitative similarities and differences between human and macaque vision, using behavioral search tasks to probe comparative perception across classical phenomena such as amodal completion, mirror confusion, and global advantage. Furthermore, their research investigates fundamental visual computations, examining how object-selective cortex tracks visual homogeneity to solve tasks involving symmetry or repeated items. Finally, they are studying the visual foundations of reading by investigating how early learners develop shape familiarity and visual search efficiency for letters prior to acquiring explicit phonetic knowledge.

papers.title: Natural behavior elicits reliable neural signatures in high-level sensory and motor regions of freely moving monkeys
papers.abstract: Using wireless neural recordings in freely moving macaques, the authors compare natural actions such as eating with controlled screen-based tasks. They find that high-level visual and motor regions show reliable, invariant neural signatures during natural behavior rather than noisy, mixed sensorimotor activity. The apparent mixing of visual and motor information is argued to arise from the correlation between what is seen and how the animal moves.
papers.authors: Sini Simon, Shubhankar Saha, Surbhi Munda, Jason Joby, Thomas Cherian, Georgin Jacob, Jhilik Das, Debdyuti Bhadra, SP Arun

papers.title: Do monkeys see the way we do? Qualitative similarities and differences between monkey and human perception
papers.abstract: Monkeys were trained to do an oddball visual search task on natural images, then tested on controlled images designed to probe a range of perceptual phenomena, and their behavior was compared with humans. Monkeys resembled humans in object relations, Weber's law and amodal completion. Unlike humans, they showed no mirror confusion and no global advantage, giving a first broad map of where monkey and human perception agree and diverge.
papers.authors: Thomas Cherian, Georgin Jacob, SP Arun

papers.title: Dynamic tracking of social variables in simultaneous brain recordings from socially interacting monkeys
papers.abstract: Wireless neural recordings were made simultaneously from two macaques interacting freely. Neurons in each animal encoded social variables such as grooming state, partner identity and joint movements. High-level visual cortex neurons tracked a running favor signal (grooming given minus received), offering a neural basis for reciprocity, and activity was predicted by the partner's posture and neural activity, especially while giving grooming.
papers.authors: Sini Simon, Debdyuti Bhadra, Shubhankar Saha, Surbhi Munda, Jhilik Das, SP Arun

papers.title: Visual homogeneity computations in the brain enable solving property-based visual tasks
papers.abstract: The paper defines a 'visual homogeneity' signal that distinguishes displays of repeated items from heterogeneous ones, and shows it predicts response times in visual search, same-different and symmetry tasks. Brain imaging localizes this signal to object-selective cortex. Property-based tasks with no obvious feature space can thus be solved with one shared homogeneity computation.
papers.authors: Georgin Jacob, RT Pramod, SP Arun

papers.title: Early readers know letter shape without knowing letter names
papers.abstract: Three hundred children just starting to read Kannada were tested on letter-shape familiarity, letter recognition, letter visual search and rapid digit naming. They were highly familiar with letter shapes despite knowing few letter names, and this familiarity was tied to faster visual search among letters. Print knowledge thus includes a shape-familiarity component beyond letter naming.
papers.authors: Jhilik Das, Sonali Nag, Usha MN, SP Arun

E373.name: Aditya Murthy
E373.bio: Aditya Murthy is a Professor at the Centre for Neuroscience, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, where he heads the Movement Control Lab. His lab studies the computations the brain uses to decide on, plan, execute and correct goal-directed movements, including saccadic eye movements, reaching and eye-hand coordination. The group combines psychophysics, computational and optimal-control modeling, high-density surface EMG of motor units, and non-invasive brain stimulation (tDCS/TMS). It works with healthy volunteers and with patients who have movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease, and earlier work used primate frontal eye field neurophysiology. He earned his PhD with Allen Humphrey at the University of Pittsburgh working on visual motion processing, and did postdoctoral work on primate visuomotor systems with Jeffrey Schall at Vanderbilt University.
E373.research_direction: Dr. Murthy's recent work investigates the neural and biomechanical mechanisms of motor planning and execution, exploring how cortical preparation translates into peripheral muscle activity before a movement even begins. To study this, they have been combining delayed-reach tasks with high-density surface electromyography and transcranial direct current stimulation to measure how individual motor units are recruited to reflect spatial movement plans and vigor. Their research also examines the kinematics of goal-directed actions, analyzing trial-to-trial variability to understand how the motor system balances pre-planned arm trajectories with rapid online corrections and how redundant joints are coordinated during whole-arm reaches. Additionally, Dr. Murthy has recently been investigating the intersection of cognition and motor learning, using dual-task paradigms and state-space modeling to test how task-relevant cognitive load modulates the fast and slow processes underlying visuomotor adaptation.

papers.title: Signatures of rapid trajectory control during finger and arm movements
papers.abstract: Asks whether goal-directed hand movements follow planned trajectories or arise purely from trajectory-free online control. By analyzing how trial-to-trial kinematic variability evolves over time in finger and whole-arm reaches, the authors find task-dependent regulation toward an average trajectory, with signs of rapid correction beginning about 60 ms (finger) and 70 ms (arm) into the movement. Control strength peaks in early and late movement phases, implying a trajectory plan combined with fast feedback.
papers.authors: Niranjan Chakrabhavi, Varadhan SKM, Ashitava Ghosal, Aditya Murthy

papers.title: Task-Relevant Cognitive Load Modulates Fast and Slow Processes Underlying Motor Adaptation
papers.abstract: Manipulates cognitive load with an easy or hard decision-making task performed alongside visuomotor adaptation, while attention stays on the motor task. High load attenuated steady-state learning, and dual-rate state-space modeling showed a larger fast component under high load and a larger slow component under low load. This fits a competition account in which a shared error signal is split between the two processes and links fast explicit adaptation to action-selection processes.
papers.authors: Vyaas Ramasubramanian, Somesh Nana Shingane, Aditya Murthy

papers.title: Transcranial direct current stimulation of the supplementary motor area modulates behavioral and peripheral electrophysiological measures of motor preparation
papers.abstract: Combines anodal tDCS over the supplementary motor area with high-density surface EMG from the anterior deltoid during a delayed-reach task. SMA stimulation shortened reaction times while increasing motor-unit activity, and later raised movement velocity through recruitment of larger motor units. The results indicate that motor preparation actively engages peripheral muscle, linking cortical planning to muscle readiness and vigor.
papers.authors: Ashutosh Kumar, Ayusha Desai, Kalpajyoti Hazarika, Aditya Murthy

papers.title: Differential kinematic control and co-ordination among redundant joints during whole arm reaching movements
papers.abstract: Examines how the shoulder, elbow and wrist are controlled during whole-arm reaches, asking whether joint trajectories serve only the endpoint. Correlation and zero-crossing measures show proximal joints regulate the task-relevant space while the distal wrist regulates redundancy in the null space, so null space is selectively controlled rather than left free. A leading-joint strategy varies with reach direction.
papers.authors: Niranjan Chakrabhavi, Ashitava Ghosal, Aditya Murthy

papers.title: Context-specific early recruitment of small motor units in the shoulder muscle reflects a reach movement plan
papers.abstract: Uses high-density surface EMG of the anterior deltoid to isolate motor units during a delayed reach. Small-amplitude units ramp up early in the delay period in a spatially specific way, resembling accumulation to a threshold that predicts movement onset, whereas large units become selective only after the go cue. This delay-period activity is absent for isometric force-driven cursor movements.
papers.authors: Satya Rungta, Aditya Murthy

E374.name: Rajiv Soundararajan
E374.bio: Rajiv Soundararajan is an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical Communication Engineering at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, and Convenor of the Kotak IISc AI-ML Centre. Soundararajan earned a B.E. from BITS Pilani and M.S. and Ph.D. degrees in Electrical and Computer Engineering from The University of Texas at Austin, where the doctoral work was on information-theoretic, perception-driven image and video quality assessment, and worked at Qualcomm Research India before joining IISc. The group studies how humans perceive the quality of images and video, combining subjective studies with machine learning, and also works on novel view synthesis and 3D scene representation. Soundararajan's honors include a 2020 Technology & Engineering Emmy Award for perceptual metrics for video encoding optimization.
E374.research_direction: Dr. Soundararajan has recently been investigating how to computationally model human perceptual image quality and how to reconstruct accurate 3D scenes from highly limited visual data. Their recent work in visual quality assessment explores ways to build robust, no-reference quality predictors that generalize across diverse datasets, utilizing techniques that range from extracting cross-attention maps in prompt-guided latent diffusion models for natural video to developing new subjective human benchmarks for multispectral satellite imagery. In parallel, they are exploring sparse-view novel view synthesis using both Neural Radiance Fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting. To address the overfitting and geometric distortions that plague these under-constrained 3D representations, their research examines novel regularization strategies, such as jointly training deliberately simplified models to generate depth constraints or alternating high-capacity densification phases with aggressive pruning and depth smoothing.

papers.title: Simple-RF: Regularizing Sparse Input Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions
papers.abstract: Radiance fields, both implicit (NeRF) and explicit (TensoRF, ZipNeRF style), degrade badly when only a few input views exist. Instead of relying on depth from pretrained networks or sparse classical estimates, the authors train simplified augmented models alongside the main radiance field, restricting factors such as positional-encoding bandwidth and view-dependent radiance, and use their depth as supervision. They also add extra regularizers, and report state-of-the-art sparse-input view synthesis with both implicit and explicit models.
papers.authors: Nagabhushan Somraj, Sai Harsha Mupparaju, Adithyan Karanayil, Rajiv Soundararajan

papers.title: Image and Video Quality Assessment using Prompt-Guided Latent Diffusion Models for Cross-Dataset Generalization
papers.abstract: The paper tackles the poor cross-dataset generalization of learned image and video quality predictors. It learns quality-aware text prompts and reads out cross-attention maps from intermediate layers of a text-to-image latent diffusion denoiser to represent perceptual quality. For video, quality is estimated on a frame-rate sub-sampled version and motion information lost by sub-sampling is compensated by a distillation-style temporal module. The resulting IQA and VQA models generalize better across datasets with distribution shift.
papers.authors: Shankhanil Mitra, Diptanu De, Shika Rao, Rajiv Soundararajan

papers.title: AD-GS: Alternating Densification for Sparse-Input 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Sparse-view 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from floaters and wrong geometry, which the authors attribute to uncontrolled densification. AD-GS alternates high-densification phases, which add Gaussians aggressively and fit photometric detail, with low-densification phases that prune by opacity and regularize geometry using pseudo-view consistency and edge-aware depth smoothness. This controls model capacity growth and reduces overfitting, giving strong results on sparse-view benchmarks.
papers.authors: Gurutva Patle, Nilay Girgaonkar, Nagabhushan Somraj, Rajiv Soundararajan

papers.title: Quality Assessment of Multispectral Remote Sensing Images: A Subjective Study and No Reference Algorithms
papers.abstract: The paper builds a subjective benchmark of multispectral remote-sensing images, collecting human pairwise quality rankings across distortions relevant to satellite imagery. It then tests whether existing no-reference quality models designed for natural images transfer to this domain and proposes new no-reference algorithms tailored to multispectral data.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
papers.authors: Aakanksha Bharti, Nithin C Babu, M Naveen Sai Kiran, Aditi Prasad, Neeraj Badal, Rajiv Soundararajan

papers.title: SimpleNeRF: Regularizing Sparse Input Neural Radiance Fields with Simpler Solutions
papers.abstract: Few-view NeRF training is under-constrained, and depth supervision from pretrained networks may generalize poorly. SimpleNeRF learns its own depth supervision by training augmented, deliberately simpler models (less positional encoding and view-dependent radiance) jointly with the NeRF. The simpler models' depth regularizes the NeRF, yielding large gains in sparse-input novel view synthesis.
papers.authors: Nagabhushan Somraj, Adithyan Karanayil, Rajiv Soundararajan

E375.name: Richa Verma
E375.lab_name: Neuroanatomy Lab, Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre
E375.bio: Richa Verma is Chief Scientific Officer of the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras, where she leads the centre's neuroanatomy work. She trained in optometry and earned a PhD in retinal electrophysiology at the University of Melbourne, then did postdoctoral work on primate electrophysiology and neuroanatomy at Monash University. She was a faculty member in the School of Optometry at Deakin University, teaching visual neuroscience and retinal physiology. At IIT Madras she helped build the centre's whole-human-brain histological processing and mapping platform, and her group studies the cellular-level development of the human fetal brain, including the visual pathways.
E375.research_direction: Dr. Verma builds cellular-resolution histological atlases of the developing human brain, focusing on the second trimester (about 13–27 gestational weeks). Her group processes whole fetal brains into serial 20 µm cryosections stained with Nissl, H&E and immunohistochemistry. These are combined with postmortem MRI and 3D reconstruction, producing open resources such as the DHARANI atlas, with about 500 annotated structures. She uses these datasets to describe when and how structures form. Examples include early mesial infolds that precede the calcarine, cingulate and callosal sulci; lamination of the cortical plate and subplate in occipital and parietal cortex; rotation of the lateral geniculate nucleus; and growth and calretinin/GFAP chemoarchitecture of sensory midbrain nuclei such as the inferior colliculus. Methods work runs alongside this, including optimized immunohistochemistry for fragile, non-perfused fetal tissue. The goal is a normative baseline of human neurodevelopment, including visual and other sensory pathways, against which developmental disorders can be compared.

papers.title: DHARANI: A 3D Developing Human-Brain Atlas Resource to Advance Neuroscience Internationally Integrated Multimodal Imaging and High-Resolution Histology of the Second Trimester
papers.abstract: The authors release DHARANI, an online platform of 3D histological reconstructions of five fetal human brains spanning 14 to 24 gestational weeks, built from more than 5,000 Nissl- and H&E-stained sections, postmortem MRI and an atlas of roughly 500 annotated structures. The reconstructions track when major sulci, including the calcarine and parieto-occipital, first appear and when cortical lamination begins in occipital and parietal cortex. They also describe developmental events such as rotation of the lateral geniculate nucleus and early formation of the cerebellar Purkinje layer.
papers.authors: Richa Verma, Mihail Bota, Keerthi Ram, Jaikishan Jayakumar, Rebecca Folkerth, Karthika Pandurangan, Jivitha Jyothi Ramesh, Moitrayee Majumder, Rakshika Raveendran, Reetuparna Nanda, Sivamani K, Amal Dhivahar S, Srinivasa Karthik, Ramdayalan Kumarasami, Suresh S, S Lata, E Harish Kumar, Rajeswaran Rangasami, Chitra Srinivasan, Jayaraman Kumutha, Sudha Vasudevan, Koushik Bhat, Chrisline Sam C, Sivathanu Neelakantan, Stephen Savoia, Partha P Mitra, Jayaraj Joseph, Paul R Manger, Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam

papers.title: The histological development of the fetal human inferior colliculus during the second trimester
papers.abstract: This paper describes how the human inferior colliculus, a midbrain auditory and multisensory hub, develops at five stages between 15 and 27 gestational weeks. Its volume roughly triples over this period, and Nissl staining with GFAP and calretinin immunohistochemistry tracked neuron morphology, radial glial fibres and astroglia, with calretinin concentrated in the cortical rather than the central nucleus. The results point to two major phases of inferior colliculus maturation during the second trimester.
papers.authors: Reetuparna Nanda, Mihail Bota, Jaikishan Jayakumar, Suresh S, S Lata, E Harish Kumar, Chitra Srinivasan, Sudha Vasudevan, Kumutha Jayaraman, Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Richa Verma

papers.title: Histological characterization and development of mesial surface sulci in the human brain at 13-15 gestational weeks through high-resolution histology
papers.abstract: Using whole-brain histology plus multimodal imaging, the study describes cortical organization in the human fetal brain at 13–15 gestational weeks. It reports reproducible infolds on the medial surface of the hemispheres, proposed as the earliest precursors of the cingulate, callosal and calcarine sulci, and shows that subplate and intermediate-zone cytoarchitecture already marks boundaries between orbital, frontal, parietal and occipital cortex before major dorsal sulci appear, providing a normative baseline for early cortical development.
papers.authors: Richa Verma, Jaikishan Jayakumar, Rebecca Folkerth, Paul R Manger, Mihail Bota, Moitrayee Majumder, Karthika Pandurangan, Stephen Savoia, Srinivasa Karthik, Ramdayalan Kumarasami, Jayaraj Joseph, G Rohini, Sudha Vasudevan, Chitra Srinivasan, S Lata, E Harish Kumar, Rajeswaran Rangasami, Jayaraman Kumutha, S Suresh, Goran Šimić, Partha P Mitra, Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam

papers.title: Systematic development of immunohistochemistry protocol for large cryosections-specific to non-perfused fetal brain
papers.abstract: Standard immunohistochemistry protocols developed for animal and adult human brains damage fragile, immersion-fixed fetal brain tissue and give weak antigen labeling. The authors optimized each step for 20 µm whole-brain cryosections from fetuses at 13–22 gestational weeks, from antigen retrieval through blocking and antibody incubation, and validated the protocol with six common antibodies, giving a reproducible method for mapping chemoarchitecture in typical and pathological fetal brains.
papers.authors: Karthika Pandurangan, Jaikishan Jayakumar, Stephen Savoia, Reetuparna Nanda, S Lata, E Harish Kumar, Suresh S, Sudha Vasudevan, Chitra Srinivasan, Jayaraj Joseph, Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Richa Verma

E376.name: Sridharan Devarajan
E376.bio: Sridharan Devarajan is a faculty member at the Centre for Neuroscience at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bengaluru, and associate faculty in IISc's Department of Computer Science and Automation, where they lead the Cognition Lab. Sridharan earned bachelor's and master's degrees in engineering from IIT Madras, then completed a PhD and postdoctoral research at Stanford University studying neural circuit mechanisms of attention. Sridharan has held a Wellcome Trust-DBT India Alliance Fellowship and a Ramalingaswami Fellowship. The lab combines psychophysics, EEG, fMRI, neurostimulation and computational modeling to study attention and decision-making.
E376.research_direction: Dr. Devarajan’s recent work explores how complex cognitive phenomena—such as spatial attention, visual working memory, reward expectation, and the attentional blink—can be formally decomposed into distinct subcomponents of perceptual sensitivity and decision bias. Using multidimensional signal detection models paired with multialternative tasks, they have recently been investigating the dissociable neural signatures of these processes across both human and non-human primate visual systems. To achieve this, their lab employs a diverse methodological toolkit, including EEG, fMRI-guided brain stimulation (TMS/tACS), and macaque V4 population recordings, to probe how specific cortical regions and neural dynamics independently govern sensory processing versus choice behavior. By isolating these components, they are investigating the precise neural mechanisms driving spatial reorienting, reward-modulated perception, and distractor interference in working memory.

papers.title: Neural bases of space-specific distractor biases in visual working memory
papers.abstract: The study examines how distractors presented during a visual working memory delay bias memory for items at the same location. Behavior and EEG show that distractors induce space-specific biases, and identify neural signatures that account for the bias separately from general memory sensitivity. It extends the lab's bias-vs-sensitivity approach to working memory.
papers.authors: Deepak V Raya, Sanchit Gupta, Devarajan Sridharan

papers.title: Reward expectation yields distinct effects on sensory processing and decision making in the human brain
papers.abstract: The paper tests whether reward expectation improves sensory processing, decision making, or both. Behavioral modeling of a multialternative task with EEG shows reward independently modulates sensitivity and choice bias, with distinct neural markers such as steady-state visual responses and ERP gain for the sensory effect versus alpha lateralization for the decisional effect. A double dissociation results.
papers.authors: Ankita Sengupta, Devarajan Sridharan

papers.title: Distinct neural bases of subcomponents of the attentional blink
papers.abstract: The attentional blink is decomposed into a perceptual sensitivity deficit and changes in decision bias using signal detection modeling. EEG shows these subcomponents have distinct neural signatures, with the sensitivity deficit localized in time and the second-target processing stages. It clarifies which mechanisms cause the temporal limit of attention.
papers.authors: Swagata Halder, Deepak Velgapuni Raya, Devarajan Sridharan

papers.title: The right posterior parietal cortex mediates spatial reorienting of attentional choice bias
papers.abstract: Using a multialternative change-detection task with a model that separates perceptual sensitivity from choice bias, the study asks which of these two components the right posterior parietal cortex controls when attention must be reoriented to an unexpected location. Combining EEG, fMRI-guided TMS and tACS, the authors show that the right PPC causally and selectively mediates reorienting of choice bias, not sensitivity, and that frontoparietal beta coherence tracks this process. It gives causal evidence that attention is not a unitary process.
papers.authors: Ankita Sengupta, Sanjna Banerjee, S. Hari Ganesh, Shrey Grover, Devarajan Sridharan

papers.title: Dissociable components of attention exhibit distinct neuronal signatures in primate visual cortex
papers.abstract: Applying the lab's multidimensional signal detection framework to V4 recordings from monkeys performing a multialternative attention task, the authors ask whether attention's effects on sensitivity and choice bias have separate neuronal correlates. They find that bias and sensitivity map onto distinct firing-rate and correlated-variability signatures in V4 populations. This links the behavioral dissociation to single-neuron and population physiology.
papers.authors: Adithya Narayan Chandrasekaran, Ayesha Vermani, Priyanka Gupta, Nicholas A. Steinmetz, Tirin Moore, Devarajan Sridharan

E377.name: Tyler Bonnen
E377.bio: Tyler Bonnen is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania, with a joint appointment in Computer Science. Their lab integrates methods from neuroscience, psychology and computer science to develop unified models of perception and memory, two interlocking cognitive functions that are often studied in isolation. Bonnen earned a PhD at Stanford University (2023) with Anthony Wagner and Daniel Yamins and was a UC Presidential Postdoctoral Fellow at UC Berkeley with Alyosha Efros, Angjoo Kanazawa and Jitendra Malik. Their work links deep learning models of the ventral visual stream to medial temporal lobe function and human behavior.
E377.research_direction: Dr. Bonnen studies how perception and memory work together, building unified perceptual-mnemonic models that connect behavior to neural function in the ventral visual stream and medial temporal lobe. Recent work shows that perirhinal cortex supports object perception by integrating over sequences of glances, and that apparent human-monkey discrepancies in lesion data disappear when a stimulus-computable model of the ventral stream is used to measure perceptual demands. The lab also benchmarks humans against vision models on multiview 3D shape inference, finding that humans outperform models such as DINOv2 and CLIP, and shows that networks trained on a multi-view visual-spatial objective can match human 3D shape accuracy and predict error patterns and reaction times. A further line of work uses data augmentation as a computational framework for hippocampal contributions to generalization.

papers.title: Human-level 3D shape perception emerges from multi-view learning
papers.abstract: The study builds a modeling framework that predicts human 3D shape judgments for arbitrary objects directly from experimental stimuli. Neural networks are trained with a visual-spatial objective on naturalistic data: given images taken from different locations in a scene, they learn to predict camera location and depth, with no object-specific inductive biases. Evaluated zero-shot on an established 3D perception task, these multi-view models match human accuracy, and independent readouts of their responses predict human error patterns and reaction times, suggesting human-level 3D perception can emerge from a simple, scalable learning objective over visual-spatial data.
papers.authors: Tyler Bonnen, Jitendra Malik, Angjoo Kanazawa

papers.title: Data augmentation as a framework for modeling hippocampal contributions to generalization
papers.abstract: This perspective proposes that data augmentation, a machine learning strategy for improving generalization by refactoring prior experience, offers a useful framework for modeling hippocampal function. It distinguishes an offline setting, where refactored training data yield more general representations, from an online setting, where retrieved experiences are flexibly refactored at test time to support zero-shot inference, and maps both onto hippocampal functions. The authors argue these tools can supply formal linking functions between experimental evidence and theory, so one modeling approach can predict diverse hippocampus-dependent behaviors, from navigation to abstract inference.
papers.authors: Tyler Bonnen, Andrew K. Lampinen

papers.title: Medial temporal cortex supports object perception by integrating over visuospatial sequences
papers.abstract: The study tests whether perirhinal cortex supports object perception by integrating over sequences of glances. Human performance given brief viewing is approximated by a linear readout of macaque ventral temporal cortex, but people far outperform that readout with longer viewing, and brief-viewing deficits resemble those of humans with perirhinal damage. Gaze recordings show participants sequentially sample task-relevant features across saccades, and these reliable attention patterns are necessary for perirhinal-dependent inferences, pointing to complementary roles for ventral temporal and perirhinal cortex.
papers.authors: Tyler Bonnen, Anthony D. Wagner, Daniel L. K. Yamins

papers.title: Evaluating Multiview Object Consistency in Humans and Image Models
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a benchmark for comparing humans and vision models on 3D shape inference: given a set of images, participants judge which show the same or different objects despite large viewpoint changes, using both common objects and procedurally generated abstract shapes. Over 2000 image sets were run with more than 500 participants (about 35K trials, including reaction time and gaze). Humans outperform all tested vision models (e.g., DINOv2, MAE, CLIP) by a wide margin, and although human and model performance correlate, humans spend more time on difficult trials.
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024)
papers.authors: Tyler Bonnen, Stephanie Fu, Yutong Bai, Thomas P. O'Connell, Yoni Friedman, Nancy Kanwisher, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Alexei A. Efros

papers.title: Inconsistencies between human and macaque lesion data can be resolved with a stimulus-computable model of the ventral visual stream
papers.abstract: Findings on medial temporal lobe involvement in perception seem to conflict between humans with naturally occurring damage and monkeys with surgical perirhinal lesions. Using a stimulus-computable proxy for the primate ventral visual stream, the authors show that a ventral-stream-like model predicts the choices of both intact and lesioned monkeys, so a linear readout of that stream suffices for those tasks. Combined with human results, this indicates the earlier monkey data cannot count as evidence against perirhinal involvement in perception, and that the species discrepancy came from informal accounts of perceptual demands.
papers.authors: Tyler Bonnen, Mark A. G. Eldridge
